**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reprinting of All the Monuments of Catholic Tradition that Have Survived from the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, According to the Most Accurate Editions, Carefully Collated with One Another and with Several Manuscripts, and Corrected with the Greatest Diligence; Continuously Illustrated by Dissertations, Commentaries, and Variant Readings; Enlarged with All Works Discovered after the Extensive Editions Owed to the Last Three Centuries Had Been Completed; Furnished with Particular Analytical Indices Following Each Volume or Each Author of Some Importance; Adorned with Chapters Properly Arranged within the Text Itself, and Also with Titles Distinguishing the Upper Margin of Each Page and Indicating the Subject Matter Below; Enlarged with Works Both Doubtful and Apocryphal, and with Others Possessing Some Authority in Relation to Ecclesiastical Tradition; Enriched with Two General Indices: the First, of Subjects, by Consulting Which Whatever Each Father Has Written on Any Theme May Be Seen at a Glance; the Second, of Sacred Scripture, from Which It Is Immediately Evident to the Reader Which Fathers Have Commented on the Texts of the Individual Books of Scripture, and in Which Places of Their Works They Have Done So. # Saint Salvian, Presbyter of Marseilles

[Col. 0009]

## Prolegomena

### Gallandius’s Prolegomenon on Salvian

(*Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. X)

[Col. 0009A]

### I. Salvian’s life

Salvian was a Gaul by nationality, as he himself testifies [Note: [Col. 0009] Salvian, *On the Government of God*, Book VI, §13, below], and seems to have been born at Cologne Agrippina [Note: [Col. 0009] Idem, Letter 1], probably toward the end of the fourth century, if we follow Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0009] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 182]. He first married Palladia, daughter of Hypatius and Quieta, by whom, as we understand, he had an only daughter named Auspiciola [Note: [Col. 0009] Salvian, Letter 4]. Later, moved—as it is reasonable to believe—by the example of the saints who flourished at that time, namely Paulinus and Therasia, as well as Eucherius and Galla, he came to love the woman whom he had formerly had as his wife as a sister [Note: [Col. 0009] Idem, ibid. On this matter see Sirmond on Sidonius, Book V, Letter 16]. For he appears to have embraced the monastic way of life, and indeed at the monastery of Lérins, as learned men rightly conjecture [Note: [Col. 0009] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 519]. Departing from there, he was ordained presbyter of the Church of Marseilles, as Gennadius testifies [Note: [Col. 0009] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 67]. Hilary of Arles likewise celebrates him by this title in the funeral address on the life of Saint Honoratus, which he delivered in 429 or 430. [Col. 0009B] Thus he says [Note: [Col. 0009] Hilary of Arles, in Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, January, vol. II, p. 20, no. 19]: “The distinguished and most blessed man in Christ, Salvian the presbyter,” etc.

We gladly acknowledge with Baluze that our author was on familiar terms with the most celebrated men of that age [Note: [Col. 0009] Baluze on Salvian, p. 376]: namely Honoratus, bishop of Arles; Eucherius of Lyons; Agroecius of Antibes; and Salonius and Veranus, formerly his pupils [Note: [Col. 0009] Salvian, Letter 8]. To the first of these he dedicated the books *On the Government of God*. Salvian flourished around the middle of the fifth century, and it is certain that he died toward the end of that same century. For Gennadius, who was writing his book *On Illustrious Men* in 496—since he records that Pope Gelasius died in that very year [Note: [Col. 0009] Gennadius, cited work, chapter 94]—says of Salvian [Note: [Col. 0010] Idem, cited work, chapter 67]: “He lives to this day in a good old age.”

[Col. 0009C]

### II. Salvian’s writings

Our author, says the same Gennadius, instructed in both human and divine literature, wrote much in a scholarly and lucid style. Of these works, however, only three are known to survive. Among them, in chronological order, [Col. 0010A] the first place is occupied by the four books *Against Avarice*, which he composed, in all likelihood, around the year 440 [Note: [Col. 0010] Tillemont, cited work, p. 191; *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 522]. He mentions them in the books *On the Government of God* [Note: [Col. 0010] Salvian, *On the Government of God*, Book IV, §1], and sent them under the name of Timothy to the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0010] Idem, *Against Avarice*, Book I]. He discusses this matter himself in Letter 9, addressed to Salonius [Note: [Col. 0010] Idem, Letter 9].

The second work, divided into eight books, commonly bears the title *On the Government of God*; but according to Gennadius it is called *On the Present Judgment* [Note: [Col. 0010] Gennadius, cited work, chapter 67]. The author himself favors this title [Note: [Col. 0010] Salvian, *On the Government of God*, Book I, §4]. Some conjecture that these books were written before the year 451 [Note: [Col. 0010] Tillemont, cited work, p. 191]. Others, however, seem more correctly to assign them to the year 455 [Note: [Col. 0010] *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 525]. For in them Salvian reports that Rome was besieged and captured by the Vandals [Note: [Col. 0010] Salvian, *On the Government of God*, Book VI, §12], and, as is clear from Prosper’s Chronicle [Col. 0010B] [Note: [Col. 0010] Prosper, *Chronicle*, p. 754, in the appendix to the Paris edition of the works of Saint Prosper (our *Patrologia*, vol. LI)], we learn that this occurred in that very year.

Finally, Gennadius praises a third monument of Salvian’s writings: one book of Letters. Of these, however, only nine survive—obviously only a small part of those that he wrote to various people, especially if one takes into account the author’s long life. It is not worthwhile to compose a fuller account of his other lost writings, since we seem to be responsible only for those that still survive and that are consequently published through our efforts.

### III. Editions

Many editions of Salvian’s works are in circulation, and it is not the place here to enumerate them all. Among those published during the two preceding centuries, two in particular are highly valued: one by Pierre Pithou, published at Paris in 1580; the other by Conrad Rittershaus, printed at Altdorf in 1611. Later, Étienne Baluze obtained the aforementioned Pithou edition and collated it with a very old manuscript [Col. 0010C] [Col. 0011A] from the monastery of Corbie, of excellent quality, and with two Colbert manuscripts; he published the result at Paris in 1665. After revising and correcting it repeatedly, and collating it anew with two other manuscript codices used by Pithou, he issued a third edition at Paris in 1684. We have decided to commit this last, Baluze’s edition, to the press as far superior to the others.

### IV. The edition of Demetrius Barbulus

It should also not be omitted that in 1729, in this century, the same works of Salvian were published at Pesaro through the study and labor of Demetrius Barbulus, who appended alphabetical Concordances of Salvian. It is regrettable, however, that the distinguished editor imposed upon us a Salvian, bishop of Marseilles [Note: [Col. 0011C] Barbulus, in the title page of the Pesaro edition], whereas after Gennadius the most learned men recognize him as merely a presbyter. Larinus Amatius likewise asserted Salvian’s fictitious episcopate in the *Life*, or rather *Eulogy*, of that same Salvian, which appears at the beginning of the aforementioned Barbulian edition and was composed from the letters of our author [Note: [Col. 0011] Larinus Amatius, *Life of Salvian*, p. IX].

Nor are either author excused by the authority of the great Baronius. He and several others with him called Salvian bishop of Marseilles [Note: [Col. 0011] Baronius, under the year 428, §§1 and 11], having plainly been misled by corrupt editions of Gennadius’s work *On Illustrious Men*, which Erasmus and Marianus Victorius published among the works of Jerome. There, through an erroneous reading, the Marseilles presbyter is improperly dignified with such a title. But after learned men—Pagi [Note: [Col. 0011] Pagi, under the year 490, §20], Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0011] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, pp. 194 and 747, note 5, on Salvian], and the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: [Col. 0011] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 521], to omit the others—had exposed the error and openly removed the corruption [Col. 0012A], one cannot help wondering how Barbulus and his companion Amatius could still be groping blindly in so much light.

### V. On a further error of Amatius

But the aforementioned Amatius must not yet be dismissed. For it is in our interest to expose another, and by no means insignificant, error of his in the *Eulogy of Salvian* that he composed. He agrees, indeed, that Salvian was a Gaul [Note: [Col. 0011] Larinus Amatius, cited work]; but he thinks it insufficiently clear from which city of Gaul he originated. Moreover, he asserts that Baluze is not entirely consistent with himself, since at the beginning of the volume he boldly proclaims Salvian a Gaul, while later, in his notes, he states that his homeland was Cologne.

I would not have wished this to be said by a learned man. For Baluze is entirely consistent, both in declaring our author a Gaul by nationality and in conjecturing that his homeland was Cologne; and we too affirmed this at the beginning [Col. 0012B] of this chapter, following Baluze himself as well as other men outstanding in learning [Note: [Col. 0012C] Tillemont, cited work, p. 182; *Literary History of France*, cited work, p. 517].

Amatius failed to notice that Cologne Agrippina, at the time when Salvian flourished, lay on Gallic soil. When the strength of the Empire had been weakened and diminished, Childeric, king of the Franks, took and occupied it from the Romans; Sigibert the Elder, surnamed the Lame, made it the seat of his kingdom; and after his death the great Clovis added it to his other dominions, as Gregory of Tours relates [Note: [Col. 0012] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 11]. In short, Cologne Agrippina is known to have been subject to the Merovingian Frankish princes. On this matter see more fully Hadrian Valesius [Note: [Col. 0012] Hadrian Valesius, *Frankish History*, Book V, vol. I, pp. 235–236] and Dionysius Sammarthanus [Note: [Col. 0012] Dionysius Sammarthanus, *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, p. 620].

[Col. 0011]

# Schoenemann’s Historical-Literary Notice on Salvian

(*Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers*, vol. [lacuna])

## § I. Life

The homeland of this most serious and elegant writer was Gaul, and those who think that he was born at Cologne Agrippina rely on arguments that are certainly not improbable. In any case, he was not from Trier, but from a neighboring city which, unlike Trier, had not suffered destruction at the hands of the barbarians, but had merely been reduced to the status of a tributary city. The words of Salvian himself in his first letter seem, in a certain sense, to support more closely the view that makes him a native of Cologne: in that letter he recommends a young man born at Cologne and related to him.

Although he may not have been born at Trier, perhaps—indeed, all the more likely—he owed to that city the cultivation of his mind and his knowledge of the best subjects. He knows Trier and understands the character of its citizens and all their pursuits so thoroughly that it is by no means contrary to the truth to suppose that he spent some time there for the sake of study, in a city which at that period flourished in literary studies more than any other in Gaul.

It is not clear whether Salvian was a Christian from the beginning. Some maintain that he was already so when he married Palladia, daughter of a certain Hypatius and Quieta, from the same province whose metropolis was Cologne Agrippina. He later not only persuaded her to embrace the Christian faith, but, after they had had only one daughter, named Auspiciola, led her to bind herself with him by vows of continence and to live a celibate life within marriage.

Her father, Hypatius, who had hoped for male offspring from this daughter, took this very badly. He became so angry with Salvian and his daughter that for seven full years after Salvian had left him he neither saw them nor wrote to them. When those years had passed, Hypatius too gave his name to Christ. Salvian, now seeing that the causes of his father-in-law’s hostility had ceased, again asked forgiveness by letter—not out of consciousness of guilt, but from a sense of reason and the duty of charity, and so as to leave no opportunity for offense at all—and undoubtedly obtained it. When he wrote these letters, he was living far from his father-in-law; and, unless perhaps on the island of Lérins, certainly in the province of Vienne. There he attained even the dignity of the presbyterate, namely in the Church of Marseilles, supported by the friendship and favor of the most esteemed men of that region: Honoratus, later bishop of Arles; Eucherius; Agroecius of Antibes; and Salonius and Veranus, the sons of Eucherius, whom he instructed in their youth. He never attained the episcopate. His date of death is unknown; we do know that he lived into the time of Gelasius of Rome.

[Col. 0013B]

## § II. Writings

Of the many writings of Salvian that Gennadius lists, the following survive today:

1. **Four books Against Avarice addressed to the Catholic Church**, which he published under the name of Timothy around the year 440.

2. **Books On the Government of God and On the Just and Present Judgment of God**, also entitled *On Providence*. This is his principal work, written during the barbarian invasions of the Roman Empire, in 451 or 452, or, as the Benedictines prefer, in 455.

3. **Nine familiar Letters.**

The following works are lost: **Three books On the Good of Virginity**, addressed to Marcellus; **one book On Making Satisfactory Recompense for Their Reward** [Note: [Col. 0013] These words are taken from Gennadius, chapter 67, which is wholly corrupt. Others read *On the Merit of Their Satisfaction*, with an obsolete expression corrected. Trithemius, chapter 175, undoubtedly because he did not understand the passage, simply praises one book addressed to Bishop Salonius; shortly afterward he divided the exposition into two works, an exposition on Ecclesiastes and a book addressed to Claudianus] addressed to Bishop Salonius; **one book on the final part of the book of Ecclesiastes**, addressed to Claudianus, bishop of Vienne; **one book On the Beginning of Genesis up to the Creation of Man**, composed in verse in the manner of the Greek *Hexaemeron*; **several Homilies**; and **one book On the Sacraments** [Note: [Col. 0013] Thus Trithemius. Gennadius reports: “many homilies delivered to bishops, but as for the number of the books On the Sacraments, I do not remember.” In their place Trithemius praises one book of *Homilies Delivered to Bishops*, one book *On the Sacraments*, and one book of *Several Homilies to the People*. Moreover, what Gennadius reports concerning the verses on Genesis must be understood as we have explained it].

Sixtus of Siena, through carelessness, attributed to Salvian the work *Anticimenon* [Greek: Ἀντικειμένων], by an unknown author, which John Alexander Brassicanus first published together with Salvian at Basel in 1530.

## § III. Editions

From the revival of letters and the invention of printing, the books of Salvian that we have just enumerated had, as it were, three parents who first rescued them for publication: John Sichard, John Alexander Brassicanus, and Pierre Pithou. The first published the four books *On Avarice* at Basel in 1528 [Col. 0013D]. Two years later the second issued the eight books *On the Government of God* there from the Frobenian press. After a lengthy interval, Pithou finally added the third work, the book of Letters.

Whatever Salvian has owed thereafter to the ingenuity of learned men is due, in gratitude, to Pithou himself, Conrad Rittershaus, and Étienne Baluze. For Pithou not only increased the number of Salvian’s short works by adding the book of Letters [Col. 0014A], but also published all his writings transcribed faithfully from manuscripts. Although he gained few followers, he nevertheless deserved Baluze’s approval—Baluze being worth a hundred others—and would have been followed by him had sound reasons not prevented it.

Rittershaus’s work, learned and useful though it was, did not remain in vigor for long and never left Germany. After Baluze, finally, either nothing further was desired in Salvian or at least no one dared to match his learning and ingenuity.

Three periods of Salvian’s editions may therefore conveniently be described. The first extends from 1528 to 1580; during it the books *On Avarice* were joined to the books *On the Government of God*, and Brassicanus’s notes were commonly added everywhere. The old text did not, however, cease to be copied after Pithou’s recension [Col. 0014B]. The second period begins with Pithou’s edition, published at Paris by Sebastian Nivellius in 1580, and extends to 1663; it is held, as it were equally, by Pithou and Rittershaus. Yet the repetitions of Pithou’s edition became far inferior to their archetype.

Rittershaus’s edition first appeared in 1611, with an immense commentary and a text happily corrected by conjecture in certain places; it was reprinted in 1623 with a lengthy supplement. In the third period Baluze alone reigns. He collated Pithou’s text with several—and the best—manuscript copies, not once but first in 1663, again in 1669, and a third time in 1684. He thus established a new text, changing it only when the authority of the manuscripts required it, and fortified his emendations with excellent notes. How often this Baluze recension was repeated from that time onward [Col. 0014C] will be shown by the following annals.

# Sixteenth century

### 1528

Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri; folio. *Bishop Timothy’s Address to the Catholic Church Spread Throughout the Whole World* and *Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, Preface to the Book of Timothy Addressed to Bishop Salonius*; in John Sichard’s *Antidote against Various Heresies*, pp. 181, 202.

### 1530

Basel, at the Frobenian press; folio. *The Eight Books of Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment and Providence of God, Addressed to Saint Salonius, Bishop of Vienne*, edited by John Alexander Brassicanus, doctor of law, and illustrated with learned and especially useful scholia.

*Three Books of the Anticimenon*, containing questions of the Old and New Testament concerning passages that appear to conflict, by an uncertain author [Col. 0014D].

At the end: Basel, at the Frobenian press, by John Hervagius, Jerome Froben, and Nicholas Episcopius, in the month of August, in the year 1530.

John Alexander Brassicanus, doctor of law and professor of languages—first at Tübingen and later at Vienna—a man who in his age deserved the highest praise for his service to good letters, brought this work of Salvian into public view before all others, along with many other Greek [Col. 0015A] and Latin authors not previously printed, and dedicated it to Christoph von Stadion, bishop of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0015] Hendreich discussed this Brassicanus more accurately than is usually his custom in *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*. As we learn there, John Ludwig Brassicanus was a different man from him—not indeed in age or homeland, but to some extent in studies and status. For he calls him a doctor of law and suspects that he was from Tübingen. If this is true, consider whether he may have been Alexander’s brother and whether both had as their father John Brassicanus, whom Alexander writes at the end of his preface to Salvian to have once been initiated into the same sacred studies with Christoph von Stadion and to have been sincerely loved and continually supported by him. Morhof also mentions that same John Brassicanus, a Tübingen teacher, in his *Polyhistor*, p. 247; perhaps he was no other than the man whom Bock lists among the doctors of the University of Tübingen in *History of That Academy*, §85, p. 45, and whom the celebrated Saxius incorrectly confuses with John Alexander Brassicanus in *Onomasticon Litterarium*, III, 82. Note, however, that our author too calls himself a doctor of law].

Hungary, devastated by the Turks, was then presenting the world with a grievous spectacle. Among the countless public and private goods seized by their fury was that celebrated library at Buda, filled with books of every kind of writer and furnished by King Matthias at incalculable expense. Although every person with even a little learning was shaken by this grave loss, Brassicanus nevertheless felt the bitterest grief. He had seen these treasures in person at Buda, in the company of the imperial legate, and had not merely seen them but had immersed himself entirely in them. Through the munificence of King Louis he too had acquired certain Greek authors and had perhaps obtained copies of others, both Greek and Latin [Col. 0015B]. I do not know whether Salvian was among them.

Certainly, in his preface to the bishop of Augsburg—dated Vienna in Austria, March 1, 1530—he discusses not so much Salvian, or any manuscript from which he might have published him, or his own labor in editing, as he laments the catastrophe suffered by letters through the loss of that library. To prepare his readers gradually for this subject, he speaks at a distance about book collecting and about learned men and princes distinguished by their zeal for collecting books. Toward the end he names several ancient books, especially Greek ones, that remained in his own library and that he intended someday to publish; some of these, such as the books of the *Geoponica*, we know later saw the light.

The preface is followed by an hendecasyllabic poem [Col. 0015C], no less lengthy than the preface and certainly not very polished, in which he declares that he is inscribing and dedicating Salvian to the same man. His annotations, which follow immediately after Salvian’s books, chiefly illuminate words and expressions, especially newly coined ones, and are commendable for their extensive and excellent reading in authors of both languages.

It should not be omitted that the *Anticimenon* [Greek: Ἀντικειμένων], a work by an unknown author, which Brassicanus published here together with Salvian’s work, misled some insufficiently attentive readers into thinking that it was Salvian’s own.

### 1556

Basel, at the press of Heinrich Petri; folio. *The Four Books of Bishop Timothy Addressed to the Catholic Church Spread Throughout the Whole World*, and Salvian’s preface to the same; in John Herold’s *Heresiology*, pp. 579–613.

[Col. 0015D]

### 1564

Rome, at the house of the Roman People, under Paul Manutius, son of Aldus; folio. *Eight Books of Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment and Providence of God*, together with works by Maximus, Pacianus, Sulpicius, Dorotheus of Tyre, and Haymo of Halberstadt [Col. 0016A], with Peter Galesinius’s annotations added to the last three.

This edition has already been mentioned several times. Salvian’s books extend to page 81. Several variant readings were added in the margins.

### 1575

Paris, at the press of Michel Sonnius; folio. *Salvian … Eight Books On the True Judgment, Providence, and Government of God. Also Four Books Addressed to the Catholic Church under the Name of Timothy*; in the Bigne collection, volume III, p. 240 ff.

Paris, at the press of Jerome Marnef and Guillaume Cavellat; duodecimo. *Salvian … Eight Books On the True Judgment and Providence of God* [also the four books addressed to the Catholic Church], with Brassicanus’s preface and scholia. Bodleian Library Catalogue.

I do not know whether only Brassicanus’s edition was reprinted here, or whether the four books *Against Avarice* were also added. Whichever is true [Col. 0016B], it is nevertheless incorrectly listed by the Benedictines among the editions of the works.

### 1580

Paris, at the press of Sebastian Nivellius, under the sign of the Storks, on the Rue Saint-Jacques; octavo. *Eight Books of Salvian of Marseilles, Presbyter, On the Government of God and on His Just and Present Judgment, Addressed to Saint Salonius, Bishop. His One Book of Letters, Now Published for the First Time. His Four Books under the Name of Timothy Addressed to the Catholic Church. From the Library of P. Pithou, J. C.*

Rarely, variant readings differing from the printed text appear in the margins. At the end are appended various readings, partly from an old manuscript, although some of them were not admitted into the text on sound judgment, and some were omitted through the negligence of the printers; partly from published editions, which too can be tolerated. They amount to four sheets [Col. 0016C], of which very few concern the Letters and most concern the final work. In the same place Pithou also asserts that nothing in these books was supplied by conjecture, but that the whole was transcribed faithfully from a very old and carefully corrected codex. An index of noteworthy subjects and words is added.

In Pithou’s preface to Nicolas Fabri, councillor to the king—dated Paris, on the nones of October, during the vintage festivals, in the year 1579—he discusses the early flourishing of the Christian religion in Gaul and the abundant growth of Christian writers there.

The royal privilege was signed on March 24, 1579. It deserves notice that Baluze already records of this first edition of Pithou that, because of its rarity, it could be compared with a manuscript codex and was nowhere available for sale.

[Col. 0016D]

### 1589

Paris; folio. *Eight Books of Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment and Providence of God. His Four Books Addressed to the Catholic Church Spread Throughout the Whole World.* In the second edition of the Bigne collection, volume V, p. 161 ff.

[Col. 0017A]

### 1594

Paris, at the press of Jerome de Marnef and the widow of Guillaume Cavellat, under the sign of the Pelican, on Mount Saint-Hilaire; duodecimo. *Eight Books of Salvian of Marseilles, Bishop, On the True Judgment and Providence of God, Addressed to Saint Salonius, Bishop of Vienne, Edited by John Alexander Brassicanus, Doctor of Law, and Illustrated with Learned Scholia. His One Book of Letters, Now Published for the First Time, Is Added. Also His Four Books Addressed to the Catholic Church under the Name of Timothy. With a Very Full Index of Subjects and Words.*

Brassicanus’s edition was entirely reprinted, and a newly prepared index was added. The remaining material forms, as it were, a second volume—not with a new title, but separated from the first by a new pagination. It lacks an index. The words “now published for the first time,” added in the title to the book of Letters [Col. 0017B], appear to have been copied without malicious intent from Pithou’s edition.

# Seventeenth century

### 1608

Paris; duodecimo. *Eight Books of Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, On the Government of God, and the Letters; with the Annotations of John Brassicanus, from the Library of Pithou.* Barberini Library, vol. II, p. 339.

If Pithou’s edition is reproduced here, the third work, *Against Avarice*, cannot be absent.

### 1609

Trier; quarto. *The Four Epistolary Books of Salvian … Addressed to the Catholic Church, Against Avarice, with the Annotations of J. Macherentius.* Society of Jesus.

Baluze collated it for his third edition, but testifies that he derived no especially great benefit from it. For Macherentius had no old manuscript [Col. 0017C] with which to collate these books, and corrected most passages on his own authority.

### 1610

Paris; folio. *Salvian, Bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment*, etc. In the repeated edition of the Bigne collection, volume V, p. 123 ff.

### 1611

Altdorf, at the Academy of the Republic of Nuremberg, at the press of Conrad Agricola; octavo. *The Works of Salvian of Marseilles, Addressed to Louis XIII, Most Christian King of France and Navarre. Edited by Conrad Rittershaus, Doctor of Law, Who Also Added a Book of Commentary.*

*The Second Volume of Salvian’s Works, Containing Four Books Against Avarice. Addressed to the Most Illustrious Prince Philip II, Duke of Stettin in Pomerania, etc. Revised and Prepared for Printing by Conrad Rittershaus.*

[Col. 0017D]

**Conrad Rittershaus’s Doctoral Commentary on Salvian of Marseilles: Addressed to the Universities and Academies of Germany.**

Rittershaus’s name was especially famous for learning in the sixteenth century, and even now his learned annotations on various Greek and Latin authors retain their value. Yet scarcely any were more suitable than those he composed on Salvian. For while describing the customs and character of his own times, this writer draws light especially from the authors whom Rittershaus had devoted himself to reading more deeply than other learned men of his century through his study of law, and frequently from the laws themselves written in that age; he then pours that light back into his work.

He had no manuscript copies, but his fortunate ingenuity, his mastery of the Latin language as it was spoken in the fifth century, and the abundance of his reading often compensated for this lack. Certainly Étienne Baluze states in the preface to his edition that Rittershaus corrected Salvian quite successfully in several places, and remarks that his conjectures are often confirmed by the authority of ancient manuscripts; he also frequently adopts Rittershaus’s interpretations. Let us therefore see what the arrangement and distribution of his edition are.

In the first volume are contained the books on Providence and the Letters; next, an index of subjects and words is placed; then follows John Trithemius’s treatise on the Providence of God, addressed to the emperor Maximilian I; and finally Conr. Rittershusius’s Admonition concerning the shameful confusion and disorder introduced by copyists into several passages of Salvian’s Books VII and VIII, together with a catalogue of certain authors who have written on Providence.

A dissertation on the life of Salvian precedes these works, together with a general account of the contents of the eight books on the Providence, Government, and Judgment of God, and a demonstration that the four books published under the name of Timothy are Salvian’s own. An opinion is also given, incidentally, on earlier editors. There follow testimonies and encomia concerning Salvian, namely those of Gennadius (with Rittershusius’s annotation), the Chronicle of Auxerre, Ado of Vienne, Hilary of Arles, Giovanni Gioviano Pontano, John Trithemius, Joannes Alexander Brassicanus, Joseph Scaliger, and Pierre Pithou; the verses and preface of Brassicanus, as well as Pithou’s preface, are inserted among them.

Next come congratulatory pieces in prose and verse, written according to the custom of those times to the editor. The second volume contains, after the four books on Avarice, a list of the chapters into which the author of the Trier edition divided these four books quite conveniently. To fill the pages, several verses of Phaedrus on misers are appended. It also contains an index no less extensive than that in the first volume, as well as a catalogue of writers who have discussed Avarice, almsgiving, wealth, or poverty, together with epigrams on those subjects from the Greek Anthology, likewise inserted to fill the pages.

Finally, to the commentary contained in the third volume are added several various readings and emendations from Pithou’s manuscript and Brassicanus’s edition, together with a few conjectures of Rittershusius and a very extensive index to the volume. I say nothing of the dedicatory letters, which scarcely any great admirer of Rittershusius would have read, much less the princes or the friends of the princes to whom they are addressed. The third of these is addressed to all the professors of the academies of Germany, and attached to it is a catalogue of those academies arranged according to the order of their foundation and date. Finally, at the end of the entire work—although it occupies the last place, the Hymn to Christ, the Best and Greatest appears there—the editor states that he had intended to append the notes on Salvian that John Weitz, Tobias Adam, and Theodor Sitzmann had inscribed and presented to him, as well as the annotations of Brassicanus and others. But since the press could not have been made available for printing them, he promises to publish them on another occasion.

[Col. 0019A]

Around the same time. Frankfurt, at the shop of Nicolaus Roth; octavo. The same edition reprinted. The Benedictines, in the *Literary History of France*, cite it on the authority of Boldianus in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 52; Fabricius, however, argues that this testimony is not very trustworthy and consequently places this edition among the fables. Perhaps, however, it was not a Rittershusian edition that was reprinted here, but a Pithouan one.

1618. Cologne, at the shop of Antonius Hierat; folio. *The eight books of Salvian the presbyter and later bishop of Marseilles, On the Government of God; likewise the Letters to Various Persons; and Timothy, or the Four Books to the Church.* In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume V, part III, pp. 323 ff.

1623. Nuremberg, at the shop of Simon Halbmeyer, octavo. *The Works of Salvian of Marseilles, from the edition of Conrad Rittershusius and with his Commentary; second edition*, prefixed by the life of Rittershusius himself, written by Georgius F. C. R. Rittershusius. *Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris.*

In the *Catalogue of the Bodleian Library*, as also in the Barberini Library, an edition of this place and year is praised, with the commentary of Rittershusius and others. From this I infer that this edition consisted of two volumes: the first displaying Salvian’s text together with Rittershusius’s commentary, and the second, I suppose, the notes of the various commentators—Weitz, Adam, Sitzmann, and Brassicanus—as they are reproduced in the Bremen edition to be mentioned shortly. Hence, I think, arose Fabricius’s error when he confidently asserted that there was no Nuremberg edition of Salvian from the year 1623. Evidently the second volume had come into his hands separately—perhaps also into the hands of the Bremen scholars—just as only the first volume is found in the Royal Library of Paris.

For the rest, I regret the labor spent in investigating the particular edition of those notes which Rittershusius admitted had been inscribed and presented to him, especially since they are in themselves of lesser importance and are unlikely to be missed by anyone. Certainly Weitz’s little notes provide nothing but a mere heap of passages and similar material gathered from everywhere.

1624. Paris, folio. *Salvian’s eight books On the Government of God*, etc. In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume V.

1627. Rouen, at the shop of Jean Osmont; duodecimo. *Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment and Providence of God, addressed to Bishop Salonius, eight books, with the scholia of Brassicanus; the Letters and the Four Books to the Catholic Church.*

The authors of the *Literary History of France* praise this edition. It appears to have been copied from the Paris edition of 1594.

1633. Oxford; octavo. *Salvian … On the True Judgment and Providence of God, eight books; the Letters and the Four Books to the Catholic Church.* *Catalogue of the Bodleian Library.*

1635. Cologne; quarto. *Salvian’s eight books On the Government of God*, etc., in the seventh section of Jacob Merlo Horstius’s (that is, a man descended from Horst’s family) *Seven Trumpets of the Christian World*.

The complete title of the work is: *The Seven Trumpets of the Christian World, sounding the call to the reformation of ecclesiastical discipline, which must be instituted throughout the entire world, especially in Germany, as a remedy for present and more serious evils.* According to Harzheim in the *Cologne Library*, it contains seven pious little works drawn from Saint Bernard, Gregory, John Chrysostom, Prosper, Peter Damian, Peter of Blois, and Salvian, illustrated with new divisions, prefaces, and annotations, together with an appendix of various questions. Fabricius seems to indicate that Salvian’s entire work was reprinted in it. But in the *Catalogue of the Barberini Library*, at the place cited, only the eight books *On the Government* are said to be included.

1644. Paris; folio. *The eight books of Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, On the Government of God. The same author’s four books to the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world.* In the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, volume V. This edition was later issued with a new title in 1654, by three booksellers.

1645. Paris, at the shop of Edmond Pepingué; octavo. *Salvian, presbyter of Marseilles, On the Providence and Government of God and on His Just and Present Judgment, eight books. Likewise one book of Letters and Timothy’s four books to the Catholic Church, with the notes of John Alexander.* Thus the *Catalogue of the Chigi Library*.

The text was reprinted from the Pithouan edition, but, in Baluzius’s judgment, with such an unfortunate result that this edition is riddled with almost countless errors.

1647. Lyons; quarto. *Salvian … eight books On the Government of God*, under the following title: *Censorial Preliminary Statements on the Present Calamities of Europe and Their Causes*, published by Osiander Stuanus.

Certainly this title is listed among Salvian’s works in volume II, p. 340, of the *Catalogue of the Barberini Library*; the authors of the *Literary History of France* consequently repeat it. But, I confess, even from inspecting that catalogue itself I cannot determine any more clearly whether it means that the books *On the Government of God* are contained there, or the books *Against Avarice*, whose edition is proposed immediately before it.

1648. Paris, at the shop of Edmond Pepingué; octavo. A repetition of the Pithouan edition. The Benedictines, in the *Literary History of France*.

1663. Paris, at the shop of François Muguet; octavo. *The Works of the holy presbyters Salvian of Marseilles and Vincent of Lérins.* Stephen Baluzius of Tulle corrected them according to manuscript codices and illustrated them with notes.

Although the Pithouan edition had many defects, Baluzius was accustomed to regard it as the best of the earlier editions and wished to make it the foundation of this new recension. Thus, wherever this edition differs from it, the reader is to understand that everything changed was changed on the authority of manuscript codices, several of which—very ancient ones—he had obtained for the books *On Providence* and *To the Catholic Church*. For he asserts that he allowed nothing to conjecture except in one or two places in the Letters. He had obtained no ancient exemplar of any letter except the last two, in correcting which he followed the manuscripts entirely.

He declares that the chief purpose of his notes is to indicate variant readings. “If at any time,” he says, “I go beyond these limits, I can affirm that it did not happen altogether without reason, although it happens rarely. For, let me say this also, I wrote these notes in haste, as though occupied with something else. I thought it right to mention this, lest anyone should scrutinize the syllables here to the quick, or declare that these notes had been drawn straight according to the rule of Polyclitus.”

This edition is also enriched by a dissertation of Stephen Baluzius of Tulle, *On the Bishopric of Ega*, written in the form of a letter to Philippe Labbe (Paris, 19 July 1663), remarkable for the extraordinary brilliance and elegance of its type and paper.

1669. Paris, at the shop of François Muguet; octavo. *The Works of the holy presbyters Salvian of Marseilles and Vincent of Lérins.* Stephen Baluzius of Tulle corrected them according to ancient manuscript codices and illustrated them with notes. Second edition.

Not only does the text of this edition differ in several respects from the preceding one, but a considerable addition of learned notes was also made to it. First, the editor carefully reexamined the variant readings that he had written in the margin of the Pithouan edition. Then he compared the books *On the Government of God* with Brassicanus’s edition of 1530 and Galesinius’s edition of 1564; whatever was better in those editions than in the Pithouan edition or in the Corbie manuscript, against which he had previously collated the Pithouan text, he transferred into the text. If anything was doubtful or required an admonition, he states that he placed it in the Notes, and that he concealed nothing or changed anything on his own authority without giving notice of it.

He further added an appendix of ancient records mentioned in the Notes, containing:

I. A letter of Castor, bishop of Apt, to John Cassian, from an old manuscript of the Royal Library.

II. The acts of the emperors against Pelagius and Caelestius, likewise from manuscript codices, namely:

1. The rescript of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium.

2. The edict of Palladius.

3. The rescript of Honorius to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

4. The letter of Aurelius to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana.

5. The sacred letter of the emperor Constantius, father of the younger Valentinian Augustus, to Volusianus, prefect of the City, against Caelestius.

6. The edict of Volusianus for the publication of the preceding rescript.

III. The conveyance of Peter of Saint—so he is called—to the Cathedral Church of Cahors.

IV. The conveyance of William of Carbonarias to the monastery of Tulle.

V. The conveyance of Elias of Navis to the same monastery, from the chartularies of those churches and monasteries.

1677. Lyons, at the shop of the Anissons; folio. *Salvian of Marseilles, eight books On the Government of God; his Letters to Various Persons; likewise Timothy, or the Four Books to the Church; all according to the emendation of Stephen Baluzius.* In the *Great Library of the Fathers*, volume VIII, pp. 339–401.

1684. Paris, at the shop of François Muguet; octavo. *The Works of the Holy Presbyters Salvian of Marseilles and Vincent of Lérins.* Stephen Baluzius of Tulle corrected them according to ancient manuscript codices and illustrated them with notes. Third edition.

“Since the second edition too had been sold out,” says Baluzius, “and the printer wished to bring the same books again under the press, and since meanwhile I had obtained the manuscript exemplar that Pithou used in correcting the books *On the Government of God*, as well as the one with which he collated the four books *Against Avarice*, now preserved in the Colbert Library, I thought that I ought to undertake this service for this most elegant writer, collating his labors with those same ancient codices. I believe I have done so with some benefit to these studies.”

Of the records added by the appendix to the preceding edition, numbers I and II have been removed from this third edition. For the rest, although this impression too is sufficiently neat, it falls very far short of the elegance of the first. It is dedicated to Jacques-Nicolas Colbert, archbishop of Carthage and coadjutor of Rouen (Paris, 1 April of this year). The dissertation on the bishopric of Ega is absent.

1688. Bremen, at the expense of Hermann Braver; quarto. *The Works of the Holy Presbyters Salvian of Marseilles …* With the commentary of Conrad Rittershusius and the complete notes of John Weitz, Tobias Adam, Theodor Sitzmann, John Alexander Brassicanus, and Stephen Baluzius; together with the *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins, corrected and illustrated by the same Baluzius of Tulle according to ancient manuscript codices. Prefaced by G. Calixtus’s dissertation on Vincent of Lérins. With very extensive indexes, both to the authors and to the notes. According partly to the Nuremberg exemplar of 1623 and the Paris exemplar of 1669.

What was transferred from the Nuremberg edition into this one can be understood from what has been said above. Vincent of Lérins will be discussed in its proper place. The series of learned men whose notes are presented here is one thing in the volume itself and another in the title; neither has been arranged with much care. In fact, the entire Baluzius edition was reprinted, and consequently the notes immediately following the text of both authors are those of Baluzius, together with the index to that edition. Next come the commentary of Rittershusius, the notes of Weitz, Adam, and Sitzmann, and finally those of Brassicanus, with a separate index specially prepared for them.

It is strange that the bookseller chose to print the second edition of Baluzius rather than the third, when he wished to appear to have undertaken this work for anything but mere profit.

## Eighteenth Century

1728. Venice; octavo. *The corrected works of Salvian of Marseilles, presbyter, with notes by Stephen Baluzius.* *Catalogue of the Firmian Library*, volume I, p. 53.

1729. Pesaro, from the printing house of Gavelli; large quarto. *The Concordances of the Works of Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, appended to his works and arranged alphabetically, prepared through the study and labor of Father Demetrius Barbulius of the Society of Jesus, and most humbly dedicated to His Eminence and Most Reverend Prince, Cardinal Fabio degli Abbati Olivieri.* A work exceedingly useful to all students of the sacred disciplines, but especially to ascetical teachers and preachers of the word of God.

Rather, it is a foolish work, printed at the cost of paper which I wish had been less brilliant. There is perhaps one item that should not be counted in this category: the *Life*, or rather *Eulogy*, of Salvian, recently published by Larino Amatio, extracted chiefly from Salvian’s own Letters.

1774. Venice, from the printing house of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, son of Girolamo; folio. *The Complete Extant Works of Salvian, presbyter of Marseilles.* The *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins is added. From the third edition of Stephen Baluzius, a man of distinguished rank. In volume X of the *Library of the Fathers and of the Holy Ancient Church* by Andrea Gallandi, pp. 1–102.

The notes of Baluzius are not, as this editor usually places them, immediately alongside the text, but are appended at the end; consequently, the form of Baluzius’s third edition is preserved in every respect, except that the editor added biblical passages of his own in the lower margin. He discusses Salvian in the *Prolegomena*, chapter I, pp. III–IV.

## Translations

All of Salvian’s works have been translated into French more than once by Gorse, Bonnet, and others. In addition, the books *On Providence* exist in translations not only by the French but also by the Italians, as the following entries show.

### French

1575. Lyons, at the shop of Guillaume Rouillé; octavo. *Saint Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, On the True Judgment and Providence of God, translated into French by B. B. D. S.*

1655. Paris, at the shop of Caspar Meturas; quarto. *The Works of Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, containing the eight books on Providence, the four books against Avarice, and several letters, translated with notes by Pierre Gorse.*

1700. Paris, at the shop of Guillaume Valleyre; duodecimo. Two volumes. *The Works of Salvian and the Treatise of Vincent of Lérins Against the Heresies, translated into French by Father Bonnet, priest of the Oratory.*

1701. Paris, at the shop of Louis Guérin; octavo. *Salvian, On Providence, translated into French by Jean Drouet de Maupertuis.*

1734. Paris, at the shop of Jean-Baptiste Delespine; duodecimo. *The Works of Salvian, priest of Marseilles, containing his letters and his treatises on the spirit of self-interest and on Providence, translated into French by a Jesuit Father.*

### Italian

1579. Milan, at the shop of Michel Tini; duodecimo. *The Book of Salvian, bishop of Marseilles, Against Spectacles and Other Vanities of the World*, translated by Saint Charles Borromeo, together with the *Memorial of the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal of Saint Praxedes, Archbishop, to his beloved people of the City and Diocese of Milan.* Argelati, *Library of Vernacular Translations*, volume III (Milan, 1767, quarto, p. 329). I do not know, however, whether this title includes one or all of the books *On the Government of God*.

1703. Avignon, at the shop of Giovanni Robby; quarto. *Treatise of Salvian of Marseilles on Providence, in Latin, Italian, and French.* Argelati, at the place cited. The French translation is that of Maupertuis; the Italian translation was made by Guido Ronsartus, a priest.

## Manuscripts

### I. The Books on Avarice

1. The manuscript from which they were first published, belonging to John Sichardus; its present whereabouts is unknown.

2. The exemplar from which Pithou corrected them had passed into the Colbert Library, where Baluzius found it and used it in his third set of revisions. He did not, however, undertake to describe it.

3. The manuscripts of Baluzius, which he used in the very first edition and collated with the Pithouan edition, were two Royal manuscripts communicated to him in 1660 by Nicolas Colbert, bishop first of Luçon and then of Auxerre and director of the Royal Library. One was very ancient, second only to the Corbie manuscript of the books *On the Government of God*, which we shall mention immediately; the other was about four hundred years old.

In the former was Salvian’s letter to Salonius, which is usually prefixed to the books against Avarice, although Pithou had noted that it was absent from his ancient exemplar. Baluzius would likewise have found it in the more recent Royal manuscript if its opening leaves had not been lost.

### II. The Books on the Government of God

1. The principal manuscript—that is, the one from which John Alexander Brassicanus brought forth those books—once belonged to the Royal Library of Buda in Hungary and, before its destruction, came into Brassicanus’s possession through the generosity of King Louis. It was written with sufficient accuracy, as can be seen from the comparison of its text with the later editions.

2. Pithou’s very ancient exemplar, which he had most carefully copied. Baluzius later found it in the Colbert Library and used it for his third revisions.

3. The manuscript of Baluzius belonged to the monastery of Corbie; it was extremely ancient and of the highest quality. He judged that it had been written six hundred years earlier and says that it was copied by a learned hand, which demonstrated its care and diligence, among other things, by placing the punctuation almost everywhere entirely correctly. Nevertheless, it did not contain all eight books. Lucas Dacherius, a member of the Maurist congregation, had supplied it from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

### III. The Letters

1. Nothing is known about Pithou’s manuscript.

2. Baluzius’s exemplars contained only the first two and the last two letters.

[Col. 0025]

[Note: [Col. 0025A] When we first published these books after correcting them, we retained the title exactly as we had found it in the edition of the very distinguished man Pierre Pithou, supposing that he had used an ancient manuscript of good quality in which the title of bishop was attributed to Salvian. For we could obtain no assistance at this point from the Corbie manuscript, although it was ancient and excellent, because its first leaf is missing.

Later, however, we discovered that Pithou’s manuscript, now preserved in the Colbert Library, is not ancient and consequently does not possess such authority that it could compel us to retain a title contrary to the truth. For it is evident that Salvian was not a bishop. If anyone wishes to follow his authority, Salvian himself assumes only the dignity of presbyter in Letter 8, which was sent to Eucherius, bishop of Lyons.

The error arose because certain editions of Gennadius say that, after becoming a bishop, he composed many homilies, whereas the reading should be “to bishops” or “composed by bishops.” For this eloquent and learned man wrote homilies that were afterward recited in church by bishops.

As for the fact that he is called “saint” at the very beginning, although—as Bollandus notes under 16 January—he is neither venerated at Marseilles nor commonly regarded as a saint, something must be said here for the reader’s benefit. It is certain that while Salvian was alive he was called a holy and most blessed man by Hilary, bishop of Arles, and by Eucherius, bishop of Lyons. This reflects the accepted custom of those times, by which bishops and presbyters were commonly called holy and most blessed, just as today we call the Roman bishop “most holy” and “most blessed.”

The same usage continued after death, as is clear from Jerome, who complains in one place that bishops are praised in church by their successors and by the people and are called blessed after death, although their lives may have been far from holiness. This indicates the custom of Jerome’s age, in which Salvian lived.

When some people did not understand this, they took offense that Faustus, the Apollinarian bishop of Riez, was called “saint” in the title of a letter that he wrote to an anonymous person, with the author’s name also omitted. Yet this same Faustus, long before he became bishop, was called “saint” at the Third Council of Arles, held under Ravennius in 455 in the case of Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, and Faustus, then abbot of Lérins; he was also so called by Dinamius and Honoratus, or Ravennius, who wrote accounts of the deeds of Maximus, bishop of Riez, and Hilary of Arles during that period.

And long after his death, namely in the year 534, Caesarius, bishop of Arles, addressed the fathers of a certain council in the case of Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez, as follows: “And Saint Faustus, bishop, said in his letter….”

Therefore it should not seem strange that in the title of these books Salvian—whose blameless conduct, moreover, no one disputes—is called “saint” according to the custom of his age, even though he is not celebrated in the Church by public cult. For undoubtedly there are many saints in heaven who are not included in our catalogue.] 

[Note: [Col. 0025A] Some have believed that Salvian was African by nationality; most think that he was a Gaul, and each side has plausible arguments. For he describes in detail the devastation and destruction of the lands of Africa, and then, in indignation, vehemently attacks the Africans’ extraordinary drunkenness and madness, as though they were his own people. At the same time he bitterly laments the folly of the Gauls, who, after the devastation of their cities and provinces and after the most grievous disasters, still kept their minds turned toward pleasures—pleasures, I say, forbidden by divine law and always contrary to good morals.

Yet those who thought that he was born in Africa were mistaken. For in many places he himself quite clearly assigns himself to Gaul, but especially in Book VII *On the Government of God*, p. 132, where, after recounting the misfortunes of the various provinces of Europe, he adds: “But I am speaking of places situated far away and, as it were, removed into another world, although I know that even in my native land and in the Gallic cities almost all the more eminent men have been made worse by their own calamities.”

It remains, therefore, to investigate in what part of Gaul he was born. Since some think that he was Aquitanian and others that he was from Trier, I prefer the opinion of Aubert Miraeus, who writes that he was born at Cologne or in its vicinity. For Salvian himself, in Book V *On the Government*, p. 125, speaking of the people of Trier, calls them his neighbors.

And lest anyone object that Trier is not meant here because Salvian does not name the city at this point, one should consult him on pp. 135–136, where he discusses the destruction of the city of Trier. He explicitly writes that it was burned, and at the same time reproves his fellow citizens rather harshly because, although they had seen a neighboring city on fire, they were not afraid.

Miraeus’s opinion is also supported by Salvian’s first letter. In recommending to a friend a certain young man who was his relative, he writes as follows: “The young man whom I sent to you was captured at Agrippina together with his family; once a person of no small standing among his own people, of a family not obscure, of a respectable household, and someone about whom I might perhaps say more if he were not my relative. The mother of the man of whom I speak was left a widow at Agrippina,” etc.

I therefore conclude that Salvian was a native of Agrippina. Whether he was a Christian from the beginning is unclear. Certainly he was a Christian when he married Palladia, the daughter of Hypatius and Quieta. At first he invited her to embrace the Christian faith; then, when he had prevailed, he also required her to practice continence and made her his sister in place of his wife, according to the custom of that age.

Hypatius bore Palladia’s conversion to the faith of Christ heavily and resentfully, to such a degree that he not only did not see her for almost seven full years but did not even correspond with her by letter during her absence. For a man imbued with a religion that rejected continence in marriage and imposed penalties on the unmarried, it seemed extremely harsh to deprive his daughter of the care of offspring, since she was his only child, Auspiciola.

Seven years after Palladia’s conversion, Hypatius gave his name to Christ, and Quieta too, as I believe, received Christ’s grace together with her husband. When Salvian saw that the causes of hatred toward his father- and mother-in-law had ceased, he wrote to them, asking in his own name and that of his wife and daughter that their former affection be restored and that, since they were now Christians, they should no longer hate children from whom they had become estranged for no other reason than that they had converted to Christ.

At that time Salvian lived far from his father-in-law—that is, as conjecture suggests, in the province of Vienne, while his father-in-law lived in Belgica Quarta, whose capital was Cologne Agrippina. For I see that Salvian was acquainted with the most distinguished men of those regions: Honoratus, bishop of Arles; Eucherius, bishop of Lyons; Agroecius of Antibes; Salonius, to whom he dedicated the books *On the Government of God*; and Veranus, whom he instructed together with his brother Salonius when they were young.

Finally, when he was called to the clergy, he became a presbyter in the same province of Vienne, namely in the Church of Marseilles. Whether his wife was still alive at the time of his ordination is not recorded in the memory of literature, nor is it known by which bishop of the Church of Marseilles he was admitted to the presbyterate. Those who think that he was a bishop, as we have said above, are very greatly mistaken.

That he flourished in the year 439 and wrote the books *On the Government of God* not long afterward can be inferred from Book VII, p. 153, where he describes the disaster of Litorius, who fought most disastrously near Toulouse in that year, as we shall say in its proper place.

He survived into the time of Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, as Gennadius teaches; Gennadius testifies that Salvian was still living in healthy old age at that time. Gennadius lists very many of his works that no longer exist: namely, three books *On the Good of Virginity*, addressed to Marcellus; a book *On the Explanation of the Final Part of Ecclesiastes*, addressed to Claudianus, chorepiscopus of Vienne; and, in the manner of the Greeks, one book composed in verse like a *Hexaemeron*, from the beginning of Genesis to the creation of man; finally, many homilies.

These works, I say, have perished. What survive, therefore, are eight books *On the Government of God and on the Just and Present Judgment of God*, nine Letters, and four books *To the Catholic Church Against Avarice*.]

## The Eight Books of Saint Salvian of Marseilles, Presbyter, on the Government of God, Addressed to Saint Salonius, Bishop

[Note: [Col. 0026C] A bishop of uncertain see. Some think that he was from Geneva, others from Genoa, and still others from Vienne. He was the son of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, who entrusted him and his brother Veranus to Salvian’s instruction. A brief *Explanation of the Proverbs of Solomon* and a mystical *Explanation of Solomon’s Ecclesiastes* by this Salonius are extant. See below in the notes to Letter 9.]

### Preface

[Col. 0025A]

1. Salvian sends greetings in the Lord to the holy bishop Salonius.

All men who have thought it part of the cultivation of human duty to fashion some literary work by the exertion of their talents have taken particular pains to ensure that, whether they chose useful and honourable or useless and dishonourable subjects, they should adorn the mere sequence of their material with verbal brilliance and, by speaking of the very subjects they wished to treat, cast light upon them.

[Note: [Col. 0028B] Alexander Brassicanus and Peter Galesinius printed this passage thus: “They took particular pains to ensure that, whether they had chosen useful and honourable or useless and dishonourable subjects for themselves, etc.”]

Accordingly, very many writers of worldly affairs from both branches of literature devoted themselves to this task, without sufficiently considering how much more profitably they might expend themselves on their subjects, provided that whatever they said they either sang in polished and pleasing verse or narrated in splendid prose.

[Note: [Col. 0028B] Brassicanus rightly notes here that Salvian used an expression familiar in his age. For Salvian himself uses it frequently, as do other writers of that period.]

For in their writings they dealt only with their own purposes; and, caring more for their own praises than for the usefulness of others, they did not strive to be wholesome and beneficial but merely to be regarded as polished and eloquent.

[Note: [Col. 0028B] “Scholarly” speech is used here, according to the custom of that age, for polished and refined discourse, or, as Cicero would say, speech that is lively, fluent, abundant, and overflowing. Saint Paulinus, in Letter 9 to Severus, praises Rufinus because he was rich in both scholarly and beneficial—or, the reading should be “secular”—literature, in Greek as well as Latin. The word migrated from Greece into Italy, as Seneca also explains in the preface to the *Controversies*: “This second name is indeed Greek, but it has been transferred into Latin in such a way that it counts as Latin: ‘scholarly controversy’ is much more recent, like declamation itself.” For the various meanings of this word, see also Baronius under 6 February, Meursius in the *Glossary*, Rosweyde in the *Onomasticon* to the *Lives of the Fathers*, and Henri Valois on Socrates, p. 77.

Yet do not suppose that Salvian condemns this entire manner of writing. He himself wrote in a thoroughly scholarly style, as these books show, and Gennadius confirms. He condemns only those who turn their eloquence to wicked uses. It would be like criticizing Petronius for having stained his exceptionally pure Latin with an exceptionally impure work, or like Quintilian’s lament that Afranius, a writer of *togatae* who excelled in that genre of comedy, had polluted his plots with the shameful loves of boys. See also Brassicanus on this passage of Salvian.]

Thus their writings are either swollen with vanity,

[Note: [Col. 0028D] Brassicanus printed *vanity*, noting that it was written in the exemplar from which he worked; Galesinius retained this reading, whereas Pithou restored *falsehood*. Since the same word was also found in the Corbie manuscript, we too thought that it should be retained.]

or infamous through falsehood, or filthy with the foulness of words, or corrupt through the obscenity of their subject matter. Thus, while they sought only the praise of their intellects and devoted their care to such unworthy things, they seem to me truly not to have illuminated their talents so much as condemned them.

But we, who are lovers of things rather than of words and pursue what is useful rather than what wins applause,

[Note: [Col. 0028D] Below, in Book IV *On the Government*, p. 60, he will say that words are nothing without things.]

and who do not seek that empty ornaments of the ages be praised in us, but rather that the salutary benefits of realities should be praised, do not wish our little writings to contain flatteries but remedies—remedies that would please not so much the ears of idle people as benefit the minds of the sick. From either result we shall reap a great harvest of heavenly rewards.

For if this work of ours remedies some people's unsound opinion of our God, it will be no small fruit that I have benefited many.

[Note: [Col. 0028D] The Corbie manuscript begins with these words.]

But if this does not happen,

[Col. 0028B]

even this effort will at least not be fruitless,

[Note: [Col. 0028D] This is the reading of Pierre Pithou’s edition. The reading of the Corbie manuscript is also undoubtedly good; it runs as follows: “And even this, having been judged not fruitless, will not be…”—provided that it is read in that way: “And even this will have proved not fruitless.”]

because I tried to be of help. For the intention of a good and devout undertaking, even if the work begun does not achieve its effect, nevertheless receives the reward of its willingness.

From this point, then, I shall begin.

# BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0029D] This book was inscribed as follows in the Corbie manuscript: *On the Just and Present Judgment of God*. The rest was absent. Salvianus, in fact, does not argue in this first book about government, although he touches on that subject lightly as well, but about the judgment of God. Only in the second book does he undertake to write about the government of God, as will be noted there.]

## I

God is said by some to be unconcerned and almost negligent about human actions, since he neither protects the good nor restrains the wicked; and therefore, in this world, the good are generally wretched while the wicked are happy. Indeed, since we are dealing with Christians, divine speech alone ought to suffice to refute these claims. But because many people retain something of pagan unbelief, they may perhaps also take pleasure in the testimony of selected and learned pagans.

We therefore show that even those who lacked true religion—and consequently could by no means have known God, since they did not know the law by which God is recognized—did not think this way about his unconcern and negligence. The philosopher Pythagoras, whom philosophy itself looked up to as its teacher, discussing the nature and benefits of God, spoke as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0029D] In the first edition we had written *suscepit*, following the edition of Pithoeus. But since the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius both have *suspexit*, and since this latter reading is confirmed by the authority of the Corbie manuscript, we have decided to retain it.]

[Note: [Col. 0029D] The very learned Conrad Rittershusius noted that our author imitates Minucius Felix’s words in the *Octavius* here. His words are: “And God is mind, passing through and attentive throughout the whole nature of things, from which also the life of all animals is derived.” But I do not think that Salvianus took this from Minucius, but from Cicero (*On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I), whom he follows word for word. The passage is from the first book *On the Nature of the Gods*, as we noted in the margin.]

“Mind, passing through and diffused throughout all the parts of the world, from which all animals that are born receive life.”

How, then, can God be said to neglect the world, when he plainly loves it for this very reason: that he extends himself throughout the entire body of the world? Plato and all the schools of the Platonists acknowledge God as the governor of all things.

[Note: [Col. 0030D] Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 2, notes that the Stoics vigorously refuted the madness of those who thought that the gods did not exist, and taught both that the world could not have come into being without divine reason and that it could not endure unless it were governed by supreme reason. In Book VII, chapter 3, he writes that Plato taught that the world was made by God and governed by his providence.]

The Stoics testify that he remains continually within what he governs, in the role of a helmsman. What could they have thought more correctly and reverently about God’s care and diligence than to say that he resembles a helmsman? They understood, of course, that just as a helmsman at sea never removes his hand from the helm, so God never entirely withdraws his care from the world; and just as the helmsman, catching the winds, avoiding the rocks, and looking up at the stars, is wholly devoted at once, both in body and in mind, to his task, so our God neither turns away from the whole universe the service of his most worthy vision, nor removes the governance of his providence, nor takes away the indulgence of his most benevolent compassion.

Hence also that example of mystical authority, by which Maro wished to prove himself no less a philosopher than a poet, when he said (*Georgics* IV):

> For God moves through all things,
>
> Through lands and expanses of sea and the deep heaven.

Tullius likewise says: “Nor indeed can God himself, as we understand him,” he says (*Tusculan Disputations*, Book I, chapter 27), “be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, released, free, and separated from every mortal composition, perceiving and moving all things.” Elsewhere also he says: “For nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be governed by him. God is therefore obedient or subject to no nature. He himself, then, governs all nature.”

Unless, perhaps, we—the wisest of all—should think that the one whom we say governs everything both governs and neglects it at the same time. Since, then, everyone, even those without religion, compelled by the force of the matter itself and by a kind of necessity, has said that all things are perceived, moved, and governed by God, how can some now think him unconcerned and negligent, when he perceives everything through subtlety, moves everything through strength, governs everything through power, and protects everything through benevolence?

I have stated what the foremost authorities of both philosophy and eloquence judged concerning the majesty and governance of the supreme God. I brought forward the most distinguished teachers of both eminent arts so that I might more easily show either that all the others held the same view, or at least that those who disagreed did so without any authority.

And indeed, apart from the ravings of the Epicureans or of certain people who play the Epicurean, I cannot find anyone who disagreed with their judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0030D] These are the people who, as the same Lactantius says in Book I, chapter 8, unwilling to admit that the world was made by God, used to ask with what hands, what machines, what words, and by what exertion he had accomplished so great a work.]

Just as they joined pleasure to virtue, so they joined God to unconcern and torpor, making it evident that those who think in this way pursue not only the opinion and doctrine of the Epicureans but also their vices.

## II

I do not think that, in order to prove so obvious a matter, we now need to use divine testimonies in this place—especially since the sacred writings contradict all the claims of the impious so fully and clearly that, while answering their subsequent accusations, we can also refute more completely what has already been said.

They say, then, that God has abandoned everything because he neither restrains the wicked nor protects the good; and therefore that in this world the condition of the better is much worse: the good are in poverty, the wicked in abundance; the good in weakness, the wicked in strength; the good always in mourning, the wicked always in joy; the good in misery and degradation, the wicked in prosperity and honor.

First, then, I ask those who either grieve or complain that this is so whether they grieve over the saints—that is, over true and faithful Christians—or over false Christians and impostors.

If they mean the false, their grief is needless, since they are grieving that the wicked are not happy. For all who are wicked necessarily become worse through the success of their affairs, rejoicing that their devotion to wickedness is prospering. For this very reason they ought to be most miserable, so that they may cease to be wicked—claiming the name of religion for their most depraved *quaestionibus* (“questionings”),

[Note: [Col. 0031C] Rittershusius emended this by conjecture to *quaestibus* and attempted to support his conjecture by the authority of Cyprian’s *On the Lapsed*. Yet both the Corbie manuscript and Pithoeus’s edition have *quaestionibus*.]

and applying the title of holiness to the filthiest commercial dealings.

[Note: [Col. 0031C] Below, at the end of Book III, p. 59: “For it is of no benefit whatever to bear a holy name without corresponding conduct, since a life at odds with one’s profession abolishes the honor of a distinguished title through the baseness of unworthy actions.” Likewise, in Book V, p. 108, he attacks those who pretend to religion and, having inscribed themselves with the title of holiness, had indeed changed their name by that profession but had not abandoned their former behavior. From these passages it follows that those who devoted themselves to a stricter way of life were then called holy. Shortly afterward he calls them “religious”; and on p. 8, treating this same argument, he says: “Religious and holy men are not to be thought wretched.” By “religious,” as will be stated on p. 80, Salvianus understood clerics, monks, and generally those who turned from secular life to profess a stricter way of life.]

Compared with their wickedness, their miseries are less than they deserve; for, however miserable their circumstances, they are still not as miserable as they are wicked. Therefore no one should grieve on their behalf because they are not rich and happy—and much less should anyone grieve on behalf of the saints. For although the saints may appear miserable to the ignorant, they cannot be anything other than happy.

It is pointless for anyone to think that those who trust themselves to be happy are miserable because of weakness, poverty, or other such conditions. No one is miserable according to another person’s judgment, but according to his own. Therefore those who are truly happy in their own conscience cannot be made miserable by anyone’s false judgment. For, as I think, no one is happier than those who act according to their own judgment and desire.

The religious are humble: this is what they want. They are poor: they take pleasure in poverty. They are without ambition: they reject ambition. They are without honor: they flee honor.

[Note: [Col. 0032C] Pithoeus’s edition has *respuunt* (“they reject”), as do Brassicanus and Galesinius. The reading was corrected from the Corbie manuscript. Why would Salvianus, without necessity, use the same word twice within one line? It was undoubtedly a scribal error.]

They mourn: they delight in mourning. They are weak: they rejoice in weakness. For, as the Apostle says, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Corinthians XII, 10). And he judges this not without reason, since God himself says to him: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is made perfect in weakness” (ibid., 9).

[Note: [Col. 0032C] Whether Salvianus is speaking of monks or clerics, it certainly cannot be inferred from this passage that religious persons were then required to make a public profession of poverty, or what we today call a vow of poverty. For Salvianus himself will teach below, in Book III against greed, p. 256, that ownership of goods and possessions had not yet been forbidden them in those times. The sense of this passage, therefore, is that religious persons who were poor either by choice or by circumstance endured poverty with equanimity and joy, not—as most people do—with complaints and lamentation over their lot. In later centuries it was thought useful for the sake of discipline that religious persons should not be permitted to own anything of their own, to such an extent that they did not even wish the Roman pontiff to be allowed to dispense a monk from the rule concerning ownership, as was recently observed in the notes to the Councils of Narbonne in Gaul, p. 28.]

Therefore we should by no means grieve over this affliction of weakness, which we understand to be the mother of virtues. Whatever it may be, all who are truly religious must be called happy, because, amid every hardship and every harshness, no one is happier than those who are what they wish to be.

There are, to be sure, some who pursue shameful and obscene things and, although they are happy according to their own opinion because they attain what they want, are not truly happy, since they ought not to have wanted what they want. Religious persons, however, are happier than all others because they both possess what they want and cannot possibly possess anything better than what they have.

Labor, fasting, poverty, humility, and weakness are therefore burdensome not to everyone who endures them, but to those who are unwilling to endure them.

[Note: [Col. 0032D] Tacitus, *Annals*, Book VI: “Neither the evils nor the goods that the common people imagine: many who seem to struggle with adversity are happy, and many, although possessed of great wealth, are most wretched, if the former endure their harsh fortune steadfastly while the latter use prosperity recklessly.” See the notes to the second letter of Lupus of Ferrières.]

For whether these things are heavy or light, the spirit of the person enduring them determines that. Just as nothing is so light that it is not burdensome to one who does it unwillingly,

[Note: [Col. 0032D] Below, at the end of Book IV against greed, p. 295: “Everything that is imposed is hard to those who are unwilling.”]

so nothing is so heavy that it does not seem light to one who carries it out willingly.

Unless, perhaps, we should think that poverty was burdensome to those ancient men of old-fashioned virtue—the Fabii, Fabricii, and Cincinnatus—who did not wish to be rich, while they devoted all their zeal and all their efforts to the common good and enriched the growing strength of the republic through their private poverty.
