Did they endure that frugal and rustic life with groaning and pain, when they ate coarse and rustic food before the very hearths on which it had been cooked, and were not permitted to take even that food until evening?

[Note: [Col. 0032D] That is, turnips, as is clear from Aurelius Victor, chapter 33, *On Illustrious Men*. Salvianus refers to the story of the Roman citizen Curius Dentatus, whom Samnite envoys found roasting turnips and dining from a wooden dish, as Valerius Maximus says in Book IV, chapter 3. Thus, as Florus writes, he preferred his earthenware to Samnite gold. See Cicero, *On Old Age*.]

Did they find it distressing that a greedy and wealthy conscience did not weigh them down with talents of gold, when they even restricted the use of silver by law?

[Note: [Col. 0032D] The Corbie manuscript rightly has this in place of the “greedy and wealthy conscience” found in Pithoeus’s edition. That this emendation is legitimate is also confirmed by the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius, which print the passage as follows: “Did they find it distressing that a greedy conscience, separated from wealth, did not weigh them down with talents of gold?”]

Did they regard it as a punishment for temptation and desire that they did not have purses swollen with gold coins, when they judged a patrician unworthy of the senate because he had wished to be rich up to ten pounds of silver?

[Note: [Col. 0033C] Cornelius Rufinus, as Valerius Maximus teaches in Book II, chapter 4. Tertullian also mentions him in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 6: “which used to remove from the senate a patrician who had possessed ten pounds of silver, because this was considered a great title of ambition.”]

They did not despise poor clothing, I think, when they wore a rough and short garment, when they were summoned from the plow to the fasces, and wiped away their sweat-dampened dust with the splendid consular dress—perhaps with those very imperial togas which they were about to assume.

Thus, at that time, those poor magistrates possessed a wealthy republic. Now, however,

[Note: [Col. 0033C]

I agree with Rittershusius, who thinks that the term *potestas* in Salvianus here and elsewhere should be understood as the very designation of magistracy. In this sense the word may perhaps be understood in the ancient inscription first published here from an old stone that stands at Narbonne in the church of the Prior of Blessed Mary the Greater. The stone is very large, cut into an arch at the top and flat at the bottom; it is reasonably conjectured to have been placed on the threshold of some temple. On its front side the following is read:

> IMP. CAESARI. DIVI. NERVAE F. NERVAE. TRAIANO. GERM. PONT. MAX. TRIB. POT. COS. II. Q. S....ILIUS........ANUS. IIIIII. VIR. AUGUSTAL. DE. SUA. MEDIOCRITA. ................, MENTO FIERI. PONIQUE. IUSSIT.

Translation: “To the Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajan, son of the deified Nerva, Germanicus, chief pontiff, holder of tribunician power, consul for the second time. Q. S...ilius...anus, sevir Augustalis, at his own modest expense, ordered [lacuna]mento to be made and set up.”

On the reverse side, in larger letters:

> AD. URNAM. POTESTATIS.

Translation: “At the urn of magistracy.”

[Col. 0034C]

Moreover, that *sevir augustalis*, whose name has perished through half of it, may perhaps be Servilius Marcianus, priest at the temple of Roma and the Augusti at Arles, who is mentioned in an old inscription at Lyons in Sixtus’s *Pontifical of Arles*, p. 53. The words missing from the inscription should doubtless be supplied as follows: “ordered it to be made and set up from the foundation at his own modest means.”]

wealthy power makes the republic poor. And what madness—or what blindness—is it to believe that private wealth can remain standing when the republic is destitute and begging?

Such, then, were the ancient Romans; and just as those who now follow the Lord despise wealth, so they then despised it without knowing God. Yet why do I speak of those who, in their concern to extend the empire, devoted their contempt for private means to the public wealth, and, although poor in private life, abounded in common riches?

Certain Greeks, too, followers of wisdom, without any concern for public utility, stripped themselves of nearly all use of their property in their eagerness to attain glory; and not only this, but they raised their doctrine to the point of contempt for pain and death, saying that the wise man is happy even in chains and punishments.

They wished the power of virtue to be so great that a good man could never be unhappy. If, then, even those whom some wise men today do not consider miserable—because they received no fruit from their labor except present praise—are not to be thought miserable, how much less should religious and holy men be considered miserable, since they both enjoy the rewards of present faith and will obtain the rewards of future blessedness?

## III

One of those about whom we are complaining said to a certain holy man who thought according to the rule of truth—that is, that God governed everything and adjusted his moderation and governance according to what he knew to be necessary for the human race:

[Note: [Col. 0034C] Rittershusius is perhaps not wrong in thinking that this whole passage should be read and punctuated as follows: “and adjusted his moderation and governance according to what he knew to be necessary for the human race.” Yet all the editions and manuscripts oppose this, except that, instead of *necessariam*, the reading in both Pithoeus’s edition and the others, the Corbie manuscript has *necessarium*, which supports Rittershusius’s conjecture. Brassicanus and Galesinius, removing *nosset* as superfluous, print the passage as follows: “and adjusted his moderation and governance as necessary for the human race.”]

“Why, then, I ask, are you yourself weak?” This was said with the following meaning and judgment: If God, as you think, governs everything in this present life; if God orders all things, why is the sinner whom I know strong and healthy, while you, whom I do not doubt to be holy, are weak?

Who would not admire a man of such profound judgment, who considers the merits and virtues of religious persons worthy of such great rewards that he thinks health of the flesh and bodily strength ought to be the rewards of the saints in this present life?

I answer, then, not in the name of one religious person only, but of all. You ask, whoever you are, why holy men are weak. I answer briefly: they make themselves weaker for this reason, because if they are strong, they can scarcely be holy.

For I think that all human beings are made strong by food and drink, but weak by abstinence, dryness, and fasting. It is therefore no wonder that those who reject the use of the things by which others become strong are weak.

And there is a reason why they reject them, as the Apostle Paul says of himself: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should become disqualified” (I Corinthians IX, 27).

If the Apostle himself thinks that bodily weakness should be sought, who wisely avoids it? If the Apostle fears strength of the flesh, who can reasonably presume to be strong? This, then, is the reason why those devoted to Christ are both weak and wish to be weak.

But let us not suppose that religious persons are neglected by God on the basis of this very fact through which we trust that they are loved more.

We read that the Apostle Timothy was extremely weak in body.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] Below, Letter 9, p. 200: “Timothy the apostle.” Jerome, in his *Chronicle*: “The remains of the apostle Timothy were brought to Constantinople.” It is certain that Timothy was not one of those whom we commonly call the apostles. Primasius, in his commentary on the first chapter of Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, which begins “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ,” denies Timothy the apostolate when he says: “Every apostle is a servant, but not every servant is an apostle.” Yet it should be understood that the name “apostle” is general and applies to all who were sent to instruct some nation in the Christian faith, as was formerly stated at the Council of Limoges and is read in the twentieth letter of John concerning the apostolate of Saint Martial. Thus Paul calls Epaphroditus the apostle of the Philippians.]

Was he neglected by the Lord? Or did he fail to please Christ because of his weakness—the very weakness he wished to have in order to please him? The Apostle Paul himself, although Timothy was already suffering from excessive weakness, permitted him to take and taste only a little wine (I Timothy V, 23); that is, he wished him to care for his weakness but did not wish him to attain strength.

And why was this so? Why, unless because, as Paul himself says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to each other, so that you may not do whatever you wish” (Galatians V, 17)?

One man said wisely at this point that, if we cannot do what we desire because of the strength of the body resisting us, we should weaken the flesh so that we may do what we desire.

“For the weakness of the flesh,” he says, “sharpens the vigor of the mind, and when the limbs are weakened, the powers of the body are transferred into the virtues of the soul; the marrow does not burn with shameful flames, hidden impulses do not inflame an unsound mind, wandering senses do not revel in various pleasures; only the soul exults, rejoicing in an afflicted body as though its adversary had been subdued.”

[Note: [Col. 0035D] In other editions this passage had a weaker sense and read as follows: “So that, when the limbs are weakened, the strength of the body may be transferred into the virtues of the soul.” But the reading in the Corbie manuscript is elevated and worthy of Salvianus, and we have reproduced it faithfully. Salvianus himself confirms this emendation in Letter 5, from which these words are taken.]

This, then, as I said, is the reason for the weakness of religious men; and I think you can no longer deny that it is so.

## IV

“But there are perhaps other and greater matters,” you say: “that they suffer many harsh and bitter things in this life; that they are captured, tortured, and slaughtered.”

It is true. But what shall we say, since the prophets too were led into captivity, and the apostles also endured torments? And certainly we cannot doubt that they were then especially objects of God’s care, when they suffered these things for God.

“But perhaps,” you say, “you think that this very fact proves more strongly that God neglects everything in this world and reserves everything for future judgment, since the good have always suffered every evil while the wicked have done everything.”

The assertion does not appear wholly irreligious, especially since it acknowledges God’s future judgment. But we say that Christ will judge the human race in such a way that we nevertheless believe God even now governs and orders everything as he considers reasonable; and we affirm that he will judge in the future judgment in such a way that we nevertheless teach that he has always judged in this world as well.

For since God always governs, he always judges, because governance itself is judgment.

How many ways do you wish us to prove this: by reasoning, examples, or testimonies?

If by reasoning, who is so devoid of human understanding and so alien to the very truth of which we are speaking that he does not recognize and see that the beautiful work of the world and the immeasurable magnificence of heavenly and infernal things are governed by the same one by whom they were created, and that the maker of the elements must also be their governor?

He governs everything, of course, by the same power and majesty by which he created it, and directs it by the same providence and reason—especially since, even in matters administered by human action, nothing at all endures without reason, and all things draw their preservation from providence just as the body draws life from the soul.

Therefore in this world not only governments and provinces, civil and military affairs, but also lesser offices and private households, even cattle themselves and the smallest kinds of domestic animals, are maintained only through human ordering and deliberation, as though by a certain hand and helm.

And all these things are without doubt subject to the will and judgment of the supreme God, so that the whole human race might govern the parts and members of things by this example, by which God himself governs the sum of the entire body of the world.

“But at the beginning,” you say, “these things were established and arranged by God among the creatures. After the universe had been completed and perfected, however, he removed from himself all care for earthly matters and sent it away”—perhaps fleeing labor, he banished it from its place and avoided the burden of toil; or, occupied with other affairs, he left part of the world’s business because he could not attend to everything.

[Note: [Col. 0036D] This passage seems to be rightly read and punctuated as printed here. The editions have the same reading, and the sense requires that it be retained. Yet the Corbie manuscript had: “and sent away labor, namely, etc.” Before leaving this passage, I thought it necessary to warn the reader that in the same manuscript *commendavit* was written in place of *amandavit*. This alternative reading has also elsewhere been noted in the margin of Pithoeus’s edition.]

## V

“God therefore removes from himself,” he says, “care for mortals.”

What, then, is the basis of our divine religion? What reason is there for worshiping Christ, or what hope of winning his favor?

For if God neglects the human race in this world, why do we raise our hands daily toward heaven? Why do we seek God’s mercy with frequent prayers? Why do we hurry to churches? Why do we plead before the altars?

There is no reason for us to pray if hope of receiving what we ask is taken away. You see, then, how foolish and empty this assertion is. If it is accepted, nothing at all remains of religion.

But perhaps you will take refuge in saying that we worship God out of fear of future judgment and labor through every form of present service so that we may deserve acquittal on the day of the future world.

What, then, does the Apostle Paul mean when he commands that prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be offered continually to our God in the Church every day (I Timothy II, 1)? And for what purpose are all these things offered, except, as he himself says, “so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all chastity” (ibid., 2)?

He commands us, as we see, to entreat and pray to the Lord for present things—which he certainly would not command unless he were confident that the Lord could be entreated.

How, then, can anyone think that God’s ears are open to requests for benefits in the future but closed and blocked to requests for present benefits? Or how can we, pleading in church, ask God for present salvation if we do not believe that he hears us at all?

We should therefore make no petitions for our safety and prosperity. Rather, so that modesty might win the voice of the petitioner, perhaps we should say:

“Lord, we do not ask for prosperity in this life, nor do we plead for present benefits. For we know that your ears are closed to such entreaties and that you do not lend your hearing to prayers of this kind. We ask only for those things that will exist after death.”

Even if such a petition is not without benefit, how can it stand to reason? If God has withdrawn his care from the affairs of this world and closed his ears to the prayers of those who ask, then without doubt the one who does not hear us concerning present matters does not hear us concerning future matters either—unless perhaps we believe that Christ grants or withholds his ears according to the diversity of prayers: that he closes them when present things are requested and opens them when future things are requested.

But no more need be said about this. Such claims are so foolish and frivolous that we must be careful lest what is said for the honor of God appear to be an insult to God.

For sacred majesty is so great, and reverence toward it so fearsome, that we must not only recoil from the things they say against religion, but must also speak with profound fear and discipline about the things we ourselves say in defense of religion.

Therefore, if it is foolish and impious to believe that divine compassion despises the care of human affairs, then it does not despise them. If it does not despise them, it governs them. If it governs them, then by the very fact that it governs, it judges; for governance cannot exist unless judgment continually resides in the governor.

## VI

But perhaps someone may think that what reason declares is insufficient unless it is proved by examples. Let us see how God governed the world from the beginning, and we shall show that he always governed everything while also teaching that he judged.

For what does Scripture say? “Then God formed man from the dust of the earth and breathed into him the breath of life” (Genesis II, 7). And what followed? “He placed him,” it says, “in the paradise of pleasure” (ibid., 15).

What came next? He gave him a law, instructed him in commandments, and formed him through teaching.

What followed after these things? Man transgressed the sacred command, underwent sentence, lost paradise, and received the punishment of condemnation.

Who would not see in all these things both God as governor and God as judge?

He established Adam innocent in paradise and expelled him when guilty. In his establishment there is ordering; in his expulsion, judgment. When he placed him in the place of pleasure, he made provision for him; when he expelled him, guilty, from the kingdom, he judged him.

This, then, concerns the first man, that is, the father. What about the second, that is, the son?

“After many days,” the sacred Scripture says, “Cain brought from the fruits of the earth an offering to the Lord. Abel also brought from the firstlings of his flock and from its fat portions. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his offering, but he did not look upon Cain and his offering” (Genesis IV, 3–5).

Before I speak of God’s more evident judgment, I think that even in what we have already said there is a certain sentence of judgment. For in accepting one man’s sacrifice and excluding another’s, God most clearly judged both the righteousness of the one and the wickedness of the other.

But this is not enough. Preparing the way for his future crime, Cain leads his brother into solitude, accomplishes his crime with secrecy as his ally, and—both most wicked and most foolish—believes that he has secured the commission of the greatest outrage if he avoids the sight of human beings, although he is about to commit fratricide with God as witness.

Therefore I think that he already held the opinion that is now held by many: namely, that God does not regard earthly affairs and does not see the actions of criminal human beings. There is no doubt that, after committing the crime and being confronted by God’s word, he replied that he knew nothing about his brother’s murder.

[Note: [Col. 0037D] There is no doubt that this reading should be preferred to the one found in Pithoeus’s edition, where the passage reads: “He replied that he was conscious of nothing concerning his brother’s murder.” Besides the authority of the Corbie manuscript, which we used in emending this passage, the reading is also confirmed by the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius.]

He considered God so ignorant of his deed that he believed the most deadly crime could be concealed by a lie. But he learned that the matter was otherwise. For the God whom he did not think saw crimes when he killed his brother, he perceived to see them when he was condemned.

Now I wish to ask those who deny that human affairs are either regarded, governed, or judged by God whether everything in these events was the opposite of what we have said.

For I think that God is present when he attends to the sacrifice; governs when he punishes Cain after the sacrifices; is concerned when he demands the murdered man from the murderer; and judges when he condemns the wicked assailant with just retribution.

In this connection, the following point is also not inappropriate:

[Note: [Col. 0038D] I agree with Rittershusius, who thinks that there is a textual corruption here.]

Let us not be surprised, then, that holy men now suffer certain harsh things, when we see that even then God permitted the first of the saints to be killed through the greatest crime.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] That is, Abel.]

The reason why he permits this cannot be fully understood by the feeble investigation of human beings, nor is it for us to discuss it at that time. For the present, it is enough to prove that all such things happen not through God’s negligence or unconcern, but are permitted by his counsel and ordering.

Nor can we call something unjust when we cannot deny that God’s judgment is present in it, because God’s will is perfect justice. It is not unjust merely because human beings cannot grasp the force of divine justice.

But let us return to our subject.

### VII

We see, therefore, that in the matters just mentioned nothing was done through God’s negligence, but that some things divine arrangement ordered in this way, some things patience endured, and some things judgment [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “vindicated.”] condemned. But perhaps some will not think that we have proved what we say by means of a few examples. Let us see whether we can also demonstrate the same thing through all of them.

As the human race increased and multiplied, and wickedness increased with it, God, says Holy Scripture, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth and that every inclination of their heart was directed toward evil at all times, repented that he had made humanity upon the earth; and, touched with inward grief of heart, he said, “I will destroy the human being whom I created from the face of the earth” (Genesis 6:5–7).

Let us consider how, in all these statements, both the Lord’s concern and his severity are simultaneously indicated. First it says, “God saw”; second, “Touched with inward grief of heart”; third, “I will destroy,” he said, “the human being whom I created.” In the statement that God is said to see everything, his care is displayed; in the statement that he grieves, the terror of one who is angry; in the statement that he punishes, the severity of the judge.

“God repented,” Holy Scripture says, “that he had made the human being upon the earth”—not because God is subject to this emotion or lies under any passion; rather, divine speech, to convey to us more fully the meaning of the things written, speaks with us in a manner adapted to human feeling and, under the name of repentance, [Note: So below, book 4, page 71: “Since the mind and majesty of God’s nature are such that it is moved by no passion of anger.” In both places that word is used barbarously for what Latin writers call *affectus animi* or *affectio*, “a movement or affection of the mind.” That corruption of the Roman language had evidently become widespread in Salvian’s age, since the same word is used to signify an affection of the mind by Bachiarius in his letter to Januarius, Saint Ambrose, Cassian, Faustus of Riez, Caesarius of Arles, Ruricius of Limoges, Julianus Pomerius, and many others.] [Note: Faustus of Riez imitated Salvian in his letter to an anonymous recipient, where we read: “God’s anger is justice; God’s fury is the force of severity; for God to have sworn is to have determined; for God to have repented***. Yet the sentence is often changed. And when he says that he is harmed by someone persecuting him, he indicates the fault of the one harming him.” Salvian, however, says in book 2, page 29, that the countenance of a propitious Divinity is the gift of humanity’s preservation.] reveals the force of the angry God. The anger of the Godhead is the punishment of the sinner.

What followed, then? “When God saw,” he says, “that the earth was corrupt, he said to Noah: ‘The end of all flesh has come before me; the earth is filled with iniquity because of them, and I will destroy them along with the earth’” (ibid., 13).

And what happened afterward? “All the springs of the great abyss burst open,” he says, “and the floodgates of heaven were opened; and rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights” (Genesis 7:11–12). And shortly afterward: “All flesh that moved upon the earth was consumed” (ibid., 21). And thereafter: “Only Noah remained, and those who were with him in the ark” (ibid., 23).

Here I wish to ask those who call God unconcerned with human affairs whether they believe that at that time he either cared for earthly matters or judged them. I think he not only judged, but judged in two ways. For while preserving the good, he proved himself a pious rewarder; and while condemning the wicked, he proved himself a true judge.

But perhaps among foolish people these events seem to have less authority because they occurred before the Flood—that is, as though in some other age. As though God were different then, or afterward had been unwilling to exercise the same care for the world. By divine favor I could prove what I say through every generation after the Flood; but the sheer scale of the task forbids this, and certain significant examples are sufficient. Since there is unquestionably one God of both the great and the small, we must clearly understand that what is demonstrated in greater matters is also present in lesser ones.

### VIII

After the Flood, therefore, when God had blessed the human race and that blessing had produced an immense multitude of human beings, the Lord speaks to Abraham from heaven (Genesis 12:1), commanding him to leave his own land and seek a foreign one. He is called, follows, is brought there, and is settled; from poor he becomes wealthy, from unknown powerful, lowest in his pilgrimage and most exalted in dignity.

But lest the things given to him by God [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “given by the Lord.”] should nevertheless seem to have been gifts alone and not rewards for merit, the man who rejoiced in prosperity is tested by adversity. Labor, danger, and fear follow. He is harassed by migration, worn out by exile, treated with insult, and deprived of his wife. God commanded that his son be sacrificed to him; the father offered him, and, so far as the death of the heart is concerned, sacrificed him. [Note: In the margin of the Pithoean edition it is noted that elsewhere *definitio* is read, a form also found in the Corbie Codex.]

Again exile, again fear, the hostility of the Philistines, the seizure by Abimelech: many evils, but also corresponding consolations. For although he is afflicted by many, he is nevertheless avenged against them all.

What, then, appears in all these events we have recalled? Is God not at once observer, caller, guide, concerned guardian, guarantor, protector, giver of gifts, tester, exalter, avenger, and judge?

He is observer, when he chooses from among all the one whom he sees to be better; caller, when he summons him; guide, when he leads him to unknown places; concerned guardian, when he visits him at the oak; guarantor, when he promises future things; protector, because he protected him among barbarous nations; giver of gifts, because he enriched him; tester, because he wished him to be tested by hardships; exalter, because he made him more powerful than all; avenger, because he avenged him against his adversaries; judge, because in avenging him he rendered judgment.

Immediately afterward God adds to this history, saying: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave” (Genesis 18:20). “The outcry,” he says, “of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied.” He aptly said that sins contain an outcry. For unquestionably great is the cry of sinners, rising from earth to heaven.

Why, then, does he testify that human sins cry out, as it were? Clearly because God says that his ears are struck by the cries of sinners, so that the punishment of sinners may no longer be delayed. And truly it is a cry—a great cry—when God’s mercy is overcome by the cries of sinners, so that he is compelled to punish them.

The Lord therefore shows how unwillingly he punishes even the gravest sinners, saying that the cry of Sodom has risen to him. This is what he means: “My mercy indeed urges me to spare them, but the cry of the sinners compels me to punish them.”

When he had said this, what followed? Angels are sent to Sodom (Genesis 19:1 and following); they depart, enter the city, are treated kindly by the good, and suffer injury from the wicked. The wicked are blinded; the righteous are saved. [Note: That is, with his wife and children. In that age the word was commonly used to mean relatives; we may perhaps discuss this more fully in the notes to the letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges. See Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon* under the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

Lot is led out of the city with his dear ones; the city is burned with its impious inhabitants. I ask whether God burned the wicked from judgment or without judgment. Whoever says that the Sodomites were punished by God without judgment accuses God of injustice. But if he destroyed the wicked with judgment, then he judged. [Note: Other editions read: “But if he destroyed the wicked with judgment, then he certainly judged.” The Corbie Codex elegantly repeats the word “judged”; so too the Colbert Codex.]

He certainly judged—and already judged, as it were, in the likeness of the future judgment. For since it is clear that Gehenna will burn in the future as punishment for the wicked, heavenly fire consumed Sodom and the neighboring cities. In the present, God wished to disclose the judgment that is to come, when he sent Gehenna from heaven upon the impious people; as the apostle also says (2 Peter 2:6), that God condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah by overthrow, making them an example for those who would act impiously.

Yet the very thing enacted there contained more mercy than severity. His delaying their punishment for so long was mercy; that he punished them at last was justice. And therefore, when God sent the angels to Sodom, he wished to prove to us that he also punishes the wicked unwillingly: namely, so that when we read what the angels suffered from the Sodomites, and see the enormity of their crimes, the disgracefulness of their offenses, and the obscenity of their lusts, God might prove to us that he himself did not wish to destroy them, but that they themselves forced him to let them perish.

### IX

I could produce countless examples. But I fear that, while striving to prove the matter sufficiently, I may seem to have merely woven a history. [Note: The Brassican edition reads: “I fear that, while striving sufficiently to prove the matter, I may seem to have woven a history.” Galesinius reads: “I fear that, while striving sufficiently to prove the matter.” Pithoeus reads: “I fear that, while striving sufficiently to disprove the matter.” We have followed the authority of the Corbie Codex. In place of *texisse*, which Pithoeus’s edition has entirely wrongly, we have restored *texuisse* on the authority of the Corbie Codex and the earlier editions. Rittershusius made the same correction in his edition. A similar error occurred in Vincent of Lérins’s *Commonitorium*.]

Moses, stationed in the desert, tends the flock (Exodus 3); he sees the bush burning, hears God from the bush, receives commands, is elevated to power, and is sent to Pharaoh. He comes, speaks, is despised, and conquers. Egypt is struck; Pharaoh’s disobedience is scourged—not in one way only, but in many, [Note: The Colbert Codex reads: “so that the sacrilegious man might be tortured more.”] so that the sacrilegious man might be tortured all the more by the variety of his punishments. [Note: Pithoeus’s edition reads: “And what then? At last he rebels ten times,” and so forth. Here we have faithfully reproduced the Corbie Codex. This confirms the conjecture of Rittershusius, who had advised that it should be read this way.]

And what happened finally? He rebels ten times and is scourged ten times. What, then, are we to say? I think that in all these events you recognize that God both cares for human affairs and judges them. [Note: Since this passage is read in different ways, and Rittershusius had suggested that it should apparently read, “For in Egypt then the judgment of God was not simple,” we have followed his conjecture in this edition so as to give the passage a coherent meaning.]

For in Egypt at that time God’s judgment was evidently not merely simple but manifold. For each time he struck the rebellious Egyptians, he judged.

But after the events we have described, what followed? Israel is released; it celebrates the Passover; [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “is celebrated”; the Corbie Codex, “having been celebrated.”] it plunders the Egyptians; it departs wealthy. Pharaoh repents, gathers his army, reaches the fugitives, encamps, and is separated from them by darkness. The sea dries up; Israel advances and is freed through the accommodating submission of the waves. Pharaoh follows; the sea rolls over him [Note: The Corbie Codex reads “rolls over him.” Hence *volumina* is used for “waves” in the published letters of Meletius, bishop of Mopsuestia, and of Theodoret of Cyrus, in the synodical work against the tragedy of Irenaeus, chapters 119, 129, 139, and 151. Pliny, book 7, chapter 45: “Great are the upheavals of the human condition.”]; he is destroyed beneath the covering flood.

I think it is now clear that in these events God’s judgment was present—and not judgment alone, but also restraint and patience. It was patience that the rebellious Egyptians were struck repeatedly; it was judgment that those who persisted in obstinacy [Note: That is, those who remained stubborn in their defiance. Others, according to their differing views, say that this means a mind lacking generosity, while still others take it to mean a noble and lofty spirit.] were condemned to death.

After this sequence of events, the victorious Hebrew people, triumphant without battle, enter the wilderness. They make a journey without a road, travel without a path, with God preceding them; honored by divine companionship, powerful under heavenly guidance, they follow a moving column—cloud by day, fire by night—assuming suitable differences of color according to the changes of time. Thus by its yellowish darkness it distinguished the light of day, [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “light.”] and by its fiery brilliance it illuminated the darkness of night.

Add to this springs suddenly brought forth; add waters that were healed, or supplied, or transformed, [Note: The same codex reads “invited.”] preserving their appearance while abandoning their nature. Add the opened summits of mountains bursting forth with streams; add dusty fields gushing with new torrents; add flocks of birds brought into the camps of travelers by God’s most indulgent kindness, [Note: This passage was formerly read in Pithoeus’s edition and in the Corbie Codex as “by God’s most indulgent kindness.” Rittershusius had advised reading “by the kindness of God.” Since the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius preferred that reading, there was no doubt that Rittershusius’s conjecture should be retained.] serving not only human needs but also human delights; add food supplied daily for forty years by the stars, the heavens continually raining down sweet nourishment, flowing not only for sustenance but also for pleasure.

Add human beings who, in none of their bodily parts, experienced the growth and decline of ordinary bodies: their nails did not grow, their teeth did not diminish, their hair remained always the same, their feet were not worn down, their garments were not torn. [Note: In the Corbie Codex one reads *adcissas vestes*, “cut garments”; in the Colbert Codex, *cisas*, “cut.”] Human dignity overflowed even to the quality of humble clothing.

Add to this God descending to earth for the purpose of educating the nation, accommodating himself to earthly eyes, God the Son, [Note: The Corbie Codex reads this way. The Colbert Codex and all editions, however, have “the Son of God.” Once again Rittershusius dislikes the reading *visibus*, “eyes,” and prefers *usibus*, “uses.” Yet there is remarkable agreement among the editions and codices in favor of the present reading.] admitting the people of an innumerable multitude into fellowship with divine intimacy and honoring them with the dignity of sacred friendship.

Add thunder, lightning, the terrifying sounds of heavenly trumpets, the dreadful roar of the air on every side, the heavens bellowing with sacred blasts, fires, darknesses, clouds filled with God, the Lord speaking face to face, the law resounding from the divine mouth, letters cut by the finger of God, [Note: “Stone pages,” says Rittershusius, “is an elegant name for the stone tablets on which the ten words of the law were written by the finger of God.” Note also *rupices*, an adjective and a rarely used noun meaning “of stone,” whereas elsewhere *rupices* is ordinarily used substantivally for stupid or dull people.] rocky pages, a volume of stone, a people learning, and God teaching—almost one school of heaven and earth composed of human beings and angels mingled together.

For it is written that when Moses had reported the words of the people to the Lord, the Lord said to him: “Now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you” (Exodus 19:9). And shortly afterward: “Behold,” he says, “thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash, and a very dense cloud to cover the mountain” (ibid., 16). And again: “The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, upon the very summit of the mountain” (ibid., 20).

Thereafter: “He spoke with Moses, while all saw that the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tabernacle; and they themselves stood and worshiped at the doors of their tents. The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a person is accustomed to speak with a friend” (Exodus 33:9–11).

Since these things are so, does God not appear to care for human beings, granting such great things, providing such great benefits, making a humble little human being a participant in his speech and, as it were, admitting him into fellowship with the sacred assembly, opening to him his palms full of immortal riches, nourishing them with a cup of nectar, feeding them with heavenly food?

What greater care of his governance could he show them, or what greater affection could he offer, than that, while they were living the life of the present age, they should already possess an image of the blessedness to come?

### X

But perhaps someone may respond at this point that God once cared for human beings in this way, but now cares for them not at all. Why do we believe this? Perhaps because, unlike those people then, we do not eat manna every day while harvesting fields full of wheat; because we do not seize quails thrusting themselves into human hands, while we devour every kind of bird, cattle, and wild beast; because we do not catch in open mouths waters leaping from rocks, while we irrigate wine-producing houses with the fruits of vineyards. [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “receive.”]

I will add something further: we ourselves, who say that those people were once objects of God’s care while we are neglected by God, would, if we could exchange the past for the present blessings, utterly reject the choice of their condition. We would not wish to lose what we now possess in order to possess what they then enjoyed—not because we now have better things than that nation had then, but because those who were then nourished daily by the service of heaven and God preferred their former gluttony to present goods, grieving over the most shameful recollection of fleshly foods and pining with the foulest love of onions and garlic—not because what they had formerly enjoyed was better, but because they did then what we do now.

They were horrified by what they had and desired what they did not have. We praise more highly the things that existed then than those that exist now—not because, if we had the choice, we would always prefer to have those things, but because it is a customary vice of the human mind always to desire more what is lacking. [Note: The Brassican and Pithoean editions read: “This is customary to the human mind, when it looks upon those things that are lacking, to desire them more.” Galesinius reads: “This is a customary vice of the human mind, to desire more what is lacking.” He therefore deletes the words “when it looks upon.” Those words also offended Rittershusius, who thought they could more properly be omitted without harm to the sense. I am pleased that his conjecture is confirmed by the authority of the Corbie and Colbert codices, which lack those two words.]

And because, as [Note: Publilius Syrus.] that man says, “What belongs to others pleases us, and what belongs to us pleases others,” [Note: Other editions, including the Pithoean, read: “And because, as that man says, ‘What belongs to others pleases us, and what belongs to us pleases others.’ Moreover, it also happens that…” I think no one will doubt that the passage is more correctly preserved in the Corbie Codex, which we have faithfully reproduced.] there also occurred what is nearly universal among human beings: that they are always ungrateful to God. Through this implanted and almost innate evil, they all surpass one another in disparaging God’s benefits, so that they may not acknowledge themselves to be debtors.

But enough of this. Let us now return to the order of the subject begun earlier, although, as I think, we have already proved to no small degree what we proposed. Nevertheless, if you please, let us add something further, because it is better to prove more than is necessary than perhaps less than the subject requires.

### XI

Once freed from Pharaoh’s yoke, the Hebrew people transgressed at Mount Sinai and were immediately struck by the Lord for their error. For it is written: “The Lord struck the people for the error of the calf that Aaron had made” (Exodus 32:35).

What greater and clearer judgment could God have brought against sinners than that punishment should immediately overtake those who sinned? And yet, although the entire people were guilty, why was condemnation not sent against them all? Clearly because the merciful Lord struck part of them with the sword of his sentence, so that he might correct the rest by example and offer to everyone at once both discipline through correction and mercy through sparing.

It was discipline that he chastised; it was mercy that he spared—although he did the two things in unequal measure. More was then given to mercy than to severity. This was because, although the most indulgent Lord always shows himself more inclined toward mercy than toward vengeance, and although in restraining part of the Jewish army he attributed something to judgment and severity, mercy nevertheless claimed the greater portion of the people for itself: specifically, in that innumerable multitude it showed a singular mercy, lest punishment consume all those whom guilt encompassed.

Yet toward certain persons and families, as we read, God’s discipline is inexorable. Such was the case when, while the people were idle on the Sabbath, the man who had undertaken to gather wood was ordered to be killed (Numbers 15:35). Although the act itself seemed harmless, observance of the day made him guilty.

Or consider the case when, in a quarrel between two men, one who had blasphemed was condemned to death. For it is written:

“Now the son of an Israelite woman, whom she had borne to an Egyptian man, quarreled in the camp with an Israelite. And when he had blasphemed the name of the Lord and cursed him, he was brought to Moses” (Leviticus 24:10–11).

And shortly afterward: “They placed him,” he says, “in prison until they might learn what the Lord would command. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Lead the blasphemer outside the camp, and let all who heard him place their hands upon his head; and let the entire people stone him’” (ibid., 12–14).

Is it not manifest that this was God’s present judgment, and that the sentence was issued through a heavenly deliberation almost according to the form of a human tribunal? First, the man who had sinned was seized; second, he was brought, as it were, before the tribunal; third, he was accused; then he was sent to prison; finally, he was punished by the authority of heavenly judgment.

Moreover, he was not merely punished, but punished in the presence of witnesses, so that justice, rather than power, might appear to condemn the guilty person—an example contributing to the correction of all, so that no one afterward would commit what the entire people had avenged in one man. [Note: Below, page 27: “So that the punishment of all the guilty might contribute to the correction of everyone.” And book 7, page 156: “So that while one part was struck by disaster, the other part might be corrected by the example.” Tacitus, book 14 of the *Annals*: “A great example, when what is inflicted upon individuals is repaid for the public good”—as when every tenth man is beaten with clubs in the army. See Rittershusius on this passage of Salvian.]

By this reasoning and judgment, therefore, God both now acts and has always acted: so that whatever individuals suffer may contribute to the correction of all.

The same was true when Abihu and Nadab, men of priestly blood, were consumed by heavenly fire (Numbers 26; Leviticus 10; 2 Chronicles 24). In them God wished to show not merely judgment, but judgment that was present and impending.

For it is written that when fire had gone out from the Lord and consumed the burnt offering (Leviticus 9:24), Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took their censers, placed fire and incense upon them, and offered before the Lord an alien fire, which he had not commanded them to offer. Then fire went out from the Lord and consumed them, and they died before the Lord (Leviticus 10:1–2).

What else did he wish to show by this except that his right hand was extended over us and that a sword was continually impending, when he punished the error of those men at once in the very act, and punishment scarcely waited until the sinners’ crime had been completed before avenging the sin? [Note: Below, page 25: “Nor was the deed of the sinners scarcely completed before punishment avenged the sin.” See the notes to Lupus of Ferrières, page 473.]

Yet not only this was accomplished in the matter, but many other things as well. Since what was punished in them was not an impious mind but excessive and thoughtless presumption, the Lord plainly declared what punishment would be deserved by those who committed some act in contempt of the Godhead, when even those were struck by God who had sinned only through lack of consideration. He also showed how guilty those would be who acted against the command of their Lord, since even those were punished in this way who had done what was not commanded.

Moreover, by this God wished to provide for our correction through the discipline of a salutary example, so that all laypeople might understand how greatly they ought to fear God’s anger, since from the present punishment neither the merit of their parent nor the privilege of sacred ministry rescued the priest’s sons.

But why do I speak of those whose thoughtlessness in some way touched God and redounded to an injury against heaven? Miriam speaks against Moses and is punished; and she is not merely punished, but punished in the manner of a judgment. First she is summoned to judgment, then accused, and thirdly scourged. In the rebuke she receives the force of a sentence; in the leprosy she suffers the expiation of her crime.

Although this sort of correction humbled not Miriam alone but Aaron as well—for even if it was not fitting that the high priest should be disfigured by leprosy, the Lord’s chastisement nevertheless scourged him too—not only this occurred, but Aaron was also disciplined as though he shared in the guilt of the punishment that Miriam suffered. Miriam was afflicted with punishment so that Aaron might be punished with shame.

Moreover, so that we might recognize the inexorable form of divine judgment in certain cases, God did not relent even at the intercession of the one who had been injured.

For we read that the Lord said to Aaron and Miriam: “Why, then, were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” And he departed in anger. And behold, Miriam appeared white with leprosy, like snow. Moses cried out to the Lord, saying, “I beg you, Lord, heal her.” He answered him: “If her father had spat in her face, would she not at least have been covered with shame for ten days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward she shall be recalled” (Numbers 12:8–14).

Let what we have said suffice concerning this kind of division and this part of the discussion. It is endless to discuss everything, and even to enumerate everything without discussion would take too long. But let us add something further.

### XII

The Hebrew people repent of having departed from Egypt (Exodus 16) and are struck. Then they are distressed that they are wearied by the labor of the journey and are afflicted. They desire meat and are scourged. And because, while eating manna every day, they seek to satisfy the allurements of their belly’s gluttony, they are indeed filled according to their desired appetite, but even in that fullness they are tortured.

“For food,” Scripture says, “was still in their mouths, and the anger of God rose against them. He killed many of them and disabled the chosen of Israel” (Psalm 77:30–31).

Og rebels against Moses and is destroyed (Deuteronomy 3). Korah reviles and is overwhelmed. Dathan and Abiram murmur and are swallowed up (Numbers 16). “For the earth was opened,” it says, “and swallowed Dathan, and covered the assembly of Abiram” (Psalm 105:17).

Two hundred and fifty men, moreover, leaders of the people, who according to the sacred account were summoned by name at the time of the assembly, rose up against Moses. When they stood against Moses and Aaron, they said: “Let this be enough for you, since the whole multitude is holy, and the Lord is among them. Why do you exalt yourselves above the people of the Lord?” (Numbers 16:3).

And what followed? “Fire,” it says, “went out from the Lord and killed the two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense” (ibid., 35).

But while all these great things were happening, heavenly care did not bring improvement. Correction was applied very often, but amendment did not follow. For just as we, when repeatedly scourged, are not corrected, so they, though struck very often, were not reformed.

What is written? “The whole multitude of the children of Israel murmured the next day against Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘You have killed the people of the Lord’” (Numbers 16:41).

And what happened afterward? Immediately fourteen thousand seven hundred people were struck and consumed by divine fire.

Since the whole multitude of the people had then sinned, why was vengeance not exacted upon them all—especially since none had escaped from the rebellion of Korah mentioned above? Why did God there wish the whole assembly of sinners to be killed, but here only a portion?

Clearly because the Lord is full of justice [Note: The Colbert Codex reads “justice and mercy.”] and mercy. He grants much to his mercy through clemency, and punishes with severity through discipline. [Note: The editions read: “And he grants severity through discipline.” That reading is unquestionably excellent. I nevertheless prefer the reading of the Corbie Codex. Augustine, on Psalm 100: “God neither loses the severity of judgment in the goodness of mercy, nor, in judging with severity, loses the goodness of mercy.”]

Therefore, there he gave precedence to discipline, so that the punishment of all the guilty might contribute to the correction of everyone; here he assigned the matter to his mercy, so that the entire people might not perish.

Yet although he acted with such mercy, because repeated correction of part of the people produced no benefit, in the end he condemned them all to death. This event ought simultaneously to contribute to our fear and our correction, lest we, who are not thoroughly corrected by their example, perhaps be punished by their end.

For there is no doubt what happened to them. Since the entire Hebrew nation had left Egypt for the purpose of entering the promised land, no one entered it except two holy men.

For it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘How long will this most wicked multitude murmur against me? As I live, says the Lord, just as you have spoken in my hearing, so I will do to you. Your corpses shall lie in this wilderness’” (Numbers 14:26, 29).

And what followed? “Your little ones,” he says, “of whom you said that they would become prey to the enemies, I will bring in, so that they may see the land that displeased you. Your corpses shall lie in the wilderness” (ibid., 31–32).

And afterward? “All,” he says, “died and were struck down before the Lord” (ibid., 36–37).

What is absent from all these events? Do you wish to see the ruler? Behold: he corrects through his present action and arranges future things. Do you wish to see a severe judge? Behold: he punishes the guilty. Do you wish to see one who is just and merciful? Behold: he spares the innocent. Do you wish to see a judge in all things? Behold: judgment is everywhere.

For as judge he reproves, and as judge he governs. The judge pronounces sentence; the judge destroys the guilty; the judge rewards the innocent. [Note: Here book 1 ends. So the Pithoean edition. The Corbie Codex reads: “Here ends book 1, with ease.” The title of the following book is: “Here begins book 2, through the power of God.” This may perhaps seem unimportant to mention. But because of our love for antiquity, we value even trifles and half-worn stones. As the most learned men have noted, the ancients were accustomed to write *Explicit* at the end of books, intending to indicate that they had reached the end of the volume and that it had been fully unfolded and completed. Jerome, in his letter to Marcella: “When we have completed little works, we customarily insert in the middle, to distinguish the next subject, *EXPLICIT* or *FELICITER*, or something of that sort.”]

## BOOK TWO

[Column 0047D]

28 1. These examples we have cited are sufficient, by which our God is plainly and continually shown to be the most watchful observer, the most devoted governor, and the most just judge. But perhaps some less instructed person reflects: “If everything is now being done by God as it was done then, why is it that the wicked prevail, the good are afflicted, and whereas then the wicked felt his anger and the good his mercy, now the good seem somehow to feel anger and the wicked grace?” I shall answer these questions shortly.

[Col. 0048D] Since I promised to establish these three points—that is, God’s presence, governance, and judgment—by three means, namely, reasoning, examples, and testimonies, and since we have already dealt with reasoning and examples, it remains for me to demonstrate them by testimonies: 29 although the examples themselves that we have cited ought to be regarded as testimonies, since that by which the truth of things is confirmed is rightly called a testimony. Which, then, of the three matters mentioned above ought first to be established by sacred testimonies: presence, governance, or judgment? Presence, I think:

[Note: [Col. 0049C] The editions read: “Because he either will govern or will judge. Therefore, being present, etc.” Here once again Rittershusius’s conjecture is confirmed by the authority of an ancient manuscript. For after *quia* (“because”) he wished to add *qui* (“who”).]

because whoever will either govern or judge must undoubtedly be present, so that he may govern or judge whatever it is. The divine word, speaking in its books, says: “In every place the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked” (Prov. XV, 3). There you have him present; there you have him watching; there you have him vigilant in every place with care and providence. For this reason it says that both the good and the wicked are considered by him, plainly demonstrating that nothing is neglected by him who is shown to examine everything.

To grasp this more fully, hear what the same Holy Spirit also testifies elsewhere in Scripture: “The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, to deliver their souls from death and to feed them in famine” (Ps. XXXII, 18–19). There you see why God is said to look upon righteous people:

[Col. 0049B] namely, in order to preserve and protect them.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] In contrast, in Book I, p. 16, he says that the anger of the Godhead is the sinner’s punishment.]

For the gaze of a merciful God is a gift of human preservation. Elsewhere, too, the same divine Spirit says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Ps. XXXIII, 16). See with what benevolence Scripture says that God deals with his own. In saying that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, it reveals the disposition of the one who looks; in saying that his ears are ready for their prayers, it displays the generosity of the one who always hears.

Yet by saying that the divine ears are always present at the prayers of the righteous, it signifies not merely God’s act of hearing but something like God’s obedience. For how are the divine ears present at the prayers of the righteous? How, unless so that they always hear, unless so that they always heed, unless so that they promptly grant what they have heard,

[Col. 0049C] unless so that they immediately bestow what they have heeded? 30 Our Lord’s ears, then, are always ready to hear the prayers of the saints, always attentive. How blessed we would all be if we wished to hear God as promptly as we read that God hears us so readily!

But perhaps you say that the fact that God is read to look upon the righteous contributes little to the case, since the Godhead’s gaze is not general but is bestowed upon the righteous with a special benevolence. The sacred word has already testified above that the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked. But if you now want this proved more fully, consider what follows. For it adds:

[Col. 0050A] “But the face of the Lord is upon those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (ibid., 17).

See plainly that you cannot complain that God does not also look upon the unjust, since you understand that the Lord’s vision is indeed general toward all, but that there is a diversity corresponding to the difference of their merits. The good are looked upon so that they may be preserved; the wicked, so that they may be destroyed. Since you yourself are among the latter, if you deny that a human being is looked upon by God, understand clearly not only that you are seen by the Lord but also that you will perish.

For since the face of God is upon those who do evil in order to destroy their memory from the earth,

[Note: [Col. 0049D] Brassicanus and Galesinius published this passage as follows: “For since the face of God is upon those who do evil, in order to destroy their memory from the earth, from every generation, it is necessary, etc.” The words “from every generation” are entirely superfluous and were added by someone who did not understand to what passage the words concerning God’s governance should be referred—words which I easily see were present in all the manuscript copies. The distinguished Petrus Pithoeus restored the true reading, but not in its proper place. He presents the passage thus: “For since the face of God is upon those who do evil, in order to destroy their memory from the earth, concerning God’s governance it is necessary, etc.” The same distinguished man nevertheless pointed out that these words should be deleted, since they are the heading of the book and have slipped into the text. These are his words: “This is the reading of the ancient manuscript; for nothing in these books has been supplied by conjecture, but everything has been transcribed faithfully from a most ancient and carefully corrected manuscript. Since from this reading the phrase ‘their memory from every generation’ did not seem sufficiently clear, the common reading was composed. Perhaps it would be more correct to delete both. For the words ‘concerning God’s governance’ are the heading of the book, which has slipped into the text.” Yet the learned man touched the matter only with his fingertip and did not entirely detect it. The words “concerning God’s governance” must indeed be removed from the place they occupy in Pithoeus’s edition and restored to the middle of the page, as we have done, before the words “Let us now see whether,” etc. For this is how it is read in the Corbie manuscript; moreover, only at this point does Salvian begin his discussion of God’s governance.]

it is necessary that you, who deny that you behold the face of God through faith, should recognize the anger of the one who looks by experiencing destruction. Thus, these observations concerning God’s presence and gaze are sufficient.

[Col. 0050B]

## Concerning the Governance of God

II. Let us now see whether the one who looks also governs, since the very reason for looking contains within itself the purpose of governing: for he does not look in order to neglect once he has looked—indeed, the very fact that he deigns to look shows that he does not neglect—especially since the sacred word above has testified 31 that the wicked are looked upon by God for destruction and the good for salvation. In this very fact the administration of divine governance is demonstrated. For this is what it means to govern by just rule: to deal with each person according to the diversity of his merits.

Yet receive fuller testimony concerning this matter. In the psalm the Holy Spirit says to God the Father: “You who govern Israel, attend” (Ps. LXXIX, 1). “Israel” is interpreted as “seeing God.” Since Christians see God by faith and in their hearts—that is, those who believe faithfully—although God is the governor of all, governance is said to be granted especially to those who deserve to be governed especially by the Godhead. Therefore, whoever you may be, if you are a Christian, you must believe that you are governed by God. But if you do not at all think that you are governed by God together with the other Christians, you must recognize that you are outside the company of all Christians.

But if, as we have already said above, you seek what concerns all human beings rather than Christians alone, the sacred volume plainly declares that everything is daily governed by the will of the Godhead and that all things are continually administered by God.

[Note: [Col. 0050D] The author may have in mind Ecclus. XXXIX, 10, where it reads: “He himself will direct his counsel and discipline.” The context seems to suggest that it should be read in this way here.]

“For he,” it says, “loves counsel and discipline” (Ecclus. XXXIX, 10). For God is not otherwise than the one whose care is for all things. “For since you are just,” it says, “you dispose all things justly, and with great reverence you dispose us” (Wis. XII, 15). There you have God continually disposing and continually governing, although in this passage of Scripture not only sacred governance but also human dignity is being declared. In the words “you dispose us,” the power of divine governance is shown; in the words “with great reverence,” the height of human dignity is revealed.

Elsewhere, too, in the prophet: “‘Do I not fill heaven and earth?’ I,” he says (Jer. XXIII, 24). Why he fills all things, he himself declares: “‘Because I am with you,’ he says, ‘to save you’” (Jer. XLII, 41). Here indeed 32 the Lord shows not only his governance and his filling of all things,

[Col. 0051B] but also the power and benefit of that filling. For the filling of the Godhead has this fruit within itself: that it saves those things which it fills.

And therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles, blessed Paul says: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII, 28). He is plainly more than the governor of life, in whom the very movement of the living creature exists. For he did not say that we move from him but that we move in him, teaching, clearly, that the substance of us all is implanted within the sacred powers; for in him we certainly live, from whom we derive the very fact that we are.

But the Savior himself also says in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXIII, 20). He did not merely say that he is with us but that he is with us on every day. You, most ungrateful man, say that he who is with us without interruption has neither care nor regard for us? What, then, does he do by being with us? Is he with us for this purpose: not to look upon us, to neglect us? And how can both things be reconciled—that the one who grants presence to piety should assign indifference to impiety?

“For behold,” he says, “I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” We interpret God’s disposition admirably, then, if we accuse him of continually neglecting us, when he testifies that he himself continually does not leave us. By this he wished to show that he would not continually withdraw from us in affection and protection, since he would not even be absent from us in presence. We turn divine love into contempt for ourselves; we turn the testimonies of love into arguments for hatred. We want this very statement—that he says he is present—to be a testimony of hatred rather than of love.

For if the Lord had said that he would be absent, we might perhaps have had less reason to complain of the carelessness of one who was absent. It is a greater matter of contempt and disdain if he continually neglects us while continually remaining with us; and there is more hatred toward us in him if he always remains with us for this purpose: that, although he never abandons us in presence, he always rejects us in affection. But far be it from us to believe this of the most devoted and merciful God: that he should always have wished to stand beside us in order to seem to neglect us with greater disdain while standing beside us. Far be it from us to call this a crime.

No one, I think, in the entire human race is so wicked that he wishes to be with anyone because he does not love him, and desires to use his presence for this sole purpose, that he might despise one who is present with the greater fruit of hatred. Let human nature itself teach us—or, if it does not, let it overcome us—if we do not wish to be with someone precisely because we love the one with whom we wish to be. And because we love him, we wish our presence to benefit the one whom we love.

What, therefore, we cannot take away even from a wicked human being, we take away from God, making God worse than the worst human beings: saying that he declared himself to be with us for the purpose of neglecting us more disdainfully when he was present. But enough of this.

III. Since we have now proved by sacred testimonies that all things are looked upon and governed by God, it remains for us to show also that many things in this present age are judged by the Godhead.

When holy David had suffered an insulting injury from Nabal the Carmelite, because he delayed taking vengeance himself, he immediately received vengeance with God as its executor. After his adversary had shortly afterward been destroyed and struck down by a heavenly hand, he spoke as follows: “Blessed is the Lord, who has judged my cause against Nabal” (I Sam. XXV, 39).

When his persecuting son had also driven him from the kingdom, the Lord, acting as judge, soon avenged him—and did not merely avenge him, but avenged him more fully than the one who was avenged had wished. God wished thereby to show that the injury suffered by those who endure injustice is more serious in his sight than the injury suffered by those who endure it. For when he avenges the one who is avenged beyond his own desire, what else does he wish us to understand than that he himself is taking vengeance in the person whom he thus avenges?

After the parricidal son had been impaled upon a cross not made by human hands, the divine word reports that the vengeance divinely assigned to him was announced in this way: “I bring good news, my lord the king. For today the Lord has judged in your favor against all who rose up against you” (II Sam. XVIII, 31).

IV. You see how the sacred writings, through divine witnesses, prove that God judges even in the present age—not only by events, as we said above, and by examples, but also by the very name and designation of judgment.

But perhaps you will say that this was specially granted by God to a holy man, so that he might immediately judge his adversaries. The day would fail me if I wished to speak of God’s present sentences and judgments in this world. Nevertheless, so that you may clearly recognize that he grants his sacred censure and examination not so much to persons as to causes, hear how God the judge, who continually gave an evident judgment on behalf of David his servant, judged against David himself on many occasions.

[Col. 0052D]

[Note: [Col. 0051D] This is how the Corbie manuscript reads. The Colbert manuscript and the editions have *vindicarit* (“may have avenged”).]

And this was not in the affair of many people—or, what might perhaps have moved God more, of holy people—but in the case of one man, and of a barbarian,

[Note: [Col. 0052D] That is, one who was not a Jew and therefore stood outside the people of God and the number of the saints.]

and in a case where the status of so great a man had not weighed against him at all, except insofar as the cause condemned him.

After he had killed Uriah the Hittite, a man of an impious people and hostile nation, the divine word immediately came to David: “You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife as your wife, and killed him with the sword of the sons of Ammon. Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house forever. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall raise evil against you from your house, and I shall take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor. For you acted secretly; but I shall do this thing in the sight of all Israel and in the sight of the sun” (II Sam. XII, 9–12).

What do you say, you who believe that not only are the things we do not judged by God, but that they are not even seen by him at all? Do you see that God’s eyes were by no means absent even from that hidden place where David once fell? Therefore you, who—presumably as a consolation for your sins—do not think that our deeds are considered by God, understand from this very fact that you too are always seen by Christ, and recognize that you may perhaps soon be punished. For you see that holy David could neither conceal his single error in the secret recesses of hidden things nor, by any privilege of

[Col. 0053B]

[Note: [Col. 0053D] The Colbert manuscript and the editions read *majorum* (“of greater [works]”).]

his great works, escape present punishments.

For what does the Lord say to him? “I shall take your wives before your eyes, and the sword shall not depart from your house forever.” You see how immediately so great a man receives judgment for a single error. Condemnation immediately followed the fault, and the condemnation immediately punished, reserving nothing and at once restraining the guilty man, without postponing the guilt to the future.

And therefore he did not say: “Because you have done this, you shall experience God’s judgment when it comes, and you shall be tortured in the future fire of Gehenna.” Rather, he says: “You shall experience present torments and endure the sword of divine severity already hanging over your neck.”

And what follows? The guilty man recognizes his fault, is humbled, is pierced with remorse, confesses, mourns, repents, entreats, renounces his royal jewels, lays aside his garments embroidered with curling gold thread, strips off his purple, is dishonored by the diadem,

[Note: [Col. 0053D] The same manuscript reads, and the edition prints, *exoneratur* (“is relieved of his burden”). Rittershusius thought this reading could be tolerated.]

is changed in appearance and heart, casts away the entire king together with his ornaments, and takes upon himself a prudent penitent under the protection of ostentatious squalor; he is worn down by fasting, dried up by aridity, poured out in weeping, and imprisoned in solitude.

And yet this king of such great renown, greater in holiness than in power, surpassing others in the prerogatives of his preceding merits, although he pleads with such great earnestness, does not escape. The only, yet very great, fruit of such immense repentance is that he is not consigned to eternal penalties, but nevertheless does not obtain pardon in the present life.

Finally, what does the prophet say to the penitent? “Because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme, the son who has been born to you shall die” (ibid., 14). In addition to the punishment of bitter bereavement, God wished this further understanding of the supreme penalty to be added for the most devoted father: that the father himself, who would grieve, should become the cause of death to his beloved son, since the child born from the crime would in turn be killed by the very crime that had created him.

[Col. 0054A]

V. This, then, is the beginning of divine chastisement. It is a beginning, certainly, but not the only one. For a long succession of immense hardships followed, and an uninterrupted continuation of evils never withdrew from his house.

Tamar is violated by Amnon’s lust; Amnon is slaughtered by Absalom (II Sam. XIII). A great crime is committed by one brother,

[Note: [Col. 0053D] In all the editions except the one prepared by Galesinius in Rome, the reading is *a bono fratre* (“by the good brother”). The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts have the same reading. Galesinius therefore rightly emended it to *ab uno fratre* (“by one brother”). The error arose because it was customary among those ancient scribes to interchange the letters *o* and *u*, as has often already been observed.]

but it is avenged more wickedly by another. Yet amid all this, David the father is punished for the crime of both. Two sons sin, but three are destroyed through the crime of the two. In Tamar, virginity is lost; in Amnon, Absalom’s ruin is also mourned. Indeed, you do not know which of the two sons such a good father lost more grievously: the one who was killed by his brother’s hand in this world, or the one who perished by his own hand in the next.

And now, in accordance with the word of God, an immeasurable heap of evil follows. For a long time the father suffers ambushes from his son, is driven from the kingdom, and departs as a fugitive lest he be killed. You cannot tell whether the son was more impure or more bloodthirsty. Because he cannot kill his father by parricide, he defiles him by incest—and indeed by incest, in addition to the sacrilege of incest itself, he proudly increases the crime through deliberate effort. The act, which even secrecy would make abominable, the parent’s persecutor openly perpetrated, so that by this most death-dealing crime not only the absent father might be deformed, but the eyes of the whole world might also be publicly defiled by the incest.

If the appearance of his flight must also be added, what was it like when so great a king, of such great renown, higher than all kings and greater than the world, fled from everyone who belonged to him with only a very few of his own people—impoverished in comparison with his former self, alone in comparison with himself, fleeing in fear, disgrace, and mourning—“with his head covered,” as Scripture says, “and walking barefoot” (II Sam. XV, 30)?

[Note: [Col. 0054D] The Corbie manuscript rightly reads this instead of the reading found in the Colbert manuscript and the editions: “Over these things, of his former state,” etc.]

A survivor of his former condition, exiled from himself, almost already living after his own life, cast down even to the insult—or, what is worse, the pity—of his servants, so that Ziba might feed him and Shimei might not fear to curse him publicly (II Sam. XVI); so changed by God’s judgment from what he had been that a single enemy insulted to his face the man whom

[Note: [Col. 0054D] The editions of Galesinius and Pithoeus, supported by the Corbie manuscript, read: “Whom perhaps the whole world had feared.” But Brassicanus’s edition does not contain *forsitan* (“perhaps”), which appears superfluous. We have therefore removed it from this passage.]

the whole world had feared

[Note: [Col. 0054D] As it then appeared, as Salvianus will say below in Book I *Against Avarice*, p. 224.]

VI. Where are those who deny that human affairs are looked upon by God? Behold how often the sacred witnesses have taught, in the person of one man, that God not only looked upon him but also judged him. And why all these things? Why indeed, unless so that we might understand that the same judgment and correction of God would always exist in the world as had existed then?

And therefore we also read that holy men were once chastised by God’s judgment, so that we might know that we too are to be judged by God the judge even in the present age. For just as God always exists, so God’s justice always exists; just as the Lord’s omnipotence is unfailing, so his censure is unchangeable; just as God is perpetually just, so justice endures.

And therefore all the saints, placed amid the upheavals of impending dangers and the swords of persecutors, ask for God’s present judgment in the sacred books. Thus the righteous man says in the psalm: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. XLII, 1). Lest this be understood as referring to God’s future judgment, he immediately adds: “Deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man” (ibid.). He plainly asks for God’s present judgment who begs to be delivered from the hand of his persecutor.

And rightly, in the confidence of a good cause, he asks not so much for the Lord’s support as for his judgment: for the best support is always granted to a good cause when it is judged with justice.

Elsewhere also, most clearly: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me. Take hold of weapons and shield, and rise to my assistance” (Ps. XXXIV, 1–2). Here too you see that what is requested is not the severity of a future examination but the censure of present judgment. For this is what he says: “Take up the shield and seize the sword”—the shield, of course, for protection, the sword for vengeance—not because God, when judging, needs equipment, but because in this age these names of terrifying things are instruments of terrifying judgments.
