He speaks to human understanding through the signs of human things; for when he prayed to be judged and avenged against his adversaries, he expressed the force of divine chastisement through the instruments of earthly vengeance.

Finally, elsewhere the same prophet shows what difference there is between God’s present and future judgment. What does he say to the Lord concerning the censure of present examination? “You sit upon the throne, judging equity” (Ps. IX, 5). What, however, does he say concerning God’s future and eternal judgment? “He will judge the world in equity” (Ps. XCV, 13). And again: “He will judge the peoples with justice.” By these very words he distinguished the time of judgment in the two cases, using the present tense for one and the future for the other. To distinguish the future from the present, he subsequently added: “He will judge.”

[Col. 0056B] These things concerning God’s care for us, his governance, and his judgment have now been sufficiently proved by reasoning, examples, and testimonies, especially since everything that follows will also relate to this same matter. Now, if we receive from God, whose cause we are undertaking, the strength to act, we shall attempt both to present and to refute the arguments that our adversaries commonly bring against these claims.

## BOOK THREE

39 I. [Note: [Col. 0055D] Rittershusius notes that this was imitated from Cicero.]

Things are in a good state. The foundations of a work begun with devout effort and undertaken out of love for divine service have been laid. Therefore they were not placed in dissoluble clay or built with temporary stone, but strengthened by the preparation of sacred materials and made firm by the art of divine instruction:

[Col. 0055C] and, as God himself says in the Gospel, they cannot be shaken by raging winds, overthrown by the flooding of rivers, or dissolved by the pouring of rains (Matt. VII, 24–25). Since this work has, so to speak, been furnished by the hands of the divine books and made solid by the structure of the heavenly Scriptures, what has been made through the Lord Jesus Christ must be as firm as those things which made it.

[Note: [Col. 0055D] Other editions read: “As those things which made the building are firm. And therefore this,” etc.; entirely incorrectly. We have therefore followed the Corbie manuscript.]

This building, then, derives the nature of its condition from its stock, and it cannot be shaken while its authors remain safe. For just as no one can bring down the walls of earthly buildings unless he has first brought down the stones and mortar, so no one can dissolve the building we have constructed unless he first dissolves what it was built and completed from. Since this certainly cannot be shaken, we may rightly presume the safety of the building, whose condition is sustained by immortal supports.

It is therefore asked, since these things are so—if everything that exists in this world is brought about by God’s care, governance, and judgment—why the condition of the barbarians is much better than ours;

[Note: [Col. 0055D] That is, the Vandals, Huns, Franks, Goths, and the other peoples who were then attacking the Roman Empire.]

why, even among ourselves, the lot of the good is harder than that of the wicked;

[Note: [Col. 0055D] See Cassian, *Conferences* 6, chapter 2.]

why the upright lie prostrate while the wicked grow strong; why everything yields to the unjust, and especially to those in positions of power?

I can indeed say, reasonably and with sufficient firmness:

[Note: [Col. 0056D] This is precisely how the Corbie manuscript reads. The reading is truly excellent and the only correct one. The reading found in other editions should therefore be rejected: “I do not know the secret, and I am ignorant of the divine counsel.” A little farther below all the editions again read: “I am a human being; I do not understand the secrets of God, and I do not dare investigate them.” The Corbie manuscript is better, punctuating it as follows: “I am a human being; I do not understand; I do not dare investigate the secrets of God.”]

“I do not know. For I am ignorant of the secret and counsel of the Godhead.”

The heavenly oracle is sufficient for proving this case. God says—just as we have already proved in the preceding books—that he sees all things, governs all things, and judges all things. If you want to know what must be held, you have the sacred writings. The complete argument is to hold what you have read.

But do not ask me why God does the things of which we are speaking in this way. I am a human being; I do not understand; I do not dare investigate the secrets of God, and therefore I am also afraid even to attempt it. For it is itself a kind of sacrilegious presumption if you desire to know more than you are permitted to know.

Let it be enough for you that God testifies that all things are brought about and administered by him. Why do you ask me why one person is greater and another lesser; one miserable and another blessed; one strong and another weak? I do not understand for what reason God does these things; but for a complete explanation it is abundantly sufficient that I demonstrate that these things are brought about by God.

For just as God is greater than every human reason, so what I know to be done by God ought to be greater for me than reason itself. There is therefore no need to hear anything new on this matter; let God’s authority suffice for every argument.

Nor is it permissible for you to call one thing just and another unjust among those things brought about by the divine will. For whatever you see and are convinced is done by God, you must necessarily confess to be more than just.

These things concerning God’s governance and judgment can therefore be stated with the greatest ease and firmness. For there is no need for me to prove by arguments what is confirmed by the very fact that God says it.

Thus, when we read that God continually looks upon the whole earth, we prove by this very fact that he looks upon it, because he says that he looks upon it. When we read that he governs all the things he has made, we establish by this very fact that he governs them, because he testifies that he governs them. When

[Col. 0057B] we read that he administers all things by present judgment, it is evident by this very fact that he judges, because he confirms that he judges.

All other words—human words, that is—require arguments and witnesses. But God’s word is itself its own witness, since whatever incorruptible truth speaks must be an incorruptible testimony of truth.

Nevertheless, since our God has wished through the sacred Scriptures to make us know certain things, as it were, concerning the secret of his mind and thought—for the oracle of sacred Scripture is, in a certain sense, the mind of God—I shall not be silent about whatever God has wished to be recognized or proclaimed through his servants.

Yet before I begin to speak, I want to know whether I am to speak with Christians or with pagans. If with Christians, I do not doubt that I shall prove what I am undertaking to prove. But if with pagans, I decline to prove it—not because I would fail in the proof, but because I despair that what I say will be of benefit. For labor is fruitless and empty where a perverse hearer does not accept proof.

Nevertheless, since I do not think there is any person at all bearing the Christian name who does not wish to appear Christian, I shall deal with a Christian. Even if someone is of impious and pagan unbelief, it is enough for me that what I say should be proved to a Christian.

II. You complain, then, that we who believe in God as Christians are more miserable than everyone else. What the Apostle says to the churches might indeed have been sufficient for me as an answer here: “Let no one be moved by these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we have been appointed to this” (I Thess. III, 3). And therefore, since the Apostle says that we have been appointed by God to endure hardships, miseries, and sorrows, what wonder is it if we endure every evil, since we have enlisted to tolerate every adversity?

But since many do not understand these things and think that Christians ought to receive from God, as the wages of their faith, the following reward: that because they are more religious than all nations, they should also be stronger than all nations, let us accommodate ourselves to their opinion and judgment.

Let us nevertheless see what it means to believe faithfully in God. Since we wish the reward of such great belief and faith to exist in this world, we must consider what sort of belief or faith it ought itself to be.

What, then, is belief or faith? I think it means that a person faithfully believes in Christ—that is, faithfully keeps God’s commandments. For just as the servants or stewards of wealthy people, to whom abundant household goods or richly stocked storerooms are entrusted, cannot possibly be called faithful if they have devoured the things entrusted to them, so Christian people are certainly unbelieving if they have corrupted the good things assigned to them by God.

Perhaps it will be asked what the good things are that God assigns to Christians. What else, except everything through which we believe—that is, everything through which we are Christians?

First, the Law; then the Prophets; third, the Gospel; fourth, the apostolic writings;

[Col. 0058B] finally, the gift of the new birth, the grace of holy baptism, and the anointing of the divine chrism. Just as formerly among the Hebrews—that is, among God’s special and particular people—when judicial authority had passed into royal power, God called the most approved and select men to kingship through royal anointing, so all Christian people, after fulfilling all God’s commandments following ecclesiastical chrism, would be called to heaven to receive the reward of their labor.

Since, then, these are all the things on which faith rests, let us see who guards such great mysteries of faith in such a way as to appear faithful. For, as we have said, he must be unbelieving who does not preserve what has been entrusted to faith.

I am not even asking that anyone do everything commanded by the testaments of the two periods. I set aside the censure of the ancient Law; I set aside all the threats of the Prophets; I set aside even what cannot at all be set aside—the most severe instruction of the apostolic books and the doctrine of the Gospel volumes, full of every kind of perfection.

I ask only who obeys even the very few commandments of God. Nor am I speaking of those commandments from which so many recoil that they almost curse them. Such is the progress of honor and reverence for God among us that what we do not do out of devotion we even regard as deserving hatred.

Furthermore, who is willing to heed the fact that the Savior forbade us to think about tomorrow (Matt. VI, 34)? Who accepts his command that we be content with a single tunic? Who considers it not only something to do but even something to endure when he commands us to walk barefoot?

[Note: [Col. 0057D] Pithoeus noted that in his ancient manuscript the word was written *excalcios* (“barefoot”), and perhaps more correctly. Since the Corbie and Pithoean manuscripts agree substantially at this point, we have retained that reading and rejected the reading of both Pithoeus’s edition and the others, which print *excalciatos* or *excalceatos*.]

And so I pass over these points as well. For faith—the faith by which we trust—has come to this: that we judge superfluous the things the Lord wished to be beneficial to us.

“Love your enemies,” says the Savior, “do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44). Who does all these things? Who is willing to do for his enemies what God has commanded—not, I say, in prayers, but at least in words? Or even if someone forces himself to do it, he does it with his mouth, not with his mind. He performs the duty of speech, but does not alter the disposition of his heart. And so, even if he forces himself to pray for his adversary, he speaks but does not pray.

It would take too long to discuss each point individually. Yet I shall add something more, so that we may understand that we not only fail to obey all God’s words, but scarcely obey any of his commands. Thus the Apostle cries out: “For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). To our crimes we add this also: although we are guilty in every respect, we believe ourselves good and holy, and thus the offenses of iniquity are piled up within us by our presumption of righteousness.

“He who hates his brother,” says the Apostle, “is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). We can therefore understand that many are murderers who think themselves innocent, because, as we see, murder is committed not only by the hand of the one who kills, but also by the mind of the one who hates. Hence the Savior, reinforcing the standard of this commandment with still stricter judgment, says: “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5:22). Anger is the mother of hatred. Therefore the Savior wished to exclude anger, lest hatred be born from it. If, then, not only hatred but also anger will make us guilty before God’s judgment, we plainly recognize that just as no one at all is free from anger, so no one at all can be free from guilt.

The Lord continues, as though cutting away the very fibers of this commandment and all its shoots and branches, saying: “Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Racha,’ will be liable to the council” (ibid.).

[Note: Jerome, in his commentary on the fifth chapter of Matthew, says that this word in the language of the Hebrews signifies “empty” or “vacant”; “we cannot,” he says, “call him ‘without brains’ by the common insult.” Saint Gregory, *Moralia* XXI.5: “‘Racha,’ in Hebrew speech, is the word of an indignant person; it reveals the spirit of the angry speaker, but does not yet express a complete word of anger.” See Saint Hilary on the fourth chapter of Matthew, Saint Basil’s *Rule*, chap. 145, and Avitus of Vienne, first letter.]

Many do not know what sort of insult “Racha” is. But they know very well how insulting it is to call someone a fool. And so, employing their knowledge rather than their ignorance, people prefer to expiate their guilt through an insult they understand, in the fires of God, rather than through one they do not understand, before human councils.

### III

Since these things are so, and since all the commands given by the Lord are not only completely unfulfilled by us but are almost all fulfilled in the opposite way, when shall we do those greater things? “Whoever,” says the Savior, “does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). And “whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38). Whoever calls himself a Christian ought to walk just as Christ walked (1 John 2:6). Yet it is certain that these words are fulfilled not even by those who abandon worldly pleasures and displays, let alone by those who follow them.

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript. The Colbert manuscript and all editions instead read *the right of secular love*.]

For even those who seem to renounce wealth do not renounce it in such a way that they appear to have renounced it completely. And those who are thought to carry the cross carry it in such a way that they possess more dignity in the name of the cross than suffering in its punishment.

[Note: I think Salvian is speaking here of those who, after abandoning the displays and amusements of the world and then renouncing their possessions, openly professed contempt for human affairs. After renouncing everything they possessed, they either truly bore the cross or wished to be understood as bearing it, so that they might show themselves to be disciples of Jesus Christ. If they did this from the innermost feeling of their hearts, the virtue and courage of such men deserved praise. But if these things were done more ostentatiously than sincerely, they deserved to be exposed by everyone’s speech and conversation. Cassian has an elegant passage in *Conferences* 8.3, which deserves to be quoted here. It runs as follows: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” Certain of the strictest monks, indeed possessing zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, understood this literally: they made wooden crosses for themselves and continually carried them around on their shoulders, bringing not edification but laughter to all who saw them. See Innocent III, book 10, letter 121.]

Yet even if all these people were to fulfill some of these things in good faith, no one could accomplish this: to walk along the road of this life as the Savior walked. “Whoever says he remains in Christ,” says the Apostle, “ought to walk just as he walked” (1 John 2:6).

### IV

But perhaps some think that the apostles’ commands are harsh. They would indeed have to be considered harsh if they demanded more duties from others than they assumed for themselves. But if they imposed far less on others than on themselves, they must be judged not harsh teachers but most indulgent parents, who through loving tenderness remove burdens from their children’s necks while placing them upon themselves through religious devotion.

For what does one of them say to the ecclesiastical peoples?

[Note: In the Colbert manuscript and in the ancient editions, *apostles* is read instead of *peoples*, plainly incorrectly. Rittershusius recognized the error and thought that one should write *ecclesiastical peoples*. This conjectural emendation is entirely confirmed by the authority of the Corbie manuscript. We once corrected a similar error in Agobard’s *Apologetic Book*, chap. 6: “And let all the people say,” where previously it read, “And let every apostle say.” See the notes to the *Capitularies*, p. 1173.]

“My little children,” he says, “for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). And again: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:16). He commands us to imitate the one who had commanded himself to be an imitator of Christ.

That he himself imitated Christ is beyond doubt. Christ subjected himself to the world for our sake, and he subjected himself to Christ. Christ endured weariness and the heaviest labors for us, and he did so for Christ. Christ suffered insults for us, and he did so for Christ. Christ endured passion and death for us, and he did so for Christ. Therefore, conscious of his merits, he does not say without reason: “I have fought the good fight, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

Since he thus imitated Christ, let us see which of us appears to be an imitator of the Apostle. He first writes of himself that he never gave anyone cause for offense, but in everything showed himself to be God’s minister: “in great patience, in tribulations, in blows, in prisons, in wounds” (2 Cor. 6:3–5). Elsewhere, comparing himself with others, he says:

“In whatever anyone dares”—I speak foolishly—“I dare also. To speak as one less wise, I dare more: in many labors, in prisons more abundantly, in blows beyond measure, in deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck” (2 Cor. 11:21, 23–25).

Indeed, even if we do nothing about the other apostolic virtues he mentioned, in this one matter—that the Apostle says he suffered shipwreck three times—we can surpass him. For we have not suffered shipwreck only three times, since almost our entire life is a shipwreck. People live so viciously everywhere that scarcely any Christian seems not to be continually suffering shipwreck.

### V

But someone may perhaps say that the present time is not such that we should endure for Christ what the apostles endured then. That is true. There are no pagan rulers, no tyrants persecuting us; the blood of the saints is not shed, nor is faith tested by punishments. Our God is content that our peace should serve him, and that we should please him solely by the purity of unblemished acts and the holiness of an undefiled life.

For this reason our faith and devotion ought to be greater toward him, because he demands less from us and has granted us more. Since our rulers are Christians, there is no persecution, and religion is not disturbed, we are not compelled to prove our faith by more difficult trials. At least by lesser duties we ought to please the Lord more. For if necessity requires it, he judges a person who fulfills lesser things capable of carrying out greater ones as well.

### VI

Let us therefore set aside what blessed Paul endured—or rather, what we read that all Christians have endured in the books later written about religion: those who, ascending to the gate of the heavenly kingdom by the steps of their punishments, made ladders for themselves, as it were, out of torture-horses and scaffolds.

Let us see whether, at least in those acts of religious devotion that are lesser and common, which all Christians can perform in complete tranquility and at every time, we attempt to respond to the Lord’s commands.

Christ commands us not to quarrel. Who obeys the one giving this command? He not only commands it, but commands it to such an extent that he orders us to surrender the very things over which the dispute is taking place, provided that we rid ourselves of disputes. “If anyone,” he says, “wishes to contend with you in judgment and take your tunic, leave him your cloak also” (Matt. 5:40).

I ask who are the people who yield to adversaries who strip them—or rather, who are the people who do not try to strip their adversaries? We are so far from surrendering anything else along with our tunics that, if we can in any way, we take both the cloak and the tunics of our adversary at once. We obey the Lord’s commands with such devotion that it is not enough for us to refuse to yield even the smallest part of our clothing to our adversaries; if it lies within our power and circumstances permit, we must seize everything from them.

A command equal and similar to this is joined to it, when the Lord says: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (ibid. 39).

How many, do we suppose, modestly offer even their ears to this saying—or at least, even if they seem to do so, accept it in their hearts? Or how rare is the person who, if he receives one blow, does not return many for one? He is so far from offering the other cheek to the one striking him that he thinks he has won only when he has overcome his adversary by striking rather than by being struck.

“Whatever you wish people to do to you,” says the Savior, “do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12). We know one part of this saying so well that we never neglect it; the other we neglect as though we knew nothing about it. We know very well what we want others to do for us, but we do not know what we ourselves ought to do for others. And would that we did not know! The guilt of ignorance would be less, according to the saying: “The servant who did not know his master’s will will be beaten with few blows. But the one who knew it and did not do it will be beaten with many” (Luke 12:47–48).

But now the offense is greater because we love one part of the sacred saying for the sake of our own advantage, while we neglect the other to God’s dishonor. The Apostle Paul also amplifies this word of God through his preaching, saying: “Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other” (1 Cor. 10:24). And again: “Let each of you consider not his own interests, but those of others” (Phil. 2:4).

You see how faithfully he carried out Christ’s command. Whereas the Savior ordered us to think of others as we think of ourselves, Paul commanded us to care more for the interests of others than for our own: a good servant of a good master, and a distinguished imitator of his unique teacher. Walking in the footsteps of his master, he made those footprints somehow broader and more distinct by his own steps.

What, then, do we Christians do—what Christ commands, or what the Apostle commands? I think, quite simply, neither. For we are so far from doing anything for the advantage of others at the cost of our own disadvantage that we all, above all, pursue our own advantage at the cost of others’ disadvantage.

### VII

But perhaps we seem to choose the greater commands, which no one fulfills—or, as they themselves think, cannot possibly fulfill—and pass over others that can be fulfilled and are fulfilled by everyone.

First, however, we must consider that no servant is permitted to choose at will, among the orders given by his master, what he wants to do and what he does not want to do; nor, with utterly insolent abuse, to take up what pleases him and reject what displeases him. Even earthly masters consider it wholly intolerable for their servants to heed their commands in part and despise them in part, doing whatever they think should be done according to their own desire and trampling down whatever they think should be trampled.

For if servants obey their masters according to their own will, they do not obey even in those matters in which they obey. When a servant does only what he wishes from his master’s commands, he is no longer fulfilling his master’s will but his own.

If, then, we who are frail little human beings do not want to be despised at all by our servants—although the condition of servitude makes them inferior to us, the human condition nevertheless makes them our equals—how unjustly do we despise the heavenly Lord? We are human ourselves, yet we do not think we ought to be despised by people of our own condition.

Unless, perhaps, we possess such great judgment and such profound understanding that, while we do not wish to suffer injuries from servants, we want God to be subjected to our injuries, and believe that God ought rightly to endure what we ourselves think unworthy of human endurance.

And so, to return to the earlier point, if there are people who think we speak of God’s greater commands while keeping silent about the lesser ones, they should understand that they complain needlessly. There is no just grounds for preferring some commands when all must be done.

Just as, as I have already said, it is wholly unlawful for servants of earthly masters to choose which of their master’s commands they will obey and which they will not, so we, who are servants of our Lord, ought to consider it wholly unlawful either to take up what pleases us for the gratification of our minds or to trample down what displeases us through the abuse of pride.

### VIII

Still, let us accommodate those who perhaps do not want us to speak of the greater commands of the Lord because they think they fulfill the lesser ones—not because it is sufficient for salvation to do the lesser while despising the greater, according to the saying: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10).

Although doing only the small and least things is not sufficient for us, I nevertheless agree to speak of the lesser ones, so that I may show that the great majority of all Christians have not even done the small and least things.

Our Savior commanded Christians not to swear (Matt. 5:34). You will find more people who swear falsely more often than people who do not swear at all. He also commanded that no one should curse. Whose speech is not a curse? Curses are always the first weapons of anger; whatever we cannot do in our weakness, we wish for in anger. Thus, in every movement of indignant hearts, we use evil wishes as weapons. Each person thereby proves most clearly that whatever he wishes to happen to his adversaries, he would want to do himself if he could.

But because we all easily employ this wickedness of speech, we therefore also think that God, who commanded it, considers it easy. “The verbally abusive,” says the divine word, “will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10). From this we can understand how serious and destructive a curse is, since, even if other good things are present, it alone excludes a person from heaven.

Christ commanded envy to be far from us. Yet we envy not only strangers but even those closest to us; we stain not only our enemies but also our friends with jealousy. This evil reigns so nearly in everyone’s feelings; the desire to eat has a limit, but the desire to slander has none. We are always satisfied by food, but never by slander.

Perhaps the punishment for this stain is light. “The slanderer,” says Holy Scripture, “will be uprooted.” The punishment is certainly grave and terrifying, but there is no correction. So long as each person does not cease tearing another apart, he considers the matter so important that he does not even spare himself.

Yet the recompense for this evil is entirely fitting: it pursues only its author. It does no harm at all to the person whom he slanders; it punishes only the one from whose mouth the slander proceeds.

But perhaps we seem to be raving by repeating these things, and I endure being thought to rave. Did the Lord rave when he commanded: “Let all shouting be removed from you, together with all malice,” through his Apostle (Eph. 4:31)? Both of these persist continually in us, but malice more than shouting. Shouting is not always on our lips, whereas malice is always in our hearts. And so I think that even if shouting ceased in us, malice would nevertheless remain.

Our God also commanded us to be without grumbling and complaint (Phil. 2:14–15). When have these things not existed among the human race? If there is heat, we complain of drought; if rain, we complain of flooding. If the year is less productive, we blame sterility; if more productive, we blame cheapness. We desire abundance, and once we obtain it, we complain about it. What could be more wicked or insulting than this? Even in this we complain about God’s mercy, because he grants what we ask.

God commanded that every kind of stumbling block be far from his servants, even that of the eyes. “Whoever,” he says, “looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). From this we can fully understand how chaste the Savior commanded us to be, since he cut off even the license of sight.

Knowing that the light of our eyes is, in a sense, the window of our minds, and that all wicked desires enter the heart through the eyes as through natural passages, he wished them to be extinguished completely on the outside, lest they arise within and, growing lethally strong in their fibers, perhaps become established in the soul if they had first sprouted in the act of seeing.

Therefore the Lord says that the lustful gazes of unchaste people are not free from the guilt of adultery, so that anyone who sincerely flees adultery may also guard his eyes. Wishing to make his worshipers possessors of perfect and most genuine holiness, the Savior commanded them to avoid even the smallest things with the utmost care, so that the life of a Christian might be as pure as the pupil of the eye; and just as the eye, while its sight remains unharmed, does not admit the stain of dust, so our life should have no stain of impurity within it.

Hence also the Lord says in what follows: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out. And if your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off. It is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body be thrown into Gehenna” (ibid. 29–30).

If, then, according to God’s word, we are dragged into Gehenna by stumbling blocks, it is entirely right that, in order to avoid Gehenna, we should punish even our hands and eyes—not because anyone ought to deprive himself of his bodily members, but because certain relationships of domestic service are so necessary to us that we sometimes use them as eyes and sometimes as hands. We rightly withdraw from ourselves the services of present duties, lest we suffer the torments of eternal fire.

[Note: It was the belief of the ancients that there was an eternal fire in the underworld in which the damned were burned. Faustus, bishop of Riez, has an elegant passage in his sixth letter to Ruricius, bishop of Limoges: “Hence you easily despise earthly things, or distribute them as a moneylender does, while you consider that time when sinners will be burned like hay; when, by the perpetual fury of blazing Gehenna, whose smoke rises forever and ever, those who neglected what was offered will be punished by such a death that they are not permitted to die in their suffering—about to die to life, and to live without end for death.” Likewise, in his first letter: “A human being, therefore, will die to God because of mortal evils, and will live for the underworld. This will be his death: that he is not permitted to die in suffering.” Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, held the same view; in his exhortation to repentance we read: “Eternal fire itself restores the material of bodies that continually grow again.” Prosper, or Julianus Pomerius, in book 3 of *On the Contemplative Life*, chap. 12, counts among the miseries of the damned “to die to blessed life and live for eternal death”—a savage punishment that always tortures the wretched but never destroys them. As Seneca says, it is a kind of mercy to kill quickly, but cruelty to torment with prolonged suffering. Here, however, one must remember Origen.]

For when the matter concerns service and life, it is certainly better for a Christian to be deprived of service than of life.

### IX

Since our Lord has commanded us to obey him in all the things we have mentioned, where are those who obey God either in all his commands or at least in a very few? Where are those who love their enemies, do good to those who persecute them, overcome evil with good, offer their cheeks to those who strike them, or concede their possessions without litigation to those who strip them?

[Note: Christ’s command is that we should love our enemies. Caesarius of Arles presses this argument very strongly in his homilies on the love of enemies. Today, however, people have greatly departed from this command, I think, because as the Church grows old, we continually depart from the beginning of piety. Let those who make a practice of treating the laws of Christ and of the Church with contempt, or softening them through ridiculous interpretation, consider—of whom there are far too many—whether it is a great virtue to love one’s enemies when they perhaps do not love even their friends, as Salvian said on p. 51.]

Who is there to whom no pleasure at all is permitted, who harms no one by his abuse, who restrains his mouth in silence lest it burst forth into the bitterness of cursing?

[Note: All editions read this way, and the Corbie manuscript agrees with them. I would nevertheless willingly read *detractioni* (“to slander”), although *delectationi* (“to pleasure”) also yields a good sense.]

Who is there who does these smallest things—not to mention the greater things about which we spoke shortly before?

Since these things are so, and since none of the Lord’s commands is at all fulfilled by us, why do we complain about God, when God can more justly complain about all of us? What reason have we to grieve that we are not heard by God, when we ourselves do not hear God; to murmur that the earth is not regarded by God, when we ourselves do not look toward heaven; to be troubled that our prayers are disregarded by the Lord, when his commands are disregarded by us?

Grant that we are on equal terms with our Lord. What place is there for a just complaint, when each person suffers what he has done? Except that I can easily prove that we do not suffer what we do, and that God deals with us far more gently than we deal with God.

For the moment, however, let us proceed according to the rule with which we began. The Lord himself says: “I called to you, and you did not hear me; and you will call to me, and I will not hear you” (Jer. 11:11; Zech. 7:13). What could be more fitting, or more just? We did not hear, and we are not heard; we did not regard, and we are not regarded.

I ask which earthly master is content to deal with his servants according to this rule: that he merely despise them because he has been despised by them? Yet we despise God not only by this injury, by which earthly masters are accustomed to be despised by their servants, since this is the greatest contempt shown by servants—namely, their failure to do what they are commanded.

[Note: The editions read: “Earthly rulers are accustomed to be despised by their servants.” In the margin of the Pithoean edition, *carnales* (“worldly” or “human”) is written. But the Corbie manuscript has *Domini carnales* (“worldly masters”), correctly. Salvian had said shortly before: “I ask which earthly master is content to deal with his servants according to this rule,” and so on. Agobard, in his book *On the Baptism of Jewish Slaves*, writes: “We reject this because of worldly masters.”]

But we, with every effort and every exertion, not only fail to do what is commanded; we do the opposite of what we are commanded.

God commands that we should all be dear to one another; yet we all tear one another apart through mutual hostility. God commands that everyone give his possessions to the needy; yet almost everyone invades what belongs to others. God commands that every Christian keep his eyes chaste; yet how rare is the person who does not cover himself with the filth of fornication?

And why say more? What I am about to say is grievous and lamentable. The very Church of God, which ought in everything to appease God, what is it other than a provoker of God’s anger? Apart from a very few who flee evil, what is almost the entire assembly of Christians other than a cesspool of vices?

How many will you find in the Church who are not either drunkards, gluttons, adulterers, fornicators, kidnappers, revelers, thieves, or murderers? And, what is worse than all these things, almost all these offenses are committed without end.

I ask the conscience of all Christians: among the sins and crimes we have just mentioned, how many people are not guilty of at least one, and how many are not guilty of all? You will more easily find someone who is guilty of everything than someone guilty of nothing.

And what we called “nothing” may perhaps seem too severe a judgment. I shall say more: you will more easily find people guilty of every evil than people guilty of not every evil; more easily people guilty of greater crimes than of lesser ones—that is, people who have committed greater crimes together with lesser ones, rather than people who have committed only lesser crimes without greater ones.

For almost the entire ecclesiastical populace has been reduced to this disgraceful condition of morals, so that among the whole Christian people it is almost a kind of holiness to be less vicious.

[Note: Caesarius must certainly be consulted in his homily against those who think that it is sufficient for them for eternal life if they have done no evil, even if they refuse to fulfill good works.]

Thus some hold churches—or rather, the temples and altars of God—in less reverence than the house of any insignificant municipal judge. For within the doors not only of illustrious authorities but also of governors and prefects, not everyone ventures to enter indiscriminately, unless the judge has summoned him, or business has brought him there, or the dignity of his own rank has permitted him to enter.

[Note: That is, “of men of illustrious rank,” who governed the provinces in the place of the emperor. See above, p. 7.]

If anyone should enter insolently, he is either beaten, driven out, or punished with some disgrace and stain upon his reputation. But into the temples—or rather, into the altars and sanctuaries of God—all the filthy and wicked rush indiscriminately, without any reverence whatsoever for sacred honor.

This is not because everyone ought not to hasten to entreat God, but because the person who enters to appease him ought not to leave having provoked him. It is not the same duty to ask for pardon and to provoke anger.

It is indeed a new kind of monstrosity: almost everyone continually does the very things that they lament having done, and those who enter the ecclesiastical house to mourn ancient evils leave—

[Note: Something is missing here and must be supplied from what follows.]

—and what do I mean by “leave”? They are almost plotting this very conduct during their prayers and supplications. Their mouths do one thing, their hearts another; while they mourn past evils in words, in their thoughts they meditate future ones. Thus their prayer is more an author of crimes than an entreaty for pardon, so that the curse of Scripture is truly fulfilled in them: “Let them come forth condemned from their prayer, and let their prayer become sin” (Ps. 108:7).

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript. The editions and the Colbert manuscript instead read *rixa* (“quarrel”), which makes no sense. Casaubon notes in his annotations on Trebellius Pollio that *auctrix* (“author” or “originator”) is not pure Latin.]

Finally, if anyone wishes to know what such people have been thinking in the temple, let him observe what follows. When the solemn sacred rites have been completed, everyone immediately rushes off to his customary pursuits: some, of course, to steal, others to get drunk. Thus it plainly appears that, while they were inside the temple, they were meditating upon what they carry out after they have left.

## X.

But evidently some people think that all these evils and all the disgracefulness of the vices I mentioned above should perhaps be attributed to slaves or to the most degraded classes of people; but that the name of a freeborn person is not stained by such a blot of shame. What else, however, is the life of all merchants but fraud and perjury? What else is the life of courtiers but iniquity? What else is the life of officials but slander? What else is the life of soldiers but plunder?

[Note: Previously, *omnium militantium* (“of all soldiers”) was read; but we have removed this word, which does not occur in the Colbertinus manuscript, as unnecessary.]

But perhaps you think that this can also be said of persons of this sort. “This,” you say, “is their conduct and their profession; and therefore it is hardly surprising if they do what they profess.” As though God either wished anyone to commit evil deeds or profess them, or as though there were no offense against the sacred majesty if persons of lower rank appeared to commit the greatest crime—especially since in this multitude of people the larger part of the human race is involved; and unquestionably, wherever the crowd of sinners is greater, the offense against the Divinity is greater.

“But,” you say, “all nobility is free from these crimes.” That is little enough, since nobility throughout the whole world appears to be no more than one man in a great crowd. Nevertheless, let us see whether even that small number is free from guilt. First, let us consider what divine speech says about such people. For, reproving the people of God, the Apostle says:

> Hear, my beloved brothers. Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that God promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor. Do not the rich oppress you by their power? Do they not themselves blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you? (James 2:5–7)

This is a serious testimony of the Apostle—unless perhaps nobles think themselves exempt from it because only the rich are named. But either the nobles are the same people as the rich, or, if there are rich people apart from the nobles, they too are now, so to speak, nobles, since the misery of this age is so great that no one is considered more noble than the one who is richest.

But whether the Apostle spoke of one group or of both, the matter can easily be settled. It makes no difference which group was chiefly intended, since it is certain that the statement applies to both. For who among either the nobles altogether or the rich is not horrified by crimes? Although I have misstated this: many are horrified, but very few avoid them. In others they are horrified by what they themselves are always committing, strangely acting both as accusers and excusers of the same crimes. They publicly condemn what they secretly do; and thus, while they think they are condemning others, they condemn themselves even more by their own censure.

[Col. 0069A] But let us leave aside those who are more deeply guilty. Who among the rich or the nobles preserves innocence or keeps his hands from every crime? Although I have said “from every crime” unnecessarily: if only they kept them from the greatest crimes, because perhaps they wish to claim for themselves, as though by right of a special privilege, that they may commit even lesser crimes!

[Note: We had previously printed *privilegium* (“privilege”), following the Pithoean edition. Now, however, we have preferred to follow the reading of the Corbie manuscript, in which the form we have printed occurs. It may also be inferred that this was written in the archetype from which the manuscript used by Brassicanus was copied, since he printed *privilegium dicare* (“to dedicate a privilege”). The Roman edition of Galesinius likewise has this reading. In the Colbertinus manuscript, however, one reads *privilegium ditare* (“to enrich a privilege”).]

Therefore I say nothing about easier sins. Let us see whether anyone is free even from those two sins that are, as it were, capital: homicide and sexual violation. For who is not either stained with human blood or soiled with filthy impurity? One of these is enough for eternal punishment; yet scarcely any rich person has not committed both.

## XI.

But perhaps someone among this number thinks: “I no longer do these things.” I commend you, if you do not; but perhaps you did so before, and to have ceased doing something is not the same as never having done it at all.

[Col. 0069B] Yet even if that were so, what benefit was there in one person desisting from crime while many remained in their crimes?

[Note: The same manuscript reads *prodesset* (“benefit”).]

The conversion of one person does not heal the crimes of the many; nor is it enough to appease God that one person abandons his sins when the entire human race has offended him—especially since the person who is converted, in order to escape eternal death, receives great fruits from his conversion if he escapes, let alone that he could avert the punishment of condemnation from others. For it is an intolerable arrogance and a monstrous sacrilege if anyone thinks himself so good that he believes even the wicked can be saved through him.

Speaking of a certain land or of a sinful people, God says:

> If there were three men in its midst—Noah, Daniel, and Job—they would not deliver sons or daughters. They alone would be saved (Ezekiel 14:14, 16).

Yet I do not think anyone will be so shameless as to dare compare himself with such men. For although someone may now strive to please God, it is nevertheless itself the greatest kind of injustice for him to presume himself righteous. Thus every hope based on the false belief that an innumerable multitude of ruined people can be defended from present evils by the intercession of a few good people has been removed.

[Note: Salvian therefore did not think that an innumerable multitude of traitors (*proditorum hominum*) could be defended from present evils by the intercession of a few good people.]

For since no one is equal to those whom we mentioned above, what hope can there be that outsiders, innumerable and wicked, can be delivered by a very few good people, when those saints who were most intimate with God did not even obtain this from the Lord—that they should save their own members in their children?

And rightly so. For although children seem in every respect to be members of their parents, they must not be considered members of those from whom they have begun to differ in affection; for in such people the benefits of nature perish through the depravity of degenerate character.

[Col. 0070B] Hence we too, who are called Christians, lose the power of so great a name through the vice of depravity.

[Note: The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius read: “We who have said that we are Christians.” Pithoeus, from his manuscript, has: “We who say that we are Christians.”]

For it is of no benefit at all to bear a holy name without corresponding conduct, since a life at odds with one’s profession strips the illustrious title of its honor through the baseness of unworthy actions.

[Note: From this it may be inferred that, even in that age, the name “Christian” was still regarded as holy. See below, pages 59 and 79.]

Since, therefore, we see scarcely any part of all Christians, scarcely any corner of all the churches, that is not filled with every offense and every stain of deadly sins, in what respect do we flatter ourselves about the Christian name, when by that very name, which is most sacred, we are more guilty because we differ from the holy name? For this reason also we injure God more under the title of religion: because, placed within religion, we sin.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0069D] 59. I.

We therefore depart from that prerogative of the Christian name which we mentioned above, thinking that because we are more religious than all nations, we ought also to be stronger. For since, as we have said, this is the faith of a Christian person—to believe Christ faithfully—and since to believe Christ faithfully means to keep Christ’s commandments, it undoubtedly follows that the faithless person has no faith, and that the person who tramples on Christ’s commandments does not believe Christ.

[Note: The Pithoean edition reads: “For since, as we have said, this is the faith of a Christian person: faithfully to keep Christ’s commandments,” and so forth. But the Corbie manuscript has: “For since, as we have said, this is the faith of a Christian person: faithfully to believe Christ; and since to believe Christ faithfully means to keep Christ’s commandments,” and so forth. Correctly so. For above, page 42, he had said: “I suppose that a person faithfully believes in Christ, that is, is faithful to God; and this means faithfully to keep God’s commandments.” Aetherius and Beatus, Book I *Against Elipandus*: “He is not a Christian who does not rightly believe in Christ.” Athanasius, in the letter to Epictetus preserved in the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus, page 466: “Or how can those who say that the Son is one and the Word of God another be Christians?” Augustine, *Sermon 9 on the Ten Strings*, chapter 4, in the new edition: “For whoever does not think about the future age, and is not a Christian for the purpose of receiving what God promises at the end, is not yet a Christian.”]

Thus everything comes down to this: whoever does not perform the work of the Christian name does not appear to be a Christian. For a name without its action and duty is nothing.

For, as someone says in his writings:

[Note: This passage is from Salvian, Book II *To the Catholic Church*, or *Against Avarice*. But since Salvian cites the passage in words that seem to indicate that it belongs to another writer, Pithoeus was led to state that it could reasonably be doubted whether the four books written to the Catholic Church under the name of Timothy were Salvian’s. On this matter, see what is said below in our preface to those books.]

> What else is authority without the elevation of merits but a title of honor without a person? Or what is dignity in an unworthy person but an ornament in mud?

[Note: Salvian, Book II *To the Catholic Church*, or *Against Avarice*, page 252.]

Therefore, to use the same words ourselves, what else is a holy title without merit but an ornament in mud? As sacred Scripture also testifies, saying:

> A gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman without discretion (Proverbs 11:22).

The Christian name is likewise a golden ornament in us; but if we use it unworthily, we appear to be pigs wearing an ornament.

[Col. 0071B] Finally, whoever wishes to know fully that names are nothing without realities should consider how innumerable peoples, when their merits ceased, also lost their names. The twelve tribes of the Hebrews, once chosen by God, received two sacred names: they were called the People of God and Israel. Thus we read:

> Hear, my people, and I will speak; Israel, and I will testify to you (Psalm 80:9).

Therefore the Jews once possessed both names, but now possess neither. For one who long ago abandoned the worship of God cannot be called the People of God, nor can the one who denied the Son of God be called “the one who sees God,” as it is written:

> But Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me (Isaiah 1:3).

For this reason, elsewhere also our God speaks of the Jewish people to the prophet, saying:

> Call his name “Not Beloved” (Hosea 1:9; Romans 9:25).

And again to the Jews themselves:

> You are not my people, and I am not your God (ibid., 9).

Why he said this about them, he clearly shows elsewhere. Thus he says:

> They have forsaken the spring of living waters, the Lord (Jeremiah 17:13).

And again:

> They have cast away the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them.

I fear that this might have been said no more of them then than it can now be said of us, because we neither obey the Lord’s words, and those who do not obey the Lord’s words plainly have no wisdom at all within them.

Unless perhaps we believe that we wisely despise God, and that the very fact that we disregard Christ’s commandments is the height of prudence. There is indeed reason to think that we believe this. For we all pursue sins with such agreement that it is as though we were sinning by a conspiracy of supreme deliberation.

Since this is so, what reason is there for us to deceive ourselves with a false opinion, imagining that because we are called Christians, the good name can help us amid the evils we commit, when the Holy Spirit says that even faith cannot benefit Christian people without good works?

And certainly faith is much more than a name: a name is a person’s designation, but faith is the fruit of the mind. Yet the Apostle testifies that even this fruit of faith is fruitless without good works, saying:

> Faith without works is dead (James 2:17).

And again:

> For just as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead (ibid., 26).

He adds still harsher statements to confound those who flatter themselves through presumption upon the Christian faith.

## II.

But someone will say: “You have faith, and I have works. Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works” (ibid., 18).

By this he clearly indicates that good actions are like witnesses of Christian faith: unless a Christian performs good works, he cannot demonstrate his faith at all. Consequently, what he cannot prove to exist must be regarded as though it did not exist.

He immediately shows how little he regarded this as something to be counted on, when he says to the Christian:

> You believe that there is one God. You do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble (ibid., 19).

Let us consider what the Apostle wished to say here; let us not become angry with divine testimonies, but accept them; let us not contradict them, but improve. “You believe,” divine Scripture says to the Christian, “that God is one. You do well. Even the demons believe—and tremble.”

Did the Apostle err, comparing the faith of a Christian person with that of a demon? Certainly not. But wishing to show what was said above—that no one should claim anything for himself through the pride of faith without good works—he therefore says that even the demons believe in God.

[Note: This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. Pithoeus had: *Usurpare deberet. Idcirco autem a daemon.* (“He ought to claim [it]. Therefore, however, from a demon…”). Everyone, I think, can see that the reading of the Corbie manuscript is sounder.]

That is, just as the demons, although they believe in God, nevertheless persist in wickedness, so certain people possess something like demonic belief: they assert that they believe in God, yet do not cease from evil works.

He then adds, for the shame and condemnation of sinful people, that the demons not only believe in God but also fear and tremble. In effect he says:

“What are you flattering yourself about, whoever you are, with a belief that is nothing without fear of and obedience to God? The demons possess something more. You have one thing only; they have two. You have belief but no fear; they have both belief and fear.”

Why then are you surprised if we are struck? Why are you surprised if we are chastised, if we are handed over to the jurisdiction of enemies, if we are weaker than everyone else? Our sufferings, weaknesses, overthrow, captivities, and almost shameful enslavements are all proofs of a bad servant and a good master.

How are we bad servants? Because I suffer, at least in part, what I deserve. How is he a good master? Because he shows what we deserve, even if he does not inflict what we deserve.

[Col. 0073A] For in the most merciful and kindly chastisement he prefers to correct us rather than let us perish. As far as our crimes are concerned, we deserve deadly punishments. But he, showing more mercy than severity, prefers to amend us through the moderation of a lenient judgment rather than kill us with the blow of just coercion.

[Note: The Colbertinus manuscript reads *coertionis incidere* (“to fall into coercion”).]

I am quite sure that we find it unpleasant to be struck; but why are we surprised that God scourges us when we sin, since we ourselves scourge our little slaves when they sin? We are unjust judges: we do not want insignificant human beings to be scourged by God, although we ourselves scourge human beings of our own condition.

Nor am I surprised that we are so unjust in this matter. Our nature and our wickedness are servile. We want to commit offenses and do not want to be scourged. We have the same dispositions in ourselves as in our little slaves: we all want to sin with impunity.

Finally, if I am lying, I appeal to everyone. I deny that there is anyone, however great the crime of which he is guilty, who will admit that he ought to be tortured. From this it can be recognized how unjustly and perversely we are most severe toward others and most indulgent toward ourselves; harsh toward others and lenient toward ourselves. In the same crime we punish others and acquit ourselves.

This is utterly intolerable arrogance and presumption. We do not wish to acknowledge guilt in ourselves, yet we dare to assume judgment over others. What could be more unjust or more perverse than this? We consider that very crime acceptable in ourselves which we most severely punish in others.

And therefore the Apostle does not call out to us without reason:

> Therefore you are without excuse, O every person who judges. For in judging another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things that you judge (Romans 2:1).

[Note: The Corbie and Colbertinus manuscripts have precisely this reading, whereas Pithoeus’s edition had *judicas* (“you judge”). Rittershusius thought that *condemnas* (“you condemn”) should be read here. Salvian repeats the passage below, pages 65–66.]

## III.

But one of the rich will say: “We do not do the same things as the slaves do. From among slaves come thieves and fugitives, slaves continually serving their appetite and belly.”

It is true that these are vices of slaves. Yet the vices of masters are more numerous and greater, though not those of all. A few must be excepted, but very few—whom I do not name, lest by naming them I seem to praise them more than, by not naming others, to expose those others.

First, if slaves are thieves, they are perhaps compelled to steal by poverty. For even if their customary allowances are paid to them, these satisfy habit more than sufficiency; thus they fill the prescribed measure without filling satiety.

[Note: That is, the allowance customarily given to slaves.]

Consequently, poverty makes the fault itself less blameworthy, because the person who appears to have been compelled unwillingly to theft is excusably guilty of theft. Indeed, ecclesiastical Scripture seems in some way to excuse the offenses of all the wretched, saying:

> It is not a great fault when someone steals: for he steals to fill his hungry soul (Proverbs 6:30).

In Solomon:

> He steals to satisfy his soul.

Accordingly, those whom divine Scripture excuses are not to be accused by us too harshly.

[Note: These words seem superfluous and have the character of a gloss. Yet they occur in all the ancient manuscripts and editions.]

What we say about the thefts of slaves also applies to their flight—indeed, it applies more appropriately to flight, because slaves are driven to flee not only by misery but also by punishments. They fear their overseers; they fear the keepers of silence; they fear the stewards.

[Note: Rittershusius observes that Salvian here seems to allude to a certain class of slaves appointed to restrain the loquacity of their fellow slaves—*silentiarii*, so called because they imposed silence on the others.]

They are almost such that, among all these people, they are slaves of no one less than of their masters: they are beaten by everyone and crushed by everyone. What more can be said? Many slaves flee to their masters while fearing their fellow slaves.

[Note: Juretus, in his *Miscellanies on Symmachus*, Book X, Letter 10, argues that the reading should be “to their own masters.”]

Therefore their flight should be attributed not so much to those who flee as to those who compel them to flee. These most wretched people suffer violence. They wish to serve, and they are forced to flee. They do not at all wish to depart from the service of their masters, but the cruelty of their fellow slaves does not permit them to serve.

They are also said to be liars. Yet the brutality of their present punishment likewise compels them to lie. Indeed, while they wish to escape torture, they lie. What wonder is it if a slave placed in fear prefers to lie rather than be scourged?

They are also accused of gluttony and greed for food. Nor is this surprising. The person who has often endured hunger desires fullness more intensely. But suppose he does not endure hunger for bread: certainly he endures hunger for delicacies. Therefore he should be forgiven if he seeks more eagerly what is continually lacking to him.

But you, noble person, you rich person, who overflow with monstrous wealth, who for that very reason ought to honor God more through holy works, because you enjoy his gifts without interruption—let us see whether you possess conduct that is not merely holy, but even harmless.

[Note: This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. The Colbertinus manuscript and the editions have *omnibus* (“all”).]

And who, as I said above, among the rich, apart from a few, is not infected with every crime? And as for my excepting a few, if only I were permitted to except more, or even all. The innocence of the majority would be the salvation of all.

I am speaking now of no one except the person who recognizes that what I am saying exists in himself. If all that I say lies outside his conscience, then none of what I say applies as an insult to him. But if he knows that what I am saying exists in himself, he should not think that my tongue is saying it to him, but rather his own conscience.

First, to speak of the vices of slaves: if a slave is a fugitive, then you too, rich and noble person, are a fugitive. For all flee their Lord who abandon the law of the Lord.

Why then, rich person, do you blame the slave? You do what he does. He is a fugitive from his master, and you are a fugitive from yours. But you are more blameworthy than he, because he perhaps fled an evil master, while you flee a good one.

You also accuse the slave of lack of control over his belly. In him it is rare, because of poverty; in you it is daily, because of abundance. You therefore see yourself most especially—or rather, yourself alone—being scourged by the apostolic sentence, because “in judging another, you condemn yourself.”

For you do the very things that you judge—indeed, not the same things, but far greater and worse ones. In the slave you punish even an infrequent intemperance of the belly, while you yourself are swollen with continual excess.

Theft, too, you think is a servile vice. Yet you, rich person, commit theft whenever you presume to do what God has forbidden. For all who commit unlawful acts commit theft.

## IV.

But why do I speak of this so minutely and, as it were, allegorically, when the most flagrant crimes prove that the thefts of the rich are not merely thefts but robberies? For how many people are there who, beside a rich man, are not poor either in their condition or in their actual circumstances?

[Note: This reading seemed sounder than that of Pithoeus, which reads: “For how many people, beside a rich man, are either poor or untouched or safe?” Our reading is supported by the note in the margin of Pithoeus’s edition, where it is said to be read elsewhere as *auctus aut statutus*. This is the reading of the Colbertinus manuscript.]

For through the invasions of the powerful, weak people lose either their possessions or even themselves, together with their families. Thus sacred Scripture has rightly testified about both classes, saying:

> The wild ass in the desert is the lion’s prey; so the poor are the pasture of the rich (Sirach 13:23).

Yet almost the entire human race suffers this tyranny, not only the poor. For what else is the dignity of the exalted than the proscription of cities? Or what else is the prefecture of certain people, whom I shall not name, than plunder?

[Note: Sidonius, Book I, Letter 7, speaking of Arvandus: “He governed his first prefecture with great popularity, and the following one with the greatest devastation.” See the same Sidonius again, Book II, Letter 1.]

There is no greater devastation of the poor than power. For this reason honor is purchased by a few, so that it may be paid for by the devastation of all. What could be more disgraceful or more unjust than this? The wretched pay the prices of dignities that they do not purchase. They know nothing of the transaction, yet they know the payment.

[Note: Thus Innocent IV, in a letter written to the archbishop of Narbonne and the bishop of Elne, published in the supplement to chapter 17 of Book VIII of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*: “It is also reported that there are certain bailiffs, officials, and officers who purchase their offices much more dearly than usual, placing their hope of damnable profit in the services or exactions which they extort, as it were by force, from churches, their people, and ecclesiastical persons.” See Rittershusius at this passage.]

So that a few may be honored, the world is overturned. The honor of one person is the ruin of the world. Finally, the Spains know this, for only their name remains. The Africas, which once existed, know it. The devastated Gauls know it, though not devastated by everyone, and therefore still breathing a faint breath in a very few corners, because the integrity of a few sometimes sustained the lands that the plunder of many emptied.

[Note: I do not know whether Africa is elsewhere called in the plural. But Salvian, who knew that there were six provinces in Africa, thought he should use the plural in order to signify them all.]

## V.

But we have strayed too far, driven by grief. Therefore, to return to what came before, in what respect are nobles not stained by servile vices—unless perhaps because they commit, as though they were permitted, the very sins that they punish in slaves?

Finally, a slave is not even permitted to aspire to the acts of plunder which, as I said above, nobles commit. Although I am lying. Some who have risen from slavery to nobility have done equal or greater things. Yet this can in no way be charged against slaves: that the condition of slavery has turned out so favorably for certain people.

Homicides among slaves are also rare, because of terror and fear of death; among the rich they are continual, because of hope and confidence in impunity.

[Note: Lupus of Ferrières, in his *Book on Three Questions*, page 210: “The hope of impunity is a great inducement to sin.” See what we have noted there.]

Unless perhaps we are unjust in attributing what the rich do to sin, because when they kill their little slaves, they think it a right, not a crime.

[Note: The masters thought that this was permitted to them by the force of their lordly power, as Rittershusius explains at greater length. The Germans, however, were different; among them, as Tacitus writes, to beat a slave and restrain him with bonds and labor was accepted practice. They usually killed not as a matter of discipline and severity, but in a fit of rage and anger, as though he were an enemy—except that they did so with impunity.]

Nor is this their only privilege; by the same privilege they also abuse their power in practicing the filth of sexual immorality. For how many rich people are there who preserve the sacrament of marriage, whom the frenzy of lust does not sweep headlong, whose household and family are not a prostitute to them, and who do not follow the madness of their minds wherever the heat of depraved desire draws them?

This is in accordance with what divine Scripture says of such people:

> They became raging horses, each neighing after women (Jeremiah 5:8).

For what else proves that this was said about themselves than the fact that the person who wishes to possess through intercourse everything he has desired with his eyes?

As for concubines, it might perhaps even seem unjust to say something about them, since, in comparison with the crimes mentioned above, being content with a few wives and restraining the reins of lust within a fixed number of spouses is almost a kind of chastity. I said “spouses,” because the matter has reached such shamelessness that many consider their slave women wives. If only, just as they are regarded as quasi-wives, they were also treated as their only wives!

But this is more shocking and detestable: some men who have obtained honorable marriages take other wives for themselves from the servile class, deforming the honor of holy marriage through the baseness of a degraded union. They are not ashamed to become husbands of their slave women, throwing the heights of noble marriages down into the obscene chambers of female slaves—thoroughly deserving even the status of those whose society they think themselves worthy of.

## VI.

I have no doubt that many of those who are either nobles or wish to appear noble receive with arrogance and disdain what we have said, since, in considering such matters, we have said that certain slaves are less disgraceful than their masters.

But since I have said this not of everyone, but of those who are such, no one should become angry who knows that he is in no way such a person.

[Note: Tacitus: “For things that fade away when despised, if you become angry, appear to have been recognized.”]

Otherwise, by the very fact that he becomes angry, he may appear to belong to their group. Rather, any noble person who wrongly resents these statements ought to be angry with those who disgrace the name of nobility by the filthiest crimes. For although such people burden the entire Christian population, they especially pollute those of whom they are said to be a part.

We have therefore said that certain nobles are worse than slaves. We have certainly said this, and we have said it improbably—unless we prove what we have said. Behold, from this very greatest crime almost the entire number of slaves is free. Does any slave have crowds of concubines? Is any slave polluted by the disgrace of many wives, and does any slave think that he has as many wives as he has been able to subject to his lust, after the manner of dogs or swine?

[Note: The Colbertinus manuscript: “But one can reply to this.”]

But it can, evidently, be answered that slaves are not permitted to do such things. Surely they would do them if they were permitted. I believe it. But since I do not see such things being done, I cannot regard them as having been done.

[Note: The same manuscript has *quantumlibet* (“however much”) here and a little later.]

However depraved their minds may be, however evil their desires, no one is punished for a crime he has not committed. It is certain that slaves are wicked and detestable. But freeborn and noble people are all the more deserving of condemnation if, in a more honorable condition, they are worse.

Thus it is necessary to reach this conclusion in the matter—not that slaves should be acquitted of the guilt of their wickedness, but that very many rich people should be condemned by comparison with slaves.

For who could adequately describe that robbery and crime whereby, while the Roman state—whether already dead or certainly breathing its last—dies in that part in which it still seems to live, strangled by the chains of taxation as if by the hands of robbers, there are nevertheless found many rich people whose taxes are borne by the poor? That is, there are many rich people whose taxes kill the poor.

And when we say that many are found, I fear that it would be more accurate to say “all.” So few are free from this evil—if indeed any are—that in the part where we have spoken of many, we can find almost all the rich.

For consider what the remedies formerly granted to certain cities accomplished. What else did they do than make all the rich exempt and heap up the taxes of the wretched? For the rich, old burdens were removed; for the poor, new ones were added. The abolition even of the smallest public services enriched the former, while the addition of the greatest burdens afflicted the latter. The former grew rich through the reduction of what they bore lightly; the latter died through the multiplication of what they could no longer bear.

Thus that remedy most unjustly raised some and most unjustly killed others. For some it was a most criminal reward; for others, a most criminal poison.

From this we understand that nothing can be more criminal than the rich, who kill the poor through their remedies, and nothing more wretched than the poor, whom even the measures given to all as a remedy destroy.

## VII.

Now consider how remarkable and how holy it is that if someone among the nobles begins to turn to God, he immediately loses the honor of nobility. Or how great is the honor of Christ among a Christian people where religion makes a person ignoble!

As soon as someone attempts to become better, he is trampled under the rejection of the worse; and thus everyone is in some way compelled to be evil, lest they be regarded as worthless.

Therefore the Apostle does not cry out without reason:

> The whole world lies in evil (1 John 5:19).

And it is true. The whole is rightly said to lie in evil when good people cannot find a place in it. For it is so full of iniquities that those who are in it must either be evil, or, if they are good, must be tortured by the persecution of many.

Thus, as we have said, if someone of higher rank attaches himself to religion, he immediately ceases to be honored. For whenever someone changes his clothing, he immediately changes his dignity. If he was exalted, he becomes despised; if he was most splendid, he becomes most contemptible; if he was entirely honor, he becomes entirely dishonor.

[Note: Hence the complaint against Tertullian, who changed from the toga to the pallium and, as Salvian says on page 241, to the philosophy of religion. But what does Salvian mean when he says that those who attached themselves to Religion were accustomed to change their clothing? Were the monks of those times distinguished from other people by some distinctive garment? See Salvian, page 108, and the notes below on page 386 and following.]

And certain worldly and unbelieving people are surprised that they suffer God’s offense or anger, although they persecute God in all the holy people.

[Note: That is, in those who turn to God, as he said shortly before. See page 108.]

For everything has become perverse and has been changed into its opposite. If someone is good, he is despised as though he were evil; if he is evil, he is honored as though he were good.

It is therefore no wonder that we suffer worse things every day, since we ourselves become worse every day. Each day people commit new evils and do not abandon the old ones. Fresh crimes arise, and the ancient ones are not rejected.

### VIII

What ground, then, is there for complaint? However harsh and adverse the things we suffer may be, we suffer less than we deserve. Why do we complain that God deals harshly with us? We deal with God much more harshly. For by our impurities we exasperate him and compel him, against his will, to punish us. [71] Although God’s mind and majesty are of such a nature that he is moved by no passion of anger, nevertheless the exasperation caused in us by our sins is so great [Col. 0078C] that through us he is compelled to become angry. We do violence, so to speak, to his mercy, and in a certain sense lay hands upon his compassion. Although it belongs to his kindness to wish always to spare us, our wickedness compels him to punish the crimes we commit.

And just as those who besiege strongly fortified cities, or attempt to seize and destroy the firmest citadels, attack them from every side, without doubt, with every kind of weapon and engine of war, so we fight to overcome God’s mercy with every monstrous crime, as though with every kind of weapon; and we regard God as injurious to us, although we ourselves are supremely injurious to God. Indeed, every sin of all Christians is an injury to the Godhead. For when we commit what God forbids us to do, we trample upon the commands of the one who forbids it; and by this means we impiously accuse divine severity in our calamities. We ourselves, surely, are the ones who must be accused. For when we commit the things by which we are tormented, we ourselves are the authors of our torments.

Why, then, do we complain about the severity of our punishments? Each of us punishes himself. Therefore that prophetic saying is addressed to us: “Behold, all of you kindle a fire and provide fuel for the flame; walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah L, 2). For the whole human race rushes into eternal punishment in the order described by Scripture. First it kindles a fire; afterward it supplies fuel to the fires; finally it enters the flame it has prepared.

When, then, does a human being first kindle an eternal fire for himself? Clearly, when he first begins to sin. And when does he provide fuel for the fires? When he has heaped sin upon sin. [72] When, finally, will he enter the eternal fire?
