When, through the excess of his growing offenses, he has completed an irreparable sum of every kind of evil, as our Savior says to the rulers of the Jews: “Fill up the measure of your fathers, serpents, offspring of vipers” (Matthew XXIII, 32–33). They were not far from the fullness of sins when the Lord himself told them to complete their sins. Without doubt, therefore, since they were no longer worthy of salvation, they were to fill up the number of their iniquities by which they would perish.

Hence, when the old law recorded that the sins of the Amorites had been completed, it reports that the angels spoke thus to holy Lot: “Bring out of this city all who belong to you. For we shall destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy them” (Genesis XIX, 12–13). That exceedingly criminal people had long been kindling the fire by which it was to perish. And therefore, when its iniquities had been completed, it burned in the flames of its own crimes. It had deserved so ill of God that it suffered even in this world the hell that will exist at the future judgment.

### IX

“But,” someone says, “none of them deserves such an end, because none of them can be compared with their impurities.” Perhaps that is true. Yet what shall we do, when the Savior himself declared that all who despise his Gospel are worse? Thus he says to Capernaum: “If the miracles that have been performed in you had been performed in Sodom, perhaps it would have remained to this day. Nevertheless I tell you: it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you” (Matthew XI, 23–24).

If he says that the Sodomites are less liable to condemnation than all who neglect the Gospel, then there is a most certain reason why we too, who neglect the Gospel in so many ways, ought to fear something worse—especially since we are unwilling to be content with evils that have now become customary and, as it were, familiar. [Note: Codex Colbertinus: “when [they are] easier.”] [73] For the habitual offenses of many are not enough; lawsuits are not enough, nor slanders, nor robberies; drunkenness is not enough, nor revelries; falsehoods are not enough, nor perjuries; adulteries are not enough, nor murders. In the end, all these things are not enough—even though in their most inhuman atrocity they are themselves offenses against human beings—unless they also lay the hands of frenzied minds upon God in blasphemy.

“For,” as it is written concerning the wicked, “they have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has traversed the earth; and they have said: ‘How does God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?’” (Psalm LXXII, 9, 11). And again: “God will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand” (Psalm XCIII, 7).

To such people that prophetic saying may rightly be applied: “The fool has said in his heart: ‘There is no God’” (Psalm LII, 1). For those who assert that nothing is seen by God are close to taking away his very substance from the one whose sight they deny, and to saying that the one whom they claim sees nothing does not exist at all. [Note: I should gladly read *subsistentiam* (“subsistence”). Yet these two words are easily interchanged in old books.] And although no evil deed can in any way subsist by reason, since crimes cannot be joined to reason, nevertheless there is, I think, no deed more irrational or insane.

What could be more frenzied than for someone, while not denying God to be the creator of all things, to deny him to be their governor; and while confessing that he is their maker, to say that he neglects what he has made? As though, indeed, he had taken care to make all things only so that he might neglect what he had made! [Note: Thus Hrabanus, rebuking bishops who oppressed chorepiscopi whom they themselves had ordained, says in his book On Chorepiscopi: “Why, then, is the Holy Spirit invoked by the ordaining bishop to grant sanctification to the person to be ordained, if he himself, the one who invoked and ordained him, immediately after the consecration—which he properly performed—then rebukes him? Does he not mock God, whose gift he asks for, when afterward he despises the very gift?”]

I, however, say that he cares for his creatures to such an extent that I prove he cared for them even before he created them. The thing itself clearly demonstrates this. For he would have made nothing unless he had first had the intention of making it, especially since among the human race there is scarcely anyone so dull that he undertakes and completes something in order not to care for what he has completed.

The man who cultivates a field cultivates it so that he may preserve what he has cultivated. The man who plants a vineyard plants it so that he may guard what he has planted. The man who establishes the beginnings of a flock prepares them so that he may devote care to multiplying the flock. The man who builds a house or lays its foundation, even though he does not yet have a dwelling prepared, already embraces in hope of future habitation the very thing he is still laboring to make.

And why should I speak of human beings in this regard, when even the smallest kinds of animals act entirely out of desire for future things? Ants, storing various kinds of grain in underground hiding places, gather and put away all these things because, out of love for their own life, they cherish what they store. Bees, when they lay the foundations of honey in their combs, [Note: Codex Colbertinus: “of honey.”] or when they gather what is born from flowers—for what reason do they pursue thyme except from zeal and desire for honey, or certain blossoms except from love of their future offspring?

God, then, who has implanted this affection for their own work even in the smallest living creatures, deprived himself alone of love for his creatures—especially since all love of good things in us has descended from his good love? He is the fountain and origin of everything; and because, as it is written, “in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 28), from him we have received every affection by which [Note: By the term *pignora* (“pledges”) Salvian usually understands children, as on pages 110, 172, 188, 199, 209, 212, 252, 254, 260, and 264. Sometimes, however, he uses it for persons dear to us—parents, brothers, and the like—as on page 254.] we love our dear ones.

For the whole world and the entire human race are the pledge of their Creator. And therefore, through this very affection by which he made us love our own dear ones, he wished us to understand how greatly he himself loves his own pledges. For just as, as we read, “his invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” (Romans I, 20), so he wished his love for us to be understood through the love he gave us for our own.

And just as, it is written, he wished every fatherhood in heaven and on earth to be named from him (Ephesians III, 15), so he wished us to recognize in him the affection of a father. And why do I say “of a father”? Rather, it is more than a father’s. The Savior’s saying in the Gospel proves this: “For God so loved this world that he gave his only Son for the life of the world” (John III, 16). The Apostle also says: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all. How will he not also, together with him, give us all things?” (Romans VIII, 32).

### X

This, then, is what I said above: God loves us more than a father loves his son. It is evident that God loves us beyond a father’s affection for his son, since for our sake he did not spare his own Son. And what is more? I add: this was a righteous Son, an only-begotten Son, a Son who is God. What more can be said? He did this for us—that is, for the wicked, the unrighteous, the utterly impious.

Who could estimate God’s love toward us, except that God’s justice is so great that nothing unjust can happen to him? As far as human judgment is concerned, anyone would have acted unjustly if he had caused a good son to be killed for utterly wicked slaves. [Note: Codex Colbertinus: “had caused him simply to be killed.”] But precisely for that reason his compassion is more immeasurable and more astonishing. It is the power of God that the greatness of his justice cannot be understood by human beings, so that, insofar as human weakness is concerned, the greatness of justice almost seems to bear the appearance of injustice.

Therefore the Apostle, showing us to some extent the immensity of divine mercy, says: “Why, when we were still impious, did Christ die for the ungodly at the appointed time? For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person” (Romans V, 6–7). In this one statement he has plainly shown us God’s compassion. For if scarcely anyone accepts death for perfect righteousness, Christ demonstrated how much he accomplished by dying for our unrighteousness.

But why the Lord did this he immediately explains in what follows: “God commends his love toward us. For if, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us, much more, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (Romans V, 8–9). By this very fact, therefore, he commends his love: because he died for the ungodly. For a benefit bestowed upon the undeserving is of greater value.

That is why he says: “God commends his love toward us.” How does he commend it? Clearly, because he bestows it upon those who do not deserve it. If he had bestowed it upon holy and deserving people, he would not seem to have bestowed what he ought not to have bestowed, but what he ought to have repaid.

What, then, do we repay for all these things—or rather, what ought we to repay? First, certainly, what the most blessed prophet testifies that he owes and will render to him, saying: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm CXV, 12–13).

The first repayment, then, is that we return death for death, and that, for the one who died for us, we all die—although our death is worth far less than his. Consequently, even if we accept death, we still do not discharge the debt. Yet because we cannot offer anything greater, we seem to repay the whole if we take care to repay everything we can. [Note: This is the reading of the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius. Codex Corbeiensis has “that we repay by rendering”; Codex Colbertinus, “that we repay by restoring.”]

Thus, as I said, this is the first repayment. [Note: Codex Colbertinus: *redhibitio* (“repayment”).] The second is that, if we do not discharge the debt by death, we discharge it at least by love. For the Savior himself, as the Apostle says, wished by dying for us to commend his love to all, so that he might draw us to return a devotion corresponding to his devotion by the example of such reciprocal love. [Note: Codex Colbertinus: “draw us by the example of his devotion to such a reciprocal devotion.” The word “example” is absent there. Pithoeus followed his own codex and the older editions. We follow Codex Corbeiensis.]

And just as they say that there are wondrous gems of nature which, when brought near iron, suspend even the hardest steel, as though by an affection that breathes from them, so he too—that is, the supreme and most splendid gem of the heavenly kingdoms—wished that, by descending from heaven and drawing near to us, though we were exceedingly hard, he might bring us close to his affection as though by the hands of his love. Thus, recognizing his gifts and benefits, we might understand what it was fitting for us to do for so good a Lord, since he had done so much for evil slaves.

Then what the Apostle says would be fulfilled: that we should be “put to death by his love” all day long, and that neither tribulation, nor distress, nor persecution, nor hunger, nor nakedness, nor the sword could separate us from the love [Note: Thus Codex Corbeiensis. Codex Colbertinus and the editions have “the love of Christ.”] of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans VIII, 36).

### XI

Since it is therefore sufficiently certain that we owe these things to the Lord, let us see what we repay for all of them and what we offer. What, indeed, except precisely all that we mentioned above: whatever is indecent, whatever is unworthy, whatever belongs to an injury against God; wicked actions, shameful habits, drunkenness, revelries, bloody hands, the filth of lust, [Note: Perhaps we should read “raging desires.”] rapacious desires, and whatever the conscience can contain that speech cannot express. For, as the Apostle says, “what they do in secret, it is shameful even to mention” (Ephesians V, 12).

Nor is this all. This is an old matter, belonging equally to the present and former times. More grievous and mournful is the fact that we add new sins to old ones—not merely new ones, but certain pagan and monstrous practices never before seen in the churches of God. We utter profane words against God and blaspheme him insultingly, calling him unconcerned, inattentive, negligent, and not governing things; and consequently calling him also merciless, ungenerous, inhuman, harsh, and severe.

For when someone is said to be one who does not look upon things, unconcerned and negligent, what remains except that he should also be called harsh, severe, and inhuman? O blind shamelessness! O sacrilegious audacity! It is not enough for us, entangled in countless sins and guilty before God in all things, that we should also become God’s accusers. And what hope, I ask, can there be for a person who accuses the very judge by whom he is to be judged?

### XII

“If, then,” they say, “God looks upon human affairs; if he cares for them, loves them, and governs them, why does he allow us to be weaker and more wretched than all the nations? Why does he permit us to be defeated by barbarians? Why does he allow us to be subjected to the authority of our enemies?”

To put it very briefly, as I said earlier, he allows us to endure these evils because we deserve to endure them. Let us look at the disgraceful acts, the shameful deeds, and those crimes of the Roman populace that we mentioned above, [Note: That is, of the Roman people, as he will say below on page 80, and of the Roman name on page 82.] and we shall understand whether we can deserve protection while living in such impurity.

Since, then, many say on this ground that God does not look upon human affairs—that we are wretched and weak—what do we deserve? If, while we lived in such vices and such wickedness, he allowed us to be powerful, flourishing, and happy, there might perhaps be some suspicion that the God who allowed such evil and ruined people to be happy did not look upon the crimes of the Romans.

But since he commands people so vicious and wicked to be weak and most wretched, it is perfectly clear both that God sees us and that he judges us, because we suffer what we deserve. Yet we certainly do not think that we deserve it; and this is why we are more guilty and criminal still, because we do not acknowledge what we deserve.

For the arrogant usurpation of innocence is the greatest accuser of guilty human beings. Among many people guilty of the same crimes, none is more criminal than the person who thinks himself not criminal. Thus we can add this alone to our evils: that we judge ourselves innocent. [79] “But granted,” says some sinful and [Note: Corbeiensis: “most wicked.”] malicious person, “what cannot be denied is that we are better than the barbarians. And it is obvious from this very fact that God does not look upon human affairs: although we are better, we are subjected to worse people.”

Whether we are better than the barbarians we shall now see. Certainly, what is beyond doubt is that we ought to be better. And by this very fact we are worse if we are not better, since we ought to be better. For guilt is more criminal where the condition is more honorable.

[Note: Juvenal:

“Every fault of the mind bears in itself a more conspicuous crime  
in proportion as the person who sins is held in greater honor.”]

If the person who sins is more honored, the sin too is more blameworthy. Theft is an evil deed in every person; but without doubt it is more condemnable when a senator steals than when a lowly person does so. Fornication is forbidden to everyone; but it is much graver when someone from the clergy fornicates than when someone from the common people does so. [Note: Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, writes the following, among other things, in his Enchiridion of the Christian Life—which is usually published together with the canons of the provincial council held by that same archbishop in 1536—under the heading “On the Sacrament of Penance”: “The offense becomes more serious because of the person. A priest or prince sins more gravely than a layman or private person. Jokes in the mouth of a layman, as Jerome says, are jokes; in the mouth of a priest, blasphemy.” One may also add the notable passage from the eighty-fourth letter of St Leo: “For the election of priests is so exalted that actions which in other members of the Church are not considered blameworthy are nevertheless held unlawful in them.” See St Gregory, Book VII, Indiction 2, Letter 117.]

So we, who are called Christians and Catholics, if we do anything resembling the impurities of the barbarians, commit a graver error. We sin more atrociously under the profession of a holy name. Where the privilege is higher, the guilt is greater. The very religion that we profess accuses our errors.

The unchastity of one who has promised chastity is more criminal. [Note: Codex Colbertinus and the older editions: “He who is drunk is more disgraceful while displaying sobriety on his face.”] A person who becomes drunk while professing sobriety is more shamefully drunk. Nothing is more disgraceful for a philosopher than to pursue obscene vices, because, in addition to the deformity that vices possess in themselves, he is further marked by the name of wisdom. [Note: The same codex and the older editions: “the name.”]

We, therefore, have professed Christian philosophy before the whole human race, and consequently we must necessarily be believed and regarded as worse than all nations, because we live under the name of so great a profession and sin while placed within religion.

### XIII

But I know that many find it intolerable if we are said to be worse than the barbarians. And what shall we do, when this contributes nothing to our case, even if it seems intolerable to us? Indeed, it aggravates our case all the more if we are worse and believe ourselves better.

“For,” says the Apostle, “if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. Let each person examine his own work” (Galatians VI, 3–4). We ought therefore to trust our work, not our opinion; reason, not desire; truth, not will.

Since, then, some consider it unbearable that we should be judged worse than the barbarians—or not even much better than they—let us see either how we are better, or which barbarians we mean. For among every people there are two classes of barbarians: heretics or pagans. [Note: Salvianus refers to this passage below, at the beginning of Book V, page 93: “Since we have already mentioned above two classes or sects of barbarians, pagans and heretics,” and so forth. These were the names of the barbarians who at that time exercised power throughout the Roman world: Franks, Saxons, Moors, Scythians, Alans, Huns, Goths, and Vandals. The Franks, Saxons, Moors, Scythians, Alans, and Huns were pagans, as Salvianus will say on page 86; the others were Christians, but heretics, imbued with Arian perfidy. Salvianus himself excludes them from the number of pagans on page 96, where, listing the barbarians who were Christians but heretics, he says: “All those of whom we speak are either Vandals or Goths.”]

To all of these, then, insofar as divine law is concerned, I say that we are incomparably better; but insofar as life and conduct are concerned, I grieve and lament that we are worse. Although, as we have already said, I do not mean this absolutely of the entire Roman people. [Note: That is, of those peoples subject at that time to the Roman Empire, whether within Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, or the other provinces of the Roman Empire. For the expression “Roman people” should not be restricted in Salvianus to the city called Rome, since the whole world had been granted the right of Roman citizenship. At that time, as Pliny says in Book III, chapter 5, “one homeland of all nations was made throughout the entire world.” Thus Rutilius Namatianus elegantly writes:

“You made one homeland for peoples of diverse origin;  
under your rule, it profited the unconquered to be conquered.”

Nor should Lacerda be heeded, who in Book I, chapter 1 of his Sacred Adversaria, thinks that the Roman name in Salvianus means the name of a religion rather than of a people, and that Catholics were formerly called Romans in order to distinguish them by that designation from heretics. For Salvianus himself says on page 96 that there was an innumerable multitude of Roman heretics, as we have just noted; and the matter itself plainly shows that when Salvianus speaks of Romans he means those who had not yet thrown off the yoke of the Roman Empire.]

For first I except all the religious, [Note: That is, clerics, monks, and all who professed a stricter way of life, whom he immediately contrasts with secular people, as a class of human beings removed from the folly of the world. He uses the same distinction below on page 108: “And this, evidently, belongs only to laymen, not also to certain clerics; only to secular people, not to many religious.” And on page 268: “For a new madness has seized both secular people and even some who profess religion.” Likewise on page 282: “That is harder and more troublesome: that certain of your sons, as I think, under the title of religion dissent from religion, and have abandoned the world more in dress than in understanding.” Jerome writes in his letter to Nepotian on the life of clerics: “There are some monks richer than they were when they were secular.” And in the Epitaph for Nepotian to Heliodorus: “Let monks be richer than they were when secular.” Those whom Salvianus here sets against secular people under the name “religious” are called “holy” by him on page 229: “But someone may perhaps say that the holy are not indeed without debts, but that the debts of secular people are much greater, since they have more sins.” Salvianus himself teaches us that by the designation “holy” he includes monks, on page 188: “Thus, therefore, the hatred of the Africans is proved even toward monks, that is, toward the holy of God.”]

then also some secular people who are equal to the religious, or, if that is too great a claim, at least similar to the religious in the uprightness of their actions; but all the rest, or nearly all, are more guilty than the barbarians. To be worse, then, is to be more guilty. Since some regard it as irrational and absurd that we should be judged either worse than the barbarians or not much better than they, let us see, as I said, either how we are better or which barbarians we mean.

For, apart from only those Romans whom I mentioned shortly before, I say that all the rest, or nearly all, have a greater guilt and a more criminal life than the barbarians. You may be angry, reader, at these statements, and condemn what you are reading besides. I do not shrink from your judgment. Condemn me if I am lying; condemn me if I do not prove it; condemn me if I do not show that what I assert has also been said by the sacred Scriptures.

We, therefore, who judge ourselves much better than all the nations in the world—and I myself, who call the Romans worse in many respects—do not deny that they are better in certain respects. In life and sins, as I said, we are worse; but in Catholic law we are incomparably better.

But this must be considered: the fact that the law is good does not belong to us; the fact that we live badly does belong to us. It does us no good that the law is good if our life and conduct are not good. The good law is Christ’s gift; the bad life is our crime. Indeed, we are more blameworthy if we honor a good law while being bad observers of it. Rather, if we are bad, we are not observers at all, for a bad observer cannot be called an observer. No one observes a holy matter if he does not observe it in a holy way; and consequently the very law that we profess is our accuser.

### XIV

Once, then, the privilege of the law has been set aside—a privilege that either does not help us at all or even condemns us by a just judgment—let us compare the life, pursuits, habits, and vices of the barbarians and of our own people.

The barbarians are unjust, and so are we. The barbarians are greedy, and so are we. The barbarians are faithless, and so are we. The barbarians are covetous, and so are we. The barbarians are unchaste, and so are we. In short, the barbarians are full of every kind of wickedness and impurity, and so are we.

[Note: We have restored the older reading, found in the ancient editions and Codex Colbertinus. Codex Corbeiensis reads: “But someone might perhaps be able to answer.”]

“But if,” someone might reply, “we are equal to the barbarians in vice, why are we not also equal to them in strength? Since our wickedness and guilt are alike, either we ought to be as strong as they are, or they ought to be as weak as we are.”

That is true, and therefore it follows that those who are weaker are more guilty. How do we prove this? Clearly because, as we said above, we have shown that God does everything by judgment. For if, as it is written, “in every place the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked” (Proverbs XV, 3), and, according to the Apostle, “the judgment of God is according to truth upon all who do evil” (Romans II, 2), we see that we, who do not cease to do evil, suffer the punishments of our wickedness by the judgment of the just God.

“But,” you say, “the barbarians commit the same evils, and yet they are not as wretched as we are.” This, then, is the difference: although the barbarians do the same things we do, we sin with greater offense. Our vices and those of the barbarians may be equal; yet in these vices our sins must be more serious.

For since, as we have already said, all barbarians are either pagans or heretics, I shall speak first of the pagans, because their error is prior. The Saxon people is savage, the Frank faithless, the Gepid inhuman, the Hun unchaste; [Note: Thus consistently in Codex Corbeiensis. It is also read in this way in other authors. The letter c was subsequently removed, just as in Ludovicus, Lotharius, Childericus, and others. Pithoeus’s edition always has “Huns.”] in short, the life of all the barbarian peoples is vicious. [Note: Codex Colbertinus and the older editions: “one single vice.”]

But do their vices involve the same guilt as ours? Is the unchastity of the Huns as criminal as ours? Is the perfidy of the Franks as blameworthy as ours? Is the drunkenness of the Alans as reprehensible as the drunkenness of a Christian? Is the rapacity of an Alan as condemnable as the rapacity of a Christian?

If a Hun deceives or a Gepid, what is surprising? He has no knowledge at all of the fault of falsehood. If a Frank commits perjury, what new thing will he do, when he thinks perjury itself to be a kind of speech rather than a crime? [Note: Below on this page: “Is the perfidy of the Franks as blameworthy as ours?” And shortly afterward: “If a Frank commits perjury, what new thing will he do, when he thinks perjury itself to be a kind of speech rather than a crime?” Flavius Vopiscus says of Proculus: “The Franks themselves admit that it is their custom to break faith while laughing.” See Rittershusius.]

And what is surprising if barbarians believe this, since they do not know the law or God, when most of the Roman people thinks the same way, although it knows that it sins? Not to speak of any other class of people, let us consider only the crowds of merchants and of all those who deal in silk, [Note: Rittershusius advises reading “of silk merchants.” Jerome calls them “dealers in silk garments” in Book I Against Jovinianus. See Sidonius, Book I, Letter 8, and Savaron and Sirmondus in that passage.] who have occupied nearly the greater part of all the cities.

Is the life of all these people anything other than the practice of deceit and the threshing-floor of falsehood? Or do they not regard words as utterly perishable when those words benefit no one who speaks them? Such is the honor paid to God among them—even though he forbids oaths—that they consider perjury the distinctive gain in everything.

What, then, is surprising if barbarians deceive, when they do not know that falsehood is a crime? They do nothing out of contempt for heavenly commands, because they do not know the Lord’s commands; for one who is ignorant of the law does not do something against the law.

Our guilt, therefore, is particularly ours: we read the divine law and constantly violate its legal writings; we say that we know God and trample upon his commands and precepts. And thus, because we despise the one whom we believe and proclaim that we worship, the very thing that appears to be the worship of God is an injury to him.

### XV

Finally, to say nothing of other sins, is there any secular person at all, apart from a few, who does not always keep the name of Christ on his lips for the purpose of perjuring himself? Hence this is almost universally used, among both the noble and the lowly, as an oath:

“By Christ, that I do this”; “By Christ, that I do that”; “By Christ, that I shall say nothing else”; “By Christ, that I shall do nothing else.”

And why say more? Matters have been brought to such a point that, as we previously said concerning the pagan barbarians,

[Note: That is, the Franks, as was shown on the following page.]

the name of Christ no longer seems to be an oath but merely an expression. For among very many people this name is held in such little regard that they never think less about doing something than when they swear by Christ that they will do it.

[Note: We have here faithfully reproduced the reading of the Corbie manuscript. In other editions these words are not properly arranged.]

[Note: A remarkable artifice for deceiving. Thus, in Tacitus, *Annals* II, Domitius Celer said: “No one mourns the death of Germanicus more ostentatiously than those who rejoice most.” Famianus Strada imitated this in Book I of *The Belgian War*: “No one binds his good faith more ostentatiously than those who violate it most.”]

And although it is written, “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7), reverence for Christ has fallen to such a level that, among all the vanities of the world, scarcely anything now seems vainer than the name of Christ.

Finally, many people swear by the name of Christ that they will do not merely idle and foolish things, but even certain crimes. Such is the way these people speak: “By Christ, because I am taking that thing”; “By Christ, because I am beating him”; “By Christ, because I am killing him.” Matters have come to this: when they have sworn by the name of Christ, they think that they will commit even crimes religiously.

Finally, I shall tell what happened to me personally. Some time ago, moved by the entreaty of a poor man, I pleaded with a certain very powerful person, begging him not to take away the property and possessions of a wretched and needy man, and not to remove the support and alms on which his poverty depended. But that man, who had been ravenously thirsting for the other’s possessions and had already devoured the prey in imagination through his burning hope and desire,

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “most sharply.”]

looked at me and darted fierce eyes into my face, as though he thought that whatever he himself had not taken from another was being taken from him by me. He replied that he could by no means do what I was asking—as though he were doing something by command or sacred written ordinance that he could not possibly disregard.

When I asked the reason why this could not be done, he declared that it was a most compelling necessity, one that could not possibly be opposed.

[Note: The words “by Christ,” absent from the other editions, have been added from the Corbie manuscript. Entirely correctly. Observe this, reader; you will approve.]

“I swore,” he said, “by Christ that his possessions must be taken away by me.”

[Note: The words “by Christ,” absent from the other editions, have been added from the Corbie manuscript. Entirely correctly. Observe this, reader; you will approve.]

“See, then, whether I can or ought not to carry out what I said, even with Christ’s name invoked, that I would do.”

[Note: “What he himself had not at some time taken away” is found in the same manuscript and in Galesinius’s edition.]

Then I—what more could I do, when such a just and sacred pretext was being placed before me?—having heard the rationale of this most religious crime, departed.

### XVI

Now I ask all who are of sound mind: who would ever have believed that human greed’s boldness could advance to such an insult against God that people would say they would do, for the sake of Christ’s name, the very thing by which they injure Christ?

O immeasurable and monstrous crime! What will depraved minds not dare? They arm themselves for robbery in the name of Christ; they make God, in a sense, the author of their crime. And although Christ is the forbidding one and avenger of all evils, they say that they are committing, for Christ, the crime they are committing.

Yet we complain about the iniquity of our enemies and accuse barbarian paganism of perjury! How much less serious was their sin when they swore falsely by demons than ours when we swear falsely by Christ! How much less criminal it is to mock the name of Jupiter than that of Christ! In the one case, the person by whom they swear is dead; in the other, it is the living God whom they make the object of perjury. In the one case there is no human being; here there is the supreme God.

Since here the violation of the most solemn oath is involved, the perjury must necessarily be the gravest crime; whereas there, since there is almost no oath, it follows that there is no perjury. For since there is no God by whom they swear, there is no perjury when they swear falsely.

Finally, whoever wishes to know how true this is should hear the blessed Apostle Paul proclaiming these very things that we are saying. For he says: “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” (Romans 3:19). And again: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15).

By these two statements he clearly distinguished the two classes of the human race: those placed outside the law and those living under the law. Who, then, are now placed under the law? Who but Christians, just as the Apostle himself was, who says of himself: “I am not without the law of God, but am under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21).

Who, then, are without the law of Christ? Who but pagan people, who do not know the Lord’s law? And therefore he says of them: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression.”

[Note: So reads the Corbie manuscript. The Colbert manuscript and the editions have: “By which statement.”]

By this one statement he plainly shows that only Christians, when they sin, are transgressors of the law, while pagans who do not know the law sin without transgression, because no one can be a transgressor of something he does not know.

We alone, therefore, are transgressors of the divine law, who, as it is written, “read the law and do not practice it” (Romans 2:21ff.). And thus our knowledge is nothing other than guilt: we know the law only so that we may sin with greater offense, because what we know through reading and in our hearts we trample underfoot through lust and contempt.

And therefore that apostolic statement is most rightly addressed to every Christian: “You who boast in the law dishonor God through transgression of the law. For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Romans 2:23–24).

From this alone one can understand what crime Christians are guilty of: they defame the name of God. And although it is written for us that we should do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31), we, on the contrary, do everything as an injury to God.

And although our Savior himself cries out to us every day, “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16), we live in such a contrary manner that people see our evil works and blaspheme our Father who is in heaven.

### XVII

Since these things are so, we can indeed flatter ourselves greatly with the distinction of the Christian name: we act and live in such a way that the very fact that we are called a Christian people seems to be an insult to Christ.

But, by contrast, what comparable thing is there among the pagans to the things we have described?

Can one say of the Huns: “Look at what those who are called Christians are like”? Can one say of the Saxons or Franks: “Look at what those who claim to be worshipers of Christ do”? Is the sacred law blamed because of the savage customs of the Moors? Do the utterly inhuman practices of the Scythians or Gepids bring the name of the Lord and Savior into cursing and blasphemy?

Can any of these peoples be addressed in this way: “Where is the catholic law that they believe? Where are the commandments of piety and chastity that they learn? They read the Gospels, and they are immoral; they hear the apostles, and they get drunk; they follow Christ, and they rob; they lead a wicked life, and they claim to possess a good law”?

Can these things be said of any of those nations? Certainly not.

All these things are said of us. In us Christ suffers reproach; in us the Christian law suffers cursing. For what we said above is said of us: “Look at what those who worship Christ are like.”

It is plainly false that they say they are learning good things, or boast that they retain the commandments of the sacred law. For if they were learning good things, they would be good. Such, surely, is the sect as are its adherents. Without doubt they are what they are taught.

Thus it appears that the prophets whom they possess teach impurity, that the apostles whom they read have sanctioned crimes, and that the Gospels with which they are instructed proclaim the very things they themselves do. Finally, Christians would do holy things if Christ had taught holy things.

The one who is worshiped can therefore be judged by his worshipers. For how can he be a good teacher when we see that his disciples are so bad?

[Note: Tacitus, speaking of Christians: “Christ, the originator of the name, had been executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.”]

For Christians are from him; they hear him and read him.

[Note: These words are absent from the Colbert manuscript and from the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius.]

It is easy for everyone to understand Christ’s teaching. Look at what Christians do, and you can clearly learn about Christ what he teaches.

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and Pithoeus’s edition read “from Christ himself.” Wrongly, in my opinion. One or the other of these two words is sufficient. The Colbert manuscript has *Christo* but not *ipso*. Conversely, the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius have *ipso* but not *Christo*.]

Finally, how perversely and wickedly pagans have always thought about the Lord’s sacred rites is shown by the bloodiest interrogations of savage persecutors, who believed that nothing was done in Christian sacrifices except certain impure and abominable things.

Indeed, they thought that the very beginnings of our religion arose from two great crimes: first, murder; then, what is more serious than murder, incest. They believed that it arose not merely from murder and incest, but—something even more criminal—from incest itself and murder: incest with sacred mothers and the murder of innocent little children, whom they thought Christians not only killed but, what was more abhorrent, also devoured.

And all this, they supposed, was done to appease God, as though he could be offended by any crime more greatly; to cleanse an offense, as though any other offense could be greater; to commend a sacrifice, as though the Lord could abhor anything more; and to earn eternal life, as though, even if it could be obtained through such things, it would be worth reaching it through crimes so monstrous.

### XVIII

We can therefore understand either what kind of Christians the pagans believed Christians to be, if they worshiped God with such sacrifices, or what sort of god they supposed the one who had taught these rites to be.

And why was this so? Why, unless because of those who are called Christians but are not Christians, who by their crimes and disgraceful behavior defame the name of religion; who, as it is written, “profess to know God with their words but deny him by their deeds,” being “detestable and disobedient, unfit for every good work” (Titus 1:16); through whom, as we read, “the way of truth is blasphemed” (2 Peter 2:2), and the most sacred name of the Lord God is violated by the curses of sacrilegious people.

How grave and singular an evil it is to hand over the name of the Divinity to the blasphemy of the nations, we are also taught by the example of the blessed David. Although, supported by his righteous deeds, he deserved to escape eternal punishment for his offenses through a single confession, he could not obtain forgiveness for this crime even with the advocacy of repentance.

For when the prophet Nathan had said to him, as he confessed his sins, “God has taken away your sin; you shall not die,” he immediately added: “Nevertheless, because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme on account of this matter, the son who has been born to you shall die” (2 Samuel 12:13–14).

And what happened afterward? After laying aside his diadem, casting off his jewels, stripping away his purple garments,

[Note: The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius read: “When every royal dignity of splendor had been removed.” Pithoeus reads: “When every dignity of royal splendor had been removed.”]

and removing all the splendor of royal dignity, he became solitary, groaning, shut away, roughened by sackcloth, wet with tears, and soiled with ashes. He sought the life of his little child with all the resources of such lamentation and besought the most merciful God with such an abundance of prayers. Yet he could not obtain what he asked and implored in this manner, although—what is the strongest aid for those who ask—he believed that he would obtain what he was asking God for in this way.

From this it can be understood that no crime is entirely a greater offense than giving the nations cause to blaspheme. Whoever commits a serious error without causing others to blaspheme brings condemnation only upon himself. But whoever causes others to blaspheme plunges many with himself into death, and must be guilty for as many people as he has drawn with himself into guilt.

Moreover, any sinner who sins in such a way that he does not cause others to blaspheme through his sin harms only himself by the fact that he has sinned; he does not injure the most sacred name of God through the sacrilegious curses of blasphemers.

But whoever, by sinning, causes others to blaspheme must necessarily make his sin exceed the measure of human crimes, because through the insults of many he inflicts an immeasurable injury upon God.

### XIX

This evil, as I said, belongs peculiarly and exclusively to Christians, because God is blasphemed only through those who learn good things and do evil; who, as it is written, “confess God with their words and deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16); who, as the same Apostle says, “approve the law and know his will, and discern the things that are more excellent”; who possess “the form of knowledge and truth in the law”; who preach, “Do not steal,” and steal; who read, “Do not commit adultery,” and commit adultery; who boast in the law and, through transgression of the law, dishonor God (Romans 2:17ff.).

And for this very reason Christians are worse, because they ought to be better. They do not prove by their conduct what they profess, and by their behavior they attack their own profession. For wickedness is more condemnable when it is accused by the title of goodness, and the pious name becomes the guilt of the impious.

Hence the Savior says in the Apocalypse to the lukewarm Christian: “Would that you were either hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16).

The Lord commands every Christian to be fervent in faith and spirit. Thus it is written: “Be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord” (Romans 12:11). In this fervor of spirit the ardor of religious faith is displayed. Whoever possesses much of that ardor is recognized as a fervent believer; whoever possesses none at all is understood to be cold and pagan; but whoever is between the two, or is neither one nor the other, is a lukewarm Christian and hateful to the Lord.

Therefore he is told: “Would that you were either hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth.” That is to say: “Would that you either possessed the warmth and faith of good Christians, or at least the coldness and ignorance of pagans! Either a warm faith would commend you to God, or, for the present, your ignorance of the law would offer you some excuse.”

But now, because you have already acknowledged Christ and neglect the one whom you have acknowledged, although you were received as if within the mouth of God through recognition of the faith, you will be cast out through lukewarmness.

The blessed Apostle Peter also clearly explained this, speaking of vicious and lukewarm people—that is, Christians who live badly: “It would have been better for them not to have known the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back from the commandment delivered to them. What has happened to them is in accord with the truth of the proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud’” (2 Peter 2:21–22).

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “of filth.”]

To make it clear that this was spoken about those who live in the filth and impurities of the world under the Christian name, hear what he says about the same people in the same passage: “For if, after escaping the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, their last state has become worse for them than the first” (2 Peter 2:20).

The blessed Apostle Paul says the same thing in a similar manner: “Circumcision indeed profits you, if you observe the law. But if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Romans 2:25).

He himself most clearly teaches that circumcision is to be understood as Christianity, saying: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit and do not put confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3).

Thus we see that he compares bad Christians with pagans; indeed, he not only compares them but almost places them beneath pagans, saying: “If the uncircumcised person keeps the ordinances of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And the uncircumcised person who fulfills the law will judge you, who, with the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law” (Romans 2:26–27).

And thus we understand, as I said above, that we are far more culpable: we possess God’s law and despise it, whereas they possess and know neither the law nor God’s commandments. No one despises what he does not know.

“For I would not have known desire,” the Apostle says, “unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Romans 7:7). Nor can those who do not possess the law transgress the law, because, as it is written, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15).

And so, if they do not transgress the law they do not possess, they do not despise the ordinances of the law they do not possess; for, as I have said, no one can disregard what he does not know.

We, therefore, are both despisers and transgressors; and thus we are worse than pagans, because they do not know God’s commandments, while we know them; they do not possess them, while we possess them; they do not do what they have not heard, while we trample upon what we have read.

Therefore, among them there is ignorance, while among us there is transgression, because it is a lesser crime to be ignorant of the law than to despise it.

## BOOK FIVE

### I

I know that the most unbelieving people, and those incapable of divine truth, can object to what we have said as follows: if the guilt of unbelieving Christians is so great that they sin more by neglecting the Lord’s commandments, which they know, than pagan peoples who do not know them, then ignorance was more beneficial for them than knowledge, and the fact that they recognized the truth actually works against them.

To them the answer must be that it is not the truth that harms them, but their vices; not the law that harms them, but their conduct.

[Note: The same manuscript and the old editions read: “Finally, good conduct.”]

Grant good conduct, and the ordinances of the law are on our side. Remove the vices, and the law is beneficial.

“For we know,” says the Apostle, “that the law is good, if someone uses it lawfully” (1 Timothy 1:8). Use the law lawfully, then, and you yourself will have made the law good for you.

“For we know,” he says, “that the law is good, if someone uses it lawfully,” knowing this: “that the law is not laid down for the righteous” (ibid., 8–9).

Therefore begin to be righteous, and you will be free from the law, because a law that is already embodied in one’s conduct cannot come into conflict with one’s conduct.

“For we know,” he says, “that the law is good, if someone uses it lawfully,” knowing this: “that the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous, for the disobedient, for the wicked and impious, for sinners, and for whatever else is contrary to sound doctrine” (ibid., 8–10).

Thus it is not so much that the law is opposed to you, O man, as that you are opposed to the law. The law does not act against you by giving good commands; you act against the law by living badly.

Indeed, the law is for you, while you are against it. It counsels you by speaking holy things, while you oppose it by doing evil things; and you act not only against it but also against yourself. For by acting against it you act against yourself, because your salvation and life are in it. Thus, while you abandon the divine law, you abandon your own salvation.

We complain about the Lord’s law in no other way than an impatient sick person is accustomed to complain about an excellent physician: having made his diseases worse through his own fault, he accuses the physician of incompetence.

As though any instructions could cure an illness if the sick person did not obey them; or as though the observance prescribed by the physician could heal anyone if the sick person himself did not practice it.

What good is wormwood for the stomach if sweets immediately follow?

[Note: We have corrected this passage on our own authority, although both editions and manuscripts oppose us. Everywhere they consistently read: “What good is abstinence for the stomach, if …” But this error entered through the fault of copyists. Salvian intended to set wormwood against sweets, just as silence against shouting and an antidote against poison. Salvian himself confirms our conjecture on page 137: “For just as the best and most skilled physicians provide different treatments for different illnesses, and help some by sweet medicines and others by bitter ones.” From this we may meanwhile conclude that the very learned Nicolas Rigault made a most accurate observation when he noted in his preface to Tertullian that even the authority of ancient books is used to support utterly false readings. “For,” he says, “there are ancient books corrected in the most corrupt manner; nor is there any hope of recovering the truth unless we find books so ancient that they are older than all the antiquity of the correctors.”]

What benefit is there in the silence of those standing around a delirious person, when his own shouting is killing him? Or what good can an antidote do when poison is poured over it?

For us, then, the law is an antidote, but vice is poison. The antidote of the law cannot heal us, when the poisons of our vices are killing us.

But we have already said enough about these matters; and if circumstances require it, with God’s help we shall say something more after this.

### II

Meanwhile, since we mentioned above that there are two kinds or groups of barbarians—pagans and heretics—and since, as I think, we have now sufficiently dealt with the pagans, let us also address the heretics, as the matter requires.

Someone might say: Even if the divine law does not demand of pagans that they do the commandments they do not know, surely it demands this of heretics, who do know them. For they read the same things that we read; they have the same prophets of God, the same apostles, and the same evangelists. Therefore either they neglect the law no less than we do, or even much more, since, although they read the same writings as our people, they do many things worse than our people.

Let us examine both points.

“They read the same things that we read,” you say. How can they be the same things when they were badly interpolated and badly transmitted long ago by bad authors?

[Note: Pithoeus’s edition has *auditoribus* (“hearers”). Rittershusius disliked this and judged that *auctoribus* (“authors”) should be read. Since the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius, as well as the Corbie manuscript, have the reading preferred by Rittershusius, it seemed that it should be retained in this edition.]

And thus they are no longer the same, because things that have been corrupted in some part cannot properly be called the very same things. For things that have lost their fullness do not possess wholeness, nor do things deprived of the power of their sacred mysteries preserve their original condition in every respect.

We alone, therefore, possess the sacred Scriptures in full, inviolate, and complete form: we drink them either from their own source or, at least, draw them from the purest source through the ministry of an uncorrupted translation.

[Note: He is speaking about the various editions of the sacred Scriptures that were then in use. He says that Catholics possess the sacred Scriptures in full, inviolate, and complete form, while heretics have them interpolated, badly transmitted, torn apart, weakened, wounded, and corrupted by the tradition of ancient teachers.]

We alone read them correctly. And would that we fulfilled them as well as we read them! But I fear that those who do not observe them correctly do not even read them correctly, because it is a lesser guilt not to read holy things than to violate what has been read.

Other peoples either do not possess the law of God or possess it weakened and wounded. Thus, as we have said, they do not possess what they possess in this condition.

For even if there are some among the barbarian nations who appear to have the sacred Scripture less interpolated or mutilated in their books, they nevertheless possess it corrupted by the tradition of ancient teachers,

[Note: Rittershusius thought Pithoeus’s edition corrupt, because it has *traditionem* (“tradition”) here. He therefore believed that *traditione* (“by tradition”) should be read. The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius also prefer *traditionem*. We have followed the authority of the Corbie manuscript and Rittershusius’s conjecture and written *traditione*. Shortly afterward Pithoeus reads *aut per hoc* (“or because of this”), although the sense requires *ac per hoc* (“and because of this”), and the other editions and the Corbie manuscript agree in this reading.]

and therefore possess tradition rather than Scripture, because they retain not what the truth of the law teaches but what the depravity of an evil tradition has inserted.

For barbarian people, strangers to Roman—or rather, human—learning, know absolutely nothing except what they hear from their teachers; whatever they hear, that they follow.

[Note: Salvian appears to think that every Christian must be thoroughly instructed in the mysteries of his faith and must not rest in the faith of his priest. In ancient times even women were encouraged to study sacred literature. Jerome bears witness to this: in his letter to Gaudentius he wants a girl to know by heart the Psalms, the books of Solomon, the Gospels, the Apostles, and the Prophets. He praises Marcella in her epitaph because her ardor for the divine Scriptures was extraordinary, and in writing to Demetrias he urges her to determine how many hours she should devote to memorizing the sacred Scripture and how much time to reading it—not as a burden, but for the pleasure and instruction of the soul. Victor of Vita, at the beginning of Book V of *The Vandal Persecution*, likewise mentions a certain Dionysia who was fully versed in the divine Scriptures. Finally, Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, writing to his mother Sigrada, who had withdrawn into a monastery, consoles her partly by saying that, in place of the loss of worldly things, she possessed the divine sacred Scripture. Such was the simplicity and confidence of ancient times.]

And so those who are ignorant of all literature and knowledge, and know the mystery of the divine law through instruction rather than reading, must necessarily retain instruction rather than the law.

Thus the tradition and long-established teaching of their teachers is, as it were, a law for them, because they know only what they are taught.

They are therefore heretics, but unknowingly. Indeed, among us they are heretics; among themselves they are not. For they judge themselves so thoroughly catholic that they stigmatize us with the designation “heretic.”

What they are to us, therefore, we are to them. We are certain that they do injury to the divine generation because they say that the Son is less than the Father. They consider us injurious to the Father because we believe that the Son is equal to him.

The truth is with us, but they presume that it is with them. The honor of God is with us, but they think that what they believe is the honor of the divine nature. They fail in their duty, but for them this is the highest religious duty. They are impious, but they think this is true piety.

They are therefore in error, but they err with good intentions—not out of hatred, but out of devotion to God, believing that they honor and love the Lord. Although they do not possess the correct faith, they nevertheless consider this to be perfect love of God.

[Note: See the *Italian Literary Journal*, volume 24, pages 17ff., on this passage.]

How they will be punished on the day of judgment for this very error of false opinion, no one can know except the Judge.

Meanwhile, for this reason, as I think, God grants them patience: he sees that, although they do not believe correctly, they err with the devotion of a pious opinion. This is especially so because he knows that they do what they do not know, while our people neglect what they believe.

Thus the former sin through the fault of their teachers, while our people sin through their own fault; the former are ignorant, while our people are knowledgeable; the former do what they think is right, while our people do what they know to be wrong.

And therefore, by a just judgment, God’s patience supports them, while he chastises us with punishment, because ignorance can to some extent be forgiven, but contempt does not deserve pardon.

For it is written: “The servant who does not know his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with few blows. But the one who knows it and does not do it shall be beaten with many” (Luke 12:47–48).

### III

Let us not, then, be surprised that we are beaten with many blows, because we sin not through ignorance but through rebellion. We know good things, yet do not do them well; we understand the distinction between right and wrong, yet pursue what is wrong; we read the law, yet trample its ordinances.

We know the commands of the sacred law only for this purpose: that, after being forbidden, we may sin more gravely. We say that we worship God, yet obey the devil.

And after all this we want to receive good things from God, while we always add evil to evil. We desire God’s will to be done for us, while we do not wish to do his will.

We behave as though we were superior to God. We want God continually to submit to our will, while all of us continually oppose his will.

But he is just, although we are unjust. He chastises those whom he thinks should be chastised; he endures those whom he thinks should be endured.

He wills that both things contribute to one purpose: that chastisement restrain the desire to sin among Catholics, and that, at some time, God’s patience cause heretics to recognize the full truth of the faith—especially since he knows that perhaps those whom he sees surpassing Catholics in conduct are not unworthy of the catholic faith.

All those about whom we are speaking are either Vandals or Goths. For we say nothing about the Roman heretics, whose number is immense, nor do we compare them either with Romans or with barbarians, because they are worse than Romans in unbelief and more disgraceful than barbarians in the foulness of their lives.

But this does not help us at all; rather, it increases the burden under which we are already weighed down by our own people, because those whom we complain of as being such are also Romans.

From this we can understand what the entire Roman state deserves, since one part of the Romans offends God by its life, while another offends him by both its unbelief and its life.

Not to mention the fact that even the former heresies of the barbarians flowed from the perversity of Roman instruction, and consequently this too is our crime: that the peoples of the barbarians began to be heretics.

[Note: Isidore testifies in his *Chronicle* concerning the Goths that they became Arians in gratitude to the emperor Valens: “The Goths, divided at the Ister under two kings, Fridigern and Athalaric, were split into two groups. Fridigern, with the aid of the Arian emperor Valens, overcame Athalaric; and, persuaded by the same emperor in gratitude for this favor, he became an Arian from a Catholic, and then the entire Gothic people followed his error.”]

### IV

Furthermore, as regards the manner of life of the Goths or Vandals, what is there in which we can either place ourselves above them or even compare ourselves with them? First, then, to speak of affection and love—which the Lord teaches is the chief virtue, and which he commends not only throughout all the sacred Scriptures but also in his own words, saying, “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you love one another” [John XIII, 35]—almost all the barbarians who now belong to one people and one king love one another, while almost all Romans persecute one another.

For what citizen does not envy another citizen? Who shows full affection to his neighbor? All are distant from one another in feeling, even if they are not distant in place; even if they are joined by their dwellings, they are separated in mind. And would that this were found only among citizens and neighbors, though it is a very grave evil! What is more serious is that even relatives do not preserve the rights of kinship. Who makes himself close to his nearest relations? Who pays to love what he acknowledges that he owes even by name? Who has the disposition implied by the name? Who is as close in heart as in blood, in whom the livid zeal of ill will does not burn, whose understanding envy has not invaded, to whom another’s prosperity is not punishment? Who does not regard another’s good as his own evil? Whose happiness is so sufficient for him that he also wishes another to be happy?

This is now a new and immeasurable evil among very many people. It is not enough for someone to be happy himself unless someone else is unhappy. [Col. 0098A]

And indeed, what of that practice—which is so savage, so clearly proceeding from this very impiety, so foreign to the barbarians and so familiar to the Romans—that they proscribe one another through exaction? Rather, they do not proscribe one another; for it would be almost more tolerable if each person suffered what he had inflicted. What is more serious is that the many are proscribed by the few, for whom public exaction is a private source of plunder, who turn the records of fiscal debt into private profits—not only men of high rank, but almost the lowest; not judges alone, but also those who serve the judges.

For what cities, indeed—not merely cities, but also municipalities and villages—are there where there are not as many tyrants as there are *curiales*? [Note: [Col. 0097D] Shortly afterward he calls them *principales*. In the old translation of the Council of Ephesus, p. 535, and in Marius Mercator, p. 621, *curialis* is used for one who in the old translation of the Council of Chalcedon, p. 1137, is called *principalis*.] [Note: [Col. 0098D] I should certainly judge this passage to be corrupt.] Perhaps, however, they congratulate themselves on this title, since it appears to signify that they are powerful and honored. [Col. 0098B] For almost all robbers also rejoice and boast if they are said to be much more savage than they are.

Where, then, as I said, is there a place in which the entrails of widows and orphans—and, along with them, of nearly all holy persons—are not devoured by the leading men of the cities? For they regard even holy people as widows and orphans, since such people either do not wish to defend themselves out of zeal for their profession or cannot do so because of their innocence and humility.

Thus none of these people is safe, and scarcely anyone except the highest-ranking is free from the devastation of predatory robbery—unless he is equal to the robbers themselves in this condition. Indeed, matters have come to such a pass that no one can be safe unless he is wicked.

### V

But surely, since there are so many who devastate the good, there are perhaps some who come to the aid of those suffering this devastation—those who, as it is written, “rescue the needy and the poor from the hand of the sinner” (Psalm LXXXI, 4). “There is none who does good; there is scarcely one” (Psalm XIII, 1). He said “scarcely one” because the scarcity of good people is so great that there seems to be almost a single one.

For who would offer help to the harassed and afflicted, when even the violence of wicked men is not resisted by the priests of the Lord? [Note: [Col. 0098D] Below, at the end of book IV *Against Avarice*, p. 296: “Meanwhile, what are those to do to whom Christ has entrusted the duties of speaking? They displease God if they are silent, and men if they speak.” Such was the misfortune of that age: priests were not permitted to say what they wished, but had to flatter the vices of those subject to them. See what we have noted on this subject at chapter 13 of Agobard’s book *On the Privilege and Right of the Priesthood*.] For very many of them are silent, or are like those who are silent, even when they speak; and many do this not through inconsistency but, as they think, deliberately and reasonably. [Col. 0098D]

They do not wish to proclaim the manifest truth, because the ears of wicked men cannot endure it. Indeed, they not only recoil from it but also hate and curse it; and once they have heard it, they neither reverence nor fear it, but with the more arrogant defiance of stubbornness they despise it. [Note: [Col. 0098D] The Colbert manuscript and old editions read *odiunt*, “they hate.”]

And so even those who can speak remain silent, while sometimes sparing these very evils; [Note: [Col. 0098D] The same manuscript and the old editions read *male parcunt*, “they wrongly spare.”] nor do they wish to bring the force of the open truth against them, lest the truth, pressed upon them more sharply, make them worse. [Col. 0099A]

Meanwhile the poor are devastated, widows groan, and orphans are trampled, to such an extent that many of them—people born even of no obscure ancestry and liberally educated—flee to the enemy lest they die under the affliction of public persecution. They seek Roman humanity among the barbarians, because among the Romans they cannot endure barbarous inhumanity.

Although they differ from those to whom they flee in custom and language, and even—so to speak—in the stench of their barbarian bodies and clothing, they nevertheless prefer to endure an unlike way of life among barbarians rather than raging injustice among Romans.

Thus everywhere they migrate either to the Goths, or to the [Note: [Col. 0099D] Some, including Brassicanus and Galesinius, read *Bagaudas*, *Brassicanus* and *Galesinius* also giving *Boagaudas*. The Corbie manuscript consistently has *Bacaudas*. The same spelling occurs in Jerome, Hydatius, and elsewhere. The name belonged to a faction, not to a people, as can be established from Salvian himself. Joseph Scaliger notes in his observations on Eusebius’s *Chronicle* that in the language of the Gauls these men were then called *Bacaudae*, and that among authors of that period *Bacaudae* also signifies robbery, popular tumult, a rural uprising, and sedition. He proves this with many testimonies. See also Justus Lipsius, book III of Lindenbrog’s *Annals of Tacitus*; Lindenbrog’s observations on Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 181; and Rittershusius on this passage of Salvian.] Bacaudae, or to other barbarians who rule everywhere, and they do not regret having migrated.

[Col. 0099B] For they prefer to live free under the appearance of captivity rather than to be captives under the appearance of freedom. Thus the name of Roman citizens, once valued greatly and purchased at a great price, is now voluntarily rejected and fled; it is regarded as not merely worthless but almost abominable.

What greater testimony to Roman iniquity could there be than that many honorable and noble people, for whom Roman status ought to have been the highest distinction and honor, have nevertheless been driven by the cruelty of Roman iniquity to refuse to be Romans?

And hence even those who do not flee to the barbarians are nevertheless forced to become barbarians—namely, a large part of the Spaniards, no small part of the Gauls, and, finally, all those whom Roman iniquity throughout the Roman world has already made no longer Romans. [Col. 0099C]

### VI

Now I speak of the Bacaudae, who, after being stripped, afflicted, and killed by wicked and bloodthirsty judges, and after losing the right of Roman freedom, [Note: [Col. 0100D] The Colbert manuscript adds “even the name.”] also lost the honor of the Roman name. Their misfortune is charged against them; we charge against them the name of their calamity; we charge against them the name that we ourselves gave them. We call them rebels; we call them ruined men whom we compelled to become criminals.

By what other means did the Bacaudae become what they are, except through our injustices, the wickedness of our judges, and the proscriptions and plunderings of those who turned the name of public exaction into the profits of private gain and made tax assessments their own booty? They ruled those entrusted to them in the likeness of monstrous beasts—or rather, they did not rule them but devoured them. They fed not only on the plunder of men, as most robbers do, but also on their laceration and, so to speak, their blood. [Col. 0099D]

Thus it came about that people strangled and killed by the robberies of judges began to be like barbarians, because they were not allowed to be Romans. They agreed to be what they were not, because they were not allowed to be what they had been; and they were compelled at least to defend their lives because they saw that they had already utterly lost their freedom. [Col. 0100A]

Or what else is being done even now than what was done then—that is, that those who are not yet Bacaudae should be compelled to become so? As far as force and injuries are concerned, they are compelled to wish to be Bacaudae, but weakness prevents them from becoming so.

### VII

Thus virtually all the lower orders are treated in the same way. By one and the same circumstance they are constrained toward two utterly opposite ends. Overwhelming force compels them to wish to aspire to freedom [Note: [Col. 0100D] All editions read thus. But all the old books prefer: *aspirare in libertatem*, “to aspire to freedom.”], but the same force which compels the wish does not allow them the ability. Perhaps, then, it can be charged against them that they wish to become what they would desire above all else not to be compelled to wish to become.

For their greatest misfortune is what they desire. Their condition would be far better if they were not compelled to desire this. But what else can wretched people desire when they suffer the continual—indeed, unbroken—destruction caused by public exaction, when a grave and unremitting proscription always threatens them, when they abandon their homes lest they be tortured in those very homes, and seek exile lest they endure punishments?

Their enemies are gentler toward them than their tax collectors. The reality itself shows this. They flee to the enemy to escape the violence of exaction. And indeed this itself, although harsh and inhuman, would nevertheless be less grievous and bitter if all endured it equally and in common. What is more disgraceful and more punitive is that the burden of all is not borne by all; rather, the taxes of the rich weigh upon the poor, and the weaker bear the burdens of the stronger.

The only reason they cannot endure the burden is that the burden of the wretched is greater than their resources. They suffer two utterly different and dissimilar things: envy and poverty. There is envy in what they pay, and poverty in what they possess. If you look at what they pay, you might think they are wealthy; if you look at what they have, you will find them needy.

Who can assess the magnitude of this injustice? They bear the payments of the rich and the want of beggars. What I am about to say is even more serious: the rich themselves sometimes impose additional taxes, which the poor pay.

But you say: “Since their wealth is greatest, and their payments are greatest, how can it be that they themselves would wish to increase their own debt?” I am not saying that they increase it for themselves. Indeed, that is precisely why they increase it: because they do not increase it for themselves. I will explain how.

New messengers and new letter-carriers frequently arrive, sent by the highest dignitaries, commended to a few illustrious men for the destruction of many. New gifts are decreed for them; new assessments are decreed. The powerful decree what the poor must pay; the favor of the rich decrees what the crowd of wretched people must lose. [Note: [Col. 0101D] All editions read this way, and the Corbie manuscript agrees. I would nevertheless prefer *pendat*, “should pay,” which gives a clearer and more elevated sense. But since *perdat*, “should lose,” is defensible and can be understood, we have chosen not to alter it.]

They themselves feel none of what they decree. But you say: “Those who have been sent by their superiors cannot fail to be honored and received generously.” Then let the rich be first in contributing, since they are first in decreeing. Let them be first in generosity of possessions, since they are first in generosity of words. You who give from what is mine, give also from what is yours.

Even so, whoever you are who alone wish to receive the favor, you should alone bear the expense. But we poor submit to your will, rich men. What you command a few, let us all pay. What could be so just, so humane? Your decrees burden us with new debts. [Col. 0101B] At least make the debt itself common to you and to us. For what could be more unjust or disgraceful than that you alone should be exempt from the debt, when you make everyone debtors?

And indeed the wretched poor pay all that we have described, while being utterly ignorant of what reason or method they use to pay it. For who is allowed to investigate why he pays, or who is permitted to find out what he owes?

This is revealed most clearly when the rich become angry with one another, when some of them complain that decrees have been made without their advice and deliberation. Then you may hear some of them say: “What an outrageous crime! Two or three determine what will kill many.” [Note: [Col. 0101D] The Colbert manuscript reads *nocet*, “harms.” This reading may be good.] “A few powerful men decree what many wretched people must pay.” [Col. 0101C]

Each rich man is concerned for his own honor, so that he does not wish anything to be decreed in his absence—not for the sake of justice, so that he may prevent something unjust from being established in his presence. In the end, what they had criticized in others they later establish themselves, either in revenge for the contempt they had suffered or through presumption of power.

And so the most wretched poor are like people placed in the midst of a sea between battling storms: now they are overwhelmed by the waves of these men, now by those.

### VIII

But surely those who are unjust in this respect are found moderate and just in another, compensating the wickedness of one matter by the goodness of another. For just as they burden the poor with the weight of new assessments, so they support them by providing new remedies; just as the lower classes are especially oppressed by new taxes, so they are especially relieved by new remedies. [Col. 0101D]

Rather, the injustice is equal in both cases. For just as the poor are first in being burdened, so they are last in being relieved. Whenever, as recently occurred, the highest authorities have judged that tax obligations should be reduced in some degree because the cities have been exhausted, the remedy granted to all is immediately divided among the rich alone.

Who then remembers the poor? Who calls the humble and needy to share in the benefit? Who permits the person who is always first in bearing the burden to be last in receiving relief? [Col. 0102A]

And why say more? The poor are not considered taxpayers at all except when the mass of taxation is imposed upon them. But they are outside the number of taxpayers when remedies are distributed.

Do we think that we are unworthy of the punishment of divine severity, when we continually punish the poor in this way? Or do we believe that, since we are constantly unjust, God ought not to be just toward us at all?
