For where, or among whom, are such evils found except among Romans? And whose injustice is so great except ours? The Franks do not know this crime. [Col. 0102B] The Huns are free from these crimes. None of this exists among the Vandals; none of it exists among the Goths.

Indeed, the barbarians among the Goths are so far from tolerating such things that not even the Romans who live among them suffer them. Thus the one prayer of all the Romans there is that they may never be forced to cross over into Roman jurisdiction. The unanimous prayer of the Roman population there is that they may be permitted to live among the barbarians in the manner in which they now live.

And do we wonder that the Goths are not defeated by our forces, when they prefer to be among them rather than [Note: [Col. 0102D] This is the reading of all editions. The Corbie manuscript, however, has *quam apud Romanos*, “rather than among the Romans,” which is certainly a good reading. But another seems better to me, because it expresses the author’s meaning more clearly.] among us Romans?

Thus our brothers not only have no desire at all to defect from them to us, but leave us in order to flee to them. Indeed, I could wonder that all the poor taxpayers and needy do not do the same, were it not for this one reason why they do not: they cannot transfer there their little possessions, their small dwellings, and their families.

For when most of them abandon their little fields and huts to escape the violence of exaction, how could they fail to wish to take with them, if possibility allowed, the things they are compelled to leave behind? Since they cannot do what they might prefer, they do what alone lies within their power. They hand themselves over to the protection and defense of the powerful; they make themselves the dependents of the rich and, as it were, pass into their jurisdiction and control.

Yet I would not regard this as grievous or disgraceful; rather, I would congratulate the greatness of the powerful to whom the poor surrender themselves, if they did not sell these protections, and if they granted to humanity what they claim to defend in the humble, rather than to greed.

What is grievous and exceedingly bitter is that they appear to protect the poor on the condition that they strip them, and defend the wretched on the condition that they make them still more wretched by defending them. For all who appear to be defended first sell almost all their property to their defenders before they are defended. Thus, in order that the children may have the protection of fathers, they lose their inheritance.

The protection of parents is purchased through the beggary of their pledges. Behold the assistance and patronage of the powerful! They give nothing to those entrusted to them, but everything to themselves. For in this way something is temporarily assigned to the parents so that in the future everything may be taken away from the children. [Col. 0102D]

Thus certain powerful men sell—and sell at a very high price—everything they provide. And when I say that they sell, would that they sold according to the ordinary and common custom! Something might perhaps remain for the buyers.

This is a new kind of sale and purchase. The seller transfers nothing and receives everything. The buyer receives nothing and loses everything entirely. Almost every ordinary contract has this feature: envy appears to lie with the buyer and poverty with the seller, because the buyer purchases in order to increase his property, while the seller sells in order to diminish it. But this is an unheard-of kind of commerce: the resources of the sellers increase, while nothing remains for the buyers except beggary.

For what could be more intolerable, more monstrous—and something that human minds, I will not say endure, but can scarcely hear—that many of the poor and wretched, after being stripped of their little possessions and driven from their small fields, suffer the taxes of the property they have lost even after losing it? When possession has departed from them, the head-tax does not depart. [Col. 0103B] They lack property, yet are crushed by levies.

Who could assess the magnitude of this evil? The usurpers lie upon their property, while the wretched pay taxes on behalf of the usurpers.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Other editions read *Bagaudas*; Brassicanus and Galesinius read *Boagaudas*. The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius read: “After the death of the father, those born afterward, in accordance with the rights of posthumous heirs, do not possess the little fields belonging to their own right, and are killed by the burden of the fields.” Pithoeus’s edition reads: “After the death of the father, posthumous children born afterward, in accordance with the rights of their own status, do not possess their little fields, and are killed by the burden of the fields.” The Corbie manuscript reads: “After the death of the father, those born afterward, in accordance with the rights of their own status, do not possess their little fields, and are killed by the burden of the fields.” The Colbert manuscript has: “After the death of the father, those born afterward, in accordance with the rights of posthumous men, do not possess their little fields, and are burdened by the payment.” Thus the Corbie manuscript does not contain the word *posthumi*. I have no doubt that it is a gloss introduced by someone who thought the passage concerned children born after the father’s death, who are commonly called *posthumi*. It was first written in the margin of the book and afterward slipped into the text. But whoever added the word did not grasp Salvian’s meaning. Salvian means only that sons surviving their fathers, when possession of their paternal property did not pass to them but to the powerful to whom their fathers had previously made themselves dependents, were nevertheless subjected to the conditions attached to the fields and compelled to pay taxes for them as though they were their own.]

After the death of the father, those born afterward do not possess their little fields in accordance with the rights belonging to them, and they are killed by the burden of the fields. [Note: [Col. 0104D] This is the reading of Pithoeus’s edition. The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius have “are killed by the burden of the fields”; the Corbie manuscript has “the burden of the fields.” I greatly prefer the reading of the old editions. Salvian says that these sons, although they were not possessors of their fathers’ fields, were nevertheless, through the height of injustice, compelled to pay the taxes and levies that were then called *munera*, and were thus in a certain sense killed by the bitter and unjust exaction of intolerable taxes, as though their lives were being demanded from them. Below, at the end of book VI, p. 140, he says: “The gold that we pay, we call *munera*.” Nevertheless, the reading of Pithoeus’s edition, which we have retained, is good and makes good sense, although it is not so elevated as the other.]

And so nothing else is accomplished by such immense crimes except that those who have been stripped by private usurpation should die through public affliction, and that exaction should take away the lives of those from whom plunder has taken their property.

Accordingly, some of those about whom we are speaking—either more prudent or made prudent by necessity—when they lose their homes and little fields through usurpations, or abandon them after being driven out by tax collectors because they cannot keep them, seek the estates of the powerful and become tenants of the rich. [Col. 0103C]

Just as those who, compelled by fear of the enemy, retreat to fortified places, or those who, having lost the condition of free security, flee in desperation to some asylum, so these people, unable any longer to possess either the dwelling or the dignity of their birth, subject themselves to the yoke of an abject tenancy. They have been reduced to this necessity: they are exiles not only from their property but also from their own status; they are banished not only from their possessions but from themselves. They lose everything they have along with themselves, lacking both ownership of their property and the right of freedom.

### IX

And indeed, because unhappy necessity compels them in this way, this extreme condition of theirs would have to be endured somehow if there were not something still more extreme. What is more serious and bitter is that a more savage evil is added to this evil. [Col. 0104A]

They are received as newcomers but, through the prior claim of residence, are made into natives; and, after the example of that magical and powerful woman who was said to transform human beings into beasts, all those who are received within the estates of the rich are likewise changed, as though by the transformation of Circe’s cup.

Those whom the powerful receive as strangers and outsiders they begin to treat as their own; those who are plainly freeborn are turned into slaves. And do we wonder that the barbarians capture us, when we make our own brothers captives?

There is therefore nothing surprising in the devastation and destruction of cities. For a long time, by oppressing many, we labored toward this end: that, by capturing others, we ourselves should also begin to be captives.

We feel—and although much later than we deserved, we feel at last—the things we have done; and, in accordance with the sacred saying (Psalm CXXVII, 2), we eat the labor of our hands and, with God as our just judge, pay what we owe. [Col. 0104B]

We did not take pity on exiles; behold, we ourselves are exiles. We captured strangers through fraud; behold, we ourselves wander and are defrauded. Through prejudices of time we circumvented freeborn people; behold, we ourselves have recently begun to live on foreign soil, but already fear the prejudices of time.

And oh, how great is the faithless blindness of wicked minds! We endure the condemnation of the judging God, yet still do not recognize that we are being judged.

Some holy people wonder that others who have not yet endured anything of this kind are not corrected by our example, although even those who are already punished by God are not corrected by the torments produced by our iniquities.

O intolerable pride! Very many endure the punishments of their sins, yet no one deigns to understand the causes of the punishments. But there is an obvious reason that produces this pride: although we already suffer something, we do not yet suffer what we deserve.

For God’s mercy is so great that, although he wishes us to suffer some things for our crimes, he does not wish us to endure everything. He chastises the wicked; he does not render evil. He prefers that we acknowledge our sins rather than endure their full consequences.

He does this, of course, so that through holy and salutary scourges he may show us what we deserve to suffer, in accordance with the saying of the blessed Apostle: “Do you not know that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Romans II, 4–5). [Col. 0105A]

And truly we act as the Apostle says. God calls us to repentance, but we store up wrath. God invites us to forgiveness, but every day we heap up offense. Through our iniquities we use force against God; we arm the wrath of the Godhead against ourselves. We compel God, against his will, to avenge the enormity of our crimes.

We are almost preventing him from showing mercy. For although no sign or appearance of injustice can ever fall upon him, we act in such a way that, if he does not avenge the enormities of our crimes, he may appear to be unjust.

### X

But surely someone was once a sinner and is perhaps no longer one? Is there any limit to crimes, and do people depart from life before they depart from iniquity? For who does not die with his very iniquities, and who is not buried with and in those very crimes?

Thus the prophetic saying can truly and most appropriately be applied to them: “Their graves are their houses forever; and they are compared with foolish beasts and have become like them” (Psalm XLVIII, 12–13).

Would that they were like beasts! It would have been better to have gone astray through animal ignorance. What is worse and more criminal is that they sinned not through ignorance of God but through contempt for him.

And is this true only of the laity, and not also of some of the clergy? Only of secular people, and not also of many religious? Indeed, they are enslaved to secular vices under the appearance of religion. After the disgrace and crimes of their former life, they have inscribed upon themselves the title of holiness; they have changed only their name by profession, not their life, taking the garb of divine worship rather than its practice and thinking that they put off only the garment, not the mind. [Note: [Col. 0105C] Here we have followed the authority of the editions. The Corbie manuscript reads: “And they assume the appearance of divine worship rather than its practice, thinking that they have removed only the garment, not the mind.” This is how we had written it in the first edition. But now it seemed preferable to retain the old reading.]

Thus they consider themselves less blameworthy, although they are said to have done penance: just as they do not abandon their former ways, so they do not abandon their former attire.

For they do almost everything in such a way that you would think they had not so much previously repented of their crimes as afterward repented of the penance itself; nor had they so much previously repented of having lived badly as afterward of having promised to live well.

They know that I speak the truth, and their own consciences also testify to me—many others as well, but especially those religious men who ambitiously seek new honors and, after accepting the name of penance, purchase the most extensive power they had not previously possessed.

They wished to be not merely secular but more than secular, so that what they had been before was not enough for them unless afterward they became more than they had been.

How, then, do such people not regret having done penance, just as those who are said to have thought about conversion and God, while abstaining from their own spouses but not abstaining from seizing the property of others, and while professing continence of body, rage with the incontinent desires of their minds? [Note: [Col. 0105D] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. Rittershusius correctly suggested that it should be read in this way instead of the reading of the editions, *in incontinentiam*, “into incontinence.”]

This is a completely new kind of conversion. They do not do what is permitted, and they commit what is forbidden. They abstain from intercourse, but they do not abstain from robbery.

What are you doing, foolish persuasion? God has forbidden sins, [Note: [Col. 0105D] He condemns those who profess continence while meanwhile not shrinking from seizing the property of others—abstaining from permitted things while committing forbidden ones. He then adds that God forbade sins, not marriages, that is, the chaste embraces of husband and wife. Yet he does not say that it is permitted for anyone to take a wife at any time. This point has been noted lest anyone infer from it, with Bale, against the defenders of papist celibacy, that priests are permitted to marry. For Salvian is not speaking here of priests but of those who, while married, professed continence. That this was extremely common in that period could be established by many testimonies. Salvian himself should be consulted both here and below, pp. 190, 231, 235. Moreover, Salvian himself proves that at that time there was a class of people who led a celibate life, namely, religious persons. In book III *Against Avarice*, rebuking those who divided their wealth and possessions among their children in such a way that they allowed those who had abandoned the world only the usufruct of their share while denying them ownership, he says at last, p. 261, that those parents habitually defended their action by saying that nothing should be left to those who had no children to whom they could leave their possessions. “To whom,” they say, “will those without children leave the property they leave?” By these words Salvian clearly indicates that at that time there was some institution of life to which a perpetual profession of continence was attached.]

Your deeds do not correspond to your pursuits. You ought not to be friends of crimes if you say that you are followers of virtues. [Note: [Col. 0106D] The Corbie manuscript reads *adfectatores*; the Colbert manuscript and the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius read *effectores*.] What you are doing is backwards. This is not conversion but aversion.

Since, as report has it, you abandoned even the practice of honorable marriage long ago, now at last cease from crime. Indeed, justice requires that you cease from every crime. But if not from every crime—because you perhaps think that too difficult and impossible—at least cease from the greatest and most monstrous one.

Let it be so, whoever you are: your neighbors cannot remain beside you. Let it be so: the poor cannot live near you. Let it be so: you are the persecutor and devastator of many needy and wretched people. Let it be so: you afflict everyone, provided they are strangers.

At last, I beg you, spare at least your own people. And if not all your own people—because you may perhaps judge even this burdensome and difficult, if you were to spare all who belong to you—spare at least those of your own people who preferred you not only to other connections or relatives, but even to persons most closely bound to them and to their dearest pledges.

And what shall I say about your pledges and children? They preferred you even to their almost very lives and hopes—not indeed commendably, and the person who acted in this way recognizes his own error. But what does that matter to you, when the very fact that he erred conferred this benefit upon you? For you owe him more precisely because he sinned through excessive love for you.

He was made blind by his affection for you, and is marked and reproved by everyone. But you have nevertheless become more deeply responsible for this, because for your love he made himself blameworthy in the eyes of all.

XI. What, then, is there like this among the barbarian Goths? Which of them harms those who love him? Which pursues a devoted man? Which slaughters one dear to him with the sword? You persecute those who love you; you cut off the hands of those who offer you gifts; you kill those devoted to their neighbors—and you are neither afraid nor terrified? What would you do if you had not already felt God’s judgment through a punishment close at hand?

You add and attach new crimes to your earlier evils. Consider what heavier things await you, since even lesser offenses are accustomed to be punished by demons. Be satisfied now, we beg you, with the plunder of your friends and companions. Let it be enough that the poor have been harassed, enough that beggars have been stripped by you: scarcely anyone beside you can be fearless, and no one can be secure. Torrents hurled down an Alpine cliff, or fires driven by the winds, are endured more easily. Nor are sailors, so to speak, devoured as they perish by the voracity of Charybdis or by the Scyllaean dogs, as they say.

You drive your neighbors from their little possessions, your neighbors from their homes and means of livelihood. Will you, as it is written, “alone inhabit the earth” (Isa. V, 8)? This is the one thing you will not be able to obtain. For however much you occupy everything, however much you overrun everything, you will always find a neighbor.

Look, I beg you, at others whom, whether you wish it or not, you yourself respect. Look at others whom, whether you wish it or not, you yourself admire. They are higher than the rest in rank, and equal in condescension; greater in power, and lesser in humility. You yourself surely know whom we are now addressing and of whom we are speaking; and you ought to acknowledge that the very person of whom we now complain is the one whom we honor with this praise. Would that there were many who could be praised! It would be the health of all and the nobility of the majority.

But suppose you do not wish to be praiseworthy: why, I ask, do you wish to be blameworthy? Why is nothing dearer to you than injustice, nothing more pleasing than greed, nothing more precious than rapacity? Why do you judge nothing more valuable than wickedness, nothing more excellent than robbery? Learn the true good even from a pagan. “You ought,” he says, “to be enclosed by affection and goodwill, not by weapons.”

Your opinions therefore deceive you; the depravity of your perverse and blind mind deceives you. If you wish to be upright, if you wish to be powerful, if you wish to be great, you must surpass others in honesty, not in malice. I once read somewhere: “No one is wicked except a fool.” For if he had wisdom, he would prefer to be good.

You, therefore, if you can still return to sanity, cast off wickedness if you wish to possess wisdom. For if you desire either to be truly wise or to be sound, you must completely cast yourself off and change yourself. Renounce yourself, therefore, lest you be renounced by Christ. Reject yourself, so that you may be received by Christ. Lose yourself, lest you perish. For, as the Savior says, “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Luke IX, 24). Love, therefore, this saving loss, so that you may attain true salvation. You will not be wholly liberated by God unless you yourself have condemned yourself.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0107C]

## I.

We have spoken personally for a long time, and seem to have exceeded the rule of argument. For undoubtedly the reader—if indeed there is anyone who reads what has been written out of love for Christ and for Christ’s sake—is thinking, or perhaps saying to me: “Since the case he is pursuing is general, what has he contributed to this matter by heaping so much upon the person of one man?” Let it be that the man about whom he has spoken is such a person. But does one man’s crime injure another’s goodness—or, much more seriously, is the cause of all damaged by the personal crime of one man?

I can indeed prove by clear testimonies that it is damaged. Achar once secretly took away something from what had been devoted to destruction (Joshua VII, 4), and the crime of one man became a blow to all. David ordered the Israelite people to be numbered, and the Lord punished his error by the calamity of the entire people (II Kings XXIV, 1). Rabshakeh spoke certain words in insult of God, and one hundred and eighty-five thousand men were struck down because the insolent tongue of one profane man had uttered a curse (Isa. XXXI). Therefore blessed Paul the Apostle also commands, not without reason, that a pestilent man be expelled from the Church; and he shows why he commands this, saying: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (I Cor. V, 6).

[Note: Colbertinus reads Achor; Corbeiensis reads Acham.]

From this we clearly recognize that even one evil man very often becomes the destruction of many. Whoever reads this ought not unreasonably to understand that I spoke above about one evil man, since the anger of the divine majesty is very frequently recorded as having been kindled even through one person.

But I am not proceeding with the strictness implied by that statement. It is not necessary for me to think that one person harms everyone, when everyone harms one another. It is not fitting for me to think that all are endangered through one person, when all are endangered through themselves. For everyone is rushing headlong into destruction—or, to say something milder, almost everyone.

Whence comes this good fortune of the Christian people, that the number of the wicked should be either smaller than, or at least equal to, the number of the good? O miserable, tearful condition! O mournful misery! How unlike itself the Christian people now is—that is, how unlike the people it once was!

Then the chief of the Apostles, Peter, punished Ananias and Sapphira with death because they had lied (Acts V). The most blessed Paul likewise expelled one evil man from the Church, lest he contaminate many by his contact (I Cor. V, 5). Now we are content even with an equal number on both sides. And why do I say “content”? Rather, we ought to exult and leap for joy if this equality were to occur for us.

[Col. 0109A]

See to what we have fallen; see to what we have been reduced after that purity of the Christian people when all were once without stain: we now judge the Church blessed if it contains within itself as much good as evil. For how could we not consider it blessed if half the people were innocent, when we now lament that almost the whole people is criminal?

Therefore, since this is so, we spoke earlier about one evil man needlessly; we wept over the crimes of one man needlessly. For either all, or almost all, must be wept over and mourned. For either very many are such, or else—which is no less criminal—they desire to be such and strive not to appear unequal to them in the practice of evil works. Consequently, even if they commit lesser evils because they are less capable, they are nevertheless no less evil, because they do not wish to be less evil if they could help it.

Finally, in the one thing they can do, they are such in desire and will, and they do not yield; to the extent that opportunity allows, they strive to surpass the others. For, although in dissimilar matters, their rivalry is like that of the good: just as the good desire to surpass everyone in the honesty of their minds, so the wicked desire to surpass everyone in depravity. And just as it is the glory of the good to become better each day, so it is the glory of all the wicked to become worse; and just as the best desire to ascend to the summit of every virtue, so the worst desire to claim the prizes of every crime for themselves.

This is especially harmful to us—our own people, that is, the Christians—who, as we have already said, consider wickedness wisdom. Of them God expressly says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. XXIX, 14). And while the Apostle cries out, “If anyone seems to be wise, let him become a fool so that he may be wise” (I Cor. III, 18)—that is, “If anyone wishes to be wise, let him be good, because no one is truly wise unless he is truly good”—we, on the contrary, through the fault of evil minds and, as the Divinity says, through a debased sense (Rom. I, 28), reject goodness as folly and love wickedness as wisdom. Thus each day we believe ourselves wiser the worse we become.

[Note: Petronius, in the story of the Matron of Ephesus: “By a fault of the human race, he desired to know who she was or what she was doing.” Tacitus, in the book On the Life of Agricola: “It is characteristic of the human mind to hate the one whom you have injured.”]

## II.

And what hope of amendment, I ask, can there finally be in us, who are not led to evil by an error of opinion, but strive through deliberate evil will to seem always worse?

This is why I complained earlier that we are much worse than the barbarians: ignorance of the law excuses them, whereas knowledge accuses us. They, through ignorance of the truth, because they do not know what is good, love evil things as good; but we, possessing knowledge of the truth, know very well what things are good. [Col. 0110A] [Note: In the margin of the Pithoean edition the following is written: “It was noted in an old copy that something is missing here.” And indeed, who would not see that much is missing? In our manuscripts nothing of this kind is noted, nor is a blank space left. Nevertheless, since it was clear that the passage was not sound, we judged that the defect should be marked with an asterisk in this edition.] * [lacuna] ways.

First, there is scarcely any crime or outrage that is not found in the spectacles. There the highest kind of pleasure is that men die—or, what is more grievous and bitter than death, that they are torn apart; that the bellies of beasts be filled with human flesh; that men be eaten amid the joy of those standing around and the delight of those watching. That is, men are almost as much devoured by the eyes of the spectators as by the teeth of beasts.

And to make this happen, the whole world is put to expense. For it is pursued and prepared with great care. Remote places are visited, inaccessible thickets searched, impenetrable forests traversed, cloud-bearing Alps climbed, snow-bearing valleys penetrated; and so that human entrails may be devoured by wild beasts, nature is not permitted to keep anything hidden.

“But,” you say, “these things do not always happen.” True. And what an excellent defense of error it is that they do not always happen! As though things that offend God ought ever to happen; or as though evil things happen well because they do not happen continually.

Murderers, too, do not always kill; yet they are murderers even when they do not kill, because they are sometimes stained by murder. Nor do all robbers always commit robbery, but they do not cease to be robbers, because even when they do not carry out robberies in deed, they do not withdraw from robbery in their minds.

So all those who take pleasure in spectacles of this kind, even when they are not watching them, are not innocent in mind of the sacrilege of the spectacles, because they would always wish to watch them if they could.

Nor is this all; there are other and greater matters. What of it? Are not even chicks still fed according to the custom of the sacrileges of the pagans, and are omens sought from the flight of birds, and are almost all the practices carried out that those ancient pagans once considered frivolous and ridiculous? And when these things are done by the very men who give their names to the years, and from whom the years themselves take their beginning, do we believe that our years can proceed well when they begin from such practices?

Would that, just as these things are done only for the sake of the consuls, they alone were polluted on whose account they are done! But this is the most deadly and serious point: while these things are performed with public consent, the honor of a very few becomes the crime of all; [Note: In other editions one reads: “as if two were inaugurated from each year,” and so forth. The Corbeiensis manuscript reads: “and just as in each year,” and so forth. I would willingly read: “As if, just as in each year, two ...” For, as the most learned men have already observed, ancient scribes were accustomed not to repeat the same syllables, and therefore frequently omitted monosyllabic words because of this practice. A similar example occurs in the final chapter of the Gospel according to John. There both the sense itself and the Greek edition, as well as the authority of the oldest Latin manuscripts, require the reading: “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?” Yet today the most constant reading in the commonly circulated editions is: “I want him to remain,” and the word “If” has been omitted. Likewise, in Cassian, Book VII, On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 14, it is written: “it is necessary that without a mother,” where the sense itself and an old manuscript of the Royal Library show that it should be read: “as if without a mother.” Something similar, therefore, may have happened in this passage of Salvian.]

and just as two are inaugurated each year, it is almost the case that no one escapes throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0110D]

## III.

But let us consider that enough has been said about these matters, which, as you yourselves excuse them, do not always occur. Let us speak, however, about the daily obscenities which legions of demons have devised—so many and so numerous that even honorable and upright minds, although they can despise and trample down some of them, can scarcely overcome all of them completely.

For just as armies are said to lay traps in those places through which they know the enemy troops will come, either blocking them with pits, fixing them on stakes, or infesting them with caltrops—so that even if someone does not fall into all of them, no one nevertheless escapes all of them entirely—so the demons have spread so many traps of enticement throughout this life for the human race that, even if someone escapes very many of them, he is nevertheless caught by some one of them.

Indeed, since it would take too long to speak now about all of them—amphitheaters, odeons, playhouses, processions, athletes, acrobats, pantomimes, and the other monstrosities, which I am reluctant to mention because I am reluctant even to know of such evil—I speak only about the impurities of the circuses and theaters.

For such are the things done there that no one can mention or even recall them without pollution. Other crimes claim for themselves almost single portions of us: dirty thoughts claim the mind, immodest sights the eyes, corrupt sounds the ears; so that when one of these has gone astray, the others may remain free from sin.

In theaters, however, none of these is free from guilt, because the mind is polluted by desire, the ears by hearing, and the eyes by sight. All these things are so disgraceful that no one can explain or describe them without compromising modesty.

Who, while preserving complete modesty, could speak of those representations of shameful things, those obscenities of voices and words, those indecencies of movements, those foulnesses of gestures? How great a crime they are can be understood even from this: they forbid anyone to report them. For some very great crimes can still be named and condemned by one who reports them without loss of decency—murder, robbery, adultery, sacrilege, and other things of this kind. The impurities of theaters alone cannot even be honorably accused.

Thus a new situation arises for the person condemning the disgrace of these indecencies: although anyone who wishes to accuse them is undoubtedly honorable, he cannot speak of or accuse them while preserving his honor intact.

All other evils pollute those who commit them, but not those who merely see or hear them. Even if you hear someone blaspheming, you are not polluted by sacrilege because your mind dissents; and if you are present at a robbery, you are not defiled by the act because your mind abhors it.

The impurities of spectacles alone make the guilt of those who perform them and those who watch them one and the same. For while the spectators approve these things and look upon them willingly, they commit them all through sight and consent. Thus that apostolic statement applies to them with particular force: “They are worthy of death not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them” (Rom. I, 32).

Therefore, in those images of fornications, the entire populace fornicates in mind; and those who perhaps came to the spectacle pure return from the theater adulterers. They do not fornicate only when they return, but also when they come. For by the very fact that someone desires an obscene thing, while hurrying toward what is unclean, he is unclean.

## IV.

Since this is so, behold the kinds of things that all, or almost all, the Romans do. And since these things are so, we who do such things complain that we are neglected by the Divinity; we say that we are abandoned by our Lord, while we ourselves abandon the Lord.

Let us suppose that our Lord wishes to look upon us even though we do not deserve it. Let us see whether he can. Behold, countless thousands of Christians spend every day at spectacles of shameful things. Can God look upon those who are such? Can he look upon those who revel in the circuses, who commit adultery in the theaters?

Or perhaps we wish and consider it worthy that, when God sees us in the circuses and theaters, he should also look with us at the things we watch, and that he should likewise see with us the indecencies that we behold?

One of two things must necessarily happen. If he deigns to see us, it follows that he also sees the things where we are; or if, as is beyond doubt, he turns his eyes away from those things, then he must likewise turn them away from us who are there.

And although this is so, we nevertheless do these things and continue without interruption to do what I have described. Or do we perhaps think that we have a god in the theaters and circuses, after the manner of the ancient pagans? They once did these things because they believed that they were the pleasures of their idols.

How do we do these things, when we are certain that our God hates them? Or, if we know that these indecencies please God, I do not forbid us to continue doing them without interruption. But if our conscience tells us that God detests and abhors this, that these things are food for the devil and an offense against God, how do we say that we worship God in the Church of God, when we are always serving the devil in the obscenity of the games—and doing so knowingly, consciously, deliberately, and intentionally?

And what hope, I ask, will there be for us before God, when we injure God not by accident or ignorance, but after the example of those ancient giants whom we read attempted heaven with insane efforts and, as it were, lifted their steps into the clouds? Thus, through the insults that we continually inflict upon God throughout the world, we attack heaven, as it were, with public agreement.

To Christ, therefore—O monstrous madness!—we offer circuses and pantomimes, and this especially when we receive some good from him, when some prosperity is granted us by him, or when victory over our enemies is bestowed by the Divinity.

And what else do we seem to do by this than if someone were abusive toward a man who had bestowed a benefit, or struck with insults one who was flattering him, or pierced with a sword the face of one who was kissing him?

I ask all the powerful and wealthy men of this world: what crime is that servant guilty of who conceives evil against a good and pious master, who insults one who has deserved well of him, and returns an insult for the freedom he receives? Without doubt, he is considered guilty of the greatest crime who returns evil for good, although he would not be permitted even to return evil for evil.

This, therefore, is what we too, who are called Christians, do. We provoke the merciful God against us by our impurities; we injure him who is propitious with our filth; we beat him who is flattering us with insults.

## V.

To Christ, therefore—O monstrous madness!—we offer circuses and pantomimes; to Christ, in return for his benefits, we offer the obscenities of theaters; to Christ we sacrifice the most shameful victims of public entertainments?

Clearly, our Savior, who was born in the flesh for our sake, taught us to do this. He preached it either through himself or through the Apostles. For this reason he endured the shame of human birth and assumed the dishonorable beginnings of earthly origin.

[Note: Below, Book II Against Avarice, p. 227, concerning Christ: “Humbled even to the shame of human beginnings, the filth of swaddling clothes, and the lowliness of a manger.” Jerome, in his letter On the Prodigal Son to Pope Damasus: “What greater clemency could there be than that the Son of God should be born the Son of man, endure the discomforts of ten months, await the coming of childbirth, be wrapped in cloths, be subjected to parents, grow through successive ages, and, after insults of words, slaps, and scourges, also become a curse upon the cross for us, so that he might release us from the curse of the Law, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death?” This passage of Jerome should be read in this form in Agobard, Book Against Felix, chapter 20.]

For this reason he lay in a manger, he whom angels served while he lay there. For this reason he wished to be wrapped in the rags of swaddling clothes, he who governed heaven while in those rags. For this reason he hung upon the gallows, he at whose hanging the world trembled.

“For your sake,” says the Apostle, “he became poor, although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might be ennobled” (II Cor. VIII, 9). And again: “Although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself even unto death, and death on a cross” (Phil. II, 6, 8).

This is what Christ evidently instilled into us when he endured these things for our sake. We repay his passion with a splendid return, we who, having received redemption through his death, repay him with the most shameful life.

For, as the most blessed Paul says, “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ appeared, instructing us to renounce impiety and worldly desires, and to live temperately, piously, and justly in this world, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from every iniquity and to cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works” (Tit. I, 11–14).

Where are those who do the things for which the Apostle says Christ came? Where are those who flee worldly desires? Where are those who live piously and justly? Where are those who show by good works that they hope for the blessed hope, and who, living an unstained life, testify by this very fact that they await the kingdom of God because they deserve to receive it?

“The Lord Jesus Christ came,” he says, “to cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works.” Where is that pure people? Where is the acceptable people? Where is the people of good works? Where is the holy people?

Christ, says Scripture, “suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21). Clearly, we follow the Savior’s footsteps in the circuses; we follow the Savior’s footsteps in the theaters. Such an example, evidently, Christ left us—he whom we read wept, but whom we do not read laughed.

[Note: Obviously, this concerns the death of Lazarus. From this the Jews concluded that he had been greatly loved by Christ. For those final tears belong more to lovers than to mourners, although they also belong to mourners and to those who miss their friends. Let those who now command us to strip ourselves of all humanity in grief and to behave like Stoics, and who say that men who weep at the funerals of their friends have womanly hearts, go their way. See our notes on the first letter of Leidrad, archbishop of Lyons, p. 147.]

And he did both for our sake: weeping, because it is the soul’s contrition; laughter, because it corrupts discipline. Therefore he said, “Woe to you who laugh, for you will weep” (Luke VI, 25). And: “Blessed are you who weep, for you will laugh” (ibid., 21).

But for us it is not enough to laugh and rejoice unless we rejoice with sin and madness, unless our laughter is mixed with impurities and our rejoicing with crimes.

## VI.

What error is this, I ask? What madness? Can we not rejoice and laugh continually unless we make our laughter and joy a crime? Or do we perhaps consider simple joy fruitless, and find no pleasure in laughing without guilt?

What evil is this, I ask, or what madness? Let us laugh, I beg you, as immoderately as we please; let us rejoice as continually as we please, provided that we do so innocently.

What folly and madness is it to think that laughter and joy are not worthwhile unless they contain an offense against God—and indeed a very great offense? For in spectacles there is a kind of apostasy from the faith and a deadly violation of the Creed itself and the heavenly sacraments.

What is the first confession of Christians in saving baptism? What else, surely, but that they declare that they renounce the devil, his pomps, his spectacles, and his works?

[Note: Or “covenant,” as Isidore calls it in Book II, On Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 24: “The first covenant is that by which one renounces the devil, his pomps, and his entire way of life.” Caesarius, in his exposition of the faith: “For in baptism we are asked whether we renounce the devil, his pomps, and his works; and we answer with a free voice that we will renounce them.” Then, in this confession or covenant, he establishes the foundation of our faith, saying: “Therefore, if we faithfully preserve what is first and in which the foundation of the Christian religion consists,” and so forth. A little later: “Let each person examine his conscience; and if he sees that he has fulfilled what he promised—having renounced the devil and his pomps, not only in words but also in works—let him recognize that he has kept the faith intact and rejoice.” By the pomps of the devil they then understood spectacles and the follies of the nations, as even Salvian alone teaches. In later centuries, those who embraced the monastic life were said to renounce the pomps of the devil; innumerable examples of this could be produced.]

Therefore spectacles and pomps, even according to our profession, are works of the devil. How, O Christian, do you pursue after baptism the spectacles that you confess to be the work of the devil?

You once renounced the devil and his spectacles; consequently, as a prudent and knowledgeable person, you must recognize that when you return to the spectacles, you are returning to the devil. For you renounced both things together and declared both to be one.

“I renounce,” you say, “the devil, his pomps, spectacles, and works.” And what follows? “I believe,” you say, “in God the almighty Father and in Jesus Christ his Son.”

Therefore the devil is renounced first, so that God may be believed; for whoever does not renounce the devil does not believe in God. And therefore whoever returns to the devil abandons God.

The devil is present in spectacles and in his pomps; consequently, when we return to the spectacles, we abandon the faith of Christ. In this way, then, all the sacraments of the creed are undone, and everything that follows in the creed is shaken and made to totter. Nothing that follows stands if what is primary has not stood.

Tell me, therefore, O Christian, how do you think you retain the subsequent articles of the creed when you have lost its first principles? Limbs are of no use without a head, and everything looks back to its origin; if that origin is destroyed, it drags everything down with it.

When the root is removed, either the rest no longer exists, or, if it exists, it is without benefit, because nothing stands without a head. If, therefore, the crime of spectacles seems small to anyone, let him consider all that we have said. He will see that in spectacles there is not pleasure but death.

For what else is it than to incur death to lose the origin of life? When the foundation of the creed is overturned, life itself is slaughtered.

[Note: That is, the promise that we make to renounce the devil and his pomps. Caesarius of Arles calls this very thing the foundation of faith, as we were saying just above.]

## VII.

Again, therefore, we must return to what we have often said: What is there like this among the barbarians? Where among them are circuses, where theaters, where the crime of various impurities—that is, the destruction of our hope and salvation?

Even if they, being pagans, used such things, they nevertheless sinned with lesser guilt against sacred things, because, although there was impurity of sight, there was not a violation of the sacrament.

But what can we say in our defense? We hold the creed and overthrow it; we confess the gift of salvation and at the same time deny it. Where, then, is our Christianity, when we receive the sacrament of salvation only in order afterward to sin with a greater crime of violation?

[Note: That is, baptism. Cassian, Book VI, On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 18: “Recognize the sacraments of your salvation, through which you were renewed and through which you were reborn.” It was the conviction of the ancient Christians that all sins were abolished in baptism. For this reason some postponed their baptism until the end of their lives. Rempertus also testifies that this was observed among the Danes in the age of Louis the Pious, in The Life of Saint Anscharius, chapter 51: “Nevertheless, they postponed receiving baptism, judging it beneficial for themselves to be baptized at the end of their lives, so that, purified by the saving washing, they might enter the gates of eternal life pure and unstained, without any delay.”]

We place entertainments before the churches of God; we despise altars and honor theaters. In short, we love everything and worship everything. In comparison with everything else, God alone is worthless to us.

Finally, besides the other things that prove this, the very matter I am discussing also indicates it. For whenever it happens—as it often does—that an ecclesiastical festival and public games are held on the same day, I ask the conscience of everyone: which place has the larger crowds of Christian men—the enclosure of the public game or the court of God? Do they pursue the temple more, or the theater? Do they love the words of the Gospels more, or the words of the stage? The words of life, or the words of death? The words of Christ, or the words of a mime?

[Note: From this passage it is also clear that, when an ecclesiastical festival was being celebrated, ancient Christians were required to attend the sacred rites throughout the entire day. See the notes on Agobard’s book On the Insolence of the Jews, p. 20.]

There is no doubt that we love more what we place first. On every day of the deadly entertainments, if any festival of the Church occurs, those who call themselves Christians not only do not come to church, but if some happen to come in ignorance, then, while they are in the church itself, if they hear that games are being held, [Note: “It is characteristic of the human mind to take especial delight in what is forbidden and harmful, and to despise and reject what is salutary.” The Church cried out against secular and public games, declaring them impious, mockeries of our hope, and unbefitting for Christians to attend. Yet when secular games and divine assemblies happened at the same time, the temples of the supreme God could be seen deserted in comparison with the multitude of Christians rushing to circuses and theaters. Thus, even if some entertainment occurred while the people were inside the church, they all abandoned the divine services in a body to pursue the games. For this reason the African bishops thought it necessary to ask the emperors that theatrical spectacles and other games be removed on Sundays and on the other most solemn days of the Christian religion, especially because on the eighth day of Holy Easter the people gathered at the circus more than at the church. This is found in chapter 61 of the African collection. Indeed, since this evil seemed too great to holy men, at the Fourth Council of Carthage they threatened with excommunication those who, on a solemn day, neglected the solemn assembly of the church and gathered at spectacles. Whether the Africans became wiser after this is uncertain, except that since Salvian here attacks the public madness of nearly all Christians on this matter, it is probable that he was speaking of the Africans as well, whom he gravely complains in many passages of these books to have been utterly depraved at that time. See Sirmond’s notes on the fourth sermon of the sermons of Saint Augustine.]

they abandon the church. The temple of God is despised so that they may run to the theater. The church is emptied; the circus is filled. We leave Christ at the altar so that, committing adultery by the most impure sight, we may feed our eyes on the fornication of shameful entertainments.

[Note: Rittershusius considers this passage corrupt, and not without reason. The intention was clearly to omit these words up to “at the beginning,” unless the great agreement of manuscripts and editions stood in their favor. For these words certainly do not belong here. It should therefore be read exactly as follows: “Let us feed [our eyes] with fornication. And therefore, etc.”]

Afterward, however—plainly, we who are corrupted by prosperity—something must be done at the beginning [the transmitted text is corrupt]. And therefore the Lord God most rightly says to us: “Because of your filthiness you have been destroyed with destruction.” And again: “The altars of this laughter shall be destroyed.”

## VIII

But perhaps one may reply that these things are not being done in all the cities of the Romans. That is true. I add even more: they are not being done now even where they had always been done before. For this is no longer being done in the city of the people of Mainz—not because it has been abandoned, but because it has been destroyed and obliterated.

[Note: Brassicanus’s edition reads: “For this is no longer being done in the city of the people of Massilia, because it has been destroyed and obliterated.” Nicolaus Serarius likewise testifies that he read it in many books, in Book I of his *History of Mainz*, chapter 7. Galesinius’s edition reads: “For this is no longer being done in the city of the people of Mainz and Massilia.” The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts do not contain the words “and Massilia.” Learned men rightly suspected an error here, since this reading conflicts with Salvian, who speaks in the singular at that point. Moreover, there was no occasion to discuss Massilia, which no one reported as having been devastated by the barbarian invasion at that time. And even if it had been devastated, why would he name it among the cities of Germany and Belgica, so far from Narbonensis? The distinguished Hadrianus Valesius, recognizing this, advises that *Massiliensium* should be read as *Bassiliensium*. This was a city in the Rauraci, somewhat nearer to Mainz. The conjecture is plausible, unless the authority of the ancient manuscripts shows that only Mainz is under discussion here.]

It is not being done at Agrippina, because it is full of enemies. It is not being done in the most distinguished city of the Treveri, because it has been overthrown by a fourfold destruction. Finally, it is not being done in very many cities of Gaul and Spain. And therefore, woe to us and to our impurities; woe to us and to our iniquities. What hope is there for Christian peoples before God, since these evils ceased to exist in the Roman cities precisely when those cities began to be under barbarian rule? Thus vice and impurity are, as it were, a kind of kinship among Roman people, almost their mind and nature, because wherever Romans are, vices are especially found.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “iniquity” (*iniquitas*) in place of “vice” (*vitiositas*).]

But perhaps this is a harsh and unjust complaint. Harsh indeed, if false. “But how,” you say, “how is it not false, when those things we have mentioned are now practiced in almost none of the Roman cities, and most of them are no longer polluted by these impurities? Although the very places and dwellings of the ancient error still exist, nevertheless the things formerly done there are by no means practiced.”

Both points must therefore be considered: that is, what it means that the very places and theatres of entertainments still exist, while they have ceased to be theatres. The places and dwellings of shameful practices still exist because all kinds of impurity were formerly practiced there. The entertainments themselves, however, are no longer held because, owing to the misery and poverty of the times, they can no longer be held. Thus what was formerly practiced was a matter of vice; what is not now practiced is a matter of necessity.

The disaster of the treasury and the poverty of the Roman exchequer no longer permit wasted expenditures to be poured out everywhere on frivolous things. Let much still be squandered, and let it be thrown, as it were, into the mire; but such vast amounts can no longer be wasted, because there are no longer such vast resources to waste. As far as our desire and most impure pleasure are concerned, we would certainly wish to possess more, if only so that we might convert more of it into this mire of shamefulness.

And circumstances prove how much we would want to squander if we were rich and splendid, since we squander so much while beggars. Such is the corruption and ruin of present morals that, although poverty no longer has anything it can lose, vice nevertheless still wishes that more might be destroyed. There is therefore no reason for us to flatter ourselves in this matter by saying that those things formerly practiced are not now practiced in all cities. They are no longer practiced everywhere because the cities in which they were practiced no longer exist; and wherever they were practiced for a long time, they brought it about that those places could no longer exist in which such things had been practiced.

Thus God himself spoke to sinners through the prophet, because the Lord remembered these things and, he says, they rose up in his heart, and the Lord could no longer endure them because of the evil of their pursuits and the abominations they had committed; “and your land became a desolation, an astonishment, and a curse” (Jeremiah 44:21–22). Through these things, therefore, it has already come to pass that the greater part of the Roman world has become a desolation, an astonishment, and a curse.

## IX

Would that these things had merely been practiced in the past, and that Roman vice might at some time cease to practice them. Perhaps, as it is written, God would be appeased for our sins. But we do not act in such a way that he may be appeased. We constantly add evils to evils and heap sins upon sins; and although the greater part of us has already perished, we act so that we may all perish.

Who, I ask, sees another being killed beside him and does not fear for himself? Who sees his neighbor’s house burning and does not strive by every means to prevent himself from being consumed by the fire? We have seen not merely our neighbors burning; we ourselves have already burned through the greater part of our people. And what evil is this, I ask, beyond all wickedness? We have burned, we have burned—and yet we do not fear the flames in which we have already burned.

For the fact that, as I said, those things formerly practiced are not practiced everywhere is a benefit granted by misery, not the result of discipline. I can easily prove this. Restore the conditions of the former age, and immediately the things that formerly existed will exist everywhere. I add further: as far as human desires are concerned, although these things are no longer everywhere, they are still everywhere, because the Roman people would wish them to be everywhere.

When a person does not do an evil thing solely because necessity prevents him, the very desire for that shameful thing is condemned as though it were the deed. For, as I said, according to the saying of our Lord, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has committed adultery in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). We may therefore understand that, even if through necessity we do not perform shameful and condemnable acts, we are nevertheless condemned for our very desire for shameful things.

And what should I say about desire? Almost all people do these things when they can. Indeed, whenever inhabitants of any city come to Ravenna or Rome, some become part of the Roman crowd in the circus, and others part of the Ravennate people in the theatre. Therefore let no one think that he is excused by his location or absence. All who join themselves to one another through the desire for shameful things are united in the shamefulness of those things.

And do we flatter ourselves about the integrity of our morals, or about the rarity of our shameful practices? I say more: not only are those infamous stains of the entertainments that were formerly practiced now being practiced, but they are practiced much more criminally than before.

Then the Roman world still had its members intact; the public wealth had made its storehouses narrow; the citizens of all the cities were overflowing with riches and luxuries. In the midst of such an abundance of possessions, the authority of religion could scarcely maintain moral discipline. The promoters of shameful pleasures were then supported in many places, but everything was full and overflowing. No one considered the expense to the state, no one its losses, because the expenditure was not felt. The state itself seemed somehow to be looking for a place to lose what its treasury could scarcely contain.

Thus the accumulation of wealth, which had almost exceeded all measure, overflowed even into frivolous things. But what can be said now? The resources of former times have departed from us; the means of earlier ages have departed. We are now miserable, and yet we have not ceased to be frivolous.

Although poverty usually comes to the aid of orphans, whether prodigal or wasteful, and although, once they have ceased to be rich, they also cease to be vicious, we alone are a new kind of orphaned and ruined people: in us wealth has ceased, but wickedness endures.

[Note: I think the words “prodigal or wasteful” are redundant and represent a copyist’s annotation. Being uncertain which reading was preferable in the exemplar he was using—*prodigis* or *prodigiosis*—he inserted both, leaving the decision to the reader. The same thing occurs in Book IV *Against Avarice*, p. 282, at the passage “they attempt by some addition,” where a more recent royal manuscript reads “by some attraction” or “allegation.” Likewise, in Vincent of Lérins, no. 30, instead of “Saint Gregory, bishop and confessor of Nazianzus,” the manuscripts read “confessor of Nanzandus” or “Nazabos.” See the notes on Letters 3 and 122 of Lupus of Ferrières.]

We have our causes of corruption not, like other human beings, in temptations, but in our hearts; our vice is our mind itself. Thus, instead of correcting ourselves through the removal of our resources, we sin through our love of evil things.

## X

Although I have said enough thus far about the many vices of the Romans by which the barbarian peoples are not defiled, I shall nevertheless add much that has been omitted. But before I speak, I give this warning: no kind of fault that concerns an insult against God should seem at all trivial to anyone.

[Note: See below, p. 179.]

If no one is permitted to dishonor a distinguished and powerful man, and if anyone who dishonors him is brought to trial under legal decrees and rightly condemned in an action for insult, how much greater a sacrilege is it to be insulting toward God? The guilt of the one who commits an injury always increases in proportion to the dignity of the one who suffers it. For the greater the dignity of the person who endures the insult, the greater must be the offense of the person who commits it.

This is why we read in the Law (Exodus 21) that even those who seem to have committed minor offenses against the sacred command were nevertheless punished with the utmost severity. We are to understand that nothing pertaining to God should be regarded as trivial, because the injury done to the Godhead made even what seemed a small fault a grave matter.

Finally, what did that Levite Uzzah of God do against the heavenly command when he attempted to support the tottering ark of the Lord (2 Samuel 6)? Nothing had been prescribed by the Law concerning this. Yet as soon as he supported it, he was struck down.

[Note: Brassicanus reads this passage as follows: “And immediately, while he was holding it, he was struck down.” Both readings are good. For the passage is thus read in the Second Book of Samuel, chapter 6: “The Lord was angry with Uzzah, and he struck him because of his rashness; and he died there beside the ark of God.”]

He was not killed because, as it might seem, he had committed anything outwardly defiant or even with an irreverent intention; rather, in the very exercise of his duty he was irreverent, because he presumed to do what had not been commanded.

A man of the Israelite people gathered wood on the Sabbath and was killed (Numbers 15:32ff.); and this occurred by the judgment and command of God, the most holy and merciful judge, who undoubtedly would have preferred to spare rather than to kill, unless the logic of severity had overcome the logic of mercy. One careless man perished so that many others might not later perish through carelessness.

And why should I speak of individuals? The entire Hebrew people, while traveling through the wilderness, lost a part of its population because it desired its customary meat (Numbers 11:4ff.). It had not yet been forbidden to desire it; but, as I think, God wished to advance legal observance by restraining rebellious desire. Thus the whole people might more easily recognize how carefully they ought to avoid the things that God would forbid in the heavenly Scriptures, when even acts that he had not yet forbidden by law injured them once committed.

The same people also complained that it had to endure hardship (Numbers 21:4ff.), and for this reason was scourged with heavenly blows—not because a suffering person may not groan, but because the groaning was ungrateful, accusing God as the author of excessive labor. From this we should understand how greatly one who enjoys the blessing of pleasant circumstances ought to please God, since it is not even permissible to complain about things that seem burdensome.

## XI

Perhaps someone will ask what all this has to do with the matter at hand. What else, without question, but that nothing by which God is offended should be considered trivial? We are speaking of the public entertainments—mockeries, that is, of our hope and mockeries of our life.

For while we play in theatres and circuses, we perish, in accordance with the saying of sacred Scripture: “A fool commits wickedness through laughter” (Proverbs 10:23). Thus, while we laugh amid shameful and disgraceful things, we commit crimes—and not minor crimes, but crimes all the more punishable because, although they appear honorable in outward form, they are most deadly in their actual effects.

There are two supreme evils: that a person either destroys himself or injures God. Both are done in the public entertainments. Through criminal shamefulness, the eternal salvation of the Christian people is extinguished there; and through sacrilegious superstitions, the divine majesty is violated. There is no doubt that these practices offend God, since they are consecrated to idols.

Minerva is worshiped and honored in the gymnasia, Venus in the theatres, Neptune in the circuses, Mars in the arenas, and Mercury in the wrestling schools. Thus the character of the worship corresponds to the nature of its authors. Whatever impurity exists is practiced in the theatres; whatever luxury, in the wrestling schools; whatever lack of restraint, in the circuses; whatever madness, in the cages.

In one place there is immodesty, in another wantonness, in another intemperance, in another insanity. Everywhere there is a demon—or rather, in each separate place of the entertainments, every monstrous form of demons. They preside over seats dedicated to their worship.

Accordingly, in entertainments of this kind there is not merely enticement, nor merely vice. For a Christian’s participation in this superstition is a form of sacrilege, because he shares in the worship of those whose festivals delight him.

Although this is always extremely serious, it becomes still more intolerable when, beyond the ordinary pattern of life, either our adversities or our prosperity make the conduct more criminal. For God must be appeased all the more in adversity and offended all the less in prosperity. He must be appeased when he is angry; he must not be offended when he is propitious. Adversity comes to us through God’s anger, prosperity through his grace.

We, however, act in every respect in the opposite way. You ask how? Listen.

First, whenever God, won over by his own mercy—for we never live in such a way that we deserve to win him over—whenever, as I said, won over by himself, he gives us peaceful days, abundant harvests, and a wealthy tranquillity and abundance of all good things that increase beyond our hopes, we are corrupted by such prosperity and spoiled by such arrogance of morals that we completely forget both God and ourselves.

Although the Apostle says that the whole fruit of the peace granted by God consists in this: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity” (1 Timothy 2:2), we use the quiet given by God only to live in drunkenness, luxury, debauchery, plunder, and every crime and wickedness. It is as though the benefit of peace were a leave of absence for disgraceful conduct, and as though we accepted periods of tranquillity granted by God so that we might sin more freely and securely.

We are therefore unworthy of heavenly gifts, because we do not use God’s benefits well; we make a good thing merely the material for vices. Consequently, the very peace that we handle in this way is turned against us, and it is not advantageous to receive something by which we become worse.

Who could believe this? We change the nature of things through our iniquities. What God made good through the gift of his kindness, we make evil for ourselves through our evil ways.

## XII

But perhaps, although we are corrupted by prosperity, we are corrected by adversity; and those whom long peace has made intemperate, upheaval makes moderate.

[Note: Below, p. 142: “Let these be the vices both of prolonged peace and of prosperous security.” Cyprian, in *On the Lapsed*: “Because the long peace granted to us had corrupted discipline, heavenly judgment raised up the faith that was lying prostrate—almost, I would say, sleeping.” Cassian, Book V of *The Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 19: “Lest the soldier of Christ, growing sluggish in the leisure of peace, begin to forget his glorious struggles and, dissolved by the inertia of security, be deprived of the wages of his rewards and the merits of his triumphs.” The same, *Conference* 21, chapter 34: “They are loosened by the security of presumptuous freedom.” Caesarius, Homily 32: “For there are some who, after professing religion, because they seem to have gone out from the world, are loosened by excessive security.” Tacitus, Book XIII of the *Annals*: “The legions were sluggish through prolonged peace.” And Book I of the *Histories*: “The leading men of the Senate were weakened by age and idle through prolonged peace.” And in the *Life of Agricola*: “The Britons nevertheless display greater ferocity, since prolonged peace has not yet softened them.” Cassiodorus, Book III of the *Variae*, Letter 1: “The hearts of savage peoples grow gentle through prolonged peace.”]

Did the peoples of the cities who had been immodest in prosperity begin to be chaste in adversity? Did drunkenness, which had grown through tranquillity and abundance, cease at least through enemy devastation? Italy has been devastated by so many disasters. Did the vices of the Italians therefore cease?

[Note: It is uncertain which Roman siege Salvian means here: that which occurred under Alaric, king of the Goths, or that under Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, or both. For in this passage he recalls various barbarian incursions beginning in the time of Emperor Honorius. Rittershusius understood it of Gaiseric’s siege, which seems to have occurred about the time when Salvian was writing these books. For shortly afterward he writes that Sardinia and Sicily had been overthrown; Victor of Vita testifies at the beginning of his books on the Vandal persecution that the Vandals invaded them after the death of Emperor Valentinian, that is, in 455.]

The city of Rome was besieged and captured. Did the Romans therefore cease to be blasphemous and mad?

Barbarian peoples poured into Gaul.

[Note: Namely the Franks, Goths, Burgundians, Alans, Alamanni, and any others besides.]

Therefore, as far as their corrupted morals are concerned, are the crimes of the Gauls no longer the same as before?

The peoples of the Vandals crossed into the lands of Spain.

[Note: Historians relate that this occurred under the reign of Emperor Honorius. See Mariana, Book V of the *History of Spain*, chapter 2.]

The fortune of the Spaniards changed, but their vice did not.

Finally, so that no part of the world might be free from deadly evils, wars began to travel across the sea. After devastating the cities enclosed by the sea and overturning Sardinia and Sicily—that is, the imperial granaries—and cutting off, as it were, the vital veins, they captured Africa itself, as though it were the soul of the state.

[Note: Victor of Vita, in Book I of *The Persecution of the Vandals*, writes that King Gaiseric of the Vandals obtained the whole circuit of Africa after the death of Valentinian III: “And also the great islands Sardinia, Sicily, Corsica, Ebusus, Majorca, Minorca, and many others.” Idatius, in his *Chronicle*, records that Gaiseric plundered Sicily in the year 440: “Gaiseric plundered Sicily and besieged Palermo for a long time.”]

What then? Once barbarian peoples had entered that land, did vice perhaps cease through fear? Or, just as even the worst slaves sometimes become corrected for the moment, did terror at least compel moderation and discipline?

Who could estimate the extent of this evil? The weapons of barbarians resounded around the walls of Cirta and the people of Carthage.

[Note: Cirta was in Numidia, later called Constantina. Hence the bishops of Constantina, Fortunatus and Petilianus, in the Carthaginian Conference. The Council of Cirta, held in the year 305 under Secundus, bishop of Tisizus, is well known; it is mentioned in several places, including Augustine’s *Brief Account of the Carthaginian Conference*, day three, chapter 15 and following.]

[Note: The capture occurred in the year 439, as Marcellinus Comes records: “At this time Gaiseric, king of the Vandals, occupied the cities of Africa and Carthage, the capital, with his followers, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November.” Idatius, in his *Chronicle*: “After Carthage had been deceived by treachery, King Gaiseric invaded all Africa on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.”]

And the church of Carthage was raging in the circuses and luxuriating in the theatres.

[Note: That is, the people of Carthage.]

Some were being slaughtered outside; others were fornicating inside. Part of the people was captive outside to the enemy; part was captive inside to its vices. It is uncertain which fate was worse.

They were indeed captives outwardly in the flesh, but these others were captives inwardly in the mind. And of two deadly evils, it is, I think, less grievous for a Christian to endure captivity of the body than captivity of the soul, in accordance with what the Savior himself teaches in the Gospel (Luke 9:24–25): that the death of souls is far worse than the death of bodies.

Or should we perhaps believe that that people was not captive in spirit, which was cheerful amid the captivity of its own people? Was he not captive in heart and understanding who laughed amid the sufferings of his own people, who did not realize that he himself was being slaughtered in their slaughter, who did not think that he himself was dying in their deaths?

There was, so to speak, the clash of battles and entertainments outside and inside the walls. The voice of the dying was mingled with the voice of the revellers; and it could scarcely perhaps be distinguished whether it was the lamentation of the people falling in battle or the sound of the people shouting in the circus.

And while all these things were happening, what else was such a people doing except ensuring that, although God perhaps did not yet wish to destroy it, it itself would demand to perish?

## XIII

But why do I speak of places far away and, as it were, removed to another world, when I know that even in our own homeland and in the Gallic cities nearly all the leading men were made worse by their own calamities?

[Note: From this passage the Centuriators correctly concluded that Salvian was a Gaul by birth.]

[Note: The Colbert manuscript and the old editions read “more distinguished.”]

I myself saw nobles of Trier, distinguished in rank, although already stripped and devastated; yet they had been less overthrown in their possessions than in their morals. For although something of their property remained after the devastation and stripping, nothing remained of their discipline. They were such grievous enemies to themselves that, although they had already been overthrown by foreign enemies, they were being overthrown still more by themselves.

It is mournful to report what we saw: honored old men, decrepit Christians, serving gluttony and wantonness while the city’s destruction was already imminent. What should be accused first here? That they were honored, or old, or Christians, or endangered? Who could believe that such things could occur—among old men in security, among children in danger, or ever among Christians?

They lay at banquets, forgetful of their honor, forgetful of their age, forgetful of their profession, forgetful of their own name: the leaders of the city, stuffed with food, loosened by drunkenness, frantic with shouting, mad with revelry, displaying nothing less than their senses—indeed, because they were almost constantly such, displaying nothing more than their senses.

But although this was so, what I am about to say is far worse: not even the destruction of the cities put an end to this ruin.

Finally, the most prosperous city of Gaul was captured four times.

[Note: It was formerly read: “The most prosperous city of the Gauls, Trier, was captured.” But since it was established that *Trier* was a gloss that entered the text from the margin of the book, we have rightly judged that it should be removed. The following words support this correction: “It is obvious which one I mean.” Thus it is read in the Corbie manuscript, while the Colbert manuscript and the editions have “about which.” Salvian originally wrote: “Finally, the most prosperous city of Gaul was captured four times. It is obvious which one I mean.” It is as though he were saying: “There is no need for me to name it, since you understand which city I mean when I say ‘the most prosperous of the cities of Gaul,’ and since its disaster is so recent that it can be unknown to no one.” Hence someone studying the book added *Trier* in the margin. An unskilled copyist later inserted the word into the text. Salvian himself bears witness above, p. 123, to the fourfold destruction of Augusta of the Treveri, calling it “the most distinguished city.” And on p. 137, speaking of the same city, he says: “Because three destructions had not corrected you, you deserved to perish a fourth time.” The distinguished Hadrianus Valesius, in Book III of *Frankish History*, p. 113, believes that Colonia Augusta Treverorum was captured for the fourth time by the Franks around the seventeenth year of Valentinian’s reign, under King Chlodio.]
