The first captivity should surely have sufficed as a correction, so that a renewed outbreak of sins would not have renewed the destruction. But what more need be said? What I am saying is incredible. There, the constant recurrence of calamities became an increase of crimes.

Just as, according to the stories, the serpent-like monster multiplied whenever it was struck down, so in that most distinguished city of Gaul crimes increased through the very blows by which they were being restrained. You might think that punishment for their crimes had become, as it were, the mother of their vices.

And what more need be said? Through the multiplication of evils sprouting up daily, matters reached such a point that it was easier for that city to exist without an inhabitant than for almost any inhabitant to exist without crime.

So much for that city. What of another city not far away, but nearly equal to it in magnificence?

[Note: That is, Colonia Agrippina, as Hadrianus Valesius believes.]

Was there not the same ruin of both possessions and morals? For, apart from the other things, when everything had collapsed under the two chief and general evils prevailing there—avarice and drunkenness—their rabid thirst for wine finally reached such a point that the city’s leaders did not rise from their banquets even when the enemy had already entered the city.

Thus God clearly, as I believe, wished to show them why they were perishing: they were practicing, while they perished, the very thing through which they had come to ultimate destruction.

I saw there pitiable scenes: nothing, in effect, distinguished boys from old men. There was one scurrility, one frivolity. Everything was done together: luxury, drinking, ruin. All alike played, became drunk, and were destroyed; they indulged at banquets—old men and honored men—almost too weak for living, yet extremely strong for wine; weak for walking, vigorous for drinking; staggering in their steps, agile for dancing.

And what more need be said? Through all the things I have described, they sank to such a depth that the saying of sacred Scripture was fulfilled in them: “Wine and women make apostates of God” (Ecclesiasticus 19:2). While they drank, played, committed adultery, and raged, they began to deny Christ.

And do we wonder, after all this, that they suffered the ruin of their possessions, when they had fallen in their minds long before? Let no one therefore think that that city perished only through its physical destruction. Wherever such things were practiced, they had already perished before they perished.

## XIV

I have spoken of the most distinguished cities. What of the remaining cities in the various parts of Gaul? Did they not collapse under similar vices among their inhabitants? Their crimes had so weighed upon them that they did not even fear their own danger.

Their capture was foreseen, but not feared. For fear had been removed from sinners, so that it could no longer serve as a safeguard. Thus, although the barbarians were almost before everyone’s eyes, there was no fear among the people and no guarding of the cities.

Such was the blindness of their souls—or rather, of their sins—that although no one undoubtedly wished to perish, no one nevertheless did anything to prevent his perishing. Everything was possessed by carelessness and sluggishness, everything by negligence and gluttony, everything by drunkenness and drowsiness, in accordance with what is written of such people: “For the sleep of the Lord had fallen upon them” (1 Samuel 26:12).

Sleep is poured upon them so that destruction may follow. For when, as it is written (Genesis 18:20), a sinner has completed his iniquities and thereby deserves to perish, providence is taken away from him, so that the one destined to perish may not escape.

But enough of this. I have, I think, clearly demonstrated what I proposed: that not even in the utmost crisis of their circumstances did the vices of the citizens ever cease, right up to the destruction of their cities.

## XV

Perhaps these things existed in the past but no longer exist, or perhaps they have at some time ceased to exist. Certainly, if even today some city or province is either struck by heavenly blows or devastated by enemy plunder, it is humbled, converted, and corrected. In reality, nearly all the peoples of the Roman name perish before they are corrected; the vices perish within them only after the people themselves have perished.

This can be proved briefly by the destruction, through three successive devastations, of the greatest city of Gaul, when the entire city became a tomb and evils continued to grow even after its destruction.

[Note: That is, the city of Trier, as Valesius correctly explains. At the same time Cassian, in Book I of *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 2, referring to the same city of Trier, thought it sufficient to call it “the greatest city of the Belgae.”]

Those whom the enemy had not killed in the destruction were overwhelmed by calamity after the destruction. What had escaped death in the destruction did not survive calamity afterward.

Some were killed by wounds driven too deeply into them and prolonged deaths; others, burned by the flames of the enemy, were tortured even after the flames had gone. Some died of hunger, others of nakedness; some wasted away, others froze. Thus they rushed toward a single end, death, through various forms of dying.

And what more need be said? Other cities too were afflicted by the destruction of one city. Everywhere lay corpses of both sexes—naked, mangled, defiling the eyes of the city, torn apart by birds and dogs. There was pestilence among the living and the stench of the dead. Death was breathed forth from death.

Thus even those who had not been present at the destruction of the city described above suffered the evils of another’s destruction. And what after this, I ask—what after all these things? Who could estimate this kind of madness?

The few nobles who had survived the destruction were asking the emperors for circus games, as though these were the supreme remedy for the ruined city.

[Note: That is, from Honorius and Constantius, as Valesius explains.]

I wish that at this point I had eloquence equal to the task of expressing the indignity of these things—eloquence with as much force in its complaint as there is grief in the matter itself.

Who could estimate what should first be accused in those whom we have described: irreligion, stupidity, luxury, or madness? Everything is present in them.

What is more irreligious than to request something as an insult against God? What more foolish than not to consider what one is requesting? What is more depravedly luxurious than to desire luxurious things amid mourning? What is more insane than to be amid evils and have no understanding of evils?

Yet among all these things, madness is the least deserving of blame, because there is no guilt of the will where the offense is committed in frenzy. All the more, therefore, must those of whom we speak be accused, because they were sane while behaving insanely.

So you ask for circus games, people of Trier—and you ask for them after being devastated and conquered, after disaster, bloodshed, punishment, captivity, and so many destructions of your city?

What is more mournful than this stupidity, what more grievous than this madness? I confess that I thought you most wretched when you suffered your destructions; but I see that you are more wretched now that you ask for spectacles. I had thought that in your destructions you had lost only your possessions and substance; I did not know that you had also lost your judgment and understanding.

You seek theatres, then, and ask your rulers for a circus? For whom, I ask, for what people, for what city? For a city burned and ruined, for a people captive and slaughtered, which has either perished or is mourning; and whatever remains of it is wholly calamity—oppressed by grief, exhausted by tears, or crushed by bereavement. In it you can scarcely know whose lot is worse and harder, that of the dead or of the living.

The sufferings of the survivors are so great that they have surpassed the misery of the dead.

You ask for public entertainments, people of Trier? Where, I ask, are they to be held? On the tombs and ashes, over the bones and blood of the slain? What part of the city is free from all these evils?

Where has blood not been poured out? Where are there no bodies laid low, no mangled limbs of the slaughtered?

Everywhere is the face of a captured city; everywhere the horror of captivity; everywhere the image of death. The wretched remnants of the people lie upon the tombs of their dead, and you ask for circus games?

The city is black with fire, and you assume an expression of festivity? Everything mourns, while you rejoice. Moreover, through the most shameful enticements you provoke God and, through the worst superstitions, stir up the anger of the Godhead.

I am not surprised—certainly I am not surprised—that the evils which followed came upon you. Because three destructions had not corrected you, you deserved to perish a fourth time.

### XVI

All these matters, however, have been set forth at somewhat greater length for this reason: namely, to demonstrate that everything we have endured was borne not through God’s lack of foresight or neglect of us, but through justice, judgment, the fairest dispensation, and a most fitting recompense; and that no part whatsoever of the Roman world or Roman name, however severely struck by heavenly blows, has ever been corrected. Therefore we in no way deserve prosperity, because we are not corrected by adversity.

Although good things are sometimes granted even to us who are unworthy—because the Lord is good, like a most indulgent father, and although he sometimes permits us to be humbled for our sins, nevertheless does not allow us to remain afflicted for long—for this reason he now chastises his own with harsh circumstances for discipline, and now cherishes them with tranquil circumstances for indulgence.

For just as the best and most skilled physicians provide different treatments for different illnesses, helping some with sweet medicines and others with bitter ones; curing some by the burning of cauteries, others by the soothing application of poultices; applying to some a harsh surgical incision, and pouring upon others the gentle softness of oil; and yet, although the treatments are utterly different, the same health is sought through them all—[Col. 0126D] so also our God, whenever he restrains us with harsher blows, cures us as though with cauteries and incisions; but when he refreshes us with prosperity, he consoles us as though with oil and poultices. Through the varied assistance of his medicines he wishes to lead us to one health.

[Note: Pliny, Book I, Letter 8: “Healthy physicians accompany foods that are beneficial but lacking in pleasure with more agreeable words.”]

[Note: The editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius have *sectionem* (“incision”); the Pithoean edition has *praesectionem* (“pre-incision”); the Colbertinus manuscript has *prosectionem*. Both printed forms are incorrect. The Corbeiensis manuscript is correct, having *prosectionem*. Freinshemius advises that the same reading should be adopted in Tacitus, Book XVI of the *Annals*, where he speaks of Thrasea: “and when the veins of both arms had been cut,” though the common reading is “and when the veins of both arms had been stretched out.”]

Even the most wicked slaves, whom punishments have not corrected, are often corrected by kindness; and those whom blows had not subjected to their masters are subjected by benefactions. Infants and nearly all obstinate little children whom threats and the rod do not make obedient are sometimes drawn to obedience by universal remedies and caresses. From this we must understand that we are more wicked than the wickedest slaves and more foolish than foolish children: neither do tortures correct us, as they would bad slaves, nor do kindnesses convert us, as they would infants.

### XVII

Indeed, we have now sufficiently demonstrated, I believe, how no part of the Roman name has been corrected by punishment. It remains to show how neither God’s gifts nor his kindnesses correct us.

What are God’s gifts and kindnesses? What else, surely, than our peace, our repose, and the tranquility of prosperity that serves our desires and pleasures? Since the matter requires it, let us say something specific as well.

Whenever, therefore, we are in fear, distress, or danger—when cities are besieged by enemies, provinces are devastated by plundering, or the members of the state are being cut down by whatever adversities—and we beseech the aid of the heavenly hand; if, through some help of sacred mercy, cities have been saved, devastation brought to an end, hostile armies routed, and all fear removed by the gift of Divinity, what do we do immediately afterward? I suppose we strive to repay the Lord our God for the benefits we have received from him with worship, honor, and reverence.

[Col. 0127D] This is what follows naturally; and human custom also requires that gratitude be returned to those who lend favors, and that those who give gifts receive a corresponding return. Thus, perhaps, we act, and at least by human standards render recompense to our God: when we receive good things from him, we return good things.

We immediately run, of course, to the Lord’s houses; we prostrate our bodies on the ground; with joy mingled with tears, we offer supplications; we illuminate the thresholds with sacred gifts; we fill the altars with offerings. And because we ourselves are joyful through his gift, we also clothe his temples in the appearance of our festivity. Or else—which is no less pleasing to him—we renounce the former vices of our life, slaughter the victims of good works, and sacrifice offerings of a new way of life in return for our new joys. Finally, we declare holy war against every impurity, flee the madness of the circuses, curse the indecencies of theatrical games, vow a new life to the Lord, and sacrifice ourselves to God in order to obtain his protection forever.

[Note: This passage alone is sufficient against those who deny that resources should be contributed for the adornment of temples and teach that they should be distributed to the poor, who are the living temples of Christ. The needs of the poor must be relieved. Who denies this? Nevertheless, the house of God must not be neglected. See the notes on Agobard, p. 77.]

### XVIII

Since, then, these things we have described ought to be done in response to God’s recent benefits, let us see what actually is done. People immediately run to the games; they rush headlong into madness; the population pours into the theaters; the entire populace revels in the circuses.

He grants us good things so that we may be good. We, on the contrary, whenever we receive good things, increase our evils. He calls us through his benefits to uprightness; we rush into wickedness. Through his benefits he urges us to remorse; we rush into dissipation. He calls us to chastity; we rush into impurity. In splendid fashion, clearly, we respond to his sacred gifts. In splendid fashion we acknowledge and honor his gifts—we who repay him with as many insults as the benefits we receive from him.

Or is this perhaps not an insult to God? Or could anything be more disgraceful? Or is there need of many and great things? But because, through the old and deep stain of every evil within us, we can no longer be vicious in any other way than by ceasing altogether to exist—

[Note: Brassicanus and Galesinius printed this passage as follows: “Or is this perhaps not an insult to God, or could it be more disgraceful, or would many and great remedies be required? But because, through the old and deep stain of every evil within us, we can no longer be vicious in any other way than by ceasing altogether to exist.”]

—what hope, I ask, is there in us for good fruit?

Those who sin through ignorance are corrected once their error is recognized. Those who lack religion, when they change their sect, begin to change their discipline. Finally, as I have said, those who are corrupted either by excessive abundance or by security cease to be depraved when they cease to be secure.

We, however, do not fall through ignorance, nor do we lack religion, nor are we corrupted by prosperity and security. Everything is, in fact, the opposite. We know religion; we cannot plead ignorance; we do not possess the peace and riches of former times. Everything that once existed has either been taken away or changed; only the vices have grown.

Nothing remains to us of our former peace and prosperity except those crimes alone which brought about the absence of prosperity.

Where, indeed, are the ancient wealth and dignities of the Romans? Once the Romans were exceedingly brave; now they are without strength. The ancient Romans were feared; we are afraid. The peoples of the barbarians paid taxes to them; we pay taxes to the barbarians. Our enemies sell us the privilege of daylight. Virtually our entire safety consists in a commercial transaction.

O our miseries! To what have we come! And for this we give thanks to the barbarians, from whom we buy ourselves at a price? What could be more degraded or more wretched for us? And do we believe that we live after such things, when our life is maintained in this manner?

Moreover, we ourselves make ourselves ridiculous: we call the gold that we pay “gifts.”

[Note: Isaac Casaubon brilliantly illuminates this passage in his notes on Spartianus, at the passage in the *Life of Hadrian* where Hadrian complained about reduced pay.]

We say that what is a price is a gift—and indeed a price for the harshest and most wretched condition. All captives, once they have been ransomed, enjoy freedom. We are always being ransomed, and are never free.

The barbarians deal with us in the manner of those masters who hire out slaves unnecessary for their services in return for wages to be paid. For likewise we are never free from this service that we pay for. We continually pay the fees for this very purpose: so that we may pay without ceasing.

[Note: The following two books are thoroughly disordered in the edition of Brassicanus, so that passages belonging to the seventh are sometimes read in the eighth. Balduinus made a similar complaint concerning the third book of Optatus of Milevis. Galesinius therefore restored everything to its proper order in Salvianus.]

## BOOK SEVEN

### I

Since, in the conclusion of this little work, which has now ended, I have said something about the weakness and misery of the Romans, we may perhaps seem to have said something contrary to the matter we are now treating. For I know that someone might object here that this most clearly proves that God does not regard human affairs: once the Romans were pagans, yet they conquered and ruled; now they are Christians, yet they are conquered and serve.

The statements made earlier about almost all pagan peoples could indeed be sufficient to refute this objection: namely, that those who knowingly neglect God’s law sin more than those who fail to observe it through ignorance.

Nevertheless, if God grants his favor, when we come to that part of our subject in which something will be said about the ancient Romans, we shall clearly demonstrate, by divine favor, that the Lord’s favor toward them was then just, just as his severity toward us is now just; and that it was then worthy of God to raise the Romans up by his aid, just as it is now worthy that we are punished.

Would that the punishment itself were beneficial! That is much more grievous and lamentable: that after punishment there is no correction.

The Lord wishes to cure us through his chastisements, but remedies do not follow the treatment. What kind of evil is this? Animals and beasts are cured by incision; and when the rotten entrails of mules, asses, and swine have been burned with cauteries, they recognize the benefit of the medical burning. As soon as the corruption of their diseased bodies has been either burned away or cut out, living flesh takes the place of the dead.

We are both burned and cut, but we are healed neither by the incision of the knife nor by the burning of cauteries. Indeed, what is more serious, we become worse through the treatment itself. Therefore it is not without reason that what commonly happens to beasts and animals has happened to us—those that carry incurable diseases. For throughout all the regions of the world, because we are not corrected by healing treatments, we are brought to an end by death and slaughter.

Look, then, without repeating what I said long ago, at this very matter that I mentioned a little earlier: that we are at once wretched and luxurious. Let it be granted that these are the vices of the fortunate—although no one can be both disgraceful and happy, since where there is no true moral goodness there is no true happiness—but nevertheless, as I said above, let it be granted that these are the vices of long peace and prosperous security.

Why, I ask, are they present where there is now no peace and no security? For throughout almost the entire Roman world there is neither peace nor security.

[Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript reads this way, whereas the Colbertinus manuscript and the editions of Galesinius and Pithoeus have *urbe Romana* (“in the Roman city”). This is entirely wrong. Pithoeus himself correctly observed that *orbe Romano* (“throughout the Roman world”) should be restored. A different error occurs on pp. 155 and 156, where *de urbe* (“from the city”) was read instead of *de orbe* (“from the world”) and *in urbem* (“into the city”) instead of *in orbem* (“into the world”). This error arose because ancient copyists often confused the letters *o* and *u*, as those who handle handwritten books know. But this confusion is not found only in writers of a later age: ancient inscriptions preserved by Gruterus and elsewhere also contain this interchange of letters. Thus, on an ancient stone from Narbo, Rusticus, bishop of that city, is called the nephew on his sister’s side of Bishop Arator. Quintilian, moreover, writes in Book I, chapter 4 of the *Institutes*: “What if *o* and *u* were interchanged, so that they wrote *Hecoba* and *notrix*, *Chulcides* and *Pulixena*?” And lest this be noted only in Greek words, there are also *dederont* and *probaveront*. See the notes on Letter 115 of Lupus of Ferrières.]

Why do the vices alone endure? Who, I ask, could tolerate lustfulness in a destitute person? Luxurious poverty is more criminal; and “a wretched fool” is more odious still (Ecclesiasticus 25:4).

The entire Roman world is both wretched and luxurious. Who, I ask, is poor and foolish, yet thinks about the circus while awaiting captivity? Who fears death and laughs? We play while in fear of captivity, and laugh while placed in fear of death.

You might think that the entire Roman people has been filled, as it were, with Sardonic herbs.



It dies, and laughs. Therefore, throughout nearly every part of the world, our laughter is followed by tears; and our Lord’s saying has now come upon us: “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25).

### II

But perhaps, since we have spoken at such length about public amusements and indecencies, someone thinks that we are worse than the barbarians only in this respect: they do not engage in such things, whereas we do; but that we are not similarly polluted by the crime of carnal lust and the mire of deadly fornication.

Let us compare the Romans with the other nations in this respect as well. And indeed, I do not know whether they can be compared more appropriately with anyone than with those whom God placed in the very heart of the state and made the sole possessors and masters of the Roman lands.

Therefore, although nothing can be disputed concerning God’s judgment, since he has taken away from us the finest part of our lawful possessions and given it to the barbarians, let us see whether he seems to have transferred to them, by a just judgment, what he took from us.

No one doubts that the Aquitanians and the Novempopulans possessed nearly the marrow of all Gaul and the breast of its entire fertility—not fertility alone, but also what is sometimes preferred to fertility: pleasure, delight, and beauty.

There every region was almost entirely either woven with vineyards, flowering with meadows, patterned with cultivated fields, planted with orchards, beautified by groves, watered by springs, or spread through with rivers; so that the possessors and masters of that land seemed truly to have possessed not merely a portion of this soil, but an image of paradise.

What, then, should have followed all this? Without doubt, they ought to have been more devoted to God, since God had enriched them in a special way with the exceedingly abundant endowment of his benefits.

For what is more proper or more fitting than that those to whom the Lord seemed, through his gifts, to have wished especially to show favor should in turn have pleased the Lord more especially through worship and religion—particularly since God demands from us nothing burdensome and nothing difficult?

He does not call us to plows or mattocks; not to cleave the earth or dig vineyards; nor, finally, does he demand from his servants what we demand from ours. For what does he say?

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

The Lord does not therefore call us to labor, but to refreshment. What does he demand from us, what does he command us to offer him, except only faith, chastity, humility, sobriety, mercy, and holiness—things that do not burden us, but adorn us?

Not only this: they adorn the present life so that they may adorn the future life still more.

O good, O loving, O Lord of immeasurable mercy, who for this reason grants us the gifts of religion in the present, so that afterward he may reward in us the very gifts that he now grants!

All the Aquitanians, therefore, ought unquestionably to have been such people. Indeed, as we have said, they ought to have been especially such because they possessed God’s special gifts.

And what followed all this? What came next? Nothing except the complete opposite. For throughout all Gaul, just as they were first in wealth, so they were first in vices. Nowhere was pleasure more depraved, nowhere life more polluted, nowhere discipline more corrupt.

In place of sacred gifts they offered the Lord this recompense: to the extent that he had drawn them to himself through his benefits so that they might propitiate him, to that same extent they labored through their crimes to provoke him.

### III

Or is this perhaps false, and said more out of envy than truth?

[Note: We have followed the edition of Galesinius. Brassicanus had: “I shall not use the oratorical proof that others employ in legal cases, bringing forward as witnesses whatever persons they wish,” and so forth. Pithoeus had: “I do not use the approval of the matter that others employ in legal cases: that is,” and so forth. The Corbeiensis manuscript had: “I do not know from the proof that,” and so forth.]

I shall not use the oratorical proof that others employ in legal cases, bringing forward as witnesses either a few people, or outsiders, or witnesses of lesser suitability, in order to prove the matter. Let us question the people who actually carried out these deeds. We have spoken falsely if they deny it.

They confess it—and what is more serious, they confess it without grieving in the very act of confession. Their present attitude in confessing is the same as it was when they were committing these deeds. Just as they were not ashamed then to commit crimes, so now they do not regret having done disgraceful things.

Except, however, for a very few holy and distinguished men who, as one of their own number said, “redeemed their crimes by scattering money”; except, I say, for those whom I have mentioned—we rightly believe that even amid that general and overwhelming flood of vices, they were guilty of lesser crimes, since they deserved to be corrected by Divinity.

For one does not utterly injure his master when pardon remains in reserve. And what more need I say? I think that he always regarded God, even in his error, since he was able to obtain from him the grace not to remain in error longer.

But the rest, and nearly all the greater number, including the most noble—almost all alike—were nearly one whirlpool, the gluttony of all; nearly one brothel, the life of all.

And what shall I say about brothels? I think even a brothel is a lesser crime. The prostitutes who are there do not know the marriage covenant, and therefore they do not defile what they do not know. They are guilty of the offense of sexual immorality, but they are not held liable for adultery.

Add to this that there are scarcely many brothels, and scarcely many prostitutes who condemn themselves to that most wretched life.

[Note: Brassicanus had: “And few are those who live this most wretched life in them.” The reading concerning the prostitutes among the Aquitanians was rejected: “but where is that city in the wealthy part,” and so forth. Galesinius had: “And few are the prostitutes who have condemned themselves to this most wretched life in them. Among the Aquitanians, however, what city in its wealthy part,” and so forth. This is also the reading of the Pithoean edition and the Corbeiensis manuscript.]

Among the Aquitanians, however, what city in its wealthiest and noblest part was not like a brothel? What powerful or wealthy man did not live in the mud of lust? Who did not plunge himself into the abyss of the most filthy defilement? Who kept faith with his wife?

[Col. 0132D] Indeed, as far as passive submission to lust is concerned, who did not reduce his wife to the number of servant women and lower the sacraments of venerable marriage to such a degree that, in his household, no woman appeared more degraded through marital contempt than the woman who was foremost in the dignity of marriage?

[Note: The famous saying of Aelius Verus in Spartianus recurs here: “Wife is a name of dignity, not of pleasure.”]

### IV

Someone may perhaps think that matters were not entirely as I describe them: that the matrons there possessed their lawful rights and retained the honor and authority of wives. That is true. Many of them indeed possessed their full rights of dominion, but scarcely any possessed an undefiled right of marriage.

And we are not now asking what power the women possessed, but how corrupt the discipline of the men was. Yet I would not say that the matrons there even possessed full authority, because whoever does not possess the right of marriage inviolate and secure does not possess secure authority either.

A matron is not far removed from the status of a servant woman when the master of the household is the husband of servant women. Which wealthy Aquitanian was not such a man? Which one was not legally called by his shameless servant women either their adulterer or their husband?

For they were made like stallions among females, as the prophet says. “Each man neighed after his neighbor’s wife” (Jeremiah 5:8).

And those about whom we read these things were perhaps sinning with a lesser offense and, as I think, with fewer offenses and less sexual licentiousness. But these men, truly like stallions, neighed not merely after a few but nearly after all their female slaves—that is, as though after their own herds. Raging with the frenzy of heated lust, like those beasts called the husbands of herds, they rushed upon whichever woman the burning fury of their shamelessness first drew them toward.

Here I ask the wise: since such things were occurring, what do they think the households there were like, where such men were heads of households? How great was the corruption of the servants where the corruption of the masters was so great?

For when the head is diseased, nothing is healthy, and no member at all performs its proper function when the principal part is unsound. In his own household the master is, as it were, the head of his body, and his life is the standard by which all live.

The worst aspect of this matter is that everyone more readily follows what is worse; and bad training more easily corrupts the good than good training reforms the bad.

Moreover, when even good and honorable masters cannot make their servants good, how great do we suppose the stain of the households must have been where the masters were examples of impurity?

There the evil was not merely an example, but also a kind of force and necessity, because female servants were compelled to obey their most shameless masters against their will, and the lust of those in authority was the necessity of those subject to them.

From this one can understand what a mire of unchaste filth there was, where women could not be chaste under the most impure masters, even if they had wished to be.

### V

But surely this is difficult to prove, and no traces at all remain of the shameful acts and crimes of the past.

Look: even now many of them, although they lack a homeland and live in poverty in comparison with their former wealth, are almost worse than they were before. Worse, moreover, in more than one way: for even if they do the same things they did before, they are worse in this very respect, because they do not cease from crime.

Their offenses, even if they are not greater in kind, are nevertheless more numerous; and thus, although they do not increase through the novelty of their crimes, they are heaped up through their number.

Add that, as I said, they now do these things as old men; add that they do them as poor men. Both are an increase of guilt. For it is less astonishing for young men to sin, and for the wealthy to sin.

What hope or remedy is there, then, in people who are recalled from their customary impurity neither by the poverty of their miseries nor by the extremity of life?

[Note: This thought generally enters the minds of the young. “Let us use our better years,” they say, “while fate allows it. A long succession of years remains. In old age we shall correct whatever offense has been accumulated.” Certainly this is an impious thought, yet in some way it is tolerable if a person had a certain hope of long life. But what Cicero observed is most true: death threatens daily because of uncertain accidents, and because of the brevity of life it can never be far away. Thus death overtakes many who are still very young, and very many in the middle span of sound adulthood. Therefore the judgment of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, must be followed. His words are these: “For if we reserve the final period of our life for doing penance or redeeming our sins and crimes, we must fear that perhaps unexpected death may overtake us and not allow us to reach that sudden time of repentance to which, with deadly security, we wish to reserve ourselves. And therefore let us fear what is written: ‘Do not delay turning to the Lord,’ and so forth.” Augustine speaks excellently in Homily 41: “But if someone placed in the final crisis of his illness wishes to receive penance, and receives it, and is immediately reconciled, and departs from this life—I confess to you, we do not deny him what he asks, but we do not presume that he departs well.”]

Even if some foolish presumption of long life or hope of repentance to be undertaken someday consoles them, is it not a new kind of monstrosity for some people to remain vicious even in death?

Since this is so, is there anything more that can be said? Yet we add still this: many commit these acts even today while situated among enemies, captive amid daily danger and fear; and although they were handed over by God to the barbarians because of their most impure life, they do not abandon those impurities even among the barbarians.

### VI

But perhaps the enemies among whom they live are such that these things please them, and that they are gravely offended if, while they themselves are impure, they see the Romans to be chaste.

Even if this were so, another person’s wickedness ought not to make us wicked, because it is more fitting for every human being to benefit himself by being good than another by being evil. We must labor more to please God through moral purity than human beings through impurity.

Thus, even if someone lives among impure barbarians, he ought nevertheless to pursue the chastity that benefits him rather than the impurity that pleases impure enemies.

But what is added to our evils? We are impure among chaste barbarians. I say even more: the barbarians themselves are offended by our impurities.

Among the Goths, no Gothic fornicator is permitted to exist; only the Romans among them are permitted, by the prejudice associated with their nation and name, to be impure.

And what hope, I ask, do we have before God? We love impurity; the Goths curse it. We flee purity; they love it. Fornication among them is a crime and a danger; among us it is an honor.

And we think that we can stand before God; we think that we can be saved, when every criminal act of impurity and every shame of unchastity is admitted by the Romans and punished by the barbarians?

Here I ask those who think us better than the barbarians: let them say what even a very few Goths do of these things, or what all—or nearly all—the Romans do not do of them.

And do we wonder that the lands of either the Aquitanians or all our people have been given by God to the barbarians, when the lands that the Romans had polluted through fornication are now cleansed by the barbarians through chastity?

### VII

But perhaps this applies only to the Aquitanians? Let us pass also to other parts of the world, lest we seem to have spoken only about the Gauls.

What of Spain? Did not the same, or perhaps even greater, vices destroy it? Even if heavenly wrath had handed the Spanish lands over to any other barbarians, the enemies of purity would have endured punishments worthy of their crimes.

But this was added to make the condemnation of their unchastity evident: they were handed over especially to the Vandals—that is, to chaste barbarians.

Through the captivity of the Spaniards God wished to show doubly how much he hated the lust of the flesh and loved chastity: he both elevated the Vandals chiefly because of their chastity and subdued the Spaniards chiefly because of their unchastity.

For what of it? Were there not stronger barbarians throughout the whole world to whom Spain could have been handed over? There were many—indeed, if I am not mistaken, all of them.

But for this reason he handed everything over to the weakest enemies, to show clearly that strength has no power, but the cause does; and that we were then overwhelmed not by the courage of once most cowardly enemies, but conquered solely by the impurity of our own vices.

Thus that saying of the Lord to the Jews has truly come upon us: “According to their uncleannesses and according to their iniquities I dealt with them, and I turned my face away from them” (Ezekiel 39:24).

[Col. 0135C] And elsewhere to that same people: “The Lord will bring against you a nation from afar” (Deuteronomy 28:49); and, he says, “with the hooves of their horses they will trample all your streets, and they will kill your people with the sword” (Ezekiel 26:11).

Everything, therefore, that the divine word foretold has been fulfilled against us, and the punishment of all has paid the price for the force of the heavenly words.

### VIII

Yet, although almost all the barbarian peoples have drunk Roman blood and torn apart our entrails, why is it that our God has given the greatest wealth of the state and the richest peoples of the Roman name chiefly into the power of enemies who were once exceedingly cowardly?

Why? Surely so that we might recognize what I said above: that this was a matter of merit, not strength; and so that this very fact might become our humiliation and punishment—that we were handed over to the weakest, and might thus recognize the blow of the heavenly hand, since we were subdued not by the strongest enemies, but by the weakest.

For we read that whenever God wished his great works to be clearly understood as accomplished by him, the deed was performed either through a few people or through the weak, lest the work of the heavenly right hand be attributed to human strength.

For this reason the commander Sisera, whom the Hebrew army feared, was struck down by a woman (Judges 4:21); Abimelech, the conqueror of cities, was struck by a woman’s hand (Judges 9:53); and the armored ranks of the Assyrians fell with the aid of a widow (Judith 13:10).

And lest I speak only of women: Ben-hadad, king of Syria (1 Kings 20:1–20), to whom, besides countless thousands of his people, thirty-two kings and armies of the same number were subject—did not the Lord wish him to be defeated by a few attendants of the princes, so that it might be known who was the author of such a victory?

Against the Midianites also, who, as the Book of Judges reports (Judges 7:12 ff.), had filled everything like locusts, Gideon was ordered to fight with a few men—not because he did not have more in his army, but he was forbidden to lead many into battle, lest the multitude be able to claim something for itself from the victory.

When he had therefore gathered thirty thousand armed men, the Lord spoke to him in this way: “The people with you are too numerous, and Midian will not be delivered into his hands.”

And what happened next? To the man who was about to fight against countless thousands of barbarians, he left only three hundred men.

For he ordered the army to be reduced to such a small number that the few could claim nothing for themselves from the work of war accomplished by God.

Finally, the Lord himself made clear why he acted in this way, saying: “Let Israel not boast against me and say, ‘I was delivered by my own strength.’”

Let all the wicked hear this, I say; let all the presumptuous hear it; let the powerful hear it; let everyone hear what God says:

“Let Israel not boast against me and say, ‘I was delivered by my own strength.’”

## IX

Let all who utter hostile and blasphemous boasts hear this, I say; let those who place their hope in human beings hear it. God says that all who presume they can be delivered by their own strength are speaking against him. Yet what Roman does not speak thus, what Roman does not think thus? Who among our party does not almost continually blaspheme in this regard? Everyone knows that the state now has no strength; yet even so we do not acknowledge to whose gifts we owe the fact that we are still alive.

For whenever God grants us some prosperity beyond our hope and merit, one person attributes it to fortune, another to chance, another to the arrangements of commanders, another to counsel, another to a teacher, another to patronage—no one to God. And do we wonder if the heavenly hand does not grant us something, when we diminish whatever it has granted?

[Col. 0136D] What else are we doing when we assign the good things he provides either to the workings of chance, or to the abilities of commanders, or to any other trifling causes? In this way we ought also to thank the earth because we reap our yearly crops, the vineyards because we harvest grapes, the sea because we catch fish, the forests because we cut timber, the sheep because we are clothed in wool, and the other livestock because we are filled with meat. For what reason is there for us to wish to be grateful to him for some gifts, while we take away the credit for his greatest benefits? Or what person of our condition would be satisfied if someone credited him with a gift while deducting the greater part from his gifts?

So too with us: although we give God no thanks worthily for anything, it would still have been little enough if we wished to be grateful to him only for the things he has given us for the use of living. Why do we take away from him the gratitude due for the fact that he helps us in straits, delivers us in dangers, and preserves us by continual protection even though we are situated amid barbarian peoples?

But the Goths do not act thus, nor the Vandals—though they have been instructed by bad teachers, they are nevertheless better than our people in this respect also. I suspect that some are offended by what we say; but since truth must be considered more than offense, I shall say it, and say it often: the Goths do not act thus, nor the Vandals. When placed in danger, they ask help from God, and they call their successes a gift of divinity.

Our misfortune, which occurred most recently, proved this. When the Goths were afraid, we presumed to place our hope in the Huns, while they placed theirs in God. When peace was requested by them, it was refused by us; they sent bishops, while we drove them away; they honored God even in foreign priests, while we despised him even in our own.

[Note: That is, in Catholic priests. For the Goths were Arians. It is established that, with the exception of King Euric, the Goths inflicted violence on no one in Gaul on account of religion. See Cassiodorus, Book VIII, *Variae*, letter 24.]

[Col. 0137B] [Note: Hadrianus Valesius notes that this was characteristic of the people in the third book of his *History of the Franks*, p. 142.]

The outcome of events corresponded to the conduct of each side. To them victory was granted in the midst of the greatest fear; to us confusion in the midst of the greatest arrogance. Thus it was truly demonstrated both in us then and in them that saying of our Lord: “For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11). Exaltation was given to them for their humility; to us, humiliation for our arrogance.

## X

And so this was recognized by that commander of our party who, having presumed that on the very day he would enter as victor the same enemy city, entered it as a captive.

[Note: Litorius, second in authority to Aetius, was in command of the Hunnic auxiliaries. Trusting in the deceptive and empty responses of the haruspices, he had besieged Toulouse, the capital of the Gothic kingdom, in the year 439. See Rittershusius on this passage, Sirmond in the notes to the *Panegyric of Avitus*, and Hadrianus Valesius in the same third book, p. 141.]

He plainly proved what the prophet said: “A man’s way is not his own, nor is it the man’s to walk and direct his steps” (Proverbs XVI, 9; XX, 24). Because he considered his way subject to his own control, he had neither a rightly directed step nor found the way of salvation: “Contempt was poured out upon the prince,” as we read; “he was led astray in a trackless place and not on the way” (Psalm CVI, 40); and “he was brought to nothing, like water running away” (Psalm LVII, 8).

In him, apart from the very misfortune of the events, God’s present judgment was made evident: whatever he had arrogated to himself as something he would do, he himself suffered. Because he believed that he would capture the enemy without divine assistance and God’s command, he himself was captured. He arrogated to himself the height of counsel and wisdom, and incurred the disgrace of rashness. The bonds he had prepared for others, he himself endured.

And what, I ask, could have been a clearer judgment of God than that a man who trusted as a plunderer should become the booty; that one who presumed to triumph should become the triumph; that he should be surrounded, seized, bound, carry his arms twisted behind his back, see the hands he had thought warlike fettered, become a spectacle for boys and women, behold barbarians mocking him, endure the ridicule of people of both sexes, and, though he had possessed the greatest pride of a brave man, suffer the death of a coward?

[Col. 0137D] Would that this itself had been a brief remedy for his sufferings, rather than a daily endurance. But, as regards the length of his punishments,

[Note: Brassicanus and Galesinius read “length.”]

[Note: In contrast, Idatius says in his *Chronicle* that Litorius was killed a few days after he was captured.]

[Col. 0138A] he was consumed over a long period by the prolonged wasting-away of the barbarian prison and reduced to this misery: something which people generally consider even more grievous and bitter than the punishments themselves—he fell under the pity of his enemies.

And why was this? Why, without doubt, except because, as I have already said, they were humble before God while we were rebellious; they believed that victory was in God’s hand, while we believed it was in our own hand—or rather, in a sacrilegious and impious hand, which is worse and more harmful than our own?

[Col. 0138B] Finally, the enemy king himself—Theodoric, who ruled the Goths, the enemies of Rome, so that no one should think that the passage concerns the Huns—

[Note: Theodoric, who ruled the Goths, Rome’s enemies; this note is intended to prevent anyone from thinking that the passage concerns the Huns.]

as events revealed and proved, lay prostrate in sackcloth and poured out prayers until the day of battle. Before the war he lay in prayer; for war he rose from prayer. Before taking up the battle with his hand, he fought by supplication. Thus he went confidently into battle, because he had already earned victory through prayer.

## XI

In a similar way, there was also that episode concerning the Vandals. When our party, advancing against them while they were settled in Spain, carried as great a confidence in its presumption of defeating them as it had recently carried against the Goths, it collapsed with equal arrogance and an equal outcome.

[Note: This passage concerns the war conducted by the Roman commander Castinus against the Vandals in the year 622. Idatius writes in his *Chronicle*: “Castinus, master of the soldiers, brought war in Baetica against the Vandals with a large force and Gothic auxiliaries. When he had so pressed them by the force of the siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he rashly engaged in open battle and, deceived by the treachery of the auxiliaries, fled defeated toward Tarragona.” See Hard. Valesius, p. 121.]

The prophet’s saying came upon our army: “The Lord will overthrow your confidence, and you shall have no success” (Jeremiah II, 37). For we trusted in our wisdom and strength, against the command of God who says: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man glory in his strength; but let the one who glories glory in this: that he understands and knows me, that I am the Lord” (Jeremiah IX, 23–24).

Therefore we were not unjustly defeated: they turned to better sources of help than ours. For while we were proud of arms and auxiliaries, a book of divine law came to meet us from the enemy side. To this help, above all, the fear and confusion of the Vandals then fled, so that it set before us the sequence of heavenly speech and opened against their advancing rivals the writings of the sacred volume, as though they were themselves, in a certain sense, the mouths of the divine power.

Here I now ask: who among our party ever did this, or who would not have been mocked if he had thought it should be done? Mocked, certainly, just as nearly everything religious is mocked by our people.

And therefore what benefit can that distinction of a religious name bring us—that we say we are Catholics, that we boast we are faithful, that we look down upon the Goths and Vandals by reproaching them with the name of heretics—when we ourselves live with heretical perversity?

Thus that saying which the divine word spoke to the Jews who trusted in the law is most rightly addressed to us: “How can you say, ‘We are wise, and the law of the Lord is with us’?” (Jeremiah VIII, 7). “Do not trust,” it says, “in words of falsehood, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.’ For if you truly direct your ways and your practices, and do not oppress the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place, I will dwell with you in this place from age to age” (Jeremiah VII, 4–7).

This plainly shows that if we do not do these things, we flatter ourselves uselessly with the presumption of the Catholic name. But enough has already been said above about this, and perhaps more will yet be said; there is no need to discuss it further where God’s judgment is continually at work.

What God judges concerning us and concerning the Goths and Vandals, events prove. They grow every day; we diminish. They advance; we are humbled. They flourish; we wither. So that the saying which the divine word spoke concerning Saul and David truly comes upon us: “David was advancing and becoming ever stronger than himself, while the house of Saul was diminishing day by day” (2 Samuel III, 1). For, as the prophet says, “The Lord is just, and his judgment is upright” (Psalm CXVIII, 137).

## XII

Thus we are judged by God even through his present judgment. For this reason a people was aroused for our destruction and disgrace—a people that, moving from place to place and passing from city to city, laid waste everything.

[Note: This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript. All editions instead have “from world to world.” The same correction has been adopted at another place on the following page. See what was noted above at p. 142.]

First, it poured out from its native soil into First Germania, barbarian by name but Roman in jurisdiction. After its destruction, the region of the Belgians first burned; then the wealth of the luxurious Aquitanians; and after that, the body of all Gaul. Yet even this happened gradually, so that while one part was cut down by disaster, another might be corrected by the example.

But where among us is there correction, or what part of the Roman world, however afflicted, is being reformed? For, as we read, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalm XIII, 3). Therefore the prophet cries out to the Lord and says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to accept correction. They hardened their faces more than rock and refused to return” (Jeremiah V, 3).

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “they inclined.” But this reading is not good.]

How truly this also applies to us, the events themselves indicate. Gaul was devastated for a long time. Was it therefore corrected while Spain was nearby? Not at all, because there was absolutely no fear. No correction took place; Spain began to burn with the flames by which Gaul had burned.

In this lies what I called above most wicked and most serious: although, so to speak, the limbs of sinful people had burned, the vices of the sinners were not cured. Therefore God was compelled by our crimes to spread hostile blows from place to place and from city to city, and even to send across the sea peoples roused from almost the farthest ends of the earth to punish the crimes of Africa.

For what of it? Could they not, after being led away from their native soil, have remained within Gaul? Or, if they did not remain there because they feared the people whom they had ravaged unharmed until that time, what prevented them from remaining in Spain, where they had already crushed our armies in battle? Did they fear to stand or remain as victors and triumphant, when they had risen to such a height of confidence in their strength that, after the experience of war, they understood that the forces of the Roman state, even with barbarian auxiliaries, could not be equal to them?

## XIII

They could therefore have remained there, and I would not have feared them. But that heavenly hand which had drawn them there to punish the crimes of the Spaniards was also compelling them to cross over and lay waste Africa.

[Note: This is to be understood of the Vandals. See the same Valesius, p. 100.]

They themselves finally admitted that what they were doing was not their own undertaking: they said that they were being led and driven forward by divine command. From this one can understand how great our evils are, since barbarians are compelled against their will to go and devastate and torment us, in accordance with the saying of the king of Assyria, the devastator of the land of Israel: “Have I come up to this place without the Lord’s will? The Lord said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it’” (Isaiah XXXVI, 10).

And elsewhere the sacred word says: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send for and take Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant” (Jeremiah XXV, 9), “and he shall come and strike the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah XLIII, 11).

From this we can recognize that everything afflicted is struck by God’s judgment; nevertheless, as I have often said, it is overthrown on account of sins. Accordingly, whatever has been done must be attributed to sins, not to God, because an action is rightly attributed to the thing that demanded that it be done.

[Note: Below, Letter 9, p. 205: “For it is rightly said that he himself wrote through whom it was brought about that it should be written.”]

Thus a murderer, when he is killed by a judge, is punished by his own crime; and a robber or sacrilegious person, when he is burned by flames, is consumed by his own crimes. Therefore the fact that the Vandals crossed over to Africa must be attributed not to divine severity but to the crime of the Africans. For their grave and long-standing iniquity drew them there before they went.

Accordingly, we must understand that it was an act of divine mercy that God delayed the punishment long owed, but an act of their offenses and crimes that a sinful people eventually received what it deserved.

[Note: Seneca, in the preface to the tenth book of the *Controversies*: “The immortal gods are slow, indeed, but sure avengers of the human race.” See the notes to Lupus of Ferrières, p. 473.]

Unless perhaps we believe that the Africans did not deserve this, although surely no people deserved it more, since all kinds of wickedness and impurity had flowed together among them. Other people, although bound by some shameful vices, are not entangled in certain others. Although they are not free from violence, they are free from malevolence; although they burn with lust, they do not rage with rapacity. Finally, although many are accused of bodily incontinence, simplicity of character commends them.

But among almost all Africans there is scarcely anything that belongs equally to both sides—that is, to good as well as evil—for everything is thoroughly evil. Their original natural sincerity having been driven out, vices have in a certain way created another nature in them.

## XIV

Except for a very few servants of God, what was the entire territory of Africa other than one house of vices, like that bronze vessel of which the prophet says: “O city of bloodshed! A bronze vessel in which there is rust; its rust will not leave it, because blood will not leave it” (Ezekiel XXIV, 6)?

[Note: Salvianus may have written *ahenum* (“bronze”). The Vulgate at Ezekiel XXIV, 6 reads: “Woe to the city of bloodshed, the pot whose rust is in it.”]

He compared, as we see, the city to bronze and iniquity to blood, so that we might understand that in a city of the people iniquity is like boiling blood within bronze.

A similar passage occurs in the sacred word: “The house of Israel has become mixed for me with bronze, iron, tin, and lead; and silver is mixed in their midst. Therefore say this: Thus says the Lord God: Because you have all become one mixture, I will melt you together and blow upon you in the fire of my wrath” (Ezekiel XXII, 18–21).

The sacred word has mentioned metals of entirely different kinds. And how are different substances melted in the same furnace? Clearly, because the dissimilarity of human beings is represented by the varieties of metals. Therefore even silver—that is, a metal of nobler material—is consigned to the same fires, because an aptitude of nobler nature is condemned when life degenerates.

Thus we also read that the Lord said through the prophet concerning the prince of Tyre: “Son of man, take up a lamentation over the prince of Tyre, and say to him: Thus says the Lord God: You were the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of paradise; you were clothed with every precious stone—sardius, topaz, and emerald” (Ezekiel XXVIII, 11–13).

And again: “With silver,” he says, “and gold you filled your treasuries; by the abundance of your commerce you filled your storehouses” (ibid., 4–5).

Are not all these things such that they seem to have been said especially about the Africans? Where were there greater treasuries, greater commerce, or fuller storehouses? “With the abundance of your commerce,” he says, “you filled your treasuries with gold.” I add something further: Africa was once so wealthy that its abundance of commerce seems to me to have filled not only its own treasuries but those of the entire world.

And what follows? “Your heart was lifted up because of your beauty; because of the multitude of your sins I cast you down to the earth” (ibid., 17). How does this apply to African power, or how does Africa seem to have been cast down to the earth? How except because, when it lost the height of its former power, it lost, as it were, a heavenly dignity?

“And I will bring fire out from your midst,” he says; “it will devour you” (ibid., 18). What could be truer than this? From the midst of their iniquity there came forth the fire of sin, which devoured the prosperity of the former age.

“And all who know you among the nations will grieve over you” (ibid., 19). Let us not suppose that this applies to them unless the overthrow of African soil is a grief to the human race.

“You have become destruction, and you shall be no more forever” (ibid.). It is sufficiently clear that everything there has already been brought to destruction. The remaining question is whether the continuation of eternal punishment will also follow upon the penalties of present evils.

## XV

May God, in accordance with his merciful disposition, not permit this. For insofar as the merit of our crimes is concerned, the situation is such that it may seem possible for him to permit it. What kind of expiatory offense has not continually been committed there? I do not speak of everything, because they are almost monstrous, and too great to be known or spoken.

I speak especially of the obscenity of impurities and, what is more serious, of sacrileges. I pass over, in some degree, the madness of greed, a vice of the entire human race. I omit the inhumanity of avarice, which is almost the particular evil of all Romans. Let drunkenness, common to nobles and commoners, be left aside. Let pride and arrogance remain unmentioned. This is so characteristic a kingdom of the rich that they perhaps think they are losing something of their right if anyone else wishes to claim even a little of it for himself.

Finally, let us pass over almost all the wickedness of frauds, falsehoods, and perjuries. The Roman state has never been free of these evils, although this crime was especially characteristic of all Africans. For just as the bilge of a deep ship gathers the filth of every kind, so vices from the whole world flowed into their character, as it were.

I know no wickedness that did not overflow there. Yet even pagan and savage peoples, although they have particular evils of their own, do not have everything in them deserving of execration. The nation of the Goths is faithless but chaste; the Alans are unchaste but less faithless; the Franks are deceitful but hospitable; the Saxons are savage in cruelty but admirable in chastity.

Finally, all peoples possess, alongside their characteristic evils, certain good qualities as well. But among almost all Africans I do not know what is not evil. If inhumanity is at issue, they are inhuman; if drunkenness, drunkards; if falsehood, the most deceitful; if trickery, the most fraudulent; if greed, the greediest; if faithlessness, the most faithless.

Their impurity and blasphemy must not be added to all these other traits as though they were merely comparable: for in the evils mentioned above they surpassed the vices of other peoples, while in these they surpassed even their own.

## XVI

First, then, to speak of impurity: who does not know that all Africa has always burned with the shameful fires of lust, so that you would think it not the land and dwelling-place of human beings but Etna itself, filled with the flames of the unchaste?

For just as Etna burns with the internal fires of its fevered nature, so Africa continually seethed with the abominable fires of fornication. Nor do I wish my assertions in this matter to be believed without evidence: let the testimony of the human race be sought. Who does not know all Africans generally to be unchaste, except perhaps those converted to God—that is, transformed by faith and religion?

But this is as rare and extraordinary as it might seem credible for any Gaius not to be Gaius, or for any Seius not to be Seius.

[Note: This is exactly the reading of the Corbie manuscript. Tertullian, in the *Apology*, chapter 48, writes: “Yet if a Christian should promise to restore a man from a man, and even Gaius from Gaius,” he would be demanded by the people with stones, or at least with boxing gloves. And in Book I *To the Nations*, chapter 4: “I am amazed that Gaius Seius, a serious man, has become a Christian.” The reading given here by the editions of Brassicanus and Galesinius is inept, where it reads: “But this is as rare and extraordinary as it might seem rare for any reveler not to be a reveler, or for any violent man not to be violent.” The Colbert manuscript has: “For a reveler not to be a reveler, or for any savage man not to be savage.” It is remarkable how much ancient scribes allowed themselves in these names. In Optatus, Book III, one reads: “Gaius Seius or Gaia Seia, are you still a pagan?” And in Book VI: “Gaius Seius, Gaia Seia, how long will you hold yourself?” Balduinus notes that both passages were written *Gaiasei* in the German edition; he immediately adds that jurists customarily call any person Gaius, Seius, or Titius.]

For the evil of impurity is so widespread among them that whoever among them ceases to be unchaste scarcely seems to be an African. Nor will I go through individual places or examine every city, lest I seem deliberately to be seeking out and investigating the things I shall describe.

I am satisfied with one city, the chief and almost the mother of all the cities there: that city which was always the rival of the Roman citadel, once in arms and courage, later in splendor and dignity. I mean Carthage, the greatest adversary of the city of Rome and, in the African world, almost another Rome.

It alone suffices for me as an example and testimony because it contained within itself virtually everything by which the discipline of the state is administered or governed throughout the whole world. There were all the instruments of public offices; schools of the liberal arts; workshops of philosophers; in short, every gymnasium of languages and morals. There too were military forces and the authorities who directed the army; there was proconsular rank; there was the daily judge and governor—proconsul in name, but consul in power.

There, finally, were all the administrators of public affairs, and dignities differing from one another both in rank and in title; administrators of nearly every street and crossroads, governing almost all the places of the city and the members of the people.

We are content with this one city as an example and testimony for the others, so that we may understand what those cities must have been like which had smaller administrations of honorable offices, once we have seen what existed where the highest governors had always been.

At this point I almost regret my promise—that is, the promise I made above to pass over nearly all the crimes of the Africans and speak especially of their impurities and blasphemies. For I see a city, as it were, pouring forth vices; I see a city boiling with every kind of iniquity, full of crowds but even fuller of shamefulness; full of wealth but even fuller of vices.

People outdid one another in the wickedness of their crimes: some competing in rapacity, others in impurity; some weakened by wine, others swollen with gluttony; these crowned with garlands, those smeared with perfumes; all ruined by various forms of luxurious languor, and almost all prostrate in the same death of error—not all drunk with wine, but all drunk with sins.

You would have thought them a population not sound in condition, not in possession of its senses, not healthy in spirit or upright in bearing, serving drunkenness in crowds like bands of bacchants.

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “crowds of drunken revelers.” The Corbie manuscript has the same.]

And what of that other matter—how disgraceful and how grave? It is different in kind but not different in iniquity, unless perhaps it is different because it is worse. I mean the proscriptions of orphans, the afflictions of widows, and the torments of the poor. Groaning daily to God, praying for an end to their evils, and—what is most serious—sometimes, through the force of excessive bitterness, even asking for the arrival of enemies, they at times obtained from God the result that they finally endured a common overthrow at the hands of barbarians, which they alone had previously endured at the hands of the Romans.

## XVII

But let all these things be set aside, since they are practiced throughout almost the entire Roman world, and since I promised to say little about these evils in this passage.

What, then? Was the unchastity and impurity of which I am speaking not by itself sufficient to overthrow the Africans? What part of the city was not full of filth? What street or alley within the city was not a brothel? Nearly all the crossroads had become either, as it were, pits of lust, or had stretched nets across the roads, so that even those who utterly abhorred such things could scarcely avoid them.

You might have seen something like watch-posts of robbers lying in wait to seize the possessions of passing travelers. Through the dense multiplication of their ambushes they had enclosed nearly all the paths, winding passages, and side roads, so that scarcely anyone was so cautious that he did not fall into some snare of ambush, even if he had escaped from many others.

All the citizens of that city, so to speak, stank of the mire of lust, breathing into one another the foul odor of unchastity. Yet these horrors were not horrifying to them, because the same horror had infected them all. You would have thought there was one sewer of lusts and fornications, a mire collected from all the filth of the streets and sewers.

And what hope could exist there where, apart from what was in the Lord’s temple, nothing could be seen that was not utterly filthy?

Although why should I speak of the temple of God? This concerns only the priests and clergy, whom I do not examine because I preserve the reverence due to my Lord’s ministry.

[Note: He is speaking of the priests—that is, the bishops—and the rest of the clergy. He says that he does not wish to examine their conduct out of reverence for the ministers of God. Jerome writes in his letter to Rusticus: “It is neither within my humility nor within my measure to judge the clergy or to speak anything sinister about the ministers of the churches.” The same author says in his commentary on Ecclesiastes VIII that accusation of a bishop is difficult: “No one dares accuse a superior. Therefore, as though they were holy and blessed and walking in the commandments of the Lord, they add sins to sins. Accusation of a bishop is difficult. For if he has sinned, he is not believed; and if he has been convicted, he is not punished.” Saint Gregory, in Book I of *Pastoral Care*, chapter 2: “No one harms the Church more than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when, out of reverence for rank, a sinner is honored.” See the *Book of Petitions of Marcellinus and Faustinus*, p. 37.]

I regard those alone as having been pure at the altar, just as we read that, when Sodom was perishing, Lot alone was on the mountain (Genesis XIX, 30).

But as far as the people are concerned, who among that innumerable number was chaste? I say chaste: who was not a fornicator, not an adulterer—and this without interruption, without limit?

I must therefore cry out again: What hope could exist among that people, when, if one adulterer sometimes pollutes the ecclesiastical congregation, among so many thousands you could scarcely find a chaste person even in the Church?

[Note: That is, the people of the Church or city of Carthage. Above, p. 45: “ecclesiastical peoples.” Below, p. 166: “in the ecclesiastical body.” And p. 216: “the ecclesiastical congregation.”]

I shall say much more. Would that the things we have mentioned were the only ones, and that the impurity of the men there had been content to be polluted only by fornications with filthy women! More serious and more criminal was the fact that nearly everything among the Africans consisted of the practices about which blessed Paul complains with the deepest anguish of spirit (Romans I, 23 ff.): namely, that males, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense which was due for their error. And because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper.

Did the blessed Apostle say this about barbarian and savage peoples? Certainly not, but about us—that is, especially about the Romans. The Africans, since they were once unable to conquer the Romans in empire and eminence, surpassed them in the one thing they could: impurity.

Therefore, whoever thinks he has the right to be angry with me should be angry with the Apostle instead. For what we say the Africans were, he said their masters, the Romans, were.

## XVIII

But perhaps the evil of which we speak was hidden, or at least the officials took care that the city’s public discipline should not be polluted by openly exposed crimes. If this had indeed been done, although many might have been filthy in their actions, not all would nevertheless have been defiled in sight and spirit; and a disgraceful act, when carried out secretly, generally fails to establish the credibility of the crime.

But beyond every execration of monstrous wickedness lies this: to commit the greatest crime and have no shame about the crime. What, I ask, could have been more extraordinary than what happened there?

In a Christian city, in an ecclesiastical city, which the apostles had once established by their teachings and which martyrs had crowned by their sufferings, men professed themselves to be women—and this without even the shadow of shame, without any covering of modesty.

[Note: Salvianus thought that the Church of Carthage was one of the apostolic churches. It is plainly evident that he was mistaken in this. For Tertullian, an African, omits Carthage when listing the apostolic churches; he would surely not have omitted it if there had been any ancient tradition that the apostles had reached Carthage. But because, in Salvianus’s time, Catholics within Africa claimed that the Africans had received the Gospel from the apostles—a claim the Donatists stubbornly denied—Salvianus, evidently out of hostility toward the Donatists and affection for the Catholics, readily embraced the opinion of those who said that the Africans had been instructed in the Christian faith by the apostles. Moreover, he saw that the bishop of Carthage enjoyed privileges equal to those of the bishops of the apostolic churches; therefore it was easy for him to adopt the view that the African Church had been founded by the apostles. Gregory the Great shows that this was also believed by the Numidians in Book I, Letter 75, written to them. Thus, through the widespread ambition for antiquity, as each church tried to claim the most ancient origin for itself, people were found who claimed apostles for Africa—namely, Peter, the chief of the apostles, and a certain Laudatus, the first bishop of Carthage, ordained by the apostles. But the distinguished Cardinal Baronius rightly rejects these absurdities.]

And as though it were not enough for the authors of this evil to be defiled by that worst of evils alone, the public profession of the crime made the entire city guilty as well. For the whole city saw this and tolerated it; the judges saw it and approved; the people saw it and applauded. Thus, although the participation in the disgrace and crime spread throughout the entire city did not make the act common to everyone, their common approval made it common to everyone.

But did the evil perhaps finally come to an end, or was there some correction of this pollution? Who could believe—or even hear—what happened: that men had changed into feminine submission not merely their use and nature, but also their face, walk, dress, and utterly everything that belongs either to male sex or male function?

[Note: Compare Sallust in *The Catiline*: “Men enduring womanly things.” And Tacitus, concerning Caesoninus: “In that most shameful gathering, he endured womanly things.” Our Muretus, in his commentary on the second *Catiline*, notes that the Massilians, who were otherwise equipped with the best and most sacred laws, should not for this reason have been traduced by Athenaeus because they were devoted to male love, since among the Cretans and Lacedaemonians also—both of whom are thought to have used the most sacred and strict laws—the love of boys was nevertheless not regarded as disgraceful.]

Everything had been so completely turned into its opposite that, although nothing ought to be more shameful to men than to appear to possess anything feminine, among certain men there nothing seemed more disgraceful than to appear in any respect masculine.

### XIX

“But this,” you say, “was the disgrace of only a few; and what was not perpetrated by many could not harm everyone.” I have already said above, of course, that even among God’s people the crime of one has often been a plague to many: just as the people fell because of Achan’s theft (Joshua 7), just as a pestilence arose from Saul’s jealousy (1 Samuel 19), and just as death followed the census conducted by holy David (2 Samuel 24).

For the Church of God is like an eye. Just as even a small speck falling into the eye blinds the whole light, so in the ecclesiastical body, even if only a few commit filthy acts, they almost entirely darken the light of ecclesiastical splendor.

[Note: This is established from both clergy and laity. See the Notes on page 164.]

Therefore the Savior himself called the chief part of the Church “the eye,” saying: “The lamp of your body is your eye. If your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matthew 6:22–23).
