Hence the Apostle also says: “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (1 Corinthians 5:6).

Although there I should say that there was not a little of this evil, but a great deal—not because there were very many effeminate men, but because the effeminacy of a few is the defilement of many. For although few are those who tolerate disgraceful practices, many are those who are polluted by the filth of the few. Just as one prostitute makes many fornicators, so the detestable mixture of a few effeminate men defiles a very large portion of the people.

And I do not know which of them is worse before God, since they are condemned by the sacred writings with equal severity. For it says: “Neither the effeminate nor those who have intercourse with males will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:10).

What therefore must be lamented and mourned more deeply is that this crime seemed to be a crime of the entire commonwealth, and that the whole dignity of the Roman name was branded with the infamy of this monstrous deed. For when men assumed women’s dress, and broke their gait more than women did; when they attached certain tokens of monstrous impurity to themselves, and covered their heads with feminine bindings and coverings; and when this was publicly permitted in a Roman city—

[Note: That is, in the city of Carthage. He calls it a Roman city because it was then subject to Roman rule.]

—in that supreme and most celebrated city there, what else was it but a disgrace to the Roman Empire that, in the very heart of the commonwealth, the most abominable outrage could openly be committed?

A great and exceedingly powerful authority that can restrain the greatest crime seems, by knowingly allowing it to be committed, to approve that it ought to be done. For whoever has it in his power to forbid something commands it to be done if he does not forbid it.

### XX

Again, because grief demands it, I ask those who are angry: among what barbarian peoples have such things ever been done, or been permitted to be done with public impunity?

Finally, so that there may be no need for longer debate or investigation on this matter, let us compare those very devastators of Africa with the peoples of Africa. Let us see what similar deed was committed by the Vandals.

Certainly, they were barbarians swollen with pride, arrogant in victory, and made dissolute by an abundance of wealth and luxury. Even if they had always been exceptionally temperate and chaste, they could nevertheless have been changed by such good fortune, in which everything seemed to comply with their wishes. They entered—as it is written in the divine Scriptures (Deuteronomy 6:3)—a land flowing with milk and honey, fertile, extremely wealthy, and, as it were, drunk with every kind of delight. In such a land it would certainly have been no wonder if a barbarian people had given itself over to luxury, where nature itself was, in a certain sense, like one luxuriating.

Who would not suppose that the Vandals, on entering these regions, immersed themselves in every mire of vice and impurity—or, to put it as mildly as possible, at least did those things that had continually been done by the Africans, into whose jurisdiction they had entered? Indeed, if they were to be judged temperate and modest merely for doing those things, whom would prosperity itself not have made more corrupt? For how few of the wise are there whom success does not change, or in whom vice does not grow along with prosperity?

By this reasoning, the Vandals must have been extremely temperate, if, as victors, they were such as those whom they had captured and subjected. Thus, amid such an abundance of possessions and luxury, did none of them become effeminate? Does that seem a small matter? Certainly, even among the Romans this was familiar, including among the nobility.

But why should I add more? There was not even one there who was polluted by the incest of the effeminate Romans. Certainly, among the Romans this had long been regarded as such a thing that it was thought a virtue rather than a vice; and those were considered to possess the greater manly courage who had most disgracefully broken men through feminine practices.

Hence also arose the practice by which, when armies were once accompanied by boys serving as camp-followers, the rewards for their labor were decreed as though they had deserved well in the campaigns: because they were brave men, they were to transform men into women.

What an outrage! And this among Romans.

I add more: this also among Romans—not of the present age. Yet, so that we do not accuse the ancient, they were Romans but not ancient Romans: already corrupt, already dissolute, already unlike themselves and their ancestors, and more like Greeks than Romans. Thus, as we have often said, it is not at all surprising if the Roman commonwealth at some point suffers what it has long deserved.

### XXI

This impurity therefore began among the Romans even before the Gospel of Christ and, what is more serious, did not cease after the Gospel.

Who, after this, would not marvel at the peoples of the Vandals? They entered an exceedingly wealthy city where all these things were practiced openly everywhere. Yet, having obtained the luxuries of corrupt men, they rejected their corruptions of character, possessing the use of good things while avoiding the defilements of evil ones.

These things alone, even if I said nothing else, could suffice for their praise: they abhorred the impurities of men. I add something further: they also abhorred those of women. They shuddered at brothels and whorehouses; they shuddered at intercourse and contact with prostitutes.

Can anyone find it believable that Romans admitted such things while barbarians shuddered at them? Or, after what we have said, can anything more be said? Yet there is more—much more.

For when we said that they avoided disgraceful things, we said too little. A person may abhor dishonorable things without abolishing them. But this is a great and singular merit: not only to avoid being polluted oneself, but also to take care that others should never be polluted.

For, in a certain sense, he is an administrator of human salvation who not only strives to be good himself, but also endeavors to bring it about that others cease to be evil. What we are saying is great—great and extraordinary.

Who would believe that the Vandals did such things in Roman cities? For every impurity of the flesh had been removed from them.

But how was it removed? Not in the way certain Romans usually remove things: they decree that adultery must not be committed, and they are the first to commit adultery; they decree that theft must not be committed, and they steal. Although I can scarcely call what they do “theft.” Their acts are not thefts but robberies.

A judge punishes peculation in another person while he himself is a peculator.

[Note: The Corbie and Colbert manuscripts read “embezzlement” (*peculationem*). This is also noted in the margin of the Pithoean edition.]

He punishes robbery while he himself is a robber; he punishes the assassin while he himself is a swordsman; he punishes those who break through gates and doors while he himself is the destroyer of cities; he punishes those who strip houses while he himself strips cities and provinces.

Would that only those placed in positions of authority did this—those to whom the office itself grants the right to practice robbery! More serious and more intolerable is the fact that private persons who once held the same offices also do this.

The honor they have once obtained grants them so great a benefit that they always retain the right to rob. Thus, even when they have ceased to possess public authority for administering affairs, they do not cease to possess private authority for robbery. The authority they held as judges is therefore lighter than that which they possess as private individuals. In the former they are often succeeded; in the latter, never.

Behold the power of laws enacted; behold the benefit of defining statutes, which are most despised by those who administer them. Certainly, the humble and lowly are compelled to obey; the poor are forced to comply with orders, and if they do not obey, they are punished.

For in this matter they follow the same principle as in taxation. They alone serve public commands, just as they alone pay taxes. Thus, within the laws themselves and in the very just exaction of what is owed, the greatest crime of injustice is committed: the lowly are forced to observe as sacred those things that the powerful continually trample upon as though they were nothing.

### XXII

I have strayed somewhat from the order of the discourse I began, compelled by the disgracefulness of these matters. Now let us return to what came before.

We said that the cities of Africa were full of monstrous impurities, and especially that the queen and, as it were, mistress of that region was full of them; but that the Vandals were not polluted by any of these things.

These barbarians therefore arose to correct the stain of our shamefulness. They removed from all Africa the filth of effeminate men and also shuddered at the contaminations of prostitutes. Nor did they merely abhor them or temporarily suppress them: they made them cease altogether to exist.

O gracious Lord, O good Savior, how much the pursuits of discipline accomplish through you—those by which the vices of nature can be changed, as they were plainly changed by these people!

But how were they changed? It is important to state not only the results but also the causes of the results.

[Note: The meaning of this passage does not seem sufficiently clear to me. I would therefore prefer to read it as follows: “For it is useless for unchastity to be removed by word or command unless it has actually been removed; and it is useless for chastity to be demanded by word unless it has actually been demanded.” As I said, I would prefer to read the passage in this way. But the editions and manuscripts resist this reading.]

For it is difficult for unchastity to be removed by word or command unless it has been removed; and it is difficult for chastity to be demanded by word unless it has been demanded.

Knowing this, they removed unchastity in such a way that they preserved the unchaste women. They did not kill the unfortunate women, lest they stain their concern to remedy vice with cruelty and, while wishing to take away sins, themselves sin in cutting off sinners.

Instead, they corrected those who were wandering in such a way that their deed was medicine, not punishment. They ordered and compelled all prostitutes to enter the marriage bed; they turned courtesans into wives,

thereby fulfilling the Apostle’s saying and command: “Let each woman have her own husband, and each man his own wife” (1 Corinthians 7:2). Since incontinence could not be restrained without this physical union, they provided a legitimate use for bodily passion, so that incontinence would not have sin as its result.

In this they took care not only that women who could not be without men should have husbands, but also that those who did not know how to guard themselves should be kept safe by household protectors. By remaining constantly attached to the guidance of a husband, even if the habit of their former impurity tempted them toward some wicked deed, they would nevertheless be restrained from wrongdoing by marital guardianship.

They also added this for the suppression of lust: strict chastity statutes, restraining unchastity with the sword of their decrees. Thus affection within the home and marriage would preserve the purity of both sexes, while fear of the laws would preserve it in public. In this way chastity would rest upon a double protection: at home there would be something to love, and outside there would be something to fear.

Their laws, however, were by no means like those laws that remove one part of wrongdoing while admitting another part of obscenity—or like those Roman decrees that removed fornicators from other men’s wives but admitted them freely to all unmarried women: prohibiting adultery while building brothels.

Clearly, they feared that men would become too chaste and pure if they prohibited them altogether from every impurity.

But the people of whom we are speaking did not act in that way. They restrained prostitution just as they restrained adultery. They wanted women to be women for no men except their husbands, and men to be men for no women except their wives. They did not permit obscene lusts to wander outside the legitimate marriage bed. They directed their laws according to the rule of divine law, believing that they were permitted nothing in this matter that God had willed to be forbidden.

Therefore they did not think that anything should be permitted by them to any person unless it had been permitted by the Divinity to everyone.

### XXIII

I know that what I have said may seem intolerable to some. But one must proceed according to the reason of things, not according to the appetite for pleasures.

Let whoever he is who is indignant that I say these things answer me: was not Socrates always considered the wisest of all, even on the testimony of the Delphic demon, which called him, as it were, the prince of philosophers—as is the way of demons?

Let us therefore see what laws Socrates established concerning chastity, and what laws were established by those of whom we are speaking.

“Socrates says: Let no one have a wife of his own. Marriages ought to be common to all. For the harmony of cities will be greater if all men mingle indiscriminately with all women, and all women submit themselves without distinction to all men. Thus all men will become the husbands of all women, and all women the wives of all men.”

Have we ever known any madman or demoniac, raging with various forms of insanity, to say such a thing?

You say, greatest of philosophers, that in this way all men are the husbands of all women, all women the wives of all men, and all children the children of all.

But I say that in this way no man is the husband of any woman, no woman is the wife of any man, and no child is the child of any parent.

[Note: That is, any one of the children (*liberorum*), as he said shortly before.]

For where everything is promiscuous and confused, no one can claim anything as his own.

Nor, as some say, was it enough for this most wise philosopher to teach such a thing unless he himself had done it. For he gave his own wife to another man—just as the Roman Cato did, that is, another Socrates of Italy.

Behold the examples of Roman and Attic wisdom: as far as it lay within them, they made all husbands the pimps of their own wives.

Yet Socrates prevailed, since he both composed books about this matter and committed these shameful things to memory. He has even more grounds for boasting in his precepts.

As far as his teaching is concerned, he made the world a brothel. He is said to have been unjustly condemned by the judges. And that is true. For the human race ought more rightly to have condemned him for proclaiming such things, just as it undoubtedly did condemn him.

For when everyone rejected his teaching on this matter, they all condemned him not only by the authority of their judgment but, much more importantly, by their choice of life—and rightly so.

Let what he established be compared with what those established whom God commanded to rule Africa.

He decreed that no one should have a wife of his own; they decreed that no one should have a wife who was not his own.

He decreed that every woman should be subject to all men; they decreed that no woman should know any man other than her husband.

He decreed mixed and confused procreation; they decreed procreation that was pure and ordered.

He wanted every household to practice prostitution; they wanted none to do so.

He attempted to build brothels in every dwelling; they removed them even from the cities.

He wanted to prostitute all virgins; they made prostitutes chaste.

Would that this had been merely Socrates’ error, and not also that of many Romans and nearly all of them! Although they did not follow Socrates’ life in other matters, in this they follow Socratic institutions: many men have several wives each, and countless women have several husbands each.

Finally, are not all cities full of brothels and stinking with whorehouses?

And why do I say “all”? Certainly the most distinguished and exalted cities are so. Indeed, this is even considered a mark of honor in great cities: the more they surpass others in size, the more they excel in impurity.

And what hope, I ask, can there be for the Roman state when barbarians are more chaste and pure than Romans?

What little we are saying! What hope, I ask, can we have before God either for life or for pardon, when we see chastity among barbarians and still are not chaste?

Let us blush, I beg you, and be ashamed.

Now among the Goths only the Romans are unchaste; now among the Vandals, not even the Romans are unchaste.

So greatly has the pursuit of chastity advanced among them, so greatly has the severity of discipline progressed—not merely so that they themselves are chaste, but, to state something new, incredible, and almost unheard-of, they have even made Romans chaste.

If human weakness allowed it, I would wish to cry out beyond my strength, so that my voice might resound throughout the whole world:

“Be ashamed, you Romans everywhere; be ashamed of your lives! Almost no cities are free from brothels, and none at all are free from impurities, except those in which the barbarians have begun to dwell.

“And do we wonder if we are wretched, since we are so impure? Do we wonder if we are defeated by the enemy in strength, when we are surpassed by them in honor? Do we wonder if they possess our goods, when they abhor our evils?

“It is neither the natural strength of their bodies that makes them conquer, nor the weakness of our nature that makes us conquered. Let no one persuade himself otherwise; let no one think otherwise: the vices of our character alone have conquered us.”

# BOOK EIGHT

### I

I think—or rather, I am certain—that the length of this style will be tedious to many, especially because it chastises the vices of our character. Everyone wants very much to be praised; no one welcomes criticism.

Indeed, what is much worse, however bad or ruined a person may be, he prefers to be praised falsely rather than criticized justly, and to be deceived by the mockery of false praises rather than saved by the most salutary admonition.

Since these things are so, what should be done? Should we serve the will of wicked people? Or, if they too want frivolous praises to be offered them, is it fitting for us to offer them frivolous and ridiculous praise?

Especially since faithful men ought not to mock even those who wish to be mocked, just as they ought not falsely to praise even those who wish to be adorned with the very title of false praise.

[Note: If those who want to be falsely praised only understood how weighty praises cast upon the undeserving are! Sidonius, Book 8, Letter 10: “You ought to have considered that saying of Symmachus: ‘As true praise adorns, so false praise chastises.’” See the notes of the distinguished scholar Jacques Sirmond on this passage of Sidonius.]

For we must consider not so much what each of them wishes to hear as what it is proper for us to say—especially since the prophet says: “Woe to those who call sweet bitter and bitter sweet” (Isaiah 5:16).

Accordingly, truth must be held in every way, so that what exists in reality may also exist in our words: things that have sweetness in themselves must be called sweet, and things that have bitterness must be called bitter—especially now, in a sacred matter, where many ascribe our iniquities to God and, lest they themselves appear blameworthy, presume to accuse God.

[Note: Brassican’s edition: “They are regarded as sweet, as if to God; and lest they be accused, etc.”]

For when they blaspheme him as careless and negligent, and claim that he either does not govern human affairs according to judgment or does not govern them at all, what else are they doing but accusing God of inactivity, abuse, and injustice?

O blindness of human foolishness! O madness of insane presumption!

So, human being, do you call God careless and negligent? If you inflicted this insult upon any freeborn man, you would be guilty of outrageous injury.

[Note: Above, page 127: “For if you were to insult a distinguished and powerful man…”]

Certainly, if you insulted someone more distinguished and exalted, you would also have to endure the penalty of public law.

For these insults are directed especially at wards and spendthrifts. It is the particular reproach of ruined young men that they are called wasters, careless, and negligent regarding their own affairs.

O sacrilegious words! O profane insolence!

Are we therefore saying that God is what, even among human beings, we call only the most ruined people?

Nor are these the only accusations made against him. As I said above, he is also charged with injustice.

For if we do not deserve what we suffer, and are unworthy of enduring our present miseries, then we necessarily call God unjust, since he commands us to endure evils we do not deserve.

“But,” you say, “he does not so much command them as permit them.”

Let us grant that this is so. But, I ask, how far is one who permits from one who commands? Whoever knows that we are enduring these things and can prevent us from enduring them undoubtedly approves that we ought to endure whatever he allows us to suffer.

Hence we see that what we suffer is the just permission of his judgment and a heavenly sentence.

Since everything is under sacred authority and God’s will directs all things, whatever evils and punishments we endure daily is the judgment of the divine hand. Yet we ourselves make that judgment burn more fiercely and continually provoke it by our sins. We kindle the fire of heavenly wrath and stir up the flames in which we burn.

Thus, whenever we endure these evils, that prophetic saying may rightly be addressed even to us: “Go into the flame of the fire that you have kindled” (Isaiah 50:11).

Accordingly, in accordance with the sacred judgment, each sinner prepares for himself what he suffers (Psalm 7).

There is therefore nothing for which we can blame God for our calamities. We are the authors of our own calamities.

For God is gracious and merciful and, as it is written, does not wish anyone to perish or to be harmed (1 Timothy 2:4).

We therefore do everything against ourselves. There is nothing—nothing at all—that is more cruel toward us than we are toward ourselves. We ourselves, I say, even against God’s will, torture ourselves.

But perhaps I seem to be arguing against myself. Earlier I said that God punishes us because of our sins; now I say that we are punished by ourselves.

Both are true. We are punished by God, but we ourselves cause ourselves to be punished. And when we ourselves cause our punishment, who can doubt that we punish ourselves by our own crimes?

For whoever supplies the cause for which he is punished punishes himself, according to the saying: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Proverbs 5:22).

Therefore, if wicked people are bound by the cords of their own sins, every sinner undoubtedly binds himself when he sins.

### II

But since we have said much about the impurity of the Africans, let us now say at least a little about their blasphemies.

Paganism was openly professed there continually by many. Within their ancestral walls they possessed an internal crime,

[Note: Thus read the Pithoean edition and the Corbie manuscript. Quite correctly. Tertullian, in chapter 23 of the *Apology*: “That very virgin Caelestis, the promiser of rains.” Julius Capitolinus, in the *Life of Pertinax*, speaking of the proconsulship that Pertinax held in Africa: “During that proconsulship he is said to have endured many disturbances caused by the prophecies of those women who emerged from the temple of Caelestis.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 22: “The philosopher Asclepiades, when he had gone abroad to that suburban place to visit Julian, was accustomed to carry with him wherever he went a small silver image of the goddess Caelestis, and placed it upright at the feet of the statue.” Trebellius Pollio, in *Celsus*: “The Africans proclaimed Celsus emperor, adorned with the veil of the goddess Caelestis.” The distinguished Cardinal Baronius collected many other testimonies under the year 399 to show that the god Caelestis worshiped at Carthage was a goddess. Casaubon, however, in his Notes on the Life of Antoninus Caracalla, while citing this passage of Salvian, reads “that heavenly one,” misled by the authority of the editions, although he admits that she was regarded by almost everyone as a goddess. From the temple of the goddess Caelestis near Carthage there was also a “heavenly road,” mentioned by Victor of Vita at the beginning of his books on the Vandal Persecution and by Prosper in Book 3 of his *Predictions*, chapter 38. On the goddess Caelestis, see Lipsius, Book 5 of the *Epistolical Questions*, Letter 22; Casaubon, Notes on the Life of Antoninus Caracalla; Rittershausen on this passage; and Henri Valois in his annotations on Ammianus Marcellinus, page 232.]

—that heavenly one, I mean, the demon of the Africans. I suppose that the ancient pagans gave this idol the title of such a splendid name for the following reason: since it possessed no divinity, it might at least possess the name; and since it possessed no power of virtue, it might at least possess dignity through its title.

Who among them had not been initiated into that idol? Who had not perhaps been devoted to it from his very stock and birth?

I am not speaking of people who were pagan not only in life but also by profession and name—those who, just as they were profane in error, were also profane in name. Paganism is more tolerable and less criminal in people whose profession is openly pagan.

The more destructive and wicked thing was that many who had dedicated their profession to Christ served idols in their minds.

For who among those called Christians did not worship that heavenly goddess either after Christ—or, what is much worse, before Christ?

Who, full of the stench of demonic sacrifices, entered the threshold of the divine house and, carrying the foulness of those demons, mounted Christ’s altar? It would have been less monstrous to fail to come to the Lord’s temple than to come in this manner.

For a Christian who does not come to church is guilty of negligence; but one who comes in this manner is guilty of sacrilege. It is a lesser offense if honor is not offered to God than if insult is inflicted upon him.

Accordingly, whoever did these things did not give honor to God but diminished it. In a certain sense they even offered the idol the greeting due to the Church, because the service rendered to the second place benefits the one who receives the principal honors.

Behold what the faith, religion, and Christianity of the Africans—and especially of the most noble among them—were like. They were called Christians to the insult of Christ.

Although the Apostle proclaims: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:20–21),

[Note: Up to this point the authority of the Corbie manuscript extends. The rest has been partly obliterated by age and partly lost.]

this was not enough for them: they drank the cup of demons along with the cup of God, unless they even preferred the former. Nor was it enough for them to compare the table of demons with the Lord’s table. After worshiping infamous superstitions, they came to God’s temples and, guided by that diabolical spirit, breathed their most filthy stench upon the most sacred altars of Christ.

### III

“But,” you say, “not everyone did these things; only the most powerful and exalted did so.”

Let us grant that this is so. But since the wealthiest and most powerful households each make up a crowd within the city, you see that the whole city was polluted by the sacrilegious superstition of a few powerful people.

No one doubts that all households resemble their masters or are worse than they are—though it is more usual for them to be worse. Accordingly, since even good masters have especially bad servants, it is easy to understand what all the households there must have been like, when the wickedness of their masters made servants’ minds, already bad in themselves, even worse.

Let us grant, then, that the matters we have mentioned belonged to the most powerful and noble.

Were the other things, common to both noble and ignoble, any less serious? I mean the hatred and execration of all holy people.

For it is a kind of sacrilege to hate the worshipers of God. Just as, if someone beats our servants, he injures us in the person of our servants; and if someone beats another man’s son, paternal affection is tortured by the punishment of the son; so, when a servant of God is harmed by anyone, divine majesty is violated.

The Lord himself says this to his apostles: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matthew 10:40), and “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16).

The most gracious and merciful Lord makes both honor and insult toward his servants common to himself and them, so that no one, when harming a servant of God, might think he had harmed only a human being. Without doubt, the injury done to the Lord’s servants is mingled with an injury to God, as God declares to his own with the most tender affection:

“Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2:8).

To express the tenderness of his compassion, he named the most delicate part of the human body, so that we might understand most clearly that God is harmed by even the smallest insult against his saints as the sharpness of human sight is harmed by the touch of a slight blow.

The Africans therefore attacked and hated the servants of God—and in them, God.

### IV

Perhaps someone asks by what means their hatred can be demonstrated.

By those same means by which the hatred of the Jews toward Christ is also demonstrated: when they said to him, “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8:48); when they mocked him, cursed him, blew in his face, and gnashed their teeth over his head.

Hence the Savior himself, who endured these things, says in the Psalms: “All who saw me mocked me; they spoke with their lips and shook their heads” (Psalm 21:8). And elsewhere: “They tested me,” he says, “and mocked me with mockery; they gnashed their teeth at me” (Psalm 34:16).

Thus the hatred of the Africans is also demonstrated against monks—that is, against the saints of God:

because they mocked them, because they cursed them, because they attacked them, because they detested them, because they did almost everything against them that the impiety of the Jews had earlier done against our Savior, before reaching the shedding of his divine blood.

“But,” you say, “they did not kill the saints, as we read that the Jews did.”

Whether they killed them, I do not know; I do not assert it. Yet what a great defense it would be if the only thing lacking in their pagan persecution were the final stage of persecution itself!

Let us suppose, then, that the saints were not killed there. But what shall we say of those who are not far removed from murderers because they hated them with murderous intent—especially since the Lord himself says: “Whoever hates his brother without cause is a murderer” (1 John 3:15)?

They did not persecute the servants of God without cause.

[Note: That is, the monks. Below: “And if at any time a servant of God came from the monasteries of Egypt.” And on page 181: “It was scarcely possible for the servants of God to appear in the streets and crossroads without insult and execration.”]

For who could say that it was without cause when they were men entirely different from them in their pursuits of life and character, men in whom they saw nothing of their own, since everything belonged to God?

The greatest cause of discord is the difference of wills. For it is either wholly impossible or scarcely possible for someone to love in another what he himself rejects.

Thus, as I said, they did not hate them without cause: they saw in them everything that rivaled and opposed themselves.

Those people lived continually in wickedness; these in innocence.

Those in lust; these in chastity.

Those in brothels; these in monasteries.

Those almost continually with the devil; these without ceasing with Christ.

It was therefore not without cause that, within the cities of Africa and especially within the walls of Carthage, that wretched and faithless people could scarcely look upon a monk—cloaked, pale, and shorn to the skin, with the flowing locks of his hair cut off—without abuse and execration.

[Note: These, then, were the distinctive marks of monks at that time.]

And whenever some servant of God came to that city from the monasteries of Egypt,

[Note: He mentions the monasteries of Egypt; Bishop Castor of Aptonga also mentions them in his letter to John Cassian: “We regard you as especially experienced in the teaching of the Eastern monasteries, and particularly those of Egypt.” See Cassian himself.]

or from the sacred places of Jerusalem,

[Note: This was the name given to the territory of that city in memory of Christ’s life and sufferings. Jerome, in his letter to Paulinus on the training of a monk: “The blessed Hilarion, although he was a Palestinian and lived in Palestine, saw Jerusalem for only one day, so that he might neither despise the holy places because of their proximity nor, conversely, confine the Lord to a place.”]

or from the holy and venerable solitudes of the desert, and came to that city on the business of divine service, as soon as he appeared before the people he was met with insults, sacrileges, and curses.

Nor was that all: he was beaten by the most shameful laughter of disgraceful men and by the hissing of those who laughed while expressing their detestation, as though with bull-hide whips.

Truly, if someone ignorant of the circumstances had seen this happening, he would have thought that not a human being was being mocked, but that some new and unheard-of monster was being driven away and exterminated.

V. Behold the faith of the Africans, and especially of the Carthaginians. Once it was safer for the apostles to enter pagan cities, and those savage and barbarous gatherings of sacrilegious people were less hostile to their first arrival and appearance. The most superstitious people of Athens patiently listened to the holy apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, speaking about the worship and majesty of the one God (Acts 17:22). The Lycaonians, moreover, were so greatly amazed that, when they saw divine powers present in the apostles, they did not think them human beings (Acts 14:10–12). In Carthage, however, the servants of God could scarcely appear in the streets and crossroads without insult and cursing.

182. They do not consider this persecution, because the victims were not killed.

[Note: [Col. 0158B] Imitated from Marcus Tullius in the Second Philippic: “What else is the kindness of robbers, conscript fathers, except that they say they have given life to those whose lives they have not taken?”]

Robbers commonly use this proverb, claiming that they have given life to those from whom they have not taken it. But in that city these benefits belonged not so much to men as to the laws. Even the decrees of the Twelve Tables forbade killing any person who had not been convicted. From this it is clear what a great privilege the Lord’s religion enjoyed there, since the servants of God were permitted to escape for this one reason: pagan law protected them from being slaughtered by Christian hands. And do we wonder if they now endure the barbarians, when we see that holy men endured barbarians among them?

Therefore the Lord is just, and his judgment is just (Psalm 118:137). For what they sowed, as it is written, that they also reap (Galatians 6:8). Thus the Lord seems truly to have spoken of the wickedness of that people: “Repay her according to her work; according to all that she has done, do to her, because she has risen up against the Lord” (Jeremiah 50:29). Should we then wonder or be indignant that they now endure some evils from men? Those things that they previously did against God are far greater, if what they suffer and what they did are assessed according to the difference between the persons involved.

[Col. 0157]

## Letters of Salvian of Marseilles, Presbyter (C)

[Col. 0157C]

### 183. Letter I

O Love, I do not know what to call you: good or evil, sweet or harsh, pleasant or disagreeable. For you are so full of both that you seem to be both. To love our own is honorable; to harm them is bitter. And yet this sometimes belongs to the same spirit and the same devotion: although they differ in appearance, they agree in reason. Love makes us love our own; love sometimes compels us to offend them. Both are one, although one receives love’s favor while the other suffers hatred’s injury.

How grievous this is, I ask you, my dearest, or how bitter: that love should be compelled to become the cause of hatred! I fear that this has now happened often to others, and also to me: while I desire to commend to my inseparable friends this young man whom I have sent to you, attending to one person, I may trouble many, and his love may become an offense to the rest. Yet those who love sufficiently are not quickly offended. But because I fear that my recommendation may be less welcome to some, I regard even a diminution of favor as an offense. For, desiring above all to please those whom I love, I consider their distress my guilt; and unless I please them sufficiently, I undergo the punishment of one who has displeased them.

Yet this need not be feared at all in your case, since, taking all of me into yourselves, you even fear on my behalf before others. For I am so far from being able to displease your affection and judgment that you also fear with me that I might perhaps displease some, my sweetest and dearest friends.

The young man whom I have sent to you was captured at Agrippina together with his family. Once he was a person of no small standing among his own people: his family was not obscure, his household was not contemptible. I might perhaps say more about him, were he not my relative. For that circumstance makes me say less, lest, by saying more about him, I seem to be speaking about myself.

The mother of this young man, then, was left a widow at Agrippina: a good and honorable woman, of whom I might perhaps dare to say that she is truly a widow (1 Timothy 5:3). For, besides the other virtues of chastity and wisdom, she is also distinguished by faith, which is always an ornament to every adornment, since without it nothing is so adorned that it can adorn anything else.

This woman, as I hear, is in such great poverty and want there that she has no means either of remaining or of departing, since she has nothing to provide either sustenance or escape. Her sole resource is to seek a living through hired labor, offering her hands for hire to the wives of barbarians. Thus, although by God’s mercy she has been released from the chains of captivity, now that she is no longer a slave by status, she is enslaved by poverty.

I suspect, not falsely, that I possess here the favor of some holy men—for I do not deny it, lest by denying favor I become ungrateful. But just as I do not deny that I possess it, so I know for certain that I do not deserve it. Indeed, even if there is some favor in me, I am not its cause: for if there is any favor in me, it was given, unless I am mistaken, chiefly because of those whose interest it was that I should be favored. Thus I may perhaps fear that, by denying them what I began to receive because of them, I may seem to deny them not so much my own possession as theirs.

Therefore, thinking that I possess either the influence I actually have or more than I have, she sent to me this man whom I [Note: Something is missing here; the following restoration seems appropriate: “Whom I am sending to you, hoping that…”] … hoping that, through my efforts and the support of my friends’ favor, he might receive assistance from my relatives.

I therefore did what I was asked, but sparingly and before only a few, lest I use the favor itself ungratefully. I have recommended him to others; I recommend him to you, though not to others as I do to you. First, because it is enough for him to be recommended to you as one who belongs to me, so that there is no need to recommend him as though he were myself. Second, because, since you consider me a portion of yourselves, you must also regard one who is a portion of me as in some measure a portion of you. Finally, because this recommendation, just as it concerns a different kind of relationship, also concerns a higher kind of affection.

To others I have commended him bodily, to you spiritually; to others for the advantages of the present, to you in hope of the future; to others for what is brief and earthly, to you for what is eternal and divine. And rightly so: since you possess fewer bodily goods than spiritual ones, I should ask more from you for what you possess in greater abundance.

Receive him, then, I ask, as my own heart (Philemon 12), and, insofar as it lies with you, as your own. Make him welcome, entreat him and encourage him; teach him, instruct him, form him, and bring him forth. May the mercy of Christ our Lord grant that, since it is more advantageous for him, he who is now my relative and the relative of the others may begin to be yours rather than theirs.

Receive him, I ask, into those blessed and eternal dwellings; take him into the sacred granaries; open the heavenly treasures. Act and persevere in such a way that, while you store him in your treasury, you make him part of the treasures themselves. That ineffable goodness of God is powerful enough that, while you adopt him into partnership in spiritual goods, you may increase through him the riches that you pour into him.

And indeed, if there is any good natural disposition in him, his hope and salvation should not be difficult for you, even if he hears nothing from you: it should be enough for him simply to see you. Farewell.

### Letter II. To Eucherius

[Note: To Eucherius of Lyon, a man of outstanding reputation in those times, whose sons Salonius and Veranus Salvian had under his discipline, as stated above. Salvian also wrote him Letter VIII.]

To Eucherius, bishop, Salvian. Ursicinus, your fosterling, recently brought me your greeting. If he came without your command, I praise his wisdom, though I do not approve his falsehood; if he came at your command, I wonder that you preferred to entrust the duty of affection rather than write—that is, to send it through a servant rather than through yourself. I therefore criticize this and wish it corrected, provided it resulted from negligence and not from pride.

Arrogance is generally the attendant of a new dignity. Yet in your case one must not accept the general reputation of this vice, since your character and kindness are almost unique. For this reason I continually desire you even now to respond to my former esteem, lest, if your customary services have differed in some respects, it should seem that your new honors have permitted you something.

[Note: Stephen of Tournai, Letter 61: “May that common proverb, ‘Honors change manners,’ remain true of others.” Jordanus, in his letter to G., prior, in Duchesne, volume IV, p. 755: “But now I ask that the common proverb, ‘Honors change manners,’ may not prove true of you.” Arnulf of Lisieux, Letter 2: “For a new consciousness of dignity creates a new heart and new affections.” See the notes on Letter 109 of Lupus of Ferrières.]

### Letter III. To Agricius

[Col. 0160C]

[Note: Agricius was bishop of Antipolis in the second Narbonensis, not far from Marseilles; he signed the Council of Agde in 506. I do not agree with Rittershusius, who thinks that this letter was written to Agroecius, bishop of Sens, to whom Sidonius wrote around the year 473 concerning the election of the bishop of Bourges. This may also be the Agroecius who, around the year 458, while not yet a bishop, offered one thousand solidi to the Church of Narbonne to assist Rusticus, bishop of that see, who was rebuilding his church, which had long before been burned down, as is established by an old Narbonese inscription that we published elsewhere.]

To Agricius, bishop, Salvian.

If I wished to excuse my failure in duty before your holiness, I should deserve greater accusation, since through stupidity I would either fail to recognize that I am inexcusable or, through pride, refuse to admit it. I do not therefore excuse myself; for after guilt, to boast of innocence is an increase of guilt.

What, then, shall I do, when I have neither the ability to deny the offense nor to defend it? I do not dare deny what is manifest, and I cannot excuse what is excessive. I must therefore flee to the remedies of the divine Scriptures, which [the remedies] of the greatest crimes…

### Letter IV. To Father-in-law and Mother-in-law

[Note: These were the parents of Palladia, who was Salvian’s wife.]

To Hypatius and Quiet[a], Palladia’s parents, Salvian, Palladia, and Auspiciola send greetings.

The apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, teacher of faith, and dwelling-place of God, although, being a most eloquent man, he dictated all his letters, nevertheless inscribed some of them not only with his own name. In some he joined Silvanus’ name to his own; in others Timothy’s; and in certain letters the names of both were added to his. Why did he do this?

First, I believe, so that those who wrote together might be recognized as being together. Next, so that those who had been taught separately by each of them might know that the judgment of all did not differ. Finally, so that those whom the authority of individuals did not move might at least be moved by the agreement of all.

Thus we too, small imitators of great examples, write to you—whom nature has made our parents, faith our brothers and sisters, and honor our masters—not with the authority of teachers, as those apostles did, but with the humility of servants. We hope that you, who until now have not been moved by the letters of each of us individually, may now be moved by the entreaty of all of us, and that we may be your children [Note: Rittershusius thought these words should be enclosed in parentheses. I believe, however, that they do not belong here and should therefore be excised.] without undue fear; … and that you may know that we agree equally in feeling, fearing, and pleading, not because we know whether you are angry with both of us, but because we cannot be divided in our cause.

The fear is the same for us, even if the offense does not appear to be the same. Mutual affection makes it so that, although perhaps you are not angry with both of us, if one of us is guilty, the other cannot be without sorrow over the guilt.

There is one thing, however, that makes us contend and struggle with each other: although we are both equally guilty as your children, each of us fears more for the other than for himself.

Dearest parents, most revered parents, allow us, we ask, to question you. Can such loving children not be loved? What great evil have we deserved, either as your most beloved dependents or your most revered servants, that we should receive neither favor as children nor remission of offense as servants?

It is now almost the seventh year since you have sent us, living so far from you, no letter. Almost no one who has offended against God is assigned such a long period of mourning; no one who has committed the greatest crimes is so completely… [lacuna]

…so that he may love more; that is, so that a father’s anger may not be the destruction of love but its improvement, with correction bringing as much to the one person’s reform as reform restores to mutual affection.

This is more fitting for those parents who have true reasons for being angry with their children concerning certain matters. But why are you angry, since, from the time you became a Christian, you ceased even to have false reasons? Let us suppose that, when you were still a pagan, you did not accept our conversion with equanimity. At that time, because our pursuits differed, a difference of wills was also to be endured; for although love was not angry, superstition was opposed. Though a father might not hate his son, error nevertheless hated the truth.

Now the situation is entirely different. From the time you professed the worship of God, you spoke in my favor. If you are pursuing the former causes of your anger, blame yourself, since you gave your daughter to a Christian. If that is not the reason, why are you angry with me because I now desire to increase in myself the religion that you have begun to approve in yourself? Why, I ask, do you not love in me what you are, since in yourself you condemned what you were?

But I must moderate my words somewhat, because even in a good cause a child’s speech before parents ought to be humble insofar as the matter permits. Forgive me, dearest parents: affection for God makes me somewhat freer in his cause. If there are other reasons for your anger, I do not deny that I may have sinned. But if you are angry with me because I seem to love Christ, forgive me for what I am about to say. I ask pardon because you are angry, but I cannot say that what I did was wrong.

This, then, has been said to you in my name and, as it were, in a private petition. Now you, my dearest and most venerable sister [Note: He calls Palladia, his wife, by this title, in accordance with the canons and the enduring custom of the early Church. Those who advanced from marriage to the priesthood were separated from their wives’ beds and thereafter associated with them only as with sisters. See Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius, Book V, Letter 16, and Rosweyde’s Onomasticon to the Lives of the Fathers.], fulfill both your own part and mine. Pray that I may obtain forgiveness; ask that we may both prevail. Since, being absent, you cannot kiss their feet with your lips, kiss them at least through your entreaty: as a handmaid, their feet; as a fosterling, their hands; as a daughter, their faces.

Do not tremble; do not be afraid. We have good judges. Affection itself pleads for you; nature itself makes your petition; you have the support of your case in the minds of your own parents. Those who are overcome by their own love quickly assent.

Entreat them, then, and say humbly: “What have I done? What have I deserved? Forgive me, whatever it is. I ask pardon, although I do not know my offense. As you yourselves know, I have never offended you by neglect of duty or obstinacy; I have never injured you with a harsher word; I have never violated you with a more insolent expression. I was given by you to my husband; by you I was entrusted to my spouse.

“I believe I have kept your commands. The sacred secret of your pious instruction clings to my mind. You commanded me, as I think, above all to be obedient to my husband. I have followed your will; I have obeyed your command; I have obeyed him in everything to whom you wished me to be obedient.

“He invited me to religion; he invited me to chastity. Forgive me: I considered it shameful to resist. It seemed to me a modest, honorable, and holy undertaking. I confess that, when he spoke to me about such a matter, I was ashamed that I had not begun earlier. To this was added reverence for Christ and affection: I believed that whatever I did out of love for God was honorable.

“I fall at your feet, dearest parents: I, your Palladia, your little jackdaw, your little lady—the one with whom, under all these names, you once played in your most indulgent affection; the one who, under various names, was at one time your mother, at another your little bird, at another your lady, one name belonging to my sex, another to infancy, and the third to rank.

“Here I am, the one through whom you first received the names of parents and the joys of grandparents; and, what is better than either, received both happily, with the benefit of gaining and the blessedness of enjoying them. I do not claim any credit for this; nevertheless, she through whom God wished you to be happy ought not to be regarded by you as ungrateful.

“Do not, I ask, therefore be troubled that I wish to return something to God, to whom I cannot repay everything. You are full of the most delightful consolations, full of beloved pledges, full of divine blessing. Apart from the particular matter concerning me, your own situation commands me to give thanks to God: I believe that I owe it to him that he has granted you so much.”

But enough of this. We have now prayed sufficiently for ourselves, dearest sister; the rest must be done through your daughter.

Let us therefore employ—for in reconciling parents’ affection every honorable means is tried—the custom and example of those who, at the final stage of a case, sometimes presented certain things to move the mercy of judges about to pronounce sentence: grieving mothers, old men in mourning clothes, or weeping children. In this way, those who had already won their case by their words pleaded it afterward through the things themselves.

We too, therefore, offer you, dearest parents, a pledge equal to theirs in force, but more pleasing as a support. We offer a pledge not unknown but domestic; not alien but our own; not, as those orators offered, foreign both to themselves and to the judges, but common to us and to you. Her descent from your blood does not compel you to love unknown people but recalls you to affection for your own. It commends to you not strangers by what is alien, but your own by what is yours; and she does not ask you to love those whom you have never seen, but not to hate those whom, I think, you cannot help loving.

The matter is therefore yours, dearest parents; your own spirit and your own affection plead with you: do not, I ask, be so angry with us that you fail to consider even your own interests. Your common pledge, through us and together with us, sends forth almost her first voice to you on behalf of our offense.

Wretched indeed and deserving pity is her condition: she began to recognize her grandparents first through the guilt of her parents. Have pity, we ask, on her innocence; have pity on her helplessness. She is somehow compelled to plead already for the offense of her parents, though she does not yet know what it means to offend.

God, once wounded by the sins of the Ninevites, moved to mercy through the wailing of infants and the cries of children. Although we read that the whole people mourned, the lot and innocence of the little ones nevertheless merited especial mercy, when God said to Jonah: “Are you greatly grieved over the plant?” (Jonah 4:9). And shortly afterward: “Should I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right hand from their left?” (ibid., 11). He thereby declared that, because of the sincerity of the innocent, he had spared even the guilt of the guilty.

But why do I speak of God’s mercy, who not only grants what is requested but sometimes bestows even what is not hoped for—and who, if one may say so, is greater than human beings in humanity and kindness to the same degree that he is greater in power and nature?

As Livy says, a war prepared between the Romans and the Sabines—and, what is more difficult to settle, already begun—was once ended by the entreaties and intervention of beloved pledges. Although one people was naturally fierce and the other inflamed by grief, the sight of mutual affection nevertheless had such power that the Roman could no longer remember the war, nor the Sabine the injury. Those who shortly before had been fierce and half-barbarous, eager for kindred blood and prodigal of their own, began to embrace one another, because they had begun to possess a mutual pledge; and the two peoples became one, because the affection of both became one.

We are not standing in battle; we do not take up weapons; we do not use force; we do not even attempt to repel force. We judge it impious if even in this matter children oppose their parents, lest the unjust should be punished. Why, I ask, cannot the affection that once obtained something for those men on behalf of their own obtain something for us? Are we for that reason among the most unhappy of all, and for that reason less deserving of pardon, because we do not know how to resist?

What you wish us to suffer, we suffer. If you are angry, we plead. If you believe we ought to be punished, we submit. What, I ask, remains for vengeance after this? Certainly, even if parents have just reasons for anger, nothing more fortunate or desirable can happen to them than that their children should make satisfaction for their offense in such a way that they have no need to exact vengeance.

In what way, moreover, could we satisfy you more fully? We are your children, and we are the ones asking you; your granddaughter is the one through whom we ask. Spare her; forgive her. Her parents, your dearest children, plead for themselves—those whose names usually induce you to deny nothing even to strangers.

It would take too long to speak of the countless examples of piety and humanity, and it would be backwards to proceed from greater examples to lesser ones. Yet what I am about to say is apparently less important, though in reality it is no less so.

Once, in the Roman forum, Servius Galba pleaded for the danger to his reputation and safety [Note: See Cicero, Brutus, chapter 23, and Quintilian, Institutes, Book II, chapter 15.]. Because of the difficulty of the matter and the unpopularity of his action, he placed little hope not only in his case but even in his eloquence. He therefore devised a means of testing the judges’ hearts through emotion, since he could not bend them by the ambition of his pleas.

After exhausting almost every resource of oratorical art and talent, and realizing that he had made little progress, he brought forward before the benches of the audience and in the assembly and sight of the judges the little boy whom he had with him, the son of Gallus—a man considered most distinguished in those times and recently deceased—and his own little children. As he commended the boy in a mournful speech to the judges about to pronounce sentence, all their minds were broken and bent by emotion.

What more need be said? Once everyone’s feelings had been swayed, mercy granted to humanity whatever truth had denied to advocacy. O human affections, how great you are, how powerful, since you were able even to possess a place in judgment!

Learn, dearest parents—let it be said with your pardon—learn from this example at least to be broken and softened. Certainly mercy prevailed even there, where there was no legitimate place for mercy. The judges who were about to pronounce sentence, and who had sworn that they would declare nothing except in accordance with the duty of truth, nevertheless could not exclude mercy even after their oath. They were moved so greatly by humanity that, while attending to another’s case, they almost forgot their own.

We ask you for nothing harsh, nothing extraordinary. Grant to yourselves, on your own behalf, what those strangers granted to strangers against themselves. Certainly the case there was no more just, nor the person dearer, nor the audience more humane, nor the advocate more welcome. There the plea concerned a crime; here, affection. There, strangers; here, children. There, sworn judges; here, parents who have sworn no oath. There, an orator whom they were trying to entrap; here, a granddaughter who, by the simplicity of her infancy, may move you all the more because she does not yet know how to plead.

What is lacking to our case? What new and unheard-of support must be sought? Must we employ the prayers of strangers before you? There is always caution in love. No one loves better than the one who most fears to offend.

Therefore I now ask pardon, not because I know that I have offended, but so as to leave no room at all for offense; not because my conscience convicts me, but because reason and the duty of affection require it. May a blameless supplication earn greater favor for your son’s affection, and may a petition without guilt benefit love; may you have more to love in your son’s plea for pardon, if you have nothing to forgive.

Yet perhaps we flatter ourselves rashly concerning our innocence, since we do not know what you think of us. Your judgment matters more to us than the reasoning of our own opinion. It remains, then, that if something else—whatever it may be—has been committed by us, you who judge it worthy of offense should also judge it not unworthy of pardon.

You will beautifully satisfy yourself in the guilt of your own. A father loses nothing by forgiving his son, for it is much more fortunate and praiseworthy to forgive one’s own even when undeserving than to punish one’s own even when deserving. Farewell.

### 195. Letter V. To Cattura

To Cattura, his sister, Salvian.

Although, as the apostle Paul teaches, we do not know what we ought to pray for (Romans 8:26)—with the result that at times we do not know what we ought to desire or rejoice in—nevertheless, in accordance with the common feeling of the human race (by which all human beings, more piously than wisely, desire those for whom we care to remain with us as long as possible), I rejoice that, after a serious and prolonged illness, you have obtained hope even of the present life, whereas you have always possessed hope of the future life.

Blessed, therefore, is the Lord our God, who, always the guardian of your spirit, has now especially also been the guardian of your flesh. Remaining in you and guarding you, he extended his hand from your inner parts to your outward members; he preserved not only the Holy of Holies but also the vestibules of his temple and its surrounding enclosures. Pouring out his protection more widely, he caused the salvation of your soul to reach even the salvation of your body.

Yet I do not think that even this weakness of the earthly vessel which you endured has harmed you. Its strength, as you know, is always hostile to the mind. Thus I rightly consider you now so much stronger in spirit as you have begun to be weaker in flesh.

For, says the Apostle, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Galatians 5:17). Therefore, if, while the body resists, we cannot do what we wish, the flesh must become weak so that we may do what we desire. And this is true. The weakness of the flesh sharpens the vigor of the mind; and when the limbs are afflicted, the strength of the body is transferred into the virtues of the spirit. Thus it seems to me a kind of health when a person is sometimes not healthy.

For then there is almost no struggle between the spirit and the body—that is, no struggle between the divine nature and its earthly enemy. The marrow does not burn with shameful flames; hidden incentives do not inflame an unsound mind; wandering senses do not revel in various pleasures. The soul alone exults, rejoicing in an afflicted body as though its adversary had been subdued.

Rejoice, therefore, fosterling of Christ. Open the door of your mind—always simple and tranquil, but now more purified and free—and, as it is written, draw in the Holy Spirit (Psalm 118:131). I do not think you have ever been more worthy of God as an inhabitant: the weaker in body, the purer in understanding. While diseases conquered your flesh, you conquered them in mind.

Happy are you if you preserve this death of the body always for the life of the spirit. Perhaps, with all the incentives of human temptation extinguished in you, you have begun in some way to possess the nature of the soul even in the flesh. Thus it seems to me that your previous illness and your present recovery have come not only through a great dispensation of God but also through a great gift.

You were ill in order to strengthen the virtue of your spirit, perhaps now securely attaining health once the flesh has been overcome; so that, after bodily soundness has been restored, you may possess it without any weakness of soul, and the flesh may begin to be well in such a way that temptation does not rise again. Farewell.

### Letter VI. To Limenius

To Limenius, Salvian sends greetings in the Lord.

Although I know that honorable minds do not forget upright affection, because good people love good pursuits as though they were somehow their own nature, nevertheless, since it is our duty, insofar as it lies with us, to increase the love of good friends through our service, I thought I should remind you of the affection begun long ago by me and recently increased by you. Thus, when you read my letters and see in me the devotion of my love for you, you may kindle in yourself love for me.

I do not doubt that our God will grant that, while you receive the affection of Christians, you yourself may become the affection of Christ. Farewell in the Lord.

[Col. 0167A]

### Letter VII. To Aprus and Verus

To Aprus and Verus, Salvian.

Whether it was an act of duty or of presumption that I wrote to you before receiving from you the right to write, I prefer to leave to your judgment rather than assert my own position, because a doubtful and hidden matter is always better entrusted to good interpreters than to bad defenders.

But although this is truly so, and although I understand it to be so, if you think that something should be heard from me concerning the performance of duty, according to my understanding I hold this view: whenever there is a holy contest concerning the rendering of service by the lowly—as I am—to the superior—as you are—they do better if they forestall their patrons in writing than if they are forestalled by them.

For since the very regularity of writing and replying is chiefly a means of offering and returning services, it must necessarily be much more humble and obedient for someone to take care to offer his service first than to wait to receive it first. For, in accordance with what we said above, offering a service seems to flee honor, whereas concealing it seems to seek it.

It was therefore fitting and reasonable in many ways that I should write to you first. First, because, as an inferior, I would seem shamefully to have sought honor. Second, because the dignity of your character so protects you from every such suspicion that almost anything done by you is believed to have been done rightly. Finally, even if you had not written to me first with the intention that I, a sinner and a weak man, should offer services before receiving them, it ought rather to be thought that you acted from pious counsel than from arrogance.

For since you have attained the prize of nearly all humility and of almost every service, it was more credible that you did not wish to deny honor to a friend than that you wished to impose a burden on him. Although it is an honorable and religious endeavor to anticipate others in humility and to surpass them, when such a matter arises between people such as we are—that is, between the highest and the lowest—it is a sign of greater affection when the greater yields in service to the lesser.

These matters, my revered masters, I thought should be written to you according to my small opinion, not so much through confidence in my knowledge as through reverence for your dignity. If you show that you think otherwise, I shall put my hand over my mouth; and, following the example of holy Job, who after the divine voice recognized himself to be small and weak in comparison with the God who spoke, I shall judge myself to be earth, as I am, filthy, and an impure chickpea. I shall say: “Once I have spoken, I will not add anything” (Job 40:5).

And rightly so. To fall into the error of a false opinion before learning the truth is the mark of an inexperienced and simple mind; but to persist in it after recognizing the truth is obstinacy. Farewell.

### Letter VIII. To Eucherius

[Col. 0168B]

[Note: [Col. 0167C] Thus reads the old codex of the monastery of Corbie, which contains the works of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons. Pithoeus published it as: “To the lord and his beloved Eucherius, bishop, Salvianus.” The remainder of this letter has been corrected according to the same Corbie codex, which is now preserved in Paris in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

To the lord and most beloved Eucherius, bishop, Salvianus, presbyter.

I have read the books that you sent: brief in style, rich in teaching, easy to read, and complete in instruction—suited to your mind and piety. Nor do I wonder that you composed so useful and beautiful a work chiefly for the education of your holy and blessed children [Note: [Col. 0167D] Namely, Salonius and Veranius.]. For since you have built in them an outstanding temple for God, you have adorned the highest pinnacle of your building, as it were, with the teaching of a new instruction; and, so that their holy character might be illumined equally by doctrine and by life, you have adorned those whom you had formed by moral instruction with spiritual teaching.

It remains that our Lord God, by whose gift such admirable young men are what they are, may make them equal to your books—that is, may grant that whatever those books contain in mystery, each of them may possess in understanding. And since, now by divine dispensation and judgment, they too have begun to become teachers of the Churches [Note: [Col. 0167D] I do not think that they were bishops at that time. Salvianus would not have said that they had begun to be teachers of the Churches; he would have said that they were already teachers. The title “teachers of the Church” belongs first of all to bishops, but also to others, as may be gathered from the Commonitory of Vincent of Lérins. Thus Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 2: “I shall try to demonstrate these things by divine testimonies, if I first bring forward a few points concerning the praise of true priests, who are the teachers of the Churches. The first grade, then, of the teaching office, as I myself judge, was among deacons.” Philostorgius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 17, relates that Leontius, bishop of Antioch, designated his disciple Aetius for the order of deacon and charged him to teach the doctrines of the Church in the church; Aetius, however, refused to accept the diaconate, though he accepted the ministry of teaching. The same author, book IV, chapter 3, says that Eudoxius, who had succeeded Leontius in the episcopate of Antioch, designated Eunomius for the diaconate, but that Eunomius did not undertake the ministry until he had attained an exact knowledge of doctrine. From these two passages, I think it can be established that the ministry of teaching was attached to the office of the deacon—contrary to the opinion of a learned man—at least in the Eastern Church. As for the Western Church, I have so far discovered nothing certain. But since antiquity also placed deacons among the clergy, it may reasonably be inferred that their office was something greater than a simple ministry, and that authority to teach was therefore entrusted to them, just as to a bishop and presbyter, though not without the bishop’s command.], until the merciful kindness of the most gracious God grants that their teaching may be fruitful for the Churches and for you, and that, through their most excellent progress, they may adorn both him by whom they were begotten and those whom they themselves will beget through their instruction.

May the merciful God grant me this as well—not, perhaps, among all things, but certainly after all things: that those who were once my disciples [Note: [Col. 0168D] Salvianus had been, as we have already observed more than once, the teacher of Salonius and Veranius; Salvianus himself shows this both here and in the following letter. Eucherius also confirms it in the letter to Salonius that is usually prefixed to the *Questions on the Old and New Testament*. Gennadius likewise, speaking of Salvianus, says: “The teacher of the holy bishops Salonius and Veranius.”] may now daily be my intercessors. Farewell, my lord and beloved.

[Col. 0169A]

## LETTER IX. TO SALONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0169C] This heading, which is absent from other editions, was taken from a very ancient manuscript of the Royal Library, containing four books against avarice. We formerly cited a similar heading by Strabo of Fulda, from his letter to Gerungus, in the notes to the tenth letter of Lupus of Ferrières. Pithoeus observed that this letter of Salvianus does not exist in his oldest copy. Moreover, since it had hitherto been published at the beginning of the books against Avarice, in place of a preface, we judged that it properly belonged to the Book of Letters; we therefore removed it from that position and restored it among the letters.]

To the lord and most blessed disciple, son and father: disciple through instruction, son through affection, father through honor [Note: [Col. 0169D] Salonius was Salvianus’s father in honor because he was a bishop. In those times bishops generally called lower-ranking clergy, and especially presbyters, their sons. Jerome writes to Augustine: “Farewell, my dearest friend, my son in age, my father in dignity.” Sidonius, bishop of Clermont, speaking of Count Victorius, book VII, letter 17: “Whom, by secular law, I honor as patron; by ecclesiastical law, as son; as a client I revere him, as a father I love him.” Cassiodorus, on Psalm 109: “This still happens today in our way of life: a son who has become a bishop is called the father of his own father—not by the order of birth, but by honor.” Hence Jerome’s statement about bishops: “Let them remember that they are fathers, not lords.” Augustine, however, though a bishop, calls the presbyter Jerome his brother. By that time the distinction between bishops and presbyters had already been established. For although, Augustine says in writing to Jerome, “according to the titles of honor that ecclesiastical custom has now established, the episcopate is greater than the presbyterate, nevertheless in many matters Augustine is lesser than Jerome.”], to Salonius, bishop, Salvianus.

You ask me, my Salonius, my beloved, why the little books recently addressed to the Church by a certain man of our time bear the name of Timothy. You add that unless I clearly explain the reason for the name, while they are called “Timothy’s,” they may perhaps be reckoned among the apocrypha. I give you thanks, and am grateful that you judge of me in such a way as to consider this part of my concern for the faith: that I should not permit anything in ecclesiastical work to waver; namely, that a matter of the greatest benefit should not be diminished in value by uncertainty of opinion.

Thus, to exclude entirely the suspicion of an apocryphal style, it might have been enough that I indicated above that these books are works of a recent discussion and were written by a man of the present age out of devotion to and love of divine things. They are free from suspicion of being apocryphal because it is recognized that they did not belong to the apostle Timothy. But someone may ask who their author is, if he is not the apostle, and whether he inscribed his own name or another’s on the little books.

That is true. The question may be raised, and rightly so, if the inquiry can lead to some useful result. But if it is fruitless, why should curiosity labor, when knowledge will gain no benefit from curiosity? In every book, the benefit of reading is sought more than the author’s name [Col. 0169C] [Note: [Col. 0170D] Cassianus, *Conferences*, 28.1, says that the authority of all statements falters if the merit of the speaker is removed.]. Therefore, if there is benefit in the reading, and whoever he may be has something capable of instructing readers, what concern has he with a name that cannot help the curious? Thus one may most appropriately answer the inquirer with that angelic saying: “Are you asking about his homeland, or about a hired servant?” (Tobit 5:17).

Since a name offers no benefit, whoever finds benefit in the writings inquires into the writer’s name to no purpose. The reasons, then, that I have stated are sufficient. But since we can refuse nothing to you, my Salonius, our honor and support, we shall speak plainly.

There are three things that may be asked about these little books of which we are speaking: why the writer addressed them to the Church; whether he did so under another’s name or his own; and, if under another’s name, why he chose the name of Timothy above all others.

The reason why the little books were addressed to the Church is this. Their writer, as the writings themselves also testify, possesses within himself such devotion and love for God that he considers nothing preferable to God, in accordance with that saying of our Lord: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37).

Yet the most lukewarm and negligent people think that this saying need be observed only during a time of persecution. As though there were any time at all when something ought to be preferred to God; or as though one who ought to regard Christ as more precious than all things during persecution ought to regard him as less precious at every other time.

If that were so, we should owe God our love because of persecution, not because of faith; and we should be able to love him only when the impious persecute us. Yet we owe the Lord an affection that is either greater, or certainly no less, in peaceful circumstances than in harsh ones. Indeed, he ought to be loved more for this very reason: that he does not allow us to be afflicted by evils. This is the indulgence of the most loving and gentle father, who prefers that we display our faith through religious works in peace and quiet rather than prove it through punishments inflicted on our bodies during persecution.

Therefore, if nothing is to be preferred to him when he deals harshly with us, then nothing should be preferred to him when, through his indulgence, he gives us greater opportunity to earn merit. But these matters belong more properly to another occasion. Let us now complete what we have begun.

That writer, then, seeing the serious and manifold illnesses of nearly all Christians—and seeing that those placed in the Church not only failed to put everything else after God, but almost put everything before him (for drunkards seem to despise God in their drunkenness, the greedy in their greed, the shameless in their lust, the violent in their cruelty, and almost everyone in these various ways)—and seeing that this was all the more serious because these things were not only committed for a long time through the most atrocious wickedness, but were not corrected afterward even through repentance, especially since among those who are said to be repentant [Note: [Col. 0170D] So the royal codex reads throughout.
