In its place Pithoeus’s edition had: “Let the name be more repentance than its fruit.” Thus Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, one of my own bishops, says in book II, letter 12: “Repentance, dearest brother, is not to be undertaken in name but in deed.” This must likewise be read in place of what Canisius published: “Patience, brother,” and so forth. The same correction should be made in homily 35 of Caesarius, bishop of Arles, where the text now reads, “when he has closed the eyes of patience in them,” although it should read “of repentance.” Likewise in the homily of Paul the Deacon: “Every sinner, if he wishes to attain pardon, must, having cast aside all swelling of heart, regard himself in every way as earth and ashes; thus, beginning from true humility, he will be able to obtain from the Lord repentance.” Therefore “repentance” must be read.], there is more the name of repentance than its fruit—for the names of things are of little value when the things themselves are absent, and words of virtue are worthless without their powers.

For very many, indeed almost all, who abound in possessions and are conscious of their crimes and offenses, not only do not redeem what they have committed through confession and satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0171D] Below, book I *Against Avarice*, p. 221: “But how will prolonged confession help him who lies at the point of death?” Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 9: “That act which is expressed and commonly designated by the Greek term *exomologesis* is the confession by which we acknowledge our offense to the Lord—not, indeed, as though he were unaware of it, but because satisfaction is arranged through confession, repentance arises from confession, and God is appeased by repentance. Thus *exomologesis* is the discipline of prostrating and humbling a person, imposing a way of life that calls forth mercy. Concerning dress and food also it commands him to lie upon sackcloth and ashes, darken his body with filth, cast down his spirit with mourning, and treat the one who sinned with sorrowful discipline,” and so forth. See Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, where he speaks of Ananias, Azariah, Mishael, and Daniel.], but do not even deign to redeem them through gifts and acts of mercy, which are at least easy to offer. They neglect this not only in prosperity, but—what is far more irreligious—in adversity; not only when they are safe and well, but even when they are failing.

So great is human disbelief, and so grievous is the sickness of unbelieving souls, that although many leave their greatest wealth to heirs, and sometimes even to strangers, they think that they lose only what they have given for the sake of their hope and salvation.

Although this is grave in almost everyone, it is especially so in those whom a profession of holiness also accuses of the same crime of unbelief [Note: [Col. 0172D] See above, p. 6.]. Yet this disease belongs not only to secular people, but also to those who appropriate to themselves the name of religion.

Therefore, when that writer saw that this evil was common to nearly everyone, and that this stain had spread not only among worldly people but also among penitents and converts, among widows who had already professed continence, and among maidens consecrated at the holy altars—and, as I may put it, among those who should almost be counted as monsters, even among Levites and presbyters—and, what is much more savage than all these things, that it had even reached bishops, many of whom, as I have said above, having neither natural affections nor pledges, neither families nor children, assigned their wealth and possessions not to the poor, not to the churches, not to themselves, nor finally—and what is greater and more excellent than all these—to God, but especially to secular persons, the wealthy, and strangers, a zeal for the Lord arose in his heart, as it is written, “like a burning fire” (Jeremiah 20:9).

And because, with his innermost feelings burning with sacred zeal, he could do nothing else in such a fervor, he burst into a voice of grief. No recipient seemed more suitable for that voice than the Church, of which those who were doing these things were themselves a part. For it is pointless to write to one or a few when the cause belongs to everyone.

This, then, was the reason that persuaded and compelled him to send the little books of which we speak to the Church.

Now we shall discuss the second matter: why the author’s name is not present in the title of the books. Although there may be one principal reason for this, there could, I think, have been many.

The first is derived from God’s command, by which we are instructed in every way to avoid the vanity of earthly glory, lest, while we seek the empty breath of human praise, we lose the heavenly reward. From this also comes God’s command that, while instructing us to pray and give secretly, he wishes us to commend the fruit of a good work in secret; for no devotion of faith is greater than that which avoids human notice and is content with God as its witness. “Let not your left hand know,” says the Savior, “what your right hand is doing; and your Father, who sees in secret, will reward you” (Matthew 6:3–4).

This reason alone could have been sufficient for that writer to remove and conceal his name from the title: so that what he had done for the honor of his Lord might be reserved solely for divine knowledge, and so that the work might become more pleasing to God because it avoided public fame.

Yet, as must be acknowledged, the chief reason was that the writer, as we read, was humble and contemptible in his own eyes, considering himself utterly insignificant and the least of all—and, what is more important, doing so with remarkable faith: not as a matter of assumed humility, but from the truth of a simple judgment.

Thus, rightly believing that others ought to regard him as he regarded himself, he inserted another’s name into his books, lest the smallness of his person diminish the authority of writings that offered healing. For now all statements are valued according to the standing of the one who spoke them. The judgments of this age are so weak and almost nonexistent that readers consider not so much what they are reading as whose work they are reading, and think not so much about the force and power of the diction as about the dignity of the writer.

For this reason that writer wished in every way to hide and remain concealed, lest writings containing great benefit should perhaps be made less effective by their author’s name. Whoever he is who asks why another’s name was assumed now has the answer.

It remains to say why the name was Timothy’s. To explain this, we must return once more to the author. He is the cause behind all the reasons: just as humility led him to use another’s name, so fear and caution led him to write the name Timothy.

He was timid and fearful, sometimes even avoiding minor falsehoods, and so afraid of sinning that he occasionally feared what need not be feared. When he therefore wished to remove his own name from the title and insert another’s [Note: [Col. 0172D] Earlier the reading was *Timothei*, not only in the printed editions but also in the Royal codex. Since it was clear that there was an error here and that some word appropriate to a timid and fearful man had to be substituted, we followed the traces of the sound reading concealed in the word *Timothei*.], he feared falsehood in this exchange of names, considering that even in the service of a holy work a stain of falsity ought by no means to be admitted.

Placed in this uncertainty of conflicting considerations, he thought it best to follow the most sacred example of the blessed Evangelist. At the beginning of each of his two divine works, the Evangelist inscribed the name of Theophilus; although he appears to have written to a man, he actually wrote for the love of God. He judged it most fitting that his writings should be directed toward that love of God by which he himself had been impelled to write.

This writer, of whom we speak, likewise adopted that reasoning and plan. Conscious that he had done everything in his writings for the honor of God just as the Evangelist had done everything out of love for God, he wrote under the name Timothy for the same reason that the Evangelist wrote under the name Theophilus.

For just as the name Theophilus expresses love, so the name Timothy expresses the honor of the Divinity. Therefore, when you read that Timothy wrote to the Church, you must understand that the writing was addressed to the Church for the honor of God—or rather, that the writings themselves were sent by the honor of God, since one may rightly be said to have written through whom it came about that the work was written.

For this reason, then, the name Timothy was inscribed in the title of the books. The writer rightly judged that, since he was writing the little books in honor of God, he ought to consecrate their title to that very honor of the Divinity.

You have, my Salonius, my beloved, what you demanded; I have completed the task you required of me. It remains that, since I have performed my part, you should perform yours: namely, pray to our Lord God, and by praying obtain that these books, written to the Church in honor of Christ, may benefit their author before God as much as he himself desires them to benefit everyone.

Nor, I think, is it an unjust desire for someone to ask that as much be granted to him for salvation as he wishes for all others out of love.

[Note: [Col. 0173B] Pithoeus’s edition read: “Farewell, our honor and support.” The royal codex, however, reads: “Farewell, my honor and support.” The addition of *my* in the royal codex indicated that the name of Salonius should be supplied here [Col. 0172B]. Above, p. 200: “But since, my Salonius, our honor and support, we can refuse you nothing.” It was the custom of that age to repeat the same honorific titles at the end of letters, as Sirmondus observed in his notes on Ennodius, and as is evident from Sidonius, Faustus, Ruricius, and others.]

Farewell, my Salonius, our honor and support.

[Col. 0173B]

## FOUR BOOKS OF SALVIANUS OF MARSEILLES, PRESBYTER, AGAINST AVARICE

[Note: [Col. 0173C] The first edition of these books appeared at Basel in 1528 through the efforts of Johann Sichard, in a volume entitled *Antidotum*. From Salvianus’s ninth letter, which had been added to these books in place of a preface, the Centuriators concluded that Salvianus was their true author. “These four books,” they say, “are printed in the volume entitled *Antidotum*. And if it were permissible to conjecture in a doubtful matter, we would almost declare that Salvianus himself is the true author of these books, moved by the argument of this preface.” Against this, the celebrated and learned Petrus Pithoeus declared that there was good reason to doubt whether Salvianus was the author of these books, for the reason stated above: in book IV of *The Government of God*, p. 60, Salvianus cites a passage from the second book *To the Catholic Church* as though these books were not his own, saying: “As a certain man says in his writings.” But Rittershusius, in the preface to the *Works of Salvianus*, tried to remove this difficulty of Pithoeus for learned readers, and the authority of Gennadius requires us to assign those four books to Salvianus. For when Gennadius lists Salvianus’s works, he expressly includes four books *Against Avarice*. I admit that his name does not appear at the front of the work, and that the title of these books is “Timothy to the Catholic Church,” not “Against Avarice.” But Salvianus himself explains in his letter to Salonius why the author’s name was suppressed. We added the title *Against Avarice*, moved by the authority of the work and the testimony of Gennadius. Nor should the fact that he praises a passage from the second book *Against Avarice* as though it belonged to another writer trouble anyone. At the beginning Salvianus had not wished to be recognized as the author of these books, so as to avoid in every way the vanity of earthly glory and lest the smallness of his person diminish the authority of writings that brought healing, as he himself says in his letter to Salonius, p. 204. He therefore cited a passage of his own as if it belonged to someone else, in order to persist in the same purpose of remaining hidden. Thus Vincent of Lérins gave his treatise against heretics the concealed title *Peregrinus Against Heretics*, as Gennadius reports. Following this example, Faustus, bishop of Riez, cites in letter 16 a passage from his own letter to the deacon G. in this manner: “It was written in a certain letter.” Salvianus himself, in book I of *The Government of God*, p. 10, when citing a passage from a letter he had written to Cattura, a devout woman, makes no mention of his own name, but says only: “A certain man said here, not unwisely, that if bodily strength should resist,” and so forth. Let it therefore remain fixed and certain that these books belong to Salvianus. In correcting them, we used two ancient manuscript codices of the Royal Library, as stated in the preface, together with one very old codex of the Colbert Library and Pithoeus’s edition. We also compared the latter with the edition of these books published at Trier in 1609 by Johann Macherentinus, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, although with very little benefit. Macherentinus had no ancient codex with which to collate the books and corrected most passages on his own authority.]

### BOOK ONE

206

#### I.

Timothy, the least of the servants of God, to the Catholic Church spread throughout the whole world: grace and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord, with the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Among the other serious and deadly diseases of that destructive pestilence which that most ancient and foul serpent breathes into you through the gravest poison of lethal envy and that most dreadful breath from his venomous mouth, I do not know whether any plague of unbelieving souls and any more loathsome stain upon your children afflicts you more severely than this: most of your people [Note: [Col. 0175D] Earlier the reading was *existimantes*. This is wholly wrong; we have therefore corrected it.] think little of it if, in this life, they devote themselves without the fruit of mercy and humaneness to the possessions entrusted to them by God for holy work, unless they extend their avarice—that is, their enslavement to idolatry (Colossians 3:5) [Note: [Col. 0175D] See the note below on p. 225, where the editor observes that all the old books read *idolatriae*, not *idololatriae*.]—even into the future age after death [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Colbert codex reads: “with a more bitter plague of unbelieving souls and a fouler stain of your children.”].

207

Perhaps you look around and ask who these people among your own are whom I am addressing. You need no lengthy investigation to discover them. All of them—I mean, almost all—are what I am describing.

That outstanding and supreme blessedness of your primitive people has long departed [Note: [Col. 0175D] That is, of the ecclesiastical common people, or Christian populace. See above, p. 163]. In those days, all who acknowledged Christ transferred the perishable resources of worldly things into the eternal wealth of heavenly possessions, exchanging the outlook of the present for the splendid hope of the future and purchasing immortal riches at the price of present poverty [Note: [Col. 0175D] Perhaps imitated from Sallust, preface to the *War with Catiline*: “But when sloth took the place of labor, and lust and arrogance took the place of restraint and justice, fortune was changed together with morals.” And below: “For in place of modesty, restraint, and virtue, boldness, extravagance, and avarice flourished.”].

But now, in place of all these, avarice, greed, robbery, and the vices allied and joined to them by an almost kindred union—envy, hostility, cruelty, luxury, shamelessness, and treachery—have succeeded, because those former virtues serve the purposes of these vices.

Thus, I do not know how it has happened that, while your happiness fights against itself, your vices have increased almost as much as your peoples have increased; as your resources have grown, your discipline has diminished; and prosperity in your gains has arrived with a heavy interest-charge of losses.

For as the peoples of the faith multiplied, faith diminished; and as her children increased, the mother became sick. And you, Church, through the progress of your fertility, have become weaker and, as you advanced, have fallen backward, becoming at once stronger in numbers and weaker in strength [Note: [Col. 0176C] Jerome, in the prologue to the *Life of Malchus the Monk*, speaking of the Church: “For I have planned to write how and through whom the Church of Christ became known, how it grew to maturity through persecutions and was crowned with martyrdoms, and how, after it came under Christian rulers, it became greater in power and riches but lesser in virtues.” Agobard, *On the Privilege and Law of the Priesthood*, chapter 13: “This we can say about the Church without ambiguity: in earlier years it was strong for enduring sufferings, upright in the perfection of truth, powerful in the display of signs, equipped with a zeal for extraordinary continence and abstinence, watchful against the rage of wolves, and free to resist the wicked; but now it is so weakened by every infirmity of mind that it is neither safe nor possible even to speak.” Likewise James of Vitry, chapter 8 of the *History of the West*, p. 288, says that Master Fulk lost his good reputation after he began to collect money.].

You have spread throughout the whole world members bearing the religious name but lacking the power of religion. Thus you have begun to be rich in crowds [Note: [Col. 0176D] Here the Royal codices agree strongly with Pithoeus’s edition. We therefore retained *turbis* (“crowds”), whereas the earlier reading was *turpis* (“foul”).], poor in faith; the richer in multitude, the poorer in devotion; more expansive in body, narrower in mind; and, as I may put it, both greater and lesser within yourself, growing and declining at the same time through an almost unprecedented and unheard-of kind of advance and retreat.

Where now is that outstanding form of yours and the beauty of your entire body? Where is the testimony of the divine writings concerning your living virtues, which says: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he possessed was his own” (Acts 4:32)?

Now, alas and lamentation, you possess only the reading of this passage, not its virtue; and in you there is as much knowledge as there is an absence of conscience [Note: [Col. 0176D] We have followed the agreement of the ancient books. The editions read: “In whom, as knowledge is present, so conscience is absent.”].

For now the greatest portion of your children are merchants in deadly goods, and, like earthly—or rather, infernal—shopkeepers and tavern keepers, they devote themselves to markets that perish and cause others to perish at the same time.

Buying the loss of life at the price of monetary profit, they acquire what is not theirs and squander what is theirs. They entrust to the earth treasures destined to bring brief joy to their heirs and prolonged grief to their creators; they deprive both others and themselves of the use of present things; they bury infernal riches in deep caves, burying their money and their hope together, in accordance with our Lord’s saying: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:21).

Thus they begrudge themselves salvation, and they press their own souls—called to heaven—down to earth with earthly weights. For the mind of one who stores up treasure follows its treasure and is, as it were, transformed into the nature of an earthly substance—not only now, but also in the future and forever.

For since, as it is written, life and death are set before a person, and he reaches out his hand toward whichever he chooses (Sirach 15:18), each person must possess in eternity those things that here he has seized, as it were, with his own hand. Devoted to his will and judgment, he will cling in the future to those things to which he clung here in affection.

#### II.

But evidently some people think themselves free from this offense because they do not keep their gold and possessions on earth, although they keep them hidden wherever they may be. Let no one deceive himself with ridiculous opinions.

Whoever serves the increase of wealth out of earthly desire is always burying gold in the earth.

209

This is what the Savior teaches in the Gospel when he says: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matthew 6:19). And again: “But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (ibid., 20).

These words cannot be understood according to a merely bodily hearing. Do all the wicked place their bodily treasures on earth, and all the good place theirs in heaven? Certainly not.

Therefore the force of sacred speech has expressed the effects and powers of spiritual things. Since earthly and infernal things belong to greed and avarice, while heavenly and eternal things belong to mercy and generosity, the distinction between an earthly treasure and a heavenly treasure has been established so that those who store up treasure for greed and avarice may recognize that they are placing their wealth in hell, while those who store it up for mercy and humaneness may rejoice that they are preparing heavenly treasures.

He therefore named the places of the treasures according to the merits of those who store them up. For treasures are said already to be in the place where those who store them up will be in the future.

### III

But perhaps the sentence may seem harsh, calling everyone equally to perfection and compelling all under one law, since certainly not everyone’s condition is the same. It could quite rightly be said in response that, since everyone wishes to live forever, everyone ought to act so that they may be able to share in life:

> [Note: This is how the edition of Pithoeus and the manuscripts read. The Macherentinus manuscript, however, reads *perpetuare* (“to perpetuate”). That reading is not a bad one.]

For it is extremely imprudent and foolish for some to act in such a way that they appear unwilling in reality and action to do precisely what they desire in affection and intention.

Nevertheless, let us consider especially that part of the Christians—that is, of your children—which, as it supposes, is held back from perfection by certain unavoidable obstacles and insuperable bonds of family obligations. First among them, I think, are those who claim that concern for their children and, as it were, a violent love for them compels them to seek money and enlarge their wealth to the greatest possible extent.

As though all fathers must necessarily be rich, or ought to be rich; as though they could not love their children without multiplying their possessions; or as though the strength and marrow of affection were avarice and covetousness. For, according to their view, just as a body cannot exist without marrow, so love cannot exist without covetousness.

But if this is so, then without any doubt all affection is the cause of evil; it contains not the substance of good affections but incentives to vices. And where then will be that sacred oracle of divine authority: “Godliness is profitable for all things” (1 Tim. 4:8)? In this way it is not profitable for all things but almost universally harmful. For if it is the mother of covetousness, it contains much more evil than good, in accordance with that saying of Holy Scripture: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

Therefore, if covetousness is the root of all evils, and if it is engendered in the womb of affection and nourished, as it were, by its poisonous milk, then it is not so much covetousness that must be condemned—the daughter born from an affectionate mother—as affection itself, from which such a daughter is produced.

The result is that, if affection is so pestilential and harmful, it is not advantageous either to love or to be loved. Parents ought not to seek a love harmful to themselves, nor should children desire one that will injure their parents. Yet this disease is borne not only by parents but also by children: it is burdensome both to those who produce harmful inheritances and to those who are brought up as wicked heirs amid the most shameful pursuit of gain.

This is why almost all children succeed their parents not only in estates but also in vices; they inherit not only their fathers’ possessions but also their depravity. Thus, always passing into the character of their fathers, they begin to possess their wickedness before they possess their substance.

For they possess their parents’ goods only after their parents are dead; while their parents are still alive and vigorous, they possess their character:

> [211]

and thus, before they begin to hold their fathers’ possessions as their own, they have the fathers themselves in their minds; and before they possess those things falsely called goods, they possess those things truly recognized as evils.

### IV

What then? Since matters stand thus, do I perhaps seem to forbid parents affection for their children? Certainly not. For what would be so savage, so inhuman, so opposed to the law as to say that children should not be loved, when we acknowledge that even enemies should be loved? Or to forbid the affection supplied by nature, while we bestow even that which nature forbids? Or to tear away the love of the heart that one possesses, while attempting to implant in it even that which it does not possess?

It is not so. We do not merely say that children are to be loved; we say that they are to be loved especially and above all things, and that nothing at all is to be preferred to them except God alone. For this too is especially to love: to prefer to one’s children the one whom it is never right to place second.

What, then, does it mean to say that children are to be loved, and how are they to be loved? Surely in no other way than the way God himself appointed. There is no better love of children than that taught by the one who gave the children themselves. Nor can children be loved better than by loving them in the one by whom they were given.

How, then, God commanded that children be loved—I shall not say it myself. Let the divine word itself speak, addressing all fathers generally:

> “That he may declare his commandments to his children, so that they may place their hope in God, and not forget the works of their God, and seek his commandments” (Psalm 77:7).

Elsewhere also he says:

> “And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but raise them in the discipline and correction of the Lord” (Eph. 6:4).

> [Note: This passage is from chapter six of the Epistle of blessed Paul to the Ephesians and was often cited by the ancients. Cyprian, in the third book *To Quirinus*, chapter 71: “Fathers also ought not to be harsh toward their children. And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger.” Jerome, in his letter to Theophilus of Alexandria against the errors of John of Jerusalem: “And if he,” he says, “wishes to perish so that those who are lost may not perish, how much more should good parents take care not to provoke their children to anger.” Theophylact, commenting on this passage of Paul: “He did not say, ‘Love them.’ Nature itself demands this of them, even against their will. Rather, he said, ‘Do not provoke them to anger.’ That means: do not disinherit them, do not renounce them, and do not show yourselves burdensome and cruel toward them, as though they were not free persons but slaves; do not always be ill-disposed toward them.” Moreover, my fellow countryman Muretus proposes an excellent rule concerning this matter in book seven of his *Various Readings*, chapter 4, which concerns the duties of parents toward their children: “Therefore,” he says, “the reins should neither be loosened for the exultant lust of the young nor should a fierce age be further exasperated by authority harsher than is fitting. Rather, one should employ such skill that those who are reproved perceive that this is done not out of hatred for themselves but rather out of love and benevolence; and everything should be so tempered that courtesy rescues severity from hatred, and severity rescues courtesy from contempt.”]

You see what kinds of wealth God commands parents to prepare for their children: not treasuries of money, nor heavy sacks filled with gold—possessing great weight but still more iniquity;

> [212]

not proud houses rising above lofty cities; not roofs lifted beyond human sight, nor summits inserted into the clouds with an aerial inhabitant; not, finally, boundless estates exceeding even the renown of their owner, estates that consider it disgraceful to endure partners and regard a neighbor’s proximity as an injury.

God does not command these things, nor does he extend parental care into the slavish duties of managing earthly affairs. What he commands is little, but beneficial; simple, but holy; small in its injunction, but great in its fruit; brief in writing, but eternal in blessedness.

“For,” he says, “parents, do not provoke your children to indignation, but raise them in the discipline and correction of the Lord” (ibid.), so that, as the prophet said, “they may place their hope in God, and not forget the works of their God, and seek his commandments” (Psalm 77:7).

Behold what riches God loves; behold what resources he commands to be prepared: faith and fear of God, modesty, holiness, discipline—not things that perish.

How excellent they are! Since God is “the God of the living, not of the dead” (Matt. 22:32):

> [Note: That is, of those who believe in the future resurrection of the dead. For the ancient Christians called those who denied the resurrection “dead,” as was said in connection with the second letter of Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, which was published with the works of Agobard. Elsewhere: “God is the God of the dead and of the living. For all live to him,” as Saint Luke says.]

he rightly commanded that those things be prepared for children by which they might live forever, not those by which they might die in eternity.

No one doubts that, for almost all the wicked and unbelieving, worldly riches are a cause of death rather than life, in accordance with what God says:

> “How difficult it is for those who have money to enter the kingdom of God!” (Luke 18:24)

And again:

> “It is easier,” he says, “for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (ibid., 25).

Hence also that command which he gives expressly:

> “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6:19–20).

> [Note: See below, page 267.]

The preceding and following statements display two kinds of treasures: one by which fathers lay up treasure for their children, and another by which they lay up treasure for themselves.

For their children, how? By educating them in duty and the fear of God. For themselves, how? By laying up treasures for themselves in heaven.

This is wonderfully arranged: since money is perishable but discipline immortal, and since almost all parents love their children more than themselves, they should confer perishable goods upon themselves and eternal goods upon their children. Thus they will care both for their affection and for their salvation: through a twofold and immortal good, they will make their children eternal by means of eternal things, and they will convert into eternal goods, through good works, those things which naturally perish, so as to acquire blessedness for themselves.

What then, parental affection? Why are you agitated? Why do you stretch yourself out in acquiring earthly and perishable things? You can provide your children with nothing greater than that they should receive through you a good which they will never entirely lose.

It is not necessary, then, that you store up earthly treasures for your son. You will make him richer by nothing more than by making your own son himself God’s treasure.

### V

Although these things are so and are true and most beneficial, I shall not speak as though I entirely exclude children from their fathers’ goods and possessions. We shall discuss that matter later.

For now, since some people do not think they will be guilty if they do not devote their possessions to the honor of the Gospel, to their salvation, or to any service of God, but, out of lust and unbelief, transfer them indiscriminately to whatever heirs—whether irreligious or wealthy—through an impious and pagan solicitude, let us briefly examine either by whom these possessions were given or for what reason they were given. Once we have shown both the author and the purpose of the gift, we shall more easily be able to establish to whom it ought to be referred and for what use it ought to be employed.

I think no human being who can properly be counted among human beings doubts that all worldly substance is given to everyone as a divine gift. Unless perhaps someone is so foolish that, although the world itself was given by God to the human race, he thinks that the things in the world were not given by God to human beings.

Therefore, if God has bestowed everything upon everyone, no one can doubt that we ought to refer to the worship of God the things we have received as God’s gift and consume in his work what we have received from his generosity.

For this is to acknowledge God’s gift and to use divine benefits rightly: to honor him with his gifts, since you received the gifts themselves from the one who gave them.

Human examples teach this as well. If the use of certain things is granted to someone through the benefit and generosity of another person, and if, forgetting the one from whom he obtained the enjoyment of those things, he attempts to withdraw from that very person the ownership of the thing provided and to alienate it, would he not be judged the most ungrateful and faithless of all? He has forgotten the beneficent and most generous man and wishes to strip of his right of ownership the one who enriched him by granting him possession of the use itself.

We too have received only the use of the things we possess. We use resources lent by God, and we are, as it were, precarious possessors. In the end, whether we wish it or not, when we leave this world we leave everything here.

Why, then, since we are merely possessors with the right of use, do we attempt to withdraw from the Lord’s ownership and alienate what we cannot take away with us?

Why do we not use in good faith the little things given by God? We held them as long as it was permitted; we held them as long as he who provided them allowed.

What is more right, what is more honorable, than that, when the thing departs from the one who had the use of it, possession should return to the one who granted it for use?

Even the voices of God themselves command this through the tongues of the sacred Scriptures, saying daily to each one of us:

> “Honor the Lord with your substance” (Prov. 3:9).

And elsewhere:

> “Repay your debt,” he says (Ecclus. 4:8).

How compassionate and indulgent is the Lord our God, inviting us to distribute the resources of our earthly substance!

“Honor,” he says, “the Lord with your substance.” Although everything we have received from him is his, he calls it ours so that we may give it. He calls possession our property for this reason: so that the reward of the one who acts may be greater, since the giver must have more fruit where the gift appears to come from his own resources.

### VI

Yet, lest the human mind become arrogant precisely because the Lord had called this substance ours, he added: “Repay your debt.” That is, if devotion did not entice someone to give, necessity would compel him to pay; and if his own faith did not draw him toward holy work, at least necessity would constrain him.

First, therefore, he says: “Honor the Lord with your substance.” Then: “Repay,” he says, “your debt.”

This is to say: If you are devoted, give as though it were yours; if you are not devoted, repay as though it were not yours.

He has therefore rightly established both the willingness to give and the necessity of repayment. This is certainly what he says to every human being: You are invited to holy work by exhortation and constrained to it by exaction. Give if you wish; repay if you do not wish.

The Apostle, likewise exhorting to the same thing, commands the rich:

> “Let them not be high-minded, nor place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who,” he says, “gives us all things richly for enjoyment in the willingness to do good works” (1 Tim. 6:17).

In one statement he taught both matters: who gives riches and why he gives them. By saying that hope must be placed in God, who provides all things, he showed that the rich become rich through God. By adding “in the willingness to do good works,” he taught that what he said is bestowed by God only for good works.

“For he provides,” he says, “all things in the willingness to do good works.” That is, he makes people rich in substance for this purpose: that they may be rich in good works. In other words, they should exchange the riches they have received and, placing their resources in good works, make the riches of God that they possess temporarily in this world eternal by using them well.

Thus, acknowledging God’s gifts, they may rejoice in a twofold good: those who are rich in this world may also deserve to be rich in heaven.

### VII

This, then, is how riches are to be possessed, how they are to be sought, how they are to be held, and how they are to be increased.

Otherwise it is an immeasurable evil not to use well the good things given by God. For, as Holy Scripture says:

> “There is nothing more wicked than a miser” (Ecclus. 10:9);

and:

> “Riches kept to the harm of their owner” are the worst and most deadly kind of disease (Eccles. 5:12).

It is true. What is worse, or what is more miserable, than for someone to turn present goods into future evils, and for those things which God gave in order that eternal blessedness of life might be prepared through them to become the means by which eternal death and condemnation are sought?

In this connection we must also consider that, if stored-up riches are preserved for the harm of a person, how much more are they amassed for a greater harm! For how many of the rich today possess such self-restraint that, while content to guard their wealth, they no longer wish to accumulate it?

O the misery of the times and of the ecclesiastical people:

> [Note: That is, of the Christian people. See above, page 163.]

to what a condition it has been reduced! Although it is written that preserving wealth is a kind of grave crime, failing to increase it is now considered a kind of virtue.

Therefore, as we said above, how can some people not consider themselves altogether guilty if they have not provided for themselves in death through the distribution of their substance, when they are guilty even because they have preserved everything until death?

Or how will those not be guilty who have transferred their possessions to whatever people through utterly faithless vanity, when even those will be guilty who did not deprive themselves during this life of some portion of their goods for the honor of God?

Our Lord himself showed this through his Apostle and said:

> “Come now, you rich, weep and lament over the miseries that will come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust will be a testimony against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days” (James 5:1–3).

> [Note: Greek and the Vulgate have *Thesaurizastis* (“you have stored up treasure”).]

Apart from that much greater and more terrible severity of the divine words which lies hidden in the mystery, I think that what is plainly expressed is sufficient to inspire everyone with fear and trembling.

He speaks particularly to the rich. He commands them to weep, announces future evils, and threatens eternal fire. And, so that the threats themselves may be more greatly feared, this is not because of homicide, fornication, sacrilegious impiety, or, finally, other vices that slaughter souls with a deadly sword and through an endless occasion, but solely because of riches, because of insane covetousness, because of hunger for gold and silver.

He thereby showed that these things alone are sufficient for a person’s eternal condemnation, even if there were no other guilt.

What could be said more simply or more clearly? He does not say to the rich man: “You are to be tortured because you are a murderer”; “You are to be tortured because you are a fornicator”; but only: “You are to be tortured because you are rich”—that is, because you use riches badly, because you do not understand the riches given to you for holy work.

For riches themselves are not harmful in their own nature; it is the minds of those who use them badly that are criminal. Nor are possessions themselves the cause of punishment for a person; rather, the rich make punishments for themselves out of their possessions. While they refuse to use riches well, they turn the riches themselves into torments for themselves.

“You have stored up treasure,” he says, “in the last days.” After saying “you have stored up treasure,” he rightly added “in the last days”: that is, the guilt of those who store up treasure is greater because the final period of the world adds to the offense of their treasures.

“You have stored up treasure,” he says, “in the last days.” Through “treasures,” covetousness is accused; through “the last days,” unbelief:

> [218]

and thus there is a double guilt—of covetousness and of unbelief:

> [Note: The royal manuscripts read: “And thus there is a double guilt, both of covetousness and of unbelief.” The older text, however, adds the word *noxa* (“guilt”) after the word *cupiditatis* (“of covetousness”).]

for the treasures that they have stored up—although God says, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21; Rom. 7:7)—were certainly criminal to covet at another time as well, but it is unquestionably a greater crime to accumulate them through unbelief even at the end of the world.

### VIII

Perhaps someone has judged my discourse harsh up to this point. It is indeed harsh if it has admonished anyone of something not grounded in the authority of sacred testimonies. Let it be considered harsh if it contains anything like what this Apostle proclaimed.

Let us not even add that saying of our Lord in which he declared all entirely unworthy who had not renounced everything they possessed (Luke 14:33).

Since matters stand thus, should not what we have said be considered, I ask, exceedingly indulgent, moderate, and gentle? We seek at least some aid of salvation for those to whom we cannot grant perfect safety, and we attempt to lighten the death of those whose life we cannot heal.

For what is perfect health? What else but to act well in this life?

What is the final treatment? What else but to acquire, at least at the end, good provisions for the journey?

For what is perfect health? What else but to use well the things entrusted by God?

What is the last remedy? What else but at least afterward to do what you regret not having done earlier?

Perhaps someone thinks that what I say is harsh. Let it certainly be considered harsh—unless it is such that, in comparison with apostolic severity, it appears gentle and lenient.

For the Apostle calls the rich to mourning; we call them to a remedy. The Apostle calls riches fire; we desire to make water from riches, water that extinguishes fire, in accordance with the saying:

> “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33).

The Apostle testifies that condemnation lies in riches badly preserved; I desire to acquire eternal life for all from the very things which he says produce eternal death.

I do not mean, however, that anyone entangled in bodily vices should think it sufficient for eternal life, after growing old in wickedness all the way to death, to distribute everything well at the moment of dying—unless beforehand he has renounced his sins, cast off that filthy and mud-stained garment of crimes, and received from the hand of the preaching Apostle a new garment of conversion and holiness.

> [Note: Both royal manuscripts read *conversationis* (“of conduct” or “of way of life”).]

> [Note: Salvian imitated Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, at this point. In his exhortation to repentance, Ambrose is wholly concerned to show that he greatly doubts the salvation of those who, placed in the final crisis of illness, receive repentance. Concerning them he says: “But if you wish to do repentance only when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.” Augustine says the same in homily 41: “Do repentance while you are healthy. If you do so, you are secure. Why are you secure? Because you have done repentance at a time when you were also able to sin. But if you wish to do repentance when you can no longer sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you them.”]

Otherwise, the person who, lying at the point of death, withdraws from crimes only because impossibility—not will—makes him withdraw, does not cease to sin. He does not abandon his crimes; rather, he is abandoned by his crimes. Thus, although necessity has excluded him from vices, he sins, I think, even when he has ceased, because as far as his mind is concerned, he has not yet ceased, since he would still wish to sin if he could.

Therefore, the person who sins throughout life only in order to redeem the burden of his sins in death does not rely on good hopes. He thinks he will escape not because he is good but because he is rich.

As though God sought not the life of human beings but their money, and wished to receive from all those who act wickedly in the hope of redeeming their evils only coins in exchange for their crimes, demanding silver like corrupt judges in order to sell sins.

It is not so. It is certainly clear that generosity is exceedingly beneficial—but not to those who live wickedly in the final hope of future generosity, who commit crimes with confidence that exemption can be purchased. It benefits those who, deceived either by the instability of age, the darkness of error, the fault of ignorance, or finally the fall arising from human weakness, at last begin to recover, as though after death from a very serious illness, or as though after the mourning of a troubled mind.

Just as insane people return to their senses after madness, so these people return after error. They differ from one another in only one respect: the former rejoice after escaping their illness, while the latter mourn after receiving health.

And not without reason. The former rejoice all the more because they realize that they have recovered a greater measure of health; the latter are all the more ashamed because they recognize more clearly the disease of their error.

Thus it necessarily comes about that the former exult and the latter grieve: the former credit their illness to their recovery, whereas the latter attribute their error to themselves. The former are happy about their remedy, while the latter are anxious about their guilt.

### IX

Therefore I admonish everyone, but especially those whom the terror of grave offenses torments, and in whom an unhappy conscience sighs under the recollection of punishable sins.

First, although they have fallen, let them not remain in their fall, nor wallow in their filth after the manner of creatures foul in their wallowings. When such creatures have plunged their heated bellies into mud, they do not satisfy their filthy pleasures unless they completely cover their bodies with dirt.

Let sinners not follow this natural filth, nor yield to falsely flattering falls; let them not linger in the abyss of lust and bury themselves in the ruins they have themselves produced. Rather, as soon as they fall, let them rise, and let them immediately plan their recovery while still in their fall.

If the speed of repentance can accomplish it in any way, let the remedy of the one who rises be so swift that scarcely any trace of the fall can appear.

Therefore, in such cases the first work of healing is that the sick should loathe their diseases, the wounded hasten to treat their injuries, and the injured immediately pull the arrows from their bodies.

A poultice or bandage is most effectively applied while wounds are still hot, and the flesh of wounds is joined together more quickly when it is not allowed to gape for long.

For if a sore in the body becomes putrid, it spreads; and if cancer follows wounds, death must necessarily follow cancer.

These evils must therefore first be avoided by sinners. No place must be given to the devil, so that he who drove those standing into ruin may not plunge those who have fallen into death.

But if either the power of the disease or the negligence of the sick is so great that they carry the deterioration of their health to the final days, I do not know what to say, nor do I know at all what to promise.

To call those in danger back from seeking a final remedy would be harsh and impious; but to promise anything in so late a treatment would be rash.

Nevertheless, it is certainly better for hands dried up by a long paralysis to be raised at last toward heaven through some effort than to be entirely dissolved in deadly despair.

It is better to leave nothing untried than to care for the dying in no way.

> [Note: The old royal manuscript formerly read thus. But this was corrected, and *nullo* (“with nothing”) was substituted for *nulla* (“in no way”).]

This is especially so because I do not know whether attempting something at the end may be medicine; certainly attempting nothing is destruction.

And I know one thing: whoever has brought himself into this misery, the extremity of a long illness, it is impossible to say how much lamentation he owes for his errors, because he never recognized his mistakes.

> [221]

### X

And what will happen amid all this? When will the one who has lost the days of mourning mourn? When will the one who has lost the time for satisfaction make satisfaction?

Will he flee to long fasts? This is indeed something, if it is joined with almsgiving, in accordance with the saying:

> “Fasting is good with almsgiving” (Tob. 12:8).

But how will prolonged confession of sin assist him when he lies at the point of death?

Will he wear down his flesh with sackcloth and soil it with dust and ashes, so that the harshness of present hardships may make hard compensation for the softness of past pleasure, and so that the service of self-neglect, acting as an advocate, may discharge the guilt of long indulgence?

> [Note: We have corrected this from our own judgment, since previously the reading was *injuriae* (“of injury”). For just as he contrasts the softness of pleasure with hardships, so he contrasts long indulgence with negligence. Otherwise the word *injuriae* gives no good sense here. Tertullian likewise teaches in *On Repentance*, chapter 9, that it was formerly customary in the Church for the person who made confession of sin (*exomologesis*) to lie in sackcloth and ashes and to cover his body with filth. On the preceding page Salvian condemned the negligence of the sick: “But if either the power of the disease or the negligence of the sick...”]

But when will he do these great things, already shut out by his approaching death even from moderate action?

Finally, will the severity of faith’s judge subject the guilty person to crosses of various afflictions in his own body, so that he may deserve the mercy of eternal absolution by seeking it through present punishment?

But when the body is already failing, where will the censorial mind exercise the office of strict judgment? A judge cannot exercise the authority of severity when the accused can no longer endure being judged.

There is therefore one thing that can assist the wavering and abandoned person after all other aids and supports have been lost: namely, to flee to that sacred and salutary counsel of the most blessed Daniel.

Desiring to heal the Babylonian king, Daniel compounded a poultice for wounds contracted through offense from compassion, saying:

> “Therefore, O king, let my counsel be pleasing to you: redeem your sins through acts of mercy, and your iniquities through compassion for the poor. Perhaps God will be patient with your offenses” (Dan. 4:24).

Let this person, then, do what Daniel said. Let him use for his own wounds the medicine offered to another. Let him fear the example of disobedient obstinacy. Let him consider what he himself will suffer in death when he sees what the Assyrian king endured in life.

This is a clear lesson concerning pride and rebellion. Let him consider whether, if he does not listen, he will escape death, when he sees that the king who did not listen lost himself while still alive.

Let him therefore offer, even while dying, at least his substance, for the liberation of his soul from everlasting punishments, since he can now do nothing else. But let him offer it with compunction and tears; let him offer it with grief and mourning.

For offerings made otherwise are of no benefit: they please not by their price but by their disposition. For it is not the disposition of the giver that is commended by the gifts, but the gifts by the disposition; nor does money instill faith, but faith gives value to money.

Therefore, whoever wishes what he offers to God to benefit him should offer it in this way.

For a human being does not confer a benefit upon God through what he gives; rather, God confers a benefit upon the human being through what he receives, since even what a person possesses is a gift of God and his Lord.

Accordingly, in what a person offers, he does not return his own; the Lord receives back what is his.

Therefore, when someone offers his resources to God, let him not offer them with the presumption of a donor but with the humility of one paying a debt. Let him not believe that he is absolving his sins but that he is lightening them. Let him not offer with confidence in redemption but as an act of appeasement.

> [Note: The royal manuscripts read this way. The Colbertinus manuscript and the first edition have *supplicationis* (“of supplication”).]

Let him not offer as though he were repaying the entire debt, but as though he desired to repay at least a small part of a great one. For even if he hands over everything he has, according to the measure of his resources, he does not repay what he owes according to the magnitude of his sins.

Therefore, although he offers, let him pray that God may be pleased with his offering, mourning that he offers it late, mourning and repenting that he did not offer it earlier. In this way, perhaps, according to the prophet, God may be propitiated for his sins.

> [Note: In the Colbertinus manuscript, *tuis* (“your”) was first written, but it has been erased and *ejus* (“his”) written above the line. Pithoeus obscurely noted this in the margin of his edition.]

### XI

But someone says: “Then is he going to offer everything he has to God?”

Let him not offer everything he has if he does not think that he owes everything he has. I am not asking whose the thing offered is, or from whom it was received before it is returned. I say only this: let him not offer everything as a debt if he does not think that he owes everything on account of his guilt.

“Then,” someone says, “is a sinner going to offer everything?”

> [Note: The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “he says, is any sinner going to offer everything?” The old edition reads: “he says, is someone who is guilty of great crimes going to offer everything to the Lord?”—“Certainly not, nothing,” and so forth.]

Rather, nothing, if it is not offered with faith; rather, nothing, if it is not offered with eagerness; rather, nothing, if it is not offered with prayer; rather, nothing, if he does not offer it with the disposition of counting among God’s chief benefits the fact that God gave him the intention to offer, and of judging that more has been bestowed upon him in what he leaves to God than in what he previously possessed.

For what a human being possesses is temporary; what is left to God is eternal.

“Is he going to offer everything?” someone says.

But I say that even this entire offering is little. For who among human beings knows whether what has been offered compensates for the measure of his sins? Who knows whether there is as much in the duty of appeasement as there is danger in the offense?

If anyone knows by how much he can redeem his sins, let him use that knowledge for redemption. But if he does not know, why should he not offer as much as he can? If he cannot compensate for his sins by the greatness of the price, let him at least compensate through the devotion of his mind.

For he displays the perfect fruit of conscience who leaves nothing within his conscience.

Some people undoubtedly complain that these things are harsh and immeasurable, especially because the prophet of whom we spoke seems to have admonished the Babylonian king only to give much, not to sell everything.

For the moment I do not introduce the testimonies of the Gospel, nor do I flee to the voice of God speaking in the sacred books. I do not say that one thing was commanded by the old law and another by the new.

Hence the Apostle also says:

> “Behold, the old things have passed away; all things have become new.”

> [Note: The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “For all things are from God.”]

> “But all things are from God” (2 Cor. 5:17–18).

By these words he teaches that the old things are not to be done according to the letter, but that new things are to be done according to God.

For the moment I am content with what the prophet said. His speech was addressed to a king, and indeed to a king not of a single city but, as it then appeared, of the whole world:

> [Note: The same manuscript prefers this reading. The royal manuscripts read *qui itaque* (“who therefore”); the editions read *quia itaque* (“because therefore”).]

a king who certainly could not transfer the peoples he ruled by testament to the needy, or give barbarian nations to the indigent as though they were coins, or convert kingdoms spread far and wide into contributions for the poor.

Therefore the prophet says:

> “Redeem your sins through acts of mercy” (Dan. 4:24).

That is: Give gold to the needy, because you cannot give the kingdom; distribute your resources, because you are unable to extend your power.

> [Note: Thus all the old books read. The editions, however, have *facultates* (“resources”) in place of *facultatem* (“your resource” or “your means”).]

> [Note: In the old copy of the Colbertine library it was first written this way, but afterward the letter *o* was erased and the letter *e* was written above the line. From this Pithoeus produced *praerogare* (“to extend beforehand” or “to advance”).]

And so he appears to have commanded him to give everything, since the only thing he did not command him to distribute was what he could not give away.

## XII.

Perhaps we are exaggerating the matter in words and raising it too high. Let us therefore see what it actually amounts to. “Redeem your sins,” he says, “with acts of mercy.” What does it mean to redeem something? I suppose it means to pay the price of the things being redeemed. I am not asking what sins that king had committed. He himself knows how much he ought to have paid to redeem what he had done. I am addressing you, whose case is at issue; I am appealing to you, whose danger is being considered. Do what the prophet said [Col. 0187D]: “Redeem your sins with acts of mercy.” Do not leave to God only as much as you possess, if you do not think that what you possess is necessary for your sins.

Carefully assess the faults you have committed; assess the varieties of your sins. Consider what you owe for lies [Col. 0188A], what for curses and perjuries, what for negligence in your thoughts, what for impurity in your speech, and finally what for every inclination of an evil will.

[Note: The term “negligences” plainly signifies minor and light sins, which we today call venial sins, as I believe is sufficiently clear; it is also evident from Homily 32 of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and from the Rule of Saint Columbanus. Caesarius himself partly reveals in Homily 31 what sins were then considered light.]

Finally, add also any of these things that may be present within your conscience, of which the Apostle says: “adulteries, fornications, indecencies, drunkennesses, impurity hateful to God” (Gal. V, 19–20), and “greed, the servant of idolatry” [Note: All the old books read this way, both here and above. It should be observed that Latin manuscripts almost always have *idolatria*, and rarely *idololatria*. Hence the French *idolatrie*.]—and, after these, perhaps certain crimes contracted through the shedding of human blood.

When you have reckoned the number of them all, weigh the price of each. And after this, I am not asking you to surrender to God everything you possess for your sins; return only what you owe [Note: These words are absent from all the ancient manuscripts. Nevertheless, they are found in the first edition and in others.], if you can estimate what you owe.

I add, moreover, that once you have considered and assessed your offenses, you will owe all the more for your evils because you have valued your sins too cheaply [Col. 0188B].

[Note: This is absent from the more recent Royal manuscript and from the Colbert manuscript.]

How so? Because, the Apostle says, “whoever considers himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. VI, 3).

Not to mention that the king whom he commanded to redeem his sins was still going to live—and perhaps was still young—yet he was nevertheless commanded to hasten to redeem his sins. You, however, owe all the more on your own behalf because you are doing these things either while dying or when you are already on the point of death. Great will have to be the generosity and devotion capable of compensating for the fact that you return these things to your Lord only when you yourself can no longer possess them—especially since, in addition to all this, the prophet himself, who calls that king to the redemption of his crimes, by the very things he says must be done, shows him not so much the security of forgiveness as the way to seek salvation.

For when he says, “Redeem your sins with acts of mercy, and perhaps God will be gracious to your offenses,” the very word “perhaps” indicates hope but does not promise confidence. From this it can be understood how difficult it is for sinners placed at the end of life to attain complete forgiveness by any generosity, since the prophet himself, while urging that God’s favor be sought, nevertheless did not dare promise that it could be obtained.

He gives advice concerning the action, yet doubts concerning its outcome. He makes himself an exhorter to act, not an authority able to secure the result. Why is this so? Clearly because all sinners ought to try everything on their own behalf even at the end of life, although they can presume nothing.

For if that prophet does not promise the king complete forgiveness solely through the abundance of good works, the sinner may understand—without having repented of his errors—how great and how generous a munificence is needed by one at the end of life who wishes to obtain from the Lord through late devotion what he cannot claim by right.

# BOOK TWO

## I.

We have spoken of remedies for sins—or rather, of the hopes and consolations offered by remedies: first, that the sinner should repent of his error, as the foundation for seeking salvation; then, that, according to the sacred teaching, he should immediately redeem his sins with acts of mercy; and finally, if he has not done this, that at least, when dying, he should leave nothing untried, but should come to his aid by offering the last of his possessions [227].

But perhaps someone may respond at this point that, if sinful people are bound by the necessity of redeeming their crimes, then saints, who are free from crimes, are certainly not bound by it; and consequently those who have nothing that must be redeemed by generosity have no reason to give away their substance.

I hear you. But we shall now see what this amounts to.

Meanwhile, even if there are no past evils that a holy person ought to redeem with all his possessions [Col. 0189B], there are nevertheless enduring goods that he ought to acquire at great cost. But more on this later.

For now I say openly and affirm firmly that there is absolutely no saint who is not indebted to God in many respects, and consequently that whatever anyone gives to his Lord, he does not so much give as repay.

First, to speak of the general benefits: whether you are a saint or a rich person, you were first born, nourished, and brought up through the benevolence and gift of God; you were supplied with the things necessary for life; you were enriched even with things that were not necessary; your Lord granted you more for your use than the limits of use required; finally, he extended his gifts beyond your hopes—and, what is greatest and most extraordinary, his gifts even surpassed your wishes [Col. 0189C].

I add after all this that the same Lord who first brought you into being by his gift afterward saved you through his Passion. For your sake, O human being, the Lord of all things came to earth for the sake of earth and mud—indeed, for the sake of a small portion of earth and mud [Note: We had previously printed “assumed a part of all things,” because we had found it written in an old Royal manuscript. But since the other copies and editions do not contain *assumed*, and since it is superfluous, we decided to delete it.]

[Note: Thus the editions read. But this clause is found in none of the old manuscripts that we use.]—and, taking flesh and appearing in flesh, he humbled himself even to the shame of human origin, the filth of swaddling clothes, and the lowliness of a manger [Note: See above in the Notes on p. 119].

He endured the unworthy sufferings of this life: the painful alternations of eating, drinking, sleep, and wakefulness; the humiliating necessities of this fleeting existence; and finally the foul company of the human beings who surrounded him—crowds of sinners stained and covered with mud, continually guilty of the offenses of an evil conscience, exhaling the stench of shameful deeds, and therefore incapable of heavenly commandments and unable to endure the radiance of sacred brightness, because eyes darkened by sins were overwhelmed by the splendor of divine light.

Nor was this all. Add the insolent contradictions of a proud people; add insults, curses, impious persecution, false testimony, a bloody judgment, the people’s mockery, spitting, blows, and exceedingly bitter punishments [Col. 0190A]—but indignities more bitter than the punishments: a crown of thorns, a drink of vinegar, food of gall; the Lord of all condemned by human beings; salvation for the human race hanging on the gallows; God dying under the law of earthly existence [228].

## II.

Since these things are so, whoever you are—whether you are a saint or believe yourself to be a saint—tell me, I beg you: can these things alone be repaid, even if nothing else were owed?

For whatever a human being may choose to endure for God, he cannot possibly repay what God endured for humanity. Even if the Passion itself does not differ in the kind of punishments, there must nevertheless be a great difference in the persons who suffered.

But perhaps you will say that the debt in these matters is common to all human beings, and that the entire human race is indiscriminately liable for it.

That is true. But does someone owe less merely because another person owes the same thing? If the acknowledgments of a hundred people were written for a hundred *sestertii* each, would one person’s debt thereby be reduced if all were debtors for the same amount?

“For each one,” the Apostle says, “will bear his own burden” (Gal. VI, 5), and each will render an account for himself. Therefore one person’s burden is in no way lightened by another’s burden, nor is the guilty person acquitted by the fellowship of many.

Nor is anyone’s condemnation less terrible merely because the condemned person appears to have many accomplices in punishment [229].

Thus, although the debt I mentioned above is general, it is nevertheless unquestionably particular; although it is common to all, it nevertheless belongs individually to each. What reaches everyone equally is nevertheless subtracted from no one’s total.

For just as Christ suffered for all, so also for each individual; he gave himself equally for all and for each; he gave his whole self to everyone and his whole self to each. Consequently, whatever the Savior accomplished through his Passion, all owe him in full, and each owes him in full—except that, in a sense, each owes more than all together, because each received as much as all received.

Where one person receives what all receive, even if the measure is equal, envy is greater. Thus, although he receives the same thing, he appears to owe more, because one who is compared with everyone appears more deeply bound.

This much, then, on the subject, since some saints do not think themselves indebted to God because they cannot estimate the debt.

## III.

Someone may perhaps say that the saints are not indeed free from debt, but that the debts of worldly people are much greater because they have more sins.

This is like someone saying: “I am innocent because another is more guilty; I am just because another is unjust; I am especially good because another is exceptionally wicked.”

First of all, it is unworthy of a holy mind to think that its own goodness is increased by the evils of others, and to consider itself better by comparison with the worse [Col. 0191A].

[Note: Tacitus says in the first book of the *Annals* that Augustus did not adopt Tiberius as his successor out of affection or concern for the state, but because he had perceived his arrogance and cruelty, and had sought glory for himself by the most wretched comparison. See Rittershausen at this passage.]

For it is the most miserable kind of consolation to take comfort from the miseries of sinful people, when the Apostle commands us to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. XII, 15), and not to consider each person’s own interests, but those of others (Phil. II, 4).

But let us grant that such a comparison may appear just and honorable. Can it also be considered reliable? Who is sufficiently certain about that great and terrible future judgment of God? Or who can say, “I owe less; he owes more”? Finally, who can presume on himself or despair of another?

“For we shall all stand,” the Apostle says, “before the judgment seat of Christ” (Rom. XIV, 10), and “each one will bear his own burden” (Gal. VI, 5).

“Then,” someone says, “there is no difference between saints and sinners?”

There is a very great difference—almost immeasurable. But because Scripture says, “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII, 14), and because the mind of the wise is never secure concerning its own salvation, although there is a great difference between saints and sinners, I nevertheless ask all who profess religion: who is sufficiently holy in his own conscience? Who is not fearful of the terrifying severity of that future examination? Who is secure of perpetual safety?

And if no one is—nor should anyone be—let any person tell me, I beg you, why he does not strive with all the strength of his substance to redeem, even by devotion at death, whatever he has contracted through the offense of his life.

I want all readers to know that in what I am saying I am not speaking about all saints, but only about those who, although they have not professed religion, nevertheless do not abandon their riches.

As for those who, free from every burden, follow the way of the Savior [Col. 0191C], and imitate the Lord Jesus Christ not only in holiness but also in poverty [Note: All the old books have *mercantur* (“they purchase”); but shortly afterward *imitatores* (“imitators”) is written. This confirms the reading of the printed books. See below, p. 262.], there is nothing to say except what the prophet also said: “But the friends whom you have honored, O God, are exceedingly honorable to me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

I honor all such people as nothing other than imitators of Christ; I venerate them as nothing other than images of Christ; I esteem them as nothing other than members of Christ; and I remember them only so that I may become worthy of their memory.

## IV.

But what we said above may appear injurious to the religious profession [231]. For someone may say: What if a widow is rich but does not abandon widowhood despite possessing great wealth? What if she is a virgin who has professed integrity and is devoted to the holiness of an undefiled body? What if there is a marriage without marital activity, denying oneself to oneself and possessing oneself as though one did not possess oneself? What if [Note: Formerly, parents had such authority that they were permitted to devote their children to God even in childhood, and were not permitted to abandon the institution they had undertaken by paternal command. The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 48: “A monk is made either by parental devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these has bound him will hold him. Therefore we close the way back to the world to such persons and forbid every return to secular life.” Gregory III, in his fourth letter to Boniface: “You added further that, if a father or mother should hand over a son or daughter within the walls of a monastery, during the years of infancy, to regular discipline, whether it is permissible for them, after they have completed the years of puberty, to leave and marry. We altogether reject this, because it is unlawful that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for children offered to God by their parents.” That this right was widely known even in Jerome’s time is clear from his letter to Demetrias, where the following is read: “Wretched parents and Christians whose faith is incomplete commonly dedicate daughters who are deformed or disabled in some bodily member to virginity, because they cannot find sons-in-law worthy of them.” In the old chartulary of the Church of Cahors there is a formula for this paternal offering, which we shall publish after the notes in an appendix to the *Acts of the Ancients*. In the chartulary of the Church of Tulle there is an old document from which it can be inferred that, in this respect, paternal authority was sometimes extended to brothers who were still children. For in 1099 Gualterius de Navis made his brother Elias a monk in the monastery of Tulle. Fathers not only devoted children already born, but also those not yet born and still in their mother’s womb. Several notable examples of this practice survive. The earliest is the one reported by Ekkehard the Younger in chapter ten of *The Affairs of the Monastery of Saint Gall*. In 1083 Peter, son of Bernard of Corneliano, stipulated in the final provisions of his will that, if his wife, who was pregnant, should give birth to a male child, he should become a canon in the cathedral church of Elne. The *Chartulary of Elne*, book VI, chapter 3: “And if God should grant my wife a son from the pregnancy she now bears, I leave him to Saint Eulalia, together with the allod that I possess at Chexans, after the death of his mother,” etc. This will was made on the seventh day before the Ides of December, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of King Philip. About twenty years later, Peter of Tornamira of Spaniaco ordered that, if his wife should bear a male child after his death, that son should become a monk in the monastery of Tulle. *Chartulary of Tulle*, folio 209: “But if my wife, who is now visibly pregnant, gives birth to a son, I leave him to become a monk in the aforesaid place, together with the estate called Pomairol.” Testament of Louis VIII, king of the Franks, in Andrew Duchesne, vol. V, p. 325: “Likewise, we wish and command that our fifth son be a cleric, and all the others who are born after him.”] a monk serving God from the cradle? What if a cleric completes the service of sacred ministry through faithful service? Are even these people endangered in the fruit of eternal salvation if, while alive, they retain their wealth intact, or, when dying, do not leave it to the needy?

My speech and authority are too small to pronounce judgment on such a question. Let us therefore see what the language of the sacred books and the voices of the heavenly commandments say about all these matters; then we shall direct the rule of our opinion most correctly according to the standard given by God.

First, no one should now think that he can take refuge in the consolations of ancient examples by saying that some saints were perhaps rich either under the Law or before the Law [Col. 0192C]. That time has passed; the order of things has changed.

Before the Law, everyone was free to possess or even pursue whatever he wished, because at that time no one was yet chastised by the rod of heavenly prohibitions. “Where there is no law,” the Apostle says, “there is no transgression” (Rom. IV, 15).

The Law therefore made something impermissible [Note: These words are absent from the more recent Royal manuscript and from the Colbert manuscript.], according to the statement: “I would not have known coveting,” the Apostle says, “unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. VII, 7).

And so people freely possessed the wealth that God had not previously condemned. Under the Law too, almost the same right was available to everyone, because the Law did not altogether forbid a person to have whatever he wished, provided that he possessed it justly.

Thus at that time all the saints used all their resources within the limits prescribed by the Law, walking, as we read, “in all the commandments and ordinances of God without reproach” (Luke I, 6) [232].

So did those very people concerning whom these things are recorded: the prophet Anna, living in fasting and prayers; Nathanael, whom we read of as exalted by the praise of being a true Israelite and remarkable even in the testimony of the Lord and God himself; and Tobias [Note: Pithoeus notes that his old manuscript read *Tobis*, while the Septuagint edition has *Tobit*. Both Royal manuscripts, moreover, have *Tobis*.], who, surpassing the commands of the Law through the greatness of his devotion, served in the burial of the dead even at the risk of death, and cared for the needy to the point of his own need. He had reached such a degree of generosity that he assigned a portion of all his goods to his hired servant—and this while already rich.
