More remarkably still, he had become rich from poverty, because wealth acquired after want usually arouses a greater desire to possess.

## V.

Such, then, were the saints of that time: possessing everything according to the Law, and leaving everything according to the Law [Col. 0193C].

[Note: We had first printed “according to the Gospel,” etc., following an old Royal manuscript. But since the other manuscripts and the older editions prefer “the Law,” and that reading seems better, we restored it. The discussion here concerns not the time of the Gospel but the time of the Law.]

Thus everyone who obeyed the Law was perfect, and the person who then did less under the Law was as devoted as the person who now does more under the Gospel. At that time the Law was, as it were, the Gospel. Consequently, whoever then presented himself as obedient to the Law fulfilled, as it were, the Gospel.

Therefore no one should now think that he can take refuge in the Law. “The old things,” as the Apostle says, “have passed away; everything has become new” (II Cor. V, 17).

At that time there was more indulgence and more permission. Then the eating of meat was commended; now abstinence is commended. Then there were very few days of fasting in one’s whole life; now one’s whole life is almost a single fast. Then vengeance was available to the injured; now there is patience. Then the Law served those who became angry; now it opposes them. Then it handed the sword to the accuser; now it gives charity. Then the Law even indulged bodily temptation; now the Gospel does not indulge it even in the gaze.

Then bodily pleasures enjoyed a certain permission; now even the eyes are commanded to maintain restraint.

Then the Law widened one husband’s marriage-bed to receive many wives; now it constrains even the acceptance of one wife through the devotion of chaste affection. For the Apostle says: “Let those who have wives be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 29–31).

See how briefly the teacher sent by God has regulated everything and enclosed it within the bounds of perfection—not merely cutting off what is unlawful, but also restricting what is lawful: circumcising the use of marriage, the disloyalty of tears, the excess of joys, the lust for possession, the desire to buy, and finally the brief and shadowy pleasure of this world.

And why all this? Why, surely, except because, as he himself said, “the form of this world is passing away”?

How far, then, are those from God’s command who, although God orders them to renounce their wealth while alive, desire to possess it, even when dead, in their relatives! How far are they from that devotion who disinherit themselves for God’s sake but do not wish to disinherit even strangers for their own sake!

To them I would gladly say plainly: What madness is this, O most wretched people—that you make anyone else your heir but disinherit yourselves; that you leave others rich, even if only briefly, but condemn yourselves to eternal poverty?

## VI.

But someone may perhaps ask what it means that God now demands more from Christians through the Gospel than he previously demanded from Jews through the Law [Note: All the old books read, “The reason for this is certain.”].

The reason for this is certain. We now repay greater things to our Lord because we owe greater things.

The Jews once had the shadow of things; we have the truth. The Jews were servants; we are adopted. The Jews received a yoke; we receive freedom. The Jews received curses; we receive grace. The Jews received the letter that kills; we receive the Spirit that gives life. A servant was sent as teacher to the Jews; a son was sent to us.

The Jews crossed through the sea into the wilderness; we enter the kingdom through baptism. The Jews ate manna; we eat Christ. The Jews ate the flesh of birds; we receive the body of God. The Jews received the frost of heaven; we receive the God of heaven.

Although he was, as the Apostle says, “in the form of God,” he “humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross” (Phil. II, 6, 8). He was not content simply to undergo death for us, unless he also compounded that voluntary acceptance of death with the endurance of the highest punishments.

For this alone, then, what can a human being repay to Christ, who gave himself for us through the final bitterness of punishments? Or what worthy return can one make to the Lord for oneself, when one owes the God by whom one was redeemed?

This is therefore why the Lord wishes us to be more devoted to him: because he purchased our devotion at so great a price.

And therefore blessed Paul says: “Who, then, will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. VIII, 35).

The Apostle does not say that we owe God only money or only riches, but tribulation, distress, hunger, the sword, suffering, the shedding of blood, the outpouring of the soul, and finally death seasoned with every kind of punishment.

From this all religious people should understand that they do not adequately repay God even if they have given all their possessions. For although they distribute everything they own, they still owe God themselves.

And therefore, as we began to say above, if a woman is a widow, let her not think that the name of widowhood is sufficient for eternal salvation. Let her see what kind of widow God commands through the Apostle, who says: “She who is truly a widow, desolate, hopes in the Lord and persists in prayers night and day. But she who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (I Tim. V, 5–6).

In one and the same command the Apostle expressed two forms of widowhood, one of life and the other of death, when he placed death in a life of pleasure.

Therefore, without doubt, he does not wish her to be rich whom he does not permit to live in pleasure, because the entire fruit of riches consists in the use of pleasures; otherwise, when the use of pleasures is removed, no reason for possessing wealth remains.

## VII.

Since, then, the Apostle has said that death is present in a widow’s life of pleasure, it is clear that he wishes everything to be distributed for the fruit of eternal life, since he does not wish anything to be reserved for the use of death.

And therefore he says: “She who is truly a widow, desolate, hopes in the Lord” (ibid., 5), teaching that it is not enough for her merely not to be a pleasure-loving widow or merely not to be rich. She must cling to God, devote herself to prayer, be desolate of all the enticements of the world, and through all these things be truly a widow.

If this is so, then any woman who wishes to belong to life rather than death should not think it sufficient for her to renounce pleasures for God’s sake and to renounce riches, unless she also earns the right through prayer and labor to appear truly a widow of God.

For there is no doubt that, just as someone has clung to Christ in this world, so he will remain in the body of Christ, according to the words: “My soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me” (Ps. LXII, 9).

This makes clear that God’s right hand will receive in the future only the soul that has clung to God in this world.

This, then, is the rule of widowhood.

As for married people who profess continence and are full of the Spirit of God, who could doubt that they do not wish their possessions to serve worldly heirs, since they have expelled themselves from the world? How could they assign to others what belongs to them, when they deny themselves even to themselves?

Endowed with such a new virtue, and trampling underfoot, through the remarkable austerity of continence, the permitted—and, what is more, experienced—pleasures of the body, how could they fail to devote some of their possessions to God, when they have made God himself dwell within them?

In my judgment, the following can most properly be said even of such a marriage: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, for the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV, 1).

For what does not bear is barren; what has separated itself from all the enticements of the world is desolate; and what is without a husband is that which has a husband in such a way, without marital use, that it appears not to have one.

Who could doubt that such married people, while they live, live for God both in themselves and in their possessions, and that when they depart from life they migrate to God with the possessions with which they lived for him?

For if any one of them instead leaves his possessions to those devoted to the world and to the world itself, he has inscribed the name of religion on himself in vain, and he appears always to have lived for the one for whom he dies.

This is enough concerning married people.

## VIII.

Let us pass to sacred virgins, for whom the Savior himself prescribed the law of devotion (Matt. XXV, 1 ff.), in the example, of course, of the ten virgins. Of these, he says that the foolish girls are given over to everlasting punishments for this one reason: because he knows that they will lack the work of mercy [Col. 0196B].

[Note: Previously the reading was *sit* (“be”). In this edition we have preferred to follow the authority of the manuscript books.]

By saying this he taught with the greatest clarity how highly he judged generous mercy, without which he said that even virginity itself would not benefit a virgin.

But perhaps some women flatter themselves and think it sufficient if, despite possessing great and abundant wealth, they give at least a little.

[Note: These words are absent from all the ancient manuscripts.]

I do not deny that, if the situation is indeed as they suppose, it should be believed to be so. Let a little be given, if giving little is sufficient.

But I do not know that little is sufficient; rather, I know with certainty that little is not sufficient.

[Note: We followed the agreement of the old books. The editions read, “If otherwise.”]

If they know otherwise, let them know it for themselves. I know one thing: God says that the lamps of the foolish virgins were extinguished because they did not possess the oil of good works.

But you, whoever you are, think that you have an abundant supply of oil? The foolish virgins of whom I spoke certainly thought so too. If they had not believed that they possessed it, they would have made provision to possess it.

[Note: The old books likewise read thus; the editions read *providissent* (“they would have provided”).]

For when afterward, as the Lord says, they wished to borrow and sought it with every effort and ambition, there is no doubt that they would have sought it earlier as well, unless confidence in their possession had deceived them.

You too, then, whoever you are, a virgin, beware lest you not possess it even though you think you do. You bear the same name as they and belong to the same profession. You are a virgin, and they were virgins; you presume yourself wise, and they did not think themselves foolish; you judge that your lamp has light, and they certainly lost their light through presumption of a future light.

For this is also why they are said to have prepared their lamps: because they believed that they needed to be lit.

And what more can I say? I think that some light even shone in them. For when they themselves, as we read, feared that their lamps might perhaps be extinguished, they certainly possessed something that they were afraid might be extinguished.

Nor was the opinion of those who feared false. They were indeed extinguished and darkened. For it did not benefit that virginity’s integrity that the light of virginity appeared in it [Note: Both Royal manuscripts read: “Because it failed, the substance of the oil not being supplied.”], since the substance of oil was not supplied and it failed.

From this we understand that what is little is as though it were nothing, because it is of no lasting benefit for a light that is destined immediately to be extinguished to be kindled, nor does it help for something to begin to shine if, at the very moment of its rising, it already contains its setting—and if its only beginning as something living is so that it can have the beginning of something dying [Note: Previously the reading was “so that it may be able to have an end.” But all the old copies have the reading we restored.].

[Note: Pithoeus reported that his manuscript read *Plena itaque* (“Clearly, then”); the Royal manuscripts read the same. The error arose through transposition of letters.]

Clearly, then, a lamp is necessary for the light to be lasting. If even in the lamps that people use for a short time the light grows weak and fails unless oil has been poured in abundance, how great a supply of oil do you, whoever you are, need so that your lamp may shine forever?

No one, then, has enough for eternal life if he thinks that he possesses what he does not possess [238]. For foolish presumptions are causes of destruction, not of salvation. “Whoever considers himself to be something,” the Apostle says, “when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. VI, 3).

Unless perhaps the measure of generosity has been revealed to you by God, and you possess limits for giving prescribed by the Holy Spirit, limits that you think it a sin to exceed and judge it somehow a transgression to be more religious than God commands you to be.

If that is so, I do not forbid you to use the knowledge granted by the Divinity.

But if this is as false as it is frivolous, what madness is it not to do everything you possibly can through cautious and timid provision, when you are completely ignorant of what is fitting for your salvation?

## IX.

It remains to say something about ministers [Note: [Col. 0197C] These words are absent from all the ancient copies. And indeed, if one considers what follows carefully, they seem to indicate that the words are superfluous.] and priests, although perhaps some things may be said unnecessarily. For whatever has been said about all the others applies, without doubt, even more to those who ought to be an example to everyone [Note: [Col. 0197C] King Athalaric to the clergy of the Roman Church, in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book VIII, Letter 24: “Meanwhile, live according to ecclesiastical institutions, you whom our judgments revere. It is a great crime to commit an offense when it is not fitting for you even to maintain a secular way of life. Your profession is a heavenly life.”], and whom, certainly, it is fitting to surpass the rest in devotion by as much as they surpass everyone in dignity. [Note: [Col. 0197D] This entire period is missing from all the ancient copies.]

For nothing is more disgraceful than for someone to be eminent in rank [Col. 0197C] and contemptible in worthlessness. [Note: [Col. 0197D] This passage is cited above, at the beginning of Book IV of *The Government of God*, p. 59.] For what else is authority without the elevation of merit but a title of honor without a man? Or what is dignity in an unworthy person but an ornament in the mud? Therefore, all who stand prominently at the sacred altar ought to excel in merit as much as in rank.

For if God gave so complete and perfect a rule of life to men placed among the common people and to women [Note: [Col. 0197D] Previously *ipso sexu* (“by that sex”) was read, which made little sense. The Royal Codex supplied the correct reading. Salvian says that God gave the most perfect rule of life not only to bishops and clergy, but also to ordinary people, who are commonly called the dregs of the people; and not only to ordinary men, but also to women, who are weaker than the very dregs of the people.] who are themselves weaker than the dregs of the people [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Macherentinus reads *inferioribus* (“inferiors”). Entirely wrong.], how much more perfect does he command those to be from whom everyone is to be taught, so that they may become perfect—those whom God wished to be such great examples in everything that he bound them to a singular standard of life by the severity not only of the new but also of the old law?

For although the ancient decree granted everyone broad freedom to increase their wealth, it nevertheless confined all Levites and priests within a fixed limit of possessions: namely, it permitted them to have neither a field, nor a vineyard, nor any estate at all. From this it can be understood whether our God now wishes [Note: [Col. 0197D] The old Royal and Colbertine codices read, “whether God does not wish.” The more recent Royal codex and ours have neither *neque* nor *non*.] those clergy who live under the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0198C] That is, all who are established in the clergy—bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the rest. Both groups are understood by the designation “clergy,” as was stated in chapter 29 of Agobard, *On the Administration of Ecclesiastical Property*. Pope and martyr Martin teaches the same thing in his letter to Theodore. Relating how he was brought from Rome by the exarch Calliopas, he says among other things: “Let those members of the clergy who are necessary to me come with me, namely, bishops, presbyters, and deacons, and, plainly, whoever seems necessary to me.” In Sirmond’s *Collectanea* of Anastasius, p. 78.] to leave their goods to worldly heirs after them—goods which, even when they were under the law, he did not wish the Levites themselves to possess.

That is why the Savior himself, in the Gospel, imposes on them the duty of perfection not as something voluntary, as on the others, but as a command. For what do we read that he said to that lay young man? “If you wish to be perfect, sell what you possess and give to the poor” (Matt. 19:21). But what does he say to his ministers? “Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts. Do not have a bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff” (Matt. 10:9–10).

Observe how great is the difference in these two words of God. To the layman he said: “If you wish, sell what you possess”; but to the minister: “I do not wish you to possess anything.” Yet he considered it insufficient merely to take away from him the possession of greater property, unless he also removed the very bag from the apostle who was about to undertake a long journey, and restricted him to the singular possession of one tunic.

And what follows? Even this is not enough. He further commands his servants to traverse the whole world with bare feet, and took sandals away from their feet stiffened by frost. What more can be said? [Note: [Col. 0198D] We have judged it appropriate to print this in place of what the editions read, *pecuniam* (“money”). The first edition, however, has *pedum* (“of the feet”). Pithoeus was the first to restore *pecuniam*, a reading found above the line in his codex. I strongly think that *peram* (“bag”) was originally written there. In establishing the true reading, we have followed the authority of the old Royal Codex. The necessity of this emendation is also inferred from what precedes.] He snatched the bag from the apostle’s hand and left his ministers, as they traveled throughout the whole world, not even the use of a single little staff.

And after this, is it a small matter for their successors—that is, for Levites and priests [Note: [Col. 0198D] Salvian is indignant that there are certain bishops who give their property and resources to people other than the Church, taking the greatest care to leave wealthy heirs. Again, in the following book, pp. 216 and following [Col. 0199D], he attacks religious persons—including bishops—because, when they had no children or relatives to whom they could give their resources, they preferred to leave them to unrelated heirs rather than to the Churches. The Code of Canons of the African Church, chapter 81: “It has also been decreed that if any bishop prefers to the Church heirs unrelated to his family, or even heretical relatives or pagans who are related to him, let an anathema be pronounced against him after his death, and let his name in no way be recited among the priests of God.” The bishop Sextilianus of Tuni, acting in place of Primasius, bishop of Carthage, mentioned this canon in the fifth session of the Fifth Council: “I inform your holy council that in former times many bishops assembled in our province and, while settling certain matters relating to various causes concerning ecclesiastical order, decreed concerning deceased bishops who left their resources to heretics that they should be subjected to anathema after death. He also had regard to canon 22 of the same African collection, which reads: ‘And let bishops or clergy give nothing from their property by donation to those who are not Catholic Christians, even if they are relatives.’ See also canon 32 of the same collection.] who administer such great divine things—if they themselves are merely rich, unless they also leave wealthy heirs?

Let us blush, I beg you, at this faithlessness. Let it be enough for us that we seem to despise God until the end of our lives. Why do we act so as to extend our contempt for him even after death?

We have spoken about the persons and duties of each individual. And all this is because, as we said above, some who profess religion think either that they do not owe the Lord their worldly substance as others do, or at least that they owe him less; although they ought to owe him more, because “the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows; but the one who does not know it shall be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48).

Religion, however, is knowledge of God; and therefore every religious person, by the very fact that he follows religion, professes that he knows the will of God. Thus the profession of religion does not remove an obligation but increases it, because the assumption of the religious name is a pledge of devotion. Consequently, the more someone has promised by profession, the more he owes in works, according to the saying: “It is better not to make a vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill one’s promises” (Eccl. 5:4).

## X.

But perhaps someone will say: “If these things are so, then irreligion is safer than religion.” Not at all. The religious person is in debt because he professes to be religious; the irreligious person because he has neglected religion. Thus both have their own obligation, according to the difference in their condition. The religious person owes whatever he has professed that he knows; the irreligious person owes even what he does not deign to acknowledge, according to what the divine word says specifically about him: “He did not wish to understand, so that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4).

Yet since we seem to have burdened religious people by saying that the profession of the name is a pledge of religion, let us remove this burden and suppose that what I have said is not so. Let us consider, finally, not what we ought to do by profession but by reason; not what we ought to do by vow but by the very requirements of salvation.

Tell me, I beg you, all you religious people: is there any human being who does not do everything he does either for the sake of his salvation or at least for the sake of his own advantage? No one, I think. For all are led toward the desire and pursuit of their own advantage by the instruction and impulse of nature itself.

Thus those who serve in the army consider their activity honorable for themselves; those who conduct business consider it useful; and those who farm consider it profitable. And why say more? Even thieves and robbers, poisoners and assassins, and every kind of wicked way of life consider what they do suitable for themselves—not because depraved things are suitable for anyone, but because the person who uses depraved things believes that what is depraved is suitable for him.

Therefore, I think that we too pursued the philosophy of religion for no other reason than that we judged it suitable for us—thinking, of course, about the brevity of present things and the eternity of future things; how small this is and how great that is; thinking also about the coming Judge and the dreadful consequences of the terrifying judgment; about the burning valley of eternal tears in the midst of the surrounding peoples; about how not only entering and enduring that immeasurable and supreme evil, but even seeing and fearing it, is a part of the supreme evil.

We also thought, amid these horrors and punishments, about these other things, glorious and blessed: new heavens and a new earth; a more beautiful appearance of all things; an eternal dwelling-place of justice; a newly fashioned structure of creation; the golden houses of all the saints above the unworked heavens; halls polished with glittering gems [Col. 0200B] and precious with the radiance of immortal metals; a light seven times brighter there, always shining with crimson splendor; blessedness rich in ineffable goods; an everlasting life rejoicing with its inhabitants; fellowship with the patriarchs; society with the prophets; brotherhood with the apostles; the dignity of the martyrs; and, among all the saints, likeness to the angels; an abundance of heavenly riches; an overflowing supply of immortal delights; and life shared with God.

Thinking and contemplating these things, we took refuge in the worship and service of sacred religion, and adopted it, in a sense, as a supporter and advocate of most effective intercession for obtaining these goods, and in ambitious humility committed ourselves to its protection and patronage.

## XI.

Since we have both thought about and sought such great things, let us now examine and weigh most carefully whether there is anything in our actions or possessions by which we can purchase such great gifts from God.

And if there is not, why, I ask, does each one of us not offer everything he has for himself, since he cannot offer everything he owes—especially when the Savior himself and our God has declared that nothing is safer or more beneficial for anyone than to devote his property and possessions to the practice of mercy? He commanded this especially in both the old and the new law, saying that those who distribute their possessions become richer, and that mercy delivers from death (Tobit 12:9).

And elsewhere, concerning a holy man: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Psalm 111:9). In the Gospel also: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matt. 6:19). And again: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (ibid., 24). And again: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24).

To those guilty of avarice and inhumanity he also says: “Go into the eternal fire prepared by my Father for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). What their punishment will always be in the future is easily understood from the fact that their lot is assigned with the devil. Yet in those greatest torments, it is not the most atrocious crimes of fornication, homicide, or sacrilege that are punished in them, but merely avarice and inhumanity that rejects mercy.

Therefore, we ought to understand what those will suffer whom, in addition to other sins, avarice has made guilty, since those who are free from every other sin but whose sole crime is avarice will be condemned to death with the greatest punishment.

If we believe that all these things are future, we must unquestionably avoid them. If we do not avoid them, plainly we do not believe. If we do not believe, we are not Christians at all. For we cannot call anyone a Christian who does not think that Christ must be believed.

## XII.

But suppose that we, the guilty, do not fear the punishments mentioned above. Can we nevertheless hope for a reward without deserving it? Therefore, if we do not give our wealth for the redemption of sins, let us at least give it to purchase blessedness; if we do not give it so that we may not be condemned, let us at least give it so that we may be rewarded.

For even if there are no past evils from which the saints need to be redeemed, there are nevertheless eternal goods which they ought to acquire at great cost. Even if there is no punishment to fear, there is still a kingdom to seek. Thus, even if the saints have nothing from which to be redeemed, they nevertheless have something to buy.

Unless perhaps someone fears loss in the purchase—namely, that he might lend more than he receives; that, after lending great things, only small things might be returned; that repayment might not compensate for his generosity; that, once a large sum of money has been handed over as the price, the purchaser’s money might be put at risk; and that, as though he had entrusted something great to the Lord on earth, Christ might perhaps have nothing with which to repay him in heaven.

If this is the doubt, I plainly advise doing nothing, because nothing at all benefits a doubter. The action is empty if faith is not certain, and the lender lends in vain if he despairs of receiving.

For Christ, as we believe, is the retributor of all deeds. If, then, you think him either poor, unable to repay, or faithless, unwilling to repay, how will you be able to hope for repayment from one whom you yourself have condemned both for inability and for faithlessness?

But if this is not so, and you do not doubt that he will do what he has promised, what folly or error is it not to give him as much as you can, since you do not doubt that you will receive far more than you have given? What misery, finally, to prefer to receive nothing from what you leave behind, when you could possess completely everything that you believe!

But—wretched that I am—I think that God is not believed. And when I say “I think,” would that I thought it doubtfully rather than recognizing it plainly. [Note: [Col. 0201D] The two Royal Codices and Pithoeus’s edition have this reading. Entirely correctly. Previously it read: “I would perhaps struggle within myself to overcome my opinions, and…”] I might perhaps labor within myself to overcome my opinions and compel my understanding not to believe doubtful things, so that I might apply my mind to better things.

But what are we to do? We are not overcome by doubtful matters; we are constrained by things that are evident. For who believes in the Lord with his mind but does not believe in him with his resources? Who entrusts his soul to God but denies him his money? Who lends faith to heavenly promises but does not act so as to be able to share in the promises?

And therefore, when we see people failing to do these things, we are compelled to recognize openly and plainly that they do not believe. We cannot suppose that they have faith in God when they proclaim by their actions that they deny him.

In this matter, the faithlessness of almost all human beings must necessarily be mourned and lamented. O misery! O perversity! One human being believes another human being, and does not believe God. Hope is extended to human promises and denied to God.

Finally, all human affairs are conducted by hope for the future. Life itself in this world is nourished and sustained by hope alone. We entrust seed to the earth so that we may receive back what we have entrusted with interest. Great labor is expended in vineyards because the hope of the harvest consoles people. Merchants empty their treasures into purchases while hoping that they will be filled by sales.

Thus travelers at sea entrust their lives to winds and storms so that they may obtain the fulfillment of their hopes and vows. And why say more? Peace even among savage and barbarous peoples rests on hope and is secured with faith as its guarantor.

Thieves and bloodstained men themselves do not deny one another their trust; they rely on one another to keep mutually whatever they have promised. In short, as I have said, everything among human beings is conducted by hope. God alone is the one about whom people despair.

And although our Lord has made the elements themselves and the nature of the world faithful [Note: [Col. 0201D] In the old Royal Codex it is written: “Although the Lord himself has made nature and the elements of the world…” In the more recent copy, however: “Although the elements of the world and the Lord himself…”], almost everyone refuses to believe in him alone, though he alone has made it possible for all things to be believed.

## XIII.

But someone might perhaps say at this point that people sometimes use their possessions not out of faithlessness but out of necessity; that religious people do not fail to believe God, but reserve what is necessary for life and ordinary use. For many holy people are prevented from attaining the highest perfection in the distribution of wealth by their sex, sometimes by their age, or by the weakness of a frail body.

Granted, this may be tolerated. But even if it is tolerated, it must be tolerated in such a way that what is sufficient is retained according to the character of the necessities and circumstances, while what is excessive is cut away.

“For having food and clothing,” says the Apostle, “with these we shall be content. But those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6:8–9). Therefore, as we see, salvation lies only in necessary possessions; in superfluous possessions, a snare; in moderation, God’s grace; in riches, the devil’s chain. [Note: [Col. 0202D] Thus the ancient books and editions read, except for the more recent Royal Codex, which has “a snare.”]

What does the Apostle immediately add? “They plunge a person,” he says, “into ruin and destruction.” Therefore, if riches contain destruction within themselves, let us avoid wealth, lest we fall into destruction. Broad and abundant resources are said to bring ruin. Broad possessions must be avoided, lest profound destruction follow.

Accordingly, whether sex, age, or weakness requires necessities for sustenance, people ought to be content with what is sufficient, so that whatever exceeds temporary use may be consumed in religious service.

But if you, whoever or whatever you are, professing a holy vocation, devote yourself either to preserving wealth or to accumulating resources, you make an empty excuse of weakness. For surely the weaker sex can live otherwise than by having the concerns of its mind distracted through the administration of a large estate?

Surely a sacred maiden or a widow devoted to chastity can maintain the integrity of her holy profession without lying under the weight of silver and gold or knowing that she possesses such great riches as the use of their owners does not require?

Or because rest is especially necessary for this sex and for modesty alike, does some woman perhaps consider it impossible for her to preserve undisturbed quiet amid the services of a few attendants, unless the noise of a large household strikes her ears and the tumultuous clamor of surrounding crowds deafens her?

For such things are not merely a great disturbance to a holy soul that desires true quiet; in a certain sense, seeing them is also part of the disturbance. And even if someone wishes to subject them to discipline and silence, he cannot restrain their agitation without sacrificing his own peace. Indeed, even the correction of another’s disturbance is itself a disturbance of our peace. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Previously it read *ipsum commercium* (“the very intercourse”). But this reading, which is found both in Pithoeus’s edition and in the Royal Codices, now seems better because of what precedes.]

What we have said about this sex applies to everyone and is equally appropriate to every age, sex, and weakness. Therefore no one should think that riches can belong to religion or do it no harm. They are impediments, not aids; burdens, not supports.

For religion is not strengthened by the possession and use of wealth but overturned, according to what the Lord himself says: “The anxiety of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word of God, and it becomes fruitless” (Matt. 13:22).

He specifically and very aptly called riches deceitful. For they are both thought and called good; and thus they deceive people by the name of present goods, although they are causes of eternal evils.

## XIV.

But although these things are so, as God himself foretold, let us nevertheless yield to the miseries and weaknesses of certain people [Col. 0203D] who think that they cannot live at all without great wealth.

Granted, whoever or whatever you are, of holy name and profession: granted that you retain your riches, granted that you retain your resources until the end of this life—provided that at least at the end you provide for yourself. Granted that you wish to use your possessions and resources in this life—provided that, when dying, you do not forget yourself, and remember that you must devote your substance to the worship and honor of the one whose gift you acknowledge as the source of your having received it.

What is being asked of all of you, O rich people of this world, is human and even indulgent. If it cannot be obtained from each of you that you should wish to be poor in this world, at least ensure that you do not beg in eternity.

You who flee only present poverty, why do you not fear it forever? You are fearful over brief things; avoid what is long and unending. Why do you dread poverty so intensely in this life, why are you terrified? What you fear here is far less.

If you consider temporary want burdensome, what, I ask, will that want be like which will never end? We are, as it were, acting on behalf of your own minds and your own wishes. If you do not wish entirely to be deprived of the use of your possessions, act so that you may never be deprived of them.

We ask of you something pleasant and pleasurable. Since you are unwilling to be without riches at all, act so that you may always be rich, according to the saying: “Therefore, if you delight in thrones and scepters, rulers of the peoples, love wisdom, so that you may reign forever” (Wisdom 6:22).

Otherwise, what error or madness is it for any human being to live out his days amid abundant riches—which alone is enough to make him guilty—and yet, until the final day of life, not remember himself generously and beneficially even at his last departure, nor come to his own aid when his own extremity is already sick unto death?

Especially since, amid riches that accuse the Lord by their very existence, according to the saying “Woe to you who are rich” (Luke 6:24), the rich person is not lacking other kinds of sins, which have sprouted in the very bosom and womb of wealth as in a natural source of nourishment. [Note: [Col. 0203D] The ancient books read “the Lord himself.”]

Why does he not, even in his final moments, act, strive, and earn by the whole extent of his possessions that he may not depart guilty, that he may not go away guilty, and that he may not afterward leave behind a body destined for torment and a soul already being tormented?

Who, then, is so faithless or so insane as not to think about these things, not to fear them; as to provide for others from his substance more than for himself; and, deprived of every hope in this life and of every support, to lose the one plank to which he could still cling like a shipwrecked man in mid-sea—not merely to lose it, but to throw it away and drive it entirely from himself, laboring in every way to leave himself absolutely nothing by which he might escape when he is destined to perish?

## XV.

Since these things are so, tell me, I beg you, all who love Christ: can there be human beings so savage and so cruel toward their enemies as these people are toward themselves?

For there are no people so fierce or so inhuman that they do not cease pursuing enemies who are already desperate and dying. These people pursue themselves even when they are at the point of death.

Is this not persecution? Or can there be any greater persecution than for a person to be disinherited by himself, to be made an exile from every good, and, as it were, driven into exile from himself? And this not according to any ordinary or customary practice, but according to a new and most cruel one. [Note: [Col. 0204D] The material that follows, up to the word “namely,” is absent from both Royal Codices and from the Colbertinus, where it reads: “But new and most cruel, namely, where into exile…”] For all exiles, although they are banished in body, are not expelled in spirit; although they are captives in the flesh, they nevertheless remain free in heart, if they wish.

But what we are speaking of now is a new kind of exile and torment: namely, where the soul itself is sent into exile, where the spirit is disinherited from its own resources.

O how much lighter are external and bodily enemies! They are enemies only of bodies [Note: [Col. 0205A] Elsewhere, following the authority of the editions, we had written: “For they are enemies only of bodies, you of spirits; they only of limbs, you also of souls.” But now, following the agreement of the ancient copies, which omit the words “you of spirits, they only of limbs” [Col. 0206A], we too have omitted them, since they plainly do not seem to belong to Salvian.], and you are enemies of souls as well. Their hatred, therefore, is light in comparison with your crimes.

Whatever harms in the present world is easy. What is grave and destructive is what will slaughter a person in eternity. Therefore the Savior himself says: “Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28).

The hatred that injures the body but does not injure the soul is easy, because when the body is injured, the soul remains outside the harm, and the blessedness of the spirit is not interrupted by the sufferings of the flesh.

That, then, that unforgivable evil is wholly immeasurable: it is what will condemn the entire person forever. Therefore your enemies are lighter for you than you yourselves. Every enmity is dissolved by death; but you act against yourselves in such a way that you do not escape your enmities even after death.

# BOOK THREE

## I.

In the two preceding books, O my lady, the Church of God, we have spoken separately to the two parts of your children: one loving the world, the other displaying the appearance of religion. In this book, if God grants his favor, we wish to speak to both, as the case and reason require—at one time addressing either separately, at another addressing both together.

It remains that, with each of them recognizing its own part in the sequence of the reading, whatever we say out of love for God may be received with love for God.

Since, then, throughout all that we have already said, we have repeatedly declared that mercy and generosity are the particular good of all Christians, and have demonstrated, as I think, with adequate and numerous witnesses, that in them are contained especially both the merits of the saints and the remedies for sinners, I do not think anyone should expect more from us—especially since, if anyone desires more, he ought to go to the books of God themselves. They are filled with so many and such great witnesses that almost the entire body of heavenly writings forms a single testimony.

It remains to say something against the causes of the unbelieving responses that certain people commonly bring forward as a deadly excuse.

Speaking in the Gospel, the Savior says that wealth and money are lent to people by the Lord so that what has been lent may be returned with manifold interest. He says to the most avaricious debtor:

“Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter. Therefore you ought to have given my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might have received what is mine with interest. Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents” (Matt. 25:26–27).

And shortly afterward: “Throw the worthless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Although this may also be referred to another matter, it is nevertheless not unsuitably applied to this place and subject. For since the Savior’s money-changers are rightly understood as the poor and needy—because the money distributed to such people increases—whatever is given to the needy is unquestionably returned to God with interest.

Therefore, elsewhere the Lord himself more clearly commands the rich to distribute their worldly wealth and to make for themselves purses that do not grow old (Luke 12:33). And in the vessel of his election [Col. 0206B] he likewise declares that riches are given by the Lord to the wealthy so that they may become rich in good works [Note: [Col. 0202D] These words have been added from the old Royal manuscript and the Colbertine manuscript. They occur in St. Paul.] (1 Tim. 6:18–19).

Therefore I too, the least and most unworthy of God’s servants, say that the first and most beneficial duty of religion is for a Christian who is rich, while he is in this life, to consume the riches of this world for the name and honor of God; and the second is that, if he has perhaps failed to do this because of fear, weakness, or some necessity, he should at least distribute everything when he is dying.

## II.

But perhaps someone says: “I have children.”

The principal page of the treatise has already said enough about this matter, and, as I think, with appropriate relevance; indeed, the Lord’s word is sufficient for this purpose: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

There is also the prophetic statement that neither fathers are judged on behalf of their sons nor sons on behalf of their parents, but that each person is either saved by his own righteousness or perishes by his own iniquity (Ezek. 18:20). Therefore, however much wealth a person heaps up for his children, it will not benefit him at the judgment that he left behind a rich heir.

Granted, parents may perhaps be forgiven if they leave part of their inherited resources to their children—provided that they leave them to good children, provided that they leave them to holy children. Granted also that it may perhaps be forgiven if they leave something even to bad and vicious children.

They seem to possess some appearance of an excuse when they say: “Affection overcame us; the force of blood compelled us; nature itself, as though with the hand of love, drew us into its own jurisdiction. We knew what God’s justice demanded and what sacred truth required; but, we confess, we were subdued beneath the yoke of embodied kinship, and we surrendered our hands captive to the bonds of affection. Faith yielded to blood, and the laws of family devotion overcame the devotion of religion.”

Something can be said for this, although it cannot be said beneficially. It is the shadow of a little excuse that does not excuse; it gives the guilty person the appearance of a plea, not security from guilt.

I do not at all promise anyone that he can possess a firm support for any matter if he has loved something more than God, according to what is written: that the judgment will be this, that light has come into the world and people have loved darkness more than light (John 3:19). For no one doubts that whatever a person has preferred to divine love will become darkness for him in its entirety.

These things, then, are so. But granted, as I said, that parents may be indulged when they indulge nature to their own detriment.

What shall we say of those who have no children but nevertheless turn themselves completely away from concern for their salvation and from the remedy for their sins? Although they lack offspring from their own blood, they still seek out anyone to whom they may assign the substance of their own resources—that is, anyone on whom they may inscribe some shadowy name of kinship, whom they may make, as it were, adopted children for themselves as imaginary parents, and who, through the falsehood that creates them, may take the place of children who do not exist.

Thus the most wretched and impious people, although they are not constrained by the bonds of children, prepare for themselves bonds by which they may tighten the unhappy necks of their souls. Since there is no danger arising from domestic perils, they summon danger from outside; and although the causes of danger are absent, they rush as though into voluntary destruction.

How these most unhappy errors should be received and endured with what disposition of mind may seem almost uncertain to some people [Note: [Col. 0207D] This material is absent from the more recent Royal Codex and from the Colbertinus.]—whether one should be angry with such people or grieve for them. Error deserves grief; impiety, execration. Their unhappiness draws us to tears; their faithlessness to anger.

In one respect we have reason to mourn the folly of human beings; in another, to be moved on account of the love of God: namely, that any human beings should be found or able to exist who, after passing through the brief span of this unhappy life, while already hanging at its very extremity and about to go immediately before the tribunal of God, think of nothing other than their end, nothing other than their departure, nothing other than their danger; and who, neglecting their hope and their soul—though they ought to aid it in some measure even in their final moments, with every effort, every exertion, and all their possessions—think only of this, turn over only this in their minds: how lavishly their heir will consume their property.

### III

Most wretched of all, why are you anxious, why are you in turmoil, why do you yourself make yourself the author of things destined to perish? Are you perhaps afraid that, once you are dead, there will be no one to devour what you have left behind? I do not want you to fear; I do not want you to be afraid. Would that you were as easily saved as all your possessions will perish!

O faithlessness, O perversity! It has even been commonly said that everyone wishes himself better off than another. This, however, is a new kind of monstrosity: to wish to provide for anyone at all, provided only that one does not provide for oneself.

Behold, most wretched of all, you are about to go to the sacred tribunal, to that dreadful and intolerable judgment, where a wandering and anxious soul can have no consolation whatsoever except a good conscience alone, except an innocent life alone—or, what comes nearest to a good life, mercy; where the guilty man has no assistance except a generous mind alone, except fruitful repentance and abundant almsgiving, like strong hands; where, finally, according to the diversity of merits, you will find either the highest good or the highest evil, either an immortal reward [Col. 0208A] or torment without end.

And you are thinking about enriching whatever heirs you may have, sighing over the wealth of your kinsmen and relatives, considering whom you should make richest through your estate, to whom you should transfer the adornments of your varied furnishings, whose storehouses you should fill with your resources, to whom you should leave the greater number of servants! Most wretched of all, you think about how well others will live after you; you do not think about how badly you yourself will die!

Tell me, I beg you, O wretched and faithless man: when you divide your estate among many, when you enrich many with your resources, have you treated only yourself so badly that you do not even make a place for yourself among strangers as an heir?

Behold, as you are about to depart this life, the office of the sacred tribunal already awaits you; angels who torture and the dreadful ministers of immortal torments await you. And you turn over in your mind the future pleasures of worldly heirs after you; you consider the delights of others: how well, of course, your heir will dine after you on your possessions, with what resources he will fill his belly, how he will stretch his overstuffed entrails until they overflow in nausea!

Most wretched of all, what have you to do with these childish tales, what have you to do with these ravings, what with the folly of this error, what with the destruction brought by this vanity? Will this be able to help you amid the highest punishments, if the man who has greedily consumed your possessions belches contentedly after bathing and dining well? Or even—so that he may render you, who handed over all your possessions to be devoured, a greater service through his overflowing indigestion—if he vomits well?

[Note: In both royal manuscripts, and in the Colbertine manuscript, the text is absent as far as the words “But concerning these matters, etc.”]

### IV

But concerning the matters of which we are now speaking, if circumstances and reason require it, we shall add something even after this. For the present I say this in particular, and urge it with a special admonition: no one should prefer any pledge whatsoever, however dear, to his own soul.

For it is not unjust that any Christian should accumulate less in this world even for his legitimate heirs [Note: Previously, “provide for” (*consulat*) was read, as in the ancient editions. The agreement of the older books led us to prefer the reading “accumulate” (*congerat*).]—provided that in many ways he comes to the aid of himself in eternity. For it is easier here for something to be lacking to children than for parents in the future, and present want is much lighter than eternal poverty. Especially since there not only poverty but also death and punishment are to be feared, it is certainly easier here for heirs to lack something from the estate than there for testators to lack salvation; and those to whom the inheritance is left ought themselves, if they possess any piety, especially to wish that those who leave it may not perish.

If they do not wish this, they are much less worthy to have anything left to them; for it is not unjust that a wise testator should not leave what an impious heir does not deserve.

Therefore it is best that each person should provide for himself and leave everything to his own soul and salvation. Even if there are sometimes not only children, to whom it seems that more is naturally owed, but also other pledges of his, of whatever merit or status [Note: Under the term “pledges,” others besides children are here understood. This is also clear from the following page, where parents, brothers, wives, relatives, and in-laws are counted among the pledges.], so that justice itself and the worship of God may support the act of imparting and giving something to them, and so that something may be left to them not only piously but also not irreligiously.

That is, if they are unfortunate parents, faithful brothers, holy wives, or, to extend the duty of piety still farther, needy relatives, impoverished in-laws, or finally persons in need of any relationship—or, above all, persons devoted to God. For this is the chief and surpassing consideration: that what someone does as an act of piety he should do with religious devotion.

Blessed, then, is the man [Note: Previously *ipse* was read. The correction was made from the royal manuscript.] who loves his own people with the spirit of divine love, whose charity is the worship of Christ, who, within the bond of nature, thinks of God as the Father of all natures, and, turning gifts of love into sacrifices, acquires for himself such great immortal profit and blessed fruits that, while by providing for his pledges he lends to his Lord, by granting temporary generosity to his own he produces for himself an eternal reward.

But now, in a wholly different and impious fashion, less is left by people to none of their own than to those to whom more is due on account of reverence for God; piety shows the least regard for those whom religion especially commends.

Finally, if children are offered to God by their parents [Note: See above in the notes to page 231.], those who have been offered are placed behind all the children [Note: Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias on preserving virginity: “Those who seem more religious to themselves give to virgins a small expense, scarcely enough for food, and lavish their entire wealth upon secular children of both sexes. Recently a certain wealthy presbyter in this city did this, leaving two daughters who had embraced the virginal purpose in poverty, while providing abundance for the luxury and delights of other children.”]; they are judged unworthy of an inheritance because they have been worthy of consecration. Consequently, they become cheap in the eyes of their parents for this one reason: that they have begun to be precious to God.

From this it can be understood that scarcely anyone is cheaper among human beings than God, whose contempt results in parents scorning above all those children who have begun to belong to God.

[Col. 0209C]

### V

But those who do these things, evidently, give an excellent account of the reasoning behind their decision, saying: “Why should an equal share of the inheritance be left to children who have now become religious?” Nothing, then, is more just, nothing more fitting, than that, because they have begun to be religious, they should beg.

Not, indeed, because this condition will oppress them with beggary when they have renounced earthly resources while possessing heaven in hope—and soon to possess it in reality also—with their God ruling and protecting them, who, together with the immortal hope of eternal things, also rewards them with sufficient temporal gifts. Yet, insofar as it concerns the inhumanity of their parents, they are needy, since they have been left by them in such a way that they would be needy.

Certainly, even if some are not expelled entirely from their homes, and are not wholly forbidden, like exiles, access to them “by water and fire,” but are left either poor or merely usufructuaries [Note: This passage, through “so much inferior,” is absent from the royal manuscripts and from the Colbertine manuscript.], they are nevertheless left so much inferior to their brothers that, even if they do not suffer poverty, they seem needy by comparison.

You say: “Why should religious persons receive an equal share of the patrimony with their brothers?”

I answer: So that they may perform the duty of religion; so that religion may be enriched by the resources of religious persons; so that they may give and distribute; so that, when they possess, all who do not possess may have; indeed, if their faith and perfection are so great that, although they possess now, they will soon possess nothing, then it is all the more blessed, after having possessed, to possess nothing.

Why, I beg you, most inhuman parents, do you impose upon them the necessity of the most shameful poverty? Leave this to religion itself, to which you have handed over your children: it is more fitting that they should become poor by themselves. [Note: Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, book 2, chapter 11: “Clerics also, whom either choice or birth has made poor, receive the necessities of life, with the perfection of virtue, whether they live in their own homes or in a community.” From this passage it is clear that some clerics were poor by choice and others by birth. This is also gathered from chapter 32 of the African Collection: “It was likewise decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who are ordained possessing nothing, but who during their episcopate or clerical office acquire fields or any estates in their own name, should be held guilty as though of an invasion of the Lord’s possessions.” Thus the ancient Church enrolled in the clergy those who were deprived of all resources. This was evidently in accordance with the law of the emperor Constantine, who decreed that only those should be appointed to clerical positions who were poor in fortune and were not burdened by civic obligations—that is, those whose wealth was not sufficient to discharge public functions with ease (*Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 2, laws 3 and 6, concerning bishops and clerics). At the end he discloses the reason for this constitution in these words: “For the wealthy of the world ought to undergo its obligations; the poor are to be supported by the riches of the churches.” A memory of this discipline also remains in the chapters of Jesse, bishop of Amiens, chapter 6: “Sixth, that you carefully ascertain, after each presbyter’s ordination, how much each person has advanced in his ministry; for those who were poor before ordination, but after ordination purchase for themselves an estate from resources with which they ought to have served the churches, are guilty, and so forth.” Today that discipline has been changed, and no one is promoted to the priesthood unless the bishop has first established that he does not lack the necessities required for living comfortably; the poor are commonly not admitted into the clergy.], that they should become poor through you.

If you desire them to be needy to this extent, permit it to be their own devotion. Allow them, we ask, to become poor if they wish: they ought to choose poverty, not endure it. Finally, even if they endure it, let them bear it through devotion, not suffer it as a condemnation.

Why do you drive them out as though from nature and disinherit them as though from the right of blood? I too want them to be poor—but so that poverty itself may have its reward, and so that, by a splendid transformation, they may choose poverty from abundance and obtain abundance from the choice of poverty.

Yet why do I try to draw you toward humanity and piety through the very service of the holiest reasoning, when the very matter that ought to make parents more pious makes you impious? For although you ought on this account to leave more of your estate to religious children, so that something from your resources might reach God at least through your children, you do not leave it to your children for this reason: so that they may not have anything to leave to God.

With an evidently excellent plan and precaution, you are content not to acknowledge your children, lest they recognize themselves as children of God. You make a magnificent return for sacred benefits by diligently ensuring that God’s honor may possess nothing even through your own children, although you possess everything through God’s gift.

Why, I ask, do you act so faithlessly, so impiously? We do not demand that you give your own possessions to the Lord: return something of God’s own to God. Why do you act so greedily, so impiously? What you deny does not belong to you.

Do you therefore consider it unjust to make religious children equal in substance to secular children? Is this what you are doing: making those regret the religion they have begun, whom religion has made worthless in your eyes?

May the pious and good Lord preserve in them their purpose and profession. But, insofar as it lies with you, you are trying to make them worshipers of the world, since you place secular children before them. For what else is this than to prohibit religion, to hold them in contempt on account of religion?

### VI

But perhaps we seem unjust in accusing all parents equally in this matter, since not all act with equal iniquity toward their children. “There are,” someone says, “many parents who make the shares of their children equal, except that they distinguish them by one condition only: in the portions that seem to be assigned to the religious, they order that the usufruct belong to them, but ownership to the others.”

But this is much worse and more faithless. For it seems to be an impiety more tolerable when someone leaves less to his children with ownership than when he wholly removes ownership of property from them. This condition may be endured to some extent if something is left under such a law to friends, in-laws, or relatives. But whoever grants his children no ownership of property leaves them nothing.

The most unjust faithlessness of parents, however, has discovered how to exclude God entirely from their estate by taking ownership of property away from religious children. He gave them the use of it, so that they might have the means to live; he took ownership away from them, so that they would have nothing to leave to God.

O novel ingenuity of an irreligious mind! It has discovered how, through its greater impiety toward God, it might seem to provide for its children. For he has made the holy offspring, possessing the use of property but not the right of ownership, live as though wealthy but die as though beggars; and thus the most faithless testator can depart from this world with complete security, knowing that nothing of his can reach God at all.

Although, in the very matter I mentioned above—that through the use of property religious children possess some likeness of wealth—even this is not the case [Col. 0212A]; for although the use seems to possess something, conscience does not. No one can regard himself as wealthy even for a short time if he knows that he owns nothing.

### VII

What are you doing, most wretched faithlessness and, so to speak, error of pagan irreligion? Do you hate God so much that you can even refuse to love your children for the sole reason that they belong to God?

Some people leave their freedmen in a better condition than you leave your children. For it is customary in daily life for slaves, even if they have not enjoyed the best form of servitude, certainly one that is not disgraceful, to be granted Roman freedom by their masters. In that freedom they receive ownership of their peculium and acquire the right to make a will, so that while alive they may hand over their possessions to whomever they wish and, when dying, transfer them by gift.

Not only this: they are not forbidden to take from their masters’ household whatever they had acquired while in slavery.

The generosity of the patroness sometimes grants them so much [Note: Previously the text read: “The generosity of the patron sometimes grants them such a gift.” We have now judged that reading should be rejected because the royal manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript unanimously have “the generosity of the patroness.”] that she even diminishes her own legal right by granting it to the ownership of freedmen.

How much better, O whatever most faithless father you may be, how much better those masters deal with their freedmen than you with your children! What they give, they give by perpetual right; you, by a temporary one. They grant freedmen the discretion to make a will; you take it away from your children. Finally, they give their slaves freedom; you, as though condemning them, assign your children to servitude.

For what else is it than assigning them to servitude when you do not wish them to possess anything as freeborn persons? You act, then, like those who, judging their slaves undeserving because they regard them as unworthy of Roman citizenship, assign them to the yoke of Latin freedom. They order them, while alive, to live under the title of freedmen, but do not want them to possess anything when they die.

For, having denied them the right of final disposition, they cannot, when dying, give away even what they possessed while alive.

So you also order your religious children to be like Latin freedmen: to live as freeborn persons, but to die as slaves; to be bound by the law of their brothers as though by the bond of Latin freedom, so that, although they seem to be their own masters while alive, they die as though placed under the power of their brothers.

What such great wickedness do you think lies in the title of religion that you do not believe those who are religious to be your children because they have begun to be children of God? In what supposed offense against your good will have they become guilty, so that you think they should be held worse precisely because they desire to be better?

### VIII

“But,” you say, “we do not do this with that intention.” That is the same as if someone were to say that he does evil things with a good intention, or commits an impious crime with a pious mind.

What does it help, most inhuman parents, that you insist you dishonor religious children with good intentions? The deed itself rejects this; the deed refutes it. It is not enough for you to say this in bare assertions: your own actions testify against you.

Do you therefore consider it unworthy that holy pledges, pleasing to God, should be compared with children serving the world? You are right, and rightly do you think so—if only you used this judgment justly and in the opposite direction: that is, if you judged that bad children should not be compared with good ones, nor sinners with the holy; and if those who excelled before God in life and merits likewise surpassed the others in your favor and honor.

For what is more right, what more just, than that those who are better should also be more honored; that those who win in judgment should also win in reward; that those who stand first in the holy Gospel should likewise stand first in a human will; and that, at least in this respect, parental piety and parental will should agree with the will of Christ, so that those whom God had set first by his choice, parents should also place first in dignity?

But this is not merely left undone; everything is done in the opposite direction. The stained are placed before the pure, the impious before the faithful; darkness is placed before light, earth before heaven, the world before God. And do parents of this kind think that they will escape God’s judgment even in this matter, when they trample upon the worship of God and the dignity of his judgment through their own unworthiness?

### IX

But, evidently, parents say that they do these things not out of contempt for God, but for a reason and with a plan. “For whom,” they say, “will they leave the substance that they are going to leave, when they have no children?” [Note: From this it is clear that there was then a class of people in the Church who did not attend to having children, and who were known to have no offspring as soon as they professed the settled way of life that was then customary. Clerics, monks, and nuns belonged to this group. Hence it may again be inferred that Baeus is seriously mistaken when he thundered against the celibate life on the authority drawn from Salvian, as stated above in the notes to page 109. Jerome, in his book *Against Vigilantius*: “What will the Churches of the East do, what will Egypt do, and the Apostolic See, which either receive virgins as clerics, or continent persons, or, if they have had wives, cease to be husbands?”]

I shall tell you whom: I shall not name those whom I mentioned above, the poor of God—not strangers or persons far away, lest the matter perhaps seem harsh or inhuman. I mean those who are dear and inseparable, and whom you yourselves, rightly, even though you have many children, place before your children.

I mean human beings themselves, O most faithless parents—I repeat, I mean yourselves. Can anything be found nearer to anyone than himself, or dearer? We commend to each of you your own soul, your own salvation, your own hope.

And you say that you are pious because you love your children? Nothing harsher, nothing more inhuman, nothing so savage, nothing so impious can be said of you—people from whom it cannot be obtained at all that you should love yourselves.

“Skin for skin,” says the devil in the Holy Scriptures, “and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job 2:4). Even the devil did not deny that a man’s soul is most dear to him; and he who strives to turn everyone entirely away from affection for his soul nevertheless confesses that souls ought to be most dear to everyone [Note: The editions read, “that each person’s souls are dear to all.” But the word *suas* is absent from all the ancient copies.].

What madness, then, is it for your souls to be held cheap by you, when even the devil considers them precious? What madness is it for those souls to be held cheap by you which even he says ought to be dear to you, although he tries to make them cheap?

Consequently, all who neglect their souls love themselves even less than the devil’s judgment.

Since this is so, look at yourselves, you who think that religious people have no one to whom they may leave their substance. Look, even according to the devil’s opinion; see whether they do not have someone, when they have themselves.

### X

I think that what we have already said is sufficient for this part of the matter now under discussion [Note: These words through “But I have shown” are absent from the royal manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript.]: namely, that you ought to place your life, hope, and salvation before every possession and every affection.

But perhaps you wish me to demonstrate this to you not only by the intrinsic excellence of the matter but also by the authority of examples. I could indeed mention commandments of God greater than all examples, crying out daily throughout the whole world: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matt. 6:19–20).

And elsewhere: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. 6:7).

These statements apply equally to worldly people and to God’s people, to those who have children and to those who do not; for since all desire to possess eternal life, there is no doubt that, where the desire of all to possess is equal, the care required of all to earn it is equal.

Nor does it matter, for increasing the authority of divine words, whether people fulfill them or do not fulfill them; for it is certain that their power rests upon the person of the Lord, not upon the obedience of his servants. Nothing can be added to them or taken away from them by us, since their honor, through God their author, is always equal [Col. 0214C].

Nevertheless, if human weakness wishes to be helped also by human examples, so that it may more easily do now what it recognizes that others did before, we showed in the first book [Note: See above, page 230.] that these things, which are even now being done by some imitators of Christ, were accomplished not moderately but abundantly; not by very few but by whole peoples; not by the most ancient but almost by the most recent, only lately.

For what do the Acts of the Apostles say—events that are new and still almost before our eyes? “All who believed were together and held everything in common” (Acts 2:44). And again: “Great grace was upon them all; for there was not a needy person among them. For as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the prices of the things sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet” (Acts 4:33–35).

Elsewhere also: “No one said that any of the things he possessed was his own” (ibid., 32).

And this was not a small number of believers—lest the authority of the writings perhaps move someone less, if they think these were examples of only a few. What the multitude of the chief Church was at that time can be recognized from this alone: at the very beginning, eight thousand people are reported to have been added to the Church within two days (Acts 2:41; 4:4). Let it be left to calculation what multitude of every kind must have gathered on the other days, when only two days, apart from the differing ages and sexes, produced so great a number of men.

Therefore, since even then the people were so innumerable and so perfect, I ask you, all parents to whom I am speaking: among those many thousands of believers then living with such perfection of faith, were they all with children, or all without children? Neither, I think. No people of the Church is not composed of both kinds.

All Christians who have no children to whom they may leave their estates can therefore understand to whom they ought to leave them, when they see to whom those who then had no children left theirs. But if they have children, let them learn what they themselves ought also to do, when they see that parents at that time preferred the love of God’s children to their own children.

Every age, then, and every condition has something to follow. Whoever shares in the faith should make himself a participant in the blessed example.

If those people then, by giving everything of theirs for God, even disinherited themselves while alive, learn, we ask you, at least yourselves to bequeath your goods when you are dying [Note: In the royal manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript this passage reads exactly as follows: “To inherit when dying. For it is necessary, etc.” The remaining words inserted between these clauses are absent from the royal manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript.].

As I said, it is fitting that you too, O most faithless parents, should think about these matters with greater care and attention for your own sake. Believe me, you must not forget the salvation of your souls even among your children.

It is certainly clear enough that your near relations and pledges are very closely joined to you. But believe me: no one is nearer or more closely joined to you than yourselves.

Love your children, then—we do not forbid it; love them, but in the second place after yourselves. Love them in such a way that you do not seem to hate yourselves. For love that remembers another and forgets itself is thoughtless and foolish.

“The son shall not bear the iniquity of his father,” says Holy Scripture (Ezek. 18:20). And the Apostle says: “Each one will bear his own burden.”

[Col. 0215D]

### XI

Wealth left to children does not free parents from beggary. Rather, wealth left excessively to children is the parents’ eternal poverty. Consequently, no one is more harmful to parents than children who are loved too much.

While the children overflow with their father’s goods, the parents are tortured in eternity. Even if a son is so dutiful that, for the sake of relieving his father’s punishment, he later wishes to share with his father the goods left to him, he will not be able to do so.

For after death a son’s piety cannot return to his father what each person’s own lack of devotion and faithlessness denied him [Note: Rittershusius eagerly seized upon this passage, as our opponents commonly do, to show that Salvian believed that the good works of the living cannot benefit the dead by repairing what they themselves had failed to do. But how false this learned man’s interpretation is in this passage is clear from Salvian’s following words: “The flames of the wretched dead are not cooled by the wealth of their heirs.” For here he is speaking about those who have been condemned to eternal punishments, for whom we too admit that the prayers and intercessions of the living are useless.].

Therefore, in accordance with the Apostle, let each person consider his own burdens, because each person will bear his own burdens. The flames of the wretched dead are not cooled by the wealth of their heirs.

That rich man in the Gospel who was clothed in purple and fine linen (Luke 16:19 and following), who had undoubtedly himself been wealthy in this world, had also enriched his heirs by his death. But it did him no good that his brothers were enjoying his wealth and talents; he could not obtain a drop of refreshment.
