They were in abundance, but he was in want. They were in rejoicing, but he was in sorrow. They were in wealth, but he was in torments. They were perhaps continually in luxury, but he was always in flame.

O unhappy and pitiable condition! He prepared blessedness for others through his goods, affliction for himself; joys for others, tears for himself; brief pleasure for others, everlasting fire for himself.

Where were his in-laws then, where his relatives, where even his children—if he had any—or his brothers, whom he remembered and whom he had certainly loved so greatly that he did not forget them even while in punishment? What did they profit him? What assistance did they provide?

The wretched man was being tortured. While others devoured his wealth, he, burning, sought a drop of refreshment and could not obtain it. And, if anything can be added to punishment, he asked that it be granted to him by the one whom he had once despised; by the one who had rotted in filth and corruption; by the one whose stench and squalor he had kept far away; by the one who had fed the dogs with the ulcers of his limbs, whom swarms of crawling worms had gnawed even within the recesses of his body.

O exceedingly grievous and mournful condition! The poor man purchased blessedness through beggary; the rich man, punishment through wealth. The poor man, possessing absolutely nothing, purchased eternal riches through poverty.

O how much more easily the rich man could have acquired these riches through possession of so many things—he who, burning amid torments and crying out amid punishments, said: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame” (ibid., 24).

That rich man evidently did not then recoil from the hand of Lazarus, once poor, nor did he disdain his assistance. He asked that Lazarus’s fingers be inserted into his mouth and that the intolerable flames of his throat be soothed by the help of that formerly foul and filthy hand.

O what a great reversal of circumstances had taken place! He then desired to be touched by the man whom he had previously scorned even to look upon.

## XII

Let the rich therefore reflect on these things, those who do not wish to redeem themselves by their possessions lest they suffer such torments. The man about whom we are now speaking was rich; these men to whom we are now speaking are also rich [Col. 0217A]. They share one name. Let them beware lest they also share one estate.

For rich children will not rescue guilty parents, nor will a wealthy heir, abounding in luxuries, extinguish the flames of a wretched testator. It is hard for someone to leave little to children and relatives; it is much harder to be tormented throughout eternity.

I imagine that, when that rich man was being tormented, his heir’s wealth did not delight him as much as the torments of his own body distressed him; it did not delight him as much that his heir feasted well as it distressed him that he himself was being horribly tormented; it did not delight him as much that his heir abounded in exquisite luxuries as it distressed him that he himself was melting amid intolerable fires; it did not delight him as much that his heir fed parasites and gluttons from his resources [Col. 0217B] as it distressed him that he himself fed the flames with his marrow.

And I think that, if someone had then offered him a choice—whether he preferred his heirs to be rich, or preferred not to be himself in misery and torments—he would surely have wished them to be deprived of all their goods, provided that he could be freed from every evil. He would have wished to offer everything he possessed, provided that he could escape what he was enduring. He would have wished to give, for himself, all the substance he had owned, together with his temporal treasures of silver and gold, so that, if somehow he could, he might extinguish with the mass of his riches the perpetual punishments, the immortal crosses, and that everlasting fire, and might hold back the surging globes of flame by opposing to them the immeasurable abundance of his wealth—267—.

And what shall I say that he wished, in order to redeem that interminable evil, to give from his possessions [Col. 0217C]? I will say something more. He would have wished to surrender all his substance so that, lying amid the flames, he might purchase for himself even one hour’s respite. For since he desired the poor man’s finger, dipped in water, to cool the flames of his throat, how could he not have preferred to buy respite at any price, when he begged so urgently for a small drop of refreshment?

But what did these things avail him, or what benefit was it to the wretched man that he then wished to offer everything for himself, when earlier he had wickedly refused to do so? Or what did it avail him then that he desired to give everything he had already lost, when he had given nothing for himself at the time when he possessed everything?

For, as the Holy Spirit says in Scripture, repentance of the dead comes too late—indeed, it is repentance too late. How so? “There is not,” says the divine word to God the Father, “anyone in death who remembers you; and in hell who will confess you?” (Psalm 6:6). It declares that the dead sinner is entirely excluded from confession of sin, and that no one can afterward remember God who in this life forgot himself.

So completely is every hope cut off from him and every entrance to life barred, that although the one way of salvation available to the guilty is to pour out prayers to God and ceaselessly implore heavenly mercy, even this sinner is condemned by the punishment of deadly forgetfulness: not even the memory of God, from whom he ought to hope, is left to him.

Let those therefore reflect on these things who, while wishing to have rich children after their death, do not remember future punishments even in death. Let those reflect on these things who, in order to have wealthy heirs in this fleeting and brief life, condemn themselves to eternal death. In this matter, they serve their heirs less than they harm themselves; they do not love them so much as they hate themselves—because an affection that provides only for what is brief is not so salutary as the grievous hatred that will torment them in eternity.

And therefore, as we said earlier in the first book, our God commands parents to store up discipline for their children, not money; he orders them to impart things everlasting, not things destined to perish. For such a gift and holy work benefit both children and parents: children through the instruction of discipline, parents through the generosity of munificence. Discipline enables children to receive everlasting salvation, and generosity enables parents to escape everlasting death.

**Editorial note [Col. 0217D]:** In a more recent royal manuscript it is written: “All are of one estate.” “Let them beware,” and so forth.

**Editorial note [Col. 0217D]:** The words “in this matter, they serve their heirs less than they harm themselves” are absent from the royal manuscripts and from the Colbert manuscript.

## XIII

But to whom are we saying these things, or why do we say them? Where shall we be able to find open ears or seeing eyes? For nearly everyone, as we read concerning the ungodly, has turned aside; together they have become useless: “There is none who does good, scarcely even one” (Psalm 13:3).

A new madness has seized both secular people and even some who profess religion. For, as we had begun to say earlier, they now assign the possessions of their own estate—that is, the price of their redemption—not only to sons or grandsons, which might be tolerated because of the bond of nature, but also to agnates and cognates [Col. 0218C]; and not merely, as they say, to those who come in the direct line, but also to those who come through the collateral and transverse lines—indeed, rather, through an opposing and perverse line.

As it is written: “He did not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Psalm 48:8–9). And shortly afterward: “Together the foolish and the senseless will perish, and they will leave their riches to strangers; and their tombs will be their houses forever” (ibid., 11–12).

It is not now the place to discuss what distinguishes the foolish person from the senseless one; nor does it matter what difference there is between their merits, since their destruction is one and the same. What is sufficient for our purpose is this: after saying that the senseless and the foolish would perish together, let us see what he added either to the explanation or to the accumulation of their destruction. “They will leave,” he says, “their riches to strangers.”

It is true. For what could be either so foolish or so ruined as for someone not to provide for himself from what is his, especially when God says that it benefits a person nothing if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul? “Or what exchange,” he says, “will a man give for his soul?” (Matthew 16:26).

If, then, people ought to despise the whole world lest they suffer the loss of their souls, and if someone ought, for the sake of his salvation, to despise even his own profits, how faithless and foolish is the person who condemns his own soul in order to make someone else rich? Especially since the one who receives the use of temporal goods gains little, while the one who loses the fruit of blessed eternity suffers immeasurable losses.

For this reason the psalm continues: “Their tombs are their houses forever.” How miserable, then, will be the lost lot of those who, assigned as it were to everlasting tombs, suffer in their souls, in a certain sense, the same condition that they preferred for their bodies after death! Indeed, their condition would be less miserable if they suffered the same thing—or if neither perception of good things nor suffering of evil things reached them, as it does not reach senseless beasts [Col. 0219A].

**Editorial note [Col. 0219D]:** Pithoeus correctly observed that this passage might more properly be read: “if neither perception of good things nor suffering of evil things reached them as it does senseless beasts,” or “as it does beasts.”

**Editorial note [Col. 0219D]:** Here one should set down what the distinguished Petrus Pithoeus noted concerning this passage. His words are as follows:

“This passage is corrupt in all the other editions, except the first Basle edition, from which it must be restored thus: ‘nor would suffering of evils reach them. But the bitter and intolerable point is that…,’ with precisely the same sense. Since at this point we lacked the aid of an old manuscript and did not have access to that first Basle edition, we had conjectured that it should be supplied, not altogether without reason [the printed *Aprosdionysos* is uncertain]. Up to this point, Pithoeus.”

In the royal manuscripts it is read as in the edition of Pithoeus.

But this is harsh and intolerable: they perish in the same way, but they are not punished in the same way. The death of the former is eternal without consciousness; that of the latter is accompanied by pain in every respect. Thus the destruction of sinful human beings makes their condition resemble that of beasts, but their punishment is nevertheless more severe.

Let them therefore reflect on all these things that we say—or rather, on all those things that God says—those who neither provide for themselves at all before death nor come to their own aid in death, among whom there is complete forgetfulness of their souls.

And now it scarcely matters to people for whom they provide, provided that they do not provide for themselves at all. For if any of those about whom we are speaking have no children as death approaches, they most faithlessly seek out people whom they may call their relatives or connections; or, if that happens to be lacking, they seek at least certain invented names of new relationships.

As I said, it does not matter whom they remember, provided that they forget themselves; it does not matter whom they claim to love, provided that they hate their own souls; it does not matter whom they make rich, provided that they consume themselves in eternal poverty.

**Editorial note [Col. 0217D]:** This and what follows up to “and it scarcely matters” on the following page are absent from the royal manuscripts and from the Colbert manuscript. Pithoeus nevertheless observed that, even without them, the reading stands. Since, however, these passages yield a good sense, we did not wish to expunge them. It is enough to point out that in both places it is written: “They assign the price of their redemption”; and “it scarcely matters now among people,” and so forth.

## XIV

O unhappiness, O madness! What have the most wretched of all people so gravely done against themselves, I ask, that while they serve the pleasures of others, they persecute themselves forever?

For you may see some people, in the most wretched vanity, searching out new and noble relatives; you may see the shameful names of unknown agnatic relationships and the ridiculous inventions of recent and powerful connections, when someone says of an adopted and sudden relative: “I make that man my heir and my parent.”

Or some widow or unmarried girl who professes a sacred way of life says: “I appoint that man, my next of kin, as heir.” Thus some whom they had treated throughout their whole lives as strangers and outsiders suddenly regard as relatives at the point of death; and those who were always strangers to the living begin to be parents to the dead.

For they suddenly introduce into their wills people whom they never introduced into their affections—and, as I said, especially people who are wealthy, noble, or honored, and who, unless they had been powerful, would perhaps never have become relatives.

What a ridiculous ambition on the part of the wretched testator: giving the wealth of his own estate to purchase the lie of kinship, buying the name of heir at the price of an inheritance, and laboring with all the strength of his patrimony to prevent the person named as heir from denying that he is a relative. Thus the most wretched testator, through the most foolish and miserable vanity, having made a nobleman his heir because he had seemed more humble during his life, strives to appear more honored in death—271—.

O blindness, O madness! With what effort, most wretched human beings, do you bring it about that you will be miserable in eternity? With how much less care and less striving could you have secured for yourselves the possibility of being blessed forever?

I can find no other cause for this than sheer unbelief and faithlessness—that is, either that people do not think they will be judged by God, or that they do not believe at all that they will rise again. For no one who is certain that he will rise and be judged by God concerning his good and evil deeds fails either to secure for his hope and blessedness the everlasting good that follows good works, or, out of fear and concern, to avoid suffering eternal evils in return for evil deeds.

**Editorial note [Col. 0219D]:** That is, a relative who is not a parent. Properly speaking, by the word “parents” we understand father and mother. Jerome, in the second book Against Rufinus, writes: “That ridiculous claim that, after thirty years, he had returned to his parents—a man who has neither father nor mother; and those whom, as a young man, he abandoned while they lived, he longs for when they are dead.” Unless perhaps he calls relatives and connections “parents” in the military and common manner of speech. It is certain that in Salvian’s time the word “parents” also included relatives and connections.

**Editorial note [Col. 0220D]:** Erasmus, in the *Seraphic Funeral Rites*: “The dead do not perceive. Yet the living, through a kind of imagination of future pomp, anticipate some pleasure and benefit.”

## XV

But this apparently seems foreign to the Christian name: that a Christian should be said not to believe in future things [Col. 0220C].

**Editorial note [Col. 0220D]:** Other editions read: “that future eternal goods are to be said to exist.” But “eternal goods” do not occur in the ancient manuscripts written by hand, and the following words show that they are superfluous.

What, then, is the reason that, if someone believes what God has said, he does not fear what God threatens? If he does not believe the words God has spoken, let him not believe the rewards God promises. For the person who does not act in such a way as to be able to reach the rewards promised by God does not prove that he believes God’s promises.

In this very human life, if someone knows that he is to be judged by an earthly authority and brought before an earthly tribunal, he seeks advocates, appoints patrons, and purchases the favor and goodwill of officials. He does all this out of fear of the future judgment, although he cannot secure the outcome of that judgment. Thus, even if he cannot buy victory itself [Col. 0221A], he nevertheless buys the hope of victory at great cost.

Tell me, whoever you are who say that you believe in the judgment of God: if, following even the example of the people just mentioned, you believed that you were to be judged by God, would you not purchase your hope and salvation at any price?

But you do not believe; indeed, you do not believe. Although you may wish to assert your faith in words, you do not believe. For, as the Apostle says, “You confess in words, but deny in deeds” (Titus 1:16).

Finally, to prove your unbelief to you from your own conduct, tell me, whoever you are who leave your substance either to some rich relative or connection, or, if these are lacking, even to a stranger: why did you not renounce it while you were healthy and leave it to your heirs while you were safe and vigorous? Why, in the will itself, do you most carefully and anxiously write:

“When I have departed from human affairs, then you, my dearest one, shall be my heir”?

Tell me, I ask, why do you give nothing of yours and hand over nothing of yours to this dearest and most devoted person, as you call him, for as long as you think you will live, but only when you see that you are going to die?

And why do I say “when you see that you are going to die”? Rather, you carefully guard against his having anything of yours while you are still breathing or even while you are dying, but only after you are entirely dead, already deceased.

And it is remarkable that you permit even this very thing: that he should have your possessions once you have been laid out for burial, unless you have already been carried out and buried [Col. 0221D].

**Editorial note [Col. 0221D]:** In the edition of Pithoeus this passage reads: “And it is remarkable that you allow him, once you have not yet been mourned, to have something of yours: once you have been carried out and buried.” In the old royal manuscript it reads: “And it is remarkable that you allow this very thing, and that, once you have not yet been mourned, he should have your possessions: once you have been carried out and buried.” More correctly, perhaps, the recent royal manuscript reads: “And it is remarkable that you allow this very thing, so that, once you have been mourned, he should have your possessions, unless you have already been carried out and buried.” Rittershusius thought that the negative particle was unnecessary here.

Although even in what you say—“when I have departed from human affairs”—you seem to have guarded against this very thing. For to depart entirely from human affairs means that a person has wholly ceased to be present among human affairs together with his body [Col. 0221C].

Tell me, then, why do you guard against these things so carefully in your will, why do you insert them so anxiously and prudently? Without doubt, because while you live you judge your property necessary to you; because you do not wish to alienate yourself from your possessions; and because you consider it most unjust for another to become rich from what is yours while you, alive and unharmed, are consumed by poverty.

That is true, and I do not reject this reasonable concern; I approve everything you say in this manner.

But in one matter I nevertheless wish you to satisfy me adequately. Why is it that you, who consider the use of your possessions so necessary to you, do not consider the fruits and revenues of your estate necessary after death?

You will certainly say: “Because the dead have no need of anything, and nothing needs to be reserved for me for that time; because, once dead and no longer perceiving, I can neither delight in possessing my goods nor be tormented by losing them.”

The reason is evident. Therefore you assign your substance to another when you are dying because after death you yourself cannot enjoy its fruits [Col. 0222A].

But what of the fact that the Apostle Paul, God’s chosen vessel, testifies and proclaims that “whatever a person sows in this life, that he will reap after death” (Galatians 6:8), and that “the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessing will also reap from blessing” (2 Corinthians 9:6)?

From this he plainly wished it to be understood that those who sow sparingly cannot reap blessing. For when he says, “The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessing will also reap from blessing,” he has clearly placed blessing in generosity alone, and shows that miserly sowers will reap poverty, while generous ones will reap blessing.

## XVI

But perhaps these things seem to you, whoever you are, O unbeliever, either insufficiently persuasive or insufficiently clear [Col. 0222B].

What of the fact that the Lord himself most plainly teaches in the Gospel that a Christian loses nothing from good works, saying: “Whoever gives one of these little ones a cup of cold water, only in the name of a disciple, truly I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew 10:42)?

What could have been said more clearly? He said that even something which has no value in the present would have a reward in the future; and he granted such honor to his service that, through faith, something would exist there which here, through its lowliness, would be worth nothing.

Yet, lest some people perhaps flatter themselves that, possessing much, they could purchase great things with small gifts, he carefully stated that even for a cup of cold water the reward would not perish. In this he clearly showed that something great is not to be repaid for something small, but that no work of faith, whatever its size, will perish.

You therefore have an unquestionable assurance of future recompense; you have a fully trustworthy guarantor of the good works that will be received. He is not only so faithful but also so merciful and compassionate that he does not merely pay what he has promised as though it were a debt; he even points out something by which he makes himself a debtor.

For when he says that he will return a reward for a cup of cold water, he not only wishes to repay what he has received but also indicates things by which he may repay. In his piety and fullness of mercy, wishing to provide not only for the generosity of the rich but also for the small acts of kindness of the poor, he shows that even someone who has nothing at all to lend could make God in some respect indebted to him.

## XVII

But perhaps, whoever you are, O rich man, this work of the poor seems unworthy of your possessions [Col. 0222D], and you may wish to hear some promise of sacred assurance that applies particularly to you.

First, you have that statement by which God speaks to the rich man in the Gospel: “Go, sell all your goods, and you will have treasure in heaven” (Matthew 19:21).

Next, you have the command that universally forbids the contrary: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth; but store up treasures for yourselves in heaven” (Matthew 6:19–20).

Finally, you have those words by which he invites all possessors of worldly goods to an act of lavish generosity, with the hope of infinite recompense: everyone who, for the sake of his honor and love, extends a house, a field, or any other possession for works of mercy will receive a hundredfold in the future. “Moreover,” he says, “he will possess eternal life” [Col. 0223B] (Matthew 19:29).

What greater promise could he make to those who believe him, when he promised that he would return a hundredfold to his great lenders? And not only this, but, he says, “he will possess eternal life.”

This is much greater than the repayment itself of a hundredfold, because whatever someone receives a hundredfold, he will possess forever. It will not then be a fragile and fleeting possession, nor will it perish like earthly riches, in the manner of a passing shadow or a vanishing dream. Whatever God gives will be immortal; whatever is received will remain without end.

And thus, as I said, the person who receives in this way receives more than a hundredfold, because the value of the hundredfold is surpassed by this very fact: the hundredfold itself is everlasting.

**Editorial note [Col. 0223D]:** Thus the old books read it. The editions, however, have *dominicae* (“of the Lord”).

**Editorial note [Col. 0223D]:** Pithoeus advises that *superfluae largitatis* (“of lavish generosity”) should be read.

**Editorial note [Col. 0223D]:** Earlier it was read as *magis* (“more”), as in the old royal manuscript. But since the other manuscripts have *magnis* (“great”), and Pithoeus advised that it should be restored in that form, we have chosen to follow the judgment of that most learned man.

## XVIII

Since these things are so, and since without doubt the person who believes God will receive such great things [Col. 0223C], how can you suppose that after death you will use those things which you have given to God—things for which the Lord promises you not merely use, but also increase and an extraordinary abundance?

Or perhaps you do not wish to receive such great things? But reason does not permit you to be unwilling. No one among human beings, when he can be blessed, prefers to be miserable; no one, when he can possess the delights of the highest good, wishes to suffer the punishment of the greatest evil. No one at all—no one. Therefore neither do you, unless perhaps there is in you some monstrous nature, at variance with the human race, so that you alone utterly refuse to be well, you alone flee blessedness, and you alone take delight in punishments.

If that is not the case, then what reason is there that, even when dying and lying at the point of death, you do not at least perform this final act of offering, with all the striving of your possessions, so that, if you can merit it from God, you may be rich and blessed? And if you cannot do that, at least so that you may merit not to be miserable; at least so that you may not be burned, not be tormented, not be cast into the outer darkness, and not be boiled in flames that burn without end [Col. 0223D].

Since these things are so, what reason is there, as I said, that you do not in every way flee evils or wish to attain good things? What reason is there that you do not do these things? What reason is there that you do not purchase eternal goods? What reason is there that you do not fear eternal evils?

What else, indeed, except what I said at the outset: either you do not think that you are to be judged by God, or you do not believe at all that you will rise again? For if you believed, how could you fail to flee the immeasurable evil of the future judgment and avoid the torments of immortal punishments?

But you do not believe; indeed, you do not believe. Although you assert something else in speech and profession, you do not believe. For your speech and profession boast of faith, but your life and death expose your unbelief.

Otherwise, refute me; I wish to be refuted. I do not ask you to prove your faith to me by the deeds of your former life; I am content with one testimony from your final moments.

Look—look, you are already dying, about to leave the house of your body, not knowing where you will go, where you will be led, or toward what punishments and horrors you will be snatched. You have only one refuge remaining at the point of death; you are given one means of escaping the darts of eternal fire: to offer on your own behalf at least what you possess in your substance, since you no longer have anything else that you can offer to God.

And yet, forgetful of yourself and oblivious to your salvation, you think about new legatees and sigh over enriching your heir. While doing this, you say that you believe in the judgment of God—yet when you are to be judged, you do not provide for yourself even at the point of death! And you claim to say something about the salvation of your soul, although nothing is less valuable to you than your own soul; for you scarcely care whom you benefit, provided that you harm yourself—277—and you say that you believe in the coming Judge, before whom no one is less important and more despised than the judge himself!

For you despise and scorn him so greatly that you will not even provide for yourself, provided only that you disregard his commands. Refute me, then, and convict me if I am lying.

Behold, your Judge himself, who will judge you, cries out to you as you die: do not love any human being more than yourself in disposing of your goods and possessions; do not, as you die, provide more for anyone from your substance than for yourself; judge no one nearer or dearer to you than your own soul.

For what will it profit a person, says the Savior, if he gains the whole world and suffers the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul? (Matthew 14:26).

This is what he means: “What will it profit you, O most wretched human being, if you either possess the whole world yourself or leave it to your closest relatives, if you suffer the loss of your salvation and soul?”

The losses of the soul carry everything away with them; and a person who loses himself through the destruction of his perishing soul will be able to possess absolutely nothing.

Or what, he says, will a person give in exchange for his soul? This is what he means: “Do not look to money, O human being; do not look to property; and do not hesitate, at least when dying, to offer for the sake of your hope as much as you can from your goods and possessions [Col. 0224D].”

Whatever you give for yourself is cheap; whatever you offer for yourself is of little price, because your soul is more precious than all things in comparison. And therefore do not hesitate to give anything for yourself: if you lose yourself, you lose everything in yourself; but if you gain yourself, you will possess everything with yourself and in yourself.

## XIX

When your Lord, whoever you are, cries out these things to you as you are already dying, you harden your mind and close your ear. You assert your faith in bare words and think that words in place of deeds are sufficient for you; you consider that you possess enough support for your belief if you appear to honor with lying words the God whom you despise through your possessions and works.

“My son,” says Holy Scripture, “if you have the means, do good to yourself, and offer good offerings to God” (Ecclesiasticus 14:11). And elsewhere: “Have mercy on your soul” (ibid., 30:24).

See the piety of our Lord toward you; see how merciful our God the Lord is, who asks us to have mercy on ourselves.

“Have mercy,” he says, “on your soul.” This means: “You too have mercy on the one whose plight you see moves me to compassion; have mercy at last on the one whom I always pity; have mercy at least on your own soul, since you see me having mercy on another.”

And what after this, O most wretched human being? When God deals with you in this way, you do not yield. He begs you to have mercy on yourself, and you refuse! He pleads your case before you, and you do not admit him! He deigns to ask you on your own behalf, and cannot obtain this from you!

And how, whoever you are, O most wretched human being, how will he afterward hear you supplicating him in his judgment, when here you yourself refused to hear him asking for you?

But evidently you have a serious reason why you cannot hear God. Your relatives and agnates surround you while you are sick; wealthy matrons surround you; noble men surround you; a multitude, draped in silken and golden garments, besieges your sickbed.

What an immense gain of eternity it is to distribute your possessions to such beggars! Surely this is a worthy and entirely just reason for you to take away from your soul what you leave to such needy people.

But of course you are moved by compassion, and overcome by the affection of your lamenting relatives. There is a definite explanation. You see people of the most opulent and splendid appearance, anxious for you and weeping for you, displaying to you faces arranged for mourning beneath festive clothing, purchasing your inheritance through their feigned solicitude—279—.

Who would not be moved by such great affection? Who would not be moved by such grief? Or how, when you see these things, could you fail to forget yourself?

For you see tears forced out, sighs pretended, and feigned anxiety—not wishing you to recover, but waiting for the time when you will die. You see the faces of all fixed upon you, as though accusing you of delaying your death.

O unhappy and most wretched person, whose final departure so great a number of relatives desires and prays for [Col. 0225D]! Except that I know, and am fully certain, that the prayers of such people have no power whatsoever with God. For I might perhaps wonder that you were still alive when so many wished you dead.

And for the sake of these people, whoever you are—for the sake of such people—you abandon your soul, and claim that you believe in the judgment of God, while you disregard his commands in order to leave your patrimony to such persons.

“He scattered,” says the prophet concerning the one who believes in God; “he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Psalm 112:9).

And the Savior himself says to all the rich: “Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12:33). And elsewhere: “Sell what you have and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21).

Does he say, “Give to your agnates”? Does he say, “Give to your connections”? Certainly not; but to the poor, to the needy. Does he say, “To a rich relative”? Does he say, “To any powerful person at all”? Certainly not; but to the needy, the destitute, the impoverished.

And rightly so. For when you have given your substance to your wealthy relatives, will your righteousness remain forever? Or when you have added your riches to their riches, will you have treasure in heaven?

“Woe,” says the prophet, “to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20). God even forbids you to praise such people, and you are not afraid to enrich them! He does not wish words of commendation to be given to them, and you even lavish talents upon them! He forbids their life to be honored with deceptive words, and you heap up their treasures and riches—280—!

### XX

But surely you fear the faces of the relatives who surround you, and you are afraid of offending those who are present and besiege your bedside. “Do not fear them,” says the Lord through the prophet, “and do not be afraid before their faces, for they are an exasperating house” (Ezek. 2:6). Therefore you too must be fearless and steadfast. Do not dread their faces, nor be broken by their attentions. Despise those who desire your inheritance and are already dividing your property among themselves—those who love not you but your patrimony, or rather, who hate you because of their greed for your possessions. For while they thirst impatiently for what is yours, they hate you; and, judging your presence to be a rival and adversary to themselves, they think that the fact that you are alive is an obstacle and impediment to their desire.

Despise such people, then, and regard them as nothing. Let not their flatteries move you: they are poisons to you. [Note: Tacitus, Histories, book I: “Flatteries are the worst poison of true affection.” Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, in his letter to King Henry II, published in volume II of D'Achéry's Spicilegium, p. 497: “The stern counsels of one who truly loves are better than the deceptive assent of a flatterer.”] Do not heed their flatteries: they are slaughtering swords, and indeed more dreadful than swords of iron and of enemies. [Col. 226D] Everyone sees those other men; the unwary do not see these. The former, because they rage openly, are avoided; the latter, because they lie in wait secretly, kill. They are therefore more dangerous and worse by a new kind of harm: no one wishes to be wounded by those iron swords, whereas many even wish to be killed by these. A new and immeasurable deadly lure! Whoever is struck by those swords is tortured by fear and pain alike; [Col. 227A] whoever is killed by these takes pleasure in it.

Flee this evil, then; flee the flatteries that lie in wait for you; flee their harmful services [Note: A word derived from obsequendo, “to comply,” used somewhere by Plautus and by Marcellus the memorialist in the letter to Severianus and Julian which is customarily prefixed to the Acts of the Conference of Carthage: “For every compliance with the duty entrusted to us,” etc. A similar word occurs in Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, letter 13 of book II, where the common reading is vestra in Domino custodiat insequilla, “may your insequilla in the Lord preserve,” though insequela should be read. For these were times in which copyists claimed the authority of orthography; and when words of this kind occurred, they made them decline a little from their origin. Examples are querela and parentela: the former is written quaerilla in the old collection of canons and in the oldest surviving leaves of the Theodosian Code written at Paris in the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; the latter is written parentilla in the Salic Law, title 63, chapter 1. Likewise in Monasticon Anglicanum, vol. I, p. 122: “under the lordship and authority of my parentilla.” There are also many other examples.]; flee the deceptive attentions of those who court you. These are the services that slaughter you; these are the things that drag you to death. Flee the flatteries of such people; flee their assiduity. They are your executioners and torturers: in the present they surround you, but in the future they kill you, and, joining their hands, as it were, and acting like a conspiracy bound together by mutual alliance, they try to drive and hurl you into the everlasting fires of hell. Therefore do not fear them or be terrified; lift up your spirit and assume the force of holy authority.

For if they strive so greatly for you to perish, why should you not strive with greater courage to live? Take heart, then, and provide for yourself with steadfast spirit. He is sufficiently faithless and sufficiently foolish who prefers to enable others to be miserable rather than himself to be blessed, and who, in order to make others abound in temporary pleasures, delivers himself over to be burned in everlasting fires.

## BOOK FOUR

### I

It does not escape me, my lady Church, nurse of blessed hope, that what we have said in the preceding books displeases some of your sons who love Christ too little. But we do not value their opinions highly, since it is no wonder that words spoken about God do not please those whom God himself perhaps does not please; nor should it be expected that they love discourse that commends salvation and souls, when they do not love salvation itself and their own souls.

Thus, here as in other matters, the opinions and judgments of the saints alone are sufficient for us. Since they think the same among us, we are certainly assured that God himself thinks with us also: for since the Spirit of God dwells in his saints, without doubt God is there where that party is from which the Spirit of God does not depart.

The opinions of wicked people—that is, of pagans or worldly people—must therefore either be lightly esteemed or utterly disregarded. “If I were still seeking to please men,” says the Apostle, “I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10).

There is something harsher and more troublesome: certain people, as I suppose, among your sons dissent from religion under the title of religion, and have abandoned the world more in dress than in their understanding. Their view and assertion, if I am not mistaken, is that every Christian ought to consider kinship more carefully at the time of death than Christ.

And because this opinion was in itself wholly profane and execrable, they try, as I think, to conceal their most faithless teaching beneath a kind of shadowy qualification, saying that all who believe in God, so long as they are healthy and safe, ought to be devoted to Christ alone; but those who are already departing from the world ought to remember carnal kinship rather than divine duty.

As though Christian people ought to be one thing while healthy and another while departing from this world; as though some should present themselves to Christ in health and others in death, some in their former life and others in their later life. But if this is so, one person will have one Christ as a young man and another as an old man; and people ought to change their faith as often as they change their age.

For if, in the worship of God, one person is to be vigorous and another weak, one healthy and another sick, then, according as the condition of the human body is unequal, God himself will also be changeable for a person; and as often as a person’s health is altered, so often will his religion be different. As though those who ought to belong to Christ while healthy ought not to belong to Christ when dying.

And where then is the saying, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13)? Or that oracle of the divine word in Proverbs: “Wisdom is proclaimed at the end” (Prov. 1:20, according to the Septuagint)? By this it is clearly shown that, although wisdom is beneficial at every age, nevertheless all people ought especially to be wise at their departure, because the prudence of a life already passed will not deserve praise unless it is brought to a good conclusion. “Wisdom is proclaimed at the end.”

[Note: Everything up to the words “Why did he not say that it is proclaimed in childhood?” is absent from the ancient manuscripts.]

“The past work of a person is sufficient,” says this pestilential teaching, “even if he does nothing at the end.” I add much more—or at least no less, if possible: when death is near, certainly much more must be done. First, because nothing is ever too much when it is a good work. Second, because a person who is going before God’s tribunal ought to appease the Judge more earnestly, as though he were already standing in judgment. Finally, if he has done some good before his departure, he ought to do much more at the end of his life, lest the end appear worse than his earlier actions.

But if he has paid little attention to good works, it is all the more fitting that he should do much at his departure, so that what he did not repay during his earlier life he may at least pay in his final hour; and that he who is guilty because he previously neglected his duty may at least in some measure be excused before his Lord because, by a final act of devotion, he compensates for his former inhumanity.

But let us return to what came before. “Wisdom,” says the divine word, “is proclaimed at the end.” Why did it not say that it is proclaimed in childhood, or in youth, or in a state of bodily health, or in prosperity and success? Clearly, because whatever is praised in all these circumstances is uncertain. For as long as a person remains subject to change, he cannot be praised with security; and therefore, as it says, “Wisdom is proclaimed at the end.”

When someone departs from the uncertainties of danger, he will deserve a sure commendation, having escaped the vicissitudes of all things. Praise is then stable and firm, when the merit of the one praised can no longer perish.

“Wisdom,” he says, “is proclaimed at the end.” What, I ask, is the wisdom of a Christian? What but fear and love of Christ? “The beginning of wisdom,” he says, “is the fear of the Lord” (Ps. 110:10; Prov. 1:7; 9:10; Sir. 1:16); and elsewhere: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Thus, as we see, the beginning of wisdom is in the fear of Christ, its perfection in love. Therefore, if the wisdom of a Christian is fear and love of the Lord, we are truly wise only if we always love God above all things—and this at every time, but especially at our departure, because “Wisdom is proclaimed at the end.”

### II

If, then, wisdom is especially proclaimed at the end when God is loved above all things, what madness is it for someone to say that Christ ought to be preferred to carnal kinship by those who are healthy, but ought not to be preferred by those who are dying?

For why should healthy people prefer him, if dying people ought not to prefer him? Or if someone can religiously place his relatives and kinsmen before Christ at death, why could he not also religiously have placed them before him earlier? Or if there is any moment in the final stage of life when someone ought to love others more than himself and God, why should he not love them more in his earlier life as well?

And so everything is dissolved, vanishes, and perishes: no one will have anyone more worthless than himself, nor anyone lower than God. For if there is any time when God may rightly be placed after relatives or kinsmen, there is no time when he may rightly be placed before them. But if, as is true, there is absolutely no time when he ought not to be preferred, there is absolutely no time when he may rightly be placed after them. None at all.

And therefore not even at the end: for the prophet says that even a just man will perish on the day when he goes astray (Ezek. 3:20). Thus, if every error is punished by the destruction of the one who errs, and human life is endangered even by those errors through which human innocence is ordinarily and commonly stained, what do we think will happen when one sins against God himself through detestable faithlessness?

“For if,” says the Apostle, “every disobedience receives a just recompense of reward” (Heb. 2:2), “how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” No one neglects true salvation more than the person who places anything before God.

Since our salvation is the gift and mercy of God, what basis for attaining salvation can there be for someone who despises God himself, in whose mercy our salvation consists? Or since God is Judge of both the living and the dead, what hope can there be in God’s judgment for one who, even while dying, has despised him by his own judgment—him by whose judgment he is immediately to be judged?

Therefore, as the divine Scripture says, “With what judgment he judges, he will be judged” (Matt. 7:2): that is, by the judgment with which he judges concerning God, he himself will be judged by God. Nor will he be able to regard it as unjust if the Lord places him after all others in the future, since in the present he himself places God after all others; nor can he complain if God considers him more deserving of condemnation than everyone else, since he himself considers God less worthy than everyone else.

### III

But someone says that he does not do these things with the intention either of despising God or of regarding him as worthless, but because he loves those whom he has appointed as heirs, or because he honors them.

Let us grant that this is so. Nearly all other people accused of the most shameful and criminal acts also have this excuse available. For fornicators too may say that they do not commit fornication with the intention of despising God, but because they are overcome by bodily heat and weakness. Murderers can likewise assert that they do not shed human blood out of contempt for God or hatred, but commit their crimes merely out of greed.

But what good does this excuse do the wicked, since it makes no difference for what reason someone says that he sins, when every sin is an insult against the Divinity?

Nevertheless, as I said above, let us grant that this is so: that no one transfers his possessions to another rather than to God out of contempt for God, but is drawn to do so by honor for his heir or compelled by affection.

But what are we to say when this very fact more clearly proves neglect and contempt for God? For if, O whoever you are, by leaving your possessions to your heirs or to anyone else you show that you honor and love them, then clearly, because you do not leave anything to God, you show neither that you honor nor that you love him.

Accordingly, whatever you say in your defense is against you, and the love and honor you show to others belong to the contempt and insult of God. For when you leave things to others because you honor them, you clearly do not honor God, to whom you leave nothing; when you leave many things to others because you love them, you plainly leave nothing to God because you do not love him.

Look: a human being and God alike stand beside you as you die and make your testament. The matter is clear and undisputed: the one you choose is the one you have preferred. If honor belongs exclusively to one, it necessarily follows that contempt is found in the other. If the person who is preferred rejoices that you love him, God, who is passed over, necessarily grieves that he is not loved.

But perhaps you think that God does not need human generosity; and therefore, you say, “Why is it necessary for anything to be given to him by a human being, since he himself has given everything to everyone?”

Whether the Lord needs our generosity or does not need it, and in what way he either needs it or does not need it, we shall now see. Meanwhile, since even you do not dare deny that everything is supplied to everyone by him, he is undoubtedly more worthy of our generosity because he himself first gave to us; and we try to respond to him with our service all the more justly because we are more unequal to his benefits.

Nature itself and the common custom of human beings bind everyone by this general law, as it were: we owe greater gratitude to those from whom we have received some generosity. A gift received constrains us to repay what was given.

Before experiencing another’s use and generosity, a person is free and unburdened by the interest of benefits. But once they have become debtors, everyone is compelled by conscience itself to repay what has been received.

Thus we owe God all the more because we have received everything from him; and we are less able to respond to his benefits because, even if we wish to return what we owe him, we nevertheless return what is his.

Accordingly, no one should take pleasure in his own generosity. Just as everything he receives from his Lord is not his own, so everything he gives back is not his own. Therefore punishment for faithlessness is owed to the one who denies God what was entrusted to him by God; but the one who returns what he has received cannot claim the generosity as his own.

### IV

“But God,” you say, “does not need repayment.”

Nothing is less true than that he does not need it. He does not need it according to his power, but he needs it according to his command; he does not need it according to his majesty, but he needs it according to his law. In himself he does not need it, but in many he does; he does not seek generosity for himself, but he seeks it in his people. Therefore he does not need it according to his omnipotence, but he needs it according to his mercy; he does not need it in his divinity for himself, but he needs piety for our sake.

For what does God say to the pious and generous stewards?

“Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink” (Matt. 25:34–35), and other words of this kind.

And lest this perhaps seem insufficient for the matter of which we are now speaking, he added a distinction between the circumstances, saying to the avaricious and faithless:

“Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me drink; I was naked, and you did not clothe me” (ibid., 41–43).

[Note: These words do not appear in the ancient manuscripts.]

[Note: Pithoeus’s edition reads: “Where, then, are those who?” The ancient books read: “Where are those who say?” and so forth.]

Where, then, are those who say that the Lord Jesus Christ has no need of the services of our gifts? Behold, he declares that he is hungry, thirsty, and cold. Let any one of them answer whether he has no need who complains that he is hungry, whether he has no need who testifies that he is thirsty.

I add something more: Christ not only needs things along with the rest; he needs much more than the rest. For among all the poor there is not one uniform poverty. Some, even if they lack clothing, do not lack food; many lack lodging but do not lack clothing; many lack a house but not resources; finally, there are some who, although they lack many things, do not lack everything.

Christ alone is the one for whom there is nothing that is not lacking within the whole human race. None of his own people is an exile, none is tortured by cold and nakedness, with whom he is not cold. He alone hungers with the hungry; he alone thirsts with the thirsty.

Therefore, insofar as his piety is concerned, he needs more than the others: every needy person needs for himself alone and in himself; Christ alone is the one who begs among the entire multitude of the poor.

And since these things are so, what do you say, O human being, who call yourself a Christian, when you see Christ in need, yet leave your resources to those who need nothing? Christ is poor, and you heap up the wealth of the rich? Christ is hungry, and you prepare luxuries for those who already abound? Christ complains that he lacks even water, and by you the wine-cellars of drunkards are filled with wine? Christ is worn down by want of every kind, and by you abundance is amassed for the luxurious?

Christ promises you eternal rewards for the gifts you give him, and you give everything to those who will offer nothing in return? Christ sets before you immortal good in return for good and eternal evil in return for evil; and you are moved neither by heavenly goods nor by everlasting evils? And you say that you believe in your Lord, whose reward you neither desire nor whose anger you tremble before?

### V

You do not believe, then, as we have already said in the preceding book—you do not believe. And although you may appear to belong to the venerable company of the converted, although you may imitate religion by your clothing, although you may assert faith by your belt, although you may counterfeit holiness by your cloak, you do not believe at all; you do not believe.

I have said this of men of this kind as well as of women: they do not believe. Let anyone put on whatever garment bears the name of holiness and inscribe upon himself the title of sacred religion; if he takes greater care for others from his substance than for himself, he plainly does not believe.

For no believer is willing that his resources benefit others rather than himself; no one is content to purchase blessedness for others at the price of his own misery; no one wishes to undergo everlasting want in order to provide others with temporary pleasures.

Therefore the person who takes greater care for others than for himself from his patrimony does not at all believe that what he gives to God will benefit him.

Let any one of them tell me why he leaves his resources to others. Is it not because he does not doubt that they will benefit the person to whom he leaves them? Certainly it is.

Therefore, whoever you are, if you leave things to another because you are certain that they will benefit the one to whom you leave them, then surely, if you believed that whatever you bestowed in religious gifts would benefit you, you would assign it especially to yourself. For the more you love yourself than those to whom you leave things, the more you would leave them to yourself if you judged, even with the slightest glimmer of opinion, that they would benefit you.

You do not hate yourself, so that you would not want to benefit yourself; but you do not believe that what you leave to the poor will benefit you. That is why you take greater care for others than for yourself: because you do not believe that religious action will benefit you.

As you believe, so you will receive. You regard the Savior as of very little worth, and the Savior will regard you as nothing. You place Christ after others, and Christ will place you after everyone. Your Lord is of less worth to you than even people who are lost, and you will be numbered among the last of those who perish.

### VI

But perhaps, as I said earlier, you flatter yourself because of some consideration connected with your religious profession. You are all the more indebted, because by your profession of holiness you promise greater things; and therefore you will endure greater punishment, because you fulfill less of your pledge.

“For the servant,” says the divine word, “who does not know his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with few blows; but the one who knows it and does not do it will be beaten with many” (Luke 12:47–48).

And you make great promises in the outward appearance of your profession, but in reality you restore nothing. You are guilty of the crime of forgery; you lie about everything to God.

Nor without reason does sacred Scripture testify that judgment must begin from the temple of God. “Judgment,” it says, “begins from the house of the Lord” (1 Pet. 4:17). Elsewhere also: “Begin with my saints” (Ezek. 9:6).

But let us return to what came before. “Depart,” God says to the avaricious and unbelieving, “depart into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Do you suppose that you can free yourself from this evil by certain bodily goods? You boast, of course, that you loved chastity. But remember that the Savior did not accuse even those whom he handed over to immortal punishments in the Gospel of sexual impurity.

You recall that sobriety pleased you? Yet those of whom Scripture speaks are not punished for the crime of drunkenness. You say that you fasted? Nor did their meals make those people guilty.

But evidently you have a great reason for being pleased with your abstinence and fasting: you fasted, you lived sparingly and frugally, not so that after your death you might feed the needy from your resources, but so that you might enlarge the wealth of whatever heir you chose.

What great fruits of abstinence you gain! You ate less bread so that someone else might have more gold. Your belly diminished through frugality so that the treasure of some perhaps vicious person might grow.

When you come, then, to God’s judgment, you will rightly be able to charge him with your fasting, saying: “I fasted, Lord, and abstained; for a long time I deprived myself of every kind of pleasure.” And the facts prove it. For behold, my heirs now abound from what was mine; they overflow with the riches of immense wealth.

And, to borrow something from the Gospel reading, you too can say of your heirs what the Savior said of that most depraved rich man:

“They are clothed in purple and fine linen, and they feast splendidly every day; they recline upon the talents I buried; they press upon heaps of silver and gold piled up together; I also prepared for them the means of every pleasure. They are stretched out in the luxuries I left behind. Thus I abstained for a long time so that they might now become drunk.

“My frugality is their debauchery. The floors of their overflowing dining rooms swim with wine; they make mud with noble Falernian wine; their tables and carved furnishings are continually soaked and always wet with unmixed wine. They luxuriate in the tapestries I made; they commit fornication in the silks I left behind.”

And when you have said all this on your own behalf, how will you not deserve eternal repayment from Christ, for whom you have prepared such an abundance of great pleasures in these holy heirs?

[Editorial notes omitted above: All the ancient books read thus. The editions, however, have “nor is it surprising if they,” etc. — This shows that those who abandoned the world—namely clerics, monks, and nuns—wore clothing different from that of other people, so that by this manner of conduct also they might show that they had renounced the pomps and pleasures of the world. Above, book IV of On the Governance, p. 70: “For when anyone has changed his garment, he immediately changes his rank.” Book VIII, p. 181: “It was therefore not without reason that among the cities of Africa, and especially within the walls of Carthage, that unhappy and faithless people could scarcely see, without abuse and execration, one clad in a pallium and pale, with the flowing mane of his hair cut off and shorn to the skin.” Below, book VI, p. 289: “Let anyone put on whatever habit he pleases of a holy name.” Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias on preserving virginity, praises her because, in place of jewels, silk, and exquisite meals, she desired the labor of fasting, rough clothing, and restraint in food; and because she cast aside every bodily adornment and worldly dress as impediments to her resolve, so that she might be clothed in a cheap tunic and covered by a cheaper pallium. — See the notes on pp. 70 and 281. — The words from “You do not believe” through “you do not believe” are absent from the ancient manuscripts. — The words through “great in outward appearance” are absent from all the ancient manuscripts, which read: “of your pledge: great in outward appearance,” etc.]

### VII

O how much better, whoever you are, how much better and safer it would have been for you to be poor and needy than rich! For poverty could have commended you to God; riches have made you guilty. It would therefore have been better for you to be saved through need than, through your wealth, to have weighed down both yourself and others: yourself, because you leave your possessions wrongly to others; and others, because they too possess, with most inhuman use, what you have wrongly left them, and after themselves wrongly leave it to others.

If, then, whoever you are, you wish to provide for yourself, if you wish to have eternal life and desire to see good days, leave your property to needy saints; leave it to the lame, the blind, and the sick. Let your resources be food for the wretched; let your wealth be life for the poor, so that their refreshment may be your reward and their sustenance may sustain you. For if they eat from what is yours, you will be filled; if they drink from what is yours, you will quench the heat and burning of your thirst. Their clothing will clothe you; their warmth in the sun will delight you.

Do not therefore think it cheap and contemptible to leave your property to the wretched and needy: in them you will make Christ your heir. And why should I speak of Christ's name? You will indeed make Christ your heir, but you will receive the profits of the inheritance. For whatever you leave to Christ, you will possess all of it through Christ.

But you, I think, judge these things to be trifles and despise them as certain dreams and ravings. For you do not believe that Christ has spoken the truth. The matter proves that you do not at all believe him. For one who does not carry out his commands even in his last acts either thinks that they do not exist at all or condemns them as false.

In this matter all the saints ought to grieve and weep: you and others like you believe no one less than Christ. If any innkeeper promised you something, you would not refuse belief to the one making the promise. If a shopkeeper or a dealer in preserved foods asked a loan from you, you would not distrust that he would return what you had given. Indeed, things are sometimes entrusted even to liars and perjurers when security has been furnished and a guarantor supplied.

Christ has given you both the most trustworthy security and the best guarantors: the security, namely, in the Gospel; the guarantors, his apostles; and, if that is too little, his patriarchs, prophets, and martyrs—in short, the entire series of the divine writings. And do you not believe him or extend him credit? What person among human beings, I ask, could you find so extravagant and so wretched that, with so many guarantors, you would deny him credit?

You give your possessions, then, to the rich and deny them to the needy; you give to the luxurious and deny to the saints; you give perhaps to any lost person whatsoever and deny to Christ. Therefore, as you have judged, so you will be judged; as you have chosen, so you will receive. You will have no share with Christ, whom you have despised; you will have a share with those whom you preferred to him.

[Note: The more recent Royal manuscript and the Colbert manuscript read salgamarius rather than salgamentarius.]

### VIII

But perhaps someone among the unbelievers says that this matter is not worthy either to move God or to bring human beings into eternal peril. I know, indeed, that all guilty persons always consider their offenses pardonable. For thefts are slight faults to thieves; drunkenness seems harmless to drunkards; and among the unchaste, fornication is no crime. There is, in fact, no crime so great that the judgment of the person by whose deed it is committed does not mitigate it.

But if anyone wishes to learn from sinners how gravely great crimes ought to be judged by God, let him learn how the saints punish even slight sins severely in themselves. For, being already aware from God's own sayings of the coming judgment, and scrutinizing judgments through the words of their Lord, they are always occupied in God's work, always in compunction, always on the cross.

Blessed are those who, while they have compassion on everyone, never at all forgive themselves; sparing themselves in nothing, but devoting themselves wholly to God, and therefore worthy of reward in the future judgment because here they are continually guilty in their own eyes. What shall I say of their mercy and generosity, a virtue among them that is, as it were, the initiator of all virtues?

For many of them have as the beginnings and, as it were, the cradle of their conversion this practice: before entering upon the threshold of their holy profession, they leave themselves nothing from their own resources, in accordance with the saying of our Lord: “Sell all your goods, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

Those, therefore, who are to follow God's call first sell everything before they follow. Regarding riches as burdens and impediments, they do not think themselves unencumbered for following God unless they have first cast off every impediment of carnal baggage. At the same time, like people migrating, they first transfer their possessions to the place appointed for their dwelling before transferring themselves, so that, when they have transferred everything belonging to them, they themselves may then migrate—with their resources sent ahead—into the full and well-stocked house of immortal goods. They are undoubtedly confident that nothing will thereafter be lacking to them, because, when about to leave a cheap, contemptible, and already tottering dwelling, they have left nothing of their own there to perish.

This, then, is the hope and confidence of the saints. By a rich transfer of possessions they provide for themselves so as to enjoy eternal stores of immortal resources. But you, whoever you are, who, forgetful of your soul and salvation, strip yourself by your very little possessions, how will you find in the future as though stored up and prepared what you assign here to people who are not needy or even to those who abound? How do you believe that God will return to you what you yourself do not entrust to God?

[Note: These words have been added from our manuscripts.]

Finally, how do you wish to have restored what you do not wish to entrust? For no one wishes to be repaid what he has not lent; nor is anyone so foolish as to think that what he has not invested at interest must be repaid. And therefore you can in no way hope that God will repay you what, by not entrusting it to God, you yourself have been unwilling that God should repay to you.

Accordingly, the divine saying must necessarily be fulfilled in you: because you have left your riches to others or to strangers, “your grave will be your house forever” (Ps. 48:11–12). And that which the Savior says to one like you: “Because you are lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:16–17). And you say: “I am rich, I have riches, and I need nothing,” and you do not know that you are wretched, poor, blind, and naked.

[Note: These words are absent from all the ancient exemplars.]

Let no one, then, who in life, in death, in action, in gift, or in his will prefers a human being to God flatter himself on account of any prerogative of life or profession. This confidence is punitive and ruinous: presumed hopes are burdens of guilt; usurped acquittal produces condemnation. Whoever excuses himself accuses himself before God, according to the saying: “For he who thinks himself to be something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Let no one's own case, then, seem easy to him. No one escapes more difficultly than the person who has presumed that he will escape.

[Note: These too are absent from the ancient manuscripts. Titus Livy, book XXVIII: “Human dispositions are far too eloquent in lightening each one's own fault.” Velleius Paterculus, book II: “So natural is it to human beings to forgive themselves everything.” The more recent Royal manuscript reads conversationis, “way of life,” in place of conversionis, “conversion.”]

## IX.

These things may perhaps seem harsh and austere. Why should they not? For every discipline, as the divine word says, is “not of joy, but of sorrow” (Heb. 12:11). These things are harsh and austere. But what are we to do? We are not permitted to alter the natures of things; and truth cannot be expressed otherwise than the very force of truth requires. I know that some consider these things harsh, and I am quite certain of it. But what are we to do? No one reaches the kingdom except by harsh paths. “For narrow and constricted,” says the Lord, “is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 7:14). And the Apostle says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy in comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). He declares that every human work is unworthy in comparison with the future glory. Therefore nothing harsh or austere ought to seem so to Christians: for however much they offer to Christ for eternal blessedness, what is given is worthless where what is received is so great. Nothing great is paid to God by man on earth when what is greatest in heaven is obtained in exchange.

It is harsh for the greedy to give away their possessions. What wonder? [Note: See above, book I, *On the Government of God*, p. 17.] Everything commanded against one’s will is harsh. As many kinds of commandments as there are, so many are their adversaries. If the Lord commands generosity among human beings, the greedy become angry; if he demands frugality, the spendthrift curses it; the wicked regard sacred discourses as their enemies; robbers recoil from whatever is written about justice; the proud recoil from whatever is commanded concerning humility; drunkards resist wherever sobriety is enjoined; the unchaste detest wherever chastity is commanded.

Either, then, nothing should be said, or whatever is said will displease every one of the people mentioned above. [Note: As Tacitus says in the fourth book of the *Annals*, you will find people who, because of similarity of character, think that the misdeeds of others are being charged against themselves. Even glory and virtue have enemies, since they condemn what is different as though it were too close at hand. Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus, says: “I know that I shall offend very many who refer a general discussion of vices to themselves as an insult.” Sulpicius Severus, speaking of Nero in the second book of his *Sacred History*, says: “Vices are always hostile to virtues, and the best people are viewed by the wicked as though they were reproaching them.”]

Every wicked person prefers to curse the law rather than correct his mind; he prefers to hate the commandments rather than his vices. Meanwhile, what are those to do to whom Christ has entrusted the duty of speaking? They displease God if they are silent, and human beings if they speak. But, as the Apostles answered the Jews: “It is better to obey God than men” (Acts 5:29). Yet I offer advice to all for whom the law of God is burdensome and oppressive, if they are not unwilling to accept it: let them consider how they may come to take pleasure in what God commands. For all who hate the sacred commandment have the cause of their hatred within themselves. All disgust lies not in the precepts of the law, but in their own character. The law is good, but their character is evil.

Accordingly, let people change their purpose and disposition. If they make their character worthy of approval, nothing that the good law commands will displease them. For when someone begins to be good, he cannot fail to love the law of God, because the holy law of God contains within itself what holy people possess in their character.

The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

# ARNOBIUS JUNIOR

[Col. 0237]

## PROLEGOMENA

### I

#### From Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Arnobius—not the one who wrote *Against the Nations* and flourished under Diocletian, but another, the Younger, who seems to have lived shortly after Pope Saint Leo—wrote a book entitled *The Catholic Conflict with Serapion concerning the Triune and One God*; likewise, *Concerning the Two Substances in Christ in the Unity of the Person*; and also *Concerning the Harmony of Grace and Free Will*. These books have been published.

Nor is it improbable that the commentaries on the Psalms circulating under Arnobius’s name belong to this Arnobius the Younger. Concerning them, see what we said above under Arnobius, in the third century.

### II

#### To the Candor of the Reader, by F. Fr. Feu-Ardentius

[Col. 0237D]

In the year of the Lord 1593, while withdrawing from Gaul to seek the acidic springs of Spa, in order to restore my poor health, I was traveling through Liège, that most extensive city of Belgium. An old pupil, then a reader in the Franciscan community there, led me to the monastery dedicated to the memory of Saint James. While searching through its old library, I came upon a manuscript codex whose title was: “Here begins the Conflict of the Catholic Arnobius with Serapion the Egyptian,” and so forth.

I read through some of it and discovered that it was a *Conflict* undertaken concerning the greatest matter among Christians, and one never previously published in print. I asked the prior, a man of venerable piety, whether it could be copied by one of our brothers. He agreed, and they sent the copy to me at Spa. There I read it more attentively. Its brevity pleased me, as did the author’s keen intelligence; the work seemed worthy of publication. Only this delayed me: I did not know who the author was, or when he had lived and written.

For it was first of all entirely certain that he was not the Arnobius who, under the emperor Diocletian, published seven books *Against the Nations*, since the style of expression is wholly different. More importantly, the rebuking of the Arians, Photinians, and Nestorians, together with the praise of Augustine, Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Damasus, and the two Leos, reveals a different author.

Therefore, if I may judge, identify, and determine anything concerning an obscure and doubtful matter, he is the author who left short commentaries on the Psalms, since the same brevity, keenness of mind, neglected style, passages rendered in the same sense and almost the same words, and the same heresies refuted all correspond. Finally, the chronology fits perfectly—namely, the age of Leo the supreme pontiff—which can readily be recognized as the period in which the work originated.

There is also the following testimony of Alcuin, the tutor of Charlemagne, in his letter to Flavius Merius: “Arnobius, in the *Conflict* that he held with Serapion, placed *rubus* in the masculine gender,” and so forth. I find these very words here. Again, in book six against Felix of Urgel, he refers to this Arnobius as follows: “Arnobius, a man of keen intelligence, in the *Conflict* that he held with Serapion,” and so forth.

Indeed, even before Alcuin, certain writers cited him against the Arians under the name of Saint Augustine: “Augustine, in the *Debate of Arnobius and Serapion,” and so forth. These facts make it clear that he belongs to the century we have mentioned.

You will find much here still gaping and mutilated, which can be repaired only by means of more accurate copies. Some expressions are less customary among the Fathers of purer Latin and must be pardoned in the author. Everything, however, is pious, orthodox, and most useful against the new Arians, Nestorians, and Pelagians.

We have divided the work into sections so that in our notes we might indicate the reasons for certain emendations and explanations. We have appended the *Conflict* to the works of Irenaeus, both because this author also refutes numerous heresies against God and because that arrangement made its publication more convenient.

Enjoy it, therefore, in a spirit of goodwill, and favor with Christian feeling our studies and labors undertaken out of Christian piety.

Cologne, 16 September 1595.

### III

#### From Aubertus Miraeus, *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 117

[Col. 0239B]

The *Conflict of the Catholic Arnobius and Serapion the Egyptian concerning the Triune and One God, concerning the Two Substances in Christ in the Unity of the Person, and concerning the Harmony of Grace and Free Will*, divided into two books, was found by Francisco Feu-Ardentius in 1593 at Liège, in the monastery of Saint James, and was published by him with notes at Cologne in 1595.

The people of Cologne later included the same *Conflict* in 1618 in volume five of the *Library of the Fathers*. The author of this work is commonly called Arnobius the Younger and is thought to have lived during the age of Saint Leo the Great, or shortly thereafter.

Furthermore, around the time when Adrian VI was made pope, commentaries on all the Psalms of David were found in the monastery of Francondal, between Worms and Speyer. Trithemius, Erasmus, Baraeus, and others incorrectly attribute them to Arnobius the Elder, concerning whom Jerome writes in chapter 79 of his *Catalogue*.
