In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Bellarmine suspects that these commentaries are the work of this Arnobius the Younger. Whatever the case may be, they have the flavor of Pelagianism.

### IV

#### From William Cave, *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 289

Arnobius, commonly called the Younger in order to distinguish him from Arnobius the African, appears to have been a Gaul by nation. He flourished around the year 460, as may be gathered from the inscription of the Commentary on the Psalms addressed to Leontius, bishop of Arles, and Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne. He was certainly somewhat later than Leo, whom he frequently praises.

The following works survive under his name:

**Commentary on the 150 Psalms of David**, wrongly attributed to Arnobius the African. It appeared separately at Basel in 1522; afterward it was edited by Erasmus at Cologne in 1532, in octavo; finally, it was corrected by Laurentius de la Barre at Paris in 1639. It is also found in volume eight of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 203.

**Annotations on Certain Passages of the Evangelists**, published at Basel in 1543, in octavo, and revised by Scotus at Paris in 1639.

**Debate or Conflict with Serapion the Egyptian concerning the Triune and One God; concerning the Two Substances in Christ and the One Person; and concerning the Harmony of Grace and Free Will**, divided into two books.

Casimir Oudin, I do not know on what authority, places this little work among the works of Vigilius of Tapsus. Certainly, apart from the testimony of manuscript codices, Alcuin cited it under Arnobius’s name eight hundred years ago. Franciscus Feu-Ardentius was the first to publish it, appended to Irenaeus, at Cologne in 1596. It is found in all subsequent editions of Irenaeus and in volume eight of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 236.

[Col. 0239]

# THE CONFLICT OF THE CATHOLIC ARNOBIUS AND SERAPION

[Note: Below, at the beginning of the second encounter, this work is called the *Debate*, and some writers cite it by that name. But since Alcuin called it the *Conflict* many centuries ago, and since the author himself prefixed that title to his book, and since it is so frequently named thereafter, we have retained this designation.

We have added “concerning the Triune and One God,” and so forth, because the work discusses these three subjects above all. The first was attacked by the Sabellians and Arians through opposing heresies; the second by the Eutychians and Nestorians; the last by the Manichaeans and Pelagians. Their followers were still troubling Catholic doctrine in the time of Leo the Great, the Roman Pontiff, when we believe this *Conflict* began.

It is certain that Leo, while still a deacon, first suppressed a certain Julian, a propagator of the Pelagian heresy; after becoming pope, he also conquered the Manichaeans; and he refuted and condemned Eutyches in highly learned writings, as is clear from his letters to Eutyches himself, Flavian, and the people of Constantinople, and elsewhere. See Prosper under the sixteenth and twentieth years of Theodosius.]

## CONFLICT CONCERNING THE TRIUNE AND ONE GOD; CONCERNING THE TWO SUBSTANCES IN CHRIST IN THE UNITY OF THE PERSON; CONCERNING THE HARMONY OF GRACE AND FREE WILL

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0239D]

### I

[Note: In the opening he sets out the general structure of the entire *Conflict*: namely, what matter it concerned, by whom and before which judges it was begun and concluded.

It is evident from the history of that age and from the acts of the second and infamous synod of Ephesus that not only Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria—which was the chief city of Egypt—but also many bishops of that province, and even three hundred monks corrupted by the Eutychian heresy, were deprived of communion in sacred things by the judgment of the Council of Chalcedon. So greatly had that plague spread among the Egyptians.

It is fitting, however, that not only these people but all heretics should be compared in this way, since they shamelessly oppose their tricks and devices to divine truth and have much in common with demons and sorcerers. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Eusebius, and Epiphanius testify to this concerning Simon Magus, Menander, Marcus, Carpocrates, Cerdo, and other heresiarchs of earlier centuries. We have made the same point concerning those of more recent times in more than one place.

Nor can anyone deny that, because Calvinism was admitted, magical arts have gained greater strength in Gaul, Germany, Poland, Livonia, Sweden, Dacia, and England during the past fifty years than they had possessed during the preceding fifteen hundred years.]

The Egyptians who arrived—demonstrating that they were disciples of the ancient teachers of their province, namely Jannes and Mambres, whom the Apostle mentions (1 Tim. 3:8) as having resisted Moses, the servant of God, by certain magical arts—likewise resisted the truth. When they attempted to bring this accusation against us, namely, that our faith concerning the Lord’s incarnation had strayed from the path of right doctrine, we finally obtained this from them: that, with the quarrel of words suspended and the disputants on each side speaking in turn, the others sitting in the place of assessors, they would permit only individual judges, who would be allowed to give sentence according to the merits of the conclusions.

Thus it came about that Arnobius became the defender on behalf of the apostolic see, while Serapion became the disputant on behalf of the Egyptian assembly. The judges were Decius Constantius on the Catholic side and Ammonius on the Egyptian side.

### II

The matter was begun in the following order.

**Serapion said:** Before we come to the question in which we accuse you of being “Homuncionites,” saying that there are two natures in Christ and two substances, I wish to know who you are.

[Note: The title “Homousians,” imposed upon Catholics by the Arians, continued in use even in that century, as Victor of Utica shows in many passages of his books *On the Vandal Persecution*. It should nevertheless be noted that Prudentius calls and refutes not Catholics but Ebionites, followers of Paul of Samosata, and other heretics by the name “Homuncionites,” because they maintained that Christ was a mere man and possessed nothing of the divine essence or power.]

**Arnobius said:** I am plainly a servant of Christ and an advocate both of the Catholic faith and of the truth.

**Serapion said:** Declare what your faith itself believes.

**Arnobius said:** I believe in one almighty God, creator of all things.

**Serapion said:** From where do you know that this God, whom you believe to be one, is almighty and creator of all things?

[Note: Observe in Serapion the behavior of heretics in debate, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3). Tertullian likewise says: “They never handle questions in an orderly fashion,” and so forth (*On the Prescription of Heretics*).

In fact, it has been found that they never remain within the state of the question that has been proposed. Rather, according to the spirit of dizziness by which they are continually driven, they pile up one question after another, and then a fourth and a fifth, most annoyingly. Thus, with the order of disputation disturbed, they slip away like writhing serpents; or, like cuttlefish, which have ink in place of blood, they escape into darkness by pouring out obscurity when the light of truth appears, so that they do not seem defeated.

Moreover, “Where there is true faith,” says Chrysostom (*Homily 1 on the Epistle to Timothy*), “there is no need for questions.” A question, of course, removes faith: for whoever asks has not yet found; whoever has not yet found does not yet believe. Faith, however, brings the mind and its thoughts to rest.]

**Arnobius said:** Because he himself deigned to manifest himself to the human race through great acts of power.

**Serapion said:** Through what acts of power?

**Arnobius said:** To pass over the earlier events, the land of your province itself testifies that, having been struck by ten plagues [Note: Or should we read, “which he struck with ten plagues”?], it lost its king together with his army, while nearly all the elements were raging because he had rebelled against God, the creator of all things.

But to the people whom he rescued from that king’s sword by his strong hand and outstretched arm, through his servant Moses, he made known that he himself is God and that there is no other besides him. If you intend to object, state your objection.

**Serapion said:** Let us pass over those points on which our faith agrees.

**Constantius and Ammonius, the appointed judges, said:** It is clear that Arnobius has given a satisfactory account of the one almighty God and that Serapion has assented to his statement. If this is not so, let Serapion declare it.

**Serapion said:** I wish to discover whether Arnobius’s faith errs in other matters, lest, if there are other matters besides those under dispute that can properly be refuted, we should seem to have failed to take advantage of the opportunity afforded by this occasion. [Note: I would gladly read: “that we have done nothing here.”]

**The assessors said:** Let Arnobius state whether he permits Serapion to inquire about matters other than those concerning which the dispute appears to have arisen.

**Arnobius said:** I do not refuse to let him inquire about anything he wishes, lest I seem to cut off my own opportunity to inquire of him about anything I may wish.

[Col. 0242B]

### III

**The judges mentioned above said:** Let Serapion state what he wishes to learn from him.

**Serapion said:** Will you say that this one God, the liberator of the Hebrews, is the only God, or perhaps another?

**Arnobius said:** The God of the Hebrews is one God (Deut. 6:4). When you hear, “There is one God,” do not seek another God at all.

**Serapion said:** Must we therefore hold the Jewish assertion, by which the God of the Hebrews alone and singly is proclaimed and believed to be God?

[Note: The Jews, convicted by the testimonies of six hundred prophets, confess that God is indeed Father. But in the creation of this world and of all human beings they never acknowledge the generation of a coeternal and consubstantial Son. Indeed, they attribute this to blasphemy, stoning Christ because he asserted that he was the Son of God; and thus they cannot bear the teaching of a plurality of persons together with the unity of the Godhead.]

**Arnobius said:** The Jews proclaim God as alone in such a way that they deny his Son; they likewise deny that the one who was born of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary is one God together with him.

**Serapion said:** Is this one who was born of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary himself the one, or is he another?

**Arnobius said:** He is one in the Godhead; in generation, however, he is another, in such a way that the Father and the Son do not cease to be one God.

[Note: He is speaking of the eternal distinction by which the Son is truly another person from the unbegotten Father and from the Spirit proceeding from both, while nevertheless continuing with them to be the one and true God.]

For God is then truly believed to be one, and the complete divinity in him is not denied.

**Serapion said:** And how is the complete divinity in him to be believed?

**Arnobius said:** The complete divinity in him is not denied if it is not altogether denied that the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, is one God.

**Serapion said:** By drawing me out of the synagogue’s assembly, you have led me into the madness of Sabellius, who confesses one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Sabellius, unwilling altogether to agree with the Jews, acknowledged a Trinity in God, but only of names, offices, and properties, not of properly so-called persons, as Dionysius of Alexandria, Epiphanius, Hilary, Theodoret, and others testify concerning him and his followers. Let the Calvinists consider how, by perverting the true definition of person together with their Calvin, they disgracefully fall away to the Sabellians.]

**Arnobius said:** If Sabellius truly called God one, he would not deny his Son and the Holy Spirit. For he denies the true Father, since he does not acknowledge the true Son; and he denies the Holy Spirit, since he does not believe God to be complete in the complete Trinity.

**Serapion said:** I read to you Sabellius anathematizing those who dared to deny the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in order to establish the Trinity.

[Note: The old codex, having omitted Arnobius’s name, attributes this statement to Serapion. It then repeats a third time: “if the Father, if the Son, if the Spirit”; we have restored *se*. Finally, we have written *contendit* (“maintains”) for *contendis* (“you maintain”).]

**Arnobius said:** But he most impiously maintains that the Father himself is the Son himself and the Holy Spirit himself.

We, however, say and believe that the Father is the one who begot the Son; and he is the Father of his only Son, begotten before the ages.

### IV

**Serapion said:** Do not lead me into the heights; deal now with this, that he begot him before the ages. First get me out of this, because I understand you to be saying three gods.

**Arnobius said:** Your understanding is in error. [Note: An old codex reads: “For you ought to remember that I said that you confess one true and complete God, the Father,” and so forth. We judged that “the Father” should be read together with “to confess.”]

For you ought to remember that I said you confess him to be the one true and complete God when you believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God—but only if you do not call the Father merely putatively, but call him the true Father who begot the true Son.

**Serapion said:** Then there is one, and another, and another.

**Arnobius said:** There is one, and another; and yet there is one God.

**Serapion said:** This cannot stand: that the Father who begot should be one, and the Son who was begotten another, so that the Father who is the Son should not be the same, and yet there should be one God.

**Arnobius said:** I shall demonstrate to you in yourself that two persons have one substance.

**Serapion said:** Let dialectical skill cease.

[Note: Since heretics attempt to establish their errors by paralogisms and mere fallacies, it is not surprising that they generally recoil from dialectic, which teaches how to expose and refute sophisms. For this reason the Donatists were unwilling to engage Augustine, because he was skilled and well equipped in this art of reasoning.

Likewise, at the colloquy of Baden, the other chief of the new Ubiquitarians, Smidelinus, was ordered, according to the agreement, to construct syllogisms in proper mode and figure and to dispute according to the rules of dialectic. When he could not do so, he attacked this excellent discipline; and, being hissed off and driven from the stage by his fanatical opinions, he shortly afterward died, exhausted by grief.]

**Arnobius said:** Dialectical skill enters into obscure matters so that what is true may be seen to be true. But I promise that I shall show in yourself that two persons have one substance—in you, I say, because you claim that I am proceeding *dialectically* [Greek: διαλεκτικῶς; perhaps “dialectically”], and not simply.

**Serapion said:** Then plainly show me some two persons in me having one substance.

**Arnobius said:** Behold: in your one head there are two eyes, but their substance is one sight; two nostrils, but there is one sense of smell; two ears, but one sense of hearing. If these pairs in you preserve the unity of one substance, do you refuse to allow that the Father and the Son in God are truly two persons [Note: We have added the word “one”] having one substance?

**Serapion said:** The comparison is recognized as incongruous: you take bodily members as an example of what is incorporeal.

**The judges said:** You have questioned Arnobius’s example taken from bodily members to no purpose. If the bodily members of the eyes, nostrils, and ears, divided in their forms and remaining separate from one another, as it were in their own chambers, possess such unity of substance that they enjoy one light, one sense of smell, and one sense of hearing, how much more will God—who must be confessed to be incorporeal, and who has one substance with his Son—also possess one majesty of omnipotence with him?

**Serapion said:** I accept the bodily reasoning; but unless the examples are incorporeal, I do not permit them to be applied to what is incorporeal.

**Arnobius said:** I ask, judges, that you indulgently bear with him as he rejects your opinion. For I do not fear his seeking incorporeal examples, since I confess and believe the true Father, the true Son, and the true Holy Spirit to be truly three and truly one almighty God.

Let Serapion be compelled to profess silence concerning this question when, as I have produced bodily examples, I shall also produce incorporeal examples by which I shall establish that three persons exist in one substance.

**The judges said:** Let Serapion declare that, for proving this matter, the only thing still lacking is that Arnobius should produce incorporeal examples. [Note: An old codex reads: “Let Serapion declare, in rejecting this, that this alone is lacking,” and shortly afterward: “I acknowledge that the matter has been satisfied,” whereas we have placed “we shall acknowledge.”]

**Serapion said:** I shall certainly acknowledge the matter to have been satisfied when the incorporeal examples have been set forth as clearly as the bodily ones.

**Arnobius said:** Can we say that there is perfect wisdom in one human being in whom there is no memory, intelligence, or understanding?

**Serapion replied:** How can wisdom be believed to be perfect if one of these three can be lacking?

**Arnobius said:** Then, if this is so—indeed, because it is so—just as these three incorporeal persons subsist in one wisdom, namely memory, intelligence, and understanding, and, although they are three, do not make three wisdoms but one perfect wisdom, provided all three are perfect, so in our faith there will be one perfect Godhead when we believe the perfect God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—to possess one omnipotence of the Godhead.

And just as wisdom is not complete where anything is lacking from intelligence, memory, or understanding, so faith in a person is not complete if he has stumbled concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, even by as much as may be the measure of a single point.

Faith is the light of the inner eyes. And just as, if you prick a tender part of the eye with a needle, you disturb and weaken the whole light, so also, when an error has been made concerning this holy Trinity in any part, even to the extent of an atom, a moment, or a point, it turns the entire clear light of faith into cloudiness. Once the mind has been wounded, it sees nothing but darkness.

[Note: Thus also the great bishop Augustine writes concerning the same mystery (*On the Trinity*, book III): “Nowhere is error more dangerous, nowhere is anything sought with greater labor, and nowhere is anything found more fruitfully.”]

**The judges said:** Serapion refused the bodily examples because they seemed to him incapable of being applied to incorporeal things. He must therefore yield to the incorporeal examples now produced, so that he may reasonably confess one Godhead assigned to three true persons.

[Col. 0245B]

### V

**Serapion said:** Permit me, judges, to inquire of him concerning what follows.

**The judges said:** Just as you are not permitted to repeat matters that have been justly settled, so you are not forbidden to propose what has not been discussed.

**Serapion said:** By first applying a bodily comparison and second an incorporeal one to the Father and the Son, you have taught one Godhead in these two, that is, in the Father and the Son. Now I wish to know what you say concerning the Holy Spirit, since I perceive that you believe a father has two sons.

**Arnobius said:** Unless I lead you to human reasoning, you cannot reach divine reasoning.

**Serapion said:** Lead me wherever you wish, provided only that you bring me to an understanding of the Holy Spirit.

**Arnobius said:** I ask you to tell me: when a king says, “Let a forum or palace or something of that kind be built,” do you think that this word, which has proceeded from the king’s mouth, himself caused what did not exist to be made?

**Serapion replied:** It is clear that this word, having proceeded from the king’s mouth, causes what did not exist to be made.

**Arnobius said:** Therefore the Father’s word, proceeding from his mouth and full of power, makes all visible creatures.

**Serapion said:** Again you have brought me back to the Father and the Son, when I am asking you about the Holy Spirit being born from you.

**Arnobius said:** You cannot find the Holy Spirit being born, but proceeding.

**Serapion said:** Now show me that procession itself.

**Arnobius said:** Did I not tell you that you impatiently hear those things that could lead you to investigate the truth?

**Serapion said:** I shall listen patiently and follow wherever you wish. Now show me what you think concerning the Holy Spirit.

**Arnobius said:** First, you must acknowledge that the Father spoke concerning his Son: “My heart has brought forth a good word” (Ps. 44:1).

[Note: The Latin and Greek Fathers agree that this psalm is to be understood of Christ. So too does the Chaldean Paraphrast, who interprets it of the Messianic king; and, greatest of all, the Apostle Paul interprets it of the Lord Jesus, the eternal Son of God (Heb. 1:8).

Justin Martyr, writing against the Jews, says (*Dialogue*): “Certainly Christ is proclaimed in Psalm 44 in these words: ‘My heart has brought forth a good word.’”

Athanasius likewise says (*Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*): “Who, hearing these words of God the Father, ‘My heart has brought forth a good word,’ would dare to say that the Word which proceeded from God’s heart came into existence from things that did not exist?” And again (*Compendium on the Holy Spirit*): “If there is a Father and a Son, the Son must necessarily be natural and true, that is, coessential with the Father.”

Of works, the divine word says: “He spoke, and they were made”; but of the Son: “My heart has brought forth a good word.” I omit other interpreters.]

**Serapion said:** Even if I wished to deny it, all those present who hear me would refute me.

**Arnobius said:** When the Word was born from the Father’s mouth—the Word by whose power he created all visible and invisible things—the Word could never proceed without the breath of the Holy Spirit.

**Serapion said:** Then there are two sons who proceeded from the Father’s mouth: the Word and the Spirit.

**Arnobius said:** You are mistaken in what you hear. You have forgotten that I first led you to the example of a king who commanded forums, palaces, or public baths to be built; and I added that the word of his command possessed such power that things that had never existed came into being. You confirmed this before the people. Answer me now again: is it so?

**Serapion said:** It is so.

**Arnobius said:** Then, if it is so—indeed, because it is so—answer me: is it rightly affirmed that this word, born from the mouth of the one giving the command, is born?

**Serapion said:** I agree, on sound reasoning, that the word is born.

**Arnobius said:** When the word of the one giving the command was born, and, proceeding from his mouth, made what did not exist, can the breath that proceeded from the one who uttered the word likewise be shown, by any reasoning, to have been born rather than to have proceeded?

If this cannot happen in the case of a human being who gives a command, how much more is it so with God? It cannot be shown that, when the Word comes forth from the mouth of the one who begets it, the very breath, full of the Holy Spirit, is called a Son.

Rather, the Father is the one who brought forth the Word; and the Holy Spirit is the one who continually proceeds from the Father, possessing the same power as the Son. For “by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). If you remember that this is written, declare it.

**Serapion said:** No one is unaware that this is written in the first book of the Psalms.

[Note: Epiphanius observed that the Hebrews divide the Psalter into five books. From the first psalm through Psalm 40 they make one book; from Psalm 41 through Psalm 71, the second; from Psalm 72 through Psalm 88, the third; from Psalm 89 through Psalm 105, the fourth; and from Psalm 106 through Psalm 150, they count the fifth book.

Moreover, that this verse of Psalm 32—“By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established,” and so forth—also pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, who created the heavens with the same will and power as the Father, has been consistently taught not only by Arnobius here but also by the great Athanasius (*Sermon 4 against the Arians*), Pope Damasus in the Creed, Epiphanius (book I, tome II), Philastrius, Fulgentius, and other orthodox writers.]

**The judges said:** It is evident that you have been satisfied concerning the Holy Spirit; your assent proves the assertion. Now let us proceed to those matters that have not yet been discussed.

### VI

Serapion said: “See, just as in one wisdom, which is perfect, I acknowledge memory, understanding, and intelligence, so I confess that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit exist in one Godhead. But I ask you: Did the Father truly beget?”

Arnobius said:

> [Note: I would gladly read *fictum* (“made up”), so that it would correspond to this question, “Did the Father truly beget?”]

“You will find nothing made in God except what he is. That is: the Father is truly Father, the true begetter of the Son; the Son is truly Son, the Father’s true Only-Begotten.”

Serapion said:

> [Note: Alexander, patriarch of the Church of Alexandria, testifies that the Arians’ madness was of this kind, as Socrates reports from his letter to all Catholics (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 6), as does Nicephorus (Book I, chapter 8). Athanasius presents it in these words (*On the Unity of the Holy Trinity*): “Arius says that God was always Father in power, but not always in actuality; and before he begot, he was not Father, but almighty God.” Athanasius answers this insanity as follows (*On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 26): “The eternal true Son, who was born from him, declares the Father to be truly eternal; and the eternal true Father demonstrates the Son to be truly eternal. Therefore the Father was never without the Son, because the Son was always with the Father.” Augustine says: “Let no periods of time be imagined there, having a before and an after, because there are absolutely none there.” And again: “In that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown or asked whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both,” etc.]

“Before he begot the Son, was he merely God, and not Father?”

Arnobius said: “You are mistaken in your question: he was always both God and Father.”

Serapion replied: “Then he did not truly beget.”

Arnobius said: “He truly begot.”

Serapion replied: “If he truly begot, then before God begot, he was God; yet he could not also be Father at the same time before he begot—the one who begot.”

Arnobius said: “You suffer from error because you force a comparison drawn from human frailty upon divine omnipotence. Before a human being has a son, he is merely human; but after he begins to have a son, he remains human, which he was, and begins to be a father, which he could not be before he begot a son. Do not inflict this insult upon God. God is immutable and enduring; he receives nothing new into himself. He was always both God and Father, nor did the name of fatherhood accrue to him, since whatever is an accidental attribute can depart, and whatever can depart can also fail. But the Godhead, which remains immutable, receives nothing accidental into itself. What he is today is what he always was. Nothing will fail from his past, as it does for you, human being, and nothing will grow upon him from the future. Nor do periods of time dominate him as they dominate you: first you were a little infant, then a little boy, afterward a young man, later an old man, and after old age your end overtook you. If you suppose that such a process can come upon God, you will prove yourself both foolish and an execrable blasphemer.”

Serapion replied: “May God avert this blasphemy, which now, born of folly, brands the blasphemer with ridicule.”

Arnobius said: “Then is God immutable, or is he changed in any respect?”

Serapion replied: “God is immutable; yet, according to your assertion that he begot the Son, he is shown to be mutable.”

Arnobius said: “We must return to certain comparisons by which we may show that birth can occur in such a way that no division of time can exist between begetter and begotten.”

### VII

Serapion said: “I hear something new: that no intervening time can be shown to exist between begetter and begotten.”

Arnobius said: “We have assessors and judges precisely so that we may be careful not to say that we will demonstrate what we are unable to demonstrate.”

Serapion said:

> “Beware lest you again bring me bodily examples by which you attempt to fit corporeal things to the incorporeal.”

Arnobius said: “I am already afraid of offending your prudence in this matter.”

Serapion said: “Not my prudence, but that of all the assessors and judges.”

Arnobius said: “Then hear an incorporeal generation from a corporeal human being.”

Serapion said: “You are launching into a dialectical sophism.”

Arnobius said: “A dialectical sophism has two aspects: it may be used either to prove as true what is asserted, or to show that it is false in some respect. But what I am now going to say will merely display the truth and will incur no mark of deceit whatever. How, then, can the dialectical argument I introduce be refuted? Surely, if I say that the human voice is incorporeal, am I lying?”

Serapion said: “Who has ever said that a voice is corporeal?”

Arnobius said: “No one has said this, but I wish to say that the human voice is incorporeal.”

Serapion said: “You are saying what no one is ignorant of.”

Arnobius said: “Does speech arise from the voice, or the voice from speech?”

Serapion said: “Speech arises from the voice.”

Arnobius said: “Is the speech that is born from an incorporeal voice corporeal or incorporeal?”

Serapion said: “Incorporeal.”

Arnobius said: “Behold: from an incorporeal voice is born incorporeal speech, the son of the voice.”

> [Note: An old codex reads: “The son of the voice might be found to be later.” Since we could extract no meaning from this, we added, “Could it be?” Nazianzen writes concerning the Son’s eternal generation (*Theology*, Book III): “God’s begetting is to be venerated in silence. I will grant that it is a great thing for you to have learned that the Son was begotten; but I will grant that knowing how he was begotten was not given even to angels.” Ambrose likewise says (*On the Faith, to Gratian*): “It is permissible to know that he was born; it is not permissible to investigate how.” Ephrem the Syrian composed an elegant book against those who wish to scrutinize the nature of the Son of God.]

“Could he be found to be later? If you are able to find no time between speech and voice, how will you be able to find any interval of time between the immutable God the Father and the Son? In this very inquiry, the third person, the Holy Spirit, must not be omitted. For when speech is born from the voice, breath goes forth not by being born but by proceeding, and through it the integrity of the voice’s speech is preserved. Likewise, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and through whom the complete and perfect Trinity is preserved in catholic definitions, makes clear that the Father was never without the Son.”

The appointed judges said: “Arnobius’ argument has also evidently explained the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son. If there are other matters not yet stated, let them be brought forward.”

Serapion said: “If I do not bring forward the matters that move me, what has been explained will be cancelled in my mind by those things which, although not brought forward, might have reached clarification through them.”

The appointed judges said: “We too shall seem to be wearied by useless labor in listening, and you by speaking without cause, if matters already known to be settled are repeated. Therefore you must take every precaution and make every effort not to recall, like a madman, struggles of words once they have been explained and concluded.”

### VIII

Serapion said: “I shall not be able in any way to repeat what has been explained so as to reach my agreement; nevertheless, whatever conclusions arise from those matters, insofar as they have been settled, must be proposed.” And he added: “Tell me, Catholic, you who do not deny that the Son was begotten from the Father: did the Father beget him by will or by necessity?”

Arnobius said: “Neither by will nor by necessity.”

The judges said: “Explain what you have said, for it is obscure.”

Arnobius said: “Every human being who wills or does not will something, if he does not first possess wisdom, cannot will or refuse anything justly. Therefore it is prior for him to possess wisdom than the power by which he can will or refuse something; and only then does he begin to understand and will, when through wisdom he has learned that he can possess this power. Serapion therefore asks me: ‘Did the Father beget the Son by necessity or by will?’ I shall answer briefly concerning one of these. God absolutely cannot be said or believed to suffer necessity. Since, then, the question has been settled with regard to one alternative, the remaining one must be resolved in this way: I must ask the questioner whether it is prior to understand rationally or to will rationally.”

> [Note: An old codex reads, “and not virtue.”]

The appointed judges said: “Let Serapion answer what Arnobius asks.”

Serapion said: “Who is ignorant that rational understanding comes before rational willing?”

Arnobius said: “If wisdom precedes will, then the Son preceded the will and was begotten before the begetter willed or refused anything; for when the will began, wisdom—which you yourself have confessed—was already prior. And although the reasoning I offered has already been shaped by your agreement, when you said, ‘Who is ignorant that rational understanding comes before rational willing?’ I shall nevertheless confirm this reasoning by the authority of the Apostle Paul, who says of the Son of God that he himself is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24).”

The appointed judges said:

> [Note: This question—whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly, and, equivalently, whether he begot him freely or by necessity—was carefully discussed not only by the ancient Fathers but also by Lombard (*Sentences*, Book I, distinction 6). It is the question being debated here between Arnobius and Serapion. Orosius writes to Augustine: “Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity? Neither by will nor by necessity, because there is no necessity in God; but will could not precede wisdom.” Augustine likewise reports (*On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 10) that a certain extremely cunning heretic asked a Catholic whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. If he answered “unwillingly,” an utterly absurd misery of God would follow; but if he answered “willingly,” the heretic would immediately conclude what he intended, namely, that the Son was not of nature but of will. The Catholic, however, most vigilantly asked him in return whether God the Father was God willingly or unwillingly. If he answered “unwillingly,” a great absurdity and misery would follow, which it would be utter madness to believe of God. If he said “willingly,” the reply would be: then he too is God by his will, not by nature. Augustine writes again (*On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 20) that Eunomius, because he could not understand or was unwilling to believe that the Only-Begotten Son of God, the Word of God, was begotten by nature—that is, from the substance of the Father—said that the Son was not of nature or substance but of will. He thereby asserted that a will had arisen in God by which he begot him, just as we sometimes will something that previously we did not will. Athanasius also testifies (*Sermon 4 against the Arians*) that the Valentinians and Arians contended that the Son was begotten through a preceding conception and paternal will, so as to place him among creatures, which came forth not from the divine substance but from God’s good pleasure and free will.]

What, then, do the scholastic Fathers say about this? They easily untie the knot, teaching that the Son was not begotten by a will that preceded, accompanied, elicited, or produced him, as the heretics maintained, but rather with will rightly cooperating, accompanying, and approving.

They confirm the first part of this solution from these words of the great Athanasius (*Sermon 4 against the Arians*): “The Apostle proclaims the Son to be not a product of will but the proper radiance and seal of the Father’s substance, saying: ‘Who, being the radiance of his glory and the form of his substance’ (Hebrews II). But if the Father’s substance does not exist by will, it is also clear that the Son did not originate from will. Certainly the Father himself did not say, ‘This is the Son begotten by will,’ nor, ‘The one whom I obtained by my good pleasure,’ but simply: ‘This is my Son,’ etc. (Matthew XVII).”

They confirm the second part from the fact that the Father is simultaneously good, powerful, willing, and begetting, since goodness, power, and will are his substance. Thus, if he begets as good and powerful, he also produces as willing. To this belong these words of Justin Martyr (*Dialogue*): “The Father begot the Son by his will.” So too Hilary’s very weighty judgment (*On the Synods*): “The holy Church anathematizes those who say that the Son of God is from things that did not exist, and likewise those who say that the Father begot the Son neither by counsel nor by will. If anyone says that the Son was born against the Father’s will, let him be anathema. For the Father did not beget the Son unwillingly, compelled or driven by natural necessity while unwilling; rather, as soon as he willed, he manifested the Only-Begotten from himself without time.” But enough of this.

It is clear that Arnobius spoke correctly: the Father begot the Son neither by will nor by necessity, because God has no necessity; and he taught by human reasoning, and confirmed by the authority of the Apostle, that will cannot precede wisdom. If there are other matters to be brought forward by Serapion, let them be disclosed.

### IX

Serapion said: “I remember that you said there are three persons: the Father, begetter of the Son; the Son, begotten of the Father; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father. You also stated that these three persons possess their Godhead and their complete perfection.”

> [Note: Here Serapion—and above, Arnobius—speaks of the Holy Spirit as proceeding from the Father, without mentioning the Son. This was permitted to the ancients before the Church had more explicitly explained and defined her position against the error of the Greeks. This was not because they denied that he also proceeds from the Son, but because, being content with the express words of Scripture, they did not then consider it necessary to explain the matter further. Thus Theodore says: “We have learned that the Holy Spirit has his substance from God and the Father.” Cyril likewise says: “We teach that the Holy Spirit is from the substance of God the Father.” Nor are there lacking Latin witnesses: Fulgentius also says, “He is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, wholly proceeding from the Father and wholly abiding in both.”]

Arnobius said: “So it is.”

Serapion said: “Therefore the Father is not the Son, nor is the Son himself the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the Father and the Son; rather, each is perfect God in his own person.”

Arnobius said: “So it is.”

Serapion said: “What, then, do you now say in answer to my question, when I ask you and you tell me: ‘The Father is perfect God, the Son is perfect God, and the Holy Spirit is perfect God’? Do you say this?”

Arnobius said: “I do.”

Serapion said:

> “And if you say this, how do you not believe that there are three gods?”

> [Note: There were also in ancient times heretics called Tritheists, who constructed three gods out of the three persons, as may be gathered from Nicephorus and others. Even now—O the times!—they are reborn from them like beetles from dung in Transylvania, Hungary, and Poland. We refuted their madness where we refuted Beza, who distinguished the divine essence really among the three persons, and Barthasius, who tripled that same essence and invented a threefold spirit in God.]

Arnobius said: “Even if forgetfulness dominates you, it does not dominate all the assessors and judges appointed here. For they know that I have spoken of one sight from two eyes; one hearing from two ears; one touch from two hands; one step from two feet; and one speech from two lips and one tongue. I have also spoken of one wisdom from memory, understanding, and intelligence; of one substance of life from so many bodily members; and of one intellect in the five senses, which understands by seeing through the eyes, hearing through the ears, tasting through the mouth, and smelling through the nostrils.

“Since our discussion dealt with all these matters, and the question of unity was settled, what reason brings us back again to matters that have already been settled both by mutual agreement and by the judges’ decision between the parties? I said that just as memory, understanding, and intellect perform one function of wisdom, so the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit possess one enduring kingdom of omnipotence.”

Serapion said: “I did not ask about the perfection of each one’s Godhead, nor did you speak about that. I say now: ‘The Father is perfect God, the Son is perfect God, and the Holy Spirit is perfect God’—these make three gods.”

> [Note: Augustine thunders against this Arian insanity and blasphemy in these words: “Cursed is he who does not confess the undivided Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Cursed is he who confesses the proper names of the persons as three gods, three lords, or three spirits.” Elsewhere he says again: “If anyone does not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one Godhead, equal majesty and power, one glory and dominion, one kingdom and one will, let him be anathema,” etc.]

“For either one God possesses a third part, so that the three possess only one Godhead by four-ounce portions, or there are three gods if each is perfect in his own Godhead.”

Arnobius said:

> “Since I am striving for brevity, you confront me with a rambling discussion; but however much you wish to extend the matter, I shall bring it to a conclusion in brief.”

> [Note: The example related here is aptly matched by what Gregory of Tours and Sigebert report: when Arianism broke into Gaul and the bishop of Vasates was celebrating the public liturgy, three drops of water descended from above upon the altar. When he wished to gather them, they changed into three firm and transparent gems; finally, they grew together into one, so that they were no longer three but plainly a single and marvelous gem.]

“Imagine three incomparable and most precious pearls, equal in worth, placed in a dark place or in blind night. When daylight and the splendor of the sun come, however, the brighter the clarity of the light, the greater will be the splendor of these three precious stones to the eyes that observe them. I ask now: Before they were revealed by the light, did these three incomparable stones remain in their preciousness, and was their beauty in them, although they were not visible to human eyes?”

Serapion said: “So it is.”

Arnobius said: “Is the light that revealed all three stones one light, or are there two or three lights of day?”

Serapion said: “Who denies that one light can reveal them, even if they are a thousand?”

Arnobius said: “I said three, but you concede a thousand. If a thousand precious stones display the adornment of their splendor by one daylight, how can the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit fail to reveal the omnipotence of their one Godhead by one light—Godhead not to bodily eyes but to the eyes of the heart, if the window of catholic faith has been opened so that the Sun of justice may enter through it and they may shine by his light?”

> [Note: An old codex reads *inormitatem*; the intended word is uncertain.]

“Thus let three precious stones of equal worth, equal majesty, equal beauty, equal diadem, and also one kingdom, be clearly displayed—not so that you consider one good and another better, or magnify one in such a way that you judge another more magnificent to the injury of the first. Each stone is truly what it is, so that it lacks nothing by which another could be judged more truly so.”

> [Note: A novel expression, used in place of ‘lacks,’ ‘is deprived of,’ or ‘is bereft of,’ etc.]

“Only let faith open the windows of our minds, which God himself has never opened without our faith. No one will be saved unless he has subjected his belief to right faith, and that faith has opened the windows of understanding, so that you may see these three most beautiful gems constructed in one kingdom, making one diadem and possessing one dominion of majesty.”

Serapion said: “These three stones, although they are of one preciousness and one beauty, are nevertheless separated from one another.”

Arnobius said: “You have seen the separation of the three, but you do not see one kingdom of one diadem.”

Serapion said:

> “I see one diadem, but in that diadem the gems have been constructed by the art of *cataclyzomatis*.”

> [Note: Perhaps this word signifies some kind of technique for arranging, joining, carving, or painting gems, unless one prefers to read it as *catachrysomatis*, “by the art of gilding.”]

Arnobius said: “Just as, according to you, the gems have been constructed by the art of *cataclyzomatis*, so here they have been placed naturally in one treasury of omnipotence. They are manifested only to those whose faith has brought it about that complete faith opens the door of this everlasting treasury and reveals both the perfect unity of the Trinity and the utterly complete unity of that unity: the true Father, who has always been Father, and the true Son, whose Father he has always been.”

> [Note: This is an obscure passage requiring a better manuscript. I think the intended meaning is: just as no one can be called a son before he has a father, so neither can anyone be considered a father unless he has a son. For these are correlatives, which posit one another when posited and destroy one another when destroyed. It is therefore insane and impious to imagine that God the Father preceded the Son, or that the Son is later than the Father.]

“For just as, if the Son has not been his Father’s Son, he cannot become the Father of his Son. Nothing changes in him who is true God; rather, immutable, he is always the same. Since he has always been God, truly one and triune, God cannot be believed to become what he was not.”

> [Note: I think the meaning is this: God the Father was not God at some instant or moment before he was Father, but from all eternity he was simultaneously God and Father, since the Son, consubstantial and coeternal with him, always coexisted with him. Irenaeus the martyr openly proclaims this against all heresies, namely, that the Word always existed with the Father before all creatures. Athanasius also quotes Dionysius of Alexandria as writing: “There was never a time when God was not Father, because his Son, the Word, Wisdom, and Power, never was not.” Shortly afterward he says of the same one: “Since he is the radiance of eternal light, he too is eternal in every respect; for since the light always exists, the radiance also always exists.” Augustine likewise says: “Just as the Father was never not God, so he was never not Father.”]

“For from that from which God is what he is—if indeed this ought to be said—from that from which comes that whereby he is God, as the poverty of human speech permits this to be said, not according to the very principle of majesty: from that by which he is God, he is also Father, and from that by which he is both God and Father, so also is his Son. For he did not begin to possess in his substance anything that he had not possessed before. He was always with the Power, who is the Son; always with his Breath, who is the Holy Spirit.”

Serapion said: “I am satisfied with everything, and I confess that the whole Trinity has always existed. But why should I not believe the Father to be greater, since the Father is not born from the Son, but the Son is born from the Father?”

Arnobius said:

> “We have already said that speech is born from the voice, but the voice is not therefore greater because speech is born from it. In one and the same moment, the voice, speech, and breath arise together; magnitude and diminution cease, because no time intervenes between voice, speech, and breath. The Father demonstrates that the Son is speech, as Holy Scripture testifies: ‘My heart has uttered a good Word’ (Psalm 44:1). And what is as good as the Son, from whom all goodness comes? The Word of one who utters from the heart could not be born without the Spirit and breath of the one uttering. For it is the breath that proceeds when the Word is born. Hence I said a little earlier: The prophets say that ‘by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power’ (Psalm 32:6).”

The appointed judges said: “Let what Arnobius has said concerning the invisible majesty of the Trinity be regarded as spoken abundantly; from Serapion’s repeated challenges we have clearly understood the matter to have been fully treated. If Serapion has something else to indicate, let him disclose it.”

### X

Serapion said: “May it not be inappropriate, in this inquiry prompted by my mind’s impulse, for you to state who holds the first place in this holy Trinity?”

Arnobius replied: “The Father holds the first place.”

Serapion said: “What do you say about the Son?”

Arnobius said:

> [Note: It is well known both from this passage and from Athanasius, Hilary, and Epiphanius that the Arians established such inequality among the divine persons that they assigned the first place of honor and power to the Father alone, barely left the second to the Son, and the third to the Spirit. The Calvinists now attempt to revive this heresy when, with their author, they contend that the name “God” and “Creator” properly belongs by antonomasia to the Father alone and improperly to the Son; that the Son, even according to his divine nature, will be subject to the Father; that the Father is the first cause of all things, the Son the second, and the Spirit the third; and that Christ, as God’s vicar, occupies the second or next place after the Father in honor and rule, etc.
>
> Against this, divine Scripture cries: “These three are one.” And the Son of God himself solemnly and most seriously testifies: “I and the Father are one.” “We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” Hence Cyril says: “The Trinity has one Godhead, one glorification, and the same dominion.” And again: “Abraham recognized and worshiped the consubstantial Trinity in the three men whom he saw.” Leo the Great agrees in these words: “The things possessed by the Father are not one set, those possessed by the Son another, and those possessed by the Holy Spirit another; rather, whatever the Father has, the Son also has, and the Holy Spirit also has, nor has this communion ever been absent from that Trinity. Let no periods, ranks, or distinctions be imagined there,” etc. Again: “For this reason we confess the blessed Trinity to be one God: because among these three persons there is no diversity of substance, power, will, or operation,” etc.]

“He too holds the first place.”

Serapion said: “And what about the Holy Spirit?”

Arnobius said: “He too holds the first place.”

Serapion said: “Then there is no Trinity.”

Arnobius said: “It is a Trinity, but we do not say first, second, and third; we say one, two, and three.”

Serapion said: “The Father is first, the Son is first, and the Holy Spirit is first: three firsts, therefore three gods.”

Arnobius said:

> [Note: Such, for a time, were Augustus, Antony, and Lepidus, from whom the triumvirate arose. Likewise, the three sons of Constantine the Great ruled together, and afterward Honorius, Arcadius, and Gratian, although not with as much harmony of mind as would have been fitting.]

“Imagine three emperors in one kingdom, in one concord, on one throne, in one pleasant fellowship, in one affection of love, and in one power, and ask which of them holds the first place of power. Without doubt, since all three are Augusti, all three are first; they will possess a second and third place only in the order of power established among the Augusti.”

Serapion said: “Then is that emperor not first among them who first began to possess the empire among them?”

Arnobius said: “Among human beings, the emperor who first began to reign alone is indeed prior, and afterward established the others either by begetting or by choosing them. But in divine rule you will never find one of these three reigning without the other.”

Serapion said: “Why, then, did you bring forward as an example the three emperors, among whom we can speak of a first, second, and third?”

Arnobius said: “To show you that human frailty possesses such grace in a kingdom that, although a first, second, and third are clearly taught, this order is excluded by the harmony of the empire and retains only number; it does not admit order at all. For all three possess one kingdom, one empire, and one summit of imperial dignity. The one who was not first is their second, just as they themselves are first.”

Serapion said: “Does it seem right to you that this temporal kingdom should be applied to the divine and heavenly majesty?”

Arnobius said: “If this temporal and mortal empire contains such harmony of peace that one who assumed the empire after many years and only today, though younger than the others by birth and later in beginning to rule, nevertheless cannot from the hour at which he became Augustus be inferior to one who began earlier by birth, how much more is there in the divine concord of the holy Trinity, in which no one ever began to hold the rule of the heavenly and eternal throne, such unity that, although the three are counted by number and possess one empire of one power, they are called one God and one Lord?”

> [Note: An old codex reads: “So that, together with the others, he should also be greater than you,” etc.]

“For the divine nature differs in nothing from itself. If the equality of power excludes the order that earlier age admits among human beings, how much more does divine omnipotence exclude it, since in the Trinity there is no one prior—”

> [Note: This is confirmed by the Athanasian Creed, which says: “In this Trinity there is nothing before or after, nothing greater or less,” etc. The letter of Martialis to the people of Bordeaux likewise teaches that the three divine persons are of one eternity, one will, and one essence, etc.]

“—and absolutely no one later? Its unity and undivided majesty are such that, while they truly retain the number three, there truly exists one God, the source of peace, rest, and tranquility.”

The appointed judges said: “Let Serapion, if he can, bring forward something against this; otherwise let Arnobius briefly summarize the substance of his argument.”

After Serapion had remained silent for a long time, Arnobius said: “Our God is one. For although he is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, no Christian dares either to say or believe that there are three gods, since, as I have said, the divine nature differs in nothing from itself. The first, second, or third order that a first, second, or third beginning produces among human beings through intervals of time is not admitted in God, whose beginning is equal and exists before time, to such an extent that what existed before time cannot even be called a beginning.

“Since no progression through steps can be made where subordination is impossible, the Trinity preserves number but assigns one order of equality. Therefore, as I said above—”

> [Note: He means that in divine matters “first” is not said in relation to a second or third, since there is no number there that belongs to the order of genus or quantity, but only a transcendent and infinite number that is not distinct from the three persons themselves. Boethius teaches this in these words (*On the Trinity and the Unity of God*): “God does not differ from God by any accidental or substantial differences posited in a subject. Where there is no difference, there is absolutely no plurality; therefore there is no number, but only unity.” For when “God” is repeated three times, when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named, three unities do not produce a plurality of number, etc. Thus, if God is predicated three times of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, triple counting does not for that reason create a number. Augustine likewise says (*Tractate 39 on John*): “There is something ineffable in the Trinity, so that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are both a number and not a number. If there are three, what are the three? Number fails. Thus God neither departs from number nor is grasped by number. What are these three—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Three gods? No. Three omnipotents? No. Three creators of the world? No. This is the only thing number indicates: what they are in relation to one another, not what they are in themselves.”]

“—because he who is first has no second, nor does he who is second have a third; he is not born from the first. Remove distinction, and you will find the first in what you believe concerning the Trinity, so that you may rejoice in possessing one God, with no second or third.”

## XI

**Serapion said:** I confess that I have received a reasonable answer to everything I raised. But many chapters of questions still remain for me, especially concerning the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation. [Note: I would gladly add “if this is not burdensome or unwelcome,” and so forth, so that the speech might be complete.] If you do not have these matters at hand as well, command me to ask them. For just as I acknowledge that I have been satisfied by Arnobius, so you know, chosen judges of the case, that I have done nothing with legal authority. I see that throughout both the Old and the New Testament this God the Father, who is unbegotten, is placed before the one who is begotten, so that the latter holds the second place after the Father.

**Arnobius said:** Bring forth, then, testimonies from the divine Law by which you may show that the Father is greater than the Son.

**Serapion said:** [Note: Here very many testimonies of Scripture are amassed, by which the ancient Samosatenians, Arians, Photinians, and other adversaries of Christ’s divinity endeavored to force him into the ranks of created beings, as can easily be detected from the writings of Athanasius, Hilary, Epiphanius, Augustine, Fulgentius, and Vigilius. We shall discuss the true meaning of those passages in their proper places; here we shall merely make a few observations about the differing readings of certain texts. First, concerning this passage from Proverbs, “The Lord created me,” and so forth, on which the Arians based the prow and stern of their position: Basil and Epiphanius rightly judged that, according to Aquila’s translation, ἔκτησέ με (*ektēsē me*), and according to the Hebrew words *ADONAI CANANI*, it should be read “The Lord possessed me,” or “he hatched me like a chick and possessed me,” as the whole Latin Church now reads it—not ἔκτισέ με (*ektise me*), “he created me,” as the Arians argued. And indeed it was very easy for these corrupters of Scripture to transform the aorist ἔκτησε (*ektēse*), derived from the verb κτάω (*ktaō*), meaning “I possess,” into the aorist ἔκτισε (*ektise*), derived from κτίζω (*ktizō*), which means “to create, establish, and construct,” since the change from η to ι was not difficult. Eusebius of Caesarea also, who before the decree of the Council of Nicaea participated in the counsels of the Arian heresy, argues most vigorously in the third book addressed to Marcellus that the passage should not be read “He created me,” but “He appointed me” or “He ordained me,” as it is found in Socrates and Nicephorus.]

Consider the Son of God himself testifying through Solomon’s mouth: “The Lord created me at the beginning of his ways, for his works; before the ages he created me” (Prov. VIII, 12). But God the Father says of the Son through the prophet Isaiah: [Note: This passage is constructed by the Apostle in Romans IX, 23 from Isaiah VIII, 14 and XXVIII, 16, according to the Septuagint edition. I do not sufficiently see how it could serve the Arian position.] “Behold, I will place in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense; and everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isa. VIII, 14).

Thus David sings of him: “The stone which the builders rejected,” and so forth (Ps. CXVII, 22). Hence Isaiah also said: [Note: In the Septuagint one reads τῷ Χριστῷ μου Κύρῳ, “to my Christ, Cyrus.” Arnobius therefore read Κυρίῳ, “to the Lord,” instead of Κύρῳ, as did Eusebius in the sixth book, ninth chapter, of the *Preparation for the Gospel*; Tertullian in *Against the Jews*; Cyprian in *Against the Jews*, book I, chapter XXI; Lactantius in book IV, chapter XII; Augustine in the *Oration on the Five Heresies*; Cyril; and others.] “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, my Lord” (Isa. XLV, 1).

Therefore the Father himself commands the Son, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand,’” and so forth (Ps. CIX, 1). Hence Stephen also says of the Son: “I see Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts VII, 56)—namely, of God the Father, who, as the Apostle Paul testifies, “is the head of Christ; Christ is the head of the man, and the man is the head of the woman” (I Cor. XII, 3).

This is the Father who says to the Son: [Note: Athanasius, in his *Oration against the Arians*, and Fulgentius report that the Arians, interpreting this as referring to Christ’s bodily birth, brought it forward against the Catholics. They reply that it was spoken of his divine and eternal generation; and that by the name “womb,” through anthropopathic language, the fruitfulness of the divine nature is to be understood. The Synod of Seville later confirmed the same in its thirteenth act.] “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3).

Therefore it is said to Christ: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you” (Ps. XC, 1). The one who commands is consequently greater, and the one concerning whom the command is given is lesser.

Hence the Lord himself says to his apostles: “If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father; [Note: All writers testify that the Arians pressed this point most insistently against the Catholics. Alexander of Alexandria, in the letter preserved by Socrates, and other Greek writers refer it only to the fact that the Father alone is unbegotten and is the productive principle of the Son, whereas the Son is begotten and produced by the Father. Augustine, however, and all the Latins judge that it was said because he had assumed human flesh. “Insofar as he is God,” says Augustine (*Enchiridion*, chapter 35), “he and the Father are one; but insofar as he is man, the Father is greater than he.” As for the wording cited in the following verse, “greater than I,” from John, chapter X, verse 29, it is found thus neither among the Latins nor, as far as I remember, among the Greeks; rather, the text says only “greater than all,” or “greater than everything.” We shall discuss the other matters in their proper place.] for the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

And again: “The Father who gave me is greater than I” (John X, 10). The Son of God himself also says to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3).

The Son, therefore, is the second person after the Father, because he is the Son, without taking away from the Father that by which he is the one God. For if he had been unbegotten, then, when compared with the one who is unbegotten, equal parity between the two would make two unbegotten beings; and thus it would display two gods, if the Son could exist without origin as the Father does, and could be invisible and incomprehensible as the Father is.

But now whatever the Son is, he is not from himself, since he is not unbegotten; rather, he is from the Father and owes his origin to his Father, having arisen from him who has no origin. For there is one God of all without beginning, concerning whom the Son, who has a beginning, says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

To prove this he added: “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, 19). And he says again: “I have not come of myself, but he sent me” (John VII, 28). And again he says: “The works that I do testify about me, that the Father sent me” (John X, 2).

He also says: “Whoever speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but whoever seeks the glory of him who sent him is true” (John VII, 18). Hence he himself says: “Nothing of himself” (John VIII, 28), but in everything obeys the Father’s commands and instructions, so that, although his birth proves him to be the Son, his dutiful submission affirms that he is subject to the Father’s will.

Thus he says: [Col. 0258A] “I have not spoken from myself; but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment concerning what I should say and what I should speak” (John XII, 49).

Behold how he obeys the Father himself and shows that he is subordinate to him. By this it is shown that through his subjection he is a minister, while he is acknowledged as Lord of all other things; so that, rightly, God the Father is almighty God, whereas the Son is God of all the rest, having every creature subject to him, while he himself, together with every creature, is subject to the Father who subjected all things to him (I Cor. XV, 26).

For this reason he has been appointed God over all creatures, saying: “But I have been appointed king by him,” and so forth (Ps. II, 6).

## XII

**Arnobius said:** If your purpose truly tended either toward learning or teaching, you would not cut up all these testimonies from the divine books and, as though binding one bundle of your interpretation with the most twisted knots, throw it before the judges and assessors in this fashion. Therefore I address you, assessors and judges: please command that the order of the discussion already begun not be changed, and that the individual passages of Scripture—those I have mentioned and those I have not yet mentioned—be presented by Serapion in your presence one at a time. He should not be permitted to bring forward two or more at once unless the one he first presented has been explained.

**The Judges said:** What Arnobius rightly requests must be put into effect. Therefore Serapion should hasten to disentangle these testimonies, which he has presented as one mass bound together by his interpretation, so that Arnobius may answer each testimony separately.

**Serapion said:** The first objection from my testimony is one which you recognize as the voice of the Son of God from Solomon’s book: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22). From this it is shown that the Father who created is greater than the Son who was created by the Father.

**Arnobius said:** Do you therefore truly believe that the Son was begotten from the substance of the Father, and yet not so much begotten as created?

**Serapion said:** I do not deny that he is the Son of God.

**Arnobius said:** If you do not deny that he is the true Son of God, begotten from the substance of the Father, to what end did you bring forward this testimony?

**Serapion said:** [Note: From the writings of Athanasius (*On the Dispute*), Hilary (*On the Trinity*, book XII), Epiphanius (*Against Heresies*, 69), Ambrose (*On the Faith*), Augustine (*Against Maximinus* and *Against Felicianus*), and Fulgentius against the Arians, it is clear that they did violence to the unity of the most holy Trinity and detracted from the Son’s eternal divinity in more than one way. For they said that the Father alone was the invisible God, that he had no equal or coequal in the nature of divinity, that he had not always been Father, and that he alone should be worshiped and adored. Concerning the Son they said that he was not begotten from the substance of the Father but created from things that did not exist; that he was God’s Son not by nature but only by grace and adoption; that he had not always been with the Father or beside the Father; and that he was not coeternal or omnipotent, and so forth. A large part of these heresies depends upon Serapion’s assumptions: “The Son is a creature; the Son is lesser than the Father.”]

I brought it forward to show that the Son is lesser than the Father.

**Arnobius said:** You are not merely trying to show that the Son is lesser than the Father; you are attempting to demonstrate that the Son is a creature of God. [Note: I would gladly add, “only,” but also “and so forth.”]

**Serapion said:** Establish either that this testimony does not possess the full authority of divine power, or show why it was spoken. [Note: What if “praising and setting forth” were added: “I ask you,” and so forth.]

**Arnobius said:** You have now returned to the proper order, so that, God granting it, the explanation of each testimony may be granted to us.

**Serapion said:** Whose voice, then, do you wish to understand in the words, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways”?

**Arnobius said:** It is the voice of God’s Wisdom.

**Serapion said:** Who is his Wisdom, if not his Son?

**Arnobius said:** When the proper place arrives, it will be said how this Wisdom is his Son. For the moment, God’s Wisdom speaks through the wisest man, Solomon, saying: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.”

**Serapion said:** [Col. 0259B] What could be clearer than that he said, “He created me”?

**Arnobius said:** Show what you are trying to prove from the words he said, “He created me.”

**Serapion said:** As the Son, having received from the Father the beginning of creation, deserved thereby to possess primacy over the whole creation.

**Arnobius said:** [Note: He drives Serapion into this dilemma: either he must admit that the Father was for some time without wisdom, or he must acknowledge that the Son was not created—although he was arguing precisely the opposite.] Surely every creature, before it was created, did not exist?

**Serapion said:** Certainly it did not exist.

**Arnobius said:** Then wisdom began when it was created?

**Serapion replied:** It began when it was created?

**Arnobius said:** Then do you blaspheme the one who created it as foolish?

**Serapion said:** May God avert this blasphemy from me.

**Arnobius said:** Then you blaspheme ignorantly.

**Serapion said:** I do not blaspheme; rather, I praise the creator of wisdom. [Note: An old manuscript reads “the creature.”]

**Arnobius said:** You are compelled to establish one of two alternatives: either that the one who created this wisdom possessed wisdom, or that he did not possess it when he created it.

**Serapion said:** The Father was never without wisdom.

**Arnobius said:** Then he did not create wisdom.

**Serapion said:** “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI, 20).

**Arnobius said:** Who is high-minded: the one who blasphemes God, or the one who defends blasphemy?

**Serapion said:** Are you defending God?

**Arnobius said:** Whenever I hear blasphemy, I rebuke the mouth of the blasphemer, just as I rebuke your mouth and teach you that you are calling God the Father foolish. For when you said, “Before wisdom was created, it did not exist,” and affirm that this same wisdom, which was created, belongs to God, you show that the one who formed it did not possess wisdom and began to possess it only after he had created it.

**The Judges said:** This is a place of the most grievous blasphemy. Why do we delay? Our ears are being deafened, and your mouths are advancing further and further. Therefore it is fitting that Arnobius, who has exposed the blasphemy, should now explain the testimony already brought forward by Serapion.

## XIII

**Arnobius said:** Wisdom was always stored inwardly in the Father’s heart, just as rhetorical art is in the orator’s heart and grammatical art in the grammarian’s heart. An orator is said to have created a book of rhetorical art, and a grammarian to have composed a book of the arts—not because rhetoric and grammar began to exist when they were handed over to human beings for reading. For those who wrote them down, they were always in the heart from the time they learned them. But for us they were then created when our education took its beginning.

That is why I said a little earlier, appropriately, that the Son of God was Wisdom before he was made. Therefore God, who made heaven and earth and everything in them, created Wisdom in the way that, as I said, an orator creates a book of rhetorical art, bringing forth from his heart what he has possessed ever since he learned it.

He created it for us, so that what was in his heart might, through our hearing with our ears and seeing with our eyes, also take its beginning in our heart. Thus God, who learned from no one and possessed wisdom without beginning, when he wished to make heaven and earth and everything in them, first cast forth the power of his wisdom, so that it might be the very house that he wished to build.

The Father first made the air, before he strengthened the very solid ground; that is, he first made heaven, and only then solidified the earth with its mountains. But we shall speak about creatures at the proper time. Let us now speak about the Creator.

Thus Wisdom herself says: “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22). The architect, full of wisdom—or rather, Wisdom’s very fountain—brought Wisdom herself forth from himself.

But hear what Wisdom says: [Note: The Latin edition expresses this in the third person: “The Lord founded the earth by wisdom; he established the heavens by prudence.”] “I, Wisdom, founded the earth; I prepared the heavens by prudence” (Prov. III, 19).

Since times arise only from days, days from light, light only from heaven, and heaven did not arise except from wisdom, time did not exist at all before heaven except from wisdom; indeed, before heaven time did not exist at all. It is therefore established that wisdom always existed and was created in the same way that, as we said, a book is created by a supremely wise orator.

For example, Solomon composed the Book of Wisdom. Did wisdom not exist before he composed that book? You can certainly say, “Before that it did not exist”—but only in Solomon before he received it from God; afterward it always existed.

If, then, in a wretched human being by comparison with God, and one exceedingly small, wisdom, once placed inwardly in the heart, does not depart; and if whatever he believes usefully is proclaimed as wisdom—whether in writings, buildings constructed by art, or paintings, where it is itself perceived—and if it is praised in every art, how much more is this true in God, who is wholly wisdom and received it from no one?

This Wisdom, I say, which he always possessed, he then created when he undertook to bring it forth from his heart through the work of heaven and earth, so that heaven might be made together with everything that is in it. [Note: An old manuscript reads “he created.”] This did not mean that he himself began to be wise, since he had always existed as wise.

He created the earth and everything in it, which had not existed, not so that he himself might begin to have wisdom, which he had not possessed before.

But you, Serapion, who did not present the whole chapter of the passage, hear the entire passage, so that you may believe it agrees with my explanation:

“The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his work. Before the age he founded me, before he made the earth, before he established the abysses, before he brought forth the springs of waters, before he fixed the mountains: before the hills he begot me.”

Since God foresaw that the words “He created me” could lead to the danger of blasphemy, he added: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. VIII, 25). By the word “me,” Wisdom herself interpreted what she had said, “He created me.”

And it continues: “When he prepared heaven, I was with him; and [Note: In the commonly circulated Bibles we read τὸν ἑαυτοῦ θρόνον ἐπ’ ἀνέμων, ‘when he separated his throne above the winds,’ and ‘when he made the strong clouds above.’ But in Cyprian, as Arnobius has it here: ‘And when he separated his throne; when he made strong clouds above the winds.’ Hilary has it in the same way. Thus the word ‘strong’ should be referred to the clouds, not to the winds: in Greek, ἰσχυρὰ νέφη, ‘strong clouds.’ Tertullian has ‘strong clouds’; Pagninus, ‘when he made firm the heavens above.’] when he separated his throne, when he made strong clouds above the winds, and [Note: An old manuscript reads “when he made firm.” For the Greek is ἀσφαλῶς πηγάς, “firmly the springs.” Cyprian: “And when he placed the established springs beneath heaven.” Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*: “And when he placed the firm springs of that which is beneath heaven.” Here he translates the words of the Septuagint literally. The translator of Irenaeus, however, follows the words of Aquila and Theodotion, who rendered ἄβυσσον, “abyss,” in place of τὸ ὑπ’ οὐρανόν, “that which is beneath heaven.”] when he firmly placed the springs beneath heaven; and when he made strong the foundations of the earth, I was with him arranging all things, [Note: An old manuscript reads, “to whom he rejoiced in my presence.” [Col. 0262D] For the Septuagint has ἔγω ἤμην ᾗ προσέχαιρεν, “I was the one in whom he rejoiced.” Irenaeus: “I was the one in whom he rejoiced.” “And I rejoiced daily in his presence, at all times, when he rejoiced.” Tertullian, *Against Hermogenes*: “I was the one in whom he rejoiced; and daily I delighted in his presence, when he rejoiced after completing the universe.”] the one in whom he rejoiced in my presence, when he rejoiced over the completed world” (Prov. VIII, 27–36).

And he added: Let the judges now speak to the one who brought forward this testimony in order to teach that the Son of God is not a Son but his creature.
