Let him say whether, in the order I have followed, I have traversed the text of the complete statement, and whether Wisdom herself, after saying “The Lord created me,” [Note: Jerome, explaining the passage of Isaiah (chapter LIII), “Who will recount his generation?” says that this should be understood of the Son’s divinity, since it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of divine birth. Concerning this, he himself speaks in Proverbs: “Before all the hills he begot me.”] added, “He begot me”; [Note: We have corrected this to read “believe,” in place of “I shall believe,” which stood in the old manuscript.] and let him either believe that wisdom was always in the Father or demonstrate that God was without wisdom before he founded it.

**Serapion said:** I confess that I have followed Solomon’s text completely and exactly as it is written: “Before all the hills he begot me.” He therefore suitably added this, so that he might clearly show that what he had said—“He created me”—means “He begot me.”

**Arnobius said:** Surely you remember that in the earlier dispute you asked why I had brought forward incorporeal examples. Why, then, are you now content to have the beginning of God’s ways taught through mountains, hills, and visible constructions? It is because, seeing the mystical meaning of divine Scripture only as history, and investigating the beginning of the ways, you did not seek the ways themselves.

But let us teach that God is the Creator not only by the testimony of Scripture but also by the prompting of our own natural understanding. These, then, are the ways of the Lord:

The first is faith; the second, hope; the third, charity; the fourth, perseverance; the fifth, goodness; the sixth, fear of the Lord; the seventh, steadfastness; the eighth, patience; the ninth, gentleness; the tenth, rest; the eleventh, peace; the twelfth, obedience; the thirteenth, long-suffering; the fourteenth, holy solitude; the fifteenth, contempt for the belly; the sixteenth, devotion of mind; the seventeenth, chastity; the eighteenth, kindness; the nineteenth, mercy; the twentieth, justice; the twenty-first, generosity; the twenty-second, devotion to knowledge of God’s law; the twenty-third, love of the best things; the twenty-fourth, contempt for temporal glory; and the twenty-fifth, longing for eternal glory.

These are all God’s ways, in which the Father himself walked daily, as he says through the prophet: “I live, says the Lord, because I will walk among them, and I will be their Father, and they will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty” (Lev. XXVI, 22; II Cor. VI).

In all these ways of the Lord, Wisdom was created first, so that whoever began first to possess God’s wisdom would be unable to walk in any one of these ways. [Note: I confess that this allegory is exceedingly obscure to me, and I think that there are several corruptions which cannot be corrected without the aid of a better manuscript.]

There are therefore these twenty-four ways, corresponding to the number of the twenty-four elders (Rev. IV, 4), who assign the individual pounds (*libras*), and the whole of the New and Old Testament, to one pound of the twelve apostles, so that these three pounds may be offered through three classes of people to the author of the Trinity: virginity, widowhood, and marriage.

All these three pounds, walking wholly through their ways, subsist consecrated by one faith, one hope, one charity, and one baptism. Yet they cannot walk through their ways at all unless, at the beginning of the ways, the Lord has created wisdom in their minds.

Therefore, when the Psalmist said, “Make your ways known to me, O Lord” (Ps. XXIV, 4), because he knew that it was impossible to walk in these ways unless the Lord had created wisdom for him in his heart, he prayed to God, saying: “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Ps. L, 12). For wisdom does not enter a filthy [Vulgate: “malicious”] soul, nor can it dwell in a body subjected to sins.

**The Judges said:** Arnobius has more than completely answered concerning the testimony about Wisdom: both that Wisdom was always in God and that it is created in the minds of those by whom God’s ways are desired. If Serapion has anything to ask, let us hear it.

## XIV

**Serapion said:** If God first cleanses the heart and does not create wisdom, they are not at fault if they have not walked in God’s ways.

**Arnobius said:** Let the order of our discussion remain secure. We began to speak about God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and this testimony was brought forward for the purpose of showing that the Son of God is a creature. We have shown thus far that wisdom was always in God, and it is right that our discussion should proceed to the divinity and Trinity. Nevertheless, we shall also give a brief answer here.

Just as God is in no way a respecter of persons (Rom. II, 11; Acts X, 34), so he considers the minds, endeavors, and thoughts of the sons of Adam, and knows perfectly what he ought to bring forth from his treasury; [Note: An old manuscript reads, “and so his justice requires.”] and just as his justice requires, so he gives.

Therefore, as the Apostle says, “There is no respect of persons with God” (Eph. VI, 9; Col. III, 25), so he himself says: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets?” (I Cor. XII, 29; Eph. IV, 11).

Just as you are certain, then, that he is not a respecter of persons, so be certain that he is not an unjust distributor. Whatever he does concerning the human race cannot possibly be found blameworthy in any respect. [Note: An old manuscript reads “criticism.”]

Certainly David asked with tears and groans that a clean heart be created in him (Ps. L, 12). Imitate David in repentance, and by receiving a share in a clean heart you will rejoice in God, the creator of wisdom, within you. [Note: An old manuscript reads “you will give thanks.”]

But now let us return to the testimonies you presented.

**Serapion said:** I mentioned the stone which the builders rejected, because it was made the cornerstone (Ps. CXVII, 22; Matt. XXI, 42). [Note: From this passage it is evident how accurately Tertullian wrote that heretics are hunters of words. For all the Arians hunted down, collected, and pressed most insistently every passage of both the Old and New Testaments in which Christ is said, either literally or allegorically, to have been made, so that from these they might conclude, against the Catholic faith, that he was created and was not consubstantial with the eternal Father.

Such passages include: “He was made the cornerstone”; “Made from the seed of David according to the flesh”; “The one who comes after me was made before me”; “Having been made superior to the angels”; “He is faithful to the one who made him”; “Having been made a high priest forever,” and so forth.

The great Athanasius replies that these statements must be referred to the assumption of human flesh, through which he was truly created and made man, brother, minister, and our high priest—not to his divinity, through which he is truly the creator of all things, since all things were made through him.

He also says again: John, theologizing about the Son and recognizing the distinctions among the expressions, did not say, “In the beginning he was made,” or “He was created,” but, “In the beginning was the Word.” Thus, from the nature of the Begotten, the word “was” is to be understood, and he guarded against anyone imagining that an interval of time had intervened; rather, he taught that the Son always and eternally exists. Hence both the Nicene Creed and the creed of Athanasius require us to profess that the Son was begotten but not made, and so forth.

Regarding “He was made before me,” Ambrose and Chrysostom reply that this means exactly “He was placed over me and set before me,” because, as the same writer says, he was before me insofar as he is God.

As for “Having been made so much better than the angels,” Chrysostom and Theophylact understand it to mean the same as “declared” or “made manifest.”]

“This was done by the Lord; it is marvelous in our eyes.”

**Arnobius said:** Three things must be sought in this passage: who the builders are, what they were building, and who those were who rejected the stone.

The builders were the Jews, building upon the foundation of the prophets. They not only rejected our Lord Jesus Christ from the number of those included in this building, but also crucified him.

He was rejected by unbelievers (Acts IV, 11), but was made by God the cornerstone, so that he might establish the two in himself (Eph. II, 15). Thus the finished structure begun from the Law and the prophets in Moses was brought to perfection in Christ. The writings of the New Testament, having their own wall in him, were to dedicate one Church from both sides through this cornerstone—the one who said to Peter: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18).

**Serapion said:** Tell us what the gates of hell are.

**Arnobius said:** An explanation concerning the rock must still be given. When that has been completed, we shall answer concerning the gates of hell.

**Serapion said:** The completeness of the statement already made requires that you speak briefly about the gates of hell.

**Arnobius said:** [Col. 0264A] We call the gates of hell those which the rulers of this world have placed at the entrance to everlasting death through riches and passions, impieties and crimes. Through these gates idolaters enter the temples of demons, fearing not the true God but fearing the most worthless images.

They have other gates through which those who enter the council of the synagogue deny Christ the Lord as God.

They have still other gates through which people enter the sects of heretical and schismatic teaching.

And they have other gates through which sexual offenders, adulterers, fornicators, kidnappers, thieves, blasphemers, and those guilty of every kind of crime enter.

To these rulers, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit cried: “Lift up the gates,” and so forth (Ps. XXIII, 7, 9).

For those gates are truly not temporal, in which immortality reigns in such a way that the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. Through these gates the King of glory entered with all his people.

If you ask who this King of glory is, you will hear the Holy Spirit himself saying: “The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle.”

There are also gates of righteousness placed in the ears of human beings. To these the word of the Catholic faith cries out, saying: “Open to me the gates of righteousness, and entering through them I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 19).

After the word has entered through the ears into the city of the soul, it shows it the gate of eternal life and says: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous will enter through it.”

Our Lord Jesus Christ is shown to have given a narrow entrance in this world, but whoever walks along his very narrow and constricted way is affirmed to reach the broadest entrance to eternal life. For the Lord himself confirms this with his own mouth, exhorting and saying: “Enter through the narrow gate. For narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who enter through it. For broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter through it” (Matt. VII, 13).

**The Judges said:** Asked about the gates of hell, Arnobius has opened before us both the gates of hell and those of heaven. If Serapion has anything else prepared, let it be brought forward.

### XV

**Serapion said:** I will draw you back to the promised exposition; let us return to the place from which we strayed.

**Arnobius said:** The figures of the Lord’s incarnation are disclosed when he is a stone, when a mountain, when a staff, when an angel, when a man, when a priest, [Col. 0265A] and even when a testimony; there are also many other representations, which the catholic understanding, walking along clear paths and radiant with the splendor of the Holy Spirit, may discover by prayer rather than by disputation.

For the rock through which the people of God, placed in danger of thirst, were delivered in the desert, the blessed apostle Paul asserted to be Christ, saying: “Our fathers all drank the same spiritual drink; they were drinking from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 4). And in the Song of Moses it is said: “Honey flowed for them from the rock, and oil from the solid rock” (Deut. XXXII, 13). And in the eightieth psalm: “He satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX, 17). Likewise in the seventy-seventh psalm: “He brought water from the rock and led waters forth like rivers” (Ps. LXXVII, 16).

Likewise, in the twenty-sixth psalm, the Church says concerning Christ: “You exalted me upon a rock” (Ps. XXVI, 5); and in the thirty-ninth he himself says: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX, 3); and in the sixtieth psalm: “You exalted me upon a rock” (Ps. LX, 3); and in the hundred and thirteenth psalm: “He turned the solid rock into pools of water, and the cliff into springs of water” (Ps. CXIII, 8); and in the hundred and fourth psalm: “He struck the rock, and waters flowed” (Ps. CIV, 41).

And in the Song of Solomon the Holy Spirit, inviting the Church to himself, says: “Come to me, my companion, my bride, my beautiful one, and in the covering of the rock, a continuous wall [reading uncertain]” (Cant. II, 14).

[Note: We have corrected this at the suggestion of the very learned theologian and friend Fronto Ducaeus of the Society of Jesus, in place of what the old codex read: *continui te muto*.]

And in Isaiah the voice of the Son of God says: “I have set my face,” he says, “like the firmest rock” (Isa. L, 7). Likewise, in the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says: “I have made your face firm against adamant and rock” (Ezek. III, 9). And in the Gospel the Lord speaks of the wise man building his house upon a rock (Matt. VII, 24).

But what rock can this be except the one of which the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III, 11)?

There are also many other passages whose enumeration would be lengthy, and which teach that the rock signifies the unchangeableness and most steadfast will of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he exercised in his flesh: tempted by the devil, handed over by a disciple, fastened to the gallows, fed with gall, given vinegar to drink, pierced with a spear, humbled unto death—“and death on a cross” (Phil. II, 8).

And although this perfect man endured all these things, yet, imitating nothing of human impatience, he showed that God, through man, granted victory to human beings, as the Apostle asserts in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Cor. XV, 57).

**Serapion said:** [Note: The old codex reads, “will render.”] Your explanation troubles me, because in interpreting the incarnation of our Lord you strive to speak in such a way that you seem to mention a man and not God. Since, then, there are eight representations pertaining to the Lord’s *tropology*, and you have explained one of them—this one concerning the rock—by clear testimonies from the divine books, after you complete the remaining seven examples, only one explanation of the Lord’s incarnation will remain for me.

We think that he entered into this conflict for this one reason alone. For this reason I do not think you remember that at the beginning I said that I ought to deal with you as though I were one of the Arians, Eunomians, Sabellians, or Macedonians, and, while preserving my faith, support their assertions. As I said, I entered into conflict with you so that, if I found you falling into some error, I would not deal with you according to that definition on which you and I disagree.

Nothing remains for me now except that you explain these eight likenesses that you have mentioned in Christ so elegantly [Col. 0266B] and irreproachably that you also explain Christ’s complete divinity, making clear that you do not likewise present to me only part of what was divine rather than everything that existed.

Show me, then, why you mentioned only eight, when there are many other representations in Christ that could have been named, as you yourself said.

[Note: Epiphanius (*Against Heresies* 69) gathers in a few words these many names of Christ: Christ was called the door, the entrance, the way, the pillar, the cloud, the rock, the lamb, the manna, the goat, the calf, the lion, the fountain, Wisdom, the Word, the Son, the Angel, Christ, Savior, Lord, man, Son of Man, the cornerstone, the sun, prophet, bread, king, builder, farmer, shepherd, vine, and whatever other such names there are. He argues that these belong to him by *tropology*, as does the expression “creature,” which the Arians pressed with excessive obstinacy from Proverbs and Sirach.]

**Arnobius said:** I considered that many kinds of mysteries are contained in this number. First, in the Old Testament, although it is the first day on which he said, “Let there be light” (Gen. I, 3), this same day deserved in the New Testament, through Christ’s resurrection, to become both the first and the eighth.

For just as on that day the heavens were opened so that manna might be poured out (Exod. XVI, 14 and 16), so David is the eighth son, who, by defending the sheep, became the slayer of wild beasts (I Reg. XVI, 11), and, by defending the people, the slayer of the giant (I Reg. XVII, 49–50).

At first, while he was still a little child, Christ was brought forth by God Almighty. Moreover, in the Gospel, eight beatitudes are recalled from the mouth of our Lord Jesus Christ (Matt. V), although there were certainly many other virtues that could have possessed the merit of blessedness.

This example therefore seemed suitable to me: while preserving the multitude of likenesses, I would bring forward only these eight *tropologies*, confident that from those which have been set forth, the others that have not been set forth can be sought out, recognized when found, and usefully explained by reasoning.

### XVI

**Serapion said:** First, on the occasion of my objections, you explained the stone. When I then followed with the Gospel passages in which the Lord says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28), you brought forward other material. Therefore, lest you seem to have introduced these examples in order to evade those testimonies, after explaining what you have brought forward, you will give me an answer concerning those passages; only then shall we approach our particular conflict.

**Arnobius said:** We ought to discuss only this one point on which you truly disagree: namely, that you do not wish to believe, in accordance with the usefulness of the catholic faith, that in Christ our God there are two true and perfect substances, and to confess that, just as he is the true Son of God, so he is the true human Son of Man.

But how do you foresee that you will reasonably be overcome by right and by law, so that you will not grieve at being defeated alone, when you have assumed in yourself the roles of many heretics? Thus, when your fellow citizens reproach you for having been defeated, you may say that you were overcome by our victory—or rather, not ours but Christ’s—by one who was able first to open, through the wondrous and most powerful gate of the catholic faith, the sharp arguments of many heretics in you.

[Note: It is clear that this sentence is mutilated and must be restored from a better manuscript.]

**Serapion said:** A wise man then conquers unbelief when he drives it from his own entrails; and whoever conquers is twice victorious, because he receives a crown of faith for the defense of his position and wins the palm of gain from human beings.

[Col. 0267B]

**Arnobius said:** This whole matter must be attributed to the mercy of God. We can do nothing by our own efforts; rather, everything we seek we find through God’s grace and mercy.

I shall now approach the remaining seven forms of likenesses that I proposed; thereafter, with the Lord granting it, I shall explain the two questions that you brought forward from the Gospels. But you, recalling those same figures with your keen memory, begin to bring them forward one by one, so that I may show from the sacred books that I brought forth these examples.

**Serapion said:** It is sufficiently established that you explained the rock first. Second, show from the Scriptures, as you promised, that the mountain mentioned is the Lord.

**Arnobius said:** In Exodus we read: “The Lord said to Moses: Let this be a sign to you, that I am sending you to bring my people out of Egypt, and you shall serve me on this mountain” (Exod. III, 11).

**Serapion said:** This was said about Mount Sinai.

**Arnobius said:** If you seek history alone, enter the synagogue. We, however, receive the historical account so that we may explain spiritually the things contained within the history, following the apostle Paul, the teacher of the gentiles appointed by the Lord. He—as I said—so challenged our understanding and hearts that he clearly asserted that the rock which is certainly a rock, from which water was brought forth, was Christ, saying: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 5).

[Note: The old codex reads, “to assert.”]

In the same way, the mountain on which the glory of God appeared; on which there was fire that illuminated without consuming; on which God spoke face to face with man (Exod. XXXIII, 11); on which Majesty itself wrote the divine will with its finger on two stone tablets in ten commandments; on which the book of Deuteronomy—that is, of the second or repeated law—was written; the mountain where God made known to man that in the beginning God had made heaven and earth (Gen. I, 1), and all that is in them; and many other signs of holiness, whose enumeration would be lengthy—concerning this mountain the Psalmist says: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain, a mountain in which it has pleased God to dwell. For the Lord will dwell there forever” (Ps. LXVII, 16–17).

To show which mountain he meant in the fourteenth psalm, he says: “Who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” And he adds: “He who walks without blemish,” and so forth (Ps. XIV, 1–2). And who else is without blemish except the Lord Jesus Christ alone, who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (I Pet. II, 22)?

For in the twenty-third psalm he says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord?” And he answers: “The innocent in hands,” and so forth (Ps. XXIII, 3–4). Again David sings: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise,” and he adds: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north,” and so forth (Ps. XLVII, 3).

Therefore Isaiah also says: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be revealed, and all the nations will come to it” (Isa. II, 2). And in another place David says: “He who trusts in the Lord is like Mount Zion,” and so forth (Ps. CXXIV, 1). Hence also in another psalm: “Mount Zion, in which you dwell” (Ps. LXVII, 17).

And concerning this same mountain he says: “This is the one his right hand acquired” (Ps. LXXVII, 54). His right hand acquired the perfect man, the right hand of the Lord who performed the mighty deed (Ps. CXVII, 16); for “the right hand of the Father” is spoken of and demonstrated in terms of operation.

For the invisible Son himself performed this mighty work through his omnipotence, so that, by assuming manhood, he became visible in such a way that he could say: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 9–10).

**Serapion said:** Then the Jews who saw him saw the Father also.

**Arnobius replied:** The Jews saw him in such a way that the Holy Spirit says to Isaiah concerning them: “Go, say to this people: Seeing you shall see and not perceive, and hearing you shall hear and not understand” (Isa. V, 9; Acts XXVIII, 16). Therefore the Lord himself says to them: “You know neither me nor my Father” (John VIII, 19).

But to his own disciples he says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear” (Matt. XIII, 16).

Therefore, if an answer concerning the mountain seems to have been given, recall the third example that I mentioned.

### XVII

**Serapion said:** First you mentioned the stone, second the mountain, and third the tower, as a likeness.

**Arnobius said:** You remember well, if you also receive the truth well. For this is the one of whom it is sung in the sixtieth psalm that he is “a tower of strength in the face of the enemy” (Ps. LX, 4).

This is the tower of which the Holy Spirit says through Isaiah: “I built a tower in the midst of the vineyard that I planted” (Isa. V, 2). The Holy Spirit himself interprets this vineyard, saying: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Ps. LXXIV, 16).

The tower that he says he built in the midst, as Holy Scripture declares, is the Son of Man whom he established for himself. Concerning him Solomon says: “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1). For he who is the Wisdom of the Father built for himself in the Virgin’s womb the perfect man Jesus, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification (Rom. I, 4), not according to a marriage of pollution.

**Serapion said:** Do not speak of the pollution of marriage, for marriage has no pollution; fornication, rather, must be called pollution.

**Arnobius said:** Marriage has pollution, but not guilt; fornication, however, is shown to have both pollution and guilt.

[Col. 0269A]

But allow me to establish the indication of the tower. The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “A householder planted a vineyard, fenced it around, built a tower in it, and leased it to cultivators” (Matt. XXI, 33). These men did not fear to abuse with blows the servants sent to them by the householder; finally, they killed the son sent by the householder himself.

After saying this, the Lord asks them: “When the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” The Jews answered: “He will destroy those wicked men wickedly, and lease his vineyard to other cultivators.” And the Lord said to them: “Amen I say to you: The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

### XVIII

**Serapion said:** We must now seek, as the fourth point, the discourse showing the Lord prefigured by the staff, so that your promise may be explained in its proper order.

**Arnobius said:** In Exodus the Lord speaks to Moses: “I will stand at the summit of the hill, and with this staff that is in your hand I will perform all the signs of power” (Exod. IV, 17). David also says in the Spirit: “The staff of righteousness is the staff of your kingdom. Your staff and your rod,” and so forth.

And David addresses the Lord, saying: “Remember your congregation,” and so forth; “you redeemed the staff of your inheritance” (Ps. XLIV, 7). Likewise he says: “The staff of your strength,” and so forth (Ps. LXXIII, 2).

More explicitly, however, it is said concerning the Lord: “A staff will rise from the root of Jesse,” and so forth (Isa. XI, 1). All these things were fulfilled in him who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. I, 3).

**Serapion said:** Reserve the discussion of the flesh, about which we shall have a true and open conflict. For now, explain the examples you have proposed. You have already said why you placed the staff fourth; now explain, as the fifth point, in what sense you have spoken of an angel.

**Arnobius said:** Hear the Lord speaking to Moses: “Behold, I am sending my angel before you, to guard you on all your ways. Observe him and obey him, for my name is in him” (Exod. XXIII, 20).

Malachi, moreover, says: “The priest’s lips will preserve knowledge, because he is the angel of the Lord” (Mal. II, 7).

Hence also, concerning the whole people of the saints, who in this world are afflicted and are said to suffer for the sake of the holy name, it is said: “This poor man cried out, and the Lord heard him”—that is, the holy people—“and he will deliver him from all his tribulations” (Ps. XXXIII, 7, 6).

“The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him”—that is, those who fear the Lord—“and he will deliver them,” that same people of the righteous.

Likewise, Daniel recalls that an angel descended from heaven into the midst of the flames to rescue the three youths from the fire, when Nebuchadnezzar had said of him: “The fourth, whom I see, is like the Son of God” (Dan. III, 49). His testimony is not false.

David also says in his own psalm concerning God: “He himself sent his angel, and took me from my father’s sheep, and anointed me with the anointing of his mercy” (Ps. LXXVII, 70).

**Serapion said:** Hasten to the sixth, in which you have previously shown the Son of God in the likeness of a man; what has been said about the fifth is sufficient.

**Arnobius said:** [Note: Many centuries before Arnobius, Justin Martyr argued from this passage that the Son of God, who was one day to assume flesh, presented and appeared himself to Joshua; especially since Joshua worshipped him, while he said that he was the commander of the Lord’s army. Clement, Tertullian, Eusebius, and Nicephorus likewise held the same view.]

We read in the Book of Joshua that, at the time when he was continually fighting against Jericho, he saw a man standing opposite him, with a sword in his hand. When he approached him, he said: “Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?” He answered: “I am the commander of the army of God” (Josh. V, 13–14).

Likewise the prophet Isaiah says: “The people will cry out to their God in their distress, and the Lord will send them a man who will save them” (Isa. XIX, 20).

Likewise Daniel says: “I saw in the clouds of heaven one coming like a Son of Man to the Ancient of Days, and authority over the kingdom was given to him” (Dan. VII, 13).

[Note: Relying also on this testimony, Justin Martyr proves that the Son of God would become man: when Daniel speaks of one “like a Son of Man” receiving an eternal kingdom, does he not indicate this very thing? For when he says “like a Son of Man,” he recounts that a man was born and seen, but not from human seed, and so forth.]

Daniel himself also says: “There stood before me something like the appearance of a man, and he called Gabriel the archangel and told him to explain the vision that I was seeing” (Dan. VIII, 16).

Again Daniel says: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with gold” (Dan. X, 5).

Likewise Ezekiel says: “I saw above the throne something resembling the figure of a man” (Ezek. I, 26). Again he says: “I saw one ascending from above the cherubim, calling to himself a man who was clothed in a long robe and girded about his loins with a golden belt” (Ezek. X, 2).

**Serapion said:** Since abundant testimonies must be offered concerning him, because he has been called into question, proceed now, in your concern for brevity, to the seventh likeness that you mentioned, namely the priesthood.

**Arnobius said:** In the First Book of Kings, God speaks to Samuel, saying: “I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything according to my heart” (I Reg. I, 35). And David says: “The Lord swore to David, and he will not repent,” and so forth (Ps. CIX, 4).

**Serapion said:** These two testimonies that you have brought forward concerning the seventh likeness are clear. Now explain the eighth: how the covenant of God can be understood as the Son of God.

**Arnobius said:** The Book of Genesis says that the Lord spoke to Noah and his sons: “Behold, I establish my covenant with you, with your descendants after you, and with every living soul that is with you” (Gen. IX, 10).

Again, after other words, God says to Noah and his sons: “I will remember my covenant that is between me and you, and every living soul” (Gen. IX, 15).

Again, the voice of God says to Noah and his sons: “I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant that is between me and you” (ibid.).

[Note: The following testimonies from Isaiah are cited according to the Septuagint edition; consequently, in the Vulgate Latin edition they are found with the same meaning but not the same wording.]

Likewise, through Isaiah the Lord says: “My covenant shall be with life and peace; law and truth shall be in his mouth, and iniquity shall not be found upon his lips. Walking in peace, he shall dwell with you, and he shall turn many away from their iniquity” (Mal. II, 5).

Likewise, through Isaiah the Lord says: “I, the Lord, have called you and given you as a covenant to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind” (Isa. XLII, 7).

Likewise, through Isaiah the Lord says: “Hear me, and you shall eat good things; walk in his ways, and your soul shall be saved, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant” (Isa. LV, 3).

Likewise, through Isaiah the Lord says: “I will make a covenant with you in peace and faith, and I will establish for you an everlasting covenant.” All these things prefigure the one Son of God.

There are also many other kinds of figures, which, if reason requires that they be brought forward, I shall assign on the authority of the Holy Scriptures.

[Note: The old codex reads, “I shall establish.”]

[Note: This passage indicates by its obscurity that something is missing.]

**The Judges said:** What Arnobius has defended has been confirmed both by such a reasonable exposition and by the authority of law, so that Serapion, who holds the opposite position, has himself testified, while we remained silent, that everything is as he defended it.

And just as the evening hour found the dispute begun at daybreak, so, after the silence of the night’s rest has passed and the day has been mercifully restored to us by God, the confession of both parties will arise for us.

**Serapion said:** I ask that our discussion come to an end today at this point, so that Arnobius may make me understand for what reason he wished to bring forward these prefigurations of our Lord.

**Arnobius said:** How is it that some things among these prefigurations also count the very one for whom they were figured—the Son of God—while in all those things there is an image of the truth, and in this man whom the Virgin bore there is the truth itself?

Just as he is truly God, the Son of God, so he is truly man, the son of man—not mixed in such a way that an exchange between the two realities has occurred, but remaining in the truth of divinity and in his own omnipotence, the invisible Son of God having fellowship with man, and being believed to have presented to our liberation the true God, the Son of God.

For otherwise God could not have been seen by bodily eyes.

Therefore, whoever denies that God is in Christ—that is, in man—is the Antichrist (I John II, 22 and 43).

But whoever denies something concerning these likenesses may be found either blameworthy or perhaps not blameworthy. He denies the rock, denies the staff, denies the mountain, and whatever else may be said to be applicable to Christ.

But whoever denies the perfect man and the perfect God cannot be freed from eternal condemnation.

[Note: This was the heresy of Nestorius, who, as reported by Socrates, Evagrius, and Liberatus, said that there were two Christs, one God and the other man; he judged that there were two natures and likewise two persons. Eusebius of Dorylaeum, John of Antioch, Cyril of Alexandria, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius, the Roman pontiffs, together with the Fathers of the councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon, steadfastly opposed him, as will be discussed more fully later.]

Similarly, whoever dares to think or believe that there are two Sons of God—one begotten before the ages from the Father without a mother, and another born from the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary—will be struck by an eternal anathema.

[Note: We added the two preceding words; otherwise no sense appeared.]

This is the confession of our faith—that is, of the apostolic see of blessed Peter, which began with the Apostle himself: Believing in one Son of God from two perfect and wholly complete substances, from the visible and the invisible, from the corporeal and the incorporeal, from the comprehensible and the incomprehensible, from the passible and the impassible, from the mortal and the immortal, let us confess the true God and the true man, saying and believing that God in Christ, and Christ Jesus in the glory of the Father, possesses one divinity just as there is one sight in two eyes, one hearing in two ears, and one sense of smell in two nostrils. So also in these two substances, of God and man, there is one Son of God.

Certainly, so that I may recall to a new and attentive listener how I spoke of one substance of the Father and the Son, one sight in two eyes, one hearing in two ears, and one sense of smell in two nostrils: now it should not seem incongruous to you that you must believe not one substance, but one person existing in two substances.

[Note: We judged that *esse* should be restored here in place of *est*.]

For I have endeavored to show this: just as we believe that there is one substance in three persons, so we should believe that there is one person of the Son of God in the two substances of God and man.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0271D]

### I

On the following day, at the beginning of the day, when their gathering had been reconstituted and Constantius and Ammonius were seated—

**Arnobius said:** If anything remains for Serapion from yesterday’s conflict, let him bring it forward, if he wishes.

**Serapion said:** One evangelical question is known to remain, namely the one that Arius seems to regard as a decisive proof, when he says: “Why do they blame me when I say, ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John XIV, 28), since the Son himself testifies concerning himself, saying: “The Father who sent me is greater than I”?

[Note: Athanasius and Epiphanius cite several letters of Arius and a book that he called the *Thalia*, but the words that follow are not found there. Nevertheless, it is certain that he pressed this passage especially against the consubstantial equality of the Son, since the Fathers responded to him with great zeal. Referring to this, Athanasius wrote in his Creed: “Equal to the Father according to divinity, lesser than the Father according to humanity” (chap. 4). And the presbyter Faustinus, in his book *On the Faith against the Arians*, addressed to the empress Flacilla, or Placilla, says: “This was spoken by the Son concerning the duty of one who ministers, not concerning his divinity.” And again: “What he said, ‘The Father is greater than I,’ does not attack the majesty of equality, but signifies the mystery of the humility he assumed.” Augustine likewise writes in the *Enchiridion* (chap. 35): “Insofar as the Son is God, he and the Father are one; but insofar as he is man, the Father is greater than he.”]

**Arnobius said:** In the form in which the Son of the Father exists without a mother, he and the Father are one; but in the form in which the Son of the mother exists without a father, he is less than the Father.

For he assumed the nature of a servant, in which he would be less not only than God the Father but also than his mother, by as much as the age of the Virgin his mother had advanced.

**Serapion said:** Today you have given me a new answer, in which you seem to make the mother of the Lord, as the gentiles deliriously do, Mary his mother without his Father. Tell me: whose Father existed as God the begetter without a mother?

**Arnobius said:** Then yesterday, throughout the whole exchange of our words and arguments, was it not thoroughly debated that I was teaching that the Father, as begetter of his Son, is not greater than the Son?

**Serapion said:** You taught it by human reasoning, but it cannot stand by evangelical authority.

**Arnobius said:** Nevertheless, human reason has established that nothing greater exists in the Father, nothing lesser in the Son, and nothing unequal in the Holy Spirit.

**Serapion said:** If I deny this, both the judges and all those standing here will be able to prove it.

### II

**Arnobius said:** What, then, remains?

**Serapion said:** This: the most sacred assertion of Christ opposes your rational exposition when it says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

**Arnobius said:** [Note: By this testimony both Greek and Latin Fathers, with great unanimity and constancy, affirm that the Son is wholly equal and consubstantial with the Father. I append only the words of Athanasius to Arius: “Why do you reject the radiant utterance of the apostle Paul, saying of the Son, ‘While he was in the form of God, he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God’?” and so forth.]

Whatever the apostle Paul says about Christ—do you think he speaks the truth, or is he deceiving us?

**Serapion said:** If Paul deceives us, who speaks the truth?

**Arnobius said:** Do you remember that he said concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. II, 6)?

Did Paul say this, or not?

**Serapion replied:** He did say it, but you have not given the complete sentence.

**Arnobius said:** Then you know that the Apostle’s discourse was written in an epistle.

**Serapion said:** I know.

**Arnobius said:** Tell me the comma of the complete sentence that I quoted.

**Serapion said:** You said: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.”

**Arnobius said:** And of whom did he say this?

**Serapion said:** Of the Son.

**Arnobius said:** And of whom does he say that he is equal?

**Serapion replied:** Of the Father.

**Arnobius said:** Define the form of God, if you can.

**Serapion replied:** The form of God is that he is immeasurable, fills heaven and earth, and his measure extends beyond the heavens above, and below the earth, the seas, and the abysses (Isa. XL, 12).

Thus, indeed, it is read in the prophets: his palm is the measure of the whole heaven; he holds all the earth in his fist; and all the waters are the measure of his hands.

**Arnobius said:** I embrace and proclaim the true testimony of your own mouth concerning God, and I confess that it is so.

Therefore, if it is so—or rather, because it is so—you have explained in your speech that the form of God is that he is immeasurable, incomprehensible, inestimable, and invisible. Is this so, or not?

**Serapion replied:** It is so.

**Arnobius said:** Now I shall present the Apostle’s complete sentence concerning the Son of God: “Although he was in the form of God” (Phil. II, 6)—that is, invisible, incomprehensible, inestimable—and although he was equal, not lesser, in that form and in that equality in which the Father exists, he emptied himself.

**Serapion said:** How did he empty himself? Did he perhaps cease to be God?

[Note: I could not pass over at this point the explanation of Gregory of Nyssa, which Cyril also praises in his *Apology*: “He who was King of kings and Lord of lords put on the form of a servant and became subject to those who exercise authority. The Lord of creation withdrew into a cave. He who encloses the universe in his palm found no place in the inn, but was laid in a manger. The pure and undefiled one took upon himself the filth of human nature, and, having undergone all our poverty, reached even the end of death,” and so forth.]

**Arnobius said:** So that this crime of blasphemy might not creep into our judgment, he himself interpreted this statement, saying that he emptied himself in this way: although he was Lord, he took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of human beings, and was found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, and so forth.

Therefore, he who is the Son of the Father, born without beginning from that Father whose paternity has no beginning, says: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

But he who was born from a mother without a carnal father says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

**Serapion said:** Then there are two Sons of God: one from the Father without a mother, and another [Col. 0274C] from the mother without a father?

**Arnobius said:** I think you have not forgotten that I showed there are two eyes but one sight, two ears but one hearing, and two nostrils but one sense of smell.

**Serapion said:** How do you wish these two things to be one? Is it that, just as the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one substance, so the substance of God and the Son of Man is one substance?

**Arnobius said:** It is not so. Man was made God through God, who assumed him; God was not made man through the man whom he assumed.

[Note: This passage must be understood as follows: God, by the assumption, did not become a human *suppositum*, or human person, just as the assumed man became part of a divine *suppositum* or person. For in Christ the status of *suppositum* or person belongs only to God, not to man.]

### III

**Serapion said:** “By this reasoning there are two Sons of God, since you say, ‘God is God, and man is man’; the true God and the true man are two.”

**Arnobius said:** “There are two substances in the one Son of God. For this one Son of the Father, who made the first man from the virgin soil of the earth—”

> **[Note: [Col. 0274D]]** This is explained as follows in Tertullian: “The earth was still virgin, not yet compressed by labor, not yet subjected to seed; from it, we have received, man was made by God into a living soul. Therefore, if the first Adam is handed down in this way, deservedly the succeeding, or last, Adam was brought forth by God from the earth—that is, from flesh not yet surrendered to generation—into a life-giving spirit” (*On the Flesh of Christ*).

**Arnobius continued:** “With fear of God, you ought both to question me and to listen.”

**Serapion said:** “Why do you say this?”

**Arnobius said:** “Because you think you have made a plausible case when you say that there are two Sons of God: one from the Father without a mother, and another from a mother without a father. But I have told you that God, by his omnipotence, assumed the form of a servant in the Virgin’s womb, and with it assumed a temporal origin. He who has no temporal origin at all does not have this Son of God.”

**Serapion said:** “You have asserted another son of the Virgin besides Christ.”

**Arnobius said:** “I did not assert another son of the Virgin besides Christ. Rather, I said: ‘He who made the first man from the virgin soil of the earth himself fashioned, by his incomprehensible omnipotence, a man in the womb of the holy Virgin, in whom he himself would dwell,’ according to what we read: ‘Wisdom built herself a house’ (Wisdom 9:1).”

**Serapion said:** “Who is it who fashioned a man for himself in the Virgin’s womb?”

**Arnobius said:** “The invisible Son of God the Father fashioned a man for himself, in whom, dwelling as though in an incomparable house, he himself would become visible to the saints.”

**Serapion said:** “Then he became visible?”

**Arnobius said:** “I did not say merely, ‘He became visible’—”

> **[Note: [Col. 0275D]] The old codex has *tacui* (“I was silent”) instead of *tantum* (“merely”); therefore *tantum* should be written, or *et tacui* (“and I was silent”) should be added.

**Arnobius continued:** “Rather, I said, ‘Having become visible to the saints,’ that is, to believers, so that he might be seen through faith, not through sight (2 Corinthians 5:7), according to what we read: ‘We saw him, and he had no appearance’ (Isaiah 53:2). For the sight of the flesh was so open to unbelievers that, after his garments had been stripped away, he was seen whole, limb by limb, by those who stripped him, mocked him, scourged him, and placed him on the cross (Matthew 27; John 19). But because they did not have the eyes of faith, they were able to see only a mere man, not the one who was in that man.”

### IV

**Serapion said:** “Like a slippery serpent: the more tightly you are bound, the more you escape from the fists that bind you. Do you hold the Son of God to be man, or God?”

**Arnobius said:** “True God and true man.”

**Serapion said:** “Then, as I said, there are two Sons of God: one carnal and the other spiritual.”

**Arnobius said:** “Speak with fear of God; for it is blasphemous to say that there are two Sons of God.”

**Serapion said:** “Then you blaspheme, since you say that there are two Sons of God.”

**Arnobius said:** “You too blaspheme, and you cast upon me the charge of blasphemy. For I say that there is one Son of God, like fire in a mass of glowing gold.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0275D]]** John of Damascus, in *On the Two Wills and Operations in Christ* and in *On the Orthodox Faith*, uses a similar comparison to argue that in Christ there are truly two substances but one hypostasis.

**Arnobius continued:** “You see nothing in it except fire when it has been ignited, and at the same time you judge it to be pure gold; yet the hand itself catches fire when it touches it. So too, when you thrust the hand of your unbelief into this man, judging him to be merely a man, you will be consumed by eternal fire. Likewise, if you deny the gold, and deny the fire that came into it in order to become visible, although it is invisible, I ask you now: answer me. Why do you not put your hand to the glowing mass of gold?”

**Serapion said:** “Because the hand that touches it is burned.”

### V

**Arnobius said:** “Is this visible fire or invisible?”

**Serapion said:** “Visible.”

**Arnobius said:** “How do you prove that the fire is visible? Through itself, or through another material?”

**Serapion answered:** “Through another.”

**Arnobius said:** “Then the fire itself is not visible.”

**Serapion answered:** “How is the fire not visible, when it is seen and touched?”

**Arnobius said:** “By its own substance it is neither seen nor touched, neither gives warmth nor burns, unless it has been mixed with something else.”

**Serapion said:** “Then fire in itself is nothing.”

**Arnobius said:** “I do not merely say that it is nothing; rather, I say that it is a great force and an exceedingly powerful substance. Yet unless it is mixed with another substance, it remains invisible and incorporeal.”

**Serapion said:** “Then fire is God.”

**Arnobius said:** “I have told you this because you are mistaken. Is everything that is invisible and incorporeal to us likewise invisible and incorporeal to God?”

**Serapion said:** “Then fire is visible and corporeal to God.”

**Arnobius said:** “Everything whatsoever that is invisible and incorporeal is visible and corporeal to God alone, insofar as it has been created by him.”

**Serapion said:** “Then souls, spirits, and angels are corporeal.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0275D]]** It is an ancient controversy whether angels are truly corporeal, or whether they are substances so spiritual that they are wholly free from matter. Plato and all the Platonists, both pagan and Christian, embraced the affirmative position, as is evident from Apuleius, Iamblichus, Porphyry, and others, and likewise from Origen, Augustine, and others, although Augustine in these and other passages seems to hesitate (*City of God* VIII.14–16; *Peri hermeneias* II; *Enchiridion* 59; *City of God* XXI.10). I add John of Thessalonica, who likewise affirmed this in the fifth session of the Seventh Ecumenical Council, the Second Council of Nicaea. Tertullian also wrote (*On the Flesh of Christ*) that angels possess some sort of body, and John Cassian (*Conferences* 7) that they have a body by which they subsist.

Nor should Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, and Irenaeus be omitted; among the Latins, Tertullian, Lactantius, and also Augustine have at times thought, on the basis of Genesis 6—where it is written that the sons of God took the daughters of men as wives and fathered giants by them—that angels, as corporeal beings, had done this. Athanasius, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, Chrysostom, and others, however, judged that the passage should much better be interpreted of the sons of Seth.

For it is clear that the Apostle, speaking of wicked angels, denies that they are composed of flesh and blood; and throughout Scripture they are called spirits, which do not have flesh and bones (Ephesians 6; Luke 24; Matthew 8). Therefore, when Arnobius here, or the Fathers elsewhere, calls them corporeal, this is not defined properly and absolutely, but only by comparison with the divine purity and simplicity, as is made clear in this passage, where he says that God alone is incorporeal.

**Arnobius said:** “I do not want you, through your winding arguments, to remove me from God and drag me to angels, souls, and spirits. Nevertheless, so that you do not think I am evading your question, listen. Whatever has a measure is a body, though it is open not to human eyes but to divine eyes; God alone is immeasurable and incorporeal (John 4). For all angels were made by God and have a beginning; and whatever has a beginning also has an end—not visible to our eyes, as the sun, moon, and stars are, but open to the eyes of God alone.”

**Serapion said:** “Then the human soul too is corporeal.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0277D]]** The scholastics resolve this difficulty briefly and acutely by saying that the soul is corporeal by assumption and formation, but not by nature or in its proper essence. It is also observed that the souls of certain persons—Moses, Elijah, Onias, and Jeremiah—have at times appeared in various bodies. But Arnobius here asserts without hesitation that the soul is corporeal. Moreover, Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, is wholly occupied with proving that it consists of body. Certainly all who thought that the soul was produced by transmission from the parents—and these were numerous and highly respected—thereby also openly professed that it was composed of matter and bodily substance.

Yet since in sacred writings it is often called spirit, and spirit is likewise set in opposition to body, while spirit does not have flesh and bones (Ecclesiastes 7; Luke 23; Matthew 8; Luke 24); and since, moreover, the holiest Fathers—Ambrose in *Noah and the Ark* 25, Jerome in his letter to Augustine, Augustine in Letters 28 and 157, and finally Gregory the Great in *Morals* XXI.2—consistently believed and taught that it is incorporeal; and since the definitions of the Church likewise establish it as spiritual and incorporeal (Sixth Synod, sessions 11 and 13; Lateran Council, canon *Firmiter*), I consider it wicked to believe or teach otherwise.

Therefore, when Arnobius or others call it corporeal, this must not be understood simply and properly, but equivocally and by comparison with the ineffable and incomparable simplicity of our God.

**Arnobius said:** “There is no doubt that whatever touches and is touched, and is contained in some place, is a body. Since the soul is taught both to enter the body, dwell in the body, and depart from the body, how can it not be recognized as corporeal? But for the present, if you wish a longer discussion of this matter, you may propose it to me at another time. Now, however, since I say to you that fire is incorporeal, just as the soul and spirit are, I say that fire is incorporeal for us. If you have any argument by which you are stronger, oppose me.”

**Serapion said:** “I hear something new. Every day I see that we hold fire in our hands, yet by a new trick of words he wants to prove fire invisible to me.”

> **[Col. 0277B] The judges said:** “We have heard Arnobius say that fire is invisible, not in such a way as to seem to deny that it is visible through another form whenever it has been mixed with something—whether wood, iron, bronze, silver, or gold. But inquire why he says this.”

### VI

**Arnobius said:** “I give thanks to the most prudent judges—”

> **[Note: [Col. 0278D]] The old codex reads somewhat differently, namely, that they ‘showing the order of my meaning as it was spoken by me, shone forth like light in darkness.’

**Arnobius continued:** “—who, by setting out the meaning of my words in the order in which I spoke them, have shone forth like light in darkness. Say therefore, Serapion, what is true: can you see or touch this substance of fire without wood or some metal?”

**Serapion said:** “When we are speaking about the Son of God, you drag me to images and metals.”

**Arnobius said:** “Have you not heard the Apostle saying of God that ‘his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made—his eternal power and divinity as well’ (Romans 1:20)? Therefore, whether you investigate—or, as you said of me, whether you try to escape me like a crooked serpent while I hold you fast—you cannot escape the most just judges. Tell me, then: when you see fire in wood or in some metal, do you perceive one substance in it or two?”

**Serapion said:** “One.”

**Arnobius said:** “Then there is neither wood nor iron nor any kind of material there through which its power and invisibility are recognized.”

**Serapion said:** “There certainly is something through which its power and invisibility are recognized; nevertheless, fire alone is evidently the substance.”

**Arnobius said:** “This one substance of fire is recognized in air within the color of the baths—”

> **[Note: [Col. 0278D]] The old codex reads: ‘but in wood.’

**Arnobius continued:** “—but unless, when mixed with wood in the furnace, it raises flames, it gives neither warmth to the baths nor heat.”

**Serapion said:** “You are doing well to teach people what no one is ignorant of.”

**Arnobius said:** “If I were able to speak with you in the Hebrew language, would someone not call me superfluous or judicious?”

**Serapion said:** “Yes.”

**Arnobius said:** “Then if I speak with you about what everyone is ignorant of, and do not speak with you about what no one is ignorant of, by what method could I defeat you? Tell me, then: do you see two substances in fire, or one?”

**Serapion said:** “I see one, namely fire.”

**Arnobius said:** “I beg you, judges, now give judgment, and let each of us show which of us is deceiving.”

**The judges said:** “He has rejected your question without cause, and we do not understand why Serapion is afraid to say that there are two substances in fire while it is seen. Therefore, since he has evaded the question, and since you are confident that you have us not only as judges but also as witnesses, proceed in the direction toward which your speech tends.”

### VII

**Arnobius said:** “This invisible fire, entering another material, becomes visible through it. It has within itself one thing that burns and another that gives light. So too the Son, proceeding from the bosom of the Father, was received by the Virgin’s integrity in such a way as a mass of gold can receive fire; and from that very mass he brought forth a perfect man from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:2). In this entire substance, as though in golden metal, the incomprehensible fire became comprehensible, the impassible became passible, and the intangible became tangible, as I said earlier: one aspect burns unbelievers, while the other illumines all believers.

“Thus, through these two substances—the gold, which is a body, and the fire, which is not a body—there subsists one person, whose appearance we see as that of iron, bronze, silver, or gold, possessing two substances: true gold and true fire.”

**The judges said:** “We do not know why Serapion avoids giving an answer to your most evident argument. Therefore, as we said, proceed in the direction toward which your speech tends.”

### VIII

**Arnobius said:** “While trying to confirm the accusation he had brought against me, the wise man did something prudent: he remained silent, lest by refuting himself with his own mouth he convict himself. For he said that I asserted, by believing in a visible and invisible substance, that God has two sons, whereas I believe that there is one Son of God in two substances, just as I can reasonably assert that there is one mass of gold in two substances when it has been ignited.

“For the invisible Son of God, mixed with the visible son of man, made one Son of God, so that he might be visible in him. Thus fire, which was invisible, became visible in a mass of gold or some other metal without ceasing to be fire; whereas fire alone, without the material of another thing that makes it visible and perceptible, can neither be seen by the eyes nor perceived at all by bodies.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0279C]] By the word “mixture” he introduces no confusion of substances, which is the invention of Eutyches; rather, he understands only the perfect union of the man with the Word and the communication of properties proceeding from it. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine, and Vigilius did not hesitate to explain this union by that term, as we have shown in book III, chapter 21 of Irenaeus.

**Serapion said:** “I understand you to be reaching the point of saying that the Son of God abandoned the son of man and was not crucified together with him on the wood.”

**Arnobius said:** “I have never conceived this in my heart or uttered it with my mouth. Rather, together with the prophet I say that he not only did not abandon him when he was placed on the cross, but also did not abandon him when he went down to the underworld, and did not allow his holy one to see corruption (Psalm 15:10).”

**Serapion said:** “From what moment did the Godhead come into the man whom he assumed?”

**Arnobius said:** “From the moment when the angel Gabriel uttered the word and she, by believing, conceived it.”

**Serapion said:** “Then he was conceived at the same time.”

**Arnobius said:** “While the man whom the Word had fashioned—and was still fashioning so that he might remain in him—was being conceived in the womb, the one who had never had a beginning was present in him who was assuming the beginning of his own existence in the Virgin’s womb.”

**Serapion said:** “Then God has both a father and a mother.”

**Arnobius said:** “The Son of God has as father the one who begot him before the ages without a mother; and he has as mother the Virgin, who conceived and bore him without a human father.”

**Serapion said:** “Then she is the mother of God.”

**Arnobius said:** “The mother of Christ and of God.”

**Serapion said:** “What does ‘of Christ and of God’ mean?”

**Arnobius said:** “Of God, who, although he had no beginning, assumed a beginning by being born together with Christ. For Christ without God is like the other christs who existed before him.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0279D]] He means the Hebrew prophets, priests, and kings, who are frequently called christs in the sacred writings, both because they were anointed for undertaking public office and because they foreshadowed that great future Christ of ours, who surpassed them especially in this respect: that he is almighty God.

**Arnobius continued:** “But Christ our God has absolutely no natural equal. For besides him there is no one who is both Christ and God.”

**Serapion said:** “What, then, do you believe was born in Mary’s childbirth?”

**Arnobius said:** “A man who had never existed, together with God who had always existed.”

**Serapion answered:** “Then Mary is the mother of a man, and not of God.”

**Arnobius said:** “Through the man conceived and born of the Holy Spirit, she also deserved to become the mother of him who always existed in such a way that there was never a time when he did not exist.”

**Serapion said:** “Then you follow the sect of Nestorius.”

**Arnobius said:** “Nestorius denied that Mary was *Theotokos* [Θεοτόκος, ‘God-bearer’]; I believe her to be both *Theotokos* and *Christotokos* [Χριστοτόκος, ‘Christ-bearer’].”

> **[Note: [Col. 0279D]]** Socrates (*Ecclesiastical History* VII.32, 34) and Evagrius (I.2) testify that a certain Anastasius, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople under Bishop Nestorius, first disseminated this heresy: “Let no one call Mary *Deipara* [Mother of God]. For Mary was a human being; but it is impossible for God to be born from a human being.”

When Leo the Great, pope of the Roman Church, refuted this opinion as impious and blasphemous (*Letter to Pulcheria*), Nestorius raised it still more crudely against him and enlarged and propagated it with even more blasphemous additions. At the Council of Ephesus he blasphemously declared: “I will by no means name or worship God made two or three months old”—for so he called Christ the Lord.

For this reason the heresy prevailed more under the name of Nestorius than under that of Anastasius. By denying Mary to be *Theotokos*, that is, the bearer and mother of God, Nestorius completely overthrew the venerable and great mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, as Cyril calls it in his *Apology*, separating the Godhead of the Word from the substance of the assumed man and inventing two Christs: one God and the other man.

While admitting her to be *Christotokos*, that is, mother of Christ, he understood by the name “Christ” only the mere man who had been born from her and who afterward, by the gift of adoption and grace, had been called God and had been led about by the Son of God to display his divinity, so that he was found to be united to him only in appearance and not by a true personal union.

The orthodox, however, like Arnobius here, confessed her to be both *Theotokos* and *Christotokos*—that is, the true mother both of God and of Christ, who is simultaneously God and man (Cyril, *Interpretation of the Creed* and *Apology*; Euthymius, *Panoplia*).

**Serapion said:** “If he created from her what previously did not exist, then without doubt he did not create him who always existed.”

**Arnobius said:** “If you go to human reasoning and do not take faith with you, you go empty and return empty, and you will always remain empty.”

**Serapion said:** “If you know that I too cannot speak abusively with you, speak abusively.”

**Arnobius said:** “It would be abuse if the case did not, as you see, require me to say this to you.”

**Serapion said:** “Let us learn what case requires this.”

**Arnobius said:** “The entire event concerning Mary has this as its first principle: that you believe. If you possess reason but not faith, your reason will be empty.”

**Serapion said:** “Either reason will be reason, or faith will be faith.”

**Arnobius said:** “In this matter faith cannot exist without reason, nor reason without faith.”

**Serapion said:** “And what reason could teach me that the Virgin conceived, that the Virgin gave birth, and that the Virgin remained a virgin after childbirth?”

**Arnobius said:** “This is the reason: almighty God.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0280D]]** Augustine wrote this just as learnedly and elegantly: “If you demand a reason, it will not be marvelous; if you seek an example, it will not be unique. The whole reason for the deed, therefore, is the power of the one who performs it” (*Letter* III).

**Serapion said:** “I am speaking with you about a girl.”

**Arnobius said:** “I am speaking with you about the Almighty. Tell me: is the one who made heaven and earth and everything in them himself almighty, or is he not almighty?”

**Serapion said:** “You always propose one thing so that you may deal with another, and you do not answer the questions put to you.”

**Arnobius said:** “Eager to answer your question, I ask you a question. Tell me: is God almighty or not?”

**Serapion said:** “There is nothing more foolish than one who denies this. It is written: ‘The fool has said in his heart, “There is no God”’ (Psalm 13:1).”

**Arnobius said:** “Then the Son of God, by his omnipotence, wished to accomplish this: that he should become the son of man.”

**Serapion said:** “Whose son of man?”

**Arnobius said:** “Mary’s.”

**Serapion said:** “Then he wished this only apparently, and not truly.”

**Arnobius said:** “In God there is nothing apparent, nothing imaginary, and nothing false.”

**Serapion said:** “One of these two cannot stand: Mary will either be *Theotokos*, the same mother and bearer of God, or *Christotokos*, the same mother of Christ.”

**Arnobius said:** “She is both *Theotokos* and *Christotokos*.”

**Serapion said:** “Then she is the mother of two sons.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0281C]]** That this was also the position of Nestorius is clear from Vincent of Lérins’s response to him: “The Catholic Church confesses one Christ Jesus, not two, and the same one both God and man; one person in him, but two substances, because the Word of God is not changeable, so that it could itself be changed into flesh; one person, lest by professing two sons it appear to worship a quaternity rather than a Trinity” (*Against the Profane Novelty*).

“Blessed Leo likewise says: ‘The authority of the Gospel so proclaims the Word made flesh that it makes known to us not two christs or two sons, but in the one Lord Jesus Christ the truth both of God and of man; and that the properties of both substances—the saving and the saved—can neither be confused nor the persons doubled’ (*Letter to the Bishops of Gaul*).”

**Arnobius said:** “She is the mother of one son.”

**Serapion said:** “By what reasoning can you teach this, since the Son of God is the Son of God, begotten as God from God the Father before the ages, while this one has now been begotten in time as the son of man?”

**Arnobius said:** “The almighty Son of God of the almighty Father, by his omnipotence, willed this: that this son of man should become one Son of God with him.”

**Serapion said:** “Then divinity and humanity have been mixed.”

**Arnobius said:** “What is this that you wish to say: ‘They have been mixed’?”

**Serapion said:** “What mixture of flesh and Word made God and man one body?”

**Arnobius said:** “It is blasphemous to believe in this way, as though, by a process of fusion, we believed two natures had been reduced to one substance. For the corruption of both sides is evident. He who is capable is not capable of being contained; he who penetrates is not penetrable; he who fills is not able to be filled. He who is diffused everywhere and wholly present everywhere infused himself, by his omnipotence, into human nature in such a way that the flesh was perfected in the Word, not the Word in the flesh.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0281D]]** The old codex reads: “so that the flesh might perfect itself in the Word, not the Word perfect itself in the flesh.” I think the meaning is that the flesh received from the Word and in the Word the full status of hypostasis and person, but not that the Word was perfected in the flesh or from the flesh that it assumed. For what he was, he remained; what he was not, he assumed.

**Arnobius continued:** “For the evangelist does not say, ‘The Word was born with flesh,’ but ‘the Word became flesh’ (John 1:14), and he did not judge it unworthy to be born as man.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0281D]]** I cannot omit the truly golden words of the blessed martyr and apostolic man Ignatius on this passage of Saint John: “Truly,” he says, “Mary bore a body, with God dwelling in it; and truly God the Word was born from the Virgin, a body like ours, passible and without sin, which he put on. Truly he was conceived in the womb and was made in the womb, forming and making for himself a body from the Virgin without the seed of a man; and he was carried in the womb, just as we too were carried in time,” and so forth (*Letter to the Trallians*).

**Serapion said:** “If the Word became flesh, the Word ceased to be.”

**Arnobius said:** “Was not a perfect man conceived and born in the virginal womb?”

**Serapion said:** “Then a man was born together with God.”

**Arnobius said:** “If you said this piously, the dispute would be finished. But the impiety of what you say is exposed by the following. You say, ‘A man was born together with God,’ so that the very divinity of the Son of God now appears to have received a beginning.

“I too say: ‘A man was born together with God’ in such a way that God, who always exists and is without beginning, by his will—which can accomplish everything he wishes in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abyss—was pleased, while preserving his divinity whole and inviolate, to become the son of man.

“Tell me, Serapion: could he do this and did not wish to, or did he wish to and could not? Could the invisible one become one with this man whom he assumed, while preserving his own divine substance and preserving the man’s human substance? If he wished to and could not, let him cease to be almighty, since he could not fulfill his own will.”

**Serapion said:** “We ought to give God this reverence: to assign separately what belongs to God to God alone, and separately what belongs to man to man alone.”

**Arnobius said:** “That belief is impious, since it admits a fourth person into the divine Trinity. For if there are two Christs, there will be two sons; or else there will be one Christ, but he will not be the Son of God.

“And where is what we confess that we believe in the Creed of the universal Church: Christ Jesus, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary? Just as we confess that he was born from the Father before the ages, so we always confess that he was born for us from the Virgin Mary, receiving in full everything that belongs to God as man, and assuming in full, as God, everything that belongs to man. He could not be anything other than God.

“For one part, full of omnipotence, received into itself the part that did not possess omnipotence, and infused itself into it with such gentleness that, while the substance of both parts remained intact, one Son of God was born for us from the Virgin.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0282C]]** This was the impiety of Eutyches and his followers. In order to establish more contentiously one person in Christ against Nestorius, they imprudently and shamelessly confused the substances in him so completely that they asserted that the human substance had been absorbed by the divine—or rather, had been changed and poured into it so that it ceased entirely to exist.

Dioscorus of Alexandria, an especially vehement champion of this impiety, said: “I accept Christ from two natures; I will not accept two natures.” Those condemned by the Council of Chalcedon were subsequently taken under the protection of the Acephali, the Gnapheans, the Philoponians, the Monophysites, and the Monothelites. They gained such strength that they infected nearly the whole of the East and a considerable part of Africa, as may readily be gathered from Paul the Deacon, Nicephorus, Euthymius, and Nicetas.

Against these heresies Blessed Pope Gelasius writes: “We do not understand two persons in Christ by saying that there are two natures, as though we intended to divide the union and produce—God forbid—a quaternity rather than a Trinity, as the insane Nestorius thinks. Nor do we confuse these same united natures when we confess one person, as the impious Eutyches believes.” And in the Athanasian Creed it is said that Christ is one, “not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person” (*Against Nestorius and Eutyches*).

**Serapion said:** “Then there has been a migration of the human substance into God.”

**Arnobius said:** “Do you mean to say ‘corruption of the human substance’? For if I grant you this migration of substance, you will prove corruption; and God will appear, through his infusion, to have driven the substance from its state as though something enclosed had been expelled.”

**Serapion said:** “Did he not expel what had been enclosed from its state through his most humble substance, so that man might return into God, and not God be changed into man?”

**Arnobius said:** “The human substance was not expelled from its state; rather, it was strengthened in its state. For just as Mary’s virginal state, after conceiving and giving birth to a man, was not cast down from its integrity but became even more intact, so the state of the human substance, through the divine infusion, became stronger—so much so, I say, that whatever weakness it had incurred through Adam’s transgression, it no longer possessed through God’s assumption, and it held the integrity of its substance more firmly than Adam himself possessed it before his transgression.”

### IX

**Serapion said:** “Every substance, when it subsists, is either great and not small; royal and not private; immortal and not mortal; rich and not poor; divine and not human. But you, confusing everything and denying that one and two can stand together, are unable to teach us either a true God or a true man.”

**Arnobius said:** “Listen to what you have said: ‘Every substance is either great and not small.’ I shall explain it to you point by point, if you do not know. In the one Son of God I profess and establish that there are two substances.

“He has, through his humanity, that by which he is truly less than the Father (John 14:28). He has that by which he truly received a beginning in time. He has that by which he is truly impassible, and he has that by which he became passible. He has that by which he is truly immortal; he has that by which he truly died and was buried. He has that by which he never ceased to live and to distribute life to all who live according to his own will.

“He also had that by which he permitted the soul of his dead body to go among the souls of the dead into the underworld and to return (Psalm 15).”

> **[Note: [Col. 0283D]]** Gregory, Supreme Pontiff, writes almost exactly the same things in *Morals* XVIII.27 against the same Nestorius, although without mentioning his name.

**Arnobius continued:** “He had that by which he held the power of death subject to him; he had that by which he was subject to the power of death (Hebrews 2:14). He had that by which he wept for the dead man, and in him was that by which he commanded the very man for whom he wept to be raised from the dead (John 11:35, 44).

“And this is the reason for his divinity: that, although he possesses these two completely intact substances, you should believe that in these two there is only one Son of God.”

**Serapion said:** “Then he possessed some alteration in himself, by which he began to be what he had not been.”

**Arnobius said:** “It is not so. Rather, without ever departing from the Father, he, the Word of the Father, deigned to become man through his own secret mystery, known only to himself. Since he wholly received what belongs to man, he is man; and since he wholly received what belongs to God, he cannot be anything other than God.”

**Serapion said:** “And if he was incarnate, as you assert, without mixture, how was there no diminution of the divine substance?”

**Arnobius said:** “Is there anything that God either cannot do or does not know?”

**Serapion said:** “There is nothing God cannot do; there is nothing he does not know.”

**Arnobius said:** “Then if he knows and can be mixed without corruption of himself, just as he was able to assume man without receiving any increase from the assumption, he knew and was able to pour himself wholly into it without suffering any diminution.”
