> **[Note: [Col. 0283D]]** We have already observed that the ancients did not shrink from the words “to mix,” “to intermingle,” and “to combine” when they wished to explain the intimate union of the Word with flesh and the consequent communication of properties.

## X

Serapion said: What reason compels you, whenever you speak of the Son of God, who is God born from Mary, not merely to say that Mary is **Θεοτόκος**—“God-bearer”—but always to name him as the Son of Man, so that Mary is **Χριστοτόκος**—“Christ-bearer”?

**[Note: [Col. 0284D]** The old codex is also very mutilated here; for it has: “Who was born from Mary, so that Mary might be Θεοτόκος, but always naming this: that he is the Son of Man,” etc. We have supplied the rest.]

Arnobius said: Just as I never say **Χριστοτόκος** without **Θεοτόκος**, so by confessing this you confirm your faith, and the end of our dispute is reached.

Serapion said: From where has this authority for your definition come to you?

Arnobius said: Do you refuse to accept what the Apostle Paul testified: “The first man became a living soul, the last man a life-giving spirit” (1 Cor. 15:45)?

Serapion said: Tell me in what order you understand this meaning.

Arnobius said: The Apostle himself explained what I have said in his own words, saying: “Since through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead. And just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

**[Note: [Col. 0284D]** The common Latin edition reads *vivificabuntur*, “shall be made alive.” But Rufinus, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, and Tertullian, Book IV *Against Marcion*, agree with Arnobius.]

Serapion said: I see what you are contriving to establish: since in this passage the Apostle names man alone, and not God as well, he appears to have taught that the glory of our resurrection is to be celebrated through man.

Arnobius said: When you hear “Christ,” and do not hear “the Son of the holy Virgin Mary,” know that you are hearing one of the things belonging to the Jews. And for that reason we rightly affirm that this man alone is meant. But with catholic fidelity we confess the Son of the Virgin to be God and Christ in this order: that the glory which the human race had lost through the first man might be recovered a hundredfold better through this Son of the Virgin, who is God and man. For the region of paradise is read to have been taken away through the first man, but through the second man the kingdom of paradise is restored, and indulgence is granted to all.

**[Note: [Col. 0284D]** Perhaps *omnis* or *omnibus*, “all” or “to all,” should be read.]

Serapion said: Then was it man who bestowed such great benefits upon us, and not the Son of God, who is God?

Arnobius said: You wish an accusation to arise from her from whom was born the one who would free us from every evil and from every sin; and you wish to hold me bound by the very means through which we are released from bonds; and you wish to take freedom away from me by the very means through which freedom and natural liberty are generated for the enslaved and captive world.

Serapion said: From where do such good and excellent things arise?

Arnobius said: From this confession: that the Son of God came in the flesh. The Apostle says: “Whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, this one is the Antichrist” (1 John 2:22). He is therefore flesh—that is, he is perfect man—and the one who came in the flesh is the invisible Son of God; he is perfect God, the Son of God, the creator of man, with whom he deigned to become the Son of Man.

Serapion replied: Then God is his own creator.

Arnobius said: Where there has been no union with a man, who has proved to be the Creator of the one born?

## XI

Serapion said: You make me very suspicious when you repeatedly mention creature, flesh, man, and son, yet do not acknowledge that the Son of God was the Son of Mary.

Arnobius said: If the Son of God had not become the Son of Man, Mary could not be the Mother of God. Through her own Son, therefore, she became the Mother of the Son of God; through the form of a servant which the Lord assumed, she became the Mother of the Lord. Nor could she be **Θεοτόκος**, unless she had been worthy to become **Χριστοτόκος**. Listen to what she had to conceive in the womb, or what she had to give birth to, or what she had to wrap in swaddling clothes and place in a manger (Luke 2), or what she had to nurse, or what she had to take up and flee with into Egypt (Matt. 2:13), or what had to grow in age and wisdom, or what had to be circumcised on the eighth day, or what had to be baptized by John (Luke 3), unless he were perfect man, in whom there was perfect God, who fashioned him as a man in the womb.

Serapion said: This is the teaching of Nestorius.

Arnobius said:

**[Note: [Col. 0285D]** That Nestorius was certainly a prolific writer is evident not only from the passages cited by Arnobius, but also from Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 36; Socrates, Book VII, chapter 32; and the Acts of the great Council of Ephesus, where his writings are mentioned. Through the praiseworthy diligence of the ancients and divine providence, these writings, like the records of the other heresiarchs, have perished.]

I have before me what Nestorius asserts. If the judges order it, I shall read it.

The judges said: Let what Arnobius offers be read, so that Serapion’s objection may be shown, if it is true.

When the homily had been received, it was read at the relevant point as follows:

“Most holy Mary did not give birth to Deity, for what is born from flesh is flesh” (John 3:6). “A creature did not give birth to the Creator; rather, she gave birth to a minister of Deity.”

**[Note: [Col. 0285D]** The old codex reads *ministerium*, “ministry” or “service.” In the same place, instead of *non condificavit*, we read *non aedificavit*, “did not build.”]

“The Holy Spirit did not build God the Word; for, it says, ‘what was born from her is of the Holy Spirit’ (Matt. 1:20). Therefore, he built a temple for God the Word from the Virgin.”

And shortly afterward:

**[Note: [Col. 0285D]** The Acts of the Council of Ephesus read: “What was formed in the womb is not God in itself and according to itself. What was brought about through the work of the Holy Spirit is not God in itself and according to itself. What was placed in the tomb is not God in itself and according to itself,” etc. (Vol. II, chapter 7, new edition). From this it is not difficult to correct the corrupt passage in our old codex, so that it should evidently read: “He who was born in the womb was not God in himself,” etc.]

“He who was born in the womb was God in himself.”

And shortly afterward:

“Let us honor the form of the **Θεοτόκος** in God.”

Likewise, in another sermon beginning: “Often turning over with myself the fruit of life, and considering the manifold changeability of earthly things and the snares scattered throughout life, I cried out in perplexity: Who can be delivered?” A little later he says:

“The divine nature separates the Spirit, which created his humanity. Whatever was born from Mary is of the Holy Spirit, who also, according to righteousness, filled what had been created. ‘What was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit’ (1 Tim. 3:16).”

He also says:

“He who made him fearful to demons—of whom the Lord himself says, ‘I cast out demons by the Spirit of God’ (Luke 11:20)—made his flesh a temple. Hence the Baptist says: ‘I saw the Holy Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him’ (Matt. 3:16).”

Likewise, a little later:

“He who gave him his ascent into heaven,” he says, “gave commandments to the apostles whom he chose through the Holy Spirit, and afterward he was taken up into heaven” (Acts 1:2). “Thus those who think that he who granted Christ such a great economy was born fleshly separate him from the divine nature.”

Likewise, in another sermon beginning, “There is no illness worse for human minds than ignorance,” a little later:

**[Note: [Col. 0286D]** Perhaps this should be read more appropriately as *isti*, “these men.” For he attacks the orthodox Fathers and attributes many things to them, as is clear from the Acts of the same Council of Ephesus. Likewise, a little later it might more suitably be read: “when they assign a temporal mother to the Creator of times and to Deity.”]

“But they make God secondary to blessed Mary when they assign a temporal mother, the creatress of times, to Deity; indeed, they do not even allow her to be the mother of Christ, although she is also **Χριστοτόκος**. For, as they say, not human nature but God the Word was born from her, and she who gave birth is not the mother of the one born. For how can she be the mother of one foreign to her nature? But if she is a mother, as they themselves call her, then what was born is humanity, and not Deity. It is proper for a mother to give birth to something like her own essence: either she will not be a mother if she has not given birth to something like her own essence, or, if she is a mother, she has given birth to something like her own essence.

“Again, after other statements: God is the creator of months, and is not the product of months; the maker of holy Mary was not afterward fashioned from the Spirit in her. But, without the need for my teaching, hear the angel speaking to Joseph himself: ‘Take the child and his mother’ (Matt. 2:13).”

**[Note: [Col. 0286]** These words are quoted at somewhat greater length in the Council of Ephesus, from Nestorius’s twenty-first *Quaternio*, as follows: “The voice of the angels says: ‘Rise, and take the child and his mother.’ Yet it is certain that the archangels understood the mystery of the birth much more precisely; nevertheless, they do not say, ‘Rise, and take God and his mother,’ but, ‘Rise, and take the child and his mother’” (Vol. II, chapter 8).]

“Thus he said ‘the child,’ not ‘Deity.’”

Again, after this:

“Do you want another testimony added for you? ‘The days were completed for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn son’” (Luke 2:6–7). “There you have whose mother the **Χριστοτόκος** was: the mother of the child whom Mary bore, not of Deity, which encompasses all things.”

**[Col. 0287A]** Hear another testimony: “When the magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy; and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother” (Matt. 2:10–11). Everywhere the Virgin is proclaimed the mother of the child, not of Deity.

**[Note: [Col. 0287D]** Perhaps it would be more suitably read: “Why, then, do you attribute a carnal mother to Deity?” A little later, *ministrum* or *ministram Deitatis*, “a minister of Deity,” might reasonably be read. For Nestorius held that Christ the man was only an adjunct minister, or fellow-worker, of Deity, as is apparent from his own words cited at the council.]

“Why, then, do you appoint flesh as the mother of Deity?”

And shortly afterward:

“It fell to the Virgin **Χριστοτόκος** to give birth to humanity; to the Word of God, [to exercise] the ministry of Deity.”

When the judges had read these words, they said: Let what Nestorius has said suffice thus far. Let Serapion disclose what he thinks about these matters.

## XII

Serapion replied: If Arnobius neither thinks nor believes in this way, why does he frequently use **Χριστοτόκος** and **Θεοτόκος**?

Arnobius said: If I say **Χριστοτόκος** and deny **Θεοτόκος**, you rightly accuse me of being a Nestorian—or perhaps, on the slightest trace of your accusation, you accuse me unjustly.

**[Note: [Col. 0287D]** The old codex is mutilated here, having: “You rightly accuse me of being a Nestorian, or perhaps you accuse me on the slightest trace of accusation.” We have expressed the sense as best we could.]

But now the entire course of my defense attacks anyone who denies that Mary is **Θεοτόκος**; and you condemn Nestorius together with me, while Nestorius repudiates me together with you.

Serapion said: For what reason does Nestorius repudiate me together with you?

Arnobius said: Because I do not deny with you that holy Mary is **Θεοτόκος**.

Serapion said: By your argumentative use of the term **Θεοτόκος**, while asserting that she is **Χριστοτόκος**, you attack it.

Arnobius said: Do you deny that Christ is the Son of God?

Serapion said: I do not deny that Christ is the Son of God; rather, I rebuke you, because you assert that Christ is man and not the Son of God.

Arnobius said: Before he was born from Mary, did the Son of God already exist?

Serapion said: Who, except Photinus, has said such things?

**[Note: [Col. 0287D]** They report that he was born in Lesser Galatia, was educated in Greek and Latin literature, administered the bishopric of Sirmium, and, together with other orthodox men, condemned Arian impiety at the Council of Nicaea. But, through the common disease of all heresiarchs—namely pride and the desire for empty glory—he eventually fell into the heresy of Ebion, Sabellius, and Samosata, to such an extent that he asserted that God is single and solitary, and that, in the Jewish manner, one should confess not three persons but only one, although three names were attributed to the same being. He further held that Christ was merely a man, deriving his beginning from human generation, and was not begotten before the ages (Socrates, Book II, chapter 8; Book VII, chapter 32; Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 6; Theodoret, Book V, chapter 11; Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*). Athanasius, Ambrose, Jerome, Epiphanius, Prudentius, Victorinus, Nazianzenus, and many other distinguished men consistently opposed his heresies. Socrates, Book I, chapter 20, reports that Eusebius of Caesarea refuted, in three entire volumes, a book by a certain Marcellus, the teacher of Photinus—volumes that I once saw in Greek among the papers of John Curterius, whose soul may enjoy peace.]

Arnobius said: Then he always existed.

Serapion said: He always existed.

Arnobius said: Who is this one who was born?

Serapion said: The very one who always existed.

Arnobius said: Was the one who always existed born pure, or with man, or outside man, or through man?

Serapion said: I have not told you this, because you want to show that he is man.

Arnobius said: If I were saying that he was man and not at the same time God, and if I were denying that he was born at the same time without diminution of his Deity, you would rightly bring these objections.

Serapion replied: You are ashamed to say that God was born, that God was tempted, that God was crucified, died, and was buried, although Paul also says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (Rom. 1:16). You are therefore ashamed to believe that he is the Lord whom, wishing to show as the impassible God, you designate as merely a man, our liberator. Therefore I must ask you: Who suffered for us, God or man?

Arnobius said: God was born as man, and man suffered.

Serapion said: And how do you make the impassible God, the Son of God, foreign to the suffering of humanity?

Arnobius said: Just as he was born in time, although begotten before time, and yet is the Son of Man, so also, although truly impassible, he truly suffered; and although truly immortal, he truly died together with his passible nature. “For he died through our weakness, but he lives through the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

Human passibility was assumed by him who remains impassible in such a way that it was with him when he was conceived, when he was born, when he was baptized, when he was tempted, when he was sold, when he was handed over, when he was mocked, when he was struck on the cheek, when he was crowned with thorns, when he was fed with gall and given vinegar to drink, when he was crucified, died, and was buried. For he did not abandon him in hell, nor did he allow his holy one to see corruption (Ps. 15:10). Together with him also he rose from the dead on the third day; together with him he ascended into heaven; together with him he sits at the right hand of the Father; and with him he will come as judge. For at the hour of the Ascension the angels said to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way,” etc. (Acts 1:11).

## XIII

Serapion said: I consider you all the more, and with complete justification, a Nestorian because, while carrying around the books of Nestorius, you have mentioned nothing of Saint Cyril, bishop, who wrote so much in catholic language against Nestorius.

**[Note: [Col. 0288D]** Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, was born as the brother of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria. A man of outstanding intelligence, he was educated by his uncle in every branch of learning, and on the third day after his uncle’s death he was elected and installed as archbishop of the Alexandrian Church. That he was Nestorius’s most bitter and vigilant enemy, and the enemy of his errors, is clearer than need be stated—not only from the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, which he presided over in the name of Pope Celestine, but also from his letters, the *Twelve Chapters*, the *Apology*, the *Dialogues*, the *Thesaurus*, and other highly learned works. Prosper of Aquitaine calls him “the most glorious defender of the catholic faith” (Theodoret, Book V of the *History*, chapter 25; Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapters 14 and 33; Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, *On the Grace of God against the Collyridians*).]

Arnobius said: I give thanks to you, almighty God, because through Serapion’s mouth you have brought forth victory.

The judges said: In what statement do you think that victory has been brought forth for you?

Arnobius said: In his statement that Saint Cyril is a bishop who wrote much in catholic language against Nestorius. It is therefore established that, in Serapion’s judgment, the doctrine of Saint Cyril is sound and apostolic.

The judges said: If Serapion denies this, let him depart rejected not only by us but also by the holy Alexandrian Church and by the universal catholic Church that exists throughout the world.

Arnobius said: Saint Cyril, a man of apostolic memory and bishop of the Church of Alexandria, when he learned that the Nestorian doctrine was spreading in opposition to the faith, wrote throughout Egypt and sent a letter to Saint Celestine, the bishop of apostolic memory, saying that it would contribute to his praise if something were corrected by the one who held the citadel of the episcopate.

**[Note: [Col. 0289C]** It is clear from ecclesiastical histories that Celestine, the supreme pontiff of the Church, was informed by Cyril about the impiety of Nestorius, praised Cyril’s piety and zeal very highly, and admonished Nestorius by letter to abandon his impiety. If he did not do so within ten days, he would be rejected not only from communion with the faithful but also completely removed from the list of priests. Moreover, in letters sent to John of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Rufinus of Thessalonica, Flavian of Philippi, and others who were truly apostolic, he explained to them the war stirred up by Nestorius against piety and urged them, by his authority, to join the common struggle for its preservation (Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapters 33–34; Evagrius, Book I, chapter 3; Liberatus, *Breviarium*). Finally, when there was a dispute over appointing someone in place of Nestorius, he wrote to John of Antioch, Rufus, Flavian, and Proclus that there was no obstacle to transferring to Constantinople someone who was already bishop of another city, or at least had been chosen for one, so that he might restore what the impious Nestorius had undermined (Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 37).]

But Saint Celestine proved such an **ἐγκωμιαστής**—“eulogist” or “panegyrist”—of him that, in condemning Nestorius, he issued a judgment against him; and he proclaimed Cyril’s praise both before God and before all, asserting that Cyril’s teaching was strengthened by the preaching of the distinguished bishops of our province. He clearly explained that this had also been the teaching of Damasus, Ambrose, and Hilary.

**[Note: [Col. 0290C]** I believe Arnobius is speaking of a certain council convened at Rome by Celestine, which the letter of the Council of Ephesus to Nestorius mentions once and again; also of the Alexandrian synod’s letter to Nestorius and Cyril’s letter to John of Antioch, since Arnobius was not present at Ephesus but is known to have presided at the Roman council. Unless, finally, you wish to say that he participated in the Council of Ephesus by letters in which he commended his position to Cyril of Alexandria and at the same time renounced Nestorius for heresy, as Nicephorus recounts in Book XIV, chapter 34. The letters are reported in Volume II of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 14.]

For in that very council he says:

“I remember that on the day of the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, Ambrose of blessed memory caused the entire people with one voice to sing to God:

‘Come, Redeemer of the nations,  
show forth the Virgin’s childbirth;  
let every age marvel:  
such a birth befits God.’

“Does such a birth befit a man?”

And he added:

“Therefore our brother Cyril’s meaning, when he calls Mary **Θεοτόκος**, is fully in agreement with this: ‘Such a birth befits God.’ The Virgin poured forth God through her childbirth, through the power of him who is filled with omnipotence.”

**[Note: [Col. 0290C]** While preparing these passages, we carefully went through Hilary’s three books *Against Constantius*, in which we found none of these statements; consequently, those books must be mutilated, while Celestine and Arnobius possessed complete copies. Nevertheless, in Book IX *On the Trinity*, Hilary correctly teaches that, once the natures have been united in one, the reality of both natures is the same, yet neither is absent in the other, lest God should cease to be man by being born, or man should no longer be God by continuing to exist.]

Hilary too, a man of penetrating intellect, writing *Against the Emperor Constantius*, speaks thus about the Lord’s incarnation:

“The Son of God became man—God.”

And, reversing the order, he repeats:

“God, the Son of Man, became God; God did not become man, and the Son of Man became the Son of God.”

For the greatness of the Lord overcame the smallness of the servant’s form, so that the very servant’s form which he assumed ceased to be servile through the Lord who assumed it. For if those who by nature are not sons of God are made sons of God through him, how much more did he who by nature is the Son of God exalt into God the one with whom, by his own will, he was conceived and born in the Virgin’s womb, so that at his name every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10)?

**[Note: [Col. 0290D]** Between Damasus and this Celestine are placed Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface. In the first volume of the Councils there is also a letter of the same Damasus to Paulinus, bishop of Thessalonica, in which the following is read: “We anathematize those who assert two sons, one before the ages and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.”]

Likewise, my predecessor Damasus, writing to Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Antioch, says among other things:

“We anathematize those who assert two Sons of God: one begotten from the Father, and the other born from the assumption of flesh from the Virgin.”

Likewise, that man of apostolic memory, Damasus, says in another letter to Paulinus:

“We anathematize those who confess two sons in the Savior: one before the incarnation and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin, and who do not confess that the same Son of God, both before and afterward, is himself the true Christ, the true Son of God, who was born from the Virgin.”

## XIV

And while Arnobius was pursuing these points,

**Serapion said:** “I did not ask these questions without reason; rather, I wanted to see whether you were equipped for the Catholic defense against the Nestorian doctrine in the same way that you are learned in the Nestorian assertion.”

**Arnobius said:** “I have learned both that Nestorius’s error must be avoided and that Cyril’s teaching must be defended.”

**Serapion said:** “Then produce something by which you may show that Cyril asserted two substances in the one Son of God, namely, a human and a divine substance.”

At once Arnobius brought out a codex of Cyril’s letters, which at its beginning contained this letter:

> **[Note: [Col. 0290D] The title of this letter is now given in the new edition of the Council of Ephesus (vol. I, chapter 1) as follows: “Cyril to the presbyters, deacons, fathers, monks, and the others who practice the solitary life with you, and who steadfastly persevere in the faith of God, beloved and most desired brothers in the Lord, greetings,” etc. We have removed “to the parties of the monks.”]**
>
> Cyril sends greetings in God to all the bishops, presbyters, and deacons, to the fathers of the monks and to those who live the solitary life with you and are confirmed in the faith of God, beloved and dearest, and to the region of Alexandria. Recently certain men from among you came to Alexandria in the customary manner. When I questioned them, and was very eager to learn whether you too, modestly following the footsteps of the Fathers, were striving to make the orthodox and undefiled faith shine forth, and whether, adorned with an excellent way of life, you considered it a genuine resolve to endure fresh hardship anew amid the holy labors of the religious life.

> **[Note: [Col. 0291C] The new edition has: “And that you held the labors of ascetic exercise among your chief delights,” etc. From this it is apparent that *voluptatem* (“delight”) should be read here.]**
>
> And shortly afterward he says:
>
> **[Note: [Col. 0291D] This passage, which is very mutilated in the old manuscript, may be restored from Peltanus’s appended new translation of Cyril’s letter. It reads: “Our Father Athanasius, of most celebrated memory, who for forty-six full years administered the episcopal office of the Alexandrian Church with outstanding praise, and resisted the loquacious inventions of impure heretics with unconquered and wholly apostolic wisdom; and who by his writings, like some most fragrant ointment, wonderfully refreshed the whole world, and enjoyed great esteem and authority among all on account of the complete integrity of his doctrines and the soundness of his faith,” etc. Therefore, in place of *coronavit*, which is found in the old manuscript, *ornavit* should be read; and in place of *obtinebat sapientiam*, perhaps *objiciebat sapientiam* should be read.]**
>
> Our Father Athanasius, of everlasting memory, who adorned the episcopate of the Alexandrian Church for forty-six years, who possessed unconquerable and apostolic wisdom against the profane sophistries of the heretics, and who, as though with a most fragrant ointment, gladdens the whole world by his writings, whose sound faith and true knowledge of doctrine are confirmed by the testimony of all—when he was composing a work on the most holy Trinity and on the one substance, which in Greek is called **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”)—repeatedly calls the holy Virgin **Θεοτόκος** (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”) in the third book. I shall necessarily use his own words and expressions, which are as follows:
>
> **[Note: [Col. 0291D] Acts of the Council of Ephesus: “The scope and character of Holy Scripture.”]**
>
> “This,” he says, “is the meaning and character of Holy Scripture, as we have often said: that it contains a twofold signification concerning the Savior.”

When this was read aloud,

**Serapion replied:** “I do not know whether Athanasius said that there was a twofold signification concerning the Savior.”

**The judges said:** “No one could possibly lie about matters preserved in the archives of the Alexandrian Church. Therefore permit the reading to continue in complete silence. For we are certain about the writings of Cyril, the bishop of holy memory, and neither Arnobius nor anyone else could possibly lie about them.”

And the writings of Saint Cyril the bishop concerning Athanasius were read aloud.

**Arnobius said:** “Holy Scripture has a twofold signification concerning the Savior: that he was always, and is, the Son, the Word, the light, and the wisdom of the Father; and that afterward, for our sake, he assumed flesh from Mary the Virgin, the **Θεοτόκος** (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), and became man.

“Again, after other material, he says:

> **[Note: [Col. 0291D] These words occur in the fourth Oration Against the Arians; they are also reported in volume I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 1, and volume II, chapter 7.]**
>
> ‘There were also many saints who were free from sin. Jeremiah was sanctified from the womb, and John, while he was still in the womb, leaped for joy at the voice of Mary the **Θεοτόκος**, the bearer of God.’

“This was said by Athanasius, a man of the highest authority, one who must be believed and who never said anything inconsistent with the sacred writings. Nor could it have happened that so illustrious and renowned a man was ignorant of the truth. At that time he was admired above the others in the holy synod convened at Nicaea.

> **[Note: [Col. 0292C] Cyril’s translation has: “He was held in admiration by all.”]**

“He had not yet ascended to the episcopal seat but was still numbered among the clergy. Nevertheless, because of his discernment and modesty, and on account of his subtle and incomparable knowledge, he was summoned by our father, Alexander, bishop of most blessed memory. He was always present, and, like a son,

> **[Note: [Col. 0292C] In the Acts of the Council of Ephesus it reads: ‘He associated with the old man as a son with a father, offering himself as a guide in whatever had to be usefully accomplished, and showing a convenient path in everything that had to be undertaken.’]**
>
> guided his father’s counsel in the conduct of affairs and supplied a useful course of action.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0292B] Cyril, from Peltanus’s translation in the Acts of the synod, expresses the matter much more clearly: “But since it is likely that some will be found here who think that the assertions made at this point ought to be supported from sacred and divine Scripture, and who will further say that the holy and great synod nowhere called the Mother of the Lord *Theotokos*, nor made any decree at all concerning this matter, come, let us make clear, to the best of our ability, how that hidden mystery of Christ’s economy has also been proclaimed through the divine writings. Accordingly, to Arnobius’s words, insofar as they are true, the word ‘mystery’ must be added.”]**

“But since it may happen that some think we ought also to undertake such an exposition from venerable and divine Scripture, and add that the holy and great synod did not call the Mother of the Lord **Θεοτόκος**, nor establish anything at all about this matter, let us now show, insofar as it is true and understood concerning the economy of Christ, that this has also been proclaimed to us by divine Scripture.

“And since the Fathers themselves spoke while they held the holy and inviolable faith,

> **[Note: [Col. 0292D] Peltanus renders this: ‘They issued a canon of sincere and undefiled faith.’ Therefore, here *desinerent* should be read instead of *detinerent*.]**

“with the truth inspiring them through the Holy Spirit—for they themselves were not speaking, according to the Savior’s saying, but the Spirit of God and of the Father was speaking in them (Matthew 10)—a little later he says:

‘The holy and great synod says that

> **[Note: [Col. 0292D] Since Cyril’s Greek has γεγενημένον μονογενῆ, “the Only-Begotten has been begotten,” and since the most holy synod openly professes that he was begotten, not made, we delete from Arnobius’s old manuscript the words *ipsum factum*, “the Only-Begotten made.”]**

“the Only-Begotten himself was begotten from the substance of God the Father (John 1), and that for us human beings and for our salvation came down from heaven, became incarnate and man, suffered, rose again, and will come in time as judge.

“And shortly afterward he says:

‘The Word of God therefore took hold of the seed of Abraham and shared in flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14, 16), forming a body from a woman, so that he might be understood to be not only God but also man according to us, because of the union.

“Therefore, from the two realities, divinity and humanity, Emmanuel is plainly one; yet he is one Lord Jesus Christ, truly one Son, and God, and not a deified man,

> **[Note: [Col. 0293D] Since the old manuscript had *affirmando, et homo deificatus*, “affirming, and a deified man,” we have added the negation, *et non homo deificatus*, “and not a deified man,” because Cyril now reads: “He who is at once God and man, not a deified man, like those who by grace are made participants in the divine nature.” Euthymius agrees with this in part XIV of the *Panoplia*.]**

“that is, *Theopetis* [the transmitted term is uncertain], as others are by grace. But God appeared more truly in human form.’

“Again, shortly afterward he says:

‘Since it is therefore clear that Christ is not spoken of apart from the flesh, nor the Word of God as separated, and since it is more fitting to name him in this way after he became man, we prove from the sacred writings, giving faith to them, that he is God by nature and that in his union with the flesh he came together with it.’

“Again, shortly afterward he says:

‘For just as we die in Adam, so in Christ we are all made alive’ (Romans 5; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

> **[Note: [Col. 0293D] Thus Tertullian, book V *Against Marcion*, and Rufinus, in his exposition of the creed, read in the present tense *mortificamur et vivificamur*, “we are put to death and made alive.”]**

“For if he did not suffer for us in the human manner, then he did not, in the divine manner, take thought for our salvation. It is first said

> **[Note: [Col. 0293D] The old manuscript does not contain the word *mortuus*, “dead.” We have therefore added from Peltanus’s translation: ‘For he is handed over to death: first, indeed, he suffered death as man; then, because by nature he is God, he returned again to life. Therefore, if according to the Scriptures he had not endured death in the body, neither would he have been made alive in spirit, nor would he have revived.’]**

“that he was dead as a man; but that afterward he rose again, because he was God by nature. Therefore, if he did not suffer carnally, neither did he die according to the Scriptures, nor was he made alive in the spirit (1 Peter 3:18), nor did he in every respect revive. And if this is true, our faith is empty (1 Corinthians 15:14), and we are still in our sins.

“Again, shortly afterward he says:

‘I hear our same Lord Jesus Christ clearly saying concerning his soul: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have authority to lay it down, and again I have authority to take it up” (John 10:18). For he descended into death through his flesh—he who knew no death—in order that we might rise with him to life. For he revived after stripping the lower regions,

> **[Note: [Col. 0293D] Peltanus expresses it more elegantly: ‘For, when the lower regions had been despoiled, he revived, not as a man of our condition, but as God, made like us for our sake.’ [Col. 0294D] ‘Nature obtained incorruption in him as in its head.’]**

“not as a man like us, but as God in the flesh with us and above us. For nature in him first attained immortality, and death was crushed, having attacked the body of life as an enemy. Just as it conquered Adam, so in Christ it was conquered.

“Accordingly, as he ascended to the heavenly Father and Lord, for us and on our behalf, in order to make heaven accessible and ascensible to earthly human beings,

> **[Note: [Col. 0294D] Pelton: ‘He secured the way to heaven for us, the inhabitants of this earth.’]**

“the divine singer sang triumphal songs: ‘God has gone up with a shout of joy’ (Psalm 46:6). Hence Paul also says: ‘He who descended is himself also the one who ascended above the heavens, in order to fill all things’ (Ephesians 4:9).

“Again, near the end of this letter he says: ‘We are not ignorant of the glory of him who became man like us, yet remained the same God that he had been.’”

## XV

**The judges said:** “Arnobius has satisfied the matter abundantly, both by human reasoning, by the authority of divine law, and by the assertions of earlier great and holy bishops—Ambrose, Hilary, Gregory, and also Athanasius and Cyril himself.

> **[Note: [Col. 0294D] The opinions of this and many other Fathers are quoted in volume II of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 7.]**

“He has clearly shown that their doctrine was this: that two substances exist in the one Son of God, namely, divinity and humanity. Yet through these two substances they do not believe there to be two sons to such an extent that they have even read those who wished to believe otherwise as condemned by the execration of Damasus, Hilary, and Ambrose.

“It is therefore superfluous for us to delay in awarding the palm to the victor, since he has also produced many passages from Saint Cyril the bishop in which Athanasius too is read to have taught that God and man were united in the one Son of God—not in the sense that the Word who was always in the beginning and remains in his own deity ceased to be God through the assumption of man, but in the sense that man began to be God, which he had not previously been. Emmanuel was conceived in the womb, and therefore Mary is **Θεοτόκος** (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), because the man who was conceived and born began to be God in the womb from the moment of conception, and is God in the birth.

“This is Cyril’s meaning; this is the meaning of Athanasius, Damasus, Ambrose, Gregory, and Hilary; this is the meaning confirmed by Arnobius. Either let Serapion join his right hand to concord, or let him depart, having been refuted.”

## XVI

**Serapion replied:** “If everything that the mind has conceived upon consideration has not been sifted out, there will be no clear exposition of the truth. Therefore, so that I may more evidently give assent to Arnobius’s assertions, let Cyril’s complete little work be read aloud in your hearing, lest perhaps he has cut away convenient passages and thus, by mutilated statements, tried to make Cyril’s doctrine agree with his defense.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0294D] We have added *secundum*, “according to”; then, instead of *saevierit*, “has raged,” we have written *secuerit*, “has cut,” since this better answers *castratis sententiis*, “mutilated statements.”]**

**Arnobius said:** “Although there are countless volumes that teach that Cyril thought and believed this concerning the Lord Jesus: that the true God and true man must be believed in and worshiped in the one Son of God, and that Mary is **Θεοτόκος** as well as **Χριστοτόκος** (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”), nevertheless, if you command it, here is a complete book offered for reading.”

**The judges said:** “Once a mind has been stunned by contentiousness, even when the complete work has been read, it will not lack something to allege and, with needless exertion, occupy the intervals of delay. Nevertheless, since Saint Cyril’s book is at hand, let it be read.”

When the codex had been opened, the following title was read:

> **[Note: [Col. 0294D] If this concerns the letter cited above, its title is: ‘Cyril to the presbyters, deacons,’ etc. Its beginning is: ‘From those who spend their lives together with you,’ etc. The same man wrote a letter to Nestorius beginning: ‘Certain men had arrived at Alexandria,’ etc. He also wrote to the emperor Theodosius a book on the true faith in God, and again another book of the same title to the empresses Eudocia and Pulcheria, as well as a second book to them on the true faith in Jesus Christ our Lord, and other letters to various persons. In these he defends the doctrines of the Catholic faith with very weighty and numerous arguments, while refuting the heresies of Arius and Photinus, and especially those of Nestorius. Anyone can readily find and read all these works both in his published writings and in volumes I and II of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus.]**

## XVII

After this letter had been publicly read in full,

**the aforementioned judges said:** “Behold, Saint Cyril’s complete book has been read, which Arnobius is known to have produced as agreeing with his faith. If Serapion has anything remaining to allege, let him state it.”

**Serapion said:** “I am led by love of the faith, and I shall be able to glory more in being defeated than to be confounded. For a servant ought not to concern himself with his own victory when he contends with a fellow servant over the honor or dishonor of his Lord,

> **[Note: [Col. 0295D] Perhaps one should read: ‘and so that he may wish to show himself unconquered,’ etc. A little later we have added *pertinent*, “belong,” to the words *de his quae ad perpetuum gaudium*, “concerning those things which belong to everlasting joy.”]**

“and wishes to show in his words that his Lord is dishonored. The noblest kind of correction is that in which the issue is neither a monetary fortune nor matters of the sort that we shall not need after laying aside the body, but things that belong to everlasting joy or inflict eternal fire.

“I bring this forward so that, if I produce anything further against Arnobius, I may not be thought to have produced it out of love of contention, attempting to generate victory for myself through my dispute; rather, I want Arnobius to bring forth the victory of truth, sifted through all its members and shining, so that he may testify that nothing remains for me to do now concerning what I have undertaken.”

**The appointed judges said:** “Then say whether you know that anything remains for you.”

## XVIII

**Serapion said:** “This book of Saint Cyril that has been read does not teach two substances in the Son of God, but attempts to demonstrate one.”

**Arnobius said:** “Explain the one that it attempts to demonstrate.”

**Serapion said:** “Only the substance of divinity, not of humanity, so that Mary is called the Mother of God but not also the mother of man. For he wants her to be called **Θεοτόκος**, not **Χριστοτόκος**. Or, if he agrees in another respect, explain the **Χριστοτόκος**.”

**Arnobius said:** “Saint Cyril, against those who deny that holy Mary is **Θεοτόκος**, followed his earlier bishops, Theophilus and Athanasius, and showed that she was **Θεοτόκος**, lest she perhaps be thought to have an equal title when she is called **Χριστοτόκος**.

> **[Note: [Col. 0295D] Since the name “Christ,” taken generally, is derived from anointing, and since the ancients are read to have anointed priests, high priests, kings, and prophets before they undertook their public offices, they too can certainly be called “christs,” and their mothers “Christ-bearers.” For it is written concerning them: ‘Do not touch my christs’ (1 Chronicles 16:22; Psalm 104:15). Justin discusses this in his *Dialogue*, Tertullian in the *Apologeticus*, and Eusebius at the beginning of his *Ecclesiastical History*.]**

“For there were other Christ-bearers also, yet no other was **Χριστοτόκος** and **Θεοτόκος** in this way, nor did any other virgin become fruitful and pregnant as Mary did. Therefore, while mentioning what is greater, **Θεοτόκος**, he remained silent about what is lesser, **Χριστοτόκος**.

“Now, when the man who previously said that Mary had a father and a mother, and that he was a man, said this, is he to be thought to have denied that he was a man? He therefore pressed this point, which was the subject of the dispute.

> **[Note: [Col. 0295D] Vincent of Lérins expressly testifies that Nestorius denied that the Virgin Mary should be believed to be *Deipara*, **Θεοτόκος**, and wished her to be called only *Christipara*, **Χριστοτόκος** (*Against the Profane Innovation*). A letter of Nestorius to Cyril is extant in volume I of the Council of Ephesus, containing these words: ‘If we consider the matter more carefully, the sacred Virgin should be called not the Mother of God but the Mother of Christ.’]**

“For Nestorius in no way allowed that she ought to be believed **Θεοτόκος**, and therefore repeatedly asserted this in order to teach him the very thing that he had denied: **Θεοτόκος**.”

**Serapion said:** “Then show that Cyril’s meaning was such that he spoke of the one who was born from Mary as both that God and that man.”

**Arnobius said:** “We are here, and so is the book that has been read. Receive from it the passages that were read:

‘The Only-Begotten Word of God did not become man for the purpose of ceasing to be God, but so that, in the assumption also of his own flesh, we might behold the glory of his majesty.’

“If it is not enough that he first said this, listen to what he said in the second place. While situated in the flesh, he heard the Father saying: ‘Sit at my right hand’ (Psalm 109:1).

“Listen also to what he said in the third place, following divine Scripture: ‘When we join the Word of God to the created, human and mortal nature, and bring the divine nature together with it into one reality, it must nevertheless not be understood simply as a man who bears God,

> **[Note: [Col. 0296C] That is, as our humanity, created and formed in the Virgin’s womb by the power of the Most High. Tertullian likewise speaks in this way (*On the Resurrection of the Flesh*): ‘Subjected to the condition of the created world, for the created world; and worshiping the condition against the Creator, that is, the creature.’ A little later: ‘Let him not be understood as a God-bearer.’ This passage occurs in the letter of Cyril cited above: ‘Consider how Isaiah (Isaiah 15) declares the Lord to be not a man who bears God, or one breathed upon by divine power, or one assumed and employed merely as an instrument of divinity, but truly God incarnate.’ Again, in his *Scholion on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*, chapter 23, he refutes the same view. Moreover, in the fifth anathema he says: ‘If anyone dares to say that Christ is merely a man who bears God, and is not also truly God, the unique and natural Son of God, let him be anathema.’]**

“but as God incarnate, who, through the economy of the union—note what he says—claims for himself a body from the holy Virgin. For Christ is understood in this way, and in no other.

“Listen also, in the fourth place, to what he asserts: ‘In Christ we affirm that divinity and the human condition came together in one through a certain secret and ineffable manner, so that in the same person he may simultaneously be understood as man, like us, and as God, above us.’

“In the fifth place, listen to what he said concerning the Son of God: ‘Just as that pure and venerable flesh which was produced from the holy Virgin was proper to the Word himself who is from God the Father, so it had to undergo everything that belongs to flesh, except sin,

> **[Note: [Col. 0296D] He teaches that the communication of properties in Christ took place from the very first instant and moment of his conception in the Virgin’s womb.]**

“and everything, so that he might be born from his mother.’ Did you hear what he said?”

**Serapion replied:** “I heard.”

**Arnobius said:** “Explain to me what he said.”

**Serapion replied:** “Pure and honorable flesh, produced from holy Mary, was entirely such that it was born from its mother.”

**Arnobius said:** “Whatever you understand in this passage, make it known to me.”

**Serapion said:** “I think he meant that this Virgin who gave birth is the mother of the holy flesh.”

**Arnobius said:** “Do you want to see whether you have understood correctly? Consider what he added to this statement. ‘If,’ he says, ‘the divinity is understood apart from the flesh, it will itself be without a mother, and rightly so.’”

**Serapion said:** “I ask you to make clear what he is trying to assert.”

**Arnobius said:** “It is clearer than daylight that he explains Mary to be the Mother of God through the flesh, which she alone created. For he says that divinity alone has no mother, so that it may be understood that this one who was born—the one Son of God—is both God and man.

“Therefore, adding a sixth point, he says: ‘If we wish to tread the right path, it was not naked divinity but the Word of God the Father, mingled with the flesh and with the one born, that created the holy Virgin who was chosen for a venerable childbirth, so that she might give birth carnally to him who deigned to put on flesh.’”

**Serapion said:** “With the ears of my mind closed, I heard this entire book; and for that reason I did not see those two persons expressed in Cyril’s assertion concerning the one Son of God. For how could two persons not be taught as having been brought forth in the Virgin’s birth, when he says that God was born carnally, who deigned to assume flesh?” etc.

**Arnobius said:** “Certainly, flesh together with the one who assumed the flesh. For God is the one who assumed the flesh, while the flesh is a complete man. A complete man is one who has flesh and a soul. Apollinaris was condemned for this very reason: because he put God in the place of the soul as the one incarnate. Therefore we must not even recall matters condemned at the Council of Nicaea.

“Listen, then, to Saint Cyril speaking in the little book that was read:

‘If we wish to think correctly and tread the path without error, it was not naked divinity mingled with the Word of God the Father that created the holy Virgin who was chosen for a venerable childbirth, so that she might give birth carnally to him who deigned to assume flesh.’”

**The judges said:** “It is clear that Arnobius’s defense agrees with Cyril’s assertions. Therefore it is unjust to hesitate to grant victory to the one who, after the end of the dispute, deserves the palm.”

## XIX

**Serapion said:** “By your justice I beg you: since Arnobius has recalled in order what Cyril said about the matter at issue in the first, second, and third places, until he reached the sixth, now, lest perhaps he has taken other and clearer chapters from the same book that could demonstrate this very thing, grant my request.”

**The judges said:** “Say to what extent you wish him to proceed.”

**Serapion said:** “I already hold the matter as fully proved in my own mind, and with all my heart I believe that it is as Arnobius defends it.

> **[Note: [Col. 0297C] How highly the piety and learning of the divine Cyril were esteemed throughout Asia and Africa is sufficiently clear from these passages.]**

“Those who share the same city and the same ancestry, being placed in the error in which I was placed, cannot in any way be called away from this error except by this one means: that it be said and proved to them that Saint Cyril held this view.”

**Arnobius said:** “I too appeal to your fairness, asking you to deign patiently to await the end of the book of Saint Cyril while I point out its passages in order.”

**The judges said:** “Although there is no reason for delay, nevertheless, since we believe that your request ought to be granted, we allow Arnobius to point out, in abundance, the passages of the little book by which both our hearers and the readers of this proceeding may either avoid error or, if they have fallen into error, be called back from the path of error.

“The mercy of our God will be ready for these elect, so that they may return to Christ, to peace, and to the harmony of the Catholic faith—those who, thinking that the Roman Church holds the one Son of God to be divided into two parts, have miserably destroyed themselves. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself says: ‘Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause will be liable to the council’ (Matthew 5:23).

> **[Note: [Col. 0297C] Desiderius notes that in certain Greek manuscripts **εἰκῆ**, meaning “rashly” or “without cause,” is written into the Gospel text. The following words are then added: “Whoever says ‘Raca’ without cause; whoever says ‘fool’ without cause.” He further says that Chrysostom, in homily 10 on Matthew, implies that this is the reading, although it is absent from the Latin Vulgate edition. To this I add the ancient martyr Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 27.]**

“Behold, there is no cause, yet the slaughter of peoples has occurred. Blind fury proceeds throughout the entire Christian people—through bishops, presbyters, deacons, archimandrites, and almost all the crowds of monks and innumerable others.

> **[Note: [Col. 0297C] That Nestorius was above all a seditious and cruel man is clear from the libellus of Basil the archimandrite, in which he makes a grave complaint before the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian about Nestorius’s barbarity toward pious monks and clergy who refused to subscribe to his heresies: ‘He orders,’ he says, ‘the decurions to beat us. After being beaten, we are brought before the ecclesiastical tribunal; there, like criminals, we are stripped, flogged, thrown about, and attacked with kicks. After being tormented for a long time in the episcopal courtroom, we are led, exhausted by hunger, to the prison for supplicants. From there he arranged that we be handed over to the city prefect. Through him, therefore, loaded with chains, we are dragged to the public prison of criminals,’ etc. (Volume I of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 28). There it is also reported that the pious people of Constantinople publicly shouted against Nestorius on one occasion: ‘We have a rule; we do not have a bishop.’ The same Basil writes: ‘A portion of them, seized and dragged before the tribunal at that very moment, was beaten and treated with such savagery as was sometimes practiced not even among barbarian nations.’ Concerning the Nestorian satellites he also says: ‘Those whom he has once attached to his sentence, he so inflames that they dare publicly to inflict verbal abuse on whomever they please and do not hesitate openly to arouse the appearance of persecution,’ etc. And just as the Jews gnashed their teeth against Stephen, so these people gnash their teeth against Catholic Christians and strive to vent all their fury upon them. So much for the cruelties of the Nestorians at Constantinople. It is also worth recalling here how bloody disturbances they stirred up in the East from a fragment of a letter of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, inserted in the tenth session of the Council of Chalcedon. ‘Bishops,’ he says, ‘rise up against bishops in disputes, peoples against peoples,’ etc. Socrates also says of them: ‘The folly of Nestorius produced no small disturbance throughout the whole world.’ Cassiodorus likewise reports that, because of Nestorius, a sedition occurred around Miletus and Sardis, in which many died (*Tripartite History*, book XII, chapter 3). But enough of this here; elsewhere we have discussed the cruelty of the heretics more fully.]**

“So all Egypt, and all Palestine, were thrown into turmoil, so that the spilling of human blood has drenched the very earth; and the sole cause of the uproar is nothing at all, absolutely no error. For since the preaching of Saint Cyril pleases all the Egyptians and Syrians, what madness is this that rages against its own brothers and foams with anger, when the whole brotherhood of peoples shares the same faith?”

**Serapion said:** “I confess that my error took its beginning nowhere else than from this: that those who assert two substances in the one Son of God assert that there are two Sons of God, and that these substances are complete. For if the Son of God is truly believed to have been begotten from the Father before the ages, and by his omnipotence wished to enter the narrow dwelling of the Virgin’s womb, then he who had once been born from the Father before time, alone, so that he might be born again not alone but with man, plainly consists of two substances in the one Lord Jesus.

“This is just as Saint Cyril’s preaching represented it in the mass of iron that fire inflames: the iron remains in its own substance and the fire in its own nature, yet both are joined into one association and subsist in one union, so that it is not the iron but only the fire that can be perceived by human senses—by the senses, I mean, of seeing and touching, through which our reason gathers its understanding and arrives at what is true.

“Let Arnobius therefore continue what he has begun, so that at last those who unjustly persecute their brothers may blush with shame.”

## XX

Arnobius said: Up to this point the matter of the sixth chapter has been discussed; but I shall recount what was done in the seventh. She bore carnally him who became man and an infant for our sake. For he existed not according to our condition—that is, not constituted merely in our likeness—but he existed in human condition on account of the flesh; while in divinity he was heavenly and above us.

Serapion said: Of whom did he say, “He became man”?

Arnobius said: Of the Son of God, begotten before the ages and from the Father, of whom he said above: “God did not cease to be God when he assumed flesh.”

Serapion said: Did this God who assumed man make that man God through his omnipotence? Cyril taught that, from the one who assumes and the one assumed, there is one Son of God.

Arnobius said: See, I have proceeded to the eighth point. The account of the Godhead, considered naked and as though without flesh, will not in itself need the assistance of our discourse.

Serapion said: Please explain the meaning of this statement to me.

Arnobius said: If the account of the Godhead is considered naked—that is, without flesh—then, if it is considered divinely without man, it will not need the reasoning of the more human condition. For what can discourse say about the invisible God? And therefore, opening up this understanding in one chapter, he said: “But how did the only-begotten Word of God become flesh and dwell among us?” For this reason those statements refer to him. Let us now proceed and recount what he said in the ninth chapter. He calls the holy Virgin a prophetess. For, pregnant with Christ, she fulfilled the office of a prophet.

Likewise, in the tenth chapter: “For,” he says, “the divine infant was born, superior to the whole world. He was indeed in a cradle (Luke 2:7) and in the lap of his Mother according to the custom of human condition, but he was also God.”

Serapion said: When he says, “This infant who was born was also God,” he plainly expressed two persons.

Arnobius said: You have begun to open the ears of your soul. Certainly, when he said “was,” he also wished to show that an infant had indeed been born—one who was not merely an infant, but also God.

In the twelfth place as well, when he presses this matter more closely against those who deny that two substances came together in the one Son of God, he says:

“But someone says: How can it happen that human nature should contain the majesty of the Godhead, especially since God himself most plainly said to blessed Moses: ‘No one shall see my face and live’ (Exodus 33:20)? If, then, the intolerable Godhead has an inaccessible touch, how will it appear credible that God and man came together as one? I, however, would answer such a question that the explanation of this dispensation surpasses every measure and kind of miracle, and surpasses the thought and perception of our mind. Yet it was accomplished wisely, with God making his nature tolerable to our weakness.”

Serapion said: No one distinguished the divine and human nature in the one Christ so plainly as this man, when he said that those who deny that God and man came together are being rebuked. And he added: “I would answer such a question,” and so forth.

Arnobius said: You have rightly observed that he alone taught in an apostolic manner that “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:18). Indeed, you have also taken up the case against those who say that man could not come together with the substance of God.

Let us pass over the twelfth and come to the fourteenth. He says in what follows:

“As far as human reasoning and perception are concerned, the Godhead and human condition could in no way come together with one another; yet they come together in Christ, and one Emmanuel arises from both. But whoever separates the man by himself from the Son of God and considers him another person seems to me not to understand the truth and to be unable to see it.”

We shall also speak of the fourteenth. To show that two substances exist in the one Son of God, he says:

“Just as iron material, when it is melted in the midst of the furnace’s heat, glows like fire and is transformed into its appearance through the heat, imitating the flame’s victorious brilliance and brightness, so the nature of flesh, when joined to the eternal and incorruptible Son of God, ceased to be what it had been.”

Serapion said: What does “it ceased to be what it had been” mean?

Arnobius said: The following verse indicates why he said, “It ceased to be what it had been.” For he says in the following discourse: “Nor did it any longer remain in …”

[Note: The passage is so corrupt and deformed in the old manuscript that we have been unable to read it.]

Serapion said: Explain it to me, so that I may see what he means.

Arnobius said: Every nature of the human race possesses the frailty of emotions and sensations. But he never fell into this evil, nor did he ever suffer anything without his own will; rather, as it is written: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses” (Psalm 134:6).

The judges said: Since we have seen Serapion give his hands over to your victory—may this be said with his own peace—extend to us, in words of peace and in the faith of your peace, a line of explanation, so that matters worthy of remembrance may not be covered by silence.

## XXI

Arnobius, servant of Jesus Christ, said: While we confess two natures and two substances in the Only-Begotten, it is objected that we are saying that one is the Son of God and the other the son of man. We, however, say with the authority of the Apostle:

“God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

[Note: This testimony of Paul is repeatedly produced by Cyril and by other Fathers of the Council of Ephesus to confirm that Christ is one person in two substances, against Nestorius.]

For if he reconciled the world, so that he made those who believe in him sons of God—human beings who by nature were servants, not sons of God, and who in deed were also guilty, enemies through the transgression of the first man, and subject to the condemnation of the human race (Romans 5:10; 6:16–17)—nevertheless, through his grace he made these sons of God (John 1:12).

[Note: The old codex reads “of man.”]

Therefore, if he made others sons of God, how is he himself not the Son of God, united with the Word who is read to have become flesh (John 1:14)—the Word who existed before the world was (John 17:5); the Word who is not “from the beginning,” but was always in the beginning; the Word who lacks a beginning, but himself is the beginning; the Word who is subject neither to time nor to a moment, atom, or point, but is the creator of all things?

[Note: The reference is plainly to time or duration, like the angels and the other created things made from nothing, which received being after nonbeing. Yet the Son is rightly said to have been produced and begotten from the One who brought forth from the beginning, namely the divine Father: for the Father alone is from himself, whereas the Son is from the Father—not made or created, but begotten.]

This Word, without losing his timelessness but assuming a temporal and perfect man, was perfect God; he made the man born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary through his omnipotence (Luke 1:35; Matthew 1:20), because almighty God—the Father and the Holy Spirit—acted in this way.

[Note: For completeness of meaning, should we add: “Thus he willed and did”?]

Through this omnipotence, therefore, he willed that this man whom he assumed should, by being assumed in time, do what he himself had always been without time; so that two sons could no longer be spoken of—one begotten before the ages and another born in time—but only one Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Hence the Apostle said:

“And even if we have known the Lord Jesus according to the flesh,”

[Note: We have added the adverb “now” from the Apostle’s own text, and also from Cyril, who argues from it against the Nestorians. “What, I ask, does Paul mean here? Does he deny Christ after the resurrection? Did he not know that Christ, raised according to the flesh, ascended into heaven with that same flesh and would one day come from there? How, then, does he deny that he knows the Son according to the flesh? Because, as soon as he had risen from the dead, it was better to know and confess him from his divine excellence than from the weakness of the flesh. Thus Christ, Son, and Lord are one” (Book II, On the Right Faith to the Queens).]

“yet now we no longer know him” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

It is as though someone were to say: “Even if we once knew wool before it became purple through the mixture of purple dye, now we no longer know wool but purple, which among all human beings no one may use unless he possesses the dignity of an emperor.”

At this point it is objected: “Then Jesus was previously worthless wool, and the divinity that came upon him made him purple?”

We do not say this. But before the Spirit came upon Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and she conceived that which would be called holy, the Son of God (Luke 1:35–36), Mary’s womb itself, although free from sin and holy, was nevertheless, in the lowliness of humility, like the finest and incomparable wool among all the virgins beneath heaven. It was of such a kind and greatness that it could fittingly receive within itself the Godhead of the Son of God, just as wool receives the blood of the purple dye; and that wool ceased to be wool and became the true purple spoken of through the blood.

[Note: One might add: “Mary alone was merely lowly and rejected, but …,” and so forth; or else the sentence is mutilated.]

For it is not wool, but something precious, that is capable of receiving this blood!

[Col. 0302B]

If this blood elevates wool to such majesty through its admixture that no one is permitted to use it except one endowed with royal dignity, how much more, when the Holy Spirit came upon Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, did that which was born from her “of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3) become with him the Son of God, so that Mary was Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, “God-bearer”), just as she was Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, “Christ-bearer”)?

[Note: The name “David” is absent from the old codex. Moreover, Augustine, in Book II Against Faustus, chapter 4, testifies that some Latin codices read “born of seed,” as Arnobius reads here, rather than “made,” as our Vulgate edition has it.]

Before Mary there were other Christ-bearers, but they were not virgins, nor were they from the Holy Spirit, nor did the power of the Most High overshadow them. But she alone is both Χριστοτόκος, “Christ-bearer,” and Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer”: the only virgin who conceived from the Holy Spirit and through the overshadowing power of the Most High.

[Note: This too is taken from Cyril, who writes to the monks of Egypt: “From the fact that we have been anointed, we are called Christs. You have an anointing from the Holy One” (1 John 2). That anointing teaches you. Therefore one would do nothing absurd by deciding to call the mothers of any anointed persons indiscriminately Χριστοτόκους, “Christ-bearers,” and so forth. But the sacred Virgin alone is called and recognized as both Christ-bearer and God-bearer.]

## XXII

An objection is now raised concerning his temptations and sufferings: whether the Godhead itself was present in the diabolical temptation and in the Jewish Passion.

[Note: I would prefer to read “in temptation,” especially since shortly afterward it is written, “he was tempted with the tempted one.”]

To this, hear the prophet singing: “How the Lord loves judgment, and will not forsake his holy ones” (Psalm 36:28).

I add another point. If the three boys were not forsaken in the furnace of fire, but he who had always been the Son of God appeared there as the fourth among the three (Daniel 3:92), how much more did he not forsake his Holy One when he began to be conceived in the Virgin’s womb, when he was born together with the one being born, nursed together with the one being suckled, and grew together with the one growing?

[Note: Nebuchadnezzar is reported to have exclaimed: “Behold, I see four men unbound and walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.” Irenaeus the Martyr likewise judged this way, writing: “The Word of the Father was formerly seen not in one figure only, as it is written in Daniel, standing beside the three boys in the furnace of fire and delivering them” (Book IV, chapter 57). Tertullian likewise says: “This was the fourth whom the Babylonian king saw in the furnace with his martyrs,” and so forth (Book IV Against Marcion).]

[Note: We have deleted “with the tempter,” which the old codex has.]

He was certainly tempted with the tempted one, and crucified with the crucified one.

An objection is raised: How, then, do you assert that God is impassible, when you say that he was conceived, born, tempted, and suffered at the same time, and yet that he never at all forsook his Holy One?

I shall answer: You must remember the example of wool and the blood of the purple dye. When this wool has become purple through the admixture of blood, and it is woven, spun, or twisted, the wool certainly receives the majesty. Is that which is twisted forsaken by the purple color?

I add another example. Let us say, for instance, that when you strike a tree with an axe, and also strike the sun and its brilliance at the same time, you inflict a wound on the tree, and you strike the sun and its brilliance at the same time, but you do not touch the impassible heat. If the sun does not forsake the tree when it is struck, how much less did the Son of God, who is the Word, ever forsake his Holy One in the passion?

[Note: Flaccus Albinus, also called Alcuin, once tutor of Charlemagne, remembered this passage under Arnobius’s name eight hundred years ago, in his Letter to Flavius Merius: “Arnobius, in the dispute he had with Serapion, used *rubus* in the masculine gender, saying: ‘And just as truly the bush had the flame.’”]

And just as the bush truly had the flame, so truly did the Son of man suffer; and just as it truly was not burned, so truly did the Son of God not suffer.

## XXIII

Another objection is raised: You make two—the son of man and the Son of God.

The answer is: I do not make two by division, but in the one Godhead I distinguish two substances: one that had a temporal birth, and another that could not in any way be subject to time.

[Note: That is, in the one person of the Son of God I confess a human and a divine substance. This is the most certain and clear confession of the Christian faith, drawn from the Athanasian Creed: “As the rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.”]

One substance is that by which, placed as an infant in the manger and wrapped in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:7), he grew in age and wisdom (Luke 2:53); the other is that by which he himself creates those who are born and grants them to live and grow in age and wisdom.

One is that by which he is baptized by a servant, as though receiving sanctification (Matthew 3:15); the other is that by which he himself sanctifies both the water and the Baptist.

One is that by which he sleeps in the boat and is awakened by the disciples; the other is that by which he himself awakens them so that they may awaken the Lord.

One is that which is subject to winds, blasts, and storms; the other is that by which he commands the winds and orders the storms (Mark 4:38; Matthew 8:24).

One is that by which he weeps for a dead man; the other is that by which he commands death to release the dead and buried man (John 11:35, 44).

One is that by which he is sold by a disciple (Matthew 26; John 19); the other is that by which he redeems the whole world.

One is that by which he is fed with gall and given vinegar to drink (Matthew 27); the other is that by which he feeds with the bread of eternal life and offers the cup of everlasting joy (Matthew 26).

One is that by which he is sorrowful even unto death; the other is that by which he frees from sorrow and gives the joy of life.

One is that by which he dies and is buried; the other is that by which he opens the tombs, and so forth.

One is that by which he was lifted into heaven before the eyes of the apostles and sits at the right hand of the Father (Acts 1); the other is that by which he did not depart from the bosom of the Father, but was always in the Father and with the Father, and does not cease to be there.

[Note: The old codex reads “departed”; we have added the negation because the sentence and its meaning require it.]

An objection is therefore raised: When the Word was becoming flesh in the Virgin’s womb, when the infant was wrapped in swaddling clothes in the manger and grew in age and wisdom, and when he performed the other things that we know he did throughout his life, did he never depart from the bosom of the Father?

The answer is: When someone once asked an educated man, “Tell me, in what place is God now?” he is said to have given this answer: “Tell me where he is not, and inquire where he is.”

But when the prophet cries out, “If I ascend into heaven” (Psalm 138:6), and so forth, and he himself says, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24), how could it happen that he who is one with the Father and the Holy Spirit should be absent from the Father and the Holy Spirit when he was in the Virgin’s womb, when he was born, nursed, and so forth? Nevertheless, he never departed from the bosom of the Father.

When he had said this, the judges and all the hearers said: What you assert is sufficiently subtle and cannot be perceived by us unless it is clarified by certain comparisons.

[Col. 0304C]

## XXIV

“Tell me,” said Arnobius, “from where does a spring arise?”

Those who answered said: From a vein of the earth.

Arnobius said: Let this vein, from which the spring arises, suitably imprint the place of the Father upon your minds, so that the Father may be the vein and the Son the spring, who was born from the vein. From the vein and the spring the river is not born, but proceeds.

[Note: It is most certain and clear from Scripture and from the symbols of the Catholic faith that the Son of God is said and is begotten by the Father, only-begotten, and born from the same substance or Godhead from eternity. For it is written: “Today I have begotten you.” “Before the morning star I begot you.” “The only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father,” and so forth. “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” “God sent his only-begotten Son into the world.” Everywhere God the Father testifies from heaven that Christ Jesus is his beloved Son, by no means an adopted son; and Jesus, in turn, openly and confidently calls him his Father. Finally, the apostles taught, impressed upon the whole world, and confirmed in the minds of innumerable people by countless miracles and by the sufferings they courageously endured this foundation of the Christian faith.

Likewise it is open and certain that the Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the substance and Godhead of the same Father and also of the Son, because it is written: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father.” “He will receive from what is mine.” “The Spirit of my Father will speak in you through the Godhead.” “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts,” and so forth. And with Athanasius we all confess: “The Holy Spirit is not made, nor created, nor begotten by the Father and the Son, but proceeds.”

These two points, I say, are so clear and certain from Scripture and the creeds that no Christian doubts them. But why the Holy Spirit cannot be called the Son of both, since he truly exists from their substance and nature; why he should not equally be called begotten as well as proceeding; and how great the difference is between being born and proceeding—these matters are not so defined or clear. Arnobius certainly writes orthodoxly here that being born is one thing and proceeding another, and immediately afterward compares the Holy Spirit to a river proceeding from the Father and the Son as from a vein and a spring, not being born. But he does not explain how this procession differs from birth.

The scholastic Fathers bring forward something from Augustine (Book XV On the Trinity, chapter 27): that the Holy Spirit is not the Son and is not begotten because a son does not ordinarily proceed from two unless one of them is the father and the other the mother. Thus, they say, it is certain that the Holy Spirit does not proceed in that manner and therefore is not born.

Again, from the same Augustine (Book On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas, chapter 1), they teach that the Holy Spirit is not born because he is not the Son; nor unbegotten, because he is not the Father; nor made, because he is not from nothing; but is God proceeding from God the Father and God the Son.

They further gather from the same teacher that the generation of the Son occurs by way of the fruitful intellect of the Father and is therefore properly called natural birth; whereas the procession of the Spirit occurs by way of will and love and is therefore properly called breathing-forth and procession. Augustine says: “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, not as one born, but as one given, or as a gift; whereas the Son proceeds by being born and comes forth as one begotten” (Book V On the Trinity, chapter 4).

Finally, they add that confusion would arise in the most holy Trinity of the persons if two sons were spoken of instead of the only-begotten and sole Son. The Spirit, therefore, ought not to be begotten, but breathed forth and proceeding.

These men speak piously and learnedly. Yet, in my judgment, the wisest of all—Athanasius the Great, in his Letter to Serapion; Ambrose, in Book I On the Faith, chapter 5; and other ancient theologians—frankly professed that they neither fully grasped the distinction and rationale of such emanations nor could explain it to others in words. Thus the perfect knowledge of this mystery, as of many others, must be awaited until in the other age we see God face to face as he is.

From these considerations John of Damascus rightly concludes (Book I of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 2): “We have learned that there is a difference between generation and procession; but what the mode of this difference is, we have not learned at all. Although we cannot understand these things, we nevertheless truthfully confess and believe that they are so.” And Augustine says concerning a similar matter: “Let whoever can grasp it, grasp it; but whoever cannot, let him believe and pray that he may understand what he believes” (Book III Against Maximinus the Arian, chapter 10).]
