Being born is one thing; proceeding is another. Whatever pertains to giving life, healing, and washing belongs to one and the same substance. But let there be three persons, so that the Father is the vein generating the Son, whom we have called the spring; and from the vein and the spring let the river, the Holy Spirit, proceed rather than be born.

Let it proceed in a connected course with them, so that the three may be one, and so truly three that they may truly be one.

[Note: Just as Arnobius here sketches the mystery of the Trinity by the comparison of a vein, spring, and river, in which the same substance of water exists, so before him Augustine had done the same by comparisons of the sun, its radiance, and its heat, and then of fire, light, and warmth (Book I Against Maximinus and Sermon 1 On the Words of the Apostle). Athanasius likewise teaches in his fourth sermon Against the Arians that the Son proceeds from the Father while remaining in him, like a ray proceeding from light and a river from a spring.]

Therefore the Son, himself the spring of life, together with the river—the same Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son—travels through all the regions of the earth, giving drink to the thirsty, pouring into arid places, watering the lands, washing away filth, making and strengthening, and sustaining by giving life to every kind of human being, bird, cattle, creeping creature, and fish.

No one has life at all except those for whom the spring and the river, proceeding from the vein of the spring and from its own bosom, wash away filth as they circulate, pour into arid places, give drink to the thirsty, refresh those burning with heat, restore the distressed, and sustain by their draught all generations of human beings, birds, cattle, reptiles, and fish.

The vein never suffers the absence of the spring born from it beforehand or of the river proceeding from it and from the spring.

[Note: The old codex had “and.”]

If the element of water, subjected to our service, is shown to possess this power—that, running with the swiftest course through mountains, hills, the channels of aqueducts, and pipes, it nevertheless flows around without departing from the bosom of its vein, but runs while remaining there—

[Note: We preferred to read *discurrit*, “it runs,” rather than *discurrunt*, “they run,” as found in the old codex.]

how much more do the Son and the Holy Spirit, never wholly departing from that bosom of majesty, endure in unity of substance and in Trinity of persons as an inseparable and complete Trinity?

## XXV

For those wishing to inquire into the majesty and origin of this holy Trinity, the vein of a spring presents itself. Dig as deeply as you can: you will never be able to reach its beginning. A more abundant vein presents itself to you; whatever you seek by striking, the more you are prevented from investigating it, the more you seek to reach it by inquiry rather than by believing.

And if you cannot succeed in finding the beginning of this vein lying beneath your feet, how will you be able to discover the beginning of the Father?

But if you discover the beginning of the Father, you will also discover that of the Son. For if you discover when the vein began to flow, you will also discover when the spring was born from that vein; you will also discover when the river began to proceed from the vein and the spring.

But just as you cannot reach the beginning of the vein—how could the vein already be in the beginning, in which the spring was, and the spring was with the vein, and the vein was the Father of him who was in the beginning with God (John 1:1)?

For the Word of the Father is the spring, which is the Son of the vein, the spring of life, as the Psalmist sings, addressing the vein: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 35:10).

[Note: Arnobius does not contradict himself, for he also explains this passage of the psalm concerning Christ in his Commentaries. Concerning the psalm cited immediately before, he says: “The heart of the Father has poured forth the good Word; all things were made through him,” and so forth. Arnobius continues his argument.]

The river proceeding from the spring—and the vein then began to proceed when the vein poured forth the spring—for thus the Father is read to have said: “My heart has poured forth a good Word” (Psalm 44:1).

But just as you will not find the beginning of the vein, so neither will you find that of the spring; and just as you will not find the beginning of the vein or of the spring, so neither will you find that of the river.

Thus, just as the vein, the spring, and the river flow forth together, so do the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And as far as the dignity of the Creator is removed from the creature, so far is the comparison of the creature removed from the Creator.

But the more capable you are of thinking and saying something better, the more there will remain a place where the Godhead may be believed more excellently and more truly.

As has been said, a better statement does not exclude what has been said, but adorns it; whereas a bad statement is eliminated and driven out by a good one. Therefore always keep your ears open to those who say better things, and Wisdom commands your minds, saying: “Open your ear to the word of truth, and establish your heart in just sayings” (Proverbs 22).

## XXVI

Certainly one must beware, lest by falling into the understanding of the wicked Sabellius you believe the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one God in such a way that you do not think the Father the true begetter of the Son, do not believe the Only-Begotten to be the true Son of the Father, and do not believe the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be the one God who is to be believed according to sacred Scripture, which says: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6).

Thus the one God must be believed to be the true Father, the true Son, and the one and true God, the Holy Spirit.

For “God” is the name of an undivided substance, conferring the whole upon the one who receives it and diminishing nothing in the one who confers it. It is not so that the Son is regarded as the Father, nor that the Father is believed to be the Son, nor that the Holy Spirit is considered to be the Father.

[Note: Consistently, Arnobius writes in his commentary on this passage of the psalm: “Therefore, not as the condemnable Photinus believes, did the Lord take his beginning from the Virgin Mary; rather, before the morning star he was brought forth from the Father’s mouth.”]

[Note: Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius (Book VII of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6), and after him Theodoret (Book On the Fables of Heretics), report that Sabellius was by origin an African from Pentapolis. Augustine, in his book On Heresies, says that some regarded him as a disciple of the impious Noetus, who first confused the persons of the most holy Trinity; Epiphanius confirms that the sects of the two were at least similar.

Here Sabellius, reviving from the underworld not only the errors of Noetus but also those of Praxeas and Hermogenes, whom Tertullian had overthrown, preached that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person called by these three names. He taught that in the Old Testament this person had given the law under the name of the Father; in the New Testament had become man under the title of the Son; and under the designation of the Holy Spirit had come to the apostles.

Tertullian soundly refutes this heresy in his books Against Praxeas and Hermogenes, and the Fathers of later centuries likewise exposed and condemned it (Hilary, Book IV On the Trinity; Athanasius, Oration Against the Followers of Sabellius), as our Arnobius does in this passage.]

For the Father is the one who says to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm 109:4).

The Son is the one who says: “Before all the hills he begot me, and before he made anything, I was with him” (Proverbs 8:25).

But the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son (John 15:26), like a river proceeding from a spring and from the vein of the spring, is shown clearly by the Apostle Paul to be God, against the teaching of Macedonius.

[Note: Under the emperor Constantius, Macedonius was a court official and an Arian. Through the faction of the Arians and the favor of Constantius, while the Catholic people resisted, he seized the bishopric of Constantinople with such violence that approximately three thousand one hundred and fifty men, as Socrates reports, were trampled and killed when he entered the church.

Because he openly preached that the Holy Spirit was a creature, he was first called Πνευματομάχος (*Pneumatomachus*, “fighter against the Spirit”), as Basil testifies in his Exposition of the Nicene Faith. To refute and suppress this heresy, the ecumenical Council of Constantinople was summoned under Theodosius. At that time the following was added to the Nicene Creed: “And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who is worshiped together with the Father and the Son,” and so forth (Sozomen, Book III, chapter 9, and Book IV, chapter 7; Nicephorus, Book XII, chapter 30).]

Paul shows him to be the very one whom the prophet Isaiah says: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne; he said to me: ‘Go, say to this people: Seeing you shall see, and you shall not see’” (Isaiah 6:4, 9).

Paul disclosed that this was the Holy Spirit in the following manner, saying to the Jews: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly concerning you through Isaiah: ‘Go, say to this people: Seeing you shall see,’” and so forth (Acts 28:26).

This, as I have said, surpasses the sect of Macedonius, which says: “Nowhere in the sacred Scriptures is the Holy Spirit called God.” We have shown that the Apostle called this the Holy Spirit whom Isaiah calls: “I saw the Lord God almighty Sabaoth sitting upon a throne and saying to me,” and so forth.

Now I shall also show that blessed Peter called the Holy Spirit “the Lord,” and that will suffice; for just as there are two eyes in the head of a body, so Peter and Paul are in the head of the Church.

The Apostle Peter says to Ananias when he was lying: “Why, indeed, did it agree with you and your wife to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men but to God” (Acts 5:3–4).

We could set forth many other passages if the testimonies of these two, established by apostolic authority, were not sufficient.

Certainly, as we have already said and proved, he who descended from heaven for the sake of assuming man never left heaven, because it is written: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24); and he who ascended from these places into heaven never abandoned us.

For he himself promised, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Since, therefore, his descent into flesh is established, let us hold this firmly: in the one Son of God there are two births, just as there are two substances—before the ages, invisibly from the Father; in time, visibly from his mother.

Before the ages he was true God from true God; in time, true God and true man, born from Mary ever-Virgin while the Holy Spirit overshadowed her.

He was born true invisible God together with true visible man; true incomprehensible God together with true mortal man.

He was born, I say, not immaterial but bodily; not in mere appearance, but bearing flesh, bones, blood, sensation, and a soul.

One and the same was true man and true God, fulfilling the Law and the Prophets, suffering the cross according to the Scriptures, truly dying, truly being buried, and truly rising from the dead on the third day.

Yet what died in him was that which could die. For mortal man was taken up by immortal God; but it was not God who rose into man—it was man who rose into God.

Afterward he was seen on earth for forty days, and then was taken up into heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Father and will come to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1).

## XXVII

And when he said these things, all said: “Tell us, how will the living and the dead be judged?”

Arnobius said:

[Note: Justin Martyr, in his response to Question 109 of the Orthodox, interprets “the living who are to be judged” as those who will still be surviving when Christ comes for judgment. Concerning them, according to the Greek reading, it is written: “We shall not all sleep.” Assuming their person, Paul says: “We who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord,” etc. Augustine embraces both interpretations, writing: “He will come to judge the living and the dead: the living who will have survived, the dead who preceded them. It can also be understood in this way: the living, the righteous; the dead, the unrighteous.” *Book I on the Creed for Catechumens*, chapter 4.]

“The living” means believers who hold the Catholic faith; “the dead” means Gentiles, Jews, and heretics, who do not have life according to the Lord’s saying: “Whoever does not believe in me does not have life in himself” (John III, 36). And he speaks truly: “Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live” (John VI, 35). Therefore, as I said, let us follow. He will come to judge the living and the dead, the righteous and the unrighteous, the faithful and the unbelieving.

For his death makes all the deaths of believers and saints precious (Ps. CXV, 15), to such an extent that, in the same flesh in which he was born, suffered, and died, he rose again, and according to the quality of their deeds all will attain either the eternal crown of glory or eternal punishments, with God as judge.

For we must believe that our soul was made by God. Although it is destined to remain perpetually in one or the other condition, either good or evil,

[Note: These statements appear to be directed against the Manichaeans and Origenists, whom the ancients reported to have imagined souls as coeternal with God.]

nevertheless the soul is not without a beginning, since this is a peculiar attribute of God alone. Thus the soul is God’s creature, or created work. For it is written: “He who formed the spirit of all human beings, he knows all things.” And again: “The Lord lives, who made a soul for us.” And again:

[Note: Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, in the chapter whose title is given as “That the Soul and the Spirit Are One,” recalls this passage of Isaiah as follows: “The differences between spirit and soul are sufficiently declared, God himself pronouncing: ‘The spirit proceeded from me, and I made every breath.’ For the soul is breath made from spirit.” And again: “He who gave breath to the people upon the earth, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isaiah XLII), etc. Augustine, in *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 14: “The spirit will go forth from me, and I made every breath.”]

“The spirit will proceed from me, and I made every soul” (Isaiah LVII, 16). Our flesh also was made by God from clay (Genesis II, 7), and therefore both substances of the human being have one God as their author.

[Col. 0309B] Therefore all things that have been made are subject to us, because they were formed at God’s command. Hence, not by deed.

Concerning the human being, we read that God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis I, 23). Thus the Apostle proves that the human being, God’s noblest work, consists not only of soul and body but also of spirit, and is tripartite, saying:

[Note: Tertullian, in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, renders this passage of Paul as follows: “And may your whole body, soul, and spirit be preserved blameless,” etc. Irenaeus, *Book V*, chapter 9; Lactantius, *Book VII*, chapter 12, and *On the Workmanship of God*, chapters 18 and 19; and Augustine also, in *On Spirit and Soul*, discuss at length what distinction exists among these three. We too have discussed this matter in our annotation on the aforementioned passage of Irenaeus.]

“May your spirit, flesh, and soul be preserved complete at the coming of God” (I Thessalonians V, 23).

I speak specifically of the spirit that is accidental, not natural, and not the same in everyone. For the Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the spirit that is from God” (I Corinthians II, 12). The spirit that we believers receive is of divine grace; the other spirit is of diabolical intention. For the devil was not created without a beginning, as Marcion raves, but was made by the good God as an angel, and all evil took its beginning from him.

[Note: The theologians rightly teach that some things are intrinsically evil and can never be good, such as blasphemy, contempt of God, idolatry, adultery, and so forth; whereas other things are evil only because they are forbidden, such as eating unclean animals under the Law, and what Arnobius notes here concerning sacrifices and Eucharistic communion.]

That is evil which the good and benevolent God forbids to be done; even if the thing itself is good, it will be judged evil because of the prohibition of God the Lawgiver. Now what is as good as offering sacrifice to God? Yet when King Saul refused to wait for the holy Samuel and, while Samuel was delayed, himself offered the sacrifice, the Holy Spirit could no longer remain in him (I Samuel XIII, 10).

For “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom I, 5),

[Note: An old manuscript reads “useful.”]

and would that, when the Holy Spirit departed, he had not been mocked—or even tormented—by another spirit. If, therefore, we consider the quality of the act, he does a good thing; but we must not consider the quality of the act, but the pride of the one who despises. The communion of the sacrament too is holy, but it becomes a destructive act for one who has not yet been drenched with that most sacred water. There are many similar things which, although they are good works, bring destruction when they are performed not in the order in which they were instituted.

Therefore this angel, who is the devil, incurred guilt through presumption and was the first of all the angels to sin in his heart. For thus the Lord says through the prophet: “You said in your heart: ‘I will ascend above the stars of heaven’” (Isaiah XIV, 13), etc. He was therefore the first to sin in his heart. From that point all kinds of presumption began to sprout, when, following no one’s example, he gave the beginning of sin from himself.

By nature, however, he is good, just as a man is a robber when he seizes another’s possessions from their owner,

[Note: We have judged that this should be read in this way, instead of “wise in another,” which appears in the old manuscript. We have treated at length the first sin of the evil angel in our commentaries on the Epistle of the blessed Apostle Jude. A little later [the text reads], “not evil by nature.” In our judgment we have added the word “evil.” For it would reflect upon the Creator’s injury if he had created anything evil by nature.]

and a man is generous when he gives his own possessions to the needy. Both are human beings, but one is good toward others; the other is not evil by nature—for that would be an injury to the Creator—but through the zeal of a perverse will. The former is both good by nature and good through the zeal of a good will.

Hence the choirs of angels will resound with these words, so that glory might be sung to God in the highest and God’s peace sown upon earth among people of good will (Luke II, 14–15). Thus, although he was a good angel, by the choice of an evil will he turned toward evil; man followed him (Genesis III), despising the ordinances of the divine law.

But the Creator, foreknowing that both angels and human beings would become despisers, subjected them to his justice, while allowing them absolutely to belong to their own will,

[Note: Justin Martyr, a man of apostolic times, says the same in his *First Apology*: “Angels and human beings, because at the beginning, when they were created, they received free will from God, justly pay the penalty of their sins in eternal fire. For nothing would deserve praise if it were not capable of turning in either direction,” etc. Would that the Lutherans and Calvinists seriously reflect upon these and the many other things which the ancient Church most sacredly decreed, both against the Simonians, Marcionites, and Manichaeans—the first enemies of free will—and against the Pelagians, its excessive heralds! They would surely cease, at least in this matter, to trouble us Catholics.]

because otherwise the recompense of grace could not be just.

The beginning of man and of his transgression is clearly related at the opening of the book of Genesis. The prophet, however, bears witness to the beginning of the angel, saying:

[Note: We propose that the names of the gems listed below should be read according to Jerome’s interpretation of the Septuagint. They are somewhat corrupt in our old manuscript. Rufinus, Josephus’s translator, writes *ligurius*, better than Galen’s *lincurius*; this is also how it is read in Jerome’s Epistle 54. In Greek it is λιγύριος, and in the Vulgate, Exodus XXVIII, 19, *ligurius*. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book II: “He was clothed with the finest stone: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, ligurius, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx,” etc.]

“You were the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise. You had every precious stone in you: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, ligurius, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx; and you filled your treasuries and your storehouses with gold. For from the day on which you were created,

[Note: Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, Book II; Origen, *On First Principles*, Book I, chapter 5; Jerome, on Isaiah LIV; and Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book XI, chapter 25, read and interpret the prophet’s passage in this way.]

when, together with the cherub, I placed you upon God’s holy mountain, you were made in the midst of fiery stones. You walked without blemish in your days, from the day on which you were created, until iniquities were found in you,

[Note: The Septuagint reads ἀπὸ πλήθους τῆς ἐμπορίας, “from the multitude of your commerce.” Hence Tertullian: “From the multitude of your commerce.” The Latin Vulgate likewise has *in multitudine negotiationis tuae*, “in the multitude of your commerce.” It is therefore entirely clear that Arnobius should read *negotiationis*, not *cogitationis*.]

from the multitude of your commerce. You filled your storehouses with iniquity,

[Note: The old manuscript reads “and with sins.” Tertullian has: “You filled your storehouses, and you sinned.” The Latin Vulgate reads: “You sinned.”]

and you sinned, and you were wounded from the mountain of God; and he brought you out from the cherub, from the midst of the fiery stones. Your heart was exalted because of your disgrace; therefore I cast you to the earth before kings, and I gave you over to public disgrace because of the multitude of your sins and the iniquity of your commerce,

[Note: Saint Pagninus, from the Hebrew: “You profaned your sanctification.”]

because you polluted your holy things. And I will bring fire out from your midst, and that fire will devour you, and I will make you ashes upon the earth before all who see you; and all who know you among the nations will grieve over you. For you became a portent, and you shall be no more forever” (Ezekiel XXVIII, 12).

[Note: The Latin Vulgate reads: “You have been made nothing, and you shall not be forever.” Rufinus, Origen’s translator, has: “You have become destruction.” The Septuagint reads ἀπώλεια ἐγένου, “you became destruction.” It would therefore be better for Arnobius’s passage to read: “So that you became destruction,” etc.]

We must also believe that the world itself was made by God from nothing, as it is read in Maccabees:

[Note: These are the words of Salome, the mother of the seven brothers, addressed to her last son; they are reported in the sacred books in the singular number: “Look, my son,” etc. It is nevertheless probable that this courageous woman repeatedly encouraged all of them to martyrdom with the same exhortation while they were still alive. Furthermore, both from this testimony and from six hundred other testimonies of the ancient Fathers, we see that the Second Book of Maccabees possessed sacred and canonical authority. I add only that Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, asserted twelve hundred years ago that the Catholic Church had received both Books of Maccabees into the canon of the sacred volumes. Moreover, Josephus, a Hebrew by race and a priest by rank, consistently affirmed fifteen hundred years ago (*On the Maccabees*, toward the end) that the history of Eleazar and the seven brothers, which is related in the Second Book, was also counted among the sacred writings by his fellow Hebrews. Let the heretics of this latest age consider with what face and conscience they reject them.]

“Look, my children, at heaven and earth, and, seeing all that is in them, understand how God made them from nothing” (II Maccabees VII, 28).

Therefore, just as the world was made from nothing, so it will be reduced to nothing at the end, because it is written: “You, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain forever” (Psalm CI, 26; Hebrews I, 10).

Yet God’s words faithfully promise a new heaven and a new earth (Isaiah LXV, 17; likewise LXVI, 22; Revelation XXI, 1; II Peter III, 13), in which this [matter] may abide perpetually for his saints. What sort of things these will be, he alone knows who will make them, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him” (Isaiah LXIV, 4; I Corinthians II, 9).

I have obeyed your request—or rather, your command—and have explained how I believe. It remains for the love of the fear of the Lord to be granted to me through your prayers, so that I may possess at least the beginning of wisdom, and that there may be in me good understanding, manifested in upright works (Psalm CX, 10), by which I may abstain from what is forbidden and persist in what is commanded.

## XXVIII

Serapion said: “You ought to obtain this through prayers, whether your own or those of any of the saints—a thing that has not been granted to you through freedom of the will.”

Arnobius said: “And what thing has been granted to me through freedom of the will?”

Serapion replied: “That you abstain from what is forbidden and persist in what is commanded.”

Arnobius said: “He who abstains from what is forbidden and becomes free from sin is not only beyond reproach for sin; he is also worthy of praise if he persists in what is commanded.”

Serapion said: “That is so.”

Arnobius said: “If that is so,

[Note: Against this Pelagian position, admitted by Serapion, Jerome inveighs as follows in his *Letter to Ctesiphon*: “I ask, what sort of argument is this: that something can exist which never existed; that something can come to be which, as you testify, no one has done; that you attribute it to anyone whose future existence you do not know; and that you give to someone what you cannot prove existed in the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles?” Augustine likewise, in *To Quodvultdeus*: “If this were certain, the Lord would seem to have said in vain: ‘Without me you can do nothing.’”]

then a person can, through free will, become free from sin and attain divine praise.”

Serapion replied: “That is so.”

Arnobius said: “I disagree.”

Serapion said: “Then there is no free will.”

Arnobius said: “I both defend and retain free will, but enclosed within its own boundaries and distinguished by its own limits and bounds.”

Serapion said: “God willed the human being to possess free will so that the wicked might justly be blamed, because they could have been good, and the good might justly be praised, because they could have been wicked. For remove the possibility of either alternative, and punishment will find no one whom it can strike, nor will reward find anyone whom it can crown.”

Arnobius said: “Tell me, then, whether the freedom of your will can lead you to abstain from what is forbidden in such a way that you are without sin, or to fulfill the commandments in such a way that you reach the crown?”

[Col. 0313B]

Serapion replied: “And if a human being cannot be without sin, God will not count the sin against him.”

## XXIX

Arnobius said: “That which could have made him free from sin perished in the transgression of the first human being.

[Note: Augustine wrote learnedly and correctly on this matter: “We do not say that free will perished from human nature through Adam’s sin, but that among human beings subjected to the devil it is effective for sinning. For living well and piously it is not effective unless the human will itself has been freed by God’s grace and aided toward every good act, word, and thought” (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, Book II, chapter 5).]

Therefore the Creator could precede his creature with this restoration, so that, since it could no longer be freed from sin by its own powers, it might be freed by the grace of God. Hence our weaknesses gave the name ‘Lord Savior,’ our captivity ‘Redeemer,’ our miseries ‘Merciful One,’ and our servitude ‘Liberator.’

“Now I want to ask you, Serapion: Do you desire God to have mercy on you, or not?”

Serapion said: “Who is there who does not want God to have mercy on him?”

Arnobius said: “I want you to answer what I am asking, as I am asking you. Tell me, then: Why do you ask God to have mercy on you?”

Serapion said: “Obviously, because I pray and entreat God for this every day.”

Arnobius said: “Then confess that you are miserable, so that you may obtain mercy. Hear the Apostle crying out concerning this: ‘Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Romans VII, 24).

“Draw the conclusion, then, and see that, if you can be without sin, you cannot confess that you are miserable; and when you do not confess yourself miserable, you withdraw yourself from God’s mercy. Either you can so restrain yourself from sin that by your own powers you are able to abstain from what is forbidden and are not miserable, or, if you know yourself to be miserable and cannot simply confess it, you can rightly obtain mercy from God.

“For even if you should perhaps suppose that you possess something and be able to demonstrate it, the Apostle cries out to you: ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ (I Corinthians IV, 7).

“Moreover, how can you believe that the Lord is your Savior unless you acknowledge that you are weak? Or how can you ask for God’s help and assistance unless you believe that, without his help, you cannot fulfill the good you desire or avoid the evil from which you flee?

“Thus, one of two things must be conceded in your answer: either confess that you are miserable or strong, weak or healthy, so that you may hear the voice of the Lord saying: ‘Those who are healthy do not need a physician’ (Luke V, 31).

“Hence the prophet also cries out: ‘For I will not trust in my bow, and my sword will not save me; but your right hand, your arm, and the light of your face will save me’ (Psalm XLIII, 4, 7–8).

“One of two things: can you abstain from every sin, or can you not? If you can, you do not need help; you can do it. If you cannot, you rightly seek help.

“The psalmist gives this testimony concerning God’s help: ‘He who dwells in the help of the Most High’ (Psalm XC, 1), etc. Let us now see what happens to the one who believes and speaks in this way: ‘He will overshadow you with his shoulders,’ etc.”

[Note: Consistent with himself throughout, Arnobius also refutes the Pelagians’ error in his commentary on this psalm in these words: “Many think that freedom of the will can suffice for itself to such an extent that, through that freedom itself, they are confident that they can rescue themselves from invisible enemies. Yet it is dangerous to deny freedom of the will, and to strip sin bare. For if you deny it, you have loosened the reins for all; if you strip it bare, you have deceived,” etc.]

Serapion said: “What, then, will free will possess?”

Arnobius said:

[Note: Augustine asserts in these words that human free will cooperates by its consent in conceiving and retaining faith (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, Book II, chapter 32): “For what is believing except consenting that what is said is true? Consent is an act of the will; clearly, faith is in the will.” And shortly afterward: “Since faith is therefore within one’s power, because each person believes when he wills, and when he believes, he believes willingly.” The same point is made elsewhere by him (*Tractate 26 on John*): “Someone may enter the Church unwillingly, approach the altar unwillingly, and receive the sacrament unwillingly; he cannot believe unless he is willing.”]

“If you do not wish to believe in this way, do not believe in this way, but depend upon divine help. If you do wish to believe, then, with God’s help, be freed from the things threatening you through his mercy.”

## XXX

Serapion said: “I did not hear Augustine teaching in this way.”

Arnobius said: “In what respect did you not hear him teaching in this way?”

Serapion said: “The writings of all his treatises and books testify that he taught that the command of the law is not to be fulfilled.”

Arnobius said: “It pains me to bring forward his marvelous words just as they are and to demonstrate how much is granted to the command of the law and how much to free will.”

Serapion said: “I call God to witness that you will remove all ambiguity from my anxiety if you bring me clear statements from him concerning these matters, and provide evident proofs from him concerning everything that has been discussed. For I regard his assertions as so authoritative that anyone who thinks Augustine can be faulted in any expression exposes himself as a heretic by his own mouth.”

Arnobius said: “You have spoken according to my own judgment. For I believe, hold, and defend what I now bring forward from him as though it were the most sacred writings of the apostles. He says:

“‘Inquiring in the divine Scriptures what grace is—whether free will is grace, or grace is the forgiveness of sins, or grace is the commandments of the law—I recognized none of those things that pertain, through the administration of the Holy Spirit, to overcoming desires and temptations. The one who ascended into heaven pours this out upon us most abundantly, “leading captivity captive and giving gifts to human beings” (Psalm LXXVI, 19).

“‘Hence we pray that we may be able to overcome the temptations of sins, and that the Spirit of God, of whom we have received a pledge, may assist our weakness. When one prays and says, “Do not allow us to be led into temptation” (Matthew VI, 13), he is certainly not praying that he be a human being, which he is by nature; nor is he praying that he possess free will, which he already received when nature itself was created; nor is he praying for forgiveness of sins, because that is said above: “Forgive us our debts”; nor is he praying that he receive a commandment. Rather, he is plainly praying that he may fulfill the commandment.

“‘He prays that he may not sin—that is, that he may do no evil. This is what the Apostle prays for the Corinthians when he says: “We pray to God that you do no evil.” Hence it is sufficiently clear that, for not sinning—that is, for not doing evil—although free choice of the will undoubtedly exists, its power is nevertheless insufficient unless weakness is assisted.

“‘Prayer itself, therefore, is the clearest testimony to grace. Let the one who denies this confess it, and we shall rejoice whether he has become upright or has been corrected.

“‘The law and grace must therefore be distinguished. The law would be of help if there were no will; nor would grace be of help if there were no weakness. We are commanded to possess understanding where it is said, “Do not become like a horse or a mule,” etc.; yet we pray to possess understanding where it is said: “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments.”

“‘We are commanded to possess wisdom where it is said: “Fools, gain wisdom at last”; yet we pray to possess wisdom where it is said: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him.”

“‘We are commanded to possess self-restraint where it is said: “Restrain yourself”; yet we pray to possess self-restraint where it is said: “Since I knew that no one can be continent unless God grants it—and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord and entreated him.”

“‘Finally, lest it be too lengthy to go through everything, we are commanded not to do evil where it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good”; yet we pray not to do evil where the Apostle says: “We pray to the Lord that you do no evil.”

“‘We are commanded not to do evil and to do good where it is said: “Turn away from evil and do good”; yet we pray to do good where it is said: “We do not cease praying for you, that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things and bearing fruit in every good work.”

“‘If, therefore, we recognize the will to which these things are commanded, we must also recognize grace in this way: without the grace of God, the things we desire to fulfill achieve no result.’”

Serapion said: “I want to know whether this great assertion of the holy man, supported by such fairness, that no human mind can oppose it, was also established by him concerning the things we did at an earlier time, in the same sense or with the same words.”

Arnobius said: “There are many matters concerning which our disputation has reached its conclusion through debate. On what subject do you now wish to be strengthened by the authority of Saint Augustine’s words?”

Serapion said: “Concerning the birth of Jesus Christ, in which God and man have been declared to us through two substances. I have learned from your assertion and proof that in these substances Saint Mary existed as both Χριστοτόκος (*Christotokos*, Bearer of Christ) and Θεοτόκος (*Theotokos*, Bearer of God).”

## XXXI

Arnobius said: “If I wished to present his words divided into separate clauses, I would seem to have offered suspicion rather than satisfaction. Therefore I think it appropriate to provide you with his complete treatise, so that you may clearly recognize that he proclaimed two births and two substances in the one Son of God.

### A Sermon of Saint Augustine, Bishop, on the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Note: Comparing Arnobius’s work carefully with Augustine’s sermon printed at Paris in 1571, together with the remainder of Augustine’s works, we found many matters requiring correction and various readings in both texts, which we shall record here briefly and in order. Arnobius has: “Whoever marvels at that”; Augustine: “Whoever marvels at this day.” Arnobius: “The Magi invited”; Augustine: “The Magi imitated.” Arnobius: “Who gives you the gift of one fecundity”; Augustine: “Who brings you the gift of fecundity.” Arnobius: “So that he might proceed there”; Augustine: “So that he might proceed from here.” Arnobius: “He came to testify himself”; Augustine: “To have come.” Augustine has “When this birth”; Arnobius lacks the adverb “when.” Augustine: “Which pious faith recognized and held”; Arnobius: “Because faith received.” Augustine: “He did not remain silent who was speaking”; Arnobius: “Who was spoken of.”

“Furthermore, Arnobius lacked these six words, which we restored from Augustine: “Because he does not precede him by living”; “separated.” Arnobius likewise lacked these four words, which are found in Augustine: “Because they could also have children.”

“Augustine: ‘Let us transcend our souls’; Arnobius: ‘All our thoughts.’ Augustine: ‘Which the weak sight, not yet fully, palpates’; Arnobius: ‘Because the sight, perceived, palpates in the weak mind.’ Again, Arnobius lacks these eight words: ‘Through Israel, and to become Emmanuel, God with us, in the weakness of the flesh,’ which we restored from Augustine. These two words were also absent: ‘above all things’; Augustine, however, writes: ‘Without a mother, above all things.’

“Finally, where Augustine has: ‘So that, trusting in his mercy, we may triumph over the devil’s cunning,’ our old copy of Arnobius reads: ‘So that, his mercy having conquered the devil’s cunning, we may triumph,’ etc. From these points the benevolent reader will see which passages we restored, and will at the same time judge how much labor was required of us to correct many other similarly corrupted passages.”]

Our Savior, born from the Father without a day—that is, without a beginning in time—through whom every day was made, wished to have on earth this birthday, the day that we celebrate today.

Whoever marvels at this day, marvel rather at the eternal one who remains before every day, creates every day, is born in a day, and frees from the day’s evil. Marvel still further: she who gave birth is both mother and virgin; the one whom she gave birth to is both an infant and the Word (John I, 1).

Rightly the heavens spoke, the angels rejoiced, the shepherds were glad, the Magi were invited, kings were troubled, and infants were crowned.

Nurse, mother, our food; nurse the bread coming from heaven and placed in the manger as food for pious beasts of burden (Luke I, 10; Matthew II, 1; John VI; Luke II). For there the ox recognized its owner and the donkey the manger of its lord (Isaiah I, 3)—namely, circumcision and uncircumcision—by clinging to the cornerstone, whose first fruits were the shepherds and the Magi.

Nurse the one who made you such that he himself might become in you; who, by being conceived, brought you the gift of fecundity, and by being born did not take away the glory of virginity; who chose for himself, before he was born, both the day on which he would be born. And he himself created what he chose, so that he might proceed from here “like a bridegroom from his chamber” (Psalm XVIII, 6), by which he could be seen with mortal eyes and, through the annual increase of light, testify that he had come as the light of the world (John I, 9).

The prophets sang that the Creator of heaven and earth would be on earth with human beings (Baruch III); the angel announced that the Creator of flesh and spirit would come in the flesh. John greeted the Savior from womb to womb; the old man Simeon recognized God as an infant; the widow Anna recognized the Virgin Mother (Luke I–II).

These are the testimonies of your birth, Lord Jesus, before the waves were laid low as you trod upon them, before they yielded to your command; before the wind grew silent at your bidding, the dead lived when you called (John XI), the sun grew pale at your death, the earth trembled at your resurrection, and heaven opened when you ascended; before you performed these and other marvels in the age of your already youthful body.

You were still carried in your mother’s arms, and already you were recognized as Lord of the world; yourself a little child from the seed of Israel (Isaiah IX), and yourself Emmanuel, God with us (Isaiah VII).

What and of what kind is that generation of the Savior by which the Son is coeternal with the Father who begets him? When the world was astonished at this birth from the Virgin, which pious faith received and held, while unbelief mocked it and conquered pride feared it, what sort of generation was that in which “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1)?

What is this Word which, before it was spoken, did not remain silent about what it would say, and, once spoken, did not silence the one of whom it was spoken? This is the timeless Word through which times were made; the Word that no lips began by opening and no lips ended by closing. The Word that does not receive its beginning from the mouth of speakers, and opens the mouths of the mute; the Word that does not become foreign through the tongues of nations abandoned, and makes the tongues of infants eloquent.

What sort of generation is that in which the Father does not precede him by dying, because he does not precede him by living, separated from all intervals of place and spaces of time, which we are accustomed to perceive either in days or in bodies?

Let us raise our soul toward him, as far as we can with his help, if somehow we may be able to grasp both the one who begets without preceding the one who is born, and the one who is born without following the one who begets—the Father and the Son—neither the Father existing equally with the Son nor the Son equally with the Father, yet both equally eternal.

Let us consider, if we are able, that the one is eternally begetting and the other eternally born: not both begetting, not both being born, but neither living without the other; and that the Father has eternally begotten and the Son has eternally been born. If we cannot, let us believe.

This is not what we wish to say; yet it is not far from each one of us. For “in him we live, and move, and are” (Acts XVII, 28).

Let us transcend our flesh, in which parents live before their children, because they grew in order to be able to beget children, and, as their children grow, they already grow old. Parents lived before their children were born, because even when their parents have died, their children will live.

«Let us transcend our souls as well. They too give birth, by thinking something that they possess within themselves through knowing; but they can lose it through forgetting, because they did not possess it beforehand through being born.

Let us transcend all bodies, both temporal and changeable, so that we may see the one who is above all things, through whom all things were made. Our ascent is in the heart, because that to which we ascend is also near; but we are far from him insofar as we are unlike him.

His likeness, which he made and remade in us, therefore ascends to him, because the weak sight of the mind, once it has perceived it, trembles and cannot behold the ineffable brightness of eternal light. Since the mind’s vision does not yet grasp his splendor, “who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah LIII).

But “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

“This generation, therefore, whose day we celebrate today; this generation in which he deigned to come through Israel and to become Emmanuel, God with us in the weakness of the flesh, not with us in the iniquity of the heart; drawing near to us through what he assumed from what is ours, and freeing [Col. 0318C] us through what remained his own—for the Lord indeed visited his servants through mortal weakness, in order to make them free through unchangeable truth; this generation, therefore, which human frailty is capable of grasping in both respects: not that generation which remains beyond time, without a mother, above all things, but this one which came to be in time, without a father, among all things.

Let us praise, love, and adore this Son of the Virgin and bridegroom of virgins, born from an incorrupt mother and bringing forth incorruptible truth, so that, trusting in his mercy, we may triumph over the defeated cunning of the devil. The devil crept in upon us to deceive us through a corrupted female mind; Christ came forth to free us through incorruptible female flesh. He is blessed with the Father and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0318D] forever and ever. Amen.”

### XXXII

Serapion said:

“I confess that my desire has been satisfied. For he has clearly asserted both two natures and two substances. Now, so that all hesitation may be uprooted from me completely, I wish it to be demonstrated to my satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0317D] From these facts I seem not improperly to infer that this dispute of Arnobius and Serapion was either begun, or at least written down, during the time of that most holy and learned man, Pope Leo. For it mentions his predecessors, such as Damasus and Coelestine, but does not proceed beyond Leo’s period. Moreover, through his efforts and during the age of Nestorius, the stain was for the most part erased and almost extinguished. Finally, no other period presents itself as more suitable and appropriate to this dispute. A little later, where it reads *ut altoqueremur Orientales*, it might perhaps not improperly be read *ut alloqueretur*. For he wrote to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, his most celebrated letter against the errors of Eutyches, which was praised and approved by all the orthodox at the Council of Chalcedon. Then, again, he wrote to other Easterners: namely, to Eutyches himself, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, to Anatolius of Constantinople, to Maximus, bishop of Antioch, and even to the Eastern emperors Theodosius, Marcian, Leo, and Pulcheria. Finally, he also sent to the Councils of Ephesus and [Col. 0319B] Chalcedon, celebrated in the East, many learned letters against the heresies emerging throughout the East; these are printed among his other writings.] whether [Col. 0319A] my lord, the apostolic man, the venerable Pope Leo, followed his predecessors in this matter, addressing the Easterners in writing his letters.”

Arnobius said:

“Listen to what the venerable Pope Damasus, a man of apostolic memory, wrote to the holy man Paulinus of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0319B] Since in the time of Damasus, the supreme pontiff, there was one Paulinus who was bishop of Antioch and another of the same name who was bishop of the Church of Thessalonica, and since Damasus wrote letters to both, some have doubted to which of them the letter cited here was addressed. Yet both from this testimony of Arnobius and from Theodoret (*Book V*, chapters 10, 11, and 15), it is clear that it was written to the Antiochene, although Nicephorus explicitly states that it was sent to Paulinus, bishop in Macedonia, who had also been bishop of Thessalonica (*Book XII*, chapter 18). In the latest edition of the councils, Venice, 1585, the first part of the letter is addressed to the Antiochene; the latter part, whose opening is “Because after the Council of Nicaea,” to the Thessalonian.] so that you may recognize that, following ancient practice, the holy and most learned Pope Leo sent letters to the Easterners in order to recall the Churches from error.”

When Arnobius had said this, he produced a codex, from which the following was read:

“To his most beloved brother Paulinus, Damasus. Through my son Vitalis I had sent you a written reply, leaving everything to your will and judgment, [Note: [Col. 0319C] We have restored this from Damasus, and removed from Arnobius’s old codex the words *et te Petrum* (“and you, Peter”).] and through the presbyter Petronius I had briefly indicated that I had been moved to some extent when his departure was already imminent. Therefore, lest any scruple remain with you, and lest your commendable caution delay the reception of those who perhaps wish to be joined to the Church, we have sent our faith, not so much to you, who share communion in that same faith, as to those who, by subscribing to it, may wish to be joined to you—that is, to us—through you. [Note: [Col. 0319C]

Here Arnobius omits much that is contained in the same letter of Damasus and is reported in the first volume of the general councils. Since these matters contribute greatly to confirming our faith, it will not be unwelcome to pious and diligent readers if we append them. The letter continues as follows:

“Therefore, if the aforesaid son Vitalis and those who are with him wish to be united with you, they must first subscribe to that exposition of the faith which was established at Nicaea by the pious will of the Fathers. Then, since no one can apply medicine to future wounds, that heresy must be eradicated which is said to have subsequently sprouted in the East. That is, it must be confessed that Wisdom itself, the Word himself, the Son of God, assumed a human body, a soul, and a faculty of understanding—that is, the complete Adam—and, to put it more explicitly, the whole of our former human being, without sin. For just as, when we confess that he assumed a human body, we do not immediately attribute to him the human passions of vice, so, when we say that he assumed both the human soul and understanding, we do not thereby immediately say that he was subject to the sin of human thoughts. But if anyone should say that the Word took the place of the human understanding in the Lord’s flesh, the Catholic Church anathematizes him. It likewise anathematizes those who confess sons in the Savior—that is, one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin—and who do not confess one and the same Son of God both before and after.

“Whoever wishes to subscribe to this letter, provided that he has first subscribed to the ecclesiastical canons, which you know very well, and to the faith of Nicaea, you shall accept as subscribing without any ambiguity. This is not because you could not yourself propose these very things that we are writing to those who are being received, but because our agreement grants you a free model for receiving them.”

Thus far Damasus, in his letter to Paulinus of Antioch. The same source continues:

“Catholic Profession of Faith, which Damasus wrote to Paulinus, bishop of Thessalonica in Macedonia.

“‘Because after the Council of Nicaea, etc.,’ which are reported here by Arnobius, and also by Theodoret, *Book V*, chapter 15, and Nicephorus, *Book XII*, chapter 18; from these we have corrected several marked passages.”]

“Most beloved brother. Because after the Council of Nicaea, [Note: [Col. 0320C] This entire insertion, up to the words “this error became established,” appears to have been added by Arnobius, since it is found neither in Theodoret, nor in Nicephorus, nor in the letter of Damasus contained in the first volume of the councils. In addition, from the time of the Council of Nicaea until Damasus, many councils were convened at Rome. The first was under Sylvester, in the presence of Constantine Augustus; at it, whatever the Nicene Fathers had defined was confirmed by 275 bishops. The second was under the same emperor, with 67 Fathers—or, according to others, 84—assembling and condemning Sabellius, Arius, and Photinus. The third was again under the same emperor, with 284 bishops gathered at the Baths of Domitian. The fourth was under Julius, with 316 bishops, all of whom again condemned those who held the views of Arius, while receiving Athanasius—harassed by countless slanders but acquitted by them—back into communion. The fifth was under Damasus, with 90 bishops, who condemned the creed of the assembly of Ariminum and again approved the Nicene decrees. The sixth was under the same Damasus, at which the heresies of Apollinarius and Timothy were condemned by public decrees (*Sozomen*, Book VI, chapter 23; *Theodoret*, Book II, chapter 22). Which of these councils Arnobius is discussing here I leave the diligent reader to investigate.] and when a council of catholic bishops was assembled in the city of Rome, [Col. 0320A] this error became established, so that certain men dared, with sacrilegious lips, to say that the Holy Spirit had been made through the Son, we anathematize those who do not proclaim with complete freedom that the Holy Spirit is of one power and substance with the Father and the Son.

“We likewise anathematize those who follow the error of Sabellius, saying that the Father is the same as the Son. We anathematize Arius and Eunomius, who, with equal impiety, though in different language, assert that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures. We anathematize the Macedonians, who, coming from the stock of Arius, changed not their perfidy but only its name. We anathematize Photinus, who, reviving the heresy of Ebion, confesses the Lord Jesus Christ as existing only from the Virgin Mary. We anathematize those who assert two sons, one before the ages and the other after the assumption of flesh from the Virgin. We anathematize those who say that, in place of the rational and intellectual soul of a human being, the Word of God operated in human flesh, whereas the Son himself is the Word of God and did not exist in his body in place of a rational and intellectual soul, but assumed and saved our soul—that is, a rational and intellectual soul—without sin. [Note: [Col. 0320D] The translator of Nicephorus: “Those who say that the Word of God was separated from the Father by extension and contraction, and that it cannot subsist, or who blasphemously assert that it will have an end” (*Book XII*, chapter 18).]

“We anathematize those who contend that the Word of God, the Son, was separated from the Father by extension or contraction, was without substance, and would have an end. As for those who have migrated from one Church to another, we regard them as excluded from our communion until they return to those cities in which they were first established. But if, when one person has migrated elsewhere, another has been appointed in the place of the living man, let the one who has abandoned his own city remain without the dignity of the priesthood for as long as his successor rests in the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0321C] Thus we read in Theodoret, Nicephorus, and the first volume of the councils. Arnobius’s copy reads: “he was appointed.”]

“If anyone does not say that the Father has always existed and exists, the Son has always existed and exists, and the Holy Spirit has always existed and exists, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the Son was born from the Father—that is, from the Father’s divine substance—let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0321C] Nicephorus: “If anyone does not say that the Son of God is true God, just as the Father is true God,” and so forth.]

“If anyone does not say that the Lord’s Word, the Son of God, is true God [Col. 0321B] like his Father, and that he can do all things and knows all things, let him be anathema. If anyone says that, while established in the flesh, the Son of God, when he was on earth, was not in heaven with the Father, let him be anathema. If anyone says that, in the passion of the cross, the Son of God endured suffering, [Note: [Col. 0321C] Nicephorus: “Together with the soul.” Theodoret: “And not in the flesh alone but also in the soul.” Arnobius: “or the soul.”] and not the flesh together with the soul which he had assumed in the form of a servant (Philippians II), which he had taken to himself, as Scripture says, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0321C] This passage is plainly mutilated in Arnobius’s copy. It can be restored from the first volume of the councils, Theodoret, and Nicephorus as follows: “If anyone does not say that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, and tasted death in the flesh, having become the firstborn from the dead, because he is life and gives life, being God, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that he sits in the flesh which he assumed at the right hand of the Father,” and so forth.]

“If anyone does not say that he sits in the flesh which he assumed at the right hand of the Father, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is truly and properly from the Father, just as the Son is from the divine substance, and that he is true God, let him be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0321D] Nicephorus, or his translator, omitted this anathema; the first volume of the councils preserves it together with Arnobius.]

“If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit can do all things, knows all things, and is everywhere, just as the Father and the Son, let him be anathema. [Col. 0321C] If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a creature, or was made through the Son, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say [Note: [Col. 0322C] Nicephorus and the first volume of the councils add “visible and invisible”; but they lack the words that follow shortly afterward in Arnobius, “which are to be saved.”] that the Father made all things through the Son, who was afterward incarnate, and through the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

“If anyone does not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity, [Col. 0322A] power, majesty, and might, one glory, dominion, kingdom, will, and truth, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the three persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are real, equal, eternally living, containing all visible and invisible things, able to do all things, judging all things, giving life to all things, making all things, and saving all things that are to be saved, let him be anathema. If anyone does not say that the Holy Spirit is to be worshiped by every creature just as the Son and the Father, let him be anathema.

“If anyone thinks correctly about the Father and the Son but does not hold a right belief concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic, [Note: [Col. 0322C] We have added the word *quia* (“because”) from the first volume of the councils and from Nicephorus.] because all heretics who think wrongly about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the faithlessness of the Jews and the Gentiles. [Note: [Col. 0322C] Arnobius: “As if anyone should divide the Father, saying also the Son,” and so forth. Nicephorus expresses it more clearly: “If anyone divides the divinity, saying that the Father is God separately,” and so forth.]

“But if anyone divides God the Father, saying that there is God the Father, and God his Son, and God the Holy Spirit—three gods—and not one God because of the one divinity and power which we believe and know to be the true God of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and, removing the Son and the Holy Spirit, thinks that God the Father alone is to be called or believed to be the one God, let him be anathema. For the name ‘gods’ has been imposed and granted by God even upon angels and all the saints. But concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of their one and equal divinity, not the name ‘gods’ but the name ‘God’ is shown and indicated to us, so that we may believe that we are baptized only in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—not in the names of archangels or angels, as heretics, Jews, and even foolish Gentiles do. [Note: [Col. 0322C] He seems to be referring to the ancient Gnostics, who impiously and shamelessly corrupted and altered the baptismal formula handed down by Christ, as is clear from Irenaeus; we have also noted this in chapter 18 of his book."]

“This, then, is the salvation of Christians: that, believing in the Trinity—that is, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and having been baptized into it, we unquestionably believe the true and only one divinity, power, majesty, and substance of the same.”

## [Commentaries on the Psalms]

[Col. 0321]

### Notice by the Reverend Laurentius de la Barre concerning the Commentaries on the Psalms of David

He does not, as it seems, correctly attribute them to Arnobius the African.

Nothing certain is found concerning Arnobius’s origin except what Saint Jerome says in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* and in the appendix to Eusebius’s *Chronicle*: that in Africa he was a distinguished rhetorician and was regarded as a philosopher; that for several years at Sicca he trained young men—and Lactantius in particular—in declamation, until he was compelled by dreams to seek baptism. When he could not obtain it from the bishops, because they scarcely believed that one who had so often mocked the simplicity of Christians through his rhetorical art sincerely wished to profess the religion he had hitherto attacked, he, as a catechumen, labored through exceptionally eloquent books against his former religion. At last, after offering these books as pledges, he obtained the covenant of faith, in the year of the Lord 300, when Diocletian was reigning. The books that bear witness to his faith are those eight books *Against the Nations*—or rather seven, since Jerome, writing to Paulinus, does not mention an eighth. More recently, Balduinus demonstrated in a longer letter that the eighth book belongs to Minucius Felix, as will also be said in its proper place.

He also wrote Book I *On the Instruction of Rhetoric*, and some sort of brief annotations on passages from several Evangelists, beginning: “In the beginning was the Word.” While teaching at Rome he also wrote against the heresies a work cited by the Centuriators. Since all these writings are of lesser importance and scarcely display the talent of so great a man, we have readily passed them over. We have retained, however, together with that combatative disputation against the Gentiles, the *Commentaries on the Psalter*. Once a few things have been emended—things that perhaps entered through human carelessness or the violence of time—nothing is shorter or more learned, although certain men, among them Genensis in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca*, attempt by many arguments to take them away from Arnobius. They argue that these works are unpolished in diction, rhythm, and style, sometimes teeming with solecisms, and that heaven is no nearer to earth than these writings are to the seven books *Against the Gentiles*.

For this reason they suspect that there were two Arnobii, the later one being the interpreter of the Psalms. They prove this from the exposition of Psalm 109, in which Photinus, the restorer of the Ebionites, is refuted. As is clear from Book V of the *Tripartite History* and from Jerome, both in his *Catalogue* and in his *Chronicles*, Photinus began to teach the impiety of his doctrine in the year 358—that is, thirty years after Crispus Caesar, the son of Constantine the Great, had been killed. Lactantius Firmianus had trained Crispus in his youth.

They add another point: in the explanations of Psalms 108 and 117, the author attacks—or refutes—the heretical opinion of those who profess that God predestined some from eternity to blessing and rejected others to condemnation. It is established from two letters of Prosper and Hilary to Augustine that this assertion arose in Augustine’s own time, to such an extent that not a few holy men in Africa and Gaul complained that none of the ecclesiastical Fathers had ever held what Augustine was proclaiming, in a manner both novel and unprofitable, about the eternal distinction made by God between those predestined and those rejected.

He proceeds further and argues that this Arnobius lived in Augustine’s time because he dedicated his work to Laurentius and Rusticus, African bishops who perhaps are the men found together with Augustine at the Council of Carthage. For a certain Rusticus was present as a bishop in Africa, and Laurentius was bishop of Icosium and legate of the province of Mauretania.

He adds still more: that these *Commentaries* contain certain expressions commonly used everywhere among Africans in Augustine’s time. Thus, in the exposition of Psalm 131, where we read, “Upon him my sanctification shall flower,” *floriet*—“shall flower”—is a word that Augustine says was in the mouths of the populace in his own day, in Book II, chapter 13, of *On Christian Doctrine*. Likewise, in the explanation of Psalm 138, “My bone has been hidden”: the Africans themselves said *ossum meum*, “my bone”; Augustine says: “It is better that grammarians rebuke us than that the people fail to understand.”

But, to speak truthfully, nothing is established by these passages, since *floriet* was used by the Calaritan under Constantine, son of the Great;” Tertullian, who was older than the man of Calaris, also used similar expressions; and the translator of Irenaeus—or perhaps Irenaeus himself—used them as well.

Nor is it sufficient to summon chronology to our defense, since chronology offers no support; or style, which changes—or, as Quintilian says, dries out from day to day. For Saint Jerome himself, in his letter to Paulinus, does not adequately approve the seven books *Against the Gentiles*, which he criticizes as unequal in language and confused in the division of the whole work.

What if we say what is true: that Arnobius deliberately wished in these *Commentaries* to lower himself to the speech of the common people, so that, having laid aside every display of eloquence, he might declare himself a Christian with all his heart? Taking account of those with whom he was dealing, he wrote to different Gentiles in different styles: the Gentiles were led by the ornament of speech, whereas Christians, satisfied with bare truth, were addressed in a popular and humble manner. This is, by my faith, more than probable.

For when he saw Christians everywhere singing psalms in their sacred rites, he adapted himself somewhat to ordinary diction, so that people of every condition might understand to some extent what was being sung. He assumed the role of a teacher, not of an orator.

This is made clear by certain sermons and disputations delivered by Augustine to the people. It is evident from the circumstances themselves that Augustine did not write them, but that they were taken down by notaries, who recorded not only what was said but also what was done. If anyone should ask to have this fact pointed out to him with a finger, so that he might gain certain proof of it, let him read Augustine’s disputation with Maximus and compare the beginning of the disputation taken down by the notaries with the end of the work that Augustine himself described, where he says that Maximus withdrew from the disputation.

Let him read the two sermons in which Augustine clears his clergy of the rumor spread among the people. Let him read the speech in which, with the consent of the people, he designates the bishop who will succeed him and serve as his deputy in lesser matters. Let him read the song against the Donatists, which he composed to be sung publicly in the vernacular.

If anyone compares these works with what Augustine wrote for the learned—for example, *On the Trinity* and *The City of God*—he will easily understand how great the difference was between the speech of the educated and that of the unlearned multitude.

Nor, even at Rome, during the period when that language flourished most strongly, did everyone speak as Cicero spoke. Even then the common people claimed for themselves certain forms of speech by their own right, forms that educated men condemned.

Someone may say: “Why did it occur to Arnobius, a man of such eloquence, to entrust these *Commentaries* to plebeian language?”

First, in ancient times nothing was more popular than David’s Psalms. So popular were they that from them the plowman would sing something at the plow, the helmsman at the tiller, the sailor at the oar, the digger at the clod, the weaver at the warp, and the wife at the spindle. Finally, even infants would delight to sing something from them to their nurse before they knew how to speak.

Such was once everyone’s love for this divine music, which now even many Catholics disdain. Therefore Arnobius wished to be understood by everyone because he saw everyone singing. Christian charity persuaded him to do this, for charity strives to benefit as many as possible. He preferred, while stammering, to bring usefulness to many rather than to bring the praise of eloquence to a few.

The educated also understood this popular language, so that they too would not lose the benefit of mystical knowledge. Once that knowledge had been received, there was no need to demand rhetorical adornments.

Moreover, so that no suspicion might remain in the minds of simple Christians, who either hated or mistrusted that proud and artificially embellished eloquence, he laid aside in these *Commentaries* all the pomp of rhetoric at the command of two bishops, Rusticus and Laurentius, as he himself testifies in his preface.

He calls this obedience. Hence one may conjecture either that a catechumen is speaking or, at any rate, a recent Christian.

Therefore, if anyone considers for whom Arnobius was writing, he ought not to regard it as a solecism if something appears contrary to the more polished usage of speakers. Indeed, it would have been a solecism had he spoken otherwise.

For example, if someone today were to speak to the Roman populace as Saint Gregory once spoke, when popular speech was still less corrupted; or if someone speaking among the Spaniards were to use words contrary to the public usage of that nation, he would incur a double disadvantage. First, he would not be understood by those to whom he was speaking. Then, as a barbarian, he would offend and be mocked.

Thus this writer’s example offers no support to those who, while writing for educated people in a language that in our own age has no commerce with the populace, nevertheless wish to count it as praise that they overcome the ineptitude of their speech with foolish little sentences. For the chief force of eloquence lies in the discovery and arrangement of matters.

Even now, however, a clean simplicity should not be despised in a Christian writer, provided that, just as ornament and blandishment are absent, so too are filth and coarseness absent.

For Arnobius, if he were writing now, would not use the same solecisms. He would either write plainly in French if he were writing for the French populace, or pure Latin if he were writing for the educated.

The speech of the apostles was clearly of this kind—the speech in which they handed down the New Testament to us in writing. In that age charioteers and sailors spoke in this manner. Such was the language in which the books of the New Testament were first translated into Latin. If in those books certain solecisms do not offend educated ears, they should be attributed more to the accepted usage of those times than to the incompetence of the translators.

But just as it was appropriate then to write in that manner because the writing was addressed to the people, so now it is foolish to affect solecisms that benefit neither the unlearned nor the educated: they offend the latter, obscure the subject, and diminish the writer’s authority.

Moreover, just as it is sufficiently established that the people corrupted the purity of Roman speech, so it is likely that speech was corrupted differently among different nations and in different ages.

Certainly, we have detected two features in these *Commentaries* that Saint Aurelius Augustine testifies were commonly pronounced incorrectly by the people in his own age. In the commentary on Psalm 138, the author has *ossum* for *os*, “bone”—hence the genitive *ossis*, “of the bone,” and the plural *ossa*, “bones.” He also repeatedly uses *floriet* for *florebit*, “will flower,” and uses it in such a way that it is clear that this was not accidental. After saying *os*, “mouth,” he added, as if interpreting for the people, “that is, *ossum*.” For in the Greek the word is not στόμα (*stoma*), “mouth,” but ὀστέον (*osteon*), “bone.”

Thus popular speech is often more useful for signifying things than literary correctness. I would rather have someone say, with a barbarism, “My bone has not been hidden from you,” than have the meaning be less clear because the phrase is more Latin.

In Book II, chapter 13, of *On Christian Doctrine*, Augustine likewise says, while discussing faults of speech:

“That expression also which we can no longer remove from the mouths of the singing people—‘Upon him my sanctification shall flower’—takes nothing whatever away from the meaning. Yet the more skilled hearer would prefer that it be corrected, so that not *floriet* but *florebit* might be said. Nothing prevents the correction except the custom of those who sing.”

From this it may be gathered that these *Commentaries* were written both for Africans and in those ancient times. Perhaps it would also be useful to point out several other barbarisms, so that the reader, having been forewarned, may be less offended when he encounters them and may not immediately alter the text by suspecting that it has been corrupted by copyists.

The author frequently uses *poenitemini*, “you repent,” as a deponent verb. Likewise, he often uses *tribulantes*—literally, “those who afflict”—for those who are afflicted, not for those who afflict. Similarly, he uses *confundentes*—literally, “those who confound”—for those who are ashamed, as if *tribulari* and *confundi* were deponent verbs rather than passive ones.

He consistently treats *flos*, “flower,” and *ros*, “dew,” as neuter nouns, apparently following the form of *os*, “bone.” With the verbs *carere*, “to lack,” and *uti*, “to use,” he joins an accusative. He declines *manna* as *mannae*, just as we decline *anna* as *annae*. Following the example of the Greeks, he very often uses the nominative absolutely in place of the ablative, as in the commentary on Psalms 114 and 84.

Sometimes he joins a case not governed by the verb he is using but by the verb that he paraphrases. Thus, in Psalm 88, he has *memor esto apostolos*, “remember the apostles,” instead of *memento apostolos*.

He uses *attropare* in one place, evidently a word more common than correct in the speech of that time, for what would properly be *per tropologiam applicare*, “to apply by tropological interpretation.”

You will also occasionally find in him the word *paratura*, a word peculiar to Tertullian. Since Tertullian was older than Arnobius, he was likewise of the same nation.

Some similar features are encountered in Augustine’s books, especially those in which he spoke to the people—for example, *subdiacones* and *diacones*, “subdeacons” and “deacons,” and *baptismum*, “baptism,” treated as a neuter noun.

I have thought it worthwhile to record these things so that no one may find an erudite and pious work distasteful because of such faults of speech. Among those to whom the work was then written, these were not faults at all; had the author spoken otherwise, he would have been regarded as a barbarian.

Jerome does not mention this work in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Writers*. Perhaps the reason was that, since it was written in popular language, the book circulated only in Africa; or perhaps it was so familiar and so well worn in everyone’s hands that Jerome did not think it needed to be listed. Thus excessive fame caused certain works to be forgotten.

It is on a similar occasion that we now miss the titles of Origen’s works. We would likewise have remained ignorant of Tertullian’s books if God, more favorable to scholarly endeavors, had not recently brought part of them to light.

I shall offer another argument from which, apart from conjecture based on style, one may infer the antiquity of the writer. He mentions several heretics in passing—Manichaeus, Novatus, and Arius—but no one whose age was later than that of Arnobius. For it appears that the Arian heresy arose during his lifetime.

He flourished under the emperor Diocletian, around the three-hundred-and-twenty-ninth year of the world’s redemption. Yet he makes no mention of the Donatists or the Pelagians, although both plagues arose in Africa. The former clearly arose after his death, or when he was extremely old; the latter are known to have existed in Augustine’s time.

And yet this Arnobius discusses free will in one or two places. He would not have kept silent about Pelagius if Pelagius had been earlier.
