Since, then, it has been demonstrated that in the matters that alone could offend there is nothing that can or ought to cause difficulty; since the authority of Jerome and Trithemius commends the author so highly—only one of them mentions these *Commentaries*, on whose testimony Bede also relies in his exposition of the Psalms;” and since, finally, the work itself is commended by such great antiquity, I shall now briefly explain what has so powerfully carried me away into admiration of this volume.

First, it is universally acknowledged that among all the books of Sacred Scripture there is none more filled with obscure mysteries than the Book of Psalms. Nor, it seems to me, is there another book whose words are at once covered by greater darkness and more brilliantly illuminated. This combination shows the work to be that of a man equally learned, highly accomplished in eloquence, and deeply understanding the subject about which he speaks.

No one explains much in few words if he understands little. No one could bring something so obscure into clear expression unless he were thoroughly practiced in every method of speech.

Nowhere is he burdensome through the winding paths of prefaces and digressions. Everywhere he is a brilliant craftsman who hastens into the midst of things and, like a familiar guide, carries the hearer along—just as Flaccus praised Homer.

Nor is he ever ambitious in citing testimonies from the sacred books. Rather, his whole discourse is composed as though from emblems and tesserae of hidden Scripture. He frequently weaves together several verses from the psalm he is explaining, adding only a few words, so that even the verses he does not interpret may possess light. He reports them in such a way that the continuous and coherent flow of the discourse has its own grace.

Even in matters whose argument is plain—a task that is especially difficult—he teaches so openly that he allows nothing to grow cold in the affections. His discourse indicates more than it says, and, moving swiftly, leaves many thoughts and goads in the mind, so that one cannot tell whether it first causes one to understand or first carries one away.

This is not merely the mark of a learned man but also of one who loves what he teaches.

If something arises that must be drawn from the hidden histories of ancient things or from the books of those who wrote about the natures of animals or other matters, nothing is so obscure among pagan or even sacred writers that he does not indicate it in a few words. At the same time, he displays or parades no variety of learning—a habit that often troubles us even in writers of great renown.

He treats a truly sacred subject with something like apostolic simplicity and sincerity. He does not heap together extraneous material, nor anywhere do violence to divine Scripture. Whatever he adduces, one would say was born from the very passage.

He preferred to report the best things rather than the greatest number of things.

Although he abstains from jokes, which the seriousness of his subject did not permit, one nevertheless senses throughout his diction a constant cheerfulness and pleasantness. He nowhere grows weary or falls asleep; he always lifts up and refreshes the reader with the energy of his language.

He begins in such a way that he immediately refreshes; he hastens in such a way that sleep cannot creep in; he ends in such a way that he leaves the reader still thirsty and desiring more.

Now, since certain things are mixed into the books of Tertullian, Origen, and all the ancients that either contain manifest error or render their doctrines suspect, this author regulates his pen everywhere so carefully that I have found nothing in him anywhere akin to any heresy.

When he writes in the commentary on Psalm 14, “Jesus, the immaculate one, alone entered the virginal chamber and freed the tabernacle itself from carnal stains,” he is not speaking of stains that existed in Mary before Christ’s entrance, but of those that are accustomed to exist in other women, from which Christ preserved his Mother immune, increasing rather than violating her chastity.

Indeed, he appears to pay this honor to the Roman Church: that whoever is alienated from it is outside the Catholic Church, and is an exile from the true faith or an expelled deserter from the Church that holds primacy over the whole Church and that merited Peter, the chief of the apostles, as its shepherd. This passage occurs in the commentary on Psalm 106.

In the commentary on Psalm 138 he teaches that Christ granted an exceptional authority to Peter, who had denied him three times—clearly speaking of the authority to feed the sheep.

He mentions vows several times, but only those by which, in baptism, we professed Christ and renounced the world and Satan. I do not think that he despised other vows; rather, he regarded these as pre-eminent.

Nor do I doubt that in these little *Commentaries* he was assisted by the diligence of Origen, who published commentaries on no work of Sacred Scripture more frequently than on the Psalter. In several passages the author shows that he knew Greek.

I shall give one example of this in the commentary on Psalm 77. An ignorant scribe had written: “because ears in making.” Since these words conveyed absolutely no meaning, and I had long tormented myself over them, I guessed that what had actually been written was *quod auxesin faciens*, “which produces amplification.” For in many manuscripts the form of the letter *x* does not differ greatly from *r*. Thus a scribe entirely ignorant of Greek and scarcely educated in Latin had made *aures in*—“ears in”—out of *auxesin*.

Likewise, in the commentary on Psalm 105, the text read: “Let him receive the rule of repentance, with the new excluded, so that Psalm 105, etc.” By conjecture we restored it as: “with Novatus, or Novatian, excluded.” For both belonged to the same heresy, and neither admitted the penitent.

He is chiefly occupied, however, with explaining the sense that pertains to evangelical history, so that, as the Apostle Paul writes, the knowledge of Christ may be confirmed in us ever more deeply, “from faith to faith,” while we see that whatever we read as having happened in the Gospel writings was foretold in the Psalms.

This is truly the most difficult part of the task of interpretation. Once it has been rightly understood, those accustomed to the meanings found in mystical writings easily divine the remaining senses from it alone.

But, to bring this to an end at last: these *Commentaries* were brought forth from the venerable monastery situated between Worms, the city of the Vangiones, and Speyer, the city of the Nemetes, commonly called Frankenthal, around the time when Adrian VI was raised to the summit of the Roman pontificate.

[Col. 0327]

# ARNOBIUS THE YOUNGER’S COMMENTARIES ON THE PSALMS (C)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0327C]

Arnobius to the most beloved Fathers, the bishops Leontius and Rusticus.

No one is unaware that silence is a good thing. Yet silence is then judged contrary when the authority of one who commands compels us to speak. If it is permitted for you to command, it is not permitted for us to disregard you.

It is not presumption but obedience that leads us to strive to strike the veins of the Psalter rather than to open them fully. We consider that no thirsty person becomes angry with those preparing water.

Let others prepare honey fragrant with living sweetness; let others offer cups filled with nectarous liquids. We, striking the earth here and there with the thrust of our mouth’s hoe, open David’s stream—however thinly—to those suffering thirst, so that the thirsty may drink.

But let those who, with the apostles, were drunk in the Holy Spirit at the third hour of the day rejoice and flourish; nevertheless, let them permit no obstacle to be placed before those who thirst. For those overflowing with wine do not prevent those who wish to drink water.

Therefore let all readers make peace with us, even if they approve you as rustic Catholics. Let them first examine the psalm whose explanation they are reading, so that when they have read its meaning they may recognize that it belongs to the psalm to which the text of the explanation points.

You yourselves, who command this work, could have done it better. For you show not your inability but your preoccupations, since what you command us to do you yourselves would have been able to fulfill more effectively.

[Col. 0328C]

## PSALM I

*A Psalm of David.*

Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night.

He shall be like a tree planted beside channels of waters, which will yield its fruit in its season. Its leaf shall not fall, and everything he does shall prosper.

Not so the ungodly, not so; but they are like dust that the wind drives from the face of the earth. Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the ungodly shall perish.

[Col. 0328D]

### COMMENTARY

The first psalm restores blessedness precisely from the point at which it teaches that blessedness was lost.

Adam walked in the counsel of the ungodly—that is, in the counsel of the serpent and the woman. And now our Adam, that is, our consent, will be blessed if it does not walk in the counsel of the serpent and the woman—that is, in the counsel of the flesh and the devil.

Or, if it has walked there, let it not stand there; if it has stood, let it not sit—that is, let it not remain—but, remembering the law of God, let it occupy its will there.

Let it exercise both its daily and nightly activity in meditation on the divine law, so that what Adam lost by despising, this man may find by guarding. Let him remain beside the streams of the law, like a tree receiving immortality as the tree of life.

Then, at last, everything he does shall prosper.

But for them—that is, for the ungodly—it will be otherwise. They have despised. “Not so,” but this will happen to them at the end of the age, which the prophetic word threatens at the end of the psalm: eternal glory to him who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM II

*A Psalm of David.*

Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on empty things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.

“Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.”

He who dwells in the heavens shall laugh at them, and the Lord shall mock them. Then he will speak to them in his anger, and in his fury he will trouble them.

“But I have been appointed king by him over his holy mountain of Zion, proclaiming his commandment.”

The Lord said to me: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.”

And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling. Take hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way. When his anger is kindled in a little while, blessed are all who trust in him.

[Col. 0328D]

### COMMENTARY

To this day the nations rage against Christ, who brought an end to idols. For when the Lord entered Egypt, the idols of the temples fell, in accordance with the prophet Isaiah, chapter 19, who uses these words: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud and shall enter Egypt, and its idols shall be shaken before him” (Chrysostom, *On Matthew* II; Anselm, *Leviticus* XI and XIX).

The peoples—that is, the Jews—meditate on empty things, observing distinctions of foods and the sabbath festivals. The bonds of both must be broken. Meanwhile God, the inhabitant of heaven, laughs at them, but in judgment he will show his anger and fury to those to whom he will say:

“Although you denied me, the Father’s voice from heaven taught you that I am the Son of God when, after I had been placed in the Jordan, he said: ‘You are my Son.’”

When he said, “Today,” God did not mean yesterday or tomorrow, but an eternal today. For times take place under him; he does not take place under times.

The prophet teaches that Mount Zion is the Church when he says: “I, the Lord, will raise up Zion among the nations, and I will give her as an eternal festival to every nation.”

In her, therefore, the Son proclaims the Father’s commandment. In her he will rule the nations as with an iron rod. For he neither yields to the powerful of the world nor despises the faces of the wretched.

She commands kings to fear. She promises the coming anger to those who despise her, through which she threatens destruction to earthen vessels. She promises blessedness to those who trust.

All this is offered by Christ, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM III

*A Psalm of David, when he fled from the face of Absalom his son.*

Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me. Many say to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God.”

But you, Lord, are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head. With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain.

I slept and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord received me. I shall not fear the thousands of people surrounding me.

Rise, Lord; save me, my God. For you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners.

Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people.

[Col. 0330B]

### COMMENTARY

We explain the title of the third psalm in a single statement.

Absalom persecuted his father and was caught by the neck in a branch. Judas betrayed the Lord and was strangled by a noose. Just as the history indicates David’s past suffering, so the mystery announces the Lord’s future Passion.

In that Passion all denied him, saying: “There is no salvation for him in his God.” “If he is from God, let God deliver him,” they said, while the godless and obstinate Jews mocked him and treated him with many insults and reproaches.

But Jesus cried out to God with his voice and was heard, so that he received death as though it were sleep. Rising from it, he feared no longer. Now, putting on incorruption in place of corruption and immortality in place of mortality (1 Cor. 15), he does not fear the many thousands of people surrounding him.

For this is the salvation of the Lord, and it is upon us who are his people. This is his blessing, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM IV

[Col. 0330C]

*For the end, among the songs; a Psalm of David.*

When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me. In tribulation you enlarged me. Have mercy on me and hear my prayer.

Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous, and the Lord will hear me when I cry to him.

Be angry and do not sin. What you say in your hearts, be pierced with remorse upon your beds. Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord.

Many say: “Who shows us good things?” The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us. You have given gladness in my heart.

They have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil. In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same place. For you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.

[Col. 0330D]

### COMMENTARY

The title of the fourth psalm is given “among the songs,” that is, among the mysteries.

In these mysteries the God of righteousness heard his Son, placed upon the cross. Against him the Jews grow angry and sin to this day. They would not sin by growing angry if the one whom they denied were not truly the Son of God.

This happened to them because they did not sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness like Abel, but like Cain, whose sacrifice arose from ill will and envy.

But we who believe should say to the Lord: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us.” In this light gladness was given to our hearts from the time when we received grain in the body, wine in the blood, and oil in the chrism.

By offering peace, we received these things, because they were uniquely established in hope by the Lord in Christ Jesus, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM V

*For the end, for her who receives the inheritance; a Psalm of David.*

Receive my words with your ears, Lord; understand my cry. Attend to the voice of my prayer, my king and my God.

For to you I shall pray, Lord. In the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you and see, because you are not a God who wills iniquity.

The wicked shall not dwell beside you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes. You hate all who work iniquity; you will destroy all who speak falsehood.

The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit. But I, in the abundance of your mercy, shall enter your house. I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear.

Lord, lead me in your righteousness because of my enemies; direct my way in your sight. For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is empty.

Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully. Judge them, O God. Let them fall from their thoughts according to the multitude of their ungodliness; drive them out, because they have provoked you, Lord.

And let all who hope in you rejoice; they shall exult for ever, and you shall dwell in them. All who love your name shall glory in you, because you will bless the righteous, Lord. You have crowned us with the shield of your good will.

[Col. 0331B]

### COMMENTARY

The title of the fifth psalm reveals the inheritance which Christ receives. He bestowed this inheritance upon the Church when he said to the apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14).

The title therefore declares that this peace—which, as we said at the end of the fourth psalm, was uniquely established in hope by the Lord—was given as an inheritance to the Church.

An inheritance is succession to the whole right that the deceased possessed at the time of death (*L. Haereditas*, *Digest*, “On the Meaning of Things and Words”). Hence Paul says: “If we are children of God, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8).

An inheritance arises for children from the death of a parent. For unless Christ had died, this inheritance would not have been opened. It was therefore born when he died, confirmed when he rose again, and remains eternal when he ascended into heaven.

There are three things in the title: the one dying, the inheritance, and the heirs. At the beginning of the psalm there are likewise three things composed by the heir: words, a cry, and a prayer.

The words ask to be received by the ears, the cry to be understood, and the prayer to be heard.

The psalm itself says: “I shall pray to you, Lord,” namely, in the morning, when I shall have cast away the works of darkness and put on the armor of light (Rom. 13). Then I shall pray to you as one placed in the morning, when the darkness has diminished and the increase of light grows.

“In the morning I shall stand before you and see.” But what will you see? Tell us promptly. In the morning I shall see the apostles, the shining angels, and the rejoicing Marys announcing that the Lord has risen.”

We said that the Lord should be prayed to in the morning, after the darkness of sins has passed; we said that he should be seen rising in the light of the Lord’s day.

But what sort of Lord he is is expressed by the distinction of his will. “You are,” he says, “a God who does not will iniquity.”

Who had said that he willed iniquity? Without doubt, the Jews, who, rebuking the Lord for works of mercy, said: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath” (John 9).

But this man is from God, and he himself is God, who does not will iniquity. The wicked shall not dwell beside him—that is, the unbelieving people—and they shall not remain before his eyes.

Those who work iniquity are hateful to him, and those who speak falsehood perish. For everyone who denies Jesus the Son of God is a liar.

But whoever confesses him enters the house of God and worships toward the holy temple—not in stone, but in the Spirit.

The Lord will lead him in his righteousness because of his enemies, to direct his way in his sight. Why “because of his enemies”? Because his enemies show another way, which leads to death; for their sake he directs this way, which leads to life (Matt. 7).

When believers reach it, they shall exult for ever, and he will dwell in them. All who love his name shall glory in him. For there is the one who blesses the righteous and crowns him with the shield of his good will.

By one and the same action you are defended from enemies when you believe and crowned by the Lord, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM VI
In the end, with songs, for the eighth; a psalm of David.

O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled. [Col. 0332C] My soul too is greatly troubled; but you, Lord—how long? Turn back, Lord, and rescue my soul; save me for the sake of your mercy. For no one in death remembers you; in the underworld, who will confess you? I have labored in my groaning; every night I wash my bed, and with my tears I water my couch. My eye is troubled by anger; I have grown old among all my enemies. Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my supplication; the Lord has received my prayer. Let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled; let them turn back and be exceedingly, very quickly ashamed.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0332D]

The title of the sixth psalm expresses the Lord’s Day. It is the eighth when it comes to an end, and the first when it begins. For in the fifth, it begins in the morning at the resurrection—that is, at the consecration of our baptism; now, in the restoration of repentance, it is the eighth. For the sevenfold Spirit is satisfied by the eighth. The penitent therefore acts so that he may not be rebuked in anger, but may obtain mercy here, while placed in this body.

In the underworld, however, confession bears no fruit at all. Therefore the one who wishes to be saved here labors in his groaning and washes his bed every night. He washes, I say, the bed at night which he had defiled at night; and lest you should suppose that he draws just any water with which to cleanse it, he says: “With my tears I will water it.” Why? Because my eye is troubled [Col. 0333A] by anger. I have heard that eternal fire is imminent and that the anger of the just avenger presses upon me. Therefore I am troubled, because I lingered in my sins and grew old among all my enemies.

Now, renouncing evil habits and unclean spirits, I will say: “Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity,” because the one who forgave sins—the one, I say, who heard the voice of my weeping and received my prayer—said to me: “Behold, you have been saved; sin no more” (John 5). Let the vices that have hitherto lied depart from me. Let them be turned back and be exceedingly, very quickly ashamed, through the Son of God, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM VII

In the end, a psalm of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning the [Col. 0333B] words of Cush the son of Jemini.

O Lord my God, in you I have hoped; save me from all who pursue me and deliver me. Lest he seize my soul like a lion, when there is no one to redeem or save. O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands; if I have repaid evil to those who repaid me evil, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies. May the enemy pursue my soul, overtake it, and trample my life into the earth, and bring my glory down into the dust.

Arise, Lord, in your anger, and rise up at the borders of my enemies. Arise, Lord my God, according to the commandment that you gave; and the assembly of the peoples will surround you. And for its sake return on high; the Lord judges the peoples. Judge me, Lord, according to my justice and according to my [Col. 0333C] innocence concerning me. Let the wickedness of sinners come to an end, and you will direct the just, O God, who searches hearts and kidneys. My just help is from the Lord, who saves the upright in heart.

God is a just judge, strong and patient; will he be angry every day? Unless you turn back, he has brandished his sword, bent his bow, and made it ready. And in it he has prepared instruments of death; he has made his arrows fiery. Behold, he labors with injustice, conceives sorrow, and gives birth to iniquity. He opened a pit, dug it out, and fell into the pit that he made. His sorrow will turn back upon his own head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown. I will confess to the Lord according to his justice, and sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0333D]

When David’s young men had announced that they could kill Absalom, and David said, “Spare him,” David himself fled from his presence. Then Shimei appeared against him, a member of Saul’s kin, and, throwing stones after him, called him a man of blood. When they wished to kill him, David said: “Do not. Behold, the one who came forth from my loins is fighting against me. And you are surprised that the son of Shimei, from Saul’s tribe, is against me.”

Thus David spared this man, just as he had spared Saul; sparing also his tyrant son, he prays to be delivered from those who pursue him, declaring that he had not done what the other man accused him of doing, and certainly had not repaid evil to those who repaid him evil. “But if I have repaid evil for evil,” he says, “let the enemy seize my soul and bring my glory [Col. 0334A] down into the dust.” These events are read in historical narrative in the Book of Kings, through its conclusion.

Here, however, let us sing the mysteries of Christ, against whom, repaying good with evil, they cried out that he was guilty of death (Matthew 26). To him, therefore, the Church cries: “Arise in your anger,” and let us see what he will do in anger. “Rise up,” he says, “at the borders of your enemies.” But when the ungrateful perceive the Lord angry, they put an end to their impieties; and when their hostilities have ended, God is exalted at the borders of his enemies.

“Arise according to the commandment that you gave.” For you said: “On the third day I will rise, and I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me” (Matthew 28). Therefore, he says, arise according to the commandment that you gave. And after you have shown yourself to the Synagogue, lest it think that you are again arousing war, for its sake judge the peoples. When you have given judgment, [Col. 0334B] the wickedness of sinners will come to an end, and the just will be directed.

For you do not pronounce sentence for the condemnation or praise of another, since you see hearts and contemplate the secrets of the kidneys; you will save all who are upright in heart. But God is revealed as judge for those who are not upright in heart, preparing his earth for those who will not turn back.

For the righteousness of the Jews, placed in anguish of spirit, labored when it saw the Lord being worshiped by the multitude because of the power of his signs. It conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity, saying: “Crucify the one guilty of death” (Matthew 26). It therefore prepared a pit for Christ, but fell into the pit that it had made. Its sorrow turned upon its own head, and its iniquity descended upon its crown.

But when Christ rose from the dead, we confess the justice of God; and when he ascended, [Col. 0334C] we sing praise to his Most High name, penetrating the height that is above all the heavens. Through this deed every knee bows and every tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2). To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM VIII

In the end, for the winepresses; a psalm of David.

O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth! For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise, because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and avenger. For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you founded. What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man [Col. 0334D] that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field; the birds of the heavens and the fish of the sea, which pass along the paths of the sea. O Lord, our Lord, how wondrous is your name in all the earth!

## COMMENTARY

The title is fixed in the eighth psalm not for one winepress but for many winepresses. These winepresses are the voices of all the prophets, which were fulfilled when the true vine was planted by the instruments of the nails and, placed upon the wood of the cross, was struck by the spear in its side. [Col. 0335A] It poured out such power in these winepresses that the wondrous name of the Lord was proclaimed not only in Judea but throughout the whole earth.

This was confirmed when his majesty was exalted above the heavens, so that not only lawful ages but also infants and nursing children might burst forth in his praise, and that people might be destroyed who, by defending God, acted against God. For this is the people that is both God’s defender and God’s enemy: a defender in the Father, an enemy in the Son. But whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either (1 John 2).

Whoever confesses both sees that the heavens are his works of the fingers, and that he himself founded the moon and the stars. For what would man be unless he had been remembered by him, and unless he had come and taught such perfection that he made human beings, placed here in the flesh, a little [Col. 0335B] lower than the angels in heaven, granting them power of virtues and even giving them power to raise the dead? He subjected everything to the believing human being, so that he said: “I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10).

When he says “sheep,” he names the simple; “oxen,” those who labor under the Lord’s yoke; “the beasts of the field,” the lay people; “the birds of heaven,” those who think lofty thoughts; and “the fish of the sea,” those who search out the depths. Having all these subjected through Christ’s Passion, the Church confesses his wondrous name throughout the whole earth. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM IX

In the end, for the hidden things of the Son; a psalm of David.

[Col. 0335C]

I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders. I will rejoice and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, Most High. When my enemy is turned back, he will be weakened and perish before your face. For you have carried out my judgment and my cause; you sat upon the throne, judging justice. You rebuked the nations, and the impious perished; you erased their name forever and for ages of ages. The enemies’ swords have failed completely, and you have destroyed their cities. Their memory perished with a crash, but the Lord remains forever. He prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world in equity; he will judge the peoples in justice.

The Lord became a refuge for the poor, a helper in times of need and tribulation. Let those who know your name hope in you, for you have not abandoned those who seek [Col. 0335D] you, Lord. Sing praise to the Lord who dwells in Zion; proclaim his pursuits among the nations. For when seeking their blood, he remembered them; he did not forget the cry of the poor.

Have mercy on me, Lord; see my humiliation because of my enemies. You who raise me from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion. I will exult in your salvation. The nations have been fixed in the destruction they made; in this snare that they concealed, their foot has been caught. The Lord will be known when he executes judgments; the sinner has been caught in the works of his hands.

Let sinners turn back into the underworld, all the nations that forget God. For the poor will not be forgotten forever; the patience of the poor will not perish to the end. Arise, [Col. 0336A] Lord; let man not grow strong. Let the nations be judged before your face. Set over them, Lord, a lawgiver, so that the nations may know that they are human beings.

Why, Lord, have you withdrawn far away? Why do you despise in times of need and tribulation? While the impious man grows proud, the poor is set on fire; they are caught in the schemes they devise. For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed. The sinner has provoked the Lord; according to the abundance of his anger he will not seek him. God is not before his eyes; his ways are defiled at all times. Your judgments are removed from his sight; he will dominate all his enemies.

For he said in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.” His mouth is full of cursing, bitterness, and deceit; beneath his tongue are toil and sorrow. [Col. 0336B] He sits in ambush with the rich in hidden places, to kill the innocent. His eyes look upon the poor; he lies in wait secretly like a lion in his den. He lies in wait to seize the poor, to seize the poor while he draws him toward himself. In his snare he humbled him; he bowed down and will fall when he has mastered the poor.

For he said in his heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned his face away so that he may not see to the end.” Arise, Lord God; let your hand be exalted, and do not forget the poor. Why has the impious provoked God? For he said in his heart: “He will not seek.” You see, however, that you consider toil and sorrow, so that you may deliver them into your hands. To you the poor is abandoned; you will be the helper of the orphan.

Break the arm of the sinner and the wicked man; his sin will be sought, and it will not be found. The Lord will reign forever and for ages [Col. 0336C] of ages; you nations will perish from his land. The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart. Judge the orphan and the humble, so that man may no longer presume to magnify himself upon the earth.

## COMMENTARY

The ninth psalm teaches the hidden things of the Son in the sacrament of the holy creed. Whoever receives the faith hidden in the mystery first confesses it not with superficial lips but with his whole heart, and recounts all his wonders. He no longer rejoices in passing and perishable things, but says to the Lord: “I will rejoice and exult in you, and I will sing praise to your name, Most High,” because you have carried out my judgment—that is, you have judged on my behalf—and I have obtained my cause; you sat upon the throne to pronounce judgment. [Col. 0336D]

You rebuked us for being nations, and the impious devil perished, whom we worshiped in idols. You erased the name of the idols forever and for ages of ages. There they failed completely before the sword of your word, and you destroyed their cities. When their temples were being destroyed throughout the whole world, nearly every city was destroyed in its temples. For just as the churches established throughout the world are the cities of the saints, so the temples established throughout the world are known to be the cities of demons.

Their memory perished with a crash, while the Lord, remaining forever, prepared his seat in judgment to judge the world in equity. You do not receive the Lord in one way and the servant in another; rather, disregarding the persons of the rich, you became more truly a refuge for the poor, namely, for those who know [Col. 0337A] your name. For you will not abandon all poor people indiscriminately, but you will not abandon those who seek you, Lord.

Let us therefore sing praise to the Lord who dwells in Zion—that is, in the Church exalted by catholic definitions—and there let us proclaim his wonders. In her, while seeking the blood of his martyrs, the Lord is daily remembered by us, nor does he forget the prayer of the poor man who says to him: “See my humiliation, born from the hostilities of demons; raise me from the gates of death, lifting my heart away from the desires of the flesh, so that I may proclaim all your praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion and exult in your salvation.”

For the nations have been fixed in the destruction they made, worshiping the work of their hands. They will turn back into the underworld because they forget the Lord, who does not forget the poor forever and whose patience will not perish [Col. 0337B] to the end.

Now the spirit of prophecy asks that the Lord arise against human strength, so that he may judge the nations before his face; that he may remove them from idols and establish them in the Church. Let him appoint a lawgiver over them, and let the nations know that those whom they worship are not gods but that they themselves are human beings.

“Why,” he says, “have you withdrawn far away, so that you despise us in times of need and tribulation?” While the impious grows proud, the poor is set on fire. For in every judgment where poor and rich are heard, when the rich man grows proud, the poor man is inflamed. Everyone rebukes the poor man, while they praise the other—even though he is a sinner in the desires of his soul—and bless him even when he acts wickedly.

This is the sinner who provokes the Lord. For when one not only is not rebuked for acting wickedly but is even blessed, if he is questioned about anything, he makes inquiry according to the abundance of his anger. God is not before his eyes; his way is polluted at all times. Your judgments withdraw from his sight, and he dominates all his enemies, so that he says in his heart: “I shall not be moved from generation to generation, without evil.” His mouth is full of curses and contains nothing gentle. Against the poor, the labor of his tongue is directed. He sits in ambush with other rich men for no other purpose than to kill the innocent, since the rich make these plans among themselves in order to catch the innocent in their snare.

Therefore we must continually cry out: “Arise, Lord, and let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor forever,” so that, although the impious has provoked the Lord and said in his heart, “God will not seek,” he nevertheless does seek and considers everything. Acting patiently, he waits [Col. 0337D] to deliver them into his hands and take them from the hands of demons.

For the poor man is abandoned to him. Those whom everyone despises, they undoubtedly abandon to God; and to the orphan who has no father, he himself becomes a helper. He crushes the arm of the devil, who through the Pharisees sought some sin with which to accuse the Lord, but found none.

The Lord reigns forever and ever, and the nations will perish from his land. The Lord has heard the desire of the poor, and his ear has heard the desires of their hearts, so that the orphan and the humble may be judged in his Church, and so that man may no longer presume to magnify himself upon the earth—through the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0338A]

## PSALM X

In the end, a psalm of David.

In the Lord I trust. How can you say to my soul: “Flee to the mountain like a sparrow”? For behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. For they have destroyed what you accomplished; but what has the just man done? The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven. His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the sons of men. The Lord examines the just and the impious, but whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul. He rains snares upon sinners; fire, sulfur, and the spirit of storms are the portion of their cup. For the Lord is just, and he has loved justice; his face has seen equity.

[Col. 0338B]

## COMMENTARY

It could have been said to David that, like a sparrow, he should seek the inaccessible shelter of a mountain at the time when sinners were bending their bows against him—whether Saul, or his own Absalom, or innumerable enemies. But drawing these matters also toward our own edification, let us hear the counsels of the saints. Setting ascents in our hearts, let us migrate from the valley of weeping to the mountain, lest those who prepared their arrows in the quiver find us exposed in the open plain, so that they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart.

Here he used “darkness” for “hiddenness.” Those who destroy what the Lord accomplished are the ones who seek to shoot at the upright in heart. And we suffer these things because of our sins: why is the just man afflicted? Why is the just man [Col. 0338C] wearied? Why is he struck? What evil did he do? The Lord is the spotless Lamb, whom you, supposing him to be some ordinary man, handed over to human judgment.

But he is in his holy temple—that is, God is in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5). In this holy temple, having taken flesh from the immaculate Virgin, he sits in heaven at the right hand of the Father, and his throne is in heaven.

His eyes look upon the poor, to examine the just and the impious. Although sinners claim glory for themselves in this age, when judgment begins to be set in motion they will have such rain upon them as the Psalmist records: fire, sulfur, and the spirit of tempest. For then the Lord will be just, though now he is merciful; and he will see equity, though now he regards iniquity.

After his judgment [Col. 0338D] there will be no sin, nor possibility of sin, nor desire for sin, but eternal glory—he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XI

In the end, a psalm of David, for the eighth.

Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed; for truths have diminished among the sons of men. Each has spoken vain things to his neighbor; with lips of deceit and a divided heart they have spoken. May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue. They said: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips belong to us; who is our lord?” Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, “Now I will arise,” says the Lord. “I will place him in salvation; I will act confidently in him.” The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold. You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever. The impious walk around; according to your exaltation you have multiplied the sons of men.

## COMMENTARY

Again, the eleventh psalm is placed “for the eighth,” that is, for the Lord’s Day. “Save me, Lord”—that is, arise from the dead—“for the holy one has failed”: the one who believed in you has failed, and truths have diminished among the sons of men.

Behold, they even offer money to the guardians of your body, saying: “Tell people that he was stolen by his disciples” (Matthew 28). But by saying these things the Lord destroys deceitful lips [Col. 0339B] and the boastful tongue. They say: “We will magnify our tongue; our lips belong to us”—that is, “We will persuade people that he was stolen; we will arrange these things among ourselves.”

They had already said this about him when they saw the inscription, “King of the Jews.” They had said: “Who is our lord? We have Caesar as lord” (John 19). But because of the misery of the needy, for whom I suffered, “Now I will arise,” says the Lord. “And I will place him in my salvation and act confidently in him.” “Confidently” means without the capacity for suffering, yielding to no fear.

Believing these things, the Church sings in the apostles the words of the Lord. They are so true and pure that they are like silver purified by fire sevenfold. Therefore, Lord, because they said to me, “He is not our lord,” you, Lord, will preserve us and guard us [Col. 0339C] from this generation and forever.

For just as, when you humbled yourself, truths diminished among the sons of men, so when you ascended into heaven, according to your exaltation you multiplied the sons of men, so that those who had been diminished in your descent might be multiplied in your ascent—he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XII

In the end, a psalm of David.

How long, Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face away from me? How long shall I place counsels in my soul, sorrow in my heart by day? How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, Lord my God. Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death, lest my enemy say: “I have prevailed against him.” Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved; but I have hoped in your mercy. My heart has exulted in your salvation; I will sing to the Lord, who has repaid me with good, and I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High.

## COMMENTARY

From the time when the enemy of the human race obtained dominion over humankind through the transgression of the first man, the human race incurred divine forgetfulness. This forgetfulness, as I have said, occurred not through passion but through aversion, and seemed to leave exaltation to the enemy over the human race.

Yet because the coming of the Son of God was promised to exclude these adversities, the prophetic song, in the person of the whole human race, entreats him to look upon, hear, and enlighten the eyes that had fallen asleep in death, so that the devil may not say: “I have prevailed; I have obtained dominion, and I shall be lord forever.”

“Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am moved”—that is, if I despair. “My heart has exulted in your salvation,” that is, in the Lord Jesus Christ, your Son. To him I will sing, for he will repay me with good; I will praise and sing to his Most High name, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XIII

In the end, a psalm of David.

The fool said in his heart: “There is no God.” They have been corrupted and have become detestable in their pursuits; there is no one who does good, not even one. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the sons of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one.

Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they acted deceitfully; the poison of asps is beneath their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

Will they not know, all who practice iniquity, who devour my people like food, like bread? They have not called upon the Lord; there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. For the Lord is with the just generation; you have confounded the counsel of the poor, because the Lord is his hope.

Who will give salvation to Israel from Zion? When the Lord turns back the captivity of his people, Jacob will rejoice and Israel will be glad.

## COMMENTARY

The coming of the Lord, requested in the twelfth psalm, is presented in the thirteenth. But when the unbelieving people see him humble in appearance, they say in their heart: “There is no God.” Among this people all turned aside; together they became useless and devoured God’s people as though they were food, like bread.

And while persecuting the Lord himself and his apostles, there they trembled with fear where there was no fear. They observed sabbaths and the baptisms of cups and pitchers, while, as we have said, persecuting the Son of God and his disciples. They confessed that they had Abraham as father and relied on descent, not on righteousness.

But the Lord is in the just generation. Those who confounded the counsel of the poor did not consider that the Lord is his hope. Although for our sake he became poor, he himself is the one who gave salvation to Israel from Zion. Salvation did not arise from the synagogue of Satan but from Zion, which is the Lord’s Church. Through it the Lord turned back the captivity of his people, so that Jacob may rejoice in his conversion and Israel may exult in Christ Jesus, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XIV

In the end, a psalm of David.

Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain? The one who enters without blemish and practices justice; who speaks truth in his heart and has not acted deceitfully with his tongue; who has done no evil to his neighbor and has not accepted reproach against his neighbors; who regards the wicked as nothing, but glorifies those who fear the Lord; who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive; who has not given his money at interest and has not accepted gifts against the innocent. Whoever does these things will not be shaken forever.

## COMMENTARY

Every blameless person enters the Lord’s tabernacle, and there becomes blameless. But Jesus alone, blameless, entered the virginal chamber; he freed the tabernacle itself from carnal stains and gave sanctification rather than receiving it.

Since the whole Law is contained in the summary of the Decalogue, he expressed its ten forms in this psalm, by which he is shown to have taught what he was proved to have done. By entering the tabernacle, he freed it from the stains of buyers and sellers, and practiced justice by placing human salvation before sabbath observance.

He spoke truth in his heart, thinking of nothing except the Father’s will. He did not act deceitfully with his tongue, since from his tongue there came speech that gave light to the blind, healing to the sick, and life to the dead.

He did not accept reproach against his neighbor. Indeed, he received even Judas with a kiss. The wicked was regarded as nothing in his sight, since he prohibited the doing of good. But he magnified those who fear the Lord so greatly that he gave them power to become children of God (John 1).

He swore to his neighbor and did not deceive him. What did he swear? Certainly what he promised when he said: “Amen, I say to you, if you remain in my words, I will no longer call you servants but friends” (John 15). Everything he promised, he did not withhold from the neighbor who believed in him.

He did not lend his money at interest. His money was the virtues of healings, which he exercised without receiving anything from anyone; moreover, he instructed his disciples in the same way when he gave them power to heal the sick and raise the dead, saying: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10).

He not only did not accept gifts against the innocent; he himself gave himself as a redemption for all (1 Timothy 2). After completing these ten signs of virtue, he showed from heaven that perfection had been fulfilled and added, saying: “Whoever does these things”—that is, whoever imitates him—“will not be shaken forever.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XV

The inscription of the title belongs to David himself.

Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you. I said to the Lord: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods.” To the saints who are in his land he has made all my desires wondrous in them. Their infirmities have multiplied; afterward they hastened. I will not gather their assemblies from blood, nor will my lips remember their names.

The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance [Col. 0342A] to me. The measuring lines have fallen for me among splendid things; indeed, my inheritance is splendid for me. I will bless the Lord who has given me understanding; even through the night my kidneys have corrected me. I kept the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.

Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh will rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will fill me with joy in your presence; delights are at your right hand forever.

## COMMENTARY

From the fifty-fifth psalm through the fifty-ninth, all the psalms have title inscriptions, [Col. 0342B] but not pure ones. This psalm alone is preceded by a title inscription, by which it is shown to have been sung more for mystical understanding than for historical interpretation. In it we perceive the perfect man Jesus of Nazareth, going to his Passion, pouring out the prayer of this psalm.

Although God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (2 Corinthians 5), he was nevertheless subject to the conditions of suffering, for he was moved both by fear and by sorrow. Therefore, addressing and worshiping the Divinity, he says: “Preserve me, Lord, for I have hoped in you.” He was not led into arrogance, nor did he proudly take pride in his blameless conscience; rather, he said to the Lord: “You are my God.” And although all my works, words, and thoughts are good, nevertheless you who assumed me have no need of my goods. [Col. 0342C]

For the man was not assumed out of God’s necessity; rather, God was received because of the human being’s necessity. This man, assumed by God, made all his desires wondrous among all the saints, so that he surpassed everyone’s merits in immeasurable virtue and found no one at all equal to himself.

Although their infirmities multiplied, nevertheless, following the Lord’s example, they hastened toward the palm of victory. Separating them from the fellowship of evildoers, the Lord says: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood”—that is, I will separate those who believe in me from those who delight in the shedding of blood—“nor will my lips remember their names,” denying them before the Father and the angels.

The Lord is my portion and the portion of my Passion—that is, of my cup. In it the measuring lines have fallen: “the strong have fallen”; for me, among splendid things—certainly among the apostles. Indeed, my inheritance is so splendid that they remain even today the light of this world. [Col. 0342D] In them God is blessed, who granted me understanding for these things. He instructed me not only in what is clear but also in what is hidden, not from the heart but from the kidneys themselves, so that I might keep the Lord always before me.

He himself is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved, and so that what I have not sinned and what deceit has not been found in my mouth may be ascribed not to humanity but to Divinity.

Therefore my heart rejoiced, my tongue exulted, and my flesh itself rests in hope, because the Lord is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. Therefore you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you give your holy one [Col. 0343A] to see corruption, because you have made known to me the paths by which one goes to eternity. Along them, after the sorrow of the Passion, you will fill me with joy in your presence, and, ascending into heaven, you will grant delights at your right hand forever. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XVI

A prayer of David.

Hear, O Lord, my justice; attend to my petition. Give ear to my prayer, which does not come from deceitful lips. Let my judgment proceed from your presence; let your eyes see equity. You have tested my heart and visited me by night; you have examined me with fire, and no iniquity has been found in me. So that my mouth may not speak of human works, because of the words of your lips I have guarded difficult paths. [Col. 0343B] Make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be shaken. I have cried out because you have heard me, O God; incline your ear to me and hear my words. Make your mercies wondrous, you who save those who hope in you. Guard me from those who resist your right hand, as the apple of your eye. Protect me beneath the shadow of your wings, from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me. My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have shut themselves up in their fat, and their mouth has spoken arrogance. Now, as they cast me out, they have surrounded me; they have fixed their eyes on turning them toward the earth. They have received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub dwelling in hiding places. Arise, O Lord; go before them and trip them up. Rescue my soul from the ungodly, your sword from the enemies of your hand. O Lord, divide [Col. 0343C] them from the few upon the earth during their lifetime, and their belly has been filled from your hidden stores. They have been filled with sons, and they have divided their remnants among their little ones. But I shall appear in righteousness before your presence; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.

## COMMENTARY

The title indicates a prayer in which he takes from God a rule concerning justice and judgment: when one human being judges another, he should remember that the person judged was made in the image of God. He should not pronounce his judgment from the face of God with deceitful lips, but his eyes should see equity. He should not say, “This one is rich and that one is poor,” but, “This one is guilty and that one is innocent,” even if the innocent person suffers adversity, because a just judge may be wearied by factions, but not by justice.

Here, however, he has also been tested by fires, and no iniquity was found in him. Why? [Col. 0343D] “Because of the words,” he says, “of your lips,” since you yourself said: “You shall not show partiality to the powerful in judgment.” Therefore, because of what you commanded, I also believed that difficult paths must be guarded—not fearing the threats of executioners, nor fearing the loss of all possessions. Yet since the one who perseveres will be saved, I ask you to make my steps firm in your paths, so that my footsteps may not be shaken. Let me not fear unjust people, and save me from those who resist your right hand. Guard me as the apple of your eye—that is, at every hour, at every moment—and protect me beneath the shadow of your wings. “The shadow of wings” is understood as a sign of affection for the divine household.

“From the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me”: understand the ungodly as the Pharisees. “They have shut themselves up in their fat,” that is, they have become fat. [Col. 0344A] “Their mouth has spoken arrogance.” “As they cast me out”—then, from the Synagogue; “they have surrounded me”—now, in order to crucify him. For they fixed their eyes on turning them toward the earth, and, without considering the Judge of heaven, they received me like a lion ready for prey, and like a lion’s cub. He called the priestly people the lion, and the people subject to the priests the lion’s cub. While the former roared over their captive, the latter devoured him with seditious frenzy.

“Arise, O Lord; go before them,” raising up your Christ; when he rises, you will overthrow them. Envy has this downfall: it calls its object overthrown if it sees triumphant the one whom it tried to deceive. “Rescue my soul from the ungodly,” that is, from the yoke of death, “and tear the sword of the enemies from your hand.” Secular literature specifically calls *framea* [Col. 0344B] a king’s spear, but we generally understand *framea* in the sacred Scriptures as a sword.

As for his request that those who afflict him be separated from the few, the reason is this: while he was being held, he said, “I am the one you seek; let these men go” (John XVIII). Of these he himself had said: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew XX). “Therefore, separate these persecutors of mine from the few, and trip them up during their lifetime.” The one who loses his privilege is tripped up, just as Esau was tripped up by Jacob—not through Jacob’s wickedness, but through Esau’s contempt. Esau valued his birthright so little that he reckoned it worth the price of a single, utterly worthless meal.

So these people too, as though filled from God’s hidden things with swine’s flesh, refused to show reverence for his mysteries. If they had wished to scrutinize the [Col. 0344C] prophetic words with reverence, they would have received Christ as the Lamb, placing their salvation in his blood. But now, like Jews eating accursed swine’s flesh, they abused him; and, having been filled with his blood, they even transferred the remnants of their crime to their little ones, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew XXVII).

The Church, abhorring them, says that it will stand in righteousness in the presence of God and will be satisfied when his right hand appears in Christ Jesus, who reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XVII

For the end; for David, the servant of the Lord, who spoke to the Lord the words of this song on the day when the Lord rescued him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul; and he said:

[Col. 0344D]

I will love you, O Lord, my strength. The Lord is my firmament, my refuge, and my deliverer. My God is my helper, and I will hope in him. He is my protector, the horn of my salvation, and my defender. Praising him, I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies. The pains of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me. The pains of hell surrounded me; the snares of death overtook me. In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and I cried out to my God. He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry entered his ears in his presence.

The earth was shaken and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because he was angry with them. Smoke rose in his anger, and fire [Col. 0345A] blazed from his face; coals were kindled by him. He bent the heavens and descended, and darkness was beneath his feet. He mounted upon the Cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds. He made darkness his hiding place; around him was his tent, dark water in the clouds of the air. Before the brightness of his presence the clouds passed by, hail and coals of fire. The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire. He sent his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightning and troubled them.

The springs of waters appeared, and the foundations of the inhabited world were laid bare, at your rebuke, O Lord, at the breath of the spirit of your anger. He sent from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, because they had grown too strong [Col. 0345B] against me. They overtook me on the day of my affliction, and the Lord became my protector. He brought me out into a broad place; he saved me because he desired me.

And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness; according to the purity of my hands he will repay me. For I have guarded the ways of the Lord, and I have not acted wickedly against my God. For all his judgments were before my eyes, and I did not reject his righteousnesses. I shall be blameless with him, and I shall guard myself from my iniquity. And the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness and according to the purity of my hands before his eyes.

With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent. With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse. For you will save the humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud. [Col. 0345C] For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord; my God, illuminate my darkness. For in you I shall be rescued from temptation, and in my God I shall leap over a wall.

My God, his way is undefiled; the words of the Lord have been tested by fire. He is the protector of all who hope in him. For who is God besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God? God, who girded me with strength and made my way blameless; who made my feet like those of deer and set me upon high places; who trains my hands for battle—you have made my arms like a bronze bow. You gave me the protection of your salvation; your right hand received me. Your discipline corrected me to the end, and your discipline itself will teach me.

You enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footsteps did not grow weak. I shall pursue my enemies and [Col. 0345D] overtake them; I shall not turn back until they fail. I shall crush them, and they will not be able to stand; they will fall beneath my feet. You girded me with strength for war and tripped up those who rose against me beneath me. You gave me the backs of my enemies; you destroyed those who hated me. They cried out, but there was no one to save them to the Lord, and he did not hear them. I shall crush them like dust before the face of the wind; I shall wipe them away like mud in the streets.

You will rescue me from the disputes of the people; you will set me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and faltered from their paths.

The Lord lives, and blessed is my God; let the God of my salvation be exalted. God, who gives me vengeance [Col. 0346A] and subjects peoples beneath me, my deliverer from my angry enemies. You will exalt me above those who rise against me; you will rescue me from the unjust man. Therefore I will confess to you among the nations, O Lord, and I will sing a psalm to your name, magnifying the salvation of his king and showing mercy to his anointed, David, and to his seed for ever.

## COMMENTARY

The title certainly indicates a history. Anyone who wishes to know it more fully than it is sung in the psalm will find it by reading the books of Kings: how David fought and conquered, and how he escaped from the hands of all his enemies. Our purpose, however, is to mingle mystical meanings with moral ones. Then we say to the Lord, “I will love you,” when, putting an end and boundary to all [Col. 0346B] other loves, we say to him alone, “I will love you.” For then, truly rescued from the hand of all our enemies—that is, from the hand of all vices—and from the hand of Saul, that is, from the hand of the ruler of this world, we say to God, “I will love you.”

Let us nevertheless ask the Lord and say: “Who is the one who loves you?” He will answer us through his evangelist and say: “Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (John I, 4). He says: “The Lord is my firmament,” that is, the one about whom I have no doubt. He is my refuge; he is my deliverer. Praising and invoking him, I shall be saved from my enemies.

Finally, I shall speak of past things so that I may have no doubt about future ones. When groanings of death, iniquities, pains, and snares had surrounded me, I cried out to him in faith. And he heard my voice from his holy [Col. 0346C] temple, and my cry entered his ears. From this point the character of the future judgment is disclosed, whose terror purifies us if we believe. Then the earth will be shaken by trembling, so that the foundations of the mountains themselves will be troubled. When the Lord is angry, even fire itself blazes. Just as fire makes every material blaze before its face, so that fire will blaze from the face of God when he bends the heavens, descends, and darkness begins to be beneath his feet.

Whose feet? Without doubt, those of the one who mounted upon the Cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds, and who made darkness his hiding place. Here he used darkness for invisibility; hence it follows: “Around him were his tents, and dark water in the clouds of the air.” Then there will be hail together with coals of fire, when the Lord thunders from [Col. 0346D] heaven and the Most High gives his voice. He will send his arrows to scatter them, multiply his lightning, and trouble them.

Then the springs of waters will appear; then the greatness of the power of baptism will be revealed, when the foundations of the earth’s inhabited world are laid bare, at the Lord’s rebuke and at the breath of the spirit of his anger.

Then the Church will say: “He sent from on high and took me; he lifted me from the multitude of waters.” For by the sanctification of one water he willed me to be consecrated, through which he rescued me from my strongest enemies and from those who hated me, because they had grown too strong against me. They overtook me on the day of my affliction, at the time when the sword pierced the loving entrails of the mother; and the Lord became my protector.

He brought me out of narrow places into a broad expanse; [Col. 0347A] for he rescued me from my strongest enemies. He repaid me according to my righteousness, because I shall guard the ways of the Lord until death, and, without fearing the sword of human beings, I have not acted wickedly against my God. I have always kept his judgments before my eyes, and I have not rejected his righteousnesses.

Therefore his people of martyrs say: “I shall be blameless with him”—with the one who, though blameless, suffered on the cross for our iniquities. “And I shall guard myself from my iniquity,” which indeed I laid aside in martyrdom. Then the Lord will repay me according to my righteousness, according to my innocence, and according to the innocence of my hands before his eyes.

When he says, “With the holy you will be holy,” he is not referring to the common saying used among the people: “With whomever someone [Col. 0347B] associates, such will he be.” That saying is true, but it does not belong to the interpretation of the present verses. Here, if you wish to make plain the sense of the one who sings, you will recall what the Lord says through the prophet to the people: “If you walk uprightly in my presence, I too will walk uprightly with you; but if you walk perversely, I too will be perverse with you.”

Thus the Psalmist himself speaks: “With the holy you will be holy, with the innocent you will be innocent,” and so forth. Hence he adds: “For you will save the humble people and humble the eyes of the proud.”

But because he made darkness his hiding place, and we cannot see the mysteries of his Scriptures, let us cry out with the prophet: “For you illuminate my lamp, O Lord.” Just as the eye is the lamp of the body, so the mind is the lamp [Col. 0347C] of the soul. Unless Christ pours into it the oil of his grace, it will be completely unable to possess light.

Therefore the prophet cries out that his lamp be illuminated by the Lord. If it receives the material for shining, it reveals the pits into which the unwary fall and the snares placed in darkness. For unless the one walking in darkness has light, he either encounters an obstacle or cannot wholly escape the attack. Hence the prophet says: “When you have illuminated my darkness, then I shall be rescued from temptation, and in you, my God, I shall cross over walls,” just as Samson, by the power of God, crossed over the closed walls within the walls when the gates of the city had been shut.

We too cross over walls when, leaving this body, we escape those who surround us. We migrate into God if we have walked along the undefiled [Col. 0347D] way of our life. For that is God’s way, and along it he is the protector of all who hope in him.

He himself girds them with strength and makes their way blameless, so that they may flee like deer. What do they flee? Without doubt, every crime. Every sin, indeed, arises from the rejection of ‘vices’ [*vitiorum*; the sense appears to require ‘virtues’]. They will ascend to the heights of virtues, provided that he himself teaches our hands for battle, because one does not come to the refuge of the mountains without adversaries opposing the way.

Let him make our arms like a bronze bow, so that they do not fail in prayer, since, while they are extended on the cross, Amalek is conquered. If, then, he gives them strength so that, like a bronze bow, they persevere in prayers, we not only escape those who pursue us, but pursue our enemies [Col. 0348A] ourselves, overtake them, and do not turn back until they fail.

We afflict them so that they cannot stand before us but fall beneath our feet, provided that we have been girded with strength for war. Then those who rise against us will be beneath us. We shall see the backs of our fleeing enemies, not the faces of our pursuers, so that we may crush them like dust before the face of the wind and wipe them away like mud in the streets.

All these things will happen to us through the one who made his arms like a bronze bow on the cross and daily intercedes for us. For he says to the Father: “You will rescue me from the disputes of an unbelieving people, and you will set me as head of the nations.” And he adds: “A people whom I did not know served me.” The Magi believed; God did not disdain to know them. While they served him and [Col. 0348B] offered gifts, the Jews denied him and persisted in persecuting him.

“Foreign sons lied to me,” saying: “We know that you have come from God, and you teach in truth” (Matthew XXII). But these words of theirs were full of the deceit of falsehood. In this they grew old and faltered from their paths—the paths in which the prophets had taught them to walk.

But the Lord lives. Though you crucify him and see him buried, nevertheless he will rise and live, and the God of my salvation will be exalted in the heavens. He will give this vengeance to his Church: he will subject peoples beneath her, be her deliverer from angry nations and from those who rise against her, and exalt her upon the rock, so that the gates of hell may not prevail against her (Matthew XVI). He will rescue her from the unjust man, that is, from a perverse teacher.

Therefore she confesses to him [Col. 0348C] among the peoples and sings a psalm to his name—he who magnifies the salvation of his king and will show mercy to his anointed, David, when he raises up from his seed a kingdom that will rule for ever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM XVIII

For the end; a psalm of David.

The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands. Day pours forth the word to day, and night indicates knowledge to night. There are no speeches or conversations whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.

He has placed his tent in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven. His approach reaches to its summit, and no one can hide from his heat.

The law of the Lord is undefiled, converting souls. The testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones. The righteous ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts. The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever. The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.

They are more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. For your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward. Who understands offenses? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense.

And may the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart always be pleasing in your presence, O Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

## COMMENTARY

Just as earthly beings have declared the glory of human beings, so heavenly beings declare the glory of God. Thus the Magi, leaving their own region at the sign of a star, declared the glory of God. But the apostles too became heavens, possessing within themselves the Sun of righteousness, and their merits shining with varied brilliance like stars according to their differing qualities.

As they declared the glory of God, the firmament of their teaching announced the work of God’s hands—either because the cross, which is the eternal firmament, triumphed and conquered by the work of his hands, or because the sick were healed and the dead were raised: the work of his hands announces [Col. 0349B] the firmament.

When day spoke to day and night spoke to night, day proceeded from day and night spoke the word to night, and from night to night, so that its knowledge might be revealed. This is the simple interpretation.

Otherwise, the Son is the Day of the Father. The Father therefore poured forth the Word, and that Word, hidden in the night of the Virgin’s womb, indicated his knowledge while hidden in the night of the womb of the barren Elizabeth. When the apostles preached these things, there was no speech or discourse whose voices were not heard, so that people of every nation said of them: “Are not these men Galileans? And how is it that each of us hears them speaking in our own language of the mighty works of God?” (Acts II).

Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words penetrated to the ends of the whole inhabited world, [Col. 0349C] at the time when the Lord placed his tent in the sun. Not in this sun, which performs the divine service and runs through the measures of the hours according to a fixed order of times, but in the Sun of righteousness, who, born in the splendor of eternal life from a virgin womb, shone as the true light upon minds and came forth from the virgin like a bridegroom from his chamber.

He rejoiced like a giant to run his course, walking undefiled in the way, in the law of the Lord. “His going forth is from the summit of heaven”: not from the seed of a man, but from the mouth of the Father, who is in the highest heavens. “His approach reaches to its summit.” For he did not go from east to west, or as though from high places to low, but from summit to summit, from height to height, and from virtue to virtue. From summit to summit there will be no one who can hide from his heat.

There will be no nation in [Col. 0349D] this age to whose knowledge the heat of Christian faith does not reach. In that faith is the irreproachable law of the Lord, converting souls and inviting them from error to the right path, from falsehood to truth. There are the righteous ordinances that gladden hearts. For what joy of heart is as just as this: that we are commanded to do for other people everything we wish them to do for us?

This commandment is so bright that it also illuminates the eyes of the blind, provided that the fear of the Lord remains in us. Through that fear we consider the judgments of God, true and justified in themselves. We desire them more than gold and precious stone, and they become sweeter to us than honey and the honeycomb.

For the servant of the Lord keeps them and believes that the reward for keeping God’s commandments [Col. 0350A] is so great that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans VIII), provided that we make an effort to understand our falls and offenses.
