I suffered this because I was zealous for your house, because I drove commerce from your temple. I covered my soul with fasting, taking nothing for forty days and as many nights. I put on sackcloth, the form of a servant.

The King of heaven was clothed with it, and I became a proverb to them, subject on every side to verbal insults. The priests acted against me; they themselves are chosen to sit at the gates, as Jeremiah says: they hated the one who reproved them.

At the gates, therefore, these men receive the office of judging and correcting. They are spoken of as sitting at the gates, as though holding the keys of the city. And while drunk they sang derisively about me.

But I, pouring out my prayer, acted so that you might rescue me from the mud of death, so that I would not remain stuck there, so that the pit would not close its mouth over me.

The pit is used here for the devil. The pit is named from drinking; he himself gave the first human beings to drink, and through the mouth of his people he opened his mouth over them in death. Hence the saints, escaping in the Passion, say: “If the Lord had not been with us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 123). Who? Certainly the servants of that same enemy.

“I waited for one who would grieve with me, but there was none.” For the Godhead could not suffer together. Just as, if the sun is on the wood when it is cut down, it cannot at the same time be cut down, so the Godhead was present at the Passion and at the same time did not suffer grief.

“I sought one who would console me, and found none”: so many thousands fed, so many thousands saved, so many countless people taught—and not one was found to console me at the time when they gave gall for my food and in my thirst gave me vinegar.

For this reason their table before them became a snare. Here he sings of the synagogue as the table to which they go as though to be spiritually refreshed, but encounter the snare of eternal death.

Having their eyes darkened so that they do not see the light of the Church, they bend their backs toward empty walls. And therefore iniquity is added upon their iniquity, because they themselves double their iniquities.

They killed Christ, persecuted the saints, deny the Church, and nullify the voices of the prophets. Therefore they are blotted out of the book of the living and are not written with the righteous. For they have no share with Abraham, nor with all the saints of the Old Testament, because they despised the poor in his appearance—him of whom all their fathers preached.

“I am poor and suffering.” Poor, so that he might make us rich; suffering, so that he might rescue us from eternal sufferings. He became a sacrifice to God for us, making peace by his blood, whether for those on earth or for those in heaven (Colossians 1).

And he was pleasing in the sacrifice of the cross, like a young calf producing the horns of the two Testaments and the four hooves of the Gospels. When the poor see this, they rejoice.

The poor are the apostles, who have neither two tunics, nor a bag, nor money in their belts. Hence Peter said to the sick beggar: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you. In the name of Jesus, rise and walk” (Acts 3).

In these works the Lord Jesus Christ was magnified in praise. When the poor saw this, they rejoiced, because the Lord thus hears the poor and does not despise his prisoners.

The heavens praise him because he ascended; the earth because he rose; the sea because he walked upon it; and Zion because he built it without stain or wrinkle. The cities of Judah are the souls of the apostles, inhabited by Christ, and he acquired them as his first inheritance.

The seed of Christ’s servants will also possess them—those who do not possess earthly vanities. They possess, certainly, the teachings of the apostles. And those who love the Lord’s name will dwell in it—that is, in faith, doctrine, and the Church.

In it our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0422D]

## PSALM 69

For the end; a psalm of David, for remembrance that the Lord saved him.

God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me. Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame. Let those who desire evil for me turn backward and be ashamed. Let those who say to me, “Good, good,” turn back at once, ashamed.

Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you, and let those who love your salvation say always, “The Lord be magnified.” But I am needy and poor; God, help me. You are my helper and my deliverer, Lord; do not delay.

[Col. 0423A]

### Commentary

“In remembrance,” David says, “because the Lord saved me.” There he said, “Save me, Lord”; here the one who has been saved gives thanks.

What, nevertheless, did he pray? “Hasten to help me”: raise me quickly from the dead, so that those who say to me, “Good, good,” may at once be ashamed.

Let those who hope in you and seek you exult and say always, “The Lord be magnified,” those who love your salvation. It is clear that the apostles both sought and loved it.

“But I,” he says, “am a beggar and poor.” For “I emptied myself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2). “God, help me,” for human weakness does not rise again unless divine power has lifted it up.

Be my helper and deliverer, therefore, Lord; do not delay, God who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 70

A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.

In you, Lord, I have hoped; let me not be confounded forever. In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me. Incline your ear to me and save me. Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, so that you may save me. For you are my strength and my refuge.

My God, rescue me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the transgressor and the wicked. For you are my patience, Lord; Lord, my hope from my youth. I have been strengthened in you from the womb, from my mother’s belly; you are my protector.

In you is my song always. I have become like a portent to many, and you are my strong helper. Let my mouth be filled with praise, so that I may sing of your glory and your greatness all day long.

Do not cast me away in the time of old age; when my strength fails, do not abandon me. For my enemies have spoken against me, and those who watched over my soul have taken counsel together, saying: “God has abandoned him; pursue and seize him, because there is no one to rescue him.”

God, do not go far from me; my God, look to my help. Let those who slander my soul be confounded and fail; let those who seek evil for me be covered with confusion and shame.

But I will always hope, and I will add to all your praise. My mouth will announce your righteousness, your salvation all day long, because I have not known letters. I will enter into the mighty deeds of the Lord. Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone.

God, you taught me from my youth, and until now I will proclaim your wonders. Even into old age and gray hairs, God, do not abandon me, until I announce your arm to every generation that is to come: your power and your righteousness, God, even to the highest things that you have done.

God, who is like you? How many and evil are the tribulations you have shown me; then, turning, you made me alive again, and from the depths of the earth you brought me back again. You multiplied your magnificence, and, turning, you consoled me.

For I too will confess your truth to you with the vessels of the psalm, God; I will sing psalms to you on the lyre, Holy One of Israel. My lips will exult when I sing to you, and my soul, which you redeemed. My tongue also will meditate on your righteousness when those who seek evil for me have been confounded and put to shame.

[Col. 0424A]

### Commentary

The psalm, he says, is “of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.” We must see with whom David sings. He sings with the sons of Jonadab, of whom Jeremiah says that, by ancestral ordinance, they do not drink wine, and recalls the voice of the Lord reproving them, when it was said: “The sons of Jonadab keep the commands of their father and do not drink wine” (Jeremiah 35).

Let us not therefore suppose that the sons of Jonadab sang the psalter with David, but that they were men who shared sobriety and joined in singing to God. For it was not sung at will but with a groan, when the first captives poured out their tears together, saying: “My God, rescue me from the hand of the transgressor and the wicked.”

“I have been strengthened in you from the womb”—from the virginal womb, certainly. We say that Christ was strengthened in God. To many unbelievers he became like a portent, but to believers he proved to be a helper and strong.

His mouth was filled not with food or drunkenness but with praise. He was not protected at the time of the Passion, when his strength failed. Yet he was not wholly abandoned at the time when his enemies said, “God has abandoned him.”

Then God did not depart from him. When he rose, those insulting him were ashamed and confounded; those desiring his soul turned backward, knowing no other occupation than this: to enter into the mighty deeds of the Lord.

Now the outer person says to the inner: “What great things you have done, God! Who is like you? How many and evil are the tribulations you have shown me; and, turning, behold, you made me alive again, and from the abyss of the earth you brought me back again.”

By saying “again,” he raises a question. He suffered once, died once, was buried once, and was brought back once from the abyss of the earth. What does “again” mean?

By saying “again,” he excluded what is new. Thus, when we deny the restoration of penitence and leave the lions’ prey in their jaws, our shepherd here will not abandon the prey. He does not see the wolf and flee; rather, snatching the living sheep from the lions’ mouth, he presents them unharmed to his flocks again.

That is, we who were buried in him through baptism and, having put on Christ, die when we hand ourselves over to death by consenting to our enemies, who entangle us in earthly pleasures so that we seem to be submerged in the abyss of the earth.

But because he does not allow what he has bestowed in us to perish, after we have once been raised from the dead to eternal life through baptism, when we have been excluded from eternal life by the devil’s cunning, Christ again brings us back from the abyss of the earth.

In this way he multiplies his righteousness—that is, he excommunicates the offender and casts him away from the kiss of peace. Then, turning, he again consoles him, restoring the communion he had taken away and the kiss he had denied.

“And I,” he says, “will confess,” because confession is what liberates the penitent. In his prayer, therefore, he confesses his sins to the Lord his God.

But he confesses God’s truth “in the vessels of the psalm.” What are the vessels of the psalm? Those who announce God’s truth in the vessels of the psalm have the truth of right faith enclosed within the little vessel of their body.

For if someone displays the sufferings of his penitence in an incorporeal manner, abstains from sin, and remains in fasting, ashes, and sackcloth, unless he holds the truth in the vessels of the psalm, all that he has labored over vanishes.

He will come to forgiveness more easily through the truth of faith without his own affliction than he will reach it through his affliction without the truth.

Therefore, in your confession, practice correction even without sackcloth, and enclose the truth in the little vessel of the psalm. For the psalm that you sing does not reach God unless, within its vessel where it encloses the psalm—in the vessel, I say—the truth of God dwells together with it.

Then you sing psalms on the lyre to the Holy One of Israel; then your lips rejoice while you sing to the Lord, and your soul, which he redeemed, which he called back and rescued again from the abyss, rejoices. And he confounds with eternal confusion the one who sought that soul.

For its Creator alone possesses it, he who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0425B]

## PSALM 71

A psalm of David, concerning Solomon.

God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son. May he judge your people with justice, and your poor with judgment. May the mountains receive peace for the people, and the hills justice. He shall judge the poor of the people, save the children of the poor, and humble the accuser. And he shall remain with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation. He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth. In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away. And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the world. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia [Col. 0425C] and Sheba shall bring presents. And all kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him. For he has delivered the poor from the powerful, and the poor person who had no helper. He shall spare the poor and needy, and save the souls of the poor. From usury and iniquity he shall redeem their souls, and their name shall be honorable before him. And he shall live, and gold from Arabia shall be given to him; and they shall pray concerning him continually; all day they shall bless him. There shall be a firm foundation in the earth on the summits of the mountains; his fruit shall be exalted above Lebanon, and they shall blossom from the city like the grass of the earth. May his name be blessed forever; before the sun may his name endure. And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders. And blessed is the name of his majesty forever; the whole earth shall be filled [Col. 0425D] with his majesty. Let it be, let it be.

## Commentary

Those who believe that there is prophecy in the psalms hold that rule which Zechariah proclaimed, saying of God that he himself had spoken through the mouth of the prophets, that he would deliver us from our enemies. But when you read at the head of this psalm, you will find that it explains our Lord Jesus Christ. For he says in the Gospels: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Therefore the king truly fulfilled in his Son what he had promised through the mouth of the saints; at that time Solomon, bearing his image, received the name of wise man, possessing within himself a spark of wisdom.

But here Wisdom itself, coming, gave peace to the mountains—that is, to the apostles—and justice to the hills—that is, to the peoples. He judged the poor with justice, disregarding the persons of the rich. He humbled the accuser, that is, the Jewish people. He remains with the sun, indeed above the sun, because he remains seated at the right hand of the Father, and before the moon forever. In this passage he mentioned the moon not on account of the nature of the moon, but with reference to the eternity of the Lord Jesus Christ.

And he descended like rain upon fleece, that is, upon fleeces of wool, just as Gideon received the sign of victory in fleeces of wool. For the Father also commanded that his Word be awaited like rain: “Let my Word be awaited,” he says, “like rain.” Therefore the one whom in Deuteronomy he commanded to be awaited like rain, in the Gospels he presented as rain. Not, certainly, as a firstborn bursting forth from below through human seed, but as the Word of the Father, arising from the heights of heaven and coming like rain. Arising, I say, as light for the upright of heart in the darkness of the world.

Justice arose in his days, and abundance of peace. “My peace I give you” (John 14)—not such as this world possesses, but that peace of mine which the heavens possess, in which Christ rules from sea to sea, that is, over the whole earth surrounded by the waters of seas and rivers.

The Ethiopians shall fall before him: Ethiopians surrounded by the blackness of unbelief, not in the skin of the flesh but in the perceptions of the soul. For this reason they shall fall before him, and his enemies shall lick the earth, so that they may deserve to obtain forgiveness from him.

But the kings of Tarshish and the islands offer gifts—that is, those who rule securely in their own bodies and offer gifts. The kings of Arabia and Sheba bring presents: those who rule over barbarous ways of life. These bring their souls as gifts, so that they may hand them over to him for worship, together with the kings of the earth who rule over earthly pleasures.

All nations, however, shall serve him, because he delivers the poor from the powerful. Observe the reason: therefore, he says, all nations shall serve him, because he delivers the poor—that is, their understanding—from the powerful and crafty devil, who persuaded them to fear and worship the works of their own hands.

He delivered their souls from usury and iniquity. Usury was increasing upon their souls, because what was owed to God was handed over to idols—and to those receiving it, if it may even be said that they receive it, since they neither receive anything nor refuse anything. Thus, when demons received what was owed to God alone, both the debt and the interest accumulated for these people.

The compassionate one, to whom the Father entrusted his judgment, seeing that they were poor enough in making repayment, judged this: “Human beings, forgive one another your debts, as your heavenly Father forgives you.” And he added: “If you do not forgive, neither will he forgive you.”

O you who deliver souls from usury and iniquity, truly glorious is your name to us, you who live forever and ever. You live, and gold from Arabia shall be given to you. For the gold of that land is great; you receive tested, shining gold in the apostles, in the martyrs, in the confessors, and in the virgins. You receive gold in which no deception can be made against you.

Your firm foundation shall be in the earth of our bodies, not in the valley of weeping. Your fruit shall be exalted upon the summits of the mountains, and shall surpass even the height of Mount Lebanon, and it shall blossom (sic) in the heights of the apostles.

Let us hear what shall blossom: “Like grass,” he says. Therefore, in that praised height, grass shall blossom. It blossoms in the Church to this day, so that animals may be fed; nothing is done there with the people concerning divisions. There, then, grass is produced for the animals. For the more substantial food belongs to the perfected.

Since, therefore, the mountains blossom with grass, let no one flee the Church. Let everyone come, so that God may be blessed there—the God of Israel, who alone does wonders—and so that the name of his majesty may be blessed there forever, and the whole earth may be filled with his majesty. Let it be, let it be. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXII

[Col. 0427B]

The hymns of David, son of Jesse, have come to an end. A psalm of Asaph.

How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart. But my feet were almost moved; my steps were nearly poured out. For I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners. For there is no regard for their death, and their strength remains in their affliction. They are not in the labor of human beings, and they shall not be scourged with humankind. Therefore pride held them fast; they were covered with their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity came forth as though from fatness; they passed over into the desire of the heart. They thought and spoke wickedness; they spoke iniquity on high. They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed through the earth. Therefore my people shall turn here, and full days shall be found in them. And they said: “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?” Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in the world, they have obtained riches. And I said: “Then in vain I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent.” And I was scourged all day, and my chastisement came in the mornings. If I said: “I shall speak thus,” behold, I have rejected the generation of your children. I considered how I might understand this; it is a labor before me. Until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand their final destiny. Yet because of their deceits you set them [there]; you cast them down when they were being lifted up. How they have become desolation! Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquity. Like the dream of those who awake, Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing. For my heart was inflamed, and my kidneys were changed; and I was reduced to nothing, and I did not know. I became like a beast before you, and yet I am always with you. You held my right hand, and in your will you led me, and with glory you received me. For what is there for me in heaven, and what did I desire from you upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God, the God of my heart, and my portion is God forever. For behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish; you have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you. But for me, it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God, so that I may proclaim all your praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion.

## Commentary

Since God is good to all and is evil to no one, why did he wish to say: “Good to those who are upright in heart”? This expression must be applied to the human perceptions of those who criticize God’s judgments, saying: “That one is faithless, that one unjust, filthy, savage, insane. But this one is innocent, chaste, and humble; he is worn down by insanity, shaken by weakness,” and similar things. These are regarded as the seeds of virtue in the upright of heart. In them, approved faith may receive its harvest in the loveliness of eternal life, and, placed in this world as though in a glacial winter, they may await the flowers of the first resurrection, as though the first flowers of spring [perhaps “of spring”].

Thus, while sinners rejoice in their peace, while pride holds those who are not scourged with human beings, let them become fat; let iniquity come forth from their fatness; let them set their mouth against heaven and speak iniquity on high; let them say that there is no knowledge in God. Yet let us hear what they are: “These,” he says, “are sinners and, abounding, have obtained riches in the world. But my feet were almost moved, and my steps were nearly poured out from the straight path, because I said in my heart: ‘Then in vain I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent.’”

But when I considered that all the things supplied to sinners are temporal, that they suddenly fail and perish because of their iniquity, and that they pass through this life like a dream; and because God in his city, Jerusalem, which he prepares for the saints, will reduce their image to nothing—then my heart was inflamed with the love of God, and my kidneys were loosened, that is, released from the bond of an evil example into the freedom of chastity.

For this reason I was reduced to nothing, thinking these things, because I did not know that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory. After I learned this, although I was regarded as a beast and placed like cattle for slaughter, nevertheless I remained always with you. You held my right hand; in your will you led me, and with glory you received me.

These things were fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ. He himself held the right hand of the human race, already dead and already stinking; he led it from the will of the devil to his own will, and received it into glory. He could boldly say: “What remains for me in heaven?” That is: “Placed upon earth, I practiced heavenly life in such a way that, when I ascend into heaven, nothing remains for me that I had not fulfilled while placed upon earth.” For I desired nothing besides you upon earth—even if my heart failed, and my flesh was given over to sufferings; my portion, because it is God, did not fail but remains forever.

For none perish except those who distance themselves far from God their protector; and he destroys only those who commit fornication away from him—that is, those whose soul leads another as its god, or who mingle themselves with falsehood, away from the marriage of truth.

But when each one of us has been proved by these things, let him say: “For me, it is good to cling to God and to place my hope in the Lord, so that I may proclaim all the praises of God at the gates of the daughter of Zion.” The daughter of Zion is the soul believing in Christ, which at the end of the psalm will find the praises that it testifies in the title to have failed it. Its praises failed because it was jealous over sinners; it will find them at the end if it clings to the Lord and places its hope entirely in him, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0429A]

# PSALM LXXIII

For the end; an understanding of Asaph.

Why, God, have you rejected forever? Has your anger raged against the sheep of your pasture? Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning. You redeemed the rod of your inheritance, Mount Zion, in which you dwelt. Lift up your hands against their pride forever; how greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the sanctuary. And those who hated you gloried in the midst of your solemn feast; they set up their signs as signs, and they did not understand, as at the entrance above. Like men cutting down trees in a forest, they cut down its doors together; with axe and hatchet they cast it down. They burned your sanctuary with fire upon the earth; they profaned the dwelling-place of your name. They said in their heart, their whole kindred together: “Let us cause all the feast-days of God to cease from the earth.” We have not seen our signs; there is no longer a prophet, and he will not know us any longer. How long, God, will the enemy reproach you? Will the adversary provoke your name forever? Why do you turn your hand away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom, forever? Yet God is our king from before the ages, working salvation in the midst of the earth. You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of dragons in the waters. You crushed the heads of dragons; you gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians. You tore open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan. The day is yours, and the night is yours; you made the dawn and the sun. You made all the boundaries of the earth; summer and spring, you formed them. Remember this: the enemy reproaches the Lord, and a foolish people provokes your name. Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you, and do not forget forever the souls of your poor. Look upon your covenant, because those who have been darkened upon the earth have been filled with houses of iniquities. Let the humble person who has been made ashamed not turn away; the poor and needy shall praise your name. Arise, God; judge your own cause. Remember the reproaches against you, those made by the foolish all day long. Do not forget the voices of your enemies; the pride of those who hate you continually rises up.

## Commentary

The Lord was angry with Israel when the ark of God was at Shiloh, while Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, were neither rebuked nor corrected for their sacrifices and fornications. The ark of the covenant was also handed over to its adversaries, [Col. 0429D] and those who hated him gloried in the midst of his court. Like men cutting down trees in a forest, they cut down the doors of the fortifications. They burned with fire wherever they found a sanctuary, that is, a place of prayer constructed by them. And they caused the feast-days of the Lord to cease upon the earth, saying: “There is now no prophet in Israel”—clearly hearing that Eli and his two sons, who held the highest priesthood, had been killed in battle. Samuel was still a little child, and his reputation had not yet begun. Therefore the enemy people of the nations seemed to reproach and insult; in this situation he asks that the Lord not forget the souls of his poor forever, but rise up and judge his own cause, because the pride of those who hated him was rising exceedingly high.

Thus far the historical account has reached its end. For there is also in you an ark of the Lord’s covenant, which enemies strive daily to seize: namely, steadfastness of spirit, which wages war against vices in defense of virtues. Therefore, if the priests of this ark—that is, my body and soul—worship in agreement, the Lord rests upon it, and neither demons nor warfare will dare remain in the flesh.

But when this has withdrawn through the negligence of the priests, it is captured by adversaries; the enemy acts wickedly in the sanctuary, and those who hate the Lord glory in it. After this, the Lord must be entreated with tears, so that he does not forget the souls of the poor. May the Lord not turn away forever, having been made humble and ashamed, so that the soul confessing to him may not be handed over forever to beasts; may he remember his creature, because those who have been darkened upon the earth have been filled with houses of iniquities.

Therefore let the Lord arise and judge his own cause, since through the occasion of my sins the enemy reproaches the Lord. “Remember,” he says, “Lord, your reproaches, those made by the foolish all day long, so that you may not forget the voices of those seeking you through repentance; and let the pride of those who despise you rise up to you, so that you may repay the proud and spare us who confess”—you who reign forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXIV

For the end: “Do not destroy” or “Do not corrupt”; a psalm of a song of Asaph.

We shall confess to you, God; we shall confess and invoke your name. We shall recount your wonders when I receive the appointed time; I shall judge judgments. The earth melted, and all who dwell upon it; I established its pillars. I said to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly,” and to sinners: “Do not exalt your horn.” Do not raise your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God. For neither from the east nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains—for God is judge. He humbles one and exalts another, because there is a cup in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine, mixed. He inclined it from this side to that, yet its dregs were not emptied; all the sinners of the earth shall drink. But I shall proclaim forever; I shall sing to the God of Jacob. And I shall break all the horns of sinners, while the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.

## Commentary

We passed over certain matters in Psalm 73 for this reason: we believed they would be better explained in Psalm 74. “We shall confess to you, God,” he says. If we confess our sins, we do not confess them so that he may know what he does not know; we confess them so that he may forgive what he knows perfectly. For we confess him and invoke his name. The confession of the penitent does not look toward forgiveness if the invocation of God’s name in right faith does not follow it; in this confession all his wonders are recounted, as the text of the holy creed sets forth.

But because, as I said, I passed over certain matters in the preceding psalm, what must be supplied here is this: recount all his wonders against Manichaeus, and do not say that the world is governed by opposing and contrary powers—one lord of light, another of darkness, another of night, another of day. Rather, confessing one and the same Lord, let us recount all his wonders, saying: “The day is yours and the night is yours; you made the sun and the moon; summer and spring, you made them. You established the sea by your strength; you crushed the heads of dragons in the waters,” that is, the heads of demons in baptism.

When he said “in the waters,” he wished to show that one baptism can be celebrated in all waters: rivers, sea, springs, torrents, and pools. There the heads of demons are crushed—that is, in all waters.

But the Lord will crush the head of the great dragon in repentance, and give him as food to the Ethiopian people. Ethiopians are black from the southern region. Therefore those who suffer the ruin of the southern demons become black before God, and on account of that blackness of unbelief they are called Ethiopians.

Thus, when they were baptized, because the heads of the demons had been crushed in the waters, all poison vanished in the flowing waters. But after he had presented them cleansed, placed now upon dry ground and purged of every poison, the great dragon himself, the prince of dragons, came to them. By feeding him with their wicked deeds, they blackened themselves again with his poison.

Yet because the help of divine mercy comes to the penitent, the head of this dragon is also crushed upon dry ground. There the only water is that of tears. And because there are no rivers leaping around him to wash away such great sacrilege, he is given to them as food, and it is said to them: “When the heads of the dragons were crushed for you in the waters, you tasted and saw how sweet the Lord is. Now, because you have abandoned the Lord, taste and see how bitter the devil is. There you tasted honey and milk; here taste ashes for bread, and mix your tears in your cups. There you had bright and clean garments; here, dirty garments of sackcloth. There you had joy; here, amid sighs, utter bellowing and groaning.”

Thus you will cease to be Ethiopians, and your former whiteness and brightness will be restored to you. For there the springs and torrents will again burst forth for you, where the rivers of Ethan were dried up.

The rivers of Ethan were found in the desert of Sinai. Whoever tasted from them was not filled with bitterness as from myrrh [variant: mulberry], but was immediately seized by swelling and exposed to the danger of death. Therefore, when did he turn solid rock into pools of water and stone into springs of water (Psalm 113)? By God’s command these rivers of Ethan were dried up.

This event points to the fact that for the penitent the rivers of Ethan are dried up. And from the hopeless stone and the hardest rock, placed in the desert and in barren places, springs and torrents alike burst forth. This our King did—the God who exists before the ages and is himself.

This the King did, who worked salvation in the midst of the earth (Psalm 73), in our Lord Jesus Christ. He said to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly, and do not exalt your horn, you sinners; do not raise your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God.”

But if someone says to you, “Behold, here is Christ,” or “Behold, there,” do not believe it, because he will come neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains, but like lightning, since God is judge.

He does not come as a human being comes, but as God the judge, to humble the proud as he promised, and to exalt the humble, carrying a cup in his hand, full of wine mixed with something, from which he pours from this side to that.

Wine has two kinds: one by which it heals the sick, another by which it weakens the healthy. From one and the same wine, it is administered to the righteous for salvation and to sinners for destruction. It is like fire to the righteous; yet the dregs of the cup are not emptied, so that not a few but all the sinners of the earth may drink. From one and the same cup salvation comes to some and destruction to others—even today, when those who taste and drink unworthily consume it. From it, as the Apostle says, they take judgment upon themselves.

But knowing these things, if we wish to rejoice forever and ever, let us sing to the God of Jacob in such a way that we break all the horns of sinners—that is, break the agitations of vices by despising them—and exalt the horns of virtues in our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXV

For the end: in songs; a song for the Assyrians; a psalm of Asaph.

God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel. And his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion. There he broke the powers: bow, shield, sword, and war. You illumine wondrously from the eternal mountains; all the foolish in heart were troubled. They slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands. At your rebuke, God of Jacob, those who mounted horses fell into slumber. You are terrible, and who will resist you? From then on is your anger. From heaven you caused judgment to be heard; the earth trembled and became still. When God arose for judgment, to save all the gentle of the earth. For the thought of the human being shall confess to you, and the remnants of thought shall keep a feast for you. Vow and repay your vows to the Lord your God, all you who, around him, bring offerings—to the Terrible One, and to him who takes away the spirit of princes; terrible is he among all the kings of the earth.

## Commentary

We begin a song against the Assyrian, that is, against the devil. For against him God became known in Judea, reconciling the world to himself in Christ (1 Corinthians 5). “In Israel his name is great.” Israel is the Jewish man. Therefore, when the man saw God and believed in God, his name was first made great in that man, so that he might say to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” And because the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matthew 16).

There he broke the horns of bows, and the shield, and the sword, and war; he made his place in peace, and his dwelling in Zion, and illumined it from the eternal mountains—from the prophets who existed from the beginning.

Against this, all foolish in heart are troubled to this day. And those who die in their sins, sleeping the sleep of their death—that is, sleeping their own sleep—there found nothing in their hands, all the men of riches. For what they find here while being born, they leave here when dying.

Not only do the rich sleep, but also the strong who mounted horses. For God is terrible, and no one can resist him. Then, in his anger, when judgment begins to be hurled from heaven, the earth will tremble and become still, when God begins to rise in judgment, in which he will save no others except all the gentle of the earth.

There the thought of the human being shall confess to him, and the remnants of thoughts shall keep a feast for God. Thus will all the days of the righteous be, just as for us the holy day of Easter is once a year. Therefore all the saints shall keep feast-days for God.

And you, he says, if you wish to rejoice with the saints, vow and repay your vows to the Lord your God, all you who offer gifts around him. They must remember what they have vowed, or to whom they have vowed. For in the consecration of baptism they vowed to hand themselves over and to renounce all the works of the devil. Repay this to the Lord your God, keeping it before your eyes, because he will also take away the spirit of princes when they depart from their vow. And he is terrible even to the kings of the earth. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXVI

For the end; for Jeduthun; a psalm of Asaph.

With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice to God, and he attended to me. In the day of my tribulation I sought God; with my hands at night toward him, and I was not deceived. My soul refused consolation; I remembered God and was delighted, and I was exercised, and my spirit failed. My eyes anticipated the watches; I was troubled and did not speak. I considered the ancient days, and I held eternal years in my mind. And I meditated at night with my heart, and I was exercised, and I swept my spirit. Will God cast us off forever, or will he not again become more favorable? Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to show mercy, or restrain his mercies in his anger? And I said: “Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High.” I remembered the works of the Lord, for I shall remember your wonders from the beginning. And I shall meditate on all your works, and I shall exercise myself in your inventions. God, your way is in holiness; what god is great like our God? You are the God who does wonders. You made your power known among the peoples; with your arm you redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph. The waters saw you, God; the waters saw you and were afraid, and the abysses were troubled. The multitude of the sound of the waters; the clouds saw your voice. For your arrows also passed through; the voice of your thunder was in the wheel. Your flashes illumined the world; the earth was shaken and trembled. Your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footsteps shall not be known. You led your people like sheep, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

## Commentary

In this psalm the prophet promises that he will remember all God’s wonders from the beginning, and he explains the reason for this recollection. While remembering past blessings, he complains about present evils: “I cried,” he says, “to the Lord in the day of tribulation. And I stretched out my hands before him at night, and I was not deceived.”

But now the Lord delays so greatly in bringing help that I say: “Will God forget to show mercy forever, or will he restrain his mercy in his anger?” And I said: “Now the change of the right hand of the Most High has begun.”

And in order to show, he says, that it has only now begun, I shall remember his wonders from the beginning, in which he delivered his people. For what god is as great as our God, whom the waters of the sea saw and feared? The abysses were troubled, giving a dry path to the feet of the children of Israel and Joseph.

After this the clouds gave forth their voice. For there was a voice in the pillar of cloud when the arrows of God passed over the Egyptians. “The voice of his thunder was in the wheel.” Moses is compared to a wheel. Although a wheel rolls upon the earth, yet while it stands, a large part of it is separate from the earth, and only a small part of it rests upon the earth. Therefore the voice of God is in the wheel: he who is content with small earthly things seeks all that is above and proceeds to where Christ is.

His flashes illumined the world when he made a way in the sea, and a path in many waters, when he led his people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXVII

An understanding of Asaph.

Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will speak declarations from the beginning. How many things we have heard and known, and our fathers have declared to us. They were not hidden from their children, from one generation to another: recounting the praises of the Lord, his powers, and his wonders that he performed. And he raised up a testimony in Jacob and established a law in Israel. How many things he commanded our fathers to make known to their children, so that the next generation might know them—the children who would be born, rise up, and declare them to their own children—so that they might place their hope in God, not forget the works of God, and seek his commandments.

Let them not become like their fathers, a perverse and provoking generation: a generation that did not direct its heart, and whose spirit was not faithful with God. The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle. They did not keep God’s covenant, and they refused to walk in his law. They forgot his benefits and his wonders that he had shown them.

In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis. He split the sea and led them through it, and made the waters stand as in a wineskin. He led them by a cloud during the day, and all night by the illumination of fire. He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink, as from a great abyss. He brought water from the rock and brought forth waters like rivers.

Yet they continued to sin against him and provoked the Most High in the waterless place. They tested God in their hearts, asking for food for their souls. They spoke evil of God, saying, “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed, and torrents flooded forth. Can he also give bread and prepare a table for his people?”

Therefore the Lord heard and delayed; fire was kindled against Jacob, and anger rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not hope in his salvation. He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven. [Col. 0435A] He rained manna upon them for food and gave them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels; he sent them provisions in abundance. He transferred the south wind from heaven and brought in the African wind by his power; he rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. They fell in the midst of their camp, around their dwellings. They ate and were filled exceedingly, and he brought them what they desired; they were not deprived of their desire.

While their food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them. He killed their fat ones and struck down the chosen men of Israel. In all these things they continued to sin and did not believe in his wonders. Their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste. When he killed them, they sought him, returned, and came to him at dawn. [Col. 0435B] They remembered that God was their helper and that God Most High was their redeemer. They loved him with their mouth, but with their tongue they lied to him. Their heart was not right with him, nor were they considered faithful to his covenant.

Yet he is merciful and will be propitious toward their sins, and he will not destroy them. He abounded in mercy so as to turn away his anger, and did not kindle all his wrath. He remembered that they were flesh: a spirit that goes away and does not return. How often they provoked him in the wilderness and angered him in the waterless place. They turned back and tested God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his hand on the day when he redeemed them from the hand of the afflicter.

As he set his signs in Egypt and his wonders in the field of Tanis, he turned their rivers into blood, and their rainwaters, so that they could not drink. He sent among them the dog-fly, and it devoured them; and the frog, and it destroyed them. He gave their fruits to the rust, and their labors to the locust. He killed their vines with hail and their mulberry trees with frost. He delivered their cattle to hail and their possessions to fire.

He sent upon them the anger of his indignation—indignation, anger, and tribulation—an assault through evil angels. He made a path for his anger; he did not spare their souls from death, and enclosed their cattle in death. He struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor, in the tents of Ham.

He took away his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness. He led them in hope, and they did not fear, while the sea covered their enemies. He brought them to the mountain of his holiness, the mountain that his right hand had acquired. He drove out nations before them and divided the land among them by lot, with a measuring cord of distribution. He made the tribes of Israel dwell in their tents.

Yet they tested and provoked God Most High and did not keep his testimonies. They turned away and did not keep the covenant, just as their fathers had turned aside like a crooked bow. They provoked him to anger on their hills and aroused him to jealousy with their carved images. God heard and despised them, and utterly rejected Israel. He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle where he had dwelt among human beings. He delivered their strength into captivity and their beauty into the hand of the enemy. He enclosed his people in the sword and despised his inheritance. [Col. 0436A] Fire consumed their young men, and their maidens were not lamented. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows were not mourned.

Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a warrior revived from wine. He struck his enemies in the rear and gave them everlasting disgrace. He rejected the tent of Joseph and did not choose the tribe of Ephraim. But he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loved. He built his sanctuary like a unicorn on the earth, which he founded forever.

He chose David his servant and took him from the flocks of sheep; from following the nursing ewes he took him, to shepherd Jacob his servant and Israel his inheritance. He shepherded them with the innocence of his heart and led them by the understanding of his hands.

[Col. 0436B]

## Commentary

What he promised to God in the seventy-sixth psalm, he here delivers to human beings in the seventy-seventh. There he said to God, “I will remember from the beginning your wonders.” Here he says to the people, “I will speak declarations from the beginning,” his powers and the wonders that he performed, so that the next generation might know them and the children who would be born might rise up. Let them declare them to their children, so that they may not place their trust in the profits of the world or in the earthly desires of the age, but place their hope in God alone, not forget the works of their God, and seek his commandments.

Let them not become like their fathers, a crooked and most bitter race. When he says “race,” consider carefully what precedes. God does not condemn the creature in things deserving condemnation, but the will. Seeing, therefore, that by censuring the race he had created a difficulty, he removed this [Col. 0436C] statement from any insult to the Creator and explained that the fault lay not in the race but in the will. For he continued, saying, “A race that did not direct its heart.” And as though asked how they had failed to direct their heart, he replied: “Because they did not keep the covenant of God and did not wish to walk in his law.” By saying “they did not wish,” he excluded blame from the race and demonstrated the guilt of the will, through which they forgot the benefits and wonders of God: when he divided the sea so that they might cross, and made its waters stand here and there as in a wineskin; when he led them by a column of cloud during the day and by a column of fire at night; when he split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great abyss. Although they had drunk, they gave no thanks, but continued to sin.

Thus they spoke evil of God, saying, “Look, he brought water from the rock; can he give bread?” They said this because they did not believe in their God and did not hope in his salvation. “And he commanded the clouds above, and opened the doors of heaven.” “Doors” is used figuratively, as in the statement about the earth, “It opened its mouth.” The purpose of opening required him to name an opening a mouth on earth and doors in heaven. “And he rained manna upon them for food.” Manna, in Latin, is what we call “What is this?”—as the Hebrew says.

When heaven rained it down like coriander seed, the children of Israel, asking what it was, gave it its name while they were asking. For when they said, “What is it?”—that is, manna—the species itself received its name from the word with which they asked, a word that, by enlargement, they added. “He gave them the bread of heaven.” Through the occasion of the manna, the bread that descended from heaven was named. [Col. 0437A] “Man ate the bread of angels.” Whatever provides eternity in drinking and eating is angelic, since it does not involve foul and excremental digestion.

All beings have the substance of life; whether angels or whatever lives in heaven, they do not suffice for themselves without nourishment. They are led by hunger and thirst—or rather, by hunger and thirst for the Lord’s praise. They hunger and thirst for his righteousness, by which they grow fat and hold the eternal summit. Conversely, apostate angels hunger and thirst for unrighteousness, and are fattened by that work.

When the Lord says that the angels in heaven rejoice over one sinner who repents, he wished to show that, through righteousness, the one who had fattened the bellies of demons through unrighteousness had returned to their refreshment. There are also many things in bodies that restore without excremental digestion: a good report, an excellent fragrance, a wondrous sight, the favor of great people, and an excellent reputation, which is also said to “make the bones fat.”

We have said this to show that everything in heaven and on earth, invisible and visible, has its own measures, because God alone is immeasurable; that all things subsist through the structure of their qualities, because God alone is incorporeal; and that they live through another substance, because God alone needs nothing. He, however, is necessary to all, while no one is necessary to him.

Yet because, in the excess of his gracious goodness, he loves his creation in all things, he deigns to invite human beings through the law, through the judgments of virtues, through compunction of heart, and through the greatness of human works. Therefore he grants not only the bread of angels but also the flesh of countless birds [Col. 0437C] to those who desire it, even to the ungrateful.

And so that posterity might fear the crime of ingratitude, lest it go unpunished, while their food was still in their mouths the anger of God came upon them, because they did not believe his wonders. “Their days failed in vanity, and their years in haste.” But, as I said, if you are unwilling to do good unless compelled by evil: “When he killed them,” he says, “they sought him, and turning back they came to him at dawn.” Then they remembered that God was their helper and protector.

But when they said, “You are our God,” he says that they lied to him with their tongue alone, while their heart was not right with him. Hence the Lord also says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). Why this? Because faith was not held in his covenant. But, as the Apostle says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11).

Let us examine briefly which covenant is meant. Hear the Apostle: “No one,” he says, “annuls a human covenant or adds conditions to it.” It was said to Abraham, “In your seed I will inherit all the nations.” He did not say, “in seeds,” as though in many, but “in your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. 3). This, then, is the covenant that God made with Abraham, their father, and, while fulfilling it in his Son, “faith was not held in his covenant.”

Yet he is merciful; even while placed upon the cross, he is propitious toward their sins and, although he could have destroyed them, did not. Thus he asked his Father to forgive them also. For he remembered that they were flesh, knowing nothing in the spirit, and that they were spirits passing away and not returning. [Col. 0438A] Therefore the Lord often leaves sinners in this world the joy, abundance, and power that they have taken for themselves, because he knows what they will suffer in the fire of Gehenna; and, having compassion on them, he turns his anger away from them in this age.

Considering that, once they depart, they will go into the destruction of eternal fire and will not return, he says: “How often they provoked him in the wilderness,” not remembering the day when the Lord delivered them from the hand of the afflicter, first striking their enemies with ten plagues, then drowning them in the sea, while he himself led them out like a shepherd leading sheep in the wilderness, brought them to the mountains of his holiness, and drove nations out before them.

And after all this, what did they do? “They turned away,” he says, “and did not keep the covenant, as their fathers had done,” even to the point of provoking him to jealousy with their carved images. “For this reason,” he says, “he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh.” This passage refutes the heretics who say that, because of the sin of the two sons of Eli, the just God delivered the entire people of Israel to the Philistines. But the Holy Spirit, exposing the crime of the entire people, says that they turned away from God and did not keep his commandments, just as their fathers had done.

“Therefore,” he says, “he utterly rejected Israel, and therefore he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh; therefore he turned their strength into captivity.” And their beauty—that is, the ark of the Lord’s covenant—he delivered into the hands of the enemy. He enclosed his people in the sword and despised his inheritance, so that their priests fell by the sword, fire consumed their young men, their maidens perished without lamentation, and their widows died without mourners.

We now come to the passage that urges us from the historical sense toward a mystical and moral understanding. “The Lord awoke,” he says, “as from sleep.” Whenever captivity comes, whether carnal or spiritual, let us know that the Lord is sleeping; and he sleeps so long as those who dare to awaken him are not found fit to do so.

This is what our Lord Jesus Christ enacted in the boat while crossing over. An excessive and incomparable storm drove the boat in which he was with his disciples, so that nothing remained except that they should be submerged in the waves. The disciples approached the sleeping Lord and awakened him with a great cry, saying, “Teacher, we are perishing” (Matt. 8). But he arose, commanded the winds, and they grew still; the waves became calm. [Col. 0438D]

The Lord does not sleep, therefore, as though sleep holds him. He is always watchful and will never sleep completely, nor slumber. But when we impose on him such silence that he might say: “You are silent in the way that silence is customarily imposed upon the master of the household”—so that he may rest—“Look, I rest; look, I am silent; look, I sleep. I am not struck by the groans of prayers, I am not disturbed by the voices of psalms, nor awakened by constant supplications. In this great silence of yours I sleep. And while I sleep, a storm comes upon you, spiritual, as I have said, or carnal, so that, compelled by it, you flee to the king, in order to be freed by the watchfulness of the one whose sleep has seized you.”

Finally, awakened by the prayers of the saints, hear what he did: “He struck,” he says, “all his enemies in the secret place of their hind parts.” [Col. 0439A] So great was the multitude of mice that none of them remained whose anus was not gnawed by mice, so that, as the First Book of Kings says, their prominent *extales* [anal swellings?] protruded. This, then, is what he now says in this psalm: that the Lord, awakened, struck his enemies in their hind parts.

“He gave them everlasting disgrace,” he says, “and rejected the tabernacle of Joseph in the kingdom of Saul.” These two tribes held the royal power, namely Joseph and Benjamin. Hence he added, “He did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,” implying “for the kingdom,” but “he chose the tribe of Judah” for the kingdom. Although this had then been established by covenant in David, it was fulfilled in Christ.

“In Mount Zion, which he chose,” where he built his sanctuary like a unicorn: there he was born, there baptized, there tempted, there manifested in his powers, there suffered, there died, there was buried, there rose from the dead on the third day, and there ascended into the heavens. “In the land that he founded forever”—that is, in Zion, that is, in the Church of the saints.

For there he had chosen David his servant, when he took him from the flocks of sheep, to shepherd Jacob and Israel, his inheritance. The Son of God shepherds them to this day without malice of heart, and in the understanding of his hands he will lead us. For this reason he raised his hands upon the cross, so that in the glory of his hands he might direct us, he who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXVIII

### A Psalm of Asaph

O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem into a guardhouse for fruit trees. They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, and the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

We have become a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and derision to those around us. How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your anger upon the nations that do not know you, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon your name. For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his dwelling.

Do not remember our former iniquities; may your mercies quickly anticipate us, for we have become exceedingly poor. Help us, God our savior, and for the glory of your name deliver us; be propitious toward our sins for the sake of your name. Lest they perhaps say among the nations, “Where is their God?” let the vengeance for the blood of your servants that has been poured out enter into your sight; let the groaning of the prisoners come before you.

According to the greatness of your arm, take possession of the sons of those put to death. Repay our neighbors sevenfold in their bosom for the reproach with which they reproached you, Lord. But we, your people and the sheep of your pasture, will give you thanks forever; from generation to generation we will declare your praise.

## Commentary

The seventy-eighth psalm, following the summit of its predecessor, pours out lamentation to God together with prayer. Its historical account explains the former slaughter of the Philistines; its prophecy recalls the future of Nebuchadnezzar; and its moral sense concerns our present spiritual battle.

It must truly be said that it mourns that the nations have come into God’s inheritance. The First Book of Kings, concerning Solomon, also recalls the ark of the covenant. And Jeremiah, concerning Jerusalem and the temple, explains this psalm if you seek its prophetic meaning.

But we, who call our soul our Jerusalem—provided that the peaceful king rests in it—understand that when, through its own consent and negligence, it is overcome because it does not resist, and when, by sinning against God, it has departed from him through its offence, nations come against it. They come against the one whom Christ possesses as his inheritance, and they defile his holy temple, his holy body made so in baptism. They make Jerusalem into a guardhouse for fruit trees. They leave it so deserted that you might think that great city has been changed into a cheap gardener’s hut.

“They have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven.” Here the birds are called unclean spirits, of whom the Apostle says, “the spirit of this air.” Like birds, they devour the flesh of your holy ones through luxury. The beasts of the earth also devour them if they pour out their blood like water around Jerusalem itself. And there is no one to bury them, since no one is present who, by the example of his life, might hide them from the destruction of death.

Then we become a derision to all the demons, who are called our neighbors and enemies because, being placed near us, they never withdraw from hostility even for a single moment. In this situation the Lord must be asked to pour out his anger upon them. For these are the kingdoms that do not call upon his name, but daily devour Jacob and turn his dwelling—which had been adorned with virtues—into a wilderness.

These things happen to us if the Lord remembers our iniquities—would that they were former ones and not new ones. But because a remedy is necessary for the wounded, may your mercies quickly anticipate us, O God. For we have become exceedingly poor: we have lost the gold of chastity and the silver of a good conscience. We ourselves have become the prey of our enemies.

For the honor of your name, Lord, deliver us, and be propitious, lest unbelievers rejoice and say, “Where is their God?” Defend the blood of your servants that has been poured out. For just as demons rejoice in the ruin of human beings, so angels rejoice in our restoration. The most wicked spirits suffer destruction when the groaning of prisoners enters into the sight of God—if such a groaning for sins can be made only when it enters into God’s sight.

And the Lord begins, according to the greatness of his arm, to take possession of the sons of death, so that those who were sons of death may begin to be sons of life as well. When he repays the enemies sevenfold, because what was promised by the sevenfold Spirit at the time of baptism has been denied at the prompting of these enemies by those who had made the promise, let us make satisfaction to the Holy Spirit whom we received at our consecration and say to him:

“We are your people and the sheep of your flock, or of your pasture; we will give you thanks forever, and from age to age we will declare your praises”—you who reign with the Father and the Son, Holy Spirit, now and forever, unto eternal ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXXIX

### For the end; for those who will be changed; a psalm for the Assyrians; a testimony of Asaph

O ruler of Israel, attend; you who lead Joseph like a sheep. You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself before Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. Stir up your power and come, that you may save us.

O God of hosts, restore us and show your face, and we shall be saved. Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry over the prayer of your servant? You will feed us the bread of tears and give us drink in tears by measure. You have made us a contradiction to our neighbors, and our enemies have mocked us.

O God of hosts, restore us and show your face, and we shall be saved.

You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were its guide; you planted its roots, and it filled the land. The mountains were covered by its shadow, and its branches were like the cedars of God. It stretched its branches as far as the sea, and its shoots as far as the river.

Why have you destroyed its hedge, so that all who pass along the way pluck it? The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary beast has devoured it. O God of hosts, turn again; look from heaven, see, and visit this vine. Perfect the vine that your right hand planted, and [look] upon the Son of Man whom you strengthened for yourself.

What has been burned by fire and dug up at the rebuke of your face will perish. Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you strengthened for yourself. We will not depart from you; you will give us life, and we will call upon your name.

Lord God of hosts, restore us and show your face, and we shall be saved.

## Commentary

Again, in this psalm, he sings the same things concerning the destruction and the same tribulation of the people. He asks that the one who rules Israel attend and stir up his power, because no one worthy is found who dares to awaken him. Let him, therefore, stir up his own power; let him come and save us.

But because he is invisible and cannot be seen by anyone at all, let him take a form through which he may deign to show his face. If he shows it, we shall be saved—just as those placed in icy danger, where the force of cold threatens death, are undoubtedly delivered if the sight of the sun is shown to them. How much more shall we be saved when God’s face is shown to us in our Lord Jesus Christ?

If, then, we perceive the captivity of the Lord’s vine, which he brought out of Egypt through water and the Holy Spirit, and which he planted after driving out the demons; who was so much the way before us that he said, “I am the way” (John 10); who planted our roots so firmly in his faith that he might fill the whole land of our body; and if the true vine was in us, whose branches covered mountains, superior to all the saints, whose shoots were more excellent and higher than the cedars of God—this vine the boar of the forest, the unbelieving people, ravaged in the Passion, and the solitary beast devoured it.

Christ first suffers this tumult in us also when we permit the rage of demons to enter our heart, where we have received Christ. Therefore our food ought not to be joy, but the bread of tears, and our drink tears, if we perceive that we have become a reproach to our neighbors and that they themselves have mocked us.

For when we remain in tearful prayer, the God of hosts looks from heaven, sees, and visits this vine. He directs the vine that his right hand planted in us through the Son of Man, Jesus, whom he strengthened for himself by fire kindled and a hand dug through, when Abraham, with fire kindled and sword-bearing hand, was ready to slaughter his son before the Lord.

Then he swore to Abraham that he would so establish his son for himself that in him he would inherit all the nations. Therefore remember, Lord, what you swore, and restore what you granted, so that we may not depart from you. For we shall not depart from you if you are made alive. We, however, shall always call upon your name.

We have no other hope than that you restore us by giving good counsels in our hearts and showing us your face. May we be saved by its sight, in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXX

### For the end; for the winepresses; a psalm of Asaph; for the fifth day of the week

Rejoice in God our helper; shout joyfully to the God of Jacob. Take up a psalm and give the tambourine, the pleasing psaltery with the lyre. Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your feast. For it is a statute in Israel and a judgment for the God of Jacob.

He established it as a testimony in Joseph when he came out of the land of Egypt; he heard a language that he did not know. He turned his back away from burdens; his hands served with the basket. You called upon me in tribulation, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the water of contradiction.

Hear, my people, and I will testify to you. Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god for you, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

But my people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me. So I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they will walk in their own inventions. If only my people had heard me, if only Israel had walked in my ways. Perhaps I would have reduced their enemies to nothing and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them.

The enemies of the Lord lied to him, and their time will endure forever. He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock.

## Commentary

In the seventy-ninth psalm the vine is restored; in the eightieth, the winepresses are treated. “Rejoice in God our helper,” because his vine has risen. “Shout joyfully to the God of Jacob”: his vine has been restored. For he has risen whom the unbelieving people ravaged.

The people ravaged the very one who said, “I am the true vine” (John 15), the one who said, “They have ravaged my hands and my feet” (Matt. 28). The people who ravaged him were more savage than the wild boar; behold, he has risen.

You who mourned there, rejoice here; you who were silent there, shout joyfully here; [Col. 0443A] you who were anxious there, rejoice with one another here in psalms and hymns, and on the notable day—that is, on the day of the Lord’s redemption. For this is the day of our feast, on which the Lord deigns to give a command as a testimony to Joseph, because the Lord was about to visit them with a visitation.

Therefore he established a testimony concerning himself in Joseph when he came out of the land of Egypt. He heard a language that he had not known, after four hundred and thirty years. Through the night Moses heard the voice of God, the descendant of Abraham, just as had been promised to him, when he turned his back away from the exceedingly heavy burdens, when his hands served with the basket in mud and brick.

Then the Lord says to Israel: “You called upon me in tribulation, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the storm. I heard you and drowned your enemies. I tested you at the water of contradiction,” amid the worst murmuring, in which Moses, the blameless servant, also appeared to have given offense.

Hear now, my people. I will speak to Israel and testify to you: I, whom you crucify, am God. And what God? The one who brought you out of the land of Egypt (Num. 20). “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.”

Why do you command so insistently that the criminal and unbelieving people who crucified the Lord open its mouth? “Open your mouth,” he says, “and I will fill it.” O most merciful Savior and most evident restorer of the human race: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” If you wish to escape the death into which you have fallen, drink the blood that you shed.

But what follows? “My people did not hear my voice, and Israel did not attend to me.” Therefore I let them go according to the desires of their heart, and they went in their own inventions.

I came to this people, to this people; and before I came, I sent prophets. To this people alone I sent apostles before I suffered, but it utterly disdained hearing me. For if it had heard me, or if it had walked in my ways, I would have humbled its enemies to nothing and laid my hand upon those who afflicted it.

But the chief priests, the scribes, and the Pharisees, who were enemies of the Lord Jesus Christ, lied to the people, saying, “He is not from God.” Those wretched people, to their own destruction, believed those who lied to them. They denied the one who had come to free them.

Yet their time will be forever. For when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11). Then they too will feed on the fat of wheat and be satisfied with honey from the rock, believing in the one from whom they fell through envy. For the Lord is able to graft them in again.

Let us remain in his faith, so that he may reduce our enemies to nothing and lay his hand upon those who afflict us, whether spiritual or carnal enemies, through Christ our Lord, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM LXXXI

### A Psalm of Asaph

God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods. How long will you judge unjustly and take the faces of sinners? Judge for the needy and the orphan; justify the humble and the poor. Rescue the poor and deliver the needy from the hand of the sinner.

They did not know, nor did they understand; they walk in darkness. All the foundations of the earth will be shaken. I said, “You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Yet you will die like human beings and fall like one of the princes.

Arise, O God; judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all the nations.

## Commentary

Everything that can generally be called by an honorable name belongs specifically to God, through the nature of his incomprehensible majesty by which he is God. Yet it is said to a human being, “I have made you a god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7); and the Lord is also said of a human being, although God alone is Lord. A human being is called holy, although God alone is holy; a human being is called good, although no one is good except God alone.

What is God-like in human beings is that a human being receives in image what God possesses naturally, being the more like him as, in conduct, he imitates his likeness more fully. Hence in the present psalm God himself speaks to those to whom he has granted the power of judging: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. Yet you will die like human beings and fall like one of the princes.”

“One of the princes”—that is, the devil, the traitor Judas, Saul, Jeroboam, or one of those who held authority. You too will fall, because you judge unjustly and take the faces of sinners. You do not judge for the orphan and the needy; you have not justified the humble and the poor; you have not rescued the poor and the needy, nor delivered them from the hand of sinners.

Although these statements are generally made about judges and the poor, nevertheless the prophecy of the song resounds against the Pharisees together with the chief priests. For “they did not know, nor did they understand,” because it was said to them, “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” If they had believed, they would have understood that the one whom they denied was their Lord, and that they persecuted with unjust hatred the one who loved them.

Even if, according to your unbelief, he was not Lord, he was nevertheless a brother: a Hebrew from Hebrews, and you yourselves said that his parents were your brothers. Say, then, what was the cause of your hatred. “Why,” they say, “does he heal the weak on the Sabbath?” Does a physician deserve hatred for bringing health to his brothers, or deserve to be harassed by your detestable conduct because of his love?

But because “the one who hates his brother walks in darkness” (1 John 2), and “all the foundations of the earth will be shaken” when God rises to judge the earth, let us withdraw from hatred of our brothers. For “the one who hates his brother does not know where he is going” (ibid.), because darkness surrounds him.

Let us therefore attend carefully to the end of the psalm, so that when the Lord rises to judge the earth, he may also receive us into his inheritance among all the nations—he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM LXXXII

### A Song; a Psalm of Asaph
God, who is like you? Do not be silent or restrain yourself, O God. For behold, your enemies have made a noise, and those who hate you have lifted up their heads. They have plotted wickedly against your people and have conspired against your holy ones. They have said, “Come, let us destroy them as a nation, so that the name of Israel may no longer be remembered.” For they have conspired unanimously; together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of the Edomites and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, the foreigners together with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assyria also has come with them; they have become an aid to the sons of Lot. Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor; they became like dung upon the ground. Make their leaders like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna— all their leaders who said, “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.” My God, make them like a wheel, and like chaff before the face of the wind. Like fire that consumes a forest, like a flame burning up the mountains, so pursue them in your storm, and in your wrath throw them into confusion. Fill their faces with disgrace, and [Col. 0445B] they will seek your name, O Lord. Let them be ashamed and terrified forever and ever; let them be confounded and perish. Let them know that you alone are called Lord, the Most High over all the earth.

## COMMENTARY
