The eighty-second psalm does indeed contain the names of nations fighting against the Israelites, against whom the Most High is entreated—the one God who is Lord over all the earth. It says that these nations rose up against the Hebrews: Moab from Lot, Amalek from Ham. They were in the tents of Edom, and the Ishmaelites joined them. They were attempting to hold God’s sanctuary captive. Against them the Lord is entreated not to be silent or restrained.

Therefore at the beginning it says, “God, who is like you?” and at the end, “You alone are the Most High over all the earth.” For those who trust in their gods are stirred up against us, while we have you as God, and you have no equal. You alone are the Most High over all the earth.

But since we believe that all these nations, having been taken possession of by the apostles, have been enrolled in Christ’s inheritance, and that they have been made fellow citizens of the holy ones by grace and members of God’s household, let us not say of them, “Your enemies have made a noise, O Lord,” but rather of the demons, whose counsels shake the whole world carnally and weary it spiritually. Yet we would not be overcome carnally by visible enemies if we overcame the invisible ones spiritually. For no one enters the house of a strong man and carries off his possessions unless he has first bound the strong man.

The spiritually strong, therefore, are human beings whose vessels are their outward bodies; human beings are the ones with whom the demons wage war in their inner selves. When the demons have conquered them and taken possession of their vessels—that is, their bodies, which they had used as weapons of war against their enemies—then, having taken possession of them, they stir up the nations, because they know that they entirely lack those who were accustomed to fight against them spiritually and to overcome them with the weapons of prayer and a pure conscience. Let one spiritual person come forward, confident in his conscience, and recite this psalm against a hundred thousand nations, and you will immediately see victory take place.

But since we still have a struggle with those whom we are attempting to overcome spiritually—for we have not yet conquered them, even if we think that we have—for if we had conquered them spiritually, as I said, we would certainly not be overcome carnally, let us act so that, as earthly provinces are overcome and occupied for us, spiritual homelands may not be denied us. Thus, at least at the end of our life, we may be found engaged in a good purpose, because they plot against us, saying, “Let us destroy them as a nation, so that God may remember their name no longer.” For the demons know that if we sin, we shall be hateful to God just as they are.

Let us ask the Lord that, just as fire consumes forests and a flame consumes mountains, so he may pursue them in his storm. For they say, “Let us take possession of the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.” God’s sanctuary is where the sacred mysteries are stored: there is the heavenly flesh, there the divine blood, there the power of the charism, there the everlasting fountain and the divine law. All these things are within us, who through faith have become God’s sanctuaries. Therefore let us stir the Lord to zeal, saying to him: “Lord, those whom you redeemed with your blood, whom you deigned to make your sanctuary, are being attacked by those who have conspired against your covenant. Fill their faces with disgrace, so that they may be confounded and perish forever.”

For when those who hinder the knowledge of the Lord have perished, then every nation will know that you alone are the Most High over all the earth. Thus, when temples and idols have finally been cast down everywhere, the Lord reigns over the whole earth in the Church; the Lord Jesus Christ reigns over the body that is ours. He is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and he alone is the Most High, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 83

A psalm of the sons of Korah, for the end, concerning the winepresses.

How beloved are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and languishes in the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God. For the sparrow has found a home for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young. Your altars, O Lord of hosts, my King and my God! Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you. Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place that he has established. For the lawgiver will give a blessing; they will go from strength to strength, and the God of gods will be seen in Zion. O Lord God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob. Look upon our protector, O God, and look upon the face of your Christ. For one day in your courts is better than thousands. I have chosen to be despised in the house of my God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. For God loves mercy and truth; the Lord will give grace and glory. He will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things. O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.

## COMMENTARY

Since in the eighty-second psalm those who wished to seize God’s sanctuary have been confounded and have perished—those who produced weariness and obstacles to chastity, to reading, to singing psalms alike, and to thinking about good things—now, with the Lord reigning within us, we who were the sons of Korah the transgressor become sons of God, after this evil father has been swallowed up by the earth.

And we who formerly drank alien fire, not from God, and thought of enduring greed, now, kindled by the fire of divine love, say: “How lovely, how beloved, and how beautiful are your dwellings, in which you dwell, Lord God of hosts.” What are these dwellings of which he says, “My soul longs for and languishes in his courts,” in which the heart and flesh of this new lover also rejoice? In them, he says, Christ the sparrow found a home for himself; and in them the turtledove—that is, the Church—found a nest where it might gather its young.

“Where,” he says, “are your altars, O Lord of hosts”—that is, your mysteries—“my King and my God”? Blessed are those who reach them, because they will praise you forever, the sweet solace of misery. For there, having your help, they establish ascents in their hearts—not at banquets of those who laugh, but in the valley of tears. There they receive a blessing from you, from whom they received the Law, and in these things they see the God of gods in Zion—that is, in your Church.

There, O Lord God of hosts, you will hear prayers—not the prayers of vices: “God, let him love me; let me obtain this; let me possess that.” The Lord of hosts rejects such prayers of vice. What, then, does he embrace? “Give me chastity, wisdom, contempt for the world, patience, charity, and a good opinion of my neighbor.” If these are kinds of virtue, and the God of hosts is the one whom we pray to, he certainly approves those things by which he will make us sharers in his nature.

When he looks upon the face of Christ and sees the human being seated at his right hand, through whom one day will be better because it will be eternal and will have no night, it will be a day of joy for believers. This one day in his kingdom will be better than thousands of years consumed upon the earth. Whoever believes these things chooses rather to be despised in the conduct of believers. For God’s house does not consist of cement and lime, but in the believing person who keeps God’s commandments.

Among us, therefore, it is better for me to be regarded as despised than to be regarded as a king in the tents of sinners, where the Lord loves mercy and truth, and, after seeing mercy and truth preserved by the one to whom the Lord gave them, will give grace and glory, so that he may possess them without succession. For he will not deprive those who walk in innocence of good things.

To this let us all say: “O Lord God of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes in you.” When you say “man,” you have not distinguished sex but the mind. A woman will act as a man in virtue. The king loves the one who is rightly called a man, when, through the faith of her mind and by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, she has cast down the vices that make even a man a woman. He reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 84

For the sons of Korah, for the end.

You have blessed your land, O Lord; you have turned away the captivity of Jacob. You have forgiven the iniquity of your people; you have covered all their sins. You have softened all your anger; you have turned away from the anger of your indignation. Convert us, O God our Savior, and turn your anger away from us. Will you be angry with us forever, or will you extend your anger from generation to generation? O God, when you have turned, you will give us life, and your people will rejoice in you. Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation. I will hear what the Lord God will speak within me, for he will speak peace to his people, to his holy ones, and to those who turn their hearts toward him. Yet his salvation is near to those who fear him, so that glory may dwell in our land. Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed one another. Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven. For the Lord will give goodness, and our land will give its fruit. Righteousness will walk before him, and he will set his footsteps upon the way.

## COMMENTARY

The eighty-fourth psalm is likewise applied to the sons of Korah. The sons of Korah are those whose father is removed when he wishes to place alien fire upon the altar, while Christ is bestowed as their Father through grace. For just as that fire is lust proceeding against God and against Moses, that is, against the Law, so this fire kindles the hearts of believers in the embrace of mercy and truth, so that righteousness and peace kiss one another.

If you ask when these things took place, listen. When the Lord blessed his land by his coming, then he turned away the captivity of Jacob. Then he forgave the impiety of his people, softened all his anger, and turned away from us the anger of his indignation, showing us his mercy and giving us his salvation in Christ.

Let us hear what he speaks who came and blessed his land: “My peace,” he says, “I give you” (John XIV). See how he speaks peace to his people: first to the holy ones, that is, to the apostles; afterward to those who are converted to him through the apostles. For his salvation is near to those who fear God, if glory—that is, the Holy Spirit—dwells in our land, that is, in our bodies. When he dwells there, mercy and truth meet one another within us in loving embraces, and righteousness and peace kiss one another.

For truth, which is Christ, has sprung up from the earth—that is, from Mary—and this was accomplished by a just judgment, which, when it took place, taught us that righteousness had looked down from heaven. When the Lord gave this blessing to Mary, in whom, as in our earth, he gave his fruit from our own substance, he gave his own perfect human being, from the seed of David according to the flesh. Before him righteousness walked in John the Baptist, so that he might set his footsteps upon the way. He himself was the voice promised by Isaiah’s prophecy, crying in the desert of this age: “Prepare the ways of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isaiah XL).

For Zechariah also says to John: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke I). In him, therefore, righteousness walked before the Lord, so that righteousness itself might, through Christ, set its footsteps upon the way by which one travels to heaven. Let us follow the traces of him who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. To him be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 85

A prayer of David.

Incline your ear, O Lord, and hear me, for I am needy and poor. Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I have cried to you all day; gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul. For you, O Lord, are gentle and mild, and rich in mercy toward all who call upon you. Give ear, O Lord, to my prayer, and attend to the voice of my petition. On the day of my tribulation I cried to you, because you heard me. There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there is nothing like your works. All the nations that you have made will come and worship before you, O Lord, and will glorify your name. For you are great and perform wonders; you alone are God. Lead me, O Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth; let my heart rejoice so that it may fear your name. [Col. 0449B] I will confess to you, O Lord my God, with all my heart, and I will glorify your name forever. For your mercy is great toward me, and you have delivered my soul from the lowest underworld. O God, the unjust have risen up against me, and the assembly of the powerful have sought my soul; they have not set you before their eyes. But you, O Lord God, are compassionate and merciful, patient, rich in mercy, and truthful. Look upon me and have mercy on me; give your authority to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid. Establish with me a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see and be confounded, because you, O Lord, have helped and comforted me.

## COMMENTARY

Whereas in the eighty-second psalm he said, “God, who is like you?” now, in the eighty-fifth, he says, “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord.” If he had asked the former question as though ignorant, here he has been instructed.

There he spoke against all the nations; here he says concerning all the nations that you made: “They will not come and wage war,” as he had said there, but, “They will come and worship before you, O Lord.”

From where do you derive this confidence? “If you incline your ear,” he says, “and hear me, and guard me because I am holy”—that is, because I have been sanctified—and if you gladden me because I am your servant; if, on the day of my tribulation, you hear me crying to you; if you lead me in your way, and I walk in your truth; if you deliver my soul from the lowest underworld; and if you confound these unjust, unclean spirits who have risen against me—then my heart will rejoice over the victory, and it will fear your name because of the battle.

For in this battle I had this one and only consolation: I gloried that I feared you as my Lord, while those who had risen against me had not set you before their eyes. But because you are compassionate and merciful, and because you are forbearing, you will not kill. As you are merciful toward them, be truthful toward me; give your power to your servant Jesus Christ, and save the son of your handmaid, Mary.

For when he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, we, his apostles and disciples, together with all who believe, will have the sign of his cross for good, so that they may see your sign upon our foreheads and be confounded, whether the enemies are visible or invisible. For by this sign you help us, and by it you console us, you who reign throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0450A]

# PSALM 86

A psalm of a song, for the sons of Korah.

Its foundations are in the holy mountains. The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God. I will remember Rahab and Babylon among those who know me. Behold, the foreigners, Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians—these were there. Will Zion not say, “A human being, and a human being, was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her”? The Lord will recount in the Scriptures of the peoples and of the rulers, of those who were in her: “The dwelling place of all who rejoice is in you.”

## COMMENTARY

Nearly all the psalms that are entitled “for the sons of Korah” are full of joy. For they did not follow their father’s iniquity and take up lustful fire alien to God; rather, loving what the Lord loves, they speak of the glorious city.

Let us inquire, however, what beginning the spirit of prophecy gave to the eighty-sixth psalm. “Its foundations.” You have not yet said whose, and already you say “its.” From this it is evident that God showed you the city, whose position, while you were singing to the Lord, you named; and, answering your thought, you suddenly exclaimed: “The foundations of that city which I am contemplating, whose gates the Lord loves above all the tents of Jacob, of which glorious things have been spoken by the prophets—its foundations are in the holy mountains.”

There are the foundations of the city: those whom Christ made lofty mountains, whose summits strike the heavens; in them they are transfigured in splendor; in them Moses and Elijah appear with him; in them the Law and the Prophecy agree with Christ; in them, when the heavens were opened, the Father cried out concerning his Christ: “This is the one in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew XVII). Upon these mountains the foundations of the Church have been placed.

But no one can lay another foundation there except the one that has been laid (I Corinthians III). A solid rock has been laid. If anyone lays something other than what has been laid, he has laid it upon sand.

But perhaps you say: “Since the Apostle mentions one foundation, how can you mention several foundations here?” Consider this in response: if you say that Christ alone is king, you are told, “He is King of kings”; if you say “Lord,” you will be answered, “He is Lord of lords”; if you say “holy,” he is “Holy of holies.” Thus, if you mention only one foundation, you cannot deny the foundation of foundations.

Therefore the same Apostle desires and earnestly wishes that believers be built upon Christ, upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians II).

In this city, then, I will remember Rahab, who received the messengers, and Babylon, which led captives away—namely, the filthy peoples of the nations in fornication, like Rahab, and the proud in their strength, like Babylon. “I say,” he says, “that these will come to this city, so that they may know you.” For there are foreigners; there are Tyrians; there also the people of the Ethiopians will cry out concerning the apostles, saying: “We have heard them speaking in our own languages of the mighty works of God” (Acts II).

There we came to know Zion, the mother, saying that a human being and a human being was born in her. In the province of Zion, the mother of the Hebrew citizens says: “We nations have learned that the first human being, Adam, was made from the earth into a living soul; now another human being, the last Adam, has been born from a virgin into a life-giving spirit. The first human being generates children who possess the earth; the second human being generates those who possess the heavens.”

“Behold, a human being and a human being”—how do you nations know this? In Zion, that is, in the city whose foundations are in the holy mountains. There it was said to us: “The Lord will recount this in the Scriptures of the peoples and of the rulers who were in her.” And we learned that in her dwelling there will be no one who troubles, no one who sighs, no one who weeps, and no one who is afflicted; rather, the dwelling of all who rejoice will be in her.

Because their joy could not be expressed in words, it has been distinguished by comparison, so that as much joy as all of us who are in the world can gather into one totality is founded in one inhabitant of that city, through him who founded it, the Most High, reigning with the Son, the Father, and the Holy Spirit throughout eternal ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 87

A song of a psalm of the sons of Korah, for the end, concerning Maheleth, for responsive understanding, of Heman the Ezrahite.

O Lord, God of my salvation, I have cried out by day and by night before you. Let my prayer enter into your presence; incline your ear to my petition. For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to the underworld. I have been counted among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead. Like the wounded who sleep in tombs, whom you remember no longer, and who have been cut off from your hand. They placed me in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death. Your wrath has been confirmed against me, and you have brought all your waves over me. You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves. I have been handed over and could not escape; my eyes failed because of poverty. I cried to you, O Lord, all day; I stretched out my hands to you. Will you perform wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up and give thanks to you? Will anyone in the tomb recount your mercy, or those placed in destruction acknowledge your truth? Will your wonders be known in darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? But I have cried to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer will come before you. Why, O Lord, do you reject my prayer and turn your face away from me? I am poor and in labors from my youth; yet, when exalted, I was humbled and thrown into confusion. [Col. 0451D] Your angers have passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They have surrounded me like water; all day they have surrounded me together. You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery.

## COMMENTARY

The title of this psalm does indeed name the sons of Korah, but the psalm directs its song concerning Maheleth and gives understanding to Heman the Ezrahite. They call Maheleth, that is, “the destitute”; Heman they call “the needy.” Therefore the speech is addressed to the destitute and the poor.

I believe it is addressed to that destitute one whom the disciples abandoned, leaving him alone in the hands of his enemies and fleeing. But to which poor man could it refer except the one of whom the Apostle says: “Although he was rich, he became poor for our sake” (II Corinthians VIII), so that his eyes were weakened because of poverty?

He was poor, not possessing the riches of immortality in his passion. His eyes were closed in death because of that very weakness. In that death he says that physicians cannot raise him; there he says that he was placed in the lowest pit, in darkness and in the shadow of death. It was at the time when they made him an abomination to themselves, when he was handed over by Judas. “Then,” he says, “when I was handed over, I could not escape. I did not demand the cup of suffering from the hands of those who bound me. Then my eyes were weakened because of poverty.”

For I was not making use of the salvation of divinity; rather, I was suffering the weakness of the humanity I had assumed. Let us therefore hear what that assumed human being himself speaks: “You caused me to be born from a virgin, so that, as they recount your wonders, human beings might believe and, fleeing unbelief, attain life. You caused me to walk over swelling waters with dry feet, to command the winds, to restore light to the blind, health to the sick, and the life they had lost to the dead. Why do you now permit me to go to death? Will they recount your mercy in the tombs? Or will those placed in destruction acknowledge your truth? Or will those brought back to the land of forgetfulness know your righteousness?”

These are the things about which I cried to you in my prayer when I said: “If it is possible, let this cup of suffering pass from me.” But because it cannot pass unless I drink it, “your will be done” (Mark XIV). Let me be exalted on the cross, humbled before the judge, and seem confounded in death; and in this way let me be exalted, humbled, and confounded.

But because I am free among the dead, in the morning my prayer will come before you, and they will see the one rising whom they had seen all day stretching out his hands upon the cross. After this, when he had been placed in the tomb, every friend and every neighbor had been put far from him because of the misery of his suffering. His prayer does indeed enter into the presence of God. He inclined his ear to his peace, and let his life, which had drawn near to the underworld, rise from the dead.

For when morning came, his prayer immediately went before him, fulfilling the promise of the resurrection, so that he might show himself not only alive but also ascending into the heavens. To him be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 88

The understanding of Ethan the Ezrahite.

I will sing the mercies of the Lord forever. From generation to generation I will proclaim your truth with my mouth. For you said: “Mercy will be built forever in the heavens; your truth will be prepared in them.” I have established a covenant with my chosen ones; I have sworn to David my servant: “I will prepare your seed forever.” And I will build your throne from generation to generation. The heavens will confess your wonders, O Lord, and your truth in the assembly of the holy ones. For who among the clouds will be equal to the Lord? Who will be like the Lord among the sons of God? God is glorified in the counsel of the holy ones, great and terrible above all who surround him. O Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are powerful, O Lord, and your truth surrounds you. You rule the power of the sea; you still the movement of its waves. You humbled the proud as one wounded; with the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies. The heavens are yours, and the earth is yours; you founded the world and its fullness. You created the north and the sea. Tabor and Hermon will rejoice in your name, and your arm with power. Let your hand be strengthened and your right hand exalted. Righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne. Mercy and truth will go before your face. Blessed is the people that knows the shout of joy. O Lord, they will walk in the light of your face; they will rejoice in your righteousness all day, and in your name they will be exalted. For you are the glory of their strength, and by your good pleasure our horn will be exalted. For our exaltation belongs to the Lord, and to the Holy One of Israel, our king.

Then you spoke in a vision to your holy ones and said: “I have placed help in one who is powerful, and I have exalted an elect one from my people. I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. For my hand will assist him, and my arm will strengthen him. The enemy will accomplish nothing against him, and the son of iniquity will not add to harming him. I will cut down his enemies before him, and I will put those who hate him to flight. My truth and my mercy will be with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted. I will place his hand upon the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers. He will call upon me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the protector of my salvation.’ And I will make him firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth. I will preserve my mercy for him forever, and my covenant will remain faithful to him. I will establish his seed forever and ever, and his throne like the days of heaven.

“But if his sons abandon my covenant and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my righteous ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows. But I will not scatter my mercy from him, nor will I harm him in my truth. I will not profane my covenant, and I will not make void the things that proceed from my lips. Once I have sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David. His seed will remain forever, and his throne like the sun before me, and like the full moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

Yet you have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ. You have turned away the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary on the earth. You have destroyed all his hedges; you have made his covenant a terror. All who pass along the road have plundered him; he has become a reproach to his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of those who oppressed him; you have gladdened all his enemies. You have turned away the help of his sword and have not assisted him in battle. You have destroyed him from purification and have cast his throne to the ground. You have shortened the days of his time; you have drenched him with confusion. How long, O Lord, will you turn away forever? Will your anger burn like fire? Remember what my substance is. Surely you did not establish the sons of human beings in vain. Who is the man who will live and not see death, or deliver his soul from the hand of the underworld? Where are your former mercies, O Lord, as you swore to David in your truth? Remember, O Lord, the reproach of your servants, which I have kept in my bosom, from many nations. Remember what your enemies reproached, O Lord, what they reproached concerning the exchange of your Christ.

Blessed be the Lord forever; let it be so, let it be so.

## COMMENTARY
From the time when the people were counted, the historical meaning of this psalm is made clear. Its mystery, however, extends to the passion of our Lord. Let us therefore first state the historical sense, and from this turn to the mystical sense.

The Hebrews call Ethan “humbled.” King David is therefore humbled through the reduction of the people. The whole song arouses a recollection of the Lord’s mercies. He says that he will sing of the Lord’s mercies forever; he says that God declared that he would build mercy forever; he says that the heavens confess the Lord’s mercies; he says that God swore to him, his servant, and prepared this truth in the heavens, when he established his covenant with the elect, and then swore to David, his servant. What he had sworn he discloses below. “But if his sons,” he says, “forsake my law, I will visit their sins with the rod and with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them, nor harm my truth.” And he added: “Once I have sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David.” But you, Lord, rejected, expelled, and delayed your Christ—that is, King David. For on account of one action of his, the whole people dies. And therefore he says: “Have you established the children of men in vain? Who is the man who lives and will not see death? Or who will rescue his soul from the hand of the underworld? Where are your ancient mercies, Lord, as you swore to David in your truth?” [Col. 0454B]

Let the historical discourse suffice for us; let us ascend to the mystical sense. For in Christ an eternal mercy has been built—not a building made by hand, but one composed by the Holy Spirit. Its truth was prepared in the heavens in such a way that, when he had established the covenant of his law, he swore to David, his servant, that he would place upon his throne one from the fruit of his womb, one like whom there would be none among the sons of God, one who is great and greatly to be feared above all who surround him. For they are all his servants.

He gave a sign that the Lord was himself Jesus Christ when, placed in a boat, he himself ruled over the power of the sea, calmed the movement of its waves, humbled the proud devil himself like one wounded, and by the power of his arm scattered all the demons. Then he showed his heavens to be his own when he gave the blind the light of heaven. He showed the earth to be his own when he commanded it to return the buried dead. He also showed that he had created the north when he commanded its winds. Tabor and Hermon rejoiced in his name when they saw the inhabitants of those mountains, which are near Jerusalem, having their sick saved, paralytics cured by him, lepers cleansed, and the dead raised.

Those mountains themselves—that is, Tabor and Hermon—will rejoice in Jesus’ name, saying to him: “Your arm and your power, for your hand is strengthened, and let your right hand be exalted above every healing of the sick.” We rejoice, not only because you do these things, but also because we see your disciples, Lord, walking in the light of your countenance, since [Col. 0454D] you are their glory and power.

For yours, God, is the taking up of man, as sacred Scripture, which has spoken and declared through the mouth of the saints, bears witness: “I will choose the chosen one from the people of God,” in whom “the glory of your hand” may glory, who would say to you, God, in truth: “You are my Father.” Of him you also would say: “I will make him firstborn, so that at his name every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth may bend, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II). He established his throne forever and ever, faithfully preserves his covenant with him forever, and promises that his days will be like the days of heaven.

Yet this one, seized by his enemies on account of our sins, had his holiness profaned on earth. He does not permit the assistance of the sword to be offered even by one disciple, but cries out to him: “Put your sword back into its sheath” (John XVIII). And although he could have provided him with more than twelve legions of angels, he did not wish to assist him in this battle, but shortened the span of his days and covered him with such great shame that, counted among the impious, he was compelled to undergo the cross in the midst of murderers. This is not the action of an angry God, but of one who shows mercy.

Yet what does he say because he suffers? “How long will your anger burn like fire? Remember, Lord, that you formed me from the Virgin, and remember what my substance is. For when all human beings die in their sins, so that there is no one who lives and does not see death, and scarcely anyone who rescues his soul from the hand of the underworld—for all things have been shut up in unbelief, so that you may have mercy on all” (Rom. XI)—let your promised mercies come, Lord, and remember the apostles whom I held in my bosom, gainers of many nations, whom your enemies reproached, Lord, whom they reproached as a substitute for your Christ, while expecting another Christ and denying the one who suffered. [Col. 0455C]

But let us who know the jubilation walk in the light of his countenance. Let us rejoice in him whom we mourned in his suffering, now risen from the dead, and, worshiping him, let us say: “Blessed are you, Lord, forever; let it be, let it be.”

Let us pray that this confession may benefit us at our end, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM LXXXIX

[Col. 0455D]

## A Prayer of Moses, the Man of God

Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation. Before the mountains came to be, or the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are God. Do not turn man toward humiliation, and you said: “Turn back, children of men.” For a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday, which has passed, and like a watch in the night; their years will be counted as nothing. In the morning, like grass, may he pass away; in the morning may he flourish and pass away; in the evening may he fall, grow hard, and wither. For we have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled. You have set our iniquities before your sight, our age in the illumination of your countenance. For all our days have failed, and in your anger we have failed. Our years [Col. 0456A] will be reckoned like a spiderweb; the days of our years are in themselves seventy years. But if there are eighty years in strength, even more than these are labor and sorrow. For gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be corrected. Who knows the power of your anger, and, because of your fear, can count your wrath? Make your right hand known in this way, and instruct those who are learned in heart with wisdom. Turn back, Lord—how long?—and be entreatable toward your servants. We have been filled in the morning with your mercy; we have rejoiced and been glad throughout all our days. We have rejoiced for the days in which you humbled us, for the years in which we saw evils. Look upon your servants and upon your works, and direct their children. And let the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us; direct the works of our hands over us, and direct the work of our hands.

[Col. 0456B]

## Commentary

The eighty-ninth psalm sings of our Lord, who has become our refuge in Christ Jesus. It sings of the one who made the mountains and established the earth and the world, who already reigned from age to age, before these things came to be.

Question David, and say to him: “How do you know this—that your God was already God and reigned before the earth came to be?” He will answer you: “That great prophet Moses, who spoke with God face to face, as though speaking with his friend, learned this from the mouth of God himself, and he himself taught us.”

Why have we said these things? Because we read in the title: “A Prayer of the Man of God.” What he had therefore learned from him, he consecrated to him under his own name.

Why, however, does the psalm proceed toward the mystical sense? Because he foresaw that accursed heresies would arise, saying that the Son of God, who has become our refuge in Christ, did not exist before the world came to be and the circle of the earth was established. Against these he says: “From age to age you are God.”

“Do not turn man toward humiliation”—that is, do not condemn man who has been placed in a state of humility, because you said: “Turn back, children of men.” This means that you declared yourself to resist the proud and to grant grace to the humble. Do not turn away the man who has been placed in humility, who rises like grass and is like a flower: what rises in the morning withers in the evening.

With you, a thousand years are like one day, or like a watch in the night. The watch in the night is one quarter of the night, which the shepherds divide among themselves, so that, while some keep watch for three hours, others rest.

When he recalls that “we have failed in your anger,” he recalls what the predecessor sang in the psalm: “After the numbering of the people, we failed in your anger,” because you placed our iniquities before your sight, and our age in the light of your countenance.

Against grass and spiderweb, and against the flower of hay, Lord—you who have always had mercy on human beings—why are you moved? A thousand years appear to you as one night watch appears to us. But our years, which are meditated upon like sand, scarcely amount to eighty years at most, and in them there is for us labor and sorrow.

Why has such gentleness come upon the wretched? Why are we corrected so severely? Who does not know the power of your anger? Did I not know that you would be angry if I counted the people? It would have been enough that you made one hindered in heart understand.

Turn back, Lord, for a little while, and be entreatable toward your servants. Whenever the darkness of sins passed over us through correction, you showed mercy to us as though we were placed in the sea. Through this mercy we rejoiced and were glad throughout all the days in which you humbled us and throughout the years in which we saw evils.

Do the same now, because you have already made your right hand known, instructed us, and caused us to understand what we had failed to understand. Do not take pleasure in our death, you who said to sinners: “Turn back, children of men,” because you do not take pleasure in the destruction of the living.

Look, I beg you, upon your servants and upon the works of your hands, because, as it is written, we are all the works of your hands, and our fathers, corrected by your indignation, failed. Let their children be directed through the coming of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0457B] Christ, your Son, so that the splendor of the Lord our God may be upon us, through whom the works of our hands are directed. Through him the whole course of discipline has been set straight, the law amended, perversity corrected, and righteousness fulfilled. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XC

## A Song of Praise, to David

He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide in the protection of the God of heaven. He will say to the Lord: “You are my protector and my refuge; my God, I will hope in him.” For he himself has rescued me from the snare of hunters and from a harsh word. He will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope. His truth will surround you with a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow flying by day, nor the activity that walks in darkness, nor the assault and the noonday demon. A thousand will fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not approach you. Nevertheless, with your eyes you will observe, and you will see the repayment of sinners. For you, Lord, are my hope; you have made the Most High your refuge. Evil will not approach you, and a scourge will not come near your tent. For he has commanded his angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways. They will carry you in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone. You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon. For he hoped in me, and I will rescue him; I will protect him, because he has known my name. He will call upon me, and I will hear him; I am with him in tribulation, I will rescue him and glorify [Col. 0457D] him. I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.

## Commentary

Many think that freedom of choice can suffice for them to such an extent that, by that freedom itself, they may confidently rescue themselves from invisible enemies. Both to deny freedom of choice is perilous, and to strip it bare is sinful. If you deny it, you have loosened the reins for everyone; if you strip it bare, you have deceived them.

You deny it if you say: “If God wishes, I am good; if he does not wish it, I am not good,” although it is established that God wishes all human beings to be saved and that each person is wicked by his own choice. But you strip it bare when you give so much to choice alone that you deprive it of the realities of divine assistance.

For he who dwells in the help of the Most High, who abides in the protection of the God of heaven, and says to the Lord, “You are my protector and my refuge,” also says: “I will hope in him,” because he himself will rescue me from the snare of demons and from the harsh word of their suggestions.

If you say this, if you believe this, then at last he will overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you will hope. The wings of God are his angels, to whose guardianship we have been entrusted.

“His truth will surround you with a shield”—the shield of the body, blood, and chrism, by which shield we are both defended and crowned. For another psalm asserts that he crowns us with the shield of good will. This is also affirmed in this psalm, so that we may not fear the terror of the night: namely, the pleasure of lust, whose arrow flies by day. What is desired in the sight of light is carried out in darkness, or is completed in ruin, or in the noonday demon.

But if you dwell in the help of the Most High, a thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand. The left side is not named in the one who acts under God’s protection; only the side against which a thousand rise is explained, while ten thousand rise at the right hand.

This left side, which he did not wish to name, is free choice, against which the lesser battle is waged; but in the right hand is God’s assistance. Therefore he named the side first, because it lies within choice that you should believe first, so that, when you have believed, you may obtain grace.

You will find in the right hand such a numerous battle-line of virtues and aids. It arms the forehead with the trophy of the cross; it takes up the breastplate of the mysteries; it receives the remedies of salvation; it expresses the signs of the one who speaks.

For what the Wisdom of God also recalls—that the Lord knows the ways which are at the right, whereas those at the left are perverse—may perhaps have been intended to show that, when we conquer, we are entrusted to the virtues of the right side, but when we are conquered, we are joined to the weaknesses of the left side.

God’s help is not conquered, but our freedom of choice is overcome. If we incline more readily toward the right, he commands his angels concerning us to guard us in all our ways, so that, if we walk upon the asp and the basilisk—that is, upon the devil and his kingdom—we may be able to trample both lion and dragon.

For the Lord says this: “Because he hoped in me, I will rescue him; I will protect him, because he has known my name. He called upon me, and I will hear him. I am with him in tribulation; I will rescue him and glorify him. I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XCI

## A Psalm of Song for the Sabbath Day

It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praises to your name, Most High, to announce your mercy in the morning and your truth throughout the night, with a ten-stringed psaltery and song upon the lyre. For you have delighted me in your creation, and I will meditate upon the works of your hands. For your works have been magnified, Lord; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. An unwise man will not know, and a fool will not understand these things. When sinners have arisen like grass and all who work iniquity have appeared, it is so that they may perish forever and ever. But you, Most High, are forever, Lord. For behold, your enemies, Lord—for behold, your enemies will perish, and all who work iniquity will be scattered. And my horn will be exalted like that of a unicorn, and my old age will be in abundant mercy. And my eye has looked down upon your enemies, and my ear has heard of those who rise against me, the malicious. The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will multiply like a cedar of Lebanon. Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of the house of our God. They will still multiply in abundant old age, and they will endure well, so that they may proclaim: The Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him.

## Commentary

On the Sabbath the Lord’s enemies perish, so that on the Lord’s Day the Lord’s friends may rejoice. For on the Sabbath the Lord lies dead in the tomb, and on the Lord’s Day he is worshiped alive among the angels.

In this matter his thoughts have become exceedingly deep, which the unwise man does not know and the fool does not understand. But it is good for us if we confess our sins daily and sing praises to his most high name; if, freed from the darkness of sins, we announce his mercy in the morning; and when the night of questions comes upon us, we do not presume to speak at will about what we do not know.

For we must fear speaking about God even when what we say is true, because it is dangerous. Therefore the things that are clear in the holy Scriptures ought not to suffer prejudice from obscure passages. Let us offer something briefly, from which the whole matter may be understood.

You have a clear statement that there is no acceptance of persons with God. Peter, Paul, and all the evangelists testify to this. Even if they had not said it, the definition is so clear that we would believe it even while they were silent.

What now? Against this, a question arises from an obscure passage: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau,” and “He has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens” (Rom. IX), along with many similar statements.

Placed in these matters, you have entered the night. You cannot bring the darkness of this night into the light of day, nor introduce the force of darkness into the middle of my day. If you have something to say, announce the truth in the night; otherwise, let your finger be upon your mouth.

For even if you should find a thousand such questions, you will never prove that the Lord, by choosing one person, wishes one and rejects another. It is another matter if you demonstrate that Esau was good in his works and was unjustly hated, or that Jacob, guilty of evil works, was unjustly chosen.

But let us break off the delays caused by another’s work, and let the Lord delight us with the ten-stringed psaltery in his creation and in the works of his hands, which he stretched out upon the cross. In these works, I say, let us rejoice. For in them his works were magnified, which the unwise man did not know.

The unbelieving Jewish people, who arose like grass, prepared themselves by working iniquity to perish forever and ever. While the Lord remains forever, they will perish and be scattered over the whole face of the earth—all the Jews who work iniquity.

But Christ flourishes like a palm tree. Planted in his house, he will flourish in the courts of the house of our God, and he will multiply in abundant old age. Here he recalls not Christ’s own old age, but the old age of the world, because the ages come to an end and decline in old age. The Lord, however, remains forever.

Nor should you receive with displeasure the fact that he compared him to a flowering palm, because what is compared is less than that to which it is compared. He is not himself a flowering palm; rather, Christ’s divinity is compared with the ever-flourishing palm, which, seated at the right hand of the Father, extends its branches to the victorious, granting a crown from its flowers and imparting nourishment through perpetual refreshment from its fruits.

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XCII

## A Song of Praise of David for the Day before the Sabbath, When the Earth Was Founded

[Col. 0460B]

The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty. The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself. For he established the world, which will not be shaken. Your throne has been prepared from that time; from age to age you are. The rivers have raised up, Lord; the rivers have raised up their voice. The rivers have raised up their waves, from the voices of many waters. The risings of the sea are wonderful; the Lord is wonderful in the heights. Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy; holiness befits your house, Lord, throughout the length of days.

## Commentary

“The Lord has reigned”—that is, he assumed his kingdom upon the cross. He clothed himself with beauty in the resurrection. For he clothed himself with weakness in power, girded himself with eternity, and made the earth firm in his resurrection.

Having a prepared throne, he ascended into heaven and sat at the right hand of the Father. The rivers of the holy Scriptures proclaimed him beforehand; over him they raised their voices, “from the voices of many waters”—that is, crying out more powerfully than the nations.

For all the Scriptures of the nations have voices and powers: these Scriptures command kings, whereas those serve them. Therefore, when the rivers raised their voices, Christ became wonderful to the rising of the sea—that is, to the kings and exalted ones of this world—not only to these, but also wonderful in the heights.

When the Lord ascended into heaven, then the testimonies of God became exceedingly trustworthy. For he gave power so that healings might be performed for the human race in his name. When they proclaimed the Son of God, and, while performing these signs, his testimonies became exceedingly credible, [Col. 0460D] his house—which the Pharisees said could not receive the holy commandments—received the laws of the Old Testament. And the holy of holies befits it, so that they may dwell there forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XCIII

## A Psalm of David for the Fourth Day of the Week

God of vengeance, Lord, God of vengeance has acted openly. Exalt yourself, you who judge the earth; repay the proud. How long will sinners, Lord, how long will sinners boast? Will they utter and speak iniquity? Will all who work injustice speak? They have humbled your people, Lord, and afflicted your inheritance. They have killed the widow and the stranger, and murdered orphans. [Col. 0461A] And they said: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.”

Understand, you foolish among the people, and you fools, learn wisdom at last. He who planted the ear, will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, does he not see? He who corrects the nations, will he not reprove—the one who teaches man knowledge? The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain.

Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and whom you teach from your law, so that you may give him relief from evil days until a pit is dug for the sinner. For the Lord will not reject his people, and he will not abandon his inheritance, until justice is turned toward judgment, and all who are upright in heart follow it. Who will rise up for me against the malicious? Or who will stand with me against those who work iniquity? If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in the underworld. [Col. 0461B]

If I said: “My foot has been moved,” your mercy was helping me. According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul. Does the seat of iniquity cling to you, you who fashion labor into a commandment? They hunted the soul of the righteous, and condemned innocent blood. And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope. And he will repay them for their iniquity, and in their malice the Lord our God will destroy them; he will destroy them.

## Commentary

It proclaims God as the avenger of his people to judges for whom it seems a slight matter, in judgment, to show partiality to sinners over orphans and the needy; but those who exalt the Lord in their hearts and judge the earth in their bodies render recompense to the proud.

We can apply the testimony of the Apostle, who says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. XI). We judge ourselves when we put an end to vices and establish the beginning of virtues.

If we do not do this, we humble the people of God—that is, virtue—and despise his inheritance, which is promised to us, killing the widow and the stranger.

The widow is the soul that has no husband, word, or understanding of prudence. If you deceive her either by your word or by your example, you kill the widow whom you ought to have set free.

The stranger is one who does not know how to be a citizen of the saints. If you show yourself to him as a lover of the world, you remove from him faith in the future city; and, as though you had killed him spiritually, you are accused by the present psalm.

Orphans are likewise killed. Orphans are those who do not believe that, by living holily, they can have God as their Father. You are wise here, and you know that believers can become children of God; but if you offer a contrary example and cause them to despise becoming children of God, you have killed orphans.

For if he is speaking about these orphans, strangers, and widows, then whoever kills married people, citizens, or children who have a father and mother escapes the guilt of the crime. Or if the psalmist were silent about this, who would ever accuse criminals of such an act?

But because we ourselves, who think that we are wise while doing these things, imagine that the Lord neither seeks nor understands these small matters of ruin brought about by us—things that we do not wish to understand—the cry is directed at us: “Understand, you who are foolish,” that is, “you who, placed among the people, have become unwise while following one another’s examples in contempt of the Lord”; and, “you fools, learn wisdom at last.”

When those to whom it is commanded “learn wisdom” are addressed, it is shown that they do not possess wisdom by their own choice. For they say: “Will God now really concern himself with this, so that he hears each of our words and sees each of our actions?”

They are answered: “Then he who gave you hearing does not hear? He who granted you sight does not see? He who infused into you the taste of knowledge does not possess wisdom?” He is wholly wisdom, and he sees the thoughts of human beings who seem wise to themselves, because their thoughts are vain.

Blessed is the man whom the Lord would instruct in this very matter—not by choosing the negligent, but by teaching his law to the believer. He will be given relief in evil days, when demons prepare pits for sinners.

Then the Lord will not reject his people—that is, those who presume upon his help—and he will not abandon his inheritance. Rather, he will protect them from temptations, giving them endurance through the promised inheritance of eternal life.

He makes them await repayment until he turns justice toward judgment, and until all who are upright in heart hold to it—that is, to justice itself.

But because those who administer malicious counsels to minds persist, we must fight against them with sufficient courage. The one who knows that battle must be waged sharply against every suggestion cries out: “Who will rise up with me to fight against those who work iniquity?”

I ask you, most courageous athlete: tell me by what order you escaped the assault of the enemies. Hear the answer: “If the Lord,” he says, “had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in the underworld.”

If I said with tears to the Lord, “My foot has been moved,” and had turned away from the right course, at once his mercy helped me so much—and even more—as he saw the multitude of sorrows in my heart, and with his consolations gladdened my soul.

Perhaps you will say, listener: “This is a great labor.” But this labor is temporary, while the reward of labor is eternal. The seat of iniquity does not cling to God. For the one who creates weariness, labor, or sorrow in a commandment—whether for the labor of combat or for the labor of martyrdom—has not denied the reward of eternal joy.

When sinners hunt the soul of the righteous who confesses God and condemn his innocent blood, then the Lord becomes his refuge, [Col. 0462D] and God becomes the help of his hope, so that he may repay them for their iniquities and destroy his persecutors in their malice—he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XCIV

## A Song of Praise, to David

Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us shout for joy to God our Savior. Let us come before his face with confession, and let us shout to him in psalms. For the Lord is a great God and a great king above all gods, because the Lord will not reject his people. For in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and the heights of the mountains are his. For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.

Come, let us worship and [Col. 0463A] fall down, and let us weep before the Lord who made us, because he is the Lord our God. We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as at the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the desert, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works.

For forty years I was offended by that generation, and I said: “They always go astray in heart.” And they did not know my ways, so I swore to them in my anger: “They shall not enter into my rest.”

## Commentary

This is the praise of the song: that we rejoice not in empty pleasures, but in the Lord. Before we are overtaken, let us ourselves come before his face with confession of our sins, believing that he will not reject his people who confess to him—he who is great above all things, whose are the heavens and whose are the mountains, who established the earth with his hands.

Come, let us worship him, not considering him merely in the form of a servant and supposing him to be a mere human being. The one who made all these things is in him. Come, let us worship the Lord; let us weep because he is merciful; he is the one who made us.

He is the shepherd whose sheep we are. Let us hear his voice and follow him wherever he goes. For the shepherd sends out his voice to the sheep so that, hearing him, they may follow. Either he provides pasture, or he strives to rescue them from the ambushes of wild beasts.

Therefore the cry is directed at us today: if we hear his voice, let us not harden our hearts, as the children of Israel did for forty years in the wilderness. And because they did not hear his voice, they did not enter into his rest.

But let us hear our shepherd and follow his footsteps, so that, escaping the death of this wilderness, we may deserve to enter with Jesus into the land flowing with milk and honey. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM XCV

## A Psalm of David, When the House Was Built after the Captivity

Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord and bless his name; announce his salvation from day to day. Announce his glory among the nations and his wonders among all peoples. For the Lord is great and exceedingly praiseworthy; he is terrible above all gods. For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens.

[Col. 0463D] Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary. Bring to the Lord, families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory for his name. Take up sacrifices and enter his courts; worship the Lord in his holy court. Let the whole earth be shaken before his face; say among the nations: “The Lord has reigned.”

For he has set the world right, and it will not be shaken; he will judge the peoples in equity. Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult; let the sea and its fullness be shaken; the fields and everything in them will rejoice. Then all the trees of the forests will exult before the face of the Lord, because he has come—for he has come to judge the earth. He will judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth.

[Col. 0464A]

## Commentary

We who wept as penitents in the ninety-fourth psalm should rejoice in the ninety-fifth. There we mourned our house, believing that through his mercy we could again attain the building of this house.

Therefore the title also agrees with this meaning, since it records that the house itself was to be built after the captivity. Christ, building it, gives joy to the whole earth. Hence it is said that all the earth should sing a new song to the Lord and bless his name.

The world had been held captive through Adam. After Christ transformed that captivity, he built a most glorious house, having neither spot nor wrinkle. As he built the house, all the temples were destroyed. For it was proved that all the gods of the nations who were placed in temples were demons dwelling in them.

But the one who built the house is himself the one who made the heavens. Through his confession everyone is born; whoever does not confess the Lord Jesus is despised with accursed foulness. Those who confess him, however, will shine like the sun before God. Holiness and magnificence are in this very holy confession of him.

Therefore all the families of the nations are invited: “Come, bring to the Lord.” What shall we bring to the Lord? Bring the glory that you once offered uselessly to idols. Bring the honor with which you honored the priests of idols in vain. Take sacrifices away from the idols, enter here into the house that he built, and worship him in his holy court.

Let nation say to nation: “One Lord reigns from the wood of the cross.” For through the wood of desire the kingdom of God had departed from human beings; now through the wood of the cross the kingdom of God has returned. He established it throughout the world so that it would not be shaken.

In this Church he judges the peoples in equity and the nations in his anger. For this work the heavens rejoice in the saints, and the earth rejoices in us sinners.

For this joy the sea is moved—the ignoble and wavering multitude—and its fullness, that is, the rich filled with possessions. They are moved while laughing at Christ’s humble people and counting his psalms and teaching as cold dirges.

But the trees of the forests, who appear wooden and savage to the wise of the world, will then exult before the face of the Lord when he comes to judge earthly things. For he does not judge by accepting the persons of the powerful; he judges the whole world by equity alone and confirms the peoples in truth [Col. 0464D] throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM XCVI

## A Psalm to David, When His Land Was Restored to Him
The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice, and let the many islands be glad. Clouds and darkness surround him; righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne. Fire goes before him and burns up his enemies round about. His lightning flashes have illuminated the world; the earth saw and was shaken. The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord, all the earth. The heavens proclaimed his righteousness, and all peoples saw his glory. Let all who worship carved images be confounded, and those who glory in their idols. Worship him, all his angels. [Col. 0465A] Zion heard and rejoiced. And the daughters of Judah exulted because of your judgments, O Lord. For you, Lord Most High, are exalted above all the earth; you are exceedingly exalted above all gods. You who love the Lord, hate evil. The Lord guards the souls of his saints; he will deliver them from the hand of sinners. Light has dawned for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice, righteous ones, in the Lord, and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness.

## COMMENTARY

You sing confidently in the ninety-sixth psalm, since in the ninety-fifth you came to know the Lord. In this psalm the earth rejoices over the resurrection of the saints, and the islands—not all of them, but those inhabited by saints—rejoice. For behold, he will come, as he promised in the preceding [Col. 0465B] psalm; he comes to judge: clouds and darkness surround him, and righteousness and judgment are the direction of his throne. Fire goes before him, fire destined to perform two functions. For in one and the same appearance it illuminates the souls of God’s people and sets his enemies aflame. When his lightning appears to the whole world, then the mountains will melt like wax before his face; and at the face of the Lord the earth will tremble. When all things fear, dread, and quake, all who worship idols will be confounded, when they see the glory of the Lord Jesus Christ in the resurrection. Then only Zion will rejoice, that is, the Church. The daughters of Judah will also exult, that is, all the synagogues that possessed prophets before the Lord’s advent, proclaiming the Lord’s advent. Because of the Lord’s just judgments, they will not have the condemnation of the latter time. For the same Lord who now shines forth, and who then shone forth in the synagogues before the Lord’s advent, is himself alone above all gods.

Therefore, whoever loves what is good in the Lord, hate everything that is evil. For the love of the good is proved by hatred of evil. But if some have persecuted you out of love for the good, be secure: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10). For the Lord guards the souls of his saints and delivers them from the hand of sinners. The fire that will set the transgressors aflame becomes light for the righteous and joy for the upright in heart. Do not, then, preserve righteousness out of fear of punishment, but out of the joy of love, so that even in this world you may already rejoice in the Lord and give thanks to the remembrance of his holiness, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XCVII

*A psalm of David.*

Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done marvelous things. His right hand and his holy arm have brought salvation for him. The Lord has made his salvation known; before the nations he has revealed his righteousness. He has remembered his mercy and his truth toward the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God. Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and chant psalms. Chant psalms to the Lord with the lyre, with the voice of a psalm, with trumpets of beaten metal and the sound of the horn. Shout joyfully before the King, the Lord; let the sea and its fullness be stirred, the inhabited world and those who dwell in it. Let the rivers clap their hands; [Col. 0466A] let the mountains rejoice together before the Lord, for he has come to judge the earth. He will judge the inhabited world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.

## COMMENTARY

The psalm itself explains the reasons for the present song. It says: I exhort you to sing a new song because he has done marvelous things. And, as he said, sing because he has done marvelous things—as though someone had said to him: “The Lord has always done marvelous things; therefore the song of singing of divine marvels is not new but old.” To this he replies: “New marvels demand a new song.” Say, then, “new.” If you ask what new marvels there are for us, listen.

When the Lord was placed upon the cross, the Jews said: “Let him save himself” (Matt. 27). [Col. 0466B] But his right hand and his holy arm saved him when the Lord made his Savior known, raising him from the dead, and revealed his righteousness before the nations. For he remembered the mercy that he promised to Jacob, saying: “And I will make you into a great nation” (Gen. 12). He fulfilled this truth toward the house of Israel when all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of the Lord, the God of Israel.

And although all the provinces see the Lord’s salvation, let this not pass idly before the observer: when earthly thoughts have reached their end, thoughts of heavenly things are born. These themselves cause the salvation of the Lord our God to be seen. In this devotion shout joyfully to the Lord, the whole earth—that is, offer all the members of the earthly body in the service of holy conduct. [Col. 0466C] Do not exult with sadness, but sing; and chant psalms on the lyre, whose player invites the hearing, and with the voice of a psalm, whose mysteries stir minds; with beaten trumpets and the sound of the horn, by whose voices the victory of war is proclaimed.

Shout joyfully before the King, the Lord, proclaiming the Lord’s presence throughout the ages. Do not fear, even if the world is shaken like the sea and its fullness, the inhabited earth, and all that is in them. Then the rivers will clap their hands together as one, because scarcely any river exists in which remission of sins has not been granted; there is no water that has not brought forth from itself a living soul for eternal life. In this event the mountains will exult, from whose depths springs issue that make the rivers—the mountains whose summits strike the heavens, whose inhabitants are near heaven. [Col. 0466D] These will exult when the Judge comes to judge the inhabited earth in equity and the peoples in truth. All the saints will rejoice, because the one who rewards holiness has arrived, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XCVIII

*A psalm of David.*

The Lord reigns; let the peoples rage; he who sits upon the cherubim reigns—let the earth be shaken. The Lord is great in Zion and exalted above all peoples. Let them give thanks to your great name, for it is dreadful and holy; and the honor of the king loves judgment. You have prepared uprightness; you have carried out judgment and righteousness in Jacob. Exalt the Lord our God and worship the footstool of his feet, [Col. 0467A] for it is holy. Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who invoke his name. They invoked the Lord, and he heard them; he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud. They kept his testimonies and the commandment that he gave them. Lord our God, you heard them; you were a forgiving God to them, yet taking vengeance upon all their inventions. Exalt the Lord our God and worship at his holy mountain, for the Lord our God is holy.

## COMMENTARY

Let the peoples rage, and in their pride let them look upon our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the one who has reigned, though they do not think that he should reign over them. He sits upon the cherubim, however much the earth may be shaken. He will be great in Zion; [Col. 0467B] he will be exalted above all peoples.

It is fitting for us to know clearly that “the honor of the king loves judgment.” For only those fear judgment who know that they have something deserving punishment by right—namely, the deed by which God was dishonored. But those who have preserved the Lord’s honor in their minds love judgment. Conversely, those fear it who know that, to the king’s dishonor, they have violated the rights of his law, in which this king established equity. Therefore, those who guard equity honor the king, and this honor does not fear judgment; indeed, it even loves it.

Yet the one who will judge is himself the one who carried out righteousness and judgment in Jacob, who had Moses and Aaron as his priests, and Samuel as one like them. He is the one whom they invoked and who heard them, speaking to them in the pillar of cloud. [Col. 0467C] They kept his testimonies and the commandments he gave them. Whoever imitates them will not only not fear the coming judgment but will also love it.

Let us therefore say to our Lord Jesus Christ: “You are the Lord who spoke with Moses and Aaron; you heard them; you were gracious to them; you took vengeance upon all their devoted endeavors.” Let us therefore exalt the Lord God in Christ. And let us worship at his holy mountain, in the height of his faith, which in its loftiness pierces the clouds, while we believe that he is the Lord our God, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM XCIX

*A psalm of thanksgiving.*

Shout joyfully to God, all the earth; serve the Lord with gladness. [Col. 0467D] Enter his presence with exultation. Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves. We are his people and the sheep of his pasture. Enter his gates with thanksgiving, his courts with hymns; give thanks to him. Praise his name, for the Lord is gracious; his mercy is everlasting, and his truth endures from generation to generation.

## COMMENTARY

The whole earth is invited to shout joyfully, so that the call may be understood to accept no distinctions among persons: “Come, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11), and enter his presence with exultation.

Know that the Lord Jesus Christ is none other than the one who spoke with Moses. He is the God who made us, of whom Moses spoke when he said that he made the human being. He made us; for we human beings are all his handiwork.

Indeed, many who desire children do not have them because God does not give them. Many who do not desire them, because they are unwilling to sow and do not want the fruit, and because they unwillingly act against the proper order, even because they do not want it unjustly—God justly commands the creature to give a response to the seed. Thus it is proved that he himself made us, since children are neither given nor denied according to our choice.

Therefore, because we are his people, let us become the sheep of his pasture, recognizing the shepherd who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Let us enter his gates with thanksgiving for unity, praising his holy name because he is gracious; believing that his mercy is everlasting toward those who believe, and that his truth concerning his promises remains for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM C

*A psalm of David.*

I will sing mercy and judgment to you, O Lord. I will chant psalms and understand in the blameless way, for you are coming to me. I walked in the innocence of my heart within my house. I did not set any unjust thing before my eyes; I hated those who commit transgressions. A perverse heart did not cling to me; I did not know the one who turned away from me and was wicked. I pursued the one who secretly slandered his neighbor. The one with a proud eye and an insatiable heart—I did not eat with him. My eyes were upon the faithful of the earth, so that they might sit with me; the one who walked in the blameless way served me. The one who practices pride will not dwell in the midst of my house; [Col. 0468C] the one who speaks wickedness did not direct himself aright before my eyes. will not dwell in the midst of my house; the one who speaks wickedness did not direct himself aright before my eyes. In the morning I killed all the sinners of the earth, in order to destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity.

## COMMENTARY

“Judgment without mercy awaits those who have not shown mercy” (Jer. II); but those who show mercy escape judgment. Do you know, human being, how you will be placed at the shepherd’s right hand? Show mercy and judgment; you may await securely.

For he does not say to those placed on the left, the unjust: “Go into eternal fire because you lied, because you committed fornication, because you committed various crimes,” but rather: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not receive me; [Col. 0468D] I was sick, and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25). Since fire is owed to crimes, why is the punishment for crimes not charged to those through whose mercy the crimes might be forgiven? “Go, then,” he says, “into eternal fire” (ibid.), because you despised the means by which the fire is extinguished. For you have heard it written that almsgiving delivers from sin (Tob. 12). You have heard that just as fire is extinguished by water, so all sins are taken away by almsgiving.

“Go, then, into the fire,” because you yourselves made it live for you. But I caused mercy to be sung for you upon the face of the earth together with judgment, so that the one who did not deny mercy might escape judgment.

Therefore I will chant psalms and understand in the blameless way, and I will understand when you come to me, so that if I see you as a stranger I may receive you, and if I see you hungry, [Col. 0469A] I may refresh you. I will understand when you come, so that I may not regard you as just any person and refuse you. For if I walk in the innocence of my heart, I do not set an unjust thing before my eyes. It is unjust for me not to have mercy on one who shares my nature, in whom you dwell, Christ.

But I will hate those who commit transgression; let no perverse heart cling to me. I will not acknowledge the wicked who turn away from me; I will pursue secret talkers; I will not share in the company of the proud and envious. But my eyes will be upon the faithful of the earth, who faithfully preserve the earth of their body, so that they may sit with me. The one who walks in the blameless way will serve me.

I will not seek to obtain anything from those who live blameworthily in my house. Let no one who practices pride dwell there—that is, let no enemy dwell in the house of my body who persuades me to despise the Lord. For this is the root of pride.

But in the mornings I will kill all the sinners of the earth—that is, I will kill sins as they arise at their very birth and will not allow them to live—so that all who practice iniquity may perish from the city of the Lord.
