The city of the Lord is our soul, in which the king and the saints dwell, the foremost citizens of God, who are born from him.

Therefore, when sinful thoughts are born in the soul, let them be killed as soon as they are born. Let all who practice iniquity perish from the city of the Lord, so that the Lord may rest in his city with the whole company of virtues, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CI

*The prayer of the poor person when he was anxious and poured out his prayer before the Lord.*

[Col. 0469C]

Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me; on whatever day I am troubled, incline your ear to me. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly. For my days have vanished like smoke, and my bones have dried like kindling. I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up, because I forgot to eat my bread. Because of the sound of my groaning, my bone has clung to my flesh. I have become like a pelican in the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling. I kept watch and became like a solitary sparrow on a roof. All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who praised me swore against me. For I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with weeping. This was because of the face of your anger and indignation, for although you lifted me up, you struck me down. My days [Col. 0469D] have declined like a shadow, and I have dried up like grass.

But you, Lord, remain forever, and your memorial from generation to generation. You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is the time to have mercy on her, for the time has come. For your servants have loved her stones, and they will pity her earth. And the nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory. For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory. He has regarded the prayer of the humble and has not despised their prayers. Let these things be written for a later generation, and the people who will be created will praise the Lord. For he looked down from his height; the Lord looked from heaven upon the earth, to hear the groaning of the prisoners, to release the children of those who were slain, to proclaim the name [Col. 0470A] of the Lord in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem, when peoples and kings gather together to serve the Lord.

He answered him in the way of his strength: “Tell me the shortness of my days. Do not take me away in the middle of my days; your years endure from generation to generation.” In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment. Like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail. The children of your servants will dwell there, and their offspring will be established forever.

## COMMENTARY

We read that the cry of the people of Sodom rose up to God, and that at last they were burned by a rain of sulfur. [Col. 0470B] Before, then, we turn our minds to weeping and fasting for our sins, let us not dare to say, “Let my cry come to you,” lest it happen that our cry is not of such a kind as to obtain mercy. Perhaps it contains anger, accusation, cursing, flattery, slander, insult, lying, and other things resembling these acts. When our cry resounds with such very wicked vices, God must be asked that this cry not reach him.

But while we are established in certain wicked deeds, let us ask, saying: “Do not turn your face away from me.” We must say to him: “Turn your face away from my sins.” Let us therefore renounce all vices and passions, become poor in spirit, and mourn our past deeds. Let us pour ourselves out in prayer through the song of this psalm, so that our cry may reach him and he may not turn [Col. 0470C] his face away from us.

Yet how we who pray for our sins should weep is taught to us in these verses: “My days,” he says, “have declined like a shadow”—that is, I have lost what I lived, because I dried up like grass in sins. Grass, straw, and wood are fuel for fire. Therefore I am troubled, because my bones too have been burned like a frying pan—that is, like a dry bundle of brushwood—and are prepared for the fire of Gehenna.

“I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up.” I have been struck by compunction over the coming punishment, and for this reason I forgot to eat peace. Because of the sound of my groaning, my bones have clung to my flesh. I have become like a pelican in the wilderness—that is, like the bird called the pelican, which lives only in deserts and has food full of the poison of the wasteland and uncultivated bitterness.

[Col. 0470D] “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.” The raven is dark because of its blackness; already it is almost blacker by night, and the darkness doubles its blackness. Therefore I too, he says, lamenting within myself a doubled blackness of sins, direct my cries like a night-raven, calling alone, like a solitary sparrow in a building.

All day long my enemies reproached me, and those who formerly praised me now swore against me—that is, “I will not live after his death.” How could you live, so that they would swear this against you? “They swore this,” he says, “because I ate ashes like bread and mixed my drink with tears.” Why was this? “Because of the face of your anger and indignation.” Whose anger? That which is deserved at the judgment because of sins. Those who are lifted up and exalted here must necessarily be struck down there.

[Col. 0471A]

Since the whole human race dies in sins, what remains except that the person of the whole age pour out prayers to you in tearful speech? No one will be saved unless you, Lord, arise and have mercy on Zion. For the time has come for you to come and have mercy on Zion.

“For your servants have loved her stones.” These are surely the stones of which it is written: “The stones of the righteous are rolled within her.” For those who are God’s servants rightly love all the books of the Old Testament, which contain within them one cornerstone.

They have not only loved her stones, but they will also pity her dust. The dust of the stones is the bodies of souls. If we are God’s servants, we do not love only the holy souls; we also reverently pity their very bodies, in which they were afflicted, tortured, burned, and tormented by various punishments. [Col. 0471B] How do we pity them? Their affliction and the punishment they suffered cause us sorrow, while their perseverance, because they conquered, causes us joy.

Therefore, when you, Lord, come, and your saints suffer for the testimony of your name, then the nations will fear, and all the kings of the earth your glory. Then your Church will be built in Zion, and you will be seen in your majesty, when you look down from your height, Jesus Christ, to hear the groaning of the prisoners and release the children of those who were slain.

All our fathers who preached Christ to us were slain. We, therefore, were bound by Satan, because those who begot us by the word of life were slain. But when we came to know that they rejoiced in heaven and possessed the glory of Christ, Zion was built in us, and the Lord was seen in his majesty. [Col. 0471C] We rejoice because he regarded their prayers and did not despise their supplications.

We have written their sufferings for later generations, and the people who will be created praise the Lord in his saints forever. There peoples and kingdoms gather together to serve the Lord. Through them the shortness of our days is governed, and it is announced to us that the end is near; it remains that those who use this world should live as though they did not use it. For “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7), and when its form has passed away, Christ the truth will come. To him we say: “Your years endure for ages of ages.”

In the beginning you yourself founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. Therefore we do not worship a new Lord in Christ, but the one who is and is always the same, whose years will not fail.

When he says of heaven and earth, “They will perish,” he confirms that promise by which it is assured that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, in which the children of Christ’s servants will dwell. Paul was a servant of Christ, and likewise all the apostles were servants of Christ. We who have believed through them are children of his servants. And if we follow in their footsteps, as they followed Christ, we will dwell with them in the new heaven and the new earth.

[Col. 0471D]

Then the seed of the word that gave us hope as believers will bear fruit in our reward. It will no longer have an end, but will remain established by God, irrevocable. At the middle of days, youth is first found, and old age at the end of days. There, therefore, they will neither come to an end in the middle of their days nor die in old age. For the new heavens pour forth the dew of immortality, [Col. 0472A] and the new earth has no bosom of death but possesses life, the Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CII

*A psalm of David.*

Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses. He is the one who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities, who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with mercy and compassion. He fills your desire with good things; your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.

The Lord performs mercies and judgment for all who suffer injustice. He made his ways known to Moses, and his will to the children of Israel. The Lord is compassionate [Col. 0472B] and merciful and merciful, patient and exceedingly merciful. He will not be angry forever, nor will he threaten eternally. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. For as high as heaven is above earth, so he has strengthened his mercy over those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us.

As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him, for he knows our formation. He remembered that we are dust. Man is like grass; his days will flower like a flower of the field. For the spirit will pass through him, and he will not remain; he will no longer know his place. But the mercy of the Lord is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him, and his righteousness upon the children’s children, upon those who [Col. 0472C] keep his covenant and remember his commandments in order to do them.

The Lord prepared his throne in heaven, and his kingdom will rule over all. Bless the Lord, all his angels, mighty in strength, doing his word, obeying the voice of his words. Bless the Lord, all his powers, his ministers who do his will. Bless the Lord, all his works, in every place of his dominion. Bless the Lord, O my soul.

## COMMENTARY

We bless the Lord when we do some work of such a kind that the Lord’s name is blessed. For how can God be blessed by a human being except through this one thing alone: that a work must be done from all our inward parts? [Col. 0472D] If we are compassionate from our very depths, and he is blessed by us, he will forgive all our iniquities, heal all our infirmities, fill our desire within us, and crown us in his kingdom because of his compassion and mercy.

For to the compassionate he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). In that kingdom there will be no death, nor will harsh old age weaken strength; rather, youth will be renewed there like the eagles. There the Lord will show mercy to the compassionate, and judgment to all who suffer injustice.

He is, of course, the God who made his ways known to Moses, the one who showed his will to the children of Israel. He is God in Christ, whether reconciling the world (2 Cor. 5), [Col. 0473A] rewarding the saints, or showing mercy to the compassionate. He is patient, and he is exceedingly merciful. If he sees us patient and compassionate, he will not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our injustices; rather, as high as heaven is above earth, he confirms his mercy over us. As far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our iniquities from us.

As a father has compassion on his children, so he will have compassion on us if we are compassionate. If we consider our formation in human beings who weep, or who are needy, or who suffer want, then in the measure with which we measure the needs of others, he will measure to us.

“I was not compassionate in another’s case; he will not be compassionate toward me in mine. I helped the needy; I am helped. I forgave the sinner; I am forgiven. [Col. 0473B] I considered myself to be of the same formation as one living in soft circumstances, and I grieved over the naked person and clothed him. I had compassion on the hungry person and fed him.”

Therefore, because I considered myself and the needy person to have one formation, he too considers my formation and remembers that I am earthly flesh and dust. From this, if he deigns to do so, he can raise us up. For if this were not so, who would count as anything a human being who flowers like the flower of the field, whose spirit passes away from him, who is no more, and who no longer recognizes his place?

But if we practice temporal mercy toward our brothers, we will obtain eternal mercy, which the Lord will perfect upon those who fear him. His righteousness is upon the children’s children—those who, because they could not care for the materially poor, cared for the spiritually poor, [Col. 0473C] so that by word or example they might call spiritual beggars to the riches of righteousness.

If you wish to see the rich person and the beggar, read the Apocalypse of the holy apostle John. To him, therefore, are like all those who are rich in gold and silver, yet beggars in faith or in works of righteousness. The righteousness of God is upon the children’s children. The children of the apostles are all teachers of good counsels. As they themselves are their children, so those who hear them are the children of their children, keeping God’s covenant and remembering God’s commandments—not so that they may be puffed up by knowledge, but so that they may do what they know by heart.

Let us now look upon the one for whom the Father in heaven prepared his throne. “The Lord prepared it for the Lord.” And “the Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). There he sits, reigning, and his kingdom will have no end.

[Col. 0473D]

Because it may be asked: “If the Son was always with the Father, how did he prepare it for him beforehand, and afterward say, ‘Sit’?” We must therefore understand that God prepared his throne for the Son of Man. For the Son of God, who assumed this Son of Man, was always in the bosom of the Father, is there, and will be there.

Just as a river, although it passes through many provinces of the earth, never leaves the bosom of its spring, so the invisible Son of God may rejoice with Jacob, shine in the bush, be in the pillar of cloud, be in the pillar of fire, be in the cloud, be in the leader, and be in whatever form he chooses for the salvation of human beings, yet he does not leave the bosom of the Father. For you do not read, “the one who was in the bosom of the Father,” but “the one who is in the bosom of the Father”—he has made him known.

The angels bless him, powerful in strength and obedient to his word. [Col. 0474A] The powers hostile to him also bless him; for they do his will. All his works bless him in every place of his dominion. Wherever any creature exists, that is a place of his dominion, because he created everything.

May our soul bless him through these works at all times, him who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for all ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM CIII

*A psalm of David.*

Bless the Lord, O my soul. Lord my God, you are greatly magnified. You have put on thanksgiving and splendor; you are clothed in light as in a garment. You stretch out heaven like a skin; you cover its upper parts with waters. You make the cloud your ascent; you walk upon the wings [Col. 0474B] of the winds. You make your angels spirits, and your ministers burning fire.

You founded the earth upon its stability; it will not be moved forever and ever. The abyss covered it like a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled; at the voice of your thunder they were afraid. The mountains rise, and the plains descend to the place you founded for them. You established a boundary that they will not cross, nor will they return to cover the earth.

You send springs into the valleys; the waters pass through the midst of the mountains. All the beasts of the field drink; the wild asses await them in their thirst. Above them the birds of heaven will dwell; from the midst of the rocks they will give voice. You water the mountains from your upper chambers; the earth will be satisfied with the fruit of your works.

You produce grass for cattle and vegetation for the service of human beings, so that you may bring bread from the earth and wine [Col. 0474C] to gladden the human heart, so that you may brighten the face with oil and bread may strengthen the human heart. The trees of the field will be filled, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. There the sparrows will nest. The house of the heron is their leader; the high mountains are for the deer, and the rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs.

He made the moon for appointed times, but he knows its setting. You set darkness, and night came; in it all the beasts of the forest pass through. The young lions roar as they seize prey and seek their food from God. The sun has risen, and they gathered together and will be placed in their dens. A human being goes out to his work and to his labor until evening.

How magnificent are your works, Lord! You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your possession. This is the great and spacious sea; there are reptiles without number, small animals with large ones. There ships pass through. [Col. 0474D] This dragon, whom you formed to sport therein. All things wait for you, that you may give them food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness. When you turn your face away, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust. You will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.

May the glory of the Lord endure forever; the Lord will rejoice in his works. He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke. I will sing to the Lord in my life; I will chant psalms to my God as long as I exist. May my speech be pleasing to him; but I will rejoice in the Lord. May sinners and the wicked perish from the earth, so that they are no more. Bless the Lord, O my soul.

[Col. 0475A]

## COMMENTARY
We have come to Psalm 103, which contains the entire structure of the world, in which the Lord is greatly glorified. But when it recalls the structure, it reveals the coming of the Lord. Before the Son of God came, the Lord was not the Lord of human beings, clothed with confession and beauty. For all had withdrawn from God, placing their hope in their gods and images, and in empty inventions. Finally, the Apostle asserts this very thing when he says that, when the Lord came, he confined all things in unbelief so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. 11). Through him, God put on confession and beauty, through the mediator between God and human beings—the mediator who is the Son of Man.

Whose son is he? The Son of David, the Son of Abraham. Thus you read at the beginning of the Gospel: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). But who this Son of Man is—lest you think him to be such as Moses, or Jesus the son of Nun, or Elijah, or one of the great men—he is not so. For he is their Lord, and they are his servants.

He is clothed with light as with a garment. He is the one who stretches out heaven like a skin, and stretches it out so far that it may receive prostitutes and publicans—those whom it did not formerly receive except as immaculate. And because, when a skin is stretched, water is sprinkled over it, so here, when he was about to stretch out the heavens like a skin, he covered their upper parts with waters. They could not be stretched out and reach even to sinners unless they were covered with the water of sacred baptism. To those very heavens he set the clouds as a means of ascent. In the sight of the apostles, he walked upon the wings of the winds. For the winds move in the clouds, and there was no other way by which he could have his ascent to heaven unless he walked upon the wings of the winds.

Then he made his angels spirits. In Latin speech, angels are called messengers, and the Gospel is explained as “good news.” Therefore he made his angels—that is, the apostles—spirits when he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit, and preach the Gospel to every creature.” And then he made them a burning fire, when the Holy Spirit himself, like fire, sat upon them.

Then he founded the earth upon its firm foundation—that is, the earthly minds of the nations, which had been divided in the building of the tower. Now restoring them to their own stability, he strengthens them in the one word, Jesus Christ, and so founds the Church in them upon this rock that it may not be shaken forever and ever.

The abyss of this earth, moreover, is clothed like a mantle. Let philosophers pursue their fruitless investigations and say, with great labor, that they can learn that beneath the earth there is an abyss with which it is covered as with a mantle. Let us direct the attention of our discourse to this earth, which is founded upon the stability of the Church.

For the abyss surrounds it. The height of the riches of wisdom that surrounds it has no end. “And upon the mountains its waters will stand.” Whoever have their hearts above are mountains, and upon them the waters stand. The sanctification of baptism stands upon them; they stand firm in the right faith and are not carried about by every wind of doctrine.

But listen carefully to who these mountains are. They are those who flee from God’s rebuke. They certainly flee from the deeds that are rebuked by God, and they fear the voice of his thunder. They fear the threatening everlasting fire, and they withdraw their deeds from everything forbidden.

They ascend the mountains when they contemplate the kingdoms of heaven; they descend the mountains when they consider how to direct their earthly actions toward the place that the Lord founded, where God set a boundary and commanded that it not be crossed. He does not cross the boundary that has been set, so as to cover the earth as Adam covered the earth. He covered the earth with fig leaves and hid himself. These do not cross the boundary that the Lord established, and therefore they do not cover the earth.

And because it is not covered, the Lord waters it from above. For if he finds it scattered open, rain waters it, coming from above. But if it has been covered and is hidden from heaven, it is not watered from above. If, however, it lies open to the heavens and heavenly rain pours upon it, it will produce grass for cattle. It will give the simple such teaching for the nourishment of their souls as they are able to receive.

It will give grass for the service of human beings. At the beginning, when they come to God, it will bring forth grass for them. For they cannot be nourished by more solid foods. Solid food belongs to the perfected, who are able to possess discernment between good and evil.

After grass it will give the ear of grain, and it begins to bring bread forth from the earth. For just as milk comes from the breasts, so through grass one reaches the ear of grain from the earth, and from the ear one arrives at bread, which descends from heaven through rain.

Therefore, through an unfailing spring, bread comes to you from the earth of the Virgin Mary. Hear how this rain that came upon Mary came. The angel says to her: “The power of the Most High”—that is, coming from above—“will overshadow you” (Luke 1). And bread came forth for us from the earth.

Let us therefore return to ourselves, who receive this rain coming from above, if the spring coming from above finds us open to it. We receive bread that strengthens our heart. We receive wine that gladdens our heart. And, having received these two strengthenings of the heart, our faces are gladdened with the oil of chrism, so that through the wood of the cross all the trees of the field may be satisfied—that is, the entire crowd of the simple, among whom are the rich and the highest powers, whom, because of their loftiness, he called the cedars of Lebanon.

Among these the sparrows build their nests. He did not say that sparrows would build their nests in all of them. For there are some who love Christians and support them with their assistance. Resting in these, they build nests for God. They are called sparrows because, seeking heavenly and lofty things, they so associate with human ways of life that they flee human beings themselves, in whose houses they are nevertheless seen to build their nests.

Among these sparrows that build their nests, the house of the coot is their leader. The coot remains in the water, nests in the water, lives in the water, and the water is its house. Thus the house of the coot of these sparrows—that is, the water itself—is their leader.

There are the lofty mountains, for deer fleeing the devil and fleeing the world. There is the rock offering refuge, whether for the young of hedgehogs, because, having smaller quills, they are not afraid of dogs, or for hares, because both hares and hedgehogs flee dogs.

Those, therefore, who flee these dogs, about whom Paul cries, “Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers” (Phil. 3), find a rock for refuge and, placed beside the path, escape the bites of dogs.

Now we have passed beyond the mountains and forests, and the face of heaven shines upon us. In it we see the moon made, shining in the darkness at the time of the Passion.

But explain at what time. We said, “At the time of the Passion.” How so? Because at that time the Sun of righteousness set its setting at the sixth hour of the day; it brought darkness, and night came to be. In that night all the beasts of the forest—the ferocity of the Pharisees—passed through, as did those who devour God’s people like bread: both spiritual beasts and carnal ones.

But for this reason he gave the moon in the night, so that, possessing heavenly light, we might escape the bites of wild beasts. In its very darkness the cubs of lions abound—that is, the sons of demons, all heretics who do not teach holiness, but roar in order to seize and seek to take food for themselves from God.

But when the Sun of righteousness rose—whether the Lord’s rising from the dead for the Jews, or his rising through Catholic affirmation against the heretics—when this sun rose, all the beasts that lay in ambush fled and settled in their dens: the Jews in their synagogues, and the heretics in their synedria.

There they gather, and as long as the Sun of righteousness shines upon us, they sleep in their dens and do not dare come out into the light. For everyone who does evil hates the light. Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness; he is a beast. He too sleeps with the Jews and heretics: the Jews placing themselves and sleeping in the dens of unbelief, and the heretics in the dens of false belief.

Thus a dark night of hatred presses upon their eyes from within, and, seeing nothing but darkness, they sleep in hatred.

But whoever is a human being and not a beast goes out to his work, believing and believing rightly. As the Sun of righteousness shines upon him, he works at his labor until evening—that is, as long as he remains in this light. And, not attributing this to his own powers, he cries: “How greatly magnified are your works, O Lord! You have made all these things in wisdom,” whether visible things, according to the Apostle, or invisible things (Col. 1).

For the earth has been filled with his creation. We have come to the ends of the earth; let us now enter the sea.

“This sea is great and spacious.” The psalmist patriarch—or rather, the Holy Spirit speaking through those in whom he speaks—does not teach you this for the sake of a great prophetic utterance, but intended to teach us that the sea is great and spacious, and that in it are creeping things whose number is beyond counting.

Large and small living creatures are there, and ships pass through it. He did not teach what no one is ignorant of; rather, he wanted us to know that the great and spacious sea is the whole law of the New and Old Testament, and that in it are creeping things whose number is beyond counting: in the law, Jews; in the law, Samaritans; in the law, heretics; and in the law, Catholics; in the law, kings, consuls, rich and poor. Small and great are there.

Ships pass through it: only the Churches of all the provinces, which carry passengers upward to the kingdoms of heaven, from earthly cities to the city of Jerusalem, our mother.

But whoever is found in this great sea without a ship will find the dragon that was formed to mock them. It must nevertheless be noted that God is told: “There is,” he says, “the dragon which you formed.” For the Manichaeans say that the prince of darkness has his origin from himself. Therefore, so that the creature may be assigned to God, it is said to God: “Whom you formed.”

What follows—“to mock them”—refers to those who refuse the ships and, like creatures without a Catholic teacher leading them and transmitting the tradition of the law from the apostles, surrender themselves to the waves and depths.

Therefore, because they are outside the Church, wandering among small and great animals, they find the dragon mocking them so completely that they think themselves wiser than Catholics. Following their own will, they find the destruction of everlasting death when they have descended into the depths.

Yet what do you do, Lord, patient and greatly merciful? Jews and heretics, and the ungrateful together with your servants—all, as long as they are in this body, wait for you to give them food at this time: at this time of present life. For if you do not give it, no one gathers anything.

You open your hand over the good and the wicked, and fill every living creature with blessing. But when you turn your face away, they are troubled; when you take away their spirit, they fail and return to their own earth, from which they were taken.

But when the time of resurrection has come, your spirit will come, and those in whom you have renewed the face of the earth will rise again: those who have walked in newness of life, who have walked in newness of spirit, and have not remained in the oldness of the letter, in whom all old things have passed away and all things have become new (2 Cor. 5).

In them there will be the glory of the Lord forever and ever, when he is blessed in his works, which he now performs with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He looks upon the earth—that is, the bodies of the faithful—and makes them tremble before the future judgment.

“He touches the mountains, and they smoke.” The smoke of the mountains makes clouds. Therefore the Lord will touch those who raise their understanding toward heavenly glory, so that they appear diminished among human beings on earth but may be found exalted in the future. They will give forth the smoke of their mouths, bringing forth speech. They are clouds to the eyes, and they will make many weep for their sins, many wash them away through almsgiving, and many hasten to the sacred fountain.

Thus, at God’s touch, the mountains smoke for the overflowing of the clouds, which, giving rain, both wash away filth and provide crops and trees with the means of growth.

Let us therefore sing to the Lord our God in our life, and sing psalms to him as long as we live. May our praise be pleasing to him, seasoned with Catholic affirmations, carrying nothing of the disease of the Jews and nothing of the disease of the heretics. Then we too shall rejoice in the Lord when the heretics, or the Jews, and the wicked begin to fail from the earth, so that they are no more. Then our joyful soul, blessing the Lord at all times, will give thanks to him, whose glory is forever and ever. Amen.

## Psalm 104

### Alleluia

Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name; proclaim his works among the nations. Sing to him and sing psalms to him; recount all his wonders. Praise yourselves in his holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually.

Remember his wonders that he has done, his signs and the judgments of his mouth: the offspring of Abraham, his servant, the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones. He is the Lord our God; his judgments are throughout all the earth.

He remembered his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations: the covenant that he established with Abraham, and his oath to Isaac. He established it with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac; he appointed it for Jacob as a commandment, and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying: “To you I shall give the land of Canaan, the allotment of your inheritance.”

When they were few in number, very few, and strangers in it, they passed from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people. He did not allow anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

And he called famine upon the land, and destroyed every support of bread. He sent a man before them: Joseph was sold into slavery. They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul, until his word came. The word of the Lord inflamed him. The king sent and released him; the ruler of peoples set him free.

He appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to instruct his princes like himself, and to teach wisdom to his elders.

And Israel entered Egypt, and Jacob became a sojourner in the land of Ham. He increased his people greatly and strengthened them against their enemies. He turned their hearts so that they hated his people and dealt treacherously with his servants.

He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he chose. He placed in them the words of his signs and wonders in the land of Ham. He sent darkness and made it dark, and they did not rebel against his words. He turned their waters into blood and killed their fish.

Their land brought forth frogs in the inner chambers of their kings. He spoke, and the dog-fly and the gnats came throughout all their borders. He made their rains hail, with burning fire in their land. He struck their vines and their fig trees, and shattered the trees of their borders.

He spoke, and the locust and the young locust came, whose number was beyond counting. They consumed every plant in their land and consumed all the fruit of their soil. He struck every firstborn in their land, the first fruits of all their labor.

He brought them out with silver and gold, and there was not a feeble person among their tribes. Egypt rejoiced at their departure, because the fear of them had fallen upon it.

He spread out a cloud as their protection, and fire to give them light by night. They asked, and quail came, and he satisfied them with the bread of heaven. He broke open the rock, and waters flowed; rivers ran through the dry land.

For he remembered his holy word, which he had spoken to Abraham, his servant. And he brought out his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness. He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labor of peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.

## Commentary

The Alleluia in this psalm took its beginning from this point. Since it is interpreted as “glory to God, the creator of all things,” the interpretation is correct. For he commands that his glory be proclaimed to all nations, and that all his wonders be recounted: how he was born from a virgin; how he taught by example and word; how he exercised powers; how he hung upon the cross; how he died, was buried, and rose again; how he confirmed once more after his resurrection the things he had taught before his Passion; how he ascended into heaven; and how he sent the Paraclete, who, in the sight of the nations, dispersed like fire, opened the tongues of all the nations then present through the apostles, so that what had been commanded in the present psalm was fulfilled by the Holy Spirit himself.

Then those very nations said about the apostles: “Are not these,” they said, “Galileans? And how have we each heard them speaking in our own languages of the mighty works of God?” (Acts 2).

Then they confessed the Lord to the nations and called upon his name—the name that Judaea alone had retained. Then they proclaimed his mighty works among the nations. Then, rightly and for the first time, the Alleluia was sung at the coming of the Holy Spirit, in whom they recounted all his wonders and taught the nations in this order:

“Do not boast in the power of your kings, nor in the strength of your battles. Lay aside the power of bows, shield, sword, and war, and take up peace. Join Christ, whom we preach to you, to your name, so that you who are called nations may be called Christians, and may be praised in his holy name.

“And let your heart rejoice, you who seek the Lord. Seek Christ and be strengthened. And because he has ascended into heaven and prepares everlasting joy for you, seek his face continually, until you attain to him.

“Remember his wonders that he has done”—the wonders we mentioned above; “the judgments of his mouth,” whatever the apostles and the four evangelists testify—not those coming from the nations, but from the offspring of Abraham, his servant, who are the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.

“For Christ is not a recent God, nor an outsider, nor a newcomer. He is himself the Lord our God, who has always existed. And he who had established ceremonies only among the Hebrew people now wills that his judgments be throughout all the earth.

“What do you say now, Jews? Speak, if you wish. We accuse you knowingly, and we say to you: You possess false Scriptures. If it was truly God who spoke with Abraham, why could he not fulfill what he promised? If he could not, he is not omnipotent; if he could and did not wish to, he lied.”

To this Paul cries out—Hebrew of Hebrews—“It is impossible for God to lie.” Therefore show that what God swore has been fulfilled when he swore by himself, saying: “In your seed I shall inherit all the nations.” He established this with Abraham, and his oath with Isaac; he appointed it for Jacob as a commandment and for Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying: “To you indeed I shall give the land of Canaan, the allotment of your inheritance.”

And when did this happen? When they were still few in number, very few, and strangers in the land of Ham. Then they passed from nation to nation, from the kingdom of the Canaanites to the people of Egypt. Yet he did not allow anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings for their sake, as he did Amalek and the others. He said to them: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.”

Accordingly King Amalek said to Abraham: “Unless God had warned me by night in a vision, I would have sinned against you; but he rebuked me in the vision and warned me to ask you, and for you to pray for me.”

Up to this point we have treated both the mystical and the historical sense, but one little question seems to be in our hands. For it is asked how this word—“he commanded for a thousand generations”—which he established with Abraham, is to be understood.

To teach these thousand generations of nations would require a sufficiently lengthy account. But, as we are able, with the Lord’s help, let us proceed phrase by phrase.

“From nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people.”

Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. To Shem, the firstborn, a portion was assigned from Persia and Bactria as far as India, and as far as Rhinocorura. These stretches of land contain twenty-seven languages in barbarian speech. Within these languages there are 406 ancestral territories—not different languages, but, as I have said, different homelands.

For example, although there is one Latin language, under that one language there are different homelands: those of the Bruttians, Lucanians, Apulians, Calabrians, Picentines, and Tuscans; and if we mention other homelands of this kind, there are similar distinctions.

Ham, Noah’s second son, extends from Rhinocorura to Cadiz. He has twenty-two languages: Punic in the region of the Garamantes, Latin toward the north, barbarian speech toward the south, the languages of the Ethiopians and Egyptians, and various speech among the interior barbarians. These comprise 394 homelands.

Japheth, however, has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia, with 200 homelands of varied speech and twenty-three languages.

Thus all the languages together amount to seventy-two, while the homelands of the generations amount to a thousand. They are situated in this tripartite world in the following order.

As we have said, Japheth has the river Tigris, which divides Media and Babylonia. Shem has the Euphrates, while Ham has the Gihon, which is called the Nile.

Among these tripartite nations flowing from one human being, the Trinity appeared through our Lord Jesus Christ as a perfect human being. He alone encountered these thousand generations through the language of his Passion, because he remembered the word that he had sworn for a thousand generations, saying to Abraham: “In your seed I shall inherit all the nations.”

And just as Joseph came to the aid of the children of Israel when they were suffering famine—Joseph who had been sold and, after being sold, rose to royal power, carefully aiding several nations and homelands that were perishing from hunger by storing grain—so Christ, sold by Judas, was exalted in the triumph of the cross.

Before this he suffered the synagogue as a false witness, just as Joseph suffered his mistress, a prostitute. Afterward, rising from the dead, he received the kingdom, so that at his name every knee might bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2). And when these thousand generations were perishing from hunger, he came to their aid by opening the storehouses with the most abundant generosity of his hands, supplying them not merely with the form of grain, but also with wine and oil. He freed them from all adversities.

For he called famine upon their land—upon those who had previously trusted in idols—and destroyed every support of bread for them, because they did not know the true bread that would descend from heaven.

But when the perfect man came, the one who had been sold into slavery, after iron had passed through his soul because the word of the false witness had inflamed anger against him, then the king sent from heaven and released him. The ruler who is God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ (2 Cor. 5), released him, freeing him from every bond of weakness.

Immediately he appointed him lord of his house: lord in heaven and in the Church, and ruler of all his possession, of all holiness. He did so that he might instruct the apostles like himself, he who had advanced in age and wisdom, and teach wisdom to his elders—these very fathers of all believers—and what was hidden in the ministry.

Then Israel entered Egypt, seeing God: the apostles among idolaters. Jacob became a sojourner in the land of Canaan, and he increased his people greatly, so that thousands of human beings had one heart and one soul. He strengthened their heart against all their enemies who denied him.

For, despising them, the apostles turned to the nations. The heart of the nations was turned so that they hated his people and, by killing the martyrs, dealt treacherously with his servants, until Moses and Aaron came to them, until the law of God reached their understanding and they placed in their minds the words of the signs and wonders that they had either recognized by reading or heard from those who recounted them.

For they began to fear that, if they did not believe, they would suffer what Egypt and its king had suffered: darkness, waters turned to blood, frogs, locusts, young locusts, gnats, dog-flies, hail, and the fiery wind that burned their vines and fig trees and every tree within their borders.

After this came also the striking of the angel against every firstborn of their land and the first fruits of all their labor.

Therefore, all yielding fear to the might of the conquering God, they fled the unbelief of the Egyptians and, following the faith of the apostles, were brought out with silver and gold: with the two Testaments, silver representing the Old and gold the New; with what is good and what is better. None of those who passed through the water was found to be weak among them.

For among all these thousand generations of baptized people, no one is found to have sin at the hour of baptism. Otherwise, if he has sin, he did not believe and was drowned with the Egyptians.

For all who believed, from the hour when they crossed over and came to receive the seal, are found not to be weak among their tribes. All are strong; all have been strengthened.

Egypt rejoiced. Egypt—the whole world, though living in sins—nevertheless rejoices on the holy day of Easter at the departure of those who, fleeing Pharaoh and following Moses, passed through the water in order to find where they might hear the voice of the Lord.

Fear fell upon the unbelievers, and they did not dare to be without observance on that very day. If they do not rejoice as believers in God, they keep the feast because they fear the kingdom and the Christian people. Therefore they rejoice, because their fear has fallen upon them.

For God spread out a cloud—that is, his Church—for their protection, and the fire of faith, which shines for them amid the darkness of the world. When they asked for flesh, they received the *ortygometra*, a quail. For flesh was given to them then: quails, flying creatures indeed and desiring heavenly things. Flesh was given to them—the flesh that ascended above the cherubim and flew—and they were filled with the bread of heaven.

When he broke open the rock and waters flowed, rivers ran through the desert of the whole world, because he remembered his holy word that he had spoken to Abraham, his servant.

Therefore he led out his people with rejoicing, with Alleluia, in white garments, and his chosen ones with gladness. He gave them the regions of the nations and the cities of peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.

For he says: “Baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Amen.

## Psalm 105

### Alleluia, alleluia

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Who shall speak of the powers of the Lord? Who shall make all his praises heard? Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times.

Remember us, O Lord, in the goodwill of your people; visit us with your salvation. Let us see the goodness of your chosen ones, let us rejoice in the joy of your nation, so that you may be praised with your inheritance.

We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they did not remember the abundance of your mercies. They provoked you as they went up to the sea, the Red Sea.

And he saved them for his name’s sake, to make his power known. He rebuked the Red Sea, and it was dried up; he led them through the depths as through a desert. He saved them from the hand of those who hated them, and protected them from the ambush of the enemy. He redeemed them from the hand of the enemy.

The water covered those who afflicted them; not one of them remained. And they believed his words, and sang his praise. They acted quickly; they forgot his works and did not wait for his counsel.

They desired desire in the desert and tested God in the waterless place. And he gave them their request and sent abundance into their souls.

They provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the congregation of Abiron. Fire burned in their synagogue; flame consumed the sinners.

They made a calf at Horeb and worshiped a cast image. They exchanged their glory for the likeness of a calf that eats grass.

They forgot God, who saved them, who had done great things in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrible deeds at the Red Sea. He said that he would destroy them, had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him to turn away his anger, lest he destroy them.

They treated the desirable land as nothing. They did not believe his word and murmured in their tents; they did not heed the voice of the Lord. He raised his hand against them to overthrow them in the desert, to cast down their offspring among the nations, and to scatter them throughout the regions.

They were initiated into Baal-peor and ate the sacrifices of the dead. They provoked him by their inventions, and destruction was multiplied among them.

Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased. It was counted to him as righteousness, from generation to generation, forever.

They provoked him at the water of contradiction, and Moses was afflicted because of them, because they embittered his spirit. He spoke rashly with his lips.

They did not destroy the nations that the Lord God had commanded them. They mingled with the nations and learned their works. They served their cast images, and it became a stumbling block for them.

They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. They poured out innocent blood—the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the cast images of Canaan. The land was polluted by blood and defiled by their deeds, and they committed fornication in their inventions.

The Lord was enraged with fury against his people, and he abhorred his inheritance. He delivered them into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands.

Many times he delivered them; but they provoked him by their counsel and were humbled by their iniquities. He saw when they were afflicted and heard their prayer. He remembered his covenant and repented according to the abundance of his mercies.

And he made them objects of mercy in the sight of all those who had taken them captive.

Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, so that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise.

Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, from age to age. And all the people shall say: Amen, amen.

## Commentary
Alleluia first brought about the baptism of believers. The second Alleluia brings about the reconciliation of penitents. There he received his people with rejoicing, and his chosen ones with gladness. Here he hears the penitents and grants them mercy in the sight of all who had taken them captive. Blessed, therefore, are those who keep justice. For they do not come to this end: to be captured by their enemies. But those who have been captured cry out to the merciful, saying: [Col. 0484C] “We have sinned with our fathers; we have acted unjustly; we have committed iniquity.”

Nor do I want you to regard without some qualification what I said: that all who do not keep justice are captured by their enemies. Regard as enemies, rather, those who are certainly known to exist but cannot be seen with certainty. And when you attend to them with the mind’s eye, you will see that person more completely possessed by his enemies who, after sinning, rejoices, having been struck by no scourge.

But because that person is a true Christian who daily pleads for his sins, let him accept the rule of penance, [Note: [Col. 0483] I think that “excluding Novatian” should be read; for Novatian did not receive penitents.] with Novatian excluded. [Uncertain text: *Nova ita non* appears corrupt in the supplied text.] Let him therefore join the hundred-fifth psalm to the hundred-fourth, and not reject the one who weeps in the fifth, whom he received rejoicing in the fourth. And just as the one sang “Alleluia,” so let this one also sing “Alleluia.”

There the rich man, made wealthy in silver and gold, goes forth rejoicing; here, having become a beggar, he returns weeping. There Alleluia was sung, and here Alleluia is sung. There it was said, “Give thanks and call upon his name”; here it is said, “Give thanks, for he is good.” Declare your sins, by which you provoked the Lord. For he pronounced sentence against you, in order to cast you among the nations and scatter you through the regions. Give thanks to the Good One; give thanks to the One willing to pardon.

But they say: “We have sinned with our fathers.” “We have sinned with our fathers”—he does not specify a time. For they sinned with their fathers when, going up at the Red Sea, they provoked him—when the water covered those who afflicted them. [Col. 0485A] After they had believed God’s word and sung his praise, they immediately forgot his works. They lusted with lust in the wilderness—for the pots of Egypt—and provoked him in the parched land. Their request was granted them, and satiety was given to their soul. Luxury followed satiety, and the Lord was provoked by the proud Dathan, Korah, and Abiron. Whether on account of strange fire or on account of the pride they displayed against Moses, the earth was opened and swallowed them alive.

But the people, delivered and forgetful of their deliverer, remembered the superstitions of Egypt. Remembering them, they poured out their gold in the likeness of a calf and worshiped the works of their hands. For they forgot the one who had delivered them. When the Lord therefore wished to destroy them on account of this deed, Moses stood and said: “Lord, erase me from your book, if you do not spare these people” [Col. 0485B] (Exod. 32).

Do you suppose, Moses, that you are more merciful than the One who, when manna was blasphemed, rained it down, and when he was despised, brought waters forth from the earth? You are not more merciful; rather, the Lord wished your devotion to be recounted to the leaders of the people, so that they might act toward sinners as they know you acted: not condemn them quickly, but by their prayers bend the Lord, who wished to condemn them.

Hear what you sing: “He said,” it says, “that he would destroy them, had not Moses stood in the breach and in the rebellion”—the one by which the people had begun to be admonished and provoked to action. “He stood,” it says, “in his sight, to turn away his anger, lest he destroy them.”

Now, if you please, since the psalm is long, let us pass from the history of the Jews to our own case. For all these things happen to us after the consecration of baptism. Through baptism we enter a land flowing [Col. 0485C] with milk and honey. After this, however, we regard the desirable land as nothing when we defile the land of our body. For we do not truly believe the words of God, who threatens everlasting fire [Note: [Col. 0485] I judge that it should be read thus: “to the One threatening [eternal fire] for wicked temporal deeds.”] in connection with deeds committed in the present.

And because we do not believe God, we murmur in the tabernacles of our minds, because we have not heeded the Lord’s voice. With what face do we say to God, “Hear our voice,” when we do not heed the Lord’s voice? Moreover, we consecrate ourselves to Beelphegor, serving the belly and lust; or we honor those who worship our bellies, or those whose person is welcomed by the world. Though we know them to be either shameful in their deeds or unjust in judgment, nevertheless, because they are joined to the friendships of the powerful—or are themselves powerful—we consecrate them to the priesthood. We proclaim them worthy and just, through whom we eat the sacrifices of the dead.

For those who offer either money or gifts to the churches, and who are dead in their sins, offer precisely so that they may come back to life through our prayers. But we, committing worse crimes, eat the sacrifices that those dead people offer; they, meanwhile, remain in their death, because they will not be recalled by our example. Thus it happens that we provoke the Lord by these pursuits of ours, and ruin is multiplied upon us.

Cities perish; provinces perish, because discipline perishes. It remains for Phinehas to stand and intercede for us—that is, for the people of martyrs to stand, who, like Phinehas, did not fear to shed blood. May the devastation cease among us through their prayers, and may what we escape—not through any righteousness of our own—be reckoned to the righteousness of those who pray, from generation to generation forever.

Now we must see how we also, like them, provoke the Lord at the waters of contradiction, so that Moses is vexed on our account, because we embitter his spirit. Thus, as I said, this psalm is clear in its historical sense, so that it does not need an expositor at all. But because we have entered beneath the letter from the letter, let us see how the Lord is provoked at the waters of contradiction.

After baptism, one water of contradiction arises for us: the water of baptism is contradicted to us. For “there is one God, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4). There we vex Moses. Moses is the law of God; [Col. 0486B] we vex his law by despising his commands. Moreover, we embitter his Holy Spirit, in whom we were sealed for the day of redemption.

We do this when we do not destroy the nations whom the Lord commanded us to destroy, but nourish our vices; when, loving what the Lord hates, we mingle among the nations, doing things like—or worse than—the nations that do not know God. We serve their idols, having the belly as our god and glorying in filth. From this scandal arises for us—that is, lust.

Then we sacrifice our sons and daughters to demons—that is, our senses, which are born from us as children. We hand our thoughts over to demons. We pour out innocent blood—that is, the blood of simple souls who sin because of our example. We sacrifice their blood, certainly, to the idols of Cham. Cham is the mocker of his father. Therefore we sacrifice those who sin because of our example to those who mock the law of our God.

For they lie before their mouths: they speak of them, laugh at them, joke about them, and find every kind of insult in them. “That monk did this; that cleric did this; that nun did this.” Thus the earth is slain by blood—that is, earthly minds are slain in this manner—if one who has been called holy and *nonnus* [Note: [Col. 0486] I believe Jerome used this Egyptian word] says, “If he does this, who am I, or how important am I, not to do it?” Thus the earth is stained with blood by our vice and polluted by our deeds.

For we fornicate in our observances—that is, although placed in a holy undertaking, we fornicate either in heart or in deed. Therefore the Lord is angry with his people and has rejected his inheritance. Therefore he has handed [Col. 0486D] us over to the power of our enemies, and those who hate us rule over us. Our enemies afflict us and humble us beneath their feet. We have often said, “Spare us, Lord,” and often he has delivered us.

But we, delivered again, have once more burned with our thoughts. Nothing remains for us except to depart from this body. If we have despised what we have suffered, we despise what we will suffer. For there suffering has no end. Let us repent wholeheartedly at last. For just as, by despising God, we made God despising toward us, so, when we repent from the heart, we make God repentant toward us.

We repent because we despised him; he repents because he pronounced the sentence. You renew your deeds; he renews his sentence. You repent, and he repents according to the multitude of his mercy. Removing his anger from us, he grants us mercy in the sight of all who took us captive.

Let us therefore cry out wholeheartedly to the Savior, saying: “Save us, Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations” (Ps. 105), so that we may no longer serve sin. Let our ways not be like those of the nations. For even if we are scattered among the nations, like Daniel and the three young men, we are not among the nations if we do not mingle with them in conduct.

Rather, we glory in his praise. When people see our works, they will praise and bless the God of Israel, and all the people will say: “Let it be, let it be”—that is, “Let it be, let it be: may there always be such a work in which God is blessed,” who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 106

Alleluia, alleluia.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let those whom the Lord has redeemed now say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions—from the rising and the setting of the sun, from the north and the sea.

They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they did not find a road to a city of habitation. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. And he led them by a straight way, so that they might go to a city of habitation.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. For he satisfied the empty soul, and he filled the hungry soul with good things.

Those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron, because they embittered God’s words and provoked the counsel of the Most High. Their heart was humbled by toil, and they became weak, and there was no one to help. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. For he shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars.

He received them from the way of their iniquity, for they had been humbled because of their injustices. Their soul abhorred every kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he delivered them from their distresses. He sent his word and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. Let them offer a sacrifice of praise and proclaim his works with rejoicing.

Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon the great waters: they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and the storm-wind arose, and its waves rose up. They went up to the heavens and descended to the abysses; their soul languished amid evils. They were troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.

And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted, and he led them out of their distresses. He made its storm into a breeze, and its waves were silent. [Col. 0488A] And they rejoiced because they were silent, and he led them into the harbor of their desire.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people and praise him in the seat of the elders.

He made rivers into a wilderness and springs of water into thirst; fruitful land into saltiness, because of the wickedness of those dwelling in it. He made the wilderness into pools of water and dry land into springs of water. And he settled the hungry there, and they established a city of habitation. They sowed fields, planted vineyards, and produced the fruit of their harvest.

And he blessed them, and they multiplied greatly, and he did not diminish their cattle. Then they became few and were afflicted by the tribulation of evils and sorrow. Contention was poured out upon princes, and he made them wander in a trackless place and not on a road.

And he helped the poor in their poverty and made families like sheep. The upright will see this and rejoice, and all iniquity will shut its mouth. Who is wise and will keep these things, and understand the mercies of the Lord?

## COMMENTARY

The third Alleluia is sung in the hundred-sixth psalm, in which our daily experience is unfolded anew. Hear, Novatian; hear what it is speaking about. For in this psalm the Holy Spirit wishes to act especially against you.

You say: “Those who have not yet been redeemed can reach pardon through penance.” We say: “They reach pardon through faith alone. But those who have already been redeemed do not reach the mercy of the Redeemer through faith alone—for they have already believed—but through penance.”

Finally, hear what it says: “Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord speak,” whom he redeemed from the hands of enemies—clearly through baptism—and gathered from the regions—clearly to the faith—from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea. [Col. 0488C]

They wandered—that is, they departed from the straight course—suffering dryness on the way, that is, walking in Christ, because he himself is the way. They suffered dryness of speech, while no one taught and no one exhorted, or while there was no one whose example could pour strength into them. Suffering dryness, they wandered and did not find a city of habitation. They did not find anyone whose example would enable them to live spiritually. But, suffering the wilderness of this world, hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.

For they had no food of God’s word or of a good example. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted—that is, while they were repenting [Col. 0488D]—and he delivered them from their distresses. He brought them back to the straight way: through penance they were recalled to Christ, so that through him they might reach the city of habitation and be refreshed by holy teachings.

Let them give thanks to the Lord for his mercies and for his wonders to the children of men. For he satisfied the soul that was perishing from hunger, and the hungry soul. What hungry soul? The soul hungry for the good things it did not possess. Therefore he filled the penitent with good things, the one sitting not in the world’s displays, not boasting in public, but sitting in darkness and in bonds, in poverty and in iron.

“Why this?” worldly people say. “What do these religious people mean by weeping, sitting in bonds, sitting in darkness? Where is it written?” Behold, it is written here: God regards that soul which sits in darkness and in bonds because it embittered the Lord and despised the counsel of the Most High. They humble their heart through toil and fasting.

Since, therefore, God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart, hear what follows: “They cried out,” it says, “not when they were feasting, but when they were afflicted.” For they themselves impose upon themselves the yoke of affliction, lest, while they seek to reach pardon for their past deeds, they fall into present ones. A joyful spirit easily falls into what a sorrowful and afflicted spirit finds difficult.

Let our heart therefore be humbled by toil and fasting. Let wines not make it joyful. Showing our weakness to the heavenly physician, let us cry out to him. For he himself will lead us out of darkness and the shadow of death. And he will break our bonds, [Col. 0489B] so that we may give thanks to him because he has shattered for us bronze gates.

The bronze gates are vicious habits, which shut us in so tightly that they almost enclose even the freedom of our will. For example, although we have become accustomed to swearing, we no longer wish to swear; but, like a closed gate of this habit, it does not allow the one who wishes to leave to depart. Thus it happens that, even unwillingly, I bring an oath forth from my mouth. Consider the same to have been said concerning all vices.

For in those very vices, as though against bronze gates, we stumble; though we flee and wish to leave, we cannot. But when, in our affliction, we cry out to Christ, he will break the bronze gates and crush the iron bars. The iron bars are unclean spirits, which close the gates of an impious habit against us.

If the Lord withdraws himself here, the very freedom of our will [Col. 0489C] vanishes. But the Lord does not withdraw himself unless he is entreated with tears in a troubled spirit [Note: [Col. 0489] *Tribulanti* is said in Greek of one who is afflicted.]

For he will send his word, just as he previously sent his Son. He sends him and heals us; and just as he redeemed us from the hand of the enemy, so now he rescues us from our destruction.

Let them therefore give thanks to the Lord in the plural for his mercies, and let them proclaim his wonders to the children of men, so that they may offer a sacrifice of praise. Therefore let them announce his works with rejoicing and not with affliction.

“Those who go down to the sea in ships”—those who dwell in this world in holy conduct go down to the sea in ships. For they do their work upon great waters: by their word and example they are said to perform the work of those who either hear or imitate them upon great waters.

They see the works of the Lord daily. They devote themselves to seeing the works of the Lord, which this world, while enjoying it, does not see. But they not only see the works of the Lord; they also contemplate his wonders in the deep.

Yet because no righteous person passes through without temptation, hear what is said about them: “They go up,” it says, “to the heavens.” What does “they go up” mean? Learn from Peter, so that what you find in him you may see in everyone.

Peter went up to the heavens when he said to the Lord, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26). He descended to the abysses when he denied him. After this he was so troubled and shaken as a drunken man. And all his wisdom was so swallowed up that, unless he had cried out to the Lord when he was afflicted [Col. 0490A] and wept most bitterly, he would not have escaped those distresses.

He therefore wept, and he made the storm a breeze for him. Hear the Lord saying: “Peter,” he says, “Satan asks to sift you like wheat on the threshing floor; but I have interceded for you” (Luke 22)—as though he were saying, “I made the storm a breeze for you and caused its waves to be silent before you.”

Peter rejoiced because they were silent, and he led him into the harbor of his desire, clearly into the Church. Where do they exalt him in the assembly of the people? And in the seat of the elders they praise him, because he made rivers in the wilderness—that is, as he traveled through the wilderness of this age until he reached Rome, he preached the baptism of Jesus Christ, in which all rivers are blessed by Peter to this day.

He himself made springs of water in thirst, so that whoever goes outside Peter’s Church may perish from thirst. [Col. 0490B]

He made fruitful land into saltiness. Just as saltiness withdraws the earth from fruitfulness, so the world’s letter withdraws minds from spiritual fruitfulness. But through Peter he made Rome, placed in the saltiness of letters, bear fruit.

He also explained how that land itself came to have saltiness: “Because of the wickedness,” he says, “of the people dwelling in it.” And he added: “He made,” he says, “the wilderness without waters”—the waters that wash away sins—“into pools of water.” The waters of baptism, martyrdom, penance, and almsgiving abound in this wilderness, which before Peter’s arrival was dry and parched. Now it has been cultivated, when the city of the Church was established in it, in which fields are sown and vineyards planted daily, so that they may produce the fruit of their harvest, which God blessed and caused to multiply.

But after this persecution arose, and they became few. [Col. 0490C] For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). Few, indeed, were deemed worthy to attain the palm of martyrdom. This was when contention was poured out upon the princes of the world. Then they led them astray in a trackless place and not on the way—that is, among idols and not in Christ, who is the way.

But the Lord helped the poor in their poverty and looked upon them, because the believing people could not bear the temptations at all. He helped them from the unreliability of their strength and established families like sheep over the whole face of the earth, appointing shepherds and pastures for them. When the upright see these things, they will rejoice.

But the unrighteous will murmur. Every iniquity against the Church of God, and against the sheep and shepherds, has now shut its mouth. Whoever is wise understands these things, and when he has understood them, he understands nothing else except the mercy of the Lord, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 107

A psalm-song for David.

My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; and I will sing and make melody in my glory. Awake, psalter and lyre; I will awake at dawn. I will give thanks to you among the peoples, Lord, and make melody to you among the nations. For your mercy is great above the heavens, and your truth reaches to the clouds.

Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth; let your beloved ones be delivered. Save with your right hand and hear me. God has spoken in his holy place.

I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of the tents. Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine, and Ephraim is the protection of my head. Judah is my king; Moab is the cauldron of my hope.

Upon Idumea I will extend my sandal; foreigners have become my friends. Who will lead me into a fortified city? Who will lead me as far as Idumea? Is it not you, O God, who rejected us, and will you not go forth, O God, with our armies?

Give us help in tribulation, for human salvation is futile. In God we shall act bravely, and he himself will bring our enemies to nothing.

## COMMENTARY

The hundred-seventh psalm is shown to have been constructed from the endings of two psalms, partly from the fifty-sixth and partly from the fifty-ninth. If spiritual understanding carefully attends to this arrangement, it sees that the heart is sufficiently necessary to God: separating from him all the world’s opportunities, it makes itself ready for God, alluding to him in the psalm and repeating the words.

For what does it mean to say, “My heart is ready, O God,” except to say to him: “Come, Lord; my heart is ready, and enter into the thing prepared for you, so that I may sing and make melody in my glory”?

And he added what glory he meant as his own: “Awake,” he says, “my glory, with psalter and lyre, so that I may rise at dawn into that very glory.” As soon as your shining help has driven away from me the darkness of my sins, then I will give thanks among the peoples and say: “Because of my sins I am not worthy to be called your servant, I will not boast in pride even when, through your pardon, I acknowledge myself to have been commanded.”

Thus the one who, having become a chosen vessel, cried out: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15). And after confessing this among the peoples to the Lord, he began to recite the psalm among the nations.

Which psalm did Paul sing among the nations? Certainly this one: “For his mercy has been magnified to the heavens.” He came into this world to save sinners, “of whom,” he says, “I am the first” (1 Tim. 1). And his truth reached to the clouds—that is, the truth reached as far as the apostles, who is Christ.

The prophets are now silent; only the apostles speak, and the disciples of the apostles. What do they say? That God the Son has been exalted above the heavens, and that, seated at the right hand of the Father, his glory is proclaimed over all the earth, so that those who are his beloved may be delivered throughout the entire world. In them the Church cries: “Save me with your right hand and hear me.”

[Col. 0491D] For unless his right hand draws our soul up from the lower regions—that is, from lower thoughts—we are not released from those descending into the pit; that is, we are not rescued, but are entangled in the snare of fornication. Yet just as we are not rescued except through his right hand, so his right hand does not rescue us unless we say in faith: “Save me with your right hand and hear me.”

To this, God, it says, spoke in his holy place—that is, God spoke in the Lord Jesus Christ. “I will rejoice and divide Shechem.” It is a city that the Hebrews humbled with the sword, because their sister had been violated there. But now, because their mind has been corrupted, God sent his Son among the nations, to take this city of the nations away from the power of the Hebrews. I will divide it among the apostles, and I will measure its valleys of tents into three parts, so that I may join those three parts into one kingdom, and the Trinity of God may exist in the trinity of the peoples—the Hebrews, the Greeks, and the Latins.

From these three let people go forth into all parts of the world, so that all may be ours through faith, since without faith they cannot be ours. Let Gilead and Manasseh be ours among the nations, and let Ephraim be the strength of our head in blessings. Let Judah be my king in Christ; let Moab be the cauldron of my hope.

Moab is the daughter of Lot, from whom the Moabite peoples descend; she, under the guidance of angels, escaped the fiery rains coming from heaven. For her he asks that she not burn in the flames of Sodom, but burn fervently in the Holy Spirit, and that, with her children—that is, with the nations that do not know God—she may be the cauldron of my hope.

“Upon Idumea,” he says—that is, into the dwelling-place of the nations—“I will extend my sandal.” Let my disciples not flee from there, shaking the dust from their feet, but let them go there extending their sandal, so that it may be said of them: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Rom. 10).

These things will also happen to us, so that we may escape the heat of Sodom and be kindled by the flames of the Holy Spirit, if we strive to overcome the Philistines and, whenever they take up arms against us—that is, unclean spirits—strive to subdue them, so that we may rightly say: “The Philistines are subject to me.”

When they have been subjected, who will lead us into the fortified city except the Son of God? Or who will lead us into Idumea except the Lord Jesus Christ? For he himself gives us help.
