From where does he give us help? From rejoicing or from tribulation? “From tribulation,” he says, as though saying: “No one deserves to obtain help who does not show himself afflicted to Christ and believe that human salvation is futile.”

In God we act bravely. What kind of bravery? So that vices may be subdued through habit and the virtues of the soul raised up. Applying ourselves to these pursuits, let us act bravely in God, and he himself will reduce to nothing those who afflict us, he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 108

For the end; a psalm of David.

O God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded me with words of hatred and attacked me without cause.

Although they ought to love me, they slandered me; but I prayed. They repaid me evil for good and hatred for my love.

Set a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand. When he is judged, let him go out condemned, and let his prayer become sin. Let his days be few, and let another receive his office. Let his children become orphans and his wife a widow. Let his children be moved from place to place and beg; let them be cast out of their dwellings.

Let the creditor search out all his substance, and let strangers plunder his labors. Let there be no helper for him, nor anyone to have pity on his orphans. Let his descendants be destined for destruction; in one generation let his name be blotted out.

Let the iniquity of his fathers return to the memory of the Lord’s sight, and let the sin of his mother not be blotted out. Let them be before the Lord always, and let their memory perish from the earth, because he did not remember to show mercy.

He pursued the poor and needy man, and the brokenhearted, in order to put him to death. He loved cursing, and it will come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it will be far from him. He put on cursing like a garment, and it entered his inward parts like water and his bones like oil.

Let it be for him like a garment with which he covers himself and like a belt with which he always girds himself. Such is the work of those who slander me before the Lord and speak evil against my soul.

But you, Lord God, act with me for your name’s sake, because your mercy is sweet. Deliver me, for I am needy and poor, and my heart is troubled within me. Like a shadow when it declines, I have been taken away; I have been shaken off like locusts.

My knees have become weak from fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of the oil. I have become a reproach to them; they saw me and shook their heads.

Help me, Lord my God; save me according to your mercy. And let them know that this is your hand, and that you, Lord, have made it. They will curse, but you will bless. Let those who rise up against me be put to shame, but your servant will rejoice.

Let those who slander me be clothed with disgrace, and let them be covered with their shame as with a double cloak. I will give great thanks to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him, for he stood at the right hand of the poor, to save my soul from those who pursued it.

## COMMENTARY
We come to Psalm 108, which the apostle Peter interprets as referring to Judas Iscariot. Let us follow the path he himself opened and walk in it. [Col. 0493C] The perfect man addresses his inner self, saying: “O God, do not keep silent about my praise,” as though he were saying: “Men are stirring up false accusations against me; you, my God, do not keep silent about my praise.” Return to your conscience, O man of God, who follow Christ. And when the mouth of the sinner and deceiver has been opened against you, rejoice and be confident. For the sinner’s mouth is opened on earth for your disgrace, while the mouth of God is opened in heaven for your praise.

Let them speak against you, as the Pharisees spoke against the Lord with a deceitful tongue; let them surround and assault you with words of hatred, and let them attack you without cause. Understand that “without cause” means that it is not because of your fault, not because of your guilt, but that their lie serves your truth. For falsehood serves truth if you do not fear human reputation. A false witness accomplishes nothing [Col. 0493D] except to stain it itself. If you fear this, you have become a slave; if you do not fear it, you are free. Fear God alone, therefore, and, relying upon a good conscience, let reputation recognize that it is the servant of your purpose; compel it to serve virtue rather than command it. For if you fear reputation, you will be the slave of all who can slander you. You will fear speaking the truth, lest falsehoods about you arise.

Perhaps you will say: “What shall I do if they wound my reputation?” Do what the man whose song you are expounding did: “Instead of loving me,” he says, “they slandered me, but I prayed.” He shows you what to do.

Now, as we approach the curses, let us beware of the outcome of these matters, lest we direct them against human beings and think that we have been given this rule so that we may curse those who persecute us with unjust hatred. The evangelical Teacher altogether prohibited this; therefore we must in spirit have recourse to the prince of malice. And whenever you sing the curses, you must sing them against the one whom the Lord cursed.

For he sets evils against us in place of good, either when we are doing good, because through his jealousy he stirs up evils against us, or when he displays idols: then he displays evils in place of good. Or when he agitates the desires of the flesh—for all the works of desire are evil—he displays those very evils as good and implants hatred in place of love, so that he seems to us to love and cherish us when he grants opportunity for sin.

“Appoint a sinner against him.” How this can stand, listen carefully. He appointed my disciple against me; let his disciple be appointed against him. Let the one who had become Christ’s persecutor be the devil’s persecutor, and let the devil stand at his right hand to be refuted and convicted. The devil stood at Paul’s right hand, so that Paul, judging him, caused him to depart condemned and counted all his speech and counsel as sin.

He made his days few. While Paul was preaching to the nations, the devil did not retain his authority in the temples for long. After this he ceased to be prince over the nations, and his teaching was received by the one who said: “I am the teacher of the nations in faith and truth” (1 Tim. II). For the devil had been the teacher of the nations in unbelief and deceit.

Then those to whom the Lord had said, “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII), when the king of unbelief had been cast down, became orphans, and the devil’s wife [Col. 0494C] also became a widow. For just as the Church was betrothed to one husband through faith, so through unbelief the power of unbelief is not a bride but a wife; it granted the priestly authority of ruling to the priests of the temples, whether of the Synagogue or of the churches of the heretics. When the devil has been cast down, this power becomes a widow, so that her children are expelled under anathema and forced to beg.

Our Lord the creditor searches all her property and demands from her—that is, from this very power—the interest of the word of wisdom, which she has used badly. Strangers seize all her labors; she is shown to have taught unjustly, written unjustly, and constructed unjustly. And all these things are seized by strangers from the fellowship of that same power, a power which, having failed in the devil himself, has no God as helper at all.

Nor is there anyone who has pity on her orphan. In one generation—that is, in the Christian people alone—her name is erased. There the iniquity of her fathers returns to memory. Every day it is read in the Church in the sight of God how many evils they committed against Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs; and the sin of her mother, that is, the sin of her power, is not erased, but is always turned against the Lord, and she will lose her memory from the earth.

Behold, the power of the persecutors has perished, because those who were lords of things are themselves servants of Christ. Therefore that power has perished from the earth. It did not remember to show mercy, but persecuted a man. Which man? “The poor man,” he says, “and the beggar”—Christ, certainly, both in his Passion and in the martyrdom of his people.

He loved the curse of Adam, which is taken away through Christ, and it will come upon him; he did not want the blessing that is brought through Christ, and therefore it will certainly be removed far from him. Observe that this happened by his own choice, on account of the heresy that says that God predestined some to blessing and others to cursing. For he is shown to possess the curse through his own love, and by his own will not to possess the reward of blessing.

Hence he added that he himself had clothed himself with the curse as with a garment. For just as we are told, “You have put on Christ” through faith (Gal. III), so through unbelief a man puts on the accursed one—that is, the devil—who enters the holy as water to liberate them, but enters them to destroy them. And just as oil brings gladness to the holy, so to the impious it brings affliction. Thus the curse itself becomes for them like the garment with which they are clothed and like the belt with which they gird themselves.

This is the work of those who slander the catholic faith and seek evils against the holy and against orthodox definitions, through which the Lord shows mercy because of his name. For even if someone is a sinner, whoever is nevertheless of right faith obtains mercy on that account.

If his heart has been troubled by fear of judgment, if he has been shaken from the hand of sin like a locust, if his knees have grown weak through fasting, and if his flesh has been changed, deprived of fatness, then he will find mercy. Though he may say—and say truly—“They saw me and shook their heads,” this is what the Pharisees did to Christ, and what demons do to the Christian. While Christ was suffering, the Pharisees shook their heads in mockery; and while the Christian is weighed down by sufferings, the demons see him consenting and mock him.

But the shrewd servant of God cries out: “Help me, O Lord, my God, so that they may know that your hand is with me, and that you, O Lord, have done this.” [Col. 0495C] Understand “this” in this passage as the Lord said to Pilate: “You would have no power unless it had been given you from above” (John XIX). In the same way, we too are left to a small temptation. And therefore he says: “You, O Lord, have done this,” so that they may shake their heads over me.

But because you are faithful and do not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, cause them to be clothed, as with a double cloak, in confusion. A *diploidis* is either a *chlamys* with a fourfold covering, or any other kind of garment that is double in front and double behind. Thus demons are clothed in fourfold confusion when we take up the fourfold deliverance of the Gospels, in which we confess the Lord greatly with our mouth and praise him in the midst of many while confessing him.

And because it is Christ, the Son of God, who stands at the right hand of the poor man in order to save our souls from those who persecute them—he who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 109

A psalm of David.

The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet.” The Lord will send forth from Zion the scepter of your power; rule in the midst of your enemies. With you is sovereignty on the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you. The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” The Lord is at your right hand; he has shattered kings on the day of his wrath. He will judge among the nations; he will fill them with ruins; he will crush the heads in the land of many. He will drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he will lift up his head.

## COMMENTARY

Christ also puts the opening of Psalm 109 to the Pharisees as a question, saying: “If David in the Spirit calls Christ ‘Lord,’ saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,’ then,” he says, “if David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. XXII). This is the objection of one asking a question, not of one denying the truth.

For we believe that he is the Son of God, begotten as God from God before the morning star, and we confess him to be David’s son through his birth from the Virgin Mary. Having ascended into heaven, he sits at the right hand of the Father, from which place he will come as judge. He will have his enemies as a footstool for his feet, as the Apostle also says: “When he has abolished every principality, power, and authority, then he must reign until he places all his enemies under his feet” (1 Cor. XV).

If you ask whose enemies they are, he will answer you: without doubt, they are his whose scepter of power the Lord sent forth from Zion. The scepter of power is the body of the man born from the Virgin. The Lord sent this scepter from Zion so that he might rule in the midst of his enemies. Therefore, as the condemned Photinus believes, he did not take his beginning from Mary’s birth; rather, before the morning star he was brought forth from the Father’s mouth. Through the mystery of bread and wine he became a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, who alone among the priests offered bread and wine when Abraham returned victorious from battle.

Let us now see how kings were shattered at his right hand on the day of his wrath. A thief was fixed beside the Lord, placed on the cross at his right hand; the kings and princes of darkness claimed him for themselves. He shattered these powers on the day of his wrath—the day, certainly, of the wrath of those who were crucifying him.

After shattering these princes, he crushed many heads, so that notorious criminals said: “A murderer has been saved by faith in a single word. Why should we not believe as well?” That one man placed upon the cross converted many of us on earth in great number. Through him who drank from the torrent on the way: he drank the cup of suffering from the torrent of the Jews’ anger. Walking on the undefiled way, while established bodily on earth he crushed the heads of demons.

And he lifted up the head of man, raising it from confusion—certainly from the confusion of the first transgression. And unless the Son of God had drunk on the way, he would not have lifted man’s head, cast down to the earth. Therefore do not say that because he crushed the heads of crimes, Christ himself lifted up his own head. For he did not say, “He lifted up his own head,” but simply said: “Therefore,” he says, because God judged among the nations and filled the ruins of the demons, “where sin abounded, the grace of Christ abounded still more” (Rom. V).

And because he drank the cup of suffering from the torrent of revolt, on that way of which he says, “I am the way” (John XIV), therefore he lifted up the head in the freedom of the wood of the cross, which had been cast down through the transgression of the wood of desire.

Let us therefore give thanks to him, who with the Father is one God with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0497A]

## PSALM 110

Alleluia.

I will confess to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the assembly. Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his desires. Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness endures forever and ever. The merciful and compassionate Lord has made his wonders memorable; he has given food to those who fear him. He will remember his covenant forever; he will proclaim the power of his works to his people, so as to give them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are truth and judgment. All his commandments are faithful, established forever and ever, made in truth and equity. The Lord sent redemption to his people; he commanded his covenant forever. Holy and terrible is his name; the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Good understanding belongs to all who do it; his praise endures forever and ever.

## COMMENTARY

In the council of the saints, Psalm 110 confesses the great works of the Lord: his birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. These are great works of the Lord, great and sought out in all his desires. All his works have indeed been great from the beginning of the world, but these are not only great; they are also sought out in everything that he willed and did from the beginning.

The confession of the Trinity and the magnificence of the Godhead is his work. His righteousness, unchanging, endures throughout the ages of ages. In this righteousness he made his wonders memorable, saying: “Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.” When did the merciful and compassionate Lord say this? Without doubt, when he gave the food of his body to those who fear him.

And the Lord will remember this covenant forever, through which he proclaimed the power of his works to his people; through which he gave them the inheritance of the nations; through which he did not act in appearance—as the accursed Manichaean dreamed—but in truth and in judgment. Whatever commandments of his are read are faithful and holy, confirmed in Christ and enduring forever and ever, because they were made in truth.

They were completed in our Lord Jesus Christ himself and preserved in his equity, when he sent redemption to his people through the apostles, saying: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII). Because all his commandments are faithful, his name is so holy and so terrible in those commandments that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

For whoever is without fear falls into evil, while whoever possesses the fear of God possesses the head of wisdom. Through this fear he will have good understanding, so that his praise may endure forever and ever. Remaining—or rather, persevering—in the fear of God, he will have praise in Christ, and that praise itself endures throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 111

Alleluia of the return of Haggai and Zechariah.

Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments. His offspring will be powerful on the earth; the generation of the upright will be blessed. Glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever. Light has risen in darkness for the upright: the merciful, compassionate, and righteous man. The man who has mercy and lends is gracious; he orders his words with judgment, for he will never be shaken. The righteous man will be in everlasting memory; he will not fear an evil report. His heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is strengthened, and he will not be shaken until he looks down upon his enemies. He has scattered and given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever and ever; his horn will be exalted in glory. The sinner will see and be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners will perish.

## COMMENTARY

When the prophet Ezra, a man of God, was recapitulating the whole Law, he added certain things at God’s command. Hence he also dedicated this title to Haggai and Zechariah.

Let us therefore sing Psalm 111 and give its praise, as though in one perfect man, to all the saints, so that what we say of one may be said of all, and what has been explained individually may be received by universal holiness.

“Blessed is the man who fears the Lord.” He placed the conclusion of the preceding psalm at the beginning of the present one. What he said at the end of that psalm—that the praise of the one who fears the Lord endures forever and ever—he applies here at the beginning to the one who fears the Lord, declaring both the nature and the deeds of his blessedness.

Who, then, is the one who fears the Lord? Without doubt, the one who greatly desires his commandments. His offspring will be powerful in the land—not in rocky ground, nor beside the road, nor among thorns, but in good soil (Matt. XIII). The generation born from that seed is powerful and will always be in blessing.

“Glory and riches are in his house.” Let us hear the Wisdom of God addressing us: “And if riches are loved in this life, what is richer than wisdom, which possesses all things?” Whoever has deserved to have wisdom within the house of his body has glory within. He also has riches—not fleeting riches, not those which the moth destroys or thieves steal, but the riches which he says endure forever and ever. Through them, light will arise in the darkness of this world for the upright in heart. Seeing their works, people will glorify the Father who is in heaven.

Let a man be merciful and compassionate toward his fellow human being, as he wants the Lord to be toward himself. Let him be kind and gracious; let him show mercy and lend; and in judgment let him neither shame the poor man nor favor the powerful. If he does not do this, he will never be shaken.

His memory will be everlasting. When the trumpet begins to sound from heaven, when the fire of Gehenna begins to roar and spew forth flames in crackling globes, he will not fear at all. Why? Because his heart was always ready to hope in the Lord. Therefore, with his heart strengthened, he will not be shaken until he sees his enemies cast into the fire—namely, all unclean spirits, who never cease their hostility as long as we are in this body.

But since, as I said, if this work names one particular blessed man, it will apply to all who perform a similar deed, I shall speak of blessed Lawrence as having both fulfilled and received all these prophecies. For he scattered everything and gave it to the poor; he did not store it up or conceal it, but scattered it and gave it to the poor. Therefore his righteousness is not temporal but endures forever, and his horn—that is, his Christ, who reigns in him—is exalted in glory.

[Note: Blessed Lawrence suffered under Gallienus in the year 261. Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 13.]

This the most bitter king, the sinner, saw. He saw that Lawrence had scattered and given to the poor; he began to gnash his teeth and waste away, but the sinner’s desire perished. The desire of the righteous martyr, however, endures throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 112

Alleluia, alleluia.

Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord. Let the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and forever. From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise. The Lord is exalted above all nations, and his glory is above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly in heaven and on earth? He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to place him with princes, with the princes of his people. He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children.

## COMMENTARY

Come, children; do not wait, do not say: “We are not yet old.” There is an order of being born, but there is no order of dying. Come, therefore, children—not to some labor, but to praise. Praise the Lord, children; praise the name of the Lord in Christ. In him the name of the Lord is blessed from this time forth and forever.

The name of the Lord has become worthy of praise in Christ, not in Judea alone but throughout the whole earth, from the rising of the sun to its setting. Previously there were as many sects as there were nations, and as many gods; but from the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ all these superstitions have been renounced by the nations, and they praise one God and confess him in Christ.

For he is the Lord exalted above all nations. Although his great humility appeared on earth, his glory is great above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly? He does not look upon the earth as though from a roof, but, although he was in the form of God and did not consider equality with God something to be seized, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. II), so that he might raise from the earth the needy one to whom he had said in anger: “You are earth, and you will return to earth.”

He raised this needy man from the earth because he had lost the riches of eternal life and of paradise. In Christ he lifts him from the dungheap and places him with the princes—that is, with the apostles, who are the princes of God’s people. And who is it that placed him there? Without doubt, the one who assumed him: the Son of God, who assumed the Son of Man.

Where did he place him with the princes of the people? Certainly where he made the woman who had been barren dwell in a house—made her herself become the house—and said to her: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. LIV). And he made her a mother rejoicing in her children.

This is the holy Church, in which the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—reigns in the unity of the Godhead, now and always and throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 113

Alleluia, alleluia.

When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judea became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion. The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back. The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep. What ails you, sea, that you fled, and you, Jordan, that you turned back? Mountains, why did you leap like rams, and hills like lambs of sheep? The earth was shaken at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turned the rock into pools of water and the cliff into springs of water.

Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth. Let the nations never say: “Where is their God?” But our God is in heaven; he has done everything that he willed. The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands. They have mouths and do not speak; they have eyes and do not see. They have ears and do not hear; they have nostrils and do not smell. They have hands and do not touch; they have feet and do not walk; they do not cry out with their throat. Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.

The house of Israel has hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. The house of Aaron has hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector. Those who fear the Lord have hoped in the Lord; he is their helper and protector.

The Lord has remembered us and blessed us. He has blessed the house of Israel; he has blessed the house of Aaron. He has blessed all who fear the Lord, small and great. May the Lord add to you—to you and to your children. You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men. The dead will not praise you, O Lord, nor all those who descend into the underworld. But we who live bless the Lord, from this time forth and forever.

## COMMENTARY

Let us see, in Israel’s departure from Egypt, how the house of Jacob went forth from a barbarous people, and how Judea became his sanctuary.

Christ was born in Bethlehem of Judea. He sanctifies those who flee from Pharaoh and, following Moses—that is, the law of God—come to the water. Crossing through it, they go out to a place of rest and silence, which is elsewhere called the desert place. It is deserted, certainly, of the crimes of the world; there they find manna coming from heaven.

When they came to the sea in faith, the sea saw them and fled. It fled so as to provide a passage for those who believed and to prepare destruction for their enemies. Likewise the Jordan turned back behind itself, also in order to prepare a passage for God’s people. For without water neither can the land of Egypt be fled nor the promised land entered. We have explained why the sea fled and why the Jordan turned back.

Now let us see why the mountains leap like rams and the hills like lambs of sheep. Do the mountains, earth, and rocks themselves leap? No, the mountains are the prophets, who see their words fulfilled in Christ and who spoke of the heights of God. The prophets rejoice like rams; they rejoice in everything, seeing the shepherd born who lays down his soul for the sheep (John XI), and thus they rejoice like rams.

The hills, however, rejoice like lambs of sheep. These hills are those who occupy a humble place in knowledge, knowing nothing except perhaps how to sign the forehead or invoke the name of the Lord; thus they rejoice like lambs of sheep. Sheep possess knowledge both of themselves and of their shepherd’s voice; they hear him, recognize him, and follow him wherever he goes. Lambs, however, understand the voices of their sheep because they are still unable to understand the shepherd; nevertheless, through their sheep—that is, their mothers—they too follow the shepherd, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Before his face the earth was shaken when he turned solid rock into pools of water—that is, when he caused rocky hearts to produce waters from their interior, leaping up to eternal life—and when he turned the cliff, that is, the inaccessible rock of the breast of unbelieving nations, into springs of water.

These things happened figuratively, as the history of Exodus relates and this psalm bears witness. But, the Apostle says, these things were written not for their narration but for our edification (2 Cor. XII). In that edification we cry out to the Lord, saying: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.” Not on account of our merits, but because of your mercy, grant that unbelievers may not say: “Where is their God?” Rise from the dead and ascend upward into heaven, for you are the one who reigns in heaven and on earth and performs everything you will.

For the idols of the nations, made from whatever metal, are mute, deaf, and blind; let those who trust in them become like them. But all we of the house of Israel hope in you, O Lord, so that you may deign to be our helper and our protector. You remembered us and, descending from heaven, blessed us.

You blessed the house of Israel by being born from Mary. You blessed the house of Aaron by pouring out the priesthood. You blessed all those who fear the Lord by choosing the apostles, the small together with the great. There were James and John with the great, although they were themselves small.

“May the Lord add to you.” May he add Paul to you, to you and to your children. May he add to you the believing people. “You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” You proclaim the one who made them. “Heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men.” Whatever is heavenly in minds, actions, and thoughts must be attributed to the Lord. Whatever is earthly, as mortal and wretched, must be despised, even if it is without fault. For whatever comes from the earth is mortal; in such things the Lord does not deign to be praised.

Nor does he wish to be praised by those who descend into the underworld—that is, those who dwell in the lower actions of life—but by those who live in him who says: “I am life.” We bless the Lord, provided that we live by withdrawing from every mortal work. We bless the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 114

Alleluia.

I have loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer. Because he has inclined his ear to me, I will call upon him throughout my days. The pains of death surrounded me, and the dangers of the underworld found me. I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord. O Lord, deliver my soul. The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God has mercy. The Lord guards the little ones. I was humbled, and he delivered me. Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt kindly with you. For he has rescued my soul from death, my heart from evil affections, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. I will please the Lord in the land of the living.

## COMMENTARY

The psalmist explains the reasons for his love of the Lord in this song: “I have loved the Lord,” he says, “because when the pains of death surrounded me, and the suggestions of demons besieged me, I went toward tribulation, sought it, found it, and thus called upon the name of the Lord.”

For some reason, I do not know how, when we find joy we invoke the name of the Lord only with the tips of our lips. But when we either stir up tribulation for ourselves through abstinence and repentance or encounter it by some accident, such a cry is forced from our hearts that it reaches the very ears of the exalted God.

Yet let us see what he did in order to deserve the Lord’s deliverance. We who wish to be delivered need to know what the one who announces his deliverance did. Tell us, what did you do so that the Lord might deliver you?

“I was humbled,” he says, “and he delivered me.” This statement agrees with the Gospels. In the Gospels, the teacher and Lord of this deliverance says that everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled (Matt. XXIII). Humility must be held fast; from it eternal deliverance and exaltation are obtained.

Through humility the soul is rescued from death, and the eyes are freed from tears—that is, they admit nothing for which they must repent. The feet too are freed from falling. The humble stand firm in their purpose of holiness. In order to please the Lord in the land of the living, they persevere in standing in the land of mortals, so that they may pass from death to life through our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0502D] who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 115

Alleluia.

I believed; therefore I spoke, but I was greatly humbled. I said in my alarm: “Every man is a liar.” What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord before all his people. Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints. O Lord, for I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid. You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise and call upon the name of the Lord. I will fulfill my vows to the Lord in the sight of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord, in your midst, Jerusalem.

## COMMENTARY

Before saying what he spoke, he sets forth his faith: “I believed,” he says. What did you believe? That he was born and suffered. And because I believed, therefore I was greatly humbled.

When I believed, I said this: If the Lord of all emptied himself and took the form of a servant for me, wretched as I am, what shall I do? What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? However much a man may say that he serves in return for his benefits, every man is a liar. What worthy thing will a man render to the Lord, unless perhaps he compensates suffering with suffering?

“I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” For precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints—provided that in death itself he shows himself to be a servant of God and the son of his handmaid. God’s handmaid is holy discipline.

Whoever at the end of his bodily life truthfully says to the Lord, “O Lord, I am your servant”—that is, “I have not despised you”—and, “I am the son of your handmaid”—that is, “I have obeyed your discipline as a son”—the Lord will break the bonds with which he is entangled by the devil. He will sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, so that he may fulfill his vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people—that is, in the sight of those who are God’s people, not the people of this world.

He will not appear before human beings for the destruction of his holy labor, but before the saints who glory in your midst, Jerusalem, in which Christ is emperor, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 116

Alleluia, alleluia.

Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. For his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.

## COMMENTARY

“Praise the Lord, all nations.” The Jews are excluded—the Jews who took away the key of the kingdom of heaven, neither entering themselves nor allowing you to enter. “All,” praise the Lord, who, without respect of persons, wishes all people to be saved (1 Tim. II).

“All nations, praise him, because his mercy has been confirmed over us.” For he excluded our merits and brought his mercy upon us, confirming it over us through the forgiveness of all sins, promised to those who believe and repent.

The Lord’s truth itself remains forever. In this the confirmation of his mercy and goodness is shown: when we correct our sin, pardon and forgiveness accompany us. And our ceasing from sin is God’s act of forgiveness. To him be glory throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

## PSALM 117

Alleluia, alleluia.

Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever. Let Israel now say: “He is good, for his mercy endures forever.” Let the house of Aaron now say: “He is good, for his mercy endures forever.” Let those who fear the Lord now say: “His mercy endures forever.” From tribulation I called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered me in spaciousness. The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man can do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon my enemies. It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes. All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them. Surrounding me, they surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them. They surrounded me like bees and blazed like fire among thorns, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them. I was thrust down and overturned so that I might fall, but the Lord upheld me. My strength and my praise is the Lord, and he has become my salvation. The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous. The right hand of the Lord has shown strength; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me; the right hand of the Lord has shown strength. I shall not die, but live, and I shall recount the works of the Lord. The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death. Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering them, I shall confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it. I shall confess to you, for you answered me and became my salvation. The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This has come from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes. This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it. O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper me well and happily. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord. God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. Establish the solemn day amid the dense foliage, up to the horns of the altar. You are my God, and I shall confess to you; you are my God, and I shall exalt you. I shall confess to you, for you answered me and became my salvation. Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.

## Commentary

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.” Although his mercy reigns forever, nevertheless confession can benefit sinners in this present age. After this age, confession will have no power at all to obtain forgiveness. Therefore, while there is time to confess to the Lord, let us confess. For his mercy is most ready in this present age.

If you wish to learn that this is so, both the house of Israel and the house of Aaron can teach you. Throughout all the Scriptures of the Old Testament you read that whenever the people turned to confession and repented, they obtained mercy. If you seem incapable of learning this by reading, seek out those who fear the Lord, and they themselves will show you how his mercy is prepared for those who confess. I too, in my tribulation, confessed and called upon the Lord, and he answered me in spaciousness.

But because we ourselves are also our own enemies whenever we desire something contrary to our salvation, while outside us we likewise have other enemies, visible and invisible, let us pray that the Lord may deign to be our helper against the hostilities we have mentioned. Then, at last, we shall not fear our enemies.

For it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. Christian, recognize the trust you ought to hold. Do not trust in yourself; do not say that you possess free will in such a way that you can trust yourself in yourself. You do indeed possess free will, but do not presume upon it; presume upon God, because he cannot be conquered, whereas free will can be conquered.

“It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man or in princes.” For if you trust in the Lord, then you can say: “All the nations surrounded me, and in the name of the Lord I took vengeance on them.” The freedom of the will cannot say this—or, if it does say it, I shall openly prove it to be lying. Or let it show me, from the beginning of the world, anyone who escaped visible or invisible enemies without God’s help.

Consider also what happens to those who are placed under attack yet receive help: “I was thrust down,” he says, “I was overturned so that I might fall, and the Lord upheld me.” Let him add, if he can: “My strength and my praise is free will, and it itself became my salvation.” If it cannot say this—or rather, because it cannot say this justly—let it say that it is upheld by the Lord and ascribe all its strength to divine assistance.

For it was his right hand that showed strength, if we possess any strength within us. His right hand exalts us from the lowest underworld. He himself makes us live and not die, so that we may recount his works. He chastises and chastises us in mercy, and he will not hand us over to death.

Perhaps now someone who teaches predestination and weakens human choice will hear me and think that I exclude free will in such a way that I consider sinners to sin because God rejects them. The fact that we sin will be shown to belong to our choice; the fact that we despise grace will also be shown to belong to us. Consider how great is the freedom of your will: a servant may deny the Lord, so that a human being says to God, “I do not wish to believe you,” and makes for himself a temple in which to worship an idol, or a synagogue in which to deny his Savior.

What evil do we therefore do? Through our freedom we incur it, because the just Lord does not approve compelled service. But if we do something good, let us attribute it to the giver, who grants every good thing to those who flee to him, according to what he himself deigned to promise: “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Luke 11).

Let us therefore knock, and with the prophet in this psalm let us sing: “Open for me the gates of righteousness, and entering them I shall confess to the Lord.” We cry out these words with divine supports and aids; from them we seem to hear their answering voice: “This gate at which you knock has not been granted to man by free will, but has been established in the Lord’s help, and only the righteous shall enter through it.”

Let us therefore confess to the Lord, because he himself answers us, and he himself becomes our salvation.

Let us now come to the stone which the builders rejected. This stone is read of in Daniel as cut out without hands (Daniel 2), that is, born of the Virgin without the work of a man. The builders were the Jews alone throughout the whole face of the earth. For all the nations remained in the destruction of idols, while the Jews alone, under the almighty and true God, cultivated the building of the law and the prophecy. Through Moses, from the beginning of the world, God made known to them what he had done concerning the human race and what human beings had done concerning God. He also made known that in the last times he would raise up for them from the thigh of Judah the king Christ, of whom Moses himself would say: “You shall hear him as you hear me in all things”; of whom God the Father swore to David, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I shall place one upon your throne” (Psalm 31); concerning whom he swore to Abraham: “In your seed I shall inherit all the nations” (Genesis 22); and concerning whom God said through Isaiah that a Virgin would conceive in the womb and bear Emmanuel (Isaiah 7).

You will find many such things in the ancient books, and the Jews, reading them for the building up of the people, were called builders. While building, they came to the cornerstone, which would embrace two walls and establish two in itself (Ephesians 2). But because they wished to stand in one wall, they rejected the stone that was suited not for one but for two.

Seeing the unjust rejection by human beings, God himself ordained what he had approved, despite their unwillingness, and himself placed this stone at the head of the corner, so that from the two Testaments and the two peoples a building might arise. The unbelievers abandoned it and were abandoned by God. But believers build upon this foundation, which, having been placed at the head of the corner from the angular stone, binds and contains both sides.

Having this marvelous stone before their eyes, they confess that this is the day which night does not follow, which the hours do not divide, and which no shadow obstructs. Let us therefore rejoice and be glad in it, because it has shone forth from the true light in order to drive away our darkness. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Luke 13). God the Lord has blessed us in the house of the Lord, and he has shone upon us.

Let us therefore establish the Lord’s day amid the assemblies, up to the horns of the altar. On that day let us say to God: “You are my God, and I shall confess to you; you are my God, and I shall exalt you.” I shall confess, groaning over my sins; I shall rejoice, glad in your forgiveness.

Thus the text continues: “I shall confess, because you answered me and became my salvation.” And, as though encouraging his companions so that, just as forgiveness had been granted to him when he confessed, it might also be granted to them when they confessed, he says: “You too, confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever”—he who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0506D]

# PSALM CXVIII (verses 1–48)

## Alleluia

Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who examine his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart. For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways. You commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly well. Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances. Then I shall not be put to shame when I have looked upon all your commandments. I shall confess to you with an upright heart, in that I have learned the judgments of your righteousness. I shall keep your ordinances; do not utterly abandon me.

How does a young man correct his way? By keeping your words. With my whole heart I have sought you; do not drive me away from your commandments. In my heart I have hidden your utterances, so that I may not sin against you. Blessed are you, Lord; teach me your ordinances. With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth. I have delighted in the way of your testimonies as in all riches. I shall exercise myself in your commandments, and I shall consider your ways. I shall meditate on your ordinances; I shall not forget your words.

Repay your servant; give me life, and I shall keep your words. Reveal my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law. I am a sojourner on the earth; do not hide your commandments from me. My soul has desired to long for your ordinances at all times. You rebuked the proud; cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments. Take away reproach and contempt from me, because I have sought your testimonies. For princes sat and spoke against me, but your servant was exercising himself in your ordinances. For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsel.

My soul clung to the pavement; give me life according to your word. I declared my ways, and you answered me; teach me your ordinances. Make me understand the way of your ordinances, and I shall exercise myself in your wonders. My soul became drowsy from weariness; strengthen me in your words. Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law. I have chosen the way of truth; I have not forgotten your judgments. I have clung to your testimonies, Lord; do not put me to shame. I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.

Set before me, Lord, the law—the way of your ordinances—and I shall always seek it. Give me understanding, and I shall examine your law and keep it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it. Incline my heart toward your testimonies and not toward greed. Turn my eyes away, so that they may not see vanity; give me life in your way. Establish your utterance for your servant in your fear. Cut off my reproach, which I have suspected, because your judgments are delightful. Behold, I have desired your commandments; give me life in your righteousness.

Let your mercy come upon me, Lord, your salvation according to your word. Then I shall answer the one who reproaches me with a word, because I have hoped in your words. Do not utterly take the word of truth from my mouth, for I have hoped exceedingly in your judgments. I shall keep your law always, forever and ever. I walked in spaciousness, because I sought your commandments. I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame. I meditated on your commandments, which I loved. I lifted my hands toward your commandments, which I loved, and I exercised myself in your ordinances.

## Commentary

“Alleluia” begins with the alphabet. The alphabet is God’s instruction in the Alleluia and the teaching that is to be handed on to human beings. Let us therefore call blessed and undefiled the disciples of Christ, who are still in the way, which is Christ. For the one who said that he was the way himself also said to them: “Remain in me, as I also remain in you” (John 15).

Therefore these blessed ones remain, because they are the undefiled apostles, since they obey in all things; they are in the way because they are in Christ. They will walk because their holy teaching, which is in the law of the Lord, walks throughout the whole world.

The first degree of blessedness was completed in the apostles; the second has been reserved for us. For just as in the first psalm, “Blessed is the one who will meditate on the law of the Lord day and night,” he did not wish the reader to be negligent. For if someone reads without knowing what he is reading, he will be negligent. God wishes all the mysteries of his writings to be known. Just as, if you seek something that is not written, you stumble upon it, so, if you do not inquire into what is written, you will be accused.

You cannot be perfect in blessedness unless you have examined his testimonies and sought him with your whole heart [the printed text has *exquirunt*; read *exquiras*, “you seek”]. Those engaged in military service, business, and earthly concerns cannot occupy themselves with these studies; they have no leisure for them. They guard the world and perform all its functions.

What do you do, Christian? If you serve a human master, examine his law, because if, in ignorance, you incur something unlawful, you will die; for no one is permitted not to know the law. Are you a merchant? Inquire into the established prices, because if, through ignorance, you incur something unlawful, you will not escape. Are you Christ’s servant? Examine his testimonies.

If you have no time for them, you who profess to be a cleric or a religious person—if perhaps you do not wish to make time even there—let God answer to whom he ought to entrust his law.

I know that many say at this point: “Then simple people will not see the kingdom of God, since they cannot examine these matters.” Listen, beloved: God will ask no one for what he cannot do. A mute will not be condemned for silence, nor will a sick person be blamed for labor. The will alone is sufficient for God. Where ability is lacking, that same will makes a person guilty or holy, according to what he truly wished and truly could not do.

Thus we have freed you from the hook of the objection and have in some measure rescued you from the case of simple people. Now I shall discuss the matters I mentioned, since you know how to examine things, since you know the varieties of clothing, the varieties of wine, the varieties of food, and the varieties of silver. Even if you do not possess these things, you nevertheless know them, and you examine both what deception they contain and what truth they possess.

You do not wish to be unaware of what your neighbors are doing; you ask what strangers are saying, what the judge of the city thinks, what the emperor has newly decreed, what the people of the East are doing, what those of the West are doing, and what peasants are seeking throughout all the countryside [the printed passive *quaerantur* is uncertain; perhaps read *querantur*]. You examine these and many similar matters. Then you come to God’s commandments, withdraw yourself, and say: “Nothing is better than to live simply.”

Does someone live simply through a cunning conceived from contempt? And who keeps the commands of his Lord, which he cannot keep unless he has first learned them? The Holy Spirit says through the prophet: “Unless someone has learned righteousness upon the earth, he will not practice truth.”

Just as doing God’s will is greater than knowing it, so knowing it comes before doing it. In this order, the one rightly precedes the other. It can happen that someone offends while wishing to obey because he has not first learned how he ought to obey.

Therefore, when we desire and say, “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping God’s ordinances,” we shall not be put to shame when we look toward all his commandments, provided that we confess to the Lord with an upright heart, in that we have learned the judgments of his righteousness. For only as much is required as we understand—not as much as we do not understand; indeed, as much as we are able to understand, not as much as we are unable to understand.

But because, he says, you wish your commandments to be kept exceedingly well, “do not utterly abandon me.” For there is no other way in which I can correct the ways of my youth except by keeping your words.

Let us now consider the prayer. The one who prays does not lie to God in the words of his prayer: “With my whole heart,” he says, “I have sought you.” If you speak truly, he will not drive you away from his commandments.

“In my heart,” he says, “I have hidden your utterance, so that I may not sin against you.” I did not therefore labor to attain knowledge and retain God’s precepts by heart so that I might appear clever and, puffed up by knowledge, become fit for rebuke because of pride. I did so in order not to sin against you.

“Teach me, therefore, Lord,” he says, “your ordinances.” The one whom you pray to, asking him to teach you his righteousness, will answer you: “This is my righteousness: that whatever you wish a human being to do for you, you do the same for that human being.”

If you embrace God’s righteousness, you will say: “With my lips I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth, and in them I have delighted as in all riches.”

Let us now see what follows: “I shall exercise myself in your commandments.” Just as military training exercises the body, so divine precepts train the soul. For they teach it how to receive blows cautiously and how to return them courageously.

“And I shall consider your ways,” he says—that is, I shall attend to how you conquered, and I shall imitate those examples. For the one who taught us says: “Be imitators of me, as I am also of the master [Christ].”

“I shall not forget your words.” You see that forgetfulness is a defect, not a matter of nature.

“Repay,” he says, “your servant.” What do you wish to be repaid? “The affection of love,” he says, “so that I may live.” And if I give you life, what will you do? Perhaps he said: “I shall live, feast, rejoice, build, cultivate fields, plead cases, and perform the other things that perish with time.” He did not say this. What does he say? “I shall live and keep your words.”

But because I perceive treasures hidden among your letters, which I cannot find, “you, Lord, reveal my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law.”

It must carefully be understood what he adds: “I am a sojourner,” that is, a pilgrim, “with you on the earth.” In other words, I seek nothing earthly; do not hide from me what I seek. “Do not hide your commandments from me.”

For my soul desires nothing except to long for your ordinances. And because I know that you rebuke the proud, “take away reproach from me.” The proud are those who despise the Lord when he commands, and cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments.

He says “your” commandments because, while we act devoutly, the princes of the air devise our overthrow. Therefore he adds: “Those princes,” he says, “spoke against me. But I, your servant, exercised myself in your ordinances.” For your testimonies are also my meditation, and your ordinances are my counsel.

Let us see what counsel you followed in the Lord’s ordinances. “My soul,” he says, “clung to the pavement”—that is, I lay upon the pavement, entreating and imploring you, Lord: “Give me life according to your word.”

For what did God promise? “God promised,” he says, saying: “Because he hoped in me, I shall deliver him” (Psalm 90). Behold, because I hoped in you, I have already clung to the pavement. You who raise the needy from the earth, give me life according to your word.

“I declared your ways, and you answered me.” Consider what he says he did in order to be answered. What is “I declared your ways”? It means: wherever I had the ability to speak, I showed them the paths along which footsteps proceeded. For through them one escapes death and arrives at life.

Therefore, when I declared your ways, then you answered me. Christian, you have learned the art of being answered. If you wish to be answered, proclaim God’s ways: teach chastity, humility, contempt for the world, and whatever you ask will be granted to you.

And when you ask the Lord to teach you, and ask what you should teach your fellow servant, say: “Because I wish to declare your ways so that you may answer me, make me understand the way of your ordinances, and I shall exercise myself in your wonders.”

To exercise oneself is to reason subtly. “I shall be keen-witted,” he says, “not sluggish.”

What are you promising so greatly? Behold, one temptation arises, and you are shaken, so that you say: “My soul has become drowsy from weariness.” Sleeping belongs to the body, not to the soul. How great a sleep has overtaken your body, that it compels even your soul to grow drowsy!

But he says: “These things happened to me because I presumed upon myself. Awaken me, Lord, because I am asleep.” You awaken me if you strengthen me in your words. You strengthen me in your words if you remove from me the way of iniquity—that is, the tempter himself.

For unless you drive him far from me, I shall remain in the sleep of the soul and in the weariness of my mind. Therefore remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me in your way.

It is mine to choose the way of truth; it is yours to grant the accomplishment of this choice. And because I have clung to your testimonies, believing that everyone who asks receives, I ask, Lord: do not put me to shame.

Naturally, shame arises when what is requested is denied, especially by one who proclaims that he will deny nothing to the one who asks. Therefore he too, desiring to be freed from this shame, cries out: “Lord, do not put me to shame.”

But let us see what you ask. Why do you run in the way of the commandments? Why do you ask for understanding so that you may examine God’s law? Why do you seek a guide for God’s way? Explain what you ask.

“Incline,” he says, “my heart toward your testimonies and not toward greed.” Therefore your soul was growing drowsy from weariness because you were thinking about greed, attending to the things that are seen and that consist in vanity: while they are thought to be held, they flee away.

Pray, therefore, that he turn your eyes away, so that they may not see this vanity, whether in the ambitions of the world or in the desires of the flesh. And say to the Lord that he establish his utterance for his servant in his fear and cut off the reproach that you feared.

For what had you supposed when you grew drowsy from weariness? You said: “What shall I eat? What shall I drink? What shall I wear?” But when the Lord inclined your heart toward his testimonies, he freed you from greed, and you began to seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, believing that all these things would be added to you.

Now, therefore, you ask that the reproach of this fear be cut off from you. For it is a reproach to believe that a human being is concerned about his servant while God neglects the one serving him.

“I sinned, Lord, because I supposed this; pardon me, because your judgments are delightful.” Behold, I believe; behold, I desire nothing except your commandments. Make your mercy come upon me, if your salvation comes upon me, according to your utterance, which you promised: “Seek the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke 12).

When, therefore, you complete your salvation according to your utterance, I shall answer the one who reproaches me with a word, because I hope in your words. Do not therefore utterly take the word of truth from my mouth.

Behold, they are placing strong denials against God. Does God therefore take the word of truth from anyone’s mouth? The devil does this: he removes truth and sends falsehood.

“Show me, therefore, what I should say to God.” “I wish,” he says, “to answer the one who reproaches me with a word, because, hoping in God’s words, I have thought nothing about the belly but about the mind, nothing about earth but about heaven.”

When I said, “God prepares everything for his servants,” those unbelievers—or the unclean spirits—were turning the truth of this proclamation into falsehood. Therefore, Lord, when you fulfill what I promised about you while I believed, I shall answer the one who reproaches me with a word, and the word of truth has not been removed from my mouth forever, because I did well to hope in your words.

I shall not guard my coins, my riches, or empty glory, but I shall always keep your law forever.

We have now heard what he means when he says that he walked in spaciousness because he sought God’s commandments, although spaciousness leads to death. This spaciousness is not understood in that way. Do you wish to know how a person walks in spaciousness? By seeking God’s commandments.

The one whom the affections of the flesh do not bind walks in spaciousness; the one whom the burden of possessions does not constrict moves freely. He speaks of God’s testimonies even in the presence of kings, and no one says to him in confusion: “You possess things—why do you preach contempt for the world?”

There is no trembling, because he expects neither glory nor wealth from the world, but raises his hands to God alone, whom alone he loves, and exercises himself in his ordinances—the God who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# PSALM CXVIII (verses 49–80)

Remember your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope. This has comforted me in my humiliation, because your utterance will give me life. The proud acted wickedly to the utmost, but I did not turn aside from your law. I remembered your judgments from of old, Lord, and I was comforted. Faintness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law. Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage. At night I remembered your name, Lord, and I kept your law. This happened to me because I sought your ordinances.

My portion, Lord, I said, is to keep your law. With my whole heart I pleaded before your face; have mercy on me according to your utterance. I considered my ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies. I am prepared and am not troubled, so that I may keep your commandments. The cords of sinners entangled me, but I did not forget your law. At midnight I arose to confess to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness. I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments. Your mercy, Lord, fills the earth; teach me your ordinances.

[Col. 0512A]

You have dealt well with your servant, Lord, according to your word. Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge, because I have believed your commandments. Before I was humbled, I sinned; therefore I kept your utterance. You are good, and in your goodness teach me your ordinances. The iniquity of the proud has multiplied against me, but I shall examine your commandments with my whole heart. Their heart has thickened like milk, but I have meditated on your law. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your ordinances. The law of your mouth is good for me, better than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.

Your hands made me and fashioned me; give me understanding, so that I may learn your commandments. Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped exceedingly in your words. I know, Lord, that your judgments are righteous, and in your truth you have humbled me. Let your mercy come, so that it may comfort me, according to your utterance to your servant. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation. Let the proud be put to shame, because they unjustly committed iniquity against me; but I shall exercise myself in your commandments. Let those who fear you and those who know your testimonies turn toward me. Let my heart be undefiled in your ordinances, so that I may not be put to shame.

## Commentary

Up to this point there is one continuous sense. The text of the one praying now begins differently, saying: “Remember, Lord, your word to your servant, in which you gave me hope.”

In this prayer he was lamenting the whole human race. The whole human race had perished through Adam’s transgression, and it had been promised that the Word of God would come in the flesh and, through him, restore our race to something better.

Therefore the cry is made: “Remember your word to your servant,” that is, to the human race, “in which you gave me hope.” This hope comforted me in my humiliation, while the proud acted wickedly to the utmost—that is, while the unclean spirits acted so arrogantly that they built high capitols and temples for themselves.

I remembered your judgments, because you promised that your Word would come for their destruction. I remembered this and was comforted. Yet in the present, faintness of spirit held me because of sinners abandoning your law and going over to the law of demons, which was practiced in the temples.

Nevertheless, your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage, where I was shown to be a foreigner. Indeed, take a Christian suddenly and place him among Jews or Gentiles: does he not appear to be a foreigner, even if he remains in his own city?

“There,” he says, “your ordinances were songs to me, and I did not remain silent before those acting unjustly.” At night I remembered your name, Lord—that is, placed amid the dark councils of human beings, I remembered your name—and I kept your law. The examples of the many did not draw me back from the straight course.

This alone became my portion, because I sought your ordinances while learning to keep your law. This alone became my portion. For while they divided fields, houses, vineyards, and the various glories of the world among themselves, they left me unarmed and outside their fellowship, saying: “If you cannot live on bread but on the word of God, let this alone be your portion.”

And I said to you: “Lord, have mercy on me according to your utterance. You promised that we should seek none of these things. Let my sins not obstruct your promise to me, because I considered your ways and turned my feet toward your testimonies.”

Now I am prepared and am not troubled. Let nothing trouble me: there is no wheat in the granary, no oil in the vessel, no coin in the purse, no garment in the storerooms. I am unburdened; I am prepared; and in this poverty I am not troubled.

And what are you prepared for? “To keep your commandments,” he says. And although the sinner stretches out a cord amid the darkness, even though I was surrounded by the cords of sinners and placed amid the deepest darkness, I arose to confess to you, proceeding according to the judgments of your righteousness.

For I desired to become a companion of those who fear you and keep your commandments. I nevertheless considered my sins, but I thought more fully about your mercy and said: “Your mercy fills the earth.”

What does “the mercy of God fills the earth” mean? It is medicine for the soul. But when medicine is applied to wounds, unless it fills them, the wounds are not healed. Therefore the earth is our body, which, contracting spiritual wounds through all its members, needed a Savior, whose mercy would fill the earth and who would teach his ordinances to those he had saved.

Thus the text continues: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.” “Because I believed your commandments,” he says, “I who sinned before I humbled myself before you.”

But now, because your mercy fills the earth, therefore I have kept your utterances. And although the iniquity of the proud is multiplied against me—that is, although the suggestions of demons are multiplied against me—I nevertheless shall examine your law with my whole heart.

And although their heart becomes thick like milk, I have nevertheless meditated on your law. It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments.

Bodily affliction is not to be counted among miseries if it comes upon us even against our will. See what he said: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments.”

Let others possess things and glory in their wealth; for me the law of your mouth is better than thousands of pieces of gold and silver.

For your hands made me. Remember this: although you made everything by your word, your hands fashioned me according to your likeness. Therefore give me understanding, and I shall learn your commandments.

Those who fear you will see me, desiring and longing for these things, and rejoice, because I have hoped in your words. In them I have learned that your judgments are righteous.

“And in truth you humbled me”—that is, there was a true reason why you humbled me. For you rebuked me because of iniquity.

Now let your mercy come, so that it may comfort me, according to your utterance to your servant. Let your mercies come to me, and I shall live, because your law is my meditation.

We must carefully guard and foresee this: whenever God’s law is our meditation, then the proud work iniquities against us. For the more humbly we wish to act before God, the more wickedly the proud behave toward us.

“Let the proud be put to shame,” he says, “because they unjustly committed iniquity against me.” But I did not withdraw from patience; rather, continuing what I had begun, I examined your law with my whole heart.

But since we must pray that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life (1 Timothy 2), let these people be turned away from me. Let those who fear you and those who know your testimonies turn toward me, because through the companionship of the good our heart becomes pure in the Lord’s ordinances, so that we may not be put to shame.

This is granted by him alone, who is at the right hand of the Father and intercedes for us; to him be glory together with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Godhead, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM CXVIII (verses 81–176)

My soul has failed in longing for your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word. My eyes have failed in longing for your utterance, saying, “When will you comfort me?” For I have become like a wineskin in the frost; yet I have not forgotten your statutes. How many are the days of your servant? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute me? The wicked have told me tales, but not according to your law. All your commandments are truth; the wicked have persecuted me—help me. They almost destroyed me on the earth, but I did not abandon your commandments. According to your mercy, give me life, and I will keep the testimonies of your mouth.

Your word, O Lord, remains forever in heaven. Your truth is from generation to generation; you founded the earth, and it remains. By your ordinance the days continue, for all things serve you. If your law had not been my meditation, I might perhaps have perished in my humiliation. I will never forget your statutes, because through them you have given me life. I am yours; save me, for I have sought your statutes. Sinners have waited for me in order to destroy me; I have understood your testimonies. I have seen the end of every consummation; your commandment is exceedingly broad.

How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all day long. Through your commandment you have made me wiser than my enemies, for it is mine forever. I have understood more than all who teach me, because your testimonies are my meditation. I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your commandments. I have restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your words. I have not turned aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me. How sweet your utterances are to my throat—sweeter than honey to my mouth. From your commandments I have gained understanding; therefore I have hated every way of iniquity.

[Col. 0514D]

Your word is a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths. I have sworn and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice. I have been humbled exceedingly, O Lord; give me life according to your word. Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord, and teach me your judgments. My soul is always in my hands, and I have not forgotten your law. Sinners have set a snare for me, but I have not strayed from your commandments. I have acquired your testimonies as an inheritance forever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart. I have inclined my heart to perform your statutes forever, because of the recompense.

I have hated the wicked, but I have loved your law. You are my helper and protector, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word. Depart from me, evildoers, and I will scrutinize the commandments of my God. Receive me according to your utterance, and I shall live; do not put me to shame in my hope. Help me, and I shall be saved, and I will meditate continually on your statutes. You have despised all who depart from your judgments, for their thought is unjust. I have regarded all sinners of the earth as transgressors; therefore I have loved your testimonies. Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments.

I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me. Receive your servant for good; let the proud not slander me. My eyes have failed in longing for your salvation and for the utterance of your justice. Deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, so that I may know your testimonies. It is time to act, O Lord; they have destroyed your law. Therefore I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz. Therefore I was directed toward all your commandments; I hated every crooked way.

Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul has scrutinized them. The unfolding of your words gives light and grants understanding to the simple. I opened my mouth and drew in breath, because I desired your commandments. Look upon me and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name. Direct my steps according to your utterance, and let no injustice rule over me. Redeem me from the slanders of men, so that I may keep your commandments. Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes. Streams of water have run down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.

You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright. You commanded justice—your testimonies—and your truth exceedingly. My zeal has consumed me, because my enemies have forgotten your words. Your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire, and your servant has loved it. I am young and despised; I have not forgotten your statutes. Your justice is justice forever, and your law is truth. Tribulation and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation. The justice of your testimonies is eternal; give me understanding, and I shall live.

I cried out with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord. I will seek your statutes. I cried out to you; save me, so that I may keep your commandments. I anticipated the dawn and cried out, because I placed my hope in your words. My eyes anticipated the dawn, turning toward you, so that I might meditate on your utterances. Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Lord, and according to your judgment give me life. Those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity; they have gone far from your law. You are near, O Lord, and all your ways are truth. From the beginning I understood from your testimonies that you founded them forever.

See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law. Judge my judgment and redeem me; for the sake of your utterance give me life. Salvation is far from sinners, because they have not sought your statutes. Your mercies are many, O Lord; according to your judgment give me life. Many are those who persecute and afflict me, but I have not turned aside from your testimonies. I saw transgressors and wasted away, because they did not keep your utterances. See that I have loved your commandments, O Lord; in your mercy give me life. The beginning of your words is truth; all the judgments of your justice are forever.

Princes have persecuted me without cause, but my heart has feared your words. I will rejoice over your utterances like one who finds abundant spoils. I have hated and abhorred iniquity, but I have loved your law. Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your justice.
