Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling block for them. I awaited your salvation, O Lord, and I loved your commandments. My soul kept your testimonies and loved them exceedingly. I kept your commandments and your testimonies, for all my ways are before you.

Let my prayer draw near in your sight, O Lord; according to your utterance give me understanding. Let my petition enter your sight; according to your utterance rescue me. My lips will pour forth a hymn when you teach me your statutes. My tongue will proclaim your utterance, because all your commandments are justice. Let your hand come to save me, for I have chosen your commandments. I longed for your salvation, O Lord, and your law is my meditation. My soul shall live and praise you, and your judgments shall help me. I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.

## Commentary

One and the same sense has run up to this verse; now another begins, descending from that preceding course. Thus the whole human race began in this sense by saying: “He remembers your word, in which you gave me hope of recovery.” This hope consoled me when the proud acted wickedly against me. Now, complaining that he has again reached this same failure of expectation, he cries out once more: “My soul,” he says, “has failed in longing for your salvation, and I placed my hope in your word. My eyes have failed in longing for your utterance, saying: ‘When will you come? When will you restore me? When will you comfort me?’ For through Adam’s transgression I have become like a wineskin in the frost, empty within but contracted on the outside; nevertheless, I have not forgotten your statutes.”

But because human life on earth is short, how many days remain for the world, your servant, before it comes to an end? When will you execute judgment on those who persecute it? For the idolaters tell tales, but not according to your law; wicked demons persecute it. Help it, O Lord. Behold, the end of the world is near, and in a little while the world itself will be brought to completion on earth. Come, O Lord, for I—the chorus of all the saints—who suffer over these things, have not abandoned your commandments, so that I may live according to your mercy and keep the testimonies of your mouth. You promised that, as we were perishing, you would send us a Savior.

For I am certain that your word will remain forever in heaven. Although it may be seen among human beings, as you promised, it never departs from heaven. Just as a river, when it enters the sea and encircles the lands, is never absent from the bosom of its source, so undoubtedly your word, when it has come to us, never departs from your bosom, holy Father. Why do you delay sending him who, coming here to earth, never departs from heaven? Let the promise come by which we may be freed—the promise that cannot lie.

[Col. 0517A]

For your truth is from age to age. You founded the earth, and it remains; yet the human being for whom you founded the earth does not remain. Behold, by your ordinance the days continue, yet the human being for whom you made the days does not continue. All things continue because all things serve you; the human being does not continue because he does not serve you as all things do. As soon as he withdrew from your service, when, through transgression, he fell from the height of a good conscience and was humbled, he was destined to perish in that very humiliation. He was destined to perish in that humiliation because perseverance was granted to these things, since by obedience (obtemperando; the sense is difficult in context) the security of life withdrew from him; and he was so humbled that he thought he would perish in his humiliation and that the human race would no longer have stability.

In this person’s present abasement it is said to God: “I am yours; save me.”

[Col. 0517B]

Let the one who saves him come, because unclean spirits await his destruction in the persistence of idolatry. While the Savior delays, let the consummation of the age come. But while they wait for the world to perish, I—that is, the chorus of the prophets—have understood your testimonies. I have seen the end of every most wicked consummation, but your commandment is exceedingly broad.

Broad, because it occupies all the spaces of the earth, encompasses the boundaries of body and soul, leads the one who obeys it upward to the heavens, and casts down into hell the one who despises it. Its rule is exceedingly broad, since it commands both the powerful and kings and all nations. “This commandment,” says the chorus of the saints, as I have said, “I did not fear, but loved.” For “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4), and, he says, “I loved it” so that it was my meditation all day long.

[Col. 0517C]

Let us now see what he reports to have happened to him through love of the commandment: “Through your commandment,” he says, “you have made me wiser than my enemies, for it is mine forever.” Here he has mentioned both invisible and visible enemies. “I have understood more than all who teach me, because I have sought your commandments.” Note carefully, most learned reader, that although he was wiser than his teachers, he assumed the role of a disciple. “I have also understood more than the elders, because I have not forgotten your law.”

Let no one suppose that forgetfulness is a matter of nature when it arises from the fault of negligence. Therefore, he says, because I have not forgotten your law, I restrained my feet from every evil way, so that I might keep your commandments—that is, I withdrew from evil and thus approached the keeping of your commandments. And when I had approached, I did not turn aside from your judgments, because you established your law for me, which, as I turn it over in my mouth, I find sweeter than honey.

[Col. 0517D]

And understanding how many good things come to me through love of your law, I began to hate every way of iniquity. Just as a lamp in the darkness shows a person’s feet the pits and obstacles that must be avoided, so your word is a lamp for the steps, or feet, of my heart; it is a lamp for my feet and, correspondingly, for my perceptions.

Thus, seeing that through it I had escaped the darkness of the devil and found shining paths, I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your justice. What does “I swore” mean? I established a law, or set down a rule, in which I resolved to keep the judgments of God’s justice. For this reason I was humbled exceedingly. I was so humbled that I was not permitted even to harm a contemptuous servant who injured me; when I suffered insult, I remained silent.

[Col. 0518A]

When I suffered slander, I remained at peace—not by striving against it, but by despising everything that happened, I was humbled. For I could not keep what I had resolved to keep unless I were humbled exceedingly and became like refuse to this world.

But because they threaten death while stirring up infamy, he says: “O Lord, give me life according to your word”—and according to what I resolved, since I resolved it by voluntary judgment, not under compulsion. “I pray,” he says, “that you make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord, and that you teach me your judgments.”

“Let my soul always be in your hands, and I will not forget your law.” This is what the Greeks sing: “My soul is always in my hands,” according to that saying: “If you remember your last things, you will never sin” (Ecclesiasticus 7).

[Col. 0518B]

Thus, while this person holds his soul in his own hands, always considering that it will depart, he does not forget God’s law. Even if sinners set snares for him, he will escape them at once, because, having a lamp for his feet, he escapes by means of the law through which the snares of the unclean are exposed.

He added to this good deed that he would strengthen the keeping he had once begun by swearing to it. “By doing these things,” he says, “it happened to me that I acquired an inheritance forever.” An inheritance is not spoken of unless the one who established the heir has died. Therefore, when the Lord died for me, I acquired as an inheritance his testimonies forever, because his testimonies are the rejoicing of my heart. He testified to me that I would find perpetual life and escape eternal death.

[Col. 0518C]

And I, believing, hated the wicked and loved your law. Therefore I said to the unclean spirits: “Depart from me, evildoers, so that I may scrutinize the commandments of my God.”

Notice how you have scrutinized the law, and scrutinize it in the same way. Say also to the unclean spirits: “Depart from me, so that I may scrutinize the commandments of my God.” They themselves impose an obstacle on you when they see your mind intent upon attentive study.

Let losses of possessions, and various adversities or prosperities, come. Hear the angels crying out: “Take heed to your soul, Lot; do not look back.” Do what you are doing, because if you wish to stand, you recall what you are passing through.

[Col. 0518D]

Therefore, do not yield to occupations that call you back from holy scrutiny, but cry out with the prophet to God: “Help me, O Lord, and I shall be saved, and I will meditate forever on your statutes”—that is, day and night, as was promised in the first psalm: “For you have despised,” he says, “all who descend from your justice.” Their thought is unjust.

For this reason he says: “I have regarded all the sinners of the earth as transgressors, because I have loved your law.” But because “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5), I pray that you may fasten my flesh to your fear. For I have feared your judgments. Unless my flesh is fastened to the fear of God, laughter arises in us and we do not fear God’s judgment. And while we do not fear the Lord, we are handed over to our enemies and persecutors.

Therefore he added: “I have practiced judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who persecute me.”

Explain to us what judgment this is and what justice is: “My flesh,” he says, “wanted to become the mistress of my soul; I chastened it and reduced it to servitude. This is judgment. I practiced justice by giving the soul dominion over it, because the proud slandered me through the flesh.”

[Col. 0519A]

Choose, I beg you, O Lord; choose the servant—that is, the whole world. Choose it for good—that is, in Christ. Let the proud, that is, the unclean spirits who hold the document of sin, not slander it. Come, O Lord, and erase it, removing the hostility of the proud.

For my eyes have failed in longing for your salvation. The one who always waits watches so that he may see the one who is coming; while he delays, he says: “My eyes have failed in waiting for him.”

Deal, I beg you, with your servant—that is, with your age—according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. It is time for you to come: your law has been utterly destroyed by the wicked—that is, by the Jews, who, after receiving it, destroyed it by establishing their own precepts, as the Lord rebukes them, and by keeping human traditions while despising God’s law.

[Col. 0519B]

The wicked have destroyed your law; no one believes, all have turned aside. Come, O Lord, for it is the time to show mercy; bring all things to completion in faith, so that you may have mercy on all (Romans 11).

Remember, reader, that we have said that here the voice of all the prophets is speaking. They wished their proclamations to be brought to fulfillment through the Lord’s coming and assistance to be given to the human race.

Here, then, the chorus of the prophets and saints speaks: “I have loved your commandments more than gold and topaz”—that is, more than gold and a precious stone. He repeated this in the one hundred eighteenth psalm just as he had already said it in the eighteenth. “And therefore,” he says, “I was directed toward all your commandments. I hated every way of iniquity, because your testimonies are wonderful.”

[Col. 0519C]

Paint, paint before your eyes, you who sing these things, some buildings. What kind? Those that the apostles admired. Paint baths; paint marketplaces and walls rising upon a lofty summit. And while you contemplate these things, remember some little hut woven from a hedge of leaves. Will it not seem all the more contemptible to you the more you marvel at those splendid structures?

Therefore, whoever wishes to regard God’s law as reason and understanding despises the whole world as though it were a worthless hut. Since his testimonies alone are wonderful, his soul scrutinizes them. When the unfolding of his words has illumined him in eternal realities and granted great understanding through their humble considerations, he will open his mouth in praise of God and draw in breath—that is, become absorbed in sighs—because he desires God’s commandments.

[Col. 0519D]

He begins to desire them so greatly that, through desire, he does not sleep; withholding food, drink, and joy from himself, he cries out from the desire of his heart: “Look upon me and have mercy on me according to the judgment of those who love your name.” This prayer is poured out by the whole human race.

Hence it continues: “Direct my steps according to your word, and I shall live.” Through Adam I sent my steps crookedly and found death. Come, O Lord, and through yourself direct my steps according to your word, which he transgressed, so that through you I may find the life that I lost through him.

I await you, O Lord; come, and do not put me to shame in my hope. For if you come, all iniquity—namely, that of the demons—will not rule over me. Unbelieving human beings, however, slander believers, saying: “Why do you deny the gods of the nations and await the son of a Virgin? When will the Virgin conceive in her womb and bear Emmanuel for you?”

[Col. 0520A]

Come, therefore, O Lord, and redeem me from the slanders of men, and I will keep your commandments, not the commandments of men. When you make your face shine upon your servant—that is, upon your age—then through your Son you will teach us your statutes.

Let us now consider the highest degree of prayer. The highest degree of prayer is reached when, while engaged in prayer, you pour out prayers and tears together. For it is impossible that your eyes have not incurred sin. Everything that is in the world, as the apostle says, is the desire of the eyes and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father (1 John 2).

Say, therefore, with the prophet: “Streams of water have run down from my eyes, because they did not keep your law.” He did indeed speak of your mercy, and all my hope is in it. But what shall I do? I know that you are righteous, O Lord, and that your judgment is upright. You commanded your justice and your testimonies, by which you threaten eternal fire, and I know that there is exceedingly great truth in your utterance.

[Col. 0520B]

Therefore my eyes pour forth waters that may wash away through weeping what they polluted through desire. Yet I am zealous for your world against idols, because your enemies rejoice over it and rage on every side, so that these enemies of the human race have forgotten your words.

They know and understand the voices of the prophets, in which your words promise the coming of our Redeemer. But you delay so long, O Lord, that my enemies have forgotten the very words of this promise.

Moreover, your utterance is exceedingly refined by fire. It is a burning love, excluding deadly loves and enclosing the loves of eternal life. After saying that it was refined by fire, he added: “And your servant loved it.”

[Col. 0520C]

“I am younger,” he says, “and despised by those who fight against me.” They are older than the whole world and are known to be more ancient than all the ages of antiquity. Therefore I am regarded by them as younger and despised while I seek your statutes.

For your justice—I am certain—is justice forever. And I know that your law is truth; therefore tribulation and distress have found me. For your commandments are my meditation.

Demons do not cause tribulations and distresses except especially for those who meditate on the Lord’s commandments. Therefore I cried out with my whole heart: “Hear me, O Lord; I will seek your statutes.” Arrange my conduct in your love so that I seek nothing from this world, but only your statutes.

[Col. 0520D]

For I anticipated the dawn and cried out. I was a child, then an adolescent, and afterward a young man; now, behold, I have already grown old, and, looking toward the end of my life, I cry out at this mature age. My eyes anticipate you at dawn—that is, before anyone else begins to pray to you. My eyes anticipate the very light of the coming day as they turn toward you, so that you may hear my voice according to your great mercy, because those who persecute me are near.

Iniquities are near me because they have gone far from your law—that is, the demons in idols and the unclean spirits in evil thoughts. They have drawn near to persecute me, thinking that you are still far away. But you are near, O Lord, and all your commandments—by which you commanded that your coming be awaited—are truth.

From the beginning I understood from your testimonies that your promises are so firm that you founded them forever.

[Col. 0521A]

See, therefore, my humiliation. The chorus of the saints intercedes for the whole world: “See my humiliation and rescue me, because I have not forgotten your law”—the salvation promised through your coming.

“Judge my judgment and redeem me for the sake of your utterance,” so that you may make that truth manifest to all who do not believe. For the sake of your utterance, rescue me.

Salvation is far from sinners, whether those who do not believe that you will come or those who do not believe that you have already come. Salvation is indeed far from them, because they have not sought your statutes.

But your mercies are many, O Lord, when you seek those who do not seek you and hear those who despise you. Therefore, since you show mercy to those who have not sought your testimonies, how much more will you have mercy on me, who have not turned aside from your testimonies?

[Col. 0521B]

As we often say, the chorus of all the saints bears witness to this. It also added: “I saw those who did not keep the covenant, and I wasted away, because they did not keep your statutes”—as Moses wasted away among the transgressing people; as Phinehas did; as Caleb son of Jephunneh did; as Joshua son of Nun did; as Samuel did in the case of Saul.

Thus the entire chorus of the saints before the Lord’s coming, seeing those who did not keep the covenant, wasted away and said to the Lord: “See that I have loved your law; in your mercy give me life.”

This, as we have said very often, was the declaration of all the saints from Abel to Mary and Joseph. All pleased God under the Old Law: from Abel to Abraham, by keeping the law of nature; from Abraham to Moses, by keeping the law of nature and circumcision; from Moses to the Lord Jesus Christ, by keeping the law of nature, circumcision, and the Law.

[Col. 0521C]

All these were already then laying the foundation of the Church, whose founder and fulfiller they awaited—the Lord who would fulfill what he had sworn to his servant Abraham, namely, that he would inherit all nations in his seed.

This chorus of all the saints had already learned that the Son of God was born from the Father’s mouth, so that it could say plainly to the Father: “The beginning of your words is truth.” What less than the Gospels did he declare here? Thus Christ already then reigned with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For they could not have desired and confessed him unless they had seen his beauty with the eyes of their minds. Therefore in them the Church of Christ already foretells future things in such a way that it seems to recount past things: “Princes,” he says, “have persecuted me without cause, but, despising their persecution, my heart feared your words”—those words in which you said: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna” (Luke 12).

[Col. 0521D]

Thus, possessing fear and joy in your words, like one who finds abundant spoils, at the time when I hated iniquity—that is, when I refused to sacrifice to idols—and, seeing iniquity, abhorred it, to the point that I endured various torments and escaped, I said praise to you seven times a day.

At that time, in the sevenfold Spirit, I was constructing the structure described above for the seven churches. For just as we said that Christ worked in the foundation of the Church among the ancient saints, so he worked in the new walls, through which towers of that one and same foundation rise until the end of the age.

[Col. 0522A]

In them there is great peace for those who love your name, O Lord, and there is no stumbling block for them. In them your salvation is awaited, and your commandments are kept. In them our petition enters your sight, O Lord, and according to your word you free us. In them our lips pour forth a hymn when we are taught your statutes. In them our tongue proclaims your utterances, and is taught that all your commandments are justice. In them your hands—the very hands that were fastened to the cross—save us, if we love your commandments, long for your salvation, and make your law our meditation.

We believe that our soul will also live in our body and praise you; we believe that your judgments will help us. We confess that we have gone astray like that sheep which perished, and we ask you to seek it, place it upon your shoulders, and restore it to the enduring flock according to your promise, Lord Jesus Christ, who reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.

Amen.

# Psalm 119

## A Song of Ascents

To the Lord I cried when I was in distress, and he heard me. O Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue. What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, for a deceitful tongue? The sharp arrows of the mighty, together with desolating coals.

Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged! I have lived among the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long-time sojourner. With those who hate peace I was peaceful; when I spoke with them, they attacked me without cause.

## Commentary

The songs of ascents are songs of climbing. It is as though a ladder were placed for someone who had fallen into a pit, so that he might gain the ability to climb out. Thus, when the Israelite people had descended into the pit of captivity, “when I was in distress I cried out to the Lord,” and he was heard. Hence he also laments, saying: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has become long.”

And he added: “I have lived among the inhabitants of Kedar.” Kedar was one of the sons of Israel who obtained the wilderness in the eastern region, which extends from the desert of Palestine to the lands of the Persians. The Saracens now inhabit that region, and a reading of Genesis will show that their father was Kedar, the son of Ishmael.

[Col. 0522D]

These people are proved to hate peace to such an extent that, from the time they arose until the present day, they have never entered into a treaty of peace with any nation.

Comparing this people with demons, I approach my captive. Fleeing the delays of historical narration, I explain this psalm to the one who has fallen into the pit of sin. I say to him: “Be distressed, because you rejoiced in evil. And when repentance has made you distressed, cry out to the Lord, believing that he will hear you. Say to him: ‘Deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.’”

[Col. 0523A]

The demons say to him: “Even if I have cast the sinner into the sewer, for now I postpone his cry; time remains for you in which you can climb out.” They disseminate such notions for this reason: whoever listens to them dies while still hoping.

Prepare powerful arrows for these lying lips and for this most wicked tongue—arrows tempered by prayers and sharpened by fasting, together with coals kindled by divine fire. Apply yourself to the step and place ascents in your heart, from the valley of weeping to the mountain of refuge.

Do not merely avoid creating delays for yourself; consider the delays imposed upon you. With a plaintive voice, lament amid sighs that you have lingered in sins: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have lived among the inhabitants of Kedar.”

[Col. 0523B]

I lived among those who persuaded me not to make peace with the word of God; there my soul was a long-time sojourner. He rightly said “soul.” For flesh, because it is from the earth, is in its own land wherever it may be. Yet although I remained among those who hated peace, I was at peace with the word of God.

When I spoke to them of my desire to approach the step of ascent, they attacked me without cause. As soon as the sinner begins to hasten toward repentance and to climb from the pit of death to the mountain of the life above, let him recognize the attacks of demons that he will have to endure, if he truly believes that the Wisdom of God has said to him: “When you approach the service of God, stand in fear and trembling [in justice], and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Knowing this, the Lord included our discourse in the words of our prayer, so that we might cry out: “Let him not allow us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6), he who reigns forever and ever.

Amen.

# Psalm 120

## A Song of Ascents

I lifted my eyes to the mountains; from where will my help come? My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. May he not allow your foot to be moved, and may he not slumber who guards you. Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, the one who guards Israel. The Lord guards you; the Lord is your protection, at your right hand. By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night. The Lord guards you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul. May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure, from this time forth and forever.

[Col. 0523D]

## Commentary

The ascent of the one hundred twentieth psalm is clear: “Lift your eyes to the mountains.” Why do you linger in the valleys? Believe that if you lift your eyes to the mountains, you will escape death and find life.

But you must lift your eyes to the mountains and remove them from contemplation of those concerning whom it was said: “They fixed their eyes on turning toward the earth” (Psalm 16)—that is, they resolved to look downward upon earthly things and to love the earth. But the Apostle cries out to us: “Seek the things that are above; think on the things that are above” (Colossians 3). And the priestly voice cries out to us all, summoning us to receive the mysteries: “Lift up your hearts.”

Do not be afraid, therefore. You will not be abandoned to your own strength. If you have resolved to climb, help will come to you from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. Only do not let your foot be moved—that is, do not decide not to climb, but climb without hesitation.

For the one who guards you does not sleep. He himself will also be your protection at your right hand; that is, he will extend his hand to you as you desire to climb. He will grant that you not be burned by the sun during the day; he will grant that the light of the sun not drive the fire of desire against you or burn you with its sting.

[Col. 0524A]

For if you hasten wholeheartedly to the help of God, he himself guards you from every evil. The Lord guards your body, and he also guards your soul. He guards your entrance into repentance and your departure from the body—from this point, that is, from the day on which you turn in faith.

The Lord Jesus Christ now guards you, he who reigns forever and ever.

Amen.

# Psalm 121

## A Song of Ascents

I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: “We will go into the house of the Lord.” Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem. Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose fellowship is in unity. For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, as a testimony to Israel, to confess the name of the Lord. For there thrones were set for judgment, thrones over the house of David. Pray for the things that are for the peace of Jerusalem, and abundance for those who love you. Let there be peace in your strength and abundance in your towers. For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors, I spoke peace concerning you. For the sake of the house of the Lord our God, I sought good things for you.

## Commentary
Having ascended the second step, approach the third. Good things have been promised to you on this step, if you believe; take up the psalm and utter the song. We know that you have believed when you rejoice in the things that have been said to you. And, abandoning the company of sinners, you will go into the house of the Lord, and there your feet will stand in the courts of Jerusalem, where the building of the future city is being erected within its walls. To it the tribes of the Lord ascended as a testimony to Israel. The twelve apostles are understood as the tribes of the Lord: they first ascended these mountains to confess the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and there thrones were set for judgment, thrones over the house of David. They ask for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem and for abundance for those who love you—that is, for those who love Jerusalem. [Col. 0524D] For there the peace of Christ was confirmed, and it has been spread throughout the whole world. There it was said to them: “I give you my peace” (John 14). To that city the Lord Jesus Christ says: “For the sake of my brothers and my neighbors.” “Who,” he says, “are my brothers and my neighbors, except those who do the will of my Father?” (Luke 8). For their sake, therefore, I speak peace concerning you; I shall promise that in heaven—which is where you are truly built as a city—I shall promise that I will have a share in you as one united whole. And my brothers and my neighbors will reign with me in it. For the sake of the house of my God, I have sought good things for you—eternal good things—so that your citizens may reign with you not temporally, but forever. To him be the glory who promised these things, [Col. 0525A] who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 122

*Song of Ascents.*

To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant look to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us. Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we have been filled exceedingly with contempt. For our soul has been filled exceedingly: with reproach for those who abound, and with contempt for the proud.

## COMMENTARY

Let us gradually reach the heavens from the mountains. For if we have already lifted our eyes to the mountains and rejoiced in everything that was said to us, let us now lift our eyes to the heavens—or rather, to him who dwells in the heavens. This is why we sing the songs of ascents: so that little by little we may rise from the pits of sins. Let us remember that we are servants, because we were created by him; servants, because we are shown to have been both created and redeemed. And as the eyes of servants look to their master, or as the eyes of a maidservant look to her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.

But because we lie in the reproach of proud demons, and because, when we wish to escape crimes, vices, and sins, our own actions oppose us, therefore we ask: “Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us.” For our soul has been filled exceedingly with the reproach of those who abound—of those who overflow in wickedness. And the contempt of the proud goads us, in circumstances in which we believe that only your mercy can come to our aid. You reign for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 123

*Song of Ascents.*

“Unless the Lord had been with us,” let Israel now say, “unless the Lord had been with us. When people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their anger raged against us, perhaps the water would have engulfed us. Our soul passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water. Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us over as prey to their teeth. Our soul was rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare was broken, and we were set free. [Col. 0525D] Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

## COMMENTARY

Whatever unbelieving people did to the martyrs during the persecutions, invisible enemies do the same to us in temptations—provided, that is, that we render service to God. Therefore, when you read of their visible battles, consider your own invisible battles. And oppose in your mind the spirit that suggests what is unjust, just as they opposed the man who persuaded them to offer sacrifice. Conquer from the same source from which they conquered. Their victory was death; let your victory be life. There persuasion and force were at work; suppose that the same thing is happening to you, and that persuasion and violence are fighting against you, although only persuasion is at work against you, O most Christian teacher.

For if you speak with me according to a just judgment, you will admit that you are resisting persuasion alone. But I grant that both persuasion and the violence of demons are wrestling against you. You have the means by which to conquer; assistance is ready. Begin the battle—the Lord is with you. Indeed, the Lord was in you as he was in those who, after this victory, sang this psalm to the Lord, saying: “Unless the Lord had been with us,” let Israel now say, “unless the Lord had been with us. When people rose up against us, perhaps they would have swallowed us alive. When their anger raged against us.”

Why would they not have been angry? Why did they resist them with their objections and not fear those who threatened, beat, tortured, and took away life itself through many and elaborate punishments? Suppose that the same thing is happening to you. “I strike the hoof of the heart; I strike the assaults of the mind”—cry out: “I do not consent.”

For they offer opportunities for sinning: the sweetness of conversation, a woman’s elegance, opportunities for profit, the piety of a bodily action. “It is pious to see the judge, to defend your case, to present a petition, to pour out prayers, while meanwhile you dine; let today be a cheerful day; tonight there are no vigils,” and all the other things by which a combatant is rendered unarmed. Do not believe it; you are being led astray. Believe one who speaks from experience: pray, keep watch, cry out, hold to your purpose; declare yourself a follower of the martyrs.

Cry out at each suggestion: “I do not consent,” and the Lord will be with you. Through him your soul is rescued from the snare of the hunters, so that with the saints you may sing sweetly: “The snare was broken, and we were set free. Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” To him be glory [Col. 0526C] forever. Amen.

# PSALM 124

*Song of Ascents.*

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem will not be shaken forever. Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people, from this time and forever. For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners over the lot of the righteous, so that the righteous may not stretch out their hands toward iniquity. Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart. But those who turn aside into obligations [that is, into bonds] the Lord will lead away with those who work iniquity. Peace be upon Israel.

## COMMENTARY

Let the one who trusts in the emperor serve in his entourage; the one who trusts in the powers of the world has officials for his protection; the one who trusts in his possessions has money in his hand. But the one who trusts in the Lord has mountains around him; he who trusts as Mount Zion does, which follows the law of God—for from Zion the law proceeds.

Therefore, the one who trusts while holding the catholic faith will not be shaken forever. No sect, no heresy, and no disputant will twist him away from his more upright course. Mountains surround him, and the Lord surrounds his people—that is, the testimonies of the holy Scriptures surround him for the defense of the simple people whom Christ acquired with his own blood.

The Lord himself surrounds his people from the time when he suffered for them, as he himself said, “until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). He himself will not abandon the rod of heretics over the lot of Catholics. For the rod of our law proceeds from the hand of the lawgiver, and, having become a dragon, it devoured their rod, so that the orthodox might not stretch out their holy hands toward empty heresy—that is, might not extend their works to heretics.

But since there are some whose hearts the heretics corrupt, the Holy Spirit intercedes for those who are upright in heart. Those who turn aside into the bond of anathema he will lead away on the day of judgment with those who work iniquity. Let there be peace in Israel through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns in the unity of the Godhead with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 125

[Col. 0527B]

*Song of Ascents.*

When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who were comforted. Then our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation. Then they will say among the nations: “The Lord has done great things for them.” The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful. Turn back our captivity, Lord, like a torrent in the south. Those who sow in tears will reap in exultation. Going forth, they went and wept, carrying their seeds. But coming, they will come with exultation, carrying their sheaves.

## COMMENTARY

The songs of ascents are the gates of an open heaven. Jacob, resting, sees in his vision the Lord above, reclining with the heavens open: its upper part leans upon heaven, through which the Lord looks; its lower part is on earth, where the man slept.

What does the ascent of this ladder to the Lord say? “Do good, Lord, to those who are good and upright in heart.” For they heard the priests cry out to them, “Lift up your heart,” and they said to God: “To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 122). Ascend, because the Lord does good to those who are good and upright in heart. But those who turn aside and depart from God he leads into bondage and assigns a place with those who work iniquity.

Arise, Israel, you who have slept; wake up. Anoint the cornerstone with the oil of joy; peace be with you. For your sons, freed from captivity through Christ, sang this song of ascents, saying: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who were comforted.”

Step by step we ascend from the tribulation of the first song to joy, and we who there sowed tears shall here reap joys. We who there groaned in captivity, saying, “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged” (Psalm 119), here have our mouth filled with joy and our tongue with exultation.

For behold, they say among the nations: “The Lord has done great things for them. The Lord has done great things for us; we have become joyful.” We must remember that we said we would apply everything to the building of our own edifice—everything which, through a mystical course, either leads to the Lord or draws us toward his martyrs. It is known that these things apply to all the saints.

But let us rejoice that, drawing a stream toward ourselves from their passion, we have escaped our captivity through repentance, believing that the Lord will do great things with us. [Col. 0528A] And from the condition in which we presented ourselves to him weeping and sorrowful, may he himself make us joyful and glad.

For if we have sown the tears of repentance, surely a fertile harvest of forgiveness will arise for us. From it, when we depart from the body and come to the Lord with exultation, we shall be with the saints, carrying our sheaves. For where they rejoice as crowned, we shall exult as freed, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 126

*Song of Ascents of Solomon.*

Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain. It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord: sons; the reward: the fruit of the womb. As arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have been cast out. Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire through them; he will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies at the gate.

## COMMENTARY

Many who explain the beginning of this psalm badly preach idleness instead of labor. They say that holy people are occupied with pursuits in a futile struggle. They also turn the medicine into a wound by fostering the vain hope that a person can obtain something through his own efforts, saying in this way: “Unless the Lord has built, you build in vain. Unless the Lord has guarded, you keep watch in vain.”

I could, through an elaborate discussion of this building, demonstrate its foundations, walls, roofs, and fortifications; but the matter is being treated with another purpose. From the beginning we have undertaken to speak briefly and concisely. Nevertheless, I shall make a small digression and quickly return to you, who are waiting for the psalm.

From the beginning of the world, all who lived as saints built a city for the Lord. Indeed, the saints will be the walls of the future city. Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua son of Nun, and all the saints built the house and guarded the city.

But unless the Lord—that is, the Son of God—had come and built everything that they had built (his saying is proved: “I have not come to destroy, but to fulfill” [Matthew 5]), then, if he had not come while they were laying the foundations and building the walls, to construct the roof and adorn everything within, they would have labored in vain, building the house.

For this reason the Synagogue is vain today: it has the buildings of walls but has no roof, and it does not dwell under the protection of the God of heaven. It has the walls that the saints built, but it does not have the roof that Christ completed. It has a threshold, but it does not have the blood of the Lamb on the threshold.

When it begins to rain upon sinners a snare of fire and sulfur, these people, being without a roof, are exposed to this rain. When the angel begins to strike the first fruits, these people do not escape the angel who strikes through the blood of the Lamb.

What, then, are you building, Jews? Why do you keep watch, heretics? You do these things without cause, because the Lord neither builds nor keeps watch with you. But you, orthodox Christians, loving Christ in incorruption, do not be afraid; build securely, because the Lord builds with you.

For you are God’s building, God’s cultivation (1 Corinthians 3). Keep watch, because he not only keeps watch with you, but also awakens those who sleep, saying: “Keep watch with me; keep watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26). It is as though he said: “You would keep watch in vain if I did not keep watch with you.”

But now it is most unjust that, while I keep watch with you, you should be occupied with sleep. Hence the Apostle also cries out: “Build one another up” (1 Thessalonians 5). The building, therefore, would be vain if the Lord did not build. The vigils would be vain if the Lord did not guard; but the Lord guards, and they are not vain.

“It is in vain for you to rise before the light”—that is, Christ is the light, and for you who rise before him, it is vain to rise before him, you who eat the bread of sorrow. For unless the one who gives the bread of joy comes, you have risen in vain.

When will he come? “When he gives,” he says, “sleep to his beloved”—that is, he will come when those who are now saints have received the sleep of peace.

Why will he come? So that at the resurrection the inheritance of the Lord may be revealed, in which all the sons of God receive an inheritance—provided that they have been sons of his womb, that is, provided that they have been baptized in the font of the catholic faith.

Where is the womb of the Church, which gives birth to her sons? They wound the enemy as an arrow shot from the hand of a mighty man, when they fulfill their desire in good things, so that they are not put to shame when they depart from the body. For then they find their enemies at the gate, when they leave the body in which they overcame the devil.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that the title reads, “Song of the ascent of the house of Solomon,” so that you may retain the historical sense of what was then said to Solomon: “O most prudent Solomon! You are indeed building a house for God, but unless the Lord builds the house, as you yourself said—for Wisdom builds herself a house and sets up [or: cuts down] seven pillars” (Proverbs 9)—unless, therefore, the one who is called Wisdom builds the house, you have labored in vain.

For in the house that you built, “not one stone will be left upon another.” But the house that the Lord builds ascends into the heavens, and in it the King, the Lord, will be glorified for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 127

*Song of Ascents.*

Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you. Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house. Your sons shall be like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed. May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life. And may you see your children’s children. Peace be upon Israel.

## COMMENTARY

It is of no value if you fear the Lord, since the demons also fear him. But you will be blessed if you fear the Lord in such a way that you walk in his way. For if you walk in his way—that is, in the catholic faith—there you will eat the labors of your fruits, the flesh of the Son of Man, so that, possessing enduring life within you, you may be blessed and it may be well with you.

Then your wife—that is, your flesh—will abound like a vine on the sides of your house. Then, I say, just as a vine produces clusters of grapes, so your sons will advance from the actions of your body. And as you advance like a vine in the blood of Christ, they will advance like olive shoots around your table, wherever you provide them a feast from the words of God.

Thus every person who fears the Lord will be blessed—that is, the one who acts in this way will be blessed, so that the Holy Spirit may say to him: “May the Lord bless you from Zion,” that is, from his Church, “and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.”

And just as you have begotten sons for God, so may your sons beget, so that you may see your children’s children in the presence of the Lord, when Israel has received peace, when this time of war has drawn near [Col. 0530B] and the time of peace has come. Glory to the Eternal, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 128

*Song of Ascents.*

Often they have fought against me from my youth—let Israel now say. Often they have fought against me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me. Sinners built upon my back; they prolonged their iniquity. The just Lord will cut the necks of sinners. Let all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward. Let them become like the grass of the rooftops, which withers before it is plucked up. Of it the reaper does not fill his hand, nor the one who gathers sheaves his bosom. And those who passed by did not say: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we have blessed you in the name of the Lord.”

## COMMENTARY

No one endures battle unless he is placed in youth. Therefore, you who, according to the interpretation of the name Israel, are beginning to see God through purity of heart, must endure the battles of demons.

But be confident, because the Lord fights for you in such a way that he will cut their necks—provided that you do not cease to fight, so that you may say: “They could not prevail against me,” although sinners built upon my back; that is, although, placing heavy burdens of tribulations upon me, they bent me down and prolonged their iniquities—that is, they delayed their afflictions, by which they troubled me.

But the Lord will cut their necks by his just judgment. Let the Pharisees and all heretics who hate Zion—that is, who hate the Church of Christ—have a share with them.

Let them become like the grass of rooftops or buildings, which withers before it is plucked up. Here he names a rooftop or building because the greatest numbers of heretics go over to prominent persons, where they seem to escape the sickles of priests cutting hay; but there they will wither before they are plucked up.

For the one who reaps will not fill his hand with anything from them, nor will those who gather their sheaves fill their bosoms. For among all those who have passed by—from the apostles, the holy ones, down to the present day, whether those who exist now or those who have passed away—no one has blessed them in the name of the Lord.

And whoever has not received a blessing from the blessed Apostle Peter, or from the apostles, or from their successors, and has thus taught the little communities whom he deceived—because he usurped a blessing, he incurred a curse—through that curse, before he is plucked up, he withers. That is, while he appears to live in the body, he has already withered in spirit.

Separated from them, and holding the catholic faith in complete integrity, we find eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord, who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 129

*Song of Ascents.*

From the depths I cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice. Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplication. If you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who will endure? For with you there is forgiveness, and because of your law I have waited for you, Lord. My soul has waited for his word; my soul has hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord. For with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him. And he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities.

## COMMENTARY

My penitent, now established in goodness, recalls his former cries. For hear the wise man saying to him: “My son, you have sinned; do not add again, but also pray for your former sins.” That servant is useful who always recalls his faults. For he will not otherwise remember the good patience and mercy of his lord unless he has recalled his own impatience and iniquity: “I did this; I committed that, against the command of my lord.”

“Lord, if you wished to consider our contempt, long ago you would have erased the world; but with you there is abundant forgiveness: because of your law I have waited for you, Lord.” For I had withdrawn from you; I had not awaited you. But your law told me concerning you that you do not wish anyone to perish, but wish all human beings to be saved [or: to become saved] (1 Timothy 2).

Therefore my soul waited for your word—that is, for your Son who was coming, who is promised as coming for this purpose: to take away the sins of the world. He will come from the morning watch. One watch is a quarter of the night. Thus the first watch begins in the evening; the second reaches the middle of the night; the third passes with the crowing of the rooster; the fourth is the morning watch, which is completed at the rising of the light. In that watch the angels announced the Lord’s birth to the shepherds.

But let us call the morning watch remembered at the birth of the light, in which light Israel should hope in the Lord from morning until night—that is, until it comes to an end, until then—or let the human being hope for as long as he is in the body, because with God there is mercy.

Let him do penance; let him cease from sin from the morning hour until the evening of his life, from the time when the illumination of the Savior arose for him. He will in no way perish if he ceases from sin and repents, because great is the mercy with God, and he himself will redeem Israel.

For he will redeem no other except Israel—that is, unless one is baptized, he will not redeem him. For if someone should perhaps repent of evil deeds and show himself remarkable in good works, yet if he is not Israel, if he has not been baptized, he is not redeemed from his iniquities.

For there are some who think themselves Christians without Christ, although a person is taught to have done whatever good he has done for his own honor, whereas whatever he has believed rightly belongs to the honor of God. Great is that servant who has acted vigorously for his own honor and neglected the honor of his master. A most insignificant Christian sinner will be placed above him, one who believes that through faith he reaches the mercy of him who reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 130

*Song of Ascents.*

Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been raised up. I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me. If I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul. Like a weaned child upon his mother, so is the recompense in my soul. Let Israel hope in the Lord, from this time and forever.

## COMMENTARY

There is a common saying among the people that says that a household is arranged according to the customs of its master. If this saying had its proper effect between masters and servants, as it does between Christ and Christians, we would rightly call ourselves servants of Christ.

Although he was Lord of heaven and earth, he “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, and, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), said: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted.”

Act, servant, according to the customs of your master. Since he is humble by nature, why are you exalted? That judge is reported as humble, while we are proud; he without glory, while we, by contrast, are glorious. He does not walk in great things; we walk among important persons, and we glory in the fact that nobles worship or love us—if indeed they love us and are not merely making a joke at our expense, as though we were unaware of the saying: “The mouth that kissed us when we came, how greatly it tears us when we depart.”

But we dishonor the poor person in whom Christ assumed his own person. We do not walk in small things, but in great things and things too wonderful for us, and we sing that we think humbly and do not exalt our soul, forgetful of the Apostle’s exhortation: “Desire the milk like little children, so that you may grow through it” (1 Peter 2).

If we did this, we would certainly be like a weaned child upon his mother. The mother, the Church, recognized her nourishment in us, and, as to one weaned upon his mother, Christ rendered to us the effect of his love for his Church. In him Israel hopes—that is, the pure in heart, because he is Israel, which is interpreted as “seeing God.”

For his only hope is to attain the divine vision. Then he will be satisfied, when the glory of him who reigns for ages of ages appears to him. Amen.

# PSALM 131

*Song of Ascents.*

Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness. As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob: “If I enter the tent of my house, if I ascend upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.”

Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest. We shall enter his dwelling; we shall worship in the place where his feet stood. Arise, Lord, to your rest—you and the ark of your sanctification. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your holy ones exult. For the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your Christ.

The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate it: “From the fruit of your womb I shall place one upon your throne.” If your sons keep my covenant and these testimonies of mine that I shall teach them, their sons also will sit upon your throne forever.

For the Lord chose Zion; he chose it as a dwelling for himself. “This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I chose it. Blessing I shall bless her widow; I shall satisfy her poor with bread. I shall clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones will exult with exultation. There I shall bring forth the horn of David; I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. I shall clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him my sanctification will flourish.”

## COMMENTARY

“Remember, Lord, David”—not so that God may pass from forgetfulness to remembrance. God is reminded by a human being, but the human being is taught how the Divinity delights in human vows: namely, that, having laid aside ferocity—which generates anger, nourishes discord, and gives birth to pride—he may become meek under the Lord’s burden.

The burden is light; bear it meekly; the yoke is easy (Matthew 11). Draw it, Christian. The Lord will remember in you that, for carrying his commandments, you present to Christ your meek sheep—that is, your body—not one that resists.

The Lord will remember you if your meeknesses have knocked upon his memory through holy intercession. If you have progressed in meekness, progress also in devotion.

“He swore,” he says, “to the Lord, and he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob.” Hear the concern of the one making the vow, and then show yourself to be a participant in the one who sings.

After he vowed his vow to God, he did not enter the tent of his house, he did not ascend the bed of his couch, he did not give sleep to his eyes or slumber to his eyelids, until he found a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob.

The complete and perfect concern that the one who makes a promise must preserve before God endures until he finds a place for the Lord. The Lord is eternal, and his place cannot be temporal. Why do we seek temporal places, when we seek an eternal inhabitant?

But if what we seek with concern and vigilance is eternal, it is shown to be everlasting. We do not cease to seek with the greatest diligence until we deserve to find what we seek.

Let us nevertheless see what the most holy Psalmist seeks. “A place,” he says, “where the God of Jacob may dwell.” And he added: “We heard of this dwelling in Ephrata.”

The Ephratean Elkanah, who holds the beginning of the royal books, was the father of Samuel. In him we heard the voice of the Lord saying: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who will do everything according to my heart; and I shall build him a house, and he will walk before my Christ forever” (1 Samuel 2).

This voice, therefore, which we then heard in the Ephratean, we now find in the fields of the forest, where the angels addressed shepherds of sheep, saying: “We announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today the Lord has been born for you, who is the Savior of all. And this will be a sign for you: you will find a child wrapped in cloths and placed in a manger” (Luke 2).

The shepherds attained this dwelling, where God dwells forever, when the angels pointed it out. And they were not shepherds of just any kind of animals, but only of sheep; nor were they sleeping, but keeping watch; and they were found not sleeping, but keeping watch; not negligent, but concerned; not careless, but fearful.

Finally, the angel began to address them at the point where he recognized the terror of their fear: “Do not fear,” he said—as though saying: “Because you keep watch and are concerned for the flock of meekness, and you pasture in the fields of your hearts.”

For there are the fields of the forest. Since, therefore, you diligently guard the flock throughout the night, lest a meek sheep—whether patience, charity, hospitality, chastity, or their other companions, which you pasture by the word of God—be seized by the ferocity of wolves, and because you fear the Lord of the flock and are concerned lest the wolves’ fierceness invade you, now do not fear, because such a shepherd has been born, one who lays down his life for his sheep (John 10).

Now we ask you, O shepherds: tell us whether you found the child as the angels indicated. In response they said: “We entered his dwelling; we worshiped in the place where his feet stood.”

Certainly you went to see him lying in the manger; how can you testify that you saw him standing? “We,” they say, “saw him standing, because we believed, not lying.” To unbelievers and doubters he is shown lying and wrapped in cloths; to believers the crowned king is revealed.

Finally, we saw such a radiance of his royal dignity that we did not dare to worship him himself, but worshiped those footprints in which his feet had stood.

“What, then, did you worship—the earth?” “The holy earth of the body of Jesus,” they say, “in which the footprints of God were shown to us, when we saw an infant brought forth by virginal birth, for whom the angels led choirs, singing that through him there would be peace for heaven and earth.”

To him we say every day: “Arise, Lord, to your rest.” God’s rest in Jesus is evident and distinctive. In him is the ark—that is, the mystery—of God’s sanctification. Through him the apostles have been clothed with righteousness, and all the saints exult, for the sake of David, God’s servant, because from the fruit of his womb God placed one upon his throne.

Through him his sons keep God’s covenant—that is, the apostles who came according to the flesh from the lineage of Judah. They not only kept the covenant of our Lord Jesus Christ, but also his testimonies, which he taught them. Their sons sit upon their throne to this day, themselves possessing the power to bind and loose.

This was granted to them because the Lord rejected the Synagogue of falsehood and chose holy Zion—namely, the Church of right faith—which, in his foreknowledge, he had chosen beforehand as a dwelling for himself. In it is God’s rest forever and ever; in it he dwells, because he chose it beforehand; in it widows are blessed in chastity; in it the poor are satisfied with the bread of piety; in it priests are clothed with righteousness; in it the saints exult with exultation; in it the horn has been brought forth.

Therefore, let the kingdom of David be established. This is the lamp that, placed upon the lampstand, shines for all who are in the house—that is, who are in the faith of Jesus Christ.

By contrast, every assertion apart from this one does shine in words and possesses materials for human acclamation and admiration; but, placed under a measure, it does not shine for those who are in the house, but for those whom it finds beneath the measure.

For those who use the measure of right faith upside down dwell beneath the measure. They are enemies of the lamp that the Holy Spirit prepared through the apostles for his Christ, our Lord.

Therefore he clothes his enemies with the shame of anathema, while upon Christ his sanctification will flourish, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 132

*Song of Ascents.*

Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one! It is like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends to the edge of his garment. It is like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion. For there the Lord commanded blessing and life forever.

## COMMENTARY
In the first Song of Ascents, placed in captivity, we cry out in tribulation to God, and he hears us. In the second ascent, we lifted our eyes to the mountains, from which the Lord’s help comes, by which we are guarded from every evil. On the third ascent, climbing upward, we came to the house of the Lord. Having undertaken the fourth ascent, we then lifted to the heavens the eyes that we had raised to the mountains. On the fifth, we encounter the persecutions of human beings and God’s defense. On the sixth, the Lord commands heretics who deviate in bondage to be handed over. On the seventh ascent, we who had previously been weeping became joyful. On the eighth ascent, we find Christ, who builds the holy house, without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5). On the ninth ascent, we see those who fear the Lord and walk in his ways. On the tenth ascent, we endured battles and, with God’s help, won the victory. On the eleventh ascent, we find such great mercy from God that through it we are redeemed from all our iniquities. On the twelfth ascent, we find contempt for the world, in which our heart is not exalted. On the thirteenth ascent, we find in the fields of the forest the one whom we had heard of in Ephrathah. There we find the Son of God exulting with his saints in exultation. There the lamp is prepared, full of the oil of gladness, overcoming the darkness of the world, so that those who had been separated by pressing darkness and divided from one another through the building of the proud tower may now all come together as one, so that that evil counsel may be shown to have been corrected by God’s counsel.

Seeing this, the Holy Spirit cried out: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together as one!” For they have the ointment of chrism, which descends from the head into the beard—that is, from Christ into the virtues. Just as the hairs of the head and beard are drenched with ointment, so all the virtues that daily struggle against vices, so that they may be able to conquer, are infused with Christ’s help. Observe, however, the mysteries of chrism in the ointment of the head, and apply the dew of Hermon descending upon Mount Zion to the stream of the fountain of perennial water. For there the Lord commanded blessing and eternal life, forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 133

### A Song of Ascents

Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place, and bless the Lord. May the Lord bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth.

### COMMENTARY

The ascent has reached charity, and it found no place to go higher. For whatever the fourteenth ascent accomplished, the fifteenth advances in those who are ascending. In charity, the brotherhood that had been divided by discord returns, and all become good who had all been evil.

Now tell me: why have you all come together as one, you who are called brothers, or from where do you all come? Show it. “From one Father, Christ,” he says, “and from one mother, the Church.” Therefore we have come together as one because we have acknowledged ourselves to be servants of the Lord.

The answer is given to us, and it is said: “Now, therefore, because you have all come together as one, bless the Lord”—“all,” he says, “you servants of the Lord.” And because it could be said that all human beings are servants of the Lord, he replied: “I am speaking to you servants who stand in the house of the Lord, who have deserved to enter the house in which God rests with his friends and feasts with his apostles.”

Will only those who are inside the house bless the Lord? “No,” he says, “not they alone, but also those who still stand in the courts of the house.” And you, catechumens—yes, you who stand in the courts of the house of our God, who do not yet dare to enter inside—you too should lift your hands together within the Holy of Holies, and together bless the Lord, raising holy hands under the banner of the cross, without anger and disputation, in the night of this age, shining like lights, so that through you the Lord may be blessed from Zion, he who made heaven and earth, who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 134

### Alleluia

Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, servants. You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing praises to his name, for it is pleasant. For the Lord chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his possession. For I have known that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.

Whatever the Lord desired, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses. Bringing up clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightning into rain. He who brought forth winds from his treasuries, who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from human being to beast. And he sent signs and wonders in your midst, Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. He who struck many nations and killed mighty kings: Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan. And he gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people.

Lord, your name is eternal; Lord, your memorial is from generation to generation. For the Lord will judge his people, and he will be entreated on behalf of his servants.

The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths and will not speak; they have eyes and will not see. They have ears and will not hear, for there is no spirit in their mouth. May those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them.

House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord. Blessed be the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.

### COMMENTARY

This ladder, whose top reaches heaven, has fifteen steps in the five books of Moses and in the ten commandments of the law. There the stone beneath Jacob’s head was anointed; here that anointed head itself is directed toward the dew of Hermon—not toward all the dew of Hermon. For the mountain’s dew has streams descending all around it; we reach that dew which descends upon Mount Zion, seeking only the source of this dew after the ointment of chrism. It flows in channels onto Mount Zion—that is, into the height of the Church’s position—and thus joins the Trinity in one Godhead, so that I may truly say that there are three persons and truly say that there is one substance.

Thus the Lord is praised by his servants. Thus his name is proclaimed truly worthy of praise, when unity is spoken with the mouth and held in the heart within the Trinity, and the Trinity within unity. Then we affirm that the Lord is good and kind. For if the Father is said to assume a greater share of the Godhead for himself, or to claim for himself a rank above the Son, he is not praised as good but blasphemed as a rival.

Therefore nothing is greater in God, because the Father never grows old. Nothing is less in the Son, because he never grows. For where there is something greater and something less, old age threatens decline to the greater, while age promises growth to the lesser. The Godhead is free from these stages, because God is not later than time. If any times existed before God, they would make him greater who is the Father and lesser who is the Son. But if he was begotten before all things, time could in no way impose necessity upon him, because time itself took its beginning from him in order to exist.

Thus the Lord’s praise is celebrated, and in that praise we must sing that “the Lord chose Jacob for himself.” He chose this one, he says, who supplants the pleasure-loving counsel, and he possesses this one who strives to see God with a pure heart. For just as Jacob is called “supplanter,” so Israel means “seeing God.”

He then recognizes that the Lord is great when he possesses the purest heart. But if it is not pure, this age appears great to him, and he either marvels at persons or is stunned by unlawful beauties. When the mind is pure, it judges nothing worthy of wonder except God alone, and it will marvel at this God above all gods.

How “above all gods”? Listen carefully, singer. The gods of the nations are demons. They want us to marvel at perishable beauties—for example, in buildings, in persons, in the glories of the world, and in fleeting desires. When, therefore, we embrace this God of ours above all others, who shows us eternal things, then we honor him above all gods, rejecting their counsels and embracing God’s counsels.

For he made whatever he desired in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in the abysses. He brought forth clouds for us from the ends of the earth—that is, those who bring earthly occupations to an end—and he presents them to the world as clouds. Therefore he made lightning into rain: that is, so that in fiery lightning he might kill the enemy, and with the water of rain wash away the sinner.

And who does this? Without doubt, he who brings forth winds from his treasuries—that is, apostles from his own perceptions. For as winds are to ships, so apostles are to souls. When the winds blow, ships reach their desired destinations; when the apostles preach, souls arrive at Christ, who is truly the harbor.

He struck the firstborn while hanging upon the cross, and he struck them in such a way that he considered neither human being nor beast to be spared. Whatever is Egyptian is drowned together with Egypt’s ruler; it perishes with Pharaoh and with all his servants.

When we had come to the water that opened for us the way of salvation, and that covered all who were pursuing us, then we confessed the name of the Lord forever and received his memorial, so that, as believers, it might be in us forever and ever—the judgment that is to come, in which, when he has judged the living and the dead, he will console his servants alone. For there the Christian fornicator will be found better than the most chaste idolater.

The idols in which he placed his hope possess all the limbs but no sensation, and a container but no spirit. Those who trust in them will be like them—that is, they will be melted in a similar fire, not so that they may be reduced into some forms, but so that they may be consumed in eternal fire.

The house of Israel alone, founded in those who see God with a pure heart—that is, in the apostles—will itself be delivered. In this house Aaron blesses in the priests, and Levi in the ministers, together with those who fear the Lord—that is, with the entire Christian people, who sing “Alleluia” in David’s songs, blessing the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.

We believe that Jerusalem, which is to come from the heavens, is proclaimed by the prophets and apostles, and that in it the Father reigns with the Son and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 135

### Alleluia, alleluia

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for—. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for—. To him who alone does great wonders, for—. To him who made the heavens with understanding, for—. To him who established the earth upon the waters, for—. To him who made the great lights, for—. The sun to govern the day, for—. The moon and the stars to govern the night, for—. To him who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for—. With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, for—. To him who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for—. And led Israel through its midst, for—. And shook Pharaoh and his army into the Red Sea, for—. To him who led his people through the desert, for—. To him who struck great kings, for—. And killed mighty kings, for—. Sihon, king of the Amorites, for—. And Og, king of Bashan, for—. And gave their land as an inheritance, for—. An inheritance to Israel his servant, for—. For he remembered us in our lowliness, for—. And redeemed us from our enemies, for—. To him who gives food to all flesh, for—. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for—. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his mercy is forever.

### COMMENTARY

We have come to the “Alleluia” that is written twice. In it I consider this: neither flesh without the soul nor soul without the flesh can give thanks to the Lord. Therefore let the two in one sing two “Alleluias,” so that, while they are together in the passage of this life, they may maintain the proper order of thanksgiving: let the flesh say its “Alleluia,” and let the soul say its own. The human being is twofold; the “Alleluia” is twofold.

Let each of the two give thanks to the Lord: first, because he is good; and afterward let the confession of our faith be good. Then let us say: “His mercy is forever.” The confession of one who accuses his sins in this age cannot perish. Without doubt, the one who has offered his confession to God will find God’s compassion. If he receives our confession daily, he daily grants us his goodness. And if we do not grow weary in confessing, how will he cease to show mercy?

We have sinned; we cannot deny it; we have many sins. We shall not be free of them in any other way unless we daily ask the Lord that they be forgiven us. For this is his teaching: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6). Let us confess that we are debtors to the one to whom we owe a debt, for we too are debtors to God, and God is our debtor. Let us ask that what we owe not be demanded of us. Let us ask that he not repay what he owes. Woe to us if he demands what we owe. You say nothing, as though the almighty God did not owe the kingdom of heaven that he promised. Woe to us if he repays what he owes.

But because he is merciful, and is God of gods and Lord of lords, as one who needs nothing, he must be asked to forgive. Indeed, you who plead for mercy should know that you will not find it unless you have been adorned with the confession of the true faith.

Confess, therefore, that this is your God, who made the heavens with understanding, so that their appearance alone may shine beautifully for us; who founded the earth upon the waters, so that our body might be washed by the water of holy baptism; who alone made the two great lights, one for the day of the New Testament, which shines like the sun upon those who act in the light, and the other for the night of those living according to Judaism.

For in the New Testament what is read openly is illuminated as in daytime, in the letter itself, by Christ, who is the true Sun of righteousness. In the Old Testament, however, placed as though in the night beneath the covering of the letter, it is revealed by the moon—that is, by the Church. For she is the moon that waxes in the saints and wanes in sinners; she shines upon those placed in the darkness of ignorance, and she also has stars in her degrees.

For she shines one way in a bishop, another way in a presbyter, another way in a deacon, and another way in the other clergy, in whom the Lord is proclaimed. He struck Egypt with its firstborn—that is, the earth filled with superstitions, together with the demons who dwell in it. They are called firstborn because nothing is older or prior to the demons in sin.

After they have been struck, Israel is led out from their midst. For whoever has seen God reconciling the world to himself in Christ (2 Corinthians 5), having become Israel—as one who sees God—is led out from the land of Egypt that the Lord struck.
