And how is he led out? “With a strong hand and an exalted arm,” he says—certainly with the arm raised on high in the cross, by which he shook off Pharaoh and his army, that is, in the abyss where eternal darkness dwells in the depths.

And he leads his people through the desert, namely, to a purpose removed from all worldly cares. There he also brings water from the rock of the cliff, and strikes against them many armed nations—that is, wicked thoughts—and mighty kings—that is, the rulers of this world’s air.

And Sihon, king of the Amorites. In the Hebrew language, “Amorites” is interpreted as “foreigners.” Therefore the Lord kills the king of the Amorites—that is, of the foreigners. And the king of Bashan. The Hebrews say that Bashan means “deep.” Therefore Christ also kills the king of the deep, who wishes to lead us from higher things to lower ones, and he kills all his kingdoms, for “Ham” is interpreted as “a mocker.”

Therefore, when the Lord has killed all these for us, he gives us their land—that is, our bodies, in which they reigned—as an inheritance, provided that, having become Israel, we desire to see God through faith and not through sight.

After this, let him see our lowliness and deliver us from the hand of all our enemies. Thus he also says in another psalm, in which he sang that he had been delivered: “I was brought low, and he delivered me” (Psalm 114).

Let us see where the two remaining verses are directed: “He who gives food to all flesh. And give thanks to the God of heaven.” It is as though he were saying: “Heavens, you are witnesses that all flesh—birds, human beings, cattle, and creeping things—is fed by God. Confess this, O heavens: that the Lord gives food to all flesh.” Or: “You human beings, believe that the God of heaven created everything and feeds all things.” The accursed Manichaean denies this, saying that all flesh was constituted by the devil as its author and is fattened through his service.

Let us, however, confess that this is the God of heaven, who gives food to all flesh. And as this psalm has done, so let us do, so that through each word of our confession we may sing: “For his mercy is forever”—that is, the mercy of our God and Father and of the Son, who reigns in the unity of the Godhead, before all things, now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0540D]

## PSALM 136

### A Psalm of David. Alleluia

By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments. For there those who had taken us captive asked us for the words of songs. And those who had led us away said: “Sing for us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land? If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten. May my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you. If I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy. Remember, Lord, the children of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, those who say: “Empty it, empty it, down to its foundations within it.” Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the recompense with which you repaid us. Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock.

### COMMENTARY

Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” and the first confusion occurred nowhere except in our parents according to the flesh—that is, in Adam and his wife. In them we sat and wept until the one came who would take us away from captivity to the devil and his ministers.

In saying this, we do not prejudice the prophet, who foretold the rage of the Assyrians and the barbaric ferocity by which captives were to be led away. It happened: they were led into Babylon, and everything that the holy man Jeremiah wrote came to pass.

Nevertheless, when the captivity of sins comes upon us, we cease from all that former practice of singing psalms. We have been confused, Babylon besieges us, and we have no confidence to open our mouth in God’s praises. There we hang our instruments upon the rivers of Babylon, upon the streams of crimes.

O Lord, break our bonds, so that we may be able to offer you a sacrifice of praise. For there those who took us captive asked us for the words of songs, and those who led us away asked us for a hymn.

Let us open the eyes of the mind, and we shall see demons mocking us after sin, as though they were adding voices to these words of their mockery: “Sing as you used to; sing psalms as was customary for you.” Let us, miserable people, at least show them our eyes washed away by weeping, if we cannot produce our voices. Let them see us weeping if they cannot hear us singing: “There,” he says, “we sat and wept.”

Let us weep as much as we can, so that by the rivers of our tears we may overcome the rivers of Babylon. For our instruments have been hung up; the voice of joy has failed; and, placed in a foreign land, we cannot sing the Lord’s song. Our bodies have indeed been made foreign to God by those who took us captive.

Let our mother Jerusalem come to mind—sweet in chastity, pure in simplicity, gentle in correction, clean in conduct. Let us see in our mind what we have lost and what we have found, and amid our tears let us cry out, saying: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten. May my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you. My joy will have no beginning unless I return to you.”

After saying these things, giving voice to the groaning and sigh of our inmost heart, let us cry out to God, saying: “Remember, Lord, the children of Edom”—that is, the children of Esau. They are your enemies, who rose up against us.

This gives us consolation, because you never loved those who took us captive. You always loved Jacob, and you hated Esau—that is, you love your servants in the likeness of Jacob, whom you loved, and you abhor the children of Edom in the likeness of Esau, whom you abhorred.

Behold, those whom you hated and hate rule over those whom you loved and love. Rise up, Lord; remember the wickedness of those who say to one another concerning your Jerusalem, which had poured its love into us. They say to one another: “Empty it, empty it down to its foundations”—that is, reach down to their faith, so that they may not again build towers of strength in the face of the enemy (Psalm 60).

Come, blessed one; come, Lord Jesus Christ. Come invisibly against the invisible ones, and repay them with the recompense with which they repaid us. Seize and dash not only those gigantic warriors but also their little ones against your rock, upon which you founded the Church, so that you may kill in us not only those enormous crimes but also the little one—what appears to be less than all sins—and even that.

Give us the counsel that, as soon as sins are born, we should dash them against the rock and not allow them to grow, lest, when they have grown, they generate barbarity for us again.

We shall do this if he who is our strength fixes the minds of our definitions with his own true teachings, setting the point of his cross upon them, so that when they reach us as tempters, they may depart in confusion.

For if those who flee to bronze statues of kings escape their pursuers (Codex, book 1, unique title, *Concerning Those Who Flee to Statues*, *Digest*, title *On Punishments*, law “Capital Punishments,” section “To the Statues”), how much more can those who flee to the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ not be seized by their adversaries, but through him—who conquered on the cross—become conquerors themselves.

To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM 137

### A Psalm of David

I will give thanks to you, Lord, with all my heart, because you have heard all the words of my mouth. In the sight of the angels I will sing to you; I will worship toward your holy temple, and I will give thanks to your name. Because of your mercy and your truth, for you have magnified your holy name above every name. On whatever day I call upon you, hear me quickly; you will multiply strength in my soul.

May all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord, because they have heard all the words of your mouth. And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord. For the Lord is exalted and regards the lowly, but he knows lofty things from afar.

If I walk in the midst of tribulation, you will revive me; and against the anger of my enemies you have stretched out your hand, and your right hand has saved me. The Lord will repay on my behalf. Lord, your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of your hands.

[Col. 0542D]

### COMMENTARY

The one who has handed over all twelve ounces of his heart to Christ and has granted no part of his mind to superfluous and transient things proves himself to be confessing with his whole heart. The confession of such a person reaches the divine hearing.

The one who had offered praises to God purely in the sight of human beings begins, after laying aside the body, to sing psalms in the sight of the angels and to worship the holy temple—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells.

He gives thanks to his name because at the name of Jesus every knee bows, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2). What does he confess concerning the holy name? “Your mercy,” he says, “and your truth.”

The soul confesses nothing else to God in the sight of the angels except the mercy by which it was redeemed and by which it was taught the truth. What truth? Without doubt, the truth in which his holy name was magnified above all things. For this is the name that is above every name (Philippians 2).

Let us now see by what order it can be reached. “On whatever day,” he says, “I call upon you, hear me quickly.” And because my soul has been diminished through its weakness, you multiply it by your strength.

For the soul cannot rescue itself from hidden snares and blind pits in which vices rule over those who have fallen into them. Therefore, if we wish to be rescued from the lordship of vices, let us trust in the strength of the Lord, so that he himself may multiply our soul in his strength.

May all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord—that is, all the apostles. They rule over earthly pleasures; for this reason they are called “kings of the earth” in this passage. They are the ones who heard the words from your mouth, Lord Jesus Christ.

They also sing a song to the Lord in songs. He sings of two things: the victory of one side and the destruction of the other. Let them sing, therefore, because great is the glory of the Lord, when, dwelling on the heights of the cross, he looked upon the lowly things of the underworld and knew the heights from afar.

For afterward he saw the underworld and became distant—not only from the heavens but from the earth itself. Descending, he split the depths of the abyss, because he would return from there to those above, and because from the proud he would return to the heavens.

Thus he knew the heights from afar when he deigned to revive us, as we walked in the midst of tribulation, by visiting us, and stretched out his hands against the anger of our enemies, bearing the punishment of the cross, when his right hand saved us.

To him we say: “Lord, repay on my behalf.” For on my behalf you were both born and suffered, Lord. Your mercy is eternal. You did not redeem us by a temporary benefit, but freed us by the eternal help of your mercy.

Do not abandon the works of your hands. We are the works of your hands, because we are your creation. And because the works of your hands had been destroyed through the works of our hands, your hands were fastened to the cross for our sins, so that the works that had perished through the wood of desire might be restored again in the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ by those same hands that had created them and that now, through the wood of the cross, restored them.

He reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0543D]

## PSALM 138

### For the End. A Psalm of David

Lord, you have tested me and known me; you have known my sitting down and my rising up. You understood my thoughts from afar; you investigated my path and my cord. And you foresaw all my ways, because there is no word on my tongue. Behold, Lord, you have known all things, the last and the ancient; you formed me and placed your hand upon me.

Your knowledge has become wondrous through me; it has been strengthened, and I cannot reach it. Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present.

If I take up my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest ends of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me.

And I said: “Perhaps darkness will trample me, and night will be illumination in my pleasures.” For darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illuminated like day; its darkness is like its light.

For you possessed my reins; you received me from my mother’s womb. I will give thanks to you, because you have been greatly and fearfully magnified; your works are wonderful, and my soul knows this exceedingly well.

My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, nor my substance in the lower parts of the earth. Your eyes saw my imperfect state, and in your book all will be written; days will be formed, and no one will be in them.

But your friends, O God, have been honored exceedingly by me; their rule has been strengthened exceedingly. I will number them, and they will multiply beyond the sand. I arose, and I am still with you.

If you kill sinners, O God—men of blood—depart from me. For you say in your thought: “May they receive their cities in vanity.” Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord, and waste away over your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me.

Test me, O God, and know my heart; question me and know my paths. And see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the eternal way.

### COMMENTARY
Lord, you tested me when I entered your service, and you knew that I was your soldier when I fought. But who is a soldier of God is indicated by the blessed Paul, when he approves as God’s soldier the one who withdraws himself from worldly affairs. But since in nearly all the moral Psalms we have set forth a mystical meaning, let us now show its effect in the apostle Peter.

“Lord, you tested me”: you tested me when you called me; you recognized me when I presumed and dared to say, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matthew XXVI). But you knew all my thoughts long before I thought them. You examined my path and my direction; you foresaw and tested all my ways, and that there was no deceit in my tongue when I said, “Even if I had to die with you, I will not deny you” (ibid.).

But you formed me and placed your hand upon me. By your foreknowledge you strengthened me, knowing that I would deny you, and you placed your hand upon me so that sin would be followed by tears. Your foreknowledge became wondrous; it was strengthened from me, and I could not attain to it. I tried not to deny you; I promised that I would even choose to die rather than incur the crime of denial. But your foreknowledge was so firmly established that I could not overcome it.

What shall I do now? I denied the Lord and Master. Nor, as some suppose, did I deny merely a man: I denied the one to whom I had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of God” (John XI); I denied the one whom I had experienced walking upon the waves; I denied the one whom I saw, by his voice alone, calling the dead from the tomb; I denied the one whom I saw, with the heavens opened, together with Moses and Elijah, and over whom I heard the voice of the Father from heaven: “This is my Son; hear him” (Matthew XVII). I denied the one who by his touch enlightened the blind, who cleansed lepers by his word, who by his command [Col. 0545A] cast out demons, and who displayed many works of his divinity.

What shall we do now, Novatian? Shall we cast away the apostle Peter, or shall we receive him when he returns to Christ? Behold, Christ received him, while you cast him out. But Paul cries out against you: “If God justifies, why do you condemn?” (Romans VIII).

You certainly say that baptized people who repent ought not to be helped. Behold, the repentant apostle is helped—he who is the bishop of bishops—and a higher rank is restored to the one who weeps than was taken away from the one who denied. To demonstrate this, I point out that none of the apostles received the name “shepherd.” For the Lord Jesus Christ alone said: “I am the good shepherd”; and again: “My sheep follow me” (John XI).

Therefore, after his resurrection, he granted this holy name and the power of this name to the repentant Peter, and the one who had been denied granted to his denier the power that he alone had possessed. Thus Peter was shown not merely to have recovered what he had lost, but also, by repenting, to have acquired much more than he had lost by denying.

This good teacher gives an example in his chosen one: if Christ’s disciple sins with a wholehearted disposition, he must reject sin; and if it happens that he falls, he must likewise repent with a wholehearted disposition. He must not permit the fault to grow within him, since it is overcome all the more quickly the sooner it is resisted.

Certainly all holiness leads to God, and every sin leads to the devil. Since we have been placed under a good Lord, how can we believe that we have been granted the possibility of going to the devil but denied the possibility of returning to the Lord?

I add another point: certainly God does not wish a human being to withdraw from him through sin, and God wishes the sinner to come to him. If what God does not wish could happen, how much more can what God does wish happen?

Finally, the thought of sin was not prohibited by God through nature, but through the command of his precepts, so that, when the struggle of labor fell upon humanity, a reward might arise from the contest. For God wished to leave human beings the toil of action, lest he prevent the reward in some respect by removing the struggle.

No one is unaware that there are two peoples, of the good and of the wicked. We call believers good, and unbelievers most wicked; unbelievers are under the devil, and believers are under God.

Great indeed is your preaching, Novatian: you call the devil’s servant to yourself, and drive away God’s servant from yourself—as though you wished God to gain what he does not possess and to lose what he possesses. Add this also: that God can raise the dead but cannot save the sick. For unbelievers are dead, while believers, although they are sinners, live in their weakness.

And if our Savior possesses—indeed, because he possesses—the skill to raise the dead, how can he not possess the ability to heal whatever weaknesses there may be?

You blaspheme from both sides when you deny repentant people the benefit of restoration. If you teach that he can heal the illnesses of the soul but does not wish to, you prove him impious; if you perhaps say that he wishes to but cannot, you exclude him from divinity. From both sides condemnation remains for you, since you deny that help can be given to the perishing members of God’s household.

Thus far I have spoken with Novatian. Let us return to the repentant apostle, who weeps most bitterly [Col. 0546A] and says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? I know that you are the Christ, the Son of God; and this knowledge was not revealed to me by flesh and blood, but by your Father who is in heaven” (John VI).

“Where shall I flee?” I know you as God and have acknowledged you as almighty. If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. For there you descended in a particular way through your passion, while by your power you are present there as everywhere in general.

“If I take my wings before the light.” Here he uses “wings” for thoughts, which by sudden flight are everywhere—in heaven, on earth, in the abyss, and wherever the seas end.

“If, therefore,” he says, “I go also into the light of your resurrection, wherever remoteness ordinarily hides a fugitive, so that I may be able to go there, your hand will lead me, and your right hand, as though I were a fugitive, will hold me.”

Here he places “before the light” before the Savior’s resurrection. For the entire world was in darkness while the Lord lay in the tomb, during which time the repentance of the apostle Peter was taking place. At that time he also said: “Perhaps darkness will trample me.”

By his three denials he indicated that three avenues of flight were closed to him, if he were to flee there: in heaven, in hell, and at the farthest limits of the sea. Thus “darkness” means denial, and fleeing is the trampling of darkness.

Fearing this—that, once seized by them, he might be trampled by the darkness itself, and, as though subjected to darkness, might become devoted to the works of darkness, bearing everlasting guilt, continual tears, and eternal sorrows—he says that in this way the darkness of this death is trampled, the death by which we die bodily.

But if, while dying, he says, I am not trampled by the darkness [Col. 0546C] but reach the delights of the saints, that very night of death will become illumination in my delights. There I shall have my light, my Christ, who does not suffer the darkness of shadows; in whose presence night will be illuminated like day. “As its darkness is, so is its light.”

This is directed against Mani, who says that darkness belongs to one ruler and light to another. But of our God we both sing and believe that, as his darkness is, so also is his light.

Darkness does not make all creatures obscure. Nearly all beasts, indeed, and also nocturnal cats [Latin *cartae noctium*, perhaps corrupt], suffer no obscurity; and there are many birds that fly at night. From this we learn that our eyes have received from the Creator this nature: that they cannot see in darkness. For God established nights for human rest, so that provision might be made for the repose of the human race.

Therefore the darkness belongs to the one to whom the light belongs, which Mani denies. He is also the Creator of our bodies, against whom the repentant Peter now says: “You possessed my inward parts; you received me from my mother’s womb.”

Just as, when we speak with our mouth and work at some task, we display the thoughts of our heart, so what we think in the heart is generated in the inward parts before it is revealed by speech or action—according to what we say to God in another Psalm, that he searches not only hearts but also inward parts.

Therefore, when the repentant man says to God, “For you possessed my inward parts,” he says to him: “For nothing in me is hidden from you, so that you consider not only the thoughts that are in the heart, but also the thoughts that are to be conceived in the inward parts—you, Lord, who received me from my mother’s womb. Thus you know whatever I may have sinned from my birth, even in the words of my half-speaking, babbling infancy.”

In this also I confess: “You have been wondrously made terrible to me.” Your works are marvelous; I saw them with my eyes, and I recognized you, Lord Jesus Christ, exercising your power. My soul knows this exceedingly well. Within me is what I have believed—not merely on the surface of words, but inwardly, in the depths of my soul. That this is so is not hidden from you.

Indeed, not even my mouth is hidden from you—that is, my bone, which you made in secret. If even my bone is not hidden from you, which you willed to exist naturally, what will be hidden from you in the heart, when you have commanded it to be revealed?

We are led to higher things when we discuss the bones and the substance that is in the lower parts of the earth. For here the day of resurrection is being described:

“Wherever,” he says, “my bone may be, and wherever my substance may be in the lower parts of the earth, your eyes will see my imperfect state.” My imperfect state—without sinews, without skin, without spirit—your eyes will see; for by the mere sight of your eyes it will rise.

In the book of resurrection all human beings who have been born are written—all who will be formed for that day—and there is no one among them who is not written there.

In that book, no one is dear or honored to me except your friends, O God. For you promise that their dominion will be greatly strengthened, since you promise that they will share in your eternal kingdom.

Nor, as the heretics say, ought the world not to have continued through the one who foreknew that human beings, through their sins and crimes, would be destined for the eternal fires of Gehenna. If you think things ought to have happened in that way, you judge that it would have been more beneficial for the guilty than for the saints.

For if the world had been recalled from its course, none of the saints would have shared in the kingdom. While the wicked were being protected so that they would not come to destruction, the good would have been prevented from reaching glory; and, so that the wicked would not perish according to their deserts, the good would have received this sentence: that they should not even receive temporal life, although eternal life was owed to them.

But let us rejoice with the prophet in God’s saints, and with the Apostle remember the Lord’s friends with the honors they deserve. Their number is so great that they are known to have multiplied beyond the sand.

What, then, if the Lord kills sinners? He killed Nero, and after him all the bloodthirsty men who killed the Lord’s saints.

If God had followed your counsel, O heretics, so that Nero, Diocletian, and the other killers of the saints would not perish, he would not have caused apostles or martyrs to be born. There would have been the same judgment for the unjust and the just, and one sentence would have gone before them all, by which they would all have appeared to be punished before they were born.

But you, bloodthirsty men, withdraw from us—you who say that human beings received their cities in vain, that is, that they became mortal without purpose, and that everything perishes with the world, including destruction itself.

It is not so. All are written in the book. All rise again, but to some there will be given the fragrance of life unto eternal life, and to others the fragrance of death unto perpetual death (II Corinthians II). To the latter belong those of whom it is said: “Have I not hated those who hate you, O God, and was I not wasting away over your enemies?”

Peter speaks these words in the Church, and the Church pronounces them in Peter. “With perfect hatred,” he says, “I hated them; they became enemies to me.” Therefore, after anathematizing them:

“Test me,” he says, “Lord, and know my heart: ask me what I think about you, what I believe about you, and know my paths. Let your concern be for your Church and for your sheep. See whether the way of iniquity is the devil, who offers himself to walk in that way among unbelievers and heretics.

“Look,” he says, “upon your people, lest there be anyone in whom the way of iniquity offers a path to error. And, excluding the way of iniquity, lead me in the eternal way, so that the gates of death and hell may not prevail against me, according to your word” (Matthew XVI), Lord Jesus Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXXXIX

A Psalm of David, for the end.

Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man; rescue me from the unjust man. They who planned iniquities in their heart established battles all day long. They sharpened their tongues like serpents; the venom of asps is under their lips.

Guard me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and rescue me from unjust men. They who planned to trip my feet hid a snare for me, in their pride. They stretched out cords as a snare; beside the path they placed a stumbling block for me.

I said to the Lord: You are my God; hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication. Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you overshadowed my head on the day of battle.

Do not hand me over, Lord, to the sinner’s desire. They have plotted against me; do not abandon me, lest they be exalted. The head of their circuit, the labor of their lips, will cover them. Coals will fall upon them; you will cast them into the fire; they will not endure in miseries.

A man of many words will not be directed upon the earth; evil will seize the unjust man in destruction. I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the poor and vengeance for the needy. Nevertheless, the righteous will confess your name, and the upright will dwell in your presence.

## COMMENTARY

We must take care lest our understanding go to the place where praise of the creature rests by an innate impulse. For the evil one is not himself the devil through creation. If even the devil is not evil by nature, how much more will a wicked human being be proved evil by action and not by birth?

Every nature is the work of God. Every sin, however, is the work of the one who despises him; yet sin itself is not evil by its own nature. For the evil is produced not by the action alone, but by transgression. When forbidden things are done, they are assigned to the wrath of the one who prohibited them and condemned by his judgment.

Indeed, the forbidden acts themselves make the perpetrator guilty, whether they concern good or evil matters. Murder occupies the highest place among human evils, while mercy occupies the highest place among goods; yet both can be charged as crimes.

Cain is cast away from God’s presence for having killed; Saul is excluded from the kingdom for not having killed. You may say that these matters could perhaps have been established among the ancients. But now, in every person, mercy is proved to be a virtue, while we teach, on the contrary, that under the spiritual judgment of the present time one is punished more severely than formerly by the sword.

For by the sword life is taken—at most, a life of fifty years; but by the slaughter of anathema, eternal life is taken away and perpetual death is inflicted.

Who could doubt that the one who spares heresiarchs or preachers of falsehood, and does not slaughter them with the sword of his faith, will suffer what happened to Saul? Or who could deny that the one who thinks he is showing mercy to those who persist in heresy will likewise be excluded from the kingdom of God, just as Saul is shown to have been excluded from the human kingdom?

Who, moreover, would doubt that Cain is his partner, since he dared, through envy, to condemn the righteous? For the authority of apostolic speech affirms that everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (I John III).

The scale of just judgment, therefore, weighed in an equal balance, shows that when it kills the guilty and frees the innocent, it displays both unjust mercy toward the wicked and cruelly inflicted slaughter toward the godly.

When a deed committed by the wicked is condemned, God is shown to have been despised. The deeds are rightly condemned not according to the quality of human action, but according to the authority of divine command: if they were forbidden, they are rightly condemned; if they were commanded, they are rightly praised.

Thus murder is evil in Abel but good in Goliath. A lie is good in Judith but evil against Susanna. The use of marriage is good among the married, but evil among adulterers. Serpentine cunning is good against the wicked but evil against the good.

Every work, even a holy one, is a crime when undertaken presumptuously, even if it appears suited to the mysteries themselves. For what is as holy as receiving the communion of Christ? And what is as wicked as an unbaptized person receiving it? Or what is as magnificent as celebrating the divine sacraments? And what is as harmful as having them celebrated by one who has received no rank of office?

Having been given this opportunity to address the wise, we have made it clear in every respect that nothing is evil except what God prohibits, and nothing is good except what God commands. When a person commits what is prohibited or disregards what is commanded, the action makes him evil.

Therefore, when he said, “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man,” he set forth the evil man’s actions, so that wicked people might be revealed not by the quality of their nature but by the wickedness of their deeds.

He says: “Lord, free me from those who have planned wickedness in their heart.” The accusation of birth ceases where the perversity of thought is rebuked.

“All day long,” he says, “they established battle.” When you hear “battle,” beware of the combatants, whether you see them or not. For you should know that those whom you see are aroused through those whom you do not see. Those whom you see are human beings; those whom you do not see are evil spirits.

Therefore fight against those who are fighting. And if you seek help from the king, show yourself resisting.

Tongues fight against you, sharpened by heretics like serpents. Be like a clever serpent toward them also, and show yourself simple as a dove to your fellow citizens—that is, to Catholics alone.

But toward heretics and all who come against the truth, be more cunning than the serpents themselves. Do not fear: your Lord has commanded you. Cunning against wickedness is as good as benign simplicity toward justice.

Kill the heretics, and destroy the enemies of your Lord with his spiritual sword. For what do the enemies of God—that is, unclean spirits—do? They wish to exclude the Lord from his temple, that is, the Holy Spirit. They themselves wish to dwell there—that is, in you. You are the temple of God.

And what do heretics attempt? They wish to exclude truth from you and to shut deception within you. Kill both: overcome false assertions with true assertions, and conquer the suggestions of demons with the judgments of divine law.

But since you have learned that demons can be overcome by fasting and prayers, maintain the order of battle, as the present Psalm teaches you.

“For the proud have hidden snares for me.” Why “proud”? Because they despise God. How have they hidden them? They make what is bitter appear sweet and what is evil seem good.

“And they have stretched out cords as a trap for my feet.” You are clearly instructed about the feet of the mind. The cords are the assertions of heretics, with which they try to fasten bonds to holy steps through syllogisms, so that what is false may appear true to you.

The cords are also the suggestions of demons; whoever consents to them will be bound by them.

“Beside the path,” he says, “they placed a stumbling block for me.” Along the path of one walking in chastity comes the goad of fornication. Along the path of one pursuing truth comes the assertion of falsehood.

What shall we do about this? Cry out: “Overshadow my head, Lord, on the day of battle.” Be my helmet, covering my head, so that I may not be handed over to the sinner’s desire.

“For they have plotted against me. Do not hand me over, lest they ever be exalted. The head of their circuit—but the labor of their lips will cover them,” so that they may be convicted by their own assertions.

For example, demons say through their suggestions: “A sweet embrace, a pleasant kiss, delightful fornication.” I shall say to them: “It is the pleasure of one hour—or rather, of one moment—but it is destruction leading to eternal death.”

For example, heretics say in their assertions: “The Father is greater; the Son is lesser.” I shall answer: “The one who is greater grows old and declines; the one who is lesser grows young and likewise grows greater, so that he may cease to be lesser.”

But God is neither lesser nor greater, because just as he has no end, so he had no beginning. The Father was always unchangeable, and there was always one of whom he was Father; he was never without the Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Father was never without goodness, which is the Son; he was never without holiness, which is the Holy Spirit.

By these assertions of yours, then, the labor of their lips will cover them, and coals of fire will fall upon them, in unclean spirits, so that they may be burned in heretics and schismatics and return to their Lord.

But if the perverse advocate persists in his assertions, and the man of many words is not directed upon the earth—that is, while he is in the body, if the man of many words does not turn his tongue away from wicked assertions—then, having become unjust, he will be followed by a sentence corresponding to his injustice, so that evils may cover him unto eternal destruction.

For I know that the Lord will execute judgment for the poor—certainly for those who fall into error simply, who, worn down by poverty of understanding, receive the poisonous food of heresy as nourishment.

What, then, shall we think? Will the future judgment strike only those who hand poisonous food to the hungry? I think the sentence applies even more to those who do not refresh them with healthy food.

For if Catholic teachers refreshed them, heretics would not be able to snatch them away. Thus this speech threatening judgment touches us more than them.

It is we—yes, I say, we—who are roused by this goad of warning, by which God is said to execute judgment for the poor and vengeance for the needy.

For, as the prophet testifies, he will say: “Behold, you ate the milk, and clothed yourselves with wool” (Ezekiel XXXIV), while my sheep were attacked by wolves; and because you did not provide healthy pastures, poisonous grasses were provided for them by my enemies.

Therefore let all who can give useful food to the hungry beware. Let them beware, I say, because if they do not receive life-giving nourishment from these people, they will receive deadly food from their enemies; and we shall be judged in the judgment that will be judgment for the poor and vengeance for the needy.

Then, without doubt, the righteous will confess the holy name, and the upright will dwell with Christ, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXL

A Psalm of David.

Lord, I have cried to you; hear me. Attend to my voice when I cry to you. Let my prayer be directed like incense in your presence; let the lifting of my hands be an evening sacrifice.

Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth and a door of enclosure around my lips. Do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness, to make excuses for sins with men who work iniquity; and I will not share in their chosen things.

The righteous man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let the sinner’s oil not fatten my head. For even now my prayer is directed against their good pleasures. Their judges, joined to the rock, have been swallowed up.

They will hear my words, for they are powerful, just as the richness of the earth bursts forth upon the earth. Our bones have been scattered beside hell, because my eyes are toward you, Lord; in you I have hoped. Do not take away my soul.

Guard me from the snare they have hidden for me and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity. Sinners will fall into his net; I alone remain until I pass over.

## COMMENTARY

The sequence of the Psalm, having taken up the theme of faith, extends into the text of the present Psalm. There he said: “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man,” and so forth. Here: “Lord, I have cried to you; hear me.”

And to show that he had spoken about heretics, who plan wickedness in their heart, here he says: “Do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness, but set a guard over my mouth and a door of protection over my lips,” lest, while zealously attempting to defend the truth, I try to produce many speeches, offend someone, and share in the lot of those who work iniquity.

But since I ask not to associate with their chosen ones, grant me your correction, so that there may be a righteous man who commands me, whose example may correct my error.

God’s gift is incomparable when any righteous person is shown to us upon the face of the earth. God, rich in all things, has servants—kind and righteous servants, I say—but we are not worthy to know them.

Blessed is the person who is permitted to know a servant of God who corrects in mercy and rebukes in the love of God.

But woe to me and to those like me, because we anoint one another’s heads with oil, flattering one another while we live in the present, calling ourselves saints when we are not. When absent, however, we bite and strike one another so that we may rightly be compared to dogs.

“Let their oil,” he says—that is, their flattery—not anoint my head. Rather, let my prayer concern their good pleasure: I pray that I may not approve what pleases those who have been swallowed up beside the rock.

Their judges are heretics beside the rock, not upon the rock. For if they were upon the rock, they could not be swallowed up. But now, abandoning the foundation of the solid rock, they build beside the rock upon sand; there they construct their nests and are swallowed up together with their young.

“Let them not excuse themselves,” says the prophetic speech, “but let them hear my words, for they are powerful.” They possess meaning, intelligence, and understanding. Let them hear my words and lay aside their own. Let them hear and open their ears to my words.

Just as the richness of the earth erupts upon the earth wherever the soil is thin and mixed with dust and sand, so that it does not burst forth, but fertile earth opens itself so widely that it displays its mouth open toward heaven, eagerly receiving whatever is sent from heaven—so, he says, let them hear my words as the richness of the earth erupts in the produce of grain, wine, and oil, and as its fertility below erupts above it.

“Our bones have been scattered beside hell.” The Greek says, “their bones.” Therefore, whether our bones or their bones, they are scattered when placed beside hell.

Just as wax placed beside a fire softens, while in the fire the mass melts and disappears, so our bones, placed beside hell, soften; but in hell the masses melt.

For they are beside hell when we are beside those who provide us with fuel for sinning: when we do not resist thoughts that shamefully thrust themselves upon the mind; when the difference of sex disturbs our society; when we join ourselves to those who do not approve the course of Christian discipline; or when we join ourselves to heretics and, under the appearance of friendship, seem to enter into conflict with them, rather than fighting with open face as Romans fight against barbarians.

There our bones, placed beside hell and situated next to hell itself, are scattered. But if we are joined to any of these through such proximity, not only our bones but our very soul is scattered.

Let us therefore say with a cry: “To you, Lord, Lord, my eyes are turned; in you I have hoped. Do not take away my soul.” Do not take it out of the book of life, where the Catholics are, and insert it into the book of death, where the assemblies of heretics are condemned.

“But guard me from the snare they have set for me and from the stumbling blocks of those who work iniquity.” There they have stretched out a net in order to catch people in one of the ways mentioned above—there where sinners fall. Having been made separate from them, may I live alone until I depart or pass over.

For it is better for me to have a solitary way of life that possesses life than, by living among a multitude, to incur death. One must live alone where the society of the present life opposes the benefits of eternal life.

Let us pray earnestly to escape from that net, so that our prayer may be directed in the presence of God like the incense of perfume. For in Greek it is sung thus: “Let our prayer be directed in the presence of God like incense”—that is, so that he may receive the sacrifice of our prayer as a pleasing fragrance.

Let our sacrifice be an evening sacrifice—that is, toward the end of this light, at the hour when we depart from this light. Then we are in the evening sacrifice. There we must place the entire intention of our thought, so that, raising our hands in the sign of the cross as we go to the Lord, we may rejoice in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns in the unity of the Godhead with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXLI

An understanding of David, when he was in the cave: a prayer.

With my voice I cried to the Lord; with my voice I pleaded with the Lord. I pour out my prayer in his presence, and I declare my tribulation before him.

When my spirit failed within me, you knew my paths. Along this way in which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me. I looked toward the right and saw, and there was no one who knew me. Refuge has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul.

I cried to you, Lord; I said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. Attend to my supplication, for I have been humbled exceedingly. Deliver me [Col. 0553C] from those who persecute me, for they have grown strong against me.

Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may confess your name. The righteous await me until you repay me.

## COMMENTARY

When David was hiding from Saul’s presence as a fugitive in a cave, he is said to have sung this Psalm.

“With my voice,” he says, “I cried to the Lord, and with my voice I pleaded with the Lord. I pour out my prayer in his presence and declare my tribulation before him.”

“For in the failing of my spirit,” he says, “there you knew my paths.”

There, Christian, cry out; there pour out your prayer in the presence of God; there declare your tribulation—not over lost possessions, wealth, the boundaries of fields, or those things that are utterly unnecessary to us once the body has been laid aside, but in the failing of your spirit. There be concerned.

For there your paths are known. The failing of our spirit occurs when the necessities or pleasures of bodily things invade us. There snares have been hidden for us by the devil and his ministers.

Then we look toward the right—that is, toward reading, prayer, and the Psalm—and we take no pleasure in them. We return so sorrowful that we can scarcely recognize ourselves. The very letters of the sacred writings become foreign to us, and, as though placed outside ourselves, we are unable to recognize ourselves.

Then refuge has perished from us, and we do not pass by with deaf ears that which the Apostle cries to us: “Flee fornication” (I Corinthians VI). For evil is within; the enemy is within.

Then, when this flight has perished from us, there is no thought or compunction arising from any affection that seeks the soul. Nor does it return to my understanding so that I may seek my soul and say to it: “Come, do not lose my deeds, for which you have labored so long.”

This is what I now say. Why? Because my spirit failed within me at the time when, along the way in which I walked, they hid snares for me.

And because refuge has perished from me, I shall have nothing else by which I can escape unless with all my strength I cry to you, Lord: “Let everything in the world perish; you are my hope; you are my portion in the land of the living.”

Attend to my prayer, for I have been humbled exceedingly. My sins hold me, and they have placed their yoke upon me—the leaders of vices and crimes through my sins.

You, deliver me from those who persecute me, for they have grown strong against me, and bring my soul out of prison.

Our soul suffers imprisonment when worldly occupations or bodily pleasures close us in from every side, shutting us off from reading, prayer, or a good course of life.

Nor do we dare, as some think, to call the human body a prison, since the apostle Paul testifies that it is the temple of God (II Corinthians XVI). Rather, we suffer imprisonment when we take no pleasure in praying, when we grow weary of spiritual food, and when we fail, confined now by the barriers of earthly necessities, now by the doors of pleasures.

The true prison of the soul is within you. For this reason we must cry to Christ with all our strength, so that he may lead our souls out of this prison to confess his name.

Then the delight of confession may begin to cultivate the soul that has been abandoned, since the cultivation of prayer, reading, and spiritual exercise has ceased.

Therefore, when you have led my soul out of this prison and I have begun to confess your name in an upright course, then the righteous will await me until you repay me in Christ Jesus our Lord, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## PSALM CXLII

A Psalm of David, when his son Absalom was persecuting him.

Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness. And do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight. For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has humbled my life to [Col. 0554D] the earth. He has placed me in dark places like those who have been dead from of old, and my spirit has been distressed within me; my heart has been troubled within me. I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works, and I pondered the deeds of your hands. I stretched out my hands toward you; my soul is like earth without water before you. Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall become like those descending into the pit. Make your mercy known to me in the morning, for I have hoped in you. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you. Deliver me from my enemies, Lord, for I have fled to you; teach me to do your will, for you are my God. Your good Spirit will lead me into a straight land; for your name’s sake, [Col. 0555A] Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness. You will bring my soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy you will destroy all my enemies. And you will destroy all who trouble my soul, for I am your servant.

## Commentary

Thus the Psalmist began, in order to put the whole human race in fear. For who would dare say to God, “Hear me in your truth, and in your righteousness”? It is indeed true and just that whoever has sinned should be punished most severely. You began, prophet, with such an opening, joining to it something that follows, so that we who sing the psalms may breathe again. “Do not enter,” he says, “into judgment with your servant.” This, then, is what you wished to say: Your righteousness is that you, Lord, should disdain to enter into judgment with your servant. For who [Col. 0555B] will be justified in comparison with you, even if a person is holy, chosen, pure, and praiseworthy in your sight—that is, in comparison with you? Neither divine judgments nor human judgments can establish such a person. For every beauty is deformed in your presence; every strength is weakness in your presence; all riches are poverty in your presence; all human righteousness is unrighteousness in your presence.

And so that you may cease to seek a human righteousness near to your righteousness, I ask this: since the enemy has pursued my soul, he has humbled my life to the earth—that is, in the body—and has placed me in darkness like one dead from of old. He surrounded me with so great a darkness of his deceit that, I believed myself dead before God and thought that I would find no hearing for recovery before your righteousness. [Col. 0555C] Therefore my spirit was distressed within me, and my heart was troubled within me.

I began to remember the days of old, how often you deigned to come to the aid of the afflicted because of your mercy. And I meditated on all those works by which I learned that you help all who entreat you. Therefore I stretched out my hands toward you, because my soul had become dry in sins like earth without water, as though it had no water of baptism.

“Hear me quickly, Lord; my spirit has failed”—that is, spiritual life within me has failed. “Do not turn your face away from me, and I shall be like those descending into the pit”—that is, I shall be like those condemned to death. Yet I shall not be a partaker of their fate, but only like them: like them because I have sinned, but not a partaker because I have fled to your mercy.

Therefore make your mercy [Col. 0555D] known to me in the morning, for I have hoped in you, Lord. He said “in the morning” because we suffer night and darkness for as long as divine compassion pierces us and the kindness of mercy grants forgiveness. But when the voice of the penitent begins to be heard and the light of the one who forgives is revealed, every night departs and the beginning of light draws near. In that light we do not wander; rather, placed as though in the daytime, we walk honorably.

For he will make known to us the way in which we should walk in the light, if we lift up our souls to him. Just as those placed in darkness need light, so those placed in the light need a guide who will free them from error. Therefore those who are in the light must say, “Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for I have lifted up my soul to you. Deliver me from my enemies, for I have fled to you.”

Whoever goes to a patron [Col. 0556A] asks to be delivered by him in this way: he entreats him that he may know the patron’s will. For the one received by a patron is uncertain if he has not also declared his will. And therefore, after saying to God, “I have fled to you,” he added, “Teach me to do your will.” Do you wish, then, O human being, to have the Lord as your patron? Learn his will. Do what he wills, and he will do what you will.

We have therefore said to our patron, “Deliver me from my enemies.” Unclean spirits are our enemies; they flee from us when they perceive the Holy Spirit within us. Therefore the Holy Spirit must be entreated to lead us into the land. For the land of our body is straight when the Holy Spirit is in it. And whenever the evil spirit offers us his own way to walk, he will lead us into a straight [Col. 0556B] land. And if our merits are lacking—indeed, because they are lacking—he nevertheless gives us life in his righteousness for the sake of his name.

By this judgment of his righteousness he determines to destroy all our enemies, who are our enemies for this reason: because we strive to be servants of the Lord. “For this reason,” he says, “you will destroy all my enemies: because I am your servant.” We do not therefore have enemies because of anything else, nor adversaries on account of merely earthly actions; rather, we suffer the hostility of demons and human beings because we strive to be servants of the Lord.

Let us not fear their hostility, because when they perish we shall be delivered by Christ our Lord, who reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and forever, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 143

*A Psalm of David against Goliath.*

Blessed is the Lord, my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war. He is my mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer; he is my defender, and in him I have hoped, who subjects my people beneath me.

Lord, what is a human being, that you have made yourself known to him, or a son of man, that you regard him? Human beings have become like vanity; their days pass away like a shadow.

Lord, incline your heavens and descend; touch the mountains, and they will smoke. Flash forth lightning and scatter them; send out your arrows, and you will trouble them. Send out your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me from many waters and from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand [Col. 0556D] is a right hand of iniquity.

God, I will sing a new song to you; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to you. You give salvation to kings; you have redeemed David, your servant. Deliver me from the evil sword, and rescue me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

Their sons are like young plants in their youth; their daughters are adorned and decorated like the likeness of a temple. Their storehouses are full, overflowing from one thing to another. Their sheep are fertile and abundant in their folds; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passageway, and no cry in their streets. They have called that people blessed which possesses these things. Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.

[Col. 0557A]

## Commentary

“Blessed is the Lord, my God, who taught my hands for battle.” At the time when Moses lifted his hands to God, the multitude of the Philistines who were fighting was defeated; but when he lowered them, those who had been defeated began to conquer. He therefore taught our hands to fight in battle, not with weapons but with prayers.

He also taught our fingers for war, so that whenever we perceive the warfare of visible or invisible enemies, we may arm our foreheads with our fingers with the triumph of the cross and fight with a secure spirit, saying to the Lord: “You are my mercy; you are my refuge; you are my protector; you are my deliverer. For you will place peoples beneath me.” You will place beneath me the hostile people of evil thoughts rising against me.

But why is fighting [Col. 0557B] mentioned? Why battle? Why war? And what did the eternal God wish to make known to humanity, if humanity has become like vanity? It dies, and its days pass away like a shadow. What, then, is the law? What is the threat to sinners? What is the terror for unbelievers, if a life lasting only a few days reaches its end and will have no further effect?

Hearing this, the apostle Paul rebukes us, saying: “If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore hear what the present psalm understands. It is as though it says: Because human beings do not believe your prophets and preachers when they proclaim that there is eternal life, you yourself incline your heavens and descend.

When did he incline the heavens? When he was in the form of God and was equal to God the Father, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. [Col. 0557C] 2). He inclined the heavens—as one might say to an emperor, “When you humble yourself, you incline the whole palace.” He therefore inclined the heavens and descended, so that he might touch the mountains and they might smoke.

The smoke of the mountains creates clouds, which God brings forth from his treasuries and pours upon the earth, so that the earth may produce every kind of fruit with which the bodies of the hungry are nourished. When God descended in Christ to reconcile the world to himself (2 Cor. 5), he touched the mountains and they smoked. That is, he touched his apostles, and they gave forth the smoke of clouds. Their rain was so abundant throughout the whole world that the channels of the springs were filled, by which every crime was washed away and every sin cleansed.

But since the ruler of this world prevents us from reaching him, together with his spirits and the human beings who [Col. 0557D] worship him, send your arrows against him and deliver me from many waters, so that I may enjoy the one fountain of baptism. Deliver me from the hand of the Philistines, whose mouth speaks vanity and whose right hand is not a hand of mercy, since it strips the clothed and deprives them either of temporal riches or—what is more bitter—of eternal riches.

“When you have delivered me from them,” he says, “Lord, I will sing to you in a new song,” that is, walking in newness of life. “On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to you,” receiving the ten commandments of the law and fleeing Egypt, struck by the ten plagues. I will sing praise to you—yes, I will sing praise to you—who give salvation to kings, that is, who give eternal life to the conquerors of vices. For those are truly kings who are believed to share in the kingdom of God.

Who [Col. 0558A] else, then, delivers them except the same God who delivered David, his servant? Marcion denies that this is the same God; likewise Apelles, Valentinus, and Manichaeus. Unbelieving and wretched, they do not fear eternal damnation, although they refuse to be delivered by the Lord himself. May the one who delivered David himself deliver us from them, because their mouth speaks vanity and, as we said above, their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.

Here he certainly asserts that they speak vanity because they ridicule and abuse the poverty of those who serve God, saying: “Why do those who worship the Lord suffer hunger? And why do those who despise him abound in riches?” They do not understand that the physician commands frugality and prescribes abstinence for those in whom he detects health in the movement of their veins. But those whom they recognize as destined to die, they allow to indulge in all their [Col. 0558B] pleasures.

How can you say of such people that they rejoice in strong sons, adorned daughters, full storehouses, fertile sheep, and fat oxen? Although they possess every temporal thing, they do not deserve to have the Lord, who is eternal, favorable to them. When they have reached the end of temporal joy, they take upon themselves the punishments of eternal sorrow.

By contrast, those whom you see mourning and weeping, and who live in the fear of God in poverty, when they have finished weeping, are received by the fruit of eternal joy. Let unbelievers call blessed the people who abundantly possess the things of the world; but let us call only that people blessed whose God is the Lord throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 144

[Col. 0558C]

*A Praise of David.*

I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name forever and throughout the age of the age. Every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name forever and throughout the age of the age. Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness.

Generation after generation will praise your works, and they will declare your power. They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of your holiness, and they will recount your wonders. They will proclaim the power of your fearful deeds, and they will tell of your greatness. They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they will rejoice in your judgments.

The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundantly merciful. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works. Let all your works give thanks to you, Lord, and let your holy [Col. 0558D] ones bless you. They will speak of the glory of your kingdom, and they will proclaim your power, so that they may make your power known to the sons of human beings, and the glory of the magnificence of your kingdom.

Your kingdom is a kingdom throughout all ages, and your dominion is in every generation and generation. The Lord is faithful in all his words and holy in all his works. The Lord raises up all who fall and lifts up all who have been cast down.

The eyes of all hope in you, Lord, and you give them their food at the proper time. You open your hand and fill every living creature with blessing. The Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth. He will do the will of those who fear him, and he will hear their prayer [Col. 0559A] and save them.

The Lord guards all who love him, and he will destroy all sinners. My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and throughout the age of the age.

## Commentary

God is exalted by a human being when that person does not humble the Holy Spirit, whom he received within himself through the consecration of sacred baptism, with earthly and lowly thoughts, but exalts him with heavenly desires and lofty aspirations. Thus he blesses the Lord every day and, as one who has only recently begun, serves him without weariness. Generation after generation confesses him: the generation of the Jews and the generation of the nations.

The former, in the law of Moses and the prophets; the latter, in the teaching of the Gospels [Col. 0559B] and the apostles, will proclaim the power of your fearful deeds, so that they may make your power known to the sons of human beings. They will show that your kingdom, Lord, is a kingdom throughout all ages, and that your dominion extends through every generation and lineage, so that there is no nation or kingdom in which your Son is not proclaimed.

For you are faithful, Lord, in the words by which you promised that you would give us one who would raise up all who fall in this world and lift up all whom the enemy had cast down. The eyes of all believers hope in you, Lord. “By hope we were saved” (Rom. 8), and you gave them food at the proper time when you opened your hands on the cross. You took our curses upon yourself and gave us your blessings.

You are near to all—to all, I say, who call upon you [Col. 0559C] in truth, that is, to those who call upon you in our Lord Jesus Christ. For he is the truth. You will do the will of those who do not despise you, and you will hear their prayer, in which they entreat you for eternal things.

“The Lord guards,” he says, “all who love him.” Let us see who those are who love him; let us ask him, and let him himself say who those are who love him. Let us hear him saying: “Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (Matt. 7; John 14). But those who do not do them he will reject from himself and destroy—all such sinners.

Therefore let our mouth speak the praise of the Lord; let all slander depart from it. Let us remember those things that we know are worthy of praise in our brothers. Let other people find witnesses for the sins of others; but let us become our own accusers and our own reprovers alone, [Col. 0559D] always occupied with the praises and blessings of God, giving thanks to him throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 145

*Alleluia.*

Praise the Lord, my soul. I will praise the Lord during my life; I will sing praise to my God as long as I exist. Do not trust in princes, nor in the sons of human beings, in whom there is no salvation. His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish.

Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. He keeps truth forever; he executes judgment for those who suffer wrong; he gives food [Col. 0560A] to the hungry.

The Lord releases those in chains. The Lord gives light to the blind. The Lord raises up those who have been cast down. The Lord loves the righteous. The Lord guards strangers; he will receive the orphan and the widow, and he will destroy the ways of sinners. The Lord reigns forever, your God, Zion, from generation to generation.

## Commentary

Our soul praises the Lord when our works are exercised in the praises of God. We praise the Lord in our life—that is, in our conduct. Let us therefore sing praise to our God as long as we are in this body, not trusting in human beings who rule today and are buried tomorrow. Their spirit will go out, and they will return to the earth from which they were taken; on that very day their thoughts perish.

Those are the thoughts that [Col. 0560B] did not allow them to rest: “Let us buy, let us sell, let us build, let us fight.” These and similar kinds of thoughts perish in a single sudden moment.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who places his hope in the Lord God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them. For he keeps truth forever. At the time when deceitful people think they can conquer through falsehood, he guards the truth, so that he may execute judgment on those for whom truth does not perish, either in this age or in the age to come.

For this reason we also believe that he will come as judge: because he guards the truth, so that he may then execute judgment for those who suffer wrong. He who now gives food to the hungry himself raises up those cast down through Adam, and through that same one he releases those in chains. He gives light to the blind; he directs the righteous; he guards strangers.

These are those who present themselves as foreigners in this [Col. 0560C] world and long for the homeland for which they have been reborn. He will guard the orphan who, for the name of God, abandons the parents of his flesh. He himself, who is your God, Zion, will destroy the devil, who is the way of sinners.

He is the God of the catholic Church, one in Trinity and triune in unity, who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 146

*Alleluia.*

Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good; let praise be sweet and beautiful to our God. The Lord builds Jerusalem; he will gather the dispersed of Israel. He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.

Great is our Lord, and great is his power; [Col. 0560D] there is no measure of his wisdom. The Lord receives the meek, but he humbles sinners to the earth. Sing beforehand to the Lord in confession; sing praise to our God on the lyre.

He covers the heavens with clouds and prepares rain for the earth. He brings forth grass on the mountains and plants for the service of human beings. He gives their food to the beasts and to the young ravens that call upon him.

He will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse, nor will the legs of a man be pleasing to him. The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy.

## Commentary

Let us praise the Lord, for the psalm is good. The [Col. 0561A] psalm is good in which there is rejoicing for our God. For the Lord builds Jerusalem and gathers the dispersed of Israel. Every day the Lord builds her; every day he builds his Church through believers. Calling back to her those who have been dispersed from her, he joins them again to the congregation.

He heals repentant people who are brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls all of them by name. Although the power of his might is prepared for these works, and no one doubts that he can do them except one who does not believe him to be omnipotent, nevertheless let us understand him to number the multitude of the stars in the saints: those who, placed in the darkness of the world, direct their courses through heaven, giving the comfort of their luminous appearance to those who look toward heaven. [Col. 0561B]

These stars shine more or less brightly according to the merit of their deeds. In them our great Lord is shown, and his great power. For through a human being he is magnified by human beings, and through a human being he is blasphemed by human beings. Just as those through whom the Lord’s name is blasphemed are under a woe, so those through whom his great power is displayed and his immeasurable wisdom is declared are blessed.

Through this wisdom he casts down the proud, receives the meek, and humbles sinners to the earth, so that he may raise them from earth to heaven. For “everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14)—that is, whoever repents and confesses his sins to the Lord.

Begin, then, with confessions to the Lord, and sing praise to him on the lyre. The lyre has the wood of the cross; it has strings from the innermost parts of sheep; it has a plectrum from the Gospels. Let this lyre sound and announce the rain coming from heaven.

For he covered the [Col. 0561C] heavens with clouds—that is, he entrusted the appearance of his heavens to his apostles and commanded them to give rain to the earth, drenching all earthly nations with heavenly rain in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

This rain brings forth on the mountains grass with which the simpler people may be nourished, since the greater part of them is approved among the people of God. Those who are occupied with earthly actions, though they appear to be members of the Church, cannot be nourished with spiritual food.

These mountains—that is, the apostles—offer the solid food of heavenly things from the heights of their minds. “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Heb. 5). Who could debate with them concerning perseverance in fasting, occupation by day and by night joined to divine learning? Who could debate with them concerning the subtleties of suggestions? Who concerning contempt for all passing things? Who concerning contempt for all [Col. 0561D] vices?

Who could discuss with them invisible progress, so that a person may be a bishop of God or a priest of Christ through the invisible efforts and steps established in his heart, ascending as long as he departs from this body and never descending, offering his body to God as a living sacrifice? Each day he joins himself to the body of Christ in such a way that, according to the Apostle, his body, mixed with the body of Christ, becomes one body (1 Cor. 10).

These and similar things are given as food to those who can say with Paul: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6).

As we have therefore shown the solid food of spiritual things belonging to mature men, let us now show the grass of the beasts that the mountains mentioned above [Col. 0562A] produce.

“Whatever is sold in the marketplace, buy [eat], without asking questions” (1 Cor. 10). Again: “Who are you, that you grieve your brother by eating?” Again: “Whoever cannot exercise self-control should marry” (1 Cor. 7). Again: “He who gives his daughter in marriage does well” (ibid.). Again: “I want younger widows to marry” (1 Tim. 5).

This grass the mountains, which are close to heaven and, placed on earth, say, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3), produce for beasts, over which carnal custom alone exercises command. And a law is imposed upon that carnal custom: following it, a wife pleases her husband, a slave pleases his master, carnal children their carnal parents, and carnal parents their carnal children.

Grass is offered and given to these beasts as food, and to the young of ravens that call upon him. For our fathers were ravens, who [Col. 0562B] remained in the blackness of idolatry and never returning to the ark. But we are their young, and we call upon the Lord.

“He will not take pleasure in the strength of a horse.” For one who does not fight against us with earthly strength cannot be conquered by earthly strength. The strength of the horse, therefore, is earthly strength, in which God did not wish anyone to glory in self-confidence, but permitted him to hope in God’s mercy.

“Nor,” he says, “will the legs of a man be pleasing to him”—that is, confidence in his own dwelling. Accordingly, the Greek does not say “in dwellings” but “in legs.” Thus, whether a person trusts in the running of a horse or presumes upon his own legs, the Lord will despise him.

We express the meaning more broadly as follows: Whoever trusts in the freedom of his will, thinking that by means of it he can flee, encounters the one pursuing him. Whoever trusts in the strength of his [Col. 0562C] spiritual running, thinking that he can remain immovable by standing on his own legs, does not remain.

In saying this I do not exclude the command, “Strive to stand”; rather, I warn you not to think that you can flee by free will alone. Let the horse run; let it be prepared for battle. For it is written: “The horse is prepared for the day of battle, but the Lord grants salvation” (Prov. 21).

Yet while you run, say: “God gave strength to my horse, so that it might run. God gave perseverance to my legs, so that I might stand.”

Do not therefore think that your freedom of will possesses you in such a way that it is like a ship by which you wish to escape the barbarians from the shore, by which you wish to escape the waves of the sea, and by which you wish to reach the homeland you desire. But if the Lord commands favorable winds and gives silence to adverse blasts; if he reveals hidden shallows, takes away sleep [Col. 0562D] from the sailors who steer, and brings the ship into harbor without injury, then afterward give thanks to God, not to the ship; give thanks to God, not to the sailor (Rom. 10).

In saying this we do not exclude the ship and the sailors; rather, we adorn both the ship and the sailors by confessing God as their ruler. For if there had been no ship, there would have been nothing for the Lord to steer. If there had been no sailors, there would have been no one for the Lord to rouse. If there had been no sails, there would have been nothing upon which he could bestow favorable winds.

Let us therefore say: If there is not in you the freedom of a good will, the peace of God will not be with you. For on earth there is peace of God among people of good will.

It is objected to this passage that we speak in such a way as to appear to show that human will precedes the grace of God. Act [Col. 0563A] attentively, not maliciously, and observe the general grace of God poured out over the entire human race.

Grace precedes everyone, diffused in manifold generosity. God descended from heaven when humanity did not will it. He taught by example and word when humanity did not ask. He performed many signs and mighty works to reveal himself, even when humanity opposed him. He assumed our mortality while humanity was ignorant. Mocked, crucified, killed among murderers, buried, he rose again and ascended into heaven.

Christ carried out all these things for human salvation, human liberation, human redemption, the human crown, and human glory. Take note, malicious critic, that I say: “for the salvation of a human being who neither wills nor runs.”

What, then, is it that we read? We have shown that the general [Col. 0563B] grace of God precedes the good will of all human beings. Take note, predestinarian, of what I am saying: the grace of Christ, in the order we have described, precedes the good will of all people in general—if indeed he was born for all, if indeed he suffered for all; if you do not deny that he died for all; if, with the Apostle, you affirm that he wills all human beings to be saved (1 Tim. 2).

Now leave general grace and approach the particular, and cry out with the Apostle in the same way: Not every human being in general will be saved, but “every person who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Go, then, to the physician’s workshop, to the one who came of his own accord to our city. Without our asking, the physician came to all of us, opened his workshop, and sent forth a voice with which, as though proclaiming like a herald, he said: “Come [Col. 0563C] to me, all” (Matt. 11).

Now, after this voice, the will precedes grace. For he says: “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land. But if you are unwilling, the sword shall consume you” (Isa. 1).

Therefore, just as grace preceded human will in its self-revelation and in the opening of truth, so human will precedes the grace of God. For you are not first baptized and then begin to wish to believe; rather, you first present your perfected will to the priest, disclose your confession with your lips, and only then approach the grace of God in order to receive it.

Having received it, you will confess that you obtained all God’s gifts by believing and desiring.
