And then at last you will sing the final words of this psalm: “For the Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him and in those who hope in his mercy [Col. 0563D].” Wishing to exclude human self-exaltation, he expressed the will of the Divinity.

For God knows that our enemy can creep upon us when he finds us without divine fear. Therefore, as a remedy for us, he pronounced this saying, as though he were saying: “God takes pleasure in those who are delivered from the devil.”

God is not moved by a feeling that he should be feared by human beings; rather, being wholly devoted to showing mercy to humanity, he wishes what he knows with certainty will benefit humanity to be brought about through the authority of fear.

Just as teachers of letters instill fear and terror in their pupils—not because the teachers need this, but because it will greatly benefit the students—and just as they declare that they love those who fear them and hope in their instruction, while they abhor those who are without fear and without hope, since they know that such people cannot attain learning, so this human comparison [Col. 0564A] is as far removed from God as humanity is far removed from divinity.

Human nature, being weak, can accomplish no good at all without the aid of the divine will. But let this comparison, offered to clarify what has been said, urge us toward hope and divine mercy, so that it may make us participants with those upon whom the Lord’s good pleasure rests—he who reigns throughout the ages of ages. Amen.

# PSALM 147

*Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah.*

Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion. For he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has [Col. 0564B] blessed your children within you. He has established your borders in peace and satisfies you with the fat of wheat.

He sends forth his utterance upon the earth; his word runs swiftly. He gives snow like wool; he scatters mist like ashes. He casts his ice like morsels; who can stand before his cold? He will send forth his word and melt them; his spirit will blow, and the waters will flow.

He declares his word to Jacob, his ordinances and judgments to Israel. He has not done such things for every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them.

## Commentary
Praise, Jerusalem, the Lord. The Lord is not praised by the holy city for a single reason. Therefore it hears the reasons for his praise explained by the one exhorting it to praise him, as though the city itself were questioning him. He says: “Praise him because he has strengthened the bars of your gates.” You see, therefore, that, as we said above, it is our task to bar the gates when enemies are making an assault, but it is the Lord’s task to strengthen the bars of Jerusalem’s gates. Thus Jerusalem is the city in which the prophets dwell, in which Christ preaches and exercises various powers, in which he suffers the cross, and in which every kind of virtue has been accomplished. Whoever meditates on all these things within his soul day and night, having within himself the prophets, Christ, and the apostles, becomes the city of Jerusalem; he closes his gates against the enemy and his angels, and must fasten the bars of faith upon the closed entrances. For faith, hope, and charity are three bars set against the devil. Yet faith fails, hope grows weak, and charity grows cold unless they are strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“When the bars of your gates have been strengthened, your children will be blessed in you.” Your children are those formed according to your example, whether for good or for evil. “They,” he says, “will be blessed in you if the bars of your gates have been strengthened in you.” Your end is established in peace when the day arrives for you to depart from the world and bring all your deeds to an end. Your end will be peace with God; when you begin to depart in that condition, “he will satisfy you with the fatness of grain.” He himself does this who sends forth his utterance to the earth—that is, who sent his Word into Mary. And his speech runs so swiftly that, although God had been known for so many thousands of years in Judaea alone, now within a few years not even the Indians in the East, nor the Britons in the West, are unaware of him. His speech runs swiftly everywhere.

“He gives snow like wool.” He wished wool to be understood as a covering. “Though your sins,” he says, “be like scarlet, I will make them like wool” (Isa. 1). Thus he teaches that those who are satisfied with the fatness of grain will one day appear white throughout the whole world in white garments. To these the Lord scatters mist like ashes. The mist that is scattered like ash is the frost that fattens all the crops enclosed within the earth’s depths; the longer it lies upon them, the more abundantly they flourish in their ears of grain. We therefore understand the frost among those whom the Lord satisfies with the fatness of grain as the afflictions of temptations, through which they will make greater progress in the future the more they have suffered in the present.

Next, hail is sent like pieces of bread. By this crystal he recalls the stoning of God, which he compares to broken loaves and small pieces of bread. Believers are struck like material of any kind of metal, not so that they may die, but so that they may be restored to the condition from which they had fallen. It is added that no one can withstand the presence of his cold. Yet because he is faithful and will not allow them to be tempted beyond what they can bear (1 Cor. 10), “he sends forth his word and melts them”: that is, when they have been reborn, the Holy Spirit breathes, and waters flow from their eyes, so that these waters may wash away every impurity and cleanse the stains of sins.

And who is it who does these things? Who else, certainly, but the one who proclaims his word to Jacob, his righteousnesses and judgments to Israel? Wherever Israel is—that is, wherever there is one who sees God—there God will display his righteousness. For just as God is gracious in forgiving those who weep and repent, so he is just in rendering recompense to those who labor for righteousness.

“He has not dealt thus with every nation,” as he has with this one—namely, the nation that day and night displays its hope in God and its charity. He manifests his judgments to no one except those who regard the Lord’s commandments, believing that he will judge us worthy of being helped in his judgment. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# Psalm 148

## Alleluia of Haggai and Zechariah

Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his powers. Praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all stars and light. Praise him, heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created. He established them forever and for ages of ages; he gave a commandment, and it will not pass away.

Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all the abysses. Fire, hail, snow, ice, storm wind, which carry out his word. Mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars. Beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds. Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth. Young men and maidens, old men together with the young, let them praise the name of the Lord, because his name alone is exalted. His confession is above heaven and earth, and he has exalted the horn of his people. A hymn belongs to all his saints, to the sons of Israel, the people drawing near to him.

## Commentary

Custom—or rather, a certain natural force—commands chicks to divide the night from the night by their song. They cry out, indeed, to awaken others, but they themselves sleep while everyone else is awake. Therefore, to our shame, what shall I say about us, who awaken those in heaven to the praise of God, saying: “Praise the Lord, you who are in the heavens; praise him, you also who are in the heights”? We also command the sun, the moon, the stars, the light, the heavens of heavens, and the waters that are above the heavens to praise the Lord. Yet we ourselves sleep when we do not perform such works in which God is praised and his name blessed.

But what is worse—and what cannot be said without a groan—is that through us the name of the Lord is blasphemed when we show partiality in judgment, when we pay attention to clothing, rings, and human honors, and reject the persons of the poor. The one whom you think silent groans: despised, rejected, and regarded as nothing, he assails the blessed name with blasphemies.

Why, then, do we awaken the angels and everything that is in the heavens to the praises of God; why do we call forth from the earth even the dragons, serpents, birds, fire, hail, and storm wind; why do we invite the mountains and hills, all fruit-bearing trees, kings and princes, all judges, all youth and old age, maidens and young men, and everything beneath heaven? We awaken, summon, and exhort everyone to the praise of the Lord, while we ourselves, wretched ones, sleep.

Would that we were sleeping the sleep of the flesh and were not weighed down by the torpor of our thoughtlessness! Behold, everything we have awakened has gathered together as one. The dragons, serpents, beasts, and all cattle will rebuke us, saying: “Why do you awaken us to the praises of God? We came together to praise God with you, and we found that through your fault widows blaspheme the holy name. You favored the injustices of the rich against the poor, orphans, and all those who could not stand up for themselves against the powerful. You despised their persons; you raised your eyes toward the world’s high places, offering your cheerful and welcoming looks only to them, while you rejected the poor as though God had commanded that they be abused.”

These words are addressed to us by all creatures—addressed, I say, to us, who every day, with the trumpet of this psalm, throughout the whole world, as soon as the dawn begins the day, summon everything in heaven and on earth to praise and bless God.

Yet just as the lack of self-restraint of a physician who is ill nullifies medicine and does not allow its benefit to be displayed, introducing the failure of his own restraint, so we employ all these things, although we show by our contempt that they do not please us when they are read. Somehow we cannot at all be persuaded not to abuse, with the utmost negligence, the person of any sinner, even if he is righteous. Let us therefore beseech the Lord that this vice may be cut away from us.

For he assents to those who ask for correction of their conduct, and he is so generous in these gifts that he himself commands what is to be requested: “Ask,” he says, “and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11). The grace of God goes before the human will, and he wishes the human will to go before God’s grace in asking. But when he gives to the one who asks, he follows the will: “For everyone who asks receives.”

Let us therefore ask that we too may share with all the angels and with all his powers in divine praises. And just as it is said of them, “He gave a commandment that will not pass away,” so let us preserve the Lord’s commandment.

Of every creature it is said that “he spoke, and they were made”—that is, they were made through the Word of God, with the Father speaking, the Son creating, and the Holy Spirit giving life. They were established for eternity and for ages of ages: that is, for as long as this age exists, they remain throughout the age of ages. All these things carry out his word—that is, the elements of fire, hail, snow, and storm wind. All these serve God’s will and do what his word has commanded.

Finally, he commanded the storms, and they were still; he commanded the blowing winds, and they were silent, showing that this is the one whose name alone is so exalted that his confession is above heaven and earth, and in whose name every knee shall bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2).

He also exalted the horn of his people, so that hymns are sung throughout the whole world to all his saints and to the sons of Israel, the people drawing near to him. In the sacred writings, sons are called imitators, whether in a good example or a bad one. Thus, although it was clear that those who thought they could circumvent our Lord Jesus Christ by cunning and deceit were sons of Abraham, he says to them: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). When they said that they had Abraham as their father, he replied: “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would do the works of Abraham.”

Therefore these are now the sons who receive the hymn: those who follow Israel’s example. And just as Israel, progressing through patience and faith, deserved to see the Lord God face to face—hence he was called Israel, that is, “seeing God” (Gen. 32)—so those who desire God hear the exhortation addressed to them: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Thus a hymn is commanded to be sung for those who have become his sons through imitation of him, because through purity of heart they deserve to see God drawing near to the one who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# Psalm 149

## Alleluia

Sing to the Lord a new song, his praise in the assembly of the saints. Let Israel rejoice in him who made him, and let the daughters of Zion exult in their king. Let them praise his name in the choir; with the tambourine and the psaltery let them sing to him. For the Lord has been pleased with his people, and he will exalt the meek for salvation. The saints will exult in glory; they will rejoice upon their couches. The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples, to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron handcuffs, to carry out among them the judgment that has been written. This glory belongs to all his saints.

## Commentary

We sing a new song to the Lord when we walk in the newness of life in the assembly of the saints and, by the example of our life and conduct, offer edification to the Lord’s congregation. We rejoice not in the glory of the world or in the riches of the age, but in the one who made us when we were born. For it is then evident that we are sons of Zion—that is, of the Church—if we exult in our King and Lord, praising his name in the choir, that is, with the whole people, and with the tambourine, that is, in the stretching of our bodily skin. For it sounds well when it is sober, clean, and chaste.

Nor should we sing to him only with the tambourine, but also with the psaltery. Chastity and abstinence do not lead us to God if the integrity of faith deserts us; that faith is signified by the ten strings of the psaltery. Then we recognize that the Lord is pleased with his people, when he has humbled the proud for condemnation and exalted the meek for salvation.

Then, I say, we shall acknowledge what we now believe, when the saints exult in glory—those who now rejoice upon their couches, awaiting the day of recompense. For those who now had the exaltations of God in their throats did so when they confessed the glory of Christ, who was exalted on the cross, exalted in the resurrection, and exalted in heaven. For whoever has had these exaltations of God in his throat, the faithlessness of ungodly people will perish. Therefore, neither fearing the executioner nor terrified by the threat of blows, they did not keep silent about these exaltations of the Lord. Indeed, the more severely they were afflicted, the more fully they continued to confess.

They will have two-edged swords in their hands—that is, sentences of eternal death and everlasting punishment—to execute vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples, to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron bonds. To them the Lord now says: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

These, therefore, carry out among them the judgment that has been written. They will judge the world for its ungodly deeds—those who were afflicted by the world for their works. And when the saints have judged those kings by whom they themselves were judged, then this will be glory for all his saints.

Now it is said to each person: “If you believe that you will see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, wait for the Lord and act courageously” (Ps. 26). If you believe, do not cease to watch; and if you recognize that you desire with certainty what you believe, do not cease to desire it. We shall then rejoice that this glory has come to all the saints if, placed in whatever distress, we do not wholly change our mind, but wait daily for the Lord and, through patience, give thanks to him who reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# Psalm 150

## Alleluia

Praise the Lord in his saints; praise him in the firmament of his power. Praise him in his powers; praise him according to the multitude of his greatness. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with the psaltery and lyre. Praise him with the tambourine and choir; praise him with strings and pipe. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation. Let every spirit praise the Lord.

## Commentary

We praise the Lord in his saints when we imitate their examples, follow their admonitions, and maintain their rule. We praise him in the firmament of his power when we display a firm struggle of faith and, just as the saints despised punishments and visible enemies, so we cast away the pleasures imposed by the invisible enemy.

We praise him with the sound of the trumpet when, if the occasion requires it, we proclaim from the housetops what we have heard in the ear, not fearing those who kill the body (Matt. 10). We praise him with the psaltery and lyre if on the lyre we embrace the wood of the cross and in the psaltery we hold the catholic confession. For that which is not approved as catholic sounds hoarse.

We praise him with the tambourine and choir when, placed in a way of life that must be rendered back, we adorn the tambourine of our body with the finest examples. We praise him with strings and pipe when we exercise the intact strings of the cords that are in our lyre. We also cleanse chastity, with the little reeds of self-restraint, from every rust of sin and offer to God mellifluous sounds.

We praise him with well-sounding and well-ringing cymbals when we adapt our lips to good persuasion and spiritual explanation. We invite every spirit to praise the Lord when, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, we grant nothing to the flesh, but dedicate everything it desires wholly to the spirit and imitate the examples of spiritual people. Following in their footsteps, may we believe that we shall reach the Lord’s mercy, to whom belong glory and dominion throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# Notes on Certain Passages of the Gospels

## Testimony of Gilbert Cognatus, who wrongly attributes these notes to Arnobius Africanus

The antiquity of the archetype from which these Notes of Arnobius on passages of the Evangelists were taken, and its excellent reliability in the transcription of a book written in worn characters and with great difficulty, commend this little work. The characters are so closely connected with one another that, not to say sentence from sentence, it is laborious for anyone not accustomed to it to separate even one word from another.

Commentaries by this same Arnobius on the Psalms of David have long since been published. There is also another work, the celebrated seven books Against the Nations, which Blessed Jerome mentions in his catalogue of illustrious writers.

## Notes on Certain Passages of the Gospels (C, G, S)

# From John

## Chapter 1

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made.”

The Beginning is God, who wished to be the originator of all things. Therefore, in this Beginning was the Word, that is, Christ, concerning whom he says: “The Word was with God, and the Word was God.” He shows that Christ proceeded from God. Of him the paternal voice also spoke in Psalm 44: “My heart has uttered a good Word”—that is, Christ, through whom all things were made, except idols, which were made without Christ’s will. Concerning these the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing.”

## Chapter 2: On the Wedding

“On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited, together with his disciples, to the wedding; and they had no wine,” and so forth.

All these things took place, but they possess a spiritual meaning. The wedding, namely, is the union of Christ and the Church, that is, of the tradition of the new law. The seven stone water jars signify the seven Churches founded upon the rock. “They were full of water,” he says: this is the grace of baptism. When he says, “holding two measures each,” these are those who are joined in marriage. Those holding three measures are the spiritual and continent, who are filled with the powers of the Trinity. The master of the feast is Moses; the new bridegroom is Christ; the water changed into wine signifies the blood of the Passion.

## Chapter 3: On the Blind Man

“Jesus went out from the temple, and while he was walking he saw a man blind from birth. His disciples asked him, saying: ‘Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?’ Jesus answered them: ‘Neither did this man sin nor his parents, but this happened so that the works of God might be revealed in him.’ Having said this, he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and anointed his eyes with the clay. Then he said to him: ‘Go to the pool of Siloam and wash your eyes.’ He went, washed, and returned with his sight.”

When he spoke of the blind man, he signified the race of the Gentiles, and we, who from birth wandered in blindness. Siloam is interpreted as “the fountain of light”; this is baptism, through which we enlighten the eyes of the heart.

## Chapter 4: On Lazarus

“There was a certain sick man named Lazarus, from the village of Mary and Martha, his sister. This was the Mary who had anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother was sick,” and so forth.

All these things took place, but they possess a spiritual meaning. Lazarus signifies the human race, which previously slept in death before Christ came. Martha and Mary signify the Church and faith, asking Christ to raise Lazarus. The stone rolled away from the tomb signifies the hardness of humanity removed from the heart. The raising on the fourth day signifies the form of the Gospels, which drive hardness of heart away from us. When he said, “Jesus wept,” he was referring to the unbelief of the Jews.

## Chapter 5

“Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you; for whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going. While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may become sons of light.”

The light of which he speaks is the law of God, in which we ought to walk. The darkness of which he speaks is ignorance. Christ is the light, while the Antichrist is darkness.

## Chapter 6: On the Vine and the Branch

“I am,” he says, “the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he will cut off and cast into the fire.”

Christ is rightly the vine, since he brought life to us. His Father is also rightly the cultivator, because he is the governor of the world, administering rains and seasons like a good husbandman. The fruitful branch of which he speaks signifies our people. The fruitless branch is a figure of the heretics, whom the fire awaits.

## Chapter 7: On Abraham

“Abraham your father rejoiced that he was to see my day; he saw it and was glad.”

Before Christ came, Abraham died two thousand years earlier. How, then, did the Lord say, “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced”? It was when Isaac carried the wood to the sacrifice, and he provided a ram worthy of sacrifice, and received his son back with joy. Then he exulted, because he saw the wood of the cross and recognized that Christ would suffer.

## Chapter 8: On Peter’s Sword

“Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear,” and the rest that follows.

Since earlier the Lord had commanded his disciples not even to carry a staff on the road, how then did Peter draw a sword and cut off the priest’s servant’s ear? The Lord said to him: “Put your sword back into its sheath.” The sword, namely, is the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle Paul mentions in the Letter to the Ephesians. The severed ear is the hearing of the Jews, as Isaiah said: “Lord, who has believed our report?” The sheath, moreover, was Peter, in whom the Spirit of God was hidden.

# From Matthew

## Chapter 1

“Opening their treasures, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Having been warned in a dream, they did not return to Herod, but went back by another way.”

At that time the Magi, under the prophetic guidance of the Spirit, were bringing gifts to Christ: gold, namely, as to a king; frankincense, as to God, or because it signified the offering of the Passion; and myrrh, which displayed the sign of burial. The Magi themselves were a type of believers. Herod signifies a figure of the devil. When the Magi were told not to return to Herod, this means that those who come from the Gentiles to Christ must not return again to the devil.

## Chapter 2

“A voice crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low, and crooked things shall become straight.’”

The valley of which he speaks signifies this world, filled with Christ’s teaching. The mountains and hills brought low signify the unbelief of the devil and the worship of idols, which were humbled and cast down at Christ’s coming. When he said, “Crooked things shall become straight,” he was speaking of the perversity of the Gentiles, who now walk along straight paths.

## Chapter 3: On John’s Food

“John’s food was locusts and wild honey.”

The locusts of which he spoke signify the multitude of peoples who were coming to John. The honey signifies the fruit of their sweetness, by whose belief and faith John was satisfied.

## Chapter 4: On the Winnowing Shovel and the Threshing Floor

“He has a winnowing shovel in his hand; he will cleanse his threshing floor and gather the grain into his barns, but he will burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

By the threshing floor he understands this world. The grain signifies the saints and the faithful. The winnowing shovel signifies the cross. The barn is paradise, where the saints are gathered. The chaff signifies frivolous and ruined people, who are cast into Gehenna and consumed by fire.

## Chapter 5: On Fasting and the Temple

“When Jesus had fasted, afterward he was hungry. The tempter said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.’ But he said to him: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’ Then the devil took him and set him upon the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here, for the angels will receive you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’”

While Christ was fasting, he was hungry for us, whom righteousness will satisfy. We were the stones that possessed hardness of heart. The temple signifies Christian people, as the Apostle Paul says: “You are the temple of God.” The summit of the temple is charity, through which Christ ascends in Christians.

When the devil said to Christ, “Throw yourself down from the temple here,” he was urging Christ to descend from our charity. “Lest,” he says, “you strike your foot against a stone”—that is, as though we were unbelieving and possessed the hardness of stones. Thus he was setting our stumbling before Christ.

## Chapter 6

“Be reconciled quickly with your adversary while you are with him on the way, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the attendants, and you be thrown into prison.”

The adversary of whom he speaks signifies the outer person, that is, the carnal person, with whom we make our journey. The way signifies the passage through this age. We should therefore be reconciled with this adversary—that is, live chastely with him—lest perhaps, because of unlawful deeds, he hand us over to the judge, that is, to Christ. “And the judge,” he says, “to the attendants,” that is, to the angels; and the angels will hand us over to prison, that is, to Gehenna.

## Chapter 7

“Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret.”

We are the right hand because we worship Christ, who sits at the right hand of the Father. The Jews and heretics are the left hand. Therefore, let the left side not know what the right hand is doing.

## Chapter 8

“Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moth and eating destroy them, and where thieves break in and steal. But store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where thieves do not break in and do not steal,” and so forth.

The earth of which he speaks signifies the dwelling place of our body. The treasure is faith. Therefore, “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” means: do not treasure up things in the flesh, where “moth,” he says, consumes—that is, greed or lust—and where thieves break in—that is, the devil, who steals faith.

Rather, “Store up,” he says, “treasures in heaven,” that is, in the spirit, which is understood as heaven. As the Apostle Paul said: “Whoever sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit.”

## Chapter 9

“You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not consider the beam in your own eye.”

He said this concerning the heretics, who dare to quarrel with the Jews. They think they remove from the Jews’ eyes the speck—that is, the splinters of that crown of thorns—so that they do not perceive the beam in their own eyes, that is, the offense of the cross.

## Chapter 10

“Do they gather grapes from thorns or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruits, but an evil tree produces evil fruits.”

The thorns and thistles of which he speaks signify heresies, from which no one gathers the fruit of righteousness. That is, no one remembers martyrs arising from the heretics. The evil tree is the old person, who produces evil fruits—that is, sins, lusts, and greed. The good tree is the cross, which brought the fruit of life to believers.

## Chapter 11

“Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon rock. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears my words and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain descended, the winds blew, they struck that house, and it fell, and its fall was great.”

The rock is Christ, the author of the apostles. The house of which he speaks is the dwelling place of our body. Therefore, let us build our house upon this rock—that is, upon Christ; let us sanctify our body—so that when the rivers and wind come, that is, the assault and storm of persecution, we may not fall when struck.

The sand signifies nothing other than heresies, which are rolled about by every storm. Therefore, whoever builds his house upon this sand—that is, upon heresy—is foolish. As soon as the rivers and winds arrive—that is, the assault of persecution—he will immediately fall.

## Chapter 12

“The children of the bridegroom cannot fast as long as the bridegroom is with them. But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast in those days. No one places a patch of new cloth on an old garment, for it removes its fullness from the garment, and a worse tear results. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wine bursts the wineskins, and the wine is lost, as are the wineskins. Rather, they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved.”

The bridegroom is Christ; we are the children of the bridegroom. Therefore, if someone persists in reading, he does not fast, because the bridegroom, who is Christ, is with him; Christ said: “I am the bread of life.” Then they will begin to fast.

The new garment signifies the new person; the old garment signifies the old person. Therefore, if someone joins the inner person—that is, the spiritual person—to the outer person, that is, the carnal person, he makes a worse tear.

The new wine, namely, is the sacrament. The old wineskins are the Jews. The new wineskins are we who drink from this must.

## Chapter 13

“Behold, a woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. She approached from behind and touched his garment, for she said within herself: ‘If I touch only his garment, I shall be saved.’ But he said to his disciples: ‘Who touched me? For I felt power go out from me.’ When the woman who had touched his garment saw that she could not remain hidden, she fell at his feet, saying: ‘Lord, I touched you, because I was afflicted by a flow of blood.’ He said to her: ‘Daughter, your faith has saved you.’”

All these things took place, but they possess a spiritual meaning. The woman transformed into a flow of blood signifies the Church. In her image, the Maccabean woman was already being slaughtered at that time, and her blood flowed as an image of the Church. When Christ came, her blood was transferred from a flow of death to the glory of martyrdom.

The garment of Christ that she touched is the body of Christ, which we too touch and by which we are healed. The twelve years signify the number of the apostles.

## Chapter 14

“Behold, I send you like sheep among wolves. Be wise,” he says, “like serpents, and simple like doves.”

The wolves of which he speaks are our persecutors. We are the sheep, who during persecution are restrained by wolves. But “be crafty,” he says, “like serpents, and simple like doves.” This means: just as a serpent hides its head when death is necessary, but hands its body over to death, so let us honor our head—that is, Christ—by confessing him, while handing our body over to the wolves.

The dove is the Church. Whenever her children are killed for the name of Christ, they rejoice and exult.

## Chapter 15

“Are not two sparrows sold for an as? And not one of them will fall to the ground without the will of your Father who is in heaven.”

The two sparrows of which he speaks signify the spirit and the soul, as he said in the Psalm: “Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters.” The as of which he speaks is the denarius of faith, by which we purchase him. The earth is the human being himself, who cannot receive either soul or spirit without the Father’s will.

## Chapter 16

“Jesus entered the synagogue and found there a man who had a withered hand. Jesus said to him: ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He stretched out his hand, and it became sound like the other.”

All these things took place, but they possess a spiritual meaning. By the withered hand he signified the person of the unfruitful man. Therefore, the Lord said to him: “Stretch out your hand,” so that with mercy we may extend our hand and offer alms to the poor.

## Chapter 17

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it hidden, he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.”

This field is the world. The treasure hidden in the field is Christ, who lay hidden during that three-day Passion. Alternatively, the field is paradise, and the treasure is eternal life. Therefore, let us sell whatever we have in this age, so that we may reach that field.

## Chapter 18

“He compelled the disciples to go up into the boat and proceed across the sea until he dismissed the crowds. The boat was already in the middle of the sea, tossed by the waves, for the wind was contrary. During the fourth watch of the night he went to them, walking on the sea. When they saw him, they were troubled. Simon Peter said: ‘Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.’ He said: ‘Come.’ Peter descended from the boat and walked upon the water to come to Jesus. But when Peter saw the strong wave coming toward him, he was afraid, and when he began to sink, he cried out, saying: ‘Lord, save me,’” and so forth.

The sea, of course, is the present age; the ship, however, into which the apostles embarked, is the Church. By saying that it was thrown into confusion by the waves, he means that the Church is battered by persecution. The contrary wind is the devil, who is opposed to the Church. By saying that he came to them during the fourth watch of the night, walking upon the sea, he means that he brought us the light of the Gospel, who were lying in the ignorance of night. By saying that Peter was troubled when he saw the storm, he means that he was troubled in Christ’s passion, so that even by denying him his faith might be submerged. [Col. 0576A]

## CHAPTER XIX

Jesus said to his disciples: “Amen, I say to you, it is difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. Again I say to you: it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.”

By “the rich man” he meant the Jewish people, who came out of Egypt with riches; concerning them he said in the Psalm: “The rich have become needy and hungry.” We were the camel, however, who had nothing upright in us, but who have now laid down the burden of sins and entered through the eye of the needle—that is, through the narrow and constricted way that leads to life. For Judas Iscariot was rich from the price for which he betrayed Christ, but he did not enter the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0576B]

## CHAPTER XX

“The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard, and agreed with each of the laborers on a denarius for the day. Going out also at the sixth and ninth hours, he did the same; but going out at about the eleventh hour, he found others standing there and said to them: ‘Why are you standing here idle?’ They answered him: ‘Because no one has hired us.’ And he said to them: ‘You also go into the vineyard.’ When evening came, the lord said to his steward: ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last and proceeding to the first.’ When those who had been called about the eleventh hour came, they received a denarius each. The first also came, expecting that they would receive more; but when they too had received a denarius each, they began to murmur against the householder, saying: ‘These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have endured the burden of the whole day.’” [Col. 0576C]

The householder is Christ, who hires laborers—that is, who gathers believers so that they may receive their wage. The vineyard is the cultivation of the Law. The denarius is eternal life. Those whom he said had worked at the first hour are virgins, who say that they have endured bodily labor and the heat of the flesh. The marketplace signifies this world; those who came to the work late are the abstinent. By saying that they received their wage in the evening, he means that at Christ’s coming the chaste will receive the reward of their labor.

[Col. 0576D]

## CHAPTER XXI

“And they brought the colt of a she-ass, and he sat upon it; and laying their garments on the road, while others were cutting branches from the trees, they were throwing them before him. And the crowds went before him, saying: ‘Hosanna to the Son of David.’”

The colt of the she-ass that he mentioned signifies the new people—that is, our people—who also recognized the manger of their Lord, namely, the altar where we gather food. The crowd that he described as casting down its garments signifies that the multitude of believers, stripping off the old man, will cast themselves down. The trees are those same people. The branches cut from the trees are the sins that were growing strong within us.

[Col. 0577A]

## CHAPTER XXII

“Hear another parable,” he says. “There was a householder who planted a vineyard, surrounded it with a hedge, dug a pool in it, built a tower, leased it to tenants, and went abroad. When the time of the fruits approached, he sent his servants to those cultivators, to receive his fruits from them. But the tenants seized his servants: one they beat, another they stoned, and another they beheaded. Again he sent other servants, more than the first, and they treated them in the same way. Finally he sent them his only son, saying: ‘Perhaps they will respect my son.’ But they seized him also and struck him down.”

The householder whom he mentioned reveals the likeness of the Father. The vineyard that he said had been newly planted is the new Law. [Col. 0577B] The tower is the Church. The winepress is baptism. The tenants are the Jews. The hedge is faith; the servants whom he said were killed are understood to be the prophets. The later ones whom he said were sent are the apostles, one of whom was beheaded, namely, John. Finally they killed the Son, that is, Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIII

“Give back,” he says, “to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

In persecution we are commanded to give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s—that is, the body over which he has power—and to give back to God the things that are God’s, namely, the spirit and faith.

## CHAPTER XXIV

“There were,” he says, “among us seven brothers. The first of them, [Col. 0577C] having taken a wife, died without leaving children and left his wife to his brother. Likewise the second, and the third, and the fourth, down to the seventh; finally, the woman also died. In the resurrection, therefore, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife.”

The seven brothers whom he mentioned signify the seven patriarchs, who are the seven books of Moses. Their wife is the Synagogue. Although the seven patriarchs came together with her and poured in the seed of the name of Christ, she never conceived faith.

## CHAPTER XXV

“Kingdom will rise against kingdom and nation against nation, and there will be famines and earthquakes in various places. But all these things will be the beginning of groaning and anguish. [Col. 0577D] Then they will hand you over to death. Then many will be scandalized, and they will hand one another over to death; many false prophets will arise and lead many astray; and because wickedness will abound, the charity of many will grow cold. But whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

The kingdom rising against kingdom means that the devil dares to raise heresies against the kingdom of Christ. Famines and earthquakes mean that certain people—who are understood by “earth”—suffer hunger; that is, having neither the Spirit of God nor understanding, they are driven toward heresies. “They will hand themselves over,” he says, to death; and “false prophets will arise,” such as Amapobius, who deceived many.

[Col. 0578A]

## CHAPTER XXVI

“Then,” he says, “let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is in the field not turn back for his garment. Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days. Pray, however, that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath.”

Judea, of course, is the holy land—that is, chaste people who have sanctified their flesh. “Let them flee,” he says, “to the mountains,” that is, to the teaching of the apostles. “And let the one who is in the field not turn back for his garment”; that is, let the one who is in the world not return to the old man. “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing”: woe to the one who, like a pregnant woman, has conceived the avarice of the brothers or of the priests. The one who nurses is he who has not taught Christ’s commandments correctly; [Col. 0578B] he has given drink, not with food, but with milk. By “winter” he indicated the time for capturing people; likewise, just as Jews are not permitted to flee on the Sabbath. But now he does not permit them to withdraw from the city. Thus let us also pray that we may be able to flee the world, lest we be overtaken by the Antichrist as by winter or the Sabbath.

## CHAPTER XXVII

“Then the kingdom of heaven will be likened,” he says, “to ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish and five wise. The foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them in their vessels. But the wise took oil in their vessels along with their lamps.”

The ten virgins whom he mentioned are identified by the names of the five wise ones: hope, faith, charity, chastity, and almsgiving. [Col. 0578C] Their vessels are their dwelling places, that is, the people in whom they dwell. “Full of oil,” he says, meaning spiritual grace. The lamps are vigilance of the Spirit. They go out to meet the bridegroom, that is, Christ. The foolish are the opposites of these: those who hope in what they see; another, unbelief; a third, lack of charity; a fourth, carnality; and a fifth, unfruitfulness. The lamps of these too are extinguished, because they do not have oil—that is, spiritual grace.

# FROM LUKE

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0578D]

“Therefore a son will be born to you; you will call his name John; and many will rejoice at his birth; and he will drink neither wine nor strong drink.”

The wine that John is forbidden to drink signifies luxury. Strong drink is the juice of dates; by it he understands nothing other than the sweetness of the flesh. Therefore let spiritual people flee this kind of drink.

## CHAPTER II

“Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ But I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Indeed, the axe has already been laid at the roots of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.”

The stones that he mentioned are understood to be the Jews, because of their hardness and unbelief. From them he raised up children for Abraham—that is, the apostles; or else he means the hardness of the Gentiles, from whom he crowned martyrs. The trees are understood to be human beings, against whom the axe has been laid: that is, the sharpness of both Testaments, whose handle is understood to be the cross.

[Col. 0579A]

## CHAPTER III

“No one,” he says, “lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel or under a vessel. Rather, he puts it on a lampstand, so that all who enter may see.”

The lamp is Christ, who said, “I am the light of this world”; or else it is his commandments, which illuminate our hearts. The vessel signifies this world. The bushel signifies heresies. The lampstand is the truth that displays the light. Therefore let us not hide this lamp—that is, the commandments of Christ—from the world, but let us place it on the lampstand, so that it may shine, he says, for all who enter the house, that is, the Church.

[Col. 0579B]

## CHAPTER IV

“Jesus went up onto the mountain to pray; and while he was praying, the appearance of his face became altered, and his garment became white, shining like snow. And behold, two men were speaking with him: Moses and Elijah, appearing in glory. And they were speaking of his departure, which he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem. But Peter and those who were with him were weighed down by sleep; and when they awoke, [Col. 0580A] they saw his glory and the two men standing with him. And they said to Jesus: ‘Master, it is good for us to be here; let us make three tents, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah,’ not knowing what they were saying.”

Christ on the high mountain of wisdom is understood, believed in, and worshiped as God the Word, through the practice of spiritual discourse, according to the form of God. His garment, which became shining like snow, is the sayings and writings of the Gospels, with which Jesus is clothed. Moses, that is, the Law, and Elijah, that is, the prophets, are speaking with Jesus.

If someone understands the spiritual Law as agreeing with Jesus’ sayings, and the wisdom hidden mystically in the prophets, that person sees Moses and Elijah in glory when [Col. 0580B] he sees them as one with Jesus. For if Christ, the Law, and the prophets are one, then Christ is also proved to be the Son of God; and the Law and the prophets are found to have prophesied truly, since the Law and the prophets bore witness to Christ, foretelling what was to come concerning Christ. Christ, in turn, bore witness to the Law and the prophets, since they prophesied truly, fulfilling their prophecy in the events themselves.

“It is good for us to be here, and let us make three,” and so forth: that is, let us adhere to these three joined together—namely, Christ, Moses, and the prophets. For every judgment stands on the testimony of these three. Those who strive to separate them will be found not to know what they are saying.

# THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF THE *PRAEDESTINATUS*

[Col. 0579]

## PROLEGOMENA: GALLAND’S PROLEGOMENON ON THE ANONYMOUS AUTHOR OF THE *PRAEDESTINATUS*

(Galland, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. X.)

[Col. 0579C]

### I

Who the author of the *Praedestinatus* was has been the subject of many conjectures among learned men, but the plan of our work does not allow us to report them individually at length. Yet, lest we seem entirely to fail in our duty, we shall bring forward only those considerations that sufficiently reveal what ought to be thought either about the author himself or about his work.

Sirmond, who first brought our anonymous writer to light, found that the old manuscript, otherwise of the best quality, did not disclose the author’s name. Therefore, lest the book appear without any title at all, he invented an added title and prefixed the work under the name *Praedestinatus*. Then, indulging in conjecture, he guessed that the author of the book was Arnobius the Younger, whose commentaries on the Psalms survive, on account of the affinity of style and ideas. [Col. 0580C] For this reason he appended Arnobius’s excerpts to the end of the *Praedestinatus*. Later, the editor of Sirmond’s works enlarged them in about twenty other places from the same commentaries of Arnobius, which Hardouin had pointed out to him.

We know that Petavius too approved Sirmond’s conjecture. For after observing that the author of the *Praedestinatus* seemed earlier than Faustus of Riez [Note: [Col. 0579] Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, vol. IV, part II, book XIII, chapter 6, §3], and that although he appeared to wish to defend the position of Saint Augustine against the Predestinarians and Pelagians, he had plainly acted treacherously, since he had inserted many things that smacked of Pelagianism, Petavius finally concludes [Note: [Col. 0580] Id., ibid., §11]: “Arnobius the Younger in his Commentary on Psalm 147 is of a similar character and disposition, so that both works may appear to have proceeded from the same author; and learned men [Col. 0581A] rightly suspect this.”

This same opinion is known to have appealed both to Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0581] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 21] and, above all, to the authors of the *History of French Literature* [Note: [Col. 0581] *History of French Literature*, vol. II, pp. 349–351].

### II

Holstenius adopted a different view. As Baunius reports [Note: [Col. 0581] Baunius, preface to vol. I of Sirmond’s works, §7], he informed Sirmond from Rome that, in an old manuscript of the Barberini Library, the work of the *Praedestinatus* was attributed to Primasius. He thought that the authority of this manuscript was confirmed also by the testimony of Isidore, bishop of Seville, who reports [Note: [Col. 0581] Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 9] that Primasius, an African bishop, composed three books on heresies in scholastic discourse, addressed to Bishop Fortunatus.

Rigaltius held the same opinion, for he cites the book of the *Praedestinatus* once and again under the name of Primasius [Note: [Col. 0581] Rigaltius, notes on Cyprian’s letters 49 and 55]. Mabillon likewise testifies that he saw Sirmond’s *Praedestinatus* [Col. 0581B] in the library at Augia [Note: [Col. 0581] Mabillon, *German Journey*, in the *Analecta*, p. 15, folio edition], with the following title, written in somewhat lighter ink but by an ancient hand: “The work of Saint Primasius, a disciple of Augustine, on heresies, number 90.”

Yet both from a proper understanding of Isidore’s words and from the letter that Sirmond wrote to Holstenius—printed by the editor of Sirmond’s works at the beginning of the *Praedestinatus*—it is sufficiently clear that the books of our anonymous author were entirely different from those that Isidore reports as having been composed by Primasius.

Moreover, Piccinardus published a careful historical-theological inquiry concerning the work of the *Praedestinatus*, and at the same time thought that its author was either a certain Vincent, a presbyter and a Gaul by nationality, whom Gennadius mentions [Note: [Col. 0581] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 80], or rather Vincent Victor, against whom Saint Augustine wrote books *On the Soul and Its Origin*. But learned men have stated what should be thought of his views [Col. 0581C] [Note: [Col. 0581] Baunius, preface to vol. I of Sirmond’s works, §7; Balterius, *Observations*, book II, chapter 10, in vol. IV of Noris, p. 922].

I shall not linger over the conjectures of others concerning the author of this work, whether Hardouin’s—that the book was written by Reginbald, a Benedictine monk, more than 850 years ago, an assertion brought forward without any witness [Note: [Col. 0582] Hardouin, *Dissertation on Baptism*, §13, in the selected works, p. 235]—or Oudin’s, who persuades himself that its author was Vincent of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0582] Oudin, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, p. 1247]. The authors of the *History of French Literature* have solidly refuted the latter above all [Note: [Col. 0582] *History of French Literature*, vol. II, p. 313 and following]. But enough on this small matter.

### III

As for the work itself, we shall use the words of learned men [Note: [Col. 0582] Baller, cited work, pp. 921 and following], so that readers may recognize it more intimately:

> “Thus the author, whoever he may finally have been, divided his work into three books. In the first he compiled a catalogue of ninety heresies, which he says were excerpted from Hyginus, Polycrates the African, and Heliodorus, [Col. 0581D] whom no one before him had named as writers on heresies. Nor does he mention Augustine, from whose book *On Heresies* he copies everything good that he reports; for the rest either seems to have been fabricated [Col. 0582A] from his own imagination and is wholly unknown to all antiquity, or, if cut open to the living tissue, is found to be doubtful or false.

> “In the second book he presents a short work that contains the errors of the Predestinarians. He writes that this was attributed to Augustine by the Predestinarians, so that they might secure the patronage of so great a doctor for their opinion. Yet, he says, when Celestine read it, he was so horrified that he ordered it to be condemned to perpetual silence.

> “Father Piccinardus suspects Evodius of Uzalis to have been the author of this little book [Note: [Col. 0582] See Baunius, preface to vol. I of Sirmond’s works, §7]. He conjectures that Evodius cultivated the Predestinarian heresy, which he agrees with Sirmond had arisen in the monastery of Hadrumetum. Furthermore, he supposes that when this book of Evodius was brought into Gaul, the name of Augustine was written upon it, and that Vincent’s objections, which Saint Prosper answered, were taken from it; he draws many other conclusions [Col. 0582B] of that kind, which we do not think will win the approval either of us or of anyone else.

> “For Noris sufficiently clears the monks of Hadrumetum from suspicion of the Predestinarian heresy [Note: [Col. 0582] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 15, in vol. I of Noris’s works, p. 441]. Evodius, who firmly held Augustine’s doctrine, ought not to be dragged into such criticism by the weakest conjectures. The remaining claims that rest upon these foundations are no less feeble, so that there is no need to refute them.

> “We believe that this book was fabricated by the Semipelagians. If, according to Prosper’s testimony, they invented a little catalogue of diabolical errors and attributed them to Augustine, why should we not suspect that they themselves wrote this book, overflowing with errors, and published it under Augustine’s name? But when the author of the *Praedestinatus* tells the story that this book was offered to Celestine and condemned by him, he seems equally to have fabricated it; [Col. 0582C] for Saint Celestine touched on nothing of the kind in the letter that he wrote near the end of his life in defense of Prosper and Hilary.

> “Moreover, it is unbelievable that neither Saint Prosper nor the other disciples of Saint Augustine and defenders of the Catholic faith ever refuted a book that brought such a calumny against Augustine and such danger to the faith, in order to defend Augustine’s faith and doctrine [Note: [Col. 0582] See Pagius on the year 490, §13].

> “Finally, while the third book rejects the work mentioned above, it inculcates several errors of the Pelagians and Semipelagians. It preaches grace in agreement with Pelagius; with the Semipelagians it attributes the beginning of faith and good will to the will; like Julian, it calls concupiscence good; and it uses almost the same words as those found in fragments of Julian. From this it is evident that the author must be classed with the heretical Pelagians and Semipelagians [Col. 0582D].”

Thus far the learned men. Nor should Tillemont be omitted on this matter [Note: [Col. 0582] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 20].

### IV

Sirmond published the *Praedestinatus* at Paris in the year 1643. In the following year, 1644, a very sharp criticism of this work appeared there [Col. 0583A] in French, entitled: *Censure du Praedestinatus du P. Sirmond, par le sieur Auvray* (“Censure of Father Sirmond’s *Praedestinatus*, by Sieur Auvray”). It is said to have subsequently been committed to the press in Holland, translated into Latin, together with the *Praedestinatus*, in the year 1645.

Under the name of Monsieur Auvray, some thought that Arnauld was concealed, while others thought it was Blondel, as Grotius supposed [Note: [Col. 0583] Grotius, part II, letter 699]. But we have learned that the true author of the criticism was Monsieur de Barcos, the nephew of Jean Vergerius, the famous abbot of Saint-Cyran [Note: [Col. 0583] *History of French Literature*, vol. II, p. 350].

This was the cause and occasion for Sirmond to write the *History of Predestinarianism*, which we have appended to the books of the *Praedestinatus*. Various judgments of learned men circulate concerning this work. The editor of Sirmond’s works lists those who approved the same history with their endorsements [Note: [Col. 0583] Baunius, preface to vol. IV, §5].

But the eminent author judged otherwise, and delivered the following judgment concerning this history [Col. 0584A] [Note: [Col. 0584] Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 4, in vol. I of the works, p. 440]:

> “What Sirmond wrote about the Predestinarian heresy, he wrote in exhausted old age, when he was more than eighty years old. In this he departed so far from the truth that his own *History* was called, by Gilbert Maguin, a distinguished man and counselor to the king of France, deeply learned in sacred and profane history, a disgraceful fable. This writer so solidly and vigorously refuted the first three chapters of Sirmond’s *History of the Predestinarians* that Louis Cellot, in his *History of Gottschalk*, in which he undertook to refute Maguin, when he treats of the Predestinarians in book II, chapter 2, was unable to offer even a word in Sirmond’s defense against Maguin.”

Thus far the distinguished man. Tillemont likewise held the same opinion [Note: [Col. 0584] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 19].

# SIRMOND’S PREFACE TO THE *PRAEDESTINATUS*

[Col. 0583B]

Whenever the words of teachers reach you, O lover of God, the Lord’s commands must immediately be recalled—those by which he deigns to order us to beware of those who come to us in sheep’s clothing, lest under this covering the rage of wolves invade the simplicity of the flock.

Would that it were enough for me to have said these things in words, and that it were not—something to be remembered with a sigh—manifest that beasts have been mingled with the Lord’s flock: men who have insinuated themselves among Catholics [Col. 0583C] by such subtlety and secret gaping that those who are proved to be enemies of the Church and most treacherous foes are themselves regarded as citizens of the saints and members of the household of faith.

They say that people are so predestined to death by God’s foreknowledge that neither Christ’s passion, nor the redemption of baptism, nor faith, nor hope, nor charity can help them. Let them pray and occupy themselves with fasts and almsgiving: they say that they can in no way be freed, because they were not predestined to life. Conversely, let those whom foreknowing predestination has assigned to life neglect and despise righteousness and flee from it. Thus these people are dragged unwillingly to life, just as those who wish to attain life are driven out into death. Thus what is not requested is given to these, while what is requested is denied to those. These, without seeking, will find; those, though seeking, cannot find. The door of piety is opened to these without their knocking; [Col. 0583D] to those it can in no way be opened, even though they knock and cry out.

Who, holding this faith, would wish to bow his head to the blessings of priests, or believe that their prayers and sacrifices could bring him help? For if people begin to believe that these things help neither those who wish them to help nor harm those who do not wish them to harm, all the efforts of God’s priests will cease, and all the aids of admonition will appear to be empty fictions. Thus each person will be so occupied with his own vices that he will regard the pleasure of his crimes as God’s predestination, and will not believe that he can find a passage from evil to good either [Col. 0584B] through God’s priests, through his own conversion, or through the Lord’s Law.

I would have remained silent, I confess, and would not have exposed these things with my running pen, if, after being so often admonished to keep silent, they had at least moderately restrained the force of their contention. But they have also boldly published books under Augustine’s name and wounded the members of our immaculate mother, the Church, with the darts of their writings.

What son would not grieve to see his mother beaten? What child would not weep to see his mother wounded? Shall we remain silent while she suffers? But our silence will be judged guilt, and our taciturnity will appear to be consent. For what you consider the patience of silence, another regards as complicity in perversity—especially if you yourself remain silent and perhaps compel the one who wishes to speak in defense of our common mother [Col. 0584C] to be silent.

Since divine wisdom has established a time for keeping silent and a time for speaking, so that there might be both modesty in silence and reason in speech, lest anyone either put forth or restrain his tongue beyond the bounds of propriety, and so that there might be either importunate loquacity or obstinate silence—for both become vices, speaking when one ought not and refusing to speak when one ought—therefore I show, with due consideration, that this has been guarded on both sides. Against the book that directs ambushes against Mother Church, I seize the weapons of the divine mouth and, like David against Goliath, trusting in the Lord, cut off its neck with its own sword.

Whoever is saddened by this will be exposed by his own judgment, like a mouse, when by his murmuring he reveals himself to be a Philistine. But everyone who is not an alien will rejoice with me.

Thus, while it was carefully concealed, secretly read, and cautiously copied, the book finally reached our hands—not so much published as apprehended. [Col. 0584D] It falsely claims Augustine in its title, while revealing itself as heretical in its text. For who does not know that Augustine was always an orthodox teacher, and that both by writing and by disputing he confronted all heretics? [Col. 0585A]

Therefore, wishing to introduce an enemy of our faith among the brethren, they placed a Catholic title above the threshold of their book. The book is like a foul-smelling tomb: outwardly it is whitened with Augustine’s name, but inwardly it pours forth the worms of the dead.

When this book was once offered to the most blessed Pope Celestine, he held it in such abhorrence that he ordered it to be condemned to perpetual silence. The more the spirit of the heretics was inflamed by this, the more secretly they passed it around to be read in various houses. The more it was forbidden to be read publicly, the more they asserted that it had been written with invincible equity.

Thus they formed their treacherous plan: that it should be handed down to certain people in the manner of a creed—not to be examined, but to be believed. [Col. 0585B] Accordingly, we have undertaken its refutation, so that against each of its blasphemous statements we may fight with both rational truth and the authority of the Law.

We have not torn this book apart, but, transcribing it whole from beginning to end, we have cast it into the forest of the ninetieth heresy, exposing it as a most wicked tree, at whose root an axe has been laid, so that it may be cut down and thrown into the fire. Wherever the sayings of that book occur, they are indicated by lines placed behind the verses. Although, because of their perversity, they reveal themselves readily to readers, we nevertheless took care that truth should be distinguished from falsehood not only by rational words but also by rebuking *alogiai*—exposures of irrationality. [Col. 0586B]

Indeed, we mention the writings of the Catholic Greeks [Col. 0586A] that fight against the sects of heretics, and we set down all the heresies individually and in order, though briefly, so that the inventors of this new heresy may know that we oppose the definitions of all heretics and do not use the agreement of any of them against it.

Let every evasion cease, and let the cleverness of those who bark, like a dog, swallow its vomit again. We uncover, accuse, and condemn all the heresies that began with Simon, and we show that they have been overcome by both reason and authority.

In exposing falsehood and defending the truth, therefore, we have followed the footsteps of the Catholics. We have arranged matters so that in the first book the superstition of the ancient heresy may be fully exposed; in the second, the poisons of the new invention may not remain hidden; and the third book may hand over to all the Churches the tomb of the conquered heresy and the trophy of the faith.

Clement, therefore, bishop of Rome, disciple of Peter, and most worthy martyr of Christ, taught that Simon’s heresy had been overcome by the apostle Peter together with Simon himself. All the holy orthodox men followed him, and each in his own time wrote, in many books and many thousands of lines, about the origin, struggle, and end of each heresy. We have abridged these writings and, with the Lord’s help, enclosed them in this single little book.

May the holy studies that, through our labor, reach the rest from their cares pray for us.

[Col. 0585]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE HERESY OF THE PREDESTINARIANS

## TIRO PROSPER, IN HIS CHRONICLE, FROM THE LIBRARY OF SAINT VICTOR

The heresy of the Predestinarians, which is said to have received its beginning from Augustine, began to spread in these times.

[Note: [Col. 0585] What was written in Tiro’s *Chronicle* as “from Augustine,” Sigebert interpreted, most correctly, as “from books of Augustine wrongly understood.” For this is what Prosper testifies, in responding to the Gallic Chapters concerning Augustine’s detractors: that they criticized his teaching either because they did not understand it or because they did not wish it to be understood.]

[Col. 0585C]

## ARNOBIUS THE YOUNGER, ON PSALM 108

“He loved the curse,” namely, Adam’s curse, “which is taken away through Christ, and it will come upon him; and he did not wish for the blessing that is brought through Christ, and it will certainly be removed far from him.”

Note that this happened by free choice: he did not wish it, because of the heresy that says that God predestined some to blessing and others to cursing. Thus he is proved to have the curse because of his own love, and because he did not wish it he does not have the reward of blessing.

## FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF RIEZ, TO LEONTIUS OF ARLES

By your pastoral concern, blessed Pope Leontius, in convening a council of the highest bishops to condemn the error of predestination, you have rendered a service to all the Churches of Gaul.

[Col. 0585D]

## GENNADIUS OF MARSEILLES, IN HIS BOOK ON HERESIES

The Predestinarians are those who say that God did not create all people for the purpose that all might be saved, but so that the world might be adorned by the multitude of human beings.

Although he says in a general proclamation, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28), nevertheless he does not call all with the intention that all should follow the one who calls. Nor are all who, inspired by him, obey the call said to receive perseverance in carrying out a good work. Rather, after many labors and fruits of righteousness, if they are not among the number of those to be saved, [Col. 0586C] the strength to act is withdrawn from them, so that they do not continue in goodness.

Conversely, those who are predestined to eternal life, even if they roll for a long time in unbelief or in every kind of sin, will receive an opportunity by which they will both believe in God and live according to God’s commandment, so that they may possess fellowship with the saints.

By such a definition they strive to teach that God is a respecter of human persons; that he draws some, even unwilling, to salvation after many evil works; and that he rejects others after good works and compels them into evil, so that they may perish eternally.

## JOHN SCOTUS ERIUGENA, AGAINST GOTTSCHALK, BOOK I, CHAPTER 4

This Gottschalkian heresy, then—if it may be called by that name—has been established midway between two other heresies opposed to one another: [Col. 0586D] plainly, between the one called Pelagian and the one opposed to it. One of these diminishes the gift of divine grace; the other condemns free choice.

The Pelagian sect commends the freedom of rational nature to such an extent that it is sufficient, without the gift of grace, for perfecting human righteousness. The opposing sect, however, confirms the gift of gratuitous grace, so that, with grace alone operating in a person and every effort of free choice despised, [Col. 0587A] every believer may attain the summit of righteousness.

## SIGEBERT OF GEMBLOUX, IN HIS CHRONICLE, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 414

The heresy of the Predestinarians began to spread at this time. They are called Predestinarians because, while disputing about predestination and divine grace, they asserted [Col. 0588A] that the labor of good works benefits neither those who live piously if they have been predestined by God to death, nor does it harm the impious who live wickedly if they have been predestined by God to life.

This assertion both drew the good away from good works and incited the wicked to wickedness. This heresy is said to have taken its beginning from books of Augustine that were wrongly understood.

[Col. 0587]

THE HERESY OF THE PREDESTINARIANS, OR OF THOSE WHO TEACH PREDESTINATION, AND A REFUTATION OF THE BOOKS RASHLY ASCRIBED TO SAINT AUGUSTINE, DIVIDED INTO THREE BOOKS.

(From the edition of Sirmond, in Galland, *Bibliotheca*, vol. X.) (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0587B]

A synopsis of Hyginus’s *Ecdicesis* against the heresiarchs, and of Epiphanius’s *Categories* against the sects, and of Philaster’s *Expositions*, who, translating these works from Greek into Latin, published them when the Arians were being condemned. First came Hyginus, then Polycrates, the African, Hesiod, Epiphanius, and Philaster; at different times these men composed accounts of different heresies.

### I

The first heresy took its beginning from Simon, who said that chastity had nothing to do with God, that God had not made the world, and similar things. He was publicly defeated by the blessed and holy apostle Peter so completely that, after falling at his feet, he was utterly unable to rise again.

### II

The second heresy was that of Menander and the Menandrians, who declare that the world was made not by God but by angels. Saint Linus, the second bishop after the apostle Peter, expelled them from our fellowship and way of life and inflicted eternal condemnation upon them [Col. 0589A], teaching reasonably, in accordance with the holy Scriptures of the Old Testament, that the God who spoke with Moses is the creator of all things, and that among all created things there is nothing which, according to its nature, can be blameworthy. For everything judged culpable is culpable in its action, not in its condition.

### III

The third heresy was that of Basilides and the Basilidians. They say that there are three hundred and sixty-five heavens and, contrary to Moses, accept this claim; they name the God of these heavens Abrasax. The value of this name, when calculated according to the Greek system of letters, reaches the following total [Col. 0589]:

**ΑΒΡΑΣΑΞ**, that is: Α, one; Β, two; Ρ, one hundred; Α, one; Σ, two hundred; Α, one; and Ξ, sixty—making 365 in all. The Church, counting them as possessed persons, condemned them not by disputing with them but by casting them out.

[Note: Read according to the Greek reckoning with Cotelerius, on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VI, chapter 8, note 9.]

### IV

The fourth heresy, that of the Nicolaitans, was devised by Nicolaus, who had been ordained by the apostles as one of the seven deacons. When he was reproached on account of the jealousy aroused by his exceedingly beautiful wife, he began to teach that one ought to use wives indiscriminately—not only laymen, but also those serving in the priestly office. Saint John the apostle and evangelist condemned them and ordered that anyone who had entered into conversation with them, even briefly, should for that very reason be deprived of communion. He taught reasonably that, from the beginning of the world, chastity had been exceedingly pleasing to God; but that now Christ, the Son of God, had also consecrated the glory of chastity in himself: possessing a virgin mother and remaining a virgin, he permitted none of his disciples to engage even in lawful marital intercourse, saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

[Note: Nicolaus the deacon had both accusers and defenders. Cotelerius carefully lists both, at the place cited above, note 16.]

### V

The fifth heresy is that of the Saturninians, from Saturninus. He taught that seven angels made the world, and that they were intent on implanting lust in it, so that, while the sexes desired one another, the world, restrained from reaching its end, might be able to continue forever. The blessed Thomas, apostle of Christ, anathematized them, teaching reasonably that the world had a beginning and, because it had a beginning, would come to an end. He taught also that angels cannot possess omnipotence and therefore could not have established the world [Col. 0589D]. The creator of the world, he said, is the one God whom Moses proclaimed to have made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them.

### VI

The sixth heresy is that of the Gnostics, who wished to call themselves Gnostics, as though on account of superior knowledge, although they were judged to be more wretched than those whom we have mentioned above [Col. 0590A].

The blessed apostle Paul taught reasonably that they did not serve God but their own belly and lust, that they were puffed up, knew nothing, and were diseased with respect to questions and quarrels about words.

[Note: The Augsburg manuscript has *appellari*, “to be called.”]

### VII

The seventh is the heresy of the Carpocratians, devised by Carpocrates. He taught that the powers of darkness could not pass over anyone except those who had joined themselves to every kind of shamefulness. They asserted that our Lord Jesus had been begotten from both sexes, but that he had received such a soul as knew the things above in the heavens. Denying the resurrection of the body, they condemned the prophets of the Old Testament.

They had a certain Marcellina [Col. 0590B], who placed images of Jesus, Paul, and the philosopher Pythagoras in the midst of the people whom she was deceiving, and made them offer the honor of divinity and incense to these images. The blessed Barnabas, disciple of Christ, condemned them in Cyprus, teaching that they were ministers of Satan and decreeing that a Christian ought to have absolutely no conversation with them.

### VIII

The eighth heresy is that of the Cerinthians, from Cerinthus. They said that the world had been made by angels; that the flesh ought to be circumcised; and that the precepts of the Old Testament ought to be observed according to the letter [Col. 0590C]. They maintained that Jesus had been merely a human being, had not risen again, but would yet rise in the future. The blessed apostle Paul condemned them in Galatia with an eternal anathema. Finally, he refers to them in his Epistle to the Galatians.

[Note: In the Augsburg manuscript this chapter is tenth and reads as follows: “The tenth heresy is that of the Nazarenes. Although they confess the Son of God, they nevertheless observe all the practices of the Old Law, which Christians, through apostolic tradition, have learned not to observe carnally but to understand spiritually.”]

### IX

The ninth heresy is that of the Nazarenes. They confess the Son of God, but preserve the entire rite of the Old Testament in the Jewish manner. The blessed apostle Paul taught them that the Scriptures ought to be understood spiritually; he discovered them in the churches of [Note: Perhaps “Galatia.”] Galatia and decreed that those who did not agree with his teaching should be anathematized.

### X
