The tenth heresy is that of the Ebionites. They assert that the Lord Jesus Christ was merely a human being and establish that the commandments of the Law are to be kept in the Jewish manner. The evangelist Luke, finding them in the church of Antioch, condemned them, teaching that the angel had said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

[Note: In the Augsburg manuscript this chapter is ninth.]

### XI

The eleventh heresy is that of the Valentinians, from Valentinus [Col. 0591A]. Scattered throughout the East, they grievously wounded the Church of God, saying that the Deep and the Height had been mingled with one another. From these two, as if from a marriage, the world came forth. They called the Height the Father and the Deep the Son, and said that he had taken nothing from the virgin Mary, but had passed through her like water through a channel or pipe, without assuming any flesh. They utterly denied the resurrection of the flesh.

The blessed Zacchaeus, bishop of Caesarea, anathematized them, teaching that our Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man, passed through the virgin’s hidden womb, from the seed of David according to the flesh; that he was truly born as a man [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “truly”]; truly suffered; truly died; truly rose from the dead; and truly ascended into heaven.

### XII

The twelfth heresy [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “of the Evandrians.”] is that of the Secundians [Col. 0591B]. They differ from the Valentinians in this one respect: they add to this sect bodily shamefulness, which those pseudo-chaste people pretend to avoid. Bishop Diodorus of Crete condemned them.

### XIII

The thirteenth heresy is that of the Ptolemaeans [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Ptolemites”], from Ptolemy, a disciple of Valentinus. By arguing more aggressively, he disseminated this same heresy; at the same time he was condemned by the aforementioned holy Zacchaeus, bishop of Caesarea. Nevertheless, he spread the most wicked heresy through extensive regions of the East.

### XIV

The fourteenth heresy was devised by a certain Marcus. Denying the resurrection of the flesh, he attempted to establish that Christ had not truly suffered but only apparently. Saint Clement, bishop of Rome and most worthy martyr of Christ, refuted him with firm and complete arguments, exposed him before the entire congregation in the church, and punished him with eternal condemnation.

He taught that our Lord Jesus Christ was truly born and truly suffered, maintaining that nothing had been done by him in mere phantasy, and clearly showing that truth, being hostile to falsehood, could contain nothing false within itself—just as light cannot contain darkness, blessing cannot contain a curse, and sweetness cannot contain bitterness. Even if these things could be mixed, he taught that it is nevertheless impossible for God to be mixed with a lie.

### XV

The fifteenth heresy is that of the Colorbasians [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Colobrasian”], devised by Colorbasus [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Colobrasius”]. He attempted to establish that the whole life of human beings was placed in the seven stars, and that these were the seven churches and the seven golden lampstands.

Saint Theodotus, bishop of Pergamum, held a synod of seven bishops and anathematized him, teaching that the seven churches were consecrated in a sevenfold Spirit. “The first form,” he said, “is when a person is restored to the form which the first man had lost. The second is when one who was sinful is made immaculate. The third is when the dead body will be raised from the earth. The fourth is when the soul is rescued from the prison of hell. The fifth is that the soul rejoices in the dwelling of paradise until it receives its incorruptible body. The sixth is that he makes children of God those who were children of Adam [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “of God.”]. The seventh is that he makes a human being a participant in the kingdom of heaven.”

These, he said, are the forms of the Holy Spirit, placed in the seven churches, in the seven eyes, and in the seven golden lampstands.

### XVI

The sixteenth heresy was devised by Heracleon and is that of the Heracleonites. It taught that a baptized person, whether righteous or sinful, was to be counted as holy; and it declared that sins did not harm the baptized, saying that just as the nature of fire does not receive frost into itself, so the baptized person does not receive sin into himself.

For just as fire dissolves snow by its very sight, however much may lie nearby, so one who has been baptized once does not receive the guilt of sins, no matter how greatly his sins may have been mingled with his deeds. He began teaching this in the regions of Sicily.

Against him the Sicilian bishops Eustachius of Lilybaeum [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Eustasius”] and Theodorus of Panormus took action. They summoned a synod of all the bishops throughout Sicily and decided to hear him formally; then, sending all his assertions to Saint Alexander, bishop of the City, they asked him to arrange something for refuting him.

Saint Alexander then drew from the sheath of divine law, one by one, individual swords of the Word of God against each head of the hydra. He composed a book against Heracleon and sent the presbyter Sabinianus, exceptionally fervent in intellect, who refuted him by both the written arguments of the bishops and his own reasoning so effectively that Heracleon fled at midnight under the protection of a ship, and no one ever knew where he went.

[Note: Baluzius mentions this Sicilian synod in his new *Collection of Councils*, following the authority of our author: at the year 125 (vol. I of Labbé’s *Councils*, p. 555, Venetian edition). On this matter Pearson’s criticism must be examined in his posthumous works, p. 231.]

[Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “of the bishops.”]

### XVII

The seventeenth heresy is that of the Ophites. They were named from the serpent, for “serpent” is called *ophis* in Greek. They therefore keep a serpent accustomed to lick their loaves with its tongue and thus, as it were, sanctify them as an Eucharist. They call this serpent their Christ.

Against them the priests of the province of Bithynia—that is, Theocritus and Evander, the bishops of Chalcedon and Nicomedia—took action, publicly defeated them by refuting them, and then attacked them through their various associations. In the regions of Bithynia, as I have said, they secretly went through the estates where these practices were being carried out, expelled their priests, killed their serpents, and, giving an account before the entire people, freed most of the populace from this danger.

### XVIII

The eighteenth heresy is that of the Cainites [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Caianites,” as does Theodoret]. They were so called because they honor Cain, saying that he possessed the strongest virtue. At the same time, they think that Judas the betrayer was something divine and reckon his crime as a benefit, asserting that he had foreknown how greatly Christ’s passion would benefit the human race and had therefore handed him over to the Jews to be killed.

The priests of the churches of Mesopotamia in Syria [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “of the Mesopotamian churches”] wrote to their fellow bishops that these people had arisen. Thirty-two bishops residing at Antioch, together with Theodorus, the bishop of that city, refuted and condemned them on the spot, saying to them what the Holy Spirit spoke through the prophet: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness” (Isa. 5:20).

It is therefore clear that you have condemned yourselves, since you wish those whom God has destined, according to the character of their deed, for the eternal fire of Gehenna to be counted great and righteous.

### XIX

The nineteenth heresy is that of the Sethians. They received their name from Adam’s son called Seth, claiming that he was born from a heavenly mother, whom they say had intercourse with a heavenly father, so that another divine seed might be born from which God would choose righteous people for himself and call them his children.

They arose in the regions of Achaea. Against them Saint Perigenes, bishop of the city of Argos, took action, showing them that from the one holy and true righteous man Isaac two twin sons were born, brought forth from the same womb: one penetrated into the higher things of divine grace, while the other descended into the lower regions of hell.

“Therefore,” he said, “either one of the two is a son of an evil nature, and both are to be condemned for what they were born to be [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has ‘both, in accordance with what they are, are to be condemned’]; or they are sons of a good nature, and according to the character of their deeds, justice crowned one with blessing and condemned the other with a curse.”

When Saint Perigenes asserted these and similar things, some who believed were converted from this most wicked error. Those who did not believe and were not converted were cut off by the sword of anathema.

### XX

The twentieth heresy, in Crete, is that of the Archontics, who took their name from the rulers. For they boast that they worship the rulers whom they say created this world.

Saint Dioscorus, bishop of Crete, condemned them, teaching that the one true God cannot in any way be divided into substantial parts. He is the God who showed himself to the prophets and delivered from every danger those who believed in him: Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the children of Israel, Jonah, Susanna, and the three youths. God displayed countless signs of power toward those who believed in him, by which he showed himself to be the only God.

He received those who yielded to the truth, but punished those who dissented with eternal condemnation.

### XXI

The twenty-first heresy arose from Marcion. He affirms that there were two principles, one of good and one of evil [Col. 0594A]. Epiphanius said that he taught three principles—the good, the just, and the evil—but Eusebius writes that a certain Syrinus, not Marcion, was the author of the doctrine of three principles and natures [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Synerus,” as does Eusebius. See Cotelerius on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VI, chapter 8, note 12; and Huetius in the notes to Origen’s *Exegetica*, vol. II, p. 7.].

The Marcionites [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Marcionists”], while they were staining the universal Church of the East, were overcome and refuted by Origen and condemned in each individual city. Again, after some years, when they had already been defeated and exposed, they began to flourish in the regions of Africa. Tertullian so completely overcame them in every way that he made them publicly preach against their own sect.

### XXII

The twenty-second heresy is that of the Apellites, whose leader is Apelles. He introduces two gods but admits one principle: that is, the second was made by the one first principle [Col. 0594B]. Since this second principle was an evil creation, it was cast away by the good one. Having been cast away by the good principle, this principle, which acted wickedly against the will of the good principle, made the world in its wickedness.

Hence, he says, nature makes us more ready for evil than for good, and we take greater pleasure in vices than in virtues. They assert that our Lord Jesus Christ received flesh from the elements, returned it to the air when he ascended, and entered heaven without it.

Origen overcame them so completely that he became a *periodeutes* on their account and went through every city in the East preaching against them. Because the volumes of his expositions are innumerable, the heretics, having been defeated, altered his books with extremely clever argumentation according to their own desires, so that they could say to those whom they wished to deceive that Origen had defined matters in this way in his expositions [Col. 0594C].

Therefore, whoever reads Origen even today, if he knows how to distinguish his work by careful reading, detects the passages corrupted by the heretics. That this is so was demonstrated by the holy martyr Pamphilus in his *Apology* [Note: The author attributes the *Apology for Origen* to the holy martyr Pamphilus both here and below, chapter 43. We have discussed this matter elsewhere, namely in the *Prolegomena* to vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, chapter 1, §4, p. 4.].

### XXIII

The twenty-third heresy, that of the Cerdonians, took its beginning from Cerdo. He taught two opposed principles and said that the God of the Law and the prophets was not the Father of Christ, that God was not good but just, while the Father of Christ was good. He asserted that Christ himself had neither been born from a woman nor possessed flesh, and that he had neither truly died nor suffered anything, but had only pretended to suffer.

Saint Apollonius, bishop of the Corinthians, took action against him and condemned him together with the entire Eastern synod [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “and the entire Church together with the synod”]. He gave as the reason that this is the God who is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, of whom Moses says at the beginning of his book: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1).

He approved all the blameless people of the Old Testament according to the Apostle, saying: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns?” (Rom. 8:33).

When the priests condemned the heretics for these and similar reasons, they seemed by reasonable speech to satisfy them—either in order to recall them from the precipice or to show that they condemned sects, not human beings. Human beings, however, condemn themselves when, embracing condemned sects, they depart from the truth.

### XXIV

The twenty-fourth heresy is that of the Severians, who arose from Severus [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Severianus”]. They do not drink wine, because in their fanciful folly they assert that the earth caused the vine to sprout from the seed of Satan. Together with the Old Testament, they also reject the resurrection of the flesh.

Saint Euphranon, bishop of Rhodes, condemned them; for their superstition arose at Rhodes. He convicted them by the reasoning of the holy Scriptures, in which it is written that God brings bread out of the earth to strengthen the human heart, and wine to gladden it (Ps. 103:15–16).

It is not the necessary use of wine but its excess, which is hostile to salvation, that must be condemned. He also taught clearly that the resurrection of the flesh was promised by the one who in the present raised the dead; for if he had lied, he could certainly not have raised the dead.

He taught that the passages of the Old Testament are holy, like the foundations of a house, saying:

“The foundations of a house are laid around filthy places, so that the upper parts may suffer no insult from dung. The upper parts of the house are therefore raised with gilded ceilings, painted walls, and varied marble. But the lower parts, lying close to the earthly moisture, are arranged so as to support the whole of the upper structure. What, then, shall we do? If we remove the lower parts, the upper parts collapse. Yet if the lower parts had to be destroyed, no one other than the Son of God could do this. Let us therefore see whether he himself destroyed what we say remains: ‘Do you think that I have come to destroy the Law or the prophets? I have not come to destroy the Law but to fulfill it’” (Matt. 5:17).

By saying these and similar things, Saint Euphranon, the bishop, converted many. Those who persisted in their error he deprived of communion by perpetual decree.

### XXV

The twenty-fifth heresy is that of the Tatianists, instituted by a certain Tatian. They are also called Encratites. They condemn marriage and make it altogether equal to fornication and other corruptions. They do not admit into their number anyone—male or female—who uses marriage [Col. 0595D].

They do not eat meat and utterly abominate it. Against them Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, took action, citing the first epistle of the apostle Paul to Timothy, because they have a seared conscience, forbid marrying, and teach abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth:

“For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4:2–5).

We praise our Catholic abstainers for this reason: when they do not receive certain foods [Note: The Augsburg manuscript does not have “when”], they do not do so as people who say that receiving them is evil; rather, they say that receiving them is good and best, but assert that they are unworthy to partake of such food.

Thus the apostolic rule is preserved, which says: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, and let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat” (Rom. 14:3). For he does not accuse the creature, but declares that he himself is such that he does not deserve to be refreshed by this food [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “who says that he is such.”].

### XXVI

The twenty-sixth heresy is that of the Cataphrygians. They took this name from a province, not from a doctrine. Their authors were Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla.

They assert that the coming of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord was fulfilled in themselves rather than in the apostles. They regard second marriages as fornication. Therefore, they say, the apostle Paul permitted them because he knew in part and prophesied in part. For what is perfect had not yet come. They foolishly claim that this perfection came upon Montanus and his prophetesses whom we mentioned above.

So much may be said about the Cataphrygians. I pass over the remaining allegations as uncertain. We mention that they are said to receive the blood of an infant so that we may not appear to be unaware of everything said about them; for those who wrote against them make no mention of this matter at all.

Saint Soter, pope of the City, wrote a book against them, as did Apollonius, bishop of Ephesus [Col. 0596C]. Tertullian, a presbyter of Carthage, wrote against these men. Although he wrote everything else well, excellently, and incomparably, he made himself blameworthy in this one respect: he defended Montanus, acting against the aforementioned Soter, pope of the City. He asserted that the reports about infant blood were false, and that they shared with us the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead, penance for the lapsed, and the same mysteries and one Easter.

“We differ only in this,” he says, “that we do not accept second marriages and do not reject Montanus’s prophecy concerning the future judgment.”

Some object to Tertullian that he said the soul is derived from another soul—*ex traduce*, that is, that a soul is generated from a soul just as a body is generated from bodies. The Catholic faith vehemently rejects this.

[Note: Dodwell proves the testimony of our author concerning Pope Soter’s writing against the Cataphrygians in his separate dissertation *On the Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 14, §2. The distinguished Abbé de Longuerue should also not be omitted, in his dissertation *On the Heresy of Montanus*, §8, p. 259.]

### XXVII

The twenty-seventh heresy is that of the Pepuzians, who were named after a certain place. Epiphanius calls it a deserted city; but they, thinking it to possess something divine, call it Jerusalem.

They grant women so much authority that they are honored among them even with priesthood. For they say that there are two churches in the same city of Pepuza, those of Quintilla and Priscilla. They are one with the Cataphrygians. They despise them, however, because these Pepuzians consider themselves better than the others.

They say that Pepuza was a village belonging to Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and that because they began preaching there and lived there, they called the place Jerusalem. And because they are inhabitants of the place, they count themselves better than the others [Col. 0597A]. The bishop Apollonius of Ephesus overcame them.

### XXVIII

The twenty-eighth heresy calls its adherents Artotyrites; their offering gave them this name. For they offer bread and cheese, saying that from the first human beings offerings to God were made from the fruits of the earth and from sheep.

Epiphanius joins them to the Pepuzians. No one deigned even to speak against them.

### XXIX

The twenty-ninth heresy is called the Tessareskaidekatites, because they celebrate Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, whatever day of the week it may fall on [Col. 0597B]. If it falls on the Lord’s Day, they fast and keep vigil on that very day. This alone distinguishes them from us; there is nothing else.

Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, overcame them in many cities by the following reasoning. He went with his clergy and celebrated Easter with them, saying: “Just as we have celebrated Easter with you, come and receive it with us.” When he obtained this from them, they began to share one conviction and to celebrate the day with us. For they proved that they held the whole rule of faith as we do, and that they believed as we do.

### XXX

The thirtieth heresy is that of the Alogians. They are so called because they do not wish to accept that the Son is the Word of God, to such an extent that they say the Gospel of Saint John is not his, and they do not accept the Apocalypse of that same John [Col. 0597C].

What more need be said? They agree with us in everything except that they utterly abominate the Word of God, the Son of God, as though it were blasphemy [Note: I have no doubt that something has dropped out here, namely: “They agree with us in everything except that the Word …” Thus the sentence will cohere perfectly. Wesseling, *Probabilia*, chapter 30, p. 266.]. Bishop Philo often overcame them.

### XXXI

The thirty-first heresy is that of the Adamites, who took their name from Adam and imitate his nakedness in paradise, as it was before the sin. Hence they also reject marriage, because Adam did not know his wife before he had been expelled from paradise.

They therefore believe that marriages would not have existed if no one had sinned. Men and women therefore meet naked, hear readings naked, pray naked, and celebrate the sacraments naked. For this reason they regard their church as paradise.

The holy presbyter Polycarp exposed, overcame, and expelled them [Col. 0597D].

### XXXII

The thirty-second heresy is that of the Helcesites. A certain false prophet named Helci deceived them; from his lineage, it is said, two women were worshiped by them as goddesses. Epiphanius asserts that in other respects they held beliefs similar to those of the Ebionites. The presbyter Papias of Achaea overcame them.

[Col. 0598A]

### XXXIII

The Theodotians hold the thirty-third place among the heresies. They were instituted by a certain Theodotus [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Theodotion”], asserting that Christ was merely a human being and the Son of God. The same Theodotus is said to have taught this because, having lapsed during persecution, he thought he could avoid the disgrace of his fall in this way—if he appeared not to have denied God, but only a human being.

Bishop Craton of the Syrians overcame them.

### XXXIV

The Melchisedechians devised the thirty-fourth heresy. They think that Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, was not a human being but the power of God, following the passage in the Epistle to the Hebrews which says: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy” (Heb. 7:3).

Dionysius, bishop of Jerusalem, confronted them, saying that Melchizedek had both a father and a mother. He said that the Apostle spoke in this way because neither his genealogy nor his maternal or paternal ancestry was recorded in the order in which the law of the Hebrews was written, although the generation of the Hebrews was certainly pleasing to God.

### XXXV

The thirty-fifth heresy is that of the Bardesanites, led astray by a certain Bardesanes [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “Bardesan”]. Bardesanes is said to have been a completely orthodox Catholic, but afterward, through a disciple of Valentinus, he fell into the error of calling the creation of human flesh evil and the soul good.

The bishop Theocritus condemned him in Cappadocia, teaching that the good God made and joined both together, and that it is not the nature of the human flesh but its transgression that must be blamed.

### XXXVI

The thirty-sixth heresy is that of the Noetians [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has “of the Anoetians”]. They say that Christ is himself the Father and the Holy Spirit [Note: The Augsburg manuscript has: “that Christ and the Holy Spirit are the same, not in substance.”], not in substance, as we do, but in person, so that the Holy Spirit is said to be so merely in appearance, not truly.

He was condemned by Tranquillus, bishop of the Chalcedonians of Syria. Tranquillus demonstrated that the Father is true, the Son is true, and the Holy Spirit is true. He affirmed that one God is to be believed in one substance, but three persons by distinction.

### XXXVII

The Valesians fall into the thirty-seventh heresy. These wretched people castrate both themselves and their guests. In this way, they say, the saying is fulfilled: “Those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:11).

They are also said to teach other heretical and shameful things, but neither Epiphanius himself mentions what these are, nor have I been able to find them anywhere. They were condemned by a synod of Achaea.

### XXXVIII

The thirty-eighth heresy is that of the Cathars, who arrogantly called themselves by this name as though on account of purity. They do not admit second marriages and deny penance.

They follow the heretic Novatian and are therefore also called Novatians. Against him the blessed Xystus, martyr and bishop, and the venerable Cyprian, martyr of Christ and then bishop of Carthage, wrote a book against Novatus, *On the Lapsed*, teaching that through penance people could recover the grace which they had lost by falling, whereas Novatus asserted that this was entirely impossible.

### XXXIX

The thirty-ninth heresy is that of the Angelics. They wished to be called Angelics. For they say that angels ought to be worshiped and honored in spirit, and that prayers should be poured out to them, so that the angels whom they know to be able to do more may themselves assist human wishes and petitions.

Epiphanius testifies that they have now completely disappeared, having been overcome by Theophilus, bishop of Apamea [Col. 0599B].

### XL

In the fortieth place appeared the Apostolics. They arrogantly wished to be called by this name because they do not receive into their communion those who use marriage or possess private property—things which the Catholic Church has, including many monks and clerics.

They are therefore heretics because, separating themselves from the Church, they think that those who use the things they themselves lack have no hope. The Church confronts them with the testimony in which the Apostle says: “Even if I discipline my body not only by abstinences but also hand it over to the fire to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

[Col. 0599C]

### XLI

The Sabellians fall into the forty-first heresy, from Sabellius. They confess the Father as himself, the Son as himself, and the Holy Spirit as himself.

These are also called Praxeans, because at the beginning they had a certain teacher named Praxeas. They are also called Hermogenians, because they had Hermogenes as a companion of Sabellius.

Bishop Dositheus of Seleucia confronted them, teaching that Sabellius denied the whole Trinity while thinking that he was defending unity. For the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, coequal in all things with the Father and the Son. The Godhead so accepts unity of substance that it does not lose distinction of person.

[Col. 0599D]

## XLII

The forty-second heresy was begun by the Origenians, [Note: [Col. 0599] Huetius sharply attacks here and shortly afterward this writer, who invents two Origens, in *Origenianus*, Book I, chapter 1, § 7, p. 3. He also observes that Baronius expressly denied this, while he carefully investigated the reasons why a second Origen was fabricated, at the year 256, § 47. After Huetius, the same point was noted by Cotelerius, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. I, p. 778, and by Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. V, p. 213, note a.] by a certain Origen—not the one known to almost everyone, but another, a certain exceedingly wicked Syrian. Epiphanius says of him that he taught such shameful things that they ought not even to be handed down in writing to our descendants.

## XLIII

The forty-third heresy was immediately followed by other Origenians, [Col. 0600A] as Epiphanius says. They also deny the resurrection of the dead; but they say that the Holy Spirit is a creature of Christ, while affirming that paradise and the heavens are allegorical expressions. These two Origens [Note: [Col. 0600] The Aug. manuscript has: “the evil things that have been written. Heretics.”] wrote every kind of evil. Heretics and perverse teachers mixed them with our Catholic Origen, the interpreter of Scripture, so that what the Lord says in the Gospels might be fulfilled: “Did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, [Note: [Col. 0600] The Aug. manuscript has: “does it have these weeds?”] are these weeds?” He answered: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII, 27).

For this reason, when reading Origen, we find him Catholic, fighting against and defeating heresies; yet, when reading Origen again, we find him heretical and asserting things opposed to the faith. Letters convey words and meanings; if they could also display the faces of those speaking, no one could fall into error concerning the identity of the teacher. For one must also guard against what a certain Ampullianus, a Bithynian arch-heretic, taught in the Church of God after Origen. He fell into such a heresy that he said all criminals, together with the devil and demons, were to be boiled in Gehenna until, once purified, they could emerge from it clean and spotless, and thus be restored again to their own Creator, to the state in which they had previously been free from guilt.

When he was challenged by the universal Church, he began producing books of Origen that he himself had corrupted and saying, “See, Origen thought this way”—especially in the four books of *Periarchon* (“On First Principles”). But a person of sound judgment, possessing [Note: [Col. 0600] The Aug. manuscript has: “the bright eyes of the mind.”] bright eyes, sees and recognizes that these evils were added to Origen’s little works just as one might see white pieces of cloth, or pieces of any other color, sewn onto a scarlet covering. That this is so is taught by the holy martyr Pamphilus, who, before attaining the crown of martyrdom, held the episcopal chair [Note: [Col. 0600] The author incorrectly reports that Pamphilus the martyr was a bishop.] without reproach and ministered sound doctrine to the peoples of God.

He published an *Apology* and removed all the lies that Catholics, in ignorance, [Note: [Col. 0600] The Aug. manuscript has: “ignorantly.”] utter about Origen. He showed that the objectionable things found in Origen’s works were not Origen’s, but belonged to those whom he himself had overcome; whereas the other things that are wholly perverse belonged to two other heretics, who possessed Origen’s name but neither his faith nor his conscience.

## XLIV

The forty-fourth heresy, invented by Paul of Samosata, [Col. 0600D] formed for itself a Paulian people. They say that Christ did not always exist, but began from Mary, and that he was nothing more than a human being. This heresy had previously belonged to Artemon; when it had declined, it was restored by this Paul of Samosata. Likewise, although after many years, when the perverse defense had failed together with its advocates, the Church took action against him; then, when it was renewed again by our bishop Photinus, it produced a Photinian people.

Whether, therefore, you hear of Artemonians, Paulians, [Col. 0601A] or Photinians, know this one thing: just as we call people Donatists, Montenses, and Parmenianists [Note: [Col. 0601] Perhaps “Montenses.”], we call them Donatists after Donatus, Montenses after the hiding place in the mountain, and Parmenianists after Parmenianus, who traveled throughout Africa composing books against us and producing new psalms; against him our Optatus wrote.

But let us return to the Paulians. [Note: [Col. 0601] The Aug. manuscript has “Paulinianos.” But more correctly, surely, “Paulianos,” namely from Paul of Samosata, as also Augustine in *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus; from that book the author of the *Praedestinatus* copied this enumeration of his heresies almost word for word.] It is known to everyone that we do not rebaptize heretics who come to us, but extend the hand of reconciliation and thus hand them over to the divine people to be joined to them. Concerning the Paulinians, however, the holy Council of Nicaea established that they must be baptized outright and only then joined to the Catholic people. Hence I believe that they do not possess the rule of baptism intact, and that this decree was established by the bishops of Christ for that reason.

## XLV

The forty-fifth heresy is that of the Photinians, from Photinus, whom I said to have been our bishop just as Judas Iscariot was our apostle. He formed his own people. He taught that Christ was a mere human being and, with Paul of Samosata, believed that Christ began from Mary; but he maintained that the Holy Spirit had always existed. In this alone he differed from the forty-fourth heresy: he named the people whom he had perverted after himself.

## XLVI

The forty-sixth heresy, begun by Manes, formed the sect of the Manichaeans. This Manes, although a Persian citizen, and although he claimed while teaching in Persia to be an apostle of God, also made his way to Greece. His Greek disciples, avoiding the name associated with madness, decided that he should be called “Manichaeus,” that is, as though he were “pouring out manna.” [Note: [Col. 0602] Restore *Mannichaeus*, with Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. I, p. 171, note (**).]

He constructed two principles, mutually different and opposed, and likewise eternal and co-eternal—that is, existing always—and, following certain other ancient heretics, he held that there were two natures and substances, namely, of good and of evil. They assert, according to their doctrines, that there is conflict and mixture between these, that the good is purified from the evil, and that the good which could not be purified is condemned with the evil forever. They tell many stories about these matters, all of which would take too long to set out.

They say that good souls are of the same nature as God. Accordingly, they do indeed confess that the world was made by the nature of the good, that is, by the nature of God; but they say this resulted from the mixture of good and evil, which occurred when the two natures fought against each other. They say that God’s power carries out the purification and liberation of the good from the evil not only throughout the whole world and from all its elements, but also through the food that their elect consume.

They maintain that God’s substance is mixed with those foods, just as with the whole world, and that it is purified in their elect by the manner of life lived by the Manichaean elect, as though this were holier and more excellent than that of their hearers. For they wished their church to consist of these two classes, namely, the elect and the hearers.

In other people, including their own hearers, they believe that this portion of the good and divine substance, which is held mixed and bound in foods and drinks, is especially tightly and filthily bound in those who beget children. Whatever light is purified from every side, they say, is returned to the kingdom of God, as to its proper dwelling places, by certain ships, which they identify as the moon and the sun. They say that these ships were fashioned from the pure substance of God, and that this bodily light, which lies before the eyes of mortal living creatures, is God’s nature.

They assign five elements, which they say produced their own rulers, to the race of darkness. They call these elements by the names smoke, darkness, fire, water, and wind. Animals with two feet were born in smoke, from which they believe human beings derive their origin; creeping animals in darkness; four-footed animals in fire; swimming animals in water; and flying animals in wind.

They say that five other elements were sent from the kingdom and substance of God to conquer these five evil elements, and that in this conflict they became mixed: air with smoke, light with darkness, good fire with evil fire, good water with evil water, and good wind with evil wind.

They distinguish those ships—the two heavenly lights—in this way: they say that the moon was made from good water, but the sun from good fire. They also say that holy powers are in these ships, transforming themselves into males in order to entice the women of the hostile race. When their desire is stirred by this enticement, the light that they held mixed with their bodily members escapes from them, is received by the angels of light for purification, and, once purified, is placed in those ships to be carried back to its proper kingdoms.

On this account their elect are compelled to consume what is spread like a Eucharist together with human semen, so that the divine substance may be purified from it as well, just as from the other foods they receive. But when they denied that they did this, they were exposed. For they were also exposed in the church at Carthage.

Finally, at an assembly of bishops before the entire people, a girl not yet twelve years old confessed this unspeakable depravity and disclosed many things, asserting that she herself had been subjected to violence for the sake of their wicked sacrament. When at first no one believed a single girl acting alone, she named many women who knew of this crime. These women, driven from various houses where they were being hidden by clerics, through the assistance of Ursus the tribune, who at that time was in charge of the imperial household, were brought to the Restituta church. It is reported that they too had suffered this very thing for that reason, and confessed only with difficulty and under compulsion.

Then the whole most shameful crime was brought into the open: flour is placed underneath to receive and mix the semen of those having intercourse. What is said and heard with boundless shame has also recently led to some of them being brought to the church, as the episcopal acts drawn up there testify.

Thus they have three groups: the Catharistae, [Note: [Col. 0603] The Aug. manuscript has *Mattari*. Augustine has the same reading. The manuscript copies, however, have *Mattari* and *Mattarii.] the Macharii, and the Manichaeans. Nevertheless, it is clear that all three forms were written down by one teacher, that same wicked Manes. In the end, they all read Manichaeus, and all his books are without question held in common by them.

These books teach that the ruler of both sexes, the prince of darkness, is dissolved through sexual desire, and that the divine substance, which they believe is held in pollution in human semen, escapes from them once liberated. Hence they are also called Catharistae, as though “purifiers.”

Although they do not eat meat, they are so polluted that, together with all their adherents, they consume human semen, even though they do not accept eggs either; for they say that eggs themselves expire when they are broken. They also do not use the nourishment of milk—not because they think that no divine substance is mixed into it, but because their error is inconsistent with itself.

They also do not drink wine, saying that it is the gall of the prince of darkness; yet they eat grapes, although they do not take even a finger dipped in must. They believe that the souls of their hearers pass back into the elect; but they assert that all other souls—not those of their hearers—return into animals and into everything fixed by roots and nourished in the earth.

They believe that there is life in herbs and trees in such a way that they feel and experience pain when injured. Therefore, in their madness, they accuse agriculture—which is the most innocent of all arts—as guilty of countless murders, especially when they see a field being cleared of thorns. They believe their hearers are forgiven for this reason: that they provide food from it for their elect, so that the divine substance, purified in the elect’s belly, may obtain pardon for those whose offering is used to purify it.

Thus the elect themselves do no work in the fields, pick no fruit, and pluck no leaves, but wait for these things to be brought for their use by their hearers, living, according to their own vanity, from so many and such great murders committed by others.

They also warn their hearers that, if they eat meat, they should not kill animals, lest they offend the princes of darkness, who are bound in the heavens and from whom they say all flesh derives its origin. And they use their wives [Note: [Col. 0603] The Aug. manuscript has: “and thus let them use them.”] in such a way as to avoid conception and generation, lest the divine substance entering them through food become bound by bodily bonds [Note: [Col. 0604] The Aug. manuscript has: “in offspring.”] in the child. For they believe that souls enter all flesh—that is, through food and drink.

Hence they condemn marriage without hesitation and, insofar as they can, prohibit it, since they prohibit generation, for which marriages are joined. They assert that Adam and Eve were born from the princes of smoke. Their father, they say, was named Saclas; he devoured the offspring of all his companions and, having intercourse with his wife, bound within the flesh of his offspring, as though with the strongest chain, whatever divine substance he had taken from that mixture.

They affirm that Christ was the one whom our Scripture calls the serpent. They say that he illuminated their eyes so that they might distinguish good and evil, and that this Christ came in the final times to liberate souls, not bodies. They say that he was not in true flesh, but presented the appearance of flesh to deceive human senses, falsely simulating not only death but also resurrection.

They assert that the God who gave the law through Moses and spoke in the Hebrew prophets is not the true God, but one of the princes of darkness. They read the Scriptures of the New Testament as though they had been falsified, accepting from them whatever they wish and rejecting whatever they do not wish; and, as though they possessed the whole truth, they prefer certain apocryphal writings to them.

They say that our Lord Jesus Christ’s promise concerning the Paraclete was fulfilled in their arch-heretic Manes. Hence, in his own writings, he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ, because Jesus Christ promised that he would send him; and therefore he is his apostle because the Holy Spirit was sent in him.

For this reason Manes himself also had twelve disciples, in imitation of the apostolic number; the Manichaeans continue to preserve this number today. From among their elect they have twelve whom they call teachers, and a thirteenth who is their leader. They have seventy-two bishops, ordained by the teachers, and presbyters, ordained by the bishops, in an indefinite number. The bishops also have deacons. All the rest are simply called elect. Yet even those who appear suitable are sent to this error, either where it is to be increased or where it has not yet been sown.

They claim that baptism in water brings no salvation to anyone, and they do not believe that any of those whom they deceive should be baptized. By day they pray to the sun as it travels in every direction; by night, to the moon if it is visible, but if it is not visible, toward the north, where the sun, after setting, returns to the east. They pray standing.

They attribute the origin of sins not to the free choice of the will, but to the substance of the hostile race, which they teach is mixed with human beings. They assert that all flesh is the work not of the Divinity but of an evil mind, which is co-eternal with the opposing God.

They wish carnal desire, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, to be an opposing substance, clinging to us in such a way that, when we are liberated and purified, it is restored again and continues to live immortally in its own nature. They say that in one human being there are two souls and two minds, opposed by nature—good and evil—and that they are in conflict with each other.

When this age has ended, after the conflagration of the world, they say that this substance of evil will live in a certain globe, as in a prison. They assert that something made from souls naturally good, but unable to be cleansed from the contagion of the evil nature, will approach and remain forever attached to that globe, as though serving as its covering and roof.

## XLVII

The forty-seventh heresy was instituted by Hieracas, the Hieracites. They deny the resurrection of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0604] The Aug. manuscript has: “They receive only monks.”] They admit only monks and nuns, and those who do not have marriages, into communion. They say that little children do not belong to the kingdom of heaven because they have no merits from the struggle by which vices are overcome.

The holy Aphrodisius, bishop of the Hellespont, opposed him, asserting that the resurrection of the flesh is established by both the New and the Old Testament. He also said that infants are already human beings: just as one who kills them incurs the charge of homicide, so one who consecrates them by baptism gains a reward for the salvation of a human being. Communion is to be denied to no one except those who, having set aside their own spouses, seek others’ spouses.

## XLVIII

The forty-eighth heresy is that of the Meletians, from a certain Meletius. They formed a schism because they refused to pray with those who had fallen during the persecution. The holy bishop Basil of Cappadocia resisted them, saying that the greater charity of hope and faith endures all things, and that a hand should rather be extended to the fallen. He also urges that those in despair should be encouraged to recover and return, since even in heaven one repentant person causes greater joy among the angels than ninety-nine who have not sinned (Luke XV, 10).

## XLIX

Arius arose as the forty-ninth arch-heretic. He established the Arian peoples, who refuse to say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one and the same substance. They wish the Son to be a creature, but the Holy Spirit to be a creature of a creature—that is, created by the Son.

Epiphanius reported that Arius also believed Christ had assumed flesh without a soul. For this reason he speaks of the Father as greater than the Son, as though he were the Son’s creator, and of the Son as greater than the Holy Spirit, as though he were the Spirit’s creator.

They rebaptize our people—that is, Catholics—when they come over to them. Whether they do this also to others, that is, to non-Catholics, is nowhere recorded. The holy Hesiodus, bishop of the Corinthians, was the first to oppose them; he is also said to have raised the dead. Thus people, paying more attention to his holiness than to argument, came to detest Arius. For Arius himself is said, while sitting in seclusion, to have expelled all his intestines at once together with his feces through his own prayers.

Both Eastern and Western bishops have written against his sect. They assert that he blasphemed in each individual article of his doctrines.

## L

Epiphanius mentions the Audiani as the fiftieth group [Note: [Col. 0605] The Aug. manuscript has *Valdiani*. Augustine has *Vadiani*.], not indeed as heretics but as schismatics. Others call them Anthropomorphites, because they imagine God with carnal thought, in the likeness of the image of corruptible humanity, saying: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous” (Ps. XXXIII, 16); “The heavens are the work of God’s fingers” (Ps. VIII, 4); “God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. XLVI, 9); and “God stood in the assembly of the gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 1), along with other passages that can be understood in terms of visible form.

Since they err in no other respect, Epiphanius, dealing more gently with them, did not wish to call them heretics, granting pardon to their rusticity. But because they do not communicate with us, they loudly proclaim that our bishops possess riches, which Christ commands even laypeople to despise. They celebrate Easter with the Jews. Zeno, a bishop of the Syrians, acted against them.

## LI

The fifty-first heresy is that of the Eunomians, from Eunomius. Filled with the spirit of the ancient serpent, they assert not only that the Son is lesser, but that he is not even of similar essence. The presbyter Ammonius acted against them.

## LII

The fifty-second heresy is that of the Macedonians, from Macedonius. Our people throughout the East call them Pneumatomachi, because they dispute concerning the Holy Spirit. They think correctly concerning the Father and the Son, but refuse to believe that the Holy Spirit is God, calling him a creature. Philaster writes that Macedonius called the Holy Spirit the divinity of the Father and the Son; by saying this, he appears to deny the Holy Spirit his own proper identity. [Note: [Col. 0605] The Aug. manuscript adds: “The Council of Nicaea acted against them.”]

## LIII

The fifty-third heresy is that of the Aerians, from a certain Aerius. He is said to have grieved, while a presbyter, because he had not been ordained a bishop. He began to teach that offerings should not be made for the departed, and that established fasts should not be observed; rather, one should fast whenever one wished, lest one appear to be under the law. He also taught that there should be no distinction between presbyter and bishop, [Col. 0606C] and that no one should be admitted to their communion except those who abstained from marriage.

## LIV

The fifty-fourth heresy is called Aetian, after Aetius. Together with Eunomius, they confess that the Son is entirely unlike the Father [Note: [Col. 0606] The Aug. manuscript has: “they say while confessing.”]. They also say: “Let all who agree with our faith know that no sins whatsoever committed by them can harm them” [Note: [Col. 0606] The Aug. manuscript has: “that no sins can harm them.”]. A synod of twenty bishops acted against them in Achaea.

## LV

The fifty-fifth heresy is that of the Apollinarists, begun by Apollinaris. They deny that Christ was a complete human being, but say that the assumption of flesh took place in such a way that divinity was within the human being in place of a soul. They wished to teach that the flesh and the Word were of one and the same substance. Citing with extreme insistence the words, “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14), they wish to teach that something of the Word was changed into flesh. Moreover, they affirm that nothing was assumed from Mary’s flesh in the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. A synod in Antioch acted against him.

## LVI

In the fifty-sixth heresy, the heretics were called Antidicomarianites [Note: [Col. 0606] Augustine has *Antidicomarianitae*.]. They contradict Mary’s virginity to such an extent that they assert she had intercourse with a man after Christ was born. Theodotus, bishop of Cyprus, acted against them.

## LVII

We find the fifty-seventh heresy, that of the Messalians. This name comes from the Syriac language; in Greek they are called Euchites, named from prayer. They do not sing psalms but pray continually. But because this is all they do, possessing neither charity nor conversation nor humanity, they were refuted as heretics by a holy synod.

They also condemn those monks who engage in anything other than reading and prayer, whether a craft or agriculture. Epiphanius reached this point and fell silent. I believe that he lived only up to that time. Human curiosity can report past and present matters, but God alone can predict the future.

But because Philaster himself, in the books in which he set out the histories of various people, also included heresies that arose in later times, we now extract from his books and present only those heresies. Ephrem, a Syrian presbyter, acted against them.

## LVIII

The fifty-eighth heresy was begun by the Metangismonites. In Greek, ἀγγεῖον (*angeion*) means “vessel,” while μεταγγισμός (*metangismos*) refers to one vessel within another. From this expression they derived their name, saying: “The Son is in the Father as a smaller vessel is within a larger vessel.”

The Church therefore rejects them because they think carnally about what is incorporeal, speak of what is incomprehensible in limited terms [Note: [Col. 0607] The Aug. manuscript has: “in a bounded way.”], and establish degrees within the equality of the Divinity. Diodorus, bishop of Nicomedia, acted against them.

## LIX

The fifty-ninth heresy is that of the Seleucians, who arose from Seleucus. They say that the matter of the elements from which the world was made was not made by God, but is co-eternal with God. They do not attribute the soul to God the Creator; rather, they wish the angels to be creators of souls, from fire and spirit.

They assert that evil comes sometimes from God and sometimes from matter. They deny that the Savior sits in the flesh at the right hand of the Father; instead, they say that he stripped it off and placed it in the sun, taking their occasion from the psalm where it is written: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII, 6).

They deny a visible paradise, do not accept baptism in water, and do not believe that there will be a resurrection; rather, they assert that resurrection occurs daily in the generation of children. Our discipline of faith does not permit them to engage with us in disputation, but commands that they be consigned to anathema for their definitions.

## LX

The sixtieth heresy was formed by the Proclinianists, from Proclinus. They say that the Son of God appeared on earth as the angel Raphael or Gabriel, not having assumed flesh but only appearing to do so.

They mingle with the people of God in such a way that they are not recognized. Finally, because they suffer from no other error, they communicate with us; and this is what is worse, because they make any simple people they encounter think and believe in the same way.

They assert this crime, which is profoundly hostile to our salvation, as follows: “So, then, did God have to endure those filths inflicted by natural conception, childbirth, and the woman giving birth? Did the Son of God have to possess a belly that expelled and washed away its waste, moisture from the nostrils, saliva from the mouth, filth in the ear, feces in the stomach, and foulness in the breath?”—and other things of this kind, which madness of mind devises.

Tertullian vigorously opposed them, showing that the Son of God is impassible, and that these things bring not injury but praise to the Divinity.

It is like a king who, wishing to retrieve a gold ring with a gem from a sewer, puts on a slave’s tunic and descends into the sewer, so that the tunic may receive the filth; then, reaching in and rescuing the gold ring with its gem, he washes it with water and places it on his royal finger after climbing out.

So, without doubt, the Son of God, assuming the form of a servant, came not only to the lower regions of heaven, where we are who appear to live in the world, but also to the deeper lower regions, which are farther below us than we are below heaven. In order to rescue the human race from there, he endured the squalor of every kind of filth—not his own, but ours.

For the living, he lived as we who live do, differing in nothing except that he practiced an immaculate life, having God within him. For the dead, he died in the same way, differing in nothing except that he rose from the dead on the third day; and he descended for this reason, to rescue the saints from there and bind the prince of death.

That he placed the gold ring with the gem he explained in the following reading, declaring that the ring signified the body and that the gem enclosed within it signified the soul. Thus Christ lifted this ring from ancient filth and from the sewer of this world, drenched it with baptismal water, and washed it of every stain, causing it to shine in the hands of his saints.

For it is written: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis. III, 1). And again: “Place me like a ring upon your hand” (Song VIII, 6). And: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. XXX, 6). There are countless similar passages in the sacred writings; omitting them for the sake of brevity, let us proceed to the sixty-first heresy.

## LXI

The sixty-first heresy was formed by the Patricians, taking its beginning from Patricius. They say that the substance of human flesh was created not by God but by the devil, and they so detest it that they call the person perfect who is able resolutely to kill himself. Some of them even ask strangers whom they meet to kill them.

This madness began long ago in the regions of Upper Numidia and Mauretania. The wretched Donatists later followed them and began to hurl themselves down mountain precipices as though they were going to become martyrs, so that those who abandon eternal life in the Catholic faith might find, as *viothanati* (seekers of a violent death), eternal death. Optatus is said to have acted against them.

## LXII

The sixty-second heresy is that of the Ascites. The Ascites are named from a leather bag, for ἀσκός (*askos*) means “leather bag” in Greek. Although these people have nothing evil concerning the Trinity, they place an enormous leather bag beside the altar, inflate it while empty, cover it with linen cloths, and worship it, because they add there what has been made from the Lord’s blood, citing the Gospel saying: “They put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matt. IX, 17).

## LXIII

The sixty-third heresy is that of the Passalorynchites. Whenever they gather in their church, they cultivate such silence that they place a finger on their nostrils and lips, lest they injure even the silence itself with their breath.

I do not know why those who composed this name preferred to signify the finger by *palus* (“stake”), since in Greek πάσσαλος (*passalos*) means “stake,” δάκτυλος (*daktylos*) means “finger,” and ῥύγχος (*rhynchos*) means “nose.” It seems better to me that they should be called Dactylorynchites.

The devil has found for himself, within God’s law, people whom he could make into Pythagoreans, observing the Apostle’s words: “I will pray with the spirit, I will pray also with the mind; I will sing a psalm with the spirit, I will sing a psalm also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV, 15). They therefore teach people what they should say outside the church in their hearts while inside the church.

As though the same Apostle had not said: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). I say that the person who undertakes the labor of replying to such people wastes his time foolishly; and I judge it right that by remaining silent we should conquer those who are silent.

## LXIV

The sixty-fourth heresy is that of the Aquarians, who are called Aquarians because they offer water in the sacramental cup. They say that wine is a thing of drunkenness, through which murders, fornications, and other crimes are committed, although it is clear that everything excessive causes guilt and produces vice.

Crimes are therefore committed not by drinking wine, but by excess. What is there that does not incur blame when taken excessively? Let water be drunk excessively, and let us see whether it does not harm. Let bread be eaten excessively, and let us see whether it does not produce indigestion.

Thus, while maintaining the proper measure in all things, we also anathematize these people because, separating Christ’s blood from its source through the prejudice of fornicators and murderers, they boldly violate the rule established by Christ. [Note: [Col. 0609] The Aug. manuscript has: “weaken.”]

## LXV

The sixty-fifth heresy, that of the Coluthians [Note: [Col. 0609] Augustine has the same reading. The Augiensis codex has *Colutanorum* and *Coluthano* instead of *Colutho*.], arose from a certain Coluthus. They say that God created both evils and good things, understanding literally what is said: “I am God, creating evils and making good things” (Isa. XLV, 7).

God had promised through the prophet that he would make them live without the sword of their enemies and would make the earth produce its growth and an abundance of every crop if they kept his commandments; but if they were transgressors, they would suffer the sword and famine. To these words he added: “I am God, creating evils and making good things.”

They transfer this from the sphere of circumstance to that of substance and assert that God is the creator of evils. Since no creature is evil, as I see it, they can blaspheme a perverse God who says to the people: “If you walk uprightly, I too will walk uprightly with you; but if you walk perversely, I too will walk perversely with you” (Lev. XXVI, 23).

## LXVI

The sixty-sixth heresy is that of the Florians, from Florianus, who says that evil and good souls are created by God. “Therefore,” he says, “those who are malicious are evil and do not change, while good people who live simply are not driven into the audacity of wicked men.”

Theodore briefly defeats this statement as follows: Judas was good and became a traitor. At the very time when the worst of prostitutes was watering his feet with tears and seeking mercy, if the woman had possessed an evil soul, why did she not persist in the crime of prostitution at that time? It is therefore clear that good souls were created by God. The Creator graciously implanted in them by nature the capacity, while they are good, not only to improve through their own actions, but also to be turned into wickedness itself: diligence brings about the former, while negligence incurs the latter.

## LXVII

The sixty-seventh heresy is that of the Satannians, from Satannius. They say that after the resurrection of the dead people will not remain in the same condition in which we now are, nor will they be changed in such a way that there will be a new heaven and a new earth, as holy Scripture promises (II Peter III, 13). The writings of both Testaments contend against them.

## LXVIII

The sixty-eighth heresy is that of the Gymnopods. They always walk barefoot because the Lord said to Moses: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exod. III, 5), and because the holy Isaiah is read to have walked barefoot (Isa. XX, 2). For this reason they form a schism, since they condemn those who wear shoes.

### LXIX

The sixty-ninth heresy was originated by the Donatists, from Donatus. Because Caecilianus, bishop of the Church of Carthage, had been ordained against their will, they created a schism, charging him with unproved crimes, and especially with having been ordained by traditores—those who had handed over the divine Scriptures. But when they were convicted of lying about this, they turned the schism into a heresy.

As though, even if the crimes alleged against Caecilianus had been true, the Church throughout the whole world could have lost its status on account of one man’s guilt—whether that guilt was real or, as appeared more clearly to the judges, false—and as though Donatus alone could have preserved the Church’s status in the African region, while throughout the whole world the labor of the holy apostles and the suffering of the martyrs had been erased. Indeed, it would seem that the blood of our Savior himself had failed to preserve the assembly of the Catholic faith, which Donatus alone, together with a few little asses of the Byzaceni, obtained.

[Note: Byzaceni who plowed with a donkey. Pliny is witness to this, Book XVII, chapter 5.]

And therefore they dared to rebaptize Catholics. In this undertaking they proved themselves both presumptuous and condemnable, since they know that the universal Church has approved that the power of baptism is not violated even in heretics themselves.

We read that the founder of this heresy was Donatus. Coming from Numidia to Carthage and dividing Christ’s people against Caecilianus, he joined to himself bishops of the same faction and ordained at Carthage, for his own party, a bishop named Majorinus.

[Note: He is also called Majorinus in Augustine; in the Augiensis manuscript, however, Majurinus.]

Another Donatus succeeded this Majorinus in the same division. By his eloquence he so strengthened this heresy that many think the Donatists took the beginning of their heresy from this Donatus rather than from the former one. His writings still exist today, in which it is shown that he embraced, concerning the Trinity, [views] contrary to the Catholic faith.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “it is shown [that] his *integritas* (that is, perhaps, ‘defense’) against, etc.”]

Although he says that God the Father in the Trinity is of one substance, he nevertheless attempted to assert that the Father is greater than the Son and the Son greater than the Holy Spirit. But no one among his people paid attention to this error, because the parties had another issue in view.

These heretics are called Montenses in the regions of Italy, Parmeniani in inner Africa, and Donatists in the Carthaginian region. In the regions of both Numidias they have what are virtually monks, whom we call Circumcelliones: rustic and exceedingly audacious servants of demons. They rage fiercely not only against others but also, in their misery, spare themselves not at all. For they customarily kill themselves by various forms of death, especially by leaps from heights, by water, and by fire; and they seduce as many as they can, of either sex, toward this end.

Sometimes they even ask those whom they find to kill them, threatening death if they do not do so. It is true that many Donatists dislike such people—but in word, not in deed. For if they truly disliked them, they certainly would not share communion with such persons, while they themselves cast the crime of one Caecilianus upon the Churches throughout the whole world.

They also frequently had disagreements among themselves. Finally, at Carthage, in the time of Count Heraclianus, when Maximianus—ordained against Primianus by nearly one hundred bishops of the same error—had been condemned by the remaining three hundred and ten bishops, who brought charges against his ordination, he taught the people who followed him that the baptism of Christ could be given even outside the Church.

Consequently, whoever went either from Primianus to Maximianus or from Maximianus to Primianus was not baptized again by the one who had been ordained against the will of the other; rather, they were acknowledged by the one whom they had certainly condemned. They did not reject them, refuse them, or alter the sacrament of baptism. Whether someone was baptized or ordained cleric by Primianus or by Maximianus, it was treated as though it had been done by one person, not by two opponents. In whatever rank someone came from one to the other, he remained in that rank: baptism was not changed, nor was rank taken away, because the division was shown to have arisen not from a dispute over baptism but from a dispute over ordination.

For they began by disagreeing about Caecilianus’s ordination; they did not cut themselves off from the Church because of any transgression concerning baptism or faith.

### LXX

The seventieth heresy is said to have been begun among the Spaniards by Priscillianus. They affirm that souls are of the divine nature. They say that, in order to undergo a kind of voluntary contest on earth, souls descend through seven heavens and through certain principalities arranged in stages, encounter an evil prince whom they wish to have made this world, and are then sown by that prince through various bodies of flesh.

They also assert that human beings are bound to the stars by fate, and that our very body is composed according to the twelve signs of heaven. Precisely as those commonly called mathematici establish a ram in the head, a bull in the neck, twins in the shoulders, a crab in the chest, and then run through the remaining signs by name down to the feet, so they have migrated from the sign of Christ to the signs of astrology.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “of astrology.”]

They invent many other fabulous and empty things of this kind. They separate wives from husbands whenever they can. Like the Manichaeans, they shun meat. They accept apocryphal Scriptures together with the canonical Scriptures and turn them allegorically toward their own interpretations. As for the Trinity, like the Sabellians, they confess that the Father is himself the Son and himself the Holy Spirit.

### LXXI

The seventy-first heresy was begun by the Adelophagi. They say that a Christian ought not to eat food in such a way that another person can see him while he is eating. This is the only reason known to separate them from the Church. For they confess the Trinity to be of one substance. The bishops of Ephesus dealt with them.

### LXXII

We find, as Philaster writes, that the seventy-second heresy of the Rhetorians was begun by Rhetorius. They have fallen into such great vanity that they say all heretics walk rightly before God, because this has been given to their minds: they worship God as they are able.

Their error appears reprehensible to us; before God, however, they say, it is neither error nor blameworthy. Their teachers instruct them to enter, apart from temples and synagogues, wherever Christ, born of the Virgin, is invoked, and to make themselves participants with heretics.

### LXXIII

The seventy-third heresy is that of the Theoponites. They say that, while Christ was suffering, the Divinity felt pain in the same way that a soul can feel pain when the body is subjected to punishments.

Of these Bishop Gregory says: “The wretched and unhappy do not see that, when trees are cut with iron, the sun is indeed in the trees. Does the splendor of the sun not suffer, when the blow of the iron reaches it before it reaches the wood?”

God, therefore, is light; and how can light be cut? That it is the soul which feels pain in the body we understand from this: when the soul departs from the body, the body can feel nothing at all, whether adverse or favorable.

In the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, the soul of his humanity experienced suffering, the soul which he assumed together with the body—not the one who assumed it, just as the sun itself did not suffer in the tree which, as we have mentioned, it illuminated. Even if the light of the sun in a tree can be cut by one striking it, the Divinity in Christ cannot be touched by one who inflicts suffering, because the sun’s light is a creature, whereas Christ is acknowledged and proved to be the Creator.

That the soul of his humanity experienced the Passion, the Lord himself says to his disciples: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). Let this much have been said; let us proceed to the others.

### LXXIV

The seventy-fourth heresy was embraced by the Triscilidae. They assert that God is three-formed, so that one part of him is the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit, and that in this way there is a Trinity in unity.

Of them Gregory says: “The wretched and unhappy do not see that they are blaspheming the whole Trinity itself. For there is no God except the one who is perfect in himself. The perfect Father therefore begot from himself a perfect Son, and the perfect Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Behold: three perfect realities do not make three gods, but one, because the Godhead is one.

“For the Godheads are not three in the same way as the persons are three. There are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but one Godhead, one majesty, one power, one will, and one substance to be confessed.”

### LXXV

The seventy-fifth heresy was produced by the Hydrotheites, who say that water is God, having neither beginning nor end, washing away filth, forgiving sins, and possessing the Holy Spirit.

The Catholic faith rightly condemns them as blind, since they do not see what filth water serves, or how God could serve such impurities; nor do they understand what importance water has without consecration.

The living Word gives it life; the holy Word sanctifies it, so that the Holy Spirit may deign to dwell in it and so that it may be able to cleanse the sins of believers. And just as, through blessing, it receives the power of this thing so that it can cleanse all sins, it cannot cleanse the sins of one who has not first offered his faith to God in complete belief.

The Holy Spirit is therefore poured into human beings not through the one who merely washes but rather through the one who believes, and forgiveness of sins is granted.

### LXXVI

The seventy-sixth heresy was produced by the Homuncionites, who say that the image of God is in the human body, not in the soul.

[Note: On this passage see Cotelerius, notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VI, chapter 10, note 4.]

Gregory therefore says: “Since the image of God ought to be sought in the great and primary things that are in a human being—in memory, understanding, knowledge, and in those faculties by which a human being is moved toward piety—these things are established in the soul, not fashioned in bodily features. A person is all the more like God the more purely he is able to possess the things we have mentioned.”

### LXXVII

The seventy-seventh heresy was established by the Ametrites, who say that there are innumerable worlds. Whoever has not read the philosophers thinks this a new teaching; for some pagan philosophers said this long ago.

We, however, accept Moses as sent by God, and from him we have learned what we should think and believe about the world.

### LXXVIII

The seventy-eighth heresy was occupied by the Psychopneumones, who say that the good souls of human beings are changed into the spirits of angels, while the evil souls of human beings are changed into the spirits of demons.

### LXXIX

The seventy-ninth heresy is held by the Adecerdites.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: Adicerditae.]

[Note: Greek: Ἀδηκερδῖται, “those concerned with gain,” because of the profit of salvation in hell. Philaster, *On Heresies* 122: “There are other heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and proclaimed himself there to all even after death, so that those who confessed might be saved there.” We owe this observation to Cotelerius, in his notes on the *Shepherd of Hermas*, Similitude 9, §16, volume I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 120, Cler’s edition.]

They say: “When Christ descended to the underworld, the entire multitude of souls met him, believed in him, and was liberated.”

### LXXX

[Note: This name appears in the list as Metagenetae; in the manuscript there is no name, as Sirmondus states.]

The eightieth heresy says that the Son of God was begotten later, after the Father willed it; if the Father had not willed it, he would not have begotten him. Let us grant, they say, that the Son is equal to the Father; but for him to be equal is not a matter of nature but of grace. The Father willed this, and therefore everything belongs to the Father, not to the Son.

We, on the contrary, say: just as a spring begot a river from the same substance from which the spring itself exists, so the Father begot the Son from the same substance from which he exists. And just as a spring begot a stream not by willing or not willing, but by begetting, so the Father, not by disputing, willing, or not willing, but just as the nature of a spring is such that from its fullness it pours forth, begot the Son by pouring him forth from his fullness.

And just as a river encircles the whole world and enters the sea, yet does not depart from the bosom of the spring, so the Son never departed from the bosom of the Father—not even when he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.

Thus he appeared among us through his assumption, but by his majesty he never departed from the bosom of the Father. For in order that this might happen, neither possibility nor will was lacking to God. If either of these had been lacking to God, he could not be called God. Whoever does not will what is good is evil; whoever cannot do what he wills is not omnipotent.

Condemning this blasphemy in the heretic we have mentioned, let us proceed to the others.

### LXXXI

We do not accuse Lucifer of the eighty-first heresy, but we charge him with schism.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “in Lucifer.”]

They are Catholics in every respect, but by making peoples Luciferian and by separating themselves from the Church, charity excluded them from their faith.

[Note: Same manuscript: “excluded charity.”]

The Apostle says: “If I have faith so as to remove mountains, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

They boast that they have not deviated from the faith. Yet we rightly charge them with no small crime, because they were unwilling to have charity with the Church of God.

### LXXXII

The Jovinianists are found to have taken up the eighty-second heresy from a certain Jovinianus. Like the Stoic philosophers, they say that all sins are equal. They also say that a person cannot sin after receiving the washing of regeneration, and that fasting or abstinence from particular foods provides no benefit.

They destroy the virginity of Saint Mary, saying that it was violated when she gave birth. They equate the merits of the virginity of holy women, the chastity of those practicing continence, and of men who choose a celibate life with the marriage of chaste and faithful people. It is said that, after hearing this teaching, certain consecrated virgins already advanced in age married in the city of Rome, where he was teaching these things.

Jovinianus himself, however, neither had nor wished to have a wife. He said that this practice would not benefit the future life, but applied it to present convenience.

Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, took up the case against him and published a book destroying all his inventions and arguments.
