After it had been read in the Roman assembly—that is, in the Lateran church—the Roman people and the priests together, with one voice, pronounced anathema against the Jovinianists and Jovinianus himself, at the very beginning of Lent, under Bishop Anastasius.

Finally, during that very authentic week of Easter, they were found feasting and holding banquets with pork, to such an extent that the people hung a roasted pig, which they had found on their table, around his neck and made him carry it through the entire city.

Jerome the presbyter also wrote certain books against them. Whoever reads them more fully learns how many good things virginity, continence, and abstinence possess, and shudders at how many evils gluttony and luxury contain.

### LXXXIII

Our historian Eusebius places the eighty-third heresy in the sixth book. Neither Epiphanius, nor Polycrates, nor Africanus, nor Hesiodus—who, writing in Greek and describing all the heresies, composed volumes of many books—mentions it anywhere.

In the sixth book, then, as I said, Eusebius relates that there were heretics in Arabia. Since he does not mention their founder, we can call them Arabians. He says that they taught that souls die and are dissolved together with bodies, and that at the end of the age both are restored.

Eusebius adds that a large part of them were recalled from this position through Origen’s disputation.

### LXXXIV

We record that the eighty-fourth heresy was held by the Helvidians, from Helvidius. They contradict the virginity of Saint Mary to such an extent that they say she bore other children by Joseph after Christ’s birth.

These people arose only recently—that is, under Siricius, bishop of the Romans—and sent their disciples through Italy and Gaul.

The outstanding teacher Jerome wrote two books against them.

[Note: The greatest teacher wrote not two but one book against Helvidius, as Vallarsius notes in the preface to volume I of Saint Jerome’s works, p. XXIII, no. 33.]

When these books were read at the appropriate time, they condemned them with a fitting execration.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “they will anathematize.”]

Our Epiphanius, investigator of heretics, also wrote a short work against them, who at that time were putting forward this assertion filled with blasphemies; he judged that they should be called Antidicomarians.

### LXXXV

The eighty-fifth heresy is said to have been begun by the Paterniani. They think that the lower parts of the human body were made not by God but by the devil, and, granting license for every kind of crime involving those parts, they live in the utmost impurity.

When Bishop Damasus condemned them after they had been discovered in their crime, he wrote the following about them in his report to Valentinian the Elder:

“We wish your Piety to know that the Venustians, discovered in a most shameful crime, have been condemned by the Apostolic See.”

[Note: Saint Augustine speaks of the Venustians in *On Heresies*, chapter 85, and in Book V of *Against Julian*, chapter 7, no. 26. From this passage of the *Praedestinatus*, Baluzius judges that the Venustians were condemned by Saint Damasus at the Second Roman Council, convened in 367. See the *Collection of Councils*, volume II, p. 1038, Venetian edition of Labbé. For further information about these heretics, if desired, consult the distinguished Wesseling, *Probabilia*, chapter 3, p. 29; Petrus Horreius, *Critical Miscellanies*, Book I, chapter 7, pp. 105 ff.; and the scholar who recently published at Rome the writings of Saint Damasus, in his review of that pontiff’s minor works and deeds, chapter 7, §4, p. 38.]

He also sent their confessions along with the report. Later a special law was issued against them, providing that wherever they were found they should be dealt with by the sword of punishment.

### LXXXVI

We read that the Tertullianists were formerly condemned by Soter, the Roman pope. The reason we call them practitioners of the eighty-sixth heresy is as follows.

A certain Octaviana came from Africa. Her husband, named Hesperius, appeared to be closely connected with the general Arbogastes, who had also possessed great influence under the tyrant Maximus. This Octaviana brought with her a certain slippery and crafty demon, against whose loquacity scarcely a hundred people could prevail, so confident was he in addressing human beings.

[Note: Manuscript: “Octavia,” formerly “Octaviana.” Sirmondus.]

When he claimed to be a Tertullianist presbyter, he obtained through a sacred document permission to build himself a community outside the walls of the City. After he had obtained this from the tyrant Maximus, he expelled from the place of our saints—that is, the place of the two brothers Processus and Martinianus—saying that they had been Phrygians and had therefore followed the law which Tertullian had followed. In this way, under the pretext of the martyrs of God, he was leading the people astray.

But when God, through Theodosius the devout Augustus, granted victory, and Maximus’s henchman—whose power the Tertullianist had boasted of—had been punished, he immediately fled with the matron who had come with him, and the rumor of neither the living nor the dead was renewed.

God restored the watch of his martyrs to the Catholic festival.

Tertullian was a citizen and presbyter of Carthage. He published very eloquent and fervent little works in defense of the truth. At Carthage he had a basilica where the people gathered around him. That basilica remained until Bishop Aurelius.

For when Augustine, bishop of Hippo, engaged them and argued with them reasonably, they were converted and handed over their church to the holy Church.

The Catholic authority reproves Tertullian, however, because he says that a soul is born from a soul; because he defends Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla against the Catholic faith and against Apollonius, bishop of the East, and Soter, pope of the city of Rome—as we said above when we exposed the Cataphrygian heretics.

Later he separated from them. So that the people would not seem to exclude the name of Montanus because of the name of Tertullian, he poured out from himself all the vanity of Phrygia and propagated the assemblies of the Tertullianists, though he changed nothing in the faith.

For he also condemns second marriages, as we have said; he asserts that the soul comes by generation; and he labels us Catholics “Psychics.” Whenever you read *Tertullian Against the Psychics*, understand that he is acting against Catholics.

### LXXXVII

In the eighty-seventh heresy we name the Abeloites. Although they were earlier than almost all the heretics, they have now come to an end in our times.

They derived their name from Adam’s son: that is, they wished to be called Abeloites from Abel. They did not have sexual relations with their wives, yet the sect itself did not allow them to live without wives.

A man and a woman therefore lived together under a profession of continence and adopted a boy and a girl for themselves, who would become successors in the compact of that union. When any of them was overtaken by death, others were substituted, provided that two persons of different sex succeeded two others in the association of that household.

Whenever one parent died, the children served the surviving one until that person also died. After the latter’s death, they too adopted a boy and a girl in the same manner.

They never lacked people from whom to adopt, because neighbors were continually having children and willingly giving their needy children to the hope of another’s inheritance.

This alone was the difference between us and them: they reproached our people because marriages were not practiced according to our law in such a way that those who marry might be as though they did not marry.

### LXXXVIII

The Apostolic See taught, under the holy pope Innocent, that it had discovered the eighty-eighth heresy in Pelagius. This occurred when Caelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, was teaching at Carthage that human beings could be without sin by the sufficiency of human nature alone.

A certain Paulinus, a deacon and defender and procurator of the Milanese church, opposed him. In an assembly of priests he brought many propositions against the Catholic faith before him, which Caelestius declined to condemn, saying: “It does not concern me to answer the matters he has raised, where my name is involved but the crime belongs to someone else.”

Then they presented him with his own books, in which he said that human nature itself could be sufficient for perfection; that is, that a human being could practice so much righteousness that he could be without sin if he wished.

They taught that Adam was made mortal and that, whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. They taught that the Law led to the kingdom just as the Gospels did. They confessed that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins solely because of the rule of the universal Church. They taught that Adam’s sin had harmed nothing in the human race.

All these kinds of propositions were brought forward against Caelestius for condemnation. But he said that many things among them were held by his faith and that, because of these, he could not condemn the rest.

Then, in response to the report of nearly all the bishops of Africa, Pope Innocent wrote a condemnation of both Pelagius and Caelestius.

Whether before they were condemned by the universal Church or after they had been condemned, they did not cease writing that a human being could be without sin; that Adam had harmed nothing in the human race; that the Law had led to the kingdom just as the Gospels did; that infants were not baptized because they could possess original sin; and that nature had been so well made by God that it was sufficient by itself to be free from sin.

A certain teacher named Constantius took up the case against them without writing. After him, Augustine, bishop of Hippo, and Jerome the presbyter of Bethlehem wrote against them.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “Bethlemites.”]

The Pelagians, or Caelestians, nevertheless became mingled with the Catholic people because they have no other church. Therefore, wherever they happen to be, they do not refuse communion.

They say that in this matter—where the Eucharist is celebrated—they share one confession; that they are separated not over communion but over a question. Because of this presumption, they are exposed to danger both from our people, if they are discovered, and to execration among their own. For they have their own presbyters and bishops.

Pelagius himself writes as follows in his commentary on Romans, while treating the passage where the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Referring to Caelestius, who was the first to write against the transmission of sin, he says:

“Those,” he says, “who oppose the transmission of sin attempt to attack it in this way: If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s grace also benefits even those who do not believe.

“They add this as well: If baptism removes that original sin, then children born of two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin. For how do they transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess at all?”

We have set down these words as Pelagius himself wrote them.

Concerning the claim that a human being can be without sin, the following objection was put to them: Either he can, and therefore does not seek assistance; or he cannot, and therefore seeks assistance. For whenever assistance is sought from someone, the person admits that he cannot accomplish what he wishes to do. Otherwise, he absurdly asks for assistance in accomplishing alone the very thing for which he requests assistance.

For example, if I wished to lift ten pounds of some object and sought assistance, I would appear ridiculous in making such a request. But if I wished to lift two hundred pounds or more, because I could not accomplish it, I would call for help and seek assistance with enormous pleas—especially if the condition of my life seemed to depend upon this weight, so that I could not attain life unless I lifted the weight I have mentioned.

As to the claim that one born of two baptized parents has nothing from the faith of the parents, the following reasoning teaches us.

Those who have been baptized have two births: one by which the flesh generated them, and another by which the Holy Spirit generated them. Born from these two generations, they transmit two generations to their descendants: one from the flesh, through the ministry of marriage; the other from the Spirit, through the consecration of baptism.

I ask you, then: this person who is born of baptized parents, from what is he born? From the flesh—that is, from the first generation—or from the spirit—that is, from the second generation?

If he is born from the Spirit, he ought not to be baptized. Why? Because the Holy Spirit caused him to be born, not the lust of marriage.

But if he is born from carnal marriage—that is, from a male and a female—it remains that those who were regenerated from Christ and the Church should regenerate their offspring again.

From the first comes what we are born as Adam; from the second comes what we are recreated as, as the holy Apostle says: “The first man Adam was made a living soul, the last Adam a life-giving spirit. Yet the spiritual was not first, but the natural; afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. Therefore, just as we have borne the image of the earthly”—that is, just as we have created children carnally—“let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:45).

That is: those whom we have created carnally, let us recreate spiritually; or let us who were created carnally by the Creator’s command be recreated spiritually by his grace.

“But this I say,” the Apostle said, “because flesh and blood”—that is, human beings born only through the first generation—“cannot inherit the kingdom of God unless they have deserved to receive divine grace. Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (ibid., 50).

### LXXXIX

The eighty-ninth heresy is said to have been embraced by Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople.

It is customary for the bishop of Alexandria to send one of his sermons to Constantinople, to be recited at Easter, and for the bishop of Constantinople to send his sermon to be recited at Alexandria.

In his sermon Nestorius of Constantinople wrote that Mary was not *Theotocon* (“God-bearer”) but *Christotocon* (“Christ-bearer”): that is, that she had not given birth to God but to a human being.

Cyril of Alexandria rebuked this statement in a letter, expressing himself in such a way that, if Nestorius had perhaps been mistaken, he might correct what he had said.

From the very fact that Cyril had rebuked him, Nestorius began to call Cyril a heretic. A council was held at Ephesus.

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “at Thessalonica.”]

Even then Nestorius did not wish to correct himself by saying that Mary had borne God and man, but said only that she had borne a human being.

“For if we say that she gave birth to God,” he said, “we make her [Note: Same manuscript: “mother of God.”] the mother of God, like the pagans.”

“Mary,” he said, “gave birth to a temple for God, not to the one who dwells in the temple.”

He was given a period of grace in which either to condemn his statement and return to his episcopal see, or, if he refused to condemn it, to be unable to return afterward. He refused and remained in the same confession.

The council at Ephesus condemned him. In that condemnation Pope Coelestinus wrote, and all the bishops of the East and West subscribed together with him.

### XC

The ninetieth heresy, which in our preface we said had falsely taken the name of Bishop Augustine, adopted the name of the Predestinati. They define the election of the good and the rejection of the evil as determined by God, not by human beings, whether they strive or neglect.

They do not wish God’s ordinances either to be guarded by those who strive or violated by those who are negligent. They say that even if someone predestined to evil wishes to do good, he will not be able to attain the good; for whoever is predestined to good will be brought to the good even against his will, even if he is negligent.

They say that the water of baptism does not cleanse all sins. They say that grace precedes free will in such a way that a person receives before he asks, finds before he seeks, and has the door opened before he knocks.

They say that no one comes to faith in Christ unless he has been drawn by the Father against his will, attending to the statement: “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him” (John 6:44).

They say that all things occur not in reality but in hope, so that they apply even to the mysteries the Apostle’s statement, “Hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8:14), and say: “Things that are perceived appear indeed to exist, but they do not exist.”

They say: “Adam did more harm in injuring the human race than Christ did in helping it.” For, they say, what Adam harmed remains in such a way that neither Christ’s Passion nor the sanctification of baptism can remove it.

But why are we causing you delay, holy and diligent reader? We present their entire book to you in this volume, exactly as it was published. By reading it, you will learn that its definitions were devised by the surveyors of Antichrist.

Whenever we took up the case against them, they said that we were arguing against them from the sophistries of heretics. Seeing themselves overcome so completely that they could scarcely breathe, they continually brought this accusation against Catholic efforts: fearing to be branded heretics, they sought to restrict the speech of truth in silence.

For their sake, therefore, we have exposed all the heresies from Simon down to this point, so that we might prove that we alone are in agreement with the Catholic faith.

We ask you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, who with your Son and the Holy Spirit possess the majesty of one truth, the Godhead of one majesty, and the Trinity of one Godhead, to help us as we take up weapons against your enemies.

Let them have the camps of Goliath, arrayed in the battle line of the Philistines. Let us Hebrews, taking up the shepherd’s bag of your servant David, fight with your cornerstone, so that we may confidently say with your Apostle: “Thanks be to our God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 13:17).

Let there be peace for all Catholics, and let them cry out together with the angels in one voice, singing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

## BOOK TWO

[Note: Augiensis manuscript: “Book II, Primasius to Fortunatus, On Heresies.” Nevertheless, in another manuscript copy of the Augiensis codex, which the distinguished Mabillon most kindly communicated to me, these two words, “To Fortunatus,” appear neither here nor anywhere else. The fact that several copies of the *Praedestinatus* existed in the Augiensis monastery seems sufficiently indicated by the subscription found in Mabillon’s copy: “There follows now, in order, the ninetieth and final heresy, formerly written out by our most reverend and distinguished fathers at Augia Dives.” In the Holstenian copy, however, the subscription is entirely different, as we have just presented it.]

FABRICATED UNDER THE NAME OF AUGUSTINE, containing the ninetieth heresy, which asserts that sins are committed by God’s predestination.

The exhortation of spiritual brothers invited me to become a participant in your purpose, you who defend the truth. Therefore, briefly inserting myself into your efforts, I have avoided an expansive style and confined ideas that seek a broad field of contest to a narrow space, so that I might remove from you the weariness of reading, provide an opportunity for defending the truth, and refute servants fighting against the will of their own Lord—namely, those who say that, against God’s wish and will, human choices are set in motion, and that the power of the immortal God is diminished by the power of mortals. To this they add that human beings become holy through their own will and reach friendship with God by their own judgment.

You will see these men collapsing at a light push, since they have assigned human concern both the better and the first place, so that, with God excluded, it is said that a human being can save himself by his own will rather than by God’s ordinance. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “takes the parts.”]

But you, sons of charity, retaining in your minds the zeal of faith marked upon them, be secure concerning God’s ordinance, which he established by predestination. And let this sentence, spoken by the apostolic mouth, stand firmly in our minds: “For God has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. It is not therefore of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 19, 16); because “the potter has authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (ibid., 21). [Note: The same manuscript reads, “another for dishonor.”] Hence also it is that “the flesh is opposed to the spirit, and the spirit to the flesh. These,” the Apostle says, “are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. V, 17). [Note: The same manuscript reads, “are opposed to one another.”]

For in his work God foresaw all human beings beforehand and, by foreseeing, established what was fitting for each. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “foresaw beforehand.”] This is the singular sign of his majesty, in which he has no equal. [Note: “God” is absent in the Augia manuscript.] For God alone foresaw what all would think, say, and do; and because he generally foresaw the deeds of all before they occurred, he beheld their merits as though they had already been accomplished, arranging them beforehand. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “distinguishing them.”]

And therefore, when he foresaw them, he predestined matters as though they were visible to his eyes and placed openly before him, and he established those who would be conformed to the image of his Son, “so that he might also be the firstborn among many brothers.” “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29–30). [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “these he also called.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads, “these he also justified.”] [Note: In the same manuscript, “and” is absent.]

Hence the prophet also says: “A man’s way is not his own” (Jer. X, 23).

What do you think, frail, perishable, wretched, mortal human beings? If you do anything good, are you to be praised—or, perhaps, if you offend, are you altogether to be condemned? For the law speaks for this reason: to instill fear. Otherwise, nothing exists except what God has willed. Whomever God wills to be holy is holy; there will be nothing else. Whomever he foresees to be unrighteous will be unrighteous; there will be nothing else.

For God’s predestination has already established both the number of the righteous and the number of sinners, and it will necessarily be impossible for the established limit to be exceeded. But he established this not as one who shows partiality toward persons, but as one who foreknows all future things. [Note: In the same manuscript, “of all” is absent.] For God fixed and established his predestination not through partiality toward a person, but through foreknowledge.

Those whom he foresaw would in no way be converted, he predestined to death; those whom he foresaw would be converted in every way, he predestined to life. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “those whom he foresees will certainly be converted.”]

I am astonished that testimonies of the Old Testament are customarily brought forward against the authority of the New. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “They customarily produce the testimonies of the holy prophet Ezekiel, saying,” etc.] For they customarily invoke the testimony of the holy prophet Ezekiel, who says:

“Thus says the Lord: When I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he turns from his wickedness, ‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘he shall surely live’” (Ezek. XVIII, 27).

As I said, this is written in the old law for the time of the captivity, for the reason on account of which that captivity occurred, and for the person of the people upon whom it was imposed, so that, placed in captivity, they might learn that because of their sins they were subject to the yoke of the Assyrian king.

Certainly captivity occurred because of sin. And why did the righteous suffer captivity together with sinners, unless it is because the mysteries of God cannot be thoroughly known by our frailty? This mystery, therefore, was written in the old law. But in the New the Apostle cries out: “Vessels of wrath fit for destruction” (Rom. IX, 22).

And for this reason he recalls that God said through his foreknowledge: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. IX, 13). For although they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil (ibid., 11), it was said through foreknowledge that one would be hated and the other loved. [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “good or evil.”]

These things have not been invented by us; nor do we say anything beyond what the Apostle preached. He himself recalls that predestination was made through God’s foreknowledge. He himself says of God: “Those whom he called, he predestined” (Rom. VIII, 30).

If you read in the Apostle of the one who foreknows, predestines, and calls, why do you bring a charge against us because we say that God predestined human beings either to righteousness or to sin? Otherwise, it might seem that he made without foresight human beings who would do what he did not wish. For God remains unconquered in his will, while the human being is continually overcome.

If, then, you confess God to be unconquered, confess this also: that those whom the one who created them wished them to be cannot be otherwise. Hence we conclude in our minds that those whom God once predestined to life will be brought to life against their will, even if they are negligent, even if they sin, even if they do not wish it; but those whom he predestined to death labor in vain, even if they run, even if they hurry. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “that those whom God,” etc.]

Do not accept this without instruction from an obvious example. Judas heard the word of life every day, clung to the Lord every day, was occupied with virtues every day, and every day heard the very Son of God as his teacher. Yet, because he was predestined to death, he suddenly perished in a single stroke.

Saul was every day a persecutor, every day a stoner of Christians, every day a devastator of churches; yet, because he was predestined to life, in a single sudden stroke he became a vessel of election. [Col. 0623C]

Why, then, do you who remain in sins tremble? If God has deemed you worthy, you will be holy. Or why do you who live in holiness become anxious, as though your anxiety preserved you? If God does not will it, you will never fall. Be secure concerning God, both of you. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “You will certainly never fall. Certainly be secure concerning God.”]

You who are holy and anxious lest you fall, who attend to prayers day and night, occupy yourselves with fasts, diligently devote yourselves to divine readings, give yourselves to exhortations, and daily apply yourselves to every holy pursuit—will you be saved by this effort of yours? Will you be holier than Judas, who received power to heal the sick, drive out demons, raise the dead, and tread upon serpents and scorpions; who was a companion of the apostles and a disciple of Christ? Yet, because he was predestined to death, he found eternal death.

Cease, human being—cease, I say—from being anxious about your own virtue, and trust securely in God’s will alone. For you will obtain nothing good from God against his will. But if God deigns that you remain in the good, you will be saved.

And you who are shaken by a vain despair while living in sin, learn from the Apostle Paul. Who was ever able to be found his equal in crimes? Could you ever have committed sins worse than those he committed? Yet, because he was predestined to the apostleship, he suddenly escaped all his crimes and ascended from the lower hells to the upper realms of those above. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “from the lower depths to the heights above.”]

Therefore, all whom God knows to be worthy of the salvation of his redemption, he predestined to salvation; and he saves only those whom he knows he predestined to salvation. For God’s salvation does not serve the human will; he himself knows what he does for each person.

Nor does the freedom of human choice precede God’s grace; rather, God’s grace precedes the will of human choice. For the human will is vain and fruitless, and the judgment of the human will is vain.

He is mistaken who thinks that he can reach Christ through the good he wills, when Christ himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John VI, 44).

You who understand better than Christ, say whether Christ lied; and only then assert that we have established this sentence against Christ’s rule. For if Christ spoke the truth, what we say—that the predestined are drawn to life—does not lie, because he himself is life.

But if the force of the Gospel testimony weighs you down, you who come against our position, and if, weighed down by the burden of the sentence, you cannot give us a reply, at least explain to us the Apostle’s definition, which says: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

However much strength the human will may exert in its own effort to build, it strives in a fruitless contest. Or how does human frailty think that its vigilance will benefit its eternal desires, when the prophet cries out with clear proofs, saying:

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1–2).

What is it that anyone hopes, against the divine writings and against his own conscience, to devote himself to building, when these sacred writings teach that human construction is not secure but vain?

But if you come against us, you do not come against us; you come against the one who said: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain.”

Did he therefore not know that it was not useful for God’s people that these things should be written down and transmitted through succeeding generations to the end of the ages? You, then, who criticize these things, remove them from the Book of Psalms, because, as you say, those who read and sing these verses cannot be built up.

But how do such people think that by their own will they can attain the fruit of edification, when not even the vessel of election himself asserts that he was able to fulfill his own will? For the Apostle says of himself: “I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will” (Rom. VII, 19).

If, then, the Apostle is unable to accomplish the good that he wills, how do these people say that by their own will they can reach the fruit of grace? [Note: The same manuscript reads, “to be able to attain grace.”] These are the Apostle’s words; we add nothing of our own. He himself says of himself: “I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will.”

And you blame us because we say: “They are called only if they are predestined”? [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “God’s grace precedes.”]

For God’s grace precedes the human will. God is first in what is good for a human being; but a human being, even if he is at his best, is scarcely found to be last in every good. Give the first places to God, so that you may empty human pride.

But if you wish to nourish pride in human beings, it is clear that you seek the ruin of the human race, because you teach that in a good work it is not God who precedes, but human will. Thus human beings appear to admonish God by their suggestions to do good, as though he would not do good unless they had told him to, although it is certain that God, without anyone suggesting or asking, bestows good things upon all.

For the Apostle does not say, “when we were asking,” but: “when we were enemies,” he says, “we were reconciled to God, not through our will, but through the death of his Son” (Rom. V, 10).

Where, then, is human will? It has been excluded. Why? Because not everyone who wills is saved; for if everyone who willed were saved, no one could be excluded from salvation. [Note: This entire clause, “because not everyone who wills is saved,” is absent in the Augia manuscript.] Every human being wishes to be saved, but not every human being is saved. Rather, the one whom God wills is saved—yes, I say, the one whom God wills—so that, with human will excluded, he may display his own grace in its fullness and integrity. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “his full and complete grace.”]

But if God wills someone to be good, and he is not good, then the human being overcomes God. For he overcomes God if God wills him to be good and he is not good. God’s will, therefore, is effective in what is good for a human being.

For it was not when we were asking or when we were requesting, but “when we were enemies,” he says, “we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son.”

But when you read “the death of his Son for all,” I am astonished at how you understand “all,” when you scarcely see a few reaching salvation. Whenever you read “all,” you wish “all” to be understood in a general sense, although often “all” is shown to mean only a part. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “you wish all to be understood”; it also reads *irrogaret* for *inrogaret*, *illiciens* for *inliciens*, *subjicere* for *subicere*, *corruere* for *conruere*, *illustris* for *inlustris*, *collatum* for *conlatum*, and so forth. By this very fact the greater antiquity of the Reims codex used by Sirmond is revealed.]

For when it says: “All have turned aside” (Ps. XII, 2), nevertheless not all have turned aside; and “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV, 11), nevertheless not every human being is a liar, since we read of someone: “He was a truthful man.” And also: “Lying men will not remember him, but truthful men are found in it” (Eccli. XV, 8).

Thus “all” appears to signify the greater part, although it is plainly established that “all” should not always be understood universally.

And I am astonished that, with your eyes closed, you pass by the enemy’s ambushes—you who say that human will can acquire some virtue—not considering how great the ruin of chastity brought about by the devil is, and how many crimes of lust, greed, envy, and faithlessness are committed every day. If you saw these things, we would not have to labor to show you the losses of virtues and the victories of vices.

For if freedom of choice were intact, these things would not occur. Through the transgression of the first human being, therefore, freedom of choice perished from human beings.

But you renew the Pelagian heresy when you say that through freedom of choice human beings can put an end to sins. For you exclude grace through freedom of choice. Either we are liberated by free choice, or we are rescued by God’s grace. Choose what you will say. If you attribute everything to grace, we hold the same belief; if to free choice, know that we cannot agree with you.

But from where does one person have greater freedom of choice in the good, and another less, unless they are judged according to God’s dispensation? [Note: In the same manuscript, “is judged” is used.] In one person grace shows itself slight, in another abundant and generous, according as grace itself wills, not as we will, who have departed from the order of our creation.

Finally, we have recognized that human nature was so corrupted through Adam’s transgression that it obtained its restoration through Christ not in reality but in hope, as the Apostle says: “We were saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. VIII, 24).

If, then, we have been saved in hope, we have not yet received the reality in the present age. Therefore, even the baptized again experience carnal desire and suffer those bodily impulses, because they have obtained the aid of restoration in hope, not in reality.

For if they had obtained it in reality, after the grace of baptism there would be neither the possibility nor the will to sin. But although the power of baptism is so great that it wipes away all sins, the growth of sins is not washed away by the water of baptism; for it is taught that this growth naturally exists through Adam.

For those members that, at the hour of baptism, are free from shame afterward recover their shame, by which they avoid everyone’s gaze and seek privacy in modesty. What God had made members, the transgression turned into shameful parts; and they are not called members, but shameful parts.

These shameful parts become members at that moment of baptism, but soon again the members become shameful parts; for they have been restored not in reality but in hope.

For the concupiscence of the flesh, which through Adam’s transgression reigns in the body like the law of sin, again lays claim to the baptized person and strives to overthrow his entire mind. This is the root of that wound which Christ saved.

He saved it in the manner the Apostle says: “We were saved in hope.” And he commands us to turn our minds toward contemplating invisible things and not to fall through presumption concerning what is seen. Therefore he says: “Hope that is seen is not hope.”

Otherwise people might think that sins are removed through baptism in such a way that the very roots of sins are uprooted at the same time. That impulse of pollution, which invaded nature through the transgression, remains in the baptized person just as the root of a hair remains when the surface has been cleansed and shaved with a razor.

It has been shaved so that the place might be cleansed; it has not been uprooted, lest it grow again. For if all the frailty of Adam’s transgression were removed completely through baptism, none of the baptized would be drawn to crimes by any impulse of heat, no one would be stained by human filth, and no one would be pricked by the goad of concupiscence.

But because “we were saved in hope,” we patiently await what we do not yet see. [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “The time will come.”]

A time is coming when they will neither marry nor take wives, but will be like the angels in heaven (Matt. XXII, 30). For when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption, and this mortal thing has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass:

“Death has been swallowed up [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “in victory”] in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (I Cor. XV, 54–56).

Then we shall say: “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., 57).

[Note: In the Augia manuscript, immediately after “Jesus Christ,” the book ends without a title, etc.]

## PROLOGUE OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK

The book hostile to human beings, fabricated against the Catholic faith, is finished: a deceitful book, surrounded by frauds, a corrupter of sound doctrine; and, as Saint Cyprian says, “it displays falsehoods in order to steal away truths.” Published under the appearance of piety, it acts against the institutions of all the saints.

As we mentioned in the brief preface, we have gathered the sects of all the heretics into one book because of this book, so that its defenders may know that we oppose every heresy and use the agreement of none of them against them.

Therefore, O holy mother Church, mother of pure faith, raise up our strength against your hidden enemies, against new barbarians who pretend to wear a peaceful guise, against those who take up arms through you against you. Help us who desire to enter the contest, especially against those against whom no one has yet fought in writing, although by their writings they have already wounded almost the entire world under the name of the priest Augustine, producing corrupted books and circulating various letters that they falsely claim belong to the bishop of Hippo.

And we beseech all you defenders of the Catholic faith, setting aside every distraction, to attend more intently to our battle. Keeping the future Judge of your judgment before your eyes, defend fully what must be defended, and condemn fully what must be condemned.

But why, leaving aside their other corruptions, have we brought forward this book alone? The reason is that they hand it over in the manner of a creed to those whom they have deceived.

We therefore judged that the whole of it should be written out in order, lest it appear that the passages which could easily be defeated had been torn from their book, while those passages that could cunningly defend the book itself against the charge brought by us had been omitted.

We have omitted nothing. Rather, by exposing its entire body in these writings, we bring against it the sword of God’s word. Cutting it into parts, we lay each of its limbs bare before the eyes of Catholics, showing what poisons it has in its head, what it twists in its mouth, and what arrows it sends forth from its breast.

By exposing its adversarial cunning through each function of its limbs and casting it captive at the feet of the Catholic Church, we make it manifest to everyone, so that anyone who, abandoning Catholic doctrine, wishes to corrupt his own assent by the contagion of this book may thereby become his own condemner. [Note: The Augia manuscript reads: “Here ends the book fabricated under the name of Augustine concerning the Predestined. Then begins the book of the Catholic bishops against the same book of the heretics, defending the Catholic and orthodox faith and refuting their errors.”]

## BOOK THREE

Containing a refutation of the preceding book fabricated under the name of Saint Augustine.

Up to this point the forests of all the heretics have been set ablaze; in them treacherous faithlessness has plundered the riches of faith, the Church has suffered robbery, and the blood of souls has been poured out.

But because it is customary for thorns to sprout again after a fire, let us hold the sickle of divine judgment, so that we may cut off the revived heads of the thorns, which rise against heaven. There will not be lacking, by God’s providence, cultivators for this field, so that the blessed—“blameless in the way, blameless in faith, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 1)—may reach without the impediment of thorns the place toward which they proceed. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “blameless in the way, that is, blameless.”]

The Predestined have produced the ninetieth heresy, displaying false books that they fabricate as Augustine’s, although his statements are read in many places and are strongly opposed to these books.

Catholics therefore have genuine grounds for suspecting that such wicked statements cannot belong to an orthodox man. For, joining hands with the astrologers, these statements say that the human race is so subject to divine predestinations that all the evils committed in the world are said to be committed by God’s will. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “of the aforesaid orthodox man.”]

Lest human fear or shame make us participate in their error, we have dealt with the concerns of all the heretics and have found that no one could have erred more grievously than those who say that all evils and crimes are committed through God’s predestination.

Let all the heretics, then, have one book in which we have condemned them not on the basis of power but on the basis of true reason, so that the Predestined may know that we consent to no heretic.

Let the Predestined also have one book in which God himself refutes them—he who knows that he predestined no one to evil, but predestined everyone to good—so that we may approve what is good as belonging to him.

For all the good things that human beings do now, or have done from the beginning, or will do, we say are accomplished by God’s grace, God’s mercy, God’s help, and also God’s predestination.

But by predestination we do not mean one by which God forces unwilling people to do good; rather, we mean one by which he never changes his judgment of goodness, is continually ready for those who wish the good, and is unprepared for those who wish evil.

For when people come toward the good, he immediately displays the reward of their faith, granting forgiveness of sins and making them children of God. But when they go toward evil, he does not immediately inflict the punishment they deserve; instead, he graciously grants them the delays of his patience.

This purpose of God we confess to be predestined and fixed. Therefore, while evils are being committed, God has not withdrawn his purpose; rather, the human being has introduced his contempt. Sin was never committed with God’s will; it was committed through human negligence.

The human race sinned to such an extent against God’s will that he was always angry with those who practiced sins and came to the aid of those who practiced righteousness.

Finally, when the whole world had turned away from righteousness and deserved to perish in the shipwreck of the Flood, God is shown to have wished to save it through his correction.

For what does the Apostle Peter mean when he says: “The patience of God waited for those who had been unbelieving in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built” (I Pet. III, 20)?

Tell us: what was the patience of God awaiting? The predestined destruction, or a conversion that had been invited?

The construction of the ark of the Flood therefore became a preacher. The axe cried out, the hammer resounded, the saw bore witness; the tools themselves preached the Flood to the unbelievers.

Thus, after a hundred years of delay had been granted, the law went before it, declaring that those who were about to perish could escape through repentance. Predestination did not prevent this law by denying that they could be saved through correction.

For if predestination has fixed a limit for its boundaries, then the law is unjust when it seeks to invade boundaries belonging to another. Therefore, if you establish predestination, refute the commandments; reject the law, so that you may introduce the reign of predestination. For the law has always wished to command everyone and never to serve anyone. [Note: The Augia manuscript reads, “to serve no one.”]

If, then, predestination empties the authority of the law, and the law disturbs the rights of predestination, one of the two exercises tyranny. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “one of the two.”]

Choose now, Catholics, to which we should bow our necks.

If we choose the law, let us deny that predestination excludes the law from its authority, because the law says: “Keep my commandments, and you shall live”; but predestination says: “Vessels of wrath already fitted for destruction, and vessels of mercy which are called to life.”

Both are written. What are we to do now? Choose.

If vessels of wrath have already been prepared by God so that they may sin, and vessels of mercy have been prepared for life so that they may live, let us all submit to the command of predestination and expel the law together with its preachers.

And lest you perhaps think that this sin is something new, committed with such criminal audacity, every crowd of sinners has done this from the beginning. [Note: The same manuscript reads, “lest you perhaps think this sin new.”]

For why were the prophets, the apostles, and the entire multitude of saints killed, unless for this reason: that, forcing God’s law upon human understanding, they reproved vices in sinners?

If they had wished to introduce the reign of predestination with the voice of flattery, excluding the law of righteousness, no one would have been killed.

For they said to them, as it is written: “Do not preach hard things to us” (Isa. XXX, 10).

What does “Do not preach hard things to us” mean? Without doubt it means: “Do not preach punishments to us through the threatening law.”

They would have replied: “If you had listened to the teachers of our time, they would have had to flatter you with these words and, as you do, deceive you by misinterpreting the testimonies of the law.” [Note: In the Augia manuscript: “Here begin the words of the heretics’ book concerning Predestination. Whoever reads that book should read it carefully because of the serpent’s poisons, until the Catholic [book] begins.” In Mabillon’s copy, which we have already mentioned, the words “whoever reads that book,” etc., occur not here but somewhat earlier, at the end of the Prologue to Book Three.]

[Note: [Col. 0630] The same manuscript: “I. HERETICS. Be secure,” etc.]

## I.

“Be secure concerning God’s ordinance, which he established by predestining. God has mercy on whom he wishes, and hardens whom he wishes. For it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy. The potter has power over the clay to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. The flesh opposes the spirit, and the spirit the flesh. These oppose one another, so that you do not do the very things you wish. God has already predestined those whom he foreknew; and those whom he predestined, he called; those whom he called, he justified; and those whom he justified, he glorified. His way is not in man. What you think deserves praise in you because you act well is nothing, since the Law speaks precisely in order to inspire fear. Otherwise, nothing exists except what God has willed: whom he has willed to be holy is holy; he will be nothing else. Whom he has foreknown to be wicked is wicked; he will not be otherwise. For God’s predestination has already determined both the number of the righteous and the number of sinners, and it will be necessary that the appointed limit cannot be passed.”

[Note: [Col. 0630] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. If you had said these things,” etc.]

If certain people of the present age had said the things you say, they would indeed have escaped human anger for a time, but they would have encountered God’s eternal punishments. They did not say this, however. They said:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you.’ For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. 1:19–21).

And again:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘Because you have departed from me, I also will depart from you, and I will hand you over to the Assyrians for plunder. They will kill your sons with the sword before your eyes, and they will lead away your wives, because you despised my Law and chose what I did not wish.’”

And again:

“Thus says the Lord: ‘Have I become a disgrace to the house of Israel, because they abandoned me and counted my commandments and ordinances as nothing?’”

And again:

“Because I called and you despised me, I too will laugh at your destruction and rejoice when sudden calamity comes upon you” (Prov. 1:26).

Those who said these things and others like them were killed by various punishments. Therefore the Lord also cries out to the people of the city in which the prophets had been killed, both through the prophets and in his Gospels, saying:

“Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37).

“You were unwilling,” he says, “to do what I wanted; you wanted what I did not want.”

If, therefore, God did not want what they wanted, either he established predestination under compulsion from some more powerful being, or, if he established it himself, he acted unjustly. For why does he say to a person, “I wanted what you did not want,” if he knows that he predestined that person not to want it? According to your blasphemy, human guilt is excluded and God’s injustice appears; the one who commits the offense is proved innocent, and the one who punishes it unjust.

The sinner ought therefore to be pitied rather than angered, because he suffered violence from divine predestination when he plunged into the precipices of crimes. For this was willed by the one who created him; and the one who created him is the one who predestined him. If this is so, it is clear that the fault of the one who sins is not his own at all. If, therefore, the fault is not his own when he sins, it is clear that everything condemned by the just God is foreign to him; and whose deed it is, that person’s sin it will be found to be.

No reasoning permits one person to be called the predestiner and another the transgressor; nor does the equity of the good and just God allow him to make a crime belonging to another into his own predestination. Therefore, if you punish the sinner, show the predestiner; identify the author of predestination, so that you may be able to show the judge of the sin, because you cannot show the same person as both predestiner and condemner.

[Note: [Col. 0631] The Augian manuscript reads: “and sinner.”]

For if God is the author of predestination and himself established our actions, show someone else who punishes the sins that were predestined; or, if, as though he were just, he condemns the unjust actions of human beings, show another predestiner of this injustice. For whoever is displeased by an act could never have established that it should be done.

It is exceedingly foolish if you confess that the same person is both the predestiner and the condemner of actions. No one is so impious as the person who recoils from something preordained by himself and punishes the deed that he himself preordained to occur—unless perhaps, turning his mind toward better things and changing his plan, he judges what he previously did worthy of condemnation, and the person who acts is driven on by the instruction of a better course.

But he who stands in the power of omnipotence, who knows neither an equal nor fears a superior—tell us: under whose compulsion did he condemn his own predestination? For if the works of the predestined person are guilty, much more criminal is the ordinance of the predestiner. If the one who has been predestined is guilty through predestination itself, how much more is the one whose predestination was made called to account?

I beg you, take care lest the weeds of an adulterous seed be scattered over the Church’s pure doctrine. Sin is not directed by the one who predestines; it is committed by the one who transgresses.

[Col. 0632A] Let empty arguments of words therefore withdraw. The transgression of the delinquent and the predestination of the avenger have absolutely nothing in common: sin lies in the transgressor’s will, whereas predestination has been ordered in the redeem­er’s power. For the one who created did not predestine anything else except that human beings should be able to live according to his will. It is impious and exceedingly criminal to believe that human presumption arises from God’s predestination, and to regard the fault of the delinquent as the preordination of the future judge.

[Note: [Col. 0631] The same manuscript: “II. HERETICS. At this point they respond,” etc.]

At this point they respond and say:

“God established his predestination through foreknowledge. For those whom he foreknew would in no way be converted, he predestined to death; and those whom he foreknew would certainly be converted, he predestined to life.”

[Note: [Col. 0631] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. Let us now see.”]

Let us now see whether, by wicked evasions, you are not dragging God’s judgment toward prejudice against justice. So human beings have not yet been created, and already they suffer prejudice from the just God? It seems to me that you would have discovered another god for yourselves—one so impious that he would circumvent the mass of the human race through prejudice, determine the merits of a human being not yet born by sorting them out, bind him to sin by the chain of his predestination, prepare eternal punishments for one who has not yet even been conceived, and prepare perpetual penalties of darkness for one to whom he has not yet given the fleeting gifts of this passing light.

Seek for yourselves, as I said, another god about whom you may say these things. You will never provoke this God of ours, who is kind and merciful, to do this to you, not even if he were stirred by your blasphemies. For if he patiently tolerates you, I do not know whom he would not pardon when he sins.

Every day he helps us when we act unjustly, and continually bestows more recent gifts of his indulgence upon our more recent offenses; yet you say: “Before the foundation of the world, already angry because of our future sins, he predestined his sentence against us.” In the present he grants pardon to those who blaspheme him, while you say: “Already then, enraged against those who would sin, he predestined them to death, when he formed the first outlines of human generation.”

So already then he exercised judgment upon the world, before he established the world itself, so that after the end of the age he would find no one left to punish. Perhaps he wanted to spare himself the trouble, so that he would not have to judge human beings after their deeds: before they were created for life, he predestined them to death. And yet, if he himself created those whom he predestined for punishments, he anticipated the merit of killing them; and one who had not yet begun to live had already received a sentence of eternal death.

Our God never did this. If there is some other god of yours, inflict these blasphemies upon him.

Of our God the prophet says:

“‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘when I say to the sinner, “You shall surely die,” and the sinner turns away from his evil way and from his most wicked practices, “As I live,” says the Lord, “he shall surely live, and he shall not die in the offense he committed.” And when I say to the righteous, “You shall surely live,” and afterward he turns away from his righteousness, “As I live,” says the Lord, “he shall surely die.” His righteousnesses shall not save him on the day when he turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity; in his iniquity he shall die’” (Ezek. 33:13ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0633] The Augian manuscript reads: “his righteousness will not free him.”]

You see our God warning the righteous on both sides, so that he may not fall through security, and addressing the sinner so that he may not fail to rise through despair.

[Note: [Col. 0633] The same manuscript: “through despair.”]

If anywhere you have read concerning God, “As I live,” says the Lord, “the one whom I predestined to life will have no other fate, and the one whom I predestined to death will certainly die,” who could tolerate you teaching such things? Behold, God speaks against your sentence, and you do not believe God himself when he bears witness about himself.

Nor should the righteous be secure, he says. If I say to him, “You shall live,” yet if he turns away from righteousness, he will die in iniquity. And when I say to the sinner, “You shall surely die,” and he turns back, “As I live,” says the Lord, “I will not remember his iniquities; he shall live. For I do not desire the death of the dying, but only that he turn and live.”

[Note: [Col. 0633] The same manuscript: “III. HERETICS. They respond to us again,” etc.]

## III.

They respond to us again, crying out:

“This is written in the old Law, but in the New Testament the Apostle cries: ‘Vessels of wrath prepared for destruction’” (Rom. 9:22).

[Note: [Col. 0633] The Augian manuscript: “CATHOLICS. Therefore, if before the coming of mercy,” etc.]

Therefore, if mercy already overflowed before the coming of mercy, how much more now, when Mercy itself accepted a sentence of condemnation on behalf of the impious, in order to absolve the impious from their guilt and call them back to the grace of indulgence?

Let us therefore see in what manner the vessels of wrath are prepared for destruction. Hear the Apostle, who applies this not to God’s preordination but to human negligence or diligence. “In a great house,” he says, “there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; and some indeed are for honor, but others for dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to God, prepared for every good work” (2 Tim. 2:20–22).

Therefore the vessels prepared for wrath unto destruction, if they cleanse themselves from those things for which they were prepared for destruction, will become vessels sanctified for honor and useful to God, prepared for every good work. This accords with what he said above to the prophet: “When I say to the sinner, ‘You shall surely die’” (Ezek. 33:34)—that is, “When I say, ‘You will be a vessel prepared for destruction’”—and this sinner turns away from his iniquity; that is, when, though he is a vessel prepared for destruction, he cleanses himself from those things, he will become a vessel sanctified for honor.

After you have defeated them here, they flee to the more obscure passages of Scripture, so that they may shoot in the darkness at those who are upright in heart.

## II.

[Note: [Col. 0634] The same manuscript: “IV. HERETICS. Do you not know,” etc.]

They say:

“Do you not know that it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’? For since they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, it was said from foreknowledge that one would be hated and the other loved.”

[Note: [Col. 0634] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. It will be necessary for us.”]

It will be necessary for us at this point to kindle the light of this little interpretation from the light of the sacred Law, so that you may be exposed as fixing yourselves in obscure passages for no other reason than to strip Catholics, who walk simply, of their gilded clothing and dress them in rags full of heretical filth.

In the book of Genesis it was said concerning Rebecca:

“Two nations and two peoples will come forth from your womb, and one people will surpass the other people, and the elder will serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23).

The prophecy, therefore, does not concern those who were being born according to the flesh, but the two peoples, the Jews and the Gentiles. In this prophecy the greater people, the Jews, will serve the lesser, that is, the Gentiles. For the Apostle continues in this way:

“It was said by the one who foreknew: ‘The elder will serve the younger’” (Rom. 9:12).

Why did you say this, blessed apostle Paul? I ask you to answer. Did you say this so that predestination might bring prejudice against those who would be born? The Apostle answers in this way:

“For this reason I said, ‘The elder will serve the younger’: so that the election might come from the Gentiles.”

Therefore, if the Apostle interprets the mystery of this prophecy for us, who are you to explain this meaning otherwise than our true teacher explained it, when he said that even if an angel from heaven should preach to you something other than what we preached to you, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8)?

## III.

[Note: [Col. 0634] The same manuscript: “V. HERETICS. At this point they respond,” etc.]

At this point, with the dispute renewed, they say:

“We are not saying anything other than what the Apostle preached. He himself recalls that predestination was made through God’s foreknowledge; he himself says of God: ‘Those whom he called, he predestined’ (Rom. 8:30). If you read in the Apostle of one who foreknows, predestines, and calls, why do you charge us with a crime?”

[Note: [Col. 0634] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. We do not charge you,” etc.]

We do not charge you with a crime; we prove it. For whether you claim to be learned, we show that you ought not to cut apart the Apostle’s meanings in this way; or whether you prove yourselves ignorant, we rebuke you for presuming, in your ignorance, that you ought not to do so and for promising to teach what you have never wished to learn.

If you had wished first to learn and then to teach, fleeing from these interpretations, you would never have departed from God’s justice, nor would you say that God does not wish all human beings to be saved. But our Apostle, learned in the Law, says that he became all things to all people, in order to win all sinners (1 Cor. 9:22).

For he had already learned that “God imprisoned all things in disobedience, so that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). He had learned that every mouth ought to be stopped and that the whole world ought to become subject to God (Rom. 3:19); and therefore he said:

“I say, by the grace that has been given to me, to everyone who is among you” (Rom. 12:3).

And again:

“Admonishing every person and teaching every person” (Col. 1:28).

And again:

“The same God is rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. 10:12).

And again:

“The grace of God has appeared to all human beings, instructing and teaching us” (Tit. 2:11), so that every person may be perfect in Christ (2 Tim. 3:17).

And because he knew that the Son of God was born for all and suffered for all, he cries out:

“This is pleasing before God our Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:3).

Therefore the Lord himself also cries out to us daily in his Gospels, saying:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. 11:28).

And in order to teach that he repels no human being from his generosity—ready, liberal, abundant, never giving less—he says in his Gospels:

“Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. 7:8).

The Scripture of the Old Testament also, inviting all nations to listen, said:

“Hear these things, all you who inhabit the world, you earthly-born and sons of human beings, both rich and poor together” (Ps. 48:3).

And therefore the same Apostle, seeing that God wishes all human beings to be saved, though not all human beings wish God, recalls the future judgment and cries out:

“We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10).

The apostle Peter likewise says:

“The grace of God is upon all and in all of you.”

All the prophets call; all the apostles call; Christ calls everyone. Throughout the whole world, countless priests of God call everyone to the grace, mercy, and indulgence of God.

Only two or three little men, with blind hearts, come forth with these apostate books. Pretending to be Catholic men, they wound the whole world. Introducing a new kind of blasphemy, they say that God does not wish all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Suffering from the obscurity of a single passage, they attempt to cast the darkness of their own shadows upon so great a light and such immense splendor.

But because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness cannot overcome it” (John 1:5), with the Lord’s help, drawing from his treasures, we have explained the passage that they think extends a hand to their heresy.

Let us now speak both of foreknowledge and of predestination. God foreknew and foretold that all nations would be blessed in the seed of Abraham, that is, in Christ. When this occurred, the Jews bore it with great displeasure. For this reason they seized the apostles and kept them in custody, saying to them:

“We strictly charged you not to preach this name, yet you have filled everyone with your teaching” (Acts 5:28).

The Apostle Paul, seeing that the Jews were failing because the Gentiles were entering the faith and excluding the Jews from the privilege of the Synagogue through the privilege of the Church, addresses them so that they may not be distressed, saying (1 Thess. 2:16):

“Why do you now prevent us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, when you know that God said to Abraham, ‘In your seed I will inherit all the nations’?” (Gen. 22:8; Acts 3:25).

[Note: [Col. 0635] The same manuscript: “that they would deny his Son.”]

For God foreknew that the Jews would deny his Son and that the peoples of the Gentiles would believe in him. Therefore he says:

“Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8:29).

The Jews are taught to be sons of Abraham through circumcision, whereas the Gentiles become sons of God through baptism, and the Son of God is their firstborn brother. The only-begotten Son of God, specifically the Son of God, becomes the brother of those who are adopted generally as sons of God. Hence he also says to the Father:

“I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Ps. 21:23).

These peoples of the Gentiles, then, as we have said, God foreknew would sincerely receive his Son, whom the Jews were going to crucify, and worship him as was fitting for the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0636] The same manuscript: “VI. HERETICS. Therefore, those whom,” etc.]

“Those whom he foreknew, therefore, and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that his Son might be the firstborn among many brothers—these he predestined; and those whom he predestined, he called.”

[Note: [Col. 0636] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. If you ask,” etc.]

If you ask the Apostle when he predestined them, he tells you: at the time when he said to Abraham, “In your seed I will inherit all the nations.” Therefore through the prophet it is said:

“Hear these things, all nations” (Ps. 48:2).

He says to the Jews:

“Let it not seem to you that God has done something new, since he wished to fulfill for our father Abraham what he had promised: that all nations would be inherited in his seed.”

Therefore, because he predestined all nations, he imprisoned all nations in disobedience so that he might have mercy on all (Rom. 11:30).

Thus those whom he predestined, he called; those whom he called, he justified by taking away all their sins; and those whom he justified, he also glorified, that is, he made them sons of God.

Why, then, do you murmur, O Jews, preventing us from addressing the Gentiles? “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31–32)—that is, why do you lay hands upon us and take offense at the apostles of God?

For if God did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, mark well, O Predestinarian, what he says: “He handed him over for us all.” By saying “he handed him over for all,” he removed the stumbling block from the Jews and excluded your intention.

I am astonished at your wisdom in reading this passage in such a way that you were afraid to approach the verse immediately preceding it. When you came to this passage, thinking that your intention had been satisfied, you refused to look back at the verse that convicted you, namely, “He handed him over for all.” Instead you closed the book and began to cry:

“God does not call everyone to his grace; he does not invite everyone.”

And when our people said, “Then does he not call everyone?” you answered, “He does not call everyone.”

Our people, astonished and anxious because they were hearing something that no heretic had ever said, questioned your expertise:

“How do you prove that God does not call everyone to his grace? Does God himself not wish to call them? Or does he wish to call them but cannot? Or do they not deserve it?”

If he wishes but cannot, he is blasphemed as powerless. If he can but does not wish to, he appears unjust. If they themselves do not deserve it, then grace is no longer grace, and calling is a matter of human merit, not God’s grace. But if it is God’s grace and not human merit, he calls everyone.

For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God,” as the Apostle says (Rom. 3:23); and he adds:

“Therefore they are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ” (ibid., 24).

Behold: freely; behold also: redemption.

I say boldly: wherever there is presumption concerning human merit, there is no grace of divinity. For we cannot attribute to our merits everything that we believe belongs to God’s grace.

Therefore, if it is grace and not merit, how can you say that some are not called because they are unworthy of his calling? If no one is called on the basis of his own merit but through the gift of God’s grace, and one person is called while another is rejected, then God is blasphemed as a respecter of persons.

The apostles are also accused of being false witnesses in this matter. For blessed Peter the Apostle cries out:

“In truth I have discovered that there is no partiality with God” (Acts 10:34).

And blessed Paul says:

“There is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:11).

And again the Lord says concerning servants:

“Do the same for them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Lord and yours is in heaven, and there is no partiality with him” (Eph. 6:9).

If this is so—and indeed because it is so—how do you prove that he does not call everyone to his grace? Or whom does he not wish to save, when he prays for those who crucified him?

In this heresy the devil rages with the fury of his tyranny, so that with a deadly wound he may almost injure the whole world. It wages war between the creature and the Creator and says that God predestined what he punishes, and established for execution what he prohibited.

How impious and sacrilegious this is, anyone, however unlearned, will recognize. For sin is rightly called sin only when both the guilt of the delinquent and the equity of the judge are shown, since the merit of the deed always precedes the punishment of sin. No one makes a person guilty unless that person was able to avoid sin.

Distinguish sin, therefore, between the one who predestines and the one who acts, so that the one may condemn or correct the evil deed of the other as something alien to himself. Everything condemned by the just God is alien to him.

Therefore, if predestination is shown in the sinner, the sinner is proved to owe nothing to the just Judge; for the one whose predestination is asserted is also shown to be the author of the action.

[Note: [Col. 0637] The same manuscript reads: “Do you see?”]

Do you see, I beg you, how gravely God is blasphemed by these assertions? For if the force of his predestination is carried so far that sin is said to arise from his preordination, a bad fruit can come only from an impious root.

There will therefore be, according to Manichaean teaching, one god of evil things and another of good things, so that what is good may be ascribed to the good god and what is evil to the evil one. Otherwise, we would seem to cry out a blasphemy worse than that of the Manichaeans if we judged that the one and same God whom we confess to be good and just had predestined all crimes.

Let empty arguments of words therefore withdraw. The transgression of the delinquent and the predestination of the avenger have nothing in common: sin consists in the transgressor’s contempt, whereas vengeance rests upon the judge’s equity.

Remove one of these two alternatives: either remove predestination from the Judge, so that you may prove him just, or show that another judge will come. For no one who judges can punish what he himself established. If you assign evil to God’s predestination, you cannot assign it to the human will.

Either accuse the human being of guilt and withdraw from blaspheming God, or, if you assert that predestination was established by God for the sinner, you have removed guilt from the sinner but charged God with crime.

Certainly sin is nothing other than human transgression, and predestination nothing other than God’s ordinance. How, then, could things so different and so contrary come together into a single structure, so that what belongs to God as good becomes evil in the human being, and the transgressor’s fault is called the preordination of the one who prohibited it?

Why do you not consider this, you who think that human beings consent to sins through God’s predestination? The devil certainly desires and wishes every sin to occur. Do you believe that God subjected his predestination to the devil’s desire and to the destruction of humanity? Did he wish his predestination to serve the devil’s will, so that, at the demons’ pleasure, he would already condemn human beings as guilty to their enemy before they had earned guilt through their own will?

Let it suffice to have exposed the blasphemies of this passage. For with fearful heart I collapse in intolerable trembling. We wrote down eighty-nine heresies in the first book, but we saw none that had so loosened the reins of crime for human beings; we found none that so asserted blasphemies against God.

I confess, Catholic confessors,

[Note: [Col. 0638] The same manuscript: “Catholics, openly confessors.”]

that their blasphemies increase in this defense. I therefore ask the purity of your faith to assist me with your prayers as I contend against those whose every word is blasphemy.

I confess, dearest ones: all the limbs of my body grow numb; my spirit fails; my hearing trembles; my face is disfigured by pallor; a crop of hair bristles upon my head; my mind within, together with its deliberations, is battered by trembling fear; my very tongue cannot move in its own chamber, because we are speaking against those who say that God serves the devil’s will.

## IV.

They say:

“God has already predestined human beings either to righteousness or to sin; and therefore, since the Creator willed them to be what they are, they cannot be anything else.”

When you ask them why they utter so much blasphemy, they say that the Apostle said:

“Those whom he predestined, he called” (Rom. 8:30).

## V.

Therefore they say that those whom God once predestined to life will be brought to life against their will, even if they are negligent, even if they sin, even if they do not wish it; whereas those whom he predestined to death labor in vain, even if they run and hasten.

[Note: [Col. 0638] The same manuscript: “VII. HERETICS: Those whom God once predestined,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0638] The same manuscript: “CATHOLICS. Who would not see,” etc.]

Who would not see that this statement removes from the righteous the anxiety of fearing lest they fall and cuts off from sinners the possibility of hoping that they may rise?

We have escaped the blasphemies concerning God and have come to the ruin of human beings. For if it is so, that each person is what he has been predestined to be, the Law ceases, the priest ceases, the devotion of the people ceases; the hall of refuge is closed, the bosom of the Church is emptied; no one bends a knee before God, no one bows his head for blessings.
