The books of God are closed, and all the pursuits of virtue simultaneously vanish.

[Editorial notes omitted above: Col. 0630, the same manuscript reads *in depraedationem* (“for plunder”), rather than the printed *in depraedatione*; it reads “when it comes.” Col. 0631, the Augian manuscript reads *constitui* (“to be established”), rather than *constitutum*; the same manuscript’s heading supplies “certain people of the present age.” Col. 0632, the same manuscript reads “we would have found another God,” “ours, however, never,” “at least,” “against sinners,” and “whom he might punish.” Col. 0633, the same manuscript reads “for honor.” Col. 0634, the same manuscript reads “you do nothing except”; it reads *recesseritis* (“you would depart”), where the printed text has *recesseratis* (“you had departed”). Col. 0635, the Augian manuscript reads “upon so great a light and such immense splendor”; the same manuscript reads “let us explain,” “you have filled the whole world,” and “whom they had crucified.” Col. 0636, the same manuscript reads “it is said,” “he shut all nations up in unbelief,” and “for.” Col. 0637, the same manuscript reads “what he prohibits,” “from blasphemy,” and *ad libitum* (“at will”).]

VI. [Note: [Col. 0639] The Augiense Manuscript: VIII. THE HERETICS. “For however much,” etc.] “For,” they say, “however much anyone may strive, and however much he may not withdraw either from the Church of God, or from the priests of God, or from divine studies, if God has once predestined him for death, he cannot be saved. Judas heard the word of life every day, clung to the Lord every day, was occupied with virtues every day, and every day heard the Son of God himself as his teacher; yet, because he was predestined for death, he suddenly perished at a single stroke. Saul was a persecutor every day, every day a stoner of Christians, every day a despoiler of churches; and because he was predestined for life, at a single stroke he suddenly became a vessel of election.

“What then,” they say, “are you, who persist in sins, afraid of? If God deigns it, you will be holy. Or why are you, who live in holiness, made anxious? If God does not will it, you will never fall. Let both of you be secure regarding God.”

Are you, who are holy and anxious lest you fall, who attend to prayers day and night, occupy yourself with fasts, diligently apply yourself to sacred readings, devote yourself to exhortations, and daily press on toward every holy discipline—will you be saved by your own will? Will you be holier than Judas, who received power to heal the weak, to drive out demons, to raise the dead, and to tread upon serpents and scorpions; who was a companion of the apostles and a disciple of Christ; and yet, because he was predestined for death, found eternal death?

“Cease to be anxious, and rest secure in God’s will, since, if God deigns that you should remain, you will be holy.”

But you who are a sinner, learn from the apostle Paul. Could you ever commit worse deeds than he committed? And yet, because he was predestined for apostleship, he suddenly escaped all sins and rose from the lowest depths to the heights above.

[Note: [Col. 0640] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “This is the whole sum,” etc.] This is the whole substance of your counsel. By this you deceive the world; by this you enter houses and take captive little women weighed down with sins, who are led about by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of God (II Tim. III, 6–7).

Therefore, with the Lord’s help, that spirit which tore apart the plans of the false elders who acted against Susanna—[Note: [Col. 0640] The same manuscript: *futuorum senum* (perhaps “of the future elders”; the reading is uncertain).]—that spirit will now divide you, who deal falsely against the immaculate Church of God. And just as those men were found to be full of deceit in their own accusation, so you will withdraw from your own objections, overcome by them.

Accordingly, we repeat the very words you yourselves used at the beginning, but we draw a different conclusion from those same words. We say to the righteous man:

“Certainly Judas was an apostle and did not withdraw from Christ’s footsteps. Day and night he received counsels of salvation from his mouth; he performed signs of power and obtained all the insignia of apostleship. Yet, because he was negligent, he fell. Keep watch lest you fall; be anxious, because your adversary, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour” (I Pet. V, 8).

But do not suppose that Judas’s fall was due to God’s impiety. God did not want him to be wicked. Rather, because he was a thief and kept the money-box (John XII, 6), and because avarice—the root of all evils—was in his heart (I Tim. VI, 10), he therefore, wretched man, fell and burst open in the middle (Acts I, 18). He had neglected such great divine gifts; while the physician was present, he strove not only not to heal his wounds but even to enlarge them.

In Judas’s sin we ask you to judge yourselves. For, with Christ’s help, we will so confute you that you will overcome yourselves by your own judgment. In Judas’s sin there is a great sacrilege, an incomparable crime, an immense offense. Tell us: to whom do you wish this crime to be attributed—to Judas the betrayer, or to God the predestiner?

If you prove that this sin—which it is worse to name than any other sin Judas committed—is the sin of God the predestiner, I confess that you have won. But if it belongs to Judas the betrayer, our defense has carried the day; for God neither predestined him to be such nor wished him to be such.

Let us therefore defend the holy and immaculate Lord from accusation. Let us not accuse through injustice the one whom Judas betrayed through avarice; and, removing Judas’s crime, let us call the Lord to account. For if he became such because God predestined him to be such, and not because he himself was negligent, then we indeed free Judas from every burden of guilt, but, removing ourselves from the condemnation of the human betrayer, we accuse the craftiness of God the predestiner—who, as though he had wished him to become an apostle in order to make him a betrayer from an apostle; who, as though he had wished to raise him to heaven in order to hurl him down from on high; who, as though he had wished him to cast out demons in order to hand him over to the power of demons.

Why do we delay? You have both men before your eyes, you interpreters of our age: the servant and the Lord, the Master and the disciple, the good God and the evil man. Accuse whichever one you wish. If you accuse God the predestiner, Judas is innocent. If you accuse Judas the betrayer, you will in no way be able to prove that God predestined his crime, because God’s predestination is good, whereas Judas’s betrayal is evil.

The good one therefore performed a good work, since he must never be believed to have done evil. And if God’s predestination is good, while Judas’s betrayal is utterly evil, the evil deed of Judas and the good deed of God could not belong together. For darkness and light, good and evil, life and death, truth and falsehood cannot have fellowship together.

Therefore, restore Judas’s sin to Judas alone in its entirety, and offer God the full honor of his righteousness; then give us also the kiss of charity. For you labor in a vain struggle when you excuse and defend all sinners on account of Judas, while accusing God’s justice.

Now let us come to the good and truly blessed teacher Paul, and, setting aside the madness of evasion, let us explain what is true and cannot be denied in its entirety.

It is one thing to persecute an innocent person out of malicious zeal, as Cain did; it is another thing to persecute out of zeal for God, as Elijah did. He not only persecuted, but also ordered many people to be killed by the sword in his presence. Cain killed one man and was punished with eternal condemnation; Elijah killed many and was carried away to everlasting glory.

Paul therefore did not imitate Cain, as you suppose, but, moved by zeal for God, followed Elijah.

Perhaps you will say: “How do you prove this?” Read his own testimony in the Epistle to the Galatians, where he says: “I was persecuting the Church of God and ravaging it; I was advancing beyond many of my contemporaries in my nation, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (Gal. I, 13–14).

Is it not known to all Catholics that the God of the Hebrews is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ? Whom, then, was Paul defending? The Father, without doubt, because his priests had told him that the one whom they had crucified was not the Son of God.

Believing, therefore, in his law and in the priests of the living God, he received letters from them so that, going to Damascus and its synagogues, he might bring Christians in chains (Acts IX, 2). A most prudent and most wise man, who knew that he was acting out of zeal for God, undoubtedly appeared to himself to be persecuting the enemies of God. For he was running on behalf of God’s faith and truth.

He had not learned that the Lord Jesus Christ was the Son of God; rather, as he had heard from his teachers and priests, he considered him a seducer and deceiver of his people. Possessing Elijah’s spirit, not Cain’s, he therefore applied himself resolutely against the new worshipers of God; and, while ignorant, he practiced what he thought virtues but what were actually crimes.

God, however, the examiner of the heart and observer of faith, caused him to find mercy, because his innocence demonstrated that he had acted in ignorance.

How do we prove this? He himself says to Timothy: “I was a persecutor and insolent; but I obtained mercy because I acted in ignorance.” Do you see, then, that where there is ignorance there is no envy? From God’s justice, instruction is given to the ignorant; but judgment is pronounced upon the one who knows and despises.

Thus Paul, walking through the darkness of ignorance, thought that he was persecuting the enemy of his Lord. He burned in persecution, because, as a good servant, he strove to please the Lord. He did not rest; he raged, showing himself more abundantly zealous for the traditions of his fathers.

Whose fathers’ zeal did he possess? Abraham’s, Isaac’s, and Jacob’s, without doubt—and the God of these men was, without doubt, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, striving to please him, he thought he was pursuing his enemy, suffering from the darkness of his priests, to whom he was giving the testimony of his faith by submitting to the authority of the divine law.

Everyone knows what darkness contains. Can experience itself not teach us that darkness has this nature: that it presents the known and the unknown, the parent and the stranger, the citizen and the barbarian, in the same way before the eyes, so that, unless he speaks, it is impossible to know fully who he is?

Thus, like a good keeper of the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, the house of Israel, like a good watchman—[Note: [Col. 0641] The same manuscript: *circuitor*.]—with a staff in his hand he went around through the night of ignorance, so that, wherever he found people gathering the Lord’s harvest, he might ravage it with Elijah’s spirit.

Therefore, while the good servant watched over his Lord’s vineyard, while the servant persecuted out of zeal for faith, while the servant imitated Elijah, while the servant struggled for truth in the darkness of ignorance, while the servant—who knew that he had been told to struggle for truth even unto death—was laboring and, in darkness, persecuting the faith—[Note: [Col. 0642] The same manuscript: “persecuting faith.”]—and did not know that the one whom he thought to be the enemy of his Lord was himself his Lord, the Lord came to his aid, saying: “Stop; I am your Lord.”

Now judge for yourself. If you enter your vineyard at night, and your manservant or servant, in the darkness of night, senses you and begins to come to seize you, tell me, I beg you, speak the truth from your mouth: do you not remain silent and allow yourself to be seized by one whom you know is pursuing you not out of zeal or enmity, but in defense of you? While he thinks you are a thief, he pursues you for your own sake.

Such a servant deserves both praise and reward. For when you say to him, as he pursues you and wishes to strike you, “Stop; I am your master,” he immediately casts the club from his hand, prostrates himself at your feet, and asks pardon for his ignorance. At that moment he will do whatever you command him.

So at that time blessed Paul, sent by the priests of God and already full of apostolic merits, was a vessel of election. Within himself he possessed Elijah’s spirit, and he persecuted—as it seemed to him—the enemies of God’s law. The one whom he thought to be a thief in his Lord’s vineyard was himself his God. He was suffering through the night whose darkness had been produced in him by the priests’ unbelief.

But the just Lord was pleased with this very persecution, which Paul endured for the Lord’s righteousness, because the Lord himself had given the law that Paul was observing.

The Lord therefore did not, as one who shows partiality, seize an unwilling man and make him willing; seize an unbeliever and make him faithful; seize an enemy and make him a friend; seize an evil man and make him good. Rather, he addressed his own faithful servant, who was laboring for him, and said: “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4).

And he replied with the very words usually spoken in darkness: “Who are you, Lord?” (Ibid.). And the Lord said: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting” (Ibid.).

Immediately he believed, and immediately he transferred himself from the Synagogue to the Church—not by changing his Lord, but by recognizing that it was the same one whom he had always worshiped; not by coming from one God to another, but by proving that the God whom he had always worshiped was the same; not by coming from unbelief to faith, but by possessing the very faith that he had rightly held.

The just Lord recognized his servant, as the Apostle himself says to Timothy: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 56). But to those whom he sees boasting that they are his servants not in defense of truth but out of empty glory and some desire, he cries: “Depart from me, for I do not know you” (Matt. VII, 23).

But why do we linger here, when you inflict upon the Apostle not only this insult—that you say he was dragged unwillingly—but also read him saying of himself in a single statement: “If I do this unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship; but if I do it willingly, I receive a reward” (I Cor. IX, 17)?

Exclude him from his reward and say: “Because you do this unwillingly, seized unwillingly, dragged unwillingly, you are not running; for you gain nothing from your running. Be secure now. Know that, even if you wish to sin, you cannot.”

He himself replies to you: “I therefore run, not as uncertainly” (Ibid., 26); “I hasten every day and stretch toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. III, 14). “Although I am conscious of nothing against myself, I am not thereby justified” (I Cor. IV, 4). “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked” (Gal. VI, 7). “For unless I persist in many fasts, mortify my flesh, and bring it into servitude, I myself will be made reprobate” (I Cor. IX, 27).

O good teacher! O wise architect and instructor in every good thing! Thus he builds the Church, wishing to offer an example of salvation. He does not make those who strive in the good race recline backward, so that they may think they will reach God by removing from their minds the effort to please God and saying:

“We will not please him through our effort—why do we strive? We will not please him through our running—why do we run? We will not please him through our will—why do we will? We will not please him through our watchfulness—why do we watch? We will not please him through our prayer—why do we pray? If we are predestined for life, we will not be reprobate.”

The apostle Peter excludes this when he cries: “Be watchful, because your adversary, like a roaring lion, prowls about, eager to devour one of you” (I Pet. V, 8). And the apostle Paul says: “Do not consent to the unfruitful works of darkness; rather, even reprove them” (Eph. V, 11).

“Do not consent,” he says. You see how carefully he shapes our consent. For he knows that through consent each person may be deceived, and through consent each person may be saved.

By consent I mean the consent that we give to the physician who, wishing freely to heal us, cries to us every day: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28).

You hear him calling so that you may present yourself as one who responds. He who cries for everyone to come to him did not know your doctrine. For he would not have said, “Come to me, all”; rather, he would have said: “Let those who are predestined for salvation come to me, so that they may be saved; let those who are predestined for death depart from me, so that they may be punished.”

But it is not as you teach. For if a person withdraws his consent from God’s call, he perishes.

This physician of ours heals freely, but he commands observance. Anyone who is not saved either despised the one calling him, rejected the one inviting him, or neglected those things from which he was commanded to abstain.

This is what we say about the perfect physician. What do you say? Say what you wish. If you praise the physician and blame the sick person, you demonstrate the physician’s diligence and the patient’s negligence.

VII. You do not say this, but you say what you have written in your book of deceit. [Note: [Col. 0643] The Augiense Manuscript: IX. THE HERETICS. “Everyone whom he knows,” etc.]

“Everyone whom God knows to be worthy of the salvation of his redemption, he predestined for salvation. He saves only those whom he knows himself to have predestined for salvation. For God’s salvation does not serve the will of man. He himself knows what he does for whom. For freedom of choice does not precede God’s grace; rather, God’s grace precedes freedom of choice.”

[Note: [Col. 0643] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “These are your writings,” etc.] These are your writings; these are your sayings, with falsehoods mixed into truths. We answer each point.

If he calls all whom he knows to be worthy, then he predestined all for salvation, because he does not cease calling all every day.

If he saves only those whom he knows himself to have predestined, then he predestined all for salvation, because he is the Lord and Savior of all.

If God’s salvation does not obey the will of man, but God’s grace anticipates the will of man, show us who has unwillingly received the holy mysteries of baptism and afterward, through grace, began to will what he had not willed; or who has ever unwillingly performed penance and, after being reconciled, began to repent in such a way after receiving forgiveness.

These two things are the means of human salvation: sacrifice and confession. Yet we sacrifice to God voluntarily, and we confess voluntarily. The sacrifice by which we are redeemed through Christ’s blood and drenched by the water from his side; and confession, by which, confessing our error, we once more merit pardon for our sins.

Therefore, let us examine these two forms—the only ones we know can aid the human race—which, as the Holy Spirit says, are performed voluntarily. Let us see whether, as you say, they are demanded from an unwilling person or sought from one who offers voluntary obedience.

If from an unwilling and reluctant person, we surrender to you: you have won. If from one who consents, desires, and wills, then the consent of truth has granted us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

For we sacrifice to God voluntarily and confess to his name, because he is good.

VIII. [Note: [Col. 0644] The same manuscript: X. THE HERETICS. “It is not so,” etc.] “It is not so,” they say. “The will of man is empty and fruitless; the freedom of human will is empty.”

[Note: [Col. 0644] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “If you said this by comparison,” etc.] If you said this by comparison with divine grace, we would say one thing. For we do not place human will above divine grace. Everything that is good we attribute not to a man who is proud but to God who shows mercy.

Yet, while saying these things, we cannot say what you both say and write: “The will of man is empty.” We say instead: The will of man is not empty. For if it is empty, it neither obtains a reward when worthy nor deserves punishment when unworthy.

But lest you be so dull that, by neglecting or failing to hear what we assert, you do not understand it, go with your catechumens and penitents to the bishops of all the churches. If you see them giving the grace of baptism to unwilling people, or laying a hand of penance upon unwilling people, know that you are Catholics.

But if they have not dared to give the grace of baptism unless they have first examined a true and complete will, nor to lay a hand upon a penitent unless he shows voluntary confession, what madness, drawn on by the emptiness of your folly, makes you say here: “Grace precedes the will”?

God’s grace is indeed greater than human will; but in this matter the will comes first in sequence, while grace comes first in merit. The former precedes by merit, the latter by order.

I know what clouds you are accustomed to raise here for the ignorant, and how you chatter about this statement with the slanderous cleverness of your cunning. “Look,” they say, “they say that the will comes before grace.”

In these two matters we say that the will comes before grace: in receiving baptism and in conversion to penance. We say this so that people, led by your counsel, may not begin to incline their hearts toward making excuses for sins (Ps. CXL, 4), while one says:

“If God wills it, forgiveness of sins will come to me; and if Christ wishes to add me to the number of his flock, it will happen.”

To such a person we say:

“Unless you wish to believe with all your heart, forgiveness will not come to you, nor will this grace come to you, so that you may become a participant in the divine flock.”

Likewise, when it is said to those who remain in sins, “Repent” (Matt. III, 2; IV, 17), “for the kingdom of God is near”—[Note: [Col. 0645] The Augiense Manuscript: “for it will draw near.”—]—and they say:

“If God deigns to forgive sins, it is in his power,”

we say to them:

“Unless you wish to repent with all your heart, God’s pardon will never reach you.”

In these two matters, therefore, we say that the will of man precedes God’s grace.

Yet we also say how this very human will is preceded by God’s grace: it would not possess even this desire to will unless the Only-Begotten, coming from heaven for us all, had opened to everyone the workshop of his grace.

For, coming on behalf of all human beings, he suffered. Thus, in this order, God’s grace precedes the will of man.

We say this in order to exclude you on two counts. For when you say, “Grace precedes the will,” you sound good, but you strike wrongly.

You say, “Grace precedes the will,” in order that a person may not even begin to will what is good, but may wait to be dragged along; may wait to become good unwillingly; and, while being evil, may say: “God wills this, because his grace does not come to me.”

Here we confront both you and the one who says this, declaring: “The will of man precedes God’s grace.”

For the Lord did not say: “You will receive first, and then ask; you will find first, and then seek; it will be opened to you first, and then knock.” Rather, he said: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives” (Matt. VII, 7–8).

By saying “everyone,” he established a universal principle and excluded the particularity of predestination; and by saying “the one who asks receives,” he demonstrated that human will comes before the gift of grace.

And yet the will of man comes first before grace, and God’s grace also comes first before the will. For we did not go to the Holy One as sinners; rather, the Holy One came to sinners. Nor did we ask him to come; he came without being asked.

And so that man might ascend to God, God descended to man. He emptied himself so that he might fill us; humbled himself so that he might exalt us; became poor so that he might make us rich; hungered, the living bread, so that he might refresh us; thirsted, the everlasting fountain, so that he might drench us, parched as we are, with the water of the honey-bearing and eternal fountain.

He was seized so that we might be released; bound so that we might be saved; sold so that he might redeem us; received a crown of thorns upon his head so that he might remove the thorns and thistles of the first curse; was stripped so that he might clothe us; and was hung upon the cross so that he might remove us from the torments of eternal death.

By condemning the wood of concupiscence from the wood of the cross, he stretched out his immaculate hands in place of hands extended in uncontrolled desire. In place of the taste of concupiscence, food mingled with gall was received; and the death of Life was inflicted for the life of death.

For he conquered on our behalf, not for himself. He was always utterly victorious, and he is and will be so forever.

But because in Adam we all lost life and paradise, through Christ we obtain paradise, eternal life, adoption as sons of God, and an everlasting kingdom.

Here we vehemently condemn the one who says, “The will of man precedes God’s grace.” Yet we condemn him in such a way as to say that, from the time of the Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven—when grace has already been spread throughout the world and all the gifts of divine grace have been placed in the bosom of the Church—if anyone does not run to these great gifts of God, but, instead of going to the Church of God, waits for the Church of God to come to him, we call that person insane.

Here we say to such people:

“God’s grace, without distinction of persons, has been placed in the bosom of the Church. If anyone wishes to seek it, he finds it; if anyone knocks at it, it will be opened to him. But divine grace is not given to those who are unwilling or who desire it lukewarmly, according to what the apostle Philip says to the eunuch: ‘If you believe with all your heart, you may be baptized’” (Acts VIII, 37).

Grace did not exclude our willing; it stirred it up, and every day awakens our sleeping will.

Now, with grace placed—as it is written—in the middle of the earth, it cries: “Come” (Matt. XI, 28). This word of God anticipates the one who comes; “ask”—this word anticipates the one who will ask; “seek”—this word anticipates the one who will seek; “knock”—this word anticipates the one who will knock.

If a person seeks and finds, it is God’s grace, because God invited him to seek and God caused him to find. If you do not seek, you will not find; this belongs to your free choice.

For you have such great power of free choice that you are even able to despise the Lord who calls you.

Whoever, therefore, is saved owes it to God’s grace, which established the desire to will; which, through the prophets, through himself, and through his apostles, invites you every day to will. If you will and listen, you will receive the eternal good things of his land.

Thus what you will is God’s, what you ask is God’s, and what you obtain is God’s, because in this respect grace precedes the will.

You would not know what you should will unless he himself, through himself and through his servants, called you, and taught you both to ask and how to ask.

If this is so, what shall we now do with you, who do not ask? Did God not will you, or did you not will God? Did God not will you to perform what is good, or did you not will to perform what is good? Did God not will you to be righteous, or did you not will to be righteous?

I ask you this, O most holy predestinarian, so that you may do one of two things. Either you will admit that you have been defeated, or you will be convicted of blaspheming God.

If you allow yourself to be defeated, say with us:

“Man did not will what was good, and therefore he is evil; for if he wishes to ask, God’s grace will be given to him.”

When you say this, you surrender to brotherhood and reconcile yourself to the Godhead through reverence.

But if you say, “He is evil because God willed this, not because man was unwilling,” you will be shown to have blasphemed God, whom you affirm to have willed evil; and the Church will necessarily anathematize you for blaspheming God.

IX. Let us now state the false inventions that follow in your book. [Note: [Col. 0647] The Augiense Manuscript: XI. THE HERETICS. “He is mistaken who,” etc.]

“He is mistaken who thinks that, by willing what is good, he can come to Christ, since Christ himself says: ‘No one comes to me unless the Father draws him’” (John VI, 44).

You who are wiser than Christ, say whether Christ lied, and only then assert that we have established this opinion against Christ’s rule. If Christ spoke the truth, we are not lying when we say that the predestined are drawn to life, because he himself is life.

[Note: [Col. 0647] The same manuscript: “to have fabricated the statement.”]

[Note: [Col. 0647] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “It is not new,” etc.] It is not new that fools can be deceived by the sound of a word. Thus the vain Arius, following the sound of the word, says that the Father is greater than his Son. He says to us the same thing you say: “If you believe the Son himself, listen to him.” For he says: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

Whoever attends to the sound of the word is joined to the vanity of the Predestinarians just as to the Arian heresy.

For who does not know that no one can come to the Son unless the Father has drawn him? Yet before the Lord reveals to us the hidden mystery of this passage, we expose your meaning.

You cite this testimony so that no one may receive the priests’ exhortations with attentive ears; no one may hasten to the bosom of Mother Church and grow strong at the breasts of the two Testaments; everyone may flee the house of God and occupy himself with whatever vice he chooses, waiting for the Father to send his hand from heaven, drag him unwillingly, reluctantly, and resisting, and make him chosen and holy without his consent.

This is shown to be your assertion and your doctrine.

We, however, say that although a person may be holy—whether he is an apostle, a martyr, a prophet, or a righteous man—he does not possess the power of his own nature to ascend to Christ.

For the Lord alone, by his own power and in accordance with his divinity, ascended into heaven and sits at the Father’s right hand.

However holy a person may be, however much he may be a friend of God, he does not possess the power to ascend into heaven. And because the Son says to the Father, “Father, I wish that where I am, these also may be with me” (John XVII, 14), explaining the harmony of the Godhead, he says:

“No one comes to me”—that is, no one can come to me by his own power. It is not possible for human holiness to ascend to me, where I sit at the Father’s right hand, unless the Father has drawn him.

Therefore, in the person of the whole assembly of the saints, he says to God:

“You have held my right hand; in your will you have led me, and with glory you have received me” (Ps. LXXII, 24).

And he added:

“For those who distance themselves from you will perish” (Ibid., 27).

He did not say, “Those whom you distance from yourself will perish,” but “Those who distance themselves from you will perish,” showing that destruction comes to man not from God’s rejection but from man’s own withdrawal.

[Col. 0648A] [Note: [Col. 0647] The same manuscript: XII. THE HERETICS. “But now hear what the book *Predestinatus* says,” etc.] But now hear what the book *Predestinatus* says.

X. But if the force of the Gospel testimony weighs heavily upon you, and, oppressed by the weight of the statement, you cannot give us an answer, at least explain to us the Apostle’s statement, which says:

“It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

[Note: [Col. 0648] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “We have explained both the Gospel,” etc.] We have explained both the Gospel testimony through true assertions [Note: [Col. 0648] The same manuscript: “we shall explain.”] and now make this statement of blessed Paul clear through evident reasoning.

First, however, we expose your meaning, so that the reason why you misuse the sacred testimonies may be detested.

You wish no one to will what is good, no one to run toward what is good, but everyone to say in his heart:

“However much I may will, however much I may run, nothing can benefit one who wills; nothing can benefit one who runs. For it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

We, however, affirm that no one obtains God’s grace unless he has run in faith. Once he has obtained it, he is forbidden by the Apostle’s admonitions to become exalted.

For he did not receive God’s grace according to his running or according to his will. His running and will, however great and extensive they may be, nevertheless have a measure; God’s grace has no measure.

Therefore, even when the righteous man has reached the crown, he is not permitted to exalt himself in his crown. For the Holy Spirit says: “He crowns you, not according to your merit, but according to his mercy and compassion” (Ps. CII, 4).

Thus the Apostle says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

He therefore extends his running and his will toward receiving from the giver; but the gift, because of the grace of the giver, surpasses the merit of the one who labors.

Our willing toward God is like the relationship between a beggar and a giver. The one who gives alms wishes to give to everyone, since this giver of ours, the giver of grace, cries every day: “Come to me, all.” And again: “Ask, and you will receive.”

For example, a poor man runs and receives from the giver; after receiving riches, he begins to be wealthy, though he had been needy and poor. What will he say now?

“I am rich through my own labor, because I willed it, because I ran”?

He does not say this. Rather, he says:

“I am certain that I possess nothing on account of the merit of my will or my running; everything belongs to the grace of the one who gave.”

Having said this, he can truly say with the Apostle: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16).

We have spoken of the one who willed and ran, because God’s gifts are so great that they surpass both human running and human will.

For human running and effort, unless they are aided by God’s invisible supports, vanish. Indeed, the Apostle, after fighting the good fight, completing his course, and keeping the faith, and now awaiting only the crown (II Tim. IV, 7), says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV, 10).

And again he says to us: “By grace you have been saved” (Eph. II, 5, 8).

Greatly wretched is the person who thinks that he obtains God’s gift by the merit of his own will.

“Every good and perfect gift is from above, from the Father of glory” (James I, 17). We claim nothing for human power; everything that is good we attribute to God’s mercy.

Yet we say that all good things are God’s gifts in such a way that we attribute all the evils we do to our own negligence. For we do not merit forgiveness unless we truly show that we sinned through our own fault, not through the Creator’s prejudice.

And just as we said of the good—that all the good he does belongs to God’s grace—so let him regard whatever evil he does as belonging to his own negligence.

Therefore the Holy Spirit cries:

“If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling, the sword will devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things” (Isa. I, 19).

Thus, by exploiting a good testimony through an evil interpreter, you say:

“Do not will, because it is not of the one who wills.”

The Holy Spirit says:

“If you are willing.”

You say:

“Do not run, because it is not of the one who runs.”

The Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0649] The Augiense Manuscript: “says: Run in this way.”] says:

“Run so that you may all obtain” (I Cor. IX, 14).

The Lord Jesus Christ cries:

“Run while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John XII, 35).

Therefore, rejecting you, we adhere to the Holy Spirit. For, as the apostle Peter says: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V, 29). [Note: [Col. 0649] The same manuscript: “to obey more.”]

But what are we doing? Once again the doctrine of your books grows worse, in which it is written—
## XI. [Note: [Col. 0649] The same manuscript: XIII. HERETICS. “However much,” etc.]

However greatly human will may exert the strength of its zeal in building, it strives in a fruitless contest. Or what does human frailty think its vigilance can contribute to eternal desires, when the prophet cries out with clear testimony, saying: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have watched in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1)?

What is it that anyone hopes to pursue in building, against the divine words and against his own conscience, when he is taught by these sacred utterances that human building is not certain but vain?

[Note: [Col. 0650] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “First of all I ask,” etc.]

First of all, I ask what sort of building you mean. If you are speaking of cement and mud, discuss such matters with the Egyptians. We, however, understand “building” here as the building up of the word of God. The word of God is presented throughout the whole world by God’s priests for the building up of God’s churches.

Is the speech of the bishop therefore vain? Is the doctrine empty? Is the endeavor empty? And if the building of this work is vain, why is it commanded by the Apostle? For the Apostle Paul says: “Build up one another; let all your affairs be done for building up” (I Thess. V, 11). And again: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (I Cor. XIV, 26). “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, the work of each person—what sort it is—the fire will test” (I Cor. III, 10–12).

And in the Gospel the Lord praises the wise man because he builds his house upon the rock, so that it is not overthrown by the force of either winds or rivers (Matt. VII, 24).

Are priests therefore building the Church in vain, and watching in vain so that they may rescue the simplicity of the sheep from the bites of wolves? And how do they guard Christ’s flock, striking all heretics with eternal anathema? Everywhere the sheep of Catholics are pastured, and amid the flourishing pastures of pure faith “the mountains leap like rams and the hills like lambs of the sheep” (Ps. CXIII, 4).

Everywhere, from the rising of the sun to its setting, there is one flock and one shepherd, by whom the wolves are killed lest they harm God’s flock. And still you do not see that the building of good will is not vain but certain?

Every day God’s house is built through good speech, holy example, and excellent devotion. Every day the Lord cries out through the prophet: “Build houses for yourselves” (Jerem. XXIX, 5)—not mud houses that may be shaken by the wind, but houses that may remain firm upon the solidity of rock.

But all these things that we have said appear to you empty and vain. For your books say: “Human building is not certain but vain.”

From the beginning all the saints have applied building-up to their minds. For example, Abel, the first, built righteousness; Noah, innocence; Abraham, faith; Isaac, sacrifice; Jacob, zeal for holy things; Joseph, chastity; Moses, priesthood; Jesus son of Nave, steadfastness of spirit; David, the defense of God’s people; Solomon, wisdom; John, repentance.

We have recalled these briefly from among many, so that, by recalling through them the others whom we have passed over in silence, the reader may inquire whether they were human beings. If they were human beings, how do their books say: “Human building is not certain but vain”?

Therefore, we now deal with the statement of the heretics by Catholic conclusions: either they were not human beings, because their building remains; or they were human beings, and the assertion of these men has vanished.

## XII. [Note: [Col. 0650] The same manuscript: XIV. HERETICS. “But if,” etc.]

“But if you come against us,” they say, “you are not coming against us, but against the one who said: ‘Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain.’ And: ‘Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it have watched in vain’” (Ps. CXXVI, 1).

“Therefore, did he not know that it was not useful to God’s people for these things to be written and transmitted to later generations until the end of the age? You who criticize these words, remove them from the Book of Psalms, since, according to your claim, those who read and sing these verses cannot be built up.”

[Note: [Col. 0650] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “We praise the prophet’s saying,” etc.]

We praise, approve, confess, affirm, and sing the prophet’s saying; and in accordance with the Catholic rule we explain it as follows.

From the beginning, as we have said, from the holy righteous Abel to Zechariah and John, all built a house—not with cement, as we have said, but with holy examples. Nevertheless, unless the Lord Jesus Christ had come and himself built this house in which they labored, those who built it had labored in vain.

For they also diligently cared for the flock; but unless the Lord Jesus Christ had provided his protection, those who guarded it had labored in vain.

Hence the verse also follows: “It is in vain for you to rise before the light” (Ps. CXXVI, 2). For Christ is declared to be the light by the prophets, evangelists, and apostles.

All the prophets therefore rose before the light—that is, before Christ’s birth. For them it was in vain to rise before the light; they were not able to show the truth to those suffering through the night.

But the light came and revealed the hidden things of darkness; and only then did praise begin to belong to each person from God. Therefore, unless he himself had come and built the house, those who built it had labored in vain.

Now, therefore, because he came and built the house, those who build it no longer labor in vain. And because he came to guard the city, those who guard it no longer watch in vain. And because the light came and shines in the darkness, we no longer rise before the light in vain. And because the bread of joy descended from heaven, we no longer eat the bread of sorrow.

For this reason the following verse occurs in the psalm. “You,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0651] The Augiense manuscript: “You build in vain, you watch in vain, you rise before the light in vain.”] “rise before the light in vain, you who eat the bread of sorrow.”

But we who do not eat the bread of sorrow, but the bread of salvation, should build our house upon the rock and keep watch as we await the Lord, because we do not know the day or the hour (Matt. XXV, 13). Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching (Luke XII, 37).

If it seems good, let us proceed to what remains.

## XIII. [Note: [Col. 0651] The same manuscript: XV. HERETICS. “But what do these men suppose,” etc.]

But how do these men suppose that by their own will they can attain the fruit of building, when even the chosen vessel himself asserts that he was unable to accomplish his will?

For the Apostle says of himself: “I do not do this good which I will, but I do that evil which I do not will” (Rom. VII, 19).

If therefore the Apostle is unable to accomplish the good that he wills, how do these men say that by their own will they can reach the fruit of grace?

[Note: [Col. 0651] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “He never hastens toward forgiveness,” etc.]

He who wants what he sins to be prolonged never hastens toward forgiveness. Grant us forgiveness, teacher of the nations, we ask, lest you allow us to share in your injuries.

Let us see, then, what the Apostle wanted to do but was unable to do, and what he was compelled to do although he did not want to do it.

He wanted to speak the truth and utterly did not want to lie; therefore he was lying. He wanted chastity and abhorred unchastity; therefore he was defiled. He wanted contempt for the world and cursed all worldly glory; therefore he was vainglorious—that is, desirous of empty glory.

Finally, he wanted every good thing and utterly abhorred everything evil; therefore the Apostle did none of the good that he wanted, but committed everything most wicked.

For you say: “The Apostle says of himself: ‘I do not do this good which I will, but I do that evil which I do not will’” (ibid.).

Do you see, I ask, into what pit of blasphemies your blind understanding has thrown you? You want to show that the Apostle was overwhelmed by crimes, so that no one would sigh over being a sinner, no one would utter a groan from the depths of his heart for his crimes, and no one would strive with tearful eyes to wash away what he had polluted through desire—when he hears that the chosen vessel, that teacher of all the churches, declares that he committed not the good he remembered willing, but the evil he asserted he had not wanted.

You have opened gates, not of justice but of iniquity, to all human beings, and from the Apostle’s words you have taken up wars against the Apostle. You want to be teachers, although you show that you have never been disciples; and, attending to the sound of the letter, you have suddenly begun to be teachers to yourselves.

What are we to do now, since we cannot endure your blasphemies? If we remain silent, you appear to have spoken rightly—not merely to have spoken, but also to have written rightly.

We speak, with the Lord’s help, fleeing human glory, teaching the ignorant, instructing the diligent, bringing joy to those who know, and exposing you.

Your book’s writing exists; what is worse, it does not die when you die, but creeps like a cancer toward the overthrow of the unwary. Let us see what follows in the book composed by your vanity.

[Note: [Col. 0652] The same manuscript: XVI. HERETICS. “These are the Apostle’s words,” etc.]

“These are the Apostle’s words; we add nothing of our own. He himself says of himself: ‘I do not do this good which I will, but I do that evil which I do not will’” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0652] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “Arius in his third book,” etc.]

Arius placed the following epigram in his third book, saying:

## XIV.

We have received the words of the Son of God, and we believe them true; we also confess them to be true. He himself says: “The Father is greater than I,” and: “I and the Father are one,” because “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”

He did not want to read further. For he could have joined these two statements—“The Father is greater than I” and “I and the Father are one”—and, when he had joined them, he would have found the Son of Man and the Son of God.

For every kind of passibility, removed from the Godhead, could belong only to the Son of Man. God is neither lesser nor greater, but is what he is, always the same, without increase and without diminution. He never advances by growing, nor declines by diminishing; rather, he is the same before all things as after all things, and remains immutable in all past, present, and future things.

Let these matters be understood as though they had been said in another work. For we have mentioned that the condemnable Arius said this at the beginning of his third book, in the same order in which the Predestinarians spoke: “These are the Apostle’s words; we have added nothing of our own. He himself says of himself: ‘I do not do this good which I will, but I do this evil which I hate’” (ibid.).

We now question your judgment. We read that the Apostle said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me; and what I now live in the flesh, I live in the faith of God” (Gal. II, 20).

What do you say now? Was this man carnal or spiritual?

If you say “carnal,” you will be convicted; for he cries out: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me.” If you agree that he was spiritual, you will explain this passage with us.

For you will find the beginning of this passage in these words: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal” (Rom. VII, 14).

If you are carnal, blessed Apostle, how do you rebuke the carnal, saying: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (I Cor. III, 1)? And again: “Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal?” (ibid., 3). And again: “As many of us as are spiritual, let us think these things.”

We are taught by your writings, man of God, that not only were you yourself spiritual, so that while placed on earth you rightly said that your manner of life was in heaven; we are also taught that your disciples were spiritual.

For you say to them: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual, correct such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI, 1).

What, then, are you saying to us now: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal” (Rom. VII, 14)?

To this he himself will deign to give us an answer: “I became as a carnal person to carnal people, so that I might win those who were carnal.”

[Note: [Col. 0653] The Augiense manuscript: “who are carnal.”]

The truth has revealed itself to us, and deception has been excluded by the truth. The spiritual teacher therefore assumed in himself the person of a carnal man. And so that he might not repel his hearer as an insulting teacher, he rebukes himself in order to correct another.

Hence he also recalls this elsewhere, saying: “Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted?” (II Cor. XI, 7).

What then? “I,” he says, “am carnal.”

[Note: [Col. 0653] Perhaps: “Who are you?”]

“I,” he says, “who have been sold under sin” (Rom. VII, 14).

Are you, Apostle, sold under sin, you who, long ago redeemed by Christ’s blood, redeemed an innumerable people for God through Christ?

It is therefore clear that in this passage the Apostle wished to reveal not his own person but that of another—that is, of a carnal man.

[Note: [Col. 0653] The same manuscript: “to be declared.”]

That man is sold under sin who has not yet been redeemed by Christ’s blood, who is [Note: [Col. 0653] The same manuscript: “still called carnal because he is a son of flesh, and therefore says, ‘What I do.’”] still carnal; and therefore it is said: “What I do, I do not understand” (Rom. VII, 15).

For the Gentile does not understand that his activity is directed against his salvation. Although he is a Gentile, he wants good to come to him, to attain good, to possess good, to acquire good—the good of his salvation, the good of his life. But he does not practice the good he wants; he does the evil that he hates.

He hates death, but practices the works of death. He hates danger, but his activity is full of danger. He hates every evil, but he practices the things he hates.

Why? “Because good does not dwell in my flesh,” he says—that is, the true God does not dwell in me. “For willing is present in me”; it is certain that I want the true God, “but I do not find what I want” (ibid., 18).

All these things confront me—the carnal man, the man sold under sin, the man who does not understand what he does, the man who does not do the good he wants but does the evil he does not want, the man in whose flesh good does not dwell. They confront me so that I do not find how to accomplish good.

“Nevertheless, I delight in the law of God according to the inner man” (ibid., 22)—that is, my inner man, in which my understanding resides, delights in the law of God, which says that the one invisible God must be worshiped.

Although I am carnal, I know that wood and stone cannot be God. But I see another law opposing my understanding, opposing the law of my mind, which says and proves that these things cannot be gods. Yet this carnal law resists the law of my mind and leads me captive into the law of sin—a law that is not in my mind but in my members.

For I am led by the body where I do not consent in mind.

“Wretched man that I am!” Paul does not say this about himself. For he was not wretched, but blessed and holy.

“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 24).

The grace of holy baptism will therefore come, make this carnal man spiritual, and redeem from sin the man sold under sin; and he will no longer say: “What I do, I do not understand.”

For he will not do the evil that he hates, but will do the good that he wants. For he knows that good now dwells in his flesh—that is, the Holy Spirit—through whom willing is present in him and he will find how to accomplish it according to his good will.

Now he is secure, and he delights in the law of God according to the inner man, because he does not see another law in his members. For he has in himself only the law of Christ, which does not resist the law of his mind and does not lead him captive into the law of sin, but leads him free toward eternal life.

He is no longer a wretched man, but a blessed man, because he has escaped all these evils and found all these good things.

But who has granted this to me, if you ask? “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And so that the ambiguity of this interpretation might not remain, whereby it might be thought that the Apostle had said these things about himself, he sets down words that must be read in an admonitory manner, saying: “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid., 25).

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus who walk according to the flesh” (Rom. VIII, 1).

That is: If I, who am an Apostle, am considered carnal, will those who live carnally have no condemnation?

And he added: “But the law of the Spirit and of life has freed you from the law of sin and death” (ibid., 2).

Hence elsewhere he says: “When you were slaves of sin, you were free with respect to righteousness. But now, having been freed from sin, you have become slaves of God” (Rom. VI, 20).

God, however, glories in the servitude of all, because the servitude he possesses can be compared with no other servitude. For all other servitudes are known to be coercive; but God’s servitude cannot stand unless it is voluntary, according to what is written: “The Father draws no one unwillingly.”

Hence the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out: “With my will I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. XXVII, 7). And again: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily” (Ps. LIII, 8).

But let those opposed to all these things bring forth a book surrounded by blind ambiguities and, as though unaware of itself, repeating the same things again and saying:

## XV. [Note: [Col. 0654] The same manuscript: XVII. HERETICS. “They are called only,” etc.]

“They are called only if they are predestined; for the grace of God precedes human will. God is first in the good of a human being, whereas a human being is scarcely ever found last in every good.

Give the first places to God, so that you may empty out human pride. But if you wish to nourish pride in human beings, it is evident that you are seeking the ruin of the human race, since you teach that in a good work God does not precede, but human will does, so that they themselves appear to admonish God through their suggestions to make them good—as though he would not do good unless they had told him to—although it is clear that God, without anyone suggesting or asking, bestows every good upon human beings.

For the Apostle does not say: ‘When we were asking, seeking, running, and keeping watch, we were reconciled’; rather: ‘When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God—not through our will, but through the death of his Son’” (Rom. V, 10).

Where is human will? It has been excluded.

Therefore, not everyone who wills is saved. For if everyone who willed were saved, no one could be made alien to salvation. Every human being therefore wants to be saved, but not every human being is saved.

For the one whom God wills is saved. Indeed, I say, the one whom God wills—so that, with human will excluded, he may manifest his own full grace entirely.

[Note: [Col. 0655] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “I call our predecessors blessed,” etc.]

I call our predecessors blessed, because they had no knowledge at all of the practice of such a great crime. Who would ever have suspected that one should act against goodness by means of good things, and fight against justice with the weapons of justice?

“They are called only if they are predestined,” he says. And we say with you: “They are called only if they are predestined.”

For the one who commanded his disciples to call all nations, saying, “Go, baptize all nations” (Matt. XXVIII, 9), predestined all of them before his coming.

He therefore predestined all nations for life, because he called all nations to life. Whoever comes will attribute it to the divine clemency, which both predestines and calls; whoever does not come must attribute it to his own negligence, since he both despises and refuses.

It does not belong to divine predestination that the destruction of a human being should occur; nor is it God’s will when the devil’s will is fulfilled. For these wills are hostile and contrary to one another, and one cannot be fulfilled without the contempt of the other.

But if some are not called to life, in those who are not called the devil’s will is fulfilled. And I marvel with what boldness you enter the Church of the one whom you do not fear to say is subject to the devil’s will. For the one who does not want all human beings to attain salvation is proved to fulfill the devil’s will.

Just as those whom he wishes to save are believed to fulfill his will, so in those whom he does not wish to save the devil’s will is fulfilled.

But the good God wants all to be good; and here you fall into error, because all those whom he wants to be good are not good.

You are accustomed to say: “Those who are not good are evil because God repels them from himself,” so that those who sin may appear not to be sinners through their own fault.

If you fall into error here because God’s will is not fulfilled, why do you not rather render judgment here upon those who sin, so that God may be praised for the patience of his mercy, and the human being blamed for the impatience of his own will?

## XVI. [Note: [Col. 0655] The same manuscript: XVIII. HERETICS. “For you say,” etc.]

For you say: “Therefore the human being conquers God.”

He conquers God if God wants him to be good and he is not good.

[Note: [Col. 0656] The same manuscript: CATHOLICS. “What, then,” etc.]

What, then, are you attending to here? Do you see God and the human being wrestling, so that you say these things? If you saw them wrestling, you would rightly award victory to one side.

But now, since the Savior of human beings, holding to the physician’s rule, gives instructions—not necessary for his own usefulness but beneficial for our salvation—he commands certain things to be done so that you may obtain life, and forbids certain things to be done so that you may escape death.

If you listen, you will attribute your life to the Savior; if you despise him, you will attribute it to your own negligence when you begin to feel the torments of death.

But if you say that the sick person’s death occurred through the physician’s incompetence, we teach that the physician is perfect in every respect. If, however, you say that the destruction through death came about by his will, he himself cries out to you, saying: “I do not want the death of the sinner” (Ezek. XXXIII, 11).

If you should be worthy to question him and say, “If you do not want this, show what you do want,” he will answer: “I want him to turn and live.”

Therefore we also formulate a Catholic conclusion that counters your tricks:

If a human being can sin against God’s will, how much more can a human being, with God willing, put an end to sins?

If a human being can will what God does not will, how much more can a human being will what God wills?

If a human being can perish against God’s will, how much more can a human being be saved with God willing?

If a human being could, against God’s will, fulfill the devil’s will, how much more can a human being, with God willing, fulfill God’s will?

If a human being could despise God’s predestination through his aversion, how much more can a human being fulfill God’s predestination through his conversion?

God therefore said: “I do not want this; I want that”—that is, he said: “I do not want the death of the one who dies; I want him to turn and live.”

What he said he wanted, he predestined, for he predestined nothing unwillingly. What he said he did not want, he abandoned.

If a human being can will and do what God does not will, how much more can he both will and do what God wills?

The issue here is the destruction and salvation of the human being. God wants us to be saved; the devil wants us to perish.

If the destruction of a human being, which the devil wills, can occur through our negligence, how much more can the liberation of a human being, which God wills, occur through the diligence of a good and most faithful will?

## XVII

[Note: [Col. 0656] The same manuscript: XIX. **HERETICS.** “But he says,” etc.]

“But,” says your book, “the grace of God precedes the will of man.”

[Note: [Col. 0656] The same: **CATHOLICS.** “We say,” etc.]

We say: It not only precedes, but also follows the will of man. Before we show, however, how it precedes and how it follows, we shall explain what you wish to establish.

You say, then: “The grace of God precedes the will of man,” so that, when a person hears such a worthy and truthful statement, he will not consider what follows, but will learn from your explanations that human will must cease; before he has begun to will, he seems to provoke God to jealousy. Let him wait until grace first comes—grace that drags the unwilling, compels the reluctant, and holds the fugitive. Let a person roll in filth, become the dregs of the sewers, and be submerged in whirlpools of crimes, yet remain secure in his vice. For if preceding grace comes, the person will withdraw from crime. [Col. 0657A] For the human being will not precede God’s grace; rather, God’s grace will precede the human will.

We have exposed this purpose of yours. Now it is necessary to demonstrate by sound assertions what we Catholics hold against it. Remember that we agree with you when we say: “The grace of God precedes the will of man.” We have said, then: It both precedes and follows.

It precedes because, when we were not asking, not entreating, and not even willing it, the Son of God came to rescue the whole world from death; and, as we have already said, so that man might ascend to God, God descended to man. He came to invite the hungry to a feast, the thirsty to a spring, the wretched to strength, beggars to riches, the sorrowful to joy, the sold to redemption, slaves to freedom, and captives to rest.

Behold, here we teach [Col. 0657B] that the grace of God precedes the will of man. Now let us see how that same grace, which preceded, also follows by continuing after it. For the grace that preceded shows what you should ask, whom you should ask, and how you should ask; it shows what you should seek, how you should seek, and where you should seek; it shows what you should knock at, where you should knock, and how you should knock. It excluded no one from this inquiry.

It not only excluded no one, but also invited everyone universally: “For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. 7:7). And again he said: “If a son asks his father for bread, will he offer him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he offer him a serpent? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (ibid., 9–11). [Col. 0657C] To those who ask, certainly.

Therefore, just as I said with you in the preceding passage that the grace of God precedes the will of man, so now say with me in this passage: The will of man precedes the grace of God—not by becoming proud, but by asking; not by exalting itself, but by seeking; not by wrestling, but by knocking.

For unless a gentile wills to believe in faith, no one grants him the gift of baptismal grace; unless, I say, he wills in faith to believe, he will not share in forgiveness; unless he desires it in faith, he will not be able to reach the gift of God.

If a gentile comes to Christ and says, “I do not wish to be baptized,” he cannot be baptized. If a sinner comes seeking the fruit of repentance and says, “I do not wish to be reconciled,” he cannot be reconciled. Priestly discipline examines both of them, and can confer no grace upon them unless it has learned from their mouths their completely sincere will. Or, if it has dared to do so, you yourselves know the result.

Let us say something greater. Even if the force of illness takes away the ability to speak, the abundance of God’s grace can in no way be given to one who remains silent. For unless the secret of the mind has been declared through the tongue as its messenger, it cannot be obtained. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

Since, then, the Lord says, “Everyone who asks receives” (Matt. 7:7), the will of the one who asks appears to precede, so that the grace of the giver may be granted to those who ask.

And lest I seem to have left you wavering at this point—you who attribute every good thing to grace, yet do not agree with me—[Col. 0658A] I shall say not only that grace preceded at the time when God, disdaining not to join himself to man, graciously came when we did not ask him; even to this day the will of God precedes the will of man. For he wills that we be saved, and we do not wish it.

Woe to me and to those like me, because every day grace, invitation, the will of God, compunction, the promise of everlasting joy, and the fear of eternal punishment precede our wills. Every day, then, the grace of God, full of innumerable aids, goes before our wills; but our will does not follow all these gifts of God.

[Note: [Col. 0657] The Augiensian manuscript: XX. **HERETICS.** “What, then, does he say?” etc.]

What, then, does your book say? “The will of God precedes the will of man.”

[Note: [Col. 0658] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “And what did we say?” etc.]

And what did we say? It both precedes and follows. Why, then, have we labored in speaking, since you say only that it precedes and deny that it follows?

[Col. 0658B] You say that it precedes for this reason: so that a person placed in crimes may make his own will cease and wait for grace to come to him first, lest he begin to place his will before God’s grace.

But we Catholics abhor this and say: Grace precedes the will of human beings by showing eternal life, in which they may delight, and showing everlasting fire, by which they may be frightened, so that they may be called back from the pleasures of sins.

Grace, I say, precedes our wills every day; but—what is worse—our will does not follow. That is why we weep while praying and groan while repenting: we do not follow the one who precedes us; we despise the one who invites us; we honor neither the Father who gently entreats us as sons, nor fear the Lord who terrifies us as servants.

Therefore he himself also speaks to us through the prophet: “A son honors his father, and a servant fears his lord. If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my honor?” (Mal. 1:6).

Let us ask now: Does preceding grace demand something from us, or does it not demand anything? Without doubt, it demands something. What does it demand? Certainly, the very thing that you yourselves say: the will itself.

Grace, then, precedes. What is grace? That you receive freely what you have asked for. Therefore he did not say, “Buy, and it will be given to you,” but, “Ask, and it will be given to you.”

And so that the simplicity of our brothers may recognize this meaning more clearly, let us offer some comparison. Wisdom was shown to Solomon: behold, grace. Now listen to Solomon himself speaking about what he did when it was shown to him. “I became a lover,” he says, “of her beauty; I sought to take her for myself, and I ran after her; [Col. 0658D] all the more she withdrew from me” (Wis. 8:2).

Does this not seem to you like a most beautiful girl enticing and provoking her lover to run? Why, then, should we wish to mention this example?

Listen to the grace of God. Let us imagine a father’s daughter. Know, O man, that she has been revealed to you by her father through evident signs, so that you may see her and become a lover of her beauty. He also shows how great are her riches, how great her affection, how great her graciousness, and how great her fidelity. She is beautiful, rich, faithful, wise, and also the daughter of the highest king.

The father has displayed her before your eyes, O man, so that, having become her lover, you may ask to take her in marriage, and through her beget children for God, as did the one who said: “Though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15).

From what wife did Paul beget us for God? Certainly from the grace of Christ, whose lover he became, and for whose love he declared that he regarded every suffering as sweet.

Take, then, a comparison from the example of the fleshly girl, so that you may reach the spiritual meaning more effectively. The girl has been shown to you by her father: behold, the father’s grace has preceded your will. Now begin to will.

The grace of the one who showed her has indeed been displayed, so that you may consider how much you ought to believe that he loves you: in order to make you his own, he showed you his daughter—beautiful, rich, and wise—so that, having become her lover, you might take her for yourself in marriage.

Behold grace preceding the will; behold grace stimulating the breast; behold grace enticing the mind; behold grace awakening the sleeper.

What do you now command the father to do for one who does not ask, does not entreat, does not desire, and does not show the warmth of his love? Should he take his daughter and join her to you while you are occupied with aversion or surrounded by other loves? He does not do this.

But unless you seek her as silver, unless you search for her as a treasure, unless you will in faith, unless you run in faith, and unless you show your true love, you will not receive her at all.

Let it be enough for you that, although you are a beggar and she is rich, she enriches you with her wealth; although you are low-born and she is the daughter of the highest sovereignty, she ennobles you with her nobility.

Listen carefully to what her father says to the lovers of his daughter. “Whoever loves father and mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). He did not say, “Whoever is poor, low-born, or wretched”; but, “Whoever loves anything more than me is not worthy of me.”

[Note: [Col. 0659] The Augiensian manuscript: “Behold preceding grace.”]

O grace preceding the will, demanding only love! O man, love and receive; but if you love, show it by your deeds.

Everyone who loves wishes, desires, asks, keeps watch, runs, hastens, and exerts himself through friends,

[Note: [Col. 0659] The same manuscript: “through acquaintances.”]

through children, relatives, servants, and through himself—at a convenient or inconvenient time, with entreaties, promises, a fixed agreement, and an undivided sign of love.

And to open your eyes for you, you who think that you can be joined to divine grace unwillingly and without desire: when the father gives her, why is preceding grace expressed through her relatives? The one who receives her is asked how he will come and whether he renounces all the loves of the world and all the pomps of the enemy. If he has not expressed his will in words, is the grace he requested given to him?

What, then, did the man wish for, what did he run after, what did he desire? To obtain grace. And what does he promise? “I renounce all the pomps of the devil and his pleasures.”

He shows that he does not want what he wanted, and begins to want what he did not want. Then he begins to delight in sharing in grace, through which he is called both rich and a son of the king.

Behold, we have shown you the grace of God, both preceding [Col. 0660A] and following. It precedes because it calls, provokes, and invites you to come; it follows because, when you have come, willed, and asked, it gives.

Let us now see where your argument is heading. For that damnable book, composed by your

[Note: [Col. 0659] The same manuscript: “concocted by your vanity.”]

vanity, says:

## XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0659] The same manuscript: XXI. **HERETICS.** “For not,” etc.]

“For we were reconciled to God not when we were asking or seeking, but when we were enemies—not through our will, but through the death of his Son.”

[Note: [Col. 0660] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “Then you command,” etc.]

Then you command people not to ask God to be reconciled to him, but to become his enemies, so that the statement of the apostle Paul may stand; nor should they submit their will to good efforts, because you say of the reconciliation of human beings to God: “The Apostle said that we were reconciled to God not through our will, but through the death of his Son.”

[Col. 0660B] According to you, then, is the one who has been God’s enemy the one who must be reconciled to God, the one who must be saved? Are those who crucified Christ the ones who must be saved, and those who said, “We do not want this man,” the ones who are to be delivered? But those who were not enemies, but friends, and who wished to place their souls in his love—will they be under the curse of the Most High?

You prove that you blaspheme more fiercely than all heretics. Unwilling to enter the straight path, you have handed yourselves over to winding ways full of errors.

For the Apostle does not invite us to hostility toward God, but to charity. He says: “God commends his love toward us, in that, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son; much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. 5:8).

Therefore, by this work he commends his love toward us, so that, at least in this way, by offering him our love wholly, we may seem to repay in the desire of love what we are unable to repay by our strength.

For God’s love for us benefits us; if we love God, we cannot benefit him. God needs no one: he is exalted by no one’s honoring him and cast down by no one’s despising him.

Why, then, does he commend his love toward us? So that we may say: “If, while we were enemies, he loved us so much that he even allowed his only Son to be killed for the salvation of us all, how much more, now that we have been reconciled to him, will he save us unto his own life?”

Therefore, excluding your special defense, he introduced a universal grace, saying: “Considering this, that one died for all.” And he added: “Therefore all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14–15).

At this point your deranged book confronts us and says:

## XIX

[Note: [Col. 0660] The same manuscript: XXII. **HERETICS.** “You,” he says, “wherever,” etc.]

“You,” he says, “wherever you read ‘all,’ wish it to be understood universally, although ‘all’ is often taught to mean only a part. For when it is said, ‘All have turned aside’ (Ps. 13:3), not everyone had turned aside. And, ‘Every human being is a liar’ (Ps. 115:11), yet not every human being is a liar, because we read of someone: ‘He was a truthful man.’ Therefore ‘all’ appears to signify the greater part, since it is certainly established that not everyone is meant.”

[Note: [Col. 0661] The Augiensian manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “We find no place,” etc.]

We find no place in your book without blasphemies. What does this assertion seek? It seeks to have those who agree with you say that Christ did not suffer for everyone.

If you do not want “all” to be understood in this way, then in this passage the Apostle did not use “all” to mean a part, but mentioned all universally.

Correct your book, then, because Christ suffered for everyone and hastens to help all human beings. He calls everyone; he invites everyone. Whoever is saved will attribute it to the grace of God, who calls, invites, and comes to his aid. Whoever is not saved will attribute it to himself, because he was negligent, despised the invitation, and likewise abandoned it.

For all good things are bestowed upon us by the Lord’s grace when we ask; but all evil things are inflicted upon us by the devil when we despise God.

The devil cannot exercise his power over those who live by divine protections. Can a captive subject the vessels of his conqueror to himself? The Lord says: “No one enters the house of a strong man and plunders his vessels unless he first binds the strong man; then he will plunder his vessels” (Matt. 12:29).

You make the strong man the enemy; but we believe that he has been bound and subjected to the trophy of the cross. You call him crafty, but we show that his plots have been exposed.

Can the defeated one prevail against someone protected by the sign of victory? Can the blows of arrows invade one surrounded by the Lord’s shield, clothed in the breastplate of faith, and fortified with the helmet of hope and salvation (Eph. 6:16–17)?

A person is not conquered by the devil unless he has withdrawn from his own defender, as the Apostle says: “Submit yourselves to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7).

He is an invisible enemy, but he is struck down by an invisible defender. Yet here too your deranged book contradicts us and has dared to say that the devil has such power that he can drag people against their will—even those whom Christ, redeeming them with his own blood, made children of God.

## XX

[Note: [Col. 0661] The same manuscript: XXIII. **HERETICS.** “You have passed,” etc.]

“You have passed by the enemy’s ambushes with your eyes closed—you who say that the will of man can acquire some power—without considering how much harm God suffers every day

[Note: [Col. 0661] The same manuscript: “how much he suffers.”]

from the fall of souls, how many collapses of chastity are caused by the devil, and how many lusts for crimes arise. If you saw these things, we would not labor to show you the damage done to virtues and the victories of vices.”
