[Note: [Col. 0661] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “Tell us, I beg,” etc.]

Tell us, I beg you: the harms that God suffers every day—does he suffer them because the devil conquers, or because man despises him?

If you say that he suffers them because the devil conquers,

[Note: [Col. 0661] The same manuscript: “we return your blasphemy.”]

we return your blasphemy upon your own head. If you say that he suffers them because man despises him, our assertion has won.

For the devil is neither lord, nor creator, nor father. God, however, deigns to be our lord, creator, and father.

He joined his most victorious body to our body, in order to exclude the fragility of our body. He mixed his blood with our blood, so that the fervor of our natural heat might be stilled by being tempered with divine blood. By the power of his chrism [Col. 0662A] he anointed us, so that we might conquer the devil who struggles against us.

He promises that he himself will protect us with the shield of his good will: “Whoever hopes in me, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he has known my name” (Ps. 90:14).

Therefore the prophet also said earlier concerning him: “Whoever dwells in the help of the Most High” (ibid., 1)—the one whom neither the arrow that flies by day, nor the danger that stalks in darkness, nor ruin, nor the noonday demon, and so forth, can assault.

These indications make clear that the devil has power when he finds us negligent, when he finds us sleeping in faith. “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord in faith will be saved” (Rom. 10:13).

But what benefit is there in our showing that the human race is freed from the devil by God’s victory, while human beings are captured through their own fault? Another point of opposition is now added to us.

[Note: [Col. 0662] The same manuscript: XXIV. **HERETICS.** “For the book says,” etc.]

For their book says:

## XXI

Through the transgression of the first human being, freedom of choice perished from humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0662] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “But we,” etc.]

But we say: Through the transgression of the first human being, freedom of choice was made manifest, since it was able to make a person will what God does not will.

If freedom of choice perished, then from where are we sinful human beings? We are sinful for no other reason than that we want what God does not want and do not want what God wants; we commit what he forbids to be done, and do not wish to do what he has commanded to be fulfilled.

Through what do we commit such great evil if we do these things unwillingly? Someone else is acting through us; therefore the law ought to have been given to him, not to me.

The law is not given to a sword so that it may not kill a person; it is given to the one who cuts a person’s throat with the sword. For whether the sword kills or does not kill, it remains the same; it gains no praise by resting, nor incurs guilt by killing.

If, then, we too are driven rather than acting, we are excluded from sins while we sin and excluded from faith while we believe.

Having been defeated at this point, they turn to slander. For their book says:

[Note: [Col. 0662] The same manuscript: XXV. **HERETICS.** “You renew,” etc.]

“You are renewing the Pelagian heresy when you say that through freedom of choice human beings can put an end to sins (Matt. 7:7; John 16:24).”

[Note: [Col. 0662] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “The Church did not,” etc.]

The Church did not condemn Pelagius for this. Rather, it charged him with having exaggerated freedom of choice to such an extent that he rejected God’s help.

## XXII

But we say: Through freedom of choice we commit every sin; but from every sin we are freed by God’s grace with the consent of our choice.

We have shown from this passage that God does not give his grace to those who do not ask, because he himself says: “Ask, and you will receive.”

It has been shown to us, although we were not asking, what we should ask; it has been shown to us, although we were not seeking, what we should seek; it has been shown to us, although we were not knocking, what we should knock at.

If we do not wish to ask, we will not receive; if we do not wish to seek, we will not find; if we do not wish to knock, it will not be opened to us.

“For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. 7:8).

Freedom of choice, then,

[Note: [Col. 0663] The Augiensian manuscript: “The freedom of choice is so complete and so perfect in us.”]

is so vigorous in us that it can obey God; yet it is so weakened in us that it can even despise God, by whom that freedom itself was given.

It was given, of course, for this purpose: so that the devil alone might be despised through it.

For if freedom of choice had ceased through the transgression of the first human being, the law would certainly have ceased, since it can speak only to one who is able both to despise it and to hear it.

But the law did not cease—whether the natural law, through which Abel, Enoch, Noah, Shem and Japheth, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and the others pleased God.

They pleased him through the impulse, certainly, of the natural law. Conversely, those displeased him whom the whirlpool of the flood swallowed, as well as those whom the sulfurous flame consumed.

Neither the former would have pleased him, nor the latter displeased him, if the natural law had not existed and freedom of choice had not been present in them.

What, then, are we doing? We do not escape the accusation unless we say that grace alone belongs to God. For their book barks, saying:

## XXIII

[Note: [Col. 0663] The same manuscript: XXVI. **HERETICS.** “You exclude grace,” etc.]

“You exclude grace through freedom of choice. For either we are freed by free choice, or we are rescued by the grace of God. Choose what you will say. If you attribute everything to grace, we are of one mind; if to free choice, know that we cannot agree with you.”

[Note: [Col. 0663] The same manuscript: **CATHOLICS.** “Listen, slanderers,” etc.]

Listen, slanderers, and listen to precisely what you fear. We say that free choice exists where divine grace exists. Without the grace of God, choice is not free but captive. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

We do not hand this freedom over to human pride, but define it as belonging to the grace of God and to his glory. Grace grants so much that some do more good than it has commanded, from which it also follows that others do more evil than it has forbidden.

The hand that can strip a clothed person, which God forbids, can also clothe a naked person, which God commands.

What do you say? Is it one and the same hand that clothed the naked and stripped the clothed? It is blamed when it stripped, because it could clothe; it is praised when it clothed, because it could strip.

Take away free choice in both matters, and it incurs neither blame from vice nor praise from virtue.

To distinguish freedom of choice for you: choice is in the soul, freedom is in the body. Freedom without choice does not sin, while choice can sin without freedom.

For example, if you have caught a thief and confined him, you have taken away his freedom to steal

[Note: [Col. 0663] The same manuscript: “you have removed it.”]

but not his choice; you have bound his hands, not his mind.

If someone becomes blind who had been devoted to the desires of the eyes, the freedom of his eyes is indeed bound, but choice remains within its own jurisdiction; for desire is exercised according to the mind’s choice.

Therefore Christ calls one who looks at a woman in order to desire her an adulterer even though he has not committed adultery (Matt. 5:28). He has choice, although he lacks freedom.

By his choice he becomes guilty without an act; for a complete will is counted by the just judge as the deed itself. One is said to have fulfilled everything when he has done what he could.

The body is prevented from doing the thing by the impossibility of the act, because the choice of the mind is not restrained.

What, then, does grace do? It does not take away free choice; rather, it heals, enlarges, adorns, instructs, and exalts it. Yet it does not exalt the unwilling, but the willing.

For unless you will in faith and run in faith, you cannot otherwise be freed by grace.

Let us therefore be certain that grace does not reject us while we sin; rather, we reject grace when we sin. For here the judgment of the one who judges considers one of two things: either grace being rejected, or man despising it.

If grace rejected him, it would have freed the person from sin. Is someone to be blamed for not dining with one who refused him from his own banquet? Would he not rather be shown worthy of compassion, since the other invited some but refused him?

It is monstrous cruelty if he was forbidden to dine with those who were dining, and then ordered to be killed by the one who had refused to let him dine together with them.

At last your vain book seems to concede freedom of choice, but on this condition: that it deal with degrees, not with kind.

## XXIV

[Note: [Col. 0664] The same manuscript: XXVII. **HERETICS.** “From where,” he says, “does the greater freedom,” etc.]

“From where,” he says, “does one person have greater freedom of choice in doing good, and another less, unless it is determined by God’s dispensation? For in one person grace shows itself scant, in another abundant and generous, according to what we wish.”

[Note: [Col. 0664] The same manuscript: “I contend with you.”]

I do not contend with you here; here both Christ and Paul defeat you.

For Christ says: “To the one who loves more, more is forgiven; to the one who loves less,

[Note: [Col. 0664] The same manuscript: “less is forgiven.”]

less” (Luke 7:47).

And Paul asserts, saying: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6).

Grace, then, does not operate through God’s acceptance of persons, but through the love of the human being in the mind—whether that love is great or small.

For who can love God more and be loved less by God? Rather, to speak more truly, one who does not love God is loved by God.

But how God can be loved, the Lord himself teaches when he says: “Whoever hears my words and does them is the one who loves me” (John 14:21). Therefore he also says to his disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (ibid., 15).

Let us therefore see, O man, what freedom of choice itself does, so that it may seek God’s grace perfectly.

It empties its own freedom and makes itself God’s servant. The Apostle himself teaches that we do this by our own choice, saying: “Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey, whether of iniquity unto sin or of righteousness unto sanctification?” (Rom. 6:16).

Therefore, whoever has placed himself under God’s yoke has emptied his freedom of choice, so that he may be freed through the freedom of divine choice.

Does it not seem to you that the one who denies himself bread when he is hungry, drink when he is thirsty, and sleep when he is drowsy is emptying his freedom of choice?

But he cannot be worthy in these matters unless he proves himself willing. “Not from sorrow,” the Apostle says, “nor from necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7).

Therefore the prophet also says to God: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. 53:8). And again: “My flesh has blossomed again,” he says, “and by my own will I will confess to him” (Ps. 27:7).

Of the unjust person we read: “He was unwilling to understand, so that he might do good” (Ps. 35:4).

Therefore blessed Jacob also says: “Simeon and Levi completed iniquity according to their own will” (Gen. 49:5–6).

If, then, before our true and complete freedom came, the Lord Jesus Christ, the righteous one, willingly sacrificed to God and confessed by his own will,

[Note: [Col. 0665] The Augiensian manuscript: “He willingly confessed his sin and by his will.”]

and the sinner sinned by his own will, how much more now, with freedom restored to us through Christ, has everything been returned to our own authority—not with nature ruling, as Pelagius and Coelestius defined, not with human nature ruling, but with the grace of Christ forgiving?

We do not attribute it to our own strength, but rely on God’s aids; we do not claim anything for ourselves, but attribute everything to God’s grace.

Everything, I say—I said everything; I repeat: everything, but everything good. Evil, however, we incur through our own fault, through our own negligence, and through our own will.

Why do you turn your head toward slanders and bring Pelagius’s doctrine against us?

[Note: [Col. 0665] The same manuscript: “We anathematize. But both are correctly said.”]

We anathematize all who say that, once God’s help has been removed, a person can be without sin if he wishes; we anathematize those who say that neither death came through Adam nor life through Christ; we anathematize those who say that one born of two baptized persons cannot need baptism; we anathematize those who say that infants ought not to be reckoned among those sanctified by baptism for the remission of sins; we anathematize everything that the Church condemns in all heretics; and we anathematize, together with you, your book, which says:

XXV. [Note: [Col. 0666] The manuscript has the same reading: XXVIII. HERETICS. “So greatly corrupted ...”]

We acknowledge that human nature was so corrupted by Adam’s transgression that it received its restoration through Christ not in reality but in hope, as the Apostle says: “We have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24). If, then, we have been saved in hope, we do not yet possess the reality in the present age. Therefore, after baptism, the baptized still experience carnal concupiscence and suffer those bodily impulses, because they have attained the help of restoration in hope, not in reality. For if they had attained it in reality, after the grace of baptism there would be neither the possibility nor the will to sin. Yet because the power of baptism is so great that it wipes away all sins, the growth of sins is not washed away by the baptismal water; for it is taught that this remains naturally present through Adam. Those members which at the hour of baptism are free from shame afterward recover their shame: they avoid public sight everywhere and seek privacy in modesty. For the transgression turned into shameful parts the members God had made; and they are no longer called “members,” but “shameful parts.” These shameful parts become members at that moment of baptism, but soon afterward the members again become shameful parts. They have not been restored in reality, but in hope.

For the concupiscence of the flesh, which through Adam’s transgression resists in the body like the law of sin, again claims the baptized person for itself and strives to overthrow his whole soul. This is the root of that wound which Christ saved; but he saved it in the manner the Apostle says: “We have been saved in hope.” And he commands us to turn our minds toward contemplating invisible things, lest by presumptuously relying on what is seen we fall. Therefore he says: “Hope that is seen is not hope”—lest people should suppose that sins are removed through baptism in such a way that the very roots of sins are likewise thought to be torn out.

That impulse of pollution which invaded nature through the transgression remains in the baptized just as the root of a hair remains when the surface has been cleansed and shaved with a razor. It has been shaved so that the place might be cleansed; it has not been uprooted so that it would never grow again. For if all the weakness resulting from Adam’s transgression were completely removed through baptism, none of the baptized would be drawn to crimes by any impulse of heat, none would be pierced by the goad of concupiscence, and no one would be stained by human filth. But because we have been saved in hope, we await with patience what we do not yet see.

The time will come when women will neither marry nor men take wives, but they will be like the angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30). For when “this corruptible” has put on incorruption and “this mortal” has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up [Note: [Col. 0666] The manuscript has the same reading: in victory.] in victory; where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, while the power of sin is the law. Then we shall say: “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 15:54–57).

[Note: [Col. 0666] The manuscript has the same reading: CATHOLICS. “This is your little book ...”]

This is your little book, which you give no one permission to read except under oath. Take care not to disclose it or give it to the unlearned to read; the kingdom of God belongs to the few. It becomes evident that God has predestined you to life if you preserve this little book as you preserve your own soul. The greater part of the women who are among you deserve to receive this little book from you. Finally, the woman who disclosed it—a woman in body but a man in spirit—had received this little book from you under oath. While reading what was written, she recoiled in horror and gave it for examination to those whom she knew to be Catholics.

We too have read it, which you always feared; and, with the Lord’s help, clearly exposing its blasphemies, we admonish all Catholics to flee this little book, execrate it, and strike it with an eternal anathema. For its damnability has advanced so far that it empties all the mysteries of the Savior. It says that Christ’s baptism has absolutely no fruit at all when it is administered. “Hope,” it says, “that is seen is not hope”—that is, the remission of sins; and whatever is promised in the present does not exist, because it is reserved for the future; nevertheless, it is not received here, that is, in this world. For the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope.”

Did the Apostle, then, say this according to the meaning you assign to it? First, therefore, we shall explain the meaning of blessed Paul with the reverence due to him; and only then shall we cut apart, piece by piece, the feet of your book, in those matters concerning which its conclusion presumes to have found a complete ending against us.

The Apostle, bringing consolation to the children of God, says that they should seek nothing in this world. Otherwise, seeing the impious and unbelieving prosper in their affairs, while they themselves are afflicted, they might say: “Behold, these sinners, who abound in the world, have obtained riches” (Ps. 72:13), whereas “up to this very hour we are hungry and thirsty, naked and beaten with blows” (1 Cor. 4:11). Removing, therefore, consideration of the present age, he promises future joys. “And although,” he says, “you are wearied by great sufferings, the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). And therefore, he says, “we have been saved in hope” (ibid., 24).

Notice the words “we have been saved”: he did not say “we are to be saved,” but “we have been saved.” He put salvation in the past tense: when we believed, we were saved. Why “in hope”? Because we hope that we shall rise; for we have not yet risen. Since, then, we hope to receive rewards for good deeds and to be able to incur the punishments of Gehenna for evil deeds, being hopeful of good things and fearful of evil ones, we have been saved; and we who were children of wrath have become children of God (Eph. 2:3). Hence another Apostle cries out: “Beloved, we are children of God” (1 John 3:2).

Adoption as children, therefore, is not promised in baptism but bestowed. Yet concerning what we have already received you say: “Hope that is seen is not hope.” For us, hope appears wholly to consist in the sanctification of baptism; therefore, what appears to us as hope is not hope. In the anointing of Christ’s chrism we see the foundation of our hope; therefore, hope that is seen is not hope. We see the body of Christ as our hope; therefore, hope that is seen is not hope. We regard the blood of Christ as our redemption; therefore, hope that is seen is not hope.

You have emptied all the sacraments and made the mysteries void. Like faithful and capable surveyors of Antichrist, you have prepared a place for him to enter after expelling us. For what the Apostle says about the joys of this world—“Hope that is seen is not hope”—you have transferred to the divine mysteries. What he mentions concerning perishable and passing things, you yourselves have attributed even to holy baptism.

May we have no share with you forever, and may our understanding never again be stained by these blasphemies.

XXVI. “Therefore,” they say, “the baptized are again polluted and experience carnal concupiscence because they have attained the help of restoration in hope, not in reality.”

[Note: [Col. 0667] The Augsburg manuscript reads: “we direct our hope toward.”]

We, however, direct our hope toward future rewards in such a way that we do not deny what we have received in the present. For the one who does not acknowledge what he has received does not deserve to attain further benefits. If you now deny what you have received, you are exposed as ungrateful. Therefore, if you have not yet received grace but are going to receive it, why do you secretly communicate with us? Wait for another body of Christ and another blood of Christ; for you claim that this one exists not in reality but in hope.

XXVII. [Note: [Col. 0667] The manuscript has the same reading: XXIX. HERETICS. “For if in reality ...”]

“For if we had attained it in reality,” they say, “after the grace of baptism there would be neither the possibility nor the will to sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0667] The manuscript has the same reading: CATHOLICS. “Therefore you wish ...”]

Therefore you wish to show that the grace of baptism has not bestowed the reality, because after baptism we can still both will evil and do evil. And to whom would God’s law have been given if the possibility of evil had been removed? Or who would seek a reward for keeping God’s commandments if he could not transgress them? Just as a mute is not praised for silence, nor a eunuch for virginity. Those who are denied passage to evil lack praise in the good.

We therefore say that the possibility of evil is good for those who reject it. I shall give a brief response under each heading. Someone could strip those who are clothed: there is evil that was possible; but because he did not wish to do so, the possibility of evil became good for him, since he rejected it by wiser deliberation. Someone could steal money entrusted to him; he could commit adultery: there is the possibility of evil. The person who rejected it was praised both for not stealing the money and crowned for preserving his chastity.

We have discussed one heading, namely, that the possibility of evil is good for those who reject it. Now let us see, conversely, how the possibility of good becomes evil in those who reject it. Someone has money set aside: there is the possibility of good, for he can assist all who suffer need. But when he rejects this possibility of good, it becomes a possibility of evil—and so evil that it is proved to be “the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

But what are we doing? The state of baptism is placed in danger, while we are discussing the poison of avarice. Everyone knows that the crime of avarice is extremely serious; but that the grace of baptism is being emptied by faithless people has only recently begun to become known and has only recently begun to be proclaimed to Catholics.

XXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0667] The manuscript has the same reading: XXX. HERETICS. “For they say ...”]

For they say that sin is removed through baptism as hair is removed by a razor. “It has been shaved,” they say, “so that the place might be cleansed; [Note: [Col. 0668] The manuscript has the same reading: “but it is not uprooted.”] it has not been uprooted so that it would not grow again.” “If all the weakness resulting from Adam’s transgression were completely removed, none of the baptized would be drawn to crimes by any impulse of heat, nor would anyone be pierced by the goad of concupiscence.”

[Note: [Col. 0668] The manuscript has the same reading: CATHOLICS. “Therefore you empty ...”]

Therefore you empty the sacred mysteries of baptism, since, as you yourselves say, concupiscence is the law of sin, and it again claims the baptized person for itself. If, then, you are excluded from this concupiscence, both the remission of sins and the true [Note: [Col. 0668] The manuscript has the same reading: “bestowal of graces.”] consolation of graces will be complete in baptism.

I used the plural “graces” because, although grace is one, just as one vine becomes many through its branches and as many vines are spoken of as there are shoots compressed from one vine, so grace produces many graces. From the one baptismal font, therefore, the remission of sins is bestowed in the present and the kingdom is promised in the future; the son of man becomes a son of God; he becomes a son by adoption; he becomes a sharer in the kingdom; he becomes a citizen from an alien; he becomes freeborn who had been the enemy’s slave; he becomes wealthy who had previously been a beggar; and he who had long been without distinction begins to be both distinguished and great.

But your book empties all these things, and you say:

XXIX. [Note: [Col. 0669] The manuscript of Augsburg has: XXXI. HERETICS. “If the things promised were given ...”]

“If the things promised in baptism were given, no one after the waters of baptism would be pierced by the goad of concupiscence.”

[Note: [Col. 0669] The manuscript has the same reading: CATHOLICS. “Let us therefore see ...”]

Let us therefore see whether this concupiscence becomes, as you say, the law of sin. We say that concupiscence is a matter of natural struggle, and we say that it was implanted by God the Creator in the very entrails of human beings for the propagation of the race. For the first human beings had not yet tasted the tree of transgression when God blessed them, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). He who, by blessing, commanded the human race to multiply before sin undoubtedly implanted in this nature the means by which it could propagate. For the sexes could in no way have multiplied if they did not possess the increase produced by natural concupiscence.

“It is not good,” says the Lord, “for man to be alone; let us make him a helper” (Gen. 2:18). Do you wish this helper of the opposite sex to have been made by the Lord for consolation or for generation? For if concupiscence is evil, as the material of generation demonstrates, then according to you it is clear that God made woman not as a helper for good but as an occasion of sin.

But if you say that woman’s help was granted not for reproduction but for some sort of consolation, the opposite sex was created without cause by him of whom we read that he made all things in wisdom (Ps. 103:24). Yet because the authority of the Old Testament perhaps does not persuade you, listen to what our Lord Jesus Christ himself said about the first human beings. “He who made them,” he says, “male and female blessed them and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’” (Matt. 19:4–6). And after these words he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate.” We read, therefore, that they were made by God, blessed by God, and joined together by God.

XXX. [Note: [Col. 0669] The manuscript has the same reading: XXXII. HERETICS. “And I wonder with what face ...”]

And I wonder with what face you say that this concupiscence, through which marriages are celebrated, was inflicted upon the human race by the devil.

[Note: [Col. 0670] The manuscript has the same reading: CATHOLICS. “For who would doubt ...”]

For who would doubt that a bad thing—if indeed it is bad—could not have been bestowed by the good God upon human beings? If it was given by God, it is recognized as good; but if it is evil, it is clear that it was infused by the devil. For your book says:

XXXI. “The members that God made, they made shameful by transgressing.”

If what God created is not present in the members, and the enemy appeared above God’s workmanship and, against God’s will, made his creature contain another order—not the one God himself established—then marriages are accursed, and the whole mass of the human race, proceeding from that curse, exists under the devil’s authorship.

Choose one of the two alternatives. Either human generation is good and concupiscence is good, or marriages are evil and concupiscence is wicked. Correct, then, the rule of the Church; condemn the priests throughout the whole world who bless the beginnings of marriage, consecrate them, and join the spouses in the mysteries of God.

I wonder with what face you enter the church when you know that everything done there is opposed to your sects. You deny, then, that God gave this concupiscence from which we are born. Therefore we are not his creation, if conjugal concupiscence is not his creation. Take away this concupiscence, which you call the law of sin, and let us see who can cling to a wife.

But he who had given the power of seed for blessing also implanted love in concupiscence for the multiplication of offspring, and wished what he had ordained to multiply to be loved. Natural concupiscence is the increase of the race. But if, as you say, it is the entire cause of sin, then the one who wished posterity to multiply through love created the crime in the race and commanded the wife to be loved above the claims of paternal affection.

Finally, when our Lord Jesus himself says, “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 10:6), it is as though he were saying: “You may not hate the wife whom, with me as author, you began to love.” For he was jealous that the union made by him should be stained by conjugal hatred. What strange perversity! When hatred of a wife is punished by God, human beings condemn the concupiscence of husbands.

But the just Judge does not condemn natural desire, since he implanted love for the purpose of multiplying offspring. When the question of marriage and divorce was being discussed, the Lord then pronounced this sentence: “What God has joined, let no human being separate.” He said this specifically to show that the union of marriage is from God. For there could be neither intercourse without union nor union without intercourse.

“If marital concupiscence comes not from the Creator’s creature but from sin,” they say, “then according to you God joined in blessing what the devil implanted through transgression.” But if this is so, the devil was not God’s adversary but his helper: if God wished certain people to be one flesh, the devil made them inseparable through concupiscence, and what God commanded to increase and grow, the devil discovered a means by which that very command might be fulfilled.

O what unhappy impiety has been invented by the Predestinarians, so that what was implanted by the Creator’s blessing is said to have arisen from transgression! You call this the law of sin; we, however, affirm it to be the law of the race, which you accuse as a crime. We say that it is the cause of virtues, whereas you wish to show it to be the source of vices.

For while its assistance makes parents fruitful in offspring, its struggle makes the continent and virgins glorious. And lest you suppose that it is harmful in any respect, it bestows greater gifts by resisting than by helping: by helping, it produces the fruit of the race; by resisting, it confers the reward of chastity. There it works without guilt; here it wages battle with its own gift.

Take away concupiscence, and marriages cease; take away concupiscence, and the rewards of chastity cease. What kind of evil is this, I ask, which is shown to be the cause of a twofold good, which presents some with the joy of generation and others with the triumph of virtue? Some lawfully act through it; others gloriously fight through it.

But if it is said to be sin in everyone, it follows that married people, the continent, and virgins must all be condemned through it, since it is known to exist in everyone by nature. We do not think so. Rather, we praise it when it preserves its proper order and shows reverence to God. Therefore, in the baptized also, it is itself blessed, not driven away, and adorned rather than removed.

For he who has now blessed the fountain of perennial water so that we might be reborn spiritually also then blessed spouses so that we might be born bodily. We have therefore received this movement of concupiscence, like all the other members, from the Creator.

If concupiscence is evil because adultery is sometimes committed through it, then the hand too is evil because murder is committed through it. Accuse the tongue as well, because God is blasphemed through it; condemn the foot too, because it has led a person to a brothel. In this way not only concupiscence but all the members would be condemned by you.

I shall answer you with a Catholic mouth: just as the hand was made not for killing but for working; and the tongue not for blaspheming but for the glory and praise of the Creator; and all the members not to serve vices but to attend to divine commands; so concupiscence is implanted in nature not for committing adultery but for generating. We have certainly proved that it can bring not only the assistance of fertility to married people but also the palm of virtue to the continent.

Do you wish to know that this concupiscence is good? I shall compare it with the divine mysteries. For not only desired evil things but also good things presumptuously taken are condemned. Suppose that someone had presumed to take the body of the Lord before the illumination of baptism: would he not be condemned for presuming upon a good thing? What brings salvation to some when bestowed according to order brings condemnation to others when received out of order and out of season.

Likewise, if a layman usurps the priesthood or presumes to offer sacrifice, would he not be condemned for a power not granted to him? If presumption regarding such holy things makes a person guilty, rather than the act itself, how much more, in the case of concupiscence, is it not the act that keeps its proper order but the act that goes beyond that order which is called criminal—and which makes the one who goes beyond the order accursed, although the Creator placed him blessedly within his own order?

Since this is so—or rather, because this is so—why do you, unhappy people, endure this? In your desire to empty the restoration of baptism, you say that this concupiscence remained so that all sins might not appear to have been fully forgiven to human beings. Why should you not rather suspect from this that it is not sin, since it is not removed from baptized persons? For if it were sin, it would certainly be removed like the rest.

Therefore, by striving through concupiscence to empty the gifts of baptism, you show that the devil is the creator of concupiscence. Through him you also teach that the Creator failed in his work when he created it and that the one who grants baptism was unable to provide complete assistance.

Those who willingly admit you to themselves will share your portion. For it is written that not only those who commit iniquity are guilty, but also those who are shown to have consented to them (Rom. 1:32).

[Note: [Col. 0671C] NOTE. After the three preceding books, Sirmond has two excerpts from Arnobius the Younger’s Commentaries on the Psalms, in which the closeness—indeed, the identity—of doctrine between Predestinarian and Arnobius is demonstrated. Since we have already brought forward the work cited for this purpose, we refer the reader back to it. Let the Commentaries on Psalms 117 and 147 be consulted above, cols. 491 and 564. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0671C]

APPENDIX. TO THE READER

Those who, after the publication of our Predestinator, which was the first of all to engage the ancient Predestinarians, and after the letters of Rabanus, who again suppressed those same people when they were reborn in Gottschalk, now think that it must be asked whether such people ever existed at all are voluntarily closing their eyes in such clear light. In my judgment, they do not so much fail to see what is true as pretend that they do not see it.

Therefore, in rendering them this service as well, by arranging the principal events in the history of Predestinarianism and setting them before their eyes in a single view, I am not trying to establish the credibility of the matter as though it were doubtful to them. Rather, I wish them, by themselves, as they listen to the testimonies of the ancients who count the Predestinarians among the heretics, and to the councils that condemn them, to Augustine’s testimony that he corrected their error at its very beginning, and to the reports that Prosper and Hilary complained about the same people both to Augustine by letter and in person at Rome before Celestine—to acknowledge, even against their will, that this cause has more witnesses in its favor and rests upon more supports than they had thought.

No one in former times thought otherwise—for whom will they produce from the memory of those days who raised an objection? Let them be ashamed that they alone resist. I do not doubt that there will be some who will at last acquiesce and yield to the truth. Let those who continue to object consider with what hope and with what weapons they will thereafter fight.

For concerning the Predestinarians—both that they actually existed and that they were heretics—there will, as I hope, be no doubt or obscurity in your judgment, reader, after so many and such certain documents that prove that those who contradict cannot prevail against them.

[Col. 0673]

JANSSEN OF YPRES’S CONJECTURE CONCERNING THE HERESY OF THE PREDESTINARIANS  
(From Augustine, volume 1, book 8, chapter 23)

[Col. 0673A]

Therefore, to state my suspicion freely and submit it to the judgment of readers, I believe that there never was in nature a Predestinarian heresy or Predestinarian heretics. Rather, I believe that the Catholic doctrine taught by St. Augustine and Prosper was maliciously misrepresented by the people of Massilia under the name of this heresy.

Thus those Predestinarian heretics were none other than St. Augustine, Prosper, Hilary, and all who followed their doctrine. The Semipelagians designated them by that name and placed them among the heretics without expressing their names; and a credulous posterity rejected certain people as Predestinarian heretics.

[Col. 0673A]

JACQUES SIRMOND, PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS  
HISTORY OF THE PREDESTINARIANS: BY WHAT BEGINNINGS IT AROSE, AND BY WHOM ABOVE ALL THE HERESY OF THE PREDESTINARIANS WAS ONCE DEFEATED AND SUPPRESSED

[Col. 0673B]

CHAPTER ONE. The Beginnings of the Predestinarians in Africa among the Monks of Hadrumetum, Detected by Augustine and Evodius

Hincmarus, in his letter to Pope Nicholas (Epistle 17) and in his book On Predestination against Gottschalk, states that the Predestinarian heresy, which arose from a misinterpretation of St. Augustine’s words, first began in Africa. Prosper himself had indicated the same thing when, writing to Augustine about what was then troubling the Gauls concerning Augustine’s view of predestination, he said that some people within Africa had already raised similar questions.

Neither of them, however, explained what was being said in that part of Africa. Augustine, for his part, explained it in the penultimate chapter of the Retractations: namely, in the province of Byzacena, among the monks of Hadrumetum.

When St. Augustine’s one-hundred-and-fifth letter to Sixtus, a priest of the Roman Church, had been brought to them, some of the monks were led by reading it to believe that Augustine preached grace in such a way as to deny that human beings possess free will. They consequently adhered to this doctrine, which later became that of the Predestinarians, while the others fought in defense of free will.

When the monastery had been thrown into turmoil by this disagreement and conflict, two monks went to Augustine to seek his advice, while Florus, who had been the cause of the misguided interpretation and the disturbances, was sent to him as well. The most holy and gentle man was not content merely to teach those who had come the true and correct meaning of his book, which they had not understood. To benefit everyone, he wrote through them two letters to Valentinus the abbot and the other monks, and added two books: one On Grace and Free Will, the other On Correction and Grace.

In these works, refuting their error, he teaches that human free will was not extinguished by Adam’s sin but wounded, and that it is not destroyed in us by the breathing of divine grace but healed. He further teaches that this is the Catholic faith: it neither denies free will, whether toward an evil life or a good one, nor grants it so much power that it can accomplish anything without God’s grace. In the first of these errors the Pelagians fell; in the second the Predestinarians went astray.

Accordingly, he warns them to avoid both pitfalls in these words in Epistle 47: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” That is, do not defend free will in such a way as to attribute good works to it without God’s grace, as the Pelagians did; nor defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works, as the Predestinarians did not shrink from doing.

These, then, were the first beginnings of the Predestinarians among the monks of Hadrumetum, although, as Hincmarus observes, they did not yet have this name. Although after Augustine’s most certain testimony it would be superfluous to seek further evidence concerning them, I shall nevertheless add another testimony that readily presents itself and that, I believe, Augustine himself would not reject.

It comes from a man closely joined to him in character, teaching, and companionship of life: Evodius, bishop of Uzalis. Several of his letters are known among the Augustinian letters, and we have learned from the Corbie manuscript and others that the book On Faith against the Manichaeans, which is commonly attributed to Augustine, belongs to him.

When Evodius had been informed of the disturbance at Hadrumetum of which we are speaking, he likewise wrote a letter to the same Valentinus and his monks. In it, following the sense or example of St. Augustine, he briefly indicates what they ought to think about free will and warns them, from the writings of the ancients, not readily to criticize what they do not understand.

“Honorable brothers,” he says, “have reported to us that I do not know what questions have arisen among you concerning free will and the justice of God. We praise your zeal, but we do not wish it to be contentious. For contention arouses disturbance, whereas zeal requires piety.

“Man, I mean Adam, when first created, possessed the fullest exercise of free will. But when free will itself was wounded, it was weakened. Therefore free will still exists in human beings, but it is wounded. Hence it is said: ‘My strength has been weakened through poverty, and the light of my eyes is not with me’ (Ps. 30:11; 37:11).

“For the recovery of this, the physician Christ the Savior was sent, so that he might save what had perished and heal what had been corrupted.”

And later:

“Let the saints of God, therefore, read the sayings of the ancients, as I have already said—those who possess a pious disposition toward the divine gift. When they do not understand, let them not quickly criticize, but let them pray that they may understand.”

I omit the remainder, which is contained in the manuscript of St. Maximinus of Trier. All of it is not unworthy of publication, except that it has been insufficiently corrected. But what I have said is enough for our purpose.

Now, when we have observed that the heresy of the Predestinarians was detected among those monks and censured by Augustine, who cannot see the error of those who maintain that this very doctrine was Augustine’s own and, although Augustine himself testifies that his book was misunderstood by them, do not hesitate to assert that it was correctly understood by them?

These events took place in Africa. What followed took place in Gaul.

CHAPTER TWO. When the Predestinarian Heresy Emerged among the Gauls, Prosper and Hilary Seek Augustine’s Assistance by Letter

The disturbances that had arisen in Africa soon broke out in Gaul, considerably more serious and more lasting, in the year of Christ’s birth, as is conjectured, 429, on account of Augustine’s doctrine concerning God’s absolute predestination. Many people—and among them not a few distinguished for piety and learning—strongly rejected this doctrine at Massilia and elsewhere, both because it seemed new and unusual, as they said, and because it appeared exposed and vulnerable to the Predestinarian heresy, which had already begun to grow in Gaul.

This was especially the reason why Prosper and Hilary thought they should write to Augustine, seeking his counsel and assistance in a difficult matter. This is shown above all by those objections which Prosper recalls as customarily being brought forward and urged from the standpoint of his opponents.

“This purpose of God’s calling,” he says, “by which, before the foundation of the world, or in the very creation of the human race, a distinction between those to be chosen and those to be rejected is said to have been made; by which, according to what pleased the Creator, some were created as vessels of honor and others as vessels of dishonor—this purpose removes from those who have fallen the care of rising again and gives the saints an occasion for sluggishness. For labor in either direction is superfluous if the rejected person cannot enter by any diligence, nor the chosen person fall away through any negligence.

“However they may conduct themselves, nothing other than what God has determined can happen to them. Their course cannot be steady under uncertain hope, since, if the election of the predestining God determines one thing, the intention of the one striving is futile. Thus all diligence is removed, virtues are taken away, and under the name of predestination a kind of fatal necessity is introduced.”

Since all these ideas plainly belong to the opinions of the Predestinarians, whose author they wished Augustine to be regarded as, it is clear that Prosper was speaking about them. Hincmarus therefore did not go astray when he stated that the Predestinarian heresy, once it had arisen in Gaul, was made known to Augustine through Prosper and Hilary, and that Augustine published his books On the Predestination of the Saints and On the Gift of Perseverance against the same heresy in response to Prosper and Hilary.

Therefore those who, in order to favor the Predestinarians of our own age, cunningly try to transfer the matter elsewhere are dissembling in vain, as though the disturbances mentioned by Prosper and Hilary concerned not the question of predestination but other matters concerning which they later disputed with the remnants of the Pelagians. Prosper’s words that we have quoted, together with others with which he concludes his letter when explaining what he desires from Augustine, refute this futile invention most clearly.

“Grant,” he says, “best father, that you may deign to disclose what is more obscure in these questions. How is free will not impeded by this preceding and cooperating grace? How, through this proclamation of God’s purpose, is none of those who ought to be exhorted impeded, nor given an occasion for negligence if they despair of being predestined? How may it be explained that, when the opinions of earlier writers on this matter are reviewed, nearly all are found to have the same and one judgment, by which they accepted God’s purpose and predestination according to foreknowledge?”

What else does Prosper demand from Augustine in these words and throughout his letter except that he explain the knots and difficulties of divine predestination? The subject, then, was predestination, and this alone—or almost this alone—accounts for all Prosper’s responses to the objections of the Gauls.

If Prosper and Hilary, together with the others who stood on the good side in Gaul, were distressed that the doctrines of the Predestinarians—which they rightly abhorred—were attributed to St. Augustine or derived from his books, and if they labored to learn from Augustine how they might defend him against this charge, what judgment would those people make about them today, if they were alive, who do not distinguish the Predestinarian heresy from Augustine’s doctrine?

Augustine did not fail to answer their desire; as we have already said, he wrote two books for this purpose. Nor did Prosper cease, so long as Augustine lived, and after he had been received into heaven, to advance and defend Augustine’s position to the best of his ability, explaining that each point criticized in Augustine’s books was either misunderstood or falsely attributed to him. But as the evil grew stronger, and after Augustine’s death spread more freely and dangerously, Prosper judged that stronger remedies must be sought from Rome.

CHAPTER THREE. The Predestinarians, at the urging of Prosper and Hilary, Are Restrained by Pope Celestine through a Letter to the Bishops of Gaul
## On Prosper and Hilary’s Journey to Coelestine, [Col. 0676B] Why It Was Undertaken, and What Was Done There

If we ask the Predestinarian writers of our own age, and above all their chief champion, why Prosper and Hilary undertook this journey, they will reply that they went to Rome to destroy the remnants of the Pelagians. For this is what they loudly assert everywhere, and they had reason to represent the matter in that way as a justification for their enterprise. But here we prefer to listen also to Hincmar, who relates that they went, on behalf of the Predestinarians, to lodge complaints against them, and obtained from him a condemnation of the new heresy, in his letter to Pope Nicholas, which we have already mentioned. He says:

> From the ancient Predestinarian heresy, which first arose in Africa and afterwards in Gaul, at the same time when the Nestorian heresy also emerged, and which, in the time of Pope Coelestine, was overcome by his authority and through the prompting of the holy Prosper.

For where and when was it overcome, or when did Prosper press his case before Coelestine, if we deny this? We cannot fail to know that the Predestinarian heresy became known to Coelestine, and that he disapproved and rejected it. Whoever the author of our *Predestinarian* may be, he does not allow us to be ignorant of this, when in his preface he speaks of the pseudonymous book that they had falsely attributed to St. Augustine in these words:

> At last a book came into our hands which falsely bears Augustine’s name in its title, while it reveals itself as heretical in its text. For who does not know that Augustine was always an orthodox teacher? This book, once presented to the supreme pontiff Coelestine of blessed memory, he held in such abhorrence that he ordered it to be condemned forever to silence.

Tell me, I ask, why did he abhor the book, why did he judge it unworthy of Augustine, unless because of the heresy it contained?

Let us now show that Coelestine’s letter, which he wrote to the bishops of Gaul after hearing the embassy, cannot be twisted into another meaning. What does he write? I shall state it briefly, and only so much as is sufficient for our purpose:

> Our sons Prosper and Hilary, whose concern for our God is worthy of praise, have reported to us that, I know not by what license, certain presbyters there—men devoted to stirring up dissension among the Churches—bring undisciplined questions before the people and persistently claim that these men preach doctrines opposed to the truth. But we more justly attribute the matter to your Belovedness, since they have the opportunity to dispute before you. Therefore let such men be corrected. If matters stand thus, let novelty cease to attack antiquity; let disturbance cease to trouble the peace of the Churches.

And elsewhere:

> Yet we cannot be surprised that these men now dare to attempt such things against the living, since they strive even to scatter the memory of their departed brethren. Augustine, a man of holy remembrance, we have always held in our communion, in accordance with his life and merits, and never has even a false rumor of sinister suspicion touched him. We remember that he possessed such great learning that, even before my predecessors, he was counted among the best teachers. Therefore all together judged rightly concerning him, since everywhere he was both loved and honored by all.

Here, I say, I appeal to fair-minded judges: what were the “undisciplined questions” that, according to Coelestine, these presbyters brought forward, apart from those concerning which Prosper had written to Augustine and to which Augustine himself had replied in his response to the chapters of the Gauls—questions which we have shown all to have concerned predestination? And what else was that “novelty attacking antiquity,” as he says, if not the teaching that was being charged against those who advanced new and unheard-of doctrines concerning predestination?

Finally, when Coelestine takes Augustine’s part and testifies that he had never been touched by any rumor of sinister suspicion—that is, that he had never been accused of any heresy—who does not see that this was said on account of the Predestinarian heresy? The Predestinarians both openly proclaimed Augustine their author and falsely represented him as such in fabricated books.

But let us also hear the patriarch Photius. His words on this subject appear in chapter 54 of the *Bibliotheca*:

> Μετὰ μέντοιγε θάνατον τοῦ ἐν ἁγίοις Αὐγουστίνου, ἤρξαντό τινες τῶν ἐν τῷ κλήρῳ, τὸ μὲν δυσσεβὲς κρατύνειν δόγμα· κακῶς δὲ λέγειν Αὐγουστῖνον, καὶ διασύρειν, ὡς ἀναίρεσιν τοῦ αὐτεξουσίου εἰσηγησάμενον· ἀλλὰ καὶ Κελεστῖνος ὁ Ῥώμης ὑπέρ τε τοῦ θείου ἀνδρὸς, καὶ κατὰ τῶν ἀνακινούντων τὴν αἵρεσιν, τοῖς ἐγχωρίοις γράφων ἐπισκόποις, τὴν κινουμένην πλάνην ἔστησεν.

> After the death of the holy Augustine, certain members of the clergy began to establish the impious doctrine, to speak evilly of Augustine, and to attack him as though he had introduced the destruction of free will. But Coelestine, bishop of Rome, writing to the bishops of that region both on behalf of the holy man and against those who were reviving the heresy, checked the error that was arising.

I am not unaware that Photius mentions these matters together with those that belonged to the Pelagians. But since, apart from other considerations, there was no new Pelagian error at this time, it is clear that these words cannot be understood of the Pelagians. Everyone knows that it was specifically the Predestinarians’ calumny against Augustine that, according to his teaching, there was no free will in human beings and that free will was entirely removed by him. These statements must therefore refer precisely to them.

Let what we have established, then, stand: the subject here is the Predestinarians, who were condemned by Coelestine, at the urging of Prosper and Hilary, through a letter sent to the bishops of Gaul.

## CHAPTER IV. The Author of the *Predestinarian* Is the First to Attack the Predestinarian Heresy; His Name Is Absent from the Rheims Manuscript and Falsely Supplied in the Augia Manuscript

Until now we have seen the case of the Predestinarians conducted silently and more by deeds than by words. For although their doctrines were debated and rejected in Africa and Gaul, the name of heresy had not yet been heard, nor were their adherents called Predestinarians. Afterwards the matter broke into the open: it was publicly classified among the heresies, refuted in the writings of many, and finally condemned and suppressed by synodal decrees.

The first to wield his pen against them was, by his own testimony, the author of the *Predestinarian*, whose book came to light a few years ago from the library of St. Mary of Rheims. When he discovered these men hiding among the Catholics with whom they had mingled, and obtained the book that they had falsely fabricated under Augustine’s name to support their heresy—a book that they treated as a kind of creed—he published it in full and refuted it, prefacing it with a catalogue of all the heresies and adding to them the Predestinarian heresy, which he describes in these words:

> The ninetieth heresy, which we said in our preface had been falsely attributed to the name of Bishop Augustine, has received the name of the Predestinarians.

> They define the election of the good and the rejection of the evil as determined by God, not by whether a human being strives or neglects to strive. They do not want the rights of God either to be preserved by those who strive or violated by those who are negligent.

> They say that even if the person predestined to evil should wish to do good, he cannot attain to good; for the person predestined to good will be brought to good even against his will, even if he is negligent.

> They say that the water of baptism does not cleanse all sins.

> They say: Grace so precedes free will that a person receives before asking, finds before seeking, and has the door opened before knocking.

[Col. 0678A]

> They say that no one approaches faith in Christ unless he has been unwillingly drawn by the Father, attending to the statement: “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him” (John 6:44).

> They say that everything comes to pass not in reality but only in hope, so that they apply even to these mysteries what the Apostle says: “Hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 7:24), and say: “Things that are perceived do indeed seem to exist, but they do not exist.”

> They say: Adam did more harm in bringing injury upon the human race than Christ did in coming to its aid. For, they say, what Adam inflicted remains in such a way that neither Christ’s Passion nor the sanctification of baptism can remove it.

Struck and stunned by so clear a testimony against themselves, the defenders of the Predestinarian doctrine had only one argument by which to weaken it: they claimed that its author was, as they wished, a Semipelagian; they apply the same label to the others who support him. These foolish men do not perceive that this has nothing to do with the question before us, in which we ask only whether the Predestinarians were ever counted among the heretics.

Even if the orthodox assert this, we embrace it with the greater religious seriousness; nevertheless, it does not immediately become false if those who affirm it happen to hold a false doctrine. What then? Are we to remove all authority from Eusebius of Caesarea, or from Socrates and Sozomen, among ecclesiastical historians, merely because the former was an Arian and the latter two Novatians? If we do not reject them in the histories they relate, why should we refuse to accept the author of the *Predestinarian* and the others in a historical matter, even if they were what their opponents claim?

Finally, without now asserting that those whom they accuse were free from every stain, what particular reason do they have for raging against them in the cause of the Predestinarians, if it is clear that whatever view any of these men held concerning the Predestinarians was also held by others whom they cannot regard with suspicion?

Unless, perhaps, they consider St. Augustine insufficiently orthodox because he rebuked the monks of Hadrumetum, who—as we have said—denied free will in human beings; or the thirty bishops who assembled at the Council of Arles to condemn the error of predestination; or Caesarius and his colleagues, who pronounced an anathema at the Second Council of Orange against those who believed that some people were predestined to evil.

If they do not dare to criticize these men, let them cease abusing our author, and instead regret that his name—which deserved to be brought into the light—remains unknown.

For Hincmar’s calling him Hyginus is an error. The copy of Hincmar’s work that we reproduced in our edition had no author’s name. The name Hyginus, which is found at the beginning of the first book, belongs not to the author—as we stated in our preface—but to one of those who compiled catalogues of heresies.

In the wealthy library of Augia, however, there is a copy whose exemplar we later saw at Rome. In it the author’s name is indeed written, but falsely: it gives the name Primasius. Nor is this a recent error. As the antiquity of the manuscript proves, it arose long ago through the carelessness of some critic who, having noticed in Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* that the African bishop Primasius had published three books *On Heresies* addressed to Bishop Fortunatus, rashly guessed that these three books were our *Predestinarian*. He therefore arranged that Augia manuscript so as to place the title “Books of Primasius to Fortunatus” before each of the individual books.

This was utterly absurd, since Primasius lived a full century later, and Isidore’s words make clear that the character of the two works was entirely different. They say that a third copy exists in the Flemish monastery of Dunes, but, as I think, without a title. Thus it remains entirely unknown who wrote our *Predestinarian*.

## CHAPTER V. The Name and Origin of the Predestinarian Heresy in Prosper’s Chronicle—not in the Chronicle of Prosper Tiro of Aquitaine, but in That of Another Man of the Same Name and Period

Among those who placed the Predestinarian doctrine among the heresies, Prosper occupies second place, in the Pithoean *Chronicle*, that is, the edition published under the care of Pithoeus.

Whether this was the same man as Prosper of Aquitaine or another, we shall shortly see. For the moment, it is certain that they bore the same name. The ancient copies acknowledge this, and Sigebert of Gembloux calls him by this name when writing about the death of St. Martin.

His words concerning the Predestinarians and their origin are therefore as follows:

> The Predestinarian heresy, which is said to have received its beginning from Augustine, began to spread at this time.

The manuscript of the Library of St. Victor, from which Pithoeus’s edition appeared, is open to everyone’s inspection. In Paris, without requiring any external evidence, another copy also agrees with this manuscript: it formerly belonged to Antonius Oiselus and is now in the possession of his heirs.

But why, they ask, did Pithoeus decide to publish “from Augustine’s books,” when the manuscript reads “from Augustine”? For my part, if I must say so, I wish he had not done it. Nevertheless, when this sharp-minded man found both readings in the Oiselian manuscript and knew that both conveyed the same meaning, what is there so very objectionable in his preferring the reading less vulnerable to calumny?

It is as though they believed the author of this *Chronicle* so foolish and careless that he would want Augustine to be regarded as the leader and founder of the very heresy he himself called a heresy. Yet these men simply cannot tolerate the reading which teaches that Augustine was misunderstood by them.

For us, however, after the example of the monks of Hadrumetum, it is firmly established that, however much they flatter themselves about having correctly understood St. Augustine’s books, and however freely they invent and reinvent his positions and opinions, they will never succeed in making him favor their errors except through a false and corrupt interpretation.

But to return to Pithoeus’s *Chronicle*: what shall we say to those who deny that it belongs to Prosper? On what grounds do they deny it? “Because,” they say, “he is called Tiro.”

Those who reason in this way do not know that this was the surname of Prosper of Aquitaine. Pithoeus was not unaware of this, but although the copy of St. Victor that he used contained only the name Prosper, he added “Tiro” on his own initiative because he had come to believe that the same man was the author of both chronicles.

Here, although we reluctantly depart from the opinion of so great a man, those who oppose him have our support. This *Chronicle* was not the work of Prosper Tiro, but it was nevertheless the work of Prosper, as has been said. There is no sufficient reason why the same man should have written two chronicles of the same period; nor is it credible that, if he had done so, he would have written them so differently—not to mention that the statements concerning the Predestinarians found in this Prosper cannot belong to Prosper of Aquitaine or suit him.

There were therefore two men. Two Prospers, I say, living in the same period and in the same region of Gaul, both wrote chronicles and both carried their works to the same endpoint: the eighth consulship of the emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius, when Rome was captured by Genseric.

The difference between the two chronicles is this: Prosper Pithoeanus seems merely to have added an appendix to Eusebius and Jerome—that is, he composed no more than what Pithoeus brought to light. Prosper Tiro, however, according to the testimony of Victor, Gennadius, and Cassiodorus, began from Adam and the origin of the world and carried his work down to the Vandal sack.

As the facts show, this *Chronicle* is a mere epitome of the Eusebian *Chronicle* for as far as it extends together with Jerome’s supplement. For this reason it is sometimes called an epitome of the chronicles, or excerpts from the chronicles, since Prosper had extracted everything from them—except that he inserted in their proper places the consular fasti, which his predecessors lacked, beginning with the baptism of Christ, and subsequently composed the rest from his own material down to the end of the work.

Just as Prosper continued the history of Eusebius and Jerome, so Victor of Tonnona, bishop in Africa, continued Prosper’s history. He began his own appendix where Prosper had ended the first edition of his *Chronicle*, namely, with the consulship of the emperor Theodosius XVIII and Albinus, which is reckoned as the year 444 of Christ.

That the first edition did not proceed beyond this point would be sufficiently established by Victor’s testimony, who says that Prosper left off at this consulship, and by the copies of his work published up to the present, all of which stop there. Therefore the eleven years remaining before the capture of Rome must be acknowledged to have been added in a second edition.

[Col. 0680A]

## CHAPTER VI. Gennadius of Massilia’s Testimony Concerning the Predestinarian Heresy, and the Refutation of Jansenius, Who Attacks Gennadius in Vain

Gennadius of Massilia follows Prosper. Although he did not write before all the others, he was the first among those who branded the Predestinarians with the mark of heresy to appear publicly.

He summed up their doctrines in these words:

> The Predestinarians are those who say that God did not create all human beings so that all might be saved, but so that the world might be adorned by the multitude of human beings. And although he says in a general proclamation, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28), they say that he does not call everyone with the intention that all should follow his call.

> They also say that not all who obey the call under his inspiration receive perseverance in carrying out good works; rather, after many labors and fruits of righteousness, if they are not among the number of those who will be saved, the power to act is taken away from them so that they may not continue in goodness.

> Conversely, those who are predestined to eternal life, even if they roll for a long time in unbelief or every kind of sin, will receive an opportunity through which they may believe in God, live according to God’s commandment, and possess fellowship with the righteous.

By such a definition they strive to teach that God is a respecter of persons: that he draws some to salvation against their will after many evil works, while rejecting others after good works and compelling them to evil, so that they may perish eternally.

As soon as this statement was brought to light, it is incredible to say what disturbances and consternation it aroused among the modern patrons of the ancient error. They left nothing unattempted by which they might diminish Gennadius’s reliability—since they could not refute his testimony—and weaken his authority.

But what, finally, do they have to oppose? If you question the chief of their school, he accuses Gennadius of having been the first of all to dare to place the Predestinarians in the catalogue of heretics.

But this is false, because before him—as I shall say nothing of others—Prosper and the author of the *Predestinarian* had already done so. Moreover, what fault is there in professing what is true before others?

“They show that it is not true,” they say, “because Isidore rejected and corrected Gennadius’s book under this title.”

Jansenius says:

> For this reason St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, when he had seen this book and had described several heresies in exactly the same words, added the Pelagians, whom Gennadius had omitted, and omitted the Predestinarians, whom Gennadius had included.

This is what he says in volume I, book VIII, chapter 23.

How many frivolous and fabricated claims are packed into these few words—claims that are at once overturned by a single statement! For it is established that Gennadius published no book *On Heresies*, but merely appended a list of four heresies to St. Augustine’s book.

Let us hear Hincmar, who relates matters much better known and more accurately, in book I, chapter 1 of his work *On Predestination*:

> The same remarkable teacher Augustine also wrote concerning eighty-eight heresies, to which he finally added the heresy of the Pelagians. Then Gennadius of Massilia, a highly learned priest, placed this Predestinarian heresy after the Pelagian heresy as the ninetieth. After that he places the Nestorian heresy as the ninety-first, then the Eutychian, and after this the Timothean.

Yet why should we need Hincmar’s support, when we have suitable witnesses in the ancient books, among them the manuscript of the Library of St. Victor in Paris? In that manuscript, after the end of St. Augustine’s book *On Heresies*, the appendix of Gennadius that we mentioned is added in this form:

> Here ends the account of the bishop St. Augustine concerning heresies. The following items, however, were set down by the holy Gennadius, presbyter of Massilia:

> XC. The Predestinarians are those who say that God, etc.

> XCI. The Nestorians say that the holy Virgin, etc.

> XCII. The Eutychians say that the Lord Jesus, etc.

> XCIII. The Timotheans say that the Son of God was indeed born a true human being from the Virgin Mary, but not so as to be one, etc.

[Col. 0681A]

Then follows:

> Here ends the book *On Heresies*.

Thus there can be no doubt that Gennadius proceeded no further, and that he included these four heresies.

For this reason I cannot sufficiently wonder by what accident or policy it came about that, in the celebrated Louvain edition of St. Augustine’s works, when this Gennadian appendix was reproduced from the Gembloux manuscript—even though the author’s name was silently omitted—its Predestinarian section was left out and only the other three were printed.

Moreover, since the foregoing makes it clear that Gennadius, even if he may have intended to do so, did not in fact write any book *On Heresies*, it is evident with what reliability Jansenius says that a book which never existed was plundered by Isidore. With what right does he complain that Gennadius omitted the Pelagians, as though he were suspected of that heresy, when Gennadius had no reason to repeat the Pelagians whom Augustine had already included? Nor was there any reason for Gennadius to hesitate to mention the Pelagian heresy, since in his catalogue of illustrious ecclesiastical writers he openly called Pelagius himself a heresiarch (chapter 42).

Finally, with what futile and empty guesswork does he declare that Isidore omitted the Predestinarians whom he had found in Gennadius? Where had he found them? Not in the book *On Heresies*, which Gennadius had never written. Therefore, in the appendix. But he had not even seen the appendix.

Read and compare what the two men wrote concerning the Nestorians and the Eutychians: you will not find even a single letter that that great rival of your Gennadius could have borrowed from Gennadius. Why, then, does Isidore not mention the Predestinarian heresy among the heresies? Because he had not read Gennadius.

These, therefore, are deceptive and ridiculous fictions. If they do not deceive ears somewhat more cautious, they are certainly pitiable fare for the ears of Marcellina and Priscilla, who become accustomed to stories of this sort among them.

## CHAPTER VII. The Council of Arles, at Which the Predestinarian Heresy Was Condemned by a Decree of Thirty Bishops, and the Council of Lyons, by Which It Was Again Proscribed

[Col. 0681C]

Of all the wounds inflicted upon the Predestinarians, none was more severe than the wound they received from thirty bishops at the Synod of Arles, and again afterwards at Lyons.

Although the acts of neither council survive today—which they share with very many other councils—some documents from Arles nevertheless remain, and they also support the authenticity of the Council of Lyons.

First there is the letter of Faustus, bishop of Riez, to Lucidus, a presbyter of the Predestinarian sect. It was written while the Council of Arles was being held, about the year 475, as we have conjectured. Next comes the little book presented by Lucidus to the same council. Finally there is another letter of Faustus to Leontius of Arles, who presided over the council.

We shall set out these three documents in order, since in some fashion they can make up for the loss of the acts. First, then, comes the letter of Faustus to Lucidus mentioned above, in which he urges him to retract his errors and warns that otherwise he will be condemned by the council. It runs as follows.

[Col. 0681D]

### Letter of Faustus of Riez to Lucidus the Predestinarian, Urging Him to Retract His Errors

To my most devoted lord, my specially beloved, venerable, and welcome brother Lucidus the presbyter: Faustus.

It is a great act of charity, with God’s help and grace, to wish to cure the error of a brother who is insufficiently cautious, rather than—as the chief bishops are considering—to suspend him from unity. How can I speak in letters with you concerning this opinion, as you say, in harmony with you, when, though present with you, I was never able to draw you back to the path of truth through much gentle and humble conversation?

When we speak, therefore, of God’s grace and human obedience, we must establish this absolutely: that, turning neither too far to the left nor obstinately to the right, we should walk rather along the royal road.

I was surprised that your Reverence said that no one who made a religious profession had ever written or preached against the Catholic faith, since many people who gloried in the Christian name have believed that their various and profane errors should be inserted into written records.

I shall therefore say briefly, as much as I can say to one who is absent, what you ought to hold together with the Catholic Church. It is this: that you should always join the work of the baptized servant to the grace of the Lord, and that you should detest, together with the doctrine of Pelagius, the person who asserts predestination while excluding human labor.

Therefore:

> Anathema to the one who, among the other impieties of Pelagius, presumes to maintain with condemnable arrogance that a human being is born without sin and can be saved through labor alone, and who believes that a person can be liberated without the grace of God.

Furthermore:

> Anathema to the one who asserts that a person solemnly baptized with a faithful confession, professing the Catholic faith, and afterwards having fallen through the various delights and temptations of this world, perished in Adam and in original sin.

Furthermore:

> Anathema to the one who says that, through God’s foreknowledge, a human being is driven down into death.

Furthermore:

> Anathema to the one who says that the person who perished did not receive the possibility of being saved—that is, a baptized person, or a pagan of such an age that he could have believed but did not wish to believe.

[Col. 0682C]

Furthermore:

> Anathema to the one who says that a vessel of dishonor cannot rise to become a vessel of honor.

Furthermore:

> Anathema to the one who says that Christ did not die for all, nor wish all human beings to be saved.

When you come to us in Christ’s name, or when you have been summoned by the holy priests, then, if the Lord commands, we shall present the relevant testimonies in their proper places. Through them what is Catholic will be made clear and what is contrary to Catholic teaching will be destroyed.

For our part, enlightened by Christ, we assert truthfully and confidently both that the person who perished through fault could have been saved by grace, if he had not denied obedience in labor to that very grace, and that the person who by grace reaches the goal of good perfection through obedient service could fall through negligence and perish through fault.

Therefore, walking midway with Christ as our guide, we assert, after grace—without which we are nothing—the labor of dutiful service. But we entirely exclude the arrogance and presumption of labor, so that, while toiling with all our strength lest grace be emptied in us, we declare that whatever we have received from the hand of the Lord is a gift, not a payment.

We know that the fruit of this labor is a matter of duty, not merit, saying with the Evangelist: “We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke 17:10).

Your unanimity should answer in a renewed exchange whether it receives or rejects these points, which have been briefly stated because of the letter’s brevity.

But whoever does not follow this measure of truth, with grace going before and effort rising to meet it, will deserve to be kept away from the sacred thresholds.

For my part, retaining your indivisible goodness on the road in the full embrace of sincere kindness, I desire that you remain within the womb of Mother Church after rejecting this error. If it is quickly rejected, it will appear to have been ignorance; but if it is stubbornly defended, it will be judged blasphemy.
