For we bring a serious charge against the author of the error if we say that the one who perished did not wish to give him the possibility of attaining salvation—provided only that he was already able to exercise free choice—when we cannot at all deny that he will condemn the transgressor of the commandment when he examines him in his judgment.

For how can one who is not liable for what he received be guilty of what he lost? Thus, by sinning against God—whose grace we have first asserted—we would ultimately appear to attack his justice.

I retain a copy of this letter with me, to be produced before the assembly of the holy bishops if necessary. If your Fraternity thinks it should be accepted, send it back to me at once with your own signature; or reply in writing that you altogether reject it.

If you do not wish to send it back signed, as I have said, you will openly confirm by your very silence that you still persist in error. Consequently, you will force me to expose your position in public assemblies.

Accordingly, reply in accordance with what I have sent: without evasions, say whether you acknowledge or reject these statements.

And in another hand:

> I have reread and signed this copy of my letter.  
> Faustus.

[Col. 0683C]

This is the true and genuine subscription of the letter, bearing the sole name of its author, which alone both Hincmar and all the best ancient manuscripts reproduce.

The other subscription, found in the editions published up to the present, which adds the names of Auxanius and other bishops—nine in all, together with Faustus—is undoubtedly spurious and foreign to the letter, although it is not unsupported by the testimony of certain ancient manuscripts.

It led some people into error, causing them to believe that Faustus’s letter had been signed either by the Council of Arles or by the Council of Lyons. It also gave our opponents an opportunity for slander, enabling them to say that we attributed the name of a council to this one letter of Faustus. This is entirely false.

Stirred by this letter of Faustus, Lucidus came to his senses. What he had long hesitated over, he recognized as error and retracted in accordance with the judgment of the council, presenting the council with a little book of the following kind:

### Copy of the Little Book of the Presbyter Lucidus Retracting His Former Errors

[Col. 0683D]

To the most blessed and most reverend Fathers in Christ, the bishops Leontius, Eufronius, Fonteius, Viventius, Mamertus, Patiens, Verianus, Auxanius, Faustus, Paulus, Megethius, Graecus, Eutropius, Leontius, Claudius, Marcellus, Crocus, Basilius, Claudius, Ursicinus, Praetextatus, Pragmatius, Theoplastus, Leontius, Viventius [Note: [Col. 0683] Leocadius, as it is read in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul* and in Hincmar, chapter 1 of book *On Predestination*.], Julianus, Amicalis, John, Opilio, and Licinius, bishops: Lucidus the presbyter.

Your correction is the salvation of the community, and your judgment is medicine. Therefore I regard it as the supreme remedy to excuse myself by accusing my former errors and to cleanse myself through a salutary confession.

Accordingly, in agreement with the recent decrees of the council that are to be proclaimed, I condemn with you the opinion that says that the labor of human obedience must not be joined to divine grace; the opinion that says that, after the fall of the first human being, the power of choice was entirely extinguished; the opinion that says that Christ the Lord and our Savior did not undergo death for the salvation of all; the opinion that says that God’s foreknowledge violently compels a human being to death, or that those who perish perish by God’s will; the opinion that says that, after receiving lawful baptism, whoever sins dies in Adam; the opinion that says that some are appointed to death and others predestined to life; the opinion that says that, from Adam to Christ, none from the nations was saved by the first grace of God—that is, by the law of nature—in expectation of Christ’s coming, and that they lost free will in their first parent; the opinion that says that the patriarchs and prophets, or any of the greatest saints, lived within paradise even before the time of redemption.

I condemn all these opinions as impious and filled with sacrilege.

I assert God’s grace in such a way that I always join human effort and striving to grace. I declare that human freedom of will was not extinguished but weakened and impaired. I affirm that the person who is saved can be endangered, and that the person who has perished could have been saved.

I also affirm that Christ God and Savior, insofar as concerns the riches of his goodness, offered the price of his death for all, and that, since he does not wish anyone to perish who is the Savior of all, especially of the faithful, he is rich toward all who call upon him.

And because conscience must be satisfied in matters of such importance, I remember having previously said that Christ had come only for those whom he foreknew would believe, following the Lord’s statements in which he says: “The Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” And this: “This is the cup of my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins.” Or the Apostle’s statement: “Just as it is appointed for human beings to die, so Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many.”

But now, by the authority of the sacred testimonies abundantly found throughout the breadth of the divine Scriptures, and by the reasoning made clear through the teaching of the elders, I willingly confess that Christ also came for those who were lost, because they perished against his will.

For it is not right to confine the immense riches of goodness and the divine benefits to those alone who appear to have been saved. If we say that Christ brought remedies only to those who have been redeemed, we shall seem to acquit the unredeemed, whom we know to be punished because they despised redemption.

I also assert that, according to the order and succession of the ages, some were saved under the law of grace, others under the law of Moses, and others under the law of nature, which God wrote in the hearts of all, in hope of Christ’s coming. Nevertheless, from the beginning of the world they were not absolved from the bond of original sin except through the intervention of the sacred blood.

I also profess that eternal fires and infernal flames were prepared for capital deeds, because divine judgment justly follows persistent human guilt; those who do not believe these things with their whole heart justly incur that judgment.

Pray for me, holy and apostolic lords and Fathers.

I, Lucidus the presbyter, have signed this letter with my own hand. I affirm what is asserted in it, and I condemn what is condemned.

From this letter of Lucidus to the Synod of Arles we have learned not only the names of the thirty bishops who took part in it, but also the principal doctrines they sanctioned against the Predestinarians.

There remains the third document we listed: the letter of Bishop Faustus to Leontius of Arles, or the preface to his books *On Grace and Free Will*. This document shows both that the council was convened against the Predestinarians and that Faustus composed his books at the command of Leontius and the council in order to arrange and explain the matters brought forward by the council.

Accordingly, Faustus prefixed to them a title that identifies the Predestinarians and their errors in these words:

> Profession of faith against those who, while saying that some are drawn to life by the will of God alone and others driven down to death, thereby affirm fate together with the pagans and deny free will together with the Manichaeans.

The beginning of the preface is therefore as follows:

### To the Most Blessed and Most Reverend Leontius, Pope: Faustus
That, out of pastoral concern, you, blessed Father Leontius, assembled a council of the chief bishops to condemn the error of predestination, you have conferred upon all the Churches of Gaul. But when you entrusted to my weak shoulders the task and care of arranging what you had most learnedly set forth in public discussion, you gave too little consideration to your holy reputation, burdening me by a judgment of charity and yourselves with the risk of your choice. These are the words with which it concludes:

“In this little work, after the subscription of the Council of Arles, the Synod of Lyons required that certain additions be made because new errors had been detected.”

From these facts it is clear that, of the three works which we said concerned the Council of Arles, Faustus’s letter to Lucidus was written while the council had already begun; Lucidus’s little book was presented while the council was still in session; and Faustus’s books, together with their preface, were composed after the council had ended.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Faustus of Riez and his books on Grace and Free Will, and on what should be thought concerning the stigma with which some customarily brand him

At this point the pursuit of truth and love of innocence admonish us to grieve over the plight of Faustus of Riez and to ask, with the reverence due to it, pardon for a holy bishop of such illustrious name. Who, indeed, would not find it difficult to bear that Faustus—who in his own age was admired and honored by everyone; whom Sidonius (*Book IX, Letter 8*) called a man of salutary and singular learning; whom Ruricius called an outstanding teacher and an excellent shepherd; whom, while he was still an abbot, Hilary of Arles honored so highly that he placed him between the bishops Theodore and Maximus; whom all his fellow bishops revered as a bishop; and whom the pontiff Hilary judged worthy to preside with him at the Roman synod—should now, because in these books he refuted the errors of the Predestinarians in accordance with the judgment of the synod, be harassed and widely denounced by many as a heretic?

This was done at the instigation—and, something they cannot conceal, under the leadership—of John Maxentius, a Scythian monk, one of those who secretly cherished the heresy of Eutyches and attacked the Council of Chalcedon, by covert devices, in opposition to Hormisdas and his legates. This is the Maxentius who, at Constantinople, more than forty years after the Council of Arles, first stirred up controversy over Faustus’s books, loudly proclaiming that they were heretical. Others, however, led by Possessor, an African bishop, maintained that they were orthodox. When Hormisdas was consulted by Possessor about these books and replied more mildly than Maxentius wished, that deranged man became so furious that he attacked Hormisdas himself and did not hesitate to call him a heretic.

Nor did the hatred of Maxentius and his associates end there. Indeed, they attempted to incite the African bishops exiled in Sardinia against Faustus and even sent these books to Sardinia so that Fulgentius might refute them. It was evidently not difficult to expect such a response from the Africans, among whom, as has been said, the Predestinarian heresy—once born there—still clung to the minds of many. Those who were free from this stain were nevertheless mostly so disposed that everything said against the Predestinarians seemed to them suspicious and offensive, as though it were directed against Augustine.

What else did those hostile to Faustus’s books press more vigorously than the charge made by the deacon Peter and the others with him in their letter: that these books had been written against the doctrine of predestination? But what has this to do with Augustine? Faustus did not deny that he had written against the doctrine of predestination; he maintained only that he had written against the kind of predestination that either asserted fate or denied free will. That both of these positions are contrary to Augustine’s mind, even the men in question did not deny; and Prosper, in his letter to Rufinus, bears witness that both are commonly imposed upon Augustine by slander.

They further say that Faustus’s speech was cunning and deceitful, agreeing with Pelagian depravity, and that Fulgentius, Avitus, and others exposed and convicted it. What more suitable or truthful answer can be given on Faustus’s behalf than that familiar saying of Faustus himself: “It is not so”?

For we cannot determine, since the works no longer exist, what deceits Fulgentius detected in Faustus’s writings or by what method he exposed in his seven books the deep cunning with which they reproach him. We know that Avitus of Vienne did not praise certain things in other books of Faustus; but whether he wrote anything against these books, as Ado seems to have thought, is uncertain.

Who does not know that, in the judgment of many, Maxentius’s objections against Faustus were deceptive and wholly insincere? Nor is there any reason why we should listen to him about Faustus rather than to Gennadius or Possessor, one of whom pronounced the work excellent and the other these books Catholic.

Even in our own age—and in the immediately preceding century—there have been and still are men of the greatest learning and most exact judgment who have adopted their position. Among them, not to mention more, are the two brightest lights of the illustrious University of Louvain, John Driedo and Ruard Tapper, both of whom call Faustus, and not without honor, a Catholic teacher of the Church.

This is not because, as I think, they failed to notice in Faustus’s books those passages in which he seems to have attributed somewhat more than was proper to our nature with respect to the beginning of faith and other matters. Rather, they understood that what he wrote at a time when it was permissible to speak in that way was not of such a character that the Catholic name ought to suffer on its account.

Otherwise, what would become of so many Fathers, both Greek and Latin, whose case is comparable? What would become of Augustine himself, who, writing about the predestination of the saints, confessed that he had once held the same view concerning the origin of faith (*Chapter 3*)? Either they must be condemned together with Faustus by the same judgment, or, if the same consideration absolves them, Faustus must likewise be absolved—or else a distinction must be shown.

Since this is so, let the theologians of our age now see where they are driving themselves when, together with Maxentius and Maxentius’s imitator Gottschalk, they do not fear to number Faustus among heretics. Out of the reverence they owe to truth and to a holy bishop, if a judgment concerning Faustus’s books is to be made, let them not wish to be wiser than the Apostolic See, or than Gelasius and Hormisdas, who were content to call them not works of the highest authority—that is, apocryphal—not heretical.

[Col. 0687A]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Second Synod of Orange, in which the Predestinarian heresy was also condemned

Among those who, following Prosper’s example, took up the cause of divine grace in Gaul after his death, the foremost was Caesarius, bishop of Arles. He was devoted not merely to the teaching of Saint Augustine but also to Augustine’s person, so much so that, out of love for Augustine, when near death he wished that his last day of life might fall next to the day that had been Augustine’s last. This wish was granted.

Applying himself, therefore, with the greatest zeal to this concern, he turned to uprooting the errors of those whom Prosper called the remnants of the Pelagians and who later received the name of Semi-Pelagians in the schools of theologians. Although they were not wholly Pelagian and were wholly opposed to the Pelagians, they nevertheless indulged free will more than was proper. To refute or instruct them, Caesarius presented for approval, and arranged to have subscribed by hand, propositions on grace and free will drawn from the preceding councils, from the responses of the Apostolic See, and from various works of Saint Augustine. He had summoned neighboring bishops and leading men on the occasion of dedicating a basilica.

This, plainly, was the later Synod of Orange, held in the year of Christ 529. Although it was convened by chance and for another purpose, the Church approved it in such a way that it possesses foremost authority among all. For although there were many who held differing opinions and opposed Caesarius’s teaching on grace, all their efforts nevertheless proved fruitless and empty, when Pope Boniface, as Cyprian relates in the *Life of Caesarius* (*Book I*), confirmed the decrees of Caesarius and of this synod.

He relates the matter as follows:

“Many rivals indeed arose who resisted his teaching concerning grace. But, O happiness worthy of imitation! A groundless suspicion arose in the regions of Gaul against the preaching of the man of God, through the whispers and malicious interpretation of certain persons. For this reason the bishops of Christ who lived beyond the Isère, gathered together in the love of charity, assembled in the city of Valence. There, too, blessed Caesarius was unable to hasten to them as he had arranged, because of his customary illness. Nevertheless he sent distinguished men from among the bishops, together with priests and deacons.

“Among them Saint Cyprian, the great and renowned bishop of Toulon, shone forth. He confirmed everything he said concerning divine matters from the sacred Scriptures and proved it from the ancient traditions of the Fathers: no one can seize anything for himself in the progress toward divine things unless he has first been called by the prevenient grace of God.

“But while they sought to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God, not remembering that the Lord had said: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John XV, 5, 16). And: ‘No one has anything unless it has been given him from above’ (John XIX, 11). And the Apostle Paul: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (I Corinthians XIII, 10). And elsewhere: ‘Every good gift is from above’ (James I, 17). And the prophet: ‘The Lord will give grace and glory’ (Psalm LXXXIII, 12). And that a human being will truly recover free will at the time when he has been redeemed by Christ’s liberation, under which release he can attain the effect of perfection.”

To their arguments the man of God gave a true and evident answer from apostolic tradition. For Boniface of blessed memory, pope of the Roman Church, having learned of the same struggle, trampled down the contention of the disputants and confirmed the advocacy of Saint Caesarius by apostolic authority. Thus, with Christ granting the increase, the bishops of the Churches gradually received what the devil had wished to bring to an end by sudden violence.

Moreover, in this very synod, which was wholly formed from Augustine’s positions, the Predestinarians were also condemned and struck with anathema. Let those who do not distinguish Augustine’s position from the Predestinarian heresy learn from this, at least, to recognize their own folly.

“These are the words of the synod, chapter 25: ‘We not only do not believe that anyone has been predestined by divine power to evil, but we also declare with complete detestation anathema against those who wish to believe that so great an evil exists.’”

“But why,” you will ask, “were the Predestinarians censured in a place so apparently unrelated, when the remnants of the Pelagians are being discussed?” I think the reason is that, just as the Predestinarians, when attacked, were accustomed to stir up hatred against their opponents by making it seem that they held Pelagian views, so the Semi-Pelagians, when pressed, in turn aroused suspicion of the Predestinarian heresy against those who were pressing them.

Therefore, in order to remove this suspicion from itself, the synod cursed that most dreadful head of their heresy. The author of the *Predestinarian* also describes it in these words:

“They say: ‘Even if the one who has been predestined to evil should wish to do good, he will not be able to attain the good.’”

Thus, among the synods that condemned the Predestinarian heresy, the Synod of Orange must rightly and without controversy be numbered as well.

## CHAPTER X. The Predestinarian error concerning free will also refuted in Italy at that time by Ennodius of Pavia

Although I did not intend to pursue the Predestinarians outside Gaul, the opportunity invites us to turn for a while to nearby Cisalpine Gaul. A few years before the Synod of Orange, Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, ceased to live. Among his other works there survives, in Book II, a letter to Constantius in which, without naming him, he refutes someone who asserted that free will had been given to human beings only for the worse.

This was the Predestinarian error which Augustine, at the very origin of the heresy, had censured in the monks of Hadrumetum, as has been said, in his book *On Rebuke and Grace*, teaching that we possess free will for doing both good and evil. Since Ennodius likewise proves and confirms this point fully and at length in the letter I have mentioned, I thought the whole passage ought to be inserted here.

“Therefore,” he says, “as you testify in writing, a man has been found who, taking this opportunity, would sift the servants of Christ in the way Christ himself promised they would be made, asserting that, concerning freedom of the will, permission to choose had been given only in one direction, the worse one.

“O schismatic proposition, bearing blasphemies written upon its forehead, according to the Apocalypse (Revelation XIII, 1)! What kind of freedom is this, if he can explain it, when it is granted only to will what brings punishment? Or why should he call it choice when he asserts that only one direction has been granted?

“If this were supported by truth, there would be no place for divine judgments. For what good would our God rightly seek from us, when he had removed from the will our desire for him? But, according to the Apostle: ‘Is God unjust? By no means’ (Romans III, 5).

“Among human beings, anyone who demands from subjects what he has not granted them the power to do is at odds with a concern for justice. Consider with what conscience this may be thought of God. Where is that saying of the Apostle, crying out and bearing witness to the freedom of the will: ‘To will is present with me, but to accomplish it I do not find’ (Romans VII, 18)? What else does this mean than: ‘I know how to choose the right path; but unless heavenly grace helps the one who enters it, I shall grow weary’?

“No one doubts, no one condemns, that when the author of grace grants assistance, the path of righteousness itself is opened by divine power. For grace is the leader and forerunner of good things when we are invited to rest by manifold exhortation, when it is said to us: ‘Come, children, listen to me’ (Psalm XXXIII, 12); ‘Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you’ (Matthew XXIV, 34); ‘Where I am, there also will my servant be’ (John XII, 26).

“But unless, in response to such admonitions, our will—which is free—and our labor offer obedience, we descend to danger and Gehenna, not by any command but willingly. Thus either devotion produces reward or contempt produces punishment.

“Otherwise there will be no just retribution: either punishment will be imposed upon those who sin by necessity, or a good reward will be offered for a work to which people are dragged unwillingly.

“Therefore we owe it to grace that, by hidden paths, the taste of life is poured into us unless we resist. Yet it belongs to our choice that we follow the benefits once they have been shown to us.

“The way of crimes is not read as our mistress but as our servant, since it is said of sins: ‘Their desire shall be under you’ (Genesis IV, 7).

“What does the prophet’s entire utterance, adorned as though with garlands, mean: ‘Do not emulate those who do evil’ (Psalm XXXVI, 15); ‘Do not put your trust in princes’ (Psalm CVIII, 2); ‘Do not become like a horse and a mule’ (Psalm XXXI, 9)? And the Apostle: ‘Do not become slaves of human beings’ (I Corinthians VII, 23).

“What does ‘Do not’ so often signify in the heavenly admonition, if it was not permitted to will otherwise?

“Moreover, although spoken in the person of Christ, the testimony of that same prophet supports our freedom of will: ‘To do your will, my God, I have willed it’ (Psalm XXXIX, 9). And elsewhere: ‘I will sacrifice to you voluntarily’ (Psalm LIII, 8). And: ‘I will repay my vows to the Lord’ (Psalm CXV, 5). And again: ‘Vow and repay’ (Psalm LXXV, 52).

“As for that example of the blessed Apostle by which he believes himself fortified, it helps us too, if he notices what follows. When the enemy of boasting had said, ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (I Corinthians XV, 10), the wise architect immediately added, lest, by fleeing glory in that way, he should depart too far from the truth: ‘I labored more abundantly than all of them, and the grace of God in me was not empty’ (ibid.). This is as though he had said: ‘Christ found in me something that he might worthily or abundantly reward.’

“For divine grace is not poor, but is thought to be weakened by a certain leanness or thinness of our merits. It is then not judged to flow through its own channels when the stream of our dryness receives nothing from its courses.

“O that the narrowness of a letter permitted the secrets of the sacred books to be disclosed! But I fear that the person who, with God inspiring him, will be unable to find any slander against our faith may complain about the length of the page.

“What does he receive with what state of mind: ‘Behold, water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish’ (Ecclesiasticus XV, 17)? What of the other passages which you yourself, its copious advocate, have repeated? I believe that, as they say, he passed them by with his ear closed like an asp.

“I see how far the poisons of the Libyan pestilence extend. The sandy serpent does not have only those harmful things which it reveals; what it confesses must be brought to the estimation of its hidden crimes.

“For he wishes to reach the point of saying that no one perishes through his own fault or negligence if a human being is deprived of the power granted over both good and evil. He boasts that only those could have been saved, without any labor and without friendship with the commandments, whom heavenly favor alone rescued as they wandered away from merit. Therefore, in referring this to himself, he understands that those whom grace did not wish to save have perished.”

## CHAPTER XI. The Predestinarian heresy renewed in Gaul by Gottschalk and again crushed by Rabanus and Hincmar in two synods

For more than three hundred years the Predestinarian heresy had been silent in Gaul when, in the age of Charles the Bald, it was revived by the priest Gottschalk. He was a monk of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons. After leaving the monastery and crossing into Italy, he scattered the seeds of perverse doctrine in the territory of Verona. He was refuted by two letters from Rabanus, recently published: one to Notingus, bishop of Verona, and the other to Eberard, count of that region. In the latter we read, among other things, the following concerning Gottschalk:

“It is reported,” he says, “that a certain minor scholar named Gottschalk is staying among you. He teaches that God’s predestination so constrains every human being that even if someone wishes to be saved and strives for this with right faith and good works, so as to come by God’s grace to eternal life, he labors in vain and fruitlessly if he has not been predestined to life.

“It is as though God, who is the author of our salvation and not of our destruction, compelled people to perish by his predestination. And already this sect has driven many into despair of themselves, so that they say: ‘Why must I labor for my salvation and eternal life? If I do good and have not been predestined to life, it benefits me nothing; but if I do evil, it harms me nothing, because God’s predestination causes me to attain eternal life.’”

From Italy he proceeded to Germany and presented Rabanus with a little book containing his error. Rabanus and the bishops of Germany condemned him and sent him back to the metropolitan see of Reims, at the Council of Mainz in the year 848. The following is a copy of the synodal letter containing the sentence of condemnation:

“To our most reverend brother and fellow priest, Hincmar, archbishop, Rabanus, servant of Christ and of his servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

“Let it be known to your affection that a certain wandering monk named Gottschalk, who claims that he was ordained a priest in your parish, has come to us at Mainz from Italy, introducing new superstitions and a harmful doctrine concerning the predestination of God and leading peoples into error. He says that God’s predestination exists in evil just as it exists in good, and that there are certain people in the world who, because of God’s predestination—which compels them to go to death—cannot correct themselves from error and sin. It is as though God had made them incorrigible from the beginning and destined to go to destruction liable to punishment.

“Having heard this opinion from him recently at the synod held at Mainz and finding him incorrigible, with the consent and command of our most pious king Louis, we have decreed that he, condemned together with his pernicious doctrine, be sent to you. You are to retain him in your parish, from which he first departed disorderly, and not permit him any longer to teach error or lead the people astray.

“For, as I have heard, he already has many deceived and less devoted to their salvation, who say: ‘What will it profit me to labor in the service of God? If I am predestined to death, I shall never escape it; but if I do evil and am predestined to life, I shall go without any doubt to eternal rest.’

“We have therefore written these few things to you, making known what sort of doctrine we found in him. You will also be able to hear more fully from his own mouth what he thinks and to decide justly what ought to be done. May almighty God graciously preserve your holiness in good health and praying for us forever.”

After this, another synod was held against Gottschalk at the palace of Quierzy. There he was heard again and again condemned by the bishops, and a sentence of the following kind was issued against him:

“Ecclesiastical sentence issued with ecclesiastical severity against the most obstinate Gottschalk, because of his incorrigible obstinacy, at the synod held at Quierzy by twelve bishops.

“Brother Gottschalk, know that the holy office of the priestly mystery, which you irregularly usurped and which, in all your morals, evil deeds, and perverse doctrines, you have not feared until now to abuse, has, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit—whose gift of grace the priestly office is—and through the power of the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, been taken away from you, if in any manner you received it, and that you are entirely forbidden to exercise it any further.

“Furthermore, because, contrary to the purpose and name of a monk, you have contemptuously disturbed ecclesiastical and civil affairs and presumed upon ecclesiastical rights, we decree by episcopal authority that you be chastised with the harshest blows and confined in a prison according to the ecclesiastical rules. And so that you may not presume thereafter to usurp the office of teaching, we impose perpetual silence upon your mouth by the power of the eternal Word.”

[Col. 0691A]

At the same synod, or certainly at the same place, four chapters were also established in opposition to the same number of chapters which Gottschalk had composed to establish his heresy.

The silence imposed upon him by the synod agrees with what Rabanus privately advised concerning Gottschalk when he wrote to Hincmar:

“But I, insofar as I dare, advise you to prohibit these controversies from being carried on among the Christian people and not to permit Gottschalk himself, the author of this error, to harm many any further either by writing or by speaking.

“For I am astonished at your prudence: you permitted this harmful man—that is, Gottschalk, who has been found blameworthy in everything, who observed neither the vow of a monk nor the life of a sacred order, and who did not properly fulfill the office of preaching—to write anything. In this office he could do more harm than by speaking aloud.

“Thus, in many places, as I have heard, he has intoxicated not a few with the cup of his poison and turned them toward the madness of error.”

## CHAPTER XII. The Church of Lyons and the Synod of Valence did not support the Predestinarian errors in the case of Gottschalk

Some are troubled when they see that the Church of Lyons took up Gottschalk’s cause and that two synods, which had condemned him at Mainz and Quierzy, were opposed by two others—the Synod of Valence and the Synod of Langres—which appear to favor him. They would indeed have good reason to be troubled if this favor extended to protecting Predestinarianism and defending the heresy. But the matter is otherwise.

However much they may perhaps differ in other respects, they agree in this: both are enemies of the Predestinarians. Although the Synod of Valence opposed four chapters to Hincmar’s four chapters, with which he had demolished Gottschalk’s four chapters; although these very chapters of the Synod of Valence were later confirmed at the Synod of Langres and presented and reread at Toul, near Savonnières; and although, when they reached Hincmar, they were carefully refuted by him and the positions of his own which they attacked were firmly reestablished, the people of Lyons nevertheless never concealed, amid such a varied and uncertain controversy, that they could neither approve nor accept the errors of the ancient Predestinarians which Hincmar censured in Gottschalk.

There were chiefly two errors: one concerned predestination itself, the other the freedom of the will. Gottschalk taught that the reprobate had been predestined by God to destruction; Hincmar maintained that this was falsely said. Explaining why he held this view in chapter 15 of his work *On Predestination*, he said:

“The ancient Predestinarians confess the predestination of the reprobate to destruction, whom, just as they say they were predestined by God to destruction, they also say were predestined to sin. The modern Predestinarians alter this position in appearance, but they retain its odor and flavor. For they say: ‘God predestined the reprobate to destruction, not to sin,’ although destruction can be reached only through sin.”

For this reason he did not approve of calling them predestined to destruction: once this was admitted, he judged that it necessarily followed that they were also believed to have been predestined to sin, which had been the error of the ancient Predestinarians.

The authors of the Synod of Valence, although they did not shrink from saying with Gottschalk that the ungodly are predestined to death, since they did not think that this conclusion followed, nevertheless so abhorred the predestination to sin which the Predestinarians introduced that, following the Synod of Orange (Canon 3 of the Third Synod of Valence), they pronounced anathema against those who believe that anyone is predestined by God to evil.

[Col. 0692A]

Moreover, the same Church of Lyons and its bishop Remigius, in the book *On Three Letters*, responding to Hincmar’s letter against Gottschalk, although it endeavors to interpret more leniently what Hincmar had said about those predestined to destruction, nevertheless equally and utterly rejects the necessity of doing evil and predestination to sin which the Predestinarians taught and which Hincmar not without reason attributed to Gottschalk.

“If there are any,” he says (*Chapter 8*), “who appear to be scandalized by this, as though the words of predestination signified that the necessity of doing evil had been imposed upon someone, they ought rather to have been instructed that God predestines no one to sin, but to endure punishment for sin, and that by this predestination he does not compel anyone to do evil.”

From this it is clear that the people of Lyons, as far as this point is concerned, by no means support the errors of the Predestinarians.

But what of the other error, which undermines free will? Shall we admit that they supported it? On the contrary, they do not favor this error either to such an extent that they detest it and do not believe that it could have fallen upon Gottschalk.

For they reason as follows:

“It is added,” they say (*Chapter 21*), “that in that letter the wretched monk said that, after the first human being fell through free will, none of us can use free will for doing good, but only for doing evil. This is not only astonishing and unheard of; as far as we can judge, it is also incredible that a man raised and instructed among the faithful and by the faithful, and considerably exercised in the writings of the ecclesiastical Fathers, could say or think that after the fall of the first human being no believer can use free will for doing good, but only for doing evil.

“It is as though free will existed in us only for evil, while for good the grace of God alone worked in us without free will. If he had said generally, ‘No human being,’ and had added, ‘without the grace of God,’ and then had asserted that a person can use free will well, the sense would have been Catholic and the assertion altogether Catholic.

“But when he is accused of having said that none of us—that is, none of the faithful—can use free will except for doing evil, what else is asserted by such a statement and such presumptuous novelty than that the freedom of the human mind—which before sin was free to love, desire, and enjoy the true good—was so corrupted and destroyed when the first human being sinned that thereafter free will remained in human beings only for evil? For doing or possessing good, there would be no free will of the human being, but only a gift of divine grace.

“We do not remember having known or heard this kind of error either among heretics or among any Catholic. Thus, as we have already said, this too appears incredible to us.

“Should anyone believe that those who exaggerate this error with such a wealth of words, through so many circumlocutions and roundabout paths, and refute it so zealously, wished to appear its patrons or defenders? Since, in explaining Catholic teaching concerning free will, they transmit precisely what Hincmar transmits, who does not understand that in this controversy they were seeking and pursuing opportunities to rebuke Hincmar and defend Gottschalk—whether provoked by the private hatred of Ebo of Grenoble against Hincmar or moved by some other matter—rather than having actually found grounds for doing so?

“Therefore those who now labor, by comparing and setting against each other the assertions of the people of Lyons and those of Rabanus or Hincmar, to persuade us that the Predestinarian errors which Hincmar notes in Gottschalk were wrongly censured by him and were held and defended by the people of Lyons as Catholic doctrines, are laboring in vain.”

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 470. MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, PRIEST OF VIENNE.

[Col. 0693]

# GALLAND’S PROLEGOMENON ON MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS

*(Galland, Old Library of the Fathers, vol. X.)*

[Col. 0693A]

### I.

That Mamertus Claudianus—or, as others prefer, Claudianus Ecdicius Mamertus—was from Vienne, Baluzius infers from Claudianus’s own letter to Sapaudus, where the following is read:

[Note: Baluzius, preface to vol. VI of the *Miscellanea*, final page.]

“You should also be reminded of the ancient nobility of the city of Vienne, whose citizen and teacher you are. You will not discharge your double obligation through idleness, since from you a response is sought in two directions, either to your ancestors or to your native land.”

[Note: Ibid., p. 537.]

After first professing the monastic discipline in the vigor of his youth, as Sidonius writes in his epitaph, he later became a priest of Vienne under Saint Mamertus, his elder brother in age and bishop of the city. He was that bishop’s energetic assistant, as the same Sidonius testifies.

[Note: Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 11.]

“Bishop Mamertus,” he says, “held Claudianus in very high esteem, having in him an adviser in judgments, a deputy in the churches … a companion in readings, an interpreter in expositions, and so forth.”

[Col. 0693B]

Hence, in Claudianus’s epitaph, which follows the Sidonian letter just cited, he is called “the bishop in the second rank.” That is, according to Sirmond’s interpretation, he assisted his brother, the bishop Mamertus, in very many matters, so that although he was only a priest, he himself seemed in a certain way to be a bishop.

These final words of Sidonius, however, perhaps insufficiently noticed, may have been the reason why Gennadius called our Claudianus a bishop.

[Note: Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 67.]

Unless, as others prefer, that passage of Gennadius is corrupt, since afterward he calls Claudianus a priest.

[Note: Id., ibid., chapter 73.]

Trithemius later repeated this error.

[Note: Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, no. 178.]

And, what may surprise you, so did Canisius.

[Note: Canisius, *Thesaurus*, vol. I, p. 361, note.]

Although he had been instructed by Baronius, whom he cites, he could have guarded himself against the error.

[Note: Baronius, under the year 490, § 39.]

For the rest, Claudianus flourished toward the close of the fifth century. It is established that around the year 470 he dedicated his three books *On the State of the Soul*, about which we shall soon speak, to Sidonius the patrician, who had not yet been elevated to the bishopric of Clermont.

[Col. 0693C]

He seems to have died in the year 473 or 474. When Sidonius went to Vienne and learned that Claudianus had died, he composed, as he himself testifies, a mournful poem over the bones of his brother in soul.

[Note: Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 11.]

For both dates, however, the most learned authorities should be consulted.

[Note: Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, pp. 213, 245; *Literary History of France*, vol. II, pp. 448, 445.]

[Col. 0694A]

### II.

What kind of man Claudianus was, and how great he was, whether one considers his character or his intellect, Sidonius, whom we have cited, teaches us clearly. First, he says:

[Note: Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 11.]

“Who,” he says, “could raise him up with praise proportionate to his merits? Since he remembered the human condition in everything, he consoled the clergy through his works, the people through his speech, the sorrowful through exhortation, the destitute through consolation, captives through payment, the hungry through food, and the naked through clothing.

“Likewise, I judge it superfluous to repeat more concerning these matters. For he took greater care to conceal his merits, by which he enriched a wealthy conscience with the resources of poverty, in the hope of future recompense.”

These are the few things he says about Claudianus’s piety.

Admiring his intellect as well, Sidonius wonders whether anyone comparable to him will arise.

[Note: Id., ibid.]

“For he was,” he says, “a prudent, wise, learned, eloquent, vigorous man, and the most ingenious of the men of his age, place, and people; a man who philosophized unceasingly while preserving religion.”

And shortly afterward:

[Col. 0694B]

“Good God,” he says, “what was it like whenever we met simply for the sake of consultation? How readily and without disdain did he immediately open everything to everyone, considering it the greatest pleasure if, perhaps, through the labyrinthine insolubility of some questions that had arisen, the treasures of his knowledge might be brought to light!

“For who would unwillingly consult such a man about hidden matters, from whose fellowship in discussion not even the questioning of ordinary and ignorant people was rejected?”

These observations about Claudianus’s learning we have summarized from Sidonius, who elsewhere as well as here expands at greater length upon his praises.

### III.

Among the surviving literary monuments of this most flourishing intellect—some others, indeed, mentioned by the ancients, having perished, not without loss to ecclesiastical antiquity—the three books *On the State of the Soul*, written against Faustus of Riez, stand out. For this bishop published a two-part letter, from which Gennadius makes two separate books [Note: [Col. 0694] Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 85]. In the first part, to be sure, he refutes the Arians and Macedonians; in the second, he contends against those who say that something incorporeal exists among created things. The latter part of Faustus’s letter appears in the libraries of the Fathers, prefixed to Claudian’s books under the title indicating that our Viennese presbyter undertook to refute it. Canisius was the first to publish that same letter in full [Note: [Col. 0695] Canisius, *Thesaurus*, vol. I, pp. 361–365]; thereafter it passed into the Paris [Note: [Col. 0695] *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1644, vol. III, pp. 359 ff.] and Lyon [Note: [Col. 0695] *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, vol. VIII, pp. 548 ff.] libraries of the Fathers.

But to return to Mamertus: the bishop of Clermont repeatedly praises his three books against Faustus with the highest commendations. From these we select only the following [Note: [Col. 0695] Sidonius, book V, letter 2]:

> “Mamertus Claudianus,” he says, “that most skilled Christian philosopher and foremost of every kind of learned man, took care to adorn and cultivate the book *On the State of the Soul*, distinguished in three volumes, with all the limbs, arts, and departments of the philosophy it pursued, showing that the nine whom they call Muses are disciplines, not women. For in his pages the watchful reader will find the truer names of the Camenae, which themselves generate their own designation. There grammar divides, oratory declaims, arithmetic counts, geometry measures, music weighs, dialectic disputes, astrology foreknows, architecture constructs, and metrics modulates.”

So far he. But the bishop of Clermont himself augments these same books with still more abundant praise in a letter addressed to the author, Claudianus, which you will find below interwoven with two other letters of our Viennese presbyter. And Claudianus is rightly exalted by such praises; for, as the great Baronius says [Note: [Col. 0695] Baronius, under the year 490, § 38], he excelled not only in theological disciplines but also in the other sciences, so that you may clearly recognize that Sidonius was an assertor of truth, not a flatterer.

[Col. 0695C]

### IV.

One point, however, may perhaps usefully be noted here: namely, that Claudianus held the opinion [Note: [Col. 0695] Claudianus, *On the State of the Soul*, book I, chap. 14] that an angel consists both of body and spirit, formed with the highest dignity among created things. Concerning this passage Huetius remarks [Note: [Col. 0695] Huetius, *Origeniana*, book II, chap. 2, question, § 8, p. 71]:

> “Mamertus seems to have been deceived by his own reasoning. For he will either say that the vital spirit itself is incorporeal or corporeal. If he wishes it to be incorporeal, there is no reason why he should not likewise admit the whole nature of the angel as incorporeal. If corporeal, since according to his opinion no body can live by itself, it must necessarily be brought to life by another spirit. The same question will then recur concerning that third spirit, and likewise concerning a fourth, and so on to infinity.”

Thus far the distinguished man. The opinions of that same Mamertus concerning the bodies of angels are also criticized in the Brasichellan *Index of Expurgated Books* [Note: [Col. 0695] Brasichellus, *Index*, vol. I, pp. 141 ff., Roman edition, 1608]. Moreover, we know that quite a few of the ancient Fathers inclined toward the same opinion. On this matter, besides the Huetius already mentioned, one may also consult Muratorius [Col. 0696A], where he inquires what should be believed concerning the question whether angels are corporeal or incorporeal [Note: [Col. 0696] Muratorius, *On Moderating Genius*, book I, chap. 13, pp. 106 ff., Paris edition].

### V.

We have committed to the press an edition of these three books of Claudianus, which Andreas Schottus revised after John Wowerius had collated them with the Plantinian manuscripts. He compared them both with the copy published at Basel in 1520 through the efforts of Petrus Mosellanus from the German library at Celle, and especially with an older manuscript from Tournai belonging to the Benedictine library at Saint Martin. Having carried out this task, he declares that almost innumerable passages were restored for him:

> “For at Paris,” he says, “the typographical work twice or three times disfigured this author in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, so that nothing sound or whole could be read or understood in that appalling mode of expression, much less could it invite anyone to grasp those subtleties.”

Schottus’s edition of this kind first appeared in 1618 in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, and was subsequently reprinted in the Lyon edition of 1677. Since the Cologne edition was not available to us, we used the Lyon edition [Note: [Col. 0696] *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, vol. VI, pp. 1045–1074]. Nevertheless, finding it ill-treated in many places, we compared it with the edition found either in the Paris *Library of the Fathers* [Note: [Col. 0696] *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, vol. IV, part I, pp. 599–658] or in the *Orthodoxographs* [Note: [Col. 0696] *Orthodoxographs*, pp. 1250–1305]. As a result, not only were many typographical errors removed, but many passages were also restored to their integrity, as will become clear from the comparison and from the notes appended below.

Moreover, for easier reading, we divided the longer chapters into sections. An additional and especially useful feature was that from the same Paris library [Note: [Col. 0696] *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, cited work, pp. 654–658] [Col. 0696C] we took a short commentary addressed by the same Claudianus to Sidonius and relating to the same subject, *On the State of the Soul*. It is surprising that such a commentary was omitted from the Lyon edition—and perhaps also by Schottus from the Cologne edition—although both the *Orthodoxographs* of Heroldus and of Grynaeus, published at Basel in 1555 and 1569, present it. We have therefore carefully revised our text against those copies.

### VI.

The three books *On the State of the Soul* are followed by two letters of Mamertus Claudianus. One is addressed to Sidonius, and is followed in turn by the letter in which Sidonius replies to Claudianus; the other is addressed to Sapaudus, a Viennese rhetorician. Writing to him, Sidonius himself [Note: [Col. 0696] Sidonius, book V, letter 10] praises him so highly that he does not hesitate to compare him with the great rhetoricians Quintilian and Palladius.

Baluzius was the first to bring this most elegant letter of Claudianus out of darkness from the royal archive at Paris [Note: [Col. 0696] Baluzius, *Miscellanea*, vol. VI, p. 535], although he left it less corrected in certain places, as we indicated in the margins of the pages [Col. 0697A]. For further learned observations concerning Sapaudus, see the authors of the *Literary History of France* [Note: [Col. 0697] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 498].

To these two letters we have added the hymn *Pange lingua gloriosi praelium certaminis* (“Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious struggle”), which the same Sidonius seems to mention in a letter to Claudianus himself in these words [Note: [Col. 0697] Sidonius, book IV, letter 3]:

> “Now, if you ask what I think of your hymn, it is rich in clauses, copious, sweet, elevated, and surpasses every lyric dithyramb in poetic charm and historical truth ... The breadth of its introduction exceeds the regular limits, and, like a great gem scarcely contained by a small setting of gold, etc.”

Concerning this passage Sirmondus says:

> “A certain scholiast had noted that the hymn meant was the one beginning *Pange lingua gloriosi praelium certaminis*. Indeed, it bears a more polished style than Fortunatus usually has, yet the ancient writers and manuscripts attribute it to him. Moreover, everything praised by Sidonius fits it remarkably well. It is written in trochaic verses, into which pyrrhic rhythms are sometimes inserted. It is rich in clauses, divided by frequent and suitable cola, with thoughts that are not abruptly interrupted but fall smoothly together with the verse. Finally, not only does the ancient scholiast whom I mentioned claim this poem for Claudianus, but so does Gennadius—not in the form in which he has been published, but as he appears in a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael of the Tomb, where the passage concerning Claudianus is fuller and reads as follows: ‘He also wrote several other things, among them a hymn on the Passion of the Lord, whose beginning is *Pange lingua gloriosi*. He was the brother of Mamertus, bishop of Vienne.’”

So far Sirmondus. Most recent writers attribute other poems to Claudianus as well; yet these acknowledge either Pope Damasus or Paulinus of Nola as their author. The learned writers of the *Literary History of France* clearly establish this, following Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0698] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, p. 126] [Note: [Col. 0698] *Literary History of France*, vol. II, p. 453].

[Col. 0697]

# THE THREE BOOKS OF MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, PRESBYTER OF VIENNE, ON THE STATE OF THE SOUL (C)

## Preface

### CLAUDIANUS SENDS GREETINGS TO THE PREFECTORIAN PATRICIAN, THE MOST LEARNED AND EXCELLENT MAN, GAIUS SOLLIUS SIDONIUS

[Note: [Col. 0697] Some have thought that *Praefecto praetorio* (“to the prefect of the praetorium”) should be read. But nothing should be changed. Sidonius, book I, letter 7, p. 858: “Away with you, degenerate men, unworthy of prefectorian fathers.” Sirmondus likewise reads the same heading at the beginning of Sidonius’s works and elsewhere.]

You commanded me to publish the little books that I composed *On the State of the Soul*, though I am a cautious judge in withholding speech and a measured arbiter in speaking. It was right for me to yield either to the expertise of the most learned and most loving man, or to trust his friendship. But, as you yourself know exceedingly well, many others, and with them men of the highest distinction, have imposed this same task upon me—one which I would not rashly have undertaken unless I had judged that rejecting it would be more dangerous than carrying it out would be laborious.

Although it was also my duty, according to my ability, to assert the truth even without being prompted, insofar as my powers allowed. I have therefore written these few things, as it were certain seeds of arguments. If any earnest student takes them up without idleness, he will, as I think, be able to draw much from them; and although they flow through narrow channels, they will nevertheless swell into great rivers through a longer course.

For my part, deprived of time [Note: [Col. 0698] Alternatively: “deprived of time ... and of spirit”], and occupied in mind, I was content, insofar as the importance of the matter required, to indicate briefly and, as it were, with a finger either what should be avoided or what should be followed. Certainly, that little work published without an author, thoroughly searched out in every direction, brought out in its full array and led into battle against us in close combat—whether it has conquered or yielded, you, above all eloquent men, must pronounce judgment.

But so that every reader may perceive from the preface the sequence of our style:

The first book, at its beginning, briefly establishes that the impassible Divinity is subject to no affection whatsoever. It then alternates a varied struggle with the opponent concerning the state of the soul. From that point onward, in order to instruct the reader in matters that are more obscure, it modestly and moderately, and as sparingly as possible, offers a preliminary treatment of certain philosophical principles drawn from geometry, arithmetic, and dialectic, together with some others insofar as they were useful. It repeatedly engages the opposing side, and thus, with several additions of our own and without interpolating foreign material, the book reaches its conclusion.

The second book, after its opening, discusses measure, number, and weight—not idly and, as I suppose, not without profit. If an attentive student is present, he will, with piety as his aid, advance through the degrees of different creatures toward a certain firmness concerning the Trinity that created all things—if not yet the blessedness of contemplating it, at least a stronger faith in it. From that point onward, until its conclusion, the entire book uses witnesses.

The third book argues somewhat at its beginning. Afterwards it pursues the wounded men wandering from the opposing line. Finally, it neither rejects peace nor fears the conflict of an unknown adversary.

Behold, most learned man, you have read what you are about to read. Only see to it that you remember that what you command to be published ought not to emerge without concern for you. I would have no doubt about the weight of the matter, but about the lightness of the undertaking. Therefore uphold and defend your counsel, since if I am endangered in these matters by the writing [Note: [Col. 0700] Alternatively: “in the composition ... in the publication”], you are endangered by the publication. Farewell, and flourish in good strength, restorer of ancient eloquence.

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER I. On the ignorance of the unlearned and their obstinacy in defending their opinions

A great vice among the human race, dear brother Sollius Sidonius, is arrogant ignorance and obstinate persistence in wrongly defending opinions rashly adopted. For most mortals either deceive the vision of the mind with images drawn through the bodily senses from corporeal things, as though with certain shadows of reality, or, through the convictions once formed in the tender years of their infancy, become childish again in old age.

If they possess any facility in speaking, they neglect the causes of things, reject the soul of reason, and cherish the bodies of words. Since there are two ways of arriving at the truth—either to submit our credulity to an authority already prejudged, or to strive toward knowledge through reasoning—they hold nothing in highest regard, whether authority commands it or reason advises it. Scorning the few learned, they deride the unlearned, who form the great majority.

Yet they themselves are deceived by a reciprocal deception on the part of those whom they deceive. For they are praised, and they believe those who falsely praise them; by this the soundness of the mind is placed in the greatest danger. Added to this is the ever-active purpose of assailing envy, both the guilt and the punishment of an envious mind.

For if something true is brought forward for the public benefit by those whom they attack with unjust hatred, they immediately assert the contrary, even if they hold the same opinion. Thus, with their hatred strengthened and inexhaustible, they do not fear having sacrificed the truth together with those whom they have made it their practice to hate. They hate their neighbor, and they hate God as well.

Since in these two matters they have rejected the fullness of all the commandments and of the whole law, it is not surprising if they have no sound thoughts either about God or about man, since by means of hatred they distance both from themselves. Yet although I am moved by this punishable vice of theirs, I am moved less strongly, because although they prepare weapons of ill will against others, they themselves are more grievously pierced by their own blows and suffer the wounds they try to inflict. For they are punished first by the goads of the hatreds whose authors they are.

The far greater and much more dangerous crime is that they foolishly conceive opinions hostile to Catholic soundness, foolishly bring them forth, proudly assert them, write them with rashness, and defend them with a perverse intention. And because they have fallen through human imprudence, they choose to defend the guilt of their boldness by obstinate persistence, lest they appear to have been capable of sinning.

Thus they openly assert their opinions while secretly muttering, and with seductive flatteries diligently entreat the ignorant to assent above all to their own opinion and to agree with themselves. They confirm, even while raving, that whatever they teach is full of truth and conducive to salvation.

If you seek authority, they reply that the secrets of such matters cannot be approached except by the most subtle investigation of reality through reason. If you demand that same reason at the decisive point, they add that authority ought rather to be obeyed, and that one should not enter the sea of disputation, which is threatened with shipwreck because of certain hidden reefs in the arguments.

Thus they elude reason by means of authority, and authority by raising the objection of reason; they use both of these for the purpose of using neither. But if the confinement of a more rigorous disputation encloses them somewhat more tightly, they say that there are certain saints for whom it is very easy to resolve questions of this kind; that they themselves depend more upon the authority of others; and that they will chiefly follow whatever another has established.

Who could endure this, or judge that it could be endured in any way—that someone should both deny knowledge and claim learning? When no examiner is present, they assert their thoughts; when one is present, they conceal them. But, you ask, where is this speech going?

I have prefaced my subject at rather greater length than I intended, because I am weary and disgusted with those who make rash assumptions. Recently I encountered certain men who were reading a little pamphlet with considerable zeal. Since it is the habit of the human race to be enticed by the discovery of a new work, they had applied their minds diligently to grasping it. They freely pressed the same task upon me as though it were necessary to know it, and I did not at all refuse to examine it.

## CHAPTER II. On his having encountered a book without an author

The first appearance of the little work, scarcely hovering at the threshold of a most exalted question concerning the unbegotten and begotten God, displayed no small degree of Catholic character, though its opinion was argued with very unequal force. Thus the gravity of the subject outweighed, in my judgment, the weakness of the reasoning.

When, as my reading progressed, I came to the remainder of the work, I noticed that through certain circumlocutions it was striving with great effort to assert that its own author should be believed to hold the Divinity passible. I asked for the name, but it was disclosed neither in answer nor in writing.

I confess that I began to regard the style of such a page with considerable suspicion. As we are accustomed to do in places made treacherous either by the continual washing-away of moisture, or slippery through a slight downward slope, or hanging over a hollow, or rough with stakes, I preferred to test the unknown path with a cautious step rather than run along it—until I entered the third part of the question, as it is arranged there.

Here the opinion appeared not merely to require investigation but outright rejection, and it was expressed with no measured speech. It was earnestly striving, if it could somehow do so, to make the soul appear to be a body. Thus, without any force of argument, without any law requiring it, without any reason persuading it, the worn-out discourse comes to an end in this futile undertaking.

My first concern is to ask what reason there could have been for someone about to undertake such important arguments and speak about such lofty matters to avoid being known. If you argue with a good conscience, why conceal your name? If you fear recognition, why publish the work? Not to mention: why write these things?

Are you perhaps following examples of evil in this matter? But I see that prophets, evangelists, apostles, and afterwards the interpreters of many authoritative writings have prefixed their names to their own volumes [Note: [Col. 0701] Alternatively: “of very many”]. Others have even begun the opening sections of their works with their own names, as in: “Peter, an apostle of Christ,” and “Paul,” as well as various other founders and teachers of the Church. Clearly they knew that the empty or harmful fabrications of apocryphal writers had to be guarded against.

Yet even in this way the fabrications of rash deceivers could not be avoided. Hence the Catholic soundness of our Church does not accept many works prefixed with the names of Paul and many saints [Note: [Col. 0701] Alternatively: “The soundness of our Catholic faith does not accept them”], because it does not evaluate the merit of a work by the enticement of a name but is won over to its author by the truth of his style.

Indeed, the fact that this page is being made public while its author is concealed gives clear indication that the same man who composed it has been condemned. For no one seeks concealment except one who fears recognition. Yet I cannot sufficiently wonder why, in the same matter, there was no concern to avoid the offense even though there could have been a decision to suppress the name.

## CHAPTER III. That the impassible Divinity is subject to no affection whatsoever

### I.

But let us return to our subject and set down the very words of the work prefaced above—addressed, that is, to the person for whom such things are intended, whom he was as eager to keep concealed as himself. He says:

> “You ask me how it can have been said, in accordance with the substance of God, in a certain letter.”

Here he did not wish to indicate whose letter it was, to whom it was addressed, or what it concerned. He continues concerning God:

> “He perceived nothing with the sensation of one suffering, but with the affection of one suffering together.”

He adds:

> “The philosophers were not ignorant of this either, because,” he says, “in man different activities—that is, justice, mercy, holiness—are accidental realities, and therefore they are called affections. God, however, is not affected by these passibly.”

O “not passibly”! O “is affected”! By what is he affected, if he does not suffer? Why is your memory so quick to forget even what you yourself have said?

You said that justice and mercy are affections in man because they are accidental. Therefore, if they are affections in man because they are accidental, they are not affections in God because they are not accidental. He therefore did not perceive with the affection of one suffering together, since in him, because there was no accident, there could be no affection.

But you add:

> “Therefore what is affection and grace in man is virtue and nature in God.”

And when the virtue that is in God has been given to man, is it not virtue? God is undoubtedly virtue. If he is immutable, then even when he has given himself to man, virtue is in man. Therefore what is virtue in God is also virtue in man. The only difference is that there it exists substantially, here by accession.

Hence the Lord says to the apostles:

> “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:43).

And the prophet:

> “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:1).

Yet you say that God is virtue in himself, but is not virtue in man. The reason for such an opinion, however, is clearer than daylight. It follows, of course, that if you say he is affected, you must assert that he is changed.

### II.

For me, the proper meaning of this word must first of all be examined most carefully. *Affectus*—“affection”—is so called because it affects something. Whatever is affected, however, suffers. But to suffer belongs only to a passible and created substance.

Since the human soul was called out of nothing by the highest essence, which is God, in order to exist, it stands midway between that out of which it was made and him by whom it was made. It can therefore be affected by higher things so that it may advance, and by lower things so that it may decline. I am speaking, of course, about the human soul.

Thus neither nothingness can be affected in any way, because it has no substance, nor God, because he experiences no losses and receives no increases. Intermediate things are affected, as was said above, either by advancement or by decline.

Indeed, no sound-minded person will deny that whatever is affected suffers, and that whatever suffers is not God, because the two are reciprocally related. Nothing mutable can be other than passible, and nothing passible can be other than mutable.

When he says, however, on the testimony of the philosophers, that mercy, justice, and good affections of this kind belong to a passible creature, but that the same things exist in God essentially and not by accession, he does not intend to utter statements contradictory to himself. For an affection is an accession. But nothing accrues to God; therefore he is not subject to affection.

For whatever is affected is exposed on every side to passion, alike to contrary and corresponding conditions. Accordingly, if the highest Divinity perceived with the affection of one suffering together, it would also be subject to the stimulus of evil passion.

“You say that it perceived”—but perception is certainly an accident of one who previously did not perceive. Since eternity knew the Passion of Christ eternally, as it was itself the one who ordained it, nothing new entered eternity at the time of the Passion that it might know, let alone perceive.

### III.

But why should I now discuss affection and demonstrate by argument that it is impassible, when the very person whom we oppose has undoubtedly confessed that God suffered together with the crucified man?

What, I ask, is the meaning of this statement: “He did not perceive with the sensation of one suffering, but he perceived with the affection of one suffering together”? What does “he perceived” mean, and what does “he did not perceive” mean? Or how did he suffer, if he did not perceive?

If someone says, “That man walks, and the other walks with him,” or “That man speaks, and the other speaks with him,” does this not mean that the one who speaks together with him speaks and the one who walks together with him walks?

Or if someone says, “That man has died, and the other has died with him,” does this not affirm that both have died? For one who dies with another certainly dies.

Therefore one who suffers together certainly suffers. If the Divinity suffered together, then it suffered; and consequently perhaps it also died. But if even to think this is impious, then God did not suffer; and therefore he was not affected. Where, then, is the affection of one suffering together?

### IV.

Afterwards he adds:

> “What the various saints of old prophesied figuratively, in the prophetic Spirit, for the overthrow and restraint of those who think carnally and humanly, was said in this way: ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger’ (Psalm 37:2). And: ‘The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent’ (Psalm 109:4).”

Previously, by means of the philosophers, he does not impute accidental qualities to God; here, through the prophets, he imposes even the necessities of vices upon him. For unless things that must be understood figuratively are examined attentively within, one does not reach the life-giving Spirit but remains in the dead letter.

It follows, of course, that we must believe the undefiled essence of the exalted Divinity to be passible if we consider the prophecies of the prophets only in the body of the letter, though they are animated by allegorical mysteries. For when the prophetic oracles speak of God as becoming angry or repenting, the effects of these passions, not the passions themselves, must be considered.

Moreover, because this recent writer claims that his little reflections ought to be weighed according to the example of prophetic speech, he is professing himself not an interpreter but a prophet, since he has watched at the mouth of the prophets [Note: Possibly “at the birth,” though immediately afterward another reading has “the mouths of the prophets”] [Col. 0703C], as though he had unlocked their prophecies.

It is therefore contrary to reason to weave rhetorical periods in the mystical style of the prophets. The result is that he who promises to expound the words of others cannot himself be expounded. Either do not use the words of prophets, or prophesy.

Prophecy is wholly unsuitable either to the present time or to an interpreter. Therefore whatever you have borrowed from prophetic speech in defense of your position works against you rather than helps you. Either the defense you sought admits its own weakness, or an unsuitable defense does not cleanse the error.

### V.

The undefiled Divinity, therefore, is not rightly said to be affected, since effect belongs to the craftsman, affection to the work. Whenever God temporarily punishes someone, it is the one who is punished who suffers according to the eternal plan.

God too would suffer something if he came to know someone’s sins temporally, or if anger moved him to exercise justice. For immutable and abiding eternity encompasses every temporal, mobile, and mutable thing: affecting some things beneficially, others judicially, and allowing others to be affected, while remaining itself sufficiently removed from every affection and movement of time and place.

It possesses only that movement which is called stable, from which, through which, and in which everything exists that is moved by time alone and by it alone, and everything that is moved by it both through time and through place, not through time alone. But these matters belong elsewhere.

For now, setting aside matters of this kind—which are plainly such, whether in merit or in strength, that it is just to disapprove them but unnecessary to attack them—let us come to those testimonies that he has borrowed from the Apostle in defense of his position.

He says:

> “Why could it not be said, ‘He perceived with the affection of one suffering together,’ when the Apostle thought it necessary to say, ‘They would never have crucified the Lord of glory’ (1 Corinthians 2:8)? Just as light cannot perceive any blow of a wound, so the author of light felt no pain of suffering.”

It may therefore be said: “But he perceived with the affection of one suffering together”?

It may indeed, because everything is permitted; but it ought not to be said, because not everything builds up (1 Corinthians 6:12).

### VI.

Yet I can scarcely restrain my laughter at this kind of comparison and way of speaking. A little earlier you had asserted that God ceases to be virtue and is therefore changed. Now, with your argument likewise weakening, you declare that just as light cannot perceive any blow of a wound, so the author of light felt no pain of suffering.

Therefore light alone does not perceive a blow. Does earth, water, or air perceive the blow of some wound? Or perhaps light is animate? Or can any lifeless body perceive? Or is there any body that, although it does not perceive a wound, cannot be wounded?

Light can therefore be wounded even if it cannot perceive, because just as night is broken by the admission of light, so light is wounded by darkness. Hence the very well-known poet Asclepiades made a most delightful jest when he said:

> “The rival night drives away the absent day,  
> whom light, defeated, flees with torn robe.”

What do you mean by saying that, just as light does not perceive a blow, so the Divinity did not perceive a wound in the Passion? If that is so, then it could have been wounded even though it could not perceive; insensibility would be one thing, corruptibility another.

For it did not feel pain because of incorruptibility; it could be wounded [the supplied text appears to omit “not”]. Since light is insensible, it was likewise vulnerable. See whether perhaps this is the very error into which you have fallen more deeply, the one you think should be reproached to us.

You declare that corporeal light, common alike to man and beast, is so compared with God—who does not feel an inflicted wound—as is any body, however beautiful; yet you do not merely liken a body to the highest incorporeal reality, but make it equal to it. In so punishable an opinion, you claim for yourself not merely the privilege of innocence but also praise.

And because we say that the likeness of God is incorporeal, just as God himself is incorporeal, you declare that we are outside the faith. But these matters will be treated later.

### VII.

For the moment let us discuss affection. Was Christ crucified in such a way, then, that the incorruptibility of the highest Divinity—undefiled in every respect—should be believed crucified? Tell me, if that is not an insult.

It is permitted to believe that after the humiliation of death he was exalted by the highest God, that is, by the Trinity itself; that the name which is above every name was bestowed upon him (Philippians 2:9). I think this refers to the one who, having become obedient unto death because of the obedience of ineffable humility, was ineffably exalted into the glory of God the Father.

Will you dare not confess that he is the Lord of glory whom you confess to be the Son of man? Yet you will use the statement, “They would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8), for the purpose of making it unquestionably believed that the Divinity itself can be affected, if it could be crucified.

Thus you have revealed your opinion in an open statement. For although you think you have said without reproach that God is affected because the Apostle says that the Lord of glory was crucified, and although truth urges that “the Lord of glory was crucified” be understood in such a way that the Divinity is not believed to have been crucified, you nevertheless argue with all your might that the Divinity is affected, driven by your zeal to defend your error.

You do not notice that you are saying that the punishment which the crime of the persecutors inflicted upon the man Christ was itself inflicted upon the inviolable Divinity. If this is so, then God could suffer for human beings without assuming a human being. For if he could be passible in man, he could also be passible outside man.

But perhaps you will contend that he was changed through contact with the human substance and therefore became passible after assuming man. God, then, is not incorruptible. For whatever can be made worse can certainly also be corrupted.

But the Divinity cannot be corrupted or changed; therefore it cannot suffer either.

## VIII
