Now, therefore, what remains is this: since Christ is true man and true God, one person from two substances, both God-man and man-God; since he is likewise the Lord of glory, he was not crucified in respect of his inviolable divinity, but was crucified in the manhood for the unity of his person. Thus, in a wondrous and inconceivable manner, the man-God suffered, while the divinity did not suffer.

[Col. 0705C] Consider now, therefore, that you have claimed the Apostle’s testimony only for this purpose—not so that your opinion might derive strength from it, but so that the perversity of your savage opinion might not remain concealed. You say, as though truth itself were supporting you through the Apostle, that the divinity is affected; but the Apostle compels us to understand “the Lord of glory crucified” in that part of him which could be crucified. [Variant: “in what manner.”]

For you, therefore—for you alone—this opinion remains: that the undefiled and inestimable divinity was beaten with whips, pierced with nails, stabbed with a lance, afflicted with pains, and consumed by death, because you refuse to believe that in the one and same Christ one thing was subjected to death and another to suffering. [Variant: “because we should believe.”] But, pressed by the truth, you alter your words, saying that whatever affects created substance is in God substantially, not adventitiously.

Continue to speak in this way; may ignorance, presumption, and falsehood not stain sincerity within you. To err is human; to repent of an error is human. No one sins more dangerously than one who defends sins. For you do not hesitate, as you yourself declare, to agree with the philosophers that the essence of the supreme divinity is impassible and subject to no affection. Therefore drive this inward conflict from your mind. Let it be certain to you that truth cannot be mixed with falsehood, just as substance cannot be mixed with nothing.

[Col. 0706A] Yet you say that he is affected whom you deny to suffer. For if he is not without affection, your deceptive declaration of his impassibility is false. The one contradicts the other without restraint. One who says, “He felt with the affection of one who suffers together,” does not say that he felt nothing in the suffering.

But you say that God is not affected passibly; therefore he is affected not passibly. This is as though someone were to say, “This man stands while running; that one sleeps while keeping watch”—a contradiction that the difference between opposites plainly does not permit. What, then, is gained by your addition of “passibly,” when it can be said with the greatest truth and completeness, “God is not affected”? This two-headed expression cannot escape suspicion of defect. You do not say that God suffers, but you say that he is affected. “Affection” and “suffering” signify one and the same thing. Either remove both, or preserve both in the one term.

Therefore one must not say, “God is not affected passibly,” but, “God is not affected.” If he is not affected, he did not feel with the affection of one who suffers together. If he felt with the affection of one who suffers together, then he is consequently affected.

[Col. 0706B]

## IX

I say, “The divine substance is affected by nothing”; you say, “God is not affected.” Let us be reconciled. Let the slanderer who casts upon you the charge—perhaps rightly apparent—of ignorance or carelessness be driven from our midst. But you add to this and declare that the Apostle also said of Christ, already placed in heaven: “We have such a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses” (Heb. 4:15).

And as though nothing here needed to be examined or discussed, you boast that you have satisfied your purpose and are ready to pass to the third question. Therefore, to give the briefest possible answer: I believe that this high priest is the one who, in the first place, offers sacrifices on behalf of the human race before the divinity of the supreme Trinity, expiates sins, and commends vows.

[Col. 0706C] He is therefore the true priest. For if the Son of God, inasmuch as he is equal to the Father, does not so much offer prayers as hear those who pray, then here we must understand the man whom the Apostle calls the high priest and declares to sympathize with our weaknesses. Of him also he says:

[Note: These words are omitted by some other editions.]

“Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who was also raised—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34).

That high priest, therefore, sympathizes with us who also intercedes for us. But the one who assents to the intercessor—the Trinity itself—would certainly have no need of anyone to intercede with it, if it could in any way suffer or be affected.

[Col. 0706D] Do you now understand that the testimony of truth has rather been taken up in opposition to the truth and employed in defense of falsehood? For if anything of this kind is found in the divine books, as we said above, it must be referred to the unity of the person. Just as soul and body, though of different substances, are one man, so God and man, though of different substances, are one Christ.

Accordingly, since he is one from different substances, in a certain manner he asks of himself; in a certain manner he hears himself on our behalf. There are innumerable things that could readily be said on this subject. But since matters that collapse of their own accord do not need to be laboriously demolished, let these remarks suffice for the present.

## CHAPTER IV. The state of the human soul

The present state of the human soul—that is, of the divine image—is now called into question. This is that third question in which my worthy opponent, having undertaken to distinguish the causes of the natures, declares the spirit of life to be a body. He claims that he can produce on this matter the authoritative judgments of the Fathers; yet he says that they did not so much define something known to them through intellectual apprehension as hold certain opinions.

[Col. 0707A] And because he himself, insofar as he speaks, has yielded not so much to tested reason or undefiled authority as to human and mistaken opinion, he labors with all his might to make us assent to him with our eyes closed, as they say, after setting aside divine authority and abandoning clear reasoning.

But whoever has thought truthfully and piously about God understands as a necessary consequence that nothing which ought to have been created was not created by him. For the goodness of the Creator is the cause of created things. He who was able to create all things that he wished would have exercised no goodness if he had created nothing; and he would have used only half-full benevolence if he had fashioned something only half-full.

[Col. 0707B] It would seem strange for something to be lacking from the fullness of created things if the little flower of the rose did not exist, yet not to be lacking if incorporeal substance had not been created. Therefore, lest something not merely minor but even most important should be absent from the fullness of creation, incorporeal substance also ought to have been created.

But perhaps this may be regarded as an injury to the Creator, if he is said to have fashioned something incorporeal and like himself, since nothing like God is found among bodies. Yet the human soul is called by God himself the likeness of God; whereas no divine likeness can exist in a body. Therefore what is like God will be incorporeal; but the human mind was made according to the likeness of God. [Col. 0707C] The human mind, therefore, is incorporeal.

## CHAPTER V. That the incorporeal is superior in dignity to the corporeal, and the nonlocal to the local; concerning the great good and the supreme good

### I

Everything incorporeal is preferred in the dignity of nature to the corporeal; everything nonlocal to the local; everything indivisible to the divisible; and everything living to the nonliving.

[Col. 0707D] Indeed, if the most powerful and most benevolent Creator did not create a substance superior to every body and like himself, although it has now been established that such a substance ought to have been created, then either he did not wish to create it or certainly could not. If he wished to create it but could not, he lacked omnipotence. If he could but did not wish to do so—which even to think is impious—then he was envious. Yet omnipotence cannot be unable, nor can goodness be envious.

Therefore he both could and wished to create the incorporeal; consequently, he created it. Unless perhaps you say that what he could wish ought not to have come into being—he who could not wish anything except what he ought to do. Why, then, do you now insist that something was not created which you do not doubt ought to have been created?

[Col. 0708A] It is certainly established that it ought to have been created, because, just as the incorporeal Creator is the supreme good, and created incorporeal substance is a great good, and created body—since it does not exist except as created—is some good from the supreme God, who is the supreme good [variant: *bonam*, “good,”], so, just as some good body was created, some great incorporeal good ought also to have been created.

For it would not befit the omnipotent Good, who made all things “very good” (Gen. 1:31), to leave the perfection of the fullness of things truncated even in the smallest matters—not to mention failing to create what is most excellent.

But perhaps someone may assert either that an incorporeal creature is not a good, or that a good ought not to have been created, or that what ought to have been made could not be made. Yet the supreme good is the incorporeal Creator, and an incorporeal creature is a great good. Therefore a great good ought to have been made by the supreme Good. And the omnipotent one could make what the good one ought to wish.

Therefore he created an incorporeal substance, since he could not fail to make what ought to have been made. Unless perhaps it is said that something ought to have been made [variant: *decuisse*, “to have been fitting”] which he did not make. The consequence, then, will be that he made something which he ought not to have made.

### II

[Col. 0708B] But you will say to me: “If something incorporeal was created, it therefore equals the Creator.” We are asking about the true man—that is, about the human soul. It is not equal to God, but like him: like him insofar as the incorporeal is inferior to the incorporeal, insofar as the created is inferior to the Creator; like him insofar as intellectual light is like intelligible light; unlike him insofar as mutable creation is unlike the immutable Creator.

For truth is one thing, and the image of truth another. But just as there can be no image of a corporeal thing except a body, so an image of the incorporeal can in no way be found in a body.

[Col. 0708C] For when Moses speaks of the creation of man, he says: “And God said, ‘Let us make man according to our image and likeness.’ And he made man according to his image and likeness. In the image of God he created him, male and female” (Gen. 1:26–27).

This declaration of divine authority cannot be evaded by eloquence, deceived by argument, overcome by power, or corrupted by artifice. If the human soul is the image of God, it is evidently the image of the incorporeal. If it is the image of the incorporeal, it is itself certainly incorporeal. But if it is not incorporeal, it is not at all the image of the incorporeal. Yet it is the image of the incorporeal; therefore it is incorporeal.

[Col. 0708D] Since it is created, it is not God. Since it is the image of God, it is not a body.

## CHAPTER VI. That although everything incorporeal is invisible, not everything corporeal is visible

### I

But you add that you have been taught by certain people whose names you conceal from us, that some things are incorporeal and others invisible. What formidable experts these are, who have penetrated so deeply into the secret! If some things are incorporeal and others invisible, then incorporeal things are not invisible.

[Col. 0709A] The incorporeal must therefore be placed below every corporeal thing, because Truth says through the Apostle: “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

But you distinguish the creating and created substances in such a way that some are incorporeal and others invisible. Therefore everything corporeal is invisible, and everything incorporeal is visible.

Here I dare to ask: Is God invisible or visible? If you deny that he is corporeal, you do not refuse to call him visible. If you call him invisible, you confess him to be corporeal. According to your opinion, then—an opinion that should be far from both you and us—the eternal, invisible, incorporeal God will either be incorporeal and visible, or corporeal and not eternal.

Someone was able to think this, but was not able to express it. He was evidently ignorant of obvious causes; I believe he was attempting to say that there are certain corporeal things which cannot be seen, whereas it is proper to every incorporeal thing not to be seen. Thus certain corporeal things can be invisible, while incorporeal things cannot be anything but invisible.

[Col. 0709B] For although everything incorporeal is invisible, not everything invisible is incorporeal. A voice, for example, is not seen, yet it is a body. Indeed, because of the preeminence of sight, we also say that things belonging to the other senses are “seen,” as when we often say, “See what it sounds like,” although sound belongs to hearing, not to sight.

Yet we do not say, “Hear what is shining,” because sight, being more preeminent than the other senses, abusively claims for itself what belongs to inferior senses, without mingling its own power with their powers.

Accordingly, all things that can be perceived by any bodily sense are also “visible,” if we refer everything to sight. But not everything is visible if we restore to each sense what is proper to it.

Hence all the principal bodies called elements are undoubtedly visible, as we experience. From their measured proportion, when their dimensions have been duly combined, a living body is formed by the animating soul.

[Col. 0709C] Although there are many things that are not animated and yet cannot be denied to live, we are speaking here of things that not only live but also perceive, such as animals without reason. After postponing discussion of these for a little while, let us speak about ourselves.

### II

Since, then, we consist of soul and body, and just as a body cannot be a mind, so a mind cannot be a body: the mind that perceives in the body, even if it perceives through what is visible, perceives invisibly.

[Col. 0709D] Sight is one thing, and the eye another. The ear is one thing, hearing another. The nostrils are one thing, smell another. The mouth is one thing, taste another. The hand and touch are likewise not the same thing.

By touch, therefore, we distinguish hot and cold things, but we do not touch the sense of touch itself. For there is neither cold nor heat in it. By taste we perceive sweet and bitter things, but we cannot taste taste itself. There is nothing bitter or sweet in it.

We receive odors through the nostrils; yet by smelling we do not grasp smell itself, because smell has no odor. We draw in voices through the ears, but since hearing itself produces no sound, we do not hear hearing.

[Col. 0710A] We look at colored and formed shapes with our eyes, and because they are colored and formed, we perceive them with our eyes. But we do not see sight, because it is neither colored nor formed. If sight itself shone, we would see continually; if hearing itself sounded, we would always hear; if smell itself gave off fragrance, we would smell perpetually; if taste itself had flavor, we would taste without weariness; and if touch itself touched itself, we would touch eternally.

To say nothing of the rest: if taste could itself be tasted, no one could be fasting, nor would external things need to be applied for the sense to exercise itself, if it perceived itself.

Therefore the bodily member through which we perceive is one thing, and the sense through which we perceive is another.

[Note: Orthodoxus has: “between the invisible.” The Paris edition of the Fathers has the wording as we printed it. The Lyon edition reads: “Because between the visible incorporeal and the visible body there is that visible corporeal thing,” and so forth.]

Between the invisible incorporeal and the visible body there is that invisible corporeal thing which, in us, is sight, smell, taste, hearing, and touch. Since these exist only in an animated body, through the interaction of the two distinct substances they are both corporeal and invisible: they derive from the visible body the fact that they are corporeal, and from the incorporeal soul the fact that they are invisible.

[Col. 0710B] According to your opinion, therefore, it will not be the case that what is not incorporeal is invisible, as though it were proper for the incorporeal to be visible and the corporeal invisible. For nothing belonging to the body would be invisible unless the invisibility of the incorporeal made that visible thing invisible.

Thus, in the same man, as we said above, the soul is an invisible incorporeal, while there is also an invisible corporeal, through which the soul acts invisibly upon the visible body.

## CHAPTER VII. That the body consists of the four elements, and how they correspond to the five senses

### I

Whatever we touch through the bodily senses is so assigned to each of them individually that the others are not admitted into the fellowship of what properly belongs to it.

[Col. 0710C] Among all corporeal things, therefore, the light of the sun is unquestionably superior. It belongs to that highest element within the corporeal universe which is called fire.

This is why sight also holds the principal place among all the senses in the human body. From the inward heat of the heart and liver, certain little fires, continually sparkling, rise into the chamber of the head, as into the heaven of our body. From these, rays poured through the middle of the eyes and mingled with the external light, rebounding from the bodies upon which they fall, return and absorb their colors and forms.

You observe, therefore, the highest fire among the elements, the most beautiful light among colors, and sight as the chief of the senses.

[Col. 0710D] Hearing rightly follows sight in excellence and power. It corresponds to that element [variant: *compos.*; abbreviated and uncertain] which the Greeks call *aether*, which, although it belongs by nature to the air, nevertheless—because it sorts certain impurities downward from its highest regions as though into a basin—is purer and subtler than this stormy air, naturally productive of clouds, and surpasses it both in place and dignity.

This is why the purest air makes hearing easier and carries it farther. For just as the eyes cannot contemplate without the forms of bodies and external light, so the ears perceive only if the air is struck or is blowing. The same applies to the sense of the nostrils.

Just as air is affected by sounds so that it produces hearing in the ears, so it is likewise affected by odors so that it produces smell in the nostrils.

[Note: Another reading: “which are naturally understood to be present in them, but are not perceived unless air is drawn in.”]

[Col. 0711A] The sense of taste clearly cannot operate without the aid of moisture, as is shown by the fact that nothing flavorful is perceived when it is received by a dry tongue. Touch, I think, is evidently most similar to the element of earth.

### II

Let us now return to the matter for which we have discussed these things. Sight sees and perceives both light and other bodies contemplated through the same light. Does hearing claim anything for itself from this? Again, the passages of the ears receive sounds and articulated voices. Does sight claim anything from this?

Through the cavities of the nostrils we receive odors of countless kinds. Hearing certainly has no power to perceive any of these. Does taste perhaps share with smell in the examination of flavors? Or does touch allow taste anything in perceiving rough or smooth things?

[Col. 0711B] Behold: a voice is not perceived by sight, the more eminent sense; light is likewise not heard; a voice is certainly not apprehended by the nostrils; fragrance is not received by taste; flavor alone is perceived in the mouth.

## CHAPTER VIII. That every soul was made from no element whatsoever, nor from any body

Behold: the entire variety of body is mixed into the structure of the human body from all the elements, by modes scarcely conceivable and according to the principle of harmony of that eternal music.

Choose now from what kind of bodies the soul is, if the soul is a body. For if it is a body, the soul is either from one of these bodies, from some of them, or from all bodies; or else it is not a body.

[Col. 0711C] But what shall I do now? Where shall I turn, having been forestalled by the intelligence and skill of this most acute and learned disputant? He understands, of course, that no body can exist except either as created originally from nothing, as the elements of bodies are, or as formed from these by a proportionate arrangement. Yet, while deciding that the soul is a body, he preferred to judge it made from one of the principal bodies rather than composed from all of them.

Cautiously employing a crafty intelligence, he did not wish to gather the substance of the soul from a mixture of many bodies, lest, if it were said to have been formed from the same principles from which an external body was formed, it should likewise appear capable of dissolution.

[Col. 0711D] For this reason he chose air, declaring that the soul is either made from air or like air. He added the testimony of some author of his—I do not know which—whose words are these:

“Some natures are spiritual, such as angels, archangels, and the other powers; our own soul also, or certainly this subtle air. Nevertheless, they are in no way to be considered incorporeal.”

Are such words entrusted to parchment? Is this the business we are undertaking?

Setting everything else aside, the whole issue rested on this point: if careful examination should show that the soul was either made from air or like air, I would then, as they say, go over completely to the opinion of the opponent, and at that point to the opinion of the teacher; having begged pardon, I would announce myself as the messenger of my own error.

[Note: Another reading: “and, without asking pardon, I would set aside my error.”]

[Col. 0712A] But if, by the right of disclosed truth, I claim for myself what reasoning will prove—that not merely the human soul, but every soul whatsoever, consists neither of air nor of any body at all—then it will be permissible for you either to agree with us or to forgive us.

## CHAPTER IX. That the soul consists of no body whatsoever

It was already made clear above that the element of fire surpasses the element of air not only in place but also in power. This is clearly shown by that earthly fire which, with movement scarcely comprehensible, is carried upward by its natural weight, as though toward its own region.

If this could not be recognized from that fact, it may be plainly understood from the following: all air grows bright in the presence of the sun and darkens in its absence.

[Col. 0712B] There is also this point of the greatest importance: air suffers fire in order to become warm, yet fire suffers nothing from air that would make it cold. Air can be enclosed and contained in any vessel; this never happens to fire.

Fire is therefore plainly superior to air.

Now sight comes to us from fire, and sight is certainly a sense shared by human beings and animals. Yet some irrational creatures surpass human beings in sharpness of vision.

If, therefore, it cannot be denied that sight comes from fire, while according to your reasoning the soul comes from air, then the eye of an animal is superior in the dignity of substance to the human mind, because the former comes from fire and the latter from air.

[Col. 0712C] It is therefore not without reason that one who judges the soul to be airy regards it as local and confines it within the prison of the body. You must now choose one of two alternatives: either the soul is inferior to an animal’s sight, if it is airy; or it is not airy, if it is superior.

You see how easily the fiction of unlearned presumption has vanished, apart from the fact that countless further arguments on this matter are readily available.

For if the soul is airy, then its darkness is the departure of this corporeal sun, and its light is likewise the arrival of this same sun. The statement pronounced by the Evangelist would then be false: “That was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

[Col. 0712D] So too would be false what the prophet speaks in the person of sinners: “Therefore the light of justice did not shine for us, and the sun did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6).

Did these people not see this corporeal sun while they were living in this world? But incorporeal eyes were seeking an incorporeal sun.

It would be very strange if this light has eyes which it illuminates, while that true light has none. Or, if it has them—as it truly does—from where could it be seen to be incorporeal? I believe that it is not only not airy, but not corporeal at all.

## CHAPTER X. That what is already a form or substance cannot be called matter

What is one to make of this? At the very beginning of your discussion you thought it necessary to warn the reader to prepare his mind for subtler reflections, yet now you try to lead our reason downward from the highest things to the lowest, from incorporeal things to corporeal ones.

[Col. 0713A] And as though teaching us to prepare the eye of the mind for subtle matters, shortly afterward you add and say: “Whatever has been created appears to be matter,” by which you determine it to be corporeal.

If creation is still matter, then you have not yet been formed. For Scripture says to God: “Who created man from formless matter.”

[Note: This passage occurs at Wisdom 11:18, but with a different meaning. The Greek there speaks of the omnipotent hand of God: *κτίσασα τὸν κόσμον ἐξ ἀμόρφου ὕλης*—“which created the world from formless matter,” or, as the Vulgate has it, “from invisible matter.”]

The world is full of forms, whether less or more beautiful according to their quality or kind. Matter, however, is formless, whereas the world is formed. Therefore creation is not matter.

## CHAPTER XI. That nothing whatsoever, whether incorporeal or corporeal, can be called uncreated

After this you argue and say: “For this reason nothing incorporeal was created: because whatever is comprehensible to its maker cannot be incorporeal.”

[Col. 0713B] According to this reasoning, God himself is unknown to himself. For if he created nothing incorporeal for this reason, and if nothing created exceeded the Creator’s knowledge, since nothing corporeal or incorporeal came into existence except through the prior knowledge of the Creator—because he made nothing in ignorance—then he knows himself least of all, since he surpasses incorporeally every substance that he created.

Consequently, he is greater than himself, since he is incapable of comprehending himself. Since reason does not permit this to be said, it follows that he created something incorporeal so that nothing created could be incomprehensible to him, since the supreme incorporeal one cannot be unknown to himself. [Variant: “may not have created.”]

[Col. 0713C] See how with little effort the warmth of truth melts the frosts of frigid words.

And since you cannot distinguish matter from what is created, the formed from the formless, or spirit from air, you pronounce upon the image of God as though you were an expert in the most important matters, although you are shown to be ignorant of lesser ones.

Now, driven especially by the great lack of testimonies, you append a chapter from a certain work of Saint Jerome—one which it is clear you did not understand. He says: “They suppose that the spheres of the stars are embodied spirits.”

[Col. 0713D] It is beyond doubt that anyone who merely supposes is wavering. Yet you say that blessed Jerome reports the opinion of certain people concerning embodied spirits. If he perhaps follows the opinion of those who suppose—that is, those who doubt—then follow him together with them.

Since the doubt of one who supposes proceeds only from ignorance, you acknowledge that, when we seek the truth from you, you have brought us, in place of the knowledge you promise, the ignorance of many.

For when you use as an almost fully proved testimony that of a man who, while uncertain about the matters on whose testimonies he relies, presents as witnesses those who themselves doubt, what are we to think you are able to assert? You yourself are now doubting for the third time: following the doubtful author of your author, who himself doubts.

## CHAPTER XII. That the author of that work, not understanding the philosophers, supposed the spheres of the stars to be embodied spirits and declared angels to be bodies; against this he uses the Apostle’s testimony concerning the resurrection

### I

[Col. 0714A] I nevertheless find philosophers saying that, in certain discussions, they maintain that the very spheres of the moon and sun are animated by incorporeal spirits, under a certain divine mind.

But you ought to recognize that this same testimony not only contributes nothing to your opinion against us, but is of the greatest value against it and in our favor. This has happened to you because, without understanding the philosophical opinion, you placed on your side something which, when properly understood, can support only our position.

For if the philosophers had said that spirits are corporeal, the entire foundation of your argument would still have tottered under the authority not of those who define but rather of those who merely suppose.

[Col. 0714B] But since they said knowingly and without doubt that spirits are not corporeal but embodied (*corporati*), does it not become clear that whatever is embodied is not itself corporeal?

Otherwise they would have said that spirits are corporeal, not embodied. For that is corporeal which an incorporeal spirit animates; but that is incorporeal by which a body is animated.

Therefore, since they clearly distinguished the body that is given life from the incorporeal thing that gives life, it seems to me that this advocate of the body either did not understand the philosophical opinion concerning incorporeal substance, or ought not to have brought it forward in his own interest under the very name of Saint Jerome.

### II

[Col. 0714C] He continues and adds: “If angels, and even heavenly bodies, are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think man must be considered?”

As far as I can see, this most violent disputant does not understand this either. He believes angels to be of one substance, so that he may hold a better opinion of the stars, which he judges to be embodied spirits.

Would the learned Jerome here be judged to have said anything other than that the bodies of angels, by their aptitude and power, greatly surpass human bodies?

Likewise, when he said, “If angels,” and added, “even heavenly bodies,” he wished two things to be understood: angels and heavenly bodies. For since angelic spirits are embodied, there are in heaven certain things which are bodies alone.

[Col. 0714D] Therefore he clearly shows that no body, however supreme in place or powerful in movement, can be placed above incorporeal things.

Again, advancing by comparison, he says that man cannot be compared with divine beings, so much so that he cannot even be compared with angels.

He also distinguishes body from flesh. For although all flesh is body, not every body is flesh. Hence the Apostle says: “There is one flesh of birds, another of fish, and another of human beings. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Cor. 15:39–40). He clearly shows that an earthly body is also flesh, whereas a heavenly body is not also flesh.

[Col. 0715A] Perhaps here we should apply what he remembers Jerome himself to have said: “They suppose that the spheres of the stars are embodied spirits.” Thus the stars themselves—or the bodies of angels—are certainly heavenly bodies, while the spirits embodied in them are not corporeal.

So also we say that God became incarnate, and likewise that the human soul becomes incarnate when it takes on flesh to administer it.

Although what Scripture testifies may happen to it—“The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15)—it must not therefore be believed to be changed into a body, however heavily it may be burdened by the weight of flesh. For a body will likewise never be changed into the nature of the soul, however much it may be moved by the soul that animates it; otherwise it would no longer be a body.

[Col. 0715B] Accordingly, when the Apostle said, “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Cor. 15:40), whether he wished this to be understood of angels, of the stars, or of all manner of earthly bodies—about which there is no dispute—will become clear from what follows.

For he immediately adds, without interruption: “There is one glory of the heavenly, and another of the earthly” (ibid.). And to show clearly what those heavenly bodies are, he says: “There is one brightness of the sun, another brightness of the moon, and another brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41–42).

He teaches, of course, that the difference found in the quality of the stars will correspond to the difference among resurrected bodies according to their merits.

[Col. 0715C] Here, without ambiguity, the teacher of the nations is discussing only the resurrection of human bodies, using comparisons of this kind. For he begins his treatment of the subject as follows: “Someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’” (ibid., 35).

From this point all the way to the comparison with the stars, he pursues the same subject without introducing any other matter, making no mention of the soul—lest anyone, perhaps with a harsh judgment, should think that what he had said about the differences among the bodies of the sun, moon, and stars, that is, the heavenly bodies, had been said about souls.

[Note: Another reading: *servo* (“as a slave”); perhaps *laevo* (“perverse” or “sinister”). This variant concerns the preceding “harsh judgment.”]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the resurrection in greater detail
Now then, if the human body—earthly, that is, and mortal—will be transformed into such glory that it becomes spiritual instead of carnal, according to the Apostle, who says, “The natural body is sown; it will rise a spiritual body” (ibid., 44), and if the human soul is now spiritual in such a way that it is nevertheless a body, then human flesh will be transferred into the dignity of the soul when it has become a spiritual body. And the soul, which rightly ruled the body, which devoutly served the Lord, which faithfully believed in God—or perhaps even knew him—will itself, once its flesh has been made equal to it, advance no further in accordance with the quality of its substance. And what of the saying that the one who has cleansed not the eye of the flesh [Col. 0715D] but the eye of the heart will see God? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Therefore perhaps the body will be blessed according to its own measure, and the soul likewise according to its own measure. The body will be changed so that in every respect it serves at the command of the spirit, against which it often rebelliously resisted. And the soul will be changed so that it sees God, for whom it yearned with the ardor of chaste love.

And since the Apostle distinguished spirit, soul, and body, saying, “that your spirit and soul and body may be kept entire” (1 Thess. 5:23), because after the resurrection one is not to live in a natural manner—namely, where there is no eating [Col. 0716A] or drinking, no sleeping or sexual intercourse—the entire natural body will pass into a spiritual body, because the entire soul too will pass into spirit, and the whole will be a spiritual body because of the indwelling spirit. Now if that spirit in this life desired against the flesh, and did not yield to the flesh that desired against it, then rightly in eternity it will feel none of the difficulty whose difficulties it overcame by the power of heavenly assistance. Nor will the one who yielded unwillingly to it be equal to the Lord, nor will the one who overcame willingly remain in the condition of a servant.

Accordingly, it is understood that just as in this life the substance of the human soul, by the dignity of its nature, surpasses the natural body incorporeally, so after the resurrection and recompense it will surpass the spiritual body. But whatever is superior to a spiritual body, I think, is not a body. Therefore, according to the argument of this treatise of mine, which determines that angels are bodies only, human substance will be inferior to the angelic nature. For we firmly retain, on divine authority, that the bodies of the saints which will deserve to be changed will be made equal in glory to angelic bodies, since the Lord says: “And they will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30). If, therefore, angels are only spiritual bodies and are of one substance, and the human body will be advanced to the dignity of an angelic body, a human being will be made equal to an angel in the quality of the body, but will surpass him in the dignity of the spirit.

But if this—as it certainly is—seems absurd, then the angelic substance, like the human, is twofold: possessing a body of the greatest facility and beauty, which is made to appear to human beings when commanded [Col. 0716C], and possessing an incorporeal element by which it always sees God. This accords with the Gospel saying: “For their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10).

## CHAPTER XIV. That spiritual things cannot be seen by bodily eyes

I am greatly astonished that any Christian, especially one occupying the position of a teacher, should define that God will be contemplable by any beautiful or sublime body, provided it is still a body, and that he can universally be seen locally, when to see God is to understand him. We also recognize by understanding that the understanding itself is not local. For if the understanding is local, then what is understood will also be local. Nothing is local that is not itself also a place. But if the understanding is local, and God is in this respect local because God is what is understood, then God is local. Since this is contradictory, we must understand that a human being consists of body and incorporeal substance, both of which are to be reformed for the better; and that an angel consists of body and spirit, formed with the highest dignity among creatures. [Note: [Col. 0715] In both cases “its,” that is, the angel’s. But another reading: “That spirit … that body.”] The spirit in an angel is more powerful than every created spirit; its body is more exalted than the most exalted of all the elements, in accordance with the prophetic passage where the angelic substance is plainly declared to be twofold: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4 [LXX 102:4]). It is manifest that fire is not spirit, and likewise that spirit is not fire. For this must not here be taken allegorically, as in the passage where the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), when he was speaking of the Holy Spirit. For it is not right to believe that human souls are inflamed to divine love by participation in an angelic spirit, because a human being is good by the same gift by which an angel is good, and both are blessed by the same gift. Both desire the same thing with the same will—that is, with the same spirit [Note: Alternatively, “they grasp”]. Both perceive this same thing through an incorporeal capacity. Thus human being, angel, and God become one spirit, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The one who adheres to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

But I do not see how a body can be brought into conformity with the incorporeal, so that it can rightly be called one spirit. For if the soul is a body, then what is bodily will be changed so that it can be one with the incorporeal. And so we necessarily return to that argument by which it is said that something incorporeal could have been created. For if something incorporeal can be made from something corporeal, then it could also have been created from nothing. Unless perhaps it is said that the immutable God somehow becomes bodily in order to be one with the body. But let this be the belief of certain ruined people. For if it is good for either an angel or a human being to adhere to God, the immutable Creator will not deteriorate into a creature; rather, the mutable creature will advance toward the Creator. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “Father, let these be one in us, as we are one” (John 17:21).

## CHAPTER XV. That all corporeal things become greater by the addition of themselves, and many greater than few; but that the incorporeal soul is neither increased among many nor diminished in individuals

Nor can it be believed that the conjunction of any bodies imitates the unity of the Trinity, or that bodies can be mingled with it without confusion. It is plainly evident that any one body is doubled by the addition of an equal body. There are in it an upper and a lower part, a right and a left, a front and a back. According to its magnitude, it has length, breadth, and height. But in God, whose likeness we are told to imitate by being one and united with him, we do not posit parts and spaces resulting from divisibility and locality in the Trinity itself. He himself, as we read in the apostolic Acts, says that “the multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul” (Acts 4:32).

Nevertheless, I do not think that many souls were so joined to one another that from many souls some greater soul came to be, since it is through and with the Trinity that all good souls become one [Note: Orthodox. “Nor is any one”]. Nor is any one person of that same Trinity lesser than the three, nor are the three greater than each one. So too the substance of the human soul, in imitation of the one whose image it is, is neither greater among many according to any bulk nor lesser in individuals according to any bulk. For they are powers, not bodies.

The creative power rightly surpasses created powers, above all precisely because it created them. We often experience and say that one soul is superior to another. Yet we do not believe that the soul which we call superior in power is greater in bulk—a bulk which it does not possess. I also do not think that you will deny that however many perfectly wise souls there may be, they do not know more than one perfectly wise soul; nor that what one soul wills in every respect is willed more strongly because many souls will it in every respect; nor that whatever one remembers perfectly is remembered better by many through the tenacity of their memory.

A body, however, has more weight when it is large than when it is small; a multitude of bodies is stronger than a few; and many hands hold, support, or push something more forcefully than individual hands. Let us now examine what follows.

[Col. 0718B]

## CHAPTER XVI. That souls are incorporeal

“Souls,” you say, “have in themselves a body by which they subsist, although it is much and incomparably more tenuous than our bodies.” Let it be accepted in that way, if that is so. But I should like you to answer this: Who is the one who says, “The soul has a body incomparably more tenuous than our bodies”? If these are the soul’s words, what body does it say is its own—the body that it itself is, or that which animates and gives life to the flesh? For the soul itself says: “The body of the soul is more tenuous than my body.” What body does the soul call its own, unless it is that which the soul itself is, if the soul is a body? Therefore either the soul is a body, and it does not rightly call this fleshly body its own, because that which it itself is is rather its own; or, if this body is the soul’s body, then the soul itself, as must be understood, is not a body.

It then speaks as follows to the one consulting it: “You object to me that the soul is not corporeal because it is neither local nor constituted by quality or quantity. We shall show in what danger it lies to believe this in what follows. But for now, after the matter has been examined at this stage of our treatise, the conclusion will depend on this: if it is neither local nor subject to quantity, you should unquestionably believe it to be incorporeal. But if we demonstrate that it is determined by quantity and enclosed by place, then you too should no longer doubt that it is contained by a body. You have placed the position of your treatise in the condition of this point, so that if the soul can be proved to be local and subject to quantity, it would consequently also be believed to be corporeal.” Yet shortly afterward you assert that within the workshop of the breast it invents the variations of its thoughts and sets its movements in motion.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the soul gives life to the body without any local distinction

First, I ask you to answer this: In what place of the body is the soul? Is it in the whole body or in a part? If it is in a part, how does it move and animate the entire body everywhere? If it is in the whole, how does it invent its thoughts and exercise its movements within the workshop of the breast alone? Or perhaps it is not only in the breast but also in the head; not only in the head but also in the sole of the foot and in the bones? And wherever you believe the soul to be locally present, you will also admit that it understands locally and thinks locally.

And since, if it is corporeal, it is present in the body in such a way that, just as water fills the smaller parts of a smaller vessel with a smaller part of itself and the larger parts with a larger part, it necessarily follows that a greater thought is in the breast and a lesser one in the finger. Thus, whatever portion of the living body someone cuts away, he also cuts away an equal portion of the animating soul. Consequently, the soul—now certainly weakened—will possess no such great power either of thinking or of remembering. No one doubts that air, from which or like which you declare the soul to be, is divisible and capable of being cut. For when we inhale and exhale, we draw in and give back its particles, which the veins—called by the Greeks ἀρτηρίας, “arteries”—receive as nourishment for the whole body; through them that same air is distributed, by the tireless movement of the lungs, in a balanced mixture of the three elements.

But if inhaled air, according to your opinion, belongs to the soul’s nourishment, because an airy thing is suitably nourished by air, then, as was said above, when the body which it animates is divided, it too receives division. The power of memory certainly belongs to the soul as a whole, without question. Every body, however large or small, can surely be cut; and this happens to it because it consists of parts. For whatever has a part can certainly be divided, because one part can be torn away from another.

Therefore, if the soul is a body, it receives division; if it receives division, it receives diminution; and if it receives diminution, then when any part of a living body is lost, a part of the soul is also lost. With a part of the soul, a part of the memory perishes. Therefore a soul whose substance has been diminished ought to remember less. Consequently, if the soul is local, it can be reduced by division in many ways and destroyed by repeated diminution.

But since a sound mind—not to mention an educated one—does not accept this, let us discuss movements, so that the soul’s non-locality may become more apparent insofar as we can set it forth with divine assistance. For it will not be doubtful that just as that which moves locally is a body, so that which does not move locally is not a body.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Three kinds of movement

[Col. 0719D]

I. It is already known, then, that there are three movements: stable, non-local, and local. Stable movement belongs to God, non-local movement to the soul, and local movement to the body.

Stable movement is this: God did not always make the creature, yet he did not will to create it at the time when he created it by a new will, because he always willed to create it when he made it. “Then” signifies time; “always” does not pertain to time. Therefore “then” pertains to the beginning of time, not to time, because temporal movement is enclosed by the stability of the eternal will. Accordingly, to will “then” always is stable movement.

Here you must understand that nothing can move except through something unmoved. To teach this by an example: we cannot move a finger unless the hand is stationary; the movement of the arm proceeds from the stability of the shoulder. And, not to linger over the matter, in walking one foot must certainly be fixed so that the other can advance. Hold on to this: for a little while we distinguish the movement of the soul from the movement of the body [Note: Alternatively, “when we have distinguished for a little while”].

For just as God moves stably, as was said above, so the soul moves temporally. That is temporal which was proud a little earlier and is now humble; which was previously joyful and is now sad; which loved before and now hates; which earlier forgot something and now remembers it. In such movements the soul does not communicate with the body, since it moves while the body nevertheless remains unmoved. Hence it is understood that the soul moves non-locally through time, and that by the same soul the body is moved both temporally and locally, while the soul itself is moved locally by the body.

II. To make this very point clear in words, if I can, I need a reader who will pay close attention. Suppose that the soul’s command is directed toward moving the hand so that something may be written or fashioned. The soul sees incorporeal forms non-locally; inseparably joined to them—or placed above what is subordinate, or subordinate to what is above—it moves the whole limb as a whole and animates the whole variety of forms.

Therefore, when it is intent upon those eternal and ever-identical forms, and attempts through the body to produce, after their models, a bodily square, hexagon, or circle, what happens if it turns its mind—its eye, so to speak—in another direction? For example, if it wishes to make a square but thinks of making a circle; or if it wishes to write the name Paul but thinks of the name Simon: is not the movement of the limb immediately directed toward expressing or shaping that to which the soul’s command has passed in thought?

The soul, then, remains stationary in contemplation of the forms so that it may move the body in the shaping of things capable of being shaped. The truth of these forms is not visible except to a rational being. For every soul remains in rational desire and deliberation. It is not believable that when the writer’s hand is moved to write by the soul’s command, the soul itself is also moved by the agitation of the hand. Unless it viewed the forms of the letters immovably and non-locally, it could not form those same letters locally through the movement of the fingers.

III. But perhaps you say: “That part of the soul which is in the writer’s fingers moves, while the rest does not move.” Those who think that the soul is divisible make this claim, although, by an inseparable chain of reasoning, if it were corporeal it would be divisible. For whatever is corporeal is divisible, and everything divisible is corporeal.

Let us therefore inquire whether the mind can be divided into parts, and whether one part of it can be removed in proportion to a bodily part. First and foremost, this must be the point examined in our investigation: if the mind has parts, it can be cut into parts.

Let us observe with our mind that no body can be touched all at once in its entirety, nor can it touch another body in its entirety all at once. But the soul is wholly present at once in each of its movements and actions. For, as we argued above, every body, however great or however small, has length and height. According to the number of its parts, it is subject to six movements. Every body moves upward and downward, to the right and to the left, forward and backward. It also moves in a seventh movement, as does a wheel or a sphere; this movement is accomplished as an indication of eternity—from itself, through itself, and in itself.

Every body, then, as we have said, having six parts and being subject to six movements, necessarily has something intermediate according to its thickness. For there would be no exterior parts in bodies at all if there were no interior parts as well. Therefore, even if any body is touched throughout its exterior by a hand that encloses it, it is certainly not touched in its interior. From this it is clear that no body can be touched in its entirety all at once.

Nor can even the smallest body be wholly in one place—for example, a poppy seed, or any part of such a seed—since where it has its upper parts it does not have its lower ones; where it has its right side it does not have its left; where it has its front it does not have its back.

The soul, however, sees through the whole body, recalls everything seen with its whole self, hears with its whole self, and remembers sounds with its whole self. It smells with its whole self and remembers scents with its whole self. Through the tongue—and, as some maintain, through the palate—it senses flavors with its whole self and distinguishes them with its whole self. It touches all smooth and rough things with its whole self; with its whole self it approves and disapproves.

It seems remarkable, given the necessity of locality in temporal things, as I discussed above, that the soul animates the entire body with its whole self, while, although the entire body is alive and perceives with its whole self, the soul receives all at once through the smallest part of the body—the organ of sight—the forms of visible things. Through that same body-part, the organ of hearing, it receives voices all at once with its whole self. Through the tiny membrane of the nostrils it senses fragrances with its whole self. Through the sense of taste it distinguishes differences of flavor with its whole self. It distinguishes something hot or cold with its whole self through the very tip of a finger.

If, therefore, the whole soul is locally present to the eye in order to see, how is the whole soul not absent from all the senses simultaneously, so that it perceives everywhere with its whole self, animates each part of the body not with its parts but with its whole self [Note: Alternatively, “animates itself”], and through different organs perceives different things all at once with its whole self? When you have persuaded me that the soul performs all these activities locally, then you will persuade me that it is local or divisible. Yet all these things are still common to human beings and animals.

[Col. 0721D]

## CHAPTER XIX. That the soul is not subject to quantity

If the soul’s non-locality has appeared even to some extent, although I have not yet discussed what is most important—that is, our rational faculty—in which its incorporeality and non-locality will certainly shine forth more clearly, let us discuss how the soul is not subject to quantity. [Note: Alternatively, “Although also where, etc.”]

Where there is no locality, there cannot be quantity, since these two are so mutually connected that either both can exist in something or neither can. The divine essence is subject to none at all of those Aristotelian Categories. The human soul, again, is not subject to all of them. Any body, on the other hand, is subject to them all.

For we do not say of God what sort he is, because he cannot be compared as though to something else, so that one might say, “He is such-and-such.” Nor do we say how great he is, because he is not great by bulk. Nor do we say what he possesses, because he possesses everything. Nor do we ask how he is, because he himself is the mode of being. Nor do we investigate his state, because he contains all things. Nor do we ask about his place, because only a body is in a place. Nor about his time, because he is eternity. Nor about his activity, because he acts in repose. Nor about his suffering, because he does not suffer. The tenth category—or rather the first—is substance itself, from which these predicates are woven.

## CHAPTER XX. That the soul is subject to quality

[Col. 0722B]

The human soul, however, just as it does not receive quantity, is subject to quality. For if we inquire of some body what sort it is, its quality is indicated in this way: “That one is blond,” “he has eyes,” “that one is pale,” or “he is dark.” But if we inquire about the soul, its quality is shown to us in this manner: “It is proud,” “it is humble,” “it is angry,” “it is tranquil”; “it remembers very well,” or “it forgets quickly.”

Likewise, if the quantity of a body is asked, we are rightly told that its length extends to five feet, that its breadth is likewise two feet, and that its thickness is the same. Is the quantity of the soul indicated by such measurements, or is anything long, broad, or thick found in it? If so, then the greater a body’s capacity, the greater the soul of the person who possesses it will be. Yet we would never truly call a person of a very small body great-souled, while we often call people of enormous bulk small-souled.

Thus we say, “Great-souled was Moses when, as an undaunted leader, he entered the pathways of the Red Sea”; and “small-souled was the people who did not believe, although God promised, that this very thing would be extremely easy to accomplish.” Here we plainly call the soul of one man greater than the soul of an entire people—greater, obviously, in virtue, not in bulk.

For if bulk made one mass greater than another, then the mass of two souls would be greater than that of one, to say nothing of many. There is therefore quality in the soul, but not quantity: whatever is subject to the mutability of affections receives quality; whatever has no bulk has no quantity.

Hence, when every living body dies, it does not lose the soul but releases it, because what is not enclosed does not go out, and what is not held is not lost. For if it is held, it is not lost; and if it were not lost, no one would die. Thus Papinius Statius says, not poetically but philosophically [Note: Statius Papinius, Book 8 of the *Thebaid*, at the end]:

> … I hate these limbs and this fragile use of the body,  
> abandoned by the soul.

To make this clearer, let us examine the matter more carefully and proceed in ordered stages from the lowest kind of living beings to rational life, so that we may see those three things—memory, deliberation, and will—which constitute the unity of the human soul, although remembering is common to rational and irrational beings alike.

## CHAPTER XXI. That memory is common to the rational and irrational soul; and that every creature is a human being

I. Hence it is not without truth that it is said: “The boundary between human beings and animals lies in memory.” For storks and swallows return to their nests after a year; horses return to their stalls; and dogs recognize their masters. But although the souls of animals naturally retain images of places, they do not possess knowledge of their own substance. They necessarily remain in recollection of bodily things which they have taken in through the bodily senses, and, lacking the eye of reasoning, they cannot see anything above themselves—not to mention seeing themselves.

Therefore let the whole human being give thanks to his Creator—not as much as he ought, perhaps, but as much as he can—for in the generosity of ineffable goodness he has given him existence together with stones, seminal life together with herbs and trees, sensory and likewise animal life together with beasts, and rational life together with angels.

To make it clear, then, that the life of herbs and shrubs is also incorporeal, and that it is not lost by the body but released from it, I ask you: Do you deny that herbs and trees live, or will you perhaps say that some souls are present in these living things so that they may live? But if they were animate, they would not lack self-directed movement, since there are things that move without self-directed movement. They would also feel an inflicted wound. But we know that such things are not present in them from the cutting of bones and the trimming of hair and nails [Col. 0723C], which we cut away without any sensation of pain. There is therefore life even where there is no soul.

II. Now observe that, in bringing about the life of a tree, the seeds of all the elements have come together in their several ways. There is earth in its density, water in its moisture, air in its growth, and fire in its sprout. But if the soul is from air, or is like air, as you assert, then you will not deny that a tree is animate, because it is evident that a nature resembling air is present in it.

The lower things are affected by the higher according to an ordered balance of things. After the winter cold has passed through the turning of the heavens and the return of the stars, the heat that follows first affects the air, which is close to it in both place and nature. And because air yields to fire to the same degree that it rises above water, through the roots of trees and certain sprouts it draws water from the inner parts of the earth. For the element of fire, naturally snatching everything toward itself, draws warmed air toward itself; and through the tree’s marrow it draws air, just as air draws water and water draws earth.

That is why we too can easily draw up water through a tube or some kind of pipe by inhaling air. And from the depths of wells, by means of a cleverly constructed mechanism, the heavier water is forced upward by its nature; aided by air and driven by force through the narrow passages of tubes, it is brought out and flows over the rim above the top of the well [Col. 0724A].

Thus the discord of contrary bodies is compelled, by the Creator’s command, into a kind of harmony so that every living body may exist. From these four elements, which combine with one another in a moderate and harmonious balance to produce the life of a tree, if something has either remained beyond measure or has been lacking, the tree first becomes sick and afterward dies, as though overcome by weakness.

You see here that when the parts of a body fall out of harmony with the unity of the whole, life rather deserts the body than the body is released from life. It follows, therefore, that all life neither departs from the body locally, nor exists in the body as in a place, nor approaches the body locally.

III. If you attend here to the hidden principles of causes, you will observe that although a soul is scarcely absent from these living things, incorporeal life is not absent. To select one example from the whole class of seeds, we know how large a grain of wheat is, and we measure its bulk according to its capacity [Note: Alternatively, “its size”]. If we wish to see something corporeal within it, once it has been split we see nothing except as much white grain as the small capacity of its very thin skin encloses.

There you have, within corporeal space, the total extent of a grain of wheat. Now show me corporeally, within this same little grain, the swellings of sprouts, the greenness of herbs, the stalks of straw, the bristling of ears, the smoothness of chaff, the richness of crops, and from these the seeds of seeds for their tireless multiplication—all of which are stored in that little grain in the hidden principles of causes.

Now either show corporeally within those same seeds everything that comes forth from seeds, or acknowledge that the life of herbs too is incorporeal. And, if you wish, assert that the human soul is corporeal and that the life of a shrub is corporeal. Since no person of sound judgment can endure this, let us pass to living creatures which not only live but also perceive.

IV. In an animal, then, there is a corruptible body and a mortal soul, which neither precedes nor survives the life of the body [Note: “To delay” is an unusual expression. A passage of Claudian was noted by Du Cange in the *Glossary*]. You see, therefore, that in an animal’s body the soul grants to the seminal life which we find in herbs and trees sensation and movement through its appetites, provided that the body itself is in good condition through the harmonious proportion of the elements, and that it responds to the soul’s commands with a concordant obedience of movement.

But how does it happen that the soul moves a healthy and an impaired limb by the same command in different ways? Suppose that the man is strong in his left hand but has lost the use of his right through a blow, as commonly happens. The remaining hand, although attached to the body and retaining the same form though not the same strength, does not obey the soul’s commands.

What shall we say? Has the soul been locally driven out and departed from that hand? Where did it go? Where did it depart from there? Perhaps it withdrew into its remaining part, but the soul was already filling the entire body. Nothing can be added to what is full without overflowing. Therefore perhaps some portion of the soul must be exhaled or belched out, or somehow digested, because an incomplete body cannot contain a complete soul.

These conclusions necessarily follow, without ambiguity, if the soul is a body. Since this cannot happen at all, consider instead that the soul has not lost the power of commanding, but that the hand has lost the strength to serve. Through some disturbance—for example, a rush of blood—when the harmony of the cooperating elements is disrupted, the body loses the capacity to serve, difficulty in ruling comes to the mind, and what had been useful begins to be a burden.

Yet the soul has not lost the power of moving, even if the limb does not offer itself suitably to the movement required. In anyone who has been deprived of sight, as far as the soul is concerned, the power of seeing corporeal things through the body remains; but the bodily organs fail, through which it might exercise its powers in perceiving corporeal things.

Therefore, just as clear reason plainly demonstrates that it is not the soul which has been locally driven from a weakened limb, but the limb, languishing as though near to death, which has become discordant with the soul’s active command, so when the body of some animal perishes through its own discord, as particles of the elements return to their proper regions, the soul, having no means by which to express its commands, perishes from the animal, while the human soul comes to rest. Yet it has departed only from those movements by which it moved the body through places; it itself has moved non-locally through time.

V. Let no little bodies, as it were, now present themselves to the eyes of your mind, so that we should believe that souls, once they have laid aside their bodies, occupy certain places of the air or of any element. If you can, understand your own intellect, to which alone, together with the angel, it has been granted to see such things.

Do you see anything long, broad, or high in your intellect? Does the brilliance of any corporeal light shine there? Does any modulated song whose sound flows through time resound there, or does the sweetness of a vanishing fragrance breathe there, or does anything corporeal have taste there, or is anything soft or hard touched there locally?

Its sight grows bright through wisdom and dark through folly. Its hearing is offended by falsehood and soothed by truth. Justice gives off a non-local fragrance there; iniquity reeks. It wastes away through vanity and grows rich through virtue. It is wretched in the company of folly and blessed in the embrace of wisdom.

It is therefore wholly an eye, because it sees wholly, and it sees wholly whatever it observes. But no body is wholly seen, nor does any body see wholly. It is wholly hearing, because it wholly hears whatever it hears. But no body hears anything wholly. And it wholly smells, tastes, and touches, although such unity and power cannot exist in a body.

This belongs to it by its very nature because in it seeing is the same as hearing, hearing the same as smelling, smelling the same as tasting, and tasting the same as touching. But fantasies of bodies confront the soul. Affected by them through the bodily senses, it is circumscribed not by places but by deceptions. And because it remembers only those things whose forms it received through the body, it believes that whatever has not been such a thing does not exist.

Nor can it long for that homeland from which it was deservedly cast into this pilgrimage, since it does not know that it is on pilgrimage. It cannot know that it is on pilgrimage in the body if it believes itself to be a body.

Hence that man, whom the nature of his own substance no longer escaped, says:

> “While we are in the body, we are on pilgrimage from the Lord. But we are confident and willing rather to be on pilgrimage from the body and to be present with the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:6, 8).

What, I ask, could be said more clearly? There is no doubt that all bodies—whether dense or heavy, such as water or earth; or thin and light, such as fire and air; or those formed from these through the seminal combination of their elements—are included under the name “body.”

Whatever kind of body something is, it may be called a lighter body, a thinner body, a more pliable body, a more elevated body, or a brighter body; nevertheless, it can be called only a body.

But what does the Apostle say? “While we are in the body, we are on pilgrimage from the Lord.” It seems to me that he would by no means have said that the soul is on pilgrimage in the body if he considered the soul itself to be a body. For if the soul is a body and is on pilgrimage in the body, then it is on pilgrimage in its own substance, and it will never be able not to be on pilgrimage, since it cannot exist without itself.

But no thing in any way loses itself, because nothing can exist after itself. Indeed, it is easier for something to be completely destroyed so that it is nothing than for it both to lose itself and to remain after itself. Either, then, the soul is a body and the Apostle was mistaken; or, if it is on pilgrimage in the body, the soul is not a body.

## CHAPTER XXII. How the soul is on pilgrimage in the body
I. You may perhaps object to this and say: How is the soul said to be sojourning merely because it is in a body? If we firmly believe in the resurrection, we too shall be in that eternal homeland, not without bodies.

You should answer: I would like to know whether the soul is now called a sojourner because it dwells in a body, or because it is in such a body. This body, as I mentioned above, weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15)—not, to be sure, by a weight that can be weighed. For with a weight of that kind, the stronger a person is, the more hunger or illness would make the body waste away. [Note: [Col. 0725] Alternatively: “had held.”] This too greatly supports our arguments: it is plainly evident that, according to that life which we share with the beasts, the human soul is more burdened by a wasted and parched body than by one that is well fed and full of vitality. This happens because a weakened body is not so capable of readily obeying the soul’s commands; what burdens the soul is not the heaviness of its weight, but the difficulty of acting.

Accordingly, if we consider the bestial life that is plainly present in us here, this body does not weigh down the soul. But if we contemplate the life that it will have with the angels, the body weighs down the soul by occupying and enticing it, fixing it upon beautiful bodies through necessities or pleasures, and drawing it away from the contemplation of supreme beauty. It is therefore clear that the soul is burdened and weighed down in proportion to the amount and difficulty of its activity, whether the activity consists in what is required for the body’s health in eating and drinking, whether the mind is needlessly occupied with trifling pleasures, or whether it is afflicted through the body by wounds and pains.

This is the sojourning of which the Apostle says: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” [2 Cor. 5:6]. But when the one who has deserved it reaches that transformation of the body of which the same Apostle says, “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51), the animal body—which will no longer exist—will not then oppose the soul’s commands; rather, the spiritual body, which will exist, will serve it in every respect. Nor will that body desire anything unworthy, nor will the soul command anything unjust.

And since the holy soul is carried toward God by chaste affection, understand that neither its sojourning nor its homeland is local. Is God not with the soul in this life, even if the soul is not with God? For it is one thing to be with God and another not to be without God, since one does not come to Him locally, nor depart from Him locally. Accordingly, that soul is with God which sees—that is, understands—God. And that soul is not with God which does not understand God. Yet God is present, without locality, both to the one who understands and to the one who does not understand.

The soul therefore sojourns here insofar as, through the pleasures and pains of the body, through places and times, and through images and phantasms, it is recalled from the contemplation of the highest good. This will no longer happen fully when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this mortal body has put on immortality” (ibid., 53). [Note: [Col. 0727] Alternatively: “to completion.”]

II. Since this is so, the soul sojourns in the body, whose corruption, weakness, and need separate it from its homeland—that is, from God. I think, however, that a substance whose sojourning is local and corporeal, and whose homeland is incorporeal and nonlocal, cannot truthfully be called either corporeal or local.

There will be no sojourning in the one who will be enticed by no desire, occupied by no resistance, and hindered by no weight. It is therefore evident, I think, that the soul does not sojourn in every body, but only in a carnal body, because the carnal body opposes it, whereas the spiritual body approaches incorporeal things.

Therefore, to discuss at last only our own substance, as we have begun to do, who can alone behold the abysses of memory and penetrate its caves? Whatever colors and forms I have seen anywhere are in it; whatever words and sounds I have received through my ears are in it; whatever odors I have drawn in through my nostrils are in it; whatever flavors I have recognized in their variety are in it; whatever I have distinguished through the testimony of touch is in it. In it, in a certain manner, grammar is stored when I discuss dialectic, rhetoric when I discuss geometry, astrology when I discuss music, and all these together when I discuss arithmetic. Through the forms of the parts of the world that I see, and with reason assisting me to know those that I do not see, I embrace the world by an incorporeal capacity.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the soul sees incorporeal things by itself, but corporeal things through the body

But you say to me: “You do not embrace the world in memory, but the world’s image.” From this, at least, understand that the soul is not corporeal, since you see that it cannot behold corporeal things corporeally.

Above the soul there is therefore an eye—not by place, but by power and capacity—which is called spirit, mind, or intellect; although the name differs, it is one and the same thing. Thus what a stone is to an inanimate living being, an inanimate living being is to an animate living being; and what an inanimate living being is to an animate living being, an animate living being is to a living and intelligent being. The irrational soul administers the animal body, plainly for its preservation; and the intellect capable of reason administers the rational soul, plainly for the preservation of the rational soul, while God administers and governs by His sovereign power and stable motion, establishing the foundation of substances: first, that they may exist; then, that according to their measure or merit they may exist in the manner in which He, who orders all things only justly, has determined that they ought to exist.

For just as it is appropriately said of bodies that they are here or there because of the necessity of locality, so it is rightly said of souls, because of their nonlocality or their quality, that they are such or exist in such a manner. Just as a bright place or temperate air is pleasing to a living body, so tranquility in thought and freedom from fear are pleasing to a life-giving spirit. Likewise, just as a dark place and harsh contact are painful to the body, so instability and fearful distress are painful to the thinking soul.

The soul is therefore affected not by place, but according to the diversity of its affections, both pleasurably and painfully. Yet it is clear that the soul, without the body and incorporeally, can be either comforted or afflicted through its affections, whereas the body without the soul cannot feel either pleasant or painful things.

Thus the embodied soul feels corporeal things through the body, and without the body sees incorporeal things. Therefore, just as an inanimate body feels nothing, so the mind without the body does not feel any corporeal thing. This is why, even while it administers and makes the body sentient, whenever the soul is raised toward the highest and unchanging reality, it in a certain manner abandons the bodily senses and departs from them without locality: it does not see what is placed before it, does not hear what sounds beside it, and does not understand the page it is traversing in reading.

The soul is present so that through the eye it may gather the signs of the letters, join them together as syllables, and distinguish them through words; yet it is absent so that it may not know what it has done through these signs. I read something aloud, and another person understands as I pronounce it, fixing the eye of his mind upon it; but I myself do not know what I have read, because the soul has departed, nonlocally intent upon something else. [Note: [Col. 0727] Alternatively: “has failed.”]
