Finally, when I return to myself, whether reminded or not, I am myself the one who returns, and I am myself the one to whom I return. I was not with myself, because I returned to myself across an interval not of place but of time. Nor was I outside myself, because I could not exist without myself.

The soul itself is there, so that through the eye it may see what is being read; and the soul itself is not there, so that it may not understand what is being read. Or does this not often happen? Whether we apply our sight to such reading or our hearing to someone’s account, although it is just as easy for these things to be understood as to be seen and heard, we nevertheless receive sounds and signs through both senses without understanding what they signify. Yet when we once more turn the attention of our mind toward what had not been understood, we comprehend the same thing without any difficulty.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That the soul is not one thing and memory, thought, or will another, since these are one and the same soul

I. But you continue and say: “The state of the soul is one thing, and the affection of thought that arises from the soul is another. Therefore it should rather be judged that, whenever the soul imagines something for itself, it is occupied more deeply with its own internal movements. And if it appears to behold something else, that thing is more deeply depicted for it in the mirror of recollection. You think that this is its nature, not its punishment. Hence your soul is deceived in recognizing itself, because it embraces things opposed to it as though they belonged to it; and, affected through the bodily senses by the mockeries of illusions, it becomes so entangled in error that, as though absent from itself, it seeks itself, although it is itself the one seeking itself.

“For the soul is not what is sought, but what seeks; whatever it seeks is outside it. It has no need to seek anything except what is not with it. But it is with itself, because without itself it is nothing. It therefore ought not to have sought itself, because it could not exist without itself. Consequently, when it seeks itself without being without itself, it necessarily encounters something else, because it cannot find itself without itself.

“This is that delusion which the person who understands it grieves over; grieving, he groans, and with the prophet laments and says: ‘All day long I went about sorrowful, because my soul is full of illusions’ (Ps. 37:7–8).

“Yet the soul suffers such illusions in memory, from which it cannot stir up and bring forth any phantasms unless it had drawn them from the forms of bodies through the bodily senses. For either it imagines for itself the very things it took in through the body, or from what it saw it conjectures and fabricates what it did not see. It is nevertheless certain that it cannot imagine within a certain inner chamber of memory anything except what it received through the body.

“These things are not natural to it, but punitive. Since the soul, enticed by corporeal attractions, flowed down from the highest good—which for it is God—into the body, it justly suffers within itself what it unjustly loved outside itself.

“Do not therefore try to persuade me that this is the soul which you see rather being disturbed. For if it had remained in the sublimity of its former state, from which it voluntarily fell away, flesh would never have desired against the spirit, nor spirit against the flesh. And if the true human being—that is, the rational soul—had understood its honor, namely, the image of God, it would never have been compared with foolish beasts (Ps. 48:13, 21), so as to live an animal life.

“Hence there is before its eyes that tumult of corporeal images, continually thrusting itself before it, so that whenever it strives by reasoning either toward itself or toward its God, it is always called away toward corporeal things by corporeal phantasms.”

II. When you say that the soul is one thing and the soul’s thought another, you might perhaps have spoken more accurately if you had said that the things about which the soul thinks when it does not think about itself are not the soul itself, but that the thought itself is nothing other than the soul. For what you said should be assumed—that the soul is accustomed to rest to the point of thinking absolutely nothing—is false. The soul can vary what it thinks, but it cannot fail to think.

What else is that which we call dreaming, except that even when the body is tired and relaxed into sleep, the soul’s power is not free from thoughts? It is wholly where it thinks, because it thinks wholly.

But you are especially mistaken about the state of the soul because you believe that the soul is one thing and the soul’s power another. What the soul thinks is its accident, whereas that which thinks is its substance.

You must acknowledge the same concerning the will. For just as the whole soul is thought, so the whole soul is will; and what wills perfectly wills with its whole being. As was said above, whatever it wills is accidental to it, while willing itself is its substance.

Hence Sacred Scripture also gives a definition of perfect will, according to which the will is judged blameworthy or praiseworthy in accordance with what a person has willed in this or that manner. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). And elsewhere, in a favorable sense, the voices of the angels say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

Behold: love, as you suppose, is some portion of the mind; but, as reason teaches, it is the whole mind. If I love something with my whole love, do I not love it with my whole mind? And where is there room for the commandment, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Matt. 22:17), if love is thought to be a part of the soul? For if the soul loves with a part of itself, it does not love with its whole being. But if it loves with its whole being, it is wholly love.

It is said, and rightly said, that “God is love” (John 4:8). But that love is of such a kind that it can love only what is good, and through it nothing can be loved except rightly.

This love, which is the human soul, can, because of the mutability of its affections, burn with heavenly charity toward higher things—which for it is God alone—or flow downward through love toward things deserving condemnation. Whatever it loves, however, if it loves with its whole love, it loves with its whole being. And when it loves with its whole being, it is wholly love. Such unity, of course, does not exist in the body.

## CHAPTER XXV. An example from geometry, arithmetic, and dialectic to instruct the reader concerning what the soul sees by itself and what it sees through the body

[Col. 0730D]

I. But you say: “When he thinks about a dear person who is absent, does he satisfy his desires as though he were actually looking upon him?”

This, as I infer and plainly demonstrate, is by far the chief reason that has driven you, ignorant of yourself, to think that the soul is corporeal. I ask you to raise yourself for a little while above the bodily senses and, if you are able, perceive what kind and how great is the power of seeing in the mind; and, if you can, distinguish the sight of the mind from that of the body.

The body certainly sees nothing, because it feels nothing at all without the soul. Thus the mind sees corporeal things through the body, but incorporeal things by itself.

Let us now set this distinction aside, insofar as the present matter requires, so that it may become clear what the mind sees through the body and what it sees without the body. I believe that anyone who has received even some education knows, in the discipline of geometry, what a point and a line are. But since among those who may deign to read this there may be someone who does not know, let us investigate the matter by discussing it briefly.

A line is—as the most learned and eminent men have not merely stated but proved by reasoning—a simple length, which cannot be found at all in a body, since every body has length but is not itself length, nor can it be long without simultaneously being broad and deep. Thus, as they say, even if you imagine a spider’s thread, you have not imagined length alone, because it is a body. In accordance with its measure, it has an inseparable breadth and depth belonging to its length.

Therefore, since truth compels us to acknowledge that length is one thing and depth another, let us set breadth aside and think of length alone. I know that this length is not clearly seen by many. When the philosopher Marcius denied that he could see it, although he saw the lines drawn by craftsmen, the mathematician Adrastus said to him: “It is certainly no wonder that you have eyes like craftsmen and an intellect unlike Pythagoras.” But those who are slower should not despair on that account, provided that we yield to authority when perhaps we do not grasp the reasoning.

II. This length, then, which I began to discuss, when begun at a point and ended at a point, is called by the Greeks γραμμή (*grammē*), and by us *linea*, “line.”

Now, if you have been able to understand what length without breadth is, and have formed a line limited in length, place two equal lines opposite each other, ἀντιστάτας (*antistatas*, “opposed”), in a corresponding position. When you have done this, understand that you have not made a figure out of two equal lines. A figure is formed when a space is enclosed by equal or unequal lines whose ends touch one another. Therefore two equal lines, whether placed opposite each other or touching at their ends, do not enclose a figure.

But with three equal lines a triangular figure is formed; and this is an eternal and unchangeable principle, clearly evident to every human mind, even without instruction. Could a figure made from three equal lines touching one another at their ends ever be anything other than triangular? Is this truth now more true than it once was? Did it begin to be true at some time, or cease to be true at some time? Or would it not be easier for the corporeal world to perish—whose swollen and local forms are images of these nonlocal and incorporeal forms—than for any of these forms to be altered in appearance, moved from place to place, aged through time, or changed in any way?

To avoid drawing you through all the minutiae of this discipline, or holding your attention in examining the principles of plane figures, cubes, and pyramids, let us speak briefly, as we have done so far, about one figure only, for the sake of the circle’s perfection.

III. A circle is made from one line. But here you will rightly be reminded that a line without depth or breadth is more perfect, although it itself has something more perfect than it.

The point is, in the first place, the origin of the line: the line begins from it and ends at it, whereas the point cannot be shown to arise from anything or to end. [Note: [Col. 0731] Alternatively: “not.”] What the point contains in figures, the one contains in numbers.

This line, therefore, which can be cut across, cannot be split lengthwise. For if it is split, it has breadth; when it is cut, it is cut by a point, although the point itself is not cut. Length is therefore more perfect than breadth, because breadth admits division both across and along. Breadth is more perfect than depth, because depth can not only be split and cut, but can also be cut from the side.

Depth, then, cannot exist without breadth and length. And where these three are present, there is unquestionably a body. Breadth cannot exist without length. Length can exist without all these other dimensions, but it cannot exist without a point. The point, however, always exists without these things and needs nothing else in order to exist, because nothing can be the principle of what is one.

A circle is therefore made from one and the same curved line. But just as in triangles and quadrilaterals there are points at the angles by which the structure of the figures is established, so in a circle its center is possessed by a point, so that the circle may be formed according to a fixed measurement. For when you fix one arm of a compass and draw the other around externally from the center, observe, as far as you can, how the power of the center, through the stationary arm, governs the arm that is revolving, and how, where the center is not locally present, it nevertheless forms the circle by its power.

IV. If you direct the purified gaze of your mind here, what the soul is should already begin to gleam for you. Consider also this: if we consult the bodily sense, we may believe that two equal lines can be drawn together through the middle of a circle; yet manifest reason proves that two cannot be drawn through that same middle unless one is shorter.

It seems to me that, just as was evident above concerning the triangle, here too the principle of the circle remains stable under indissoluble and eternal laws.

Now tell me, if the soul sees these things locally, why is it that when I attempt to form some round, triangular, or quadrangular object out of bodies in the west, the reasoning of the round or square does not fail me, without any swelling or movement on my part, while at that same moment another person in the east can construct an equal bodily object according to the same law of the round and the square?

Do you see, even from the things the soul beholds, what the mind’s vision is? Do you understand that the intelligible and the one who understands cannot in any way be separated? Do you also recognize the difference between those forms that we see bodily and those that we contemplate mentally?

You see that these latter forms are the eternal world, of which this world is an image. Hence it is divinely said: “The form of this world is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31).

You also see that, although knowing the lengths, breadths, and depths of bodies is scarcely of any importance, there is another kind of knowledge that is sufficient, concerning which the Apostle says that we ought to know “what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18).

What benefit will it bring me to investigate anywhere the height of the corporeal heaven, the διαστήματα (*diastēmata*, “intervals” or “distances”) of the plane stars, the courses of the circles, or the intervals between individual things? What benefit will it bring me to learn the spaces of the earth or penetrate the depths of the abyss?

I think the Apostle did not wish to warn me about these things, which are not only laborious but also harmful, if, although through them one must pass onward to eternal and everlasting realities, one clings to them and remains in them.

V. Return now and observe that everything long is made long by length, whereas length itself cannot in any way be called long; just as everything chaste is made chaste by chastity, whereas chastity itself cannot be called chaste.

When you wish to contemplate pure length, or when you fix the eye of your mind upon a triangle or hexagon, cast away and flee, as far as you can, not only everything corporeal but also whatever may be similar to the corporeal.

When you see that a triangle is formed incorporeally and nonlocally either by three points and three lines, and that a circle is formed by a point or a line, behold also the power and superiority of numbers. Understand that the entire corporeal world is made numerable through numbers, whereas numbers themselves cannot be numbered.

For who—not merely speak, but even think worthily—could grasp that, although number exists from one, through one, and in one, it nevertheless has neither beginning nor end? If we say that one is the beginning of number, what shall we say is the beginning of one? Behold, you have the beginning of number in the beginning, so that number may be from it.

If we wish to count, we add one to one to make two, and one to two to make three, and one to three to make four. Thereafter, as often as we multiply one, so often the units are gathered into a total, so that ten times one is called ten, twenty times one twenty, one hundred times one one hundred, and one thousand times one one thousand. Thus you recognize that every number exists through one just as it proceeds from one.

It is evident that one cannot reach the end of number, which is altogether nonexistent, because beyond every number that exists from one, through one, and in one, there is always one more.

Yet these three are eternal together when we say “from one,” “through one,” and “in one”; therefore they are wholly nonlocal everywhere. They are always equal to the infinite, because there is no true one that is greater or one that is less.

These are the beginnings, means, and perfections of numbers; they themselves are neither begun, nor numbered, nor completed. I believe this because “there is no number of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5). For since number exists from one, through one, and in one, and can be numbered only in three ways—so that through the same number we may begin, count, and finish—it is itself the whole triad through which every number exists.

Behold what dwells in the human soul; behold what it has been granted to see with the eye of the heart. Where do we flee? Where are we scattered? Why are we outside ourselves within ourselves? Why do we seek our homeland locally, although we departed from it not by walking but by sinning? Why do we believe that darkness shines, when seeing it is certainly not seeing?

We seek truth. Do not think that it ought to be sought through intervals of place, or that it can be found through anything corporeal. Whoever clings to it will sufficiently separate himself from the body, not only by touching but even by thinking. We seek the nonlocal; let us not seek it, I ask you, through the local.

Truth itself has made for itself a likeness capable of possessing it. Let us offer it within ourselves what it has made. Let us not reproach our God by saying to Him: “You could not make something like yourself.” For if I am a body, I am not like You; He Himself will convict us concerning what we are.

## CHAPTER XXVI. God’s secret speech to the soul, and how it ought to question itself

[Col. 0734B]

Truth speaks to me in silence and says to me:

“You, surely, who believe that you are a body—how do you use an incorporeal word? I suppose your word is one thing—that is, your thought or purpose—and the voice of the word another; one thing is what sounds, another what is understood. For just as there can be a voice without a word, so there is a word without a voice.

“Yet your word uses the clothing of a voice so that it may sound in the ears, just as I use the clothing of flesh so that I may appear to human beings. When you speak, the service of the voice travels only as far as the ear, whereas the word penetrates nonlocally to the soul, because it approaches the one to whom you speak without departing from you.

“If one person hears you speaking, your entire word is with you and your entire word is with him. If two hear, they hear the whole of it. If many hear, they hear the whole of it—whole for all, whole for each, and whole for you.

“Do not lose within yourself so great a gift of mine, my likeness, which I most graciously bestowed upon you, so that you would not seek outside yourself the way to strive toward me.

“‘No one comes to the Father except through me’ (John 14:6); and ‘No one comes to me unless my Father draws him’ (John 6:44). And no one comes either to me or to the Father unless love is poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit, who is given only to one who believes well, hopes well, and seeks well.

“You were made human unto that Trinity in which we are one God, when it was said: ‘Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness’ (Gen. 1:26).” [Note: [Col. 0733] So the Paris edition. But the Lyon and Orthodox editions read: “Toward this reality, in which we are one God, you became human. Toward the Trinity,” etc.]

“Look within yourself, O human soul, and strive toward me. See your mind, see your word, see your will. For everything you think is in the mind; and whatever you remember wholly at once, you think wholly at once. And to wish to think and remember is to love to possess mind and thought.

“When you embrace your thought together with your mind—that is, when you remember that you are thinking—you certainly comprehend the whole of your thought with your whole mind. And when you think of your whole love or your mind with your whole thought, as you think that you love or remember, you think your whole mind with your whole thought. And with your whole love you love that same whole mind and that same whole thought, when you love to remember and to think.

“Yet there is no one who does not love to remember and think, and to love this very act itself. When the memory of your thought and love is present to you in your mind, if you remember as much as those things contain, your mind is as great as they are. And when you think of your love or your mind, if you think of them as fully as they are, your thought is as great as they are. And if you love your mind or your thought according to its measure, they and your love are certainly equal.

“If each of these three loves, thinks, or remembers itself wholly and all at once, the three together will not be greater than either the whole mind remembering all together, or the whole thought knowing all together, or the whole love loving all together. [Note: [Col. 0735] Alternatively: “the whole of it.”]

“By my radiance you recognize that these things are in you and, more precisely, that you are these things, if you bring to me those eyes with which I am worthy to be seen. No one sees me, even though incorporeal, unless purified; therefore, if you are a body, do not suppose that I can be seen by you.

“I and the Father and our love are one God; you, a rational mind, and your word or love, are one human being, made in the likeness of your author, not created equal to Him—created, indeed, not begotten. You yourself were formed; you are not the one who forms.

“Withdraw from those things that are beneath you, less formed—that is, less beautiful—than you are. Approach the forming form, so that you may be more beautiful, and join yourself to it continually; for you will receive more of its beauty the more deeply you impress yourself upon it by the weight of love.

“From it you will obtain the unchangeable state of this image, from which you received your beginning.”

Truth speaks these and similar words to the ear of the heart within, admonishing us to recognize that, because we were made in the likeness of the incorporeal God, not in the likeness of the corporeal world, we are incorporeal—not only because we are like the incorporeal God, but also because we are unlike the corporeal world.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That anyone can see a dear person who is bodily absent with the mind

Behold: concerning the state or vision of the rational soul, I think I have given a sufficient answer regarding the soul’s nonlocality and incorporeality, touching briefly upon causes rather than investigating them fully, since the magnitude of the question would require an infinite number of arguments.

Now, clearly understanding bodily vision, which is so different from and inferior to the vision of the mind, do not allow yourself to be further tossed about by this uncertainty: if, as you yourself say, you think of your dear person while he is absent, do not for that reason believe him absent because he does not appear bodily to you.

For if he is dear to you in that part of himself in which both of you are human beings, and through which you love one another with reciprocal love, he is as present to you as you yourself are to yourself. Whatever you are substantially, he is also.

The vision of the intellect belongs to the soul. If you see yourself, you see him who is nothing other than yourself. If he were bodily present, he would certainly make himself known to you through bodily signs. If, from those signs, you happened to receive an indication that he was rather your enemy, your soul, repelled by the disparity of your affections, would in a certain manner recoil from his soul; and although you were bodily in one place, indeed in the same, if that can be said, you would be sufficiently separated by the difference of your wills.

Since this is so, I do not think that souls are divided by bodily separation, when we see that they can be separated even while their bodies are joined together. Accordingly, it is of little value that bodies effect mutual representations of souls, unless either the image of God is sought in one another through those very bodies, or the souls themselves are sought.

For it is miserable and wholly contrary to truth that the image of God—that is, the true human being—should be sought through the body rather than through itself. It is sought and recognized through itself if it is sought through the image of God. Every rational soul is the image of God.

Therefore whoever seeks the image of God seeks both himself and his neighbor. And whoever recognizes it by seeking it within himself recognizes the same image in every human being.

You are not unjustified, however, in complaining that your dear person is absent from you when you love the body in him. You can love nothing other than the body in one whom you believe to be nothing except a body.

Love your God; love your dear person in your God, the image of your God. Let him, in turn, by loving you, love God in God. If both of you seek one thing, you strive toward one thing; you will always be with one another, because you abide in one.

I do not see how it could happen that bodies placed together can be present to one another, while souls cannot be present to one another in one thing.

But since this book demands an end, and since, although I have touched upon certain matters superficially, I have passed over many things for the sake of brevity, yet have not passed over everything that the eminence of the subject requires, let us begin at the start of the second volume the matters that remain to be discussed.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0735D]

## CHAPTER I. Why God so often allows the truth to be attacked

When I repeatedly considered with myself how the highest truth could knowingly have so many enemies, after much treatment of this same question a not implausible reason, as I think, appeared: everything is better recognized by comparison with its opposites.

Thus light is more pleasing when set against darkness, life against death, and truth against falsehood. It was therefore necessary that these distinctions should receive defenders corresponding to their qualities, so that the defender of falsehood would not remain hidden, nor the champion of truth lack an opponent. In this way the former would not do greater harm by remaining concealed, nor would the latter grow sluggish through idleness.

## CHAPTER II. How the philosophers investigated the truth of the world and gradually reached God at last
## I.

And since it has been given to the mortal race by nature to seek hidden things more earnestly, to desire what is denied more avidly, and to love what is attained more deeply because it was attained slowly—and since truth is loved more ardently the longer it is desired, the more laboriously it is sought, or the more slowly it is found—this has consequently come about: philosophers too, possessing outstanding intellects, employing many-sided disciplines, and holding conflicting opinions, have continued through long ages to seek the same truth, beginning with the Italian Pythagoras or the Ionian Thales. Among them there have always been some who, despite the disagreements of others, discerned or judged something worthy of so great an inquiry, at least in part of their work.

Hence the Apostle to the Gentiles does not so much judge philosophers ignorant of the truth as accuse them of despising what they have known, saying: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are perceived and understood through the things that have been made; likewise his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse: for although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. 1:20–21). Therefore they knew him, and the human mind entered into the secret of the hidden divinity. Having passed beyond all corporeal things and traversed them, it saw that he was the creator of the universe—one who not only surpassed all corporeal things, as an irrational soul does, nor even surpassed that irrational soul, as a rational soul does, but who far excelled all these together by an incorporeal power.

For the mind saw that the body is moved through places and times, whether it moved from one place to another or changed its age through the passage of time. It therefore paused for a little within itself and, contemplating with no small dread its own power, doubted whether it ought to seek something above itself or remain established within itself. But, while doubting, it could not doubt that it was not God, since ignorance was the cause of its doubt; yet no one would doubt unless ignorant. God, however, would be ignorant of nothing and therefore could not doubt.

[Col. 0737C]

## II.

Moreover, the soul perceived that it necessarily remained ignorant and consequently doubted, with this added consideration: even if it was not subjected to motion through place, it was moved through time by affection. Nor could it be the principal foundation of things if it could be moved either by place or by time, since nothing can be moved except through something else. That in which the universe would stand would itself stand in itself. Thus, reasoning more deeply about its author, it recognized what I mentioned in the preceding book: that nothing can be moved except by what is unmoved.

Therefore the soul must stand in order to move the body through time and place; and God stands in himself, moving the soul through time and the body alike through place and time. And since there can be no beginning of a beginning, something must be understood here concerning immensity and eternity. For just as God began from no one, so he stands in no one. The soul therefore judged that it must pass, not without some intermediary, from the lowest things, which are corporeal, to the highest, which is God.

It found itself situated midway between the extremes: it was not like any body, since that would make it like God; nor could it be equal to God, since, although it had begun from him, it was not made from his substance.

## III.

It also perceived, in the fullness of things, that one thing exists which judges according to truth but is not judged; another which both judges and is judged; and another which is judged but does not judge.

According to truth, God judges and is not judged; the soul judges and is judged; bodies are judged but do not judge.

The judge is least deceived when it adheres to that according to which it judges, and most deceived when it collapses toward that about which it judges.

It also understood that, because of the immutable force of contraries, just as darkness is contrary to light and nothingness to being, so body is contrary to what is incorporeal. It saw that the likeness of anything cannot exist in its contrary, since the unmoved order of things does not permit something dead to live, something blind to see, or a substance to be simultaneously both being and nothingness.

Understanding, then, that something in the human soul is like God—for God is illuminating light, while the soul is light capable of being illuminated—it concluded without doubt that it was incorporeal. It added this consideration: if the soul were a body, and this same likeness to God existed, then God would consequently be corporeal. It rightly preferred, therefore, on account of the likeness of the Creator, to exalt the creature rather than humble the Creator on account of that same likeness. For it knew with certainty that the bond between two similar things is indissoluble: either both are incorporeal or both corporeal.

It also recognized that among substantial things there are some which are not merely dissimilar in appearance but contrary in natural force, as water and flame are; yet both are corporeal. It would therefore be astonishing if two dissimilar and mutually contrary things, such as water and flame, could both be corporeal, but two similar and mutually agreeing things—God and the soul—could not both be incorporeal.

[Note: [Col. 0737] Another reading: “according to which it had judged and would judge.”]

[Note: [Col. 0738] Another reading: “to be judged by the judging truth.”]

## CAPUT III. Greek Philosophers Are Used as Witnesses Concerning Corporeal and Incorporeal Things, with the Example of the Camel and the Ant.

### I.

Having therefore examined, as far as I could, the books of the philosophers who employed such arguments, and having rejected the base rabble, I selected the better ones to bear witness to the truth for the present. It would indeed be easy to produce their opinions in abundance—not because we lack arguments of our own, but because it is more remarkable that our own people should fight against us and outsiders fight on our behalf.

Nor would I have cared to take anything from them in return, unless this friend of the body had displayed to us certain scarecrows of deeper learning merely by mentioning the name of philosophy. From those whom he calls against the truth, then, let him receive the voice of truth. Let him first hear the loud, many-toned trumpet of Pythagoras and the clarion of Plato, the twin instruments of Greece. Let him not swell with the mere vanity of names, but grow rich on the many-sided truth of their arguments.

Since Pythagoras himself wrote nothing, his opinion must be sought from his successors. Among them I find Philolaus of Tarentum especially distinguished. In many books he discusses, with considerable obscurity, the intelligible structure of things and what each thing signifies. Before deciding about the substance of the soul, he argues wonderfully concerning measures, weights, and numbers according to geometry, music, and arithmetic. Through these he affirms that the whole universe came into existence, agreeing in this with the statement of Scripture addressed to God: “You have ordered all things by measure, weight, and number” (Wis. 11:21).

I am astonished that our adversary has thrown this statement from divine reading at us. For he says in these words:

“God indeed made all things from nothing. Just as he established them by his work, so he incorporated matter into all things, among which the soul too is reckoned. Just as he distributed weight, number, and measure, so he assigned quantity.”

### II.

Observe, my good expert, this eloquent and learned teacher of the present age: he does not wish anything incorporeal to have been created, and he says that everything corporeal has been incorporated. Into what, I ask, is that which is a body incorporated? If you perhaps used *in* instead of *not*, so that you intend *incorporated* to mean “not corporeal,” you freely grant us more than we ask.

For if the author of things, who made all things, did not make them corporeal, then whatever exists is without a body. Indeed, whatever exists without a body must necessarily be incorporeal—what the Greeks more elegantly call *asōmaton* (ἀσώματον), “incorporeal.”

But if you used this kind of expression straightforwardly, you fell unknowingly into error concerning the truth. Yet through the same ignorance you slipped by only one grammatical particle: you said that everything had been incorporated, although it is sufficiently clear that the substance of the twofold creation was composed according to such an orderly law that everything created is both incorporeal and incorporated, but not everything is corporeal and animate.

Accordingly, an incorporated body could not be called “incorporated” in the sense of having been put into a body. For incorporation plainly belongs to that nature which, before being incorporated, was not a body and, after being incorporated, is not a body.

But if by saying that everything had been incorporated you perhaps meant something which could plainly be said, although it ought not to have been said—namely, that everything had been made corporeal—then you have departed alike from the proper meaning of the word and from the reasoning of truth. For if every creature is corporeal, nothing has been incorporated; but if something created is incorporeal, then not every creature is corporeal.

### III.

But one and the same cause entangles you in this multiplicity of error: namely, great ignorance of things combined with astonishing presumption of knowledge. Hence it comes about that you either believe spirits which have been incorporated to be bodies, or define bodies as incorporated.

In these dialectical conclusions of yours, always remember that reproach of profound error which you seek to brand upon others. The divine word also warns you that one must first remove one’s own beam, so that one may remove the speck from another’s eye (Matt. 7:3–5; Luke 6:41–42).

Therefore, since you do not challenge people as though they were uncertain opponents in battle, but strike the peaceful with the sword of insult; and since you have said that measure, weight, and number are implanted in every part of creation—for these are plainly present together in all bodies—and since you decide that the soul is a body, I ask: what is its measure, what its number, and what its weight?

If the measure of the living body makes the measure of the soul that animates it, because an external body, like a vessel, encloses the soul as a lesser body, then, as you say, the soul’s quantity must be judged according to the quantity of the body.

### IV.

Oh, if it were possible for me to speak with you face to face and openly about these matters, I would act generously and concede certain things to you from my own position. I would not immediately inquire about the human being, but would first ask you, as one supposedly skilled in these matters, to admit the truth in a clear answer.

Would you judge the souls of the ant and the camel according to intelligence or according to bulk?

If according to intelligence, it would be clearer than daylight that the camel’s soul surpasses the ant’s soul in such a way that the camel is almost as much smaller than the ant in soul as it is greater in body.

If bulk pleased you in such a comparison, I would repeat the same argument and nevertheless ask: if the measure of the soul is the measure of the body, why does the camel fall below the measure of its body in intelligence, while the ant rises above the measure of its body?

Perhaps the grand words which now safely fly from you would come to a halt. I would present this same double alternative and offer you whichever one you preferred.

If you chose bodily bulk, I would set against it the ant’s tiny body. But if you chose the power of the soul, I would prove that this same power has no correspondence with bulk, since I could establish nothing of it in the corporeal magnitude of the camel.

Here too I would bring against you that line of Maro—most truly spoken of bees:

> They turn mighty spirits within a narrow breast.

[Note: [Col. 0739] Virgil, *Georgics* 4.23.]

### V.

When I began to discuss the condition of the human being, I would demand from you, as a new geometer, a ten-foot measuring rod for judging and distinguishing the minds of all persons.

If you perhaps wished to use this refuge, saying that invisible things cannot be measured by visible things, I would immediately reply that, from the magnitude of the body which enclosed the soul, it would be possible to measure the soul which filled the body.

If you said that this was impossible, I would ask most insistently why something could not be done with one kind of body which could be done with all bodies.

If you agreed that it was possible, I would say to you in prophetic language: “Go to the ant, you sluggard, and observe her ways, and emulate them” (Prov. 6:6)—that is, her foresight.

Unless perhaps we should believe that we were instructed by the heavenly oracle for this reason: so that we might learn the art of walking from the ant. In this address, however, do not trouble yourself about the care of walking, but about skill in action:

> And just as the ants, remembering winter,  
> plunder a great heap of grain  
> and store it in their shelter,

[Note: [Col. 0740] Virgil, *Aeneid* 4.402.]

so every human being, having fallen through the first-created man’s sin into embodiment among irrational creatures, must provide—lest winter come upon your flight (Matt. 24:20)—through the warmth of faith and devotion in action. At the same time, understand that mighty spirits are enclosed in the small bodies of the ant and the bee.

For no great thing occupying a place can be contained by a small thing occupying a place. The bee has a small body and a great soul. It is therefore not contained by a body outside itself; consequently, it exists, but nothing can exist outside itself. It is therefore wholly in the body. Yet something corporeally great cannot be contained by something corporeally small, because each thing occupying a place fills as great a place as its magnitude requires.

Either, then, the soul is without place and will therefore be incorporeal, or it will not be wholly with itself. But nothing can exist except with itself. Therefore a great thing is present without occupying a place in a small thing. The soul is not, then, local; and nothing without place is corporeal. Therefore the soul is not corporeal.

Whatever is not corporeal is not to be judged by bulk. The magnitude of the soul, therefore, is not inferred from the magnitude of the body.

### VI.

Let us now see where you will escape. The bee denies you the magnitude of the body, and the camel denies you the magnitude of the soul. Do you see whether your preferred opinion begins to collapse under arguments of this kind?

The magnitude of the soul cannot be subjected to numbers, weights, and measures according to corporeal quantities. It is both small within something great and holds the whole, and great within something small without overflowing.

But perhaps the soul cannot be measured corporeally, though it can be weighed. Let the person dare to say that he knows how many pounds a soul can weigh, when he claims to comprehend how many feet long it is.

The traces of numbers in bodies are recognized in three ways. First, in place: for a body to be greatest or smallest, it must be one—that is, it must derive this from number.

Second, in how many parts it consists of. As we have already said, these parts are right and left, above and below, front and back.

Third, in how many parts every body can be divided according to the aforesaid differences among its parts. Each part of those bodily parts will likewise, because of the primordial force of number, be one body, consist of the same number of parts, and in turn be capable of division into parts.

Now you must consider whether, although there is one soul in each living creature, this same soul can be divided so that each part of the soul is again a soul, just as every part of a body is a body.

Since I believe that no sane person can say this, there is no reason to spend time discussing causes which by their very nature are so clear that they seem rather to be obscured by minute argument.

## CAPUT IV. On the Measure, Number, and Weight of the Body.

### I.

Now, unless you despise it, direct your attention more closely to this point, so that the divine power of measure, weight, and number may be disclosed to you insofar as it deigns to be seen.

We read that it is said of God: “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 10:11). You used this testimony especially for the purpose of wishing to prove from it that certain corporeal quantities have also been implanted in our souls.

Let us see, then: where and when did this measure, this weight, and this number exist or begin to exist, so that God might form all things according to their pattern?

If nothing is uncreated except the Creator, then these things were created. If they were created, God did not order all things by measures, numbers, and weights, since he did not form these things according to such measures, numbers, and weights.

But it is impious to oppose divine authority. Therefore all created things were made according to numbers, weights, and measures.

Measure, weight, and number, then, were not created, since all things were not created according to them if they too were created.

Here we must strive with all the powers of thought to recognize, in whatever way possible, that the principal weight is not what is weighed, but that by which it is weighed; nor is the number the thing that is counted, but that by which it is counted; nor is measure the thing that is measured, but that by which it is measured.

Likewise, magnitude is not the same as what is great, equality is not the same as what is equal, and beauty is not the same as what is beautiful. For nothing created is great in itself; rather, something is called great by comparison with something smaller.

Hence we call a mountain small and a grain of millet large; we call a fly large and an ox small. But when we come to the magnitude of the Creator himself, since it cannot be compared, it is neither greater nor smaller.

The same reasoning applies to those principal forms which Plato calls ideas. According to the same law of the square, we make both a square table and a square marketplace. Even when the marketplace is a larger square, it is not more square.

From this you ought to recognize that unweighed weight, immeasurable measure, and innumerable number are three things which together are co-eternal, always undivided, wholly present everywhere and wherever they are: the one God.

### II.

For all bodies by which we count, weigh, or measure anything are countable, weighable, and measurable. The number of bodies has a definite limit; the balance has a definite weight for its weights; and the ten-foot rod has a definite measure.

From the magnitude of the ten-foot rod one may proceed downward to ounces, half-ounces, and the smallest possible unit, below which nothing exists. One may also proceed upward to the greatest magnitudes, even to the currently inaccessible spaces of the universe itself to our senses.

Whatever is finite has a definite limit of magnitude. The entire mass of the universe, therefore, since it is composed of finite bodies—for one body sets a boundary to another—is undoubtedly itself finite and therefore measurable.

If the human mind thinks of spaces beyond it, it does not doubt that they can be treated according to the same principle of measure through corporeal forms—provided that some place exists outside the universe. But since there cannot be a place outside every place, local measure does not extend where there is no place.

And when there is nothing that can be measured, that by which it can be measured nevertheless remains, since an immeasurable measure is not lacking for what is finite and measurable. So too the principle of weight does not perish when that which can be weighed ceases. Nor does number end with what is finite and countable.

Therefore, if the splendor of immeasurable light glimmers upon us with some radiance, you will necessarily be warned by it to set aside for a little the deception of corporeal visions and tell us: to whom among us is the form of a corporeal ten-foot measure visible?

[Note: [Col. 0741] Another reading: “to whom is it not visible?”]

But since you will not deny that this can be contemplated by a body—unless perhaps you are excessively angry—I consequently ask whether you say that the immeasurable measure of which we spoke above is perceptible by the soul or by the body.

But truth will not so abandon anyone that he should claim that divine things are visible to the body, since the body cannot even see bodies unless the soul knows them—or, to speak more accurately, since the body itself perceives nothing independently, but the soul perceives things through the body.

There are therefore two powers of seeing in the soul. It sees measure, weight, and number through itself; it sees measurable, countable, and weighable things through the body. Through the body it sees what is like the body—that is, bodies; but it sees incorporeal things through itself, since it is itself like them.

### III.

Now, if you please, since all things have been ordered by measures, weights, and numbers, let us seek their signs in created things.

The lowest of all the elements is certainly earth. In a round body, that which is at the center is evidently the lowest, since there is no lowest point at the outermost edges of a sphere.

Therefore every portion of earth, whether large or small—a little stone, or the finest speck of dust that cannot be touched by a visible point—has measure according to its own size and number according to the arrangement of its parts, by which upper things are separated from lower things, right from left, and front from back.

Hence even the smallest thing can be divided into two, because it is a body.

Its weight is perceived from this: when even the smallest particle is lifted from its origin and released into water, the element above it, it does not cease its tireless motion until by its natural weight it reaches the ground of the earth.

The same path of reasoning must be followed with the remaining bodies. A drop of water which you lift with a dipped finger has measure according to its size and number according to the separation of its parts; if you release it into the air according to the law of weight, it does not remain there but reaches its proper place.

The same reasoning applies to air, none of which can remain beneath water or be carried above fire. If this happens in some way, the necessity of weight will cause it either to burst out naturally from below or to fall spontaneously from above.

That air is measurable and numerable according to the number of its parts is also clear, as I think, from the fact that people know that the corporeal universe can be measured, of which air is one-third.

The element of fire likewise stands in fourth place. It receives numbers according to its parts and is subject to measures according to its extent, since it is finite.

This terrestrial fire has as its weight a kind of seed of the higher fires, directed upward. The more abundant the fuel by which it is nourished, the greater its power. As though making its way toward its homeland, it breaks through large masses of densely packed air by its subtle nature; and unless it were overcome by the depth of that other element toward which it is naturally borne, it would reach it.

## CAPUT V. On the Measure, Number, and Weight of the Soul.

[Col. 0743D]

It is now clear that nothing corporeal lacks measure, weight, and number. Since these three likewise involve divisible unity, local weight, and measurable magnitude, let us ask whether they exist in the soul to the same extent as in the body.

We call a body great according to length, breadth, and height, and we judge its space to be large or small according to its capacity. Thus anything that receives any body receives as much as it is capable of containing according to its size.

Now, passing beyond the level of lower creation, observe the higher creature and measure the magnitude of the soul according to its capacity.

The human soul is capable of wisdom, for it is capable of that by which it understands. Therefore, just as it cannot be called capable of wisdom before it has acquired wisdom, so it cannot be called wise before it becomes a participant in wisdom.

Here, then, I ask you: do you judge this to be an extent of place, or something without place by which wisdom is contained?

I judge it thus: if the wise soul is capable of wisdom according to spatial extent, then wisdom is great according to bulk. But since truth does not permit this to be said [Note: [Col. 0743] Another reading: “because it permits.”], what contains wisdom is without place, so that what is contained may also be without place.

Here you have the magnitude of the human soul without bulk.

Now consider the nature of number.

### II.

You have observed, I suppose, that the signs of numbers in bodies consist in this: bodies are numerable when, according to the pre-eminent equality of number, their parts correspond to one another through equality. Just as there is complete equality between one and one, two and two, and three and three, so we call that body numerable which is formed according to a fixed proportion.

Thus, for example, the human body has its paired parts arranged opposite one another so that they do not differ in magnitude, space, or position, as with the ears and the eyes. The individual parts, such as the nose and mouth, likewise occupy the middle position.

And in order that they may be beautiful, they imitate the harmony of perfect equality.

To the extent, then, that we find the truth of number in the human soul, the soul itself must first harmonize its manner of action with itself according to the equality of the virtues, so that justice corresponds to wisdom and fortitude to temperance. This equality is indeed numerable, since anything is closer to number insofar as it is more harmonious.

But I judge that what is more properly numerable in the soul is that by which it is scientifically acquainted with number—not numerable through parts, as the body is, but capable of recognizing number itself and judging according to it.

That three and four make seven, and that three and seven make ten, no one except the human soul either can know or will be able to know.

Therefore, just as it was clear concerning measure, so it is sufficiently evident concerning numbers: they are present visibly in the body, but intellectually in the soul.

### III.

It remains now to discuss weight.

It has become clear that the weight of bodies is that by which they are naturally carried toward the regions from which they originally arise, and that they do not rest until, having traversed the space of another element, they reach their own.

The weight of the soul, however, is its will, which is more properly called love. Through it the soul loves either itself or anything else. Whether it loves incorporeal things, such as true wisdom, or desires corporeal things for the body, such as beautiful bodies, it is carried by the weight of love, which has no place, until it possesses what it loves.

Therefore the weight of a body, wherever it carries the body, draws its measures and numbers inseparably along with it.

Likewise, the weight—that is, the love—of the soul compels memory and counsel to accompany it toward what it loves, because it can remember or think of nothing except that for which it burns with love.

Hence it is divinely said to humanity: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Matt. 22:37). The meaning is that, just as the body is compelled by its weight toward its proper place, so the soul may be brought by its weight toward its homeland.

By this weight, however, the soul is not only joined to other things; it is also itself made solid, because through the love which lies between counsel and mind, the mind is loved by counsel and counsel by the mind.

## CAPUT VI. On the Measure, Number, and Weight of the Divine Trinity, and How the Trinity Itself Is These Three.

Thus, too, the most exalted unity of the supreme Trinity, surpassing all things incorporeally, is, as they say, measure without measure, weight without weight, and number without number.

The weight by which these same three are ineffably one with one another is the love of the Father and the Son. The Apostle expressly identifies this with the Holy Spirit when he says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). He clearly shows that, by this weight—namely, divine love—that ineffable number and that measure are borne in stability wherever such a weight is present.

These three are therefore inseparable in the body, but much more so in the soul; and they are undivided in the soul, but much more so in themselves.

And just as nothing came into existence without the one Creator, that is, the Trinity itself, so nothing at all can exist which does not subsist in a threefold manner and yet remain one. Every body, therefore, is one, measurable, countable, and weighable.

Every rational soul subsists through three undivided realities—memory, counsel, and will—and through them is capable of measure, weight, and number.

According to these it judges all measurable, weighable, and countable things—that is, bodies. If it were a body, it would certainly not contain incorporeal things, just as a body could itself be judged but could not judge concerning bodies.

Thus the pattern of the united Trinity flows from the highest, which is God, through the middle, which is the soul, to the lowest, which is the body. It impresses its signs upon bodies and grants knowledge of itself to souls: forming the former visibly and the latter intelligibly.

Therefore, when nothing but absence can contain substance, and nothing becomes one except through three, as we argued above—when there is as much unity in the body, that is, in the vestige of the Trinity, as there is in the soul, that is, in the image of the Trinity; and again when there is as much in the image as in the Trinity itself.

[Note: [Col. 0745] Another reading: “to the lowest, which is corporeal.”]

[Note: [Col. 0745] Orthodox text: “nothing receives substance except essence.” Perhaps read: “nothing receives substance except essence.”]

## CAPUT VII. Pagan Witnesses Are Used to Show That There Are No Corporeal Measures or Local Weights in the Soul.

### I.

But since this is not now a suitable time to discuss at greater length the pre-eminence of this question, I have lingered over these matters only as long as I think sufficient for prudent people to recognize fully that there are no corporeal measures in the soul, no local weights, and no spatial extension of parts. Rather, the soul perceives that which no place contains, no weight moves, and no division diminishes.

Now, learned judge [Note: [Col. 0746] Another reading: “ignorant of what is just.”], once you have proved that you are capable of delivering a just judgment, decide whether something which receives what has no place is itself a place; whether something which cannot be cut apart is divisible; or whether something which contains the infinite is measurable.

I now return to Philolaus, from whom I digressed a long way earlier. In the third book of his work entitled *On Rhythms and Measures* (περὶ ῥυθμῶν καὶ μέτρων), he speaks thus about the human soul:

“The soul is inserted into the body through number and an immortal and likewise incorporeal harmony.”

And again, after other remarks:

“The body is loved by the soul because without it the soul cannot use the senses. After it has been separated from the body by death, it leads an incorporeal life in the world.”

I am not now retracing the path of the arguments through the most intricate minutiae of the questions by which Philolaus made these propositions plausible, whoever may oppose them. If anyone should burn with curiosity or zeal concerning them, let him draw from the very source itself.

For my purpose, it is enough that, in order to establish authority, I have brought forward the testimony of so great a philosopher, just as it will be appropriate to present briefly the testimony of the others hereafter. It is unjust to demand of anyone both argument and testimony at once.

### II.

Archytas of Tarentum, likewise a Pythagorean, in the work which he magnificently published under the title *On the Nature of Things*, after a subtle and extensive discussion of numbers, says:

“The soul has been composed according to the pattern of unity. It rules the body without occupying a place, just as unity rules among numbers.”

What, I ask, could be said more precisely? What more truly?

It has been composed according to the pattern of unity because it was made according to the image of unity. For this reason unity is the principal pattern of forms: things capable of being formed receive forms from it, while it received form from no one.

Eromenes of Tarentum, from the same school of Pythagoras, after presenting indissoluble arguments in support of his position, declares concerning the soul:

“The soul is altogether different from the body. It remains vigorous when the body is numb; it sees when the body is blind; it lives when the body is dead.”

But whence, if this is so, does he say that he does not know by what principle it is so?

I am not now pursuing the opinions of all the philosophers of the Pythagorean family in such a way that, by piling them up at greater length, I should make my own work out of books belonging to others. I consider it sufficient that I have brought forward clear teachings from the Pythagorean school concerning the present question.

I am certain that no learned person will deny that Archippus, Epaminondas, Aristeus, Gorgiades, Diodorus, and all the successors of Pythagoras held and committed to writing this same opinion. If I wished to set forth the multitude of their names—not to mention their opinions—in the same way, I would produce a whole volume.

### III.

Let Plato now come forward. From him it truly becomes clear how great a good the human race neglects in itself, especially in our own age. In this age, when sayings and deeds have been issued from heaven, religion has been proclaimed to such an extent that, with labor almost removed for believers, in the time of faith it attains the fruit of knowledge and receives the reward of labor without the work having been accomplished.

For this reason I cannot sufficiently wonder at the soul of this Plato, who so many ages before the Virgin’s childbirth, before God’s incarnation, before the resurrection of humanity, and before the ineffable unity of the supreme Trinity had been proclaimed among the nations, sought out, discovered, and proclaimed—with admirable daring, astonishing intellect, and inimitable eloquence—the One and three persons in the divinity: God the Father, the paternal mind, art or counsel, and the mutual love of these two, one supreme, co-eternal, and undivided divinity.

He taught and demonstrated not merely that this ought to be believed, but that it is so. He did not merely teach that this ought to be believed; he proved that it is so.

I cannot persuade myself that this philosopher’s soul was corporeal. And if, perhaps through a precipitous fall into folly, any soul is to be judged a body, I would judge those souls corporeal which believe themselves to be bodies.

By this I do not disparage the race of souls; rather, against my own inclination, I mark certain people because of the wickedness of their opinion. I indicate what becomes of human beings when ignorance holds them so completely that they do not know themselves to be unlearned, while nevertheless claiming for themselves the privilege of knowledge.

While they spit the froth of childish words into untrained ears, they deceive themselves by one and the same falsehood concerning their own knowledge, and deceive others by teaching them. They are like Lysias, whom Plato himself rebukes in the *Phaedrus* for pouring out empty words about things. Plato argues there that it is worse to be skilled in words but ignorant of causes than, while ignorant of things, not to know the words for them. He would rather have uninstructed silence than talkative incompetence.

Hence Cicero too says in the first book *On the Orator*: “Eloquence is knowledge of comprehending very many things; without this, fluency of words is empty and ridiculous.”

And shortly afterward:

“For speech ought to blossom and overflow from knowledge of things. If the orator has not apprehended and understood the subject underlying it, his speech is empty and almost childish.”

But more on this elsewhere.

IV. In the *Phaedrus*, however, Plato declares concerning the soul: “The soul,” he says, “is immortal; it is always moved by itself and is the cause of motion for other things. But a body is not moved by itself.” He does not merely say, “it moves other things,” but “it is the cause of motion for other things,” observing, as a man of outstanding intelligence, that there are some things for which movement is proper, but which are the cause of motion in something else. For whatever moves voluntarily is generally itself the cause of its own movement. But whatever is moved either unknowingly or unwillingly has the causes of its movement in one who knows or compels it.

Nor does this conflict with our earlier arguments, in which we say that the soul moves itself, although we say that the principal pivot of movements is in God. For that very capacity—to move voluntarily—comes almost from God; namely, just as the cause of the mind’s movement is its will, so God is the cause of the substance that exercises the will. For although the power to will is from God, not every movement of our will will be from God. Or so, at least, I think: when we sin by our will, the cause of our movement is from ourselves, lest we make God the author of sins.

Therefore, if a body is not moved by itself, and what is the cause of its own movement is not a body—because the soul possesses within itself the causes of its movement—the soul is not a body.

V. The same Plato, in the book he wrote *On Nature* (περὶ Φύσεως), says: “The soul of every living creature is not corporeal; it moves itself and is also the mover of other things that are moved naturally.”

In the *Phaedo*, moreover, Socrates speaks thus before the same Plato, with Simmias, Cebes, and other philosophers: since we see there statements that agree very closely with our own views and are exceedingly suitable to them—not merely supported by the prejudice of authority but also strengthened by the power of reason—we should observe that, beyond the natural vigor of the human mind, these souls, which pursued such remote matters, entered such closed places, and saw such hidden things so knowledgeably, were for this very reason inspired by the light of truth, so that a doctrine might one day be divinely proclaimed to the whole world for the salvation of the human race [Note: [Col. 0747] Others: “published”; others: “would be published”]; and that among the uneducated minds of the nations it might employ the testimonies of the gentiles. Thus the gentile world, blinded by the denser darkness of ignorance and hardened into a kind of ice by the cold of unbelief, might yield to the warmth of evangelical truth, if that same truth had resounded from the mouths even of its opponents.

Or why should we not believe that these very things, which we recognize as useful for refuting the ignorance even of our own people, were divinely provided for our use through philosophers? Thus, in the *Phaedo*, he persuades Socrates and says that true reason speaks as follows:

“So long as we have a body, and our soul is mingled with this evil, we shall never fully attain what we have long desired. Now we desire knowledge of the truth. For, first, the body imposes upon us innumerable and endless occupations by which we are worn down because of the necessary provision of food and daily nourishment. Then, if illnesses have attacked us, they prevent us from being able to seek and discover the truth. For the body is burdened with innumerable desires and fears, with visions of various things and their objects of appetite, and with a kind of boundless madness, so that, in comparison with it, we cannot even think wisely about anything.

“And whenever we have or have made some free time for philosophizing, even then the body intrudes into our very thoughts, bringing a crowd of errors into the mind, so that, because it blinds us, we cannot clearly perceive the truth. Accordingly, one point alone, and that most evidently, is proved to us in every inquiry: if we ever wish to know anything in good faith, we must withdraw from the body and consider things in the soul itself.

“For then we seem likely to attain what we desire and what we profess to love, when we have died; for while we live, we must despair. Indeed, if it is established that the soul, while mixed with the body, can perceive nothing pure, it follows that one of two things must be true: either it is never and nowhere possible for a human being to attain true knowledge, or it is possible only after we have departed from life. For the soul of the dead is free and released from the body.

“While we live, therefore, we shall approach and draw near to knowledge only if we use the body not at all, or as little as possible, and do not surrender the soul to its society except insofar as necessity requires. In this way we shall be least filled with the vicious and turbulent nature of the body; rather, insofar as we are able, we shall be pure from its contamination. And if we act thus, departing incorrupt and sincere, we shall come to all things incorrupt and sincere.”

[Col. 0749A]

VI. I thought these words should be excerpted verbatim from the dialogue of a philosopher of such eminence and inserted into our own volume. I did not think that anyone accustomed to resisting the bodily attractions of deceit would, while experiencing these contradictions within himself, fail to agree with the testimony of this man—by far the greatest among philosophers—on the distinction between the different natures of body and soul, as he himself attests to himself, and would not dispute by the authority of reason between his soul and his body.

What, then, is that thing which, as they say, prevents a corporeal soul from every discovery by the obstacle of a foreign body that continually confronts it? Or why should it arraign a foreign body for holding it back from contemplation of the truth, when it is itself an impediment, if it is a body?

But I shall not argue these matters further. [Col. 0749B] Truth itself plainly shines forth and needs no external ornament or assistance; indeed, when naked, it is both more beautiful and stronger. For this reason I have judged that I should use the testimony of my witnesses, whose evidence has hitherto remained undefended, since we shall doubt the guarantors of this truth only among those who are wholly body in every part of themselves.

VII. But what this same Plato declared concerning the soul in the *Hipparchus*, the *Laches*, the *Protagoras*, the *Symposium*, the *Alcibiades*, the *Gorgias*, the *Crito*, and the *Timaeus*—even in that work which is a kind of citadel and summit of philosophy [Note: [Col. 0749] Others omit “a certain”]—I omit for the sake of the brevity I have chosen. For the recognition of truth does not depend on asking what someone has said repeatedly about the same matter, rather than what he has believed. In repeated statements, knowledge of things is no richer than the burdensome length of the words.

Therefore, in establishing the truth, we should consider more carefully what many have believed once than what one person has said often. Nevertheless, because my opinion rightly regards Plato as the foremost of all philosophers, I have repeatedly called him as a witness in the present matter, drawn to him by admiration, although, when compared with the innumerable things he discussed concerning the soul, you may judge the several passages you read here to be very few.

Nor did the Platonist Porphyry, many centuries after Plato, anywhere dissent from his teacher in this same matter. In a celebrated utterance, he reminded the human race of its dignity: “If we wish to be blessed,” he says, “all body must be fled.” There is therefore something incorporeal in us, opposed to which is the contamination of the whole body. And what can this be except the image of God? And what is the image of God except the human soul? If it cannot be blessed in a body, and is not incorporeal, it will never be blessed, since it will not be without itself.

CHAPTER VIII. He uses Roman philosophers as witnesses to the incorporeality of the soul.

We have used many testimonies of many philosophers in the present matter, and we could produce many more from that same Greece, if either the case demanded or reason allowed it. But lest we seem to have sought the truth locally—as though it could be seen among one nation alone and were unknown to others—since human substance possesses the truth not by region but by kind, let us also call Roman philosophers as witnesses. Among them Sextius the father and Sextius the son devoted themselves with exceptional zeal to the practice of wisdom and philosophized with distinction; concerning every soul they offered the following judgment:

“Every soul is incorporeal and without location, a power that cannot be grasped, which, without occupying space, receives and contains the body.”

These men, unless I am mistaken, entered more sharply into the hidden principles of things than certain of our own people. These, in bedroom disputations concerning the investigation of lofty causes, yawn drowsily in their little beds over some soporific matter; driven on by an abundance of lukewarm inanities, they sleep away the musty suspicions of old-womanish opinions under the praise of a foolish flatterer, and decide that the soul, joined to the entrails, is enclosed and held within the body’s prison.

But this fiction, empty of the truth because of ignorance, we have already refuted, as the circumstances of the discussion required, in the preceding book; and now, by bringing forward the great testimonies of the highest authorities, we refute it also by the powers of reason, with truth itself assisting us in its own cause. [Note: [Col. 0749] Others: “by blows.”]

M. Varro, the most learned man of his age and, according to Cicero, without question the most learned of all, what did he argue with a kind of divine reasoning in his books on music, arithmetic, geometry [Note: [Col. 0750] Others omit “what in”], and philosophical works (φιλοσοφουμένων), except that he might draw the soul from visible things to invisible, from localized things to nonlocalized, and from corporeal things to incorporeal ones, by the wondrous methods of eternal art [Note: [Col. 0750] Others: “of eternity”], and restore it to possession of itself after it had dispersed into bodies—that is, into things opposed to it? If it were a body, it could not be opposed to a body.

Why should I now bring forward, in defense of the truth, the opinions of Zoroaster, of the Brahmans from India, of Anacharsis from Scythia, of the Catos, of M. Cicero, or of Chrysippus, who from almost the very beginning of his work grants the soul the right of domination and imposes upon the body the law of servitude? Why should I demonstrate what judgment the whole world makes concerning the condition of the soul, at least among those who have deservedly shone forth?

CHAPTER IX. He uses ecclesiastical teachers as witnesses to the incorporeality of the soul.

I. This would certainly be easy for me, if a crowd of witnesses, compelled by necessity, did not prevent me from adding anything, and if the time or the argument did not now urge me to disclose the divine oracles. And so, in order to approach the very sources of the heavenly books, under the guidance, for the most part, of those who drew more abundantly from them, Gregory of Nazianzus, in his *Apologeticus*, loudly declares that there is a great distinction between soul and body; and that just as the body is fed by corporeal things, so the soul is nourished by incorporeal things.

Blessed Ambrose, speaking to the people in the church at Milan in language most learned and erudite, says: “Let us separate ourselves from the body, against which, if we wish to be saved, there is a continual struggle for us.”

One outstanding judgment, expressing the same thing, must be understood in the same sense and handled in the same language. I shall therefore say now what I remember often saying when I reached this point: Ambrose persuades us that we ought to be separated from the body. I ask, then, who this is whom it is appropriate to separate from the body. For we consist of soul and body. And therefore, since the soul cannot be separated from itself, there is nothing in us that can be separated from the body, if the soul is a body.

Why, holy Ambrose, why do you teach in this manner? Why do you smear Christ’s bride with the filth of falsehood? Why, by the force of a savage preaching, do you drive her from the way of truth into precipitous byways? Why do you assert that a body ought to be separated from a body? What benefit, I ask, would this bring to a human being? Is it because the nature of the inner human being is subtler—although it is nevertheless only a body—that it ought therefore to be cast apart and separated?

Because, in the structure of this worldly mass, some things are subtler and lighter, while others are denser and heavier, is it therefore appropriate for the thinner things to break apart the entire cohesion of this solid structure? Or will the air be happier if it is not joined with water and earth?

To such false-speaking prattlers he gives the following response: “A certain doctrine has arisen among us—bare of words, devoid of virtue, foreign to reason, empty of truth, hollow with vanity, swollen with pride, a teaching of this recent schism without an author, raised with an arched brow, cast down by falsehood, filled with abuse, stealing power from the Creator and dignity from the image. By a wondrous kind of folly it disgraces the image through comparisons with corporeal substance.

“It asserts, namely, that it would benefit the soul as little to be separated from the body as it would benefit the air to be separated from the denser bodies of the worldly mass. But if there are anywhere among the nations people whose minds have penetrated the secrets of causes, come swiftly and punish yourselves for your ignorance. Marvel at the new doctrine: the soul’s dignity is acquired within the solid world—the fourth part of the worldly body. This, then, is plainly the greater soul of all souls, and, because of its bulk, the wiser. Thus a person will now possess wisdom all the more abundantly the more of this air he has absorbed according to his capacity.

“And deservedly the human race has blamed nature, which, the larger the oxen of the forest it has produced for human beings, has made them happier in proportion to their greater capacity.”

Ambrose has said enough for the present; indeed, he alone would certainly be enough. Nevertheless, I shall also grant others a place to testify.

II.
