Aurelius Augustine—by the sharpness of his intellect, the abundance of his subject matter, and the magnitude of his work, like a kind of Chrysippus in argumentative power, a Zeno in subtlety of meaning, or our Varro in the vastness of his volumes, and certainly so constituted by nature, attention, and discipline that he not undeservedly differed from the bodily Epicureans or Cynics of our age as a spiritual sophist—declares in his book to Jerome concerning the origin of the soul:

“Although it may be difficult to persuade those who are slower of understanding that the soul is incorporeal, I confess that I myself am persuaded of it.”

And although he proves this by powerful arguments and an unanswerable demonstration, and asks Jerome’s opinion on the matter, he receives from Jerome only writings that praise his own position: indeed, Jerome says without doubt that nothing truer can be thought concerning the soul and nothing more perfectly argued.

There you have two men, outstanding in the superiority of their virtues and learning, who agree with us concerning the condition of the soul, and who overthrow you, stripped of the weight of authority and the strength of reason. By separating bodies through the vanity of wisdom, you wish to make two souls one.

For this reason I am greatly surprised that Jerome was called as your witness, since the chief of commentators was scarcely able to argue both for the soul and against the soul. Yet what you have set forth from him against us without understanding it serves us to such an extent that you appear to have been craftily arranged not as an opponent but as a disguised traitor: as though, by a collusive act of agreement, you had made us prevail by means of your own witnesses.

For it is a glorious kind of victory to take weapons from the one with whom you are fighting, to seek a witness from your opponent’s side, and then to throw him down from your own side.

III. Nevertheless, lest you think me slow to return the favor, I shall point out, as the occasion permits, that Hilary of Poitiers might have agreed with you more closely concerning your opinion. In the midst of many lofty arguments of his, he held a contrary view on one point and argued two things opposed to the truth: first, that nothing incorporeal was created; second, that Christ felt no pain at all in his passion. If his passion was not real, neither could our redemption have been real.

But because blessed Hilary erased the fault of this opinion by the strength of his confession, he endures the stroke of criticism in such a way that he suffers no loss of merit. Therefore, it is proper to give credence to commentators on the divine Scriptures only so long as they agree with the same course of truth.

Yet although I have necessarily passed over the citation of certain commentators, since I am hastening properly toward the divine oracles on which their authority depends, I have by no means passed over Eucherius, whom I knew as a living teacher and through immediate discussions in his presence, not through reports or reading. He was a man of vigorous age and mature spirit, scorning earthly things and desiring heaven, humble in spirit, lofty in merit, exceedingly subtle in intellect, full of knowledge, fluent in speech, and by far the greatest of the great bishops of his age. Having published many volumes of various works for the advancement of the faith, he also preached to the people on the condition of the soul as follows:

“Some people are accustomed to ask how man and God could have been mingled in Christ. They ask for an explanation of this mystery, which happened once, although they are quite unable to explain how something that happens continually occurs—namely, how the soul is joined to the body so that a human being comes to exist.

“Therefore, just as a corporeal thing and an incorporeal thing are joined, and the soul is mingled with the body so that a human being is produced, so man was joined to God and Christ was made. Yet, for Christ to be made, those two incorporeal things—that is, soul and God—could be joined and mingled more easily than one incorporeal thing and another corporeal thing are mingled, namely soul and body, so that the person of a human being may exist.”

I believe that those who, having been instructed equally by such teachings, have degenerated from them—destroying their own wholesome principles and making themselves subject to alien evils through an unjust hatred of those who love them—have fallen so far that they would rather choose outsiders together with falsehood and condemn Eucherius together with the truth.

IV. Here you may see some weighing the matter with a sluggish judgment, others either praising the same thing unknowingly with foolish applause or, as half-learned men, laughing at it with deceitful agreement. Among them, that man pleases himself whom no one has praised except either an ignorant person or a cunning one.

Now judgments are issued concerning individuals according not to the quality of their merits but to the quality of their wishes. Because of the praise of certain present-day fables, authors of the highest distinction are condemned. Meanwhile, that praised man, lest he seem to stand below the judgment of his praisers, gathers little scraps from the varied reading of different works and sews them, as though with coarse tow, to his own cheap materials. More disgraceful in his torn clothing, he walks about mute in eloquence, wrapped in a garment stolen without the labor of thought.

Here you may see another, foul with the accumulation of loathsome and disgraceful things, breathing out the sewer of his belly and mouth from his foul feasts and darkness, and, amid belching, twittering certain little slanders against another man, who has squandered his allowance in various all-night vigils; yet he is praised in parasitic fashion.

Among such rubbish and refuse of the same kind, can you safely say anything sober? Moreover, you will run a great danger from this sluggish crowd [Note: [Col. 0753] Something appears to be missing here in the source]: while—“For nothing at all is more unjust than command” (Terence, *Adelphoe*, act 1, scene 2, line 18)—I myself nevertheless do not fear these and such men.

And if there is now an opportunity to admonish them, I admonish and declare: whoever these men are, and whoever the others may be, who either mutter insults against great men or babble deliriously about the highest matters with their fellow-writers, let them speak openly or remain silent. Indeed, those who have hitherto hidden themselves will even now be dug out and dragged forth from the secret places of darkness, each by name.

It may be known beforehand that I shall not be silent concerning their deeds, even if I do not yet disclose their names. Let them nevertheless do what they wish and despise wholesome warnings—not with impunity, certainly. For my part, I would rather be rejected by these men together with Eucherius than be condemned by them together with the truth.

But now the place and time have come for me to proceed by a suitable course: just as we passed from philosophers to commentators, so from commentators let us advance to the authoritative sources, with most of the witnesses now urging this course by their silence.

CHAPTER X. He uses divine Wisdom itself as a witness.

[Col. 0753D]

I. Let us therefore hear what divine Wisdom declares against the enemies of its image:

“The ungodly said, thinking unsoundly: ‘Short and wearisome is the time of our life; and our body will be reduced to ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air’” (Wis. 2:1, 3).

The ungodly said these things; concerning them the same Scripture shortly afterward speaks as follows:

“For their wickedness blinded them; because God created man imperishable and made him in the image of his own likeness” (ibid., 21, 23).

Here, then, I believe you should rouse yourself more vigorously in defense of your position and, according to the merits of the case, bring against me words of approximately this kind:

“What does it matter to me that you use testimonies gathered from here and there, although they do not strike the truth of my sincere conscience? What further concern of mine is it? What does it matter that the ungodly are divinely punished for having diminished the dignity of the divine image, when I know that I am not held by the snares of this impiety? Therefore, I advise you to withdraw and not falsely brand me with the disgrace of such an opinion.”

Now, unless you object, I shall return with you to your own position and from the things that follow let us determine whether you will judge that this prophetic oracle against the ungodly has been directed against them or against you [Note: [Col. 0754] The Lyons edition omits this passage]—against you, that is, whom the pretense of a privilege of knowledge devotes to an opinion contrary to reputation, and who, contrary to your opinion, are concerned for reputation; for you defend as your own there the very things which here you reject as belonging to others.

[Col. 0754B]

II. Yet lest there be any opportunity either for me to interpret the matter differently or for you perhaps to deny it, let us examine both sides of the issue before us.

The prophet says that the ungodly say: “Our body will be reduced to ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air.”

What do you yourself say? “There are certain spiritual natures,” you say, “such as angels, archangels, and the other powers, as well as our own soul—or certainly this subtle air—but they are in no way to be considered incorporeal.”

Now, I ask you, let each of our judges attend on your behalf and decide whether there is any distinction between these statements:

The ungodly said of the human spirit—namely, of the human soul—that the spirit is dispersed like soft air.

Your advocate adds that the human soul and this subtle air are equally spiritual, but are likewise not incorporeal.

Consider the very words and the meaning. For what is called the human spirit there is called the soul here. The agreement is so complete that it is as though both had said “soul,” or both “spirit.” There the spirit is said to be poured into soft air; here it is likewise compared with subtle air.

Therefore, when it is said that the spirit is dispersed like soft air, this is equivalent to saying: “The spirit is what soft air is.” Likewise, when it is said that our soul and this subtle air are spiritual, it is equivalent to saying: “Our soul is what this subtle air is.”

Since, of these two statements, the former is the blasphemy of the ungodly, while the latter is your opinion, and since the two are united to such an extent that in matter, meaning, and wording they are indistinguishable [Note: [Col. 0754] The same edition likewise omits this passage], what follows most decisively? Either, because your opinion is similar to theirs, the opinion of the ungodly must also be praiseworthy if you believe yours should be defended; or, because theirs is punishable, yours must likewise be condemned because of its equality with theirs.

III. But why do we continue to lose our way by arguing, when the prophet has judged concerning this matter as follows?

“The ungodly,” he says, “said within themselves, thinking unsoundly: ‘Short is the time of our life; our body will be reduced to ashes, and the spirit will be dispersed like soft air.’”

A little later, after inserting an intervening discussion, he adds the judgment:

“These things they thought, and they went astray; for their wickedness blinded them.”

And as though you were asking, “What fault or error is attributed to them?”, he replies: “They thought that the human soul was corporeal, and they went astray.”

And as though someone were asking again and again what truth conceals in the belief that the soul is a body [Note: [Col. 0755] Others: “repeating” (*geminanti*)], the prophet repeats his answer:

“They went astray, yes, they went astray, because God created man imperishable and made him in the image of his own likeness.”

That is, he says: “The soul is so far from being a body that it is the divine image.”

Is there anything by which you can proceed farther from this point, exposed by your own testimony, captured by the force of truth, and convicted by the prophet’s testimony?

Let each person see to his own opinion. In my judgment, however, what we have argued thus far against the corporealists in defense of the spiritual nature would be enough, if I did not think it appropriate to bring in apostolic or even evangelical testimony for the present controversy.

CHAPTER XI. He uses the Apostle Paul as a witness for the soul’s lack of location.

Although, wherever it has been useful, I have employed the testimonies of certain Scriptures, it is nevertheless right, in the manifold joy of truth, to cut off the false-speaker’s little neck with a salutary stroke.

Paul, the teacher of the nations, the chosen vessel, says: “Every sin is outside the body. But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (2 Cor. 6:18).

If, except for the sin of fornication, every sin is outside the body, then it is in the soul. But if it is in the soul, and the soul is a body, then every sin is not outside the body. Yet the Apostle says that, apart from fornication, every sin is outside the body.

Therefore the soul is incorporeal, so that there may be something in which sin can exist outside the body.

Likewise, when he was about to pronounce judgment on the Corinthian who had been polluted by the crime of incest and had violated his stepmother’s bed—almost the bed of his mother—he says:

“Although absent in body, but present in spirit, I have already judged the one who committed this deed.”

What is this, Apostle Paul? What does this mean? How are you absent in body while present in spirit? If spirit is body, why do you not rather say that, being composed of two bodies, you are absent in one and present in the other? [Note: [Col. 0755] Others: “composed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0756] Others: “But if.”] Or, if you are wholly one body, why do you not say that you are absent in one part of the body and present in another? For when you say that you are absent from the Corinthians in body, you can perhaps be understood to mean this because, in the entirety of your being, you are wholly corporeal. But since you are wholly corporeal, and therefore absent wholly because absent in body, I do not know by what part of you—in which you are not—you say that you are present.

Either you accuse yourself of falsehood, or you convict these corporealists concerning the incorporeality of the soul. Is there anything here obscure or perhaps unclear, except that, to the extent that he is corporeal, he is absent from the Corinthians, while he is present either in no part of himself or through what is incorporeal?

Therefore the human spirit is incorporeal, through which the Apostle Paul, though absent in the whole of his corporeal being, could be present to the Corinthians.

We could produce innumerable examples of this kind, and many others, from nearly the entire body of the authoritative books.

[Col. 0756A]

CHAPTER XII. Concerning the Apostle’s statement that he was caught up to the third heaven.

I. The sound doctrine of the Catholic faith ascends by successive steps from the lowest things to the intermediate, and from the intermediate to the highest. By subjecting corporeal creation to incorporeal creation, and by subjecting that same creation, together with its lower part, to the supreme incorporeal Creator, it carries Paul’s followers into the third heaven—those who have traversed with penetrating mind the solid structure of the sensible world; who, fixing their focused gaze at the farthest edge of the lowest heaven, after recovering their strength, have crossed every created incorporeal thing by a stronger effort, according to the excellence of its substance; and who, having thereafter gathered back their strength for a brief breathing-space of rest, have stood firm in the supreme knowledge of the incorporeal Creator.

Therefore I now wish to question these corporealists carefully about what their true position is concerning this apostolic statement. Since the Apostle says that he was caught up to the third heaven, I ask first whether he was caught up locally or nonlocally; and what these three heavens are—whether there are more than these, whether all are corporeal, or whether some are incorporeal. Since the order of the discussion has brought us to this point, let us examine, with truth as our counselor, what follows from it.

II. First, let us examine the question of the number of the heavens with somewhat greater care. For we read: “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens” (Ps. 148:4).

But this may be understood both of many and of two, so that “heavens of heavens” may be taken either as many heavens belonging to many heavens or as two heavens belonging to two heavens, with the numerical distinction left unexpressed.

Behold: contiguous with the earth, extending as far as the air, is the element of water. From there extends the depth of air up to the nearest light of the lunar star. From that point lie the regions of the ethereal fires, extending to the outermost regions beyond the world, where the world is enclosed in a spheroidal globe (σφαιροειδής).

Where, then, in the complete totality of bodies shall we seek a heaven beyond the whole world?

But in this dark fog of obscured matters, let us recover answers from the inner chambers of heavenly teachings. “In the beginning”—the beginning of Genesis says—“God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1).

If we set opinions aside and seek the certainty of truth, there before you is the witness to creation itself: the author of creation. He created heaven and earth before all time; afterward, on one day, he made the light and the firmament; and, likewise, on the second day, he established it and called that heaven by an extended or figurative name, to which he subsequently attached the ornaments of the stars, arranged according to fixed limits of intervals differing in place or manner.

It is easy to observe that this visible firmament falls short of the substance of the invisible heaven by as great an interval as it surpasses the lowest parts of the earth by the distance of its location.

Therefore this firmament may be called “heaven” by an alien and transferred name, whereas the heaven created before time properly bears the name “heaven.” Indeed, this star-bearing thing that we call heaven is called “the firmament of heaven” in the book of Genesis, where it recounts the creation of the luminaries:

“God made,” it says, “two great lights, and placed them in the firmament of heaven.”

By this authority we are permitted to believe that there is one true heaven created before time, although we are not forbidden to call this firmament, of which we are speaking, “heaven,” because God called the firmament heaven.

III. But another point again causes difficulty: in the authoritative books, the heavens are often called not merely by the dual but by the plural number.

Yet it is also stated that the single body of the earth is called in Scripture the world of lands. Thus perhaps the heavens may be called many even though they are two, just as the lands are called many although it is beyond doubt that there is one.

To what third heaven, then, was Paul caught up?

Come now, leave your seat; shake off the masses of the elements, place the weights of bodies upon the scales of judgment, and weigh the world. Perhaps some heaven will leap forth from somewhere for us.

Or, if one world does not contain several heavens, let the tiny atoms, together with Epicurus, give birth to several worlds for you, so that Paul may find a third heaven.

But how does it concern blessedness that someone should ascend from one corporeal body to another, or from this to a third equally corporeal body, when what is higher in location is not thereby more blessed in merit? Otherwise human beings will yield to little birds, and each person will advance toward eternity not by progress but by steps.

IV. Therefore, since neither local preeminence makes one blessed, nor does the soul find three corporeal heavens, so that at last, exhausted by bodies, it may yield to incorporeal things, let us examine, in accordance with the reasoning previously touched upon in silence, the number and distinction of the three heavens.

Since distinction in dignity corresponds to distance of location, if they differ more in dignity than they are distant from one another as the first and second heaven, I ask what exists there. Is there a substance there, or is there nothing?

If there is nothing, no cause for a created heaven will exist, since even here, in the lowest parts of the earth, nothing would have come into being unless causes had previously existed in eternity.

But if there is there some multitude of living beings superior to earthly beings, then this supercelestial substance exists beneath the heaven, drawing from the height above it the flames of the vibrating stars and the clearer breezes of the air. This element fills the hollow of the space between the heavens, which is distinguished from the third heaven by other peoples of living beings and by other depths of intervening air.

[Note: [Col. 0757] Others: “There will be a supercelestial substance. This is beneath the heaven,” etc.]

V. Now, then, if the Apostle was carried through these regions until he reached the third heaven, what did he chiefly find there?

If it had to be sought locally, and he could not find it in the first heaven, yet he says that he was caught up to the third heaven and that he heard something divine which it is not lawful for a human being to speak.

Is it so, then, Apostle, that God is sought through places, or that truth is found only in a place? If this is so, then God will also be local, and you will locally lose the God whom you find locally; for if he exists only in the third heaven, he has therefore been left there where he was found.

But since you are blessed not by a corporeal heaven but by the Lord of heaven, and since the Lord of heaven is wholly everywhere—he who is sought neither locally nor found locally—this will truly be granted as the reason for your ascent: you ascend from the heaven of an inferior substance to the heaven of a superior substance.

For those who seek God from corporeal things to corporeal things have no ascent. In what direction will enclosed corporeality now flee?

Behold, it is true both that Paul was caught up to the third heaven and that there are three corporeal heavens is not true. Therefore you must either confess that something created is incorporeal or deny that there are three heavens.

But since both that there are three heavens and that not all of them are corporeal is taught either by unquestionable authority or proved by manifest reason, let us, with the help of one truth, investigate what is false in the same way that we have examined it, and seek what is true.

## VI. We read in the Prophet: “He who made heaven and earth. Heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the children of men” (Psalm 113:15–16).

Here we must observe that one thing is “heaven” and another “heaven of heavens.” For when “heaven of heavens” is said, it is as though “heaven and earth” were said. This earth is, in fact, the lowest part of the starry heaven. But since God created heaven and earth before all temporal things, and on the second day made this visible heaven, heaven is therefore later in time than earth, although it is so much superior in quality.

But since the creation of the world in a moment does not admit divisions and intervals of time or the delays of days—for there is now no opportunity to discuss whether the number of six days is meant more than their duration—we must understand that the prophet made as great a difference between heaven and heaven of heavens as there is almost between this heaven and earth. Thus, just as earth is the earth of this heaven, so this heaven is in turn the earth of that heaven [Col. 0758C]. Hence we should infer that the entire body of the world is divinely called “earth,” while that which has been given to the Lord is called “heaven” in its proper name. For Scripture speaks thus: “Heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but the earth he gave to the children of men.”

## VII.

What, then, shall we say? Was this visible heaven not given to human beings? Or were the sun’s radiance and heat, the waxing and waning of the lunar sphere, the wandering and regular circuits of the stars, the conjunctions and appointed progressions of the heavenly bodies through their great orbits—whether they vary the alternation of days and nights, moderate the world by the mutual fostering of heat and cold, mark the divisions of time by measured limits, or, returning without end along the same unending course of their lines, carry them back by the same circular paths—or were they not all either suitable for the use of mortal humanity or pleasing to behold?

And thus, insofar as it is corporeal, heaven is called “earth,” since it has been given to human beings. The same applies to the bodies of the waters and of the air: they are certainly not of the same density as earth, yet because they have been given to the children of men, they are called “earth,” with the added consideration that, among all beings living by sensation, touch derives principally from earth. Moreover, just as nothing can be seen without fire, so nothing can be touched without earth, because fire too is subject to touch, and the ether is fire; it is therefore not absurd that something earthly should exist there [Col. 0759A].

Consequently, everything corporeal is included under the name “earth,” and by a sound judgment everything corporeal composed together is called “earth”: for this sensible world, together with the visible heaven, is the earth that has been given to the children of men.

## VIII.

What shall we say about that heaven which was given to the Lord, not to the children of men? Let us therefore return once more to the divine utterances. The same psalmist says: “Give thanks to the Lord, who made the heavens in understanding” (Psalm 135:3, 5).

Accordingly, if the heavens inhabited by God are “in understanding,” and if the heaven given to the Lord is none other than incorporeal heaven—that is, heaven for which everything corporeal is earth—it is plainly evident that everything which understands is not corporeal. The human mind, moreover, understands substantially; therefore the human mind is incorporeal [Col. 0759B].

Here, then, you have earth: every corporeal creature. Here, too, you have heaven: incorporeal and intellectual substance. Now, if you wish to be carried, with Paul as your guide, through two heavens into the third heaven, convey the whole corporeal universe across your own incorporeal being. Then transcend even created and mutable incorporeality, with a sharper effort and swifter flight; and from there rest in the third heaven, in the most blessed contemplation of the immutable and incorporeal One. Know yourself, human soul, to be incorporeal.

By reason of its superior nature, it is at once natural and appropriate for the soul, as though it were a mediating substance between the lowest and the highest parts of yourself, either to look down upon the lowest body beneath it or to look upward toward the highest God above it.

## IX.

Now I ask whether you can offer us another account of the number and diversity of the heavens. I certainly desire one, but it is clear that no one can provide it unless the nature of corporeal substance is inserted between body and God. For if nothing exists apart from God except body, then there are not three heavens but two: all body constituting, so to speak, one heaven, and the body’s Creator another.

But since Paul was caught up not beyond the third heaven but into the third heaven, the two heavens—every corporeal and incorporeal creature—must be crossed as though in transit. To the Creator, however, as to the third heaven, one must come not in order to cross over, which is impossible, nor in order to return, which is forbidden, but in order to stand and remain.

From this comes progress and perfection: they belong to virtues, not to places. For the one who progresses runs, and the one who is perfected arrives [Col. 0759D].

## X.

Now, since we have passed through the broadest fields of a very extensive question by an exceedingly short path, supplying, as I think, several indications that distinguish the deviations of error from the straight path of truth, I inquire what the Apostle means when he says that he was caught up either in the body or outside the body.

For he says: “I know a man caught up, whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know” (2 Corinthians 12:2), and the rest, concerning which we have said what was relevant. First, after applying careful examination, let us see what the blessed Apostle declares certain and what he confesses to be uncertain. He knows that a man was caught up; he does not know whether in the body or outside the body.

Observe now that “man” is said here to be one thing and “body” another. Yet it is clearly distinguished what the Apostle says he does not know and what he says he knows. Let us therefore examine whether he is ignorant, to the same extent, whether he is incorporeal, corporeal, or composed of both, as he is ignorant whether he was caught up with the body or without the body.

“I know,” he says, “a man caught up; but whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know.” Here it is now permissible to observe that the one who was caught up knows that he was caught up, yet, perceiving that he himself is not his own body, hesitates whether he was caught up with that body or without it; nevertheless, he does not doubt that he himself exists.

And although the whole matter remains obscure, the one who is uncertain whether he was caught up with the body is nevertheless certain that he is incorporeal and has a body. If he was not caught up without the body, the body was caught up with him; yet he himself is not identical with the body with which he was caught up. If he was without the body, it is much more clearly understood that he is not a body, since he can exist without a body.

“I know,” he says, “a man caught up; but whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know.” This is as though he were saying: “I know that I was caught up, but whether with the body or without the body, I do not know.” Therefore, even if you were caught up with the body, you could nevertheless have been caught up without the body. You are therefore incorporeal even while in the body, if you could have been caught up without the body.

For the incorporeal is mingled with the body, without compromising its own substance, in order to give that body life. But the established order of things does not permit the body to exist without the body.

# CHAPTER XIII. From the Gospel he uses God as a witness to the incorporeality of the soul.

But now truth itself will bear witness through my witnesses—namely, the heralds of truth—so that the truth may testify to an indisputable faith. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28).

Why, I ask you, cannot one who can kill the body kill the soul? Unless perhaps it is because the soul is not a body. You, however, say: “It is indeed a body, but a subtler one; it is indeed a body, but a lighter one.”

I reply: Let it be subtler and lighter; nevertheless, if it is a body, it can be killed by one who can kill a body. For we are dealing with these two—namely, soul and body—of which visible man is composed. He who said, “Do not fear those who …,” did not say, “those who kill the denser body” or “the heavier body,” but “those who kill the body.” Likewise, he did not say, “the subtler and lighter body,” but “they cannot kill the soul.”

By the name “body” he plainly included living body, since nothing can be killed except what is alive. Therefore, if the soul is a living body, it can be killed by one who can kill a body. Truth says: “Those who kill the body cannot kill the soul.” The soul, therefore, is not a body, since it cannot be killed by those who can kill the body.

But since the reader’s attention must be relieved from the burden of perpetual reading, let this be the end of this volume.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0761A]

# CHAPTER I. On the lifeless body of Lazarus

Having produced, for the defense of the truth, sure supports sufficient, as I think, both in merit and in number, it remains now for us to examine without further discussion what is left from the little work of this advocate of the body. With rash confidence he declares the soul to be local, taking as an example for this purpose an instance from evangelical authority, and arguing as though decisively: The body of Lazarus, when it was dead, was without life; and when it was restored, it was again with life. From this, he says, the soul should be believed to be local, since it departed from the body and then returned to the body.

And, in order to prescribe this as a general rule for the whole race of souls, he declares that the soul of our Redeemer himself was local.

# CHAPTER II. In what respect the soul bears the likeness of God

## I.

With a formidable syllogism, as he supposes, and one that cannot be refuted: “Where the soul is, it exists; and where it is not, it does not exist”—as though we said that it is either everywhere or nowhere. For if it were everywhere, it would be God; if nowhere, it would be nothing.

The soul is not wholly throughout the entire world; but just as God is wholly present everywhere in the universe, so the soul is found wholly everywhere in the body. And just as God does not fill a smaller part of the world with a smaller part of himself or a larger part with a larger part, but is wholly in a part and wholly in the whole, so the soul is not present in a part of the body according to a part of itself.

One part of the soul does not give sensation to the eye and another give life to the finger. Rather, just as it lives wholly in the eye and sees wholly through the eye, so it lives wholly in the finger and senses wholly through the finger [Col. 0761C].

Or if perhaps it senses wholly in the finger in such a way that it is not wholly in the finger, then it senses wholly where it is not wholly present, and it exists where it is not. Either, therefore, the soul will be wholly in the smallest part of the body, even though it is wholly in the whole body, or it will sense wholly where it is not wholly present. Thus it is wholly where it is not wholly.

But I discussed this at considerable length in the first book, and prefaced not a little concerning it at the beginning of the second. Anyone who has attended carefully to those discussions will approach this passage, as it were, not as a novice.

For it is exceedingly difficult to contemplate incorporeal things, because the deceptive sight of bodily senses so clouds the eye of the feeble mind through sin that, when it wishes to contemplate either itself or God, it sees only the veil of bodily images placed before it, since it cannot see beyond it [Col. 0761D]. Whoever, therefore, is offended by the difficulty of this vision should devote effort and labor not to bringing accusations, but to becoming capable of purification.

## II.

Yet I have not so forgotten myself that I do not feel more illness than health to be present in me. Nevertheless, I am pleased to have escaped, in my childish years, from the opinion that the soul is a body; for at that time, when I held that opinion, I did not know.

To hold an opinion belongs to one who is ignorant; ignorance, moreover, is contrary to knowledge. Whoever holds an opinion, therefore, does not know. This is why I came to desire knowledge more than opinion, knowing that I did not know so long as I was merely forming opinions.

You, however, say: “When we inquire into the substance of the soul, what is above us cannot appear to us, since we ourselves are not above ourselves.” And what you deny can be known, you nevertheless judge as though it were known, confirming that the soul is a body of the body.

If you say this knowingly—for false things cannot be known—you speak truly. And if you speak truly in saying that the substance of the soul cannot be known, you are lying. Either, therefore, it is false that the soul is a body, or it is false that the substance of the soul cannot be known.

Do you see where opinion leads those who follow it? Since no one forms an opinion except one who is ignorant, and ignorance is opposed to knowledge, you who wish to derive a certain judgment from the uncertainty of opinion and to pronounce as though you knew about things you do not know are convicted of teaching what you do not know.

You therefore teach ignorance, while presuming to teach what you say cannot be known. Grant us pardon, we ask, since we do not wish to learn ignorance [Col. 0762B].

# CHAPTER III. That the soul is not contained locally by the body

## I.

You say, then, that the soul is contained by the body. Should that apostolic statement not have come to mind: “Even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet our inner man is being renewed” (2 Corinthians 4:16)?

Everything that exists, to put it briefly, is either in itself, or is a subject, or is in a subject. God is in himself. In corporeal things, the body is the subject, and the color of the body is in a subject. In incorporeal things, there are mind and discipline; these are so interconnected that, just as a body cannot exist without color, so a rational mind cannot exist without discipline [Col. 0762C].

Now you seem to believe that the soul is a body and that, being superimposed upon the subject, it is contained in the subject body. Let us see whether we can prove that what is in a subject remains when the subject itself perishes. For if the soul is contained by the body, it is itself superimposed upon its subject, and what is contained cannot remain when that which contains it perishes.

But the Apostle says that, while the body grows old, the soul is renewed [Note: [Col. 0761] Another reading: “and, when the body is corrupted, is made firm.].” If the body is corrupted, the soul is likewise made firm. The soul, therefore, is not contained by the body.

## II.

I fear that here too you may appear to be a new Academic in your opinions—one who, like the Academics, knows nothing, yet defines without hesitation what he does not know. Take care lest the body not contain the soul, but be contained by the soul.

When the body is corrupted, the soul is strengthened; and, correspondingly, the body is dissolved through the soul’s departure. The soul lives better without the body; the body cannot live, even worse, without the soul.

And so that, among these two things of which human substance is composed, what is in what may be established not by argument alone but also made clear by authority, let us bring forward a prophetic testimony as well. For it says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15) [Col. 0763A].

We must first consider whether what weighs something down is that in which something exists, or that in which something is. If what weighs something down is that in which something exists, then what is in it is lifted up [Note: [Col. 0763] Another reading: “therefore nothing is burdened by weight.].”

But if what weighs something down is that which is in something else, and not that in which something exists, then the body that weighs down the soul is more truly in the soul than the soul, which is weighed down by the body, is in the body: the burden is in the bearer, not the bearer in the burden.

Since this is so, the greatest indication that the soul possesses a great likeness to its Creator is that, in accordance with this likeness, just as the world is in God without locality, so the body is in the soul without locality.

## III.

Now I ask you to answer me as I inquire: If the soul is locally within the body, how does it contain the body? It is well known that nothing corporeal can be contained by a body unless that which contains is outside and that which is contained is inside.

But since, as you yourself assert, the soul is corporeal, how is it inside the body in order to give it life, and outside the body in order to contain it? Or perhaps does it contain externally in such a way that it is not external?

We are therefore again reduced to this difficulty: either the soul is outside the body without locality, so that it may contain the body, or, if it contains where it is not, it exists where it is not.

Perhaps this reasoning troubles you by its novelty. Wake up for a little while and, if you can, observe it; if you cannot, marvel at the power of the incorporeal, so that it moves a body while itself standing still, and reaches every place without going to places, acting without locality in those same places.

If you are able to perceive this, you will no longer set the soul of Lazarus against us as a kind of body on account of a supposedly local departure and return. Rather, you will understand that it gave life to his body by an incorporeal movement, departed from it without locality, and likewise returned to it without locality [Col. 0763C].

## IV.

If the truth of this vision has now become clear to you, you will not be tossed about by any difficulty of the question, since the soul can exist without locality in the world once it has left the body.

For it will be without locality in any part of the world just as it was without locality in the body. Yet, to the prejudice of the entire race of souls, you declare even Christ’s soul to be local and corporeal, and you say that the soul of the Redeemer is a body, although it is not the soul of an animal.

But if you insist on asking how the soul can be in a place without being local, I in turn ask you how the corporeal world can be local and yet not be in a place. If you answer that the world is in a place, I ask no less whether the place in which the world is lies outside the world or is part of the world.

If it is part of the world, then the world is not in it; rather, it itself, together with the world, is in another place [Note: [Col. 0763] Another reading: “not in the world.”]. If it is outside the world, I ask again whether the place in which the world exists is itself in a place.

Either, therefore, you will acknowledge infinite places—that is, bodies—and thereby make body equal to God, who alone is infinite; or you will concede that the world is not in a place.

Consider this reasoning carefully. Just as you perceive that there can be so many places and so many spaces without being in a place, so understand that what has no mass and no spatial extent can be in a place without locality. For if what is local is in a place, then what is non-local is still less not in a place [Col. 0764A].

# CHAPTER IV. Just as the soul departs from the body without locality so that the body may die, so the divinity of Christ departed without locality so that Christ, the Son of God, might die on the cross

Whether or not you understand this, however clear it may be, I would doubt [Note: [Col. 0763] This is how we have punctuated the passage. Another reading: “nor have I doubted that which …”]. But I cannot sufficiently marvel that the following point, which follows from so simple a consequence that its recognition is, I shall not say easy, but scarcely even avoidable, has escaped you.

You say, then, that when Christ’s body was taken up with the cross, it was animate, but that when it was placed in the tomb, it was lifeless. For this reason—which cannot be denied—you claim, as an argument of your acumen, that the soul is local, since it alternated in giving life to Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0764] We have restored the text in this form; another reading has, “And you say.”].

Under the necessity of this position, shall we therefore also believe God to be local by an impious act of daring—God who was in Christ when he was crucified and then abandoned him in his passion? The Lord himself cried from the cross: “My God, why have you abandoned me?”

For if he did not depart, he did not abandon him; if he abandoned him, he certainly departed. Now apply locality to God. The next step is close at hand: from an insult to the likeness of God you will be carried on to God himself, and, by disgracing the image, you will assail its author.

Therefore, just as God’s lack of locality is not removed when, by departing, he abandoned the man Christ, so the soul does not lose the privilege of incorporeality when it departs as the body dies.

# CHAPTER V. Mary did not see the angel Gabriel in the substance in which he is spirit, but from what he temporarily assumed from the air as a visible body

## I.

Now, in your pride, you assail the condition of angels. You choose Gabriel for yourself as a kind of prelude to your rhetoric and deliver your declamation.

That most blessed Gabriel, who testifies that he stands before God, announced to Mary that the Lord of heaven was to be infused into her womb and stood before the eyes of the Lord’s mother. Without doubt, he was absent from heaven, did not fly over the seas, and did not fill the empty and diffuse expanse of the vast air; rather, he occupied only the place in which he was present.

Setting aside for a little while the examination of this position, I confess that I am astonished at the contradiction among your statements. At one moment you call the air subtle, at another you call it vast. At one moment you describe the great place of the world, which the element of air fills in proportion, as empty with a kind of poetic license; yet you do not understand that it cannot be empty at all, because where something exists there is not nothing.

Air is not nothing; therefore, where air is, there is no void. Nor can that properly be called empty which is nothing, since what is nothing cannot receive anything. Accordingly, the void is not that which is incapable of containing anything.

What, moreover, is the point of your preferring, in the manner of poets, to call the Lord’s mother “genetrix,” and of weaving poetic rhetoric without verse? I am not asking how you speak, but what you say; and I ask you to answer [Col. 0765A].

## II.

When the most blessed Gabriel stood before the eyes of the Lord’s mother, did Mary see in Gabriel that by which Gabriel sees the Lord? For if that was visible to Mary, then what is without locality was perceptible to what is local.

But if this is so, it is not without locality. For if something is local, it sees locally, and one who looks can see only a part. It therefore sees a place, because it sees locally; a part is a place, and a place of places is certainly a part, and places are bodies.

Whoever sees a part sees a part of himself, and nothing can be seen by a part unless it is itself a part. But there is no part of God, because the indivisible has no part. Either, therefore, Gabriel does not see God, or he sees him whole; and nothing can be seen whole except by what is whole.

A body, however, can neither be seen whole nor see what is whole. It is not therefore through a body that Gabriel sees God. For by the same local means by which Gabriel saw Mary, and Mary saw him, he cannot see incorporeally.

But, to engage you on your own terms: if Gabriel in his entirety is nothing but a body, on account of the separation of his parts, then he is not wholly a foot, nor wholly a mouth, nor wholly an eye. Consequently, when he appeared to Mary, he did not speak with his foot, see with his mouth, or stand with his eye; rather, each part of his limbs performed the function appropriate to its quality. Therefore, just as he stood locally and sounded locally, so he also saw locally.

## III.

Here, now, as the conclusion of the question, I ask whether, as you suppose, the angel Gabriel, occupied bodily in contemplating Mary as a body alone, saw the incorporeal God incorporeally with one and the same sight, at one and the same time, with which he saw local Mary locally.

Since this is impossible on account of the difference between corporeal and incorporeal things, it remains either that Gabriel never saw Mary or that he ceased to see God. But this false conclusion is opposed by the sentence of truth, which says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:11).

If they always see him, they never fail to see him. But if, when Gabriel saw Mary, he ceased to see God, then the angels do not always see God. Therefore, either Gabriel ceased to see God when he saw Mary, or what Truth said will not be true.

Accordingly, the conclusion follows by an apparently indissoluble argument. Since the angel could not see God with a local sight fixed at the same time upon the contemplation of Mary, yet it is not permissible to deny that God was then seen by Gabriel—lest the nature of the angel, already established in blessedness, should fall into the misery of the devil, namely, into never seeing God [Note: [Col. 0765] This is how the Paris edition reads. The Lyon edition has: “lest, according to the devil’s case, namely, into the misery of never seeing God,” and so forth.]—there must be in him both corporeal and incorporeal substance: one by which he may be seen by a body or may see corporeally, and another by which he may behold the incorporeal incorporeally without end.

# CHAPTER VI. How far unformed matter differs from nothing, and formed matter from unformed matter

## I.

Come now, with the acumen of your excellent intellect and your knowledge of causes and things, investigate, distinguish, and pronounce: How does unformed matter differ from nothing? What is something lifeless and yet formed? What is something both formed and animate? What are place and time? In what way is local motion also subject to time, whereas what is merely temporal is not likewise subject to place? What is stable motion, and what is eternity? What is it to be nowhere, and what is it to be never nonexistent?

Ask about the hidden reason underlying all these things, within which every substance is contained. Choose something by which you may determine what angels are. Certainly they are not nothing, because whatever is something is not nothing. Nor are they unformed matter, since unformed matter lies between something and nothing. See: we have scarcely departed from nothing.

## II.

Let us now consider from what formed but lifeless thing you prefer angels to derive. Observe that, just as unformed matter, which can be formed, is superior to nothing, so what is already formed is better than what, although it can be formed, is not formed.

Likewise, just as what is formed precedes what is not formed, so any formed but lifeless thing yields to that which is both formed and animate, because just as what is formed approaches form, so what is animate approaches life.

And just as there are three things—unformed matter, formed but lifeless matter, and the form of things—so likewise there are three: what is given life, what gives life, and life.

The life of bodies is one thing, the life of lives another. A body is living, the soul is alive, and God is life; specifically, the soul, which is alive in itself, is life to the body. Thus the body does not live without the soul, just as the soul does not live without God [Note: [Col. 0766] Another reading: “itself.”].

Understand now that you attribute bodies to the holy angels but deny them life. Since every animate thing consists of a twofold substance, and you think that angels are body alone, a little worm is therefore better than an angel: for although an angel has the form of a body, he does not possess life even as a worm does.

Moreover, no body is life for itself. Body is one thing, the life of the body another. Either, therefore, there is in an angel a spirit that gives life, or an angel is worse than every living thing. But since he is superior to every created living thing, the life that belongs to him is not just any life, but the most blessed life [Col. 0766C].

# CHAPTER VII. That good and evil angels are spirits alone, not bodies

## I.

There is therefore in Gabriel both the incorporeal, by which he sees God immutably, and the body which either Mary saw or through which Mary was seen, and which he bore locally subject to the spirit, while the spirit recognized what was to be borne in the truth itself without locality.

It is sufficiently clear, I think, that blessed angels are of both substances: they are incorporeal in that aspect by which God is visible to them, and corporeal in that aspect by which they are visible to human beings. For neither can God be seen by an angel through a body, nor can an angel be seen by a human being without a body.

Since this is so, it cannot be denied that the devil too, having been made from both the incorporeal and the corporeal—as one created together with the holy angels—is of a twofold substance. After he swelled with the dropsy of pride and wasted away with the fever of envy, he fell voluntarily and without locality from holiness, and was cast down locally from heaven, though not voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0767] Another reading: “without locality.”]. He ceased to be good, not to be an angel; he lost innocence, not nature.

Therefore, just as the multitude of angels who remained will be blessed in both aspects of themselves [Note: [Col. 0767] Another reading: “who persists.”], so those who fell will be punished in both aspects of themselves. You will therefore by no means correctly deny that the devil has two substances. For even if you reject me, it will plainly be necessary for you to yield to yourself and to support one part of your argument with another, destroying what is false by what is true.

The devil therefore has a body of his own, though he himself is incorporeal, because he cannot experience corporeal torments without a body. Again, the one who experiences is one thing, and that through which something is experienced is another [Note: [Col. 0768] Another reading: “likewise.”].

If you pay attention, you will be taught the truth by your own statement. You said: “If the devil drew a body from this condensed air, then he carried a foreign body to his torments”—as though I had ever said anything of the sort anywhere.

Yet I do not deny that you have handed victory to us by this argument, though unwillingly. When you say that the devil did not carry a foreign body to his torments, you admit, of course, that he carried his own. It makes no difference to me whether he has his own body or another’s; what matters is whether he has a body.

But you not only admit that the devil has a body; you argue that he has one of his own. This, indeed, is your statement: “If the devil drew a body from this condensed air, then he carried a foreign body to his torments.”

Certainly, the one who carries is something, and what is carried is something. When it is said, “he carries his own,” one thing is signified by the one who carries and another by what he carries. The devil, therefore, is of two distinct and different substances, because when he carries his own body, he is not identical with what he carries.

The burden is one thing, and the bearer another. Therefore, do not struggle against us any longer if you believe yourself: body and that which possesses a body are substantially two things, and these two things are different. And since they are different, one will be incorporeal and the other corporeal. The devil, therefore, is both corporeal and incorporeal, being of two distinct substances [Col. 0767C].

# CHAPTER VIII. That the conversation of Lazarus in Abraham’s bosom and of the rich man in hell, with the intervening chasm, is to be understood spiritually, not corporeally

[Col. 0767D]

## I.

But if, concerning these matters, we have supplied an account at least to some extent, let us examine, under the discussion of your own chapter, that chasm which, as you argue, separates the merits of sinful and innocent souls by intervening spatially between them.

You argue as follows: “If souls are not local, how does that empty chasm, interposed with gloomy separation, distinguish sinners from the gatherings and fellowship of the righteous, so that they cannot come from here to there or cross over from there to here?”

You presented this example from the Gospel reading, removing the simplicity of the Lord’s statement, in order to establish the locality of souls. But the divine oracle, spoken plainly in its own truth, will clearly reveal what your argument has altered, corrupted, and fabricated here [Col. 0768A].

The Lord says in the Gospel: “The poor man died and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. And while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom, and he said: ‘Father Abraham, send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.’ And Abraham replied: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; therefore he is now comforted, while you are tormented. And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that no one can cross from here to us, nor from there to here’” (Luke 16:22–26).

Now explain this to me in terms of places and bodies. There, without the reciprocal exchange of air, without the instrument of the chest, without the windpipe of the throat, without the hollow of the mouth, and without the plectrum of the tongue, produce words with voices, as you claim, through a corporeal soul of whatever kind.

Here, show the hand of the soul, whose fingertip Lazarus is to immerse in water in order to cool the tongue of the burned rich man. Here, from that supposedly corporeal bosom of Abraham, demonstrate something corporeal—something narrow in proportion to the dimensions of a human body and yet capable of containing many. And let that chasm be either so small that the words of those whom it separates can mingle with each other, or so vast that it cannot be crossed.

But this is the greatest point I ask: How could that rich man, burning in the fires of Gehenna among the dead, converse with Abraham if he did not approach the locality of blessedness? And how could Abraham converse with the rich man if he did not enter hell?

You say, with a view that is not altogether implausible, that the souls of the saints dwell in the innermost seats of paradise. Accordingly, since Abraham is in paradise and the rich man in hell, separated from one another by an immense and impassable distance, yet in such a way that they not only see each other but also converse with each other as though nothing intervened, if these matters are to be judged locally, you are compelled to admit one of two alternatives: either Abraham and the rich man did not converse with or see one another, or paradise is in hell or hell is in paradise [Col. 0768C].

# CHAPTER IX. How greatly the vision of the eyes differs from the vision of the soul, since the soul’s vision is understanding; and that, if it saw corporeal things by itself, it would first have seen its own inner organs

[Col. 0768D]

## I.

But since one cannot stubbornly resist divine authority, nor can blessedness be mixed with wretchedness, let us set aside for a little while places and bodies and examine the tangled difficulty of this statement. Since, with eyes blurred by bodily imaginings, we cannot look inward, let us observe that wherever an immense distance is said to exist between persons distinguished by judgment, yet in such a way that an exchange of speech is possible, what is meant is not a distance of places but a difference of merits.

For, as far as the body is concerned, an unjust person can be locally present with a just person; but an unjust person cannot be in the innocence of the just, insofar as he is unjust. Hence, since after death no one can repent or sin, the un-crossable chaos between the saved and the lost signifies an unchangeable condition.

Your own argument, therefore, is brought against you. You now perceive that the testimony which you thought separated us is, as the discussion advances, joining with us, [Note: [Col. 0769] Others: “to assert separation.” And shortly afterward, “to be well” in place of “to become one.”] and that it closes against you, as though by an opposing door, its exceedingly narrow paths leading to the boundless spaces of regions without place. For the narrowness of bodily magnitude cannot contain the immensity of incorporeal subtleties; it cannot embrace either distance without place, speech without sound, or a bosom without spatial extent.

Moreover, whatever exists in this manner is not corporeal. But the souls of Abraham, Lazarus, and the rich man exist in this manner; therefore they are not corporeal.

The arguments resembling these that follow should have fewer watchful efforts devoted to refuting them. [Note: [Col. 0769] Thus the Paris edition. The Lyon edition has *vigidos*. This reading is repeated below in chapter 11, § 2, toward the end.] [Note: [Col. 0769] Thus also the Paris edition. Others have *cordax*; as the lexicons show, the meaning of that word does not suit this passage.] A sound-minded judge rightly considers a person defeated when what he is capable of is equal to what defeats him. Accordingly, I am amazed, and not without shame, that, in order to prove the soul corporeal, you add:

> Behold, if the soul thinks of Alexandria or Jerusalem, and if through thought it was wholly present there, let it report to us the situation of the places, the faces of the people, and the movements and actions of the populations.

Now it is shameful for the author of this statement to take the soul’s corporeality as evidence from the very point where an argument for incorporeality ought to have appeared.

## II.

Thus far I have discussed the incorporeal and placeless vision of the mind, and it has become clear that the mind beholds eternal and unchangeable things without any intervening substance. Therefore, since the rational soul by itself perceives what is incorporeal and without place, and by an entirely incorporeal vision distinguishes the truth, which is God, from falsehood, while it does not see things local and corporeal except through the body, [Note: [Col. 0770] Others: “which belong to these.”] what reason is there for believing it similar to those things in seeing which it employs the body as interpreter, and for judging it dissimilar to those things which it contemplates by itself?

The soul’s vision, as has often been said—and I do not tire of repeating it—is understanding. Corporeal things, however, cannot be understood; they can be sensed by the soul through the body. But just as the soul senses through the body, so it understands by itself. The substance of things that are sensed and understood is entirely different. Thus, because the soul is not a body and cannot sense corporeal things except through the body, it can nevertheless see by itself the things that must be understood.

Yet you, with a view altogether contrary to reason, want corporeal things to be understood and incorporeal things to be seen? But lest the human mind, which you believe to be corporeal, appear able either to see nothing or, by itself, to see only corporeal things or only incorporeal things, as is proper to its nature, let us briefly examine the obscurity of this threefold question as far as we can.

Let us therefore see whether the human mind can see by itself or not. But since almost the whole substance of this matter turns on this point, I ask for a reader who is at once alert and watchful. [Note: [Col. 0770] This word is used by Columella, book VII, chapter 12, and by Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, line 779. Sidonius likewise uses it once and again, as Cangius notes in his *Glossary*. The Paris editors therefore had no reason to replace it with *prudentem* (“prudent”).]

The mind’s vision through the body, which human beings share with animals, extends and projects itself through the points of the pupils, through the heated anterior ventricle of the brain and the invisible fires of the viscera. Flowing through rays and pores, if it encounters and apprehends anything possessing color or form, it receives it and, by the swift passages of its lines, takes it back not only on its outward course but also on its return. This, then, is what is called vision, as we discussed in the first book.

Through this vision, therefore, the human mind, like an animal, distinguishes known bodies from unknown, white bodies from black. Is this as far as human mental vision extends? How, then, does it distinguish the just from the unjust and the true from the false? Or will foolish people with eyes perhaps believe that those who are bodily sighted surpass wise men who are blind?

Let us have as witnesses, concerning this matter, either Appius from the Roman senate, Hermophilus from the Greek gymnasium, or Tobias from the company of the prophets. Appius gave the light of counsel to those whose eyes shone outwardly but were blind within; Hermophilus taught Theopompus geometry without a ray; Tobias, while opening the way through the heavens for his son, gave him an angel as companion.

The mind therefore sees without the body—not something corporeal, colored, or extended through places, but truth itself, which is supremely incorporeal and is God, it contemplates with an incorporeal gaze. It is clear, I think, that the mind sees incorporeal things both by itself and corporeal things through the body.

## III.

But for the sake of the little men of sluggish understanding, one matter remains to be examined: whether the human mind can see corporeal things by itself, without the body.

Now, therefore, be wholly present, and be as present as you can. For, as you assert, if the human mind is itself corporeal and enclosed within the body’s outer enclosure, and if it can see something corporeal by itself, nothing ought to be easier for it to see than the internal parts of the body in which it is enclosed.

Come, I ask you, direct your attention to your own viscera and to all the various parts of your body, and report to me and to us [Note: [Col. 0770] Others: “to you.”], concerning yourself, the bodily vision of the mind which you continually assert: in what manner and in what arrangement the threefold structure of the brain comes together; how the mass of the liver lies; how the spleen’s straight rule is attached; how the balance of the stomach hangs; how the plectrum of the heart strikes; what the courses of the veins and their texture are; what the origins of the nerves and their structure are; what the joining and fastening together of the bones are; what the hollows of the lungs are; what the twisted bends of the intestines are, unfolded through their knot-like passages and their ligaments, with their curves and reversals.

Behold, I think you will deny that you can return answers concerning these matters. Why, then, do you deny it? Clearly because the mind cannot see corporeal things by itself.

But why should it be unable to see corporeal things, when it has already been established that it cannot exist without vision? No one who does not possess bodily vision sees anything corporeal. But the mind, which possesses vision and sees nothing corporeal, sees incorporeally; and the ability to see incorporeally is an incorporeal vision; and no one except an incorporeal being possesses an incorporeal vision. The human mind sees incorporeally; therefore the human mind is incorporeal.

Do not, then, trouble yourself any longer with these trifles, imagining that the mind is not where it thinks because by its nature it cannot contemplate the locations of places, the faces of people, and the movements and actions of populations. These things are corporeal. But the incorporeal mind cannot see what is contrary to its nature.

Nevertheless, it is present where it thinks, insofar as it does not perceive corporeally the places that it thinks about—just as it is present where it gives life, while it does not see the internal parts of the body to which it gives life.

And if it is entirely clear that the mind cannot see corporeal things without the body and cannot see incorporeal things together with the body, let us no longer wander toward Alexandria. Returning from Egypt, having crossed the sea of errors and traversed the desert of ignorance, let us enter the homeland of truth, the land promised to us—not idle or sluggish, nor trembling. If anything born from the fault of deceitful vanity should murmur obscurely or present itself in our path, let it be struck down with Jesus going before us and assisting us.

# CHAPTER X  
## Against Those Who Say: “The Soul Is Incorporeal to Itself but Corporeal to God”

### I.

But here are certain people who, with chattering nonsense that destroys souls, delay us—not by stopping our journey, but by slowing us down. To spend a little time in this interruption is no loss; indeed, it is useful if the same truth either drives away or tramples upon whatever confronts it, whether true or contrary.

When I hear some people say that souls are corporeal, while being unable to deny that they are incorporeal, and that the souls are one thing to themselves and another to their Creator—“To God,” they say, “souls are corporeal, but to themselves they are incorporeal”—this is equivalent to saying that souls are both corporeal and incorporeal.

I call eternity to witness that it is exceedingly laborious for me to respond to these empty statements, because there is nothing here with which I might engage, nothing to draw out from the marrow, nothing with which it would be worthwhile for a trained person to contend, and nothing at all whose conquest would count as a victory.

So the soul is corporeal to its Creator and incorporeal to itself? Reason requires that these two propositions be examined carefully in the pursuit of truth.

Either it is genuinely true that the soul is incorporeal, if it truly knows this about itself; or it is likewise true that the soul is corporeal, if this is established by the soul’s author. These people say both things are true: it is true that the soul is incorporeal because it knows this in truth, and it is likewise true that the soul is corporeal because the Creator of the soul knows this.

They insist that two propositions wholly contrary to one another are both true, although nothing is contrary to truth except falsehood. A most illustrious and brilliant argument indeed: while rejecting one single truth, it discovers two truths for itself. Yet, to hold these human feet bound by the chains of their own profession, they themselves admit that the human mind is incorporeal.

### II.

Since, therefore, we agree on this part of the question, it remains for them to explain how an incorporeal substance can be corporeal to the one who created it incorporeal.

I do not initially affirm whether this is so or not; for the present I grant that it is so. But I ask how they know that it is so.

If the letters of the divine books contain this, let them read it. If some argument persuades them of it, let them teach it. If they wish to exercise dialectic, let them prove it. If none of these things is available, let them at least concede this to their own position: those who are incorporeal in themselves should not believe themselves corporeal outside themselves. For one cannot be something outside oneself if nothing can exist outside oneself.

Therefore the mind, which is incorporeal in itself, cannot in any way be corporeal outside itself. Its author does not know it as being something other than what he made it, nor can it know itself as something other than what it was made.

Accordingly, if the mind truly knows itself when it knows itself to be incorporeal, then God is deceived if he knows a mind that is truly incorporeal as corporeal. But God cannot be deceived. Therefore he knows the mind to be incorporeal, lest the truth by which the mind truly knows itself to be incorporeal be false.

The mind is therefore incorporeal to itself because it is also incorporeal to its Creator. For earth is earth to human beings precisely because it is earth to God; and water, air, and fire are these things to human beings precisely because they are likewise these things to God. Just as everything that has been truly made known to a human being is, in that person’s knowledge, what it is, so the human mind cannot be one thing and be known as another thing by God.

The Creator’s knowledge does not arise from knowledge of things; rather, the existence of things arises from the Creator’s knowledge. Consequently, unless the human mind were incorporeal to God, it could not be incorporeal. For whatever is incorporeal in any respect cannot in any respect be corporeal.

But let us not linger over these people longer than necessary. I yield, and let us now ask about what we have not examined from any angle.

# CHAPTER XI  
## That the Human Being Consists of Two Substances: an Immortal and Placeless Soul, and a Mortal and Local Body; and That, Just as the Soul Suffers Immortally, So It Also Glories Immortally and Placelessly

### I.

You say, for example:

> When the mind paints within the secrets of its own thought the image of Peter or Paul, has it immediately penetrated the innermost dwellings of paradise, where it knows them to be? Or when, from reading, it sets before itself in its heart the flames of that rich man, has it already descended to the places of his torments and to the depths of hell, inaccessible to the living?

I have already given you answers, as far as was fitting, concerning the incorporeal places of souls, hell and paradise, and the soul’s contemplation of corporeal things without the body, when we spoke about the rich man and the poor man, and when we discussed the soul’s twofold vision (*Book III*, chapters 1, 2, and 9).

But since the matter that you stated—namely, that hell is inaccessible to the living—remains unexamined (*Book III*, chapters 6 and 8), I ask what you meant when you said it. We consist, namely, of soul and body.

Although no one doubts what in us is immortal and what is mortal, I shall nevertheless proceed with you in such a way that I answer concerning whichever of the two you prefer.

If we die in neither of our substances, nothing belonging to us descends to hell, since I have said that hell is inaccessible to the living. If we die in both, then the body also descends to hell. Nor must we seek these corporeal hells far away, since the Lord’s own tomb is a place of hell.

But sound doctrine rejects both absurdities. Therefore we neither die in both substances nor fail to die in both.

The soul lives even when the body has been laid aside, although, if it is deprived of its God through sins, it may rightly be called dead. Yet it will certainly not be credible that a sinful soul loses that very thing by which it is a soul, since even a dead body does not cease to be a body. For the body dies when it loses the soul together with all life; but the soul does not lose the soul. [Note: [Col. 0773] Others: “does not lose the soul”; the *Orthodoxographi*: “the body does not lose the soul.”]

Accordingly, the soul is immortal, while the body is mortal.

But if the body does not enter hell, since it is committed to the tomb and divided among the various parts of the world according to the diversity of the elements that had gathered together in it, and if the mind does not approach hell because, according to your doctrine, hell is closed to the living, then either there is no hell, or no human being descends to it.

In that case the basis of our faith will be endangered, if the Redeemer’s soul did not unlock hell by entering and returning from it.

It is enough to say that whatever those hells may be, they are inaccessible to the living, since it is established that they can be approached only by the living.

### II.

Recall now that you placed yourself in this position in your treatise: if you could prove that the soul is subject to quantity or locality, then even the opposing side would agree with you concerning its corporeality.

But if you remember your own writings correctly, you can also observe that you proposed matters for discussion rather than discussing the matters proposed. Nor did you know your ignorance in the manner of the older Academics; rather, in accordance with the younger members of that school, you were ignorant whether you knew anything.

When someone rashly posits two things on which the entire structure of an argument necessarily depends, who would not first strive, if possible, to make each of them—or, if both cannot be established, at least one of them—not necessarily probable, but certainly credible?

These two things are required for victory, so that a worthy author may possess the soundness of a good cause. If one of them is lacking, the force of the undertaking is weakened; if both are absent, it fails altogether.

Thus deception, having found you both a forgetful and ignorant defender, has, before alert intellects [Note: [Col. 0773] The Paris edition, together with the *Orthodoxographi*, has *rigidos*. Lexicographers dislike this word. It occurs above in this book, chapter 9, § 1, where the same Paris edition has *vigiles*, as noted there.], not merely brought it about that it is clear you ought not to be believed in these matters; it has also made the truth, which must always be believed, appear clearer and more brilliant through the necessity of the conflict and the comparison with falsehood.

# CHAPTER XII  
## That the Soul Is Not Held Enclosed in the Body and Does Not Move from Place to Place, Although It Moves Temporally through Affection

### I.

You freely professed that you would assign quality, quantity, and locality to the soul, and then added:

> How can that which is inserted into the limbs and bound to the viscera not be local, when it is held enclosed, while wandering through movements according to the condition of its substance?

Error may perhaps make pardonable your having thought something wrongly and maintained that it appeared plausible; ignorance of one’s error is another matter.

But now I am utterly astonished that you have said things so contradictory and so different in almost the same moment and nearly the same words:

> Therefore it is bound to the limbs and wanders through movements.

And again:

> It wanders through movements and is held enclosed according to the condition of its substance.

If the soul moves within the enclosure of the body, as you say, then it moves while standing still; but reason does not permit this to be said. If, however, it is carried outside the body through movements, then it is not held enclosed according to the condition of its substance.

Who, moreover, says that it wanders only through movements? It is as though anything could wander while motionless—or as though it were not easier to move without wandering, which the mind does through affection, since it is subject to motion not according to place, than for something to wander without moving, which is properly characteristic of the body, since it is subject to motion through place.
