Yet you say that the soul both stands while wandering and wanders while enclosed, although, as has already been established above, it can remain at rest while the body is moved and can move while itself remaining unmoved.

### II.

This, then, is how far you have argued concerning the soul’s locality. Yet I do not accuse you of laziness in this matter. You were simply unable to accomplish what, in this present place, even the greatest orator could scarcely have accomplished. For an advocate of falsehood, however great his eloquence, can lie against evident truth, but he cannot deceive it.

As for quantity, why you promised that you would discuss it and then said nothing about it, I cannot attribute it to forgetfulness, since it is sufficiently clear that you could not even bring its name forward except from memory. [Note: [Col. 0774] The *Orthodoxographi* have “no one could [bring it forward] by it.”]

It is therefore more credible that you did not wish to speak, or that you had forgotten to say that you had found nothing to say. What sense does it make either to summon matters to discussion or to leave the propositions silent?

There will now be no controversy concerning quality, since I have not denied that the soul is subject to it. [Note: [Col. 0774] Others: *tenui*. Shortly afterward, “which certainly,” with *si* omitted.]

For if it were as free from quality as it is from quantity, it would certainly be God. And if it yielded to quantity just as it yields to quality, it would be a body. As it is, it has received an intermediate condition of created incorporeal nature: it is not God, because it has quality, and it is not a body, because it has no quantity.

# CHAPTER XIII  
## That the Sun, Moon, and Stars Are Merely Bodies and Have No Spirits; and That Just as One Body Is Preferred to a Better Body, So One Spirit Is Preferred to an Inferior Spirit

And since, as we have shown in the discussions treated earlier, the vastness of this question extends very widely and embraces the origins of principal causes, one cannot examine it inwardly unless, with the balance of judgment, one separates the substance of the twofold creation as far as is permitted to human beings.

Either we must abandon the matter altogether, or we must approach it by these lines: first distinguish body from incorporeal being; then, just as within the whole category of bodies you prefer shining things to dark, lofty things to low, and precious things to worthless, so among created incorporeal beings prefer human souls to animal souls; among human souls, prudent souls to foolish ones; and among those that possess life by nature, learned souls to unlearned ones.

Just as the sun is a body, and any stone, however unlike it, is nevertheless likewise a body, so the entire nature of every kind of living being is incorporeal. But just as one body surpasses another while both remain bodies, so one mind is preferred to another while both remain minds.

And again, an abundant subject and rich causes entice speakers to speak and, almost courteously presenting themselves, ask to be described according to their own appearance, indeed compelling it. But let those who are there—if there are any whom burning virtue has raised into the ether—approach these excellences, preeminences, and supremacies. [Note: [Col. 0775] Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, line 130.]

For the present, however, it was my task to respond to this question concerning the condition of the soul, according to the manner in which the person with whom we have engaged proposed it—and perhaps to respond at somewhat greater length. Whether I have done so rightly or wrongly, a fair and learned judge will decide.

# CHAPTER XIV  
## A Brief Recapitulation of the Preceding Books

### I.

But since a reader cannot easily retain in memory the many matters that we discussed here and there in the course of this question—what was scattered and elaborated, and what, as I believe, was proved—I have gathered them together beneath the mind’s eye, collected and briefly, as it were point by point, so that they may be reviewed and recognized at once.

### 1. On the incorporeal

God is incorporeal. The human mind, however, is the image of God, since the human being was made according to the likeness and image of God. But the image of an incorporeal being cannot be a body. Therefore, since the human mind is the image of God, the human mind is incorporeal.

### 2. On life

Everything without place is also incorporeal. The soul is the life of the body, and in a living body the smallest part of the body lives just as the whole body does. Therefore there is as much life in a part of the body as in the whole body, and this life is the soul.

Nor is something local when it is as great in the whole as in any part, and as great in what is small as in what is large. Therefore the mind is not local. Whatever is without place is not corporeal; therefore the soul is not a body.

### 3. On reason

The rational soul reasons, and reasoning exists substantially in the soul. Reason is incorporeal and without place; therefore the soul is incorporeal.

### 4. On will

The soul’s will is its substance. If the whole soul wills, the whole soul is will; and will is not a body. Therefore the soul is not a body.

### 5. On memory

Memory is likewise a certain placeless capacity. It is neither stretched by the multitude of things remembered nor diminished by their scarcity, and it remembers corporeal things incorporeally as well.

When the mind remembers, the whole mind remembers, and the whole mind that remembers is memory. Memory is not a body; therefore the mind is not a body.

### 6. On touch

A body senses touch in the part of itself where it is touched. But the mind senses through not the whole body—that is, through a part of the body—while itself sensing as a whole.

Such a sense is without place, and everything without place is incorporeal. Therefore the whole soul is incorporeal.

### 7. On approach and withdrawal

A body neither approaches God nor withdraws from God. The mind, however, draws near and withdraws from him without locality. Therefore the mind is not a body.

### 8. On motion

A body moves through place, but the mind does not move through place. Therefore the mind is not a body.

### 9. On measure

Length, breadth, and height belong to a body, and whatever lacks these is not a body. The mind lacks them; therefore it is not a body.

### 10. On right and left

Right and left, above and below, before and behind exist in every body; none of these exists in the soul. Therefore the whole soul is incorporeal.

### II.

Behold how far we have condensed from every part of our discussions whatever we undertook throughout the entire work. What we have summarized there as briefly as possible could not have been made probable without the discussions that preceded it.

Although, if the matter had found a competent advocate, he would not have dishonored the dignity of the cause with an argument so unequal to it as mine, I nevertheless could not have treated this same question at somewhat greater length and in greater detail.

It was fitting to fight only so far as the adversary was able to resist, or, once he had yielded and taken flight, to press upon his back, seize him by the hand, and disarm him with leaden daggers. To proceed farther, throw weapons into the air, and fight without an enemy is empty contention and a waste of strength—something as inglorious as it is laborious.

“What, then,” someone may say, “have you been wandering through these three volumes against a brief page, if it is sufficient to answer word for word?”

But it is not the same task to construct a deception as to destroy one. Someone may deny in a single word that the world is a sphere; but neither Timaeus nor anyone else would establish this in a single word. Accordingly, whatever more extensive discussion we have undertaken was compelled not only by the refutation of falsehood but also by the establishment of truth.

For it is one thing to teach people to unlearn harmful things and another to teach useful things. Nor is it the same to pull up a thorn from the ground as to sow grain. To uproot vice, therefore, is not the same as to plant virtue. Much more labor must accordingly be spent on both tasks than on either one alone.

Since it was my task to treat both matters, in a work so obstructed by difficulties, restraint is all the more remarkable than prolixity. [Note: [Col. 0776] Others: “of the aforesaid labor.” And shortly afterward: “whence becoming clear.”] For when the issues appeared from every side, becoming clear and displaying themselves, and gave birth to other issues in manifold ways, I prescribed a broader scope for the discussion, set its method, and fixed its limit, so that I would neither bring more forces into the battle than necessary, nor continue the settled contest longer, nor advance farther than was proper.

# CHAPTER XV  
## The Author Asks Forgiveness from His Opponent and Chooses the Judge of the Contest between Them

Whoever you are, against whose writings the injustice of your writings compelled us to speak, I beg and entreat you not to be angry with me. I have neither returned an insult nor repaid abuse. In place of your falsehood I have answered you with truth, though not with an equal exchange.

I am, and shall remain, an adversary to those things that are more harmful to you. I also urge you yourself to oppose your own arguments for your own sake. [Note: [Col. 0777] Thus the Paris edition with the *Orthodoxographi*. The Lyon edition reads: “I, all the more because your own [arguments are] more harmful to you,” etc.]

I have returned these few and slight answers, as the limited time permitted. Weigh both sides within yourself, and between me and you assume the role of judge, applying the balance of justice.

If our scale is more inclined and heavier on the side of truth, let it neither annoy nor shame you to take refuge from defection and yield from falsehood to truth.

But if—as I do not wish—you have been persuaded to employ these impious notions, that is obstinacy: publish something to be read publicly as your judgment, and do not conceal your name. [Note: [Col. 0777] Thus both Orthodoxographic editions. The Lyon edition reads: “nor do this by persuasion, as obstinacy is; publish a judgment in my favor, plainly and publicly to be read. Do not conceal your name. Since, as to how God and life are master of us, we shall from the other side undertake a peril of a hundred [things], you will experience it,” etc. The Paris reading is more felicitous, though itself also corrupt.]

For, from the other side, we have undertaken the peril of “continued roads” (*continuati viarum*; reading uncertain). You will experience, that is, how great the power of truth is in the destruction of falsehood. [Note: [Col. 0778] The Paris edition reads: “Since we have exposed you to the peril of these disputes from the other side,” which is perhaps better.] [Note: [Col. 0778] The Paris edition has: “Since we have brought you into danger in this contest of ours from the opposite side,” which is perhaps better.]

# CLAUDIUS TO C. SOLLIUS APOLLINARIS

If I were not sending you these writings, venerable man, for examination and correction, it might rightly appear excessive and presumptuous to wish to teach one whom I believe to possess knowledge, and to give a drachma from the poverty of my resources to one who abounds in a great talent of learning.

This is why the publication of the little books I sent, which I arranged through the most subtle discussion of philosophical art, made me cautious and solicitous: I resolved not merely to entrust their interpretation to judgment, but to submit them to the expertise of someone more capable. I have sent to your judgment for approval not only what I have now learned from reading them, but also what I previously committed to memory for preservation.

For your dignity knows very well that we possess no one with whose assistance we may be made firm and stable concerning matters about which we are uncertain.

Every nature that comes to God’s knowledge is called by its proper name, and for this reason the nature of each thing is indicated by its name.

The ancients therefore said that a name is so called because it makes a thing known: it introduces into the ears the images of the thing itself, which memory conveys through the senses and the body. Thus, when we speak, we understand; and, when we wish, we think about both absent things and the images retained in memory.

But there are two kinds of nature: corporeal and spiritual. Every creature is either spirit or body. We sense corporeal things through the body; we perceive intellectual things through the intellect.

Therefore, insofar as is granted in this life, every thing is known in two ways. What, then, is meant when it is said that there are three kinds of questions: whether it is, what it is, and what kind it is?

Why, I ask, is the question “whether it is” posed, when every act of knowledge that reveals a thing removes uncertainty and leaves no room for doubt? I think, however, that this question is formulated because not everything is a substance, but some things are found whose proofs reveal what they are.

For example, if it is asked whether the good is a substance or not, we answer that it is not a substance but a privation of evil. It is rightly asked in the first question whether something is a body or a spirit. In the following question it is asked what kind it is: whether it is an animal body or a spiritual one, a rational spirit or an irrational one.

The three kinds of questions have therefore been correctly defined, and, as I believe, we have now spoken sufficiently briefly about them. Let us now also see how many kinds of bodies there are, although they contain innumerable species beneath them.

There are nevertheless three kinds: a body that lives and senses; a body that lives and does not sense; and a body that neither lives nor senses.

I think that the kind of body that neither lives nor senses consists of the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. These are primary and simple, from which all compounded bodies: the living and sensing [bodies] of animals, and the living but non-sensing [bodies] of trees, shrubs, and herbs.

[Col. 0778C]

It is therefore perfectly clear how these differ from one another. With God’s help, let us inquire more attentively what they have in common.

For this is what we wish, with the Lord inspiring and assisting us: not merely to investigate his creature, but also, ascending through the things that have been made to the substance that created them, to behold it intellectually. Although we may not reach the point of being able to understand its substance and know what it is, let us at least hold with complete clarity what it is not.

Every body, therefore, is subject to quantity and quality.

A body that is in a subject is not itself a body. For a body is a subject, not something in a subject, because a body is a substance, not an accident. Accidents are in a substance, not substances in accidents.

Quantity and quality therefore happen to a body. Quantity belongs to measurements; quality belongs to colors.

The body itself is not identical with being quantitative, nor is it identical with being qualified. A body remains even when its color has changed, and in a diminished body the quantity that existed before is no longer present. [Note: [Col. 0778] Others: “or.”]

By the same reasoning, what is large is not the same as magnitude, what is long is not the same as length, what is broad is not the same as breadth, and what is colored is not the same as color. [Note: [Col. 0779] Perhaps: “The measure itself belongs to the body.”]

Measure, number, and weight likewise belong to the body. Hence Holy Scripture says that God arranged all things according to measure, number, and weight (*Wisdom* 11:21). But I see that this must be referred in another way to the rational spirit, as will be explained below.

For now, let us complete what we began concerning the body. Just as we said that what is large is not the same as magnitude, so measure is not the same as what can be measured, number is not the same as what can be numbered, and weight is not the same as what can be weighed.

A body is diminished, since throughout its whole and in its parts it has an upper and a lower side, a right and a left, a front and a back. It moves through time and place, neither judges nor is judged, and is divided infinitely into parts.

Now let us see what it is that gives the body life [Col. 0779B] but does not give it sensation. For life is more properly something equally distributed, both what receives and what gives. For that life which is not smaller in a part than in the whole, and is not smaller in a smaller part, nor provides a larger part with more and a smaller part with less, is not a body but a spirit. The spirit of an animal, which does not subsist after the body, may be passed over, so that we may come to the rational spirit.

Therefore the spirit has no quantity. If it were long or broad, it would properly be called “quantified.” It is wisely distinguished and separated from the body because it is not subject to quantity, although it is subject to quality. Disciplines accrue to the mind; justice and injustice accrue to it, chastity and lust. For there are four principal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. [Note: [Col. 0780] Others read “of the mind.”] The soul is not the same as prudence, nor the just person the same as justice, nor the temperate person the same as temperance, nor the brave person the same as fortitude. It is one thing for the soul to exist, another for a just soul to exist.

When I say “a just soul,” I understand two things. The same could be said of prudence, temperance, and fortitude, because a soul may exist without possessing any virtues whatsoever; but if it does not possess them, it necessarily possesses vice. For it follows that the soul is always the subject either of vices or of virtues; it is the subject, as we said, of disciplines, which cannot exist without it.

Indeed, the truth of number is a discipline. It will never be the case that four and two make seven, or seven and three make eleven. Likewise, the form of a circle admits no contradiction. It will never be the case that the figure of a circle is made from two or three lines, or a quadrilateral from three, or a triangle from four. For if you add or subtract anything, it will no longer be a triangle or a quadrilateral; it remains eternal and unchangeable.

The principles of these disciplines exist both in the subject, the soul, and cannot exist without it. It follows that that in which they exist is eternal, just as what exists in it is eternal. Therefore the soul is immortal; and that which lives knows and sees forever. Yet it does not always think of this, because, although it is secure in itself, it loses itself amid many thoughts and stretches itself out as though moved through time rather than through place. Nevertheless, it moves the body through time and place; that is, it judges and is judged.

See, therefore, what a great good the human soul is, while you judge bodies, while you are joined to reason, while you share in eternal truth. For you must not love those things that are beneath you; and although measure exists in you, you are not measure. Number belongs to your thought, weight to your pleasure: you yourself are neither number nor weight. Direct the will of your love toward that number without number, of which the Psalmist says, “And of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. 146:5); toward that measure without measure, toward that weight without weight, by which all things are weighed and measured.

He is the highest good, from whom all the good kinds of bodies were made. He is the highest good of rational beings, truly both good in reality and a great good. Love the highest good, the simple good—that is, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This Trinity is one God.

And yet the body and the spirit must be loved according to what they ought to be loved, as a certain most noble interpreter of the Holy Scriptures said: “You shall set down four rules of love: what is above us, what is beside us, what we are, and what is beneath us.” Let us therefore love that highest good which is above us—not in the order of place, but of nature—because creation cannot be made equal to the Creator. For the Son alone is equal to the Father, and likewise the Holy Spirit, because they are not creatures but possess one nature among themselves.

The figure placed below demonstrates these matters, which we have arranged in a brief discourse.

[Col. 0779]

TWO LETTERS OF MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, PRIEST OF VIENNE. (S)

[Col. 0779D]

FIRST LETTER.

CLAUDIANUS TO POPE SIDONIUS, GREETING.

[Note: [Col. 0779] This letter of Claudianus is the second among the letters of Sidonius, Book IV.]

If it were possible for me to meet you, my lord, even occasionally and for a little while, I would not inquire indiscriminately into the inclinations or needs of various persons, but into whatever might be of use to me in the exercise of my duty. The opportunity for visiting you is cut off in many ways and, equally, by pitiable circumstances. Indeed, the opportunity for writing is either rarely available in a suitable form or is not available at all. Whether these matters are excusable or not, you yourself must judge.

Moreover, what you so often grant in your letters to others—people who neither seek it nor, perhaps, deserve it as much as I do—I do not think can be committed with impunity against the laws of friendship. I shall also not conceal without sorrow that you have never honored with a reply those little books which you do not refuse to have ennobled by your name. But perhaps you lack the spare time which you yourself devote, in small measure, to a very great friendship.

Will you ever be so entangled in business, anywhere or at any time, that it does not rebound to the advantage of others? When you appease God with prayer, you reconcile him not only to your friends but also to strangers. When you investigate the mysteries of the heavenly Scriptures, the more diligently you fill yourself with them, the more abundantly you pour doctrine into others. When you lavish your resources on the needs of the poor, you provide most especially for yourself, but also for others.

Thus, clearly, nothing—indeed, absolutely nothing—in all your actions is so barren that it yields fruit only to you and not also, together with you, to many others. Therefore no opportunity for any impediment can even falsely be alleged as a reason why I, your special and intimate friend, should receive nothing from him who makes even the unknown partake abundantly.

But, as I suppose, in accordance with the manner of the evangelical giver, what you do not give to a hungry friend, you will give to a wicked petitioner. Further, [Col. 0781C] if even now you have become hardened in your customary way, I shall myself do something that will make you repent: for if you continue to sin by silence, I shall immediately take revenge by writing. Indeed, there is no ambiguity in this: you must be punished by my letter just as I am punished by your silence.

Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0781] This is the third letter of the same Book IV, in which Sidonius replies to the preceding one.]

SIDONIUS TO HIS CLAUDIANUS, GREETING.

You declare, my superior in our relationship, that I am violating the rights of intimacy because I have long refrained from pen and tablets with regard to what is owed to you in the way of a greeting, and because no sheet of papyrus has subsequently burdened me with any message that might convey to you my diligent expression of good health. You make these accusations beyond what is fair, if you think that any mortal—provided he cares to speak in Latin—does not tremble when he is brought in writing before the examination of your ears; your ears, I say, whose expertise, if the distinction of the years that have passed up to our age does not overwhelm me, I could not match either in the gravity of Fronto or in the weight of Apuleius’ stream of eloquence. In your presence, the Varros—whether the Atacinus or Terentius—and the Plinys—whether the uncle or Secundus—would presently appear rustic.

That volume which you yourself published on the condition of the soul and on the knowledge of things and words confirms my judgment. Since, in its preface, you address my name, I received this chief benefit from it: that the reputation of my person—although it was not worth the effort of becoming famous—might be perpetuated through the titles of its books by your favor.

But, great God, what a work it is! Its subject is enclosed, its declamation conspicuous, its proposition obstructed, its disputation unlocked; and although it is thorny because of the hooked points of its syllogisms, it is nevertheless sweetened by the flower of flourishing eloquence. [Note: [Col. 0782] In some books, “softened.”] Its words are new because they are ancient; and, when compared with them, even the style of ancient literature would rightly be made old. More precious still, its entire diction is so compressed by its clauses that it is nevertheless flowing; rich in matter and concise in propositions, it seems to teach more than it says.

In former times, not unjustly, this was regarded as the chief form of eloquence: while containing much in few words, it took care to fill the subject rather than the page. But in your books, what is this quality—that even amid continuous maturity they admit tenderness and insert a timely sweetness of judgment, so that they suddenly refresh the reader’s attention, wearied by the articulated divisions of philosophical disciplines, with pleasurable digressions as though with certain harbors of their own sea?

O book rich in many ways! O eloquence not slender but subtle in intellect, which neither swells through the springs of hyperbole nor is weakened through depressed understatement! In addition, it possesses a unique and singular learning, conspicuous in its exposition of diverse subjects. Its custom is to philosophize about each art with its respective craftsman; and, when occasion demands, it does not refuse to hold the lyre with Orpheus, the staff with Aesculapius, the measuring rod with Archimedes, the horoscope with Euphrates, the compass with Perdix, and the plumb line with Vitruvius. Nor does it ever cease investigating: with Thales, the seasons; with Atlas, the stars; with Zethus, weights; with Chrysippus, numbers; with Euclid, measurements.

Finally, no one in my age has been able to affirm what he wished in such a manner. For, when it sets itself against the person against whom it speaks, it rightly claims for itself the distinctive mark of both moral traditions and both fields of study. It thinks like Pythagoras, divides like Socrates, explains like Plato, entangles like Aristotle, flatters like Aeschines, grows angry like Demosthenes, blossoms like Hortensius, like Cethegus it excites, like Curio it urges, like Fabius it delays, pretends like Crassus, conceals like Caesar, advises like Cato, dissuades like Appius, and persuades like Cicero.

If we turn for comparison to the most holy Fathers, it instructs like Jerome, dismantles like Lactantius, constructs like Augustine, rises like Hilary, humbles itself like John; like Basil it rebukes, like Gregory it consoles, like Orosius it flows forth, like Rufinus it is concise, like Eusebius it narrates, like Eucherius it exhorts, like Paulinus it challenges, and like Ambrose it perseveres.

But if you ask what I think of your Hymn, it is compact in clauses, abundant, sweet, and elevated; in poetic charm and historical truth it surpasses every kind of lyric dithyramb. And its particular distinction is this: while preserving the feet of its meters, the syllables of its feet, and the quantities of its syllables within the limits of their space, it encloses rich words in a verse of narrow compass; nor does the brevity of its compressed song exclude the length of ornamented speech.

Thus it is easy for you, with small trochees and still smaller pyrrhics, to produce not only threefold combinations of molossians and anapaests but also fourfold combinations of epitrites and paeons. The amplitude of your discourse rises beyond the narrowness of its formal limits; and, just as a large gem can scarcely be contained in a small piece of gold, so it flashes forth like the spirit of a powerful horse. If, while it is snorting, it is restrained among rough ground and crags by the law of the reins, you understand that it lacks not so much running as space.

Why say more? I judge that in neither kind of eloquence will Athens be considered so Attic, nor the Muses so musical, provided that prolonged indolence has not deprived me of the opportunity to judge. For while, under the pretext of my adopted profession, I gradually seek a new manner of writing and unlearn the old by leaps, I have nothing more to say of a good orator than that I have begun to be more than a bad poet.

Therefore, I ask you to pardon me this fault: that, remembering me for a little while, I less often mingle my dry little stream with your river. The whole world, wherever it extends, will rightly venerate your trumpet; it is clear that it sounded with doubled success when it found neither a rival nor an equal, as it formerly spread through the ears and mouths of the peoples, with me too carrying it abroad.

For us, however, it is a great boldness to chatter even among municipal and cathedral orators or courtroom babblers; who, even when they plead their cases—without offense to their superiors—devote themselves to the most illiterate letters before a more numerous crowd. But you, for whom it is pleasing to alternate between free and bound speech, can thunder in either fashion; few whom impartial Jupiter has loved will imitate you. [Note: [Col. 0783] Apparently, this word is missing improperly from the excellent edition of Sirmond.]

Farewell.

[Col. 0783C]

[Note: [Col. 0783] This letter appears among the Miscellanies of Baluze, vol. VI, pp. 535–538.]

SECOND LETTER.

CLAUDIANUS TO SAPAUDUS, RHETORICIAN, A MOST LEARNED MAN. [Note: [Col. 0784] This letter is addressed to Sapaudus; it is the tenth letter of Sidonius, Book V.]

Greece, the teacher of all disciplines and arts, advanced to the highest distinction in noble studies and embraced almost the whole world with her manifold learning chiefly because no one there ever produced anything of good fruit without receiving an honor proportionate to his merit.

Hence certain mortals who almost surpassed the nature of mortals, extending everywhere the powers of their outstanding intellects, and with tireless care searching out what was hidden in things, grasped by investigation and skill the concealed causes of original beginnings and the fixed limits of substances fluctuating through time; they entered not only into the secrets of the world but even into those beyond the heavens.

I have reason to say this now, because, since the loss of the good arts began in the age of our great-grandfathers, the human race—despising the cultivation of the soul, by which alone it surpasses the beasts, serving pleasures and riches, and enslaved to idleness and ignorance—has finally cast down both learning and virtue. For since no one, apart from you, aspires not merely to renew something but even to unlearn, should we attribute this to human negligence or to nature?

If we attribute this evil to a defect in nature, can the human race be said to differ from the human race? Are minds no longer what they once were? Or was Cicero, the greatest orator of his age, born with the good things of his age already in his possession, rather than traveling abroad all the way to Greece to acquire richer learning, because he placed little value on domestic and civic matters? Or did Plato, the summit and pinnacle of philosophy, content with the private endowment of nature, and believing after the doctrines of Socrates that Greece was narrower in learning than in virtue, not travel as far as Egypt, as far as the Brahmans of India, and as far as the inheritors of Pythagorean teachings, an indefatigable investigator of things?

I say nothing of the others, because neither time nor the nature of this work permits it. This one thing I shall say without any doubt: our age does not lack intellects but studies. I would have buried the death of those studies, as it were, in a mournful epitaph, unless you had revived them with the same venerable profession, praiseworthy diligence, keen intellect, and flowing eloquence. This good is all the more astonishing to me because it had seemed so hopeless.

For I see the Roman tongue—not merely neglected but a source of shame to Romans—driven away, as it were, by the blows and kicks of barbarism and solecism; dialectic feared like an Amazon preparing for battle with drawn sword; rhetoric, as though a great lady, not admitted into a narrow space; music, geometry, and arithmetic despised as three Furies; and philosophy thereafter counted as something ominous and bestial.

But these remarks have been introduced in your praise. For if there were many who possessed the studies that you possess, you would presumably be—even if not the foremost of all—one among many. Hence, without doing injury to anyone else, throughout our Gaul you are the one and only equal in your profession.

Nor should what I have said be attributed to flattery or adulation. Certainly I am not able to flatter, nor do you need to be falsely praised. But the sweetness of your declamations, mingled with virtue, cannot be torn up or removed from my heart. It is like Attic honey, to which healing power, strength, and sweetness are naturally implanted; on the ridges of Hybla the winged little worker, the bee, takes it as something fallen from heaven and draws it in, then pours it into her fashioned, honey-bearing flowers, nourishing and enriching the offspring born of her virginity with the breast of her honeycombs.

So you, gathering from the highest authorities, as though from great mountains, whatever is more learned, fragrant like thyme, and more fertile, as though you were plucking flowers, fill those whose minds you imbue with the honey of your intellect and fashion honeycombs of eloquence, from which in turn is formed the multitude of your beloved pupils, as though they were your children. Imbued also with the nectar of Greek disciplines, and as though nourished on Attic honey, once they begin to beat their wings, they too will make honeycombs of eloquence.

Only see to it that you remember that the duty of teaching has come to you by hereditary descent from your great-grandfathers and earlier ancestors, and that you ought to strive all the more abundantly for knowledge because manifold learning derived from your forebears has flowed together in you.

You must also be reminded of the ancient nobility of the city of Vienne, whose citizen and teacher you are. You will discharge a double obligation not through idleness, since you are asked in two ways either to answer your ancestors or your fatherland.

Finally, I ask you with the greatest familiarity to despise the childish trifles of novel little calculations and to spend no time reading the works [Note: [Col. 0785] Perhaps “which, while …”; Fabricius reads this way, Bibliotheca mediae aetatis, vol. I, p. 1078.] in which certain writers whirl about little bull-belts of ringing chatter and emasculate oratorical strength with applauding choruses. Let Naevius and Plautus serve you in acquiring elegance, Cato in gravity, Varro in expertise, Gracchus in sharpness, [Col. 0786A] Chrysippus in discipline, Fronto in splendor, and Cicero in eloquence.

For whoever among the moderns has written anything worthy of memory did not himself read only modern authors. Those earlier writers, therefore, are to be revisited and committed to memory, from whom those whom we admire were able to profit.

In this matter I have perhaps offered this testimony of friendship somewhat too familiarly. But may the indulgence of your goodwill grant pardon to the boldness of affection.

[Col. 0785]

HYMN OF MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, PRIEST OF VIENNE, ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD. (S)

[Col. 0785B]

Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious struggle,

and upon the trophy of the cross proclaim the noble triumph:

how the Redeemer of the world, sacrificed, conquered.

The Maker, grieving over the fraud of the first-created parent,

when through the bite of the deadly fruit he fell into death,

himself then marked the wood, so that he might undo the losses caused by the wood.

The order of our salvation had demanded this work:

that by the art of the many-formed betrayer he might outwit the art,

and bring healing from the place from which the enemy had wounded us.

When, therefore, the fullness of sacred time came,

the Son, the world’s creator, was sent from the Father’s citadel,

and, made flesh in a virgin womb, came forth.

The infant cries, enclosed in the narrow manger;

the virgin mother binds his limbs in swaddling clothes;

a band tightly encircles his feet, hands, and legs.

After six lustra had already been completed, [Note: [Col. 0786] Others read “having passed through six years.”] fulfilling the appointed time of his bodily life, [Col. 0786B]

he willingly gave himself to this passion,

and the Lamb was lifted up to be sacrificed on the wood of the cross.

Here vinegar, gall, reed, spittle, nails, and lance;

the gentle body is pierced, and blood pours forth like a flood.

The earth, sea, stars, and world are washed in that stream.

Faithful cross, noblest tree among all:

no forest produces one like you in leaf, flower, or bud.

Sweet wood, sweet sign, sweet burden that you sustain. [Note: [Col. 0786] Others read “sweet nails”; and shortly afterward, “sustaining.”]

Bend your branches, lofty tree; loosen your stretched limbs,

and let that stiffness grow supple which birth gave you,

so that you may extend the limbs of the heavenly King upon a gentle trunk.

You alone were worthy to bear the ransom of the world

and to prepare a harbor for the shipwrecked world,

which the sacred blood, poured from the Lamb’s body, has anointed.

[Col. 0785]

POEMS OF UNCERTAIN AUTHORSHIP.

(From the Pisaurian Collection.) (G,S)*

[Col. 0785C]

A POEM AGAINST VAIN POETS.

I now promise myself that I shall place your songs in the sacred books

and that, inflamed with the name of Christ God, you will loosen your lips

to speak eloquently to the supreme Father.

Begin to devote your hearts wholly to divine things

and to raise your uplifted thoughts from earth to God.

Soon a new light will rise before your eyes, with heaven opened,

and the Holy Spirit will enter silently through open ways

and shake your inward being with joyful breath.

Come, then, stretch the lyre and strike your fertile breast;

let the great power that has been spent on customary songs depart,

for a greater order of things is being born for you.

You no longer sing merely of the judgment of Paris or the wars of the Giants—

let that have been your childish amusement in an earlier age;

such diversions once suited a little boy.

Now, more serious in mind, as you have advanced in years,

you should reject the Muses with mature heart,

and, as your age now fittingly demands from your chaste character

and as the venerable example of your lips requires,

take up a subject and conceive divine thoughts.

If you have gained some distinction and name from false things,

if you have drawn great renown from empty subjects

when you sang of inventions in ancient poems

or recounted earthly deeds while praising the insignia of triumphant kings,

you are not, in truth, worthy to derive praise from those works,

which you adorned more by the abundance of your words.

How much greater glory will grow for you from these beginnings,

in which, exercising your tongue, you will also educate your holy mind,

and gain both praise and life at once.

While you read wisely and write the true miracles of the supreme God,

you will learn to be nearer and dearer to God himself;

while believing, you will marvel at him;

and, beginning to love, you will rightly sink into Christ through love.

Until now the trumpet of your vain voice has sounded for vain purposes;

now let it thunder forth loftier deeds.

Learn more deeply the causes of things and the beginnings of the world.

Do not seek, with a wandering mind, the innumerable worlds of Epicurus—

worlds which, in his madness, he brings forth from atoms as parents through the void—

searching in vain through empty space.

Moses, venerable under his ancient title as lawgiver,

will release you from your empty cares as he traces the composed world

back to its first beginning, when God was establishing it.

As he tells of the human being formed from clay and breathed upon with sacred breath,

he will himself teach you by whose gift that human being is higher on earth

than all creatures that breathe.

And do not despise yourself as though you were Pyrrha’s stones or Prometheus’ clay:

the supreme hand fashioned you sublime in face and mind

and deemed you worthy of its own image.

There you will learn not to continue assigning our freedom to fate—

that judgment which has bound us to death—

or under whose law we drag out our life.

If you cast your mind higher than heaven

and desire to know what is or what existed before time,

John teaches what lies beyond both the world and the ages.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word; God rejoiced in the Word;

the Word was simultaneously God’s Word and God himself.

This Word, without whom nothing exists and through whom all things exist,

and to whom all nature, spread beneath God, serves,

the divinity of the begotten adores, as does that of the Begetter.

And now by his begotten ones we confess the Lord Jesus

as reigning in the majesty of the Father.

In his name our salvation is founded,

and our faith rests upon him, reaching toward life eternal through the ages.

Strengthened by this divine gift,

we attain, through chaste deeds, to overcome our frail nature,

to break apart the bonds of harsh death,

and to live in the body not according to bodily laws,

following the divine footprints of God’s Christ,

while the mind governs the soul and body under sacred arms.

For the mind, subject to God, takes up the weapons of salvation;

it gains dominion over its soul and flesh,

and every person becomes rightly master of himself

who, devoted to the one Lord, becomes ruler forever over his own limbs,

unconquered by vices and hating wickedness,

stronger than adversities through the virtues, in due order.

He is a true human being because he is powerful in mind,

in which he possesses the light of reason;

without struggle he governs his servant senses

and bends his breast with gentle reins.

You, whose noble mind is a fire of heavenly seed,

burning to climb with your spirit in ethereal steps,

insert your head into the bosom of the Lord.

Soon Christ, abundant, will give to you, thirsting,

flowing breasts full of sacred milk,

and will flood your mind with divine light,

so that, once great darkness has been driven away,

you may see the laws of the awesome God,

by which Christ, the wisdom of the all-parent,

always remaining in himself, renews all the forms of things.

And as God, the arbiter of his works, wills to be,

he contains and changes the forms and seasons of life;

he extends or withdraws heaven, sea, stars, and winds,

ruling by the power through which he made them.

The great outcome teaches this:

Egypt, and the tyrant drowned when the sea flowed back,

and he who himself first experienced grievous movements

through all the elements, whom all things tremble before

and whom all things serve.

For a time the common earth had the Jews,

the nation then chosen by God alone;

yet the weighty anger of God ran distinctly among the mingled peoples

against those proud enemies.

Now I know you will not say that uncertain chance drives the storms,

when you read that the sea, ordered to withdraw,

withdrew, and that a dry path opened among the rigid waves;

and that, when the sea was again released at the command

and by the staff of the holy prophet,

the waters returned to their fluid hollows.

In both instances the power of the sea obeyed,

so that a way might be given to the holy and vengeance to their enemies.

What of the prophet fleeing toward Tarshish,

who, cast into the sea by the lot of danger,

was seized by a huge creature with its spacious jaws

and vomited unharmed from its vast belly?

Does this not teach that the sea and the stars are moved by God’s authority?

For, fleeing in vain from God, whom no one escapes,

since he holds all things, he stirred the anger of both heaven and sea.

For the nature of the omnipotent Lord,

recognizing the rebel, feared, as though conscious of its own safety,

to carry the guilty man, and bound the fugitive with winds and waves.

This prophet, chosen by God to terrify peoples who sin

with a threatening warning, after he proclaimed grave destruction

and subdued the guilty, turned away the anger of the divine power;

perverse Nineveh washed away its crimes with abundant weeping

and escaped its final day.

That king did not have a fixed fate: when death was near,

he prayed to the Lord, whom he knew to be the one

who could bend his own laws,

so that he might extend his exhausted life.

He deserved to lead fifteen additional years,

himself surviving his own years and living beyond his allotted age.

Now let us marvel at Plato weaving the three Fates,

or at the numbers of Aratus and the painted stars of Manetho.

Let them say, I ask, where they then placed the rapid paths

for things coming into being, and which stars moved in which signs,

when the pious Hezekiah, praying through the power of faith,

turned the courses of the stars and disturbed the paths of heaven,

when the sun’s light was ordered to move backward.

Or when, at the command of the holy leader,

the same sun stood still, prolonging the day,

so that the victory of the sacred people might be secured,

it stood poised with the sphere turned back,

so that the increased light might encompass great triumphs.

What of Christ, the offspring, power, and wisdom of God?

Does he not sufficiently remove our cares from vain errors

and teach us by both admonitions and deeds

that one God governs all things,

and that we should suppose nothing to exist without the mind of God the ruler?

He says that not a leaf from a tree,

nor a bird from the air, falls without his command.

When the Almighty lays the sea low by his word or treads upon it,

drives away deaths by his word or presses demons,

or sends souls back into holy bodies,

and, long dead, orders them to go forth from opened tombs,

restoring the buried when life returns—

does not the Author sufficiently indicate his own power,

he who alone governs all nature and life?

To these things, I pray, devote your zeal and labor,

to reading and writing them.

Sing of the great beginnings of the Thunderer;

write of the beginnings of created things by the Word,

and of the chaos before day and the first twilight of light.

All that God thereafter said or did throughout the ages

in the various elements you will learn through the holy books:

what Moses taught, inscribed on the legal tablets,

or what the new law of the Gospel Testament sets forth: Christ,

revealing mysteries formerly hidden.

Then I shall truly call you a divine poet,

and I shall drink your songs as though they were sweet water,

when from the highest springs they offer me nectarous draughts

that retain Christ, the Lord of all things,

and testify that your mind flourishes in God,

so that from you I may receive at once the riches of speech and of mind.

And him whom I rejoice to have joined to me by a bond of kinship,

I shall congratulate as a relative under holy religion;

and, when the bonds of the mortal body must be dissolved,

I shall embrace him forever in a sacred pledge.**

TO JACOBUS, MASTER OF CAVALRY.

By the ashes of Paul, by the gray-haired threshold of Peter,

do not tear apart my verses, commander Jacobus.

So may Thomas support your breast in place of a shield,

and may Bartholomew go with you as companion to war.

So may no barbarian invade the Alps through the aid of the saints;

so may holy Susanna grant you her strength.

So may whoever, fierce, swims across the icy Danube

be drowned, like Pharaoh’s winged horses.

So may the avenging sword strike the Gothic bands,

and may fortunate weapons guide Roman hands.

So may the dying guest give you a great triumph,

and may poured-out jars conquer your thirst.

So may your right hand never be stained with enemy blood.

Do not tear apart my verses, commander Jacobus.

PASCHAL POEM.

Christ, powerful ruler of things, creator of the returning age,

voice and understanding of the supreme God, whom the Father poured forth

from his exalted mind and granted a share in so great a kingdom;

you who subdued the impious crimes of our life,

having suffered to clothe yourself in the bodily form of the world,

and to speak openly to peoples and confess yourself human;

you whom Mary enclosed in her womb, and when the divine power was seen,

her virginal breasts swelled,

and the unmarried Mother marvelled that her womb was filled

with a mysterious birth, about to give birth to her own Author.

Mortal hearts held the Maker of heaven,

and the discoverer of the world became part of the human race.

He who embraces the whole world far and wide lay hidden beneath one breast;

and he whom neither the spaces of earth, nor the wave of the sea,

nor heaven can contain, gathered himself into small limbs.

You even took upon yourself the name and bonds of punishment,

so that you might snatch us from death

and drive away death by your death.

Then, carried upward into the ethereal breezes,

you return to your joyful Father, after the earth has been cleansed.

May you favor the narrow observance, so that on festal days

the annual fast of the pure sacred rite may often be celebrated.

TO THE SAVIOR.

O you who guard the wise travail of everlasting fire,

having entered the world’s revolving necessity;

Christ, life-giving source of the divinely spoken life,

first-sown Word of the ineffable Father God;

you who, having established the great burden pregnant with maternal birth

and the self-completed offspring of unwedded marriage songs,

halted the mad delusion of the Assyrian race with its alien mind,

and destroyed the rites of empty idols bearing false names;

you have mounted the chariot of the seven-zoned heaven,

and on angelic wings you hasten through ineffable things.

Be merciful, venerable eye of the all-begetting God.

Guardian of life, savior of mortals, ruler of eternity.

TO THE LORD CHRIST.

Newly manifest, guardian of the city, ancient-born, young offspring,

ever-existing, existing before all things, most high and last, Christ,

of the immortal Father, coeval with him, wholly like him.

PRAISE OF CHRIST.

True offspring of God, older than all the years,

now begotten, who have always existed, and creator of the light

that existed before your own light;

parent of your mother, whom the coeternal Father sent from heaven,

and, poured forth as the seed of the Word,

commanded to dwell in a virgin womb,

to enter the pathways of a confined body,

and to remain in a small dwelling.

No dwelling can contain you;

you saw, in the first light, whatever you had created

when the world was coming into being.

You yourself the maker, yourself the work of yourself,

deigned to experience the unjust changes of age,

to endure the varied conditions of this body,

and to undergo humanity,

so that he might show God,

lest slippery error and the long-deceived ingenuity of the changing world

allow mortal hearts, for so many ages,

to remain ignorant of their creator.

Your conscious mother knew you through the birth,

and the startled fears of the cattle perceived you.

The Magi, scanning the new stars in heaven with anxious gaze,

saw you first in the sky and, following the light,

found you.

You release guilty hearts,

restore escaped souls to lifeless bodies,

and command life to return.

By the law of the gift received,

you enter the realm of the dead and approach the hiding places of death,

immortal.

For to you alone birth was a beginning,

and death an end.

But when night has been dispersed,

you return to heaven and to the Father,

and once more, in everlasting order,

you remove pollution from the cleansed earth.

You alone, and the innocent Spirit, companion of the Father,

are one so many times, simple in the threefold name.

What else could you be but for all?

Who could believe that you were able to die,

you who were able to restore life?

MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

An angel addresses Mary, by whose prophetic word

she may conceive God while her virginity remains intact.

The Chaldean kings give you prophetic gifts:

receive myrrh as man, gold as king, incense as God.

Christ changes water into flowing wine;

by this first deed he proves himself to be God.

Five loaves and two fish feed five thousand;

and God commands that more remain from the little.

Born from the womb blind, he perceived new light

and marvelled that he had obtained a day he had never known.

Lazarus rises from the tomb when Christ calls,

and the law of harsh death is dissolved and perishes.

The waves shake Peter as he falters; Christ, upon the deep, [Col. 0790C]

both steadies his steps with his right hand and confirms his faith with his word.

A bloodless woman touches Christ’s garment;

the blood stands still in her veins: faith becomes her medicine.

The paralytic, commanded after many years, walks,

himself the remarkable bearer of his own bed.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 450. SAINT PATRICK, APOSTLE OF THE IRISH.

[Col. 0789]

PROLEGOMENA. GALLAND’S PROLEGOMENON ON SAINT PATRICK.

(Galland, Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum, vol. X.)

[Col. 0789C]

## I

Probus, Jocelinus, and other writers of the Middle Ages committed the deeds of Saint Patrick to writing, though their authority does not rest on a firm foundation. Among more recent writers, however, Usserius,[Note: [Col. 0789] Usserius, *British Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, chap. 17, pp. 425 ff., 2nd London edition, 1687.] the Bollandists,[Note: [Col. 0789] Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, March, vol. II, p. 517 ff.] and Tillemont[Note: [Col. 0790] Tillemont, *Ecclesiastical Memoirs*, vol. XVI, pp. 452, 781 ff.] have transmitted more reliable accounts. I neither wish nor have room to pursue these matters at length here, especially if the purpose of our undertaking is taken into consideration. Yet from the blessed bishop’s *Confession* and from his *Epistle to Coroticus*, which are the first among his writings, the reader will extract much that is useful for properly distinguishing the events of his life—material which he would seek in vain elsewhere with greater certainty.

For more about our holy bishop, see John of Glastonbury, published by Thomas Hearne at Oxford in 1726.[Note: [Col. 0791] John of Glastonbury, *History of Glastonbury Affairs*, vol. I.]

For the present it will suffice to note this one point: Patrick was called by God to the conversion of the Irish around the year 431,[Note: [Col. 0791] Pagi, under the year 431, § 52.] and, after exhausting himself through innumerable labors in fulfilling that apostolic office, departed this life in the year 491, at the age of 120, according to the more common opinion.[Note: [Col. 0791] See Tillemont, cited work, p. 783, note 3, “On Saint Patrick.”]

Moreover, to use Pagi’s words:[Note: [Col. 0791] Pagi, under the year 491, § 19.]

> “The Irish owe to Patrick the fact that their homeland became the island of the saints and was at one time a center of letters and learning. For although certain seeds of Christian teaching had been scattered in Ireland before him, and for that reason Saint Palladius is said to have been sent to the Scots who believed in Christ, nevertheless the honor and title of Ireland’s conversion belong to Patrick alone. Through him, not merely a few individuals or people from the common crowd, but kings and princes and whole peoples, baptized with saving baptism, bowed their necks beneath the yoke of faith. He clothed Saint Brigid in the religious habit; he convened certain councils reported by Speelman; and through his efforts very many churches were erected here and there, with bishops ordained in them.”

Such is Pagi’s account.

## II

Now, to proceed to the examination of the little works attributed to Saint Patrick, we have followed the edition of James Waraeus, which appeared in London in 1656. He brought some of them to light from ancient manuscript codices; he revised the remainder; and finally he illustrated them all with historical notes.

First among them stands the *Confession* of the holy Father, transmitted in epistolary form to the Irish, in which he explains the course of his life and preaching. From this *Confession* Probus the Irishman, famous in the tenth century, extracted and incorporated into his two books on the life of Saint Patrick many fragments relating to history. His work is found among the writings of Bede,[Note: [Col. 0791] Bede, works, vol. III, pp. 225 ff., Cologne edition, 1688.] to whom it is wrongly attributed, as is clear from the end of Book II, where the author openly reveals his name in these words:[Note: [Col. 0791] Same work, p. 242.]

> “Behold, brother Pauline, you have from me, the humble Probus, the judgment concerning our brotherhood which you had requested, wishing us poor men to write for you something about the virtues of our most holy father Patrick, the bishop.”

The aforesaid Waraeus was the first to publish this little work, collating four ancient manuscript copies, as he himself declares.[Note: [Col. 0791] Waraeus, on the little work of Saint Patrick, p. 94.] We have compared his edition[Col. 0792A] with that which the Bollandists published from the very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Nobiliacum.[Note: [Col. 0791] Bollandists, *Acta Sanctorum*, March, vol. II, pp. 533 ff.] We have also added several annotations by which certain passages are either restored or elucidated; and we have done the same in places below, insofar as our task required.

## III

Patrick’s *Confession* is followed by his *Epistle to Coroticus*, the Cambro-British petty king—or rather, as it is correctly entitled by the Bollandists, to the Christians subject to the tyrant Coroticus.[Note: [Col. 0791] Same work, p. 538.] Waraeus observes[Note: [Col. 0792] Waraeus, preface to the little work of Saint Patrick.] that this epistle is expressly mentioned in the *Life of Saint Patrick* by Jocelinus,[Note: [Col. 0792] Jocelinus, *Life of Saint Patrick*, chap. 150.] a Cistercian monk of the Furness monastery in Lancashire. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century and composed that *Life*[Note: [Col. 0792] Same work, prologue.] at the command of the most reverend Thomas, bishop of Armagh and primate of all Ireland, and of Malachy, bishop of Down, as well as at the request of the most illustrious John de Courcy, prince of Ulidia.

After the Antwerp, Paris, and Louvain editions, the Bollandists again committed Jocelinus’s work to print,[Note: [Col. 0792] Bollandists, cited work, p. 540 ff.] and they also supplied further information about its author.[Note: [Col. 0792] Same work, p. 521.]

Waraeus compared this epistle with three ancient handwritten codices. He also observed[Note: [Col. 0792] Waraeus, on the little work of Saint Patrick, pp. 94 and 110.] that the antiquity of both little works—the *Confession* as well as the *Epistle*—is sufficiently indicated by the scriptural passages cited from the version of the Septuagint, and not from the then-recent version of Saint Jerome, which in Saint Patrick’s age had not yet been publicly received. At the same time, he adds that both little works contain some passages resulting from the carelessness of ancient copyists and requiring critical skill,[Col. 0792C] but that nothing else occurs about which anyone could rightly entertain doubt.

## IV

Let us now return to the remaining works. Next comes the *Synod of Saint Patrick*, taken from an ancient manuscript of Angers, whose copy Sirmond sent from France to Usserius. Using that copy, Speelman brought the canons of this synod to light.[Note: [Col. 0792] Speelman, *British Councils*, vol. I, p. 55.] Wilkins later published them again.[Note: [Col. 0792] Wilkins, *British Councils*, vol. I, p. 4.] Jocelinus mentions the canons of Saint Patrick.[Note: [Col. 0792] Jocelinus, cited work, chap. 185.]

Waraeus produced the following nine other canons attributed to Saint Patrick, apart from Nos. 5 and 6, which Usserius had already published, from a manuscript of the Cotton Library, as he himself testifies.[Note: [Col. 0792] Waraeus, cited work, pp. 119, 121.] He also adds that at the end of Canon 1, another collection of canons belonging to Saint Benedict’s College, Cambridge, appends the following:

> “A cleric who brings his case, whether just or unjust, before the judgment of a judge of another faith shall be excommunicated.”

The aforementioned Wilkins also had these nine canons printed.[Note: [Col. 0792] Wilkins, cited work, p. 6.]

The synod of the bishops Patrick, Auxilius, and Isserninus, previously published by Speelman,[Note: [Col. 0793] Speelman, cited work, p. 51.] was issued by Waraeus in a more accurate form after collation with the manuscript just mentioned from the library of Saint Benedict’s College, Cambridge. He also observed[Note: [Col. 0793] Waraeus, cited work, p. 123.] that Canon 1 of this synod appears in an ancient codex of the Canons in the Cotton Library as follows:

> “If anyone, by his own right, seeks the redemption of a captive without the abbot’s permission, he has deserved to be excommunicated.”

The fourth and fifth canons there read as follows:

> “If anyone receives the permission of the bishop, and the price of the captive has been collected, etc.”

Finally, in the same Cotton codex, the matter of Canon 6—namely, insofar as it concerns the tonsure of clerics according to Roman custom—is indicated in these words:

> “The Romans say that the tonsure began with Simon Magus, whose tonsure extended only from ear to ear; as an indication of superiority [perhaps *expellenda*, ‘to be removed’], it was the very tonsure of the magi, by which only the front of the forehead was accustomed to be covered.”

The sermon of Patrick testifies that the originator of this tonsure in Ireland was a swineherd of King Loiger, son of Nil (Nell), from whom nearly all the Irish adopted this tonsure. Usserius repeats the same account,[Note: [Col. 0793] Usserius, cited work, p. 479.] and reports several other matters concerning it. Tillemont, too, should not be passed over concerning these synods convened by Patrick.[Note: [Col. 0793] Tillemont, cited work, art. 7, pp. 476 ff., and p. 786, note 5, “On Saint Patrick.”]

To the acts of this synod—which Waraeus, from the Ulster annals, argues was held by Saint Patrick after the death of Bishop Secundinus, around the year 450—the same editor added three other canons, previously published by Speelman,[Note: [Col. 0793] Speelman, cited work, p. 54.] from the Cambridge manuscript of Saint Benedict’s College mentioned above. To these he further appended[Col. 0793C] some proverbs attributed to Saint Patrick from a manuscript book of canons in the Cotton Library. Jocelinus states that Patrick composed a book of proverbs in Irish.[Note: [Col. 0793] Jocelinus, cited work, chap. 185.]

Waraeus published the charter of Saint Patrick, also called the *Epistle on the Antiquity of Avalon*, from William of Malmesbury’s manuscript book *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*. He testifies that he had also compared it with other ancient handwritten codices. It is likewise extant in full in John of Glastonbury,[Note: [Col. 0793] John of Glastonbury, *History of Glastonbury Affairs*, vol., pp. 63–66, Oxford edition, 1726.] which, as we indicated above, was recently published for the general public by Thomas Hearne.

One hundred and seventy years earlier, Gerard Vossius had published an excerpt from the same charter under the title *The Mission of Saint Patrick*,[Note: [Col. 0793] G. Vossius, *Miscellanies of Various Holy Fathers*, p. 239, Mainz edition, 1604.] copied by Marianus Victorius, bishop of Rieti, while he was living in England, from a very ancient manuscript exemplar in the library of the monastery of Glastonbury.[Col. 0793D] It was subsequently taken from that source and reprinted in the Lyon Library of the Fathers.[Note: [Col. 0793] *Library of the Fathers of Lyon*, vol. VIII, p. 875.] Usserius has more about this charter of Patrick,[Note: [Col. 0794] Usserius, cited work, p. 456.] and subsequently Waraeus as well.[Note: [Col. 0794] Waraeus, on the little work of Saint Patrick, pp. 131 ff.]

## V

After the little works attributed to Saint Patrick that have so far been reviewed, we have added, following Waraeus, two others. The first is entitled *On the Three Habitations*. Boston, a Benedictine monk at the monastery of Bury Saint Edmunds, who flourished at the beginning of the fifteenth century under Henry IV, king of England, writes the following about this little book in his still-unpublished work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:[Note: [Col. 0794] In Waraeus, preface to the little work of Saint Patrick, § 4.]

> “Patrick, archbishop of Ireland, flourished in the year of Christ 424, and wrote *On the Three Habitations*, of heaven, the world, and hell. Beginning: ‘There are three.’”

As Boston indicates, that book then existed in the library of Saint John at Colchester. Elsewhere, however, the same Boston reports that the little book was attributed both to Augustine and to Patrick. The English editor excludes it from both authors,[Note: [Col. 0794] Same author, note, p. 130.] on the ground that its author repeatedly cites the text of Scripture from Saint Jerome’s version, which was not generally received in the age of Augustine or Patrick.

We have taken the exemplar of this little work from the appendix to volume VI of the works of Saint Augustine, Benedictine edition, Paris, pp. 159 ff.

As for the later little work, *On the Twelve Abuses of the Age*, certain fragments are cited as attributed to Saint Patrick in an ancient manuscript of the library of Saint Benedict’s College at Cambridge, according to Waraeus’s testimony,[Note: [Col. 0794] Same author, cited preface, § 6.] and it is praised by Cathwulf in a letter to Charlemagne preserved by Duchesne.[Note: [Col. 0794] Duchesne, *History of France*, vol. II, pp. 666 ff.]

The work is extant in full among the writings falsely attributed to Cyprian[Note: [Col. 0794] Cyprian, works, appendix, p. 275, Paris edition, 1726.] and to Augustine.[Note: [Col. 0794] Augustine, works, appendix to vol. VI, p. 211, Benedictine edition, Paris.] Yet the scriptural passages quoted in this little book are demonstrably taken from Jerome’s version,[Col. 0794C] as the same English editor correctly argues. For that reason it is neither Cyprian’s nor Augustine’s, and therefore not Patrick’s either, although it is transmitted among his writings. Fell discusses this matter to some extent in the preface to Cyprian’s works, around the middle.

Whatever the truth may be, in transcribing this little work Waraeus followed Pamelius’s edition of the Cyprianic writings. We, however, have followed the more accurate edition of Baluzius—or rather of the distinguished Benedictine Maranus, who completed Baluzius’s edition—and compared it with the same little book as prepared by the labor of his colleagues and published among Augustine’s works.

## VI

Finally, this collection of Patrick’s works is closed by the alphabetic hymn attributed to Bishop Secundinus, in praise of his uncle Saint Patrick, while the latter was still alive. Waraeus copied it from[Col. 0794D] an ancient manuscript of hymns formerly belonging to the convent of the Observant Friars Minor at Donegal and later transferred to the Usserian Library.[Col. 0795A] He compared it with another, more recently written exemplar of the same hymn and also supplied its variant readings.

This hymn is additionally extant in the *Antiphonary of the Monastery of Bangor*, published by Muratori.[Note: [Col. 0795] Muratori, *Latin Anecdotes*, vol. IV, pp. 136 ff.] We have therefore compared the edition with that of Waraeus. This distinguished scholar writes the following concerning our subject:[Note: [Col. 0795] Same author, same work, p. 125.]

> “In our Antiphonary we read the hymn of Saint Patrick, teacher of the Scots. I remember that the distinguished P. D. Bernard de Montfaucon, when he was once staying in Milan, congratulated me, after seeing the antiquity of this codex and monument, which I had shown him. For he related that in France there was a certain learned man who had come to suspect that not only the deeds of Saint Patrick but even Saint Patrick himself ought to be relegated among the Roman fables; for the history of that holy bishop had been disfigured by such childish tales.[Col. 0795B] Yet certainly this one hymn alone may suffice to confirm the truth both of Patrick’s notable works and of the celebrated reputation that has endured concerning the holy man down to our own times. For fuller material, though not equal in antiquity, consult Usserius.”[Note: [Col. 0795] Usserius, *British Antiquities*, chap. 17, pp. 425 ff.]

Such is Muratori’s account. It therefore appears that, when he wrote these words, he was unaware of Waraeus’s edition, who was the first to bring this hymn to light. We infer that the Bollandists likewise overlooked it, since they omitted the same hymn from the acts of Saint Patrick, which we know they described at great length.

As for Bishop Secundinus, reputed to be the author of this hymn, it may perhaps not be unprofitable to hear Jocelinus. He writes as follows:[Note: [Col. 0796] Jocelinus, cited work, chap. 177, in the Bollandists, chap. 18, no. 145, p. 576.]

> “Saint Secundinus, a wise and learned man, said to Saint Patrick that he wished to compose a poem about a certain holy man who was still alive. Since that holy man was Patrick, about whom he intended to write, he suppressed his name in silence. Saint Patrick said to him:
>
> ‘Truly it is worthy and just, equitable and salutary, that the peoples recount the wisdom and glory of the saints and that the Church proclaim their praise.[Note: [Col. 0796] Ecclesiasticus 39:14.] But it is more worthy and more fitting that, after the end of the light, every occasion for vainglory should have been removed. Praise, therefore, the serenity of the day—but when evening has come; the valor of a soldier—but when he has triumphed; the success of a sailor—but when he has reached harbor. For Scripture says:[Note: [Col. 0796] Same passage, 11:30.] “Do not praise a man during his life.”
>
> ‘Yet if this matter has been entirely fixed in your heart, which you intend to do, do it quickly, because death is at your doors. For of all the bishops who are in Ireland, you will be the first to depart from this world.’
>
> “Accordingly, he composed the hymn in praise of Saint Patrick. A few days later, in accordance with Saint Patrick’s words, he closed his final day. He was buried in the church of his see, in a place called Domhnach-Seachlainn, and by frequent miracles he showed that he lived with Christ.
>
> “Many Irish people are accustomed to sing that hymn every day, and they relate that many great wonders have occurred through its frequent use.”

Thus far Jocelinus.

# Schoenemann’s Historical-Literary Notice on Saint Patrick

(*Historical and Literary Library of the Latin Fathers*, vol. II.)

## § I. Life

Patrick, a Briton by nationality, whose native name was Succat, was born around the year 371 in the town of Nemthur—today Kirkpatrick—situated between the Firth of Dumbarton and the city of Glasgow. His father was Calpurnius, a deacon, the son of a certain Potitus, a priest.

Although he was born of Christian parents, religion did not greatly assist him either in the cultivation of his character or in that of his intellect. Born and raised as a rustic among rustics, he began, especially through encounters with adversity, to nurture some awareness and fear of God. This happened to him while he was still a boy, when he was several times carried into captivity by Irish raiders and repeatedly liberated.

From that time, however, not hatred but rather love and goodwill toward the Irish took root in his mind. Later, having been brought to Gaul—by an uncertain route—and sent by Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, to Rome in the year 432, he expressed to Pope Celestine his desire to convert the Irish to the Christian faith. He is said to have then been appointed their apostle and archbishop.

Having returned to his homeland after this, he crossed over to Ireland without delay in the year 447. Through preaching and baptizing, he soon spread the Christian religion far and wide, converted nearly all the petty kings of the island, founded churches, established episcopal sees, held synods, and accomplished many other things bravely and successfully for the strengthening of the Church in that region. In the year 493 of the Christian era, at the age of 122, he departed this life.[Note: [Col. 0795D] The matters concerning Patrick’s life that we have mentioned thus far, if not absolutely certain, are at least close to the truth. Certainly we have kept his *Confession* chiefly before our eyes. It testifies to his zeal in the work of conversion and explains only as much about the three captivities he experienced as a young man as can serve to connect them with the other matters handed down about him and with those he himself did not touch upon. The tales of Probus and Jocelinus, medieval British writers, have long been rejected by everyone.[Col. 0796D] Yet those judge too hastily who, because of these tales, have called all memory of Patrick’s deeds—and even his very existence—into question, claiming that it is a mere fiction woven by tale-sellers. Even after the tales have been removed, much remains in the narrative of his life whose credibility one would wish to have established by solid arguments, especially concerning his entire journey to the provinces across the sea and Celestine’s role in the matter. But take care not to diminish too arbitrarily the credibility of domestic traditions. Above all, one should read what the Bollandists wrote in volume III of the March *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 519, concerning the first and oldest acts of Saint Patrick—from which Probus, Jocelinus, and others drew—and concerning their authors.]

## § II. Writings

Patrick’s genuine writings plainly reveal themselves through their barbarous style and rough diction, arising from his neglect of the Latin language, which he had never expected to employ in writing.[Note: [Col. 0797] “Formerly I thought of writing,” he says in the aforementioned *Confession*, “but until now I hesitated. For I feared that I might fall into the speech of men; and because I had not read as others had, who had therefore rightly and excellently absorbed the sacred Scriptures in both respects equally and had never changed their speech from childhood, but had continually advanced toward perfection. For our speech and language has been transferred into a foreign tongue, as can easily be demonstrated from the awkwardness of my writing, showing how I myself have been trained and educated in speech.”]

They are as follows.

### I

The *Confession*, explained in an epistle to the Irish, in which he does not expound the faith but rather the course of his life and preaching. Probus, the tenth-century writer of Patrick’s life, incorporated many fragments from it into his own work.

### II

The *Epistle to Coroticus*, a Cambro-British petty king—or rather, to the Christians subject to the tyrant Coroticus. Jocelinus, a Cistercian monk of the Furness monastery in Lancashire, expressly mentions this epistle. He lived in the twelfth century and wrote Patrick’s *Life*. Waraeus further observes, concerning the antiquity of this and the preceding little work, that the scriptural passages cited in them come from the Septuagint version, not from Jerome’s then-recent version, which had not yet been publicly received in Patrick’s age.

### III

The *Synod of Saint Patrick*, containing thirty-one canons.

### IV

Nine other canons attributed to Saint Patrick. Of these, Usserius had already published the fifth and sixth; Waraeus discovered the remainder.

### V

The synod of Patrick, Auxilius, and Isserninus, consisting of thirty-four canons. Waraeus added three further canons, previously published by Speelman, and some proverbs attributed to the same Patrick.

The *Charter*, or *Epistle on the Antiquity of Avalon*, is uncertain, or rather not Patrick’s. Waraeus suspects that it is the work of a later author because of its style, its chronological indications, and other considerations of that kind, including the distinctly Anglo-Saxon names inserted in it.

Also uncertain are the book *On the Three Habitations*, elsewhere entitled *On the Joys of the Elect and the Punishments of the Damned*, which is also attributed to Augustine; and the book *On the Abuses of the Age*, published among the works of Cyprian and Augustine. Concerning the latter, however, Waraeus’s suspicion must not be omitted. Since certain excerpts from this book are attributed to Saint Patrick by very ancient authors, although the title of the little book is not mentioned, he says that he cannot help suspecting that it is the same as the book of *Proverbs* which Jocelinus said Patrick wrote in Irish and which is filled with much edification. Perhaps some Irishman translated it into Latin after Patrick’s death.

For in both works—in the proverbs and in the appended maxims—the Abuses of the Age are disclosed. Nor do the style or the scriptural citations from Jerome’s version prevent the book from being a product of Patrick’s intellect, even if it was translated by another.

Finally, the sermon bearing Patrick’s name was fabricated by Richard Stanihurst and published by him in *The Life of Patrick*, Books I and II, Antwerp, 1587. Cave also called attention to it, and Mesingham reprinted it at the end of the *Irish Florilegium*, Paris, 1624.

## § III. Editions

Of these works of Patrick, Nos. 3 and 5, together with part of the *Epistle on the Antiquity of the Avalonian People* and the last two works falsely attributed to him, were published before James Waraeus brought the remaining works out of manuscript codices and undertook to edit the whole collection.

After his distinguished labor, the Bollandists issued certain works newly examined against manuscript codices, while Andreas Gallandius arranged for the whole of Waraeus’s edition to be reprinted. We shall now examine the individual editions more closely.

### Seventeenth century

#### 1604

Mainz, at the press of Balthasar Lippius, at the expense of Antonius Hierat, quarto.
