*The Mission of Saint Patrick, sent by Pope Celestine I for the conversion of Ireland; or, The Epistle of Saint Patrick, Apostle of Ireland, from the library of the monastery of Glastonbury, where he himself was abbot before becoming bishop of Ireland*, in the *Miscellanies of Several Greek and Latin Holy Fathers* of Gerard Vossius, Provost of Tongeren. This work, almost a second volume, was appended by him to his edition of the works of Gregory Thaumaturgus, p. 239.

What is found there is only a fragment of the *Epistle on the Antiquity of Avalon*, which Vossius discovered among the manuscript collections of Marianus Victorius, bishop of Rieti, the editor of Ambrose. While Victorius was serving Cardinal Reginald Pole, papal legate in England, he had obtained a transcript from a very ancient manuscript exemplar in the library of the monastery of Glastonbury.[Col. 0798C] As Waraeus observes, the same material is already found in John of Tinmouth’s *Sanctilogium*, in the *Life of Patrick*, and in the *New Legend of England* by his copyist John Capgrave, printed at London in 1516.

#### 1639

London, folio.

The *Synod of Saint Patrick*, together with the synod of Patrick, Auxilius, and Isserninus and three additional canons of the same Patrick, in Henry Speelman’s *Councils of Britain*, vol. I, pp. 51, 54, 55 ff.

The earlier canons were taken from an ancient manuscript codex of Angers, whose copy Sirmond had sent from France to Usserius.

#### 1656

London, at the shop of John Crook, under the sign of the ship in St Paul’s churchyard, octavo.

*Works Attributed to Patrick, Who Converted the Irish to the Faith of Christ: Some of Which Have Now Been Published for the First Time from Ancient Manuscript Codices, the Rest Revised; All Illustrated with Notes Relating to History and Antiquities, by the Work and Care of James Waraeus, Knight Bachelor.*

The order of the contents is the same as that which we followed in reviewing the writings, except that the *Charter on the Origin of Avalon* occupies the middle position between the little works *On the Three Habitations* and *On the Abuses of the Age*.[lacuna] The first editor himself added Nos. 1, 2, and 4, for the most part, as well as the *Proverbs* and the complete *Epistle on the Origin of the Avalonian People*. He compared the remaining works anew with the manuscripts; had the book *On the Three Habitations* copied from Augustine’s works; had the little work *On the Abuses of the Age* recopied from Pamelius’s Cyprian; and added a preface, notes—partly discussing authenticity, date, and other matters concerning the author, and partly elucidating individual passages—and an index.

At the end he also appended the alphabetic hymn of Bishop Secundinus, Patrick’s nephew through his sister Davera, in praise of Saint Patrick, who was then still alive.[Col. 0799B]

#### 1668

Antwerp, at the press of Jacob Meursius, folio.

The *Confession of Saint Patrick concerning His Life and Conduct*, which Andreas Denis, of Arras and of the Society of Jesus, extracted from the very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Nobiliacum, together with the *Epistle to the Christians Subject to the Tyrant Coroticus*—for that is the more correct title here—in the *Acta Sanctorum*, March, vol. III, for 17 March, pp. 533–540.

Waraeus’s edition was unknown to the Bollandists, as Gallandius has already observed. The *Epistle to Coroticus*, as it is commonly called, followed Patrick’s *Confession* in the aforementioned manuscript without any distinction of title. The editors divided the two epistles into several smaller sections and further divided the first into five chapters. The notes supply variant readings or emendations. The *Life of Saint Patrick* by Jocelinus follows, preceded by an extensive commentary by the Bollandists on the same subject, in which each detail is carefully assessed.

### Eighteenth century

#### 1726

Oxford, octavo.

The *Charter of Saint Patrick on the Antiquity of Avalon*, in John of Glastonbury’s *History of Glastonbury Affairs*, edited by Thomas Hearne, vol. I, pp. 63–66.

#### 1737

London, folio.

The *Synod and Canons Attributed to Saint Patrick*, in David Wilkins’s *Councils of Great Britain and Ireland*, vol. I, pp. 2–7. Notes and variant readings are appended to the text.

#### 1748

Lucca, folio.

The *Canons Attributed to Saint Patrick*, from Waraeus, in John Dominic Mansi’s *Supplement to the Councils*, vol. I, p. 338.

#### 1761

Florence, folio.

The *Synod of Patrick, Auxilius, and Isserninus*, with an addition; the *Canons Attributed to Saint Patrick*; and another *Synod of Saint Patrick*, in John Dominic Mansi’s *Very Extensive Collection of Councils*, vol. VI, pp. 514–528. The canons attributed to Patrick, as though they had been omitted, were copied again at the end of volume VII, p. 1187.

#### 1774

Venice, from the press of John Baptist Albritius, folio.

The *Works Attributed to Patrick*, in Andrew Gallandius’s *Library of the Fathers and of the Ancient Saints of the Church*, vol. X, pp. 159–182, together with the hymn of Secundinus, pp. 183–184.

Gallandius transcribed all the works—genuine, doubtful, or altogether false—according to Waraeus’s arrangement, though without a separate title. He compared the Bollandists’ edition and, in the last two little works, followed the latest editors of Augustine and Cyprian, just as he followed Muratori for the hymn of Secundinus in the *Latin Anecdotes*, vol. IV, p. 136, where it is found in the *Antiphonary of the Monastery of Bangor*. Hence there arises a large supply of variant readings and emendations, which are placed beneath the text together with notes drawn chiefly from Waraeus and Usserius.

A careful dissertation on Patrick’s writings is also inserted in the prolegomena, chapter 4, pp. 7–9.

## § IV. Codices

Some of the manuscripts are native to Britain and Ireland, while others are Gallican. Waraeus chiefly used the former, namely:

### 1

One belonging to the Church of Armagh in Ireland. Besides Saint Patrick’s *Confession*, it contained the Holy Bible from Jerome’s version and a very ancient copy of Sulpicius Severus’s *Life of Saint Martin, Bishop of Tours*.

Waraeus observes that this codex was once held in such high esteem that the MacMoyer family held lands from the see of Armagh in return for safeguarding it. The popular belief that the book had been written by Patrick’s own hand naturally contributed greatly to the veneration accorded it.

This belief is supported to some extent by the words written at the end of the codex:

> “Thus far extends the volume which Patrick wrote with his own hand.”

And afterward:

> “On the seventeenth day of March Patrick was transferred to heaven.”

Waraeus nevertheless remarks that the character of the script makes it sufficiently clear that the book is not an autograph, but was copied much later.

### 2

One from the library of Sir Thomas Cotton, Baronet, written around the year 1000. Besides this *Confession* and the *Epistle to Coroticus*, it contained various monuments of antiquity relating to Ireland, as well as the *Life of Saint Fursey the Irishman* by a seventh-century author and the *Life of the Virgin Saint Brigid* by Cogitosus.

### 3 and 4

Two belonging to the Church of Salisbury in England, containing both the *Confession* and the *Epistle to Coroticus*.

### 5

Another from the Cotton Library at Westminster, in which nine canons are scattered about and attributed to Patrick.[Col. 0800D] It was an ancient book, written in Anglo-Saxon times, and formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Augustine at Canterbury.

### 6

One from the private library of Saint Benedict’s College, Cambridge, no. 221, written in capital letters, though in several places so corrupt that Waraeus admits they cannot be repaired without critical license. It contained the synod of Patrick, Auxilius, and Isserninus, previously published by Speelman—from I do not know what exemplar—and other canons attributed to Saint Patrick. By comparing the two, the aforementioned editor produced a somewhat more accurate text.

### 7

The manuscript book of William of Malmesbury, *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, preserved in the Cotton Library.[Col. 0801A] From it a complete copy of the charter *On the Origin of Avalon* was transcribed.

To these British and Irish codices used by Waraeus we shall add, in their place:

### 8

The manuscript of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, shelfmark O 20, from which Patrick’s synod was published by Wilkins.

The Gallican manuscripts are as follows:

### 1

The manuscript book of Angers, from which Henry Speelman published the synod of Patrick, copied by James Sirmond. Waraeus notes that Philip Labbe also mentions this synod in the Angers codex, and another Irish synod found in a certain codex of Fleury, in his *New Library of Manuscripts*.

### 2

The manuscript book of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Nobiliacum, Arras, from which the Bollandists published the *Confession* and the *Epistle to Coroticus*.

# Saint Patrick’s Confession, Explained in an Epistle to the Irish

*(C, S)*

## I

I, Patrick, a sinner, the most rustic and least of all the faithful, and most contemptible in the eyes of very many, had as my father Calpornius the deacon, once the son of Potitus the priest,[Note: [Col. 0801] The Bollandists, in March, vol. II, p. 533, published this confession of Saint Patrick from the very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Vedast at Nobiliacum. They read here: “who was from the village of Banavem Taberniae.” Waraeus added the following in the margin: “From the village of Bannavae, in the region of Tyburnia, not far from the Western Sea; Probus, Book I of the *Life of Patrick*.] who was from the village of Bonavem Taberniae. He had a small estate nearby, Enon, where I was taken captive.[Note: [Col. 0801] The Bollandists read: “for he had a villa.” This is perhaps less correct. Shortly afterward the same Bollandists read: “I fell into captivity.” But the common reading is confirmed again below, §§ 4 and 10.]

At that time I was about sixteen years old. I did not know the true God; and I was brought into captivity in Hiberione,[Note: [Col. 0802] Ireland is also called this in the *Itinerary of Antoninus*, as Usserius observed in his *Ecclesiastical Antiquities of Britain*, p. 431, second edition. See Wesseling on the *Ancient Roman Itineraries*, p. 509.] together with many thousands of people, in accordance with our deserts, because we had turned away from God, had not kept his commandments, and had not obeyed our priests, who warned us for our salvation.

And the Lord brought upon us[Note: [Col. 0802] Greek: *tēn orgēn tou thymou autou*, “the wrath of his anger.” 2 Chronicles 29:10. Usserius, cited work.] the anger of his indignation, and scattered us among many nations, even to the farthest end of the earth, where my littleness now appears to be among foreigners.

And there the Lord opened the understanding[Col. 0801C] of my unbelief, so that, even if late, I might remember my sins and turn with my whole heart to the Lord my God. He looked upon my lowliness, took pity on my youth and ignorance, and guarded me before I knew him and before I understood or distinguished between good and evil. He strengthened me and consoled me like a father consoles a son.

## II

Therefore I cannot, nor indeed is it fitting to do so, remain silent about such great benefits and such great grace as the Lord deigned to bestow upon me (the words “the Lord to bestow” are absent from the Book of Armagh in everything enclosed in parentheses, through the end of the Confession; Waræus. Otherwise in Bollandus): in the land of my captivity. For this is our recompense: that, after correction or recognition of God, we should be exalted and should confess his wonders before every nation that is under the whole heaven. For there is no other God, nor has there ever been, nor will there be after this one, except God the Father, unbegotten and without beginning, from whom every beginning proceeds, holding all things, as we have said (Bollandus prints after “beginning”: “for through him all visible and invisible things were made,” words that occur a little later here; the intervening passage printed here appears to have been omitted among the Bollandists through a copyist’s error caused by the repeated word “beginning”); and his Son Jesus Christ, whom we testify to have always been with the Father, before the origin of the world, spiritually with the Father, ineffably begotten before every beginning. Through him visible and invisible things were made; he became man, conquered death, and was received into heaven by the Father. And he gave him authority over every name in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, so that every tongue might confess that Jesus Christ is Lord and God (Philippians 2:10–11). We believe in him and await his coming: he will soon be the judge of the living and the dead, and will repay each according to his deeds. He has also poured abundantly into us the gift and pledge of immortality, the Holy Spirit, who makes believers and obedient people into children of God the Father and fellow-heirs of Christ. We confess and adore him as one God in the Trinity of the holy name.

For he himself said through the prophet: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Jeremiah 29:12; Psalm 80:8). And again he says: “To reveal and confess the works of God is honorable” (Tobit 12:7).

## III

Yet although I am imperfect in many respects, I want my brothers and kinsmen to know my condition, so that they may perceive the desire of my soul. I am not unaware of the testimony of my Lord, who testifies in the psalm: “You will destroy those who speak lies” (Psalm 5:7), and again: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11). And the same Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that people utter, they will give an account for it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36).

Therefore I ought to fear this judgment exceedingly, with fear and trembling, on that day when no one will be able to withdraw or hide himself, but we shall all without exception give an account even of our smallest sins before the tribunal of Christ the Lord. For this reason I formerly thought of writing, but until now I hesitated. For I feared falling into the speech of men, since I had not read as others had—those who had thoroughly and lawfully absorbed both sacred writings alike and had never changed their language from childhood, but had continually advanced toward perfection.

## IV

For our language and speech have been transferred into a foreign tongue, as can easily be proved from the clumsiness of my writing, showing how I have been instructed and educated in speech. For the Wise Man says: “By the tongue, understanding, knowledge, and instruction in truth are recognized” (Ecclesiasticus 4:29).

But what benefit is there in an excuse according to truth, especially when it is made presumptuously? Thus, in my old age, I now seek what I did not acquire in my youth, because my sins hindered me from confirming what I had not previously read through. But who will believe me? Even if I say what I have already stated: as a young man, indeed almost a beardless boy, I was taken captive before I knew what I was seeking or what I ought to avoid.

Therefore today I am ashamed and greatly afraid to expose my ignorance, because I cannot express myself with the concise eloquence of speech as my spirit and mind desire, and as my understanding and feeling show. But if such a gift had been given to me as to others, nevertheless I would not remain silent because of the recompense.

And if perhaps some people think that I am putting myself forward in this matter, with my ignorance and slower tongue—for it is written, “The stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace” (Isaiah 32:4)—how much more ought we to seek this, who, as he says, are “a letter of Christ,” for salvation to the ends of the earth, not eloquently but firmly and most powerfully written in your hearts, not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God (2 Corinthians 3:2–3).

## V

And again the Spirit testifies: “Rusticity too was created by the Most High” (Ecclesiasticus 7:16). Therefore I am the first rustic, a fugitive, that is, an uneducated man who does not know how to provide for the future. But this I know with complete certainty: before I was humbled, I was like a stone lying in deep mud. Then he came who is powerful and, in his mercy, lifted me up; indeed, he raised me high and placed me on the top of the wall.

From there I ought vigorously to have cried out, also offering something in return to the Lord for his many benefits, here and forever—benefits which the human mind cannot estimate. Therefore marvel, great and small, you who fear God (Revelation 19:5), and you ignorant people of the Lord’s rhetoric. Listen, then, and investigate who awakened me, a fool, from among those who seem to be wise and learned in the law, powerful in speech and in every matter.

He inspired me, more than others, though I was detestable in this world, provided only that, with fear and reverence and without complaint, I might faithfully benefit the people to whom the love of Christ transferred me and to whom he gave me during my life, if I should be worthy; finally, that I might serve them with humility and truth.

## VI

Accordingly, within the measure of the faith of the Trinity, we must distinguish and make known, without danger of reproach, the gift of God and eternal consolation, and boldly spread the name of God everywhere without fear, so that even after my death I might leave it to my Gallic brothers and sons, whom I baptized in the Lord—many thousands of people.

I was neither worthy nor such a person that the Lord should grant this to his little servant. Yet after hardships and such great burdens, after captivity and many years, he granted me such great grace among that people—something which I had never hoped for or imagined in my youth.

But after I had come to Hiberione, I pastured animals every day and prayed frequently during the day. More and more the love of God and fear of him increased, faith grew, and the spirit was stirred (so Bollandus also; Usserius, *loc. cit.*, p. 432, reads “was moved”), so that in a single day I prayed as many as a hundred times, and nearly as often at night. I remained in the woods and on the mountain, and before daylight I awoke to prayer, through snow, frost, and rain. I felt no harm, nor was there any laziness in me, as I now see, because at that time the spirit was fervent within me.

There, one night in my sleep, I heard a voice saying to me: “You fast well; soon you will depart for your homeland.” And again, after a short while, I heard an answer saying to me: “Look, your ship is ready.” It was not nearby, but perhaps it was two hundred thousand paces away. I had never been there, nor did I know any of the people there.

## VII

Then afterward I turned toward flight and left the man with whom I had been for six years (a harsh pagan king, with whom he had been held in slavery, according to Probus; Waræus). I came in the strength of the Lord, who was directing my way toward good, and I feared nothing until I reached that ship.

On the day when I arrived, the ship departed from its place, and I spoke so that I might find a way to sail with them. The shipmaster was displeased and answered angrily and harshly: “By no means do you seek to go with us” (that is, without payment for the fare, as Probus adds).

When I heard this, I separated myself from them in order to return to the little hut where I was staying. On the way I began to pray, and before I had finished my prayer I heard one of them shouting loudly behind me: “Come quickly, for these men are calling you.”

I immediately returned to them, and they began to say to me: “Come, because we accept you in faith; make friendship with us as you wish.” On that day, then, I ceased trying to flee because of the fear of God. Nevertheless, I hoped that they would say to me: “Come in the faith of Jesus Christ,” since they were pagans. I obtained this from them, and immediately we sailed.

## VIII

After three days we reached land, and for twenty-eight days we traveled through the wilderness. Their food ran out, and hunger prevailed over them.

One day the shipmaster began to say to me: “What do you say, Christian? Your God is great and almighty? Why, then, can you not pray for us, since we are in danger from hunger? It is difficult for us ever to see another human being.”

I clearly said to them: “Turn in faith and with your whole heart to the Lord our God, because nothing is impossible for him, so that today he may send food for you on your journey, until you are satisfied; for everything abounds with him.”

With God’s help, this came to pass. Behold, a herd of pigs appeared on the road before our eyes. They killed many of them and remained there for two nights, well refreshed. They were revived by its flesh, because many of the men had collapsed and been left half-alive beside the road.

After this they gave great thanks to God, and I was honored in their sight.

## IX

From that day onward they had abundant food. They also found wild honey and offered me a portion. One of them said: “This is a sacrificial offering.” From then on, thanks be to God, I tasted nothing of it.

That same night I was asleep, and Satan tested me fiercely; I shall remember it for as long as I remain in this body. Something like an enormous rock fell upon me, and I could not prevail with any of my limbs. But how the thought came to me, I do not know, to call upon Elijah in spirit.

Meanwhile I saw the sun rising in the sky. As I cried out, “Elijah! Elijah!” with all my strength, behold, the brightness of the sun fell upon me and immediately dispelled all my heaviness.

I believe that I was assisted by Christ my Lord (and that his Spirit was already then crying out for me), and I hope that this will likewise happen on the day of my distress, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

## X

Again, after not many years, I was taken captive. On that first night I remained with them. I heard a divine answer saying to me: “You will be with them for two months”; and so it happened.

On the sixtieth night the Lord freed me from their hands. On the journey he provided us with food, fire, and dryness each day, until on the fourteenth day we reached people.

As I indicated above, we had traveled for twenty-eight days through the wilderness, and on the night when we reached human beings we had no food at all.

Again, after a few years, I was in Britain with my parents, who received me as a son. In faith they asked me that, after so many tribulations as I had endured, I should never again leave them.

There I saw in a vision during the night a man coming as if from Hiberione, whose name was Victoricus (so also Usserius, *loc. cit.*, p. 433; but Bollandus has *Victricius*, noting that others read *Victoricuм* and *Victorem*. “This name,” they say, “is commonly given by authors to the angel who appeared so often to Patrick”). He carried innumerable letters and gave me one of them. I read the beginning of the letter, which contained the words: “The Voice of the Hiberionacians” (Usserius likewise; Bollandus has “of the Hiberionians”; Jocelinus, chapter 21, “of the Irish-born”).

As I was reciting the beginning of the letter, at that very moment I seemed to hear the voice of those who were beside the forest of Foclut, which is near the western sea. And they cried out as if with one voice: “We beg you, holy young man, to come and walk among us again.”

I was deeply moved in heart and could read no further; and thus I awoke. Thanks be to God, because after many years the Lord granted them what they had cried out for.

## XI

And on another night—I do not know whether within me or beside me; God knows—I heard words spoken with the greatest skill, but I could not understand them (Bollandus reads: “I heard certain ones in the Spirit chanting psalms within me, and I did not know who they were; whom I heard,” etc.). At the end of the prayer he addressed me in this way: “He who laid down his soul for you is the one who speaks in you” (the Book of Armagh reads: “He who gave his soul for you, he is the one who speaks in you”; Waræus).

And thus I awoke rejoicing.

Again I saw within me someone praying, and I was as though inside my own body. I heard him above me—that is, above the inner person—and there he prayed fervently with groans. During this I was astonished and wondered, asking who it was who prayed within me.

At the end of the prayer he spoke in such a way that it was clear he was the Spirit. Thus I awoke and remembered the Apostle’s words: “The Spirit helps our weakness in prayer. For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26), which cannot be expressed in words. And again: “The Lord, our advocate, pleads for us” (ibid., verse 34).

And when I was tested by some of my elders who came against my arduous episcopate because of my sins (Bollandus reads “who came and [spoke of] my sins”), on that day I was powerfully driven to fall, here and forever. But the Lord kindly spared the proselyte and stranger for his name’s sake. He greatly helped me in this trampling-down, so that I did not fall into ruin and disgrace.

I pray God that this occasion may not be counted as sin against them, for after thirty years they found me and rose up against the word that I had confessed before I became a deacon (the sentence is defective; “they rose up” or something similar must be supplied).

## XII

Because of my anxiety, I disclosed with a sorrowful heart to my dearest friend what I had done in my childhood—indeed, on one day, or rather within one hour—because I was not yet capable of much.

I do not know; God knows, whether I was then fifteen years old. I did not believe in the living God, nor had I believed in him from my childhood. I remained in death and unbelief until I was severely chastised and humbled in truth by hunger and nakedness. Every day I went unwillingly toward Hiberione, until I nearly collapsed.

Yet this was rather good for me, because through it I was corrected by the Lord, and he prepared me to be what I am today—something that had once been far from me: to care and labor for the salvation of others, when at that time I did not even think about myself.

Therefore, on the day when I was rejected by the persons mentioned above—at nightfall—I saw in a nighttime vision something written against my face, without honor. During this I heard a divine answer saying to me: “We have looked badly upon the face of the one designated, his name stripped bare” (the Bollandists read *faciem designati nudato nomine* and interpret this as a pamphlet against Patrick’s apostolate in which he was designated simply as “Patrick,” with no honorific or episcopal title; Waræus’s reading, “I saw in a vision of the night: it was written against my face … We saw badly the face of God, marked with the name stripped bare,” is judged very poor).

It did not say, “You have looked badly,” but “We have looked badly,” as though he joined himself there to me, just as he said: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2:8).

Therefore I give thanks to him who strengthened me in all things, so that this did not hinder me from the journey that I had resolved upon, nor from my work, which I had learned from Christ. Rather, through this I perceived in myself no small strength, and my faith was tested before God and human beings.

## XIII

Therefore I say boldly: “My conscience does not reproach me” (here and in the future; this is omitted by Bollandus). I have God as my witness that I have not lied in the words that I have related to you (Bollandus omits the word “to you”).

Rather, I grieve for my dearest friend: why did we deserve to hear such an answer from him, to whom I had entrusted even my soul? The Bollandists conjecture that he was Saint Germanus, before whom Patrick may have been accused at some British synod of having done or decreed something contrary to measures which Germanus himself had earlier established there against the Pelagians.

And I learned from some brothers, before that defense—which I did not attend, since I was not in Britain—that it would not arise from me, and that, in my absence, he would not be attacked on my behalf (Bollandus reads “would be struck”; Waræus has “would strike,” and shortly afterward, “and publicly dishonor me”).

He himself had said to me with his own mouth: “Behold, you are to be assigned to the rank of bishop,” although I was not worthy of it. But where did it later come from that, before all, good and evil alike, he should publicly dishonor me in what he had previously granted willingly and gladly?

The Lord exists, and he is greater than all. I say enough. Yet I must not conceal the gift of God that he bestowed upon us in the land of my captivity, because at that time I earnestly sought him and found him there, and he preserved me from every iniquity (these words are absent from Bollandus).

Thus I believe, because of his indwelling Spirit, which has boldly worked in me again to this day. But God knows: if a human being had spoken to me, perhaps I would have kept silent, because of the love of Christ.

## XIV

Therefore I will give unceasing thanks to my God, who preserved me faithful on the day of my testing, so that today I may confidently offer him sacrifice: my soul as a living offering to Christ my Lord, who preserved me from all my hardships.

Thus I may also say: “Who am I, Lord, or what is my calling, that you have bestowed such divinity upon me?” (Bollandus: “that you have unveiled such divinity to me”; shortly afterward, “that I might exalt [your name]”). So today I might confidently rejoice and magnify your name among the nations wherever I may be—not only in prosperity but also in affliction; so that whatever happens to me, whether good or bad, I ought to receive equally and always give thanks to God, who showed me that I should believe him without doubt and without end, and who heard me.

Thus, although ignorant, I should undertake in these last days this work, so devout and so wondrous, so that I might imitate certain people whom the Lord had long ago foretold would announce his Gospel as a testimony to all nations before the end of the world.

And so this has been fulfilled, as we have seen. Behold, we are witnesses: the Gospel has been preached as far as there is no farther place.

## XV

It would be lengthy to recount all my labor in detail or piece by piece. I will speak briefly of how the most merciful God often freed me from slavery through twelve dangers in which my life was endangered, besides many snares that I cannot express in words (Bollandus reads “nor do I wish to wrong the readers”).

But since I have as author the one who knows everything, even before it happens, he repeatedly admonished me through divine answers, poor and orphaned as I was. From where came this wisdom, which was not in me, since I did not even know the number of days, nor did I know God? From where came afterward such a great and saving gift: to recognize and love God?

Yet it meant that I should abandon my homeland and parents, even though many gifts were offered to me with weeping and tears (Bollandus: “and I offended there, contrary to my desire, some of my elders”). But, with God directing me, I in no way agreed or yielded to them—not through any merit of mine, but because God conquered in me and resisted all of them—so that I might come to the Irish peoples to preach the Gospel and endure insults from unbelievers, so that I might bear the reproach of my pilgrimage and many persecutions, even chains, and surrender my freedom for the benefit of others.

## XVI

And if I am worthy, I am ready to offer even my soul, without hesitation and most willingly, for his name. There also I wish to spend it unto death, if the Lord would grant this to me.

For I am greatly indebted to God, who gave me such grace that through me many peoples should be reborn to God and afterward brought to completion, and that clerics should be ordained for them everywhere, for the people newly coming to the faith which the Lord took from the ends of the earth, as he formerly promised through the prophets:

“Nations will come to you from the ends of the earth and will say: ‘Truly our fathers acquired false idols, and there is no benefit in them’” (Jeremiah 16:19).

And again: “I have appointed you as a light to the nations, so that you may be salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

There I wish to await his promise, since he never deceives, as he promises in the Gospel: “They will come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (Matthew 8:11), just as we believe that believers from the whole world will come.

## XVII

Therefore it is necessary to fish well and diligently, as the Lord warns, saying: “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4:18).

And again he says through the prophets: “Behold, I am sending many fishermen and hunters, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 16:16), and so forth.

Therefore it was very necessary for us to spread our nets, so that a great multitude and crowd might be caught for God, and so that there might be clerics everywhere to baptize and exhort the needy and desirous people, as the Lord admonishes and teaches in the Gospel, saying:

“Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:19–20).

And again he says: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16).

And again: “This Gospel of the kingdom will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

And likewise the Lord, foretelling through the prophet, says: “And it will be in the last days, says the Lord: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters will prophesy; your young men will see visions, and your elders will dream dreams. Indeed, upon my male servants and my female servants, in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they will prophesy” (Joel 2:28–29).

And in Hosea he says: “I will call ‘My people’ those who are not my people, and ‘Beloved’ those who have not obtained mercy” (Hosea 2:24; Romans 9:25; 1 Peter 2:10). “And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God” (Hosea 1:10; Romans 9:26).

## XVIII

Therefore, how has it happened that the Irish, who had never possessed knowledge of God but had always until now worshiped idols and unclean things, have recently become the Lord’s people and are called sons of God?

The sons of the Scots and the daughters of their rulers appear to be monks and virgins of Christ. There was also a blessed noble Scot, a very beautiful and mature woman, whom I baptized (the genitive word is absent in Bollandus). A few days later she came to us for a certain reason. She told us that she had received an answer from a messenger of God, who also warned her that she should herself be a virgin of Christ and draw near to God.

Thanks be to God: six days later she seized this vocation most excellently and eagerly. All God’s virgins do likewise. They do not do so with the consent of their fathers, but suffer persecution and false reproaches from their parents. Nevertheless, their number increases, and we do not know how many there are of our own people who were born there, besides widows and women living in continence.

Those who are held in servitude labor most greatly, even as they endure constant terrors and threats. But the Lord has given grace to many of his female servants; for although they are forbidden, they nevertheless imitate them courageously.

## XIX

Therefore, although I wished to leave them and go to Britain, and although I was most willing and ready to do so, as if returning to my homeland and parents—not only that, but I was also prepared to visit the brothers throughout Gaul and see the faces of the saints of my Lord—God knows that I greatly desired this.

But I am bound by the Spirit, who warns me that if I do this, he designates me as one who will be guilty; and I fear losing the labor that I have begun.

It is not I, but Christ the Lord, who commanded me to come and remain with them for the rest of my life (Bollandus: “who commanded me to come and be with them for the remainder of my life”), if the Lord wills and guards me from every evil way, so that I may not sin before him.

I ought to hope for this, but I do not trust myself for as long as I remain in this body of death, because strong is the one who daily strives to overthrow me from the faith and the proposed purity of an unfeigned religious life, which I shall preserve to the end of my life in Christ my Lord.

But the hostile flesh is always dragging me toward death—that is, toward pleasures to be illicitly pursued (Bollandus: “toward pleasures to be enjoyed in misery”).

And I know in part why I have not lived a perfect life, as other believers have. But I confess to my Lord, and I am not ashamed in his sight, because I do not lie: from the time when I came to know him in my youth, the love and fear of God grew within me, and until now, by the Lord’s favor, I have kept the faith.

## XX

Let whoever wishes laugh and mock. I will not remain silent, nor will I conceal the signs and wonders that were shown to me by the Lord many years before they occurred, as by one who knows everything, even before the ages of the world.

Therefore I ought to give thanks to God without ceasing, who often forgave my foolishness. And [I went] from place to place, though the sentence is corrupt, so that he might not be exceedingly angry with me; I, to whom a helper had been given, did not quickly comply with what had been shown to me, as the Spirit nevertheless suggested.

And the Lord had mercy on me thousands upon thousands of times, because he saw that I was prepared, though I knew no more than before what I should do concerning my state. For many were preventing this mission, and behind my back they were already saying among themselves: “Why does this man throw himself into danger among enemies who do not know the Lord?”

They did not say this out of malice; but, as I myself testify, because of my rusticity I did not understand it. I did not quickly recognize the grace that was then within me. Now I understand what I ought to have understood before.

## XXI

Now, therefore, I have simply explained myself to the brothers and fellow-servants who believed me. For this reason I previously spoke and now speak, to strengthen and confirm your faith.

Would that you too might imitate greater things and do what is better. This will be my glory, because “a wise son is the glory of his father” (Proverbs 11:1; 15:20).

You and God know how I lived among you from my youth, in the faith of truth and sincerity of heart. Even among those nations where I dwell, I have shown them faith and will continue to do so.

God knows that I deceived none of them, nor do I intend to do so, for the sake of God and his Church, lest I stir up persecution against them and all of us, and lest through me the name of the Lord be blasphemed, because it is written: “Woe to the person through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed” (Leviticus 24:16).

For although I am unskilled in everything, nevertheless I have tried somehow to keep myself whole, even in relation to Christian brothers, virgins of Christ, and religious women, who voluntarily gave me small gifts and laid them on the altar from their ornaments; and I returned them to those women.

They were offended against me, asking why I did this. But I did it because of the hope of eternity, so that I might preserve myself carefully in all things and so that unbelievers might not seize upon me under any pretext, nor find even the slightest opportunity to slander or disparage the ministry of my service.

Editorial notes not otherwise represented above: In §IV the words required for the sense, “what I did not acquire in my youth,” are supplied from Bollandus, who, a little earlier, wrongly prints “But an excuse is useful,” omitting “what.” In §V Bollandus improperly omits *sed* (“but”); the reading *et si talis essem* (“even if I were such”) is restored from Bollandus, whereas Waræus has *si*, less suitably. In §VI Bollandus omits “my death” and shortly afterward reads “although I was not worthy.” In §VIII Waræus’s reading, “and their dogs were uncovered,” printed by the Bollandists, is wholly erroneous.

In §IX Waræus’s reading, “and he took away all the strength of my limbs,” is preferable; Bollandus notes that the manuscript has “I could prevail in none of my limbs,” and conjecturally adds “to move.” Bollandus also supplies *totis* (“with all”) before “my strength.” In §X Bollandus places the sentence about the sixtieth night immediately after Matthew 10:20; it is more fitting here, since it would be intrusive there. In §XII Bollandus reads “whether I then had fifteen years,” followed by “one God”; Waræus’s *si habeam* is bad. In §XIII Bollandus omits “here and in the future,” and also omits “to you.” It reads *pulsaretur* (“should be assailed”), where Waræus has *pulsaret* (“should assail”), and later reads “and publicly dishonor me.”

In §XIV Bollandus reads *denudasti* (“you have unveiled”) for *cooperuisti*, and later *exaltarem* (“that I might exalt”); it omits the phrase “although ignorant.” In §XV Bollandus reads “lest I wrong the readers”; then, “But the Lord as author … repeatedly admonished me, poor and little as I was, by a divine response,” followed by “Whence came to me … ?” In §XVI Bollandus reads, “as we believe, [believers] are to come from the whole world.” In §XVIII Bollandus omits the genitive *Scottae* (“of a Scot woman”); it reads “who warned her,” and, for the corrupt phrase concerning those born there, “Those who were born there to Christ.” In §XIX Bollandus reads “to leave them and go to Britain, although most willingly,” “who commanded me to come and be with them,” “I hope,” “the purity of an unfeigned religious life (which I shall preserve),” and “pleasures to be enjoyed in misery.”

In §XX Bollandus prefers “shown to me, before they happened,” rather than “which had happened”; after “my foolishness” it adds “and my negligence,” and observes that the passage, corrupted by copyists’ carelessness, seems to have contained details of Patrick’s journeys. It reads *debueram* (“I ought to have”), rather than Waræus’s *debuero*; “and the Spirit nevertheless suggested”; and “I knew nothing further.” Waræus reads “not out of malice” and “now it enters my mind”; Bollandus’s readings, adopted above, are preferred. In §XXI Bollandus has “and [to] you,” and “be blasphemed”; it conjectures, for the disordered passage on gifts, “I tried to keep myself whole, accepting nothing from anyone, even from brethren.”

XXII. But perhaps, when I baptized so many thousands of people, I expected from some of them even half a [Note: [Col. 0812] Perhaps *scriptulae* (“scruples”). Bollandus has *scriptulum*, adding: “Sosipater, in the *Etymologicum* of John Gerard Vossius: *Scriptulum*, which is now commonly called a [lacuna]—namely, a *scruple*—was used by Varro in his *Plautorinus*. And elsewhere: ‘A silver coin first struck by Servius Tullius; it was four *scriptula* larger than it is now.’ A *scriptulum*, or *scrupulum*, is the smallest part of an ounce.” See Du Cange, *Glossarium Latinitatis*, s.v. SCRIPTULUS.] scruples? Tell me, and I will repay you. Or when the Lord ordained clerics through my insignificance and ministry, I distributed to them freely. If I ever asked any of them even the price of my footwear, tell me; speak against me, and I will repay you. Rather, I spent more on your behalf, so that it might cost me; and for your sake I traveled among you and everywhere amid many dangers, even to [Note: [Col. 0812] So also Bollandus; Waraeus conjectures that *extremas* (“the farthest”) should be read.] distant regions, where no one had gone farther, [Col. 0812B] and where no one had ever arrived to baptize, ordain clerics, or [Note: [Col. 0812] Bollandus: “confirm the people in the faith.”] complete the people in the faith. By God’s gift, diligently and most willingly I undertook everything [Note: [Col. 0812] Bollandus: *gessi* (“I carried out”). Immediately afterward he has: “apart from what I gave.”] for your salvation. Meanwhile I gave rewards to kings, because of which I paid compensation to their sons who traveled with me, and [Note: [Col. 0812] Waraeus thinks *non* (“not”) should be read; Bollandus’s *nihilominus* (“nevertheless”) is more correct.] nevertheless they seized nothing from me or my companions. On that day they eagerly desired to kill me, but the time had not yet come. Everything of ours that they found, they seized, and they themselves bound me with irons. On the fourteenth day the Lord released me from their power, and whatever belonged to us was returned to us, for God’s sake and because of the necessary friends whom we had previously provided for.

XXIII. You yourselves have experienced how much I paid out [Col. 0812C] to those who [Note: [Col. 0812] The manuscript has this reading, though Bollandus rewrote it in the text as *indigebant* (“were in need”).] judged throughout all the regions that I visited most frequently. For I reckon that I distributed to them no small sum—the price of fifteen men. So that you might enjoy me, and I might always enjoy you in God, I do not regret it, nor is it enough for me: I continue to spend and will spend beyond this. The Lord is able afterward to grant me that I may spend myself for your souls (II Cor. XII, 15). Behold, I call God as witness upon my soul, because I am not lying: I did not write to you, as is customary, either for the sake of flattery or greed, or in the hope of receiving your honor. The honor that is not seen but believed in the heart is sufficient for me; and the one who promised is faithful and never lies. But I see that in the present age I have been exalted by the Lord beyond measure. I was neither worthy nor such a person that he should grant this to me, since I know most certainly that poverty and calamity suit me better than pleasures and riches. Yet Christ the Lord was poor for our sake. But I, wretched and miserable, if I should desire wealth, no longer possess it, nor do I consider myself [worthy of it], because each day I expect either slaughter, or to be deceived, or to be reduced to slavery, [Note: [Col. 0813] Bollandus: “without cause.”] or some other danger. But I fear none of these things because of the promises of heaven, since I have cast myself into the hands of almighty God, who rules everywhere, as the prophet says: “Cast your thought upon God, and he himself [Col. 0813B] will nourish you” (Psalm LIV, 23).

XXIV. Behold, now I commend my soul to my most faithful God, for whom I serve as an ambassador in my lowliness (II Cor. V, 20). But since he is no respecter of persons and chose me for this office, so that I might be one of his least ministers: “How then shall I repay him for all that he has repaid me?” (Psalm CXV, 12). [Note: [Col. 0813] We follow Bollandus. Waraeus has: “But … because I see nothing.”] Or what shall I say, or what shall I promise my Lord? For I am powerless unless he himself gives it to me. But he searches hearts and kidneys, because I desire sufficiently and exceedingly, and I was ready for him to grant me to drink his cup, as he granted it to the others who love him. Therefore, may it never happen to me from my God that I should ever lose his people whom I acquired at the ends of the earth. I ask God to grant me perseverance and to deem me worthy to render him a faithful witness until my passing, for the sake of my God. And if I have ever imitated anything good for the sake of my God, whom I love, I ask him to grant me that, together with those converts and captives, I may pour out my blood for his name—even if I should be deprived of burial, or my wretched corpse should be torn limb from limb for dogs or savage beasts, or birds of the air should devour it. I am completely convinced that, if this should happen to me, I have gained my soul together with my body, because without any doubt on that day we shall rise in the brightness of the sun—that is, [Note: [Col. 0813] Bollandus adds: “We shall all be in the glory of Jesus Christ our Redeemer, like sons of God and coheirs of Christ, conformed to the image of his creation; for from him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen.” Immediately afterward: “For in him we shall reign: for this sun …”] in the glory of Christ Jesus our Redeemer, the Son of the living God, and coheirs of Christ (Rom. VIII, 17), and conformed to his future image (ibid., 29), because from him, through him, and in him we shall reign.

XXV. For this sun that we see rises daily for our sake at God’s command, but it will never reign, nor will its splendor endure. And all who worship it will come miserably to punishment. But we believe in and worship the true Sun, Christ, [Col. 0814B] who will never perish; nor will the one who does his will perish, but he will remain forever, just as Christ will remain forever—he who reigns with God the almighty Father and with the Holy Spirit, before the ages, now, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Behold, once again and briefly I shall set forth the words of my confession. I testify in truth and in the joy of my heart, before God and his holy angels, that I never had any reason—apart from his Gospel and promises—to return to that people from which I had previously scarcely escaped. [Note: [Col. 0814] Waraeus most poorly has: “that I might return, acting upon it.”] But I ask those who believe in and fear God—whoever may deign to examine or receive this writing, which Patrick, a sinner and indeed an unlearned man, composed in Ireland—that [Col. 0814C] no one should ever say that it was because of my ignorance [Note: [Col. 0814] Bollandus: “through my ignorance.”] if I did or demonstrated something small according to God’s pleasure. But judge, and let it be believed most truly, [Note: [Col. 0814] Bollandus: “that it was God’s gift.”] that it was God’s gift. And this is my confession before I die.

[Col. 0813]

[Note: [Col. 0813] In Bollandus the title reads: “The Letter of Saint Patrick to the Christians subject to the tyrant Coroticus.” This is correct, as is clear from the context.]

## The Letter of Saint Patrick to Coroticus (C)

[Col. 0813D]

I. I, Patrick, a sinner—indeed an unlearned man—declare that I have been established as a bishop in Ireland. I am firmly convinced that I have received from God what I am. Therefore I dwell among barbarians as a proselyte and refugee, for the love of God. He is witness whether this is so: not that I desired to pour from my mouth anything so harsh and severe [Col. 0814D] [Note: [Col. 0814] Bollandus: “anything from my mouth.” A little earlier in Bollandus: “a bishop established in Ireland, I am firmly convinced.”] but I am compelled by zeal for God and the truth of Christ, who stirred me up out of love for my neighbors and children, for whom I surrendered my homeland, my parents, and my life even unto death, if I am worthy.

I vowed to my God that I would teach the nations, although I am despised [Note: [Col. 0815] Bollandus: “by certain people.” Immediately afterward: “and by my hand.”] by those among whom I wrote and composed these words, to be given, delivered, and sent to the soldiers, to Coroticus. I do not call them citizens of mine, nor citizens of the holy Romans, but citizens of demons, because of their evil deeds and their hostile custom. The companions of Scots and apostate Picts live in death, [Note: [Col. 0815] So Bollandus. Waraeus corruptly has: “who desire to be made fat with the blood of innocent Christians, to bleed from blood.”] as though desiring to gorge themselves on the blood of innocent Christians, whom I have begotten in countless numbers for God and confirmed in Christ.

II. On the following day, when the chrism of the newly baptized in white garments—while faith blazed upon their foreheads—[Note: [Col. 0815] We have rewritten this passage according to Bollandus. Waraeus’s text is badly corrupt: “the chrism of the neophytes blazed on their foreheads in a white garment, while they were cruelly slaughtered and butchered by the sword by the aforesaid. And I sent a letter …”] was cruelly slaughtered and butchered by the sword by the aforesaid men, I sent a letter with a holy presbyter whom I had instructed from childhood together with the clerics, asking that they grant us something from the booty or from the baptized captives [Col. 0815B] whom they had taken. But they mocked them. Therefore I do not know whom I should mourn more: those who were killed, those whom they captured, or those whom the devil has grievously ensnared, who will be handed over together with him to everlasting punishment in Gehenna. For [Note: [Col. 0815] We have supplied this word from Bollandus; it is absent from Waraeus. A little earlier Bollandus incorrectly reads *mancipabunt* (“they will enslave”).] “the one who commits sin is the slave of sin” (I John III, 8), and he is called a son of the devil.

III. Therefore let every person who fears God know that such men are alien to me and to Christ my Lord, for whom I serve as an ambassador: parricides, fratricides, ravening wolves devouring the Lord’s people as food, as he says: “The wicked have destroyed your law, O Lord” (Psalm CXVIII, 126)—the law that, in these final times, had been planted and instructed most excellently and kindly in Ireland, by God’s favor.

I do not usurp what belongs to others; [Col. 0815C] rather, I share in the company of those whom he called and predestined to preach the Gospel amid no small persecutions, even to the ends of the earth. Although the enemy is envious through the tyranny of Coroticus, who does not fear God, nor his priests whom he chose and to whom he granted the highest, divine, sublime power: “Whatever they bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 18).

IV. Therefore I earnestly ask you, holy and humble in heart: it is not lawful to flatter such men, nor should one take food or drink with them, nor receive their alms, until, with cruelly shed tears, they have made sufficient satisfaction to God and have released the servants of God and the baptized handmaids of Christ, for whom he died and was crucified.

The Most High rejects the gifts of the wicked: “He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father” (Eccli. XXXIV, 23–24). “The riches that the unjust man has gathered,” he says, “will be vomited from his belly; the angel of death drags him away; he will be punished by the wrath of dragons; the tongue of the serpent will kill him” (Job XX, 15–16). And unquenchable fire will consume him.

Therefore, woe to those who fill themselves with what is not theirs. Or, “what does it profit a man to gain the whole world and suffer the loss of his soul?” (Matt. XVI, 26). It would be too long to examine or expound one by one, throughout the whole Law, the testimonies concerning such greed. Greed is a mortal crime: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property. You shall not kill” (Exod. XX, 17, 13). A murderer cannot be with Christ. “He who hates his brother is counted as a murderer”; or, “he who does not love his brother remains in death” (I John III, 14–15). How much more guilty is the one who has stained his hands with the blood of the sons of God, whom he recently acquired at the ends of the earth through the exhortation of our humble ministry?

V. Did I come to Ireland without God or according to the flesh? Who compelled me? I am bound by the Spirit, so that I do not see anyone from my family. [Note: [Col. 0815] Bollandus: “Do I not show loving mercy, which I practice?”] Do I show loving mercy toward that people who once captured me and ravaged the servants and handmaids of my father’s household?

By birth I was a free man: [Note: [Col. 0816] Read with Waraeus and Bollandus: *decurione* (“decurion”).] I was born the son of a decurion. I sold my nobility—I do not blush, nor do I regret it—for the benefit of others. [Note: [Col. 0816] Bollandus: “Finally, I have been handed over in Christ to a foreign people for the ineffable glory of eternal life, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord; although my own …” The intervening words are absent from Waraeus, perhaps through scribal error caused by repeated words in Christ.] Finally, I am a servant in Christ Jesus our Lord, although my own people do not know me. “A prophet has no honor in his own country” (Mark VI, 4).

Perhaps we are not from one sheepfold, nor do we have one God as Father, as he says: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI, 23). It is not fitting that “one should destroy what another builds” (Eccli. XXXIV, 28). I do not seek what is mine.

[Col. 0816C]

VI. It was not through my own merit; rather, God placed this concern in my heart, so that I might be one of the hunters or fishers whom God foretold long ago for the final days (Jer. XXVI, 16). I am envied. “What shall I do, Lord? I am greatly despised.”

Behold, your sheep around me are being torn apart and plundered by the brigands mentioned above, at Coroticus’s command and with a hostile mind—he is far removed from the charity of God, a betrayer of Christians—into the hands of Scots and Picts. Ravening wolves have swallowed the Lord’s flock, which was growing exceedingly well in Ireland with the greatest diligence. The sons of Scots and the daughters of princes were becoming monks and virgins of Christ; I cannot count them.

[Note: [Col. 0816] Waraeus’s reading is preferable to Bollandus’s: “Because of the injury done to the righteous, may he not appease you, Lord; even in hell he will not appease you.”] Therefore, because of the injury done to the righteous, may this not please you; even unto hell it will not please you.

[Col. 0816D]

VII. Which of the saints would not shudder to rejoice or feast with such men? They have filled their houses with the spoils of dead Christians; they live by plunder; in their misery they do not understand. [Note: [Col. 0816] So Bollandus. *Bibunt* (“they drink”) is absent from Waraeus, who immediately afterward printed: “They produce everlasting death and punishment.” We have supplied the missing passage from Bollandus.] They drink poison and offer lethal [Col. 0817A] food to their friends and children. Just as Eve did not understand that she had handed death over to her husband, so all who do evil bring about everlasting death and perpetual punishment.

It is the custom of Roman and Gallic Christians to send suitable holy men to the Franks and [Note: [Col. 0817] Bollandus: “foreign nations.” With him we also read *omnes interficis* (“you kill all”), where Waraeus repeatedly has the erroneous *interficis* in a different sense.] other nations with many thousands of solidi, to ransom baptized captives. You kill them all and sell them to a foreign people ignorant of God; you deliver the members of Christ as though to a brothel. What hope do you have in God?

VIII. [Note: [Col. 0817] So Bollandus. Waraeus has: “or whoever agrees with you, or whoever communicates with you in flattering words.”] Whoever agrees with you, or shares in alien and flattering words, God will judge. For it is written: “Not only those who do evil, but also those who consent to them, are condemned” (Rom. I, 32).

I do not know what more I should say or speak concerning the dead sons of God, whom the sword struck with excessive brutality. For it is written: “Weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII, 15); and again: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it” (I Cor. XII, 26).

Therefore the Church weeps and laments her sons and daughters whom the sword has not yet killed, but who have been delayed and carried away into distant regions of the earth … [Note: [Col. 0817] So Bollandus. In Waraeus the passage is corrupt and mutilated: “Where sin is manifestly [Col. 0817D] aggravated, shamelessness abounds.”] That sin may be openly charged to shamelessness, shamelessness dwells and abounds there. There freeborn Christian men have been sold into slavery, especially to the most unworthy, wicked, and apostate Picts.

IX. Therefore, with sadness and grief, I shall cry out: “O most beautiful and most beloved brothers and sons whom I have begotten in Christ, I cannot tell what I should do for you! I am not worthy [Note: [Col. 0817] This word is absent from Bollandus. Immediately afterward, the following words are also absent there: “We have become like strangers.” A little later Bollandus has: “We received one baptism and believe in one God.” “It is unworthy of them that we were born in Ireland; for this is what they say.”] to help either God or human beings.”

The wickedness of the wicked has prevailed against us. We have become like strangers. Perhaps they do not believe that we receive one baptism, or that we have one God as Father. It is unworthy of them that [Note: [Col. 0818] Ireland, which above was called *Hiberione*, is here called *Hiberia* in all the copies. Waraeus.] we were born in Ireland, as he says: “Do you not have one God? Why has each of you abandoned his neighbor?”

Therefore I grieve for you; I grieve, my beloved. Yet again I rejoice within myself: my labor was not in vain, nor was my pilgrimage empty. And a crime occurred [Note: [Col. 0818] Bollandus inserts after this word: “at that time.” Immediately afterward he has: “believers and baptized.”] so terrible and unspeakable. Thanks be to God: believing baptized people, you have departed from the world into paradise. I see it: [Col. 0818A] you have begun to migrate to the place where there will be neither night nor mourning nor death any longer (Rev. XXI, 4); rather, you will rejoice like calves released from their bonds, and you will trample the wicked, and they will be ashes beneath your feet.

X. Therefore you will reign with the apostles, prophets, and martyrs, and you will receive eternal kingdoms, as he himself testifies, saying: “They will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII, 11).

Outside are dogs, sorcerers, murderers, liars (Rev. XXII, 15), and perjurers. “Their portion is in the lake of eternal fire” (Rev. XXI, 8). Not without reason the Apostle says: “Where the righteous will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the impious transgressor of the law find himself?” (II Pet. IV, 18).

[Note: [Col. 0818] We have rewritten this with Bollandus; Waraeus’s *unde* (“whence”) is unsatisfactory.] Where, then, is Coroticus with his most wicked rebels against Christ? [Note: [Col. 0818D] So Bollandus. Here Waraeus’s text is gaping and corrupt: “Where they will see themselves, while rewards are distributed among baptized women.”] Where [Col. 0818B] will those men see themselves who distribute baptized women and the estates of orphans to their most filthy followers for the sake of a wretched temporal kingdom, which surely passes in a moment like a cloud or smoke scattered by the wind?

Thus sinners and deceivers will perish from the face of the Lord; but the righteous will feast in great steadfastness with Christ. They will judge the nations and rule over wicked kings forever and ever. Amen.

I testify before God and his angels that it will be as my ignorance has intimated. [Note: [Col. 0818] So Bollandus; Waraeus has: “through my ignorance: not my words, but …” Immediately afterward he has the Latin without the preposition *in*.] Not my words, but those of God, the apostles, and the prophets—which I have rendered into Latin—for they never lied. “Whoever believes will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 16). God has spoken.

[Col. 0818C] I earnestly ask that any servant of God who is willing to become the bearer of this letter should not have it withheld by anyone, but rather that it be read before all the peoples and before Coroticus himself. If God should inspire them so that at some time they may repent before God, or even repent late of what they have wickedly done as murderers against the brothers of the Lord, and release the baptized female captives whom they previously seized, then they may be worthy to live for God and become healthy here and forever.

Peace to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. Amen.

[Col. 0817]

# The Synod of Saint Patrick (C, S)

## Chapter One. On dwelling with sinful brothers

Concerning what you asked, about dwelling with sinful brothers, hear the Apostle saying: “With such a one do not even eat” (I Cor. V, 11); do not eat his food with him. On the other hand, if you are an ox and are threshing—that is, if you are a teacher and teach—your mouth is not to be muzzled (I Cor. IX, 9), and you are worthy of your wage (Luke X, 7). But “let the oil of the sinner not anoint your head” (Psalm CXL, 5); rather, rebuke and admonish him further.

[Col. 0819A]

## Chapter II. On their offerings

[Note: [Col. 0819] On this passage, see Cotelerius’s note on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book IV, chapter 8, note 5.]

Be content with your clothing and food; reject the remaining gifts of the wicked (Eccli. XXXIV, 23), because a lamp accepts only what feeds it.

## Chapter III. On penance after falls

It is decreed that the abbot should see to whom the power of binding and loosing is to be attributed; but, according to the examples of Scripture, [Note: [Col. 0819] Perhaps *venia* (“forgiveness”). Waraeus.] forgiveness is more appropriate. If, however, it is undertaken with weeping and lamentation and in mourning clothing, under custody, a short penance is better than a long and lax one with accommodations.

## Chapter IV. On rejecting the excommunicated

Hear the Lord saying: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII, 37). You shall not curse him, but you shall exclude the excommunicated person from communion, the table, the Mass, and peace. And if he is a heretic, “after one admonition, avoid him” (Tit. III, 10).

## Chapter V. On doubtful cases

Hear the Lord saying: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. XIII, 30)—that is, until the one who reveals the counsels of hearts shall come (I Cor. IV, 5)—so that you do not pass judgment before the day of judgment. Consider Judas at the Lord’s table and the thief in paradise.

## Chapter VI. On the Church’s punishments

Hear the Lord likewise saying: “Whoever sheds innocent blood, his blood shall be shed” (Gen. IX, 6); but this is decreed by the one who bears the sword, [Note: [Col. 0819] Perhaps: “But the dictator [or magistrate] is …” Waraeus.] or he is regarded as innocent in respect of vengeance. As for the rest, judgment is to be exercised according to evangelical law, beginning with the passage in which he says: “From the one who takes something from you, do not demand it back” (Luke VI, 30), but give willingly; if he himself returns something, receive it humbly.

## Chapter VII. On uncertain baptisms

It is decreed that those who received the tradition of the creed from anyone should not be rebaptized, because the iniquity of the sower does not contaminate the seed. But if that is not the case, it is not a matter of rebaptizing but of baptizing. Let us not believe that those who have fallen from the faith are to be absolved except through the laying on of hands [Note: [Col. 0820] Read: *accipi* (“to receive”).].

## Chapter VIII. On accused persons removed from the Church

The Church was not established for the defense of the accused; rather, judges must be persuaded to kill by spiritual death those who flee to the bosom of Mother Church.

## Chapter IX

(Missing.)

[Col. 0819D]

## Chapter X. On those who fall after receiving a rank

Hear the canonical regulations: “Whoever falls while holding a rank shall rise without that rank.” Let him be content with the name alone and lose [Col. 0820A] his ministry, unless he is one who, though sinning, has not withdrawn so far from the sight of the Lord.

## Chapter XI. On separating the sexes after a fall

Let each person examine his conscience to see whether love and desire have ceased from sin, because a dead body does not contaminate another dead body. Otherwise, let them be separated.

## Chapter XII. On an offering for the dead

Hear the Apostle saying: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for that” (I John V, 16). And the Lord says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII, 6). For if someone in his lifetime was not worthy to receive the sacrifice, how can it help him after death?

## Chapter XIII. On the sacrifice

[Col. 0820B]

On the night of Easter, if it is permissible to carry it outside. It is not carried outside, but is brought to the faithful. What else does it signify that the lamb is eaten in one house, except that Christ is believed in and shared under the one summit of faith?

## Chapter XIV. On abstinen[lacuna] from foods

[Note: [Col. 0820] Cotelerius, *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. I, p. 812, emends this passage as follows: “It was decreed that the advent of Christ, the Bridegroom, should find no fixed laws of fasting.”]

It is decreed that the advent of Christ, the Bridegroom, should find no fixed laws of fasting. What difference is there between a Novatian and a Christian, except that the Novatian abstains without interruption, whereas the Christian abstains for a period? Thus place, time, and person are to be observed in every respect.

## Chapter XV. On abandoning or teaching one’s homeland

One’s homeland must first be taught by the example of the Lord, and afterward abandoned if no progress results, according to the example of the Apostle. But whoever can make progress, even if he is in danger, should teach everywhere and make himself known. Whoever cannot should be silent and hide himself: one person is sent by Jesus to his own house, another is commanded to follow.

## Chapter XVI. On false bishops

Whoever has not been elected according to the Apostle by another bishop must be condemned; afterward he must withdraw from the rest of the people and be deposed.

## Chapter XVII. On the purpose of monks

Monks are those who live alone, without earthly possessions, under the authority of a bishop or abbot. But they are not monks; rather, they are “Vactro” experts—that is, zealous contemners [of the world]—for the perfect life at a mature age. This means that, from the age of twenty, each person ought to be bound not by public declaration but by the fulfillment of a vow, as it is written: “Let each one act as he has purposed in his heart” (I Cor. VII, 37), and “I will pay my vows in the presence of the Lord” (Psalm CXV, 14, 18), and so forth.

The place of residence constrains the life by which one lives under this vow. If there is excess, it must be avoided in every aspect of life, because they have been called to cold and nakedness, hunger and thirst, vigils and fasts (II Cor. XI, 27).

## Chapter XVIII. On the three seeds of the Gospels

The hundredfold (Matt. XIII, 8, 23) refers to bishops and teachers, who are all things to all people; the sixtyfold, to clerics and widows who practice continence; the thirtyfold, to lay people who are faithful and who believe the Trinity perfectly. There is no more than this in the harvest of the Lord; but we join monks and virgins to the hundredfold.

## Chapter XIX. At what age people are to be baptized

Catechumens are [instructed] on the eighth day; afterward they are baptized on the Lord’s solemnities—that is, Easter, Pentecost, and Epiphany.

## Chapter XX. On parishes

One must not speak with monks whose evil is unheard-of; but we have rightly accepted the unity of the people.

## Chapter XXI. On retaining or dismissing monks

Let each person enjoy his fruit in the Church in which he was instructed, unless a cause of greater progress compels him to go elsewhere with the abbot’s permission [Note: [Col. 0821] Perhaps “further.” Waraeus.]. But if he leaves, let the more useful cause be stated with a blessing: “Behold the Lamb of God,” with each person seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. II, 21). Let them not permit their subjects to wander about investigating the cause of their vocation. [Col. 0821C] [Note: [Col. 0821] Or “to examine.”]

## Chapter XXII. On receiving the Eucharist after a fall

It is to be received after examination in prison, especially on the night of Easter; whoever does not communicate on that night is not faithful. Therefore the intervals among them are brief and strict, lest a faithful soul perish through remaining so long without the medicine of fasting, the Lord saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54).

## Chapter XXIII. On the oath

Do not swear at all (Matt. V, 34). The sequence of the reading on this subject teaches that no other creature is to be invoked under oath, but only the Creator, as is the custom of the prophets: “As the Lord lives, and as my soul lives” (IV Kings II, 2, 4, 6); and: “As the Lord lives, before whom I stand today” (III Kings XVIII, 15). The end of the controversy is: “except by the Lord.” For whatever a person loves, by that he also swears.

## Chapter XXIV. On a dispute between two persons without witnesses

It is decreed that, through the four holy Gospels, before he communicates, each person should testify to what has been proved; afterward the matter should be left to the judgment of public reputation.

## Chapter XXV. On the bed of a deceased brother

Hear the decrees of the synod concerning this matter. A brother shall not ascend upon the bed of his deceased brother, the Lord saying: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24). Therefore your brother’s wife is your sister.

## Chapter XXVI. On a wife who is a prostitute

Hear the Lord saying: “He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body” (I Cor. VI, 16). Again: “Let the adulteress be stoned” (Lev. XX, 10; Deut. XXII, 22)—that is, let her die to this vice, so that she may cease what she does not cease doing: committing adultery. Again: “If a woman has committed adultery, will she return to her first husband?” (Jer. III, 1). Again: “It is not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife except on account of fornication” (Matt. V, 32; XIX, 9), as though he were saying, “for this reason.” Therefore, if he takes another wife as though after the death of the first, they do not forbid it.

## Chapter XXVII. On the will of a virgin or her father in marriage

Let the virgin do what her father wishes, because the man is the head of the woman (I Cor. XI, 3). But the father’s will must be sought together with the virgin’s, since God leaves a human being in the hands of his own counsel (Eccli. XV, 14).

## Chapter XXVIII. On first and second vows

The first vows and first marriages must be observed for the same reason, [Note: [Col. 0821] Perhaps “so that.” Waraeus.] or the first must not be invalidated by the second unless they have been adulterated.

## Chapter XXIX. On consanguinity in marriage

Understand what the law says—neither less nor more. But what is observed among us, that four degrees are to be distinguished, they say they have neither seen nor read.

## Chapter XXX. On claims that have become customary

What has never been forbidden is permitted. Nevertheless, the laws of the jubilee must be observed—that is, the fifty-year period—so that uncertainties are not confirmed by the antiquity of time. Therefore all transactions [Note: [Col. 0822] The passage is corrupt. Waraeus. Perhaps: “all business dealings.”] must be confirmed by the signature of the Romans.

[Col. 0822D]

## Chapter XXXI. On pagans who believe before baptism, and what penance they should undergo

All sins are indeed remitted in baptism. But because, with a faithful conscience, he lived as an unbeliever for a tempor[lacuna] [Note: [Col. 0822] Perhaps: “with an unbeliever for a temporary period.” Waraeus.], he must be judged as a faithful sinner.

The synod of Patrick ends.

[Col. 0823]

# Other Canons Attributed to Saint Patrick (C)

[Col. 0823A]

## I. On the judgment of clerics, so that it may not be among the wicked or unbelievers

No worldly wise man, [Note: [Col. 0823] Perhaps *etsi* (“even if”). Waraeus.] if he is wise, should judge the judgments of the Church.

## II. On the people’s subjection to the prince

You are ministers, and each one of you must fear his own prince, whom he attends and serves.

## III. On the penance of one who blasphemes a good prince

Whoever mutters words of blasphemy against a good prince out of hatred or envy shall do penance for seven days on bread and water, following the example of Mary, who murmured against Moses.

[Col. 0823B]

## IV. On the uncertainty whether a bishop may recover his former rank after a fall

Bishop Patrick says: Whoever sins while holding a rank must be excommunicated, because the dignity of this title is great. Nevertheless, after penance he can redeem his soul; to return to his former rank is difficult. I do not know whether it is not possible. God knows.

## V. On receiving an adulterous wife after penance, and on the amount of penance

If someone’s wife has fornicated with another man, he shall not take another wife as long as his first wife is alive. If she should perhaps be converted and perform penance, he shall receive her and serve her in place of a maidservant; she shall do penance for a full year on bread and water by measure, and they shall not remain in one bed.

## VI. On going to outsiders for judgment

If any disputes arise on this island, let them be referred to the apostolic see.

## VII. On performing penance at the last breath

If someone falls ill, let him perform penance, even under necessity, because God is merciful.

## VIII. On the fact that the foolish should not preside

The synod of the whole world, and Patrick, decreed: Whoever is foolish must not preside in any way, but must carry out his work under the authority of a Catholic abbot.

[Col. 0824B]

## IX. On collecting money, which is not to be condemned when necessity compels it

Patrick said: If someone has received the bishop’s permission, and money has been collected for a captive, he shall not demand more than necessity required. If anything remains beyond this, he shall place it upon the altar, and it shall be given to the needy and to captives.

Likewise, if someone collects money under the name of mercy, he must not dare to plunder the Church of God, but rather kings [Col. 0824C] and common people, for whom it is better to give than to store up.

[Col. 0823]

# The Synod of the Bishops Patrick, Auxilius, and Iserninus (C)

We give thanks to God the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit. Patrick, Auxilius, and Iserninus, bishops, send greetings to the presbyters, deacons, and the entire clergy.
