It is better for us to warn the negligent beforehand than to blame what has been done, as Solomon says: “It is better to rebuke than to become angry” (Ecclus. XX, 1). The examples of our ruling are written below, and begin as follows.

I. If anyone in the community should seek a captive for interrogation on his own authority, without permission, he deserves to be excommunicated.

II. Finally, let readers recognize individually the church in which each one is to chant.

III. A cleric shall not be wandering about in the community.

IV. If anyone has received permission and a price has been collected, let him demand no more than necessity requires.

V. If anything remains beyond that, let him place it upon the bishop’s altar, so that it may be given to another person in need.

VI. Any cleric, from the doorkeeper up to the priest, who is seen without a tunic, or who does not cover the indecency and nakedness of his belly; and if his hair has not been cut in the Roman manner, and if his wife walks about without her head veiled, they shall likewise be despised by the laity and separated from the Church.

[Col. 0824D]

VII. Any cleric who, having been ordered to do so, fails through negligence to attend the collections morning or evening shall be regarded as an outsider, unless perhaps he is being held under the yoke of servitude.

VIII. If a cleric has become surety for a pagan in any amount, and if it should happen—although this is not surprising—that the pagan, by some trick, cheats the cleric of his property, that cleric shall pay the debt. For if he fights him with weapons, he shall rightly be counted outside the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0823] Read *est*. Thus in the Cotton manuscript.]

IX. A monk and a virgin, one from one place and the other from elsewhere, shall not remain together in a single lodging; nor shall they travel together in one cart from village to village; nor shall they habitually engage in conversation with one another.

[Col. 0825A]

X. If anyone shows that he has begun a good work by chanting, yet has long hair, he is to be excluded from the Church unless he restores himself to his former state.

XI. Any cleric who has been excommunicated by someone else, and another has received him, shall both undergo an equal penance.

XII. Any Christian who has been excommunicated: his alms shall not be accepted.

XIII. It is not permitted to receive into the church alms offered by pagans.

XIV. A Christian who kills, or commits fornication, or goes, in the pagan manner, to a diviner [Note: [Col. 0825] One who examines the entrails of sacrificial victims in order to learn from them what will happen in the future. See Hadrian Junius, *Nomenclator*. WAR.], shall perform a year of penance for each individual crime. When the year of penance has been completed, he shall come with witnesses, and afterward shall be released by the priest.

[Col. 0825B]

XV. Anyone who commits theft shall do penance for half [a year], including twenty days on bread; and, if possible, he shall return what was stolen. In this way he shall be readmitted to the Church.

XVI. A Christian who believes that there is a [Note: [Col. 0825] Festus uses this term for a sorceress, who was also anciently called a *volatica* and a *strix*. ID.] Lamia in a mirror, which is interpreted as “witch,” is to be anathematized; and whoever has imposed this report upon a person’s soul shall likewise be anathematized. He shall not be received into the Church before he withdraws, with his own voice, the very charge that he made; and thus he shall perform penance with complete diligence.

XVII. A virgin who has vowed herself to God remains chaste, and afterward marries a carnal bridegroom: she shall be under excommunication until she converts. If she has converted and has abandoned the adultery, let her perform penance; afterward they shall not live either in one house or in one village.

XVIII. If anyone is under excommunication, he shall not enter the church even on the night of Easter [Col. 0825C] until he has received penance.

XIX. A Christian woman who has taken a husband in an honorable marriage, and afterward has left the first and joined herself to adultery, shall be under excommunication for having done this.

XX. A Christian who evades any debt by any pagan rite shall be under excommunication until he pays the debt.

XXI. A Christian whom someone has left, and who summons him before a tribunal rather than to the church, so that the case may be examined there: whoever does this shall be regarded as an outsider.

[Note: [Col. 0826] Perhaps “judgment.” ID.]

XXII. If anyone gives his daughter to a man in an honorable marriage, and he loves another [person] and consents to his daughter and accepts a bride-price, both shall be excluded from the Church.

[Col. 0825D]

XXIII. If any priest builds a church, he shall not offer in it before bringing his bishop, so that he may consecrate it, for this is proper.

XXIV. If a newcomer enters a community, [Col. 0826A] he shall not baptize, offer, consecrate, or build a church until he receives permission from the bishop [Note: [Col. 0826] Read “until.” ID.]. For whoever seeks permission from pagans shall be an outsider.

XXV. Whatever has been given by religious persons, during those days on which the bishop has stayed in each individual church, as episcopal gifts to be administered according to ancient custom, shall belong to the bishop, whether for necessary use or for distribution to the needy, according as the bishop himself shall regulate it.

XXVI. But if any cleric violates this rule and is caught seizing the gifts, he shall be removed from the Church as one greedy for shameful gain.

XXVII. No new cleric of the bishop entering the community is permitted to baptize or offer, or to do anything else; and if he does not comply with this, he shall be under excommunication.

[Col. 0826B]

XXVIII. If any cleric is alone under excommunication, he shall not pray in the same house with others; nor is he permitted to offer or [Note: [Col. 0826] Is the reading *conversare*, or rather *conversari*?] associate with them until he has corrected himself. If he does not do this, he shall be punished twofold.

XXIX. If any of the brothers wishes to receive the grace of God, he shall not be baptized before he has completed a forty-day period.

XXX. Any bishop who goes from his own parish into another shall not presume to ordain unless he has received permission from the one who is in authority over that place. On Sunday he shall offer only at the reception, and shall be content with this service.

XXXI. If anyone should bring one of two clerics, who are found to be at odds through some disagreement, into discord, and bring forward an enemy against one of the two to kill him, it is fitting to call him a murderer. That cleric shall be regarded by all upright people as an outsider.

XXXII. If any cleric wishes to help a captive, let him assist him with his own price. For if he violates him by theft, many clerics are blasphemed because of one robber. Whoever does this shall be under excommunication.

XXXIII. A cleric who comes to us from the Britons without a letter, even if he lives in the community, is not permitted to minister.

XXXIV. Likewise, a deacon with us who, without consulting his own abbot, absents himself into another parish without letters [Note: [Col. 0826] Read “absents himself.” WAR.] ought not to provide food; and he shall be punished by penance by his priest, whom he has despised. A monk who wanders about without consulting his abbot likewise ought to be punished.

The regulations of the synod end here.

[Col. 0827]

OTHER CANONS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. PATRICK,

Copied from a manuscript of the Benedictine College at Cambridge. (S)

[Col. 0827A]

I. On the unity of those subject to authority.

Who, then, dares to divide the unity which no human being can dissolve or censure? “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and there was no separation among them, nor did anyone say that anything of his possessions was his own; but everything was common to them. Great grace was also upon them all, and no one among them was in need. For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them, brought the prices of what they had sold, and laid them before the feet of the apostles; and distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts IV, 32–35). Then follows: “But a certain man named Ananias,” etc., up to these words: “But when Ananias heard these words, he fell down and expired” (Acts V, 1–5).

[Col. 0827B]

II. On theft committed in a church.

Whoever steals money from the holy church where martyrs and the bodies of the saints sleep shall have his hand or foot circumcised, or shall be thrown into prison, [Col. 0828A] or expelled into exile, and shall restore double. He shall swear that he will not return until he has completed his penance.

III. On true widows.

Paul on true widows: “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband” (I Tim. V, 9). Note: If she has had several husbands, she is not to be a widow.

Two canons immediately following are then added; but whether they belong to St. Patrick or to someone else is not clear from the Benedictine manuscript. The latter of them, however, is expressly attributed to an Irish synod in the Cotton manuscript of the canons, title 66.

I. On the fact that a wife is not to be repudiated if she is barren, deformed, elderly, foul-smelling, drunk, angry, or quarrelsome; she is to be retained whether one wishes it or not. However she has been received, she must be retained.

II. Every adulterer, whether from concelebration, participation at table, conversation, or companionship, is to be excluded until he repents.

[Col. 0827]

SOME PROVERBS OF ST. PATRICK. (S)

Patrick says: It is better for us to warn the negligent beforehand, lest offenses abound, than to blame what has been done. Solomon: “It is better to rebuke than to become angry” (Ecclus. XX, 1).

Patrick says: The judges of the Church ought not to fear human beings, but to fear God, because “the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX, 10).

The judges of the Church of God ought not to possess the wisdom of this world, because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I Cor. III, 19), but they ought to possess the wisdom of God.

The judges of the Church ought not to accept gifts, because “gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the righteous” (Deut. XVI, 19).

The judges of the Church ought not to show partiality in judgment, because “there is no partiality with God” (Rom. II, 11).

The judges of the Church ought not to possess worldly cunning, but divine examples, because a servant of God ought not to be cautious or crafty.

The judges of the Church ought not to be so hasty in judgment before they know how true is what is written: “Do not be a judge too quickly” (Prov. XXV, 8).

The judges of the Church ought not to be fickle.

The judges of the Church ought not to speak a lie, because a lie is a great crime. Rather, the judges of the Church ought to judge with right judgment, because in whatever judgment they have judged, judgment will be passed upon them.

Patrick says: Seek out the examples of the ancestors, where you will find no deceit.

Patrick says: Judges who do not rightly judge the judgments of the Church are not judges but falsifiers.

[Col. 0827]

CHARTER OF ST. PATRICK. (S)

[Col. 0827D]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Patrick, humble little servant of God, in the four hundred and twenty-fifth year of his incarnation [Note: [Col. 0827] The same is found in the great tablet of the church of Glastonbury. But in John of Tinmouth and John Capgrave it reads 430. It has also been corrected in another hand in the manuscript of William of Malmesbury in the College of the Holy Trinity at Cambridge. WAR.], sent to Ireland by the most holy Pope Celestine, converted the Irish, by the grace of God, to the way of truth. And when I had established them firmly in the Catholic faith, I eventually returned to Britain and, as I believe, under the guidance of God, who is life and the way (John XIV, 6), I came upon the island of Ynswytryn. There I found a holy and ancient place, chosen and sanctified by God, in honor of the undefiled Virgin Mary, Mother of God.

[Col. 0829A]

There I found certain brothers instructed in the rudiments of the Catholic faith and devoted to a pious way of life. They had succeeded the disciples of the saints Phaganus and [Note: [Col. 0829] Usserius, *Britannicarum ecclesiarum antiquitates*, p. 456, second edition, reads “Derwiani.”] Diruvianus, whose names, because of the merits of their life, I truly believe are written in heaven (Phil. IV, 3). And because “the righteous shall be held in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. CXI, 7), when I had come to love these same brothers with steadfast affection, I wished to record their names in my writing. They are: Brumban, Hyregaan, Bremwal, Wencreth, Bantommeweng, Adelwolred, Loyor, Wellias, Breden, Swelwes, Hinloernus, and another Hyn.

Since they were born of noble parents and desired to adorn their nobility with works of faith, they chose to lead an eremitical life. And because I found them humble and peaceful, I preferred to be abject with them rather than live in royal [Col. 0829B] courts (Ps. LXXXIII, 11). But because we all had one heart and one soul (Acts IV, 32), we all chose together to live, eat, and drink together, and sleep in the same house. And so, although I was unwilling, they placed me before themselves. For I was not worthy to untie the strap of their sandals (Mark I, 7).

And while we were thus leading the monastic life according to the rule of approved Fathers, the aforesaid brothers showed me the writings of the saints Phaganus and Diruvianus. In them it was contained that the twelve disciples of the saints Philip and James had built that ancient church in honor of our aforesaid Advocate, through the instruction of the blessed archangel Gabriel. It further stated that the Lord had consecrated the same church from heaven in honor of his Mother, and that three pagan kings [Col. 0829C] had given those twelve men twelve portions of land for their support. I also found in more recent writings that the saints Phaganus and Diruvianus had obtained from Pope Eleutherius, who had sent them, thirty years of indulgence [Note: [Col. 0829] The Glastonbury tablet and the manuscript of the College of the Holy Trinity at Cambridge read “ten.” ID.]. And I, Brother Patrick, acquired twelve years in my own time from Pope Celestine of blessed memory.

After a long time, taking with me my fellow brother Wellia, we climbed with great difficulty through the dense forest to the summit of a mountain that rises above the same island. When we reached it, a single ancient and almost ruined chapel appeared, yet suitable for Christian devotion and—as it seemed to me—chosen by God. When we entered it, [Col. 0829D] we were so filled with the sweetness of a fragrance that we believed ourselves to be placed amid the delights of paradise. Going out and then reentering, and examining the place more carefully, we found one volume in which were written the Acts of the Apostles together with the acts and deeds of the saints Phaganus and Diruvianus, largely destroyed. Nevertheless, at the end of the volume we found a writing that said that the aforesaid Phaganus and Diruvianus, through a revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, had built that same chapel [Note: [Col. 0829] The Glastonbury tablet reads “had built.” ID.] in honor of the holy archangel Michael, so that he might there receive honor from human beings, whom, by God’s command, he is to lead into everlasting honors.

When that writing delighted us, we tried to read it to the end. For the same writing said that the venerable Phaganus and Diruvianus had remained there for nine years, [Col. 0830B] and that they too had obtained an indulgence of thirty years for all Christians who, with pious intention, visited that place in honor of blessed Michael. Having therefore found [Note: [Col. 0830] The Glastonbury tablet reads “then.” ID.] so great a treasure of divine goodness, Brother Wellias and I fasted for three months, devoting ourselves to prayers and vigils and commanding the demons and beasts that appeared in many forms.

One night, when I had given myself over to sleep, the Lord Jesus appeared to me in a vision and said: “Patrick, my servant, know that I have chosen this place in honor of my name, so that the aid of my archangel Michael may be honorably invoked here. And this shall be a sign for you and your brothers, so that they too may believe: your left arm shall wither until you have announced what you have seen to the brothers who are in the lower cell and have returned here again.” [Col. 0830C] And so it happened.

From that day we appointed two brothers to remain there permanently, unless future pastors should decide otherwise for a just reason. To the Irish brothers Arnulph and Ogmar, who had come with me from Ireland and, at my exhortation, had humbly begun to remain at the aforesaid chapel, I entrusted this present document, retaining another like it in the chest of Saint Mary as a memorial for posterity.

And I, [Note: [Col. 0830] This word is absent from the Glastonbury tablet and the manuscript of St. Trinity, Cambridge. ID.] Brother Patrick, by the counsel of my brothers, grant one hundred days of pardon to all who, with pious intention, cut down with axe and hatchet the forest on every side of the aforesaid mountain (Ps. LXXIII, 6), so that easier access may be prepared for Christians visiting the church of the blessed perpetual Virgin and the aforesaid chapel [Note: [Col. 0830] The Glastonbury tablet and the Trinity manuscript read “who will visit, and the aforesaid chapel.” ID.].

[Col. 0831]

BOOK OF ST. PATRICK, BISHOP, ON THE THREE DWELLINGS [Note: [Col. 0831] From the appendix to volume VI of the works of St. Augustine, p. 159, Benedictine edition.]. (C, S)

[Col. 0831A]

CHAPTER ONE. On the three dwellings—the kingdom of God, the world, and hell. The goods of the kingdom of God and the evils of hell.

There are three dwellings under the hand of almighty God: the first, the lowest, and the middle. The highest is called the kingdom of God, or the kingdom of heaven; the lowest is called hell; the middle is called the present world, or the earth. The outermost of these are entirely opposed to one another and joined by no fellowship. For what fellowship can there be between light and darkness, or between Christ and Belial (II Cor. VI, 14–15)? The middle dwelling, however, bears some likeness to the outermost ones. Hence it contains light and darkness, cold and heat, pain and health, joy and sorrow, hatred and love, the good and the wicked, the just and the unjust, masters and servants, [Col. 0831B] kingship and subjection, hunger and fullness, death and life, and countless things of this kind.

Of all these, one part bears the image of the kingdom of God, and the other of hell. For in this world evil and good are mixed together; but in the kingdom of God there are no evil people, only good, while in hell there are no good people, only evil. Each place is filled from the middle. For among the people of this world, some are raised to heaven and others dragged down to hell. Like are joined to like: the good to the good, and the wicked to the wicked; just people to just angels, and transgressing people to transgressing angels; servants of God to God, and servants of the devil to the devil. “The blessed are called to the kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world, while the accursed are driven into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 34, 41).

[Col. 0831C]

[Note: [Col. 0831] The same material occurs in *On Loving God*, chapter 18, whence it was taken.]

No one clothed in flesh can speak of, think of, or understand the goods of the heavenly kingdom as they truly are; for they are far greater and better than they are thought or understood. Hence it is written: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9). The kingdom of God is greater than every fame, better than every praise, more beyond number than every knowledge, and more excellent than all the glory that is imagined.

No one can speak of or think of the evils of hell as they truly are; for they are far worse than they are thought to be. The kingdom of God, therefore, is full of light, peace, charity, wisdom, glory, honor, sweetness, love, melody, joy, everlasting blessedness, and every ineffable good that cannot be spoken or imagined. [Col. 0831D] But the place of hell is full of darkness, discord, hatred, folly, misery, disgrace, bitterness, offense, pain, [Note: [Col. 0832] The Victor manuscript reads “stench, thirst.”] burning, thirst, hunger, unquenchable fire, sadness, and everlasting vengeance, and every ineffable evil [Col. 0832A] that cannot be spoken or imagined.

The citizens of heaven are just people and angels, whose king is almighty God. By contrast, the citizens of hell are ungodly people and demons, whose prince is the devil. The vision of holy people and angels, and above all of God himself, satisfies the just. The vision of condemned people and demons, and above all of the devil himself, torments the wicked and sinners.

In the kingdom of God nothing is desired that is not found; in hell nothing is found that is desired. In the kingdom of God nothing is found except what pleases, delights, and satisfies. By contrast, in the lake of everlasting misery nothing is seen or felt except what displeases, offends, and torments. [Note: [Col. 0832] These words are absent from the manuscripts. They occur in Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 23.] In the eternal kingdom there will be life without death, truth without error, and happiness without disturbance.

[Col. 0832B]

Every good abounds in the kingdom of God, and no evil; every evil abounds in the prison of the devil, and no good. No unworthy person is received into the kingdom of God; and no worthy or just person is dragged into hell.

CHAPTER II. On the punishments of hell.

There are two principal torments in hell: intolerable cold and the heat of unquenchable fire. Hence it is read in the Gospel: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII, 51; XXII, 13; and XXV, 30). Weeping and the melting of the eyes arise from heat; but the gnashing of teeth arises from cold. Hence blessed Job also says: “From the waters of the snows they pass to excessive heat” (Job XXIV, 19).

From these two arise countless kinds of punishments: intolerable thirst, the punishment of hunger, the punishment of stench, the punishment of terror, the punishment of fear, the punishment of distress, the punishment of darkness, the severity of torturers, the presence of demons, the ferocity of beasts, the cruelty of those administering punishment, the tearing apart by immortal worms, the worm of conscience, fiery tears, sighs, miseries, pain without remedy, bonds without release, eternal death, punishment without end, and the absence of Christ after his vision [Note: [Col. 0832] Thus the manuscripts. The printed edition has “with respect to the vision.”], which alone surpasses all the things mentioned above and is more intolerable than every punishment.

CHAPTER III. On those whom the eternity of punishment does not deter from the pleasures of the world. The twofold punishment of hell. One hundred years are no portion of eternity.

Woe, therefore, to those forever who, for the pleasurable dream of a single hour, deserve to undergo all these evils even without end; for such and so great is all the glory of this world [Col. 0832D] when compared with eternal glory. It would have been better for them, as was said of the unhappy Judas (Matt. XXVI, 24), not to have been born than to endure the punishments of hell for their evil merits.

What is more foolish, what is more insane, than to be deceived and overcome, like children, by the shadow, image, and likeness of true glory, true pleasure, true beauty, true splendor, and true honor, and not to seek or desire the true glory itself? Who would choose the image of gold in water while neglecting gold itself, and not immediately be regarded by everyone as foolish and insane? Who would love the disk of the sun reflected in a mirror, or formed in any material, more than the sun itself, and not be mocked by everyone?

Thus, indeed, anyone who loves, seeks, and strives after the fleeting fragility of this world and the useless pleasure of the flesh, while despising eternal glory and neglecting the ineffable joys of the heavenly kingdom, deserves to be mocked—or rather pitied. This is truly the bargain of fools, of wretched people who do not possess a sound heart, even if the punishments of hell did not follow, punishments that can neither be spoken nor imagined.

There is, however, a twofold punishment: to be absent from the kingdom of God and always to be in hell—that is, to be condemned with the devil; to lose the presence of the angels and always suffer the terrifying presence of demons. How greatly this must be avoided, escaped, and feared cannot be expressed.

Who, in his right mind, would choose a punishment of one hundred years for the pleasures of a single day? Yet wretched people, without any wisdom, following the pleasure of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0833] Two manuscripts read *voluntatem* (“will”) instead.], do not avoid or escape intolerable punishments—not punishments of one hundred years, nor of a thousand times a thousand years, but of all the ages without end—in exchange for the pleasures of forty or sixty years, or for any corruptible delight.

But just as great as the difference is between one day and one hundred years, so much—and indeed more—is the difference between forty, sixty, or one hundred years and eternity, whether eternity is to be good or evil. For one day is some portion of a span of one hundred years, although a very small one; but a span of one hundred years is no portion at all of that eternity. For if, for example, a hundredth or thousandth part were eternity, that period would cease to be eternity after its hundredfold or thousandfold duration. Reason does not permit this of eternity; for if it could end in any way or at any time, it would not be eternity at all.

CHAPTER IV. Moving from the broad way to the narrow. The happiness, knowledge, and love of their lot possessed by the blessed. On the ineffable sweetness of the vision of God.

The pleasure of the flesh must therefore be resisted with strength; the deceptive allurements of this world must be fought with strength; and one must keep watch against Satan’s manifold suggestions. The broad way of the age, which leads to death (Matt. VII, 13), must be avoided with every effort. But the narrow way that leads to life must be approached and desired with every longing of the heart.

This narrow way is the way of abstinence, chastity, humility, and every form of religious devotion. Christ wore down this way before us, and by this way he passed into his kingdom. Let us also follow his footsteps until, after him, we arrive at the royal city [Col. 0834A] in which he himself reigns.

Whatever a human being might say about that city is like a drop from the sea or a spark from a fire. There the just will shine like the sun, as the Lord says (Matt. XIII, 43). There will be supreme peace, supreme rest, no labor, no pain, no poverty, no old age, no death, no night, no desire for food, and no burning thirst. Rather, the food and drink of all will be the vision of Christ and of the holy Trinity; the contemplation, with the pure eye of the heart, of the Divinity itself; and the continual reading, so to speak, of the book of life—that is, of eternal truth, supreme wisdom, and the Word of God, which is the vision of Jesus Christ.

There everything that is now hidden from us will be clearer. There it will be evident why this person was chosen and that one rejected; why this one was taken into the kingdom and that one reduced to servitude; why one person dies in the womb, another in infancy, another in youth, and another in old age; why one is poor and another rich; why the son of an adulteress is baptized, while at times the son of a lawful wife dies before baptism; why one who begins to live well sometimes ends badly, while one who begins badly often ends well. All these things and many others of this kind will be plain and open in the book of life.

In that same city each person’s reward will belong to all, and the reward of all will belong to each through charity. There [Note: [Col. 0833] One manuscript has “the abundance of all good things.” The printed edition has “every good.”] the good of all will be evident to everyone. There all will know one another’s thoughts. There no superior will be proud, and no inferior envious. For how could one who loves everyone as himself envy anyone, when no one envies himself?

There no one will desire to be better or higher than he will be, because it would not be fitting to be other than what he has deserved. Nor will anyone desire to be other than what he will be, because to be as he will be will be beautiful not only for himself but also for the whole body of the heavenly Church. For just as any limb of the body, if placed higher or lower than nature has established, makes the body monstrous and ugly, so surely if someone were placed higher in the kingdom of God than the skill and will of the almighty Craftsman requires, he would create ugliness, not only for himself but for the entire assembly.

In that assembly, the one who is least will undoubtedly have greater glory than one possessing the whole kingdom of the world, even if that kingdom were eternal. For it is exceedingly worthless to enjoy the elements when compared with enjoying and rejoicing in God himself, and to delight in visible and bodily things.

[Col. 0834D]

[Note: [Col. 0834] The words of Augustine, *On Free Choice of the Will*, book III, no. 77. They are absent from the manuscripts.]

For so great is the beauty of justice, so great the delight of eternal light—that is, of unchangeable truth and wisdom—that even if it were not permitted to remain in it longer than for the duration of a single day, for this reason alone innumerable years of this life, filled with pleasures amid an abundance of bodily goods, would rightly and deservedly be despised. For it was not said falsely or with slight affection: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. LXXXIII, 11).

Nothing is comparable to the delight and joy that arise from invisible and incorporeal things, from the fellowship of all the angels and the just, from certain knowledge and understanding of the divine nature itself, and from seeing God himself face to face. The angels marvel at his beauty; the dead are raised at his command; his wisdom is without number (Ps. CXLVI, 5); his kingdom knows no end; his glory cannot be told.

His light so eclipses the sun that, by comparison with it, the sun has no light. His sweetness surpasses honey so greatly that, compared with it, honey is like the bitterest wormwood. If all those confined in the prison of hell were to see his face, they would feel no punishment, no pain, and no sadness. If his presence appeared in hell together with its holy inhabitants [Note: [Col. 0835] One manuscript has “with its inhabitants.”], hell would immediately be transformed into a delightful paradise.

Without his nod, not even a leaf falls from a tree. His fire-spewing eyes penetrate the depth of hell. His ear hears the silent voice of the heart—that is, thought. His eye hears no less than it sees, and his ear sees no less than it hears, because these are not bodily organs but supreme wisdom and certain knowledge.

His delights satisfy without weariness. When the blessed find them, they nevertheless always desire them; they produce hunger and thirst without punishment and delight through ever-burning desire. His marvelous secrets are always new and wondrous to those who see them. They do not produce less astonishment in those who behold them after a thousand years or a thousand times a thousand years than when they first begin to be seen.

Although the angels have been accustomed to see these things from the beginning of the world, they marvel at them no less today than on the first day. Otherwise, after long and continual use of seeing them, they would have become cheap in the sight of the angels. The past and the future of his knowledge [Note: [Col. 0835] The manuscripts omit “not past and future but.”] are not past and future, but present.

CHAPTER V. All things are present to God, without prejudice to human freedom. God’s speech and praise. Existence before time. True evil worse than false evil. What the vision of God confers upon the blessed. God’s eternity; God’s knowledge.

Therefore he will not see the day of judgment, nor did he see the first day of the age; but he sees both. His foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin, as many who are in error say. For, they argue, if God foreknew that Adam would sin, he could not have refrained from sinning. From this error arises the claim that God is the cause of sin, which it is impious to say. Yet they too are bound by their own words. [Col. 0835D] For if what God’s foreknowledge contains must necessarily come to pass, then man sinned by his own will and not under any necessity, because God’s foreknowledge included that he would sin by his will and free choice, not under compulsion. If, therefore, God’s foreknowledge cannot be avoided, man could not have sinned otherwise than willingly, with no other force compelling him, because God thus foreknew that he would sin. If, then, he acted willingly, he was not coerced. For if he was not coerced into sinning, he could certainly have refrained from sinning if he had wished; and therefore he deserved punishment, because he did not sin unwillingly. Otherwise he would not have received from God the punishment of death.

His speech is a hidden inspiration, [Col. 0836A] by which he invisibly reveals his will and his love to minds; and, seeing this, the angels obey God in everything. His praise is that by which he will praise the elect, the manifestation by which he will display the good deeds of his chosen to all; while the continual praise with which the elect will praise him is their perpetual wonder at him.

In a wondrous manner he did not precede the world and time temporally—for he existed before the world by no interval of an hour—and yet he always existed without beginning. There was no time before time; rather, time was created together with the world. If, therefore, time began to run from the beginning of the world, it did not exist before the world was made. Thus God did not precede time and the world, which was coeval with it—or rather, slightly prior to them—in any temporal interval, as we have said; for time began to run through the world’s motion. [Col. 0836B] Whatever is moved precedes its own motion. God therefore preceded the world by ineffable eternity, not by time. Time did not exist before the world.

His light drives away the darkness of ignorance; and by some portion of that light we recognize that all the things we have mentioned are true and certain. By the same light we see that what is true is better than what is false; yet we also see that true evil, or true sin, is worse than false evil, or false sin—not because it is true, but because it is evil or sin. [Note: The manuscripts do not contain these words.] Rather, it is evil or sin because it is true evil or sin. Otherwise it could not be evil or sin unless it were truly evil or sin; for false evil is not evil, just as false silver is not silver.

Someone may say that evil or sin arose or was made from truth, and that, in a certain sense, evil is the work of truth; but this is wholly false. Everything true is from truth, and everything true, insofar as it is true, is good. It is therefore from truth that it is true for something to be evil or sin—not that evil or sin itself is from truth; for one thing is evil itself, and another thing is its being true that it is evil. Although evil itself is not good, it is nevertheless good that it truly exists as that evil. For unless it were good for evil to exist, God would in no way allow it to come about. Indeed, the Almighty brings many good things out of evils, as from the adultery of human beings he forms and makes good human beings.

If, then, by some portion of that light—as though poured through narrow cracks—we recognize that these and all the other things we know are true, with what kind and what abundance of the light of knowledge and wisdom shall we be illumined there, where we shall see the very sun of truth face to face—that is, where we shall know with certain and true wisdom? His presence makes those who are present like him. Whoever clings to true wisdom, true beauty, and true eternity will necessarily be wise, beautiful, and eternal. For his absence likewise makes them unlike him in every way.

His eternity is without beginning and without end—for if there were a time when he did not exist, who would have made him?—because he alone is God, and before him there was no other God, nor is there, nor shall there be. It is not possible that he created himself, since nothing creates itself: by what power could one who entirely did not exist make himself? It follows, therefore, that [Col. 0837A] God was not made at all. Since God was made in no way, he existed without beginning before all things. Whatever has been made has a beginning; and whatever has a beginning was certainly made—not by another than God, who was not made but makes all things.

His knowledge, without any variation [Note: The word “knowledge” is absent from the manuscript of Victor.] or any wandering to and fro, comprehends and understands simultaneously and all at once the immeasurable truth of all creatures: of angels, human beings, stars, grains of sand, hairs, words, thoughts, and every moment. God, then, is the source and origin of all knowledge: the more anyone drinks from him, the more he thirsts.

## CHAPTER VI. The knowledge of the blessed. Concerning the threefold vision: bodily, spiritual, and intellectual.

[Col. 0837B]

Incomparably, therefore, as we said above, the kingdom of the whole world—even if it were eternal—falls short of the company of the angels and saints and of being present at the vision of God himself. In this vision a threefold knowledge arises: namely, the human being who sees, God who is seen, and all the others who will see and understand everything.

For just as through a glass mirror a threefold vision is afforded us, since we see ourselves, the mirror itself, and whatever is present before it, so through the mirror of divine brightness we shall see God himself as he is, insofar as this is possible for a creature; and we shall know ourselves and the others by true and certain knowledge. Then, by seeing God, we shall see the hidden things of creatures and of hell itself. Then it will be manifest to the righteous how God is invisible, incomparable, without beginning and without end, before all things and [Col. 0837C] after all things; what difference there is between being born, which pertains to the Son, and proceeding, which pertains to the Holy Spirit—except that one was born from one, while the other proceeded from two; and how the Father did not precede the Son in time but in origin, nor did he precede the Holy Spirit.

They will also see how all the things of God are one in God, except insofar as relation is concerned. For God’s wisdom, truth, [Col. 0838A] and eternity are not different from one another but are one, as are all the other things of God. God’s wisdom is no more wisdom than it is truth, and it is no more truth than it is wisdom, eternity, or any of the other things of God; for they are one in God. Nor are these things merely identical with one another in God: they are nothing other than God himself.

They will see how the world was in God before it existed in itself—not as world, but as God; how he is wholly everywhere without being in a place, great without quantity, good without quality; and how he penetrates clean and unclean things without being polluted by them. For if this visible light illumines every place and penetrates even dungheaps without stench or self-pollution, how much more does God, who is invisible and unchangeable light, penetrate, govern, sustain, surround, and illumine all things [Col. 0838B] without any change or pollution—not only heavenly and earthly things, but also those of hell?

Then the elect of God will have a threefold vision: bodily, by which bodies will be seen—some shining like the sun, some like the moon, and others like the stars; spiritual, by which they will contemplate bodily likenesses in the spirit and not in deceptive imagination. The spirits of the righteous enjoy this vision even today, after the confinement of their bodies; and intellectual, by which, with the pure eye of the mind, they will see God in the spirit, as well as their own souls, their innermost virtues, and the angelic spirits.

Then they will give thanks to God in two ways: for their deliverance from everlasting damnation and for the ineffable recompense of good things. Then the devil, the common accused enemy of all, will be condemned in the sight of God’s elect; and his condemnation [Col. 0838C] and unbearable punishment will provide the elect with a pleasurable spectacle. Then they will love their liberator and the giver of every good thing with the most ardent love, and without end or weariness they will praise almighty, kind, and merciful God with the cry of the heart: to him be honor and glory, now and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0837]

# SAINT PATRICK’S BOOK ON THE TWELVE ABUSES OF THE AGE. (C)

(See volume IV of our *Patrology*, col. 869 ff.)

[Col. 0837]

# THE ALPHABETICAL HYMN IN PRAISE OF SAINT PATRICK, WRITTEN BY SECUNDINUS, BISHOP, WHILE PATRICK WAS STILL LIVING

(S)

[Note: This hymn also exists in the Antiphonary of the monastery of Bangor, edited by the distinguished Muratori in *Anecdota Latina*, vol. IV, pp. 136 ff.; we collated it with Waraeus’s edition.]

[Note: Saint Patrick’s nephew through his sister Darerca. Editor.]

[Col. 0837D]

Hear, all you who love God, the holy merits  
of the man blessed in Christ, Patrick the bishop:  
how, because of his good conduct, he resembles the angels,  
and because of his perfect life is made equal to the apostles.

He keeps Christ’s blessed commandments in everything;  
his works shine brightly among human beings,  
and they follow his holy and wondrous example;  
therefore in heaven they magnify the Father, the Lord.

Steadfast in the fear of God and immovable in faith,  
upon whom the Church is built, as upon Peter,  
and whose apostleship he received from God;  
against whose gate the gates of hell do not prevail.

[Note: Muratori has “upon which”; Waraeus’s reading is better in context.]

[Note: Muratori: “against whose gate.” Waraeus reports that another manuscript has: “And the gates of hell shall not prevail against him.”]

The Lord chose him to teach barbarous nations,  
to fish with the nets of instruction,  
to draw believers from the world to grace,  
so that they might follow the Lord to his heavenly seat.

He sells Christ’s chosen evangelical talents,  
and among the Irish peoples collects them with interest,  
the reward of this labor of navigation and toil,  
and will rejoice in possessing the joy of the heavenly kingdom with Christ.

The faithful minister of God and distinguished messenger  
offers the apostles’ example and pattern to the good.  
By words as well as deeds he preaches the Lord to the people, [Col. 0839B]  
so that whoever is not converted by his words may be moved by his good conduct.

He has glory with Christ and honor in the world.  
He is revered by all as an angel of God,  
whom God sent, like Paul, as an apostle to the nations,  
to provide human beings with guidance toward the kingdom of God.

Humble in spirit and body because of fear of God,  
upon whom, because of his good conduct, the Lord rests;  
he bears Christ’s marks upon his own flesh,  
and, sustained by whose cross alone, he glories in it.

[Note: The Apostle says, Galatians 6:17: “I bear the marks of Jesus in my body.” Muratori has “his own in the flesh.”]

[Note: Muratori has “and whose support he glories in”; Waraeus conjectures that the reading should be “sustained, he glories in the cross.”]

Industrious, he feeds believers with heavenly provisions,  
so that those who are laughed at may not fail on the road with Christ.  
To them he distributes, as bread, evangelical words,  
which are multiplied in his hands like manna.

He guards a chaste body for the love of the Lord,  
the body which he prepared as a temple for the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0839C]  
by whom it is steadfastly possessed through pure deeds;  
he offers it to the Lord as a pleasing and living sacrifice.

And the great evangelical light of the world, once kindled,  
raised upon a lampstand, shines upon the whole age;  
a fortified city of the king, set upon a mountain,  
in which there is abundant wealth belonging to God.

For he will be called greatest in the kingdom of heaven  
who fulfills in good works what he teaches in sacred words,  
goes before the faithful by his good example,  
and in a pure heart has confidence in God.

He boldly announces the name of the Lord to the nations,  
to whom he gives the eternal grace of the laver of salvation; [Col. 0840A]  
for their offenses he prays to God every day,  
and for them he offers sacrifices worthy of God.

For the divine law he scorns all the world’s glory,  
and regards everything as refuse at God’s table.  
He is not moved by the threatening flood of this world, [Note: Waraeus says that another manuscript reads “lightning.” Muratori likewise has that reading, and shortly before has “at whose table.”]  
but rejoices in adversity when he suffers for Christ.

The good and faithful shepherd of the evangelical flock,  
whom the God of God chose to guard his people  
and to feed his own people with divine teachings,  
for whom, following Christ’s example, he gave his life.

For his merits the Savior raised him to be a bishop,  
so that he might admonish the clergy concerning heavenly warfare,  
for whom he distributes heavenly food together with garments,  
which is fulfilled in divine rites and sacred utterances.

[Note: Muratori has “which he fulfills in divine rites.”]

The king’s messenger, inviting believers to the wedding, [Col. 0840B]  
he is adorned, clothed in a wedding garment;  
he draws heavenly wine from heavenly vessels,  
and offers the people of God a spiritual cup.

He finds a sacred treasure in a sacred volume,  
and foresees the divinity of the Savior in the flesh;  
he purchases this treasure through holy and perfect merits,  
and is called Israel because his soul sees God.

[Note: Muratori has “sees clearly”; perhaps that is the better reading.]

The faithful witness of the Lord in the catholic law,  
whose words are stored in divine oracles,  
so that human flesh and food may not rot from worms,  
but may be seasoned with heavenly flavor for sacrifice.

[Note: Muratori’s reading “white” does not seem acceptable; shortly afterward he has “the flesh and food may rot.”]

[Note: Muratori has “may be nourished”; another manuscript cited by Waraeus has “are satisfied.”]

The true and distinguished cultivator of the evangelical field,  
whose seeds are seen to be Christ’s Gospels,  
which he sows with his divine mouth into the ears of the wise,  
and whose hearts and minds he plows with the holy Spirit.

[Note: Muratori reads “whose”; Waraeus’s reading is given above.]

[Col. 0840C]

Christ chose him as his vicar on earth,  
who frees captives from a twofold servitude.  
Many whom he redeemed from the servitude of human beings,  
he released from the dominion of the stable.

[Note: Another manuscript cited by Waraeus has “of the devil.” Muratori has the same.]

He sings hymns with the Apocalypse and God’s psalms,  
and expounds them for the building up of God’s people.  
He believes the law in the Trinity of the sacred name,  
and teaches one substance in three persons.

Girded with the Lord’s belt, day and night,  
without interruption he prays to God the Lord.  
He will receive the reward of his immense labor  
and will reign with the holy apostles over Israel.

[Note: After these words Muratori adds the following quatrain:

“Bishop Patrick, pray for us all,  
that the sins we have committed may immediately be blotted out.  
Let us always sing Patrick’s praises,  
that we may always live with him.”]

## Back Matter of the Volume

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME LIII, FROM THE YEAR 426 TO THE YEAR 460, CONTAINING SEVERAL LESSER AUTHORS

## A.D. 426–432. CAPREOLUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

(From Galland.)

[Col. 0841]

## INTRODUCTION

[Col. 0841A]

I. Capreolus, the glorious pontiff and memorable teacher of the Church of Carthage, as Ferrandus, a deacon of that same Church, calls him, [Note: Ferrandus, letter to Pelagius and Anatolius, § 6, *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyon, vol. IX, p. 516 d–e.] succeeded blessed Aurelius in that see. Aurelius is known to have departed to God either in the year 429 or, most probably, 430, as we learn from Norisius, [Note: Norisius, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 8, works, vol. I, p. 355 c–d.] followed by Pagius [Note: Pagius, under the year 430, § 26.] and Tillemont. [Note: Tillemont, vol. XVI, p. 495.]

Three letters are reported by the ancients to have been written by Capreolus, and the following is said to have been the occasion for writing the first. Theodosius the Younger had sent a sacred letter to Cyril of Alexandria and to the metropolitan bishops of the provinces for the celebration of the Council of Ephesus. This letter of Theodosius is said to have been dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Theodosius for the thirteenth time and Valentinian for the third time—that is, in the year of Christ 430. At the same time, says Liberatus, the emperor wrote a sacred letter [Note: Liberatus, *Breviary*, chapter 5, p. 17, ed. Garner.] to blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius, through the *magisterianus* Ebagnius, asking him to lend his presence to the council.

When Ebagnius came to great Carthage, he heard from Capreolus, the bishop of that city, that blessed Augustine had departed from this world to the Lord. Having received from him a letter to the emperor concerning blessed Augustine’s death, he returned to Constantinople, from which he had come. Thus far Liberatus.

But Ebagnius, leaving the imperial city at the end of 430, reached Carthage in the following year, 431, during the days of Easter, as Capreolus himself testifies in his letter to the Council of Ephesus, [Note: Capreolus, letter to the Council of Ephesus, below, p. 490, col. 845b.] approximately eight months after Saint Augustine had died.

No letter survives in which Capreolus replied to the imperial sacred letter of Theodosius, except for one fragment which it will be worthwhile to quote here from Ferrandus. It is as follows [Note: Ferrandus, cited passage, p. 516d.]:

“Nothing in divine or human actions, nothing in sacred or public affairs, can possess any firmness if those matters which have been closed by the proper conclusion of a judicial sentence are presumed to be corrected, after the passage of years and whatever succession of ages, by posterity, as though it were more learned in correcting the Fathers.”

Capreolus speaks in the same vein in another letter, which must now be discussed.

II. Moved, therefore, by the emperor’s letters, although they had been directed chiefly to Augustine, [Note: Capreolus, letter to the Council of Ephesus, cited passage.] our Carthaginian bishop, unable to assemble a universal council because of the attacks of the Vandals besieging the African regions, sent his deacon Bessula to Ephesus as his legate to the council. These are the words of Liberatus. [Note: Liberatus, cited passage, p. 18.]

Capreolus himself mentions this embassy to the Council of Ephesus in his letter addressed to Vitalis and Constantius—or rather Tonantius, [Note: Capreolus, letter to Vitalis and Constantius, § 1.] about which we shall soon speak. The letter that he entrusted to his deacon to carry to that council on behalf of the African delegation survives in the acts of Ephesus, from which we have taken it. [Note: Council of Ephesus, act 1, p. 1073, cited vol. III.] In it he describes, in a lamentable narrative, the most miserable condition of the African Church because of the Vandal invasion.

From the letters that Capreolus sent to Ephesus, Ferrandus quotes an excerpt, though with some changes in wording. The passage is given below in the notes. [Note: Below, p. 491, col. 845, final line.]

Nor should we pass over here what Vincent of Lérins observes about the same letters in these words [Note: Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*, 2.31, p. 367, 3rd ed., Baluze, Paris, 1684.]:

“When the letter of Saint Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, had been read”—he says—“who intended and pleaded for nothing other than that, once novelty had been defeated, antiquity should be defended, Bishop Cyril thus addressed the assembly and issued his decision.” This too seems worth inserting here. For at the end of the proceedings he says:

“‘And this letter,’ he said, ‘which has been read, the letter of the venerable and most religious bishop Capreolus of Carthage, shall be inserted in the acts of the proceedings, [Note: Read: ‘let it be inserted’; Greek: ἐμφερέσθω. From vol. III of the Councils, p. 1957; below, p. 491, col. 848b.] for its meaning is clear. He wishes the doctrines of the ancient faith to be confirmed, but those that are novel, needlessly invented, and impiously promulgated to be rejected and condemned.’

“All the bishops acclaimed: ‘These are the voices of all; this is what we all say; this is the desire of all.’”

Thus far Vincent.

We have appended these words from the acts of Ephesus to Capreolus’s letter. Since the letter itself was written in Latin and later rendered into Greek, and since both languages were read at the same council, as its acts testify, [Note: Council of Ephesus, cited passage, p. 1073c.] we have consequently presented both texts.

III. Scarcely had the Council of Ephesus been celebrated, it seems, when Vitalis and Constantius—or rather Tonantius—Spanishmen, sent a letter through Numinianus to Capreolus concerning the one person of Christ, God and man, against Nestorius. They earnestly asked him to instruct them in what the catholic faith rightly held on this matter. [Note: Below, p. 492, col. 849c.]

The Carthaginian bishop immediately granted their request and sent them a lengthy and most learned reply, in which he showed himself truly a sublime theologian, [Col. 0843C] as the great father of ecclesiastical annals calls him. [Note: Baronius, under the year 431, § 27.]

His reputation for wisdom had spread so far and wide that the men just mentioned wrote to him from the furthest reaches of Spain in these words [Note: Below, p. 492, col. 847d.]:

“We greatly desired to write to your holy and honorable dignity through our most beloved brother Numinianus. For our smallness has discovered the outstanding fame and teaching of your holiness . . . . . . Command, therefore, that we may be watered from the good treasure of your heart with what the right catholic faith holds.”

Baronius published Capreolus’s reply in mutilated form from the papers of Pithoeus, [Note: Baronius, under the year 431, §§ 28–35.] but Sirmondus published it complete from the Herivall manuscript together with the letter of the Spaniards, on the occasion of which it had been written, among the dogmatic treatises that he brought to light at Paris in 1630.

That Capreolus wrote this letter not long after Nestorius had been condemned at the Council of Ephesus, as we have just indicated, is clear from his own words [Note: Capreolus, letter to Vitalis and Constantius, § 1.]:

“For already”—he says—“as I do not doubt has also reached your knowledge, in the regions of the East, where this pest first arose, a glorious synod of priests was assembled. Our delegation was not absent from it, and there, at the threshold, this pest, together with its author and defender, was crushed and extinguished by the ray of apostolic light.”

It is not entirely clear when our Carthaginian pontiff died. Perhaps it was shortly before the year 439, when the Vandals occupied Carthage. He was succeeded in the episcopate by Quodvultdeus, not by Deogratias, as Pagius wrote while discussing another matter. [Note: Pagius, under the year 431, § 13.] That Quodvultdeus held the see of Carthage before Deogratias is established both by Victor of Tunnuna [Note: Victor of Tunnuna, *Chronicle*, p. 2, in Scaliger, *Thesaurus Temporum*, Amsterdam edition, 1658.] and especially by Victor of Vita. [Note: Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, book I, chapters 5 and 8, and book II, chapter 3.]

As for the passage of Victor of Tunnuna, however, consult Ruinart. [Note: Ruinart, commentary on Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part 2, chapter 8, p. 495, Paris edition, 1694.]

The name of Capreolus, with the title of saint, is commemorated on the day before the Kalends of August in an old calendar of the Church of Carthage, [Note: Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 164, note d, Paris edition, 1723.] a fact which the aforementioned Ruinart says should be noted, [Note: Ruinart, cited work, chapter 3, p. 429.] since not all the other Carthaginian bishops designated in that calendar are honored with this mark of sanctity.

[Col. 0843]

# LETTERS OF CAPREOLUS OF CARTHAGE

(C, S)

[Note: It appears in the acts of the Council of Ephesus, act 1, p. 1073, Venice edition of Labbé.]

## FIRST LETTER. TO THE COUNCIL OF EPHESUS

Concerning the one person of Christ, God and man, against Nestorius.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0843D]

I. [Note: Ferrandus quotes a fragment from this letter in his letter to Pelagius and Anatolius, deacons of the Holy Roman Church, § 6, but in different Latin.] Most devout brothers, I wished that your venerable synod had been assembled in such circumstances that we too might have been able to send you a properly prepared delegation, having selected by common agreement some of our brothers and fellow bishops, rather than an apology worthy of lamentation—unless various circumstances had prevented this desire of our heart.

First, the letters of our most religious lord and son, the emperor Theodosius, reached our hands. They were of such a kind that they specifically demanded the presence of our brother and fellow bishop of blessed memory, Augustine. [Note: See Liberatus, chapter 5.] But when those letters discovered that he had already departed from this life, I received that imperial summons, although it seemed to have been directed chiefly to the aforesaid Augustine. I then sent suitable letters and customary messages to all the provinces of Africa, wishing to convene an appropriate synod, so that some might be chosen from among our brothers and bishops and sent to the venerable synod of your blessedness.

But at this time every route and avenue of travel has been closed. For the outpouring multitude of enemies and the enormous devastation everywhere throughout the provinces, which—some inhabitants having been killed and others driven into flight—presents to the eyes, far and wide in every direction, a wretched appearance of desolation, [Note: The Old Vulgate has “a pitiable appearance of destruction.”] restricts the ready possibility of coming.

Prevented by these obstacles, the bishops who had intended this could not assemble from the various parts of Africa. To these difficulties was added the fact that the emperor’s letters reached us during the days of Easter, when scarcely two months remained before the universal and venerable synod. That interval of time, even if no difficulty from the enemy had arisen in the meantime, would scarcely have been sufficient to convene an African synod.

For this reason, although we were entirely unwilling to send any formal delegation, nevertheless, out of the reverence and observance owed to ecclesiastical discipline, we have sent my son Bessula the deacon to you, venerable brothers, together with these letters of apology.

II. Therefore I wish your holiness to be entreated again and again—even though I am firmly confident that, through the help of our God, the catholic faith will remain stable and secure in every respect through so great an assembly of venerable priests—that, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, whom I do not doubt will be present with your hearts in everything you are to undertake, you may, equipped with the strength of ancient authority, drive out from your midst new doctrines previously unknown to ecclesiastical ears, and thus resist every kind of new error.

Let not the voice long ago silenced seem, under the pretext of a second disputation, to revive those errors which the Church formerly opposed and which, when they sprang up again in these times, the authority of the apostolic see and the united judgment of the priests together crushed. [Note: Ferrandus, cited passage.]

For if some new controversy should arise, it ought to be submitted to examination, so that what has been rightly said may be approved, or what deserves condemnation may be rejected. But if anyone allows matters that were judged long ago to be called back into discussion, he will plainly be considered to be doing nothing other than doubting himself about the faith that has prevailed until now.

Furthermore, for the example of posterity, so that what is now defined for the catholic faith may be able to possess perpetual firmness, everything that was established in earlier times by the holy Fathers must be preserved unshaken and immovable. For whoever wishes to retain the perpetual stability established concerning the catholic faith must strengthen his judgment not by his own authority but by the judgment of the ancient Fathers. In this way, by confirming his position partly through the decrees and judgments of the ancients and partly through those of more recent times, he must show that he asserts, teaches, and holds the one truth of the Church, which from the beginning until the present has continued in simple purity, unconquered constancy, and authority.

These things I wished to submit to your venerable ears on behalf of the present African delegation, which the necessity mentioned above prevented from being sent. [Note: Capreolus himself mentions this delegation in his letter to Vitalis and Tonantius, published by James Sirmondus from a manuscript now in the library of the Church of Paris.] Meanwhile I earnestly ask you, having regard to the calamities of the present circumstances and times, to attribute our absence not to pride or negligence but to this evident necessity.

Cyril, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, said:

“Let this letter of Capreolus, the most reverend and devout bishop of Carthage, which has been read, be inserted in the acts of the proceedings, since it contains a clear statement. For he wishes the ancient doctrines of the faith to be confirmed, but those that are new, absurdly devised, and impiously disseminated to be rejected and proscribed.”

All the bishops cried out together:

“These are the voices of all; this is what we all affirm; this is the desire of all.”

[Col. 0844D]

## Greek Version

I wished, most devout brothers, that your venerable synod had been assembled in such circumstances that we too, after brothers and our fellow bishops had been selected by common judgment, might send not an apology worthy of lamentation but rather a prepared delegation—unless various causes had impeded this disposition of ours.

For first, letters of our lord and son, the most devout emperor Theodosius, came into our hands, letters that specifically demanded the presence of our brother and fellow bishop Augustine, of blessed memory. Those aforesaid letters were entirely unable to find him in this life. Therefore I, who received that imperial communication, although it seemed to have been sent especially to the aforesaid man, wished to gather a synod by means of appropriate letters and customary communications sent throughout all the provinces of Africa, so that men selected from the number of our brothers and bishops might be sent to the venerable synod of your blessedness.

But since the entrance to the route of passage has not been opened—for the multitude of enemies that has poured in, and the widespread devastation of the provinces, which, whether the inhabitants have been extinguished or have fled, stretches far and wide into a miserable spectacle of desolation, [Note: “Of the wars.”] restrict the ease of coming [Note: “Into complete desolation.”]—the bishops who had been appointed for this purpose could not possibly gather together from the circuit of Africa.

Since the imperial letters came to us during the days of Easter, when scarcely a period of two months remained before the venerable universal synod—months that would barely have sufficed even for the African synod to assemble, had no present difficulty from the enemies arisen—it came about that, although we were entirely unable to send a formal embassy, nevertheless, because of the reverence owed to ecclesiastical discipline, we sent my son Bessula the deacon, together with these letters of apology, to you, venerable brothers.

Therefore I ask your holiness—although I firmly believe, through the help of our God, that the catholic faith will remain secure in every respect through so great an assembly of venerable priests—that, with the Holy Spirit at work, whom we trust will be present with your hearts in all that you must undertake, you may drive away by the strength of ancient authority the new teachings previously unknown to ecclesiastical ears, and thus resist every kind of new error.

Let not the voice long ago removed seem, under the pretext of a second disputation, to revive those errors which the Church formerly fought and which, when they sprang up again in these times, the authority of the apostolic see and the united judgment of the priests together buried. [Note: “Removed.”]

For if anything new should happen to arise, it requires examination, so that what has been said may either be tested or, if condemned, be rejected. [Note: Perhaps: “having been accepted.”] But if anyone should allow matters already judged long ago to be summoned into a second disputation, he will seem to be doing nothing other than doubting about the faith that has endured until now.

Furthermore, for the example of those who come after, so that what has now been decreed on behalf of the catholic faith may be able to possess perpetual confirmation, those things that have already been defined by the Fathers must be preserved. For whoever wishes what has been established concerning the catholic order to remain forever must confirm what he has thought not by his own authority but also by the judgment of the ancients. Thus, by testing what he affirms, partly from the ancient definitions and partly from those of more recent times, he must show himself asserting, teaching, and holding the single truth of the catholic Church, which from past times to the present—that is, to our own days—has continued in simple purity and unconquered authority.

These things, meanwhile, I have submitted to your venerable ears on behalf of the present embassy of Africa, which the previously mentioned necessity did not permit us to send. I earnestly ask you, therefore, that, having considered the calamities of circumstances and times, you may deign to reckon our absence not to any pride or negligence but rather to this manifest necessity.

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, said:

“Let the letter of Capreolus, the most devout and God-loving bishop of Carthage, which has been read, be inserted in the record of the proceedings, since it contains a clear meaning. For he wishes the ancient doctrines of the faith to be strengthened, but those that are new, improperly invented, and impiously stated to be rejected and cast out.”

All the bishops cried out:

“These are the voices of all; this is what we all say; this is the prayer of all.”

# LETTER OF THE SERVANTS OF GOD, VITALIS AND CONSTANTIUS, SPANIARDS, TO SAINT CAPREOLUS, BISHOP OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH OF CARTHAGE

(C)

To our lord Capreolus, venerable and most blessed in Christ, servant of God: Vitalis and Constantius, sinners.

As the first vows of our humility, we offer the fullest greeting to your holy, perfect, and venerable blessedness, and we always desire, with God’s favor, to hear that you are safe and unharmed. For although we are placed far away from your holy apostolate, with the sea between us, we are always present in your presence through the prayers of your holiness, lord and father.

We greatly desired to write to your holy and honorable dignity through our most beloved brother Numinianus. For our smallness has discovered the outstanding fame and teaching of your holiness. Through it we write to your blessedness, as the Psalmist says: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

We also ask your honor to command that what the right catholic faith holds be poured from the good treasure of your heart into our inward parts.

For there are certain people here who say that one ought not to say that God was born. This too is their faith: that a mere human being was born from the Virgin Mary and that afterward God dwelt in him. We, your humble servants, resist their assertion. It ought not to be said in that way. Rather, we confess, as the Evangelist says, when the angel Gabriel announced to Mary:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

## II.

We therefore confess that God was in the womb of the Virgin Mary, that he assumed some part of humanity, fashioned a human being for himself, and that true God and true man—the man whom he assumed for the salvation of the human race—was born, as the Apostle says:

> When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4:4).

And again:

> Think this in yourselves, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2:5–8).

And again:

> There is one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5).

For the mediator can no longer be called merely God, purely and without the human being whom he assumed, nor a human being without God, because there is a twofold meaning in the one person of the mediator: God and man. He is God from God, God; and, according to the flesh, that same one is the Son of Man. Therefore this mediator is true God and true man, just as he is of the form of God and the form of a human being.

For at the beginning of his Epistle to the Romans the holy Apostle also says:

> The gospel which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 1:2–4).

Indeed, Isaiah, the author of the prophets, says:

> Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23).

But they also say that a mere human being was suspended on the cross after being seized; they assert, “God departed from him.” To them our humble insignificance replies: God never departed from the human being he had assumed, except when he said from the cross:

> Heli, Heli, Lammasabactani: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46).

Therefore, falling on our knees, we, your humble servants, earnestly beseech your holy apostolate to instruct our lowliness in those matters in which the Catholic faith holds what is right, and to grant pardon for our foolishness or inexperience if through ignorance we have proceeded incorrectly in anything. The Lord Christ is able, through your holy prayers, to grant us pardon, so that we may not descend into the depths of evils. Pray for us, holy, venerable, and most blessed lord pope.

### SUBSCRIPTION

May our Lord Jesus preserve your venerable dignity for us in good health for a long time, holy and venerable lord pope.

## LETTER II, OR REPLY, TO VITALIS AND CONSTANTIUS

> Note: Baronius, under the year 431, §28 ff., quotes almost this entire letter; here he reads *Tonantius*. This reading is preferred even by Sirmondus himself; consequently, the same reading seems to require restoration in the preceding letter sent to Capreolus.

On the one person of Christ, true God and man, against the recently condemned heresy of Nestorius.

To his most beloved and devout sons Vitalis and Constantius, Capreolus, bishop.

### I.

Having received and read your letter, most beloved sons, which you sent through Numinianus, a devout man, I rejoiced greatly at your health and zeal, by which you hold and defend with inviolable devotion the rule of the founded and ancient Catholic faith. I perceived that the Nestorian heresy—a new and unspeakable ruin—just as it had already begun to sprout in certain places, likewise wished to cast the seeds of its tares into the hearts of the learned.

Yet I believe and trust that our Lord, the perfect farmer and creator of all things, has and has always had in every place under his dominion worthy workers of the evangelical harvest. Although unclean seeds ought not to be uprooted before the time of reaping, they nevertheless keep constant watch through continual prayers and preaching, so that those seeds, if it can be done while the time remains, may be converted and changed into wheat; or at least the enemy of the human race may not altogether succeed, through adulterous intermixture, in choking the tender kinds of grain as they grow.

For already—as I do not doubt has also come to your notice—within the regions of the East, where this plague first arose, a glorious synod of priests was assembled. Our delegation was not absent from it.

> Note: Capreolus points to the letter addressed to the Council of Ephesus, given above in the first place.

There, at the entrance, the heresy was suppressed together with its author and defender and extinguished by the ray of apostolic light.

Your charity should not be surprised if, even after its condemnation, a foul breath still blows among dying spirits. The boldness of heretics is always obstinate, and, pressed on by the weight of sins, it persists in its own destructive wickedness. If perhaps you have not yet learned this, you will be able to recognize it by an easy reading.

### Note

The reading *imperitorum* (“of the ignorant”) seems preferable.

### II.

Although the authority of the universal Church itself ought fully to suffice for Christian and devout minds, and although your own assertion in this matter does not appear weaker, as the message sent by you has made abundantly clear, nevertheless, lest I too seem to deny a necessary answer to your holy petition and inquiry, we confess that this is the one true doctrine which evangelical antiquity holds and transmits.

That is: the Son of God, true God and true man, has one entirely united and inseparable person. We do not believe that the divine fullness came to Christ Jesus from outside, as God inhabited or inhabits the other patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and other holy and illustrious men. Rather, in a certain proper and ineffable manner, the Son of God also became the Son of Man, so that he who remained and remains the only-begotten Son in the uncreated substance of the Father, by wonderfully assuming humanity, might become the firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:29); and that he who was in the beginning the Word—and the Word was with God, and God was the Word—might become flesh and dwell among us (John 1:1, 14).

When, therefore, the mystery that had been hidden from the ages in God (Col. 1:26) began to work through the angel in the Virgin’s womb, and the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke 1:35), God deigned to be born in a human being—he who always was—in order that a human being might be born who previously had not existed.

For he who was eternally begotten in heaven without a mother was himself created on earth as a human being without a father, in the Virgin’s womb, from the Holy Spirit. And therefore we believe that the person of God and man in Christ Jesus cannot in any way be separated or divided, lest there be counted not a Trinity in the Godhead but a quaternity.

### III.

When the blessed Apostle Paul was exhorting the faithful to put off the old human being and put on the new, he said:

> The first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven (1 Cor. 15:47–49).

Let them say, I ask, how this man is from heaven if God was not conceived in the womb. Or what distinction is there between flesh and blood in the man Adam and in the man Christ, if this man is not full of God?

For what does “the second man from heaven” mean? Did flesh descend after being transmitted from heaven, and not, as it is written, did the Holy Spirit come upon the Virgin? But because the Word became flesh (John 1:14), he was therefore called the heavenly man. Nor did he for that reason lack true flesh because he descended from heaven, since God assumed flesh.

The same Lord rightly said of himself:

> No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven (John 3:13).

Certainly he was still speaking on earth and had not yet ascended to the Father after the victory of his passion and the glory of his resurrection; yet he said that the Son of Man was already in heaven. He testified this with complete truth: on account of humanity, God was living on earth; and on account of God, man was dwelling in heaven.

Thus the Apostle also says:

> The one who descended is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fulfill all things (Eph. 4:10).

Elsewhere, when the Savior himself was speaking mystically about the food of his flesh and the drinking of his blood, knowing that his disciples would be offended by this and murmur:

> This is a hard saying; who can hear it? (John 6:61),

he said:

> Does this offend you? What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? (ibid., 63).
