Here too you perceive how, on account of the unity of the person of God and man, he declares that the Son of Man will ascend to the place where he was before—the one who is known to have been formed in the Virgin’s womb, so that from it he might receive the beginning of human birth.

### IV.

Therefore let no one, with sacrilegious spirit, dare to separate what he sees remaining in heaven and on earth in inseparable unity. For just as Christ Jesus the man cannot be alien to the omnipotence of the Godhead, so God cannot be separated from those things that were done to or around the man.

Thus a man was born who had not previously existed, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). In the same way, the impassible suffered through the passible nature he assumed; the immortal died; and the one who never dies rose again.

For God was not absent even in the passion from that man; otherwise the Lord of glory was not crucified (1 Cor. 2:8). Or are we to say that God was not in the man he had assumed even among the underworld? Or should we fear that the Godhead was there as though under punishment—though no quality affects it and no dimension confines it? No one can contain its greatness; no one escapes its presence; no one discovers its secret; no one reaches its splendor.

Do you fear that the immeasurable may be enclosed, the omnipotent held, the one diffused everywhere hidden anywhere? The Lord of all things could not be subjected to such a condition as to be unable, wherever and in whatever manner he willed, to “release the pangs of the underworld” (Acts 2:24).

Hear him, many thousands of years earlier, when he proclaimed through a cloud to blessed Job the works of his wonders, as though reproaching him, and added this among his innumerable demonstrations of power:

> Have you taken away light from the impious, or crushed the arm of the proud? Or have you come to the boundaries of the sea? Have you walked in the tracks of the abyss? Or, he says, will the gates of death be opened to you through fear, and, seeing you, will the gatekeepers of the underworld be terrified? Or have you known the breadth beneath heaven? (Job 38:15–18, according to the Septuagint).

If this is the voice of the Father, then nothing is difficult for the omnipotent, since he is everywhere and is nowhere absent. The prophet likewise says, in the person of someone:

> Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into the underworld, you are present (Ps. 138:7–8).

This wholly testifies and demonstrates that God, whose majesty fills all things, is also present in the underworld in a manner entirely incomprehensible and inexplicable.

But if—as is more probable—the voice of the Son of God is found in those things that were foretold about him so long beforehand and fulfilled, since all things were made through him and without him nothing was made (John 1:3), then he himself, in the man, deigned to visit the hidden places of the underworld; he terrified the rulers of death by the presence of his unconquered majesty, and ordered the gates of the underworld to be opened for the liberation of those whom he willed.

### V.

The Apostle John speaks of him in the Apocalypse:

> He placed his right hand upon me, saying: “Do not fear. I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever, and I have the keys of death and of the underworld” (Rev. 1:17–18).

On account of his divinity he is the first, because he is the beginning, who also speaks to us (John 8:25); on account of his humanity he is the last, because he did not disdain to take up the cross and die for us. Therefore, although all creatures are naked before him in his divinity, he also possesses the keys of death and of the underworld in the man he assumed.

So far is it from being possible for God, the Son of God—unchangeable and incomprehensible—to have been confined in the underworld, that we do not believe that even the soul of the assumed humanity was assumed for destruction or abandoned permanently. Nor do we believe that his flesh was infected by the contagion of any corruption.

For his own voice is found in the psalm, as the Apostle Peter interprets it:

> You will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption (Ps. 15:10; Acts 2:28).

On account of our guilt he became like a man without help (Ps. 87:6); but on account of his innocence and power he was found free among the dead. Then he truly paid what he had not taken, as it is written (Ps. 68:5).

It is therefore not astonishing if some place receives God but does not contain him; it perceives his presence but does not impede his majesty; it dreads his omnipotence but does not enclose his substance. For that supreme and perfect blessedness, that unquenchable light [perhaps: “light”], cannot be darkened by darkness, altered by places, affected by sufferings, diminished by conditions, or changed by times.

God therefore did not abandon his own Son, made man, in the underworld, nor leave him among the dead. By whose power and majesty were the ancient bodies of the saints seen to rise (Matt. 27:51–52), if God did not visit the underworld at all?

Who was it who caused the rocks to split, the earth to quake, the sun to be darkened, the day to flee, and the veil of the temple to be divided into two parts? Was it merely a human being? Was it not also God? Therefore he was not absent either on the cross, in death, in the tomb, or in the underworld.

Nor is the following said or understood in any other way, or of anyone else, than as it is written in the psalm:

> Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter (Ps. 23:7).

When they were terrified and asked, “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid., 8), the answer is:

> The Lord, strong and mighty; the Lord, mighty in battle.

In what battle, if not that in which he trampled death by death, extinguished sin by being innocently slain, and carried away the trophy of victory from the devil and his angels?

### Note

Perhaps the preposition *in* should be inserted, as the context suggests.

### VI.

But, they say, he himself said on the cross:

> My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Ps. 21:1).

This is the voice of the man who was assumed. Pay attention to where it is taken from, and there see what follows:

> Far from my salvation are the words of my sins (ibid.).

This voice is also like the one in which he says:

> My soul is sorrowful unto death (Matt. 26:38).

Had he not shortly before said to his disciples:

> You are sorrowful because I said, “I am going to my Father, and you will no longer see me” (John 16:6);

and:

> If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I (John 14:28)?

In what, then, does he command his disciples to rejoice? How is the teacher believed to be sorrowful, unless he was displaying in the man the passions and fluctuations of a true human being? For he had come to redeem, instruct, and strengthen us, and therefore endured in himself every kind of weakness that belongs to us.

> We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb. 4:15);

for, as the Apostle says, he experienced everything according to likeness, without sin.

The following saying is similar:

> Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will (Matt. 26:39).

Had he not come for this purpose—to drink this cup for us and drive out the poison administered by the serpent with such an antidote of salvation? Did he not have authority to lay down his life, and authority to take it up again (John 10:18)? Had he not himself said:

> No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (ibid.)?

And yet now he speaks as though doubting and refusing, so that divine power may appear there, while here the human condition may make itself known.

Does not the Apostle proclaim that this mystery had been hidden in God before the eternal ages (Col. 1:26)? Did Christ fear something as though it were sudden, something which he had determined with the Father in eternity was to be done at the appointed time?

Therefore, when these and similar things are said or done, they demonstrate—as has often been stated—the true weakness and frailty of the human being; but they do not thereby empty the presence of the divine majesty.

### VII.

Whoever you are, O man, who think that God Christ was separated from the man Christ during the time of his passion, do you not remember that he faithfully promised his presence to the disciples who would suffer? He says:

> When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you will speak; for what you should say will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you (Matt. 10:19–20).

Did the one who promised, granted, and displayed his divine presence to servants carrying out the Lord’s will—who, though without sin, underwent an innocent death for our salvation in order to fulfill the Father’s will—deny divine help to himself during the time of his flesh?

And did God abandon the human being whom he assumed, compelled by no necessity whatsoever to endure these things, when he was carrying out this task? He speaks as one present amid the torments of martyrs and does not permit them to devise anything for themselves, yet he abandoned himself on the scaffold of the cross?

For he is one and the same—as must often and always be repeated—and the person of God and man cannot be distinguished, although the substance in him is different. Far be it from us to believe otherwise or to think differently about the omnipotent.

The eternal one did not fear being born, the perfect one growing, the impassible suffering, or the immortal dying, without any change or corruption in himself, as has already been said. But because the Godhead alone could not suffer these things, he assumed a human being through whom he might carry out the mystery of so great a gift.

When he was received into heaven, he raised that human being to the place from which he himself had never departed.

Let us hear the Apostle proclaiming Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, the same Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

Pay attention, most beloved sons, and recognize what you already know: the very Christ who, because of the humility of the man he assumed, is said to have been a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, is himself the power of God and the wisdom of God.

Here too, surely, is the person of divinity and humanity separated or divided by the Apostle? Or did he blush to call the same one the wisdom of God whom he had said was made the foolishness of the Gentiles? Or did he blush to affirm as the power of God the same one whom he had called the stumbling block of the Jews?

Why, then, are we ashamed to confess that God was born and suffered on account of the human being and in the human being, when, by God’s gift, we do not deny that this same human being was made God? It is understood that he received this through divine grace, not through human substance.

### VIII.

A little farther on he continues:

> From him you are in Christ Jesus, who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (ibid., 30–31).

“Christ Jesus,” says the heretic, “is merely the name of a human being.” But Paul knew and had said that no one should boast in a human being; he knew Christ Jesus not merely as a human being but also as God. He believed that Christ had been made for us by God as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, and he taught those who believe in him to boast in him, because Christ Jesus is both man and God.

In keeping with this, and without verbal or philosophical self-display, as he announced the mystery of God, he adds:

> I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:2).

And so that the wicked people of the Jews might not claim that they had committed only a small sin, if they should understand that they had persecuted merely a naked human being, he says that the mystery had been hidden in the wisdom of God and testifies that it had been revealed to none of the rulers of this age (ibid., 7–8):

> If they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Here too he does not fear to preach as crucified before the rulers of the age the same Jesus Christ whom he confesses as the Lord of glory.

I exhort you to consider the whole content of this passage. You will see with what great effort and exertion the holy Apostle raises human minds from the baseness of merely earthly understanding to contemplate the divine and heavenly realities contained in this mystery. I pass briefly over everything, which you yourselves will be able to examine more fully and extensively.

For in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he says in one place:

> Whether we were beside ourselves, it was for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. For the love of Christ compels us, judging this: that one died for all (2 Cor. 5:13–14).

And shortly afterward:

> Everything is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, because God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself (ibid., 18–19).

### IX.

I ask: how did he reconcile it? Was it not by being born, suffering, dying, rising again, and ascending into heaven?

I also ask: what is the mystery of our reconciliation? Is it anything other than the sacrifice which Christ, the high priest, offered through his blood?

Let us therefore see whether a mere human being accomplished this, since, according to their belief, God departed from him in the passion. But the Apostle Paul most clearly contradicts this opinion:

> God was in Christ.

He was in Christ; he had not departed from Christ. God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.

How was he reconciling it?

> Not counting their trespasses against them.

Or do fools perhaps approve the idea that the forgiveness of sins is accomplished through a mere human being? Even the Jews rejected this, saying:

> He blasphemes. Who can forgive sins except God alone? (Mark 2:7).

The Lord himself, the Son of God and man, wished to show the unbelievers that the one they saw was not merely a human being, but also God, in whom they refused to believe. He also wished clearly to demonstrate that divine power had been granted to the man on account of the unity of his person and presence. Therefore he said:

> So that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—

then he said to the paralytic:

> Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house (Matt. 9:6).

Thus God and man, one and true Savior of souls and bodies, lifted the outward human being from bodily illness and the inward human being from the burden of sin.

God, therefore, was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, never and nowhere abandoning the human being whom he assumed through his own gracious condescension and not at all from necessity.

### X.

The same Apostle also testifies at the very beginning of his Epistle to the Hebrews:

> In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the representation of his substance, and he upholds all things by the word of his power. Having himself made purification for sins, he sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb. 1:2–3).

The Son of God and Son of Man is therefore one and the same: on account of eternity, he made the ages with the Father; on account of unchangeable light, he is the radiance of glory; on account of equality, he is the representation of substance; and on account of majesty, he upholds all things by the word of his power.

He also, on account of the passion of the man he assumed, made purification for our sins; and, on account of the reward, he has his seat at the Father’s right hand.

How, however, did he make purification for sins, unless by wiping away the written bond that had stood against us (Col. 2:14), written by the devil as our accuser? How did he wipe it away, unless by fastening it to the cross and washing it away with innocent blood?

What God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, and finally testified in the Son (Heb. 1:1–2), let us believe, hold, and defend with all our strength.

It is relevant to the case that at that time he confidently stripped the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself (Col. 2:15). This work is not at all that of a mere human being, but of divine majesty in a human being.

For it was not a strong and mighty man, but the Lord mighty in battle (Ps. 23:6).

### XI.

There also, after much discussion in which the Apostle distinguished the mystery of the New Testament from the figure of the Old, he says:

> Anyone who rejects the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as unclean the blood of the New Testament by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of the grace of God? For we know the one who said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord (Heb. 10:28–30).

I ask how the Son of God can be trampled upon. Here too you see how he neither doubts, fears, nor blushes to assert that the Son of God was trampled upon.

But since anyone who considers the blood by which he was sanctified unclean thereby tramples upon the Son of God, the Apostle did not separate the passion of the man from the majesty of God. He wants the person who regards the blood shed for him as worthless to be held guilty of this.

For the Son of God is trampled upon only when the benefit of the death he endured in the man is despised.

The Savior and Lord himself, intending to reward faith, also asks:

> Who do they say that I, the Son of Man, am? (Matt. 16:13).

When they offered him the various opinions of others, he said:

> But who do you say that I am? (ibid., 15).

That is, “Who do you say that I, the Son of Man, am?”

Peter, inspired by the same Lord and, in this confession, destined to benefit all nations as a model of right faith, answered with what great and complete integrity:

> You are the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matt. 16:16).

“You—the one who calls yourself the Son of Man—you are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Is it not also demonstrated here, whether in the Lord’s question or in the Apostle’s answer, that the two substances have one person? The Lord declares himself to be the Son of Man, which was openly visible; Peter, through the confession granted to him, reveals him as Christ, the Son of God, which was carried secretly within him.

For this reason the Lord praised him and called him blessed (ibid., 17), because flesh and blood had not revealed this to him, but the Father who is in heaven.

Therefore, may God the Father reveal through God the Son what we ought to believe, and may flesh and blood not insinuate it.

### XII.

After the resurrection, when Mary did not recognize the Lord, and he opened the way to recognition by calling her by her name, while forbidding her to touch him as she wished, let us hear what message he deigned to entrust to her for the disciples:

> Go to my brothers and say to them: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17).

Now let the heretic choose what he thinks and decide whose voice he prefers this to be. He will be struck on both sides by the sharp spiritual sword.

> I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.

If this is the voice of a man, then that man is the Son of God, for he said, “I am ascending to my Father.” If it is the voice of God, then that God is man, for he said, “I am ascending to my God.”

For he did not say, “I am ascending to my Father and the God of my man,” or, “I am ascending to my God and the Father of my God.”

Thus whoever distinguishes the person of divinity and humanity is convicted by either interpretation. Either a human being spoke, and that same one is the Son of God; or God spoke, and that same one is also the human being he assumed.

For by saying, “I am ascending to my Father and to my God,” and repeating “my” and “my,” he proves and declares one person, although he distinguishes the two substances.

The words “I am ascending to my Father” appear to pertain to the only-begotten Son; the words “to my God” appear to pertain to the one made man.

Yet in Christ Jesus neither can a created man be posited, nor can the only-begotten God be denied to have been born man.

Therefore this voice is shown to belong neither to God alone nor to man alone. God and man, one and unique Son, entrusted it to be conveyed to his disciples with an entirely inseparable and indivisible affection.

Finally, so that you may know and more fully understand that this is what is being said, observe how divine mercy watched over us when it was necessary to distinguish the Creator’s nature from the creature and to refute the devices and every slander of all heretics.

> Go to my brothers and say to them: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”

Here the person of the Lord himself—that is, of God and man—is clearly distinguished from the person of his servants, and the calling is separated according to nature.

Although what is commanded is now commanded to friends and brothers, it is nevertheless shown what is owed to the Lord and what is attributed to the other servants.

For he could have said, “I am ascending to our Father and our God,” because there is a great difference between lordship and servitude, between generation and adoption, between substance and grace.

Therefore he does not say here indiscriminately or casually, “I am ascending to our Father and our God,” but “to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”

He is God the Father to him in one way, and to us in another. Nature makes him equal to the Father; mercy humbles him. Nature casts us down; mercy raises us up.

This is what that divine humanity and human divinity accomplished, through such a great and marvelous miracle, so that the unworthy weakness of mortals might merit such grace.

### XIII.

Who could, or who would have enough space, gather at one time all the proofs of the holy pages by which this sincere and pure truth is fully taught?

But the length of this discourse, which has already exceeded its proper bounds, must eventually be restrained; nor should I labor longer with those whom I have recognized as instructed by the Lord.

Therefore, as the Apostle commanded (2 Tim. 4:2), persist in season and out of season, and with sound doctrine reprove, recall, instruct, and strengthen all who are in error—not possessing in this rule of faith the proofs that are mine, for they are none or few, but those of the divine Scriptures and of the great and most learned men who before us held these things most firmly and taught them most eloquently in numerous books.

## IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 432. URANIUS THE PRESBYTER

### [NOTICE. From Cave]

Uranius the presbyter, a disciple of Paulinus of Nola, attended him during his final illness in the year 431. At the urging of Pacatus, he wrote an account of the death of Saint Paulinus, which is found in Surius under June 22 and in all the more recent editions of Paulinus.

## LETTER OF URANIUS THE PRESBYTER

From Surius. (C, S)

## LETTER OF URANIUS THE PRESBYTER ON THE DEATH OF SAINT PAULINUS, TO PACATUS

Published from the manuscript of Troyes by Chifflet, and collated with copies of other manuscripts.

### 1.

To the illustrious lord and, by merit in Christ, venerable Pacatus, Uranius the presbyter.

I am repeatedly troubled by letters from your noble self, asking me faithfully to relate to you the death of Saint Paulinus. I shall indeed do what you command, but I fear that I shall not do as effectively as you wish what I desire to do.

Nevertheless, since you deign to command it, I shall do it faithfully and without falsehood. For I know that it is better to press the tongue into silence than to recount falsehoods to the soul’s sin, as Scripture says:

> The mouth that lies kills the soul.

And therefore I earnestly ask your reverence to deign to pardon my inexperience. Otherwise, if the poverty of my speech begins to displease you, you will more rightly blame yourself than me, since you asked water from a muddy stream that should have come from a perfectly pure spring.

But let these matters be stated briefly. Let us now come to those things that may provide material for you, who intend to ennoble his life in verse.

### Note

Vossius, in *On Latin Writers*, p. 224, writes *Paratus*, I do not know from where, since both the printed texts and the manuscripts generally read *Pacatus*. There was, as Chifflet notes, a Latin Pacatus who delivered a panegyric at Rome to the emperor Theodosius after the death of the tyrant Maximus, in the year 411. This Pacatus may perhaps have been his son—I would regard him as a secular layman rather than a cleric—and may have possessed so flourishing a poetic vein that in that learned age he undertook to praise Paulinus in verse. In this sense Uranius calls him “a most dear son” in section 5.

As for Uranius himself, who was present at the saint’s death, because he says at the end that he was hastening to sail away at the first opportunity, Chifflet conjectured that he was the man whom Saint Paulinus writes he awaited throughout the whole summer in 401 from Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux. At that time he was a young presbyter; later, as an older man, he could have sailed to Italy on some occasion to visit an old friend and written this letter from Nola to the house where Pacatus lived.

I would nevertheless prefer to regard the author of the letter as a younger man, perhaps the nephew of the other.

### Note

Surius reads *utilitati* (“for usefulness”), less correctly.

## 2

Therefore Saint Paulinus, bishop, was born in the town of Bordeaux in Gaul, but died and was buried in Campania [Note: That is, at the church of Saint Felix; he is commemorated here on 14 January. The manuscript of Melica adds “and martyr.” But although Bollandus teaches that two priests named Felix at Nola must be distinguished—one, the son of the Syrian Hermias, born at Nola; the other, a Roman—he nevertheless maintains that both were confessors only. The present passage concerns the first; the second was also the brother of another Felix, a martyr, and from this the confusion arose.] at the blessed confessor Felix, after a glorious end. We recognize his life from the merit of his death, and we prove his death from the manner of his life.

Indeed, three days before he was summoned from this world to his heavenly dwelling, when everyone had already despaired of his recovery and two bishops had come to visit him—namely, Saint Symmachus [Note: Michael the monk, in *The Capuan Sanctuary*, p. 191, testifies that he read the following words in a manuscript calendar of the Capuan Treasury: “The eleventh day before the Kalends of November: Saint Saloma, Saint Symmachus, bishop of Capua and confessor.” Because he was commemorated annually in the church of Saint Mary Major in the diocese, he displays a mosaic in which is written: “HOLY MARY, SYMMACHUS THE BISHOP.” He says that this could have been written in that form only while Symmachus was alive; and the church itself does not seem capable of being considered older than New Capua, within which it stands. The monk therefore thinks that Symmachus lived after the year 900, perhaps around 950. As though, however, some mosaic from the fifth century could not have survived in a church restored in the tenth century! Later considering this, he says in Ughellus, among the bishops of Capua, no. 38: “If anyone, moved by sound reasoning or led by a probable conjecture, should think that the name of Saint Symmachus ought to be counted among the bishops of Old Capua, I now willingly agree; and I ask him to consider whether Saint Symmachus might be that Symmachus who was present at the death of Paulinus, bishop of Nola.” Nola and Capua are separated by only twenty-one thousand paces, or seven hours’ journey; nothing could be more natural than for a neighboring bishop to be summoned in such a circumstance. Yet nothing could be more contrary to truth than that a bishop who had, and still has, so solemn a cult in such a city, as is explained there, should have lived in the tenth century, while almost nothing is known of his life or miracles. Nor should Julian be an obstacle to Capuan Symmachus: Gennadius, as published, calls Julian at this time bishop of Capua; but Chiffletius notes that the manuscript of Gennadius reads “Campanian.” This is made plausible by Prosper, who for the year 339 names Julian of Atella, an especially boastful defender of the Pelagian error.] and the blessed Acindynus [Note: Just as “holy” is used adjectivally of Symmachus, so Acindynus here seems to be called “blessed,” these being titles formerly applicable to any bishop while alive. Surius, however, took it substantively, adding the apparently adjectival name “Hyacinthinus,” for which Baronius conjectured in his *Annals* that “Hydruntinus” should be read, although Hydruntum lies nearly two hundred Roman miles from Nola. Yet “Hyacinthinus” does not seem to be the proper name of a bishop, and is found nowhere else. I therefore prefer Chiffletius’s conjecture: since the Medicean copy has *benedictus ac indignus* (“blessed and unworthy”), he suggests reading *benedictus Acindynus* (“the blessed Acindynus”). At that time Nola had neighboring episcopal cities—apart from Naples, whose bishop was John I, and Atella, governed by the aforementioned Julian: in Campania, Acerra, Cumae, and Puteoli; and in the nearer and farther principate, Nocera, Cosenza, Salerno, Avellino, and Benevento. None of these has a bishop whom one can confidently say lived in the year 431. The Julian of Puteoli, attested for the year 449, comes closest. Why, then, could Acindynus not at that time have been bishop of one of those cities?]—he was so revived and restored by their arrival that, forgetting all bodily weakness, he showed himself to them wholly spiritual and angelic.

And as though he were about to depart to the Lord, he ordered the sacred mysteries to be presented before his bed [Note: Several copies have this reading; the Trier manuscript has “ministries.” Below, it has “with the ministries” (*ministeriis*).], so that, after the sacrifice had been offered together with the holy bishops, he might commend his soul to the Lord; and at the same time recall to their former peace those whom, for ecclesiastical discipline, he had ordered to be excluded from communion in the sacred mystery.

## 3

When the holy bishop had celebrated all these things in joyful and perfect order, he suddenly began asking in a loud voice where his brothers were. Then one of those standing around, thinking that he was asking for his brothers—that is, the bishops who were present at the time—said to him, “Behold, your brothers are here.” But he replied:

“But I mean my brothers Januarius and Martin, who have just spoken with me and said that they would come to me immediately.”

Of these, Januarius, bishop and martyr, illumines the Church of the city of Naples; Martin, a man wholly apostolic, whose life is read by everyone, was a bishop of Gaul.

After saying this, he stretched his hands toward heaven and sang this psalm to the Lord:

“I lifted up my eyes to the mountains: from there will come my help. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

Then, after gathering his prayer, he was reminded by the holy priest Postumianus [Note: Here the title “holy” is given not only to bishops but also to priests; examples may perhaps be found showing that this designation was common to the whole clergy.] that forty solidi were owed for clothing that had been distributed to the poor.

When Saint Paulinus heard this, he smiled gently and said:

“Be at peace, my son; believe me, someone will not fail to pay the debt owed to the poor.”

And behold, after no long interval, a certain priest entered, coming from the regions of Lucania, sent by the holy bishop Exuperantius [Note: No Exuperantius, also called Exuberantius, is found anywhere in volume seven of Ughellus, which covers all the bishops of Lucania and Apulia who could be discovered.] or by his very distinguished brother Ursatius. Through him they had sent fifty solidi as a gift.

When Saint Paulinus had received them, he blessed the Lord, saying:

“I give thanks to you, Lord, who have not abandoned one who hopes in you.”

Of these fifty solidi he himself gave two with his own hand to the priest who had brought them [Note: Surius, followed by Baronius, remarked in the margin that one should apparently read not “two” but “ten,” as though two could not then have seemed a sufficient travel allowance. With Chiffletius, I think nothing should be changed.]; the rest he ordered to be returned to the merchants who had supplied the clothing for the poor.

## 4

Meanwhile, when night had already followed day, he rested for a short time until midnight. Then, as the pain in his side grew worse, he was awakened and exhausted by the many unnecessary cauterizations of the physicians; until the fifth hour of the night he drew a weary and labored breath.

When daylight came, the holy man recognized his customary routine. Therefore, after rousing everyone, he celebrated Matins according to the customary order.

When day had come, he preached to the priests, deacons, and all the clergy the hereditary peace [Note: By “hereditary” I understand “perpetual,” or the peace that Christ said he was leaving to his own as an inheritance, John 14:27.] after the example of the Lord.

Then, as though awakened from sleep, recognizing the time of the devotion of the Lucernarium [Note: The Latins called the prayers offered when lamps were lit at sunset the *Lucernarium*; Magrius teaches that these prayers were customarily said before Vespers. Since Vespers are now performed before sunset, Compline, said after Vespers, has taken the place of the Lucernarium.], he stretched out his hands and, although in a weak voice, sang to Christ his Lord:

“I have prepared a lamp for my Christ.”

After a period of silence, around the fourth hour of the night, while everyone present was keeping careful watch, his cell was suddenly shaken by such a violent earthquake that those attending his bed, terrified and confused, all threw themselves into prayer. Those standing outside the door, however, knew nothing of it; for it was not a public earthquake but one confined to the cell.

Received into angelic hands, he breathed forth the spirit owed to God.

## 5

We saw, dearest son—we saw, and amid tears and sobs we rejoice that we saw—we saw how the just man is taken away, and no one understands; and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers it.

No Christian ought to find it incredible if, at the passing of Saint Paulinus, one particular corner of the earth was shaken by an earthquake, since at his death almost the whole world groaned. Indeed, what place in the inhabited world is so remote or hidden that the passing of our lord Paulinus did not move it?

The Church certainly wept because it had lost such a priest; but paradise rejoiced because it had received such a saint. The peoples mourned, but the angels rejoiced. The provinces of humankind groaned, but the dwellings of the saints rejoiced—those dwellings to which he longed daily to fly when he said:

“How lovely are your tabernacles, Lord God of hosts! My soul longs and faints for your courts.”

## 6

O holy man, praiseworthy on every tongue, who lived in such a way that he lived not only for himself but for everyone!

And because he lived for many in this world, he now lives for himself in Christ—and yet not for himself alone, but also for us, because he prays for us every day.

In the end, he was a burning lamp in the house of God, not placed under a bushel but set upon a lampstand, so that by his splendid light he even made many other lamps shine.

For he was gentle and mild even while he lived amid the arrogance of the world. But when he turned to Christ, he opened his granaries to the poor and made his storerooms accessible to strangers. It was little for him merely to feed those near at hand, unless he also summoned from every direction those whom he could feed and clothe.

How many captives did he ransom! How many debt-entangled men [Note: Since all the examples here fit, I do not dare to change the reading to “those entangled in debts.” Understand “debt-entanglers,” therefore, as those who, because they realize that they cannot pay, deliberately complicate the debt itself. The joy of the creditors, freed from those troublesome complications, also seems to be intended.] he freed from their creditors by paying the money [Col. 0863A]! With one transaction of charity, he wiped away the debtors’ tears and restored the creditors’ joy.

## 7

When he had been raised to the highest rank of the priesthood, he did not wish to show himself as the kind of bishop whom anyone would fear; rather, he made himself the kind of priest whom everyone would love.

He was never so angry that he did not remember mercy in his anger. Indeed, that man could not be angry who disregarded insults and avoided hatred.

He never sat in judgment without mercy, because he knew that mercy is better than sacrifice, and that every judgment of Christians must be clothed with mercy, as the venerable Scripture says:

“I will sing mercy and judgment to you, Lord.”

He also tempered justice with more gracious considerations, knowing that, just as the Holy Spirit favors equity and justice, so benevolently he grants his own the grace of compassion. Therefore he maintained severity in the examination of justice, but displayed mercy in determining the sentence.

## 8

O admirable man, worthy to be judged by the praise of every virtue! [Note: The Medicean manuscript has “of all the saints,” which fits this passage equally well.]

For, following the examples of all the patriarchs, he was faithful like Abraham, trusting like Isaac, kind like Jacob, generous like Melchizedek, provident like Joseph, and a plunderer like Benjamin. For he plundered the rich and distributed to the poor; yet he is known to have benefited the rich more than the poor, since he benefited the poor in this world but provided for the rich in the world to come.

Therefore—as I had begun to say—he was meek like Moses, priestly like Aaron, innocent like Samuel, merciful like David, wise like Solomon, apostolic like Peter, lovable like John, cautious like Thomas, a teacher like Paul, a seer like Stephen, fervent like Apollos.

In his solicitude and care for the churches, in faith and charity, he imitated all the apostles and bishops.

He possessed all these qualities in himself and faithfully guarded them throughout the time of his life. Therefore, when he was summoned from this body to his heavenly dwelling, as I said above, the earth grieved but heaven rejoiced; the flesh wept but the spirit gloried.

## 9

Finally, not only Christians but also Jews and pagans came to the funeral of our lord Paulinus with immense weeping, even tearing their garments. All of them, together with us, mourned with one voice the patron, defender, and protector who had been taken from them.

And truly he was such a man that everyone loved him, for he lived as an example to all of the pursuit of salvation and as a source of consolation.

Nor is this merely my own testimony: all the provinces bear witness, as does the entire earth enclosed by the Roman world. The barbarian nations also bear witness, for the fame of the lord Paulinus had reached them.

Nor was he loved by everyone without reason, for he was present to everyone. Whom did he not raise up with his own right hand when lying prostrate? Whom, when appealing to him, did he not console with a compassionate voice?

For he was pious, merciful, humble, and kind: despising and looking down on no one. He gave to everyone and indulged everyone. He encouraged the frightened and calmed the violent. He built up some by his words and others by his example; he helped some by letters and others by financial support.

He admired no wealth or riches except those that Christ had promised to his saints. He defined gold, silver, and other possessions in such a way that generosity claimed them for giving, not greed for keeping.

To put it briefly, he possessed every good quality in himself because he loved Christ. He had faith, meekness, care for his neighbors, constant concern for the wretched, compassion for the weak, and regard for nothing except peace and charity. He alone begged so that everyone might abound.

Finally, what place in the inhabited world, what wilderness, what seas, did not experience the benefits of Saint Paulinus? Everyone wanted to know him; everyone desired to see him. Who came to him without joy, or departed from him without longing to return?

Those who could not see him in person at least wished to touch his letters. For he was gracious and winning in his correspondence, sweet and most pleasantly attractive in his verses.

What more shall I say? Credulity would scarcely admit whatever is said about him, were it not that his deeds drive away the charge of falsehood.

Let us be silent about the nobility of his family, brilliantly resplendent in the senatorial purple through both his paternal and maternal ancestry; and likewise about the abundance of his wealth, which he distributed to the poor for God’s sake.

Now let us turn to the matters concerning his death [Note: Here the same manuscript inserts only the material that Gregory has in his *Dialogues* concerning the enslavement by the Vandals, and presents it as written by Uranius. This deceived Possidonius in his *Apparatus*. Gregory himself, however, says that he had heard witnesses to the event, adding: “I must believe their great age with as much certainty as if I had seen with my own eyes the things they reported.” Gregory speaks differently of the earthquake by which the chamber trembled; concerning Paulinus’s death he says that an account of it was written at his church—that is, in or from this letter of Uranius. The awkward connection also shows that this passage has been sewn in from elsewhere, where it says: “Now let us turn to the events that occurred, during the time of the raging Vandals.” If a comma is substituted for the period, the rest of the sentence hangs unfinished and seems to lack its beginning. Once the interpolation is ended, the interrupted words are resumed here by repeating the earlier phrase, “But now let us turn to these matters,” and immediately adding what follows, with which we had begun to speak of his death.] .

## 10

Therefore, when Saint Paulinus had returned the spirit owed to God, his face and his entire body were affected with such snowy whiteness that everyone, amid sobs and tears, blessed the Lord our God, who leads his saints forth in magnificence, to show his servants that this is the glory of all his saints.

Therefore may his soul be praised in God, and may his works be revealed among all who fear God, because he desired the commandments of his God and understood the needs of the poor and needy, so that his seed might be mighty upon the earth and his righteousness might endure forever and ever.

## 11

Nevertheless, your reverence ought also to recognize this matter belonging to the merit of Saint Paulinus: Saint John [Note: Chiffletius, arguing at length in chapter 30, shows that this account fits John I, not John IV, contrary to certain more recent writers who think that the passage is interpolated because the letter of Uranius is found in several very old manuscripts without this account of John; Saint Gregory of Tours likewise omits it, although he describes Uranius almost word for word. But even if this letter could have been interpolated, could John the Deacon—who concluded his chronicle of the bishops of Naples with Athanasius the Younger, successor of John IV—have removed such a notable honor from the latter, whose life he describes at length, as we have given it on 1 April, and assigned it to the former, without recognizing a very recent interpolation in Uranius’s letter? John IV lived until the year 853, and the Deacon wrote toward the end of that same century. It is nevertheless possible that Uranius—whom I would hardly believe to have remained at Nola for a full year after Paulinus’s death in order to write this account there after Easter of the following year—may have added the account of John to a letter written earlier and sent to Pacatus, after news of the event at Naples had been brought to him when he had returned to Bordeaux from Italy. I do not mean the year immediately following his departure, but some later year. Hence may have arisen the variation among the copies cited by Cioccarellus. As for John Cimeliarcha’s assigning Paulinus’s apparition to John IV in another life of that John, as though correcting the Deacon’s error, this does not greatly concern us, since Cimeliarcha wrote in the year 1362 and is therefore much less reliable. I would therefore say that John I, who died on Holy Saturday and was laid to rest or buried as a saint on Easter Day itself, and is commemorated on 1 April, did not die in the year 432, immediately after Paulinus’s death, as writers commonly maintain—for that year had Easter on 3 April—but rather in the year 440, on 31 March, when Easter was celebrated on 1 April. For this reason one calendar seen by Cioccarellus places him on the last day of March, although others preferred to retain the day of his solemn burial. As for John IV, I think the exact year and day of his death are unknown, since the Deacon is silent on the matter. The date was therefore assumed on which his name was first found entered in the calendars, on the authority of John Cimeliarcha, who wanted it believed that he was buried on the fourth day. Thus the statements we made less distinctly about both men on 1 April should be corrected. I acknowledge that the more ancient cult of the first was obscured by the cult of the fourth, whose life was better known than that of the first and whose name was consequently more celebrated. But the annual veneration of the fourth must have been instituted in Cimeliarcha’s time, and indeed at the expense of the first.] , bishop of the city of Naples, is recognized as having been summoned and called by Lord Paulinus from this life to Christ.

For three days before Saint John departed from this world to the Lord, he reported that he had seen Saint Paulinus clothed and adorned with angelic dignity, wholly snowy, wholly starry, and shining with ambrosial fragrance. He held in his hand a very white honeycomb and said to him:

“Brother John, what are you doing here? Release the bonds of your weariness and come now to us, for this food that I hold in my hand is abundant enough among us.”

When he had said this, he embraced him and put a portion of that honeycomb into his mouth. Saint John said that he desired its sweetness and fragrance so greatly that, had he possessed the power during the revelation, he would in no way have departed from Paulinus’s feet.

Yet he did not long remain unaware of what was coming. Awakened from sleep, on that same day, Thursday, he rewarded all the clergy and the poor according to his custom and celebrated the Lord’s Supper in good health.

On Friday he devoted himself to prayer. On Saturday, at the second hour of the day, he joyfully proceeded to the church, ascended the tribunal according to custom, and greeted the people. When the people had returned his greeting, he delivered a prayer; and after gathering the prayer [Note: “To gather the prayer,” I think, means to conclude several prayers by adding, “Through our Lord,” and so on. Hence the prayers called *Collects* are so named because after another principal prayer in the liturgy they are read together, with a single “Through our Lord,” as ordinary speech puts it.] he breathed forth his spirit.

That night a vigil was held in the church. On the following day, Easter, with lamps lit and a great procession of newly baptized persons [Note: Chiffletius rightly asks what this procession of newly baptized persons could have been in the time of John IV, when all Naples was thoroughly Christian and baptism was not postponed until adulthood, as it had been in the time of the first John.], accompanied also by a multitude of people, he received a glorious and praiseworthy burial up to the tomb.

## 12

I have recalled these things to your nobility so that here too you might recognize the merit of Saint Paulinus. You have material for your composition, provided that faith in believing is not lacking.

Therefore I ask your nobility that, as you have graciously promised, you hasten to complete the distinguished work, destined to receive the rewards of praise and glory if you illuminate in verse the life of this holy man, for the benefit of posterity.

Would that, before I depart, you might make me worthy to read this work, for, if it pleases Christ, I intend to set sail immediately.

Saint Paulinus, bishop, died on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus, most illustrious men [Note: That is, in the year of Christ 431.]

**In the year of the Lord 450. Eustathius.**

## Notice (from Cave)

Eustathius, whom Cassiodorus calls a most eloquent man (*Divine Reading*, chapter 1), and whom Sigebertus also mentions (*On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 21), flourished around the year 440. He was a contemporary of the poet Sedulius.

He translated into Latin from the Greek the nine homilies of Saint Basil on the *Hexaemeron*, with such elegance that, as Cassiodorus says, “he seems to have matched the talent of the most learned man with the strength of his own eloquence.”

He dedicated this translation to his sister Syncletica. It exists in the editions of Saint Basil’s works published at Paris in 1603, Antwerp in 1616, and elsewhere.

Miraeus will tell you more about Eustathius and his sister Syncletica in his notes on Sigebertus, as will Casimirus Oudin, who, following his usual practice, copied Miraeus’s work in full while rarely naming him. *Supplement*, p. 87.

# Eustathius’s Latin Paraphrase of Saint Basil’s *Hexaemeron*

[Note: We find the following written in the second Colbert manuscript: “Here begins the prologue to the *Hexaemeron* of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea. Eustathius the deacon [so written] sends greetings in Christ to his sister Sindetice.” It is not unworthy of notice that the dignity of deacon is attributed to Eustathius here, although it is not attributed to him either in the printed editions, in two other manuscripts, or in the testimonies of the ancients collected by the printers at the beginning of the work. If anyone cannot be persuaded to believe that Eustathius was a deacon without stronger authority, we admit that we can offer no other evidence. The manuscript of Saint-Germain, written by a later hand, reads: “Eustathius sends greetings in Christ to his sister Syncletica, the deaconess.”]

Eustathius sends greetings in Christ to his sister Syncletica, the deaconess.

Your religious and studious spirit, my sister, desiring to know the fullness of the heavenly Scriptures, has investigated through frequent reading all the ecclesiastical libraries and the men who founded them. At last you came upon the *Hexaemeron* of the holy and venerable bishop Basil, written in Greek [Note: In the second Colbert manuscript, *conscriptum* (“written”) is corruptly read as *constrictam* (“confined”). Immediately afterward the same book has *quam dum monimentis*, and whoever wrote it—whether the copyist or Eustathius himself—seems to have had in mind the expression *εἰς τὴν ἑξαήμερον* (“for the six-day [work]”). Since this expression presents a feminine grammatical gender, he wished to use a feminine form here as well. The phrase *εἰς τὴν ἑξαήμερον* must be understood with the word *κοσμοποιΐαν* (“creation of the world”) supplied. For *ἑξαήμερος* is an adjective. See Ducaeus.], and, wishing to insert it into the monuments of the Latin language, you judged that this task should be entrusted to me.

But when I considered that you had commanded it more out of affection than judgment, I was indeed eager to obey your simple instructions, prompted by your love; [Note: The printed editions have *sed permittere* (“but to permit”), incorrectly; the second Colbert manuscript has *sed committere* (“but to entrust”), no better. Our Saint-Germain manuscript and the first Colbert manuscript have *sed promittere* (“but to promise”), correctly.] yet I did not dare to promise, considering my own childish incompetence.

Thus, torn between two thoughts, I did not know what to do. I feared that, if I preferred to refuse, I would offend a mind that was piously presuming great things of me [Note: The printed editions have *praesumenti*; our three manuscripts have *praesumentis*. The manuscript in our possession reads: “I feared that I might offend … and could not.” Not much later the printed editions have *statui operam* (“I decided the work”); the second Colbert manuscript has *statui magis* (“I decided rather”).], while, if I obeyed, I might be unable to perform the office I had undertaken.

Since this was so, I decided rather to offer my work faithfully than to excuse my speech obstinately, trusting that, if I displease you, you will pardon what you commanded. For whatever happens you will attribute not to my fault but to your judgment. For me, it is enough to have carried out your instructions.

# Book One of the *Hexaemeron*

## 1

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

As he is about to narrate the composition of the world, he has adopted a fitting beginning: the adornment of the works accomplished, making it the beginning of his discourse.

For the creation of heaven and earth must be reported as something that did not form itself spontaneously, as some have thought, but that received from God the causes of its own substance [Note: The printed editions have *nata* (“born”), incorrectly. The first Colbert manuscript has *nacta* (“having obtained”), correctly. A little later our manuscript has *ad rerum ejusmodi acceptionem* (“for the apprehension of such matters”).]

What kind of hearing, then, is worthy of the greatness of what is being reported? How must the mind be prepared for the apprehension of such things? Surely it must be free from carnal vices and not darkened by worldly troubles [Note: The printed editions have *intus carnalibus* (“inwardly carnal”). Our three manuscripts have *qui vitiis carnalibus* (“free from carnal vices”), correctly and in keeping with Basil’s meaning. In the same place the printed editions have *et aerumnis maxime saecularibus* (“and especially worldly hardships”). Our three manuscripts have *et aerumnis minime saecularibus* (“and not at all worldly hardships”). I judge the latter reading true and genuine, but only on the condition that *minime* occupies a place not its own. I would therefore prefer: “and not at all darkened by worldly hardships.” Basil’s expression, *ἀνεπισκότητον μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς*—“not darkened by the cares of life”—is what Eustathius intended to convey.], and indeed it must be laborious, diligent, and attentive to everything, so that it may draw toward itself a worthy knowledge of God.

But before we dispute the subtlety of the words and examine how great a meaning these expressions contain, let us consider who it is that speaks to us.

Although, because of the weakness of our understanding, we may be unable to reach the historian’s depth of heart, nevertheless, when we consider the authority of the speaker, we shall readily be led to assent to what has been said.

Moses, then, is the editor of this Scripture—Moses who is said to have been beautiful before God while he was still clinging to his mother’s breasts [Note: The printed editions have “before the Lord”; the second Colbert manuscript has “before God.” Basil has *παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ*, “before God.”]. Pharaoh’s daughter adopted him and generously raised him in royal fashion, appointing Egyptian philosophers as tutors for his education (Acts 7:20).

He abhorred the arrogance of tyranny and turned toward the humility of his fellow citizens, content to suffer affliction with the people of God rather than to enjoy the temporary fruit of sin. He received a love of justice from nature itself, since, before he assumed leadership of the people, he seems, from his natural hatred of wickedness, to have pursued wrongdoers even to the point of death.

He was driven into exile by those whom he himself had helped. He gladly abandoned the disturbances of Egypt and departed for Ethiopia. There, free from other occupations, he devoted himself to contemplation for forty years.

When he had reached the age of eighty, he saw God as it is possible for a human being to see him—indeed, as it was granted to no other—according to God’s own testimony:

“If any of you should be a prophet of the Lord, I shall make myself known to him in a vision and speak to him in a dream. But it is not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. I shall speak to him mouth to mouth, in appearance and not through a figure” (Numbers 12:6–8).

This man, then, who in enjoying the present visions of God had been made equal to the angels [Note: The printed editions have “had been equal to the angels.” The Saint-Germain manuscript, which we simply call “our manuscript,” and the second Colbert manuscript have “had been made coequal with the angels.” I think this is more accurate and better, since the Greek *ἐξίσου τοῖς ἀγγέλοις ἀξιωθείς*—“deemed worthy on an equality with the angels”—seems to be expressed more appropriately by it.], tells us what he heard from God.

Let us therefore hear the truth of the words, not in the persuasion of human wisdom but in the most fully tested utterances of spiritual teaching, whose goal is not the praise of those who hear but the salvation of those who learn.

## 2. “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1)

The wonder of my mind delays my discourse: as I consider what I should say first, or from where I should take the beginning of my account, shall I rebuke the vanity of secular thinkers, or rather proclaim the truth of our own teaching? [Col. 0869C] The Greek philosophers have discussed the nature of things at great length; but among them no account is held fixed and stable, since each succeeding one always overthrows the preceding. Nor is it worth our labor to refute what belongs to them, since they themselves are entirely sufficient for their own destruction. [Note: Colb. secundus reads: “for they could not know God.”]

Those who were unable to know God in no way granted that wisdom presides over mortal affairs; but, slipping through the ignorance familiar to them, they enclosed everything within various definitions. Therefore many of them reduced all things to confused and formless matter, assigning to the elements of the world the causes of everything. Others taught that nature contains atoms, indivisible bodies, bulges, and passages of visible things: sometimes, when those light and rounded little bodies converge upon one another, and sometimes when they withdraw and separate, they produce births and deaths; and they placed the combination of atoms in more enduring bodies, thinking that this more forcefully expressed the causes of eternity. Truly, those who describe such things weave a spider’s web—and so do those who inscribe such empty and vain principles upon heaven, earth, and sea.

For they did not know how to say: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Therefore, deceived by an inborn error of impiety, they said that everything is driven and carried along without restraint or governance, by fortuitous chance. [Note: Colb. secundus reads “without wonder.”] To prevent us from suffering the same fate, the expositor of the world’s creation, at the very first words of his account, illuminating our understanding by mentioning God, said: “In the beginning God made.” How good the order is! [Note: The printed editions read “he placed the first beginning”; our manuscript and Colb. secundus read “he placed the beginning first,” correctly. Eustathius proceeds in the same way, lest some should think that the world was unbegotten, since in writing this he did not attend sufficiently to the force of the Greek word ἄναρχον, “without beginning.” It is therefore better to interpret it in this way, lest anyone should think that the world is without a beginning.]

He placed the beginning first, lest some should think that the world was unbegotten. Then he added that he “made” it, to show that the work of creation is only a small part of the Creator’s power. For just as a potter, after shaping vessels, loses neither his art nor his power, so God, the maker of all things, possesses power not merely sufficient for one work, but surpassing it utterly in infinity. [Note: The printed editions read “surpassing rather by infinity”; Colb. secundus reads “surpassing utterly by infinity,” correctly. A little later, two manuscripts read “instructing us by teaching”; the printed editions read “instructing us by teachings.” But the translator has not sufficiently expressed the force of the verb προέφθασε, “anticipated.” I would therefore prefer: “he anticipates us with this instruction.”]

By the single moment of his own will he constructed the greatness of all that is seen. If, then, the world has a beginning and has been made, ask who gave it its beginning and who its maker is. But lest, while examining this with human reasoning, you should stray from the path of truth, he anticipated us by instructing our minds and, as though fixing upon them a seal of protection, immediately inserted the venerable name of God, saying: “In the beginning God made.”

Thus the blessed nature, the rich goodness, the beauty most beloved by all who possess reason, the source and ruler of all that exists, the fountain of life, the intelligible light, the inaccessible wisdom—he himself made heaven and earth in the beginning. [Note: Two ancient books and the printed editions have “the intelligible name,” corruptly. Colb. primus has “the intelligible light,” correctly. Basil has τὸ νοερὸν φῶς, “the intelligible light.” Immediately afterward the printed editions and Colb. primus read infacta esse (“to be unmade”); two other manuscripts read infecta (“to be unmade,” a variant form). Shortly thereafter Colb. secundus reads “comprehensible to our understanding.”]

## 3

Do not therefore suppose, O man, that visible things are uncreated or without providence—not because the things that move in heaven run about you, nor because the beginning of the circle itself cannot be grasped by our senses, should the nature of revolving bodies be believed to be without a beginning.

For this sphere—that is, this flat and rounded figure contained under a single point—does not, because it eludes our understanding and we cannot discover either where it began or where it ends, thereby compel us to say that it was not composed; nor, because it entirely escapes our senses, should it therefore really be thought to have begun “less from elsewhere” [uncertain]. [Col. 0871A] In the same way, do not let yourself be deceived into thinking that the world is without beginning or end simply because the things you see revolving are carried along within themselves, and because their surface is not interrupted by any intervening obstacles. [Note: Colb. secundus reads minus alicunde (“less from elsewhere”). Immediately afterward it reads feruntur haec quae (“these things which are carried along”). The printed editions and two manuscripts read interpolatur; Colb. secundus reads interponatur, and Eustathius is thought to have written this on account of Basil’s διακοπτόμενον, “interrupted.” Our codex then reads “and without end.”]

“For the form of it is passing away” (1 Cor. 7:31), and “heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:31). The preaching of all the commandments concerning the consummation of the age and the renewal of the world, according to the teaching of spiritual instruction, is made clear by what has briefly been handed down at present.

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” Everything that began in time must necessarily end in time. If it has a temporal beginning, do not doubt its end. [Note: The printed editions read “let us not doubt”; the manuscripts read “do not doubt.” Basil has μὴ ἀμφιβάλλης, “do not doubt.” In the same place the manuscripts read “and fictitious writings”; the word “and” is absent from the printed editions.]

Geometry, arithmetic, fictitious writings, and fabulous astrology—that is, the most laborious vanity: toward what end must all this be brought, when those who have devoted themselves to investigating such matters declare this visible world to be coeternal with the God who created all things, attributing to his glory this bounded sphere and this composite body, whose nature is incomprehensible and invisible?

They could not even perceive that whatever has individual members subject to dissolution and corruption must also have its whole body perish under the same conditions. But they have become so empty in their thoughts, and their irrational heart has been so darkened, that, “claiming to be wise, they became utter fools” (Rom. 12:1). [Note: The printed editions read “being wise”; Colb. secundus reads “claiming themselves to be wise,” which renders the Greek φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοί literally.]

So far did some of them dare to assert that the heaven is everlasting with God, existing without beginning or end, and that he is the author and dispenser of things established in their several parts. [Col. 0871C] [Note: The printed editions read “the author of things established”; our codex and Colb. secundus read “the originator,” which is shown to be the true and corrected reading by Basil’s αἴτιον, “cause” or “author.” Shortly afterward the printed editions and our codex read “to desire the prudence of truth”; Colb. secundus has “to conceive,” more correctly.]

## 4

For such men, when and where does secular wisdom begin to fear future condemnation—men who, although they look so sharply upon utterly vain things, have voluntarily blinded themselves against conceiving the wisdom of truth? Others count the distances between the stars and describe the northern stars that always shine, as well as how many of those that move beneath the southern pole are visible to certain peoples but unknown to us.

They divide the northern breadth and likewise the zodiacal circle into a thousand intervals; they carefully observe the courses and concealments of the stars and the principal movements of all things, and how much time each planet customarily takes to complete its own circuit. Yet they were entirely unable to discover one unified account by which they might say that God is the maker of the whole world and that he will assign to each person, by a just judgment, a recompense worthy of his deeds.

Nor, with the prospect of future examination before their eyes, did they form a fitting conception of the end of all things, considering that the world itself must also be renewed if the condition of souls is to be transferred into another mode of life. [Note: Two ancient books read necesse est (“it is necessary”); this was absent from the printed editions.] For just as the present life shares a kinship with the nature of this world, so the future way of life of souls will assume a condition suited to its own form.

Yet they are so far from believing these things to be true that they mock us everywhere when we proclaim the consummation of this world and the renewal of the age. Since, however, all things naturally have first principles, the writer, speaking of things that began in time, placed this word first, saying: “In the beginning he made.”

## 5

[Col. 0872B]

There was, as you see, a certain substance before this world, contemplable by our understanding but left unheard of, because it could not easily be grasped by those who were being instructed on account of the limitations of their senses. [Note: We have added the word “substance” from Colb. secundus. Not much later Colb. secundus reads “all works”; the printed editions have “certain works.” In that manuscript “intelligible” is also read in place of “intellectual.” Immediately afterward that same codex has “and of all intelligible things.”]

There was an exceedingly ancient ordering of creation, suited to the powers that exist beyond the world, brought forth without time, everlasting and proper to itself. In it God, the Creator of all things, established all his works—that is, the intelligible light suited to the blessedness of those who love the Lord.

I mean rational and invisible natures, and the adornment of all intelligible things, which surpass the capacity of our mind and whose names it is not possible to discover. We must understand that these filled the substance of the invisible world, as Paul teaches us when he says: “For in him all things were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, powers” (Col. 1:16), authorities, angelic armies, and assemblies of archangels.

But when it was necessary that this world should be added to existing things—a world that is especially the chastisement and instruction of human souls, and afterward a suitable dwelling-place for all things that are born and die—then the passage of time is recognized as having been generated together with the world itself and with the living creatures that are in it. It is constantly driven onward and flows away, never reaching an end in its passage.

Or should we not call that “time” whose part that has passed cannot be seen, whose future part has not yet arrived, and whose present part slips away before it becomes known to our senses? Such also is the nature of things that grow: either increasing or diminishing, their stability and foundation having nothing certain. [Col. 0873A] [Note: The Colbertine codex reads paria fuerunt (“they were equal”); the printed editions and two other manuscripts read par fuit (“it was equal”).]

The bodies of living creatures and plants were therefore alike, as though confined by the force of some torrent to an inborn necessity and subjected to that movement which leads to births and deaths and is contained within the nature of time, since mutable things possess a kindred property.

Accordingly, the narrator began by teaching us plainly about the construction of the world, saying that God made it in the beginning. “Beginning” here refers to what belongs to time, not to what pertains to antiquity, which precedes all things. Therefore he did not say, “In the beginning God made,” with reference to that antiquity; rather, after those invisible and intelligible things, he recounts the beginning of the generation of things that are seen and grasped by the senses.

“Beginning” is also used of a first movement, as when the beginning of a straight path is to do what is right (Prov. 16:5). For by righteous works we are stirred toward blessed living.

It is also used of the beginning of something made from some pre-existing material, as the foundation in houses and the keel in ships; and in accordance with the saying, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 1:7). For religion, with fear, is always set before us like a kind of defense and support for the firmness of faith.

The first part of works that are to be constructed is also called a beginning, as in the wisdom of Bezalel concerning the beauty of the tabernacle. A good outcome of undertakings likewise often becomes the beginning of actions: thus, in generosity and mercy, prosperity follows from God, and in the practice of virtues, that end is attained which has been placed in the promises. [Note: Colb. secundus reads “from some sustaining material,” which may perhaps seem better and more suited to this passage. A little later the printed editions have “but also of constructible things”; two ancient books read “of things to be built,” another “of things constructed.” Colb. secundus reads “suited to the things signified,” and so forth.]

## 6

Since “beginning” has thus been mentioned so many times, consider whether the present word is not suited to all these meanings. From the time when the world’s foundation began, you can, if you retrace your steps from the present toward the past, seek the first day of the world’s creation—when the first movement came to time. [Note: Colb. secundus reads ad praeterita repetendo (“by returning to the past”), with much the same sense.]

Furthermore, since heaven and earth were founded as though they were seats and barriers, and since the craftsman is the Word, who produced the adornment of everything that is seen, as the narrator’s account of the beginning shows, and since the world was not formed without reason or in vain: surely it was destined to provide a useful and necessary outcome, if, as we have said, it gives our minds the training of rational souls and instruction in the knowledge of God through these visible and sensible things, guiding us, so to speak, by the hand, so that we might more easily contemplate invisible things, [Note: Colb. secundus reads “and may impart sensible things”; shortly afterward it reads “from the constitution of the world.”] as the Apostle says: “For his invisible things are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the foundation of the world” (Rom. 1:20).

Perhaps, because creation was constructed with such speed that no moment of time intervened, it was said, “In the beginning he made,” since a beginning is an indivisible and undifferentiated thing. For just as the beginning of a road is not yet a road, and the beginning of a house is not yet a house, so the beginning of time is not yet full time, nor even a small part of time.

If someone should perhaps object that the beginning itself is time, let him know that he will divide it into several portions: a first, a middle, and a final portion. But to seek the beginning of a beginning is utterly ridiculous and foolish. Whoever divides a beginning must necessarily make two parts from one, or rather several, since whatever has been divided is invariably split into two portions. [Note: The printed editions read “since it”; our codex reads “because it”; Colb. secundus reads “because it is always divided.” Basil has τοῦ διαιρεθέντος ἀεὶ εἰς ἕτερα τεμνομένου, “because what has been divided is always cut into other parts.”]

Therefore, to teach us that the world came into being together with God’s will and without time, he said: “In the beginning he made.” Certain interpreters, explaining the matter more plainly, said: “God made summarily”—that is, briefly and suddenly.

Let it suffice, then, to have said this much about the beginning, out of the many things that might be said.

## 7

[Note: Thus Colb. secundus; the word sciendum (“it should be known”) is absent from the printed editions. Shortly afterward Colb. secundus reads “is displayed to those seeing”; this too is found in our codex, but only in a second hand. The printed editions read “to those visiting.”]

It should indeed be known that of all the arts, some are productive, some practical, and some contemplative. The end of contemplative arts is the mind’s mere activity, whereas the end of practical arts is bodily movement; when that movement ceases, nothing remains, nor is anything further displayed to those who see. For dancing and singing have no lasting product; the whole activity is consumed in itself.

In productive arts, however, even when the labor and activity have ceased, their work remains manifest, as in metalworking, architecture, weaving, and similar arts. Although the craftsman may no longer be present, the principle of the art itself is evident, and from the work we see we can admire the skill of each craftsman. [Note: The printed editions read “architecture and similar things”; Colb. secundus reads “architecture, weaving, and similar things.” This reading cannot be doubted, since Basil has καὶ ὑφαντικῆς, “and weaving.”]

Therefore, to make it clear that the world was perfected by art—since it lies open to the sight of all, so that through it the wisdom of its maker might be known—Moses used no other word but said: “In the beginning God made.” He did not say “constructed” or “composed,” but “made.”

Although some who had been overtaken by a vain opinion, saying that the world is everlasting with God, in no way admitted that it had been made by him, but regarded it as a kind of shadow of the divine power, they say that it was composed spontaneously. And although they confess that God is considered its author, they confess this in such a way as to affirm that it proceeded without his will, like a shadow from a body or a radiance from light. [Note: The printed editions read “for it is reported”; our codex and Colb. secundus read “they report.” Shortly afterward Colb. secundus reads “or a radiance from light.”]

Therefore, wishing to correct this error, the prophet used this precise form of words, saying: “In the beginning God made”—that is, he did not merely provide the cause for its existence, but made it: as a good being, useful; as a wise being, excellent; as a powerful being, immense.

When he says, “He made,” he unquestionably declares himself an artificer, who formed the world by arranging its individual members so that the whole would be perfectly harmonious and fitting in itself.

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” By these two highest elements, therefore, he indicates the structure of the whole substance: [Note: The printed editions read designat exstructuram; the ancient books read exstructam.] assigning more distinguished privileges to heaven, and placing earth second among created things. Whatever else lies between them was perfected together with these principal elements.

Thus, although nothing has been said about air, fire, or water, you must nevertheless understand them by your own prudence. First, because all things are mingled in all things. It is certain that water, air, and fire adhere to earth: fire is commonly drawn out of iron and stones by rubbing, and these themselves arise from the earth. [Note: The printed editions read per frictionem; our three manuscripts read per fricationem.] It is marvelous that while the flame is hidden in those bodies it remains harmless to them, but once drawn out externally it consumes the material in which it had been guarded.

The nature of water lies in veins beneath the earth, as those who dig wells demonstrate. We can also recognize that air is mingled with it from the fact that when the earth has been moistened and has received the warmth of the sun, it immediately exhales abundant vapors.
