Furthermore, if heaven has naturally received the higher position, while earth is regarded as lower, this is because lighter things are carried toward heaven, whereas heavy things are drawn down to earth. [Note: The ancient books read gravia (“heavy things”); the printed editions read graviora (“heavier things”).] The lower and upper regions are contrary to one another. What must we say, then, except that he who joined things most widely separated by the command of his will also ordered, according to his own judgment, whatever is embraced by the region lying between these two elements?

Do not therefore demand an account of each individual thing; rather, you must also infer from what has been reported those things that Scripture has passed over in silence.

## 8

“In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” The earthly substance, and the investigation of individual things exposed to our senses, give us so long a subject for discourse that many more sermons would be required for such an examination than for all the other matters that can be explained.

But no real advantage for the building up of the Church is gained from this. Let us therefore be content, concerning the nature of heaven, with what Isaiah has reported. Using simple words, he gave us sufficient understanding of it, saying: “He established heaven like smoke” (Isa. 51:6). [Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read “upon smoke,” incorrectly; Colb. secundus reads “like smoke,” correctly. The Greek is ὡςεὶ καπνόν, “like smoke.”]

That is, he did not establish in the structure of heaven a strong and dense nature. He also spoke sufficiently about its form, with praise of God: “He established heaven as a vaulted chamber” (Isa. 40:22).

We advise that the same should be thought concerning earth: let us not labor to investigate what its substance is, nor wear ourselves out with speculations about what underlies it, nor search into a nature empty and formless in its qualities. [Note: Colb. secundus reads “nor let us trust our reasonings”; this illustrates how, as in many other cases, changing a single letter often corrupts the entire sense of a passage. Basil has μηδὲ κατατρίβεσθαι τοῖς λογισμοῖς, “nor wear ourselves out with reasonings.”] It is enough for us to know that all the things we see upon the earth were ordered for this one purpose: that its substance might be filled with them.

You will therefore reach no end if you attempt in speech to pursue all its qualities. For if you distinguish its blackness, coldness, heaviness, density, and those qualities that are apprehended by the sense of taste, nothing at all will remain beneath the earth. [Note: The printed editions read “coldness, greatness”; our codex and Colb. secundus read “coldness, heaviness,” correctly. Basil has τὸ βαρύ, “heaviness.” Shortly afterward Colb. secundus reads “by the investigation of discussion”; the three manuscripts read “if you propose the earthly.”]

Let us therefore omit these questions, and let us not encourage inquiry into what the earth is founded upon. The mind will be tortured by an investigation whose course reaches no certain conclusion.

If you say that air lies beneath its foundation, you will certainly fail while considering how a fluid and diffuse nature, pressed down by so great a weight, has remained in place instead of flowing away—escaping in every direction from the earth’s density and always rising higher while remaining beneath what presses upon it.

If you posit that water lies beneath the stability of the earth, you must nevertheless ask how so heavy and compact a mass is not submerged beneath the water, but is supported by a weaker nature beneath the weight placed upon it. For the foundations of the water itself would also have to be sought, and again you would fail when you wished to discover by what resisting support its ultimate bottom is held.

## 9

But if you introduce some other, stronger body that prevents the earth from descending to the depths, you will have to imagine that this too is founded upon a similar barrier, which prevents what it carries from falling farther down. If, while inventing explanations, we can oppose something to this as well, another support must again lie beneath it.

The mind will necessarily continue its journey, and we shall be led by thought into infinity, always seeking new foundations beneath those already discovered. The farther we advance in speech, the more we shall be compelled to add a sustaining power to the earth, one capable of supporting all the things placed upon it. [Note: Colb. secundus reads “capable of carrying upward,” and adds “therefore you must set limits to inquiry.”]

Therefore you must set limits to your investigation, lest, while handling things altogether incomprehensible out of excessive curiosity, the word of Job should seem to oppose you and you should be asked: “Upon what were its circles fastened?” (Job 38:6).

And if you should ever hear in the Psalm, “I established its pillars” (Ps. 54:4), understand by the pillars the constructive power by which it is established.

When it says, “He founded it upon the seas” (Ps. 23:2), what else does it signify except that the nature of the waters, poured around on every side, encloses the globe of the earth?

How, then, since water is fluid and always tends toward lower places, does it remain suspended and not spread in one direction or another? You do not consider either that the earth itself presents us with no smaller, but even greater, difficulty, since it is held balanced in the air by so great a weight of its own.

Whether, then, you grant that it is placed upon itself, or say that it is carried upon the waters, we must never depart from thoughts of piety; rather, let us confess that all things are held together by the power of the Creator.

We ought both to persuade ourselves of this and to answer those who ask where the earth’s great and unsupported weight is fixed, saying: “For the foundations of the earth are in the hand of God” (Ps. XCXIV, 4). This answer may be found more convenient for us to believe and more useful to those who hear it.

## 10

[Note: The printed editions read “they speculate by a certain arrangement: they say that the earth remains immobile because it is situated in the world.” Colb. secundus has the reading given in the text. Basil has διὰ τὸ τὴν μέσην τοῦ παντὸς εἰληφέναι χώραν, “because it has received the central place of the whole.”]

Although some of the philosophers who study nature explain that the earth remains immobile according to a certain arrangement, they say that it is situated at the center of the world and is surrounded on every side by equal spaces; that it has no room at the top toward which it could incline more, and therefore always remains in itself; and that the surrounding equality makes it impossible for it to find any occasion to bend toward another place.

They say that the earth occupies the central region, not by chance or spontaneously, nor because it sought that position by some allotment, but because its position has been assigned to it naturally and necessarily.

Since the heavenly body has taken the farther place above, they say that whatever weights we imagine descending from the highest regions to the depths are gathered into the central place; and that the whole body must be brought to those stations toward which its individual parts have come together.

If stones, wood, and everything earthly are always driven toward lower regions, there will unquestionably be the earth’s own proper and fitting position. If anything lighter moves from the central region, it is certainly carried upward, since it is natural for the heaviest things always to seek the depths.

By “the depths” we mean the central place of the whole world. Do not therefore be surprised that the earth nowhere inclines, since it has received the central position among all things, in which it must always remain and from which it cannot be moved contrary to nature.

If any of these explanations seems plausible to you, you ought to transfer such marvels to the wisdom of the Creator, who arranged these things in this way. Their dignity will not be diminished if we uncover their rationale; but if the matter turns out otherwise, I advise that the simplicity of faith be preferred to every argument.

## 11

You will not sin if you say the same concerning heaven, although the long-winded disputation of the philosophers has discussed the nature of heaven at great length. [Note: The printed editions read plurima … disseruit (“discussed very many things”); Colb. secundus has plurimum … disseruerit (“has discussed at great length”).] Some assert that it is composed of the four elements, that it is itself invisible, and that it contains a portion of earth because of the solidity innate within it. They also say that it shares in fire, from which it is thought to be transparent, while nevertheless embracing mixtures of the remaining elements.

Others, rejecting this opinion, have added a certain fifth nature to the composition of heaven according to their own inventive judgment. They think that the aetherial body is neither air, nor earth, nor water, nor fire, nor anything else that is believed to be simple. [Note: The printed editions read “an eternal body,” very badly. Our codex has “aetherial”; two others have “aethereal,” correctly. The Greek is τὸ αἰθέριον σῶμα, “the aetherial body.”]

Their reason is that simple things characteristically possess direct motion: lighter things always tend upward, while heavier things slide downward. But neither the upper nor the lower part of the earth, in its revolving motion, maintains any entirely direct interval in relation to the roundness of the circle. [Note: The printed editions and Colb. primus read “by the motion of the vestibule,” a serious error. Two other manuscripts read “by revolving motion.” Although this is more tolerable, it does not express the force of the Greek τῇ κυκλικῇ περικινήσει, “by circular motion.”]

Whatever things have natural motions that are accustomed to change must also have changeable qualities. Nor can we believe that heaven was composed from those principal bodies called elements, because things constructed from different matter do not readily agree with one another and cannot maintain harmonious motion without some force, since their individual parts naturally possess different impulses and things composed of them are kept in continual motion only with great difficulty.

For one and the same principle cannot harmonize things that are unlike and opposed to one another, [Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read rebus interesse dissimilibus; Colb. secundus reads rebus inter se dissimilibus (“things unlike one another”). In the same place the printed editions read pugnantibus; the ancient books read repugnantibus (“opposed”).] since what is friendly to lighter things is judged hostile to heavier ones. When we hasten toward the upper and heavenly regions, earthly weight presses us down. When we sink toward the depths, we do violence to fire, dragging it downward against its nature.

The division of the elements into different parts brings causes of collapse and dissolution. Whatever is attempted violently, while nature resists, is quickly scattered, since the individual parts by which the mass is held together return to their own origin.

Because of the necessities imposed by these opinions, those who came after the earlier philosophers, having rejected their school, hastened to add assertions of their own. [Note: The printed editions read acta priorum, whose meaning is not clear. Our three manuscripts read secta priorum (“the school of the earlier philosophers”); this reading is plainly preferable if rescissa (“having rejected”) is moved to follow it. Colb. secundus reads propriam assertionem (“a proper assertion”); shortly afterward it reads siderumque substantia (“the substance of the stars”).] They maintained, as we have said, that a certain fifth nature of body exists in the substance of heaven and the stars.

Another, among the more acute thinkers, destroyed all that we have recounted and appeared to commend a doctrine of his own. If we choose to report each of these matters individually, we shall undergo the same error as they. Let us instead leave them to overthrow one another, and, setting aside all their disputation, let us follow Moses, who says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.”

Let us glorify the excellent Creator of things wisely fashioned, and from the beauty of visible things let us contemplate him who is supremely good. [Col. 0880A] From the greatness of bounded bodies let us measure him who is infinite and immense, surpassing every thought of the human heart by the greatness of his power.

Although we cannot fully comprehend the nature of creation, nevertheless the very little that is subtly presented to our understanding contains so much wonder that even the swiftest mind appears inferior to these small things found in the world. Let us therefore render to the Creator the praise due above all things with ever greater devotion:

To him be glory and honor, now and always, and forever and ever. Amen.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0879B]

### 1

With a few brief introductory remarks completed, we have discovered an intellectual depth so hidden that we might altogether despair of what follows. For if the entrance to the holy places is such, and the vestibule of the temple so beautiful and splendid that the elegance of its beauty illuminates the eyes of our mind, what must we judge the Holy of Holies to be? Who, then, would dare to handle the impossible, or who could contemplate things unspeakable, whose vision is inaccessible and whose intellectual explanation is ineffable? Nevertheless, since in the presence of the just Judge even a contemptible reward is assigned to us for our devotion alone to better things, let us not be reluctant to investigate. For although we may be thought to fall far short of such dignity, yet if we follow the intention of Scripture, with the support of the Holy Spirit we shall neither be judged unworthy nor, by the nod of heavenly grace, fail to contribute some edification to the Church.

“But the earth,” he says, “was invisible and unformed.” How, then, when both elements—heaven and earth—were constructed with equal honor, was heaven already perfect, while the earth was still unformed? Or what was the reason that it was not completed and was not visible? The earth’s complete formation consists in its own fertility: that is, in the sprouting of every kind of plant, in the abundance of fruit-bearing—or [Note: [Col. 0879] We have added “or fruitless” from the second Colbertine manuscript. Basil has καρπίμων τε καὶ ἀκάρπων, “both fruit-bearing and fruitless.”] fruitless—trees, as well as in the colors and fragrances of flowers and in the other things that, shortly afterward, produced by divine command, adorned the earth. Since none of these had yet appeared, Scripture’s discourse rightly called it unformed.

We may properly say the same also about an imperfect heaven, [Note: [Col. 0879] Thus the two manuscripts. The printed editions read “since not.” In the same place the second Colbertine reads recte, “rightly,” instead of rite, “properly.”] [Col. 0879D] since it too had not yet assumed its proper adornment, inasmuch as it had not yet been illumined by the radiance of the sun and moon or crowned with the choirs of the stars. Thus you will not seem to depart from the truth if you also call heaven unformed. “But he called the earth invisible” [Note: [Col. 0879] The two ancient books and the printed editions read “invisible,” because of the two [reasons]. The second Colbertine reads “he called the earth invisible because of the two [reasons].” In Greek: ἀόρατον δὲ τὴν γῆν προσεῖπε, “but he called the earth invisible.”] for two reasons: either because the one who would behold it—humanity—had not yet appeared, or because, lying hidden beneath the waters that then covered it, it could not in any way be seen.

For the waters had not yet been gathered into their proper [Note: [Col. 0879] The printed editions and two manuscripts read conceptaculis, “receptacles.” The second Colbertine reads receptaculis, “containers.” But whether it is read in this way or the other, the Greek word is not happily expressed. I would prefer “into their own gatherings,” εἰς τὰ οἰκεῖα συστήματα.] receptacles; afterward, when they had been collected into one place, the Lord called them seas. Thus something is invisible either because it cannot be grasped by bodily eyes, like our mind, or because it can indeed be seen by nature but is concealed by some covering drawn over it, like iron lying deep underground. For this reason, then, we should understand that the earth is here called invisible because it was covered by the surface of the waters [Note: [Col. 0880] The old books read utpote quae, “as one which”; the printed editions, utpote quod, “as that which.”]. Moreover, since the light had not yet been established, it is not surprising that it was considered invisible, since the air itself, lacking brightness, was dark.

[Col. 0880C]

### 2

But opponents of the truth, failing to follow Scripture according to its proper meaning and dragging its interpretation toward their own will, say that these words indicate the material of things: a substance that was, as it were, by nature invisible, unformed, and formless, deprived of every appearance and shape. They say that the Craftsman took this material and, according to his wisdom, gave it form, and that through it he produced everything that is seen.

If we call this material uncreated, it will undoubtedly be made equal to God [Note: [Col. 0880] The second Colbertine reads, “it will be made equal to God in substance.”] when it is judged worthy of the same honors, and will be considered deserving of the same privileges as he. What could be more impious and criminal than for something utterly confused and deformed to be judged equal in dignity to God, who is wise, powerful, supremely good, and the Creator of all things?

Furthermore, if the material is so great that it can contain all divine instruction, its substance will nevertheless appear to be equal to God’s power [Note: [Col. 0880] Again, the second Colbertine reads: “its substance will seem equal to God’s power, provided that the earth were able,” etc. The sense is no different. Immediately afterward the same manuscript reads sermo duceretur, “the argument would be led.”], provided that the earth is capable of measuring all God’s wisdom. But if the material is less than divine power, their argument will be driven into an even more atrocious blasphemy [Col. 0881A]: for, because of the inadequacy of the material, they attempt to assert that God was ineffective and idle in his works. Human weakness has deceived them into thinking such things.

Certainly [Note: [Col. 0881D] The second Colbertine and another manuscript read “certainly because”; the printed editions read “certainly how.” The second Colbertine has “having been employed,” while the printed editions have “having been employed” with a different grammatical form. Again, the second Colbertine reads “from both,” while two other manuscripts and the printed editions read “from either.”] among us every art is practiced upon some material supplied for the purpose: the smith’s craft upon iron, carpentry upon wood. In these cases one thing is what lies beneath, another is the form, and another is what is produced from the form. Material is what is taken from outside; form is what is brought forth by art; completion is what is composed from both—from form and material.

So they think it was also with divine activity: that the world received its form from the wisdom of the Creator [Note: [Col. 0881] The printed editions and the first Colbertine read “taken away”; two other manuscripts read “brought in,” which is preferable. Basil has ἐπῆχθαι, “to have been added.”], while the material had been supplied to the Creator from outside. Thus, they say, the whole world was constructed, possessing a substance sought elsewhere but receiving its form and shape from God’s power.

[Note: [Col. 0881] The printed editions read “a great occasion is given, causes,” etc., incorrectly. The first Colbertine reads “an occasion is given, causes,” etc., no better. Our manuscript and the second Colbertine read “an occasion is given to deny that God presides over worldly causes,” etc., very well. This reading is certainly such that it needs no confirmation; but, if anyone seeks one, it can be confirmed from Basil’s ἐκ δὲ τούτου αὐτοῖς ὑπάρχει ἀρνεῖσθαι, “from this it is open to them to deny.”]

From this they are given an opportunity to deny that God presides over the causes of worldly things, and to claim that he contributed only a small portion of the generation of things, as though he were [Note: [Col. 0881] The printed editions corruptly read “as though of a stock.” Our manuscript and the second Colbertine correctly read “as though of a contribution.” In Greek: οἷον δὲ ἐράνου τινὸς πληρωτήν, “as though a contributor to some common fund.” Although I strongly approve of the word stipis, “contribution,” that does not mean that I approve the whole sentence. I am firmly convinced that the sentence is defective and not complete in all its parts. It should have been written: “yet they confess that God was like the contributor of some contribution,” etc. In the first Colbertine, the first hand reads stipis; the second, stirpis, “stock.” Nor is this the only place where those who wish to correct the text have further corrupted what they intended to amend.] the contributor of some common fund. They are utterly unable, through the poverty of their understanding, to look toward the summit of truth.

They have not considered that among us art is recognized as being applied after the material, for the sake of supplying what life requires. Wool existed first, but the art of weaving was discovered afterward, so that what nature had left deficient might be supplied by art. Wood also existed first; then the carpenter’s art, taking it up and shaping it for necessary uses, brought us no small benefit. It gave the sailor an oar, the farmer a winnowing fan, and the warrior a spear.

But God, before the things that are seen came into being, comprehended everything in his mind. Desiring to bring into existence what did not exist, he considered what sort of world ought to be, and generated material corresponding to its form [Note: [Col. 0882] The printed editions read in nativitate, “in birth.” Our manuscript and the second Colbertine read in nativitatem, “into birth” or “into existence.”]. For heaven he appointed a nature suitable to it; for the form of the earth he supplied an appropriate and fitting substance. He distinguished fire, water, and air as he willed, and brought them into the order that the rationale of each required.

Although the whole world was unlike itself and composed of diversity, he bound it tightly with the inviolable bonds of a certain harmony and joined it into one fellowship and structure, so that even things widely separated from one another in position might be believed to be united through mutual combination.

Let them therefore cease from their mythical inventions and from handling, through the pitiable understanding of their thoughts, a power that the mind cannot comprehend and that human speech cannot express [Col. 0882A] [Note: [Col. 0882] The printed editions read sensui, “to the meaning.” The ancient books read sensu, “through the understanding.”].

### 3

God made heaven and earth—not each of them in half, but the whole heaven and the whole earth, that is, the substance itself together with its form. For God is not the discoverer of shapes but the Creator of the whole of nature.

Let them answer us, then: how do God’s operative power and the material’s passible nature agree, when the one, namely the underlying material, supplied nothing but what was subject and without form, while the other, possessing mastery of forms, arranged what had been offered, so that each might receive from the other what it lacked? The Creator would thus have something in which he could display the knowledge of his art [Note: [Col. 0882] The printed editions read “to display his awareness.” The second Colbertine reads “to display his knowledge”; our manuscript reads “to display his knowledge.”], while the material, having laid aside its formlessness, would assume a beautiful appearance [Col. 0882B].

But enough about these matters. Let us return to what we proposed: “The earth was invisible and unformed.”

When he said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he passed over many things in silence—fire, water, and air—which are certainly certain properties produced from those principal elements and which, as the things that complete the world, unquestionably came forth together. But the historian deliberately omitted these matters in order to sharpen our hearts toward diligent inquiry, giving us from a few indications the opportunity to investigate what is lacking.

[Note: [Col. 0882] The printed books read “Therefore, when.” The two ancient books read “Therefore, since.”]

Therefore, since it had not been said that he made the water, while it was said that the earth was considered invisible, you should reason with yourself under what covering the earth was veiled and could not appear. Neither fire could conceal it, since fire is bright rather than dark, nor air cover it, since its nature is transparent: it clearly reveals the forms of all things to those who look upon them [Note: [Col. 0882] The second Colbertine reads “clearly reveals to those who see.” The same manuscript later reads “the water had been the summit.” Two other manuscripts and the printed editions read “the water had been at the summit,” with no difference in meaning. Further below, the second Colbertine reads “but it is called empty and unformed.”].

It remains, then, for us to understand that water had been spread over the surface of the earth; for the nature of the moisture had not yet flowed into its own receptacles. For this reason the earth is called not only invisible but also unformed.

Even now the abundance of waters prevents the earth from supplying an abundance of fruits. This, then, was why it could neither be seen as dry nor be considered formed. For, as we have said, the earth’s formation consists in its natural adornment: crops waving across the plains, green meadows shining with the varied colors of flowers, highly fertile hills, and the peaks of mountains shaded by lofty trees. The earth possessed none of these things, but was still laboring to give birth to all things because of the power implanted in it by the Creator; it was waiting for the proper time to bring its conceptions into the light at the divine command.

### 4

“And there was darkness,” he says, “over the abyss.”

Again, opportunities for myths and unspeakable inventions are provided to those who twist the words of Scripture according to their own will. They do not interpret darkness as something that came into being [Note: [Col. 0883] The printed editions and the first Colbertine read “as they are known.” Two other manuscripts read “as they came into being”; this should be the reading, as is shown by Basil’s words: τὸ γὰρ σκότος οὐχ ὡς πέφυκεν ἐξηγοῦνται, “for they do not explain darkness as it came into being.” The same Colbertine later reads “a certain darkened body overshadowed.” A little later the same manuscript reads “the beginning hostile to God’s goodness.” Subsequently it has “a stain upon souls.”]—that is, as some kind of dark air or a place darkened by the intervention of some body—but say that it was a malignant power, or rather malice itself, possessing its beginning from itself, opposed to God’s goodness. They assert that this is the nature of darkness.

“For if God is light,” they say, “the power opposed to him is necessarily darkness, according to the logic of the matter—not a substance borrowing its existence from something else, but malice, the mother of itself, a stain upon souls, the producer of death, opposed to goodness.” They claim that it both exists and was made by God [Note: [Col. 0883] The second Colbertine reads “they scorn that it was made”; but neither this reading nor the common one adequately expresses the Greek. Whoever wishes to grasp Basil’s meaning precisely should consult the original source. Again, the second Colbertine reads “they are seized”; elsewhere in that book it reads rapaces, “rapacious,” instead of raptores, “robbers.”].

What impious and profane doctrine, then, is not generated from this? Will not rapacious wolves, tearing apart the Lord’s flock, take their beginning from this statement and pounce upon simple souls? From here arose the sects of Marcion and Valentinus and the accursed Manichaeans. Who could name such rottenness as belonging to the Churches without sinning? Why do you withdraw so far from the truth, O human being, seeking out for yourself the causes of your own destruction, when the statement is simple and clear to everyone?

“The earth,” he says, “was invisible.” Why? Because, clearly, the abyss had been thrown over it [Col. 0883C]. The meaning of the abyss is an excess of water possessing an infinite depth.

“But we know,” they say, “that many bodies can often be seen even through clear water” [Note: [Col. 0883] The printed editions read lucida, “bright”; our manuscript and the second Colbertine read lucidam, “clear.” In the Greek, δι’ ὕδατος λεπτοτέρου καὶ διαυγοῦς, “through thinner and transparent water”; the word λεπτοτέρου, “thinner,” has been omitted. Whether the translator or a copyist is responsible, no one, I think, could easily say.]. How, then, was no part of the earth visible through the waters at that time? Because it lacked light, and the air that still lay over the waters was darkened. When the sun’s rays penetrate the water, we often see the pebbles lying deep below; but this certainly cannot happen at night. The reason, therefore, that the earth was invisible was the covering of the waters.

He says that there was an abyss that obstructed the view, and that the abyss itself was darkened. Therefore we do not say that the abyss was a multitude of hostile powers, as some falsely argue, nor that darkness was some original, evil substance opposed to goodness.

For two things set against each other in opposition must necessarily be destructive to one another’s substance and must produce everlasting conflicts between themselves, being bound to one another by mutual struggles. If one of them prevails, the opposing side is undoubtedly consumed in defeat. But if they wish always to make malice equal to goodness, they will introduce an unceasing conflict and corruption into things [Note: [Col. 0883] The printed editions incorrectly read “an inaccessible conflict in things.” The three ancient books read incessabilem, “unceasing.” The former reading is objectionable, not because it is less Latin—for many expressions of that sort occur in this translation—but because it cannot be fitted to the Greek ἀπαύστως, “unceasingly.”], with the sides sometimes overcoming one another and sometimes yielding to one another.

But if they declare that malice is overcome by goodness, what reason is there for the nature of malice not to have perished utterly? If, however—something that it is impious to say—they declare that goodness is overcome by malice [Note: [Col. 0883] The second Colbertine reads “but if goodness is overcome by malice, which it is impious to say.” I admit that this is fuller and clearer, but I fear that the scribe added something of his own, since Basil simply has εἰ δὲ, ὃ μὴ θέμις εἰπεῖν, θαυμάζω, “but if—which it is impious to say—I wonder,” etc.], I wonder how they do not flee from such sacrilegious blasphemy when they utter it.

We establish by this reasoning that malice did not receive the beginning of its existence from God: nothing among things that are opposed to each other can generate something unlike itself [Note: [Col. 0884] The second Colbertine reads “something similar.” Literally we may translate: “because nothing among opposites is generated from its opposite.” The Greek words are διὰ τὸ μηδὲν τῶν ἠναντίων παρὰ τοῦ ἐναντίου γίνεσθαι, “because none of opposites comes from its opposite.” Shortly afterward the second Colbertine reads “established from the light,” which is not as correct. Further below the printed editions read “toward the opposite”; the ancient books read “toward opposites.”].

For neither did the origin of death proceed from life, nor is it established that darkness was formed from light, nor health from illness. Rather, in changes of condition, transitions from opposites to opposites are always effected. In acts of generation, however, each thing proceeds not from opposites but from like things.

“Therefore,” they say, “if darkness is neither generative nor made by God, where does its origin come from?” For no living person dares to deny that it is evil [Note: [Col. 0884] The ancient books read “evil.”].

What, then, do we say? Evil is not some living and animate substance, but a certain condition opposed to virtue, cast down from goodness and lodged in the minds of the most depraved.

### 5

Therefore I do not want you to consider evil something foreign, or to suppose that it possesses an original nature of wickedness. Let each person recognize that he himself is the author of his own malice [Note: [Col. 0884] The printed editions read “the agent.” The second Colbertine reads “the author.” In Greek: ἀρχηγόν, “originator” or “founder.” We corrected the same error somewhat earlier.].

Of the things that happen to us, some arise from nature, such as old age and weakness; others occur spontaneously, such as accidental events which, intruding for the most part into affairs unrelated to them, bring us either joy or sorrow. Thus, while people are digging a well, they may come upon the discovery of a hidden treasure; or, as someone is going to the marketplace, the arrival of a mad dog may confront him.

Other things, however, are within our power: restraining the desires of pleasures [Note: [Col. 0884] The printed editions read cupiditates, “desires.” Our three manuscripts read cupidines, “desires” or “lusts.”], controlling lusts, restraining anger [Col. 0885A], avoiding what incites us, following the truth, hating falsehood, being mild or harsh in character, humble or proud.

Since we are masters of these things, we do not borrow their beginnings from elsewhere. Recognize, therefore, that what is properly evil takes its origin from the acts of free choice. For if evil descended from necessity, there would not be such fear of the laws among those who sin, nor would judges assign criminals punishments appropriate to their offenses.

Let this suffice for what is properly evil. I do not yet count illness, poverty, disgrace, or the other things that usually grieve mortals among evils [Note: [Col. 0885] The printed editions read nedum, “not to mention.” The second Colbertine reads necdum, “not yet.” One manuscript shortly afterward reads “I consider among the evils.”], since the causes opposed to these are not placed among the greatest goods. Some of them are natural and generally seem to happen to us beneficially.

Therefore, for the present silencing every interpretation concerning morals that is regarded with suspicion [Note: [Col. 0885] The printed editions read suspectam, “regarded with suspicion.” The second Colbertine reads susceptam, “undertaken,” and many may think this ought to be read. But I do not doubt that the common reading should be retained, since in Basil we read πᾶσαν οὖν τροπικὴν καὶ δι’ ὑπονοίας ἐν γὲ τῷ παρόντι κατασιγάντες, “therefore, having for the present silenced every figurative and allegorical interpretation.” I think everyone can see that when Eustathius wrote suspectam he intended to express the phrase καὶ δι’ ὑπονοίας. But here, as often elsewhere, he did not grasp the meaning of the Greek words. The passage ought to have been rendered as follows: “Therefore, for the present setting aside every interpretation consisting of tropes and allegories, let us accept the notion of darkness simply and without curiosity, following the meaning of Scripture.”], let us rather draw the consideration of darkness simply and without any subtlety into our minds.

The discourse requires us to understand that, if darkness was generated along with the world, it must be considered older than light. But if this is so, why is the inferior thing considered older than the better? Although we assert that this darkness too does not consist of a substance of its own, but is a kind of defect in the air, produced when light was withdrawn, we must again ask by what light this region of the world was suddenly deprived.

For we think that, if anything existed before the establishment of this sensible and corruptible world, it was certainly in the light. Neither the dignity of the angels, nor all the heavenly host, nor whatever else is named or unnameable, nor any rational power or ministering spirit could dwell in darkness; rather, it possessed in light and joy the condition appropriate to it. I do not think anyone will contradict this.

Whoever, then, awaits that light which is above the heavens among the promises held out to the good—of which Solomon says, “Light is always for the righteous” (Prov. 13:9), and the Apostle: “Giving thanks to God and the Father, who made us fit to share in the portion of the inheritance of the saints in light” (Col. 1:12)—for if the condemned are driven into the outer darkness, those who await the reward for worthy works will undoubtedly receive as their dwelling of rest that light which is outside the world.

Since, then, it is established that heaven was made at God’s command, suddenly stretched out and enclosed around the earth in a familiar rounded form, possessing a dense and exceedingly strong body capable of separating what is outside from what is within, it necessarily left behind it a region deprived of light, since the radiance shining from above had been excluded.

Three things must come together to produce a shadow: light, a body, and a place that is darkened. Therefore we must understand that the darkness of the world arose from the shadow of the heavenly body.

Consider what we are saying by means of a clear example. If at midday you erect for yourself a tent made of very dense and opaque material, you will place yourself in voluntary darkness within it. Understand those darknesses in the same way: they were not established as an original substance but followed upon the coming forth of something else.

They say that these darknesses lie over the abyss [Col. 0886B], because the extremity of the air is accustomed to join itself to the forms of bodies. But [Note: [Col. 0885] The printed editions read “water was already for all things.” The second Colbertine reads “water was over all things.” A little later the same manuscript reads “over the waters.”] at that time water had been spread over everything; for this reason it was necessarily reported that darkness was over the abyss.

### 6

“And the Spirit of God,” he says, “was borne over the water.”

Whether he calls this diffusion of air “spirit,” understand that the writer is enumerating for you the individual portions of the world. He says that God made heaven and earth, water and air, the latter fluid and diffused.

Or—and this is what I consider more truly [Note: [Col. 0886] The printed editions read “which I consider more.” The second Colbertine reads “which I consider more truly.” The Greek has ἀληθέστερον, “more truly.” Two manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read praecipuam, “special”; another reads praecipue, “especially.”]—and what was accepted by those who lived before us, he calls the Spirit of God, that is, the Holy Spirit. Scripture reserved this name so that it might appropriately declare its special reference to him. We should not believe that any other spirit is meant unless it is the Holy Spirit, who fulfills the blessed and venerable Trinity.

If you grasp this meaning, you will find that a greater benefit is subsequently conferred upon you. How, then, was this Spirit borne over the waters? I shall tell you not in my own words, but in those of a certain man by race a Syrian, who was as far from the wisdom of the world as he was considered close to true doctrine.

He said that the language of the Syrians was more eloquent and, because of its kinship with the Hebrew language [Note: [Col. 0886] The two ancient books and the printed editions read “because of knowledge of the language.” Here too the alteration of a single letter has corrupted a beautiful meaning. We should read not cognitionem, “knowledge,” but cognationem, “kinship,” as we learn from the second Colbertine and, even more, from Basil’s words: διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὴν Ἑβραΐδα γειτνίασιν, “because of its proximity to the Hebrew language.” Again, the second Colbertine reads “having indulged more in questions.”], had devoted itself more closely to the language of Scripture.

The meaning of that statement is therefore as follows: “The Spirit,” he says, “was borne over the waters”—that is, he warmed and gave life to the nature of the waters, like a hen brooding, infusing vital power into the things that were being warmed [Note: [Col. 0886] The printed editions read “infusing into the things that were warmed.” The two ancient books read “injecting.” In Greek, ἐνιείσης, “infusing,” a word that refers to ὄρνιθος, “the bird,” so that the sense is: “like a hen brooding, infusing vital power into the things being warmed.” EDIT.].

This, then, is how the expression “was borne over” is to be interpreted: it means that he impelled the nature of the waters toward giving life [Col. 0886D]. From this it can sufficiently be established that the Holy Spirit is not lacking generative power either [Col. 0887A].

### 7

“And God said, ‘Let there be light.’”

God’s first word fashioned the nature of light, dispelled darkness, dissolved sorrow, and suddenly produced every joyful and delightful appearance. Then the sky appeared, which had until that moment been hidden by the Lord; and its beauty shone forth with such brilliance as our sight still now attests.

The air was illumined by that light which had been mingled with it, and it extended the sharp penetration of its own radiance everywhere, throughout all its boundaries. Above, it was near the ether and the heaven; in breadth, it touched the northern and southern regions, the eastern parts, and also the western, since its nature is bright and transparent. Therefore the light, passing through it, encountered no delay or interval of time.

Just as the air immediately directs our sight, without any interval of time, toward the things that are seen, so it swiftly poured the approach of light—perceived with every speed—throughout all the limits of its structure.

The ether too became more beautifully illumined [Note: [Col. 0887] The second Colbertine reads “becomes illumined,” and I would think this should be read according to grammatical rules, unless the word aether were of neuter gender in Eustathius, who in the third book, beyond the middle, wrote: “But who could doubt that ether is fiery?”], and the waters appeared brighter—not only because they were illuminated by the whiteness of the light, but also because, flashing through its reflection, they made the appearance of the air clearer.

Thus the divine word established everything as pleasing and fitting. For just as those who sprinkle oil upon the sea make its depths transparent for themselves, so God the Creator, by the breath of his mouth, suddenly established in the world the delight of light.

“Let there be light,” God said; and immediately the command was the work, and nature came into being, because nothing more delightful in enjoyment can enter the thought of mortals [Col. 0887C].

But whenever we speak of God’s voice, speech, or command, you must understand that this does not mean that a sound was sent out through a bodily movement intending to produce some noise, nor that the air was struck by a tongue and thereby became God’s speech [Note: [Col. 0887] The printed editions read “the speech of air struck by the tongue.” The second Colbertine reads “the divine speech having been struck,” while the Greek has τὸν θεῖον λόγον, “the divine word.”]. Rather, we designate the impulse of his will as a command, because we judge it useful for those being instructed to represent it in this particular form.

“And God saw that the light was good.”

With what praises, then, can we celebrate the light, when it has received such a testimony to its goodness from the Creator? Although the divine words compel our eyes to judge it equally, speech is not sufficient to explain how much the sense of sight, which anticipates language, bears witness to it.

For if bodily beauty is formed from limbs properly arranged with one another and from the loveliness of color [Note: [Col. 0887] The second Colbertine reads “from limbs and colors composed with one another, and from beauty,”], how can we adequately declare the goodness of light, whose nature is simple and everywhere identical with itself?

We call gold good not because it has been well wrought [Col. 0888A], but because it grants us great delight through its color. Likewise, the star called Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0888] One manuscript reads “not because of its exceptional arrangement.”] is called the most beautiful of all the stars—not because of any exceptional arrangement of limbs, since it has none, but because it offers our eyes a joyful and lively radiance.

This testimony of God therefore refers not only to the fact that light is good and pleasant in itself to those who see it, but also to the benefit that was afterward conferred upon mortals through it; for this reason he called it good.

“And God separated the light from the darkness”: that is, he fashioned their natures unmixed and unlike one another in opposition, setting them apart and separating them by broad intervals, as it is said: “And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night.”

8. Now, after the creation of the sun, it is called “day”—that is, air illuminated by the sun [Note: [Col. 0888] The printed editions read “made bright by the sun”; Colb. II reads “illuminated by the sun.”]—when it remains in the hemisphere above the earth. “Night,” however, is called the earth’s shadow, which is produced when the sun, having set, is concealed. At that time, then, day was made not only by the movement of the body but also by the diffusion of the principal light, which sometimes withdrew and sometimes again returned, according to the divine command, and night followed.

“And there was evening, and there was morning: one day.” The designation “evening” should therefore be understood in a general sense. For both when day is beginning and when it is tending toward sunset, night is contiguous with it by its nearness. Nevertheless, in order to preserve the privileges of the day’s birth, he mentioned evening first, saying that night accompanies day. Before light was created, night did not exist in the world, but darkness. Thus the shadowing of the earth, which we mentioned above as interrupting the day, was called night; and after its generation it was given a new name by God: “There was evening, and there was morning.” He did not say “day and night,” but “evening and morning,” so that he might evidently attribute the dignity of the designation to the better part.

For day equally embraces evening and morning, and you will find Scripture preserving this practice everywhere in its reckoning of times. We say that so many days have elapsed, making no mention of nights, as the Psalm teaches: “The days of our years” (Ps. 89:10). And again Jacob says: “The days of my life are few and evil” (Gen. 47:9). And elsewhere: “All the days of my life” (Ps. 22:6). Thus the writer established as laws for the future what had then been recorded as the reason for the narrative.

“And there was evening, and there was morning: one day.” Why, therefore, did he not say “the first,” but “one”? [Note: [Col. 0888] The printed editions read “because certainly”; two ancient books read “and certainly.” The Greek has καὶ τοίγε (“and indeed”). In the same place the printed editions read “who will go on to speak”; Colb. II, “who was going to speak”; two other manuscripts, “who is going to speak.”] Certainly it would have been more natural for one who was going to speak of a second, third, and fourth day to call it “the first day” rather than “one.”

But he said this either by defining simultaneously the measure of the day together with the night and joining the duration of both [Col. 0889A], so that the twenty-four hours might seem to constitute the span of one day [Note: [Col. 0889] Two ancient books and the printed editions read “touching both equally.” Colb. II reads “joining both equally,” which we have judged should be written so because of the Greek συνάπτων (“joining”). Shortly afterward the printed editions read “seem to produce”; our three manuscripts, “would seem to produce.”]—with the understanding, of course, that by the designation “day,” night also ought to be understood—or perhaps he said “one” because in heaven, through the fixed signs, the sun’s setting forth and return are celebrated again within the same single day. Thus, whenever evening or morning, according to the sun’s circuit, encompasses the globe of the earth, it customarily defines its proper course within no longer a period than that of one day.

Or, as a more hidden explanation teaches: when God created the nature of time, he established its measure and fixed signs according to intervals of days. He wished it to be counted by the week, and commanded it always to turn back into itself, measuring the movement of time; and he ordered the week to be completed again within the span of one day, since it turns back into itself seven times. [Note: [Col. 0889] Two ancient books and the printed editions add: “and he ordered the week to be completed again within the span of one day.” Colb. II reads as in the text. In the same place our manuscript reads “which is seven times.”]

This is the nature of revolving patterns: beginning from themselves, they are always carried back into themselves. The same is characteristic of the ages, which, continually revolving through their own tracks, never reach an end by any means. For this reason he called the summit of time not “the first day” but “one day,” so that by the designation itself its kinship with the age might be preserved.

For “one” is a name fittingly and entirely appropriately given to things that are simple and have nothing in common with others, indicating the pattern of what is singular. And although Scripture declares many ages to us, saying that there are “ages of ages,” yet even there the first, second, or third age is not numbered. Hence it is differences of causes and actions, rather than the cycles, successions, and endings of ages, that are understood.

“For,” it says, “the day of the Lord is great and very bright” (Joel 2:11). And elsewhere: “Why do you wish for the day of the Lord? It is darkness, and not light” (Amos 5:18). But he called those darknesses the darknesses assigned to the deserving. The discourse testifies that that day is unfailing and everlasting, and the Psalm also calls it “the eighth,” since it is regarded as lying outside time.

Therefore, whether you call it a day, an age, or the seventh [Note: [Col. 0889] The printed editions and Colb. I read “whether you call it an age or the seventh.” Colb. II reads “whether you call it the second seventh.” Our old manuscript reads “whether you call it the seventh age.” I suspect that all these readings contain some defect. It seems likely to me that the word “seventh” was displaced and should be restored somewhat earlier, as follows: “For it is regarded as the seventh outside time.” This conjecture is considerably supported by the wording of Basil: διὰ τὸ ἔξω κεῖσθαι τοῦ ἑβδοματικοῦ τούτου χρόνου (“because it lies outside this weekly time”). Whatever the truth may be, we have changed nothing in the text, following the authority of the ancient books. A little later Colb. II reads “as the sun in brightness.”], the meaning is drawn from the same source and is declared as singular, not multiple.

Therefore, in order to direct our thoughts toward the life to come, he rightly called the principal day—which is the image of the ages—“one,” since it is coeval with the light. I mean the holy Lord’s Day, on which the Savior was glorified by his resurrection. This is what he said: “There was evening, and there was morning: one day.”

But though the account of that evening has been treated, the present evening brings our discourse to an end. May the Father of the true light, who adorned the day with heavenly radiance and brightened the night with rays of fire, who prepared the rest of the age to come for those who are worthy, illuminate your hearts with the knowledge of truth and preserve your life undefiled, granting you to walk honorably, so that you may shine like the sun in the brightness of his saints, for my rejoicing on the day of the Lord—to whom be glory and honor, now and always and unto ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

## 1.

The works of the first day—or rather, of the one day—for it is not right for us to diminish the dignity it earned from the Creator, since it was brought forth as a singular thing in itself and was not counted among the courses of the other days—were all discussed in yesterday’s discourse. Dividing these matters here and there, it provided morning nourishment and evening joy for the minds of the listeners. Now, however, we hasten toward the wonders of the second day.

In recalling this, I do not attribute what is said to the power of the speaker, but to the grace of Scripture, which naturally possesses the ease of being understood and inspired its love into those hearts that prefer truth to excessive persuasion [Note: [Col. 0889] The printed editions read “with all things”; our three manuscripts, “with everything.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read “facility of understanding”; the ancient books, “ease of understanding.” The Greek has τὸ εὐπαράδεκτον (“readiness of reception”). A little later the printed editions read “which belongs to persuasion”; Colb. II, “which belongs to persuasion”—correctly.]—just as the Psalm, demonstrating the sweetness of truth, says: “Your words are sweet to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103).

Yesterday, therefore, while dwelling as far as possible upon the words of the Lord, we filled your senses with delight. Today we hasten forward, eager to behold the wonders of the events that follow.

Yet we could not fail to notice that many craftsmen, who live by the labor of their hands, are standing around us and urging us to compress the proposed account by brevity, lest they be kept too long from their work. To them I reply that a small portion of time lent to God not only is not itself lost, but is repaid by him with great increase.

“For all the things that produce the causes of occupations”—the almighty Lord, opportunely granting strength to bodies, joy to minds, and also the ability to carry out their tasks [Note: [Col. 0890] The printed editions read “for all things.” Two ancient books read “for every thing.” We judge that the common reading should be retained, but that some word should be supplied after “almighty Lord,” as follows: “The almighty Lord will opportunely remove [them],” and so forth. For it is obvious even to the blind that something is missing here in both the printed editions and the manuscripts.]—[he grants these things] provided that we judge spiritual matters preferable to secular ones.

And if perhaps in the present life we cannot receive the reward of good deeds, yet in the ages to come we shall undoubtedly inherit abundant treasures. Therefore I beg you to exclude all worldly thoughts from your minds and to present yourselves to me wholly and undivided. For no benefit will be gained by bodily presence when the mind, entangled in earthly cares, is believed to be absent [Note: [Col. 0891] Colb. II reads “is believed to have withdrawn.”].

## 2.

“And God said: Let there be a firmament, and let it separate between water and water.”

Yesterday we heard the words of the Lord saying, “Let there be light”; today, “Let there be a firmament.” Yet the present words seem to contain something more. For the utterance did not remain a bare command, but the reason for which the production of the firmament is sought is declared more openly: namely, that it should divide between water and water.

Let us first consider, as we examine the matter, how God speaks. Is it in our manner—that is, in the manner of human beings, who first conceive in their minds the form of a future thing; then, gathering from what lies beneath it meanings appropriate and familiar to each person, express them; and after that, making their thoughts manifest through the ministry of vocal utterance, publish the sense conceived in the heart through the striking of the air and the service of articulated speech? [Note: [Col. 0891] The same manuscript reads “through the breath of the air.”]

How, then, should one not be called insane who declares that God needs such agencies in order to explain what he thinks, when it is more pious to affirm that the divine will and the first impulse of his mind is the Word of God?

Scripture represented this under a certain form in order to show that God not only willed the creature to come into being, but also perfected it with the cooperation of another [Note: [Col. 0891] The printed editions and two manuscripts read “with some agent at work”; Colb. II, “with a cooperating agent”: word for word, since the Greek reads διά τινος συνεργοῦ (“through some co-worker”).].

For, just as at the beginning the historian could have simply reported everything, saying, “In the beginning God made heaven,” then, “He made light,” and afterward, “the firmament,” so now he seems to introduce God as commanding and speaking, hindering us by no illusion from coming, led by traces and indications [Note: [Col. 0891] The printed editions read “led by indications and signs”; the ancient books, “led through indications.”], to contemplation of him who is ineffable.

For things sought with labor are received with pleasure and preserved with the greatest care. Things whose attainment is easy are undoubtedly possessed with weariness. Therefore, having entered upon the path of true reasoning, he directs us toward the investigation of the Only-Begotten.

Certainly, a voice uttered aloud was not needed by an incorporeal nature, since the intention of thought could not be hidden from its co-worker [Note: [Col. 0891] The printed editions read “since it could not conceal from the co-worker the intention of the appointment”; Colb. II reads “since the intention of thought could not be hidden.” We have attempted to correct the passage in this way, retaining “co-worker” and taking “intention of thought” from Colb. II.]. For the fellowship of counsels is supplied by the very power itself. A voice is necessary for hearing, and hearing for a voice. But where there is neither air, tongue, ears, nor the harsher sense of touch to carry a struck sound to the sense of the head, there speech is not necessary; rather, participation in the will proceeds from thought itself, so to speak, from its very center.

Therefore, as we said earlier, in order that our mind might rise toward the investigation of the face of him about whom we are speaking, Scripture wisely and excellently adopted this kind of mode of expression.

## 3.

In the second place, it must be asked whether the firmament was something other than the heaven that was made at the beginning, although it too is called heaven; or whether there are certainly two heavens. Even philosophers, when arguing about heaven, would more tolerably agree to have their tongues cut out than concede that there are two heavens.

They assert that there is one heaven, whose nature, they maintain, does not permit a second or third to be added to it, because, they say, the whole substance of heaven has been expended in the formation of one. For they claim that it is a single revolving body, enclosed by a definite circumference, and that, since it was sufficient for the creation of the first heaven, nothing remains for the composition of a second or third [Note: [Col. 0892] The printed editions read “there is nothing left”; our three manuscripts, “nothing remains to be.”].

But in saying this they imagine that some uncreated matter was possessed by the Creator, weaving together the falsehoods of what follows from the first fable.

We ask the Greek philosophers not to criticize our views before they themselves are able to maintain agreement among themselves [Note: [Col. 0892] We have added the word “our” from Colb. II.]. For some of them assert that there are infinite heavens and innumerable worlds. When their more aggressive opponents have overcome this pernicious claim, they think that they can once again affirm, on proofs gathered necessarily from geometry, that nature does not allow any heaven other than one to be generated.

But we declare them then all the more worthy of laughter, especially since they often seem to see very many things arising even in water. Therefore there can be no doubt about the multitude of heavens, or that the living creative power of all things was sufficient for their construction [Note: [Col. 0892] The printed editions read “but we then call them all the more worthy of laughter”; the two ancient books read “but then we call them more worthy of laughter.” A little later the printed editions read “and the living creative power of all things”; Colb. II, “and whether the creative power of all things [is living].” Our old manuscript reads “and that the living creative power,” though the word “that” was added in a later correction, either by the same hand or by a very ancient one. We have judged that the word should be included.].

If we contemplate God’s power, we shall not judge the strength and magnitude of these heavens to present any greater difficulty than the flow of liquid, which, when poured into empty vessels, sometimes swells through certain expansions.

Their proposition, then, is utterly ridiculous: they are disputing the impossibility of the Almighty.

We, however, are so far from disbelieving in a second heaven that we also profess a third, whose vision blessed Paul was not denied (2 Cor. 12:2). And the Psalm, when it names “heavens of heavens,” also offers us an understanding of many heavens.

Nor does this question seem more remarkable than those seven spheres [Note: [Col. 0893] The printed editions read “those seven orders”; our manuscript and Colb. II, “those seven spheres.” The Greek has τῶν ἑπτὰ κύκλων (“the seven circles”).] according to which the seven stars are universally said to be carried. They also say that these spheres are enclosed within one another, like vessels joined one above another, and that, driven by movements contrary to one another, they blend high notes with low and produce a certain harmonious and sweet melody.

The supporters of this view, compelled to make the credibility of their assertions acceptable by the reasoning of common sense, say that, because their ears were attentive to that sound which first resounded at creation, the senses of their ears have been deafened through daily use and the constant filling of the ears, and therefore we are less able to hear the harmony—just as in a blacksmith’s workshop the hearing, battered by the repeated blows of the workers, grows dull [Note: [Col. 0893] Two ancient books read “with ears attentively”; another, “attentive with their ears.” Basil wrote one thing, while the translator wrote another. Whoever wishes to know Basil’s meaning should consult the Greek sources themselves, as I advise.].

Leaving these calculated artifices of worldly thinkers for them to discuss [Note: [Col. 0893] The printed editions read “meditated”; our three manuscripts, “calculated.”], let us return to the discourse of the Church.

It was said by our predecessors that this is not the creation of a second heaven, but an exposition of the first. There Scripture briefly reported the making of heaven and earth; here it has given us a more careful account of how each element was completed.

We, however, say that since in the second case there is both another name and a distinct use, the heaven first made must necessarily be different from the second [Col. 0893C], possessing a stronger nature that provides outstanding benefit to all things [Note: [Col. 0893] The printed editions read “that which was made first”; the ancient books, “that which was first made.”].

## 4.

[Note: [Col. 0893] The printed editions and two manuscripts read “And the Lord said”; Colb. II, “And God said.”]

“And God said: Let there be a firmament, and let it separate between water and water.”

Before we reach the root of what has been written, let us attempt to refute the objections that we think others will raise against us. They ask us, proposing the question, whether the body of the firmament is like a sphere, as vision itself testifies; and if so, how could water, which floats and always slips downward, remain upon a firmament curved into a spherical shape? [Note: [Col. 0893] The printed editions read “how could floating water always [move] downward”; the two ancient books read “how could floating water, always and continually [move] downward.”]

What shall we answer? That what appears to us, when we look within, to be revolving in every respect is not for that reason believed to be formed externally in the likeness of a sphere. We see, for example, the marble chambers of bathhouses constructed internally in a semicircular shape, while on their upper surfaces they have a flat plane.

Let them therefore cease to raise accusations against us on this matter, boasting that water cannot be contained in the higher regions.

It remains to say what the nature of the firmament is and for what reason it was established between the waters.

It is customary for Scripture, when speaking of things pre-eminent in power, to use this expression. Thus it says: “The Lord is my firmament and my refuge” (Ps. 17:5). And elsewhere: “I have strengthened its pillars” (Ps. 74:4). And again: “Praise him in the firmament of his power” (Ps. 150:1).

Secular thinkers call a firm body something condensed, and they report that the term is used in distinction from a mathematical body. For one thing is mathematical, while another exists through the extension of intervals—that is, stretched out in height and breadth. But what is firm, although separated by spaces, also possesses hardness [Note: [Col. 0894] The printed editions read “distinguished by spaces”; the ancient books, “separated by spaces.”].

Scripture, however, is accustomed to call a body that is exceedingly strong and solid “firmament.” It often uses the same term even of dense and compact air, when it says: “Who strengthens the thunder” (Amos 4:13). Since the density of the spirit conceived in the clouds and violently bursting forth produces the sound of thunder, Scripture calls the strengthening of the thunder its “firming.”

Therefore, we now too suppose that the passage and fluidity of the waters rest upon some exceedingly firm nature and are held within the barrier of this word, since it is believed to have received its origin from the generation of ordinary waters. Or at least it is appropriate to judge it similar to coagulated moisture, or to some such material that arose from the diffusion of liquid [Col. 0894C], such as the nature of crystalline stone, which they say is generated from the congealing of waters.

A stone that possesses a naturally bright transparency and is found pure according to its nature, neither defiled by any admixture of decay nor fixed at its base by any cracks [Note: [Col. 0894] Two manuscripts read thus. The printed books read “is defiled by the ruin of something”; our manuscript and Colb. II, “by some cracks.” The Greek has ταῖς διαφύσεσι (“fissures” or “clefts”). Shortly afterward Colb. II reads “which is [accessible] to our sense.”], is similar to air in color. Yet it is not lawful for us to compare the firmament with any of these things.

It is truly childish and foolish-minded to form such an opinion about heavenly things.

Nor should we suppose that the firmament is either one of the simple elements or a mixture produced from them merely because everything exists in everything—that is, fire in earth, air in water, and other things in other things—or because among the elements subject to our senses there is no mutual affinity through the communion of causes, whether intermediate or contrary. Scripture plainly commands us not to presume anything beyond what has been granted to our senses.

Let us also not pass over without examination the fact that, after God commanded, saying, “Let there be a firmament,” the historian added, not without reason, “And the firmament was made” [Note: [Col. 0895] The printed editions read “the historian adds”; our three manuscripts, “he added.” Not far afterward the printed editions read “and the firmament was made.” Colb. II likewise reads “and the firmament was made,” adding: “for God also made the firmament.” Our manuscript reads as in the text.].

For earlier he made the firmament. And again: “God divided.” Let the deaf therefore listen, and let the blind be enlightened to see.

Who is so deaf as one who does not hear Scripture crying out so openly? Or who is so blind except one who, instructed by evident proofs, does not regard the glory of the Only-Begotten?

“And God said: Let there be a firmament.” This utterance indicates the cause of the determination. But when it says, “For God made the firmament,” it demonstrates completion.

## 5.

Let the discourse now turn to what follows: “And let it separate between water and water.”

The diffusion of the waters was infinite, as far as it can be understood, flowing around the earth on every side, so that it seemed even to exceed the appointed boundaries of the other elements. Therefore, in what follows, the abyss is said to have surrounded the earth [Note: [Col. 0895] The printed editions and Colb. I read “therefore in the following passage it is called the abyss,” using a new and unheard-of manner of expression. Colb. II reads “therefore in the subsequent passages it is said.” Eustathius wished to reproduce Basil’s expression διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν (“for this reason in what follows”), but he missed the point so completely that he could scarcely have missed it more. The words should have been rendered: “Therefore above it is called the abyss,” and so forth. The expression ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν (“in what follows”) misled not Eustathius alone but also other highly skilled writers.].

A little later we shall explain the reason for the multitude of the waters. Nevertheless, none of us—not even those who are highly learned and gaze most sharply upon this corruptible and fluid nature—will be able, by conjecture, to accuse us of uttering impossible words or of attaching to the narrative certain fictions [Note: [Col. 0895] The printed editions read “impossibilities, with certain fictions attached to the narrative”; Colb. II, “either impossibilities or things joined to the narrative by certain fictions,” more verbosely, but nevertheless reproducing to some extent the Greek ἢ πλασματώδη (“or fictitious things”). Shortly afterward the printed editions read “which we can”; the ancient books, “which we may be able to.”].

Nor will he demand proofs by which we can establish upon what the nature of the waters was founded. For by the same reasoning with which they affirm that the earth, being heavier than the waters, was balanced in the midst of them, it is necessary also to say that the heavenly water, because of its natural impulse—which always tends downward—and because it is placed equally on every side, must remain stably above the terrestrial sphere.

The nature of the waters, therefore, was exceedingly vast: it was not spread out according to the dimensions of the earth but extended far more broadly and surpassed its circumference by a great amount.

Thus, from the beginning, the most magnificent Craftsman, foreseeing what would come, established the usefulness of what followed through the arrangement of what preceded.

What, then, was the reason that the abundance of water overflowed upon the earth? Because the nature of fire was necessary for created things, not only for the ordering of earthly matters but also for the completion of the whole. Everything would be extremely scant and incomplete if something were lacking from the greatest and principal elements, which we know to be contrary to one another and devourers of each other’s substance.

For fire consumes water when it prevails in power, while water, when it becomes abundant, extinguishes fire. It was therefore necessary that these elements should neither be firmly joined together nor, through the complete failure of one, provide the cause for the dissolution of all things. For this reason the governor of the world stored up a sufficient supply of moisture, so that, without exceeding the boundaries prescribed for it, it might resist the voracity of fire.

God, who established all things according to an ordering of weight and measure, and to whom even the drops of rain are numbered, as Job testifies (Job 36:27), knew how long water ought to remain upon the earth and how much nourishment he should prepare for the fire.

This is the account of the waters according to creation.

Yet who is so wholly inexperienced in living that he does not know, if only through instruction and tradition [Note: [Col. 0896] Two ancient books and the printed editions read “through the transmission of instruction”; Colb. II, “through instruction and reasoning.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read “these arts”; the two ancient books, “those arts.”], how necessary the use of fire is to human affairs?

For not only do those arts that sustain human life need the aid of fire, but the sprouting of trees, the ripening of fruits, and the birth of animals, both terrestrial and marine, would neither have begun nor continued through the ages if the benefit of heat had been absent.

The abundance of waters, too, was greatly necessary, so that fire might continually and without interruption draw its nourishment from them.

## 6.

Finally, observe creation more attentively, and you will find the force of heat powerfully clinging to all things that arise and perish.

For this reason the earth has been supplied with very abundant waters, extending farther than they appear to extend and reaching even to the earth’s depths. Hence a more plentiful supply of water is provided for the outflow of springs and wells, and the rushing courses of torrents, so that moisture might be stored in many and various reservoirs [Note: [Col. 0896] The printed editions read “the courses and moisture”; our manuscript and Colb. II, “the courses, so that moisture…,” which is excellent. The Greek has ὑπὲρ τοῦ (“so that”).].

Thus from the eastern regions, during the winter season, the river Indus proceeds, the most violent of all flowing waters, as those who have surveyed and described the position of the world’s lands have observed.

From the southern regions flow the Bactrus and the Choaspes, and the Araxes, from which the Tanais, breaking through, passes into the Maeotian marsh.

The Phasis emerges from the Caucasian mountains, and countless other rivers, from the northern regions [Note: [Col. 0896] The printed editions read “from the regions of Arradis,” a phrase whose meaning neither Mopsus nor Oedipus could have guessed. Colb. I reads “from the regions of Arcadia,” no clearer. Colb. II reads “from the northern regions.” This reading is plainly genuine and correct, as is confirmed by the Greek ἀπὸ τῶν ἀρκτῴων (“from the northern regions”).], are carried toward the Euxine Sea.

From the western summer regions, beneath the summit of the Pyrenees, flow the Tartessus and the Ister. One of them runs into the outer seas; the other, coming through Europe, is distributed into the Pontus.

Why should we enumerate those rivers that rise in the Rhipaean mountains of inner Scythia? One of them is the Rhône, which, together with many other navigable rivers, passes through the Galatians, the western peoples, the nation of the Celts, and many neighboring peoples, and mingles with the western sea.

As for those that descend from the upper south through Ethiopia—namely, the Tages, the Nisus, the Cremeas, and the Nile [Note: [Col. 0897] The printed editions and the manuscripts read “that is, Tages and Nisus,” incorrectly. I believe that the error lies not with the copyists but with Eustathius himself. When he found ὅτε Αἰγὼν (“and Aegon”; the printed Greek is uncertain) in the Greek exemplar, he ineptly joined the syllable τε (“and”) to the word Αἰγὼν (“Aegon”), thus making one word, Τεαιγὼν. It is therefore not surprising that, rendering this name into Latin, he wrote “Tages.”]—some flow into our sea, while others descend into the nearer Ocean.

Although the Nile cannot be compared with ordinary rivers, since, in the manner of the sea, it spreads during the summer season and customarily turns the Egyptian land into a marsh, the inhabited part of the world is thus entirely filled with waters. It is surrounded no less by sea waves than it is irrigated by rivers, through the ineffable wisdom of the Creator, who ordained the nature opposing heat so that it would be sufficient.

There will, however, be a time when fire will scorch everything, as Isaiah testifies when speaking to the Lord God of all: “He says to the abyss, ‘You shall be desolated, and I shall dry up all your rivers’” (Isa. 44:27).

Therefore, setting aside secular wisdom, receive with us the teaching of truth—adorned not with the trappings of eloquence, but chiefly with the reasoning of knowledge.

### 7. Therefore: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water.” [Col. 0897C]

We have explained what the designation “firmament” means: not a hard and solid nature supported by some prop or weight. For the earth would have deserved such a name much more appropriately; but because the substance of the upper regions is subtle and rare, and is apprehended by no sense, he called it “firmament,” plainly by comparison with lighter bodies, which we are unable to reach either by sight or by touch.

At the same time, imagine a certain place that separates the moisture, assigning its thinner portion to the upper regions and its thicker, muddy portion to the lower ones, so that the original adjustment might remain, accomplished by the gradual diminution of the waters.

[Note: Our three manuscripts read *minuatione confecta*, “accomplished by diminution.”]

But you do not disbelieve in the vastness of the liquid, while you pay no attention to the power of fire, which, although it appears small to the eye, is nevertheless able to consume a multitude of waters.
