For it always draws toward itself the waves beneath it, like a medicinal cupping vessel, and easily consumes them in the manner of a lamp-flame, which, licking the oil through the wick placed against it, quickly devours it.

[Note: The editions read *oppositam*, “placed opposite”; the old books read *appositam*, “placed against.”]

Who could doubt that the ether is fiery and scorching? [Col. 0897D] Unless it were restrained within the limits established for it by the Creator, it would easily consume everything. What prevents all the moisture inserted into various things from being dried up, swallowed by the sun’s heat? For this reason the heavenly water was made and gathered in the upper region: marshes, rivers, and the sea exhale it in vapors rising from themselves, so that the ethereal heat would not set fire to everything beneath it.

Indeed, we see the sun itself suddenly dry up shallow pools in a very short time during summer. Where, then, is that water? Let the clever men show us: can anyone doubt that it has disappeared, consumed by the sun’s heat? Even though they do not say that the sun is hot, they possess such a supply of eloquence for speaking.

[Col. 0898A] And consider what evidence they rely upon when they oppose the most obvious facts. “Because,” they say, “its color is white, and it is not red or purple-red, therefore the sun cannot be fiery.”

[Note: Two old books and the editions read *calor ejus*, “its heat”; the second Colbertine manuscript reads *color*, “color.” The Greek is *tēn chroian*, “its color.”]

They maintain that its heat proceeds from its rougher revolution.

[Note: The printed editions read “from its rougher circling.” Two old books read “from its rougher turning around.” In these words Eustathius intended to express Basil’s phrase, *ek tēs tacheias einai peristrophēs*, “that it comes from its swift rotation.” But he erred in reading *tracheias*, “rough,” instead of *tacheias*, “swift.”]

This is their argument for asserting that the sun consumes nothing of the moisture. But even if what is alleged is not true, I shall not reject the argument, since it supports my position. It was said that, because of the devouring nature of fire, an abundance of water is necessary; yet it makes no difference whether the heat is natural or produced, provided that it acts similarly upon the same material. Whether flame rises when pieces of wood are rubbed together, or fire kindled of its own accord consumes whatever is thrown into it, the same result proceeds from both.

[Col. 0898B] Certainly we see the regulating wisdom of God moving the sun from one region to another, so that, by not always remaining in the same places, it may not ravage the world’s adornment through its thirst for heat. At one time he leads it toward the southern zone, at another toward the signs of the solstices according to the changes of the seasons, and from there turns it toward the northern region, so that, migrating gradually through different places, it may preserve the proper tempering of earthly fruits.

[Col. 0898C] Yet let them see whether they do not appear to contradict themselves. They assert that the sea is not increased by the additions of rivers because it is absorbed by the sun’s heat; and for this reason, they say, its water becomes salt and bitter, since it loses the taste of its natural sweetness by the seizure of heat, while the heat carries off its lighter portion and leaves behind the heavier and muddy part, like some sediment.

[Note: The editions read *rapto*, “by seizure.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads *raptu*, “by being carried off.”]

Yet those who had just been making such statements about the sea change their position again and declare that no diminution of the liquid is caused by the sun.

### 8. “And God called the firmament heaven.” [Col. 0898D]

Another name would properly have suited it. Nevertheless, “heaven” very often denotes the thickened and condensed place of this air, openly presented to our eyes.

We derive more effectively from the etymology of the Greeks that “heaven” is called *caelum* from “seeing”: they call it *ouranon*, from *tou horasthai*, “from being seen.” Thus Scripture says, “the birds of heaven” (Psalm 8:9), and elsewhere, “the birds according to the firmament of heaven” (Genesis 1:20). The same is meant by the statement, “They ascend as far as heaven” (Psalm 106:26).

[Col. 0899A]

[Note: The editions read “because Moses.” The old books read “and Moses.”]

And Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph, gives a blessing from the boundaries of heaven, from the course of the sun, from the succession of the months, and from the summits of the mountains (Deuteronomy 33:13), since that region of the earth abounds in such resources.

Likewise, in the curses against Israel, he says: “May the heaven over your head be bronze” (Deuteronomy 28:23), indicating complete drought and the failure of the moisture of the air, through which the desired fertility is supplied to earthly fruits.

Therefore, whenever he says that dew or rain is sent from heaven, understand the waters that were commanded to occupy the upper region. For when vapors have gathered aloft and the air has been condensed by the breath of the winds, these exhalations, subtly inserted into the clouds, become drops through successive additions; struck together by their own weight, they are driven downward. This is the generation of rain.

[Col. 0899B] But when the moisture has been stripped of its foam and beaten back by the violence of the winds, it hardens more intensely through the cold; once the clouds have congealed, frozen snow is carried down to the earth.

And in general, according to this account, you may expect the whole nature of waters: how they gather around the air that is above us.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read “according to its moderation, you may”; the second Colbertine manuscript reads “according to this sort of reasoning, it is permitted.” The Greek is *kata ton auton logon exesti*, “according to the same reasoning it is possible.”]

Let no one, however, wish to compare the simplicity of spiritual discourses with the arguments of those who dispute about heaven. As much as the beauty of upright women is preferred to prostitute-like beauty, so much is our speech recognized as superior to secular doctrine.

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads *valet conferre*, “is able to compare.” A little below, the editions read *meretricae formositati*, “the beauty of a prostitute”; the old books read *meretriciae formositati*, “prostitute-like beauty.”]

They are accustomed to bring forward persuasion forced upon them by words; we, however, present the truth naked, without the arts of deception.

[Note: Two old books and the editions read “we present naked deception.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads “we present naked to those who deceive.” The latter reading may perhaps have arisen as follows: Eustathius wrote *fallendi artibus*, “by the arts of deceiving,” and a copyist fused these two words into *fallentibus*, “to those who deceive.” A little later the text reads *exspectare conflictum*, “to await the contest.” There I think the copyists stumbled, writing *exspectare* for *spectare*, “to watch.” The Greek is *theatas kathēsthai*, “to sit as spectators.”]

[Col. 0899C] But why do we need to provoke a contest by refuting their lies, when we can compare their own writings with one another and await their conflict without labor on our part?

Although they differ neither in eloquence, nor are fewer in number, nor inferior in dignity, they oppose their adversaries while maintaining that fire thoroughly burns and devours everything; yet again they introduce explanations for regeneration from the seeds left behind by the conflagration of fire. Hence they also introduce innumerable worlds.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read: “Hence also, in their construction, they will have been sufficient: worlds, etc.” But the second Colbertine manuscript reads: “Hence also worlds, etc.” I do not sufficiently understand what the phrase “in their construction, they will have been sufficient” means in the common editions; nor is the alternative reading a good expression of the Greek words: *Hothen kai apeirous phthoras kosmou kai palingenesias eisagousin*, “Hence they also introduce innumerable destructions of the world and regenerations.”]

### 9. [Col. 0900A]

But deprived of the truth of both professions, they seek here and there, through poverty, supports for their error. Thus, concerning those waters that the insertion of the firmament separated, they offer us certain figures by means of allegories and a higher meaning. They say that spiritual and incorporeal powers are to be understood tropically as waters, with the more worthy powers remaining above the firmament, while in the lower dwellings, as being coarser and muddy, harmful powers have been established.

[Note: The editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read “they must be understood wondrously as waters, and again upward.” In these words, *wondrously* is extraordinarily discordant, and *again* is no more suitable. Since, however, the similarity of the words deceived the copyists, I think they are to some extent excusable. The reading should therefore be taken from the other two manuscripts: “tropically … and above,” etc. The Greek is *tropikōs … kai anō*, “tropically … and above.” Although I have excused the copyists, I do not thereby excuse Eustathius; rather, I severely censure him for translating *tropikōs* inadequately as *mutabiliter*, “changeably,” when he should have translated it as “tropically,” that is, through tropes and allegories.]

For this reason they say that the waters above the heavens praise the Lord—that is, the excellent powers who, because of the merit of their purity, are worthy to celebrate the Creator with fitting praises. They affirm that those contained below are spirits of wickedness, who have fallen from their natural height into the depths of evil. Because they are turbid and seditious, tossed about by the tumult of vices, they are called “sea” on account of the variety of their purpose, which is constantly changing.

But let us leave such arguments aside as the conjectures of dreams and old women’s tales, and understand water as real water; let us accept the separation of the firmament exactly as Scripture teaches.

[Col. 0900B] And if waters are sometimes said to offer praise to the common Lord of all, they should not for that reason be judged to possess a rational nature.

[Note: The editions read “they should be judged.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads the feminine form “they should be judged,” agreeing with *aquae*, “waters.”]

For neither, because “the heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 13:1), are they in every respect animate; nor should the sensible firmament be thought to be an animal because it declares the work of his hands.

Even if someone should say that the heavens are contemplative powers and the firmament is the creative power of God, we do not reject such a statement contemptuously, although it is an invention; but we will in no way allow it to be true.

[Note: The two old books and the editions read “the heavens, indeed, are not contemptible.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads “the heavens, indeed, are contemplable,” which is correct. The Greek is *theōrētikas*, “contemplative.” In both Colbertine manuscripts, not far from here, the reading is “we speak in this manner.” The word *nos*, “we,” was absent from the editions.]

For neither dew, nor winter frost, nor cold, nor heat, since they are commanded to praise the Creator of all things—as Daniel says (chapter 3)—are to be understood as sensible or invisible natures.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read “are to be understood as sensible or invisible natures”; the second Colbertine manuscript has the reading printed in the text.]

Rather, their contemplation, wisely undertaken by beings possessing understanding, accomplishes the glorification of the Creator.

For not only does the water above the heavens, as though excelling the others in honor because of the beauty inherent in it, render praise to the Lord; those things also that are upon the earth are invited to do the same—that is, “dragons and all abysses” (Psalm 148:7).

[Col. 0900C] Thus even the abyss, which the makers of allegories strive to cast into the worse interpretation, is not judged contemptible by the Psalmist, since it too, according to its own quality, sends forth hymns to the power of the Creator.

### 10. “And God saw that the firmament was good.” [Col. 0901A]

[Note: The editions read “that it is good.” The three old books read “because it is good.”]

He did not say that it was good by an examination with the eyes. For the things established by God do not provide us with bodily pleasure, nor is their delight to be understood in the way that things appearing pleasant to mortals are enjoyed. Rather, he called the work good because it is assessed according to the reason of its craftsmanship and directed toward the end of its future usefulness.

[Note: Two old books read: “but he called the work good because,” whereas the word *opus*, “work,” is lacking in the editions.]

Therefore he set forth plainly the purpose of the things brought forth, passing through in turn those things that were subsequently produced in their several parts by the creative word of his power, and praising them as completing the world.

[Note: The printed text reads corruptly, *merito ergo quidem in rationem gignentium manifestam esse proposuit*, “therefore rightly he set forth to be manifest in relation to the reason of the things bringing forth.” The other Colbertine manuscript has *merito ergo quae destinatione gignentium manifesta esse proposuit*, no better. Our manuscript reads *merito ergo quidem in ratione gignentium manifesta esse proposuit*, likewise defective, though readily emended. For *quidem* one should read *quaedam*: “Therefore he set forth certain things plainly in relation to the purpose of the things brought forth.” The Greek is *ho toinyn enargē ton skopon tōn genomenōn prothemenos*, “he who therefore set forth clearly the purpose of the things that came to be.”]

[Col. 0901B] For the hand, eye, and other limbs of a bronze statue, when scattered and separately thrown forth, do not seem good to anyone. But when they are brought together and arranged in their proper order, and receive the appearance of a fitting form, even an uneducated person can easily recognize them.

[Note: The editions read *affecta sunt*, “were affected.” The old books read *effecta sunt*, “were completed.” Shortly afterward the editions read “hands and eyes.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads “hands and eyes”; our manuscript reads “hand and eye.” A little later the second Colbertine manuscript often reads *projecta*, “thrown forth.”]

But the Creator of the elements knew the goodness of each work even before the individual parts were arranged; and, praising each one, the Maker directs the thought of his mind toward the future outcome of what has been formed.

[Note: The editions read “toward the outcome of the future.” Our three manuscripts read “toward the future outcome.”]

Thus God is now likewise the craftsman, defender, and praiser of the individual parts; but shortly afterward, when the whole world has been completed, he will also bestow upon it all together the praise that properly belongs to it.

[Col. 0902A] Let the morning narration of the second day now reach its conclusion, so that we may grant a recess to diligent hearers. They may compare among themselves what has been said, and, by the aid of memory, carefully preserve everything in their inmost hearts for their own benefit.

[Note: The two old books read “so that they may carefully attend to everything.” The editions read “so that they may pass through everything.” Immediately afterward our manuscript and the second Colbertine manuscript read “by constant practice of meditation.”]

Let them ruminate upon the food of instruction through the habitual practice of meditation, and, after wholesome digestion, request the nourishment of the remaining discourse.

In the meantime, let us grant leisure to those who work with their hands to earn a living, so that, when their tasks are completed and their minds released from the bonds of cares, they may once again devote themselves to the evening meal.

Meanwhile, may the Lord, who made great things from nothing and has allotted to us these small offerings of words, grant you understanding of his truth, so that from visible things you may recognize the invisible; and from the greatness and beauty of creation may your mind perceive the fitting glory of the Creator.

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads *magna fecit*, “made great things”; the other two manuscripts and the editions read *magnifica fecit*, “made magnificent things.” The Greek is *ta megala*, “the great things.” A little later the editions read “from the greatness”; the two old books read “and from the greatness.”]

[Col. 0902B] Thus, in earth, air, heaven, and waters; between day and night; and in all things that are seen, may you grasp the clearest memorials of the Benefactor.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read “between day and night.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads “in day and night.”]

For neither will time be given to sins, nor will an opportunity be left for the enemy to suggest contrary things, while the Lord remains attached to your understanding. To him be glory and worship, now and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK FOUR

### A Discussion of the Gathering of the Waters and the Appearance of the Dry Land

#### 1. [Col. 0901D]

There are certain cities whose inhabitants refresh themselves by feeding their eyes on marvelous spectacles from morning until evening. They also thrust pleasant songs and wanton melodies, producing excessive luxury, upon their senses; and, delighted for a long time by listening to them, they are never satisfied.

Yet many people are accustomed to call such men blessed, because, abandoning necessary occupations and the arts by which the means of livelihood are acquired, they spend the time allotted to their life in idleness and pleasure, occupied with empty activities. They do not know that dancing, approved by the most shameful people, establishes a public and common school of vice.

[Note: The editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read “approved by the worst people”; the other two manuscripts read “approved by the most shameful people,” which better suits the Greek *akolastois*, “licentious people.” In the same place, the two manuscripts read *perficit*, “establishes”; the editions read *perfecit*, “established.”]

[Note: Our manuscripts read this way. The word *quae*, “which,” was absent from the editions.]

Lyric songs, the music of flutes, and the songs of prostitutes, slipping into the hearts of those who hear them—what else do they cause to grow upon the spectators, who imitate actors, except disgrace?

Some, seized by the frenzied passion of the circus, dream at night that they are competing in the speed of horses: at one moment turning chariots, at another transferring the charioteers to another side, and they do not cease to revolve in sleep every thought of the day.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read “marking chariots,” which cannot be doubted to be corrupt. The second Colbertine manuscript reads “turning chariots.” Eustathius certainly intended to render the Greek *harmata metazygnyntes*, “yoking the chariots together,” but did not render it successfully. It may be interpreted better as “transferring the chariots.” Immediately afterward the editions and two manuscripts read “a prolonged thought.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads “a daytime thought.” The Greek is *tēs methēmerinēs*, “of the daytime.”]

[Col. 0902D] But we, whom the Lord—who is regarded as the greatest and most wondrous craftsman of things—has summoned to behold his works, must not grow weary of their spectacles or become sluggish in listening to the words of the Holy Spirit.

Rather, let us surround this glorious exhibition of the divine work; and, reviewing the periods that have passed in our thoughts, let us contemplate heaven, raised up like a vaulted chamber, as the prophet says (Isaiah 40:22); the earth, exceedingly vast, established upon itself through its immensity and weight; and the air, naturally diffuse and fluid, supplying a suitable and unceasing nourishment to those who breathe, parting before all things that move and yielding gently through its softness.

[Col. 0903A] Let us contemplate also the water, established as the nourisher of bodies and exceedingly useful to the human race, remaining in moderation within the receptacles assigned to it.

You will approve that these things are so from what has recently been read.

#### 2.

“And God said: Let the waters beneath heaven be gathered into their gatherings, and let the dry land appear. And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of waters he called seas.”

How many accusations you might bring against me in what follows, demanding how the earth could be invisible while its color is present, since every color is apprehended by the sense of sight! Perhaps what we have said does not seem sufficient to you, because the earth was said to have been invisible not by its nature but in relation to us, on account, evidently, of the waters poured over it, which at that time had covered all the lands.

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads “all the earth.”]

[Col. 0903B] Now listen to how Scripture explains itself: “Let the waters be gathered,” it says, “and let the dry land appear.” The covering is removed so that what had not been seen meanwhile might become visible.

Perhaps someone will also ask why the discourse attributes to the Creator’s command what belongs to the nature of waters—namely, that they always strive toward lower places.

For as long as water is held in a level place, it remains stationary, finding no direction in which to descend. But when a slope presents itself, the front portion immediately breaks through, and the remaining mass quickly follows, driven onward by the pressure of the water arriving behind it. Its movement is seen to be swifter in proportion as the water flowing together is heavier and the place more sloping.

[Col. 0903C] If this is the nature of liquid, what need was there of the command by which the waters were ordered to gather into one receptacle? For, because of their natural impetus, they could undoubtedly have flowed of their own accord into hollow regions before their rearward parts had been filled; no place on earth is so level that water can remain evenly situated.

Then, they say, how was it ordered to come together into one gathering, when we know that the seas are many and are plainly separated from one another by great distances?

[Note: The old books read *hoc*, “this”; the word is absent from the editions.]

[Col. 0904A] To the first question we shall answer as follows. You came to know the movement of the fluid only after the divine command had been issued, and you know that it is always flowing around and running downward. Before it received its movement from heavenly authority, you neither saw it yourself nor learned of it from anyone who had seen it.

You must therefore understand that the word of God is the fashioner of nature, and that the command then given to creation supplied the disposition for all things that were to be brought forth. Day and night, too, were made once; and from that time until now, succeeding one another in turn, they preserve the periods of their courses divided into fixed portions.

#### 3. “Let the waters be gathered.” [Col. 0904B]

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads: “The nature of the waters was commanded to flow downward.”]

The nature of the waters was commanded to flow apart, and it never fails in obeying the commands. I say this with reference to the fluid nature of waters: some continually pour forth as springs and rivers, while others have been gathered and remain stationary. My subject now is the flowing waters.

“Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.” If, while you are standing beside a stream, a thought suddenly occurs to you and you consider by what force water proceeds from the earth, what storehouses there are from which it is poured so abundantly, or what place it is compelled to reach, or how neither the water that follows fails nor the water that came before overflows, you will certainly discover that all these things are held together by the first word; from that word their perpetual course also proceeds.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read *te stante ... reputantem*, “while you stand ... considering”; the second Colbertine manuscript reads *te stante ... reputans*, “while you stand ... considering.”]

Therefore, in every account, always remember the first command, which says: “Let the waters be gathered.” For they had to run swiftly in order to reach their proper region; and, once they had arrived, to stand in the receptacles assigned to them and go no farther.

[Col. 0904C] For this reason Ecclesiastes says: “The rivers flow down into the sea, but the sea is not filled” (Ecclesiastes 1:7). Both the fact that the course of the waters is driven onward and the fact that the sea is held within fixed boundaries are the effects of the first command: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.”

The water that flows in was not to overflow after the receptacles had been filled and inundate all the boundaries of the earth in the same way. For this reason it was commanded to draw itself together into one gathering.

[Col. 0904D] Therefore the sea, often disturbed by winds, boiling with waves, and rising into the deep, as soon as it touches the neighboring shores, dissolves the force of its surge in foam, and immediately breaks and withdraws.

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads *vicina contigerit*, “has touched the neighboring shores.” A little later the editions read “you will not fear”; the two old books read “you will not fear” in the plural. The Greek is *ou phobēthēsesthe*, “will you not fear?”]

“Or will you not fear me?” says the Lord, “who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?” (Jeremiah 5:22).

[Col. 0905A] For it is astonishing how the sand, the weakest of all things found upon the earth, restrains the violence of the sea at God’s command.

[Note: The editions read *habetur*, “is held”; the old books read *habentur*, “are held.”]

If this were not so, what could have prevented the Red Sea from invading all Egypt—which is certainly lower—and mingling with the neighboring sea, unless it had been restrained by the Creator’s command?

Since Egypt is lower than the Red Sea, we are most certainly taught this by those who wished to join the Egyptian and Indian seas. The first of these was the Egyptian Sesostris; the second, Darius the Mede.

[Note: The printed books read “we are taught by those who.” Our manuscript and the second Colbertine manuscript read “we are taught by those who.” In the same place the editions read *Aegyptum*, “Egypt”; the first Colbertine manuscript reads *Aegyptium*, “Egyptian,” which is preferable. A little later the second Colbertine manuscript reads “for this reason”; the other two manuscripts and the editions read “for this.” Immediately afterward one manuscript reads “in the first receptacle.”]

I have said this so that we might recognize the power of the divine decree: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering”—that is, let one not proceed out of another, but let what has been collected be held in the first receptacle.

#### 4. [Col. 0905B]

Then, when he said, “Let them be gathered into one gathering,” he taught that there were many waters, divided in various ways. For valley regions, naturally hollowed out into deeper spaces, contained collected water; plains too were full, presenting the appearance of the sea; and there were other regions of the same sort. From all of these the waters were commanded to flow together into one gathering.

Let no one say that, if the multitude of waters had then covered the whole earth, those places also into which the waters were afterward ordered to come together were already filled at that time. Where, then, was the water to be collected that had invaded every part of the earth?

We answer that, when the command was given for them to come together into one gathering, the place for receiving them also came into existence. At that time there was neither the sea beyond Gades nor that immense sea, navigable only by the boldest sailors, which washes the island of Britain and the western Iberians. Later, by God’s command, sufficient capacity was prepared there, so that the multitude of waters could flow together into it.

[Col. 0905C]

[Note: The two old books read “concerning which matter.” The final word is absent from the editions.]

Since this matter seems to conflict with our account of the world’s formation—because philosophers say that the water was not collected into one gathering, as we observe—we could say many things familiar to everyone. But, lest it seem ridiculous to contend with such people, although they ought also to have brought against us the existence of marshes and pools, as well as the waters collected from rains, in order by these examples to undermine our argument, let them nevertheless understand that God called the greatest and complete confluence of all waters “the gathering.”

[Note: The editions read “but not to contend with such people”; our old manuscript reads “but not to contend with such people,” with *cum*, “with,” added, whether by the same hand or at least a very ancient one.]

A well, too, is a collection of water, formed by the descent of liquid into a deep excavation made by human hands. Not every receptacle of water, therefore, displays the name “the gathering,” but that greatest and surpassing receptacle into which the entire element was suddenly collected.

[Col. 0905D]

[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads *in quem*, “into which.” The other two manuscripts and the editions read *in quam*, “into which,” feminine. A little later the second Colbertine manuscript reads “providing all with use.”]

For just as fire is scattered among small and various materials, providing each with its necessary use, yet is contained in its entirety in the ether; and just as air, although it has entered individual bodies, nevertheless embraces the whole globe of the earth; so too the nature of water, although it is held in various assigned places, is nevertheless one immense gathering that separates the entire element from the others.

[Col. 0906A] Lakes found around the northern regions, or in the Hellespont, Macedonia, or Bithynia, are certainly called gatherings. But our present reference is to that one which is so much more extensive than all the others that it equals the vastness of the earth.

Although no one denies that smaller gatherings of waters also contain a multitude, no one will properly call them seas. Certain marshes, indeed, are infected with the saltiness of the sea, such as the one called Asfaltitis in the regions of Judaea, or Serbonitis, which lies between Egypt and Palestine and touches the desert of Arabia.

[Note: The editions read *Asflaxitis*. Our old manuscript reads *Asfaltitis*. The Greek is *Asfaltitis*, “Asfaltitis.”]

[Col. 0906B] All these are marshes; nevertheless, there is considered to be one sea, as those who have traveled through all the lands assert.

Some say that the Hyrcanian and Caspian lakes are enclosed within themselves. And since we ought to examine the cosmographical accounts of historians more carefully, let us hear what has been reported about them.

They relate that these lakes, pierced by certain hidden caverns, send their channels into the great sea; hence it is also asserted that the Red Sea flows out into the sea beyond Gades.

[Col. 0906C] “How, then,” they ask, “if God called the various stations of the waters seas because they came together into one receptacle, and if all the gatherings—that is, the gulfs enclosed by the surrounding shape of the earth—are likewise called seas, namely the Arctic Sea, the Southern Sea, the Eastern Sea, and the Western Sea; and if, again, each individual sea has its own proper names—the Euxine, the Hellespont, the Aegean, the Ionian, the Sicilian, the Tyrrhenian, and many others, whose names one by one it would be excessively long and laborious to enumerate—why did God call the gatherings of waters seas?”

But the sequence of the discourse has now led us past this question. Let us return to the matter with which we began earlier.

### 5. And God said: “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear.”

He did not say, “Let the earth appear,” lest he again show it to be disordered, as being muddy, still disfigured by the inundation of the waters, and weak. At the same time, lest anyone attribute the cause of the earth’s drying to the sun alone, the Creator established the dryness of the earth before the sun’s birth. Observe carefully, then, with attentive understanding, that not only the water which had covered the earth, but also that which lay hidden in its deeper parts, obedient to the command of the Sovereign, flowed forth.

“And it was so.” This addition is therefore sufficient, declaring that the Creator’s word was brought into effect, although it is reported in many copies of the *Cosmography* as follows: “The water which was beneath the sky was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared.” Certainly, however, neither does the published text of the other commentaries make it clear that this is so, nor does Hebrew usage express it. For after the testimony asserting, “And it was so,” a repeated account of the same things would plainly seem superfluous.

“And God called the dry land earth, and he called the gatherings of waters seas.”  
[Note: The printed editions read, “he called them seas.” But our three manuscripts read, “he called the gatherings of waters seas.”]

Why, in the preceding passage, was it said, “Let the waters be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear,” when it would rather have been appropriate to say, “Let the earth appear”; and again, “The dry land appeared, and God called the dry land earth”? Because “dry land” is evidently the designation of a property, indicating that which is subject to nature, whereas “earth” is merely the name of the underlying subject. Just as rationality is proper to a human being, while “human being” is the signifying word for the animal whose property it is, so dryness is regarded as the distinctive and chief property of the earth. Therefore the element which has specifically received dryness is rightly called “earth,” just as the animal whose characteristic sound is neighing is called a horse.

This should be noted not only concerning the earth, but also concerning the other elements: a proper quality has been assigned to each, by which each is distinguished from the others and its nature is clearly recognized—that is, water retains its own quality, by which it is shown to be cold; air possesses moisture; fire, heat.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “through which each is distinguished from the others.” The two ancient books read, “through which each is distinguished from the others.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read, “water retaining its own power.” Our codex and the second Colbertine manuscript read, “water retaining its own quality.” In the Greek: *ποιότητα*, “quality.” In the same place the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “has been demonstrated.” A little later the same codex reads, “the reason for which it was said.”]

[Note: The printed editions read, “are uninjured.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “have entered,” and this is likewise read in our old book, though only in a second hand. In Greek: *κατατεταγμένα καὶ ὑποπίπτοντα τῇ αἰσθήσει*, “those which have now been arranged within bodies and fall under the senses.”]

These elements, as the primary constituents of composite things, we can contemplate solely with the mind, according to the explanation given. But those which have already been arranged within bodies and are subject to sight possess qualities joined together in themselves, and none of them can be absolute or simple, since they are apprehended by the eyes and by the senses. For earth is dry and cold; water, moist and cold; air, hot and moist; fire, hot and dry.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “and thus by these powers nature.” The two ancient books read as in the text.]

Through these qualities, nature, being set in motion, causes all things to be joined to one another by the tempering of their mutual mixture; each element coheres with its neighboring element through a shared quality, and because of the common property implanted in each, they are mingled with their contraries. Thus earth, which is dry and cold, is joined to water by kinship of coldness; but it is associated with air through water.  
[Note: The two ancient books read, “it is joined to air through water.”]

For water, placed between them, unites them by a double quality, as though by the extension of two hands: with earth through coldness, and with air through moisture. Again, air, by intervening, becomes the reconciler of naturally opposed elements, namely fire and water: it is joined to fire through heat, and to water through moisture.

Fire, because it is hot and dry by nature, coheres with air through the intervention of heat, while through dryness it shares in the nature of earth. In this way, like a certain circle and chorus joined together, the elements appear to be perfected through their mutual compatibility.  
[Note: The printed editions read *currulus* instead of *circulus*, through the carelessness of the typesetters. A little later the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “the consummator of substance.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read, “but also.” The manuscripts read, “whence also.” In the same place the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “the principal elements.”]

I have discussed these matters so that the order might become clear by reason of which the Lord called the dry land “earth,” rather than calling the earth “dry.” Dryness did not follow afterward; it was already present, since it is what completes its substance. Therefore it is rightly honored by the privileges of this name. Hence the earth, as the principal element, also assumed the causes of its designation.

### 6. “And God saw that the water was good.”

The statement does not mean that the Lord considered good only the beauty that shone forth from the face of the sea, as though goodness were judged by the beauty of creation; rather, it means that he looks upon the things that have been made with ineffable wisdom.

For the sea is truly pleasurable to us when it begins to gleam in settled calm, or when, ruffled by gentle breezes, it displays a purple color to those who behold it; and when it does not strike the earth with violent waves but, as if in peaceful embraces, kisses it.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “it shows.” Two manuscripts read, “it displays.” Immediately afterward the printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read, “to have said the writing.” Two other manuscripts read, “to have said Scripture.”]

Nevertheless, we must not think that Scripture said that the sea appeared good to God in this way; there goodness is evaluated not by appearance but according to the purpose of its making.

First, the sea is a kind of source of all the moisture that waters the earth. Spread through hidden channels, as rocky and excavated places demonstrate, when seawater flowing through them is delayed by certain mountainous obstacles, it proceeds toward the light after the barriers have been broken through by the pressure of the force driving it, having already become drinkable through filtration, with its natural bitterness deposited.  
[Note: The printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read, “through deficiency.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “through construction” (*sic*). Our codex reads, “through purification.” I think this reading is genuine and correct, but not entirely suitable. “Through filtration” would be better, since the Greek has *ἐκ τῆς διηθήσεως*, “through filtration.”]

It also acquires a hot quality when it passes through certain metals, and becomes not merely warm but burning. We find this as well on many islands and along various maritime shores, since it is agreed that the same thing occurs even in inland regions.

Why have we said this? To establish that the whole earth is filled, through hidden and invisible channels, with flowing waters that derive their beginning from the sea.

### 7. “The sea also appeared good to God”

The sea appeared good to God because of the course it makes through the depths of the earth, and because it is the receptacle of all rivers and waters that flow into it from every direction, while remaining within its own boundaries.  
[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “and a receptacle.” The word “and” was absent from the printed editions. That is, “and because it is a receptacle,” and so forth.]

It also appeared good because it is a kind of source and origin for the waters of the air.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “a certain source.” The manuscripts read, “a certain source.” Immediately afterward the printed editions and two manuscripts read *fota*, “cherished” or “warmed.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads *cocta*, “cooked,” incorrectly. The Greek has *θαλπομένη*, “warmed.”]

When these waters have been warmed by solar heat, they release the thinner moisture in delicate vapors. Drawn upward to a higher place and made cold, since they are overshadowed by clouds, these vapors produce dews and rains.

No one will be incredulous about this if he looks at pots bubbling with heat. When they have been filled with water and placed over a fire, they are often rendered empty, although it is also asserted—sailors report this—that the water of the sea itself is boiled by the rays of the sun.

For vapors exhaling from the sea are received by sponges, and thus they relieve the thirst of those who are hot.  
[Note: In place of *penicillis*, “brushes,” we learn from the Greek exemplar that *spongiis*, “sponges,” should be read; there it says, *σπόγγοις ὑποδεχόμενοι*, “receiving them with sponges.” Not far before this, the printed editions read, “nevertheless to the Lord.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “nevertheless to God.” In the Greek we read *παρὰ Θεῷ*, “with God” or “in God’s judgment.”]

The sea also appears good because it encloses the islands, providing them with protection no less than adornment; because it makes access possible for fleets and supplies merchants with the means of acquiring wealth; and because many things unknown to the inhabitants of the lands are learned through the reports of sailors. Much deep benefit to human life is also derived from the sea. For what is abundant among us we transport to other provinces and regions, and from there in turn we bring back what is less available here.

But how will it be possible for me to describe the beauty of the sea as it appeared to the Creator? If the sea is good and praiseworthy in God’s sight, how could the assembly of the Catholic Church not be judged more beautiful? In it, the diversity of every age and sex, pouring forth voices of praise to God, produces a sound like the waves of the sea. Firmly founded in the station of peace, it endures no disturbance from the storm of the heretic.

Therefore, make yourselves worthy of heavenly reward, preserving the dignity of this order in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory now and always and for ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK FIVE  
### A discussion of grass or trees

### 1. “And God said: Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder, sowing seed according to its kind, and a fruitful tree, making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself.”

Accordingly, after the earth had drawn breath, having now struggled free from the weight of the waters, it received the command first to bring forth grass and then fodder. We see this happening even now. For the voice that was then uttered, that first command, was like a law of nature and remained fixed in the earth, granting it for the future the ability to create and to bear fruit.

“Let the earth bring forth.” Germination is the first stage in the generation of things that grow; then, when the shoot has emerged slightly, it becomes grass, and when it has grown, it is regarded as fodder. Gradually becoming mature, it is divided into joints, and thus develops until the seed reaches its proper maturity. The grassy and green appearance is common to all.

“Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder.” The earth itself, evidently, was commanded to germinate, needing no assistance. Since some people think that the sun supplies the causes of growth for plants and seeds, drawing up from their lowest foundations what sprouts from the earth by the attraction of its own heat, the adornment of earthly fertility appeared before the sun, so that the opportunity to venerate the sun as the author of growing things might be removed from those who live in error—if they could nevertheless be persuaded that before the sun itself was created, the earth was already adorned with its fruits. They should consider that, in the growth of grasses and fodder, the sun is later.  
[Note: The two ancient books and the printed editions read, “is later.” Another manuscript reads, “is more recent.” Immediately afterward the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “for animals indeed.” The word “indeed” was absent from the printed editions. The Greek has *τοῖς μὲν βοσκήμασιν*, “for grazing animals.” A little later the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “for oxen.” Two other manuscripts and the printed editions read *bubus*, “for cattle,” the old form of the word.]

What, then, shall we say? Did the Creator provide nourishment for cattle but deem our race unworthy of any care or provision? Certainly not. For the one who prepared pasture for your oxen and horses has supplied you with still greater riches and an abundance of enjoyment, and has stored up the supports of your life in the nourishment provided by those animals.

What else should the production of seeds be understood to mean except the preparation of your provision? For it is beyond doubt that vegetables and the roots of wild palms provide food for human beings. Even if some kinds of grass are suited to the uses of others rather than to ours, that very fact nevertheless appears to benefit us.
[Note: The word *illud* has been added from two ancient books.] The usefulness of all seeds is assigned to us, and this is plainly the meaning established concerning the matters just stated.

### 2. “Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder and seed-bearing seed according to its kind.”

He speaks correctly, for in this way the sequence of the account will also remain coherent. That sequence now seems in some way to contradict itself, but the necessity of nature’s ordering will be fulfilled. First comes germination, then grass, after that the succession of fodder, which is immediately accompanied by the completion of the seed.

How, then, does the statement declare that everything born from the earth is seed-bearing, when neither reed, nor grass, nor mint, nor saffron, nor many other things derive their beginning of growth from seed?

To this we reply that some of the things produced by the earth are believed to possess the power of seed in their roots and foundations. Thus, after its recent growth, the reed again sends forth another offspring from its root, which will extend the renewal of the stalk into the future. This is done not only by the reed but by a thousand other things which, growing beneath the earth, preserve in their roots a returning offspring.

Thus it has been proved true that for every growing thing either seed is available for renewing its kind, or some seed-like power has been joined to it. This is what “according to its kind” means. The offspring of a reed cannot become the source of olive trees; rather, from a reed another reed arises through the likeness of kinship. In this way what the earth produced in the first generation has been preserved down to the present through the succession of posterity.

“Let the earth bring forth.” Consider how, at the sound of a small word and a very brief command, the dry and barren earth suddenly gave birth, driven toward the production of offspring. As though laying aside a mournful garment, putting on more joyful clothing, and exulting in the adornment of its own beauty, it poured forth all that it had conceived at the heavenly command.  
[Note: We have added “the wonders of creation” from our old manuscript. The Greek reads *τῆς κτίσεως τὸ θαῦμα*, “the wonder of creation.”]

I wish the wonders of creation to remain deeply fixed in your understanding, so that wherever you may be found, and wherever you stand as a spectator before any kind of growing thing, you may receive a magnificent reminder of the Creator. Above all, when you see a blade of grass or a flower, immediately turn your thoughts to the image of human nature, remembering the wise example of Isaiah: “All flesh is like grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

The brevity of this life, the very small measure of joy, and the cheerfulness of mortals over prosperous circumstances have been most appropriately compared by the prophet to the weakness of flowers. Someone may appear today with a vigorous body, a robust face, in the first bloom of life, raging with strength and irresistible in his power. On the following day he is found pitiable, either broken by old age or wasting away through illness.

Another is likewise regarded as distinguished, filled with the greatest wealth, supported by services, surrounded by a crowd of invited friends—even false ones—and by the guards of parasites or flattering relatives. From all these people, as he goes out and returns, he earns envy together with reproach. For one who stands out cannot avoid this disease.

Add to wealth civic power as well: honors conferred by princes, commands over nations, military offices, heralds proclaiming before him in a dreadful voice, and bearers of the fasces following him on either side, bringing the gravest terror to suppliants.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “with an honorific voice.” Our codex and the second Colbertine manuscript read, “with a dreadful voice.” In Basil we read *μέγα βοῶντα*, “shouting loudly.”]

Add beatings, proscriptions, auctions, chains, and prisons, from which an intolerable mass of fear is heaped upon those subject to them.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “bringing to the simple.” Our three manuscripts read, “bringing to the suppliants,” and I think Eustathius wrote this. As elsewhere, he has poorly expressed the force of the Greek verb. He ought rather to have written, “bringing terror to subjects,” since Basil has *τοῖς ἀρχομένοις*, “to those under authority.” In the same place the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “the gravest.” The final word was absent from the printed editions.]

What follows? One night, an onset of fever, pain in the side, and difficulty of breathing in the lungs—these tear a person away from humanity; his entire stage is suddenly exposed, and all that great power appears like a dream already finished. Therefore the prophet, at the proper time, compared human glory to the frailty of flowers.

### 3. “Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder, sowing seed according to its kind.”

Up to this point, then, the sequence of growing things bears witness to the first ordering. Germination precedes everything that is generated; and if anything bursts forth from a root, such as saffron or grass, it must first germinate, then appear as green fodder, and afterward be brought to mature grain, with the stalk already turning yellow.

“Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder.” When seed has fallen into the soil and has been softened moderately by moisture and heat, it is immediately joined to the earth’s womb. Then, receiving certain generative nourishments, it gradually sinks into its veins, and, spreading tiny fibers, breaks through the swelling of the earth above it as it is born. Once firmly established, it rises easily, unfolding as many stalks upward as it has extended roots downward.

Thus the tenderness of the shoot, warmed by the vapor beneath it—which has entered through the roots by the movement of heat and is applied to the nourishment of the earth—distributes part of itself into the stem, draws part into the bark, supplies part to the grains, and extends part into the ears.

In this way, once the consolidation is complete, each thing gradually reaches its proper measure.  
[Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read, “with the gathering completed,” corruptly. The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “with the consolidation completed,” and I think this should be read. In Basil we read *τῆς αὔξεως γινομένης*, which may better be rendered, “as growth takes place, with the increase completed.”]

Whether it is wheat, a legume, a vegetable, or a shrub, each can sufficiently instruct your understanding, enabling you to contemplate the wisdom of the Creator and craftsman. Consider how the straw of grain is girded as though by knees, so that, bound together by frequent joints, it can more easily carry the burden of the ears when, bent downward by the weight of ripeness, they begin to incline toward the ground.

For this reason the stalk of oats is entirely hollow: it bears no weight at its top. Nature has equipped wheat differently, however, and provided it with length; it placed its grains most carefully in husks so that they would not be snatched away by birds. Therefore it rationally added ears to it as a means of protection, like spears, whose points repel smaller creatures.

### 4. “What shall I say, and what shall I leave unsaid,”

as I behold such abundant treasures of creation? The attainment of better things is difficult, but the loss of what is omitted cannot be endured.

“Let the earth bring forth grass for fodder.” Along with foodstuffs, harmful things also immediately appear: with wheat, hemlock; among the other seeds, hellebore, aconite, mandrake, and the juice of the poppy.

What, then? Having set aside thanksgiving for the Creator’s generosity, should we accuse him because harmful causes have been produced? Certainly not. Let us consider that not everything was made for our stomach. Foods assigned to us, both readily available and well known, are sufficient for us; everything that has been generated, however, has its own reason.

The fact that drinking the blood of a bull is deadly does not mean that the animal itself ought not to have been made or seen at all, since its labor is judged extremely necessary for the various uses of our life.

But the rational faculty familiar to human beings will be sufficient for you to avoid what is harmful. If sheep and goats possess a natural sense of avoiding what is contrary to them, discerning injury by instinct alone, will you—who possess both the faculty of speech and the skill of medical art, who investigate remedies for health, and whose extensive experience of things points out escapes from evils—be able, tell me, to avoid dangers, when none of these things has been established idly or uselessly?

For either they provide food for particular animals, or, when we are sick, they bring us relief for our recovery. Starlings commonly eat hemlock, and are said to escape its poison because of the constitution of their bodies. The passages adjoining their hearts are extremely narrow, and they digest what they have consumed before the coldness reaches their innermost intestines.

Hellebore is also used as food by quails; they avoid its deadly poison through a certain tempering peculiar to their nature. Yet all these things are believed to benefit us as well. From mandrake, sleeping medicines are compounded that are useful for the most severe pains of the limbs. Some have mitigated an extremely troublesome desire to eat by means of hemlock; others have extinguished longstanding bodily disorders through hellebore.

Therefore, from the very point at which you thought you could bring a charge against the Creator, you gain instead an increase of reasons for offering him praise.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “reasons for praise.” The ancient books read, “an increase of praise,” as required by the Greek *εἰς προσθήκην εὐχαριστίας*, “for an increase of thanksgiving.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read, “and in the roots.” The two ancient books read, “and roots.”]

### 5. “Let the earth bring forth.”

How much nourishment, then, does he say is found spontaneously in the leaves, roots, and seeds of grasses, and how much is supplied through cultivation and care? Yet he did not immediately command fruit and seed to be produced; rather, he first decreed that the earth should germinate and become green, and then that it should ripen its seed, so that that first command might become a demonstration of nature for understanding what followed.

How, then, does the earth produce seeds according to their kind, when, after sowing golden wheat, we often gather black grain? We shall say that this does not belong to a change of kind but represents a certain weakness and sickness of the seed. For what has been blackened by scorching has not ceased to be grain, as we can recognize from the name itself: excessive cold has changed the cooked or ripened forms into another seed, color, and taste. Conversely, if the field proves fertile and enjoys favorable weather, it soon returns to its former appearance.  
[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “usually foul.”]

Darnel and the other adulterating species, which Scripture commonly calls weeds, mixed into the crops among the food grains, do not arise from the corruption of wheat but grow from their own origin.

This consideration should be applied to those who overturn the Lord’s commandments and do not receive the word of admonition sincerely. Corrupted by evil teaching, they dare to mix themselves among the healthy members of the Church, so that the hidden destruction of their disease may secretly grow upon sound minds.

Yet the Lord compares the perfection of those who believe in him to the growth of seed, saying:  
[Note: The two ancient books and the printed editions read, “of those who believe.” The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “of those who believe in him,” and so forth. The Greek has *τῶν εἰς αὐτὸν πεπιστευκότων*, “of those who have believed in him.”]

[Note: The printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read, “so that a man may cast.” Two other manuscripts read, “as a man may cast.” I think Eustathius wrote either “as if a man may cast” or “just as if a man may cast,” but that the word “if” was omitted by scribes. The passage is Mark 4:26: “As when a man casts seed.” A little later the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “over a period of time.”]

“As when a man casts seed upon the earth, and he sleeps and rises, by night and by day, while the harvest springs up and grows, though he does not know how. For the earth bears fruit of its own accord: first grass, afterward the ear. ‘Let the earth bring forth grass’” (Mark 4:26).

Thus, in the briefest moment of time, beginning with germination and fulfilling the Creator’s law, the earth passed through every stage of growth and immediately brought what had been born to maturity.

You would have seen at that time every woodland gleaming with the greenness of grasses; the fields too adorned with swelling crops, imitating, in a certain way, the image of a billowing sea through the movement of the ears of grain. Every kind of grass and every sort of garden plant, and whatever was shrub-like or seed-bearing, stood forth above the earth with abundant fruits.

At that time there was no despair to be feared concerning the seeds; no negligence to be blamed in the cultivators; no inconstancy of the airs; no complaint against any cause bringing corruption upon the crops; no condemnation capable of hindering the fertility of the earth.  
[Note: The second Colbertine manuscript reads, “no inconstancy of the air.” Two other manuscripts and the printed editions read, “no inconstancy of the airs.” Eustathius rendered the Greek word *ἀέρων* more scrupulously by using the plural, “of the airs.” A little farther below the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “was in itself.”]

Afterward sin arose; on account of it we were condemned to eat bread in the sweat of our face.

### 6. “Among these things he also commanded a fruitful tree to grow, making fruit whose seed is in itself, according to kind and likeness.”

At the utterance of this word, all the groves were immediately thickened; trees accustomed to rise high—namely the olive, cedar, cypress, and pine—appeared, and shrubs were clothed with leaves, while thickets put forth foliage.

Even the plants called wreath-bearing—I mean rose gardens, myrtle groves, and laurel groves—arose in a single moment of time, though they had not existed before, each with its own distinctive character. Each was separated from the other by the clearest proof and produced with a definite designation.

At that time, however, the rose was without a thorn. Later the thorn was added to its beauty, so that pleasure might evidently be accompanied by anxiety, reminding us of the sin on account of which the earth was condemned to produce brambles and thorns.  
[Note: The printed editions read *corinaria* instead of *coronaria*, as we find written in the two ancient books. The Greek is *στεφανωματικά*, “wreath-bearing.”]

The earth is indeed commanded to produce a tree making fruit, yet we see many trees that bear neither seed nor fruit.
[Note: The word *quidem* has been added from the second Colbertine manuscript.] To this we shall reply that what is more useful deserved to be committed to memory first; afterward, for those who inquire carefully, it will become evident either that all trees are seed-bearing or that they possess a power resembling seed.

The poplar, elm, willow, and other such trees appear to produce no visible fruit; nevertheless, if one investigates more attentively, he will find seed in them.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “appear to produce no visible fruit, but a clear seed.” The words are punctuated differently in the second Colbertine manuscript, and that reading is better and more consistent with the Greek.]

A grain is attached beneath their leaves, which those who devote themselves to the composition of names commonly call *mischum*; this possesses the force of seed. For those things that arise from the planting of branches very often spread roots from themselves. Perhaps even those buds that are pushed out from the trunk possess a kind of seed-nature; farmers customarily pluck them and plant them in order to renew the kind.  
[Note: We have added the word “is” from our old manuscript. In the same place the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “and this has the force of seed.”]

First, however, as we said above, those trees deserve mention which, sustaining our life with their fruits and nourishing human beings, would otherwise have made the freedom of enjoyment seem enviable: such as the vine, which produces wine that gladdens the human heart, and the olive, which bears fruit that brightens the face in mercy.

“How many other things were then emerging together in haste, as nature brought them forth.”  
[Note: The whole passage, “How many other things were then emerging together in haste, as nature brought them forth,” has been added from the two ancient books. In one it is corruptly written *urgentes*; in the other, likewise corruptly, *urguenter*. The Greek is *ἠπειγμένως*, “in haste.”]

Thus the root of the vine has green shoots in a circle, spreading across the earth. From these the first shoot arises, which becomes the wild vine; afterward, the grape.

The vine, when wisely examined, is therefore sufficient to place the remembrance of nature before you. You remember the example of the Lord’s saying, by which he declares himself to be the vine and the Father the cultivator. He called each of us, who have been grafted into the Church through faith, branches, urging us toward abundant fruitfulness, lest, accused of idleness, we be committed to eternal flames.  
[Note: The two ancient books read, “urging us.” The second word was absent from the printed editions. In the same place our three manuscripts read, “toward fruit-bearing”; the printed editions read, “toward fruitfulness.”]

He does not cease to compare human souls everywhere to vines. Thus he says: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a fertile hill” (Isaiah 5:1). Again: “I planted a vineyard and surrounded it with a hedge” (Matthew 21:33), evidently indicating human souls, which he enclosed with the protection of heavenly commandments. An angelic guard was also placed around them, as it is written: “The Lord sends an angel around those who fear him, and he will deliver them” (Psalm 23:7).

Then, as though he were setting up stakes by which we might be supported, he established in the Church, first, apostles; second, prophets; third, teachers (1 Corinthians 12:28). In this way, raising us by the examples of the ancient saints, he led us upward. He did not allow our mind, lying entirely on the ground, to become worthy of being trampled by others.

He also wants us, bound as though by tendrils of the vine—that is, by embraces of charity—and loving each neighbor, always to strive upward with the impulse of our minds, made like branches that gradually grow until they reach the highest tops of the trees.  
[Note: The printed editions read, “by certain tendrils of a vine.” The ancient books read, “by certain vine-tendrils.”]

He also requires us to undergo digging. The mind is dug over by the removal of worldly cares, which impose a heavy burden upon our hearts.  
[Note: The two ancient books read, “which fasten.” Another reads, “which complete.” The printed editions read, “which fashion.” Immediately afterward the second Colbertine manuscript reads, “and the detestable ambitions of glory or wealth.”]

Therefore, whoever rejects the allurements of bodily pleasure and despises the detestable pursuit of glory and wealth begins, shining through the cultivation of digging, to breathe freely, after every stain of earthly conduct has been wiped away.

It is also fitting that, in accordance with the meaning of the proverb, we should not flow away in luxury—that is, we should not live ostentatiously or seek the adornment of external praise—but should show ourselves fertile, presenting diligence in good works to the cultivator.

But you, like a fruitful olive tree, should not strip yourself of every hope; always preserve the green and vigorous constancy of faith. In this way you will appear to imitate the vitality and fruitful abundance of that tree, if you lavish mercy most generously at all times.

### 7

But now let us return to an examination of the artificer’s arrangement.

[Note: Col. 0916. The printed editions read: “for an examination of the artificer’s discourse.” The old books read: “for an examination of the artificer’s arrangement.” In Greek: *πρὸς τὴν ἔρευναν τεχνικῶν διατάξεων*, “for an examination of technical arrangements.” A little earlier, in place of “but also,” we have written “but now” from two ancient books.]

How many kinds of wood then existed, some of which are fertile, others suitable for throwing, and some useful for building ships, while others are necessary for fires? Again, how varied is their appearance: the investigation of their properties is difficult, as is the distinction between each kind. For some are attached to deeper roots, others to roots near the surface and shallow; some extend upward and are fixed upon individual trunks, while others are lower; and from their stocks they send out many “eyes” or shoots.

[Note: Col. 0916. The two ancient books read *exspectatur* (“is expected”). Colb. II reads *spectatur* (“is observed”). A little later, two manuscripts read *summis et lenibus* (“uppermost and shallow”).]

Those whose tops are lofty are understood to have multiple and deeper roots, spread out in a circle. Nature has set these beneath them like foundations, so that the mass placed above may be supported. How great also is the diversity in their bark! Some are smooth and shining, others knotty and rough, some simple, and still others interwoven with many trunks.

[Note: Col. 0917. The printed editions read: “some are smooth and shining, some knotty and rough, others simple, and the rest also joined with many trunks.” If anyone prefers this reading, he should read *quarum*, although the text has *aliae, nonnullae*, and so forth. The two ancient books read as in the text. In the same place Colb. II reads: “and what is more remarkable.”]

And what will astonish you still more is that in them a likeness to human old age and youth is found. The bark of young and vigorous shoots is drawn out and stretched; that of aging trees is wrinkled and rough. Some, when they have been cut off, grow again; others, as soon as they are cut down, wither, as though suffering a kind of death from the injury of the incision.

It has certainly been proved by many that pines, when burned or cut, transform themselves into a nut-bearing grove.

[Note: Col. 0917. The printed editions and Colb. I read: “the pine transforms itself into a nut-bearing grove.” Colb. II reads: “the pine transforms itself into a great-bearing grove.” Our codex reads: “the pine transforms itself into a nut-bearing [*glandiferum*] grove.” There is no doubt that the reading should be as it is written in Colb. II and as we found and recorded it; nevertheless, in place of *grandiferum*, other codices may supply *glandiferum*.]

It is also known that certain trees, treated with the care of cultivators, have been entirely freed from their natural defect. For it is said that pomegranates, which are rather sour, or bitter almonds, can in this way be softened: if, near the root, their trunks are bored through and a wedge of pinewood is driven through the middle of the channel, it removes all the unpleasantness of their unsuitable flavor by changing it into sweetness.

Therefore let no one, clouded by the darkness of wickedness, despair of his own salvation, knowing that cultivation restores the qualities of fruits to what is better, while spiritual labor is able to overcome the depravity of every disease.

[Note: Col. 0918D. Colb. II reads *suffusus* (“covered over”). Immediately afterward, the printed editions read “the qualities of the first fruits”; the ancient books read “the qualities of fruits.” Eustathius should not be thought to have written otherwise, although he ought to have interpreted it differently, since in Basil we read *τῶν φυτῶν* (“of the plants/trees”). Shortly afterward Colb. II reads: “spiritual [labor] is able to overcome everything.”]

Indeed, we see such a great difference among the fruitfulness of trees that we cannot explain it even in words. The distinction of fruits is not found only among different kinds; in each individual kind also there is an immense variety. For the skill of cultivators is said to have handed down one form of male fruit and another of female fruit.

[Note: Col. 0918. The printed editions read *quin etiam* (“indeed also”). The two ancient books read *qui etiam* (“who also”), as does the Greek *οἵγε καί*.]

They even affirm that palms have two sexes. For it is said that the one called female bends its own branches toward the male, as though seeking intercourse, so that it may conceive from his mixture. Hence ingenious farmers are said to take certain “eyes” or shoots from the male and graft them into the female; and thus, as though filled by the desired union, she immediately returns to her former state after her arms have been drawn back.

The same things are also reported concerning fig trees. For some are said to attach wild plants to cultivated ones; others even bind the fruit of the caprifig to domestic trees, to impart strength, so that they may retain their falling buds.

[Note: Col. 0918. The printed editions read: “for if you should see someone from the nations.” The two ancient books read as in the text. A little later the printed editions read *mutuata secundum*; our three manuscripts read *mutuata fecundum*.]

The figure of this, it is believed, admonishes us to recognize that we ought often to receive from foreigners also an example of faith, so that our profession of good works may be made manifest. If, then, you see someone from the Gentiles or separated from the Church of the Lord because of heresy, yet adorned with an honorable life and conduct, you must strive more earnestly and increase your zeal more and more, so that you may draw near to that fruitful fig tree which, borrowing vigor from the fellowship of wild trees, both restrained the harmful flow of its defects and seized the support of neighboring fertility.

### 8

If, then, the principle of their generation is so great that we have scarcely been able to explain a few things in place of many, who could run through the varieties, qualities, or forms of all fruits, and the usefulness found in each, when some ripen after being cooked by the sun, while others become full under the protection of coverings?

[Note: Col. 0918. The two ancient books read *decocta … defensa* (“ripened by being cooked … protected”). In this same place the printed editions read *tegmentorum praesidio* (“by the protection of coverings”); Colb. II reads *tegumentorum*.]

And why are the leaves of those that bear soft fruit stronger, as with figs, while the membrane-like covering of those whose fruit is harder is more delicate, as with nuts? The fig, evidently, because of its weakness rightly demands the assistance of greater protection; whereas a denser, darker mass of leaves could have harmed the nuts.

How rationally, too, is the vine leaf perfected with its many divisions, so that through the part by which it is covered the grape may repel the violence of the air, while through the part that is open it may receive the nourishment of the sun’s heat. We therefore see that nothing has been made by chance, nothing irrationally. In everything there is a certain ineffable and wondrous wisdom.

But what mind, or whose eloquence, would be sufficient to comprehend everything precisely, so as both to contemplate the properties and distinguish the differences of each thing, or to search out the secrets of causes entirely hidden?

How is it that one and the same moisture, drawn up through the roots of shrubs, is distributed among numerous functions: nourishing the root itself in one way, the bark in another, the trunk in another, and the pith in yet another? How does it now become a leaf, now take shape in shoots and branches, and provide nourishment for the growth of fruits?

The same material also pours out certain tears through the branches. Who could explain how greatly they differ from one another? One is the tear of the mastic tree, another the sap of balsam, and another the sweat that flows from the reeds of Egypt and Libya.

[Note: Col. 0919. The printed editions read *lacryma scini* (“the tear of the schinus”). Our codex reads *schini*. The Greek in Basil is *σχίνου*, “of the mastic tree.”]

There is also a report that amber is the tear of a certain tree, hardened in the manner of a stone. Testimony to this is provided by twigs and tiny creatures that, settling in the flowing amber sap, remained trapped when it hardened.

And in general, unless someone has learned through experience, he cannot give a complete account of their qualities: how, again, from the same moisture the vine produces wine and the olive produces oil. Nor is the marvel merely that in one place it becomes sweet and in another oily; rather, a very great multiplicity of flavor is displayed in the fruits themselves.

[Note: Col. 0919. The printed editions read *saporis imitatione* (“by imitation of flavor”). Colb. I reads *saporis mutatione* (“by change of flavor”). Colb. II reads *saporis mutatio* (“a change of flavor”), as does our ancient book in a second hand. The Greek is *ἡ παραλλαγὴ τῆς ποιότητος*, “the alteration of quality.”]

For the quality of sweetness in a grape is one thing, in an apple another, in a fig another, and in a date another. I therefore want you to examine this matter still more minutely: how moisture that is most pleasing to the sense of the lips and to taste becomes sweet in certain fruits when they reach maturity, while in others it is harsh and troubling when it turns sour.

It distresses the senses through excessive bitterness when it spreads through wormwood or scammony. In oak fruits and cornelian-cherry fruits it becomes astringent and hard; in the terebinth and the nut, however, it takes on a soft and fatty substance.

### 9

But why should we pursue distant examples, when in one and the same fig the moisture is at one time exceedingly bitter in the sap and at another exceedingly sweet in the fruit, while in the vine it is harsh when it buds and pleasant in the ripe grape?

What distinctions of colors, one might say, are there! Indeed, if at some time you look upon flowering fields, you will see the same moisture appearing crimson in one flower, but purple, white, or golden in another; and it displays an even greater difference of fragrance than of color.

But now I feel that my discourse, in its eagerness for contemplation, is spreading into boundless spaces. Unless I restrain it and bring it back to the necessities of creation, the day will surely fail me while I unfold to you the magnificent wisdom that appears through comparison with lesser things.

“Let the earth bring forth a fruitful tree, making fruit.” As soon as the command was given, the mountain ridges thickened with trees clothed in foliage; cultivated gardens appeared; the banks of rivers were filled with different kinds of leaves. Some were arranged to adorn the tables of mortals, some to provide food for cattle, and others were fitted for medicinal uses.

[Note: Col. 0920. Colb. II reads *usibus aptabantur* (“were fitted for uses”). The common editions continue: “for, to speak briefly.” But in the two ancient books we found the text exactly as we have printed it.]

To speak briefly, whatever long experience with things has gathered for us—collecting necessities from every direction—the Creator’s swift dispensation established from the beginning, foreseeing what would be needed in the future, that these things should come into being.

But when you see domestic, wild, terrestrial, aquatic, and flowering things, recognize the greater through the lesser. Do so, however, in such a way that you add love of the Creator to your admiration, asking how he makes certain kinds of wood always remain green, while others are stripped bare in winter.

Some of those that are always green are accustomed to change their leaves secretly, so that they can never be deprived of their own foliage, as with the olive or pine.

[Note: Col. 0920. This sentence has been added from the two ancient books.]
