Others he commands to remain clothed in everlasting leaves, such as the palm, which is believed to be content with the leaves received from its original sprouting until the very end.

Consider also how the tree called the tamarisk is, as it were, of an ambiguous kind, since it delights no less in moist places than in dry ones. For this reason Jeremiah (17:16) wisely compares varied and changeable dispositions to this shrub.

### 10

“Let the earth bring forth.” This small command therefore compels it, in each yearly cycle, to produce from its own powers the strength it possesses for forming and bringing forth kinds of herbs, seeds, and trees.

[Note: Col. 0920. The printed editions and Colb. I read *quantas habet, singulorum curriculis*, a very poor text. Our codex and Colb. II read *quantas habet, singulis annorum curriculis* (“the strength it possesses in each yearly cycle”). The Greek is *καθ’ ἑκάστην ἔτους περίοδον*, “in each annual cycle.” In the same place the printed editions read *ad infirmandum* (“for weakening”); the ancient books read *ad informandum* (“for forming”).]

For just as a wooden spinning top, set in motion by the blow of the first lash, traces winding circles in curved courses and, once fixed on its sharp point, carries itself around, so the order of nature, having received its beginning from God’s first command, passes through every age until it reaches the common limit and end.

Let us also hasten toward that end, filled with the fruits of good works, so that, planted in the house of the Lord, we may flourish in the court of the most merciful God, in Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and honor always and for ages of ages. Amen.

## BOOK SIX

### 1

Spectators at athletic contests ought to share in the condition of the combatants. This is readily proved by the organizers of the lustral games, who order those gathered in the stadium to sit with uncovered heads. For this reason, as it seems to me, each spectator is expected not merely to be present as a spectator but also to become a participant in the sweat.

Thus the seeker of the greatest and most excellent spectacles, and the listener to supreme and ineffable wisdom, ought to bring his own reasons to the contemplation of the subject before him and, as far as he can, share the burden of the labor with me, considering himself more a companion than a judge. Otherwise the discovery of truth may escape us, and through my fault a common loss may come upon the hearers.

[Note: Col. 0919. The printed editions and two manuscripts read *partiri laboris hujus, ut poterit* (“share this labor, as he can”). Colb. II reads *partiri laboris onus, ut poterit* (“share the burden of this labor, as he can”).]

Why have I said this? Because we have before us a discussion of the composition of the world, one whose beginning was not taken from secular wisdom, but from what the Lord taught his servant Moses, speaking to him plainly and not in figures. Therefore those most devoted to the study of great matters must attend to the questions before them, not with an untrained mind.

[Note: Col. 0921. The two ancient books and the printed editions read *inexercitatos* (“untrained”). Another manuscript reads *inexercitato* (“with an untrained [mind]”).]

Accordingly, if at some time, beneath the serenity of night, you have looked down upon the ineffable beauty of the stars, I believe that, captivated, you have asked about the creator of all things: who adorned the sky with such flowers, and how, in the things that are seen, usefulness is found together with greater delight.

[Note: Col. 0921. The two ancient books and the printed editions read *pulchritudinem desuspexisti*. Colb. II reads *desuper aspexisti*, “you looked down from above.” I know that *desuspicere* is not a Latin word, but I do not know how the reading should be corrected. Since Eustathius often uses non-Latin words, he may perhaps have used such a word here also. Let each reader adopt whichever reading he prefers.]

And if during the day, examining things with a sober mind, you have considered the daily wonders and, through the order of visible things, reflected upon him who is invisible, you have certainly come prepared to listen, showing yourself worthy of the solemnity of this honorable and blessed spectacle.

[Note: Col. 0921. The printed editions and Colb. I read *diuturna miracula* (“lasting wonders”). Colb. II reads *divina miracula* (“divine wonders”). Our old book reads *diurna miracula* (“daily wonders”), and this is clearly the reading required by the Greek *τὰ τῆς ἡμέρας θαύματα*, “the wonders of the day.”]

Therefore I shall do what those customarily do who take strangers by the hand and lead them to their destination: I shall introduce you, as people unfamiliar with the place, to the hidden wonders of this greatest city.

In this city lies our ancient homeland, from which the murderous devil led us away after luring us with his enticements. Here, as you contemplate the first generation of humanity and the death that followed us afterward, which sin brought forth—the firstborn shoot of the ancient demon—you recognize that the human being is indeed earthly by nature, yet a work of divine hands; much inferior to cattle in bodily strength, yet established as ruler of animate and inanimate things; weak in natural instruments, yet lifted even to heaven by the power of reason.

If we learn these things, we shall recognize ourselves, remember God, adore the Creator, serve the Lord, glorify the Father, reverence our benefactor, and never cease to worship the author of our present and future life. Through the riches he has bestowed upon us, he also displays the reliability of those he has promised; and by the experience of present things he confirms those that are hoped for.

For if temporal things are such, what must eternal things be? If visible things are so good, what must invisible things be? If the greatness of the heavens exceeds the measure of the human mind, who could be sufficient to estimate the nature of eternal things?

If the sun, subject to corruption, is so good and great, swift in its movement and orderly in its courses, possessing a suitable magnitude by which it cannot exceed the moderation established for all things!

[Note: Col. 0922. The printed editions read: “if the sun is subject to corruption.” Colb. II reads: “if the sun alone is subject to corruption,” as the Greek requires: *ἥλιος*, “sun.” A little later Colb. II reads “its appearance.”]

Its natural beauty, like a clear eye, provides the world with ornament. If the sight of the sun is insatiable, what must the sun of righteousness be thought to be in beauty? If it is a loss to the blind not to see it, how great a loss does the sinner suffer, deprived of the true light?

### 2

“And God said: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to illuminate the earth, and let them divide between day and night.”

Heaven and earth had preceded; light had already been made upon them; day had been separated from night; the dry land had already been revealed; the water had been gathered into the station appointed for it; and the earth had been filled with its fruits, since it had brought forth thousands of herbs and abounded in various kinds of plants. But the sun and moon did not yet exist, lest those who do not know God should call the sun the chief and father of light, or suppose it to be the source of things born from the earth.

Therefore, on the fourth day he said, “Let there be lights,” and God made two lights.

[Note: Col. 0922. The printed editions read *quia fecit* (“because he made”). The two ancient books read *et fecit* (“and he made”), as does the Greek *καὶ ἐποίησε*.]

Who commanded? Who obeyed? Do you not perceive in these words a doubling of persons? Everywhere, therefore, the doctrine of the Godhead is woven into the historical narrative by a mystical account, and the reason for creating the lights is provided: to illuminate the earth.

How, then, if light had come before, is the sun now said to have been established for illumination? First, let the simplicity of our discourse not provoke laughter in you because we do not strive after the elegance of your eloquence or follow the elaborate arrangements of rhetorical clauses. We are not accustomed to polish verbal structures or the euphony of pronunciation; rather, everywhere we place the honorable meaning of words first.

[Note: Col. 0922. The printed editions read *proponendam* (“to be proposed”). Our three manuscripts read *praeponendam* (“to be placed first”), and the Basilian expression *προτιμότερον* (“to be preferred”) shows that this is the proper reading. Shortly afterward Colb. II reads *cui superfertur* (“which is superior to it”).]

Observe, then, how nature sufficiently declared what he wished. For he calls the lights “for illumination,” and this certainly does not conflict with what was previously said about light. Then the nature of light was produced; now the solar body was made, upon which that first-created light was laid.

For just as fire is one thing and a lamp another—one possessing the power to illuminate, the other formed to supply light to those who need it—so these lights have been placed beneath that most pure and undefiled light as vehicles, so to speak, although the Apostle also calls certain people “lights of the world” (Philippians 2:15).

But there is another true light of the world, by whose outpouring the saints were illumined and became lights of the world, freeing from the darkness of ignorance those souls to whom they taught the truth. In the same way this visible sun shines, kindled by that primordial radiance.

### 3

Let no one find it incredible that we have said that the splendor of light is one thing and the body subjected to light another. First, composite things are divided into two parts: the receiving matter and the quality that has come upon it. Thus natural whiteness is one thing and that which becomes white another. In the same way, the things mentioned appear to differ from one another in nature, yet they have been joined by the Creator’s power.

And do not say to me, “It is impossible for these things to be separated from one another.”

[Note: Col. 0923. Someone might suspect that there is some defect in the text here, but in the ancient books it is read exactly as in the common editions: “these things are separated from one another.” I could easily be persuaded that a poor copyist made Eustathius speak this way.]

For I am not asserting to you and to myself that the separation of light from the solar body is comprehensible, but only that, in our opinion, it is judged divisible. Clearly, by the Creator’s will these things can easily be separated from their nature.

Indeed, it is entirely impossible for us to distinguish the sun’s heat from its splendor. Yet God, wishing to transform his servant through a wondrous vision, placed flame upon the bush in such a way as to display only the power of its brightness, with its burning heat removed.

Thus the psalm also testifies, saying: “The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire” (Psalm 28:7).

Hence, even in the punishments for the sins we have contracted in life, a more secret principle teaches us that the nature of fire is to be divided: its light will be assigned to illuminate the righteous, while its heat will serve to burn the sinners.

[Note: Col. 0923. The printed editions and Colb. I read *perficiet* (“will accomplish”). Colb. II reads *praeficiet* (“will appoint over”). Our old book reads *proficiet*. None of these words adequately expresses the Greek verb. The verb used by Basil, *ἀποτάττομαι*, would much better be rendered “will be assigned.” A little later Colb. II reads: “for when it grows old.”]

We can also readily gain confidence in what has been proposed from the phases of the moon. For as it wanes, its entire body is not completely consumed; rather, sometimes laying aside and sometimes receiving the light inserted into it, it displays to us certain appearances of its own increase and diminution.

That its entire body is not consumed as it wanes is shown by what is seen. For you may look at the waning moon in clear air free of cloudy vapors, when, according to its form, it is round, and when its globe is enclosed on its dark side by an orbit such as it has when it is full. You clearly see it whole and complete, revealed in the part where it shines.

[Note: Col. 0923. The printed editions read *quando rotunda*, but this is a construction involving the noun “form.” Colb. II reads *rotunda secundum schema est* (“it is round according to its form”), in agreement with the Greek *κατὰ τὸ σχῆμά*. In the same place Colb. II reads “on the side where it is dark.” Two manuscripts later read *et non mihi dicas*; the conjunction *et* is absent from the printed editions.]

And do not say to me that its light is adventitious, because it diminishes when it turns toward the sun and increases when it moves away from it. For it is not our purpose here to investigate this matter in that way, but to assert that its body is one thing and the cause of its light another.

[Note: Col. 0923. The printed editions read *tale quidem* (“such indeed”). The two ancient books read *tale quiddam* (“something of this kind”).]

Understand something similar to me concerning the nature of the sun, which appears to differ from the moon only in this: the sun does not lay aside the light it has once received and possesses within itself, whereas the moon, having been stripped of it more often and clothed in light again, can readily confirm from itself what has been said about the sun.

[Note: Col. 0923. The printed editions read *iterumque nudata* (“and stripped again”), a statement for which I can see nothing more inappropriate. Three ancient books read *iterumque induta* (“and clothed again”); this is established as the true and genuine reading by the Greek *καὶ πάλιν ἐπαμφιαζομένη*.]

These lights, then, were established to divide between day and night. He deprived their nature of alternating opposition, so that they might be irreproachably related to one another and that darkness might have no community with light.

[Note: Col. 0924. The printed editions and Colb. I read: “whose nature then ceased from alternating opposition.” Colb. II reads as in the text. In the same place, where the printed editions read *incomprehensibiliter* (“incomprehensibly”), our three manuscripts read *irreprehensibiliter* (“irreproachably”). From this reading one may suspect that Eustathius incorrectly read *ἀμέμπτως*, “irreproachably,” whereas Basil wrote *ἀμίκτως*, “without mixture.”]

For what the shadow is during the day, darkness is during the night. Just as every shadow is cast from bodies subjected to light—moving toward the setting sun in the morning, turning toward the East in the evening, and inclining toward the northern region at midday—so night itself, driven backward by the rays of light, withdraws.

[Note: Col. 0924. One codex reads: “for what shadow is in the night.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read *mane tendens* (“tending in the morning”); the ancient books read *mane quidem tendens* (“indeed tending in the morning”). Immediately afterward the printed editions read *meridianis horis* (“at midday hours”); Colb. II reads *meridianis se horis* (“at midday it inclines itself”).]

What else should we understand the nature of this as being except the shadowing of the world? Just as, in bright daylight, a person standing beneath the rising sun is immediately accompanied by a shadow, so when the air near the earth is shadowed, night is produced. This is what he means when he says, “God separated between the light and the darkness.”

For darkness almost always flees the approach of light, since from the first creation estrangement between them was naturally established.

[Note: Col. 0924. The printed editions and Colb. I read *est naturaliter optata* (“is naturally desired”). The other two manuscripts read *naturaliter est aptata* (“is naturally arranged”). The Greek is *τῆς ἀλλοτριώσεως κατασκευασθείσης*, “estrangement having been established.”]

Now he commanded the sun to traverse the spaces of day, while he appointed the moon, when it has completed its orbit, as the ruler of night. According to a fixed measure, these lights succeed one another. When the sun advances, if the moon is full, it is immediately led toward setting. Again, when the sun has set limits to its course, the moon begins to rise.

But if, according to other forms, the moon’s light does not equal the duration of the night, that does not concern the question before us. We assert only this: when the moon is full, it holds authority over the night, surpassing the stars with its own radiance and illuminating the earth; but in measuring time it shares equally with the sun.

### 4

“And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years.”

You will therefore find, as long experience teaches, that observations and indications of signs are necessary for human life—provided that you do not investigate them beyond what is proper. For from them we can learn many things about future rains, and very much about the vapors of the earth and the movements of the winds, whether they come in particular regions or blow everywhere generally, and whether they will arrive violently or gently.

[Note: Col. 0924. The printed editions read *possumus dicere* (“we can say”). The two ancient books read *discere possumus* (“we can learn”), as does the Greek *ἐστὶ μαθεῖν*. A little later the printed editions read *placide sunt venturi* (“they are going to come gently”); two manuscripts read *placide sint venturi* (“whether they are going to come gently”). Colb. II reads “whether they will be violent or gentle.” In the same place, where the two manuscripts and the common editions read *solis*, Colb. II reads *solum*.]

There is one indication above all that the Lord has shown us, saying that a storm is coming when the sky begins to grow mournful with fiery redness (Matthew 16:3). For when clouds rise, the obscured rays are seen with a glowing and blood-red color. The density of the air presents such an appearance to our eyes, since, not yet dispersed by the force of heat, it has been thickened more and more by the vapors exhaled within it and by the increasing quantity of water; thus it threatens the regions over which it has gathered with a most certain storm.

Similarly, this happens when the moon is surrounded by a halo, or when a ring called an *area* surrounds the sun: it announces either a great quantity of water or the future roaring of winds.

[Note: Col. 0925. One codex together with the printed editions reads *solis contrarii* (“opposed to the sun”). The other two read *soles contrarii* (“opposed suns”).]

Or when those called “opposed suns” are seen running around it, they clearly signify that certain disturbances of the ethereal region are impending. Likewise, those rods that appear in the colors of the rainbow beneath the morning clouds indicate violent rains and storms, or some disturbance of the sky in any event.

Those who have studied this science are also said to have observed many signs in the waxing and waning moon, asserting that the air nearest the earth necessarily changes according to the moon’s forms and qualities.

For when it is the third day, if it appears slender and not at all blunted at the horns, it declares settled and firm fair weather. But if it is reddish and full at the horns, it threatens excessive rains and violent south winds.

[Note: Col. 0925. The printed editions read *cum fuerit tersa* (“when it has been cleared”). The ancient books read *cum fuerit tertia* (“when it is the third [day]”), as required both by the sense and by the Greek *περὶ τρίτην ἡμέραν*, “about the third day.”]

Who does not know how much benefit the observation of these things provides to human beings? Sailors can keep their fleet inside the harbor when they foresee coming dangers; the cautious traveler, warned by the gloom of the sky, waits for a time of calm; and farmers, applying diligent care to seeds and plants, use the signs mentioned above to await the appropriate opportunity.

What is more, the Lord foretold visible wondrous signs of the dissolution of all things in the sun, moon, and stars, saying: “The sun shall be turned into blood, and the moon shall not give its light” (Joel 2:31; Acts 2:20).

[Note: Col. 0925. The printed editions read *solutiones* (“dissolutions”). Our codex and Colb. I read *solutionis* (“of the dissolution”), correctly, since in Basil we read *τῆς διαλύσεως … σημεῖα*, “signs of the dissolution.” Colb. II instead has: “they apply diligence from the instructions mentioned above.” This can more easily be reconciled with the Greek *ἤδη δὲ καί*, “and already also,” but the word *solutionis* is absent from that book. Our codex reads: “they await the appropriate time, since there are signs of the dissolution.” Immediately afterward two manuscripts read *videnda prodigia* (“wonders to be seen”).]

But these, as we have said, are signs of the consummation of the world.

### 5

But those who attempt to extend their leaps beyond the ditch bend the course of the argument back toward the doctrine of genesis. For they maintain that our life depends upon the movement of the heavenly bodies. Consequently, the Chaldeans assert that observations of the stars pertain to human circumstances, and, transferring the simple scriptural statement that they are “for signs” not to changes in the air or the qualities of the seasons but, as they see fit, to the destiny of human life, they explain it by saying that when certain wandering stars have come together with those stars that move in the circle of the zodiac according to some particular configuration—for example, *κατὰ τοιόδε σχῆμα*, “according to such a configuration”—they are accustomed to determine a specific birth; and again, if their arrangement is different, it establishes contrary decrees.

It may perhaps not be useless, for the purpose of opening up this question, to begin again somewhat earlier in the sequence of the account. I do not mean to offer something of my own, but, for the purpose of refuting them, I shall use their own statements, so that those who have been overtaken by error may receive remedies for the injury they have conceived, while the others may find some protection against suffering the same things.

The discoverers of the doctrine of natal astrology, having learned through long experience that many things escape them in the configurations, reduced the measure of time to an exceedingly narrow interval, so that even in the tiniest moment—“in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. XV, 52)—there might be a great difference between one birth and another. They assert that the person born at this instant will be king, ruler of nations, and destined to acquire the greatest power and abundant riches; whereas the person born at that moment will be a beggar and wanderer, destined to go about the doors of various people for his daily sustenance.

For this reason they divide the circle called the zodiac into twelve parts, because the sun traverses one-twelfth of the sphere—namely, the sphere called ἀπλανής, that is, “fixed” or “not wandering”—in thirty days. Again, they divide each member of those thirty-part divisions into twelve intervals; each of those portions they further divide into sixty, and they count the sixty portions sixty times over.

Having thus arranged the genesis of those who are born, let us see whether they can preserve this subtlety within the dimension of time. As soon as the infant has emerged from the womb, the midwife must inspect it and say whether what has been born is a boy or a girl, while she waits for the cry by which she may recognize that the little one is alive. How many moments, let us ask, will have passed sixty times while these things are being done?

Thus, while the child is being shown to the astrologer, how many instants do we suppose have elapsed while the answers are being given? Even if the person who records the hour of birth happens to be standing outside the doors of the chamber, he must consult his tablet, so that the course of the hours—whether they are daytime or nighttime hours—may be calculated carefully and without any interruption. How many sixtieths, then, will be thought to have passed in that very interval?

For it is necessary to discover the star not only at which part of the twelfth division of the space it stands, but also at which point of the portion divided twelvefold—or rather, at which moment among the sixtieths—it is found, since we have said that the lot of the decrees was divided among these; or, if the truth is to be investigated completely, at which of those sixtieths the portent occurs that has been restored from the first sixtieths.

But they insist that this elaborated and incomprehensible determination of time must be made for each individual planet, so that it may be known what position it held toward the wandering stars, or what configuration they formed among themselves when the infant was born. For if the hour has not been watched carefully, and something even slightly different has occurred in that most subtle calculation, the entire observation is utterly confused.

They are indeed worthy of laughter who have devoted themselves to the study of this incomprehensible discipline; but still more so are those who eagerly gape after them as though they knew something.

**Note on the text (Col. 0926A–D; Col. 0927A–B).** The printed editions read *si tale* (“if such”); two ancient books read *si secundum tale* (“if according to such”), corresponding in Greek to *κατὰ τοιόδε σχῆμα* (“according to such a configuration”). Immediately afterward the editions read *si aliter* (“if otherwise”); the second Colbertinus reads *si alter* (“if another”). It then reads *repetitam seriem* (“the repeated sequence”).

The editions read *inter gesim genesimque distantia*; an old copy of ours correctly reads *inter genesim genesimque distantia* (“a difference between one birth and another”). The Greek is *γένεσει πρὸς γένεσιν* (“from one birth to another”).

The editions read *in duodecim partibus* (“into twelve parts”); another manuscript reads *in duodecim partes* (“into twelve divisions”), which I do not deny is more suitable, although I do not think this proves that Eustathius, as a poor scribe, wrote it that way.

The editions read *locum ferae*; our codex reads *locum fere*; the first Colbertinus reads *locum fore*; the second, *locum sperae*. The last reading is so corrupt that it can easily be corrected: *sphaerae* (“of the sphere”) should be read instead of *sperae*. This is sufficiently clear in itself, but is confirmed still more by the Basilian reading *σφαίρας* (“of the sphere”).

The editions and two manuscripts read *reparata* (“restored”); the second Colbertinus reads *reputata*, perhaps for *amputata* (“cut off”).

The wording *dum manifestatur* (“while he is being shown”) was found in one manuscript. The word *dum* (“while”) was absent from the printed editions. Shortly afterward the editions and two manuscripts read *dum modice responsa redduntur* (“while the answers are being given briefly”); our old codex, in an ancient second hand, reads *dum media responsa redduntur* (“while the intermediate answers are being given”). The second Colbertinus subsequently reads *inveniet stellam* (“he will find the star”), and so on.

### 6

Accordingly, they are accustomed to predict the events and even the appearance of each individual, declaring that a person will have curly hair and be lively because his hour was situated in Aries, since that is the appearance of the animal; and that he will possess great power because Aries is a ruling sign.

They also say that he will be a magistrate and a man of profit, because this animal, the sheep, easily takes back the wool it has laid down, nature supplying the process without difficulty. But the person born under Taurus will be tyrannical and laborious, and likewise servile, since the bull is accustomed to submit its neck to the yoke.

Whoever is born under the sign of Scorpio will be regarded as wounding, as being like that creature; but whoever is born under the hour of Libra becomes just, because of the equality maintained in the balance.

What could be more laughable than these claims? Aries, then, from which you borrow the genesis of human beings, is held to be one-twelfth of heaven. If the sun stands in it, it touches the heavenly signs; Libra and Taurus likewise constitute one-twelfth of the zodiacal circle.

How, then, while asserting that the principal causes of mortal life derive from these things, can you infer the forms and dispositions of minds from earthly animals and say that a man born under Aries will be generous—not because that part of heaven produces such character, but because the nature of the sheep is such?

You are therefore urging us, under the pretext of the exalted dignity of the stars—or rather attempting to persuade us—to win assent for yourself by means of mute beasts. But if the firmament derives the qualities of character from animals, it too is subject to alien necessities, since it has obtained from quadrupeds the principles from which its causes are derived.

If, however, you say that this is absurd, you will pronounce a far greater absurdity in daring to bring forward assertions about matters that appear to have nothing in common with us.

Their arguments are like spiders’ webs: if a gnat or a fly settles upon them, it is caught and entangled; but when something stronger falls upon them, it immediately passes through, tearing apart the weak fabric.

**Note on the text (Col. 0927–0928).** We added the word *inde* (“from there”) from our old books. One manuscript reads *quippe quia* (“since indeed because”); the editions read *quippe qui* (“since indeed he”). Shortly afterward two manuscripts read *si autem hoc dicis* (“but if you say this”); the editions have *si autem dicit* (“but if he says this”). At this point two manuscripts read *pronuntiabis* (“you will pronounce”); the editions read *pronuntiabit* (“he will pronounce”).

The word *sunt* (“are”) was added from two manuscripts. Shortly afterward the editions read *tamen his quae quaque non contenti sunt*; two ancient books read *tamen his non usquequaque contenti sunt* (“yet they are not altogether satisfied with these things”), which is preferable.

### 7

Yet they are not altogether satisfied with these things; they proceed still farther in their wandering. For they apply to the necessities of the heavens things that lie within the freedom of our will—that is, virtues and vices.

Although it is laughable to contradict them, nevertheless, since many have fallen through this deception, I think it appropriate not to pass the matter over in silence. From them we ask that they acknowledge this point at the outset: do the configurations of the stars not change a thousand times each day?

For those stars called planets are always moving and wandering. Some pursue one another with swift steps; others, moving more slowly, repeatedly look upon one another and conceal themselves under the same hour.

According to their teaching, the configuration has enormous power in a birth if a favorable star has looked upon the person being born, or an unfavorable one. It often happens, however, that at the time when a favorable star has been in charge, the astrologer, unable to determine the time because he does not know one of the tiny portions mentioned above, describes the person as lying beneath the evil spirit—so that I am compelled to use their own language, in which there is great madness, but even greater impiety.

For they transfer the causes of their own wickedness from the more malignant stars to their creator. If wickedness were inherent in them by nature, their creator would plainly have been the author of malignity. But if they are most evil because of deliberate purpose, then first they must be regarded as certain living beings subject to their own will and driven by an independent and free impulse toward whatever they desire, since it surpasses every measure of madness to accuse lifeless things.

Moreover, what greater irrationality is there than to determine whether something is good or evil not according to the dignity proper to each thing, but according to the quality of its position or its relation to another, defining it as either excellent or most evil? And when a star has turned away for a little while from its configuration, they say that it has forgotten its own malignity.

But enough of this. These stars, as they say, transfer themselves at every moment of time into one configuration after another. Amid such thousands of changes, so many and so great, how many royal destinies must be thought to be formed each day?

Why, then, are princes not begotten every day? Or why is the succession of the paternal empire always preserved among them? Evidently because no one relates the fate of his children to the configuration of the stars, since kingship is conferred upon them not by the fate of genesis but by the right of lineage.

Did not Jotham beget Uzziah, and was not Ahaz born from Jotham? Yet none of them fell into the condition of slavery.

Furthermore, if the beginnings of virtues and vices are received not from our own will but from the necessity of genesis, then, as I see it, lawgivers are superfluous when they command what we must follow or avoid. Judges too are superfluous when they honor the upright with praise and punish the wicked with penalties.

The audacity of the murderer or thief must even be judged innocent, since, although they might have preferred to restrain their own hands from crime, they could not have done so because of the unalterable force of necessity.

All artisans who seek the means of life through the labor of their hands must be considered vain. The farmers’ sweat, too, is superfluous, since an abundance of crops could flourish even without their labor. A merchant likewise would become rich in idleness, since genesis would bring him money even against his will.

The hope of Christians, which is great, would be utterly removed and destroyed, since justice would be honored in vain and wickedness condemned in vain, if we are altogether permitted to do nothing according to our own judgment.

For when the power of genesis and the fatal decree bears down upon us, no place at all remains for the examination of a just judgment.

It is enough to have argued these points against them. You do not need longer speeches, being endowed with soundness of mind; nor does the time permit us to extend the limit of the discussion any farther.

**Note on the text (Col. 0928–0929).** One manuscript reads *hac seducti ratione* (“seduced by this reasoning”); the editions and the first Colbertinus, not far from this point, read *illud principii loco* (“that in the first place”). Our codex has *illud principe in loco*; the second Colbertinus has *illud primo loco* (“that first of all”). The Greek is *πρῶτον* (“first”). I think everyone sees that the last two readings correspond equally well to the Greek word; nevertheless, I believe *principe in loco* should be read, as it is written in our old book. It seems that the scribe who wrote the other Colbertinus altered and corrected some things on his own, whether he consulted a Greek exemplar while writing or did so merely by rational conjecture.

The editions read *discurrunt stellae* (“the stars wander”); the second Colbertinus reads *eae stellae* (“those stars”).

The editions read *actor exstiterit* (“he will have been the agent”); the second Colbertinus reads *auctor exstiterit* (“he will have been the author”).

The editions read *animalia quaedam putando arbitrio suo famulanti* (“thinking that certain animals serve their own will”); since this is plainly faulty, we corrected it from the second Colbertinus.

The editions read *sufficiet* (“it will suffice”); another manuscript reads *sufficiat* (“let it suffice”). Immediately afterward the editions and two manuscripts read *torqueamus* (“let us turn”); another codex reads *retorqueamus* (“let us turn back”). The Greek is *ἐπανέλθωμεν* (“let us return”).

### 8

But let us turn the discussion back to the remaining points.

“Let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years.”

We have already spoken about the signs. By “seasons” we understand the four divisions of the revolving year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These temper one another by succeeding each other in turn, according to the courses assigned to the heavenly bodies.

Winter occurs when the sun remains in the southern regions, while the darkness of night continues for a longer period around the climate that we inhabit. Hence the air nearest the earth becomes cold, and all the misty vapors gathered together produce rains, snows, and ice.

But when the sun, returning from the southern region, occupies the middle of the circuit of heaven, it then distributes equal time to days and nights. The higher it is carried above the earth, the more gradually it establishes the temperate condition through which spring advances. By its benefit, shrubs and trees put forth leaves, and all land and aquatic animals, stimulated by generative warmth, extend the propagation of their kind through the succession of offspring.

Then the sun, turning toward the summer line, passes through the northern regions, making the days longer for us. Remaining longer in the air, it makes the air itself burning and hot, while it renders the earth drier; thus it provides the desired ability to ripen seeds and fruits.

At that time it is more ardent and makes the midday shadows shorter, because from its very high position it looks down upon our region. The days are longer when the shadows are shorter, just as, conversely, the days are shorter when the shadows are longer. This happens among us, who are called *heteroscii*—ἑτερόσκιοι, “those having different shadows”—and who inhabit the northern regions.

There are some people, however, who for an entire two-day period each year are entirely without shadows when they stand beneath the midday sun. Since the sun is positioned directly above their heads and illuminates them at equal distances on every side, it permits their shadows to bend in no direction at all.

Among them even water in a well can scarcely receive the sun’s light at the narrowest depth, because of which some call them *ascii*, that is, “shadowless.”

Those who live beyond the lands of the incense-producing peoples change their shadows in both directions. For those alone who seem to inhabit our region are believed always to cast their shadows toward the south, that is, toward midday. Hence some also call them *amphiscii*, that is, “double-shadowed.”

All these phenomena occur when the sun travels toward the northern regions. From them we should consider how great is the heat of its rays and how many effects it produces for human beings.

After this, autumn follows. Holding equal portions of cold and heat, it hands us over without distress to the arrival of the ensuing winter, when the sun once more returns from the northern regions to the southern.

These are the alternations of the seasons, which are believed to regulate our life by serving the sun’s movements.

“And let them be,” he says, “for signs and for days”—not so that the sun might make the day, but so that it might govern it. For night and day came into being long before the heavenly bodies were created, as the psalm also declares: “He appointed the sun to rule the day, the moon and the stars to rule the night” (Ps. CXXXV, 8).

How, then, does the sun rule the day? Because, carrying light within itself, when it approaches the circuit that we inhabit, it dispels the darkness and supplies the day.

Therefore no one is mistaken who calls this air, illuminated by the sun’s rays, “day,” and regards this as the measure of daytime, during which the sun remains in the hemisphere that, as they suppose, lies above the earth.

“And for years,” he says, “these signs have been appointed.” When the moon has completed twelve periods of its course, it makes a year; yet it demands that one month be inserted into it, so that the complete concurrence of the hours may be calculated more accurately, as the Hebrews observed the year in ancient times, as did the most ancient of the Greeks.

The solar year is called the sun’s orderly course, when it returns from a particular sign to that same sign, retracing its steps.

**Note on the text (Col. 0929–0930).** We judged that the phrase “which we inhabit” should be added from two books. Two ancient books read *propaginationem* (“propagation”); another reads *propaginem* (“offspring”). Shortly afterward the editions read *ac aridum* (“and dry”); the old books read *torridum* (“hot”).

The editions read *aetheroscii*; our codex reads *eteroscii*. The Greek is *παρ’ ἡμῖν τοῖς ἑτεροσκίοις* (“among us who are heteroscii”).

Two ancient books and the editions read *in altum* (“upward”); the second Colbertinus reads *in alveum* (“into the channel”). Thus Eustathius translated into Latin Basil’s phrase *διὰ στομίων στενῶν* (“through narrow openings”), although he should rather have written “through the narrowness of the mouth.” See Basil, Homily 6, no. 8.

The editions read *id est umbrae nominantur* (“that is, they are called shadows”); our old codex has *id est biumbras* (“that is, double-shadows”); the second Colbertinus has *id est biumbres*. In the same place the old books read *et quantos* (“and how many”), while the word *et* (“and”) is absent from the printed editions. The editions read *efficit* (“it produces”); our three manuscripts read *efficiat* (“it may produce”).

The editions and the first Colbertinus read *sequentis hiberni* (“of the following winter”); the second Colbertinus reads *sequentis hibernii*.

The editions read *quod igitur* (“therefore, which”); the old books read *quomodo igitur* (“how, then”). The Greek is *πῶς οὖν* (“how, then”).

### 9

“And God made two great lights.”

The designation “great” has two meanings. One is absolute; the other assigns greatness to something in relation to what is smaller—for example, “a great horse” or “a great ox.” Such things receive this testimony not from the excessive size of their bodies but from comparison with something else.

How, then, should we understand the meaning of the expression “great lights”? Should we take it in the first sense, unquestionably, comparing smaller things with larger ones, like an ant or some other animal that is naturally small and is placed below the greatest things by comparison? Or rather are the lights called great because of the vastness of their form? I think the latter should be understood.

They are not called great because they are larger than the other stars, but because the extent of their sphere is such that the radiance issuing from them sufficiently illuminates the entire air and, extending everywhere, reaches all lands and seas.

When either rising or setting they stand in any part of the heavens, they appear equally to the sight of all mortals.

Their size has the clearest proof: the breadth of the earth is not measured even by comparison with the lights themselves, so that from this one might understand whether the sun and moon are smaller or larger. For things placed far away always seem small to our eyes; but when we have come near them, we more easily discover how great they are.

Yet the sun is never said to be either farther away or nearer in such a way that it regards all the regions beneath it from every side with equal balance. Indians and Britons look upon it alike.

For when it inclines toward setting, it is not perceived to lose anything of its size by those living in the East; nor does it appear smaller as it rises to those situated in the West; nor, when it holds the middle axis of heaven, does it alter its appearance for either side.

Do not, then, let the apparent smallness of its disk deceive you, nor suppose that it is truly as large as its disk seems to those who see it as only a cubit wide.

The length of things observed is ordinarily connected with the extent of the intervening distances. The power of the eyes does not reach the length of the space between by looking; rather, as though failing, it is diminished, and it touches what is seen more by estimation than by sight. Consequently, because of its own weakness, it judges that things which are large are small, attributing its own incapacity to the things it beholds.

Sight, therefore, is plainly deceived and does not possess a reliable judgment. Recall your own weakness, and from yourself you will grasp an argument for what has been said.

If at some time, from the high summit of a mountain, you have looked down upon the plain spread beneath the fields, did you not judge the teams of oxen, however large, or their plowmen, to be like ants? Likewise, when stationed on a lofty lookout, you turned your eyes toward the sea: what did the islands seem to you? Did they not appear like the tiniest pigeons? Or did not huge ships, seen from afar with their white sails swelling, seem round and black?

This happens because, as we have said, the faculty of sight, weakened by the extension of the air, cannot fully grasp what is seen.

Even the view of enormous rocks hollowed out in height appears rounded and complete, because the middle of the hollow, enclosed on every side by projecting edges, cannot be reached by the failing vision.

Thus the eye does not notice what the forms of bodies are really like; it supposes that square towers are cylindrical. It is therefore certain that at greater distances we receive not a definite but a confused vision of bodies.

So too the great lights, according to the testimony of Scripture, are greater than they appear.

**Note on the text (Col. 0931–0932).** We added the word *et* (“and”) from two manuscripts. Shortly afterward the editions and two manuscripts read *mortalium usibus* (“for the uses of mortals”); the second Colbertinus reads *mortalium visibus* (“for the sight of mortals”).

The second Colbertinus has *aspicitur* (“is seen”) in the text, but in the margin of the book we found *asseritur* (“is asserted”).

Two ancient books read *velis tumentes* (“with swelling sails”); another codex has *velis tumentibus*. The second Colbertinus subsequently reads *rotundi planique putantur aspectus* (“they are thought in appearance to be round and flat”).

The editions read *quia prolixioribus* (“because in greater distances”); two manuscripts read *quia in prolixioribus* (“because at greater distances”).

### 10

There is also this plausible proof of their magnitude: although the stars are infinite in number, the radiance proceeding from them cannot divide the density of the night.

The sun, however, spreading its light through the world, breaks and overcomes the darkness of night not only when it is seen, but also when it is expected to come, before it illuminates the earth. It surpasses the stars in brightness and dissolves and scatters the air nearest the earth, which has been condensed by cold and mist. From this the morning wind and the dewy moisture are produced when the weather is clear.

Since the earth is exceedingly vast, how could it be illuminated throughout by rays in a single moment unless an abundant light were supplied to it from the sun’s immense disk?

Here observe the wisdom of the Creator: he applied a moderate force of heat to its immensity, so that neither excessive heat could burn up the earth nor the complete withholding of warmth render it unproductive.

Understand similar things about the moon. Although its body is luminous, its full size is not always visible. Now it appears complete in its orb, now half-full, and then it is seen diminished, displaying its waning in two portions. It is found to be dark on one side when it is waxing, and on another when it is waning.

There is a more hidden reason here, revealing the Creator’s ordering. Through it the moon’s variation presents us with an example of our own nature, since nothing in human affairs remains enduring or lasting. Rather, things that are produced from nothing, when they have grown to a certain point and have been raised to the full measure of their age, gradually waste away and dissolve.

From contemplating the moon we are therefore taught to recognize mortal things. Taking their mutability into our thoughts, we ought to take care not to be lifted by prosperous circumstances into pride or arrogance; nor should we trust in temporal power or exalt ourselves in possessions and riches, which are exceedingly uncertain.

Instead, we should discipline the desire of the body, which is especially unstable, and devote our care to the soul, whose good always remains unmoved.

If the moon perhaps saddens you as it gradually lays aside its light and wanes, the soul ought to affect you still more, for it loses the honor it received from divine virtue through the fault of intemperance. It never preserves a firm purpose but continually turns about, having no supports of constancy to strengthen it.

For truly, according to the proverb: “The voiceless moon changes” (Ecclus. XXVII, 12).

I also think that the moon’s change contributes no little to the formation of animals and of all the other things that the earth produces. Their bodies are arranged differently when the moon is full and differently when it declines. At one time they appear looser and emptier as it wanes; at another they are whole and filled as it waxes, because it secretly pours into them a certain moisture mixed with heat.

Those who sleep beneath the open sky in the moonlight demonstrate that this is so: when they rise, they find their heads drenched with abundant dew.

Fresh meat likewise, if it lies beneath the moon, soon decays in flowing putrefaction. The same is indicated by the brain of sheep, by the entrails of sea animals, which are more moist, and by the pith of trees. The moon would not be able to bring all these things into conformity with its own quality unless it excelled in the magnitude of its power, according to the testimony of Scripture.

**Note on the text (Col. 0932–0933).** Two ancient books and the editions read *nec quidem perfecta videtur in globo, nec semiplena* (“nor indeed is it seen complete in its orb, nor half-full”). This must have been written by scribes thinking of something else; otherwise they would not have produced such an absurd statement. The second Colbertinus correctly reads *nunc quidem … nunc semiplena* (“now indeed … now half-full”). The Greek is *νῦν μὲν … νῦν δέ* (“now indeed … but now”).

The editions and two manuscripts read *diurnumque* (“and daytime”), corruptly. The correct reading in the second Colbertinus is *diutinumque* (“and lasting”). The Greek is *μόνιμον* (“lasting”).

The passage in Eustathius reads: “For truly, according to the proverb, the voiceless moon changes.” It corresponds to Basil’s: “For truly, according to what has been said, ‘The fool changes like the moon’” (Ecclus. XXVII, 12). Let us return to Eustathius’ proverb. If those who once undertook to collect proverbs together had known it, they would not have failed to add it to the others. I think that this new proverb arose because Eustathius read *ἄφωνος* (“voiceless”) instead of *ἄφρων* (“foolish”). Once he had been deceived by this false reading, it is not surprising that he expressed almost anything rather than what was required.

### 11

The movement of the air is also governed by these same changes, as the new moon bears witness. After a long period of clear weather, it often suddenly raises accumulations of clouds and disturbances.

The course of the whirlpools also indicates this, as does the ebb and flow—or even the reversal of the Syrtes, which lie near the Ocean. The inhabitants of those regions have reported that these are stirred according to the moon’s configurations.

**Note on the text (Col. 0934).** How ineptly the entire phrase, “or even the reversal of the Syrtes, which lie near the Ocean,” has been rendered may be seen from Basil, *Homily* 6, no. 11, not far from the beginning.

The channels of the whirlpools likewise ordinarily turn their gentle currents in either direction during all the rest of the time. But when the moon rises, they cannot remain at rest at all; they are always stirred by violent heat until the moon appears again and brings calm to the disturbed eddies.

The western sea similarly experiences frequent advances and retreats, now washing the shores with its waves, now leaving them bare. Thus, as though by certain breaths of the moon, it withdraws backward and again overflows under the moon’s impulse.

I have discussed these matters to express the magnitude of the lights, and to show that not even a single syllable can be idle in spiritual instruction, since the discussion has certainly drawn forth nothing from the more hidden matters.

A person who diligently investigates their properties and powers can discover much by reflection concerning the sun’s and moon’s size and the distances between them. Therefore each person ought rather to accuse his own weakness, so that he may not suppose that the magnificence of creation can be measured by human words.

From the few things that have been said, it is nevertheless fitting to consider how great and how remarkable are the things we have passed over. Do not, then, estimate the moon with your eyes, but rather with reason, which is better able than sight to approach the discovery of truth.

Old women’s tales, laughable everywhere, have spread abroad: that by magical incantations the moon is summoned from its dwelling and brought down to earth.

First, how could it be moved by the force of songs, when the Most High himself established it? In addition, what place could receive it as it descended?

Nevertheless, if you wish to receive proof of its size from small indications, consider this. The cities situated throughout the world are separated from one another by long distances. Their streets that face toward the East all receive the moon’s light equally.

If the moon were not visible before all of them, it would illuminate only those narrow streets positioned directly opposite it; it would not visit those that extend beyond its breadth, since they approach from the side.

A lamp lit inside a house demonstrates the same thing. If several people stand around it, the shadow of those who are directly in front extends straight out, while the shadows of the others bend to either side.

Thus, unless the moon’s body excelled in immensity and breadth, it could never reach them all at once.

When it rises from the regions of the summer solstice, it illuminates equally those who inhabit the cold region of the northern axis and those who live in the lower southern zone, embracing them with the sun’s summer heat. It thereby gives us the clearest indication of its own magnitude.

Who, then, can contradict this and assert that its body is not immense, when it extends across such great and numerous intervals of the earth?

So much for the magnitude of the sun and moon.

May he who granted us understanding, so that from the smallest things in creation we might recognize the infinite wisdom of the Maker, also grant that through greater things we may receive the greatest thoughts concerning the Creator—although, in comparison with him, the sun and moon are thought to be the size of ants.

Therefore, although these things are not worthy in themselves to provide a contemplation of divine greatness, we seem nevertheless to be instructed by certain small and obscure parables, just as we sometimes compare lesser animals or plants with immense things.

For now, let us be content with the sequence of the account: I give thanks to him who assigned me this small gift of a brief discourse, while you proclaim him the giver of spiritual nourishment, who has fed you at present, as it were, with barley bread—that is, with the meagerness of our speech—and may feed you in the future as well, granting us, according to the proportion of each person’s faith, the revelation of the Spirit (1 Cor. XII, 7).

To him be glory in Christ Jesus, now and always, for ever and ever. Amen.

## Book Seven.

1. And God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls, and winged creatures flying beneath the firmament of heaven.” After the formation of the luminaries, the water too is filled with animals, so that this element also might thereby be adorned. For the earth had long since received fitting beauty from its own sproutings; heaven likewise had assumed the flowers of the stars; and, like two eyes, it had been beautified by the conjunction of the greatest lights. It remained that a familiar adornment should also be given to the waters.

[Note: [Col. 0935] The printed editions read “before the formation of the luminaries.” But our three manuscripts read “after the formation of the luminaries.” And so, unless Eustathius was wholly unskilled in sacred Scripture, I think he wrote it thus; all the more because in Basil we read μετὰ τὴν τῶν φωστήρων δημιουργίαν, “after the formation of the luminaries.”]

The command came: and immediately lakes and rivers, each according to its own kind or nature, were made exceedingly abundant; indeed, the sea was so filled with the offspring of various swimmers that muddy marshes and shallow pools by no means retained an idle or unproductive power of generation. Frogs, flies, and gnats undoubtedly sprang from it as well. For the things now seen provide evidence of what happened in the past.

[Note: [Col. 0935] The printed editions read: “The command came, and immediately the lakes and rivers, each according to its own kind, etc.” The second Colbertinus reads: “Immediately the command came, by which the lakes and rivers, each according to its own [kind], etc.” The first Colbertinus has the reading found in the text. We have followed the first Colbertinus because it is clear from the Basilian manuscripts that the word “immediately” was misplaced in the second Colbertinus. See Homily 7, no. 1, near the beginning.]

Thus all water was compelled to serve the Creator’s commands.

[Note: [Col. 0935] The second Colbertinus reads: “to serve the commands of the Creator.” But, as we have remarked, the scribe may reasonably be thought to have corrected certain things on his own, for elegance or clarification. I therefore prefer here the common reading, in which the word is taken adjectivally, just as is the Greek expression τῷ δημιουργικῷ, “creative.” In the same place the printed editions read “whose kinds”; the second Colbertinus, “whose kinds not even.”]

For no one suffices even to explain their kinds; yet the ineffable and magnificent power of God immediately showed their life to be vigorous and mobile, and the command given to the waters was accompanied by the power to give life.

“Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls.” Now, for the first time, animals that breathe and are capable of sensation are generated.

[Note: [Col. 0936] The printed editions and two manuscripts read: “are generated, as it were, etc.” But the second Colbertinus reads as we have printed it. There is no doubt that this is the proper reading, since Basil writes: φυτὰ γὰρ καὶ δένδρα κἄν ζῆν λέγεται, “for plants and trees, although they are said to live.”]

For shrubs and trees, although they are said to live, since they have received the power of nourishment and growth, are nevertheless not thereby to be understood as living creatures. For this reason he said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” Every kind of swimmer, therefore—whether it is borne upon the surface of the waves or moves through the deep waters—has plainly received a nature suited to creeping, since its body is drawn through the water, although some also use feet and walking.

[Note: [Col. 0936] The printed editions read: “the body is drawn, although some also strive with feet and steps.” The second Colbertinus has the reading found in the text. In this same place the printed editions read: “although it is permitted to them for many a day.” Our codex and the second Colbertinus read as we have printed it.]

And although many things about them are uncertain—such as seals, crocodiles, frogs, and crabs—their chief characteristic is swimming. Therefore: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things.” In these very brief words every kind is contained.

For what is not included in the command of creation?

[Note: [Col. 0936] The printed editions read: “in the command of the Creator’s creature.” It is perhaps not difficult to say where this reading arose. A scribe seems to have been uncertain whether the text should read “of the Creator” or “of the creature”; in that uncertainty he preferred to join both readings together, so that the choice might remain with learned readers. There are many such examples, which others have already noted and which may still be noted daily. But scribes often add the little word “or” either before “Creator” or before “creature.” Hence it may be suspected that the printers omitted “or” here. Both Colbertine manuscripts read “in the command of the Creator.” Our old codex reads “in the command of the creature.” We think Eustathius rendered Basil’s τῷ προστάγματι τῆς δημιουργίας into Latin in this way, as though he had said “at the command of creation,” that is, “at the command which God used to create things.””]

Whether you call those animals that give birth to young—such as seals, torpedo fish, dolphins, and their like—or call them egg-laying animals, as are nearly all kinds of fish. The word of the command is indeed small—or rather, it is not a word but only an instant and impulse of the will; yet its meaning is as manifold as the differences that can exist among the fish themselves. To describe all of them in words is no less laborious than if you tried to enumerate the number of waves, or to explain how many jars the sea contains.

[Note: [Col. 0937] The printed editions read: “or how many jars.” Our three manuscripts read: “or how many jars.” A little later two manuscripts read “under the same [power].” The “-que” was absent from the printed editions.]

“Let the waters bring forth a creeping thing.” Among these are sea fish, shore fish, deep-water fish, rock fish, schooling fish, monstrous fish, huge fish, and tiny fish; under the same power of the command both the greatest and the least are included. Thus, when he said “Let the waters bring forth,” he demonstrated how great is the kinship of swimmers with the water.

[Note: [Col. 0937] The printed editions and the first Colbertinus read “the kinship of swimmers.” The other Colbertinus reads “the kinship of those being born with the water.” Our old codex reads “the knowledge of swimmers with the water.” All these readings are false; nevertheless, they yield this advantage: we can easily understand that the reading should be “the kinship of swimmers with the water.” In Greek: τῶν νηκτῶν πρὸς τὸ ὕδωρ συγγένειαν, “the kinship of swimmers with the water.”]

Indeed, if they are brought out upon land for a short while, they perish, for they have no breath by which they can draw in vital air. For just as air has been given to terrestrial animals, so water has been given to fish. The reason is clear: we have a loose and open lung which, drawing in air through the separation of the chest, moderates the inner heat by ventilation; but in fish, the partition of the throat, capable of being folded, now receiving, now dispersing water, performs the function of breathing.

Fish also have their own lot and their own nature, a different food, and a definite condition of life. Therefore nothing aquatic becomes tame, nor does it endure being handled by human hands.

2. “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living souls.” He commanded the origin of each kind to be brought forth now as a sort of seed, reserving the multitude for later in the offspring, when it would be necessary for them to grow and multiply.

Thus one kind consists of those called testicutes, “shell-bearing animals,” such as mussels, scallops, sea snails, and thousands of different oysters; another consists of those called mollusks, that is, lobsters, crabs, and their relatives. There is yet another kind, which the Greeks call malakia, “soft-bodied animals,” that is, those whose flesh is considered softer and more yielding, such as cuttlefish, octopuses, and their like.

Among these too there is great diversity. For dragons, moray eels, and eels, which are born in muddy rivers and marshes, are, by similarity of nature, associated more with venomous serpents than with fish.

There is another kind as well: the egg-laying; and another, the catuligenorum, “young-bearing.”

[Note: [Col. 0938] The printed editions read “another, the cataligenorum.” The old books read “the catuligenorum.”]

The weasel gives birth to young, as does the ass-fish, and all those without scales, which the Greeks call salatia. But most of the great sea beasts, dolphins, and seals also give birth to young; and they are said, when frightened for some reason, to protect and warm their newly born offspring by drawing them back again into the womb after they have slipped out.

“Let the waters bring forth creeping things according to their kind.” One kind consists of huge fish, another of small fish. Among these themselves there are likewise many differences, divided according to the quality of their kind: they have their own names, distinct foods, unequal bodily dimensions, and are separated from one another by differing forms.

Who, then, observing the multitude of tunas, could explain to us their differences, although it is asserted that, when they have seen great schools of fish, some people can identify not only their kind but also their number?

[Note: [Col. 0938] The old books read “they assert them.” A little later the printed editions read “subtle knowledge”; the ancient books, “knowledge.”]

Who could minutely disclose to us the knowledge possessed by those experts who, living along the shores and growing old in maritime resorts, know each one of them? For those who fish in the Indian Sea know some fish, and those who explore the Egyptian sea know others.

[Note: [Col. 0938] The second Colbertinus reads “the Indian [Sea].”]

The inhabitants of the islands know still others, and the Moorish fishermen others again. But the first command and that ineffable power produced them all alike, both the small and the great.

Their ways of living are greatly diverse, and there is also immense differentiation in the succession of each kind. Many fish do not brood over their eggs like birds, nor build nests, nor nourish their own young with labor. Rather, the water receives the egg and makes it an animal; and in each kind the offspring remains unchanged into another nature, without admixture—unlike the stock of terrestrial mules or of birds, which is corrupted by the intermingling of different forms.

[Note: [Col. 0938] The second Colbertinus reads “the form of manifest [offspring].” A little later the printed editions read “we see oxen”; the old books have the reading found in the text. Later the printed editions read “except the scaurus.” The first Colbertinus, in its original hand, reads “except the scarus”; since this is the excellent reading, it should not have been corrupted by an ignorant scribe, who foolishly wrote “escaurus.” In Greek: εἰ μή τὸν σκάρον, “except the scarus.” In this very passage two manuscripts read “some have reported.”]

No fish is armed with teeth on only one side, as we see sheep and oxen to be; nor does any fish ruminate, except the scarus, as some have reported. All fish, however, are furnished with a very sharp line of teeth, so that food, once worked in the mouth, may not flow away before long; for unless it were quickly torn apart and delivered to the stomach, it would easily be scattered unchanged by the waves.

3. The food of one kind is suited to one kind, and that of another to another. Some are nourished by mud; some are content with the plants that grow in water; but most are satisfied by devouring one another, and among them the smaller is always made food for the larger.

And if it should happen that the one who had caught the smaller is himself consumed by the bite of a stronger creature, both are cast into the stomach of the latter. As though we human beings were doing something different when we oppress our inferiors by power.

[Note: [Col. 0939] The second Colbertinus reads “through power.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read “otherwise, the property”; the ancient books read “another [man retains] the property.”]

Or how does a man differ from that last fish, a man inflamed by love of riches who, having captured the poor, swallows them with the unsatisfied gulfs of his own greed? One person retained the substance taken from the poor man by force. You, having surrounded him with threats and terrors, made him a portion of your patrimony, and thus became more unjust than the unjust and more rapacious than the robber.

Beware, therefore, lest the same outcome that overtakes the fish overtake you also—that is, the hook, the net, or the basket.

[Note: [Col. 0939] The printed editions read “the same hook.” Two old books read “that is, a hook.”]

For we too, stained by unspeakable crimes, must not escape the punishments of the end. Moreover, having learned that even weak animals are subject to deceits and ambushes, I prefer you to escape the frauds of the cunning.

For they say that the crab desires the flesh of the oyster. Its capture is difficult for it because of the shell coverings with which nature has enclosed the softness of its flesh; hence it is also called testicorius, “shell-covered.”

[Note: [Col. 0939] The printed editions read “for they say that the crab desires the oyster.” But the word “crab” is absent from two manuscripts. Since Eustathius uses the word cercinus both here and somewhat earlier and shortly afterward, he may be thought to have had a corrupt book in which he read not καρκῖνος, “crab,” but κερκῖνος. This may be confirmed by the fact that he rendered καρκῖνος by the Latin cancrus when, near the beginning of this seventh book, he interpreted Basil’s καὶ βάτραχοι καὶ καρκῖνοι, “and frogs and crabs.” For if he had read the same word in all these passages, it is probable that he would also have interpreted it in the same way. In the first Colbertinus too the first occurrence of the word cancrum was absent; it was later added by someone who had the Greek exemplar before his eyes.]

Since the shells are hollow, they easily protect the inner parts of the oyster by closing together; and thus the attack of its assailant is frustrated.

What does the adversary do? When it sees the oyster opening itself willingly in sunny places beneath the sun, it secretly places a small pebble inside it. Because of this obstruction it cannot close its coverings; and thus what the crab could not accomplish by strength, it was able to achieve by cunning.

This, then, is the malice of those who possess neither reason nor speech. But I wish you, having contemplated the crab’s profitable contrivances, to abstain from injuring your neighbors. Such is the person who proceeds toward his brother with a deceitful mind: he either devastates the goods of his relatives or delights in the calamities of others.

[Note: [Col. 0939] The printed editions read “proceeds toward fraud.” The old books read “toward his brother,” and the Greek requires this: πρὸς τὸν ἀδελφόν, “toward his brother.”]

Therefore cease to imitate those who are condemned. Poverty accompanied by truth is preferred by the wise to the greatest riches.

Nor will I pass over the cunning of the deceitful and thieving octopus. When it embraces some rock with its outstretched tentacles, it assumes the rock’s color; and many fish, unwittingly gliding toward it as though toward a stone, are deceived and immediately offer themselves to its malicious capture.

Such are those who continually attend upon the powerful and change with every variation of mind. They do not persist in one purpose but show themselves now as one person and now as another, practicing chastity with the chaste and lust with the lustful, and altogether adapting their own manners to the character of each person.

It is difficult to avoid them because of the wickedness that lies hidden in the pretense of service.

[Note: [Col. 0940] The printed editions and the first Colbertinus, apparently the source used by the printers, read “in likeness.” The other two manuscripts read “in pretense,” correctly. The Greek reads ἐν τῷ προσχήματι, “in the pretext.” Shortly afterward the second Colbertinus reads in the text “presenting themselves simply in their clothing.”]

The Lord called such people “ravenous wolves,” pretending by their clothing to be simple sheep (Matt. 7:15).

Flee, therefore, such variability of character, and pursue rather truth, sincerity, and innocence; for the viper too is varied, and for this reason the Lord condemned it to crawl upon its belly. The righteous person has nothing counterfeit in him, like Job. Therefore the Lord “will make those of one mind dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7).

[Note: [Col. 0940] The second Colbertinus reads “he makes those of one mind dwell in a house.”]

“This sea is great and spacious; there are creeping things there without number, living creatures small and great” (Ps. 103:25). Yet among these there is a certain wise and ordered arrangement. We ought not, therefore, to condemn all fish, but also to praise and imitate certain ones.

For observe how each kind occupies its appointed regions; none seizes the boundaries of another, but each is content with its own dwelling-place. Certainly no surveyor has distributed habitations among them that they must defend, nor marked them off with encircling walls, nor set down boundaries for them to observe. Rather, a common usefulness has been bestowed upon all.

[Note: [Col. 0940] The printed editions read “a common usefulness has been placed.” The old books read “a common usefulness has been bestowed.” A little later the second Colbertinus reads “equally for each.”]

This inlet nourishes one definite kind of fish, another inlet another. Those that abound in one place are found less frequently along other shores—not because they are separated by some exceedingly rugged mountain ridge, or prevented from crossing by intervening barriers of rivers, but because the law of nature has bound them all by its observance, imparting equally to each what is necessary, according to the use required by each.

4. But we are not like this. We boldly cross the boundaries of our ancestors; we cross the bounds of our neighbors; we join house to house and field to field; and we mutilate the rights of others (Prov. 22:26).

[Note: [Col. 0940] The printed books read “we cross the thickets of vices.” Our old codex and the second Colbertinus read “we cross the thickets of our neighbors.”]

The sea monsters know the lodging-place granted to them by nature, situated at the furthest parts of the sea, where no land at all is visible to them and which is considered wholly unnavigable. Indeed, its character has not been discovered even through historical report, since no one has ventured to cross it.

For in this place the beasts mentioned above, as large as mountains, dwell without troubling any cities or islands. Thus each kind is compelled, in the stations assigned to it by nature, to inhabit its own home, as though in the regions of the earth.

Certain fish, however, as though by a common decree of citizens, directed toward the outer sea, undertake the labor of migration; and all together, as though at a given signal, depart for distant places.

When the season for spawning begins to prevail, some from one inlet and some from another, summoned by the laws of nature, immediately set out toward the northern parts of the sea. When you see them returning in the densest masses, you will think a most violent torrent is flowing along the shore of the Propontis toward the Euxine Sea.

[Note: [Col. 0941] Two ancient books read “along the shore of the Propontis.” Another reads “along the shore of Propontis.” The printed editions have the reading found in the text. It seems quite likely to me that Eustathius wrote “along the shore of the Propontis,” but either scribes or printers corrected it to the form found in the printed editions. Where the text shortly before reads “joined in a dense mass,” two codices have “packed into a dense mass.”]

Who drives them? What authority commands them? What proclamations announce to them the appointed time? Who are their leaders? Do you not see the divine ordering filling all things and spreading even through these small creatures?

[Note: [Col. 0941] The printed editions read “diffused.” Our three manuscripts read “diffused” in the feminine form, agreeing with “ordering.” The Greek is καὶ διὰ τῶν μικροτάτων διήκουσαν, “extending even through the smallest things.”]

Fish do not resist the laws of God, while human beings scarcely receive the teaching that brings salvation. Do not despise fish because they are mute and irrational; rather, take care that you are not judged more irrational than they are by resisting the commands of the Creator.

Listen to the fish, which lack only the power to utter a voice. For they seem to speak through definite signs, since, desiring the immortality of their kind, they are compelled to undertake a profitable migration. They do not use words of their own, but possess a law of nature firmly implanted within them, showing them what must be done.

“Let us proceed,” they say, “to the northern sea, for its water is sweeter than that of the other seas, since the sun, having remained there for a short time, does not completely drain its waters of what can be drunk by its rays. For sea animals too take pleasure in sweeter waters. Hence fish coming from far out at sea are often seen ascending through rivers.

“For this reason they seek the open sea more willingly than the other inlets, because it is more suitable for them to bring forth and nourish their offspring.” When they have adequately accomplished what was appointed, they all return together in a troop to their own places.

But let us listen more attentively to the reason given by the silent ones.

[Note: [Col. 0941] Eustathius rendered παρὰ τῶν σιωπώντων as “from the silent ones.” I prefer “from those who are silent,” or “from the mute.” Thus the second Colbertinus reads: “But let us listen more attentively to what the reason is.” It is reasonable to believe that the scribe did not follow the exemplars he possessed but altered something on his own, as, I have already noted, he seems to have done in certain places. Shortly afterward the second Colbertinus has in the text “is stirred from the lowest depth,” but nevertheless gives the common reading in the margin.]

The northern sea is low and sloping, and for this reason exposed to the violence and agitation of the winds. When storms arise, it is shaken from its lowest depths, so that the sand beneath is sometimes mixed with the highest waves. It is also exceedingly cold in winter, since it is filled with many great rivers. When the fish have enjoyed it during the summer months, they are again deterred by the severity of the approaching winter and withdraw to the higher regions of the sea, which are calmer.
