5. I have observed these things and marveled at the wisdom of God, because irrational animals are regarded as provident guardians of their own safety and understand what is suitable and what is harmful to them.

What, then, shall we say, who have been honored with reason, invited by promises, and taught spiritually, yet arrange our affairs more irrationally than fish?

[Note: [Col. 0942] The printed editions read “what do we say?” Two old books read “what shall we say?” Immediately afterward the printed editions read “more irrationally than irrational fish.” Our old codex and the second Colbertinus read “more irrational than fish,” which we judge to be truer and better, in view of Basil’s τῶν ἰχθύων ἀλογώτερον, “more irrational than fish.” Not long afterward two manuscripts read “of the age to come.”]

Even they show concern for knowledge of the future. We, however, corrupted by disbelief in the future age, spend our life in the ugliest actions and unlawful pleasures.

Fish cross such vast stretches of sea in order to find what is useful. What, then, will you say, possessing an indolence joined to you, which is the chief of wickedness?

Let no one, therefore, make ignorance an excuse. For a natural reason has been implanted in us, both for desiring familiarity with good things and for avoiding the harm of things that injure. Accordingly, I will not depart from examples drawn from marine animals, since we have proposed these examples for examination.

I heard one of the inhabitants of the shore report that the sea urchin, although it is extremely cheap and contemptible, often becomes an indicator to sailors of coming calm or winter weather. For when it senses that blasts of wind are approaching, it places itself beneath a stone, supported beneath it as though by the tooth of an anchor, so that it may avoid the shaking of the storm.

[Note: [Col. 0942] The printed editions and the first Colbertinus read “as though by the tooth of an anchor.” The other Colbertinus reads the same. Our codex reads “as though by an anchor biting.” I cannot say which of these readings is more suitable or more correct, since all seem equally corrupt. Yet when I read Basil’s ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγκύρας βεβαίας, “as upon a firm anchor,” I suspect that Eustathius wrote “as upon a standing anchor,” with “standing” meaning “stable.”]

It allows itself to be pressed down for a while by the weight placed upon it, provided that it is not tossed about by the waves. When sailors see this sign, they know that the roar of the winds will soon be stirred up.

And certainly no astrologer or Chaldean, gathering the quality of the air from the rising of the stars, taught the urchin this. Rather, the Lord of the sea and of storms marked even this tiny animal with evident traces of his magnificent wisdom.

Thus nothing is unforeseen and nothing is neglected by God. That sleepless eye observes all things and is present to all, carrying remedies for salvation. If he did not leave the urchin deprived of his visitation, will he not regard you and your affairs, O human being?

Men, love your wives (Eph. 5:25). Even if the great distance of lands interposed between you may seem to separate you for a time, let the covenant of nature and the yoke of blessing be an undivided union for you.

Although the viper is the fiercest of serpents, it approaches the moray eel for mating. By hissing to signify that it has come, it summons her from the depths of the sea to proceed to conjugal union, and she soon obeys and joins herself to it.

What, then, does this discourse require? Although a man may be harsh and considered savage in character, his wife must nevertheless necessarily endure him, without allowing any circumstances to break the affection once formed. But you say that he is irascible or cruel; yet he is your husband. You say that he is a drunkard; yet by nature he is joined to you. You say that he is hard and unappeasable; yet he is regarded as the more precious part of your body.

6. Let the husband also hear an admonition suitable to him. The viper spits out its poisonous venom for the sake of reverence toward marriage; do you not lay aside the savagery and bitterness of your spirit, compelled by respect for the marriage bond?

Perhaps we shall find the viper an appropriate example for us in another respect as well, since the coupling of the viper with the moray eel commits a greater violation of nature. Let those who plot against the marriages of others recognize what sort of beast they resemble.

There is therefore one constant purpose by which the Church can be built up. For this reason I urge that the lusts of the shameless cease—lusts that must be rebuked by examples drawn from the sea and from the land.

Both the lateness of the hour and the weakness of my body compel me to bring this discourse to an end. For there would be more that we ought to add to the treatment, especially since the hearers are eager to learn, concerning the things born in the sea that are most worthy of admiration; or concerning the sea itself—how its water is congealed into salt, or how that precious stone called coral is a plant while it remains in the sea but, after it has been brought out into the air, is immediately changed into stone.

Or concerning how nature places a pearl of great value within the oysters of creatures otherwise worthless, so that the poor fisherman finds along the shore and among the rugged rocks, enclosed within the oyster’s shell, what kings greatly desire.

From where do marine pinnae nourish golden wool? Or from where do shellfish furnish purple to emperors, surpassing the beauty of all flowers by the loveliness of their own color?

[Note: [Col. 0943] The printed editions read “the waters bring forth.” Two manuscripts read “let the waters bring forth.”]

“Let the waters bring forth.” What necessary thing has not been made? Or what excellent thing has not been bestowed upon our life? Some of them benefit human uses; the marvelous contemplation of creation lays claim to others.

Some things are terrifying, clearly intended to restrain our laziness. God made great sea monsters—not because one is called great simply because it is larger than other small fish, but because, in the enormity of its limbs, it equals lofty mountains. Indeed, when it raises itself by gentle swimming to the tops of the waves, it is often thought to be an island.

[Note: [Col. 0943] The printed editions read “he made great sea monsters, not various ones, because ambergris is in their other viscera,” a reading more absurd than anything I have ever seen. The old Colbertine books are no more correct. Our codex, in a second but nevertheless ancient hand, reads: “not, however, because they are larger than other small fish, etc.” This reading too may seem corrupt to some; I judge it otherwise. I think, therefore, that the little word used here has the same force as the preposition “above,” with this meaning: the fish are called great not because of the small fish, but because they resemble lofty mountains. That the particle ab is sometimes used for the preposition prae is well known, for example from Luke 18:14: “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other,” literally “from the other.”]

It is said to inhabit the ancient sea.

[Note: [Col. 0943] The printed editions and manuscripts read “the ancient sea.” But there is no doubt that this is a scribal error, since “Atlantic” was written in Greek, τὸ Ἀτλαντικόν, and the scribes wrote antiquum, “ancient,” instead. Immediately afterward the second Colbertinus reads “swelling”; the other two manuscripts and the printed editions read “swelling” in the ablative construction.]

Such beasts, then, were formed to inspire fear and terror in us. But when you hear that huge ships, their sails swelling in the folds and flying over the sea before a favorable wind, are so delayed and held back by a very small fish that they become motionless for a long time, as though founded upon roots in the deep, will you not also recognize in this tiny creature a demonstration of divine power?

[Note: [Col. 0944] The printed books read “and this through the smallest [creature].” Two manuscripts read “and through this small creature.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read xipius; the old books read xifius. The Greek is ξιφίας, “swordfish.”]

For it is not only the dogfish, the swordfish, or the terrifying whale that is feared; the sting of the stingray, even when the creature is dead, and the sea hare are likewise avoided with equal fear, since they carry swift and unavoidable destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0944] The printed editions and the first Colbertinus read “and certain dead [things].” The other Colbertinus reads “and dead creatures.” But the scribes, falsely persuading themselves that the discourse was introducing another kind of fish, sought a knot in a reed. Our old codex reads “and certainly the dead,” that is, “and the dead indeed.” Basil has καὶ ταύτης νεκρᾶς, “and of this one even when dead.”]

Since these things are so, the providence of the Creator preferred that you should always remain watchful, so that, trusting in him, you might thereafter escape every harmful plague.

But now, returning from the sea’s depths, let us return to the land. For the successive wonders of creation that have met us, like waves repeatedly and alternately tossing themselves, have submerged our discourse.

[Note: [Col. 0944] The printed editions read “since indeed.” The old books read “and indeed.” A little later the printed editions and the first Colbertinus read “not directing their course toward a definite place”; the other Colbertinus reads “not directing their course toward a definite course.” Our old book has the reading found in the text.]

And indeed I shall marvel if our mind, occupied with more important matters, does not flee back to the earth again, just as Jonah fled into the sea.

Therefore it seems to me that the course of our discussion, entangled in many thousands of miracles and forgetful of its own modest proportions, resembles sailors on the open sea who, not directing their course toward a definite place, do not know how much distance they have covered under sail.

This has certainly happened to our discourse. While it wanders more widely through the paths of creation, it does not perceive the multitude of the things it has recounted.

But although the gathered audience is eager to hear, and the narration of the Lord’s marvelous works seems most pleasing to their hearts, here we bring our discussion to an end, intending to pay tomorrow what remains of the interest.

Now let us all together give thanks for what has been said, and ask for the completion of what we have explained inadequately. May he cause us, even amid our banquets, to remember what our speech brought forth either in the morning or toward evening; may the memory of these things remain joined to you even while you rest in sleep, and may you chew over at night also the sweetness you received during the day, so that you may say:

“I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2),

meditating day and night upon the law of the Lord, to whom be glory and honor, now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.

**BOOK EIGHT.**
### 1

And God said: “Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds: quadrupeds, reptiles, and beasts according to their kinds.” And it was so. The command came, advancing everywhere, and the earth resumed its proper course [Note: [Col. 0945] The printed editions and manuscripts read “proper course.” But I shall not readily be persuaded that Eustathius wrote this. Somehow it seems more plausible to me that, from that Basilian reading, τὸν κόσμον (“the order,” “the adornment”) he formed and wrote cosmum, that is, “ornament”; while the scribes, deceived by the unfamiliar word, changed cosmum into cursum (“course”).] order. There He commanded the waters to bring forth reptiles of living souls; here, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” Do you suppose, then, that the earth is animate, and that an opportunity will be given to the babbling Manichaeans to attribute a soul to the earth? Not at all: by saying “Let it bring forth,” He brought out what was within it; but God, who gave the command, also granted the earth the power [Col. 0945B] to bring it forth. For when it heard the command to sprout grass for hay and a fruit-bearing tree, it did not produce only the grass for hay that was hidden within it, nor did it bring upward the palms, oaks, or cypresses concealed in its recesses; rather, the divine Word is plainly the creator of things that come into being. “Let the earth sprout,” not so that it might bring out what it already had, but so that it might assume what it did not have, God supplying it with the power of operation. So also now: “Let it bring forth a soul”—not the soul that was hidden in the earth, but the soul that was bestowed upon it by God through the command.

Then the statement must be turned against the Manichaeans. For if the earth brought forth the soul it possessed, it itself has become soulless. But their detestable error is well known. Let us rather consider why the waters were commanded [Col. 0945C] to produce reptiles of living souls, whereas the earth was commanded to produce a living soul. We suppose, therefore, that the nature of aquatic creatures is thought to possess life in a certain sense imperfectly [Note: The printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read “perfectly,” against the Greek and against the evidence. Our manuscript reads “imperfectly”; the other Colbertine manuscript also reads “imperfectly.” The Greek has ἀτελεστέρᾳ, “more imperfect.”]. This is because the waters are denser. For, in the end, the hearing of creatures dwelling in water is duller, and their sight more blunted, since they see through water; nor is there among them any memory, imagination, or recognition of those close to them [Note: The printed editions read “a memorial recollection or recognition of those close to them.” Our old manuscript and the second Colbertine read “memory or imagination or recognition of those close to them,” which is expressed from the Greek terms μνήμη, “memory”; φαντασία, “imagination”; and ἐπίγνωσις, “recognition.”].

The divine Word therefore makes clear that the carnal life of aquatic creatures is governed by movements of the soul. But in terrestrial beasts, which have received a more perfect life, the soul holds primacy over the body. Their senses are indeed more vigorous; and, since animals plainly take the greatest care of present matters, they diligently preserve the memory of what has passed. Hence we must consider [Note: Two ancient books read “we must consider because,” which is less correct, but for that very reason it may be believed that Eustathius spoke in this way. A little later the printed editions read “each one itself”; the two ancient books, “each one also.”] that water produced the bodies [Col. 0945D] of fish as animate: for, as Scripture indicates, it produced reptiles of living souls; but among terrestrial creatures the soul that governs the body was commanded to be generated, since they have received a greater share of life-giving power. Although these terrestrial creatures too are irrational, each of them nevertheless expresses many things through its natural voice concerning the affections of the soul. They make their joy and grief, hunger, separation from their own kind, and various troubles known by their voices, whereas aquatic creatures are not merely [Note: The printed editions read “not only very many”; the old books read “mute”; and the Basilian expression ἄφωνα, “voiceless,” clearly shows that this is how it ought to be read.] mute, but also untamable [Col. 0946B] and uneducated, and wholly beyond human handling for every association of life [Note: The printed editions read “untamable.” The old books read “intractable,” correctly, corresponding to the Greek ἀμεταχείριστα, “not manageable.” Shortly afterward two manuscripts read “can distinguish.”].

“The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isaiah 1:3); but a fish has never been able to recognize the one who supplies its nourishment. The ass understands the familiar voice of a human being, knows the road it has often traveled, and sometimes becomes a guide for its driver when he has gone astray. Its hearing is so keen that no terrestrial creature can be compared with it. The camel always retains a tenacious memory of injuries; it is prone to anger and persistent. Indeed, if it has been struck, it conceals its pain for a long time and, when it finds a suitable opportunity, immediately repays the injury inflicted. But no marine creature imitates it.

Hear this, therefore, you angry people, who cultivate [Col. 0946C] the remembrance of a long-ago injury as though it were the greatest virtue. To what creature do you resemble yourselves, when you retain your own anger—like a certain spark lying smothered beneath ashes [Note: The word “some” was added from the ancient books. A little farther on, the second Colbertine reads “but frozen blood.”]—in your hearts until, having found an opportunity, you kindle the goads of pain, like a small ember nourished by fuel, into a flame?

### 2

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” Why does the earth bring forth a living soul? So that you may learn the difference between the soul of an animal and that of a human being. A little farther on you will learn how the human soul has been constituted; but now hear about the soul of mute creatures, because, according to Scripture, the soul of every animal is its own blood. Blood, however, commonly turns into flesh when it coagulates, and corrupted flesh returns to the earth. Rightly, therefore, the soul of beasts is subject to decay.

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” [Col. 0946D] Observe the sequence [Note: In the printed editions and in the first Colbertine manuscript the corrupt reading is “soul to blood, blood to flesh, flesh to earth.” But in the other two manuscripts we find the corrected reading “of the soul to blood,” and so on, as in the text. Basil wrote ψυχῆς πρὸς αἷμα, αἵματος πρὸς σάρκα, “of soul to blood, of blood to flesh,” and so on; the printed editions repeat this at this very passage. The old books read “by retracing,” or “going back again.”] from soul to blood, from blood [Col. 0947A] to flesh, and from flesh to earth. Then, reversing these things, go back again through the same stages—that is, from earth to flesh, from flesh to blood, from blood to soul—and you will find that the soul of beasts is earth. Do not suppose that it is older than the substance of their bodies; nor [Note: [Col. 0947D] I do not sufficiently understand the wording “nor expect it to be dissolved together with the body.” It appears that the scribes omitted the word “not”: “nor expect that it will not be dissolved together with the body.” These words are much clearer in Basil, from whom this passage comes: Μὴ νόμιζε πρεσβυτέραν εἶναι τῆς τοῦ σώματος αὐτῶν ὑποστάσεως, μηδὲ ἐπιδιαμένουσαν μετὰ τὴν τῆς σαρκὸς διάλυσιν—“Do not suppose that the soul is older than the constitution of their body, or that it remains after the dissolution of the flesh.”] expect it to be dissolved together with the body.

Avoid the anxious chatter of philosophers, who are not ashamed to assert that their own souls and those of dogs retain a similar form. Indeed, they even profess that they themselves were once women, fish, and shrubs. But if they were once fish—which I do not believe—nevertheless, while writing these things they were considered more irrational than fish.

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” Why, then, after the discourse had been proceeding everywhere, did I suddenly fall silent for no short time [Col. 0947B]? I believe that some of those present are wondering, although I do not suppose that the most attentive hearers are unaware of the reasons for the silence—for by gestures and nods they reminded one another and brought us back to the memory of what we had interrupted. We have nearly passed over without discussion a certainly not insignificant part of creation [Note: The printed editions read “we pass over”; the two ancient books, “we have passed over.”].

“Let the waters bring forth reptiles of living souls according to their kinds, and winged creatures flying beneath the firmament of heaven.” [Note: The second Colbertine reads, “We spoke above about the births of aquatic creatures.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read “they must be invited”; the old books, “they must be imitated,” which agrees well with the Greek κατὰ τοὺς ἐπιλήσμονας τῶν ὁδοιπόρων, “like forgetful travelers.”]

We spoke above about swimming creatures, as far as the evening allowed; today we pass to an examination of terrestrial creatures. Meanwhile, however, the birds escaped us in the middle of the account. Therefore we must imitate forgetful travelers who, when they have left something valuable at an inn, return even after they have covered most of the road by advancing, enduring the labor deserved by their negligence: [Note: We added the whole sentence “Thus we too must return by the same path by which we came” from our manuscripts. The Greek reads οὕτω καὶ ἡμῖν ὡς ἔοικε τὴν αὐτὴν πάλιν βαδιστέον, “thus, it seems, we too must walk back along the same path.” Soon afterward the second Colbertine reads “element of the sea,” an example that again confirms what we said: when a reading already received did not please him, the scribe repeatedly altered something on his own.] thus we too [Col. 0947C] must return by the same path by which we came. For what we omitted is not contemptible, since it is a third portion of the animal creation.

“There are three kinds of living creatures: terrestrial, winged, and marine. ‘Let the waters,’ he says, ‘bring forth reptiles of living souls according to their kinds, and winged creatures flying beneath the firmament of heaven according to their kinds.’” Why, then, did he assign the birds’ origin also to the element of the sea? Because birds and fish possess a certain kinship. Just as fish cut through the water with the movements of their fins, advancing forward, and direct their turns by the rudder of their tails, so birds too are believed to pierce the air by swimming with their wings. Therefore, since the same characteristic of swimming exists in both kinds, they also possess from the water this same kinship [Note: The printed editions read “and that same thing also”; the old books have the reading we have printed. A little later the printed editions read “even for birds of prey”; the ancient books, “but also for birds of prey.” Not much farther below the printed books read “for turning the prey”; our three manuscripts read “for pursuing the prey.”].

Their difference is that no bird [Col. 0948A] can be without feet, since birds obtain their food from the earth and therefore necessarily possess the service of feet. Birds of prey also have the sharpness of claws, adapted for carrying off prey. In the others, the services of the feet have been provided both for obtaining food and for the other arrangements of life. A few birds, however, have useless feet, suitable neither for walking nor for hunting, such as swallows and bee-eaters, whose food is supplied solely from the air. Yet the swallow usually flies lower, almost touching the earth, so that in this way it appears to make use of its feet.

### 3

There are indeed many kinds which, if someone wished to explain them in the manner in which we described part of the multitude of fish, would reveal one general name for all birds [Col. 0948B], but very many differences among them, whether of form, size, or color [Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read “whether of sizes or colors.” Another manuscript reads “whether of size or color,” correctly. Immediately afterward the printed editions read “as though, so to speak”; the two ancient books read “using various [names], as though.”]. For they are distinguished by an extraordinary diversity of dispositions, activities, and diets. Some have attempted to use various names concerning them, so that, as though through unusual seals, the distinctive character of a new and unheard-of designation might be recognized in each kind of bird [Note: Something has been omitted here either by the scribes or by Eustathius himself. See Homily 8, section 3.].

But for us the common usage of Scripture is sufficient to signify the quality of each kind and to distinguish the clean from the unclean. One kind consists of those that eat flesh, with another form corresponding to their habits: they have sickle-shaped claws, a hooked beak, and swift flight, by which they may seize prey more quickly; once it has been torn apart by their feet, it supplies easy food to the captor. Another species [Col. 0948C] consists of those nourished by seeds, and another of those that take whatever chance offers them for food.

Among these too there is a very great difference. Some are gregarious, except for birds of prey, none of which associates with others except for mating. Others live in communal groups, such as doves, starlings, cranes, and jackdaws. Some of these are without leaders and govern themselves; others are kept under direction, such as cranes. There is also another distinction among them: we see that some are visitors and others native. When winter compels them, many depart into foreign lands for the sake of food [Note: The printed editions read “for the sake of breeding”; the two ancient books, “for the sake of feeding.”].

Many become tame and patient, except the weaker ones, which because of excessive timidity cannot endure being handled. Some dwell among human beings, sharing the same homes [Col. 0949A] as they do; others delight in deserted places and mountains.

There is also great variety among birds in their voices, and each has its own distinctive character. Some are talkative and chattering, others silent; some melodious and loud, others shrill, and some have no song at all. Others are naturally imitative or have been trained through human instruction. Still others have a single sound, never changing their voice.

The cock is lustful, the peacock diligent, the dove wanton, and the hen domestic. The partridge is deceitful and jealous; at times it maliciously cooperates with hunters so that others may be captured. In every respect there is a manifold distinction among them in actions and dispositions.

### 4

There are also certain animals that are civic-minded, if civic-mindedness consists in bringing the activity of individuals to one common end [Col. 0949B]. This may be seen among bees: they have a common dwelling and a common flight, one labor for all; and, what is most important, under kings and leaders each performs its own task. They do not dare to seek the open fields before they have seen their ruler fly.

Their king is not appointed by the people, for the votes of an unskilled multitude often advance the unworthy to imperial power; nor is the kingdom bestowed by lot. The outcomes of the urn are irrational, since it often assigns the insignia of power to the lowest of all. Nor are imperial scepters handed down by inheritance from parents, since the children of rulers are easily corrupted by pleasures and luxury and become senseless and foolish. Rather, by the judgment of nature, whoever is worthy [Col. 0949C] receives the diadems [Note: The printed editions read “received”; the old books, “receives.”] of leadership. He surpasses the others no less in the stature of his limbs than in the gentleness of his character, and he has certain stings, but does not use them to injure others.

Thus nature has prescribed for them certain unspoken laws, by which they are restrained from inflicting torment on those subject to them. But if the bees themselves fail to follow the institutions of their rulers, they are punished by their own penalty. For if they sting someone, they leave their life together with the sting in the wound.

Let Christians hear this, since they have been commanded to repay evil to no one with evil, but to overcome wickedness with goodness. Therefore imitate the ways [Note: One manuscript reads “of the bees.” Soon afterward the second Colbertine reads “nor seizing the property of others”; the other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “other property.” A little later the second Colbertine reads “what is first perceived.”] of bees. They trouble no one and seize no one else’s property. They fashion honeycombs from flowers, but collect honey from the dewy moisture that rests upon the leaves of trees [Col. 0949D] and store it in waxen cells.

In the end, the honey that is first collected is more fluid; afterward, as time gradually passes, it is digested and returns to its proper thickness and sweetness. It is not undeserved, therefore, that bees receive such great praise, since antiquity called them industrious and wise [Col. 0950A]. They carefully store up their own food, whose use provides remedies of health to kings and private persons alike. And so, because they build their honey stores so wisely [Note: The printed editions read “Why so? Because so.” The second Colbertine reads “and because they build them so wisely.” Our old book reads “And so, because so,” and so forth.], they construct, within a delicate membrane, numerous compartments adjoining one another. Their compact arrangement, tightened by the finest woven interlacing and supported as though by certain barriers, holds the entire work together.

Each opening is supported by another through a mutually tightened bond and is separated by the delicate partitioning of the little chambers. These are arranged above one another in two or three layers. They did not prefer to make the depths of the cavities straight or simple, lest the moisture, compressed by its own weight, should flow outward [Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read “should remain,” ineptly. The second Colbertine reads “should flow out,” which agrees well with the Greek. In the same place the printed editions read “learn that”; the ancient books, “learn how.”].

Learn how the passion for geometry is surpassed by the wisdom [Col. 0950B] of the bees. Their waxen tubes are enclosed by six angles and as many sides; yet they are not erected vertically, lest the bottom suffer if it were deprived of the support of the joints. Rather, those six lower angles serve as a kind of seat and foundation for the structures placed above them, so that they might bear the superimposed weight securely [Note: The printed editions read “which tolerably”; two manuscripts read “by which they might tolerably.” A little later the second Colbertine reads “while the others sleep in bodily slumber.” Soon afterward the same manuscript reads “he himself”; the final word was absent from the printed editions.] and preserve the stored moisture in each cavity.

### 5

Who could carefully set forth all the peculiarities of birds? Or how could one explain the way cranes take turns keeping watch at night? While some care for their bodies in sleep, others remain awake and provide them with protection. When they have completed the period of watch assigned to them, they themselves begin to rest after giving a cry, while others take their place by lot.

They also preserve this order in flight, while they are compelled to complete the task of leading the way [Col. 0950C] by turns [Note: The second Colbertine reads “are compelled to fulfill the task of leading the way.” A little later the printed editions read “first, because”; the second Colbertine, “first indeed, because”; our manuscript, “first indeed, because.”].

Storks are certainly not far removed from those creatures to which rational prudence has been granted. For all arrive together at one time, and likewise all depart together under a single signal for distant regions. Crows support them: they escort them honorably when they set out and, as it seems to me, provide them assistance when they are about to fight against certain birds. There is clear evidence of this: first, because the crow is completely unseen at that time; and then because the returning storks display unmistakable signs of battle.

Who, I ask, imposed upon them the laws of hospitality? Or who commanded them under threat that they should not abandon storks standing in battle array [Col. 0950D], but should not leave them without their company?

Let greedy people hear this. They deny hospitality to arriving strangers, shut their doors, and do not allow them to enter their homes at night or in winter [Note: The second Colbertine reads “who deny humanity to strangers.” Shortly afterward the printed editions and two manuscripts read “allow them to follow”; the second Colbertine, “receive them.” Not far away the printed editions read “they will endure”; the manuscripts, “they will suffer.”].

The generosity shown by younger storks to aged storks [Col. 0951A] would be enough for human children, if they preferred to pay attention and become lovers of their parents. For who is so foolish that he would not consider himself marked with disgrace when he is surpassed by irrational birds in the practice of filial devotion [Note: The printed editions read “so that he does not recount”; our old manuscript, “so that he does not consider himself.” A little later the manuscripts read “and even today”; the word “even” was absent from the printed editions.]?

Those birds surround their parents when age has worn them out and the decay of years has cast down their feathers; they warm them with their own plumage, carry them food, and, in flight, placing themselves beneath them wherever they can, relieve the weariness of old age by supporting them with the help of their wings. This practice has spread so widely among all peoples that even today the repayment of a benefit received is called among the Greeks ἀντιπελαργώσις, “stork-like repayment.”

Therefore no one should excuse himself entirely on the pretext of poverty or despair of his own life, even if no resources are available at home, while he observes the resourceful swallow [Note: The printed editions read “ingenious at home”; the old books, “while observing the ingenious [bird].” Not far afterward the printed editions and two manuscripts read “as though with a kind of glue”; another manuscript reads “as though with some glue.” Here one may suspect that Eustathius wrote, from the Greek οἷον κόλλῃ τινί, “as though with some glue.”].

When building its nest [Col. 0951B], it carries straw in its mouth. Since it cannot carry mud with its feet, it moistens the tips of its wings in a river and then rolls in ashes, appearing to supply the function of mortar. Gradually, by applying mud between the twigs, it joins them together as though with a kind of glue and raises its young.

If one of them has had its eyes gouged out, its mother possesses from nature a medicine handed down to her, by which she soon restores the sight of her offspring to health. These examples plainly urge you not to turn toward wickedness on account of poverty, nor to place your hope of living in evil arts and thereby become deprived of goodness and destitute of virtue, but to flee to God. If he has given such great gifts to a swallow, how much greater things will he provide for those who implore him with the full intent of their minds [Note: The second Colbertine reads “toward wickedness.” A little later the same manuscript reads “implore him with the full intent of their hearts.”]?

The halcyon [Col. 0951C] is a certain little bird accustomed to breed on sea-shores. It lays its eggs upon the sand at the very time when the sea is stirred by many powerful blasts of wind. Yet all storms and tempests are calmed for the full seven days during which this bird is said to brood. And, for the sake of feeding the chicks after they have been hatched from the eggs, God, the giver of great things, adds another seven days to it. Sailors observe these days carefully and call them halcyon days.

This example has been set before you concerning remedies that are unquestionably life-giving and should be sought from God through prayer. For what wondrous thing would not be done for your sake—you who were made in the image of God—when, for the sake of a tiny bird, you see the vast and terrifying sea become calm in stormy weather, restrained by the divine command?

### 6

They say that if a turtledove is separated from its mate by some accident, it will never mate with another, but, while the memory of its former marriage endures, will reject a second union. Let women [Col. 0952A] hear how, among irrational birds, the continence of widowhood is preferred to repeated marriages.

The eagle is said to be unjust in raising its young. For when two have been produced, it beats one with its wings and casts it to the ground, while it keeps and cherishes the other. Thus, because of scarcity of food, it is compelled to reject the offspring it has produced; yet the bearded vulture does not allow it to perish, but takes it up, places it among its own young, and carefully nourishes it [Note: The printed editions read “beaten by many [blows]”; the old books, “punished.”].

Such are some human parents who, pleading poverty, expose their children, or do not establish an equal inheritance among them. Since they provided equal causes for their birth, it would be just for them to grant them an equal share in life as well.

Do not wish, therefore, to imitate the ways of birds of prey. When they see that their young are already confident in flight [Col. 0952B], they drive them headlong from the nests and cast them out [Note: The printed editions read “confident”; the old books have the reading printed here.], thereafter showing them no care whatsoever. By contrast, the affection of the crow toward its offspring is praised: it follows them even when they fly and supplies them with food generously.

Certain birds do not use the assistance of males to nourish and cherish their young. Some of those that fly at greater heights are entirely sterile, such as vultures, which are said to reproduce without mating, especially since they are long-lived. For they affirm that their life lasts one hundred years [Note: The two ancient books confirm this reading.].

Let this portion of natural history be noted by you, so that when you see certain people laughing at the ineffable mystery of the Catholic faith—because it seems impossible and contrary to nature that a virgin gave birth while preserving the integrity of her virgin state—you may reflect that the one who chose to save believers through the foolishness of preaching [Col. 0952C] has likewise provided us with innumerable reasons drawn from nature for believing in marvelous things.

### 7

“Let the waters bring forth reptiles of living souls, and winged creatures flying over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” They were commanded to fly over the earth because food is supplied to all from the earth [Note: The second Colbertine reads “they were commanded.” If “commands” is read, I would have you understand the word “birds.” We added the word above from our manuscripts a little later. Soon afterward the second Colbertine reads “I deliberately passed over in silence.”]. He said “beneath the firmament of heaven” on account of what we discussed above.

Here we must understand “heaven” as derived from seeing; for in Greek οὐρανός, “heaven,” is called so ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι, “from being seen.” Compared with the ethereal body, this air above us becomes dense and thick through vapors condensed from the earth.

You have, then, the pole adorned, the earth most beautiful, the sea most abundant, and the air filled with birds—all of which were brought forth from nothing into this life by God’s command [Col. 0952D]. And there are many other things that the discourse has deliberately passed over, lest by lingering longer on the same matters it should seem to exceed the proper limits of discussion.

But as you yourself ponder all these things and attentively seek the wisdom of God that is present in them all [Col. 0953A], never fail [Note: The printed editions read “you will not fail”; our three manuscripts, “may you never fail.”] to wonder, and never cease glorifying the Creator.

You also have birds of the night [Note: The two ancient books read “and of the day”; the word “and” was absent from the printed editions.] and of the day. Bats and owls are creatures that flee the light. Therefore, whenever sleep has not overcome you, examining their way of life and their peculiar nature will be enough to impel you to proclaim the wisdom of the Creator.

Consider how the nightingale remains awake while brooding over its eggs, extending its song throughout the whole night; how bats are no less four-footed than winged, and are known to be the only birds to possess teeth; how they are said to give birth to young; and how they fly through the air not with feathers but with a certain membranous skin.

They also possess by nature a great mutual affection for one another. For they cling together by alternating bonds, like certain fishing lines [Col. 0953B] [Note: The printed editions read “of a fisherman”; the old books, “of fishing.” A little later the second Colbertine reads “for just as ... sharper is ... so also theirs.” I suspect this reading because it is better and more appropriate. For, unless I am greatly mistaken, the scribe sometimes altered things according to his own judgment.]. This is not easily found among human beings, some of whom delight in individuality and solitude, separated from the company of others.

Consider also how professors of worldly wisdom resemble the eyes of owls. The sight of owls is sharper at night, but when the sun rises they are blinded. So too, although the senses of such professors are exceedingly sharp for contemplating vanity, they grow dull when searching for the true light.

During the day it is easy for you everywhere to draw admiration for the Creator. Consider how the domestic cock compels human beings to labor and work, and, proclaiming with a clear voice, announces that the sun is approaching from afar.

The race of geese is also considered vigilant and prudent, quick to detect what is being attempted secretly. They are said once to have saved the city of Rome [Col. 0953C] from the nocturnal ambushes of enemies: those who were secretly attempting to enter through hidden passages and overrun the citadel, they promptly betrayed by crying out [Note: The second Colbertine reads “through hidden entrances.”].

In what class of creatures does nature not display its own wonders everywhere? Who informs vultures of the future death of human beings? When men are soon to wage war against one another, flocks of vultures follow them and understand from the deployment or equipment of arms what kind of outcome is to be expected. This is not far removed from human reason.

How shall I also disclose to you the campaigns of locusts [Note: The printed editions read “I shall cover”; the old books, “I shall disclose.” The Greek has διηγήσομαι, “I shall recount.” Immediately afterward the printed editions read “until the divine command is given to them. How, then?” The ancient books have the reading found in the text.]? They leave their own dwellings under a single signal, establish camp in a broad field, and do not touch the places beneath them before the divine command is given to them.

How does the diver endure an insatiable appetite for feeding, through which it obtains remedies for the health of its wounds from its own belly [Note: One manuscript reads “seeks.” Soon afterward two manuscripts read “there is a reason.” The word “is” is lacking in the printed editions. A little later two manuscripts read “from the air”; the word “from” was absent from the common editions.]?

O [Col. 0953D], the wonder of heavenly power, which has transformed the frenzy of hunger into the use of medicine [Col. 0954A]! What great intelligence is also shown in the songs of cicadas, which resound more strongly beneath the burning sun, driven by the current of air that enters through their breasts as they breathe?

But now I feel that our discourse is being surpassed by the wonders of birds no less than if I myself were attempting to outrun its speed on my feet.

When you see bees and wasps, consider that they have neither a spirit nor a lung, but are continually nourished by the air. Indeed, if they are touched with oil, they immediately die, since their breathing passages are blocked; and if you sprinkle them again with vinegar, they revive, their vascular passages having been opened [Note: The printed editions and two manuscripts read “and if you sprinkle them again with vinegar, they recover.” The second Colbertine reads “and if you sprinkle them again with vinegar, they come back to life,” as required by both the sense and the Greek ἀναβιώσκεται, “comes back to life.” A little later two manuscripts read “nor hooked.”].

Thus God made nothing that is superfluous or lacking for our needs.

Again, if you wish to examine the aquatic creatures, you will find another arrangement among them. Their feet [Col. 0954B] are not split like a crow’s, nor hooked like an eagle’s, but broad and membranous, so that they may easily be carried over the waves as they swim, pushing the water away by the effort of their feet like a kind of oar.

Likewise, if you consider how the swan stretches its long neck upward and draws nourishment from the bottom depths, you can perceive the wisdom of the Creator, who for this reason gave it a longer neck than feet, so that, extending it like a kind of probe into the deep, it might be able to find food hidden there [Note: The printed editions read “because of this”; the second Colbertine, “who for this reason.” In the same place the printed editions read “longer than those”; our old manuscript reads “longer than them.”].

## 8

Thus, when the words of Scripture are examined simply, they seem to be certain syllables: “Let the waters bring forth flying creatures that fly over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven.” But when the force of the words is considered, the Creator’s wondrous work is revealed: he foresaw from afar the future varieties of birds and distinguished them according to their kinds.

My day would certainly fail me if I wished to recount to you all the wonders of the creatures of the air. Nevertheless, the earth calls us to examine beasts, cattle, and serpents. For it is ready to display kinds of quadrupeds and plants comparable to those of the fish and flying creatures: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul.”

What do you say, you who do not believe the Apostle Paul concerning the resurrection, when you see certain creatures of the air change their own form, as, for instance, the horned Indian worm, which first transforms itself into a caterpillar, then becomes a bombylion, yet does not remain in that shape, but, feathering out with softer and broader membranes, becomes winged?

[Note: [Col. 0954] The printed editions and our three manuscripts have *in verucae se speciem*—“into the form of a wart”—or *in verrucae speciem*. How absurd and inappropriate this is hardly needs to be said. But the passage is easily corrected. For, if nothing else, the Greek name itself plainly shows that *erucae*—“into a caterpillar”—should be read instead of *verucae*, since the Greek has εἰς κάμπην, “into a caterpillar.”]

Therefore, you women, when you sit unwinding their products—that is, the threads which the Seres send here for the making of delicate garments—remember the transformation of this creature, so that you may take from it a clear example of the resurrection and have no doubt about the re-formation of the body which Paul explains.

[Note: [Col. 0954] I added “and broader,” following the authority of the ancient books; the Greek agrees: καὶ πλατέσι, “and broader.”]

But now I feel that I am exceeding the proper limit of discussion. For if I look to the multitude of what has been reported, I shall seem to have strayed into infinity in my speech.

[Note: [Col. 0955] The printed editions read *perlapsus*, “having slipped away.” The old books read *prolapsus*, “having advanced too far.” Not long afterward, Colbertinus II has *judicia Domini*, “the judgments of the Lord.” Subsequently, our manuscripts have *gulosus es*, “you are gluttonous.” The word *es*, “are,” was absent from the printed editions.]

But if I turn my eyes to the diversity of creation, I think I have not even begun my account. Nevertheless, it is not useful to pass you by in haste. For what will you do until evening? Certainly, you are not pressed by diners, nor does the preparation of banquets urge us to depart, since it is a time for fasting.

Therefore, if it pleases you, let us turn bodily abstinence into the pleasures of the soul. You have often obeyed the needs of the body; let us at least devote these days to the uses of the soul, as it is written: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Psalm XXXVI, 4).

If you love riches, spiritual wealth is available to you: namely, “the judgments of God, true and justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and precious stone” (Psalm XVIII, 10). If you are ravenous and gluttonous, you have the words of the Lord, “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (ibid.).

Now, if I dismiss you and break up the gathering, some of you will immediately run off hurriedly to the gaming table, where there is swearing, violent quarrelling, and a passion for winning; and there the obscene demon stands, now raising one man up in the exultation of victory and making his opponent sad, now displaying another as cheerful and arrogant.

What benefit is there in fasting bodily if the soul is burdened with thousands of vices? Moreover, what does the man who does not play dice do when he is idle? What vanities does he not pour forth from his mouth, or what does he not hear with his ears that deserves execration? Thus idleness, without the fear of God, is the teacher of wickedness.

And indeed, I venture to suppose that you have gained some benefit from what we have said. But if this should not be so, nevertheless, remaining in a place of this kind will render you free from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0955] The printed editions have, in place of this passage, *commemoratio loco hujusmodi ... Ecclesia Dei*, “a commemoration in a place of this kind ... the Church of God.” Both Colbertinus manuscripts have the reading found in the text. A little later, Colbertinus II has *ad parvitatis nostrae possibilitates*, “according to the capacities of our smallness.”]

And the longer we keep you in the Lord’s Church, the more we separate you from evil thoughts. What we have discussed is sufficient before the most just Judge, provided that he looks not to the abundant riches of creation but to the smallness of our capacity, or to the measure for attaining the joy of present things.

[Note: [Col. 0955C] The printed editions and Colbertinus I have *super laeva capienda*, “for attaining what is on the left”; what suitable meaning these words could have, let others decide. The other two manuscripts have *super laetitia capienda*, “for attaining joy.” The Greek is εἰς εὐφροσύνην, “for joy.”]

Let this, then, be the end of our morning banquet, lest excessive fullness from what has been consumed cause you to loathe the evening meal.

The Lord, who has filled all things with the abundance of his creation and who in all things has furnished us with everlasting memorials of his wonders,

[Note: [Col. 0956] I am surprised to find the word *aeterna*, “everlasting,” in both the printed editions and the old books, although Basil has written ἐναργῆ τὰ ὑπομνήματα καταλιπών, “having left manifest memorials.”]

may fill our minds with spiritual joy in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and honor now and always, and for ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK NINE

## 1

Tell me, I beg you, what did you think of the morning table of our discourse? For I like to compare our poverty with some poor man providing a banquet, who, desiring lavishly to display the generosity of his spirit, is held back by lack of means and therefore attempts to serve his poor preparation, whatever it may be, with greater liberality, making his guests laugh at him.

Thus it happens that affected generosity is not free from the disgrace of reproach. Something similar may be found in us also, if that is how you judge us. Nevertheless, whatever our resources may be, they will not be diminished by you.

For the guests of that time did not reject Elisha as a worthless shepherd (IV Kings IV, 39); and certainly he refreshed them with rustic vegetables.

[Note: [Col. 0956] The printed editions and manuscripts have *refutabant*, “were rejecting.” We suspect that Eustathius wrote *repudiabant*, “were repudiating,” since Basil has *παρῃτοῦντο*, “were declining.” A little later, Colbertinus II has *ex me ipse*, “from myself.”]

I have therefore discovered certain rules concerning allegory—not rules which I have devised myself, but ones which I learned by examining the books of others. By these rules, those who assent to the common Scriptures say that water is not water but some other nature; and they interpret fish, serpents, and beasts, not according to the truth of the matter but according to their own arbitrary judgment, like interpreters of dreams who, after seeing various images in sleep, announce what will happen according to their own will.

But when I hear “hay,” I understand precisely what has been said. Likewise, when fish, quadrupeds, or plants are mentioned, I understand them as they have been related. For I am not ashamed of the Gospel (Romans II, 16).

Although those who have written more extensively about the world have argued in detail about the forms of the earth, describing it now as resembling a sphere, now a cylinder, now a circle, and as gathered into equal dimensions on every side, while also asserting that it is hollow in the middle—for writers of cosmography have fallen into all such opinions, cutting down one another’s doctrines—

I nevertheless am not led to say that our ordering of the world should therefore appear inferior because the servant of God said nothing about its shapes, because he did not say that the earth’s circumference contains so many thousands of stadia, or because he did not measure over what distances its shadow extends through the air when the sun follows its own courses beneath the earth and, when it approaches the moon, gives it an eclipse of light.

He wisely kept silent about all these matters, knowing that things which in no way concerned us were useless to us. Therefore, we must not suppose that spiritual words are inferior to the most empty assertions of philosophers. Rather, we should glorify God, who freed our mind from superfluous questions but arranged everything so as to benefit the awakening and building up of our souls.

Accordingly, certain ignorant people seem to me to strive, through crooked deceptions and false persuasions, to cover the divine Scriptures with some appearance of respectability by means of their own arguments.

[Note: [Col. 0957] The printed editions have *honestatis quondam*, “of a former respectability.” The old books have *honestatis quemdam*, “a certain appearance of respectability.” The word *se*, which follows shortly afterward, was added from the old books.]

What else is this to be understood as meaning except that such people profess themselves wiser than the spiritual words and establish their own sayings under the pretext of interpretation?

Therefore, let it be understood as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul of cattle, beasts, and serpents.”

## 2

Observe, then, the word of God running through all creation. It began long ago, but it continues to work and hasten toward its end even now, until the world receives its consummation.

For just as a ball, once pushed by someone, when it finds sloping spaces, is driven more swiftly by its own rolling and by the downward inclination of the place, and cannot stop before it descends to level ground, so the nature of things, set in motion by God’s command, penetrating everywhere through the generation and death of beings, preserves the offspring of each kind by resemblance to itself in equal succession, until it can reach the appointed limit.

It makes horse succeed horse, lion succeed lion, eagle succeed eagle, and brings each living creature, preserving the succession of those that follow, to the end and final issue of all things. No length of time will be able to change the properties of living creatures; rather, as though nature had been established only recently, it is carried forward fresh through time.

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” This command has remained in the earth, and in no way does it cease to serve the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0957] The printed editions read *desinet*, “will cease.” The ancient books read *desinit*, “does cease.”]

For it is beyond doubt that some creatures are born from the offspring of those first made, while we see others even now being formed and brought to life from the earth. It does not produce only cicadas from earth moistened by rain, or many other thousands of flying creatures, most of which, because of their extreme smallness, lack names; we also see mice and frogs generated from the earth.

Finally, in Egyptian Thebes, if heavier rains pour down in the summer, the whole region is soon filled with countless mice. It is also certain that eels are born only from mud; no egg or other kind of birth renews their species, but, as we have said, they receive their origin from the mud.

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” All cattle are earthly, and for this reason they incline toward the earth. But the human being is a heavenly plant: he differs from cattle as much in the dignity of his form as in his bodily appearance.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Colbertinus II has *sed aliter est ex natura coelestis homo*, “but otherwise the heavenly human being is from nature.” We have already noted that the copyist does not always follow the exemplars he had, but, when the received reading did not satisfy him, wrote something else according to his own judgment.]

[Note: [Col. 0958] Our old books have *illarum facies*, “their faces,” where, if one reads this way, the word *pecudum*, “of cattle,” may be supplied. Shortly afterward, our three manuscripts have *corporis te voluptate*, “with the pleasure of the body.”]

Their faces are bent downward and look toward the belly; they pursue whatever is pleasing to its desire. But your head is always raised toward heaven, and your eyes look upon things above. Yet if you too defile yourself with the pleasures of the body, obeying the luxury of the belly and its lower parts, you are compared with senseless beasts and have become like them (Psalm XLVIII, 13).

But you have another concern, both noble and worthy of great attention: to seek the things above, where Christ is (Colossians III, 1). It is fitting that you be carried higher than earthly things, so that, just as you were born, you may order your life according to your proper nature. “Your citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III, 20); your true homeland is the Jerusalem above; you have as citizens and companions the firstborn enrolled in heaven (Hebrews XII, 2).

## 3

“Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” The soul of the quadrupeds, therefore, was not formerly stored beneath the earth and suddenly brought forth at that moment; rather, it was created together with the command. Their soul is one, and all their beauty is placed in their form; they are distinguished individually by various properties.

Cattle are heavy and steady; asses are dull; horses are ardent in their desire for females. The wolf is untamed, the fox deceitful, the deer timid, the ant industrious, the dog affectionate and mindful of friendship. Qualities of character have likewise been fitted to the birth-natures of each kind: anger is congenial to the lion, as are solitude and avoidance of the company of others.

For, like a certain tyrant among beasts, raised up by the vice of natural pride, it shuns association with others and does not feed on daily food, although it has approached the remains of its own prey. Nature has granted it a voice of such tremendous power that, although certain quadrupeds are swifter in running, they are terrified and overcome by its roar.

The leopard is grim and sharp in attack, and its body corresponds to the movements of its spirit. Bears are by nature more sluggish; their disposition is harsh and deceitful, and is covered no less by bristles than by hostility.

[Note: [Col. 0958] The printed editions have *et minus setis*, “and less by bristles.” The old books have *et non minus setis*, “and no less by bristles.” Not long afterward, the printed editions have *fortasse quosdam incitabimus*, “perhaps we shall incite some.” Colbertinus II has *fortasse quidem incitabimur*, “perhaps indeed we shall be incited.” The Greek reads κινησόμεθα, “we shall be moved.” Subsequently, the printed editions have *credamus*, “let us believe.” The ancient books have *cred amur*, “let us be believed.”]

If, extending our discourse more widely, we wished to assert how much diligence many animals possess for preserving their own safety without anyone’s instruction, perhaps we would indeed be stimulated toward the care of our own protection; but I fear that, even in imitating the beasts, we may be judged inferior.

A bear, often pierced by a mortal wound, uses every device so that it may heal itself, especially closing its wounds with a certain herb of a drier nature. A fox, too, has often been caught bringing itself a remedy with pine sap. A tortoise, after filling its belly with the entrails of vipers, is said to escape the poison of its food by means of oregano, a remedy hostile to serpents. A snake, having eaten fennel, dispels the most severe pains of its eyes.

For the animals’ foreknowledge of future changes in the sky is believed to surpass every rational prudence.

[Note: [Col. 0959] The printed editions and Colbertinus I have *quam irrationabilem prudentiam*, “what irrational prudence.” Colbertinus II has *quantum rationabilem prudentiam*, “how much rational prudence.” Our old manuscript has *quam non rationabilem prudentiam*, “what not-unreasonable prudence.” The meaning is: “it surpasses every rational prudence.” The words which Eustathius intended to translate are: ποίαν οὐχὶ σύνεσιν λογικὴν ἀποκρύπτουσι, “what rational understanding do they not conceal?” Colbertinus II also has *imminente hieme*, “when winter is approaching.” A little later, the same manuscript has *nostri Conditoris auanta*, apparently corrupt for “of our Creator.”]

Thus a sheep, when winter is approaching, nibbles grass more eagerly, as though indicating that it is restoring itself more abundantly in order to endure the scarcity resulting from the coming weather. Oxen, when they have been shut up for a long time during the winter season, naturally sensing a disturbance in the air, all look out from the stall together, changing their expression.

Many people have captured a land hedgehog and observed that it makes two caves in its lair, so that, when it is pressed by the north winds, it may go to the southern side; and again, when the south wind blows, it opens the northern passage.

What, then, does Scripture signify to us human beings through these signs? Not only that we should contemplate in all things how great is the indulgence of our Creator toward us, but also that we should consider this: if mute cattle possess such great foreknowledge of the future, surely we ought not to defile ourselves with the pleasures of the present life, but direct our attention toward the age to come.

Will you, then, human being, not labor in this world so that you can store up for yourself resources for future rest, when you see the ant mindful of winter drawing food diligently to itself during the summer season?

[Note: [Col. 0959] Colbertinus II has *cum videris*, “when you see.”]

It is no less diligent because it has not yet experienced the dangers of winter. Rather, with every effort and wakeful care it labors and works, testing everything by ranging about, so that it may store sufficient food for itself. With marvelous prudence it takes care that the things collected do not spoil.

It cuts the grain with its teeth, lest, beginning to germinate, it provide useless food for itself. If the seed itself has been moistened by the vapor of the earth, it dries it in the sun; yet it does not always do this, but only when it senses that clear weather will remain stable.

Indeed, you will not see rain released from the clouds while the ant is exposing its seed to be dried beneath the sun.

Who, then, can speech comprehend, what hearing can grasp, or how much time could suffice to explain all these wonders? Therefore, let us also say with the prophet: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm CIII, 24).

That excuse, then, will not benefit us by which we think we can defend ourselves, saying that we have not learned from books what is useful, since we are believed to have acquired through the teaching of nature the choice of useful things.

For you know the good which you ought to do for your neighbor, and the evil which you would not wish to suffer from another. No art of medicine, nor any knowledge of herbs, taught cattle to seek remedies; rather, each animal naturally knows how to care for its own safety and, through the wisdom implanted at birth, to pursue an ineffable diligence.

## 4

There are nevertheless among us certain kinds of virtues which we obtain not from human teaching but from the transmission of nature.

For just as no instruction teaches us to hate illness, but we spontaneously feel horror toward everything believed to grieve us, so the soul also naturally possesses the duty of avoiding harmful things. Every evil is an illness of the soul, while virtue supplies the means of health.

[Note: [Col. 0959] The printed editions have *tamen apud nos*, “nevertheless among us.” The two ancient books have *tamen et apud nos*, “nevertheless also among us.” Shortly afterward, the printed editions have *institutio movet*, “instruction moves.” Our manuscripts have *monet*, “admonishes.” Not far below, Colbertinus II has *contristare videntur*, “seem to grieve.”]

Hence certain people rightly established that health is the constancy of natural movements. Who would not be judged to err if he made the same profession concerning the vigor of the soul? For the soul naturally always desires what belongs to it. Therefore chastity is to be praised by the prudent, justice is to be pursued, wisdom is to be followed, and courage is to be admired. These things are more familiar to souls than bodily health.

“Parents, love your children; children, do not provoke your parents” (Ephesians VI, 4). Did nature not command this same thing?

[Note: [Col. 0960] Colbertinus II has *praecipit*, “commands.” “For nothing new.”]

Paul therefore urges nothing new; he binds the bonds of nature more tightly. So great is its force in affection that even a wolf fights for its young.

What will the human being say who both despises the commandment and scorns nature, when either a young man disfigures his father’s gray hair with injuries, or a father, having entered a second marriage, grieves the children of his first?

[Note: [Col. 0960] The printed editions and Colbertinus I have *secundas nactus nativas nuptias*, “having obtained a second native marriage.” Colbertinus II has *secundas nactus nuptias*, “having obtained a second marriage.”]

The love of wild creatures between parents and offspring is unfeigned, because God, who created them, compensated by the gift of sensation for their deficiency in reason.

[Note: [Col. 0960] The printed editions and Colbertinus I have *quod minus illis irrationabile*, “what he granted them less irrationally.” Colbertinus II and our old manuscript have the reading found in the text, except that Colbertinus has *quae* for *quod*. The Greek is τὴν τοῦ λόγου ἔλλειψιν, “the lack of reason.” Not long afterward, the two ancient books and the printed editions have *copiosa sint et refecta*, “are abundant and replenished.” Another manuscript has *copiosa sint et referta*, “are abundant and filled.” A little later, the printed editions have *quanta videlicet*, “how great, namely.” Colbertinus II has *quantum nos videlicet*, “how much we, namely.”]

Thus, when so many thousands of sheep are present, a lamb released from the flock immediately recognizes its mother’s voice, runs joyfully to her, and seeks the sources of milk. Even if its mother happens to be less fertile, it is content with her alone and passes by the udders of another, however abundant and full they may be.

The mother likewise recognizes her own offspring amid such a great multitude. Certainly, the voice is one among the different animals, their color is one, and their odor the same, insofar as we can gather this through our own sense of smell. Nevertheless, their perception is sharper than that of human beings:

[Note: [Col. 0961D] The two ancient books and the printed editions have *ab homine*, “from a human being,” that is, “above a human being,” as I explained shortly before. Colbertinus II has *ad hominem*, “toward a human being.” But I think this was corrected by a copyist, or by someone else who did not understand the force of the little word *ab*.]

through it, each possesses recognition of its own offspring.

A puppy does not yet have formed teeth, and yet it tries to repel attackers with its mouth. A calf’s horns have not yet risen, and it already knows in what part of its body its weapons for fighting will be.

These things therefore show us that natural prudence does not use the instruction of teaching, and that nothing in created things is disordered or improvident. Rather, all things display in themselves the clearest proof of the Creator’s wisdom, who equipped cattle in this way for the defense of their own safety.

The dog is without reason, yet it is believed to possess a perception equal to reason. For the things which certain men, the secular philosophers, were scarcely able to discover while sitting at leisure throughout the long course of life—that is, the snares of syllogisms—the dog is said to have achieved through natural ability.

[Note: [Col. 0961] One manuscript has *qui vestigia*, “which tracks.”]

For, by skillfully tracking the footprints of wild animals, when it sees paths cut up in many directions, it tries them all by running back and forth, without uttering articulate speech,

[Note: [Col. 0961] The printed editions have *vocem tantum articulatim non emittens*, “not emitting only an articulated voice in detail.” Colbertinus II has *vocem cantuum articulatam non emittens*, “not emitting an articulated voice of songs.” I note in passing that here too the copyist seems to have written something different from what he found in his exemplars. Our old manuscript and Colbertinus I have *vocem tantum articulatam non emittens*, “not emitting only an articulated voice.” I suspect that Eustathius wrote *vocem tantum non articulatam emittens*, “emitting only a voice not joined to reasoning”; but even so, he did not express the force of the Greek words. They are μονονουχὶ τὴν συλλογιστικὴν φωνὴν, “almost the syllogistic voice,” that is, “emitting only a voice not joined to reasoning.” [Col. 0962D] A little later, Colbertinus II has *quo bestia quae lustratur abierit*, “where the beast being tracked has gone.” The Greek is τὸ θηρίον, “the beast.” The printed editions have *nec ullum*, “nor any.” The old books have *nec illum*, “nor that one.”]

for by what it does it clearly indicates where the tracked animal has gone. It does not leave unexamined even that place where there is no suspicion of a track, until, after retracing by scent and sorting out all the deceptive paths, it finds the lair.

[Note: [Col. 0962] The printed editions and two manuscripts have *cubile reperiat*, “it finds the den.” Colbertinus II has *civile reperiat*, “it finds the civic place.” I do not know which reading should be preferred; but I know well that neither can in any way fit the Greek expression, since Basil has written εὑρίσκει τὸ ἀληθές, “it finds the truth.”]

What more do those men do in their descriptions who, sitting idly, mark the dust with a stylus, remove two of three propositions, and find the truth in the one that remains?

Consider also the dog’s memory of a benefit bestowed on it. Does it not put to shame the ungrateful human being before his benefactor, when, even after their masters have been killed in a deserted place, many dogs have perished through keeping watch for a very long time? Others, after their masters were slain, became informers against the murderers and presented the guilty to the courts, carrying out the accusation by barking.

What, then, will those people say who do not merely fail to love God, their Creator and Shepherd, but even regard his slanderers as friends, eating at table together with them, and allow the giver of their banquets to be torn apart by the sacrilegious speech of blasphemers?

[Note: [Col. 0962] The printed editions have *lacerare*, “to tear apart.” The two ancient books have *tacerari*, “to be silent.”]

## 5

But now let us return to contemplation of creation.

It is for this reason that the weaker beasts are more fertile—hares, does, and wild sheep—so that their kind may not easily be wiped out after being consumed by predatory slaughterers. Those that devour others are found to be less fertile.

For, finally, a lioness scarcely becomes a mother: when the cubs are born with claws, they wound the womb of their mother, just as the viper emerges only after eating and tearing apart its mother’s belly, repaying its mother with a fitting reward for such a birth.

Thus nothing in human affairs is without foresight, nor is any creature exempt from the diligence appropriate to it.

If you examine the very limbs of cattle more carefully, you will find that the Creator gave them nothing superfluous and denied them nothing necessary.

To carnivorous beasts he supplied sharp teeth, since such instruments were necessary for the kind of food assigned to them. But for those to which he gave teeth on only one side, he arranged receptacles for abundant food, so that what had first been taken into the stomach might flow back again to the teeth, making it easier to grind by chewing and digest without labor.

Indeed, he did not give certain animals a throat and stomach without reason, since these provide necessary functions.

The camel therefore has a long neck so that, when it is brought level with its feet, it may easily reach the food it seeks. Bears have a short neck pressed down toward their shoulders, as do the lion, tiger, and similar wild beasts, whose food is not grassy and who have no need to bend down toward the earth, since they feed on flesh.

What shall we say about the elephant’s trunk? Although it is the largest of all beasts and terrifying to those who see it, it was fitting that it be formed with limbs of enormous size. If its neck had matched their magnitude, it would be immobile, bent downward by its very weight.

But now, by means of a few bones, its neck and head are joined to its spine, and it possesses a trunk that performs the function of a longer neck: it takes up food and draws water.

Its feet are joined by no joints of the knees, so that, like certain columns, they may support the weight placed upon them. For if its legs had been slender and unsteady, it would undoubtedly suffer constant dislocations of its joints, being insufficient to lift such a mass when it rose.

Thus you see how, like bodily towers placed before the battle line in wartime, or like living mountains set against the enemy’s defenses, they are positioned to break through the fortifications of their foes. If foundations equal to their size had not been provided for their steps, such enormous bulk could in no way be carried.

It is said that the elephant lives three hundred years and more, and that by means of its trunk it brings food to itself, as we have said. The trunk bends this way and that like a certain sinuous and slippery serpent.

Thus true is the statement that says that nothing lacking and nothing superfluous is found in the creation of things.

[Note: [Col. 0963] The same manuscript has *in rerum natura*, “in the nature of things”; nevertheless, the printed reading is recorded in the margin. Shortly afterward, that same manuscript has *idem quod docetur*, “the same thing that is taught.”]

Yet God commanded that this very enormous beast be subject to us, so that it might both understand what was being taught and endure being beaten when struck. This plainly declares that all things were subjected to us for this reason: because we were made in the image of God.

And we can contemplate his immeasurable wisdom not only in the largest animals, but also in the smallest creatures.

For just as I do not admire the peaks of great mountains sufficiently merely because, being near the clouds, they endure the heaviest storms through constant blasts of wind; nor, on the other hand, the hollowed-out caves merely because they not only avoid the roar of the winds by which high places are shaken but also rejoice in perpetual mildness—

[Note: [Col. 0963] The printed editions have *tempore*, “in time.” The old books have *temperie*, “in mildness.”]

so also, in the form of animals, I am not so astonished by the elephant’s enormous size as by the mouse, which is terrifying to the elephant, or by the exceedingly fine sting of the scorpion, which the Craftsman’s wisdom pierced like a kind of tube so that through it the scorpion might inject poison into those it wounds.

But let no one on this account criticize the Creator for having introduced venomous beasts into our life. For who will accuse a teacher of childishness when, compelling children to observe the duties of discipline, he chastises their wantonness and insolence with threats and blows?

[Note: [Col. 0963] The printed books have *ita enim et quis praeceptorem insimulabit infantem*, “for who in this way will accuse the teacher of childishness?” Our old manuscript and Colbertinus I have the reading found in the text. Immediately afterward, the printed editions and Colbertinus I have *et vanitates*, “and vanities.” The other two manuscripts have *et protervitates*, “and insolences.” The Greek is τὸ ἀκόλαστον, “the undisciplined” or “the wanton.” The two manuscripts also have *intelligamus*, “let us understand.” A little later, Colbertinus II has *confidis in Deum*, “you trust in God.”]

6. Rather, we understand the confession of faith to indicate harmful things. For if you trust in the Lord, “you will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90:13). Recall how, when Paul was gathering sticks, he was wounded by the bite of a viper but suffered no harm—clearly because that most holy man was regarded as full of faith.

[Note: Printed editions read *habeatur* (“is regarded”); two ancient books read *habebatur* (“was regarded”).]

But if you are faithless, you must fear not so much the serpent as your own faithlessness, by which you have made yourself liable to destruction.
