[Note: The printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read *sed jam sermonem humanae nativitatis* (“but now the discourse of human birth…”). Two other manuscripts read *sed jam sentio me humanae* (“but now I feel myself to be…”), which is proved to be correct and genuine by the Basilian reading ἀλλὰ γὰρ αἰσθάνομαι (“but indeed I perceive” / “but indeed I feel”). Two other manuscripts immediately afterward read *nostra quidem* (“our own, indeed”). The final word was missing from the printed editions. Not long afterward, the second Colbertine manuscript reads *hominis sensus* (“the human mind”).]

But now I feel myself pressed by the obligation of human birth, and I hear the voices of my listeners murmuring in their hearts, because we teach what our own qualities are while failing to know ourselves. It is therefore necessary to remove that cloud which darkens human understanding; for truly, of all things, the most difficult is to know oneself.

For not only is the eye, while looking upon things situated outside it, unable to behold itself; the mind itself, though sufficiently keen in contemplating the faults of others, is slower in recognizing its own vices. Hence even now, while speech swiftly runs through the actions of others, it is found duller and slower in examining what pertains to itself.

[Note: Two ancient books and the printed editions read *decursus* (“the course” or “the passing over”); our codex reads *decursis* (“when they have passed over”). The printed editions and the first Colbertine manuscript read *habetur et pinguior* (“is regarded as also more sluggish”); the Colbertine manuscript reads *habetur non purior* (“is regarded as not purer”); our old codex reads *habetur et pigrior* (“is regarded as also slower”). The latter reading is sufficiently confirmed by Basil’s words, καὶ ὄκνου πλήρης (“and full of hesitation”).]

Nor can we assess the Creator merely from the composition of the elements; we can also assess him from our own formation, provided that each person wishes to examine himself wisely, as the prophet says: “Your knowledge has been wondrous from me” (Psalm 138:6)—that is, while I contemplate myself, I learn the power of your ineffable wisdom.

“And God said, Let us make man.” Where are those Jews now who, in what follows—as though through certain caverns where the light of the Godhead shines and a second Person is mystically declared, though not yet manifestly seen—were resisting and saying that God was speaking to himself, since he himself said and himself did, “Let there be light,” and there was light?

[Note: The expression in what follows corresponds to the Greek words ἐν τοῖς κατόπιν (“in what follows”); but it ought rather to have been translated “in what precedes.” The printed editions soon afterward read *necdum tum* (“not yet then”); two ancient books read *necdum tamen* (“not yet, however”). Not much farther below, the second Colbertine manuscript reads *in promptu* (“obvious” or “at hand”), and then *quae* (“which things”).]

Their absurdities were already at hand—and even now the things they bring forward are absurd. For what blacksmith, carpenter, or leatherworker, remaining alone in his workshop, with no fellow craftsman present, says to himself, “Let us make a sword,” or “Let us join together a plow,” or “Let us fashion a shoe”? Rather, silently he begins the design that he has conceived in his mind.

Indeed, it is empty chatter for anyone to issue a strict command to himself, as though he were a judge or censor. Yet what will those who crucified the Lord not say, with tongues practiced in lying, even though their present utterance has entirely closed their mouths?

“And God said, Let us make man.” Until, therefore, there existed no one who was to be taught, the preaching of the Godhead remained hidden in the deep. But when the creation of man began to be anticipated, faith was revealed and the doctrine of truth shone forth clearly.

Listen, Jew, adversary of Christ, to how he addresses his companion in the creation of the world, through whom he made the ages, who accomplishes all things by the word of his power; but your mind does not receive words of piety.

For just as wild beasts, when shut up in cages, gnaw their own wombs with their teeth, displaying their bitterness but unable to satisfy their fury, so the Jew, adversary of the truth, constrained by the narrow bonds of his fetters, asserts that there are many persons to whom the Word of God supposedly spoke.

They claim that he said to the angels, “Let us make man.” Truly a Jewish fabrication, a story worthy of their faithlessness! In order not to accept the One, they confess many; they admit the Son into the company of servants by sharing in their dignity, and make our fellow freedmen the authors of human formation. They wish to make the perfecter of man equal to the angels, although it is absurd that any creature should be equal to its creator.

[Note: The printed editions read *et cum liberos nostros* (“and with our freeborn children”); the first Colbertine manuscript reads *et cum libertos nostros* (“and with our freedmen”); our old codex reads *et conlibertos nostros* (“and our fellow freedmen”). The Greek is καὶ τοὺς ὁμοδούλους (“and our fellow servants”). This and everything that follows to the end is absent from the second Colbertine manuscript.]

Let us also consider what follows: “Let us make man according to our image.” What do you reply? Is the image of God and of the angels one and the same? For the image of the Father must be the same as that of the Son, yet in such a way that a form proper to God is understood—not one consisting in bodily form, but in divine nature.

[Note: The printed editions read *id est, non habitui corporeo* (“that is, not in bodily form”); our two manuscripts read *id est, non in habitu corporeo* (“that is, not in bodily appearance”).]

Listen also, you who proceed from the new circumcision, commending Jewish observance under the pretense of Christianity. To whom does he say, “According to our image” (Hebrews 1:3), except to the radiance of glory and the impress of the Father’s substance, who is “the image of the invisible God”? He speaks, therefore, to his own image, who said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and, “Whoever sees me sees my Father” (John 14:9). To this one he says, “Let us make man according to our image.” For where there is unity of image, nothing can be dissimilar.

He did not say, “according to our images,” as Scripture itself also testifies: “God made man,” it says; “they did not make him.” He wisely avoided the plurality of Persons: there, indeed, he would confound the Jew; here, he would exclude pagan ritual. He mentioned unity so that you might recognize that the Son is also with the Father and avoid the danger arising from a plurality of Persons.

“According to the image of God he made man.” Again he introduces a cooperating Person. For he did not say, “He made him according to his image,” but “according to the image of God.”

And in what way it was arranged that man should possess the image of God, or how he receives the likeness of the Godhead, will be explained in what follows, with Christ granting understanding. For now it is enough simply to have said that there is one image.

But why did it occur to you to blaspheme so sacrilegiously as to say that the Son is unlike the Father? O ungrateful mind! You have yourself received the likeness of God, yet you cannot bear that your benefactor should possess it. You claim as your own what you have received from heavenly grace, yet you do not allow the Son to share with the Father the likeness naturally implanted in him by his begetter.

But evening already commands us to be silent, since the sun descended toward its setting some time ago. Therefore let us also bring the course of our discourse to an end here, content with what has been said.

[Note: The printed editions read *cursum terminemus* (“let us end the course”); the ancient books read *curricula terminemus* (“let us end the course of our discussion”).]

For at present we have discussed only as much as can sharpen your attention. A fuller treatment of the questions proposed we shall give you on another occasion, with the Holy Spirit supporting us.

[Note: The printed editions read *stipulante* (“vouching” or “guaranteeing”); our two manuscripts read *adstipulante* (“supporting” or “assenting”).]

Go now rejoicing, and, instead of abundant dishes and varied fruits, furnish your tables with the remembrance of what has been said. Let the impious be confounded, let the Jew be ashamed, let the righteous rejoice in the proclamations of truth; let the Lord be glorified, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.

## At the Same Time [Note: That is, 450.] Polemeus Sylvius

### Notice from Cave

Polemeus, or P. Annaeus Sylvius—I have not yet learned where he was born or what manner of life he followed—seems to have lived at Rome and flourished in the year 448. For he wrote under the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, after the tyrant John had been destroyed; and, as he himself testifies even more clearly, during the consulship of Flavius Zeno and Postumianus—that is, in the year of Christ 448 and at the beginning of the following year, when Asterius entered upon the consulship.

He composed a calendar comprising, for each month of the year, the festivals of Christians and pagans, and dedicated it to the most blessed Bishop Eucherius.

### The Calendar, or Index of Festival Days, of Polemeus Sylvius

(We published this calendar in volume 13 of our *Patrologia*, column 676; see it there.)

## In the Year of the Lord 453: Salonius, Bishop of Vienne

*(From the Library of the Fathers of Lyon.)*

### Prologue

Salonius, a Gaul by birth and son of Eucherius, Bishop of Lyon, was sent by his father to the island of Lérins when he was scarcely ten years old. There he was trained and instructed under the care and discipline of Honoratus, Hilary, Salvianus, Vincentius, and other great men.

He flourished in the year 453. That he was, together with his brother Veranus, a teacher of the churches while their father was still alive is attested by Salvianus (*Letter to Eucherius*). That he was a bishop is sufficiently certain, for Salvianus and Gennadius explicitly call him one (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 63). Which city he governed, however, is uncertain: some wish him to have been Bishop of Geneva, others of Genoa, and others of Vienne.

To me, however, he seems rather to deserve the title of bishop because he was appointed his father’s coadjutor in the bishopric of Lyon. Hence it may also be considered that he subscribed in his father’s place at the First Council of Orange in the year 441.

When he died is unknown. He wrote an exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon and another mystical exposition of Ecclesiastes, composed in dialogue form, with himself and his brother Veranus as interlocutors. Both works are extant in the *Orthodoxographia*, page 1010, and in volume 8 of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 401. He also wrote, together with the bishops Ceretius and Veranus, a letter to Pope Leo, which is included among Leo’s letters after Letter 51.

### The Mystical Exposition of Salonius, Bishop, on the Proverbs of Solomon (C)

**Interlocutors: Veranus and Salonius**

**VERANUS.** In what language is the word *parabolae* expressed?

**SALONIUS.** In Greek; in Latin they are interpreted as “similitudes.”

**VERANUS.** Why did Solomon give this book that name?

**SALONIUS.** To show by it that we ought to understand what he says not according to the letter, but in another and spiritual sense.

**VERANUS.** What does Solomon signify, since he spoke in parables?

**SALONIUS.** The Lord Jesus Christ, because he was going to speak in parables to the crowds of the Jews; indeed, by his very name he signifies the same Lord Jesus Christ.

**VERANUS.** How, then, is *Solomon* interpreted?

**SALONIUS.** “Peaceful,” or “lovable.” He signifies the one of whom the Apostle says, “Christ is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14). And again, “Making peace through his blood, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth” (Colossians 1:20). Moreover, because Solomon is interpreted as “lovable,” he most fittingly signifies the one to whom the Father speaks, saying, “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

**VERANUS.** What does he signify by the peaceful condition of his kingdom?

**SALONIUS.** The everlasting kingdom of Christ and the Church, concerning which it is written: “And of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

**VERANUS.** Why, according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters, are these sayings of Solomon called not *parables* but *proverbs*?

**SALONIUS.** Just as they are called parables because they signify hidden and secret mysteries, so they are appropriately called proverbs because they are things that ought frequently to be on the lips of the faithful, entrusted to memory, and retained (Proverbs 1).

**VERANUS.** What benefit do Solomon’s parables provide?

**SALONIUS.** Wisdom, namely, and discipline. This is what he says: “To learn wisdom and discipline.”

**VERANUS.** What is the difference between wisdom and discipline?

**SALONIUS.** Wisdom is knowledge of divine things; discipline is the conduct of a holy and pure life.

**VERANUS.** What, then, does it mean to learn wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** To know and understand how you ought rightly to believe.

**VERANUS.** What does it mean to learn discipline?

**SALONIUS.** To know how each person ought to live, what is fitting to do by one’s actions, and toward what one ought to direct the intention of one’s heart. It follows: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

**VERANUS.** How many kinds of fear of the Lord are there?

**SALONIUS.** Two: servile fear and holy fear.

**VERANUS.** Why is it called servile?

**SALONIUS.** Because, like servants, we serve the Lord through fear of Gehenna, lest we be led to punishment.

**VERANUS.** Why is holy fear so called?

**SALONIUS.** Because, just as a good son fears offending even slightly the eyes of his most loving father, so those who are perfect in the Church fear offending the eyes of God by sinning.

**VERANUS.** Which of these two is wiser?

**SALONIUS.** Servile fear, because whoever begins to become wise—that is, recognizes after his sins that he has gone astray—is first seized by divine fear, lest he be dragged to punishment.

**VERANUS.** What does holy fear accomplish?

**SALONIUS.** It increases wisdom, because “perfect love casts out” that servile “fear” (1 John 4:18). But holy fear “endures forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10).

**VERANUS.** What does Solomon mean when he says, “In vain is the net spread before the eyes of those who have wings” (Proverbs 1)? Surely birds are often caught in nets?

**SALONIUS.** They certainly are.

**VERANUS.** Who, then, are these winged ones?

**SALONIUS.** Holy and elect men, who have the wings of faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues by which they fly toward contemplation of heavenly things. They also have spiritual eyes, by which they foresee the snares of the ancient enemy and avoid sins.

Thus the net is spread in vain—that is, uselessly—before the eyes of the winged: that is, the snare of the devil’s ambush is set before holy and elect men. For those who have their manner of life in heaven can easily overcome the devil’s snares on earth.

**VERANUS.** What is the wisdom of which Solomon says, “Wisdom cries aloud outside; in the streets she raises her voice”?

**SALONIUS.** Jesus Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, as the Apostle says.

**VERANUS.** How, then, does this wisdom preach outside?

**SALONIUS.** She preached within—that is, in secret—before his Passion, because he revealed the mysteries of his divinity to only a few, namely, to the disciples. After his resurrection, however, he preached outside, because, having sent the Holy Spirit from above, he openly declared through the apostles to the world that he was the Son of God.

**VERANUS.** How did she raise her voice in the streets?

**SALONIUS.** Because what he had previously taught in secret and hidden away, and among only one Jewish people, he afterward openly preached through the apostles before the breadth of the common people and in the presence of all nations, according to what he commanded them, saying: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light”—that is, openly—“and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops”—that is, openly and before everyone.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “She cries out at the head of the crowds”?

**SALONIUS.** The leaders of the Jews are signified by “the head.” She cried out at the head of the crowds because, through the apostles, she openly brought to the leaders of the Jews the murder they had committed against him, recalling it to their memory and calling them to the remedy of repentance.

**VERANUS.** How should we understand what follows: “At the doors of the gates of the city she speaks her words”?

**SALONIUS.** The holy Church is signified by the city, gathered from both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles. The doors of the gates of this city were the holy teachers, who, by preaching the word of the Gospel, brought believers into it.

Wisdom therefore spoke her words at the doors of the gates of the city when Christ was speaking in his apostles.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Incline your heart to understand prudence” (Proverbs 2)? How can a person incline his heart?

**SALONIUS.** He inclines his heart to know prudence who humbles himself and cleanses his mind from sins, so that he may become worthy to receive the mysteries of the Godhead.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Do not rely on your own wisdom”? Who relies upon wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** The person who trusts that by his own wisdom or his own strength he can fulfill the divine commandments.

**VERANUS.** Again he says, “Do not be wise in your own eyes” (Proverbs 3). Who is wise in his own eyes?

**SALONIUS.** Certainly the person who exalts himself above others as though he were a teacher and boasts of what he was able rightly to know and understand from the sayings of the Fathers.

**VERANUS.** What is true human wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** To fear the Lord and turn away from evil. This is what immediately follows: “Fear the Lord and turn away from evil.”

**VERANUS.** How do you know that this is true human wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** Because it is written in the Book of Job: “Behold, the fear of the Lord—that is wisdom; and to turn away from evil—that is understanding.”

**VERANUS.** Who is the man of whom Solomon says, “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom”?

**SALONIUS.** The faithful and Catholic Christian.

**VERANUS.** When does he find wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** When he receives the teaching of truth—that is, the Gospel—with both body and heart, and strives to know the Lord’s will in the Holy Scriptures.

**VERANUS.** When does prudence abound?

**SALONIUS.** When he hears the divine commandments with great love and devotion toward his Creator and strives to fulfill them in action.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Her ways are beautiful; all her paths are peaceful”? What are these ways of wisdom, or what are her paths?

**SALONIUS.** The ways of wisdom are the actions of the Lord that he carried out in the flesh, or his teachings contained in the books of the Gospel. These ways are beautiful because they are divine.

The paths of wisdom are the Lord’s precepts and commandments, which lead to eternal peace; they are peaceful because all the Lord’s commandments lead to eternal peace.

**VERANUS.** Of what law or counsel does Solomon speak when he says, “Keep the law and counsel”?

**SALONIUS.** Of the law and counsel of the wisdom of the Lord Jesus Christ.

**VERANUS.** What is the law of wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** The law of wisdom is this: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments”—that is, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Matthew 19; Mark 10; Luke 18).

**VERANUS.** What is the counsel of wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you possess and give to the poor.”

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Everyone who mocks is an abomination to the Lord”? Who is the mocker?

**SALONIUS.** The mocker is the person who corrupts the words of God by understanding and teaching them perversely. The mocker is the person who despises simple and poor neighbors by insulting them. The mocker is the person who regards God’s great promises as though they were small and considers the punishment of eternal condemnation tolerable.

The Lord abhors all such people, but “with the simple is his conversation,” because heavenly grace illuminates them with wisdom, since they have nothing double within themselves.

**VERANUS.** Why does Solomon say, “And I was a son to my father, tender and an only child before my mother” (Proverbs 4)? How was he an only child before his mother, when a brother born of the same mother preceded him, as the Holy Scripture of the Books of Kings testifies (1 Kings 12)?

**SALONIUS.** It is true that a brother born of the same mother preceded him, but that brother died soon afterward. As though he had never existed, he departed this life without a name; therefore Solomon calls himself an only child.

**VERANUS.** Why does he say, “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left”? Who could so restrain himself that his body would not turn toward the right or the left?

**SALONIUS.** No one. Rather, the right signifies the good way, and the left the evil and rejected way. He does not forbid walking on the right-hand way, but turning aside toward the right.

**VERANUS.** Who, then, turns aside to the right or to the left?

**SALONIUS.** The righteous person turns aside to the right when he presumes upon his own righteousness and his own strength; the unrighteous person turns aside to the left when, because of the weakness of the flesh, he despairs of being able to be saved.

He turns aside to the right who wishes to be wiser than one ought to be wise (Romans 12); he turns aside to the left who serves folly.

**VERANUS.** Why, then, does he say a little farther on, “The ways that are on the right the Lord knows”?

**SALONIUS.** The holy actions and good works are signified by the ways that are on the right. The Lord knows these—that is, he directs them, and they please him.

For this reason, conversely, at the judgment he will say to the reprobate, “I do not know you”—that is, “I have not chosen you.” For you do not please me, because I do not see you in my light; I do not see you in my righteousness.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Do not give your honor to strangers, and your years to the cruel one” (Proverbs 5)? What honor does he mean, or whom does he call strangers?

**SALONIUS.** He speaks of the honor by which man was made according to the image of God. He calls demons “strangers.” The meaning is: Do not, by living badly, submit your honor—that you were created according to the image of God—to unclean spirits.

**VERANUS.** Whom does he call cruel, or of what years does he speak?

**SALONIUS.** He calls the spans of life “years,” and the devil “the cruel one.” The meaning is: Do not, by living badly, hand over to the devil the span of life that God has given you.

**VERANUS.** From what cistern does Solomon teach us to drink water, or from what well does he teach us to drink streams, when he says, “Drink water from your own cistern, and streams from your own well”?

**SALONIUS.** He calls the Catholic teaching—that is, the teaching of the Old and New Testaments—a cistern. He calls the depth and height of that same Catholic teaching a well; knowledge, water; and the streams, the abundance and overflowing of knowledge—that is, the various interpretations of Holy Scripture.

By these words he teaches us to beware of the teaching of heretics and to attend to the reading of the Holy Scriptures. The meaning is: “Drink water from your own cistern”—that is, preserve and fulfill in action the teaching that you preach to others.

“And streams from your own well”—that is, may the abundance of your discourse, or of your knowledge, overflow within you through good works.

**VERANUS.** Why does Solomon say, “Let your fountains flow out, and divide your waters in the streets,” when he immediately adds, “Keep them for yourself alone, lest strangers share in you”? If we let our fountains flow out and divide our waters in the streets, how can we possess them alone?

**SALONIUS.** Although the words may seem to sound contradictory, there is no contradiction, because these statements can be understood only spiritually.

We let our fountains flow out when we pour the power of preaching into others, when we announce the words of Holy Scripture to others. We divide our waters in the streets when we preach to the peoples.

The word “street” derives from breadth; it is a Greek expression. We therefore divide our waters in the streets when we spread the words of knowledge among a multitude of hearers and distribute the divine utterances according to the condition of each person.

**VERANUS.** If we ought to divide our waters in the streets, how can we possess them alone?

**SALONIUS.** We divide our waters in the streets when we preach the divine words broadly to others, yet we possess the waters alone because we do not seek human praise from that preaching itself.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Lest strangers share in you” (Proverbs 5:17)?

**SALONIUS.** He calls demons “strangers.” Of them the Psalmist says, “Strangers have risen up against me, and the strong have sought my soul” (Psalm 53:5), and so forth.

We make the wicked—that is, unclean spirits—our partners and associates in preaching when we swell with pride and desire empty glory from our preaching.

**VERANUS.** Of what man does Solomon speak when he says, “An apostate, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth” (Proverbs 6)?

**SALONIUS.** He calls a schismatic an apostate, one who strives to split the unity of the Church.

**VERANUS.** In what language is the word *apostate* expressed?

**SALONIUS.** In Greek; in Latin it means “a deserter” or “one who departs from the truth.”

**VERANUS.** Why, then, is a schismatic called an apostate?

**SALONIUS.** Because, following the example of the proud angel, he first swells up inwardly and falls from the state of his mind, and thus departs from the love of his Creator and from the truth. For unless he had first departed from the truth, he would not spread injustice in the Church.

**VERANUS.** Why, then, is it said of him, “He winks with his eyes, rubs with his foot, and speaks with his finger”?

**SALONIUS.** The inward guardianship of the mind keeps the bodily members externally ordered. This apostate, however, because he has lost his state and his guardianship, therefore possesses the external members of the Lord in a condition of death and has made them disorderly.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean when he says of his law, “Bind it upon your fingers; write it upon the tablets of your heart” (Proverbs 7)? How can anyone bind the law upon his fingers, or, if he did so, what benefit would there be?

**SALONIUS.** He says “upon your fingers,” that is, in your actions. Whoever strives to fulfill and adorn the law in good works binds it upon his fingers.

He says “upon the tablets of your heart,” that is, in the breadth of your thoughts. He writes the law upon the tablets of his heart who receives it with joy and entrusts it to memory.

**VERANUS.** What does Wisdom mean when she says, “Through me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just; through me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice”?

**SALONIUS.** Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.

**VERANUS.** Does Christ give kingship and authority to all wicked tyrants and rulers?

**SALONIUS.** Certainly not. Nevertheless, with his permission, wicked kings and rulers receive kingdoms or authority, because it is written in the Book of Job: “He permits the hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people” (Job 34).

But in this passage he calls the apostles holy kings, because they first knew how to govern themselves faithfully and then the Church entrusted to them. Or he calls all the saints kings, because they know how to govern themselves and others well.

**VERANUS.** Whom does he call lawmakers?

**SALONIUS.** The writers of both Testaments.

**VERANUS.** Whom does he call princes and the powerful?

**SALONIUS.** The other teachers and rulers of the faithful. For all these, through the wisdom of God the Father, possessed kingship, authority, and power—that is, they received these things through Christ, so that they might be something good. Hence he himself says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

**VERANUS.** What does Wisdom mean when she says, “I rejoiced day by day, playing before him”?

**SALONIUS.** That is, playing before the Father at all times throughout the world.

**VERANUS.** Was Wisdom—that is, the Son of God—playing childishly before the Father?

**SALONIUS.** Far from it. What he calls “playing” is to be understood as “rejoicing.” He played day by day—that is, he rejoiced that he was one, namely, of one substance with the Father, from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

**VERANUS.** How did he play at all times throughout the world?

**SALONIUS.** When the times of the world and of creation began to exist, the Son himself rejoiced, because he always remained in the Father as what he was.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9), and what house did she build for herself?

**SALONIUS.** Wisdom—that is, the Son of God—built herself a house when he himself created man in the womb of the Virgin and assumed him into the unity of his Person.

**VERANUS.** How did she hew out seven pillars?

**SALONIUS.** She hewed out seven pillars because, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, she raised up Churches throughout the world. Like pillars, they support and preserve the memory of him—that is, the mystery of his Incarnation.

**VERANUS.** Can this be understood in another way?

**SALONIUS.** Indeed it can. The house of Wisdom is the Church of Christ; the pillars of this house are the holy teachers. These pillars are rightly said to be seven because the holy teachers are filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

**VERANUS.** How, then, did Wisdom hew out these pillars?

**SALONIUS.** She hewed out the pillars because she separated the minds of the preachers from love of the present age and raised them up to bear the structure of that same Church.

**VERANUS.** Of which maidservants does he speak a little later when he says, “She sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the walls of the city” (Proverbs 9)?

**SALONIUS.** He calls the holy apostles maidservants.

**VERANUS.** Why does he call them maidservants?

**SALONIUS.** Because of their lack of learning, weakness, and poverty. He chose as apostles uneducated, weak, poor, and despised men, whom he sent to preach in the world, so that they might call faithful peoples to the citadel of eternal blessedness and to the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem.

**VERANUS.** Who is the wise son who makes his father glad, or who is the foolish son who is his mother’s sorrow?

**SALONIUS.** The person who faithfully preserves the mysteries of faith and baptism that he has received and fulfills them in action is the wise son. He undoubtedly makes God the Father glad.

But the person who corrupts the sacraments of faith and baptism that he has received through evil works or heretical perversity is the foolish son. He is surely his mother’s sorrow, namely, the Church’s, because he grieves her.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “The foolish man will be beaten with his lips”? How can a foolish man be beaten with his lips?

**SALONIUS.** In this passage, beating signifies condemnation. The foolish man will therefore be beaten with his lips because he will be condemned on account of the wicked and evil words he has spoken.

Hence Moses says elsewhere—more properly, Solomon: “Life is in the hands of the tongue” (Proverbs 18), because each person will either be condemned by his words or justified by his words (Matthew 12).

**VERANUS.** Why is the tongue said to have hands, when it cannot have hands?

**SALONIUS.** It is said metaphorically, that is, by transference, just as the winds are said to have wings (Psalms 17, 103, and elsewhere). The hands of the tongue are the words themselves, by which a person earns life through speaking good things or earns death through speaking evil things.

Alternatively, “hands” often signify works in the Holy Scriptures, as in the saying, “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Psalm 127). Thus, “in the hands of the tongue” means “in its works.” The works of the tongue are good or evil conversations, from which death or life arises.

**VERANUS.** Who is the sluggard of whom it is said, “As vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is the sluggard to those who sent him” (Proverbs 10:26)?

**SALONIUS.** The sluggard is a Catholic who lives badly and neither labors nor acts so as to deserve to attain eternal blessedness.

Through vinegar and smoke, the faithlessness of heretics is signified. Through the eyes and teeth, the preachers of the Holy Church are signified. They are rightly called eyes because they foresee the right paths. They are also fittingly called teeth because they customarily minister spiritual food to the faithful.

Thus, just as vinegar is contrary to the teeth and smoke to the eyes—that is, just as the faithlessness of heretics is opposed to good teachers, grieving them and causing them distress and tears—so the sluggard, that is, the bad Catholic, is burdensome to those same good teachers who sent him, namely, who commanded him to fulfill his faith through works.

He is even more burdensome because he destroys his faith through wicked works.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “Hand in hand, the wicked will not be innocent” (Proverbs 11:21)? How is a wicked man “hand in hand,” and why will he therefore not be innocent?

**SALONIUS.** Whoever joins hand to hand does nothing. Therefore, as long as the wicked man remains “hand in hand,” he will not be innocent. Even if for a time he withdraws his hands from evil work, nevertheless, as long as he is wicked, he cannot possess innocence of heart. Hence he says above: “A crooked heart is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 11:20).

**VERANUS.** What, then, is “hand in hand”?

**SALONIUS.** A perverse conscience engaged in evil work.

**VERANUS.** How should we understand the saying, “A beautiful and foolish woman is like a golden ring in a pig’s snout”?

**SALONIUS.** If you insert a golden ring into its snout—that is, into the snout of a pig—then, as it proceeds to turn over and dig the earth with its nose, it plunges the golden ring into the mire, and the golden ring loses the beauty it possessed.

Similarly, if a foolish woman possesses beauty of face, or receives ornaments of earrings, necklaces, and clothing, she soils her beauty and loses her attractiveness if she delights in defiling herself with the filth of lust and corrupts herself through adultery.

**VERANUS.** But how is this statement to be understood spiritually?

**SALONIUS.** Whoever attentively meditates upon the Holy Scriptures and continually examines the divine words receives the ornaments of knowledge.

But if, by living badly, he corrupts and destroys what he understands correctly, he has a golden ring in his snout. Like a pig, however, he digs in the earth, soils the ring, and plunges it into the mud, because he has stained by filthy action the ornament he had acquired through knowledge of the Scriptures.

Such a soul is a beautiful and foolish woman: beautiful through knowledge, but foolish through conduct because she is devoted to carnal pleasures.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean by saying, “The soul that blesses will be enriched, and whoever gives drink will himself also be given drink”? For there are many who give others drink but are not themselves given drink.

SALONIUS. He does not speak here of bodily drunkenness, but of the spiritual soul, which, if it blesses, will be made fat; for whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives a spiritual blessing—that is, he is increased and grows through spiritual grace. Likewise, the one who strives to make the minds of his hearers drunk with sacred discourse [Col. 0976C] is himself made drunk and filled with the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

VERANUS. Why did he not say, “The man who blesses will be made fat,” but rather, “The soul that blesses”?

SALONIUS. In the divine Scriptures, a part is often put for the whole, or the whole for a part, according to the feature of grammatical art called synecdoche. Thus, in this passage, a part is put for the whole person. The whole, however, is put for a part in the saying, “They have taken the Lord from the tomb” (John 20): “the Lord” is said instead of the Lord’s body.

VERANUS. Who is the one of whom he says, “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Proverbs 11)? Surely no one should be cursed for not distributing his grain to everyone?

[Col. 0976D]

SALONIUS. Grain means the words of holy preaching. Therefore, whoever hides this grain—that is, keeps the words of holy preaching to himself and does not wish to proclaim the divine utterances to others—will be cursed among the peoples, because he will be condemned for the guilt of silence. He could have benefited many, but because he was unwilling, he will justly be punished for the penalty of many.

VERANUS. Who are those who sell grain, of whom it immediately follows, “But blessing is upon the heads of those who sell”?

SALONIUS. They sell grain who proclaim the words of life and of holy preaching to their hearers.

VERANUS. What price do they receive from them?

SALONIUS. The price of faith and holy confession.

[Col. 0977A]

VERANUS. How will blessing come upon their heads?

SALONIUS. Because the Lord will say to each of them, “Well done, good and faithful servant, because …” (Matthew 25), and so forth.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “Whoever troubles his own household will possess winds”? How can anyone possess winds?

SALONIUS. In this passage he calls the mind a household, in which each person dwells, as it were, in a house, through his thoughts. He calls winds unclean spirits. Therefore, whoever does not fear disturbing his household—that is, his mind—with evil and harmful thoughts will assuredly possess winds, because through evil thoughts he has made a way for demons to enter and dwell within him. [Col. 0977B] He will possess winds—that is, demons—for his own condemnation.

VERANUS. How is a diligent wife a crown to her husband, and “rottenness in his bones” the woman who does things deserving of shame (Proverbs 12)?

SALONIUS. A good and chaste wife gives her husband honor in everything; and because she loves him and governs his household well, she is a crown to him, since she adds grace to his virtues, by which he is crowned by the Lord. An adulterous woman, however, although she may appear beautiful outwardly, is nevertheless rottenness in his bones, because inwardly she defiles her members with the stench of her lust.

VERANUS. How should we understand the saying, “Better is the poor man who is sufficient for himself than the glorious man who lacks bread”?

[Col. 0977C]

SALONIUS. Truly better is the unlearned and simple brother who does the good things he knows, by which he may deserve to possess eternal life in heaven, than the glorious man—that is, one renowned for doctrine and learning in the Scriptures, or adorned with the office of a teacher—who lacks the bread of love, because he loves neither the Lord nor his neighbor. Or certainly he lacks bread because he does not do what he understands or teaches.

VERANUS. Who is the crafty man who conceals knowledge? For he says, “The crafty man conceals knowledge.”

SALONIUS. Here “crafty” is used in a good sense, meaning wise and prudent. A crafty man—that is, a wise and prudent man—sometimes deliberately conceals knowledge, for two reasons. First, he cannot speak to weak hearers as to spiritual people, but only as to carnal people (1 Corinthians 3); that is, he does not dare disclose to them the great mysteries of the holy Scriptures that he knows, lest they perhaps be scandalized. [Col. 0977D] Second, he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or throw pearls before swine (Matthew 7).

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The sluggard both wants and does not want” (Proverbs 13)? If he wants, how does he also not want?

SALONIUS. The sluggard designates the one who does not wish to exercise himself in good works. Thus the sluggard wants to reign with God, but does not want to labor for God. He wants to attain blessedness, yet does not want to fulfill Christ’s commandments so as to deserve to obtain blessedness. Of him James says, “A man double-minded is unstable in all his ways” (James 1).

[Col. 0978A]

VERANUS. Of what works does he say, “The soul of those who work will be made fat” (Proverbs 13)?

SALONIUS. He speaks of those who do good works and strive to fulfill the Lord’s commandments. Their soul will be made fat with spiritual grace and with the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom.

VERANUS. Why will the soul of those who do good works be made fat?

SALONIUS. Because after the labors of the present life it will be rewarded with an unfading recompense.

VERANUS. Who is the wicked messenger of whom he says, “The wicked messenger falls into evil”?

SALONIUS. The wicked messenger is the devil’s angel. Arius, Sabellius, and the other heretics were angels of Satan. These assuredly fell into evil—that is, into the torment of eternal [Col. 0978B] Gehenna.

VERANUS. Who is the faithful ambassador, of whom it follows, “A faithful ambassador is health” (Proverbs 14)?

SALONIUS. The faithful ambassador is every catholic preacher and teacher who obtains eternal health and salvation for himself and for his hearers.

VERANUS. Why does he say, “The wicked will lie hidden before the good, and the impious before the gates of the righteous,” when in this life the good usually lie before the wicked, and the righteous before the gates of the unjust?

SALONIUS. At the last judgment, when the righteous have been crowned, the impious who afflicted them in the present life will be condemned. Therefore he says, “The wicked will lie before the good, and the impious before the gates of the righteous.” Yet when he says “before the good” and “before the gates of the righteous,” this does not concern proximity of place, [Col. 0978C] since the wicked and the good will not then be near one another. Rather, it concerns the vision of the good, because the good will always see the torments of the wicked, and therefore will render greater thanks without end to God their deliverer.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “A weight and a balance are the Lord’s judgments, and all the stones of the age are his work” (Proverbs 16)? How are a weight and a balance the Lord’s judgments?

SALONIUS. Because the Lord established all things “by weight and measure and number” (Wisdom 11). A weight and a balance are the Lord’s judgments because, just as he willed, he distributes to each person a measure of faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit.

VERANUS. Whom does he call the stones of the age?

SALONIUS. The righteous and strong in faith. For all the stones of the age—that is, holy and chosen men—are the Lord’s work, because no one was chosen by the Lord through his own strength or his own merit to be fit for the heavenly building, but solely through the Lord’s grace and mercy. [Col. 0978D]

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The crown of the old are children’s children, and the glory of children is their fathers” (Proverbs 17)? If children’s children are evil, how are they glory in this passage?

SALONIUS. He calls the patriarchs and prophets “fathers”; their children are the holy apostles, and their children’s children are the apostles’ successors, namely, the holy preachers. All these are the crown of the old—that is, of the patriarchs and prophets—because they celebrate them with worthy praise, through whose examples and prophecies they came to the knowledge of grace.

[Col. 0979A]

VERANUS. How are fathers the glory of their children?

SALONIUS. Great indeed is the glory of the preachers of the New Testament: that they have deserved to be the children of the ancient fathers, that is, of the patriarchs and prophets.

VERANUS. Why does he say, “Whoever lets water loose is the head of quarrels”? Does the person who releases confined water to flow provoke quarrels? Or is it not rather wine than water that usually provokes quarrels?

SALONIUS. This is said figuratively. For water signifies a light and flowing tongue; and whoever releases his tongue without restraint is the head of quarrels, because one who does not bridle his tongue provokes quarrels and disputes and destroys concord.

VERANUS. Tell me, please, how wisdom shines in the face of the prudent, as Solomon says, “But the eyes of fools [Col. 0979B] are at the ends of the earth”?

SALONIUS. A prudent man often displays, in the very brightness of his facial expression, the gravity of his understanding and the clarity of his intellect. Fools, however, cannot raise the eyes of their mind to imitate and pursue this gravity; instead, in complete astonishment, they seek to discover how they may reach the end—that is, the fulfillment of carnal pleasures.

VERANUS. Must we understand it only in this way?

SALONIUS. We must understand that this was said especially of Christ. In the face of the prudent one—namely, the Savior—the wisdom of divinity shone; appearing in the flesh, he demonstrated and confirmed it by the testimony of his virtues and teaching. But the eyes of fools [Col. 0979C]—that is, of the unbelieving Jews—were inflamed more by earthly desires than by his saving admonitions and teachings.

VERANUS. What does this mean: “The gift of a man enlarges his way, and makes room for him before princes” (Proverbs 18)? What is this gift that enlarges a man’s way and makes room for him before princes?

SALONIUS. This gift is the gift of charity, or of the other virtues that the faithful receive from the Lord. This gift of a man enlarges his way—that is, his activity—because the more each faithful person is inwardly filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, the more he enlarges his way outwardly; that is, he multiplies his progress in good works, because every day he grows and increases in holy desires and good works.

[Col. 0979D]

VERANUS. How does this gift make room for a man before princes?

SALONIUS. Because among the great rulers of the Church, in the public forum, it grants him the summit of honor and the glory of eternal blessedness.

VERANUS. Why does he say, “The sluggard hides his hand beneath his armpit and does not bring it to his mouth” (Proverbs 19 and 26)? Who is so lazy that, when eating or drinking, he does not bring his hand to his mouth?

SALONIUS. Whoever hides his hand beneath his armpit certainly does not wish to extend it to any work or labor. Therefore the sluggard designates every sluggish and idle preacher who does not wish to fulfill by his works what he says. [Col. 0980A] For he brings his hand to his mouth who strives to fulfill by his works what he teaches.

VERANUS. Who is the sluggard of whom he says, “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him” (Proverbs 20)? If the sluggard refuses to plow during the cold season, will he not be able during summer to find someone to give him something?

SALONIUS. Often the faithful find people to give alms to the sluggard in both the cold and the summer seasons. But here the sluggard signifies the one who, because of laziness and the adversity of this world—which is signified by cold—neglects to labor in God’s service. Therefore, on the future day of judgment he will beg, because he will not possess good works for which he may deserve to receive blessedness; for “whatever a man sows, [Col. 0980B] that he will also reap” (Galatians 6).

VERANUS. Why, then, is the day of judgment and the kingdom of God compared with summer?

SALONIUS. Because then all the clouds of our sorrow will pass away, and the day of that life will shine with the brightness of the eternal sun.

VERANUS. Of what king does he say, “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil by his glance”?

SALONIUS. Of the one who is King of kings and Lord of lords, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who sits on the throne of judgment, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He himself scatters all evil by his glance, because by the scrutiny of his power he will penetrate every evil, even hidden thoughts, so that he may repay each person according to [Col. 0980C] what he has done. Hence he says in the Gospel, “Nothing is so covered that it will not be revealed, and nothing hidden that will not be known” (Luke 12). Then, when the righteous have been crowned with the Lord, only the reprobate will suffer eternal punishments.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure, both are abominable before God” (Proverbs 20 and 21)?

SALONIUS. By “a weight and a weight, a measure and a measure,” he means a different weight and a different measure. In the literal sense, therefore, whoever has a varied weight and a varied measure in his house has them for the purpose of weighing and measuring one way for himself and another way for his neighbor. This is certainly abominable to the Lord. Hence in the law of Moses the Lord commanded, saying, “Let your bushel be equal and your sextarius just” [Col. 0980D] (Leviticus 19).

VERANUS. But how should it be understood spiritually?

SALONIUS. The person who has a different weight and a different measure in his house is the one who always seeks, in his own actions, what will cause him to be praised, while in the actions of others he investigates what will cause them to be blamed. Such a person is certainly abominable to God, since to the extent that he desires to please himself, he displeases God, who searches out all the secrets of the heart.

VERANUS. How should we understand the saying, “It is bad, it is bad,” says every buyer, “and when he has gone away, then he will boast” (Proverbs 20)?

SALONIUS. In the literal sense, a buyer is accustomed to disparage [Col. 0981A] what he wishes to buy and to say, “It is bad, it is bad”; nevertheless, if he has bought it well, he will boast when he has gone away.

VERANUS. But how do you understand it spiritually?

SALONIUS. He is truly a buyer who desires to acquire eternal rewards for himself in heaven. He strives to buy heavenly things with earthly things, enduring things with perishable things, and eternal things with temporal things. Such a buyer calls whatever he suffers in the present “bad,” because he understands that it is bad. Nevertheless, because he patiently endures every adversity for God’s sake, when he has departed from the world he will boast, because he will attain blessedness.

VERANUS. Again, how should we understand what he says shortly afterward: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end”?

[Col. 0981B]

SALONIUS. This inheritance may be understood as the acquisition of greed. Therefore, whoever desires through the wickedness of greed to multiply riches for himself in this life must lose the blessedness of the eternal inheritance in the future. Alternatively: Whoever desires to seek human praise for good works hastens at the beginning as though toward an inheritance; therefore, at the end they will lack blessing, because they will receive no reward from God. Of such people it is written, “Truly I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6 and 10).

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The ruin of a man is to devour the saints, and afterward to consider his vows” (Proverbs 26)? What does it mean to devour the saints?

SALONIUS. To devour the saints means to bind oneself by a vow. [Col. 0981C] The impious devoured the saints when they bound themselves by a vow that they would persecute and kill the saints, as did the forty Jewish men, concerning whom the Acts of the Apostles says: “They bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink until they had killed Paul” (Acts 23). And, as we often read, the pagans vowed the blood of Christians to their gods.

VERANUS. What does he mean by “and to deal with them after vows” (Proverbs 20)?

SALONIUS. To deal with the saints after vows have been made means to persecute and tear them apart and to despise them as though they were worthless slaves. [Col. 0981D]

VERANUS. How, then, is it a man’s ruin to devour the saints and to deal with them after vows?

SALONIUS. If it is a sin to harm any human being, it is much more a sin when someone persecutes, offends, or injures the saints of God. Therefore it is the ruin of the one who, by persecuting the saints, prepares destruction for himself in eternal condemnation.

VERANUS. How should we understand the saying, “As the divisions of waters, so is the heart of a king in the hand of God”? Why did he say that only the king’s heart is in God’s hand, and not the hearts of all human beings, when elsewhere it is written, “In his hand are all the ends of the earth” (Psalm 94)? If all the ends of the earth are in God’s power, then the hearts of all human beings are also in his hand.

SALONIUS. Here we should not understand “king” as one who is king in name only and rules over others temporally, but as every holy, faithful, [Col. 0982A] and devout Christian man, whose soldiers are the sacred virtues and who knows how to conquer well within himself the battles against vices. Therefore, just as God fills the broad boundaries of lands and of the air with the manifold divisions of waters, so he inclines the heart of the king wherever he wishes—that is, he turns it toward whatever good he wishes. For just as he distributes the divisions of grace to angels and human beings according to his will, so he fills the hearts of kings—that is, of the saints—with various gifts and adorns them with diverse endowments.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The man who strays from the way of instruction will dwell in the assembly of giants” (Proverbs 21)? Who are these giants, in whose assembly the one who has strayed from the way of instruction will dwell?

SALONIUS. He called unclean spirits—namely, demons—giants. Of them blessed Job says, “Behold, the giants groan beneath the [Col. 0982B] waters, and those who dwell with them” (Job 26); that is, the demons and all those whom they have deceived and who have consented to them are tormented beneath punishments.

VERONUS. Why are demons called giants?

SALONIUS. Because demons are proud and lifted up, and evil and strong, just as the giants once were. Therefore, in the assembly of these giants—that is, of the demons—all who have strayed from the way of instruction, that is, from the way of truth, will dwell, because they will be tormented together with the demons in the punishment of eternal condemnation.

VERANUS. What is the city of the strong, or who is the wise man of whom he says, “The wise man ascends the city of the strong and brings down the strength of its confidence” (Proverbs 21)?

[Col. 0982C]

SALONIUS. He calls the world a city, and the strong ones demons. This world was once the city of the strong, because, devoted to the worship of idols, it served demons and placed the confidence of its life in the worship of those who are not gods but the works of human hands.

VERANUS. Who, then, is the wise man who ascended this city of the strong?

SALONIUS. The Son of the Virgin, the power of God and the wisdom of God, who ascended this city when, born in the flesh, he appeared visibly to the world. He destroyed its strength of confidence because he overturned and removed from the world the worship of the gods in whom the gentiles trusted.

VERANUS. What does the proverb mean: “A young man according to his way, even when he grows old, will not depart [Col. 0982D] from it” (Proverbs 22)? Do not many depart from the evil way in which they walked during their youth?

SALONIUS. Indeed, very many, inspired by divine grace, turn in old age from the vices they possessed in youth. Nor does Solomon deny that this can happen. But it more frequently happens that a person does not change in old age the habits he learned in youth. Nevertheless, he does not affirm that this always occurs. Therefore he sets forth such a proverb to admonish everyone to devote themselves diligently, from their earliest age, to virtues and good works, lest in old age they be unable to learn the practice of good works that they neglected in their tender years.

[Col. 0983A]

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The mouth of a foreign woman is a deep pit” (Proverbs 20 and 23)? Who is this foreign woman whose mouth is a great pit?

SALONIUS. By “the mouth of a foreign woman” he means the mouth of a prostitute. Therefore, whoever willingly listens to the words of a prostitute and delightfully receives her kisses knocks, as it were, at the door of a deep pit—that is, of hell. Unless he quickly withdraws from her conversation or kiss, with God abandoning him he is immediately plunged into the pit of death. This is what he means when he says, “The one with whom the Lord is angry will fall into it.”

VERANUS. What does he mean by, “Apply your heart to my instruction”? And shortly afterward he adds, “Behold, I have described it for you three times in thoughts and knowledge, to show you the firmness and words of truth” (Proverbs 22). How did he describe his instruction and [Col. 0983B] knowledge three times? Or what does it mean to apply oneself to and understand instruction?

SALONIUS. He describes his instruction three times when he commands each person to strive to fulfill it in thought, speech, and deed.

VERANUS. Of what boundaries does he speak when he says, “Do not cross the ancient boundaries that your fathers established” (Proverbs 23)?

SALONIUS. By ancient boundaries he means the boundaries of truth and faith that catholic teachers established from the beginning. Thus he commanded that no one receive the truth of the holy faith and evangelical teaching in any other way than it was handed down by the holy Fathers. Or he commanded that no one interpret the words of the holy Scriptures in any other way than according to the intention of each writer.

[Col. 0983C]

VERANUS. What are the riches of which he says, “Do not raise your eyes to riches that you cannot possess, for they will make themselves wings and fly into heaven”? What wings can riches—that is, wealth or abundance—make for themselves?

SALONIUS. These riches are the mysteries of the Divinity and the secrets of heavenly mysteries. The meaning is: Do not raise the eyes of your mind to investigate the mysteries of the Divinity and the secrets of heavenly mysteries, which you cannot penetrate or understand, since these things are open only to eagles—that is, they are manifested only to the citizens above.

VERANUS. What are the storerooms of which he says, “In instruction the storerooms will be filled with every substance, precious and most beautiful” (Proverbs 24)?

SALONIUS. The storerooms are the hearts of the righteous, who through the instruction of wisdom are filled with every [Col. 0983D] precious and most beautiful substance—that is, with the gifts of virtues and good works.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again”? If he is righteous, how is he said to fall, that is, to sin?

SALONIUS. Here Solomon speaks of light and daily sins, without which no righteous person could or can exist in this life. As he says elsewhere, “I will bless the Lord at all times seven times” (Psalm 33), “seven times” also signifies sometimes, often, and frequently, which can be most appropriately understood here: the righteous man will fall seven times—that is, often [Col. 0984A]—and will often rise again. Or certainly he falls and rises at every moment, through divine grace, according to what was said above.

VERANUS. How should we understand, “Prepare your work outside and diligently cultivate your field, so that afterward you may build your house”? What is it that we must prepare outside? [The text apparently reads *quod est homo*; perhaps *quid est quod foris*—“what is it that we must prepare outside.”]

SALONIUS. He calls a good action “work,” and therefore added “your”—that is, something useful and necessary for you. We therefore prepare our work outside when we arrange our action well outwardly and order it so that it may please God.

VERANUS. How do we diligently cultivate our field?

SALONIUS. We diligently cultivate the field if we cleanse our body from the thorns [Col. 0984B] of vices.

VERANUS. After cultivating the field, how shall we build our house?

SALONIUS. If first we arrange our actions well outwardly, we build our house well when we preserve purity of life and cleanliness of thought and adorn the dwelling of our mind with devout thoughts.

VERANUS. Who is the Lord, or who are the kings of whom he says, “It is the glory of the Lord to conceal a word; the glory of kings to investigate a speech” (Proverbs 25)?

SALONIUS. This Lord is the Son of God, namely the Lord Jesus, whose glory it was to conceal the word—that is, that he was the Son of God. For when he appeared in the flesh, he wished to confess himself a man rather than the Son of God, [Col. 0984C] so that the devil would not recognize him and he might thus redeem the human race by his passion. For if the devil had known that he was the Son of God, he would never have crucified him. Thus it was the Lord’s glory to conceal the word—that is, to hide the power of his divinity in the form of a man—so that, while he displayed the weakness of the flesh, the devil would not hasten to turn him away from his passion, and so that through ignorance of the passion he might arrive at the glory of the resurrection.

VERANUS. Who, then, are the kings whose glory is to investigate a speech?

SALONIUS. These kings were the holy apostles, who diligently strove to investigate the Lord’s word, by which he indicated that he was the Lord’s. When he did not openly show that he was the Lord but wished to be understood mystically, they examined his word with the utmost diligence, as in the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and so forth. [Col. 0984D] For when he concealed the divinity of the Word and displayed the weakness of the flesh, he asked these kings, saying, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” The foremost of the kings, namely blessed Peter the apostle, investigating his saying—which he had often heard before—immediately replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

VERANUS. What does the following mean: “Heaven above, and earth below, and the heart of kings are said to be inscrutable” (Proverbs 25)?

SALONIUS. He calls prophets and apostles “kings,” who, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, deserved to know the mysteries of divinity. By the heart of kings is signified the knowledge and understanding of the prophets and apostles.

VERANUS. How, then, should we understand what he says: “Heaven above, and earth below, and the heart of kings is inscrutable”?

SALONIUS. Just as the height of heaven and the depth of earth cannot be comprehended by human beings, so the capacity of our frailty cannot comprehend or penetrate the height of the knowledge and understanding of the prophets [Col. 0985A] and apostles.

VERANUS. How do the following sayings agree with one another, or how can they be reconciled: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him,” and “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (Proverbs 26)? These statements plainly seem to be very much opposed to one another.

[Col. 0985B]

SALONIUS. They truly agree well if we consider them carefully. By saying, “Do not answer a fool according to his folly,” he admonishes us that, since a fool does not perceive wisdom, we should not imitate his folly but rather despise and reject it; and whenever we speak to him, we should speak neither disgracefully, nor furiously, nor arrogantly, but honorably, patiently, humbly, and wisely, lest we become like him. By what follows, “Answer a fool according to his folly,” he admonishes us to rebuke and refute the fool wisely and to demonstrate openly how great his folly is, lest, if he does not recognize his folly, he should think himself wise.

VERANUS. Who is the whisperer of whom he says, “The words [Col. 0985C] of a whisperer seem simple, and they themselves reach to the innermost parts of the belly”?

SALONIUS. He calls a whisperer an instigator of strife and a double-tongued person, who feigns praise in his words, and therefore his words seem to be simple. But they reach to the innermost parts of the belly because the whisperer always seeks to hear something from which he can sow quarrels, by which the stomach may be angered and all the inward parts disturbed.

VERANUS. What is the hidden love of which he says, “Open correction is better than hidden love” (Proverbs 27)?

SALONIUS. Here he calls hidden love illicit love—that is, lustful love—such as adulterous love, which is hidden because of its shamefulness, lest it be rebuked by the wise. Open correction is therefore better than hidden love, because it is far better to rebuke someone openly so that he may be corrected than secretly [Col. 0985D] to love him with the intention of sinning together.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “A sated soul will trample the honeycomb; a hungry soul will take what is bitter for what is sweet”? How does a sated soul trample the honeycomb?

SALONIUS. In the literal sense, a sated soul tramples the honeycomb because whoever is filled with food despises and rejects sweet nourishment; but whoever is hungry pays little attention even if he takes some bitterness in his food.

VERANUS. But spiritually, how should this saying be understood?

SALONIUS. The sated soul is the soul of the rich, who [Col. 0986A] possess their consolation in the present life because they abound in temporal goods. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel, “Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger” (Luke 6). The soul of the rich therefore tramples the honeycomb because, for the sake of earthly goods, it despises the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom. But the hungry soul will take what is bitter for what is sweet, because whoever hungers and thirsts for righteousness (Matthew 5) accepts every bitterness as sweetness: for the love of heavenly sweetness—that is, eternal blessedness—he patiently endures every adversity of the present life.

VERANUS. To whom does Solomon speak when he says, “Carefully know the face of your flock, and consider your herds” (Proverbs 27)? Surely he is teaching people to inspect wool-bearing flocks?

SALONIUS. No. He is speaking to the shepherd of the Church, and [Col. 0986B] the meaning is: Diligently care for those over whom you have been placed, and recognize the dispositions and actions of each one; and if you find any filth of vices, strive to correct and cleanse it quickly.

VERANUS. Why does he immediately add, “For you will not always have power, but a crown will be given from generation to generation”?

SALONIUS. So that the shepherd of the Church may continually care for the sheep entrusted to him. The meaning is: You will not always have the power to feed the Lord’s sheep, but a crown will be given from generation to generation—that is, an eternal crown has been prepared, which you too will receive if you have fed the Lord’s sheep well.

VERANUS. Why was it necessary for Solomon to say, “The meadows have been opened, the green grasses have appeared, and the hay has been gathered [Col. 0986C] from the mountains”? Who does not say or know this?

SALONIUS. Indeed, no one, if we take these words only in their literal sense.

VERANUS. How, then, should they be understood?

SALONIUS. Entirely in a spiritual sense.

VERANUS. What, then, do the meadows signify?

SALONIUS. The meadows signify the heavenly mysteries, which are called meadows because they are pastures for faithful souls. These meadows—that is, the divine mysteries—had long been hidden under legal types and figures.

VERANUS. How and when were these meadows opened?

SALONIUS. The meadows were opened because the heavenly sacraments [Col. 0986D] were revealed through the grace of the Lord and Savior, when he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). Then the green grasses also appeared—that is, the new meanings of evangelical truth and glory.

VERANUS. What do the hay gathered from the mountains signify?

SALONIUS. The mountains signify the holy Fathers who wrote the Old Testament; the hay signifies their writings. Hay was gathered from the mountains because the writings of the holy ancient Fathers were collected as food and nourishment for the Lord’s sheep—that is, for faithful souls.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “The poor man and the creditor met [Col. 0987A] one another; the Lord is the illuminator of both” (Proverbs 22)? Who are this poor man and this creditor who met one another?

SALONIUS. The poor man is the humble hearer of the word; the creditor is the one who, by preaching, entrusts the money of God’s word to the poor man—that is, to the humble hearer.

VERANUS. When do the poor man and the creditor meet one another?

SALONIUS. When the hearer and the preacher meet together in one and the same grace of divine mercy. Therefore it beautifully follows, “The Lord is the illuminator of both” (Proverbs 29), because without the grace of divine mercy, neither could the one preach nor could the other believe.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says, “When prophecy fails, the people will be scattered”? What is this prophecy [Col. 0987B], on the failure of which the people will be scattered?

SALONIUS. Prophecy is priestly instruction and teaching. Therefore, when the priests’ teaching and instruction cease, the people will be scattered, because when the priests’ admonition and rebuke are absent, the people are left to their own will and judgment and are immediately corrupted by various sins and vices.

VERANUS. How is every word of God a fiery shield? For Solomon says, “Every word of God is a fiery shield to those who hope in him” (Proverbs 30).

SALONIUS. Every word of divine authority is called a fiery shield because it kindles the hearts of the elect who place their hope in God with the fire of radiance, illuminates them with the knowledge of truth, consumes and purifies the filth of vices that it finds in them, and defends them from the ambushes of enemies [Col. 0987C] and from every adversity.

VERANUS. What is the leech whose two daughters he says there are? For he says, “The leech [Col. 0987C] has two daughters saying, ‘Give,’ and they are never satisfied.”

SALONIUS. The leech is the devil, who always thirsts for blood—that is, desires to draw human beings into sins—and continually inflames their thirst for sinning.

VERANUS. Who are the two daughters of the leech who say, “Give, give,” and are never satisfied?

SALONIUS. Lust and greed. These spiritually imitate the devil’s thirst and ardor, because just as he is never satisfied with sinning, so neither greed nor lust is ever satisfied. For the more a person indulges in lust and fornication, the more he delights in it. Likewise, the more a person amasses wealth for himself, the more he always desires to increase it.

VERANUS. Why did Solomon set forth the example of the stellio, saying, “The stellio is nourished by the hands and dwells in kings’ houses” (same passage)?

SALONIUS. To urge the lazy and dull-witted to work and to bless.

VERANUS. What kind of animal is the stellio?

SALONIUS. A kind of lizard, very lazy and of varied color. It received the name *stellio* because it is marked and variegated as though with stars—that is, with [Col. 0987D] spots.

VERANUS. What, then, does the stellio signify?

**SALONIUS.** He signifies those who are slow in understanding but who, nevertheless, through daily study and diligence, ascend with their hands into the eternal palace—that is, although they reach knowledge of the sacred Scriptures with great [Col. 0988A] labor, they are able to penetrate the secrets of heavenly mysteries. Of such people it is written in the Gospel: “To the one who has, it will be given, and he will abound” (Matt. XIII); for whoever has devoted himself to reading will be given the ability to understand.

**VERANUS.** What are the three things of which Solomon says: “There are three that walk well, and a fourth proceeds happily”?

**SALONIUS.** The lion, strongest among beasts, which fears no encounter; the rooster with his loins girded; and the ram, against whom there is no king who can stand. These are the ones that walk well.

**VERANUS.** Whom does this lion signify?

**SALONIUS.** Him of whom it is written: “The lion from [Col. 0988B] the tribe of Judah has conquered,” and so forth (Rev. V)—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the strongest among beasts, because “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. I).

**VERANUS.** What is that weakness of God?

**SALONIUS.** God’s weakness was to assume the flesh of our mortality; but this is stronger than human beings, because he himself, born as a human being from the Virgin, proved to be perfect God.

**VERANUS.** Why does this lion fear no encounter?

**SALONIUS.** Because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. II). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me.”

**VERANUS.** What does the rooster with his loins girded signify?

[Col. 0988C]

**SALONIUS.** The holy preachers.

**VERANUS.** Why are the preachers called roosters?

**SALONIUS.** Because amid the darkness of the present life they announce by preaching the true morning—that is, the true light—namely, the glory of eternal blessedness.

**VERANUS.** Why are these roosters said to have their loins girded?

**SALONIUS.** Because the holy preachers extinguish luxury and lust in their own members.

**VERANUS.** What does the ram signify, against whom there is no king who can stand?

**SALONIUS.** By the ram, holy confessors and priests are signified. Like rams, they go before the flock, because they lead the faithful people as it walks by their examples. Against these rams—if they live spiritually and rightly—there is no king able to resist them, because no persecutor, however savage, can hinder their purpose. For even when evils are inflicted upon them, they patiently endure everything for Christ.

[Col. 0988D]

**VERANUS.** What is that fourth thing which proceeds happily?

**SALONIUS.** He who appeared foolish after he had been raised on high.

**VERANUS.** Who is he?

**SALONIUS.** The Antichrist, who will be revealed on high—that is, in an exalted position. Although he will be an utterly wicked man, he will deign to call himself the Son of God and will falsely claim to be God.

[Col. 0989A]

**VERANUS.** How will he appear foolish when raised on high?

**SALONIUS.** Because in that very exaltation and pride of his, he will suddenly be struck down by the divine sword and perish.

**VERANUS.** Why does he say of the preceding three, “There are three that walk well” (Prov. XXX), but of this one, “A fourth proceeds happily”? Why did he not similarly say of this one, “He proceeds well,” but rather “happily”?

**SALONIUS.** Because everything that proceeds happily does not always proceed well, nor does everything that proceeds well always proceed happily.

**VERANUS.** What, then, are the things that proceed well, and what are those that proceed happily?

**SALONIUS.** Those proceed well which walk holily and justly; those proceed happily which possess prosperity in this life. The lion, the rooster, and the ram walk well, but not happily, because Christ fulfilled the will of God the Father in everything, yet endured many adversities and death. Likewise, the holy preachers and confessors strive to fulfill the divine will, but endure many persecutions in this life. The Antichrist, however, will not proceed well, because in his pride he will do everything against God’s will; but he will proceed happily, because, although for a brief time, he will enjoy great glory and prosperity.

**VERANUS.** Who is that King Lamuhel of whom he says: “The words of King Lamuhel, the vision with which his mother instructed him”?

**SALONIUS.** *Lamuhel* is said in the Hebrew language and is interpreted in Latin as “in whom is God.” He is indeed King Solomon [Col. 0989B] of Israel, in whom God was present; for unless God had dwelt in him, he could neither have understood nor written so many and such great divine mysteries.

[Col. 0989C]

**VERANUS.** Who was his mother who instructed him and taught him the vision?

**SALONIUS.** Literally, his bodily mother, Queen Bathsheba, may be understood, for she instructed him wisely. [Col. 0989C] But in this passage no mother is better understood than spiritual and divine grace, which invisibly instructed him in his heart and taught him the understanding of wisdom—wisdom which he himself both preached and wrote outwardly for human beings.

**VERANUS.** Who is that strong woman of whom he says: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is far away and from the remotest ends”?

[Col. 0989D]

**SALONIUS.** The holy Catholic Church is called the strong woman. She is called a woman because she spiritually generates children for God from water and the Holy Spirit. She is called strong because, for the sake of faith in and love of her Creator and Redeemer, she scorns and despises all the adversities and prosperities of this present age alike.

**VERANUS.** Why did Solomon say: “Who will find a strong woman?”

**SALONIUS.** Because through the Holy Spirit he understood that no prophet, nor any of the elect at all, would be sufficient for the redemption of the human race, except the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. Therefore he says: “Who will find a strong woman?” The implied answer is: “Except Christ.”

[Col. 0990A]

**VERANUS.** Why did he immediately add: “Her price is far away and from the remotest ends”?

**SALONIUS.** To show that Christ would come not in Solomon’s own time but long afterward, and that no one like him would come—namely, a pure human being free from the defilement of sins. Rather, at the end of the ages the Son would descend from heaven, born from the Virgin and perfect as God and human being. This is what “far away” means: long afterward. It signifies the period extending from Solomon’s days to the Virgin’s childbirth. By “from the remotest ends” he says that “his going forth is from the highest heaven.”

**VERANUS.** What price did the Lord pay for this woman?

**SALONIUS.** Himself, as the Apostle says: “He loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering [Col. 0990B] and sacrifice of pleasing fragrance” (Eph. V).
