**VERANUS.** How did the strong woman become like a merchant’s ship? For Solomon says: “She became like a merchant’s ship, bringing her bread from afar.”

**SALONIUS.** A merchant is called an *institor* because he is always intent upon acquiring and increasing his merchandise and profits. A merchant’s ship, therefore, laden with various goods that are more abundant in its own country, travels across the sea to foreign places so that, after selling everything it brought there, it may carry home more valuable goods. Thus the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—always desires to be laden with the riches of virtues and to abound in good works, sailing across the sea of this present age, so that through them she may merit—that is, acquire—greater things, namely, the gifts of divine grace.

[Col. 0990C]

**VERANUS.** Who is the builder of this ship?

**SALONIUS.** The Lord Jesus Christ, who gave the price of his blood and redeemed the Church. Thus the holy Church, following the example of her builder—that is, her Lord and Redeemer—always labors to multiply for herself the profits of virtues and good works, so that through them she may merit acquiring greater things, namely, the rewards of eternal blessedness. This is what he says: “Bringing her bread from afar,” because in all the good things she performs temporally, she desires only the satisfaction of wine and bread, since she awaits solely an eternal recompense.

**VERANUS.** What does this mean: “She made a linen garment and sold it, and gave a belt to the Canaanite” (Prov. XXXI)?

**SALONIUS.** The Church made and sold a linen garment because she gave by speaking the faith that she had woven by believing; and from unbelievers she received the faith of right conduct. Therefore she also gave a belt to the Canaanite, because through the vigor of demonstrated justice she restrained the unstable works of paganism, so that what is received may be held fast by living accordingly.

[Col. 0990D]

**VERANUS.** What does he mean when he says: “She made herself a variegated garment; fine linen and purple are her clothing”? What is a variegated garment?

**SALONIUS.** A variegated garment is one that is usually made very strong by an intricate, multicolored weave.

**VERANUS.** What, then, is signified by the variegated garment?

**SALONIUS.** The strong works of the holy Church and the various ornaments of the virtues, of which the prophet says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in variety” (Ps. XLIV).

[Col. 0991A]

**VERANUS.** How are fine linen and purple the clothing of that woman—that is, of the holy Church?

**SALONIUS.** Fine linen is a kind of very white flax. Thus, appropriately, bodily chastity and purity of holy conduct are signified by fine linen; by purple, the shedding of blood is signified. The strong woman—that is, the holy Church—clothes herself in God’s fine linen: she preserves bodily chastity and shines with the radiance of holy conduct. She also clothes herself in purple when the holy martyrs shed their blood for Christ’s name.

**VERANUS.** If fine linen and purple are the clothing of the holy Church, why does he say later: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she will laugh on the last day” [Col. 0991B] (Prov. XXXI)?

**SALONIUS.** There is no contradiction, because “strength” refers to purple, while “beauty” refers to the whiteness of fine linen. Strength, therefore, is the clothing of the holy Church because, for the sake of faith in Christ and justice, she patiently endures the wickedness and persecution of evil people. Beauty is also her clothing because she practices justice and adorns herself with the grace of the virtues.

**VERANUS.** Why, then, does he say: “She will laugh on the last day,” when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh, for you will mourn and weep” (Luke VI)?

**SALONIUS.** In the sacred Scriptures, laughter ordinarily signifies joy. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are you who now weep, for you will laugh”—that is, you will rejoice. Blessed Job also says: “The mouth of the truthful will be filled with laughter”—that is, with joy. [Col. 0991C]

Thus the strong woman—that is, the holy Church—will laugh on the last day: she will rejoice in the recompense of the heavenly kingdom.

**VERANUS.** Who are the children of the woman who proclaimed her most blessed? Or who is her husband who praised her? For he says: “Her children rose up and proclaimed her most blessed, and her husband praised her” (Prov. XXXI).

**SALONIUS.** The children of this woman—that is, of the holy Church—are all the elect; her husband is the Lord Jesus Christ. For the children of the Church, namely all the elect, will rise from the dust of the earth on the last day of judgment. Adorned with the glory of immortality, they will proclaim their mother most blessed—that is, they will praise the holy Church, which gave birth to them for God from water and the Holy Spirit. Her husband also will rise, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, when he appears openly in the power of his divinity on the day of judgment, and he will praise her, saying in judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

[Col. 0991D]

**VERANUS.** Why, then, did he use the past tense, saying: “They rose up”? He ought to have said, “They will rise.”

**SALONIUS.** What Solomon knew would be future, he held as absolutely certain; therefore, in prophetic fashion, he used the past tense in place of the future.

**VERANUS.** Of whom does he speak in what follows: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. XXXI)?

[Col. 0992A]

**SALONIUS.** He calls the churches of heretics and the crowds of bad Catholics “many daughters.”

**VERANUS.** Which daughters are called the daughters of Christ or of the Church? [Note: [Col. 0991] Salon­ius’s answer to that question appears to be missing here.] Why are they called children of Christ or of the Church?

**SALONIUS.** Because of the sacrament of faith and baptism, and the adoption as children that they received in baptism.

**VERANUS.** What riches did these daughters gather?

**SALONIUS.** Prayers, fasts, almsgiving, bodily affliction and chastity, restraint of the tongue, meditation on the Scriptures, and the riches of other good works. These are true riches if they are performed with spiritual intention—namely, for the sake of the recompense of the heavenly kingdom; otherwise, they benefit those who perform them nothing. Hence the daughters—namely, the heretics or the crowds of bad Catholics—[Col. 0992B] gathered riches for themselves in vain, because either they went astray in faith, or they performed such good works without a spiritual intention. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name cast out demons, and perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you’” (Matt. VII). But the holy Catholic Church has surpassed them—that is, she has transcended them all—because whatever she does, she performs solely in right faith and with spiritual intention.

**VERANUS.** Of what grace and what beauty does he speak when he says: “Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; the woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised” (Prov. XXXI)?

[Col. 0992C]

**SALONIUS.** Deceitful grace is human praise, which hypocrites seek from everyone. Vain beauty is the beauty of chastity or of good works that hypocrites wish to display to human beings so that they may be praised by them.

**VERANUS.** Why are this grace and this beauty called deceitful and vain?

**SALONIUS.** Because it deceives—that is, misleads—those who pretend; for while they seek their reward in this life, they will receive no recompense in the future. Even if they preserve chastity or perform some good works, everything they do is vain.

**VERANUS.** Who is the woman who fears the Lord?

**SALONIUS.** The holy Church, which remains in this life always in fear of the Lord and always desires to fulfill his commandments.

**VERANUS.** How, then, will this woman be praised?

[Col. 0992D]

**SALONIUS.** Solomon himself clearly demonstrates this at the end of this book, when he says: “Give her from the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” (Prov. XXXI).

**VERANUS.** Whose words are these?

**SALONIUS.** They are the words of her husband, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

**VERANUS.** When will he speak these words?

**SALONIUS.** On the day of judgment, when he will command the angels, after the end of this life, to lead the Church into the joys of the heavenly kingdom. Thus he will command the angels: “Give [Col. 0993A] her from the fruit of her hands”—that is, of her good works. For “hands” signify works; it is as though he openly said: “Because she took care to perform good works—namely, love, joy, peace, kindness, goodness, modesty, self-control, faith, and patience—[Col. 0994A] give her the reward worthy of this fruit.” And “let her works praise her in the gates”: that is, in judgment, or at the entrance to the heavenly homeland, let the very works that she performed praise her; that is, let her be rewarded for the good works she accomplished.

[Col. 0993]

## The Mystical Exposition of Ecclesiastes by Bishop Salonius

[Col. 0993B]

**Speakers: Veranus and Salonius**

**VERANUS.** By how many names was Solomon called?

**SALONIUS.** By three, as the sacred Scriptures very clearly teach: Solomon, Ydida, and Ecclesiastes.

**VERANUS.** Why was he called by these names?

**SALONIUS.** He was called Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because there was peace in his kingdom. He was called Ydida, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” because the Lord loved him.

**VERANUS.** In what language is *Ecclesiastes* said?

**SALONIUS.** In Greek; for in Hebrew he is called *Cohelech*.

**VERANUS.** How does *Cohelech*, or *Ecclesiastes*, sound in the Latin language?

**SALONIUS.** Properly speaking, an *Ecclesiastes* is one who gathers an assembly—that is, a church. Hence, in Latin, [Col. 0993C] *Ecclesiastes* is rightly called a *Concionator*, because he delivers a speech—that is, speaks to the people—and his speech is directed not specifically to one person but generally to everyone. A preacher, therefore, may be called a *Concionator* in the holy Church.

**VERANUS.** How many books did Solomon publish?

**SALONIUS.** Only three, corresponding to the number of his names: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs.

**VERANUS.** What does Solomon say in Proverbs, or what does he teach in Ecclesiastes or the Song of Songs?

**SALONIUS.** In Proverbs he teaches the child and, through various sayings, instructs him as a son. In Ecclesiastes, however, he forms a man already mature in age, so that he may understand that in the affairs of this world nothing is lasting, nothing glorious or great; rather, everything we see is brief, perishable, and vain. In the Song of Songs he joins a man already complete and perfect in every respect and adorned with various virtues to the embraces of the bridegroom—that is, of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0993D]

**VERANUS.** But spiritually, whom does that Solomon—Jedidiah and Ecclesiastes—signify?

**SALONIUS.** The Lord Jesus Christ, who is our Solomon, that is, the one who, making all things peaceful through his blood, made both one. “Through his blood he made both one” (Eph. II), that is, from two peoples he constructed for himself one Church. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ is our peace, who made both one.” He is also Jedidiah, that is, the Father’s most beloved Son, of whom the Father himself says to the disciples: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III; Mark [Col. 0994B] I; Luke III). He is indeed our Ecclesiastes, that is, our *Concionator*, who gathers an assembly—namely, the holy Church—from throughout the whole world. To this assembly he speaks, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). He is the Son of David, to whom the blind cried out in the Gospel, saying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David” (Matt. IX, XV, and XX). He is also the King of Jerusalem—not of the earthly Jerusalem, but of that heavenly one, which is the mother of us all.

**VERANUS.** What does Ecclesiastes mean when he says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I), when it is written in Genesis: “God saw everything that he had made, and it was very good” (Gen. I)? If everything that God made is very good, how, then, is everything vanity—and not merely vanity, but vanity of vanities?

[Col. 0994C]

**SALONIUS.** Heaven and earth, the seas, and everything contained within this sphere are good in themselves, since they were created by the good God. But when compared with God, they must certainly be regarded as nothing, because God will always remain what he is, whereas all those things will pass away. For the things that are seen are temporal, because they are transitory; but the things that are not seen are eternal.

**VERANUS.** Why did he repeat his statement twice, saying: “Vanity of vanities,” Ecclesiastes said; “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity”?

**SALONIUS.** He repeated his statement to emphasize the greatness of vanities, thereby demonstrating that all the glory of the world will wither like the flower of hay and pass away like smoke.

[Col. 0994D]

**VERANUS.** Of which generations does he say: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes” (Eccles. I)?

**SALONIUS.** Of the generation of the Jews and the generation of the Gentiles. The first generation, that of the Jews, departs because it perished through unbelief, and a generation from the Gentiles succeeds it—namely, the holy Church of the faithful, gathered together and saved through faith in Christ. It can also be understood this way: “A generation goes, and a generation comes,” that is, while some die, others are born; those whom you previously saw you no longer see, and you begin to see those who had not existed before.

**VERANUS.** Why does Solomon say: “The earth stands forever” (ibid.), when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. V and XXIV; Mark XIII; Luke XXI)?

[Col. 0995A]

**SALONIUS.** Truly, according to the Lord’s statement, heaven and earth will pass away through improvement, but not through removal; for, purified by the fire of judgment, they will be improved, since they will be renewed, but they will not be utterly destroyed. Heaven above and earth below will burn only as much as they could be defiled by the wickedness of human beings and demons together. Therefore, according to Solomon’s statement, “the earth will stand forever” (Eccles. I), because it will never be destroyed; nevertheless, it will be renewed and improved.

**VERANUS.** What did Solomon intend to signify when he said: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; rising again there, it circles toward the south and turns toward the north” (ibid.)? Who does not know that the sun rises and sets and returns by ways unknown to us to the place from which it arose, so that it may rise again?

[Col. 0995B]

**SALONIUS.** Solomon says this in order to show that the sun itself, which was given to human beings for the light of day, demonstrates daily, through its mutability—that is, through its rising and setting—the destruction of this world. Through these changes of the seasons and through the rising and setting of the stars, Solomon teaches that human life rises and sets every day.

**VERANUS.** What does the sun spiritually signify in this passage?

**SALONIUS.** The true sun, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the sun of justice, of whom the prophet says: “For you who fear God, the sun of justice will rise” (Mal. IV). This sun of justice rises daily for those who fear him—that is, for his faithful, namely holy and devout people. It also sets at midday for false prophets [Col. 0995C]—that is, heretics and bad Catholics—because on account of their sins they lose the light of his grace. It sets also for unbelievers, because they are not worthy to be illumined by the light of faith.

**VERANUS.** What does he mean when he says: “All the rivers run into the sea, and the sea is not filled; to the place from which the rivers flow, they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccles. I)? Who knows that rivers return to their place so that they may flow again?

**SALONIUS.** Ecclesiastes—that is, Solomon—knows this through the grace of the Holy Spirit. But our Ecclesiastes, namely Jesus Christ, who is the creator of these waters, knows fully, through the power of his divinity by which he is equal to God the Father, which rivers, because they run into the sea, flow down into the abyss, return through hidden channels to the heads of the springs, and begin to bubble up again from the mother abyss.

[Col. 0995D]

**VERANUS.** But spiritually, what do these rivers signify?

**SALONIUS.** By these rivers the holy preachers are signified. When they shine with virtues and flash with teachings, they truly are rivers, because through their holy preaching and works they irrigate the dry earth of carnal hearts, so that they may produce the fruits of good works.

**VERANUS.** How, then, do these rivers flow back so that they return again to the place from which they flow?

**SALONIUS.** Because in every teaching [Col. 0996A] and work they perform, the holy preachers return to the praise of their Creator, so that they may offer praise and thanks to the Lord their author, from whom they received both the ability to do such things and all their goodness. They always return to the fountain of true light, lest they perhaps wither and dry up, so that from it they may receive the water of knowledge and the grace of virtues, in order to flow again—that is, both to fill themselves with good works and to pour streams of spiritual teaching into the hearts of others. All the faithful are also rivers, and these rivers return to the place from which they flow, because through holy desires they return to the love of their Creator and offer him praise and thanks for all the good things they received from him.

**VERANUS.** Why did Solomon give his heart—that is, devote himself with an attentive heart—to knowing wisdom and instruction, and also errors and folly (Eccles. I)? It is certainly good to know wisdom and instruction, but what good is there in knowing errors and folly?

[Col. 0996B]

**SALONIUS.** Just as it is good to know wisdom and instruction, so it is truly good to know errors and folly, because the first wisdom is to be free from folly. No one can be free from folly unless he has understood it. Likewise, no one can avoid errors unless he understands them. Therefore, many harmful things have been created among earthly matters so that, while we avoid them, we may be instructed in wisdom.

**VERANUS.** Why was Solomon equally intent on knowing wisdom and instruction and, conversely, errors and folly?

**SALONIUS.** So that, while he sought some things and avoided others—[Col. 0996C] that is, grasped good things and shunned evil ones—his true wisdom might be proved.

**VERANUS.** What does Solomon mean when he says: “In much wisdom there is much indignation, and whoever increases knowledge increases toil” (ibid.)? How is there much indignation in much wisdom?

**SALONIUS.** There is much indignation in much wisdom because the more wisdom someone receives, the more he becomes indignant with himself and grieves that he is subject to vices and sins and does not possess virtues. For the more someone progresses in wisdom, the more he grows angry with himself over the evil works he has done, and he is saddened and grieves over his sins. Therefore he also increases toil, because the more he understands heavenly and eternal things, the more he labors with grief and weeping to escape the snares of errors and to be freed from the misery of this age.

[Col. 0996D]

**VERANUS.** Why does he say: “I reckoned laughter an error, and concerning joy I said, ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” (Eccles. II), when it is natural for human beings to laugh and the Lord says in the Gospel: “Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. V; Luke VI)?

**SALONIUS.** Solomon does not condemn natural laughter—that is, modest and honorable laughter. Hence elsewhere he says: “A wise man will laugh silently” (Eccles. XXI). [Note: [Col. 0995] The Vulgate scarcely reads “will laugh silently.”] Rather, he calls uncontrolled, immoderate, and noisy laughter an error; such laughter is called a guffaw. Likewise, he calls not spiritual but temporal joy a deception. Those, however, who do not mourn their past evils, nor understand the ruin caused by their sins, laugh loudly and rejoice in temporal things because they think that new and brief goods are eternal. Therefore, deceived by the sweetness of the present life, they are daily tormented by the error of this age.

[Col. 0997A]

**VERANUS.** What does he mean when he says: “I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in everything, and that nothing remains under the sun” (Eccles. II, IV, VI, VIII, and XII)? How can he say that nothing remains under the sun when he said above: “But the earth stands forever” (Eccles. I)?

**SALONIUS.** [Note: [Col. 0997] “Nothing” in place of “because nothing.”] Nothing will remain under the sun that does not pass away, because all things are vain. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away” [Col. 0997B] (Matt. XXIV). Nevertheless, the earth will stand forever because it will not be utterly destroyed but will be improved, as was stated above.

**VERANUS.** Why does he say: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness” (Eccles. II)? Are the fool’s eyes not also in his head?

**SALONIUS.** In this passage, “eyes” cannot be understood as bodily eyes but as spiritual ones—namely, the eyes of the mind, that is, the perceptions and intentions of the soul. By “head,” however, Christ is signified, as the Apostle says: “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. XI). The eyes of the wise man are in the head because the wise man directs all his intention toward Christ and places it in Christ, and he always raises the eyes of his mind to meditate on heavenly things. But the fool walks in darkness because he is obscured both by the darkness of his folly and sins and by love of this world. He hates heavenly things, and therefore, like the wise man, he cannot raise his eyes to heaven, because he does not think about the things of God but about those of this age.

[Col. 0997C]

**VERANUS.** What, then, is the difference between a wise man and a fool?

**SALONIUS.** The difference is that the one is illumined and adorned by wisdom and brightness, while the other is darkened and cast down by the error of his folly. The difference between the wise and the fool is as great as that between day and night, light and darkness.

**VERANUS.** How can there be so great a difference between the wise and the fool when their end is the same? For it is written: “The learned die just as the unlearned, the wise just as the foolish” [Col. 0997D] (Eccles. II).

**SALONIUS.** Although the end is the same, and the death of the wise and the fool is alike, and the wise person is often more afflicted in this life than the fool, their memory in the future will not be the same, nor will they receive an equal recompense. For on the day of judgment the wise person will be raised to the glory of the heavenly kingdom, while the fool will be plunged into the torments of eternal condemnation.

**VERANUS.** Who, then, is this wise man who differs from the fool as light differs from darkness? Is it the one who possesses abundance of philosophical learning alone, or who shines with eloquence in the liberal arts?

[Col. 0998A]

**SALONIUS.** Sometimes secular prudence is hostile to God, and carnal wisdom, although adorned with the flowers of eloquence, contains within itself no spiritual fruit and no fruit of perpetual blessedness. Rather, he is truly wise who loves the Lord, keeps his commandments, and, as far as human frailty permits, strives to fulfill his will in everything. Of him he says a little later: “To the good person, in his sight, God gave wisdom, knowledge, and joy” (ibid.).

**VERANUS.** Why does he immediately add: “But to the sinner he gave excessive affliction and care”? If God gave the sinful person excessive care and anxiety, what sin does he himself commit if he is afflicted by excessive cares [Col. 0998B] and anxiety over temporal matters?

**SALONIUS.** The cause of excessive care and evil anxiety is not in God but in the one who previously sinned of his own will. By the demands of his sins he deserved to have excessive care and anxiety. Therefore, when he says, “But to the sinner he gave excessive care,” it must be understood that God permitted it to be given according to the sinner’s merits—that is, because he was a sinner.

**VERANUS.** What does he intend to demonstrate by saying: “Everything has its time” (Eccles. III)? If everything has its time, does the substance of the eternal Divinity, then, have a time?

[Col. 0998C]

**SALONIUS.** Far from it. That ineffable, eternal essence of the divine majesty, which created everything from nothing, is confined neither by place, nor restricted by time, nor bounded by any space. Therefore, to show what he was speaking about, Solomon immediately adds: “And all things under heaven pass within their appointed intervals.” He intends to demonstrate that everything in the world is subject to opposites, that nothing among all the things beneath heaven is perpetual, and that these things are contained within time.

**VERANUS.** Of what planting, or of what uprooting, is he speaking when he says: “A time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted” (ibid.)? Is he speaking about the planting or uprooting of trees or plants?

**SALONIUS.** No, but about the birth and death of human beings. For what he said above—“a time to be born”—is what follows here, “a time to plant”; for to plant is to bring forth what is born. What he says above—“a time to die”—is what follows here, “a time to uproot what has been planted”; for to be uprooted is the same as to die. The rising and setting of human beings are known to God alone—that is, the time of being born and the time of perishing, the time of planting and the time of uprooting—for he himself established both the time in which each person would be born and planted for life and the time in which he would die and be uprooted from this life; that is, be eradicated by the sentence of death.

[Col. 0998D]

**VERANUS.** What does he mean when he again says: “A time to kill and a time to heal” (ibid.)? No one doubts that a time of healing is granted by God, but [Col. 0999A] God never established a time for one person to kill another. Or could he ever heal the one whom a human being had once killed?

**SALONIUS.** Certainly not. But the time to kill and the time to heal belongs only to the one who speaks through Moses, saying: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. XXXII). He indeed established the time when sinners are to be killed and the sick are to be healed—that is, those who are sick through sins. He kills when, through bodily illness or some adversity of this world, he afflicts sinners so that they may be corrected and die to sins and live for God. Often God scourges the wicked for this reason: to kill and heal them—that is, so that they may cease to be what they are and begin to be what they are not. There is therefore a time of healing when almighty God, through hidden inspiration, pierces those whom he has killed—that is, mercifully afflicted with adversities—and calls them to repentance.

[Col. 0999B]

**VERANUS.** Of what destruction or construction is he speaking when he says: “A time to destroy and a time to build” (ibid.)? Is he speaking about the building and destruction of houses? For what benefit would it be to us if he said this? Who does not know that some destroy houses and others build them?

**SALONIUS.** Here Solomon is not speaking about houses, but about the destruction of evils and the building of good things. For it is necessary first to destroy evils and then afterward to build good things, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). This, then, is what he says: there is a time to destroy evils and a time to build good things, because in the present life God has granted us time to destroy evils and build good things—that is, first to erase sins within ourselves through repentance and afterward to construct buildings of virtues through holy desires.

[Col. 0999C]

**VERANUS.** Why does he say: “A time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance” (Eccles. III)? Who does not know that at one time we weep and at another we laugh? Or what benefit was there in saying, “a time to dance”? Did he perhaps intend to show that we ought to engage in the amusements of dancing?

SALONIUS. Far be it from us; we must do nothing buffoonishly. Rather, the present life is a time for weeping, and the future life a time for laughter. Whoever, therefore, in the present life strives to cleanse himself through daily weeping and tears will laugh in the future life—that is, he will rejoice. Likewise, the present life is a time for mourning, while the [Col. 0999D] blessed life is a time for dancing. For in the movement of dancing a person displays the joy of his mind and the feeling of his spirit. Whoever, therefore, in this life strives by mourning to abolish sins will dance in the future life—that is, he will rejoice and exult in the glory of eternal happiness.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “A time for scattering stones, and a time for gathering them” (ibid.)? What benefit is there in scattering stones, or what benefit in gathering them—unless perhaps someone wishes to build a house?

SALONIUS. Solomon is not speaking of this matter, but of the dispersion and gathering of the nations. For by “stones” the nations are signified. Hence John says: “God is able, from these stones, to raise up children for Abraham” [Col. 1000A] (Matt. 3). There was therefore a time for scattering stones before the Lord’s coming, because the Gentiles did not remain in the unity of faith but, departing from God, were scattered, since they worshiped various gods and honored different idols. There was, however, a time for gathering stones after the Lord’s coming, because, as the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4). Then indeed he began to gather the stones, because, after completing the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he sent his apostles throughout the whole world, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Then, after the fortieth day had been completed, the mystery [Col. 1000B] of his ascension into heaven took place. As soon as the fame of his name had been spread far and wide throughout the world by the apostles, the stones—that is, the Gentiles, who had been scattered through their various forms of idol worship—were gathered, because, coming to their senses and rejecting idols, they came together in the unity of faith.

VERANUS. Why does he again say: “A time for love and a time for hatred,” when the Apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3), and the Gospel says: “Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life” (John 12); and again: “Whoever does not hate his father and mother, brothers and sisters, wife and children, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14)? Tell me, then, when is the time for love, and when the time [Col. 1000C] for hatred?

SALONIUS. Even now it is the time for love, since, after the Lord, we must love father and mother, wife and children, and our other relatives. It is the time for hatred, however, because for the confession of Christ we must at once despise and hate both father and mother and all our relatives, if they oppose us on the way of the Lord, just as the holy martyrs are often said to have done.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says again: “A time for war and a time for peace” (Eccl. 3)? How can it be a time for war, when the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be reconciled quickly with your adversary while you are with him on the way”; and again: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also, and whoever wishes to take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well” [Col. 1000D] (Luke 6)?

SALONIUS. Truly, for us there is always a time of war and combat as long as we are in the present life, because we must always fight against the plots of the ancient enemy and overcome the aerial powers—that is, the powers of evil spirits. The time of peace will come when we have departed from the present age, because, if we have fought well in this world, we shall be crowned in the future and shall rest in eternal peace in the heavenly Jerusalem.

VERANUS. Why does he say: “God made everything good in its time,” when above he said that everything is vanity? If everything is vain, how are they therefore good?

SALONIUS. Everything is vain because it is transitory; nevertheless, [Col. 1001A] everything is good, since it was created good by God and is indeed good—not always, however, but in its proper time. For it is good to keep watch, and it is also good to sleep; yet to keep watch always, or always to sleep, is certainly not good.

VERANUS. Why does Solomon speak hesitantly, saying: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam goes upward and the spirit of beasts descends downward” (Eccl. 3)? Who does not know that the spirit of beasts—that is, of livestock and all brute animals—is dissolved together with the body? But the spirit of the children of Adam—that is, of human beings—is not dissolved together with the body; rather, as soon as it departs from the body, it is either led to glory or plunged into punishment?

[Col. 1001B]

SALONIUS. A little earlier Solomon showed that, as far as the body’s condition is concerned, there is no difference between a beast and a human being, because just as the beast dies, so does the human being. But to show that, according to the dignity of the soul, a human being differs greatly from a beast and an animal, he therefore distinguished them by saying: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam goes upward and the spirit of beasts descends downward” (ibid.)? For he showed that this is the sole difference between human beings and beasts: the human spirit ascends into heaven, while the spirit of the beast or animal descends into the earth, because it dies and is dissolved together with the flesh.

VERANUS. Why, then, does Solomon say: “Who knows?”—as though no one could know this?

[Col. 1001C]

SALONIUS. He says “Who knows?” in order to show the difficulty of the matter. For in the sacred Scriptures “who?” usually signifies not impossibility but difficulty or rarity, as in the passage: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53)—that is, either no one or very few. For what is impossible cannot be done at all, even with great effort. Therefore he says “Who knows?” because it is very rare, or certainly difficult, to find a spiritual person who can then perfectly understand, when the spirit departs from the body, whether it ascends or is led to punishment.

VERANUS. What do these children of Adam, or those beasts, signify spiritually?

SALONIUS. The children of Adam signify holy and elect men, who are rightly called human beings because they live rationally, holily, and spiritually. By beasts, however, carnal people are represented, and they are called beasts because they live in a bestial and carnal manner, like beasts and livestock. Hence the holy prophet David says: “You will save both human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35). It often happens that those who appear to be just human beings sin and turn away from their righteousness and commit iniquity; conversely, those who are evil and impious turn away from their iniquity and practice justice and equity. Therefore Solomon says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam goes upward and the spirit of beasts descends downward?” For the condition of this life is so uncertain that the sinner who is called a beast may, converted through repentance, rise and ascend [Col. 1002A] into heaven, while the righteous person may fall from his righteousness into sin and be plunged into hell.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “The fool folds his hands together and eats his own flesh” (Eccl. 4)? Who is so foolish as to eat his own flesh?

SALONIUS. This fool should be understood as that lazy person of whom Proverbs says: “The lazy man hides his hand under his armpit and does not bring it back to his mouth” (Prov. 19). This lazy and foolish man folds his hands together and eats his own flesh because he prefers to live in idleness and sluggishness and to possess a handful of grain rather than acquire through labor what will sustain him. The phrase “he eats his own flesh” is, however, spoken hyperbolically.

VERANUS. What is hyperbole?

SALONIUS. Hyperbole is used when something incredible is stated [Col. 1002B].

VERANUS. How, then, is “he eats his own flesh” spoken hyperbolically?

SALONIUS. Because it is incredible for a person to eat his own flesh. But to exaggerate this fool’s laziness, he says, “He eats flesh,” to show that the fool would rather have his flesh waste away through starvation and perish from the misery of hunger than be sustained by the labor of his hands.

VERANUS. Who is the one of whom Solomon says: “There is one, and he has no second—not a son, nor a brother—and yet he does not cease laboring, nor are his eyes satisfied with riches”?

SALONIUS. He is one who, being alone, has no second—that is, no son, no brother, [Col. 1002C] or any relative—and never ceases to labor, that is, to amass riches, nor does he amass enough to satisfy him. Thus it is the greatest vanity to gather riches and not know for whom one is leaving them.

VERANUS. Whom does that one who has no second signify spiritually?

SALONIUS. The Lord Jesus Christ, who is by nature the only Son of God the Father and alone descended from heaven to redeem the human race.

VERANUS. How does he have neither a son nor a brother, when in holy baptism all Christians become sons of God and brothers of our Lord Jesus Christ?

SALONIUS. He alone is the proper and natural Son; all the others are adopted. Therefore they are his brothers not by nature but by grace.

[Col. 1002D]

VERANUS. How, then, does this one not cease laboring?

SALONIUS. Because he patiently bears our sins, mercifully awaits our repentance, and daily intercedes for us with God the Father.

VERANUS. How are his eyes not satisfied with riches?

SALONIUS. Because he always desires our salvation.

VERANUS. What is the threefold cord of which Solomon says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4)?

SALONIUS. The unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because in the Godhead there are three persons but only one nature.

[Col. 1003A]

VERANUS. Why, then, does he say, “It is not easily broken”? For what is difficult can be done, although with great effort. Can this cord therefore be broken?

SALONIUS. Certainly never, because the nature of the Holy Trinity is indivisible. But “difficult” in this passage must be understood as “impossible,” because it cannot happen that the nature of the Godhead be divided.

VERANUS. Who is that poor and wise child of whom Solomon says: “Better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king” (Eccl. 4)?

SALONIUS. The Lord Jesus Christ, who is called a child on account of his innocence and simplicity, because “he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Although this child was rich, he became poor for our salvation. He is truly wise, because in him dwells [Col. 1003B] the whole fullness of divinity bodily.

VERANUS. Who is that old and foolish king?

SALONIUS. The devil, who ruled over the human race from almost the beginning of the world, and therefore is called old. He is truly a foolish king, because the more people he deceives, the greater punishment he heaps upon himself. In the kingdom of this old and foolish king—that is, of the devil—the excellent child was born, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who was made King of kings and Lord of lords.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Guard your foot as you enter the house of God”? Does he perhaps warn us to guard our foot against striking stones when we enter the house of God, that is, the church?

SALONIUS. Although we must always enter the house of God honorably, with fear and [Col. 1003C] silence, he is not teaching us to guard the bodily foot but the foot of the soul, that is, the movement of the mind, so that we may pour out pure prayers in God’s presence. The meaning is this: when you enter the house of God—that is, the church—guard your foot, that is, the movement of your mind, lest you stumble through evil thoughts, so that your prayer may be directed purely to God.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Do not give your mouth so as to make your flesh sin” (Eccl. 5)? How does a person give his mouth so as to make his flesh sin?

SALONIUS. When he speaks vanities and lustful words by which the flesh is stirred to sin. But the proper meaning of this passage is: “Do not give your mouth so as to make your flesh sin”; that is, do not seek [Col. 1003D] vain excuses by which you give your flesh an occasion to sin. Do not say: “I am not the one who sins, but sin that dwells in me—that is, the frailty of my flesh.” For if you say this, you provoke the Lord to anger, as though he himself were the author of evil and sin.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “All the labor of a person is for his mouth, but his soul is not filled” (Eccl. 6)? How can it be that everything for which a person labors is for his mouth?

SALONIUS. An ecclesiastical man, wise and learned, has all his labor in his mouth, because everything he learns in the sacred Scriptures he meditates upon, preaches, and teaches daily. Yet his soul is not filled, [Col. 1004A] because what he has learned is not enough for him; rather, he always desires and strives to learn more and more.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know” (ibid.)? How does a person see what he desires, or how does he desire what he does not know?

SALONIUS. The person who discerns good and evil with the eyes of the mind sees the good that he should desire and the evil that he should reject. But whoever follows the desire of his heart and his passions often desires what he does not know, because he wishes to grasp what he cannot.

VERANUS. Of whom does Solomon say: “He who is to come has already been called by name, and it is known that he is a human being”?

SALONIUS. Of the Lord Jesus Christ, whose name [Col. 1004B] was called beforehand in the sacred Scriptures, because he was to take flesh from the Virgin; and it was known to the prophets and saints of God that the true human being was to come.

VERANUS. If this was said of the Lord Jesus Christ, what does the following mean: “And he cannot contend in judgment with one stronger than himself”? Who is that stronger one against whom the Lord Jesus cannot contend in judgment?

SALONIUS. God the Father, who is stronger, because the Son, according to his humanity, is less than the Father.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Anger is better than laughter” (Eccl. 7), since laughter is natural, whereas anger is a vice?

SALONIUS. Anger is not always a vice; sometimes it is a virtue, when we are angry with ourselves or with others who are sinning [Col. 1004C]. This anger, therefore, is better than laughter, because laughter dissipates the mind and merriment corrupts a person’s spirit; but this anger corrects and reforms sin.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Calumny troubles the wise person and destroys the strength of his heart” (ibid.)? For the truly wise person is troubled by no calumny and cast down by no adversity.

SALONIUS. In this passage “wise” should not be understood as one who is perfect and complete in wisdom, but as one who has already begun to possess wisdom and yet is not perfect. Such a wise person is easily troubled by human calumny or some adversity, and his soul’s vigor and strength are destroyed; because he does not patiently endure adversity, he is tormented by impatience.

[Col. 1004D]

VERANUS. What is wrong with saying that former days were better than those that now are?

SALONIUS. It is wrong to say this because he himself says: “Such a question is foolish.”

VERANUS. Why is it a foolish question if someone says: “What is the reason that former times were better than they are now?” (ibid.)?

SALONIUS. It is a foolish question because one God is the creator of all times and of all days.

VERANUS. Although there is one God, the creator of all times and all days, were there not nevertheless good times and bad times?

SALONIUS. Indeed there were. But virtues make times good for us, while vices and sins make times bad. Therefore we must always live so well that the present days may be better for us than those that have passed.

[Col. 1005A]

VERANUS. What does Solomon mean when he says: “Do not be excessively righteous, nor be wiser than necessary” (Eccl. 7)? What harm is there if a person is very righteous, or who can be wiser than necessary?

SALONIUS. He is excessively and too rigorously righteous whose righteousness is harsh and cruel, even provoking others to complaint and murmuring. For example, whoever sees his brother sinning and wishes rather to condemn and punish him than to correct and reform him through repentance is truly excessively and too rigorously righteous.

[Col. 1005B]

VERANUS. How does a person become wiser than necessary?

SALONIUS. When he is wise arrogantly. Hence the Apostle warns: “Do not be high-minded” (Rom. 11)—that is, do not be arrogantly wise, but fear. He is also wiser than necessary who wishes to understand things that he cannot grasp or penetrate.

VERANUS. Why does Solomon say: “Whoever fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Eccl. 7), when the Apostle James says: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. 3)? Did James or the other apostles not fear God, since they confessed that they offended in many things?

SALONIUS. They certainly feared him, and they offended in many things, because there is no one on earth who does good and does not sin.

[Col. 1005C]

VERANUS. How, then, is it true that he says: “Whoever fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Eccl. 7)?

SALONIUS. Whoever possesses holy and chaste fear of God neglects absolutely nothing, because he is neither lifted up by prosperity nor cast down by adversity, since whatever happens to him does not distress him.

VERANUS. Who, then, is the person who possesses holy and chaste fear of God?

SALONIUS. The one who wishes to offend the Lord in nothing and, insofar as the Lord deigns to help him, wishes and strives in all things to fulfill his will and his commandments.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Wisdom strengthens the wise person above ten rulers of the city” (ibid.)? What wisdom is this, or who are these rulers?

[Col. 1005D]

SALONIUS. In this passage wisdom signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God. The rulers of the city are to be understood as the holy angels, who are rulers of the city—that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem. They are also rulers of the Church, because they govern and guard it daily.

VERANUS. Why, then, are they called ten?

SALONIUS. Because there were ten [Note: He improperly calls the number of angels who fell from the nine orders a tenth order, since theologians teach that there are only nine orders of angels and that some fell from each order. See St. Thomas, part 1, question 63, article 9, reply to objection 3, and question 108.] orders of angels, but one fell through pride. Therefore the good angels always labor toward this end: that their number may be completed from among human beings [Col. 1006A] and reach the perfect number, that is, ten.

VERANUS. How, then, does wisdom strengthen the wise person above the ten rulers of the city?

SALONIUS. Because the help of wisdom—that is, of the Lord Jesus Christ—is greater than that of the angels.

VERANUS. What does Solomon mean when he says: “I found one man among a thousand, but among all women I did not find one”? Were there not many holy women, both virgins and widows, who pleased God through chastity, purity, and good works, many of whom were crowned with martyrdom?

SALONIUS. There truly were, and even now there are, many virgins and widows acceptable to God. But Solomon says this because in his own time he could scarcely find a good man among many [Col. 1006B], whereas among women he found none, because they all drew him not toward virtue but toward luxury.

VERANUS. Can this statement be understood spiritually?

SALONIUS. Certainly. For by the man is signified a good thought of the mind, while by the woman is signified a carnal and dissolute thought. Thus among a thousand one man is found—that is, one pure and clean thought, not disturbed or polluted outwardly by a perverse thought. But among women none is found who pleases God, because a carnal and perverse thought is not acceptable to God.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Whoever keeps God’s commandment will experience no evil” (Eccl. 8)? How will the person who keeps God’s commandments [Col. 1006C] experience no evil, when holy men who kept God’s commandments suffered many things in this world?

SALONIUS. It is true, because whoever keeps God’s commandments—that is, everything God ordered and commanded—will experience no evil in the future. This means that he will suffer no evil and endure no evil on the day of judgment. Although he may suffer certain evils in this life, they are light and transitory; but in the future life whoever attains the glory of eternal blessedness will suffer no evil.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “A living dog is better than a dead lion” (Eccl. 9)? What does Solomon intend to signify by the living dog or the dead lion?

SALONIUS. The living dog signifies the people of the Gentiles, while the dead lion signifies the Jewish people abandoned by God [Col. 1006D]. Thus this living dog is better before God than that dead lion, because we who believe from among the nations, being alive through faith, acknowledge God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Alternatively, the living dog is the sinner who confesses himself dead through sins and, rising through repentance, begins to live through righteousness. The dead lion is the righteous person who trusts in his own righteousness and boasts of his merits; and therefore, lifted up by pride, he is dead before God. Thus the humble sinner corrected through repentance is better than the proud righteous person [Col. 1007A], because the former is accepted by God, while the latter is detestable.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “At all times let your garments be white, and let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9)? Can anyone always have white garments? And even if someone were so rich that he could always have white clothing—which is altogether difficult—how could it happen that oil never failed from his head? Who could bear always to have his head anointed with oil?

SALONIUS. This statement must be understood not historically but spiritually. For by garments are signified the virtues with which the soul is clothed and adorned; by oil is signified the work of mercy, that is, almsgiving, or certainly spiritual joy. The meaning is this: [Col. 1007B] “At all times let your garments be white”—that is, whatever good you do, let it be clean and pure, so that it may be acceptable to God. And never cease from works of mercy; always strive to possess spiritual joy.

VERANUS. What are the flies of which Solomon says: “Dead flies destroy the sweetness of the ointment” (Eccl. 10)?

SALONIUS. Solomon certainly understands spiritual flies.

VERANUS. What are those spiritual flies?

SALONIUS. Demons, vices, and sins. All these destroy here the sweetness of the ointment—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “The heart of the wise person is at his right hand, and the heart of the fool is at his left” (ibid.)? Who has his bodily heart in his right or left hand?

SALONIUS. Certainly no one, and therefore this statement must be understood spiritually.

VERANUS. How must it be understood spiritually?

SALONIUS. By the heart is signified intention or thought; by the right hand, a good work; and by the left, an evil one. The heart of the wise person is therefore at his right hand because the intention and thought of the wise person are directed toward and labor for this: always to do good, so that on the day of judgment he may deserve to stand at the Lord’s right hand—that is, among the righteous—and rejoice with them in eternal blessedness. But the heart of the fool is at his left, because he thinks evil and accumulates evil deeds, for which on the day of judgment he will be placed on the left—that is, among the reprobate—and punished eternally with them.

[Col. 1007D]

VERANUS. Who is that spirit of which he says: “If the spirit of one who has authority rises against you, do not leave your place”? Who is this one who has authority, whose spirit, if it rises against us, we must not allow to displace us?

SALONIUS. The devil is the prince of this world; his spirit is an evil suggestion.

VERANUS. How does the devil’s spirit rise against us?

SALONIUS. By persuading us to think evil thoughts. If, therefore, through the devil’s prompting, an evil thought rises in our heart, we must not give it room [Col. 1008A], but must fight against it vigorously, lest we complete the evil thought in action. It can also be understood in this way: if you possess humility, purity, chastity, patience, and charity within you, and the devil suggests pride, lust, impurity, anger, or hatred, do not leave your place—that is, do not abandon humility and become proud. The same is to be understood of the rest.

VERANUS. Why does Solomon say: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child and whose princes feast in the morning”? Was not the land of Israel blessed, since it had a young king, namely David, who was thirty years old when he received the kingdom? Was not Josiah also a good king, who began to reign in adolescence?

SALONIUS. David was truly a good king, and Josiah was good as well. [Col. 1008B] But “woe to the land whose king is a child” means a land whose king possesses little and weak wisdom, and carnal prudence that follows youthful desires and hates justice, truth, and judgment.

VERANUS. How do the princes feast in the morning?

SALONIUS. Princes feast in the morning when they lead a luxurious life. Therefore woe to the land whose princes feast in the morning, because they love the pleasures of this age and the delights of the flesh more than the salvation of the people, and by living luxuriously they pervert judgment.

VERANUS. How is the land blessed whose king is noble and whose princes eat at the proper time?

SALONIUS. If the king is noble—that is, distinguished by wisdom, radiant with justice, and adorned with good morals [Col. 1008C] and deeds—the land over which he presides is truly blessed, because he governs it with judgment and equity and exalts it through justice.

VERANUS. Who are those princes who eat at the proper time?

SALONIUS. Those, certainly, who do not live luxuriously, who do not love the pleasures of this age, and who do not live in gluttony and drunkenness, but seek food only to sustain the body. Therefore blessed is the land that has such princes, because, while they love justice and equity, they do not pervert judgment.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccl. 11)? What are the seven or eight portions that he commands us to give?

SALONIUS. By the number seven the Old Testament is signified, because of the Sabbath, which is the seventh day sanctified in the law; by the number eight the New Testament is signified, because of the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day, sanctified by the resurrection of Christ.

VERANUS. How, then, should we understand what he says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (ibid.)?

SALONIUS. In this way: believe in and honor both Testaments—the Old, that is, and the New—with equal reverence, and strive diligently to fulfill their commandments.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north, wherever the tree falls, there it will remain” (ibid.)? Does a tree that falls toward the north or the south not often move to other regions of the world?

[Col. 1009A]

SALONIUS. No one doubts this, but the statement must be understood spiritually. For by the tree the human being is signified, since each person is like a tree in the forest of the human race. By the south, which is a warm wind, the repose of paradise is signified; by the north, which is cold, the punishment of hell is signified. The meaning is this: wherever a person prepares a place for himself as a future dwelling, whether toward the south, when he falls—that is, when he dies—he will remain forever in the repose of paradise and the glory of the heavenly kingdom. But if he prepares a place for himself toward the north by living badly, he will suffer the punishments of hell forever and ever.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “Whoever watches the wind will not sow, and whoever looks at the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11)? Who is so foolish as always to watch the wind [Col. 1009B] and therefore not sow, and always to observe the clouds and therefore never reap?

SALONIUS. This statement must be understood spiritually. For just as storms often arise through wind and clouds, so the devil is signified by the wind, and the adversities of the present age by the clouds. Therefore whoever fears the devil’s persecution or the adversities of this world does not sow—that is, he does not preach the word of God, nor perform the good that he is able to do—and he will never reap. For even if he begins some good work, he does not bring it to completion.

VERANUS. What, then, must be done?

SALONIUS. Without regard to the clouds or fear of the winds, we must sow amid the storms; that is, in every adversity we must preach the word of God [Col. 1009C] and always perform the good works that we are able to do.

VERANUS. What does this mean: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease” (ibid.)? Who can sow continually, both morning and evening, especially when no one dares to sow in freezing weather?

SALONIUS. In this passage “seed” is not to be understood as grain or any other kind of seed, but as the seed of a good work, from which grows the fruit of righteousness and the reward of eternal recompense.

VERANUS. What, then, does he teach when he says: “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease”?

SALONIUS. He teaches that at no time and at no age should we cease from good works, and that evening should find our morning righteousness, while the rising sun should once more increase our evening mercy [Col. 1009D]. In youth and in old age alike, the abundance of our virtues should always commend us to God. “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand cease” (ibid.)—that is, always exercise yourself in good works.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper will be scattered” (Eccl. 12)? What benefit was there in saying this, since no one is unaware that the almond tree usually blossoms, the locust grows fat, and the caper is scattered?

SALONIUS. This statement must be understood spiritually, and it contains a great mystery. For by the almond tree the Lord Jesus Christ is signified. Just as an almond nut consists of skin, shell, and kernel, so Christ consists of flesh, soul, and divinity. The shell of the almond signifies the divinity [Col. 1010A].

VERANUS. What is signified by the locust and the caper?

SALONIUS. By the locust, the Gentile people; by the caper, the Jewish people.

VERANUS. How, then, is this statement to be understood?

SALONIUS. “The almond tree will blossom”—that is, Christ will be born and will shine forth through miracles. “The locust will grow fat”—that is, the Gentile people will believe and be filled with spiritual gifts. “The caper will be scattered”—that is, the Jewish people will perish because of unbelief.

VERANUS. Why are the words of the wise compared with goads and nails? For Solomon says: “The words of the wise [Col. 1010B] are like goads and like nails driven deep” (ibid.).

SALONIUS. The words of the wise are most aptly compared with nails and goads, because they do not flatter the sins of sinners but prick them. Those who are truly wise undoubtedly have words that are nails and goads, because they do not soothe sinners with flattery but rebuke them with harsh correction; and, as though by pricking them, they stir their hidden consciences to pain and lamentation, so that they may be corrected.

VERANUS. What does he mean when he says: “They were given through the counsel of masters by one shepherd” (ibid.)? Who are those masters through whose counsel the words of the wise were given, or who is that one shepherd by whom they were given?

[Col. 1010C]

SALONIUS. The masters are the prophets and apostles; the one shepherd is God, from whom all the words of the wise were given, because he taught the masters—that is, the prophets and apostles—and established their counsel, since he placed the words in their hearts and mouths.

VERANUS. What does Ecclesiastes say at the end of his book: “Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole human being”? How can it be that this alone constitutes a human being—that is, fearing God and observing his commandments? For the greater part of humanity neither fears nor obeys them.

SALONIUS. The greater part is truly made up of the wicked rather than the good, because, as the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20), and the multitude of unbelievers is incomparably greater than that of believers.

[Col. 1010D]

VERANUS. What, then, does Solomon intend to demonstrate here?

SALONIUS. In these words he demonstrates this: a person who does not fear God and keep his commandments is not a human being.

VERANUS. Why is he not a human being?

SALONIUS. Because he does not preserve the measure and order proper to his nature.

VERANUS. What are the order and measure of human nature?

SALONIUS. To live rationally. For among all living creatures, the human being alone was created a rational animal, and alone received from God reason and understanding, so that he might recognize and love his Creator, fear him, and praise him with heart and mouth together.

[Col. 1011A]

VERANUS. What does it mean to fear God?

SALONIUS. To fulfill his will and to do the good things that ought to be done.

VERANUS. If, then, whoever does not fear God and keep his commandments is not a human being, what is he?

SALONIUS. He is a beast.

VERANUS. How is he a beast, when human substance and person can be seen in him?

SALONIUS. Although he appears to possess human substance and person, nevertheless, because he lives not rationally but bestially, he must be called not a human being but a beast.

[Col. 1012A]

VERANUS. How is he called a beast?

SALONIUS. If he is cruel to his household and dependents or to his neighbors, he is a lion, not a human being; if he is a robber, a tiger or wolf; but if he is an adulterer, fornicator, or impure, he is a dog or a pig; or if he is foolish, he is compared to an ass. Thus the fraudulent or hypocritical man is fittingly likened to a fox; and the same is to be understood of the rest.

VERANUS. Who, then, is truly a human being?

SALONIUS. The one who fears God and keeps his commandments.

[Col. 1011]

LETTER OF CERETIUS, SALONIUS, AND VERANUS TO HOLY POPE LEO.

(This letter may be read in volume LIV, column 887, of our Patrology, where it was long ago reprinted among the letters of Saint Leo the Great.)

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 455. PHILIP THE PRESBYTER.

[Col. 1011A]

NOTICE FROM CAVE.

[Col. 1011B]

Philip the presbyter, a disciple of Jerome, was especially distinguished around the year 440. He died while Marcian and Avitus were reigning, that is, in the year 455 or at least at the beginning of the following year. For Avitus, who became emperor on July 10, 455, laid down the purple around the following May, after holding the empire for ten months.

Besides familiar letters, very witty and especially exhortatory toward endurance of poverty and suffering—which have long since perished—our Philip’s having written a Commentary on Job is attested by Gennadius (*On Illustrious Men*, chapter 62). Indeed, under Philip’s name three books of Commentaries on Job addressed to Bishop Nectarius were published at Basel in 1527, both in quarto and in folio. Their authenticity as Philip’s is confirmed by the passage cited by Bede, in his book *On the Calculation of Ounces*, from Philip’s Exposition of Job; this passage is found today in these Commentaries, as Sixtus of Siena noted long ago (*Book IV*, p. 293). Casimir Oudin also affirms that he saw these Commentaries in manuscript in a very ancient codex of the library of Igny, in the Reims district, which had Gennadius’s authority prefixed to it. These Commentaries are also commonly included among the works of Bede and Jerome.

[Col. 1011B]

COMMENTARY OF PHILIP THE PRESBYTER ON JOB.

(We published this Commentary above in volume XXIII, column 1401, of our Patrology; see it there.)

IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 460. LEO OF BOURGES.

[Col. 1013]

NOTICE FROM CAVE.

[Col. 1013A]

Leo, bishop of Bourges in Gaul, took part in the Council of Angers in 453 and in the Council of Tours in 461. In 454, together with the bishops Victorius and Eustathius [also Eustochius], he wrote a letter to the bishops—not of Thrace, as the heading incorrectly states, but of the Third Lyonnaise, which was the province of Tours. Sirmondus correctly notes this point. The letter declares excommunicated those clerics who, having disregarded ecclesiastical judgment, have appealed to the secular authorities. It is found among the letters of Leo (to whom it was long attributed), number 96, and in volume III of the Councils, p. 1420.

[Col. 1013A]

LETTER OF LEO OF BOURGES, VICTORIUS OF LE MANS, AND EUSTOCHIUS OF TOURS TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED WITHIN THE THIRD PROVINCE. (S)

(We published this letter above in volume LIV, column 1239, of our Patrology.)

[Col. 1013]
